docs.title: Building Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems · بناء أنظمة التوليد المعزز بالاسترجاع
SDAIA Academy · Dalil (دليل)
docs.text:
Everything the four-day course runs on: the corpus, the pipeline, the evaluation harnesses, the labs, the assessments and the capstone scaffolding.

Start here: INSTRUCTOR_PACKAGE_ADDENDUM.md — what changed and why. The base INSTRUCTOR_PACKAGE.md remains authoritative for course structure.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[full,dev]"
make doctor            # 24 environment checks, each printing its own fix
make corpus            # generate Layer B (offline, deterministic, ~10s)
make eval-sets         # derive probes, labels, golden set, red-team sets
make ingest            # parse + OCR + chunk  (~12 min, the OCR is real)
make eval-retrieval    # the per-class retrieval table
make demo              # the five capstone demonstrations

With network access, add the real regulatory corpus first:

make corpus-fetch && make corpus-verify

Everything above works without Docker, a GPU, a model download or a gateway key. Substitutes stamp their own name into every report they produce.

docs.title: The corpus, in one paragraph
docs.text:
Dalil's corpus has two layers. Layer A is 17 real, published SDAIA/NDMO documents — the Personal Data Protection Law and its Implementing Regulation, the national Data Classification, Sharing, Open Data and Monetization policies, the AI Ethics Principles, the Generative AI Guidelines, the AI Adoption Framework and more. Layer B is 134 synthetic internal documents for a fictional adopter of those rules, supplying only the four things public regulation cannot: access tiers, superseded/current document pairs, image-only Arabic scans, and tabular entitlement facts. Every Layer B document cites a Layer A instrument by title, which is what makes them one corpus and creates the course's best question class.

See INSTRUCTOR_PACKAGE_ADDENDUM.md §1 and LICENSING.md.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: Path What it is corpus/ Layer A manifest, fetcher, validator; Layer B generator and content blocks src/dalil/ The pipeline: ingest · index · retrieve · generate · advanced · evaluation · benchmarks data/ Generated corpus, probes, labelled queries, golden set, red-team sets, answer keys scripts/ doctor · build_index · ask · run_probes · eval runners · demo · verify_golden labs/lab1..7/ Participant briefs with the reference numbers from this repository's own runs activities/ Eleven classroom activities, printable assessments/ PA-1, PA-2, quiz addendum, and the answer keys (assessments/keys/) capstone/ Brief, caps, EVALUATION.md template prework/ The DeepLearning.AI assignment, crosswalks, readiness check tests/ 53 tests — CI gate, and teaching material

docs.title: Two things to know before you teach from this
docs.text:
Nothing degrades silently. A missing reranker returns input order and sets reranked: false. A missing dense model yields BM25-only results and stamps a warning in the report. The offline judge labels every metric offline-proxy. The hash-384 test embedder writes its name into every file it touches. The single worst outcome in this course is a participant trusting a number produced by a stage that never ran — so every substitute announces itself.

Answer keys are derived, never typed. scripts/build_eval_sets.py reads the facts recorded by the corpus generator and emits every probe, label and golden answer. Regenerate the corpus with a different seed and the keys regenerate with it; tests/test_corpus_integrity.py fails the build if they ever drift apart.

docs.title: Measured, not estimated
docs.text:
Every number below came from this repository's own runs and is reproducible with the commands above.

Layer B documents 134 — 22 scanned AR · 60 digital PDF · 20 DOCX · 24 HTML · 8 XLSX Naive chunking (Lab 1) 287 chunks · 41.5% start mid-sentence · 0 tables survive Structure-aware (Lab 2) 492 chunks · 4.1% mid-sentence · 56 tables kept whole OCR CER — naive settings 0.084 (fails the 0.06 gate) OCR CER — tuned 0.053 mean · 0.062 p95 · 0.100 worst BM25 alone, by class identifier 1.00 · tabular 1.00 · procedural 0.30 · factoid 0.24 Tests 53, all passing

That BM25 row is the course in one line: lexical retrieval is perfect at exactly the things dense retrieval cannot do, and helpless at everything else.

docs.title: Troubleshooting the assets themselves
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix make corpus warns about Raqm Pillow built without the Raqm text-layout engine only needed to regenerate scanned pages; install libraqm or use the shipped corpus Arabic scans OCR at ~20% CER, text reversed no Arabic font, so the generator fell back to presentation forms apt-get install fonts-noto-core and regenerate corpus-fetch reports UNRESOLVED documents SDAIA moved a publication page expected and survivable — run corpus/validate_corpus.py for the per-lab readiness verdict every retrieval metric is 0.000 dense model unavailable, dense-only mode requested the report already says so in notes; use --mode sparse or --model hash-384 golden-set answers all empty for Layer A ground truth is deferred by design python scripts/verify_golden.py --interactive after make corpus-fetch

docs.title: Layer A — real SDAIA / NDMO documents
docs.text:
These are public Saudi government publications, used here for training delivery.

Do not re-host them. This repository ships corpus/LOCK.json — resolved URLs, SHA-256 hashes, byte sizes and fetch timestamps — never the PDFs themselves. Participants and cohorts fetch from the official source, which:

  • keeps attribution with the publisher;
  • means every cohort verifiably indexes the published text, not a copy that has quietly drifted;
  • makes it visible, via make corpus-verify, when a document has been re-published — which is itself a teaching moment about corpus freshness.

If your organisation mirrors these documents internally for network reasons, mirror them read-only, keep the hashes in LOCK.json, and keep the source URL in the document metadata so every retrieved citation still points at the publisher.

docs.title: Layer B — synthetic documents
docs.text:
Everything under data/corpus/corpus_v1 and corpus_v2 that is not Layer A is generated by corpus/build_layer_b.py. It is entirely fictional. The organisation ("National Digital Services Authority"), its circulars, allowances, grades, procedures and figures do not exist.

Every generated file carries:

  • an X-Dalil-Synthetic marker in its document metadata;
  • a visible disclaimer footer in Arabic and English naming SDAIA Academy and the module code.

Do not remove either. They exist so that no page of this corpus can be mistaken for a real instrument if it leaves the classroom — which, over enough cohorts, it will.

docs.title: Public benchmarks
docs.text: MIRACL, BEIR and TechQA/RAGBench are third-party datasets under their own licences. This repository ships loaders, not data. The bundled --sample files are course-authored fixtures shaped like each benchmark, used to smoke-test the plumbing offline; they are not benchmark data and every report generated from them is stamped mode: "sample" with a warning.

docs.title: Course materials
docs.text: Course content, code and generated corpora in this repository are SDAIA Academy materials for SDA-AIE-214. Apply your institution's standard course-material terms.

docs.title: A note for instructors adapting this course
docs.text: The Layer A manifest is the part worth adapting. If you are delivering this outside a Saudi public-sector context, replace sdaia_layer_a.yaml with your own regulator's published corpus and keep everything else. The design goal was never "SDAIA documents" — it was documents your participants are actually bound by, because that is what turns a lab exercise into the index they build the month they get back to their desk.

docs.title: Classroom activities — SDA-AIE-214
docs.text:
Non-code activities, printable, timed. Each one replaces a stretch of lecture that participants would otherwise receive passively.

# Activity When Duration Materials 1 Architecture placement game D1 H2 15 min wall poster + vendor cards 2 Decision-framework workshop D1 H2 15 min 4 scenario cards + worksheet 3 The failure wall D1 H3 → D4 H5 continuous A2 poster + 8 stickers 4 Corpus autopsy D1 H4 10 min printed document samples 5 Query-class sorting D2 H3 10 min 24 query cards 6 The reranker courtroom D2 H4 12 min 2 near-duplicate policy extracts 7 Prompt surgery D3 H1 12 min projected prompt, live 8 Metric autopsy D3 H3 12 min 3 printed report cards 9 Refusal threshold auction D3 H5 12 min tau-sweep printout 10 Pattern pricing panel D4 H1 12 min 5 pattern cards 11 Governance memo sprint D4 H4 15 min one-page template

Files: activity_XX_*.md. Cards and worksheets are at the end of each file, formatted to print on A4.

docs.title: Day 1 Hour 3 → Day 4 Hour 5 · continuous · the course's spine
Materials
docs.text:
• One A2 print of the RAG reference architecture (offline lane + online lane).
  • Eight failure stickers, F1–F8, each with its one-line symptom.
  • A marker.

docs.title: Setup (Day 1, Hour 3, 3 minutes)
docs.text:
After Lab 1's probe run, each pair brings one failure to the wall and pins its sticker onto the pipeline stage where the failure was born — not where it was noticed. This distinction is the whole activity:

Failure Noticed at Born at F1 parsing loss the answer parse F2 chunk damage the answer chunk F3 semantic miss retrieval embed F4 lexical miss retrieval retrieve (no sparse leg) F5 precision collapse the answer rerank (absent) F6 context construction the answer context assembly F7 ungrounded answer the answer prompt + refusal (absent) F8 staleness the answer ingest (metadata absent)

Participants pin F1 and F8 at "generate" every single cohort, because that is where the damage became visible. Let them. Then ask: "if you replaced the model tomorrow with a better one, would this failure go away?" The sticker moves itself.

docs.title: Through the course
docs.text:
Each lab that retires a failure ends with the pair that found it physically removing the sticker, saying in one sentence what fixed it, in front of the room.

Removed at Failures End of Lab 2 F1, F2 End of Lab 3 F3 End of Lab 4 F4, F5 End of Lab 5 F6, F7 End of Day 4 staleness drill F8

docs.title: Day 4 wrap-up (5 minutes)
docs.text:
The poster is bare. Walk it left to right and have the room reconstruct, from memory, which stage fixed which failure. Then the question that matters:

"Which of these eight will come back first in production, and what is the number that will tell you?"

The answers are always F8 (the corpus ages the day you stop watching it) and F1 (a new document format arrives quietly). Both are caught by numbers already in their evaluation harness — coverage and answered_stale — which is the moment the whole course closes.

docs.title: Why physical
docs.text: A slide saying "F1 is fixed" is a claim. A sticker coming off a wall in front of twelve colleagues, after the pair who found the failure has said what fixed it, is a shared memory. Cohorts that run the wall recall the taxonomy months later; cohorts that skip it recall "we did some RAG labs."

docs.title: Day 2 Hour 3 · 10 minutes · groups of three
Purpose
docs.text: Before you can report per class, you have to see classes. This activity builds the reflex that makes the rest of Day 2 land: reading a question and knowing, before you run anything, which retrieval leg will decide the outcome.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: 24 query cards (below). Six class headers laid on the table: identifier · tabular · factoid · procedural · multi-hop · unanswerable.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
1. (4 min) Groups sort all 24 cards under the headers.
  2. (3 min) For each card, write the single retrieval capability that decides it: sparse · dense · table-aware chunking · two hops · refusal.
  3. (3 min) Compare with the classifier: python -c "from dalil.retrieve.router import classify_query; ...". Where you and the classifier disagree, decide who is right. The classifier is wrong about 10% of the time, and finding those cases is the real exercise — it is a rules-based classifier and it is auditable, which is precisely why it is in the pipeline instead of an LLM.

docs.title: The cards
docs.text: # Query 1 What figure does Circular 21/2025 set? 2 ما مضمون التعميم ٤٤/٢٠٢٥؟ 3 How much is the transport allowance for Grade 13? 4 Am I allowed to paste an internal document into ChatGPT? 5 Which data classification levels does the national policy define? 6 What is the parental leave entitlement for seconded contractors? 7 ما حقوق صاحب البيانات الشخصية بموجب النظام؟ 8 Our export procedure needs an approval — which SDAIA instrument requires it, and what must it cover? 9 remote work 10 How do I report a suspected data breach, and how fast? 11 What is the difference between the Data Sharing Policy and the Open Data Policy? 12 NDSA-IT-303 13 كم مدة الاحتفاظ بسجلات الموظفين؟ 14 What is the weather in Riyadh tomorrow? 15 Per-diem for a trip to Kuwait, Grade 11 16 Who approves a remote-work request? 17 ما هي مبادئ أخلاقيات الذكاء الاصطناعي؟ 18 If I resign during my training bond, what do I repay? 19 Which vendor supplies our payroll system? 20 housing 21 Article 4 22 What must a transfer risk assessment cover before data leaves the Kingdom? 23 How many employees resigned last quarter? 24 ما الفرق بين سياسة مشاركة البيانات وسياسة البيانات المفتوحة؟

docs.title: Facilitator key
docs.text:
• identifier: 1, 2, 12, 21 → sparse. Card 21 ("Article 4") is the argument starter: it is an identifier with almost no lexical mass, and it is genuinely ambiguous without a document. Good — say so.
  • tabular: 3, 15, 20(partly) → table-aware chunking. Card 15 needs both a table and a condition; let them argue.
  • factoid: 5, 7, 13, 17 → dense, and all four are Arabic-or-enumeration cases where an English-only embedder collapses.
  • procedural: 4, 10, 16, 18 → dense, but 18 is conditional and 4 is a policy question phrased as a personal one — the phrasing gap that kills title-matching label sets.
  • multi-hop: 8, 11, 22, 24 → two hops. 11 and 24 are the same question in two languages; if a group sorted them differently, that is a finding.
  • unanswerable: 6, 14, 19, 23 → refusal. Note that 6, 19 and 23 are plausible and adjacent to the corpus while 14 is obviously out of scope. Only the first three are dangerous.
  • ambiguous: 9, 20 — deliberately not given a header. Groups that create one have understood something the header set did not tell them.

docs.title: Debrief (60 seconds)
docs.text:
"Four of these twenty-four are unanswerable. In your production corpus, what fraction do you think it is — and does your evaluation set contain any?"

Most golden sets contain none, which is why most assistants answer them.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Teach the diagnostic reflex the whole of Module 6 exists to build: read the metric, name the stage. One accuracy number cannot localise a regression; four metrics can, and this is the drill that makes it automatic.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: Three printed report cards, below. Each is a real-shaped before/after from a cohort's own runs.

docs.title: Card A
docs.text:
Metric Baseline Current Δ context_recall 0.91 0.79 −0.12 context_precision 0.86 0.85 −0.01 faithfulness 0.92 0.94 +0.02 answer_relevancy 0.88 0.87 −0.01

What changed, and why is faithfulness rising the tell?

Retrieval regressed. The evidence stopped reaching the context, so the model has less to say and says less of it — faithfully. Faithfulness measures support, not usefulness: an answer that says almost nothing is almost perfectly supported. Faithfulness rising while context_recall falls is the signature of a retriever that broke. Look at embedding model, normalisation, or the filter, in that order.

docs.title: Card B
docs.text:
Metric Baseline Current Δ context_recall 0.90 0.91 +0.01 context_precision 0.84 0.61 −0.23 faithfulness 0.93 0.81 −0.12 answer_relevancy 0.89 0.86 −0.03

Ranking regressed. The right evidence is still being fetched (recall held) but it is buried under noise (precision collapsed), so the model reads the wrong passages and drifts (faithfulness follows). Almost always: the reranker silently stopped running, or top_k was raised without raising fetch_k. Check the reranked flag in the telemetry before touching the prompt.

docs.title: Card C
docs.text:
Metric Baseline Current Δ context_recall 0.89 0.90 +0.01 context_precision 0.85 0.86 +0.01 faithfulness 0.92 0.93 +0.01 answer_relevancy 0.88 0.89 +0.01 judge judge-v1 judge-v2 —

Nothing changed. Every delta is inside the noise floor and the judge was swapped, which makes the comparison meaningless regardless. This card is the trap: it looks like a small uniform improvement, and a team celebrates a release that did nothing. The gate warns on judge change for exactly this reason — tests/test_evaluation.py::test_gate_warns_when_judge_changed.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
1. (6 min) Pairs diagnose all three cards: name the stage, name the first thing they would check.
  2. (4 min) Report out. Card C is the one to spend time on.
  3. (2 min) Closing question: "what is your judge's noise floor, and how would you measure it?" (Run the harness three times unchanged. The spread is the floor. Anything smaller is not a result.)

docs.title: Facilitator note
docs.text: Participants reliably diagnose A and B and reliably celebrate C. Let them celebrate before revealing the judge row. The embarrassment is the lesson, and it is cheap here and expensive in production.

docs.title: Day 4 Hour 4 · 15 minutes · individual, then pairs
Purpose
docs.text:
Every participant leaves with a one-page memo their own organisation could act on. This is the activity that converts four days of engineering into something a director will read — and it is the only deliverable in the course written for a non-engineer.

The corpus makes this possible: participants have spent four days retrieving over the actual instruments their organisation is bound by, so the memo is not hypothetical.

docs.title: The template (one page, no more)
docs.text:
1 · What we would ground it in. Which documents, which classification levels, who may see what. Name the access tiers.

2 · What it must refuse. The categories of question the assistant must not answer, and the measured refusal rate you would require before launch.

3 · How we would know it is still right. The two or three numbers you would watch, how often, and who sees them. Name the one that catches staleness.

4 · What we would not build. The pattern you evaluated and rejected, with the measurement that justified rejecting it.

5 · The PDPL question. Where personal data would live in this architecture, why retrieval keeps it deletable and access-controlled in a way model weights do not, and what a transfer risk assessment would be required for.

6 · The one thing that would stop us. Be specific. "Data quality" is not an answer; "62% of our HR corpus is scanned Arabic and we have not measured OCR coverage" is.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
• (8 min) Write. Alone. Phones down.
  • (5 min) Swap with a partner. Their only job: mark every sentence a director would not act on.
  • (2 min) Two volunteers read section 6 aloud.

docs.title: Facilitator notes
docs.text:
• Section 4 is the one that separates a participant who understood this course from one who completed it. Anyone who cannot name a pattern they rejected has been collecting techniques rather than making decisions.
  • Section 6 answers are consistently more valuable than sections 1–5, and are worth capturing anonymously and sending to the programme owner. Four cohorts of section 6 is a national capability gap analysis that nobody had to commission.
  • This memo is a legitimate capstone bonus artefact. It is not graded, and saying so up front produces better memos.

docs.title: Activity pack — activities 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10
docs.text: Short-form briefs. Each is self-contained; print the card block at the end of the one you are running.

docs.title: Activity 1 — Architecture placement game
docs.text:
D1 H2 · 15 min · whole room · materials: the A2 architecture poster + vendor cards

Vendor cards: managed vector DB · embedding API · "RAG-in-a-box" platform · evaluation SaaS · reranker API · document-AI/OCR service · LLM gateway · open-source orchestration framework.

Each group places two cards on the poster where the product actually sits, then defends the placement for 60 seconds. The room challenges.

The three placements that always start arguments, and what to do with them:

  • "RAG-in-a-box" spans six stages. Ask which of the six it lets you measure separately. If the answer is none, the class has just discovered why the course teaches the stages rather than the product.
  • Evaluation SaaS gets placed at the end of the online lane. It belongs across both lanes and outside them — it measures ingestion coverage too.
  • Document-AI/OCR gets placed early and then forgotten. Ask what happens to its output when it is 8% wrong and nobody measured. That is Lab 2.

Close with: "Which stage would you never outsource, and why?" Most rooms converge on evaluation, which is the right answer for the reason they will not say out loud: it is the only stage whose failure is invisible from the outside.

docs.title: Activity 2 — Decision-framework workshop
docs.text:
D1 H2 · 15 min · groups of four · materials: 4 scenario cards + the scorecard worksheet

Score each scenario on nine dimensions (freshness · citation · access control · deletion · tone/format · volume of private knowledge · cost cadence · latency · auditability), then recommend RAG, fine-tune, or hybrid — and defend in 90 seconds.

Scenario cards:

  1. Hospital clinical protocols. Updated quarterly; wrong answers are clinical harm; clinicians must see the source paragraph. (RAG, hard — citation and freshness are absolute.)
  2. Government tender-writing assistant. Must produce documents in a rigid house format; content comes from a stable regulation set. (Hybrid — fine-tune the format, retrieve the content. The clearest hybrid case in the pack.)
  3. Call-centre script generator. Tone matters more than facts; the underlying product catalogue changes weekly. (Hybrid, and the interesting argument is which half gets fine-tuned.)
  4. Legal precedent search across 40 years of judgements. Volume is enormous, attribution is non-negotiable, nothing is ever deleted. (RAG, and the useful discussion is retrieval quality at that scale, not the architecture choice.)

Facilitator note. Card 2 is where the room learns that "RAG vs fine-tuning" is the wrong framing: the right question is which layer of the output does each technique own.

docs.title: Activity 4 — Corpus autopsy
docs.text:
D1 H4 · 10 min · pairs · materials: printed samples from the actual corpus

Hand each pair four printed pages, unlabelled:

  1. a page from the real PDPL Implementing Regulation (dense, numbered, clean text)
  2. a scanned Arabic NDSA HR policy page (image only)
  3. an allowance XLSX printed as a grid
  4. an intranet HTML page including its nav and footer boilerplate

For each: what will the parser return, what will it lose, and which failure class does that loss become?

Answers: (1) fine, but numbered articles must survive as section titles or citations become useless; (2) an empty string — F1; (3) a flattened row of numbers unless tables are serialised — F1; (4) 60% navigation and footer text that will happily embed and pollute the index — F5.

Ten minutes, and it makes Module 2's lecture land on a room that has already seen the problem on paper.

docs.title: Activity 6 — The reranker courtroom
docs.text:
D2 H4 · 12 min · whole room · materials: two near-duplicate policy extracts

Print one extract from the Data Sharing Policy and one from the Open Data Policy — both real SDAIA documents, both about making data available to others, each governing a different situation.

Read the query aloud: "What conditions apply before an entity may publish a dataset as open data?"

  • (3 min) Room votes on which extract answers it. The vote splits.
  • (3 min) Run dense-only retrieval live. Both surface; the wrong one often ranks first.
  • (3 min) Run the reranker live. Watch the ordering flip.
  • (3 min) The question that matters: "What did the cross-encoder see that the bi-encoder could not?" — it read the query and the passage together, so it could weigh "publish as open data" against "share with a specified entity", which are near-identical as isolated embeddings and materially different as a pair.

This is the most persuasive twelve minutes on Day 2. Do not replace it with a slide.

docs.title: Activity 7 — Prompt surgery
docs.text:
D3 H1 · 12 min · live, on the projector

Start from the working grounded prompt. Remove one constraint at a time, re-ask the same question, read the answer aloud.

Remove What happens, live "use ONLY the context" fluent, plausible, and drawing on training data within one turn "cite [n] after each claim" the answer stays correct and becomes unauditable — ask who would sign it the refusal clause the unanswerable probe gets a confident, structured, invented answer "prefer the later effective date" the superseded circular is quoted as current "answer in the language of the question" Arabic in, English out — factually right, operationally useless

Close by putting them all back and asking: "which of these five is a prompt problem, and which is really a retrieval problem wearing a prompt costume?" (Refusal and staleness are retrieval and metadata problems. A prompt cannot refuse what a threshold never flagged, and cannot prefer a date that was never indexed.)

docs.title: Activity 9 — Refusal threshold auction
docs.text:
D3 H5 · 12 min · groups of three · materials: the tau-sweep printout

Run make tau-sweep beforehand and print the curve: tau against refusal_recall and over_refusal.

Each group must commit publicly to one τ and justify it as a business decision, given a stated context you assign them:

  • Group A: a public citizen-facing service (wrong answers reach the press)
  • Group B: an internal HR helpdesk (over-refusal generates support tickets)
  • Group C: a compliance assistant used to prepare audit responses

Then reveal that the three correct answers are different, and that this is the point: τ is not a technical constant, it is a stated risk appetite, and it belongs in DECISIONS.md with the name of the person who set it.

Sharpest question to close on: "Your τ makes the system refuse 8% of answerable questions. Who hears about those, and how would you ever find out?"

docs.title: Activity 10 — Pattern pricing panel
docs.text:
D4 H1 · 12 min · groups of four · materials: 5 pattern cards

Cards: multi-query expansion · question decomposition (2 hops) · corrective self-RAG loop · query router · HyDE.

Each group is a review board. For every card they must state, in one line each: what it buys (which query class, how much), what it costs (p95 latency, tokens per query), and what breaks if it misfires.

Then a single ruling per group: ship, ship-behind-the-router, or reject.

The intended outcome — and it lands about four cohorts in five — is that the router is the only unconditional "ship", because it is the one pattern that makes the others affordable, and every other card becomes "ship-behind-the-router". A group that rejects HyDE on the grounds that they have no measurement for it yet has understood the course.

docs.title: Day 2, Hour 5 · 25 minutes · individual · open repo, closed neighbour
The brief
docs.text:
Three retrievers are broken. Each is a real configuration that a real team shipped. For each one you must:

  1. Diagnose from the evidence — the per-class report and the telemetry, not intuition.
  2. Fix it.
  3. Verify against the labelled set, per class.

docs.title: Scoring — 100 points
docs.text:
Weight What earns it Correct diagnosis from evidence 40 You name the stage and cite the number that proves it Verified fix 40 The affected class improves and no other class regresses Per-class reasoning 20 You never quote an aggregate as evidence

Automatic cap at 70%: any answer whose justification is an aggregate metric.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
git checkout pa1-clinic
make eval-retrieval CONFIG=broken_1     # and _2, _3

Each config writes reports/pa1_<n>.json with the aggregate, the per-class table and the retrieval telemetry.

docs.title: Patient 1
docs.text:
recall@10 aggregate  0.71
  identifier  0.94    tabular  0.88    procedural  0.81
  factoid     0.19    (AR subset 0.06)
telemetry: reranked=true  fetch_k=40  top_k=6  sparse_weight=1.0

Answer space. Diagnosis: __ Fix: _ Verified by: ___

docs.title: Patient 2
docs.text:
recall@10 aggregate  0.79
  factoid     0.91    procedural  0.88    ambiguous  0.93
  identifier  0.24    tabular     0.55
telemetry: reranked=true  fetch_k=40  top_k=6  sparse_weight=0.0

Answer space. Diagnosis: __ Fix: _ Verified by: ___

docs.title: Patient 3
docs.text:
recall@10 aggregate  0.08
  every class between 0.00 and 0.14
telemetry: reranked=false  fetch_k=40  top_k=6
           context.dropped = {"access": 38, "duplicate": 0, "budget": 0}

Answer space. Diagnosis: __ Fix: _ Verified by: ___

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• You may read the repository, the reports and the tests.
  • You may not ask a neighbour, and you may not read assessments/keys/PA1_key.md.
  • Write the number that proves each diagnosis. "It looked like an embedding problem" scores zero on the first 40 points even when the fix is correct.

docs.title: Instructor logistics
docs.text:
• Pre-build the three configs and confirm each reproduces its table exactly during the T-1-week rehearsal.
  • Patient 3 is the discriminator. Most participants reach for the retriever; the evidence is in the dropped counters, and the failure is an access-control context that grants nothing. Anyone who finds it from those counters has learned the most important debugging habit in the course: read what the pipeline told you before you theorise about what it did.

docs.title: The brief
docs.text:
You are handed eight transcripts of Dalil answering questions. For each:

  1. Classify the failure (or mark it correct).
  2. Name the stage that owns the fix — M2 metadata · M3 recall · M4 hybrid · M5 refusal/context · M6 gate.
  3. Write the one-line fix.
  4. For two of the eight, state who in an organisation owns the decision — not the code, the decision.

docs.title: Scoring — 100 points
docs.text: Weight Correct classification 50 Correct stage attribution 30 Governance reasoning — who owns the refusal threshold 20

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
reports/pa2_transcripts.json, generated by:

python scripts/run_redteam.py --suite unanswerable --out reports/pa2_transcripts.json
python scripts/run_redteam.py --suite staleness --chunks data/index/chunks_v2.jsonl

Each transcript shows the question, the answer, the retrieved chunk ids, the cited chunk ids, and the lifecycle field of every retrieved chunk. Everything you need to diagnose is in the trace. No transcript requires you to guess.

docs.title: The eight
docs.text: # Shape 1 Unanswerable question, confident structured answer, three citations that all resolve 2 Correct answer, correct citation, question was Arabic and the answer is English 3 Answer quotes a figure from a lifecycle: superseded chunk; the current chunk was retrieved at rank 4 and not cited 4 Refusal on a question the corpus clearly answers; the right chunk is at rank 1 5 Answer is correct and carries citation [7]; only six passages were supplied 6 Answer merges two documents' figures into one sentence with a single citation 7 Correct, cited, grounded — and answers a question about a department the asker may not see 8 Two documents disagree; the answer silently picks one

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Diagnose from the trace fields, not from how the answer reads.
  • A transcript may have more than one failure. Name the primary one — the one whose fix makes the others moot.

docs.title: Instructor logistics
docs.text:
• Generate the transcripts during the T-1-week rehearsal and freeze them. A live generation on the day produces different traces for different participants and makes the marking incomparable.
  • Transcripts 5 and 7 are the discriminators. See the key.

docs.title: Covers the corpus redesign, the public benchmarks and the pre-work
docs.text:
Use with the base bank (Q1–Q20 in INSTRUCTOR_PACKAGE.md). Ten questions per cohort, 15 minutes, closed book. Draw at least three from this addendum.

Q21. Why does the course use real SDAIA documents rather than synthesised ones for the bulk of the corpus? → Invented corpora flatter the systems built on them — consistent vocabulary, regular structure, questions written by the same author who wrote the answers. Real regulation is heterogeneous and was not written with retrieval in mind. It is also the corpus the participants' own organisations are actually bound by.

Q22. Name two things a corpus of published public regulation cannot teach, and what the course does about it. → Access control (everything public is public) and supersession (only current editions are published). Also scanned Arabic and tabular facts. Layer B, the synthetic overlay, supplies exactly these and nothing else.

Q23. Every Layer B document cites a Layer A instrument by title. Why does that design decision matter? → It makes the two layers one corpus and creates the cross-layer multi-hop question class: hop 1 finds the internal procedure, hop 2 finds the regulation it implements. Neither alone answers the question.

Q24. A labelled query set reports recall@10 = 1.00 for BM25 alone. What is most likely wrong with the labels? → The queries restate the document titles, so the set measures string overlap rather than retrieval. Real users do not phrase questions using the document's title.

Q25. What does MIRACL-ar tell you that your own Arabic recall number cannot? → Whether your pipeline is genuinely good or your corpus was flattering you. Your labels are self-graded; MIRACL's are human-annotated by people with no stake in your result.

Q26. Why is BEIR the right benchmark for validating your metric code specifically? → All 18 datasets share one corpus/queries/qrels shape, so recall@k, MRR and nDCG code written once runs unmodified across nine task types — and each dataset has published baselines to check your implementation against.

Q27. TechQA is the only public set in this course that grades refusal. Why does that matter more than one more retrieval benchmark? → Every other benchmark rewards retrieving something. A meaningful share of TechQA's questions are unanswerable from the supplied corpus, so it measures the behaviour the capstone requires and production systems fail at.

Q28. A system scores 1.00 on refusal recall. Why might that be worthless? → It may be refusing everything. over_refusal_rate on answerable questions is the companion metric; without it, refusal recall is trivially gamed.

Q29. Why is a refusal threshold a curve rather than a number? → τ trades refusal_recall against over_refusal. The right point depends on stated risk appetite, differs between a citizen-facing service and an internal helpdesk, and is a business decision recorded in DECISIONS.md — not a constant.

Q30. Arabic text extracted from a PDF looks perfect on screen but matches nothing. What is the most likely cause? → The PDF stores Unicode presentation forms (U+FB50–U+FEFF) rather than base letters, because it was written without a bidi engine. NFKC folding fixes it. Normalise at index and query time with the same function.

Q31. Your OCR CER is 8.4% with the default settings and the gate is 6%. Name the three levers, in the order you would try them. → Page segmentation mode (the default assumes a layout right-aligned Naskh pages do not have); language pack (ara alone often beats ara+eng on a 95%-Arabic page); binarisation. Change one at a time and re-measure after each.

Q32. In RAGAS terms, what is TruLens's "groundedness"? → faithfulness. Every RAG framework renames the same four measurements; the concepts do not change.

Q33. Your gate passes but a colleague says the system got worse. Where do you look first? → git log on the baseline file. A baseline regenerated in the same commit as a quality change makes any regression invisible.

Q34. Faithfulness rose and context_recall fell. Which stage regressed, and why is the rise the diagnostic signal? → Retrieval. Faithfulness measures support, not usefulness: an answer with less evidence says less, and says it faithfully. Rising faithfulness alongside falling recall is the signature of a broken retriever.

docs.title: Do not distribute before Day 2 Hour 5 is over.
Patient 1 — English-only embedding model on a bilingual corpus
docs.text:
Diagnosis. Factoid collapsed to 0.19 with the Arabic subset at 0.06, while identifier (0.94) and tabular (0.88) are healthy. Identifier and tabular queries are carried by the sparse leg, which is language-agnostic for exact tokens; factoid queries depend on the dense leg. A dense leg that works for English and not Arabic is an English-only embedding model. sparse_weight=1.0 and reranked=true rule out the other two stages.

The number that proves it: the AR subset at 0.06 against an EN factoid subset that is materially higher. Aggregate 0.71 proves nothing.

Fix. Swap to bge-m3 (or any strong multilingual model), re-index — this is a migration, not a config change — and confirm normalisation runs on the query path as well as at ingest.

Verification. factoid recall@10 ≥ 0.85 with the AR subset ≥ 0.85; no other class regresses.

Distractor to watch for. Participants blame Arabic normalisation. It is a contributing factor and worth fixing, but normalisation alone moves this a few points; the model swap moves it thirty. Full marks require naming the model.

docs.title: Patient 2 — Dense-only: the sparse leg is switched off
docs.text:
Diagnosis. sparse_weight=0.0 in the telemetry, and the collapse is confined to identifier (0.24) and tabular (0.55) — precisely the classes that depend on exact-token matching. Semantic classes are unaffected because the dense leg is fine.

The number that proves it: the telemetry line. This one is given to them; the assessed skill is reading the telemetry before theorising.

Fix. Restore RRF fusion with the sparse leg; set sparse_weight to mandatory for the identifier class via the router.

Verification. identifier ≥ 0.90, tabular ≥ 0.85, no regression elsewhere.

Distractor. Some participants "fix" this by fine-tuning the embedder or switching models. Ask them what an embedding model could possibly do about "44/2025" versus "45/2025" that it does not already do. Cap at 70% — the fix works by accident, and the reasoning is wrong in a way that will cost them later.

docs.title: Patient 3 — Access-control filter that grants nothing
docs.text:
Diagnosis. Every class is at floor, which rules out any stage that discriminates by query type — no embedding, ranking or fusion problem is uniform across all six classes. The evidence is in context.dropped = {"access": 38}: the retriever is fetching correctly and the filter is discarding everything. The AccessContext was constructed with max_tier="public" (or an empty department set) against a corpus that is 82% internal/restricted.

The number that proves it: dropped.access = 38 with dropped.budget = 0.

Fix. Construct the context with the caller's real tier and departments. Then — and this is the part that earns the last points — add a regression test so a filter that drops everything fails the build instead of quietly returning nothing.

Verification. Aggregate returns to the Patient-2 baseline or better, and the access-control check still shows 0 cross-department leaks. A "fix" that removes the filter entirely scores zero: it trades a retrieval failure for a governance incident.

Distractor. The most common wrong answer is "the index is empty". Ask them which number would look different if it were. (fetch_k would return 0 candidates; here it returns 40 and then discards them.)

docs.title: Marking notes
docs.text:
• Award the first 40 points only for a diagnosis that cites a number.
  • Patient 3 separates the top band. A participant who solves 1 and 2 and misses 3 is competent; one who reads the dropped counters unprompted is ready for the capstone.
  • Full marks on all three in under 25 minutes is rare and worth noting for the distinction band.

docs.title: PA-2 answer key — INSTRUCTOR ONLY
docs.text: # Primary failure Stage that owns the fix One-line fix 1 F7 — ungrounded answer to an unanswerable question M5 refusal Refuse before generation when top evidence score < τ; the citations resolving is irrelevant, the passages were irrelevant 2 Language mismatch (not a hallucination) M5 prompt Add and test the answer-in-the-question's-language rule; correct-but-unusable is still a failure 3 F8 — staleness M2 metadata, enforced at M4 filter Populate lifecycle/effective_date at ingest and exclude superseded at retrieval; ranking will not save you 4 Over-refusal M5 threshold τ too high, or scores are RRF sums being thresholded as probabilities; re-tune τ against the sweep, never by feel 5 Invented citation M5 citation verification Resolve every emitted [n] against the supplied blocks and fail the answer if it does not resolve 6 Un-attributable composite claim M5 prompt + verification Require one citation per claim, not per answer; count uncited_sentences 7 Access-control leak M5 context re-check (defence in depth) Re-assert the filter at context construction; the retriever filter alone is one tuning change from off 8 Unsurfaced conflict M5 prompt + M2 metadata Prompt rule 4: prefer the later effective date, name the supersession, cite both

docs.title: Governance answers (the last 20 points)
docs.text:
Who owns the refusal threshold?

Not the engineer. τ encodes a risk appetite: how many wrong answers the organisation will tolerate to avoid how many unhelpful refusals. The engineer owns the measurement — the sweep, the curve, the two rates at each point. The business or risk owner chooses the point on the curve, and their name belongs in DECISIONS.md next to the value.

Accept any answer that separates who measures from who decides. Reject any answer that leaves the decision with the person who wrote the code — that is the failure mode this question exists to name.

Who owns transcript 7?

The access leak is a data-governance failure before it is an engineering one: someone classified a document, someone granted a tier, and the pipeline enforced what it was told. The fix is defence in depth in the code and a classification review. A participant who says "add a filter" gets half; one who says "add a filter and ask who classified this document as internal" gets full marks.

docs.title: Marking notes
docs.text:
• Transcript 5 is the sharpest single item on the paper. An answer that is correct, fluent and cites a passage that does not exist is the exact failure that makes a RAG system unauditable, and participants routinely mark it "correct" because the claim is true. Being accidentally right is not grounding.
  • Transcript 7 catches participants who have stopped thinking about access control now that the retrieval labs are over. It is graded hard on purpose.
  • Common wrong answer on 3: "improve ranking so the current document ranks first." Ask what happens the day a superseded document is genuinely more lexically similar. Ranking is a preference; lifecycle filtering is a guarantee.

docs.title: Lab 2 OCR answer key — INSTRUCTOR ONLY
Do not distribute before step 2 is over.
The measured landscape
docs.text:
Shipped scanned subset: 22 image-only Arabic policy PDFs, Noto Naskh at 200 dpi with scanner artefacts (speckle, ±0.5° rotation, 0.35px blur, edge shadow). Ground truth: data/corpus/ocr_gold/*.txt.

Configuration Mean CER Verdict lang=ara+eng, psm 4, no binarisation, 300 dpi (shipped default) 0.084 fails the 0.06 gate lang=ara, psm 4, 300 dpi ~0.075 fails lang=ara, psm 6, 300 dpi 0.049 passes lang=ara, psm 6, binarised, 300 dpi 0.046 passes; p95 0.062, worst 0.100 lang=ara, psm 6, binarised, 400 dpi ~0.074 worse — see below

The winning line:

python -m dalil.ingest.pipeline --corpus data/corpus/corpus_v1 --out data/index \
  --ocr-lang ara --ocr-psm 6 --ocr-binarise

docs.title: Why each lever moves what it moves
docs.text:
psm 6 over psm 4 — the biggest single win (−0.026). Page segmentation mode 4 assumes a single column of variable-size text; mode 6 assumes a uniform block. These policy pages are uniform right-aligned Naskh with a consistent size, so mode 6's assumption is simply correct. This is the lever participants find last and it is worth more than everything else combined.

ara over ara+eng (−0.009). On a page that is ~95% Arabic, adding the English model gives Tesseract a second hypothesis space for every glyph, and it loses more on Arabic confusions than it gains on the handful of Latin document codes. Multi-language is not free.

Binarisation (−0.003). Small but real, and it also removes the blur/speckle sensitivity that makes results vary between machines.

400 dpi is worse, not better (+0.028). This is the most valuable surprise in the lab. The source raster is 200 dpi; rendering it at 400 upsamples an image that has no additional detail, and the interpolation smears exactly the thin connecting strokes Arabic depends on. Resolution is not a monotonic lever, and "raise the DPI" is folklore, not engineering. If a participant reports 400 dpi helped, ask to see the number.

docs.title: The 0.05 stretch target
docs.text: Mean 0.046 already clears 0.05. The stretch task is the p95 and the worst document: 0.062 and 0.100. Getting the tail down requires per-document escalation — detect low mean OCR confidence and retry that document with a different psm — which is the right production pattern and roughly fifteen minutes of work for a fast finisher.

docs.title: What to say when someone reports 0.02
docs.text: Ask which documents they measured. evaluate_ocr reports documents, worst_index and worst_cer for exactly this reason. A mean over three easy scans is not a coverage number, and the habit of quoting a mean without an n is the thing worth correcting here — it will show up again in their capstone.

docs.title: The point of the lab
docs.text: Not "use psm 6". It is that OCR settings are a measurable, per-corpus engineering choice, and that shipping an unmeasured OCR stage means shipping unknown coverage. A participant who leaves with a CER number they own, and the knowledge that one plausible lever made things worse, has the lesson.

docs.title: Day 4 · 3 hours build + demo
docs.text: The rubric, milestones and mandatory scope in INSTRUCTOR_PACKAGE.md stand unchanged. This file records what the corpus redesign changes about how the capstone is executed and graded, and provides the scaffolding.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
1 · The corpus is real, so the governance requirement is real.

Requirement 7 gains a section: DECISIONS.md must include a short PDPL paragraph — where personal data lives in your architecture, why retrieval keeps it deletable and access-controlled in a way model weights do not, and what would require a transfer risk assessment. Two or three sentences. You have spent four days retrieving over the instruments that impose these obligations; this is where you show you read them.

2 · Two extension options are added, both cross-layer.

Extension What it must demonstrate Cross-layer multi-hop An internal NDSA procedure composed with the SDAIA instrument it cites, both cited in one answer, ≥ 0.80 on the multi-hop golden subset, single-hop latency flat Regulatory conflict surfacing Detect and surface a superseded-vs-current disagreement with both citations rather than silently choosing

The five original extensions remain available.

3 · The staleness drill is one command.

make ingest-v2 && make staleness

It reports answered_stale with lifecycle filtering on and off. Both numbers are required. If delta_answered_stale ≈ 0, your filter is not doing anything and you got lucky on ranking — the report says so explicitly, and a submission that quotes the passing number without noticing the zero delta is capped.

4 · The demo is scripted.

make demo

Runs all five rubric demonstrations in order — English answer with citations, Arabic answer with citations, correct refusal, the staleness toggle, the access-control contrast — and continues past any stage that fails. A demo that dies at stage 1 tells the grader nothing about stages 2–5.

docs.title: The submission
docs.text:
your-repo/
├── README.md            the runbook: a stranger runs `make demo` in 10 minutes
├── EVALUATION.md        the five tables, from YOUR runs (make report)
├── DECISIONS.md         five decisions + the PDPL paragraph
├── FAILURE_GALLERY.md   from Lab 1, with each entry struck through and dated
├── RETRIEVAL.md         the model comparison and ef sweep from Lab 3
└── reports/             every JSON your tables were built from

Tags lab1 … lab7 must be visible in the history. The history is evidence: a repository with one commit called "final" cannot demonstrate that the failure gallery preceded the fixes.

docs.title: The five decisions (DECISIONS.md)
docs.text:
Each needs: what you chose, what you rejected, and the number that decided it.

  1. Embedding model — and what the Arabic subset cost the alternative.
  2. Chunking strategy — and your mid-sentence percentage before and after.
  3. Refusal threshold τ — with the sweep, and who set the risk appetite.
  4. Retrieval budget (fetch_k / top_k / ef) — with the latency you bought.
  5. One pattern you rejected — with the measurement that justified rejecting it.

Decision 5 is the one graders read first. A capstone that adopted every technique it encountered has demonstrated enthusiasm; one that rejected a technique on evidence has demonstrated engineering.

docs.title: Grading — additions to the existing rubric
docs.text:
These do not add points. They are caps, and they exist because each one is a way to look finished while being unfinished.

Cap Trigger criterion capped at 70% any retrieval number quoted as an aggregate without its per-class table criterion capped at 70% reports/baseline.json changed in the same commit as a quality change criterion capped at 70% a refusal path that refuses > 15% of answerable golden questions (gaming the unanswerable metric) criterion capped at 70% staleness reported with delta_answered_stale ≈ 0 and no explanation submission capped at 70% any citation in the demo that does not resolve to a retrieved chunk automatic fail on the criterion benchmark numbers produced with hash-384, --sample, or judge: offline-proxy presented as results

That last row is worth reading aloud on Day 4 morning. Every substitute in this repository stamps its own name into the report it produces, precisely so that nobody can do this by accident — which means doing it is a choice.

docs.title: Live verification (graders)
docs.text:
Two questions per participant, unseen, at the demo:

  1. A fresh unanswerable question — Dalil must refuse.
  2. A fresh identifier question naming a circular — Dalil must retrieve it.

Then one spoken question, which carries more signal than either:

"Turn lifecycle filtering off and tell me what is about to happen, before you run it."

A participant who can predict the failure understands the golden thread. One who has to run it to find out has assembled a pipeline without understanding what each stage is defending against.

docs.title:
EVALUATION.md —

Generate the skeleton with make report, then fill the prose. The tables come from your own JSON; the sentences are yours. A risk officer who does not code must be able to read this and sign it.

System: Dalil · Corpus: corpus_v2 (17 SDAIA Layer A + 134 NDSA Layer B) Date: _ · Judge: ____ (temperature 0) · Judge noise floor: ± Config: embed=_ rerank= fetch_k= top_k= ef= τ=_
Table 1 — Ingestion coverage and chunk quality
docs.text:
Metric Value Gate Pass documents seen / parsed quarantined 0 unsupported formats 0 OCR documents / CER (mean, p95, worst) ≤ 0.06 chunks · tables kept whole mid-sentence starts < 8%

One sentence: what does your coverage number NOT include, and how would a user find out?

docs.title: Table 2 — Retrieval: recall and latency
