docs.title: Running without infrastructure
docs.text: Every lab has an offline path. --backend memory runs BM25 plus optional dense vectors in-process; --model hash-384 substitutes a deterministic test embedder; the golden-set runner falls back to a stub answer model. Reports produced this way are stamped with the substitute's name and must not be quoted as results — they exist so a laptop with a broken Docker install does not stop someone learning.

docs.title: Lab 1 — Naive RAG baseline and failure gallery
Objective
docs.text:
Stand up a deliberately naive pipeline over the Dalil corpus, then break it systematically. You will classify its behaviour on 12 adversarial probes into the F1–F8 taxonomy and commit FAILURE_GALLERY.md — the artefact this course refers back to for four days.

You are not fixing anything today. Diagnosis before treatment.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
make doctor                 # must show 0 failed
make ingest-naive           # 500-char blind splits, no metadata, no OCR

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1 · (10 min) Read the ingest report, do not trust the summary line.

cat data/index/ingest_report_naive.json | python3 -m json.tool | head -40

Reference run from this repository:

Parsed 122/122 docs (70 pdf, 8 xlsx, 24 html, 20 docx)
  needs_ocr 22, ocr_done 0
  unsupported 0, quarantined 22, errors 0
Chunks: 287 (avg 2.87/doc)  tables kept whole: 0
Mid-sentence starts: 41.5%

Three numbers on that screen should worry you. Write them down before you read the next paragraph.

quarantined 22 — a sixth of the corpus produced no text and the pipeline reported success. tables kept whole: 0 — every allowance figure has been shredded into loose cells. 41.5% — two in five chunks begin mid-sentence.

Now open five random chunks and look at them:

shuf -n 5 data/index/chunks_naive.jsonl | python3 -c "
import sys,json
for l in sys.stdin: print('---'); print(json.loads(l)['text'][:300])"

2 · (10 min) Ask the five friendly questions.

make probe SET=easy

It works. Record the answers. This is the feeling that ships broken assistants.

3 · (20 min) Run the 12 adversarial probes.

make probe SET=failure_gallery

For each probe capture: the answer, the retrieved chunk ids, and a failure class F1–F8 with one sentence of evidence. The runner prints a blank failure class: ____ line for exactly this reason — it will not classify for you.

Classify from the retrieved chunks, not from the answer text. An answer that reads plausibly and cites nothing is not evidence of anything. The question is always: was the right chunk in the top-k, and if not, why not?

The taxonomy:

Failure Symptom Fixed in F1 parsing loss the fact never became searchable text M2 F2 chunk-boundary damage evidence split across two chunks, neither sufficient M2 F3 semantic miss right meaning, wrong vector neighbourhood (usually AR↔EN) M3 F4 lexical miss exact identifier blurred by dense retrieval M4 F5 precision collapse right document present, buried under near-duplicates M4 F6 context construction evidence retrieved, ignored or diluted at generation M5 F7 ungrounded answer confident answer to an unanswerable question M5 F8 staleness superseded document quoted as current M2 + M6

4 · (5 min) Compare with the neighbouring pair. Resolve disagreements by opening the retrieved chunks together. Do not debate the answer text.

5 · (5 min) Commit.

git add FAILURE_GALLERY.md && git commit -m "docs: baseline failure gallery"

docs.title: Expected outcome
docs.text: Roughly F1 ×2 · F2 ×1 · F3 ×2 · F4 ×2 · F5 ×1 · F6 ×1 · F7 ×2 · F8 ×1. Nine of twelve matching the reference key is a pass. The three you argue about are usually F3-vs-F5 and F1-vs-F2, and those arguments are the lab.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix make probe says "run make ingest first" no chunks file make ingest-naive every probe answered correctly you are on a solution branch, or ran easy git checkout lab1-start; SET=failure_gallery Arabic renders as boxes in the terminal terminal font, not your data inspect via --json, or the notebook gateway 429 per-participant rate limit, by design make probe SET=... DELAY=2 answers look like [stub answer grounded in context] no gateway key set expected offline; the retrieval evidence is still real and is what you classify

docs.title: Instructor notes
docs.text:
• Resist every urge to fix something today.
  • The two F7 probes produce the strongest reaction in the room. Read fg-10 aloud — "What is the parental leave entitlement for contractors on secondment to a foreign mission?" — and then read the baseline's answer aloud. It is fluent, specific, structured, and entirely invented.
  • fg-02 is the other one worth projecting: an Arabic HR policy the parser returned as an empty string, silently, while reporting 122/122 parsed.
  • Fast finishers: vary k from 2 to 10 and watch F5 worsen as F3 improves. That tension is Module 4, previewed.
  • Answer key: data/keys/failure_gallery_key.json, or make probe SET=failure_gallery --key. Do not project it before step 4.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Parse the whole corpus with format dispatch, Arabic OCR and structure-aware chunking; attach lifecycle metadata; and prove with numbers that F1 and F2 have retreated.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
pip install pymupdf python-docx openpyxl trafilatura pytesseract
sudo apt-get install -y tesseract-ocr tesseract-ocr-ara     # or use the devcontainer
make doctor

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1 · (10 min) Implement the parser registry dispatch and run it.

python -m dalil.ingest.pipeline --corpus data/corpus/corpus_v1 --out data/index --no-ocr

Read the report. needs_ocr should be 22 and unsupported should be 0. Note that with --no-ocr those 22 documents are quarantined, not silently dropped — find the line in loaders.py that makes that true.

2 · (10 min) Wire the OCR path and measure it.

Run it with the defaults first:

python -m dalil.ingest.pipeline --corpus data/corpus/corpus_v1 --out data/index

Reference: CER ≈ 0.084 — FAIL (gate is 0.06).

Now tune it. You have three levers and about eight minutes:

  • --ocr-lang — is ara+eng helping or hurting on a page that is 95% Arabic?
  • --ocr-psm — page segmentation mode. The default assumes a layout these right-aligned Naskh policy pages do not have.
  • --ocr-binarise — threshold the raster before OCR.

Re-measure after every single change. Change one lever at a time — this is the whole discipline of the lab in one instruction.

Target: CER ≤ 0.06. Reference tuned run: 0.053 mean, 0.062 p95, 0.100 worst. Reaching 0.05 is the distinction task.

3 · (15 min) Structure-aware chunking.

make ingest
python -c "
import json; r=json.load(open('data/index/ingest_report.json')); print(r['chunk_stats'])"
Statistic Naive (Lab 1) Structure-aware (target) Reference chunks 287 — 492 tables kept whole 0 > 40 56 mid-sentence starts 41.5% < 8% 4.1% quarantined 22 0 0

If your mid-sentence percentage is still above 20%, look at the overlap code before you look at anything else. Character-slice overlap is the classic self-inflicted wound: a fix for orphaned clauses that creates orphaned clauses, because every overlapped chunk now starts mid-sentence.

4 · (10 min) Metadata and the money moment.

Verify five random chunks carry department, access_tier, effective_date and section_title. Then:

make ask Q="What is the monthly housing allowance for Grade 11?"

The figure that produced a confident-wrong answer in Lab 1 is now retrievable, because the table survived ingestion as one chunk with its header attached.

5 · (5 min) Re-run three Lab 1 probes, strike F1 and F2 off the poster, commit.

git commit -am "feat(ingest): structure-aware bilingual pipeline"

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix needs_ocr on a digital PDF text layer present but sparse lower the threshold in load_pdf; inspect page.get_text("dict") CER ≈ 0.20 and the Arabic reads backwards your OCR build is bidi-unaware, or the page was rendered from presentation forms this is a rendering problem upstream, not an OCR one — see corpus/build_layer_b.py::fix_ar_runs CER ≈ 0.14 with text truncated at line ends long lines running off the page edge wrapping, not OCR. Look at the raster, not the transcript tables still flattened loader used naive text mode confirm _serialise_table runs and kind == "table" blocks exist chunk count explodes past 5,000 overlap applied across tables overlap prose only; tables are atomic Arabic query still misses normalisation at ingest only normalise() must run on the query path too — this foreshadows M3

docs.title: Instructor notes
docs.text:
• The money moment is step 4. Project the Lab 1 confident-wrong answer beside the Lab 2 correct one, then physically remove the F1 sticker.
  • Step 2 is where data-science-background participants first feel that coverage is a number they own. Do not rush it; this is the overrun-prone lab and it is worth its full length.
  • Fast finishers: implement sentence-window retrieval (the LlamaIndex companion course, lesson 2) on one long policy and compare chunk coherence with structure-aware splitting. The honest result on policy documents is usually a wash — which is itself the lesson: don't pay for a technique without evidence.
  • Answer key: assessments/keys/lab2_ocr_key.md.

docs.title: Lab 3 — Embed, index, and measure recall
Objective
docs.text: Embed the Lab 2 chunks with bge-m3, build the Qdrant collection with payload filters, and benchmark recall@k and latency on the 138-query labelled set — proving F3 retreats against an English-only baseline.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
make qdrant                    # docker compose up -d qdrant
export HF_HOME=/course/models  # models are pre-cached; do NOT download in class
make doctor

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1 · (5 min) Build the collection.

make index
python -c "from dalil.index.collection import collection_stats; print(collection_stats())"

Confirm: vector size 1024, cosine, and the four payload indexes. Payload indexes are not an optimisation — without them a filtered search either scans the whole collection or returns nothing, and every access-control gate in this course is a filter.

2 · (10 min) Upsert, then upsert again.

make index && make index

The point count must be identical after the second run. If it doubled, your point ids are not stable — the classic cause is using enumerate() as the id instead of hashing doc_id:ordinal. Fix it now; an index that grows every time you re-ingest will poison every number you measure for the next three days.

3 · (15 min) The measurement that is the module's thesis.

make eval-retrieval MODEL=BAAI/bge-m3
make eval-retrieval MODEL=sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2

Record both in RETRIEVAL.md, with the Arabic subset broken out. The aggregate gap is embarrassing; the Arabic-subset gap is the argument:

Model recall@10 recall@10 (AR) bge-m3 ~0.91 ~0.88 all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (English-only) ~0.63 ~0.29

Before you accept those numbers, run the ablation that makes them mean something:

make eval-retrieval MODEL=... # then edit dalil/arabic.py to disable digit
                              # unification, and run it again

Which single line of normalisation is worth the most recall on this corpus? Write the answer in DECISIONS.md. (It is not the one most people guess.)

4 · (10 min) The ef sweep: recall is a purchasable quantity.

make ef-sweep

Plot recall@10 against p95 latency for ef ∈ {32, 64, 128, 256}. Pick the knee. Record the value and the reason — "we chose ef=128 because ef=256 bought 0.005 recall for 40% more p95 latency" is an engineering sentence; "we used the default" is not.

5 · (5 min) The access-control check, and strike F3.

python scripts/ask.py --tier public "What is the monthly housing allowance for Grade 11?"
python scripts/ask.py --tier restricted --departments finance "What is the monthly housing allowance for Grade 11?"

The first must not surface restricted pay data. Confirm 0 cross-department leaks across 50 queries, then commit:

git commit -am "feat(index): bge-m3 collection with filtered retrieval"

docs.title: Sidebar — MIRACL Arabic (15 min, whole room together)
docs.text:
make bench-miracl

The numbers above are self-graded: we wrote the corpus and we wrote the labels. MIRACL-ar is human-annotated Arabic retrieval by people with no stake in this course. Compare:

Your Dalil AR recall Your MIRACL-ar recall@100 What it means high in the published range for your model your pipeline is sound high far below range the corpus was flattering you low in range pipeline is fine; ingestion or normalisation is losing the Arabic

Fifteen minutes to find out whether the last two days were real.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Arabic recall near zero English-only model, or normalisation skipped on the query path use bge-m3; call normalise() in both paths recall low everywhere vectors not L2-normalised normalize_embeddings=True at index and query filtered search returns nothing missing payload index or over-narrow filter create the index; check field names against PAYLOAD_INDEXES upsert doubles the point count non-stable ids hash doc_id:ordinal p95 latency spikes ef above your knee drop to the knee value

docs.title: Instructor notes
docs.text:
• Put both model rows on the shared board and let the 0.88 / 0.29 Arabic gap sit for thirty seconds before explaining it. The silence does the teaching.
  • The ef sweep is where "recall" stops being a property and becomes a purchase.
  • Fast finishers: enable binary quantization with rescoring, measure the recall delta and the memory saving, and decide whether you would ship it. The answer is usually yes and the reasoning is the point.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Add sparse retrieval and RRF fusion, then a cross-encoder reranker, and quantify the improvement per query class. This is the lab where the aggregate metric stops being allowed.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1 · (5 min) Look at the problem before fixing it.

make eval-retrieval

Reference, BM25 alone on the shipped labels:

Query class n recall@10 identifier 60 1.000 tabular 24 1.000 procedural 20 0.300 factoid 22 0.239 aggregate 138 0.777

Dense-only inverts this table almost exactly. That inversion is the entire argument for hybrid retrieval, and you should be able to state why each cell sits where it does before you write a line of fusion code.

2 · (15 min) Sparse vectors and RRF fusion.

Implement hybrid_search. Fuse with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, not a weighted sum of scores:

score(d) = Σ over rankers   1 / (k + rank_r(d)),    k = 60

Cosine similarity lives in [-1, 1]; BM25 is unbounded and corpus-dependent. Normalising them onto a shared scale needs per-corpus tuning that rots the day the corpus grows. RRF discards the scores and fuses ranks: no tunable parameter, stable, and it degrades gracefully when one leg legitimately returns nothing.

3 · (15 min) The reranker and the two-stage budget.

Add bge-reranker-v2-m3. Fetch 40, keep 6.

A bi-encoder encodes query and document separately, so document vectors are precomputed and searched in milliseconds — and the model never sees the pair together. A cross-encoder reads them jointly, cannot be precomputed, and must run per candidate. Hence: pay the cheap stage for recall, pay the expensive stage on 40 candidates only, send 6 to the LLM.

4 · (10 min) The four-column table.

make ablation

Produce, for each query class, recall@10 under: dense-only → +sparse → +RRF → +rerank. Then answer, in DECISIONS.md:

  • Which class did sparse rescue, and by how much?
  • Which class did the reranker rescue, and by how much?
  • Is there a class where reranking cost you recall? (There usually is.)
  • What is the p95 latency price of the reranker, and would you pay it for identifier queries alone?

5 · (5 min) Strike F4 and F5.

git commit -am "feat(retrieve): hybrid RRF + cross-encoder reranking"

docs.title: The rule that starts here
docs.text:
No aggregate-only retrieval metric is accepted for the rest of the course. The capstone rubric caps a submission at 70% for aggregate-only reporting. An aggregate of 0.72 with the identifier class at 0.31 is not a working retriever; it is a working retriever for questions nobody in a compliance department asks.

tests/test_evaluation.py::test_aggregate_hides_a_collapsed_class is that rule as an executable assertion. Open it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix sparse leg returns nothing sparse vectors were never indexed the collection must be created with a sparse field; this is a re-index, not a config change identifier class still low digits not normalised on both paths normalise_identifier at index and query reranker made no difference model failed to load and the code silently returned input order check reranked in the telemetry — a silent no-op reranker is how teams ship a "two-stage" retriever that has one stage p95 latency tripled reranking the full fetch_k, or fetch_k far too large fetch 40, rerank 40, keep 6 RRF changed nothing you fused one non-empty ranking with one empty one check both legs return results before blaming the fusion

docs.title: Instructor notes
docs.text:
• The Open Data Policy / Data Sharing Policy pair is the live demo: two real, semantically adjacent SDAIA policies. Dense retrieval confuses them; the reranker separates them. Run the query on the projector both ways.
  • The two-stage budget is an economic argument, not a technical one. Retrieval is cheap and generation tokens are expensive; the reranker is the bridge.
  • PA-1 follows immediately in Hour 5. See assessments/PA1_retrieval_clinic.md.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Build the context assembler and the grounded prompt; emit citations an auditor can follow; implement insufficient-evidence refusal. Retire F6 and F7.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1 · (10 min) The context budget.

Implement assemble_context. Three behaviours, in order of value:

  • Budget, not volume. Every extra chunk costs input tokens on every query for the life of the system, and dilutes attention on the chunk that holds the answer.
  • Edge ordering. Best chunk first, second-best last, weaker ranks buried in the middle. Same chunks, same tokens, better accuracy — the cheapest win in the whole pipeline.
  • De-duplication. An Arabic and an English edition of the same clause waste budget twice and make the model's citation choice arbitrary.

Watch the Arabic token estimate. Latin text runs ~4 chars/token; Arabic runs closer to 2.2 on most tokenizers. Using the Latin ratio under-counts Arabic context by about 45% — which is how a system that works in English blows its context window the first week it goes bilingual.

2 · (15 min) The grounded prompt.

Six constraints, each defending against a specific failure:

Constraint Defends against answer from the context only ungrounded fluency (faithfulness) cite [n] after every claim unverifiable answers (audit) say so when evidence is insufficient F7 prefer the later effective date, name the supersession F8 answer in the language of the question an Arabic question answered in English quote figures, dates and identifiers exactly silent paraphrase of a legal figure

3 · (10 min) Citations that resolve.

A prompt cannot verify itself. Implement verify_citations: resolve every [n] the model emitted against the blocks it was actually given.

A citation that does not resolve is not a formatting problem. It is a fabricated source, and the capstone requires zero of them.

Report invented_citations and uncited_sentences in the trace.

4 · (10 min) Refusal, and access control in depth.

Refuse before generation when the top evidence score is below τ. That makes refusal a property of retrieval — measurable, tunable, recorded in config — rather than a mood of the model, and it saves the token spend on questions the corpus provably cannot answer.

Then re-assert the access filter at context construction, even though the retriever already filtered. The retriever's filter is one careless tuning change away from being disabled, and the capstone's "0 cross-department leaks" gate has to survive that.

python scripts/ask.py --tier public   "What is the monthly housing allowance for Grade 11?"
python scripts/ask.py --tier restricted --departments finance "..."

5 · (5 min) Commit and strike F6, F7.

docs.title: Mini-exercise — the citation that does not check out
docs.text:
An answer cites [3]. Three passages were supplied. The claim is true — you checked the source document yourself. Is this a pass?

No. The system cannot demonstrate where the claim came from, so an auditor cannot verify it, so the answer is unusable in exactly the setting that required retrieval in the first place. Being accidentally right is not grounding.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix refuses everything τ too high, or you are thresholding raw RRF sums as if they were probabilities see evidence_strength — RRF sums must be rescaled; re-tune τ whenever the retrieval stack changes refuses nothing τ ≈ 0, or the model was never told it may refuse both: fix the prompt and the threshold citations present, none resolve markers renumbered after assembly assign markers once, at assembly, and never reorder afterwards Arabic questions answered in English prompt rule 5 missing or too weak state it explicitly and test it context blows the budget on Arabic only Latin token ratio applied to Arabic see estimate_tokens

docs.title: Instructor notes
docs.text:
• Prompt surgery live: delete rule 1 from the system prompt and re-ask an unanswerable question. The model becomes fluent and wrong within one turn.
  • The dropped counters in the context stats are worth projecting — participants are surprised how much the deduplicator removes on a bilingual corpus.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Run RAGAS over the 120-question golden set, store a baseline, and wire a regression gate that fails the build. This is the lab that turns evaluation from a report into an engineering control.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
0 · (15 min, whole room) Sidebar: validate your ruler before you measure with it.

make bench-beir            # BEIR/scifact

Every BEIR dataset ships the same three objects — corpus, queries, qrels — so the recall@k / MRR / nDCG code you wrote for Dalil runs unmodified. Point your metric implementations at a dataset with published baselines. If your nDCG@10 on SciFact with a known model is far off the published figure, the bug is in your metric code, and you have just avoided grading your entire capstone with a broken ruler.

1 · (10 min) Run the golden set.

make eval-golden

Look at reports/grounding.json before you look at any RAGAS number. It answers the questions RAGAS cannot: did every answer carry citations, did every citation resolve to a chunk that was actually retrieved, did the correct document get cited rather than merely retrieved.

2 · (15 min) RAGAS, and what each metric indicts.

make eval-ragas
Metric drops Stage indicted context_recall retrieval — the evidence never reached the context context_precision ranking — the evidence was there, buried under noise faithfulness generation — claims unsupported by the context answer_relevancy generation — grounded, but not an answer to the question

That mapping is why RAG needs its own metric suite: one accuracy number cannot localise a regression, so it cannot drive a fix.

Then read the by-class and by-language breakdowns in the report. An aggregate faithfulness of 0.91 with the Arabic subset at 0.74 is not a passing system.

3 · (10 min) Baseline and gate.

make baseline          # records reports/baseline.json — its OWN commit
make gate              # exit code 1 on a regression

Three disciplines the gate enforces for you, each of which exists because a cohort got burned by it:

  • Pin the judge model and temperature. An unpinned judge turns a 0.02 delta into a coin flip, and a team that cannot distinguish signal from noise cannot run a gate at all.
  • The baseline records its config. Comparing a run at top_k=10 against a baseline at top_k=6 compares two different systems. The gate says so instead of silently passing.
  • Never regenerate the baseline in the same commit as a quality change. The capstone rubric flags it. It is the RAG equivalent of editing the test to match the bug.

4 · Measure your judge's own noise. (5 min, and skipping it costs you later.)

Run the harness three times unchanged. The spread is your noise floor. Any delta smaller than it is not a result. Put the number in EVALUATION.md; you will need it every time someone claims a 0.01 improvement.

docs.title: Offline mode
docs.text: No gateway key? make eval-ragas falls back to lexical proxy metrics, stamps judge: "offline-proxy" in the JSON, and prints a warning. The plumbing is real — citations resolve or they do not, refusals happen or they do not. The answer quality numbers are not. Never quote them.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix every metric near zero stub answer model expected offline; read grounding.json instead faithfulness high, context_recall low retrieving the wrong things and faithfully summarising them fix retrieval; faithfulness alone is not quality metrics move ±0.05 between identical runs judge not pinned pin model and temperature=0, then re-measure the noise floor gate passes but the system got worse you regenerated the baseline check git log reports/baseline.json

docs.title: Instructor notes
docs.text:
• The metric-autopsy exercise: hand out a report where context_recall dropped 0.09 and faithfulness rose 0.02. Ask which stage regressed and why faithfulness rising is the tell. (Retrieval got worse; the model is faithfully reporting less.)
  • Open tests/test_evaluation.py on the projector. Six of those tests are the module's content, executable.
  • PA-2 follows in Hour 5. See assessments/PA2_hallucination_triage.md.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Add multi-query expansion, two-hop decomposition and a corrective loop — and a router that keeps you from paying for any of them when they are not needed.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1 · (10 min) Multi-query expansion, and where it does not help.

Implement expand_queries + RRF over the paraphrase rankings. Then measure it on three classes:

Class Expected effect Why ambiguous large gain one embedding lands in one neighbourhood; three cover what the user meant identifier zero gain three paraphrases of "Circular 44/2025" are three dense queries blurring the same token; sparse fixes this, expansion cannot multi_hop zero gain expansion widens one hop; it cannot compose two documents

Report all three. The two zeros are the finding.

2 · (15 min) Decomposition and the second hop.

The question class a linear pipeline structurally cannot answer:

"Our Data Export Procedure requires a transfer risk assessment before exporting personal data — which SDAIA instrument imposes that, and what does it require the assessment to cover?"

Hop 1 lands in our internal procedure (Layer B). Hop 2 lands in the real SDAIA Transfer Regulation and its Risk Assessment Guideline (Layer A). No single chunk holds both.

Three things that separate real multi-hop from multi-query with extra steps:

  • Hop 2 is conditioned on hop 1. Retrieving both sub-questions independently and concatenating is not multi-hop.
  • Sub-questions are deduplicated before any retrieval happens. The commonest bug in this lab is a decomposer emitting two paraphrases of the same sub-question, doubling cost for identical evidence.
  • Hops are capped (max_hops = 2). Uncapped hopping is how a "smart" pipeline spends 40 seconds and real money on a question it will refuse anyway.

3 · (10 min) Corrective RAG, with a grader that can say none.

retrieve → grade → sufficient: answer
                 → partial:    rewrite once, retry
                 → none:       refuse now

Both safeguards are load-bearing:

  • An iteration cap. Everyone builds the uncapped version once.
  • A grader with a floor. A grader that always returns partial will loop to the cap on an unanswerable question and then answer it from irrelevant context — converting an honest refusal into a confident hallucination. That is the Module 7 knowledge check, and it is tests/test_advanced.py::test_grader_can_say_none_so_the_loop_can_refuse.

4 · (10 min) The router — the part that makes this affordable.

Every pattern above costs latency and tokens. Route so that only the queries that need them pay:

Class Path identifier, tabular, factoid, procedural hybrid + rerank ambiguous multi-query conditional, comparative, multi_hop multi-hop unanswerable refuse — do not retrieve, do not loop

Measure average latency across the whole labelled set, before and after. If the advanced patterns raised your average by more than a few percent, your router is not doing its job.

5 · (5 min) Commit. F8's fix is metadata, not cleverness — see the Day-4 staleness drill.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A table of: gain per class per pattern, and the cost of each pattern in p95 latency and tokens. Honest null results count for full credit. A participant who reports "HyDE bought us nothing on this corpus, here is the measurement" has demonstrated exactly the judgement the course is trying to build; a participant who bolts on four patterns and reports one aggregate number has not.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix latency doubled across the board patterns applied to every query route them decomposer returns two near-identical sub-questions no dedup _overlap threshold in decompose corrective loop never refuses grader has no "none" verdict give it a floor multi-hop finds one document twice hop 2 not conditioned on hop 1 pass hop 1's findings into hop 2's query expansion helped identifiers you are measuring noise check n per class before believing any delta

docs.title: Instructor notes
docs.text:
• Run the cross-layer question live. Watching hop 1 land in the fictional procedure and hop 2 land in real SDAIA regulation is the moment the two-layer corpus design justifies itself.
  • Ask directly: "which of these four patterns would you actually ship, and what would you tell your manager it costs?" The right answer for most teams is "the router and nothing else, until we have evidence."

docs.title: العمل التحضيري قبل الدورة
docs.text:
Two assignments. One is required and gates Day 2. One is a companion for Day 3 and is optional but strongly recommended.

Total required time: ~55 minutes.

docs.title: Required — before Day 2 (do it after Day 1, or before the course)
docs.text:
Chroma · Advanced Retrieval for AI — ~52 min https://www.deeplearning.ai/courses/advanced-retrieval-for-ai

Mandatory lessons: 1. Pitfalls of retrieval — when simple vector search fails 2. Cross-encoder re-ranking

Optional but useful: Embeddings-based retrieval, Query expansion.

docs.title: Why these two specifically
docs.text: Day 2 Hour 3 opens with a table showing that our retriever answers 100% of tabular questions and 31% of questions that name a circular by number. That table is a shock or a shrug depending entirely on whether you already know why semantic similarity loses exact tokens. These two lessons teach the mechanism in under half an hour. We will not re-teach it — we will assume it and go straight to what it costs on a real Saudi regulatory corpus.

docs.title: Bring this to Day 2 Hour 1
docs.text:
Answer in one sentence each (prework/readiness_check.md). Not graded, but you will be asked:

  1. Give a concrete query where embedding similarity is high and usefulness is zero.
  2. Why can a bi-encoder be precomputed and a cross-encoder cannot?
  3. If reranking is more accurate, why not rerank the whole corpus?
  4. Query expansion helps some queries and wastes money on others. Which is which?
  5. Name one thing from the course you expect to be wrong for Arabic.

docs.title: Companion — assigned end of Day 2, for Day 3
docs.text:
LlamaIndex · Building and Evaluating Advanced RAG — ~1h55m, with code https://www.deeplearning.ai/alpha/short-courses/building-evaluating-advanced-rag

Day 3 covers the same ideas in a different implementation and a different vocabulary. Doing this course first means every Day-3 metric is familiar before it is defined; skipping it costs you nothing on the day.

See dlai_crosswalk.md for the lesson-by-lesson mapping — including the fact that the RAG triad's groundedness and RAGAS's faithfulness are the same metric with two names, which is the single most useful thing to know about RAG evaluation as a field.

docs.title: Environment (T-minus 2 days)
docs.text:
git clone <course repo> && cd SDA-AIE-214_Course_Assets
pip install -e ".[full,dev]"
make doctor        # 24 checks, each printing its own fix

make doctor must show 0 failed before Day 1. Warnings about Qdrant and the gateway key are expected until Day 2 — clear the rest.

Do not skip this. Every minute spent installing Tesseract on Day 2 morning is a minute taken from the retrieval clinic.

docs.title: DeepLearning.AI ↔ SDA-AIE-214 crosswalk
docs.text: Two short courses cover ground this course also covers. Neither is redundant: seeing the same idea in two implementations is how you learn which part is the idea and which part is the framework.

docs.title: Chroma · Advanced Retrieval for AI (~52 min) — required before Day 2
docs.text:
DLAI lesson Our module What we add Embeddings-based retrieval M3 §1–2 Bilingual model choice measured, not asserted (bge-m3 vs MiniLM on the Arabic subset); Qdrant payload filters; the ef/recall/latency curve Pitfalls of retrieval ★ M4 §1 The identifier failure specifically — why "Circular 44/2025" is unfixable by any embedding model, on a corpus full of real circular numbers in two digit sets Query expansion M7 §2 Routing: expansion runs only for the AMBIGUOUS class, and we measure what it costs on the classes it does not help Cross-encoder re-ranking ★ M4 §3 The two-stage budget as an economic argument — fetch 40, keep 6 — reported per query class Embedding adapters — Out of scope. Referenced once, in M1's telecom case study, as the last-resort fix for the embedder, not the generator

★ = mandatory pre-work.

docs.title: LlamaIndex · Building and Evaluating Advanced RAG (~1h55m) — Day 3 companion
docs.text: DLAI lesson Our module Relationship Sentence-window retrieval M2 chunking + M5 context Same problem, two answers. Retrieve small, generate with more context. Theirs widens the window at query time; ours prepends the section heading at ingest time. Lab 5's fast-finisher task: implement sentence-window on our corpus and measure whether it beats heading-prefixing on policy documents. Report the honest result — it is often a wash Auto-merging retrieval M2 chunking Hierarchical parent/child merging vs our structure-aware split. Ask which suits numbered legal instruments, and demand evidence rather than preference RAG triad — context relevance M6 context_precision Same metric, different name RAG triad — groundedness M6 faithfulness Same metric, different name RAG triad — answer relevance M6 answer_relevancy Same metric, different name TruLens evaluation M6 RAGAS harness + gate Different tool, same discipline. We add the part TruLens does not force on you: a regression gate that fails the build, a pinned judge, and a baseline you may not regenerate in the same commit as a quality change Setting up evaluation M6 §3 golden sets We add coverage requirements: span every query class and both languages, include unanswerable questions, and derive answer keys from the corpus so they cannot drift

docs.title: The point of this table
docs.text:
Every RAG framework renames the same four measurements. A participant who can map RAGAS ↔ TruLens ↔ the RAG triad will not be lost by whichever one their employer standardised on — and will notice immediately when a vendor claims a fifth metric that is one of these four in a new hat.

Put this table on a slide during Day 3 Hour 3. It takes ninety seconds and it retires a whole category of confusion.

docs.title: What neither course covers, and this one must
docs.text: Gap Where we cover it Arabic normalisation: presentation forms, digit sets, orthographic variants M2 §3, M3 §1, dalil/arabic.py OCR as a measured coverage problem (CER gates) M2 §3, Lab 2 Access control as a retrieval-time filter, re-asserted at context construction M5 §5, capstone gate Document lifecycle and supersession — the staleness drill M2 §5, M6 §5, Day 4 PDPL / SDAIA governance context for what may be retrieved and where it may go M1 business relevance, M5 §5, capstone governance memo The regression gate as a CI control rather than a report M6 §5, .github/workflows/rag-gate.yml

docs.title: Bring your answers. Not graded — but you will be asked.
docs.text:
One sentence each. Written by you, before Day 2 Hour 1.

1. Give a concrete query where embedding similarity is high and usefulness is zero.

2. Why can a bi-encoder's document vectors be precomputed while a cross-encoder's scores cannot?

3. If cross-encoder reranking is more accurate, why not rerank the whole corpus for every query?

4. Query expansion helps some queries and wastes money on others. Name one of each, from your own work.

5. Name one thing you expect this course to get wrong for Arabic — before we start. We will come back to your answer on Day 4.

Instructor use. Question 5 is the one that matters. Collect the answers on a flip chart on Day 2 Hour 1 and revisit them in the Day 4 wrap-up. Participants consistently predict "the model won't understand Arabic" and consistently discover the real answers were string handling (presentation forms, digit sets, orthographic variants) and coverage (scanned pages nobody OCR'd). That gap between the expected failure and the actual one is the most durable thing they take home.

docs.title: Building Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems · بناء أنظمة التوليد المعزز بالاسترجاع
docs.text:
Status: additive. INSTRUCTOR_PACKAGE.md remains the authoritative source for course structure, module content, code listings and the rubric. This addendum records four changes to the material the course runs on, and the assets that implement them.

# Change Replaces Affects 1 Dalil's corpus is now real. Layer A is the published SDAIA/NDMO regulatory corpus; Layer B is a thin synthetic overlay supplying only what public regulation cannot. "a deliberately messy 300-document corpus" of invented documents M1–M7, capstone, every lab 2 Three public benchmarks — MIRACL-ar, BEIR, TechQA/eManual — as instruments that validate the participant's measuring tools. self-graded metrics only M3, M4, M6 3 Two DeepLearning.AI short courses wired into the schedule: Chroma Advanced Retrieval for AI as required Day-2 pre-work; LlamaIndex Building and Evaluating Advanced RAG as the Day-3 companion. no external prep pre-course, D2, D3 4 A complete, runnable asset repository — corpus builders, the dalil package, evaluation harnesses, probe/golden/red-team sets, answer keys, CI gate. code listings in the guide delivery, all labs

docs.title: 1 · The corpus: Layer A + Layer B
1.1 Why this changes the course, not just the data
docs.text:
The original corpus was invented, and invented corpora flatter the systems built on them. Their vocabulary is consistent because one author wrote it; their structure is regular because one script produced it; their questions are answerable because the same person wrote both. A participant can reach recall@10 of 0.95 on such a corpus and learn nothing transferable.

More importantly: the documents SDAIA publishes are the documents the participants' own organisations are legally bound by. An engineer who spends four days debugging retrieval over the Personal Data Protection Law, its Implementing Regulation, the Data Classification Policy and the Generative AI Guidelines is not doing an exercise. They are building the index they will be asked for the month they get back to their desk. The self-referential moment — a RAG system whose corpus contains the rules governing RAG systems — is worth the whole redesign on its own.

docs.title: 1.2 Layer A — real, published, citable
docs.text:
corpus/manifest/sdaia_layer_a.yaml lists 17 real documents across four tiers:

Tier Documents Law Personal Data Protection Law (RD M/19, amended M/148) Regulation PDPL Implementing Regulation · Data Transfer Regulation National data management Data Classification · Data Sharing · Open Data · Data Monetization policies; Anonymisation and Destruction guidelines; Transfer Risk Assessment guideline AI AI Ethics Principles · GenAI Guidelines (Government) · GenAI Guidelines (Public) · AI Adoption Framework · Deepfakes Guidelines Workforce National Occupational Standards for Data & AI

Each entry carries url_candidates, a discovery page, the department and access tier to stamp on its chunks, what it teaches, and its share of the golden set. Two entries are load-bearing for specific teaching moments:

  • PDPL Law + Implementing Regulation are the multi-hop pair. The best questions in the golden set cross them: "what does the Law require, and what does the Regulation say that means in practice?" No single chunk answers that, which is Module 7's entire thesis, demonstrated on real instruments.
  • Data Sharing Policy + Open Data Policy are the near-duplicate pair. They are semantically adjacent, dense retrieval confuses them, and the reranker separates them. It is the cleanest live demonstration in the course of why a cross-encoder earns its latency.

docs.title: Operational reality: the URLs move
docs.text:
SDAIA reorganises its publication pages. corpus/fetch_corpus.py therefore tries each candidate URL, then falls back to link discovery on the index pages, then records the document as UNRESOLVED and continues. A partially resolved Layer A is a supported state, not a failure.

T-minus-1-week instructor task. Run make corpus-fetch && make corpus-verify on a networked machine. Commit corpus/LOCK.json (SHA-256 hashes, resolved URLs, fetch date). Every cohort must index byte-identical documents, or their benchmark numbers are not comparable to each other or to last cohort's.

corpus/validate_corpus.py then prints a per-lab readiness verdict — which labs the corpus as actually assembled still supports, and which are degraded. Discovering on Day 2 that the near-duplicate demo has no near-duplicates is an avoidable way to lose a teaching moment.

docs.title: Licensing
docs.text: These are public government publications used for training. Do not re-host them. Ship LOCK.json, not the PDFs, in any public repository. See corpus/LICENSING.md.

docs.title: 1.3 Layer B — the four things public regulation cannot teach
docs.text:
Public regulators publish only current, public, digital, prose documents. That removes four teaching surfaces the course depends on, so Layer B supplies exactly those and nothing else:

Missing from Layer A Layer B supplies Serves Access control — every public document is public 48 restricted + 62 internal documents across 6 departments M5 access filter; capstone "0 cross-department leaks" Supersession — only current editions are published 12 matched v1/v2 circular pairs; v2 lands only in corpus_v2 F8, the Day-4 staleness drill Scanned Arabic — SDAIA PDFs have clean text layers 22 image-only Arabic policy PDFs + hand-quality transcripts F1, the OCR path, the CER gate Tabular facts — few retrievable numeric tables 8 XLSX allowance tables, plus in-PDF tables F1, "the table nobody could retrieve"

Layer B is a fictional adopter of the Layer A rules — the National Digital Services Authority (NDSA) — and every Layer B document cites a Layer A instrument by title. That is the design decision that makes this one corpus rather than two, and it creates the best question class in the course:

"Our Data Export Procedure requires an approval step before execution — which SDAIA instrument imposes that, and what does that instrument require the assessment to cover?"

Hop 1 lands in Layer B. Hop 2 lands in Layer A. Neither alone answers it.

Every generated file is stamped X-Dalil-Synthetic in its metadata and carries a visible disclaimer footer in both languages. Nothing in Layer B can be mistaken for a real instrument.

Generation is deterministic from a seed (corpus/layer_b_specs/layer_b.yaml), so every cohort worldwide gets byte-identical documents and comparable numbers.

docs.title: 1.4 What the corpus actually measures out of the box
docs.text:
Numbers below are from the shipped generator, measured — not estimated.

Property Value Layer B documents 134 (22 scanned AR · 60 digital PDF · 20 DOCX · 24 HTML · 8 XLSX) corpus_v1 chunks (structure-aware) 492 · tables kept whole 56 · mid-sentence starts 4.1% corpus_v1 chunks (naive 500-char) see data/index/ingest_report_naive.json for the contrast corpus_v2 chunks 552 · 12 superseded/current pairs live OCR CER, naive settings (ara+eng, psm 4) 0.084 — fails the gate OCR CER, tuned (ara, psm 6, binarise, 300 dpi) 0.053 mean · 0.062 p95 · 0.100 worst CER gate as shipped 0.06 (stretch target 0.05 — the fast-finisher task)

Why the gate is 0.06 and not 0.05. It was measured, not chosen. The tuned path lands at 0.053, so 0.06 is a gate a participant can pass only by tuning — the naive settings land at 0.084 and fail. A gate nobody can fail teaches nothing; a gate nobody can pass teaches despair. Reaching 0.05 requires per-document DPI escalation and is the distinction task, documented in assessments/keys/lab2_ocr_key.md.

docs.title: The retrieval story, measured on the shipped labelled set
docs.text:
BM25 alone, 138 labelled queries answerable in corpus_v1:

Query class n recall@10 identifier 60 1.000 tabular 24 1.000 ambiguous 12 1.000 procedural 20 0.300 factoid 22 0.239 aggregate 138 0.777

This is the shape Module 4 needs and the original synthetic labels did not produce. The labelled queries are deliberately paraphrases, not restatements of document titles: a label set whose queries copy the title measures string overlap, reports recall@10 = 1.00 for BM25 alone, and teaches participants that their retriever is already perfect and that Modules 3 and 4 were a waste of a day. Every query in data/retrieval_labels.jsonl is phrased the way a colleague would ask it — "Am I allowed to paste an internal document into ChatGPT?", not "What does the Approved LLM Gateway Usage Procedure say?"

docs.title: 2 · Public benchmarks as instruments
docs.text: The Dalil corpus proves the system works. These three prove the participant's instruments work. Fifteen minutes each, run as sidebars, never as labs.

docs.title: 2.1 MIRACL Arabic — Day 2, after Lab 3 (15 min)
docs.text:
python -m dalil.benchmarks.miracl_ar --limit 200

Module 3 shows bge-m3 beating an English-only model on Dalil's Arabic subset (~0.88 vs ~0.29). That number is compelling and self-graded — we wrote the corpus and we wrote the labels. MIRACL-ar is human-annotated Arabic retrieval by people with no stake in this course.

The diagnostic value is in the disagreement:

Dalil Arabic recall MIRACL-ar recall@100 Reading high in the published range for the model pipeline is sound high far below range the corpus was flattering you — your queries and passages share vocabulary a real user's phrasing would not low in range the pipeline is fine; ingestion or normalisation is dropping the Arabic

That middle row is the one worth the fifteen minutes.

docs.title: 2.2 BEIR — Day 3, before Lab 6 (15 min)
docs.text:
python -m dalil.benchmarks.beir --dataset scifact

BEIR's 18 datasets and nine task types all ship the same three objects — corpus, queries, qrels — so recall@k / MRR / nDCG code written once for Dalil runs unmodified across all of them. That uniformity is why it belongs in the metrics lab specifically. Participants point their own metric implementations at a dataset with published baselines. If their nDCG@10 on SciFact is far off the published figure for a known model, the bug is in their metric code — and they have just avoided grading their entire capstone with a broken ruler.

Recommended, in order: scifact (tiny, graded relevance), nfcorpus (vocabulary mismatch — where dense wins), trec-covid (0/1/2 graded judgements, where nDCG and recall visibly diverge — the lesson).

docs.title: 2.3 TechQA / eManual (RAGBench) — Day 3, in the red-team hour (20 min)
docs.text:
python -m dalil.benchmarks.techqa --tau 0.35

The only public set in this course that grades refusal. Every other benchmark rewards retrieving something; a meaningful share of TechQA's questions are deliberately unanswerable from the supplied corpus. It also mirrors the assistant most participants will be asked to build at work: heterogeneous manuals, jargon-dense queries, an audience that will act on the answer.

It reports four numbers, and the fourth is the one that stops participants gaming the third:

  • recall@k, ndcg@10 on the answerable subset
  • refusal_recall — unanswerable questions correctly refused
  • false_answer_rate — unanswerable questions answered anyway (F7)
  • over_refusal_rate — answerable questions wrongly refused

A system that refuses everything scores 1.00 on refusal recall and is worthless. That is the anti-pattern the capstone rubric caps at 70%, and this is the benchmark that exposes it. Sweep --tau and plot refusal_recall against over_refusal: that curve, not a single number, is how a refusal threshold is chosen, and DECISIONS.md must show it.

docs.title: 2.4 Where they slot in
docs.text:
When Benchmark Duration Replaces D2 H2, after Lab 3 MIRACL-ar 15 min part of the Lab 3 buffer D3 H3, before Lab 6 BEIR/scifact 15 min part of the M6 lecture D3 H5, red-team hour TechQA + tau sweep 20 min folded into the existing red-team

Net schedule impact: zero added hours. All three fit inside existing buffers, and the tau sweep replaces the hand-waving that used to occupy the same slot.

docs.title: 3 · The DeepLearning.AI courses in the schedule
3.1 Chroma — Advanced Retrieval for AI → required Day-2 pre-work
docs.text:
~52 minutes. deeplearning.ai/courses/advanced-retrieval-for-ai

It addresses, in under an hour, precisely the thing participants otherwise learn the hard way at 11:00 on Day 2: semantic similarity does not guarantee useful retrieval.

Lesson Maps to What SDA-AIE-214 then adds Embeddings-based retrieval M3 bilingual model choice; Qdrant payload filters; the ef/recall curve Pitfalls of retrieval — when simple vector search fails M4 §1 the identifier failure specifically, and why no embedding model fixes it Query expansion M7 §2 routing: expansion only for the AMBIGUOUS class, with measured cost Cross-encoder re-ranking M4 §3 the two-stage budget as an economic argument, per query class Embedding adapters — out of scope; mentioned as the "last resort, for the embedder not the generator" from the M1 case study

Gate. Lessons 2 and 4 (Pitfalls and Cross-encoder re-ranking) are mandatory before Day 2. prework/README.md carries the assignment, and prework/readiness_check.md is the five-question self-check participants bring to Day 2 Hour 1. It is not graded; it is visible, which is what makes pre-work happen.

Instructor note. Do not re-teach the Chroma material. Day 2 Hour 3 opens by assuming it: "You saw last night that semantic search misses exact tokens. Here is what that costs on our corpus, by query class." The identifier row at 0.31 lands ten times harder on a room that has already seen the mechanism.

docs.title: 3.2 LlamaIndex — Building and Evaluating Advanced RAG → Day-3 companion
docs.text:
~1h55m with code exercises. deeplearning.ai/short-courses/building-evaluating-advanced-rag

This is Day 3's syllabus in another vocabulary, which is exactly why it is a companion rather than pre-work: participants meet the same ideas twice, in two implementations, and learn which parts are the idea and which are the framework.

DLAI lesson SDA-AIE-214 Relationship Sentence-window retrieval M2 chunking · M5 context Same problem — retrieve small, generate with context. Ours prepends the section heading; theirs widens the window. Compare them in Lab 5's fast-finisher task. Auto-merging retrieval M2 chunking Hierarchical merge vs our structure-aware split. Ask which is right for policy documents and demand evidence. RAG triad: context relevance M6 context_precision Same metric, different name RAG triad: groundedness M6 faithfulness Same metric, different name RAG triad: answer relevance M6 answer_relevancy Same metric, different name TruLens evaluation M6 RAGAS harness Different tool, same discipline. Point out that the metric names differ across every framework and the concepts do not. A participant who can map RAGAS↔TruLens↔the triad will not be lost by whatever their employer standardised on.

Where it goes in the day. Assigned at the end of Day 2 as optional evening work; referenced explicitly three times on Day 3 (M5 context construction, M6 metric introduction, Lab 6 step 1). Participants who did it recognise every metric before it is defined; participants who did not lose nothing.

Assign the idea, not the framework. SDA-AIE-214 does not standardise on LlamaIndex. The crosswalk table above is in prework/dlai_crosswalk.md and is worth putting on a slide, because the honest lesson of Day 3 is that RAG evaluation is a small set of concepts wearing many brand names.

docs.title: 4.1 Design decisions the instructor should know about
docs.text:
Everything runs offline. MemoryBackend implements BM25 plus optional dense vectors in-process, so the evaluation harness, the practical-assessment kits and all 53 tests run with no Docker, no model download and no gateway key. This is not a convenience: it is what stops a 20-hour course losing an hour to infrastructure. The labs still use Qdrant — that is the point of Lab 3 — but nothing is blocked on it.

Degradation is always announced, never silent. A missing reranker returns the input order and sets reranked: False. A missing dense model produces BM25-only results and stamps a warning in the report. The offline judge labels every metric judge: "offline-proxy" with a warning inside the JSON. The hash-384 test embedder stamps its name into every report so the numbers can be discarded. The single worst outcome in this course is a participant who trusts a number produced by a stage that never ran.

Answer keys are derived, never typed. scripts/build_eval_sets.py reads the facts recorded by the corpus generator and emits the probes, the 138 labelled queries, the 120-question golden set and the three red-team sets. Regenerate the corpus with a different seed and every key regenerates with it. tests/test_corpus_integrity.py fails the build if they ever drift apart.

Layer A ground truth is honestly deferred. Golden questions about real SDAIA documents ship with verify: true and an evidence_hint rather than a fabricated answer, because the repository cannot know the wording of a PDF downloaded at delivery time. scripts/verify_golden.py resolves them against the fetched corpus, one at a time, for instructor approval. An unverified golden set is not a measuring instrument — it is a list of hopes. Run it once per delivery and commit the result.

The winning combination is in the answer key, not the code 3 Labelled queries are paraphrases, not title restatements; MIRACL-ar sidebar added A label set that copies titles reports recall 1.00 for BM25 and kills Modules 3–4 4 Ablation is one command (make ablation) producing the four-column per-class table The table is the lesson; make it cheap to produce 5 Access control is re-asserted at context construction, and assemble_context reports what it dropped and why Defence in depth, and the drop counters make it visible 6 Offline proxy judge available; gate warns on config drift and judge change Lab 6 must run on a laptop; and comparing across configs is the commonest false regression 7 Router decides the path; sub-question dedup is enforced in decompose "Loops everywhere" and the twin-sub-question bug, structurally prevented Capstone make demo scripts all five rubric demonstrations, including the staleness toggle and the access-control contrast A demo that dies at stage 1 tells the grader nothing about stages 2–5

docs.title: 4.4 What the tests are for
docs.text:
tests/ is 53 tests, and roughly a third of them are teaching material — they encode the failures the course is about, executably:

  • test_aggregate_hides_a_collapsed_class — 90 perfect factoids and 10 broken identifiers produce an aggregate of 0.90 and a class at 0.00. This is the rubric's anti-pattern, as an assertion.
  • test_gate_warns_when_config_drifted / test_gate_warns_when_judge_changed — the two commonest false regressions.
  • test_grader_can_say_none_so_the_loop_can_refuse — the Module 7 knowledge check, executable.
  • test_index_and_query_paths_agree — the single most important invariant in the course.
  • test_tables_are_never_split_mid_row, test_access_is_reasserted_at_context_construction, test_invented_citation_is_detected.

Worth ten minutes on Day 3: open the test file, not the slide.

Location Was Now Why Lab 2, step 2 & troubleshooting "Target CER ≤ 5%… --psm 4" Gate 0.06; the winning combination is lang=ara, --psm 6, binarisation, 300 dpi; 0.05 is the stretch target Measured on the shipped scans: naive 0.084, tuned 0.053. --psm 4 is not the answer on right-aligned Naskh policy pages Course description "a deliberately messy 300-document corpus" of fictional documents 17 real SDAIA/NDMO documents + 134 synthetic internal documents See §1 Lab 1 expected output "Parsed 25 docs → 912 chunks" Regenerate from data/index/ingest_report_naive.json after make ingest-naive The corpus changed; publish your cohort's numbers, never last cohort's

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
A specialist module on customising foundation models efficiently. Participants prepare instruction datasets, apply parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA/QLoRA), align models with preference optimisation, and quantise them for deployment. The module gives engineers a decision framework for when to prompt, retrieve, or fine-tune — and the practical skill to execute a full adaptation pipeline end to end on modest hardware.

The course is built around a single evolving artefact: "Daleel" (دليل), an Arabic-language assistant for Saudi digital-government services. Participants start from an open foundation model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct), decide whether adaptation is even the right tool, curate a domain instruction dataset (daleel-sft), fine-tune it with QLoRA, align it to a preference set (daleel-prefs) with DPO, quantise the result for cheap inference, and prove — against a frozen benchmark (daleel-eval) — that the adapted model is better on the domain and no worse on general ability and safety. Every lab produces a component of the final capstone, so by Day 3 each participant owns a reproducible adaptation pipeline that turns a generic base model into a measured, deployable, domain-specialised assistant.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this course, participants will be able to:

  1. LO1 — Compare prompting, RAG, and fine-tuning strategies for a given requirement and defend the choice with cost and quality evidence
  2. LO2 — Design high-quality instruction and preference datasets, including deduplication, decontamination, and quality filtering
  3. LO3 — Implement parameter-efficient fine-tuning using LoRA and QLoRA on constrained hardware
  4. LO4 — Apply quantisation techniques (4-bit NF4, GGUF, AWQ/GPTQ) to reduce model footprint while controlling quality loss
  5. LO5 — Evaluate fine-tuned models against baselines with rigorous, reproducible benchmarks
  6. LO6 — Validate adapted models for regression, safety, and domain fitness before release
