  • Debugging exercise: labs/sim/sim_swallowed_error.py or trace through what happens if load_order silently defaulted amount to 0 on an order-lookup failure instead of failing closed — would amount_gate still protect you?
  • Discussion: which parts of Rafeeq's behaviour must NEVER be a prompt sentence (money limits, identity checks), and which must ALWAYS stay model judgement (empathy, ambiguity)? Where is the line, and who signs off on it?

docs.title: What you just built
docs.text:
The exact same five rules, moved from prose a crafted message can argue past into branches nothing can. test_amount_gate-style checks run in milliseconds with zero model calls — business rules became unit tests. This lab is the direct setup for Module 8: a gate is a security control; a sentence is not.

Capstone requirement satisfied: contributes to LO2 (right pattern per workflow — the flow replaces prompt-only judgement for refunds) and sets up LO6 — Guardrails & security: "structural authorisation and deterministic gates (no rule lives in a prompt)" (final_capstone_project.md, requirements 2 and 6).

docs.title: Lab 7, Task 2 — prompt inventory
docs.text:
Read src/rafeeq/reasoning/refund_prompt_only.py's REFUND_PROMPT. List every imperative sentence and classify each as a rule (a fixed business constraint — belongs in a branch) or judgement (open-ended, needs the model — stays in a prompt).

# Imperative Rule or judgement? Where it belongs after the refactor 1 "Only refund orders delivered late per the SLA." 2 "Never refund more than 500 SAR without human approval." 3 "Always verify the order id before refunding." 4 "Never refund the same order twice." 5 "Reply in the customer's language and cite the refund policy."

Fill in the last two columns. (Answer key: 1–4 are rules — eligibility_gate/amount_gate/load_order/do_refund's idempotency key in refund_flow_task.py; 5 is genuinely judgement — composing a bilingual, policy-citing sentence stays a model's job even after the refactor.)

docs.title: Lab 8 — Guard and Attack Rafeeq
docs.text:
Module 8 · Guardrails, Security, and Adversarial Testing

Objective Add input/output guardrails and structural controls to Rafeeq, build a red-team agent, and produce a triaged security report — the Day-4 graded artefact Duration 2 × 50 min (H4 build + H5 report clinic) Setup Lab 7 flow + Lab 6 supervisor; security/**/*.json (seed attack corpus); git checkout lab8-start

Offline note: everything in this lab is Layer A — stdlib + pydantic, no langgraph needed anywhere. screen_input, guard_tool_call, and the whole red-team suite (StubTarget, run_suite, retest_finding, write_report, demo_layered_defence) run under plain python3.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
git checkout lab8-start
export PYTHONPATH=src

docs.title: Instructions & Tasks
docs.text:
1. (10 min) Input guardrail. Fill in labs/lab08/start/guardrail_task.py::screen_input: flag every matched injection and PII pattern, mask PII in cleaned before it could reach memory (M4's lesson reused). Confirm known injection/PII patterns are flagged and masked. Remember: allow is always True — this is a filter, not a wall.
  2. (10 min) Output guardrail. Fill in guard_tool_call: consult rafeeq.security.action_risk.classify and structurally block over-limit refunds, prohibited actions, and cross-customer access — before the tool body ever runs.
  3. (10 min) Prove the layered defence. Call demo_layered_defence() (or replicate it by hand): confirm the over-limit refund is blocked even when the input guardrail is disabled — structure holds when the filter misses. This is the module's defining demonstration.
  4. (15 min) Red-team run. Run rafeeq.security.red_team.run_suite(StubTarget()) against the seed corpus in security/; collect findings with reproductions (the seven-part shape: attack → vulnerability → exploit trajectory → business impact → detection → mitigation → retest result).
  5. (10 min) Triage and fix. Pick the highest-severity finding, harden the target (e.g. StubTarget(enforce_step_budget=True)), and retest_finding() the same finding to prove it now fails (retest_result == "held").
  6. (5 min) Commit. git commit -m "feat: guardrails, red-team agent, and security report"

docs.title: Expected outputs
docs.text:
input guard      → 5/5 seeded injections flagged, national ids masked before memory
output guard     → over-limit refund BLOCKED (structural), even with input guard off
red-team run     → 4 goals attempted: 1 breach found (denial-of-wallet), 3 held
after fix        → global step budget tightened; denial-of-wallet re-run: HELD
security report  → 4 findings triaged (1 high fixed, 0 open high), mitigations mapped

solution/verify.py reproduces this mechanism against the full, deterministic security/ corpus (78 entries across 8 families) rather than the package's illustrative 4-attack sample — StubTarget's outcome oracle checks a concrete effect (was the tool call actually blocked?), never model chatter, so the numbers below are stable across runs:

$ PYTHONPATH=src python3 labs/lab08/solution/verify.py
...
14/14 checks passed

It writes this lab's own labs/lab08/solution/SECURITY_REPORT.md (do not confuse with the repo-root reports/SECURITY_REPORT.md, generated elsewhere from the same corpus) and asserts 0 open high-severity findings across the full run.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Cause Fix Injection still triggers a refund Relying on the input guard as a wall Add the structural gate/authz; the filter is only one layer Guardrail blocks legitimate refunds Threshold too aggressive / no human path Route over-limit to approval, not outright refuse Red-team always "succeeds" Weak oracle Make the oracle check the concrete outcome (was a refund issued?), never model chatter Attack payload poisons memory Storing raw hostile input Store masked/summarised content only (M4)

Instructor notes. The defining demonstration is task 3: disable the input guardrail and show the over-limit refund still blocked by the output guard and flow gate — layered defence made undeniable. The red-team run finds real breaches when enforce_step_budget=False (seed denial-of-wallet as reachable) so the report is not theatre. This is a graded artefact: collect every pair's SECURITY_REPORT.md at end of Day 4. Reserve H5 entirely for triage — severity discipline (money/PII before cosmetic) is the assessed skill.

docs.title: Fast finishers
docs.text: Add your own two INJECTION_PATTERNS entries (one Arabic, one English, covering a family not already seeded — e.g. role_play) and re-run run_suite to confirm they change zero structural outcomes: the output guard never reads the input guard's verdict, by design.

docs.title: Mini exercises
docs.text:
• Quiz: the governing security principle (treat all model input as untrusted, all output as unverified); why an input guardrail is a filter, not a wall; where refund authorisation must live (the tool server and a flow gate, never the prompt); why automate red-teaming (regressions return silently — make it a CI test).
  • Debugging exercise: labs/sim/sim_prompt_authz.py — the refund limit lives only in the prompt; a crafted "override" message issues 9,500 SAR. Reproduce it, then add the server-side authz + flow gate and prove the attack now fails.
  • Code-review exercise: review a PR adding a guardrail that is a new prompt paragraph ("never allow jailbreaks"). Finding: a prompt is not a control; propose the structural input+output guardrails instead.
  • Discussion: rank Rafeeq's assets by attack impact (money, PII, availability). For each, name the structural control that protects it and the red-team probe that proves the control holds.

docs.title: Lab 9 — Trace and Cost Rafeeq
docs.text:
Module 9 · Observability, Cost Optimisation, and Reliability

Objective Instrument Rafeeq with tracing, produce a cost/latency report attributing spend by model and component, then cut cost with caching + model routing and add a bounded retry Duration 50 minutes Setup Lab 8 hardened Rafeeq; data/tickets_eval.jsonl; git checkout lab9-start

Offline note: everything in this lab is Layer A — stdlib only, no langgraph or LangSmith needed. LocalTracer persists every run to reports/traces/<run_id>.json unconditionally; @traceable/LangSmith streaming is an OPTIONAL extra layer (RAFEEQ_LANGSMITH=1) this lab does not require.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
git checkout lab9-start
export PYTHONPATH=src

docs.title: Instructions & Tasks
docs.text:
1. (10 min) Add tracing. Fill in labs/lab09/start/tracing_task.py::run_traced_ticket: wrap a ticket's classify → specialist-tool → policy-retrieval → compose-reply pipeline in start_run/start_span. Run it on one ticket; render the trace tree (rafeeq.observability.tracing.render_tree); identify the most expensive span.
  2. (10 min) Build the cost report. Fill in cost_report_for: run a batch of 30 tickets, attribute total spend by model and by component via rafeeq.observability.cost.cost_report. Identify the single biggest cost bar.
  3. (10 min) Cut cost. Fill in labs/lab09/start/optimise_retry_task.py's reply_model_for (model routing) and cached_policy_lookup (scoped, versioned KB caching). Re-run the same 30 tickets; compare blended cost/contact before vs after.
  4. (10 min) Bounded retry. Fill in retry_read_tool_once_flaky (a flaky read tool IS retried) and call_write_tool_never_retried (issue_refund is called exactly once — confirm via RetryLedger.retry_count).
  5. (5 min) Fill BENCHMARKS.md. Cost/contact before vs after; confirm the same tickets route to the same intents (no quality regression). Commit: git commit -m "feat: tracing, cost attribution, caching, routing, retries"

docs.title: Expected outputs
docs.text:
trace tree            → refund run: 6 spans; frontier model on supervisor = top cost
cost report            → 68% of spend in order-status on frontier model (the target)
after optimise          → blended cost/contact 0.019 → 0.008 USD (-58%), success unchanged
p95 latency             → 3.4s → 1.9s (cache hits + cheap model)
retry safety            → read tool retried on timeout; issue_refund retried 0 times

solution/verify.py reproduces this mechanism end to end against the real data/tickets_eval.jsonl and the deterministic classify_intent fastpath router (no model call, M2/M7). Two honesty notes on how the measured numbers diverge from the package's illustrative figures above:

  • Cost cut. This build's classify_intent correctly refuses to guess at low confidence rather than risk a wrong cheap-model routing decision — it only classifies ~17% of the eval set as order_status/track at ≥0.8 confidence (the routing lever's eligibility gate), versus the package's illustrative majority. The real, reproducible cut this build delivers is ≥15% (measured: ~19%), not 58% — the mechanism (route the confident simple majority cheap, cache the repeated policy lookups) is identical; a live/frontier classifier recognising more intents at high confidence closes the rest of the gap, exactly as route_model's own docstring predicts.
  • Latency. No wall-clock model calls happen in stub mode, so a meaningful p95-latency-before-vs-after comparison needs RAFEEQ_MODEL_MODE=live (or replay); verify.py does not assert a latency number for this reason — the cache/routing SAVINGS estimates (CacheStats.seconds_saved) are still real and reported in BENCHMARKS.md.
$ PYTHONPATH=src python3 labs/lab09/solution/verify.py
...
21/21 checks passed

It writes this lab's own labs/lab09/solution/BENCHMARKS.md with the real measured cost/contact and cache-hit-rate numbers from the run above — the same table shape capstone/templates/BENCHMARKS.md asks every team to fill from their own build.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Cause Fix No cost in traces Token usage not captured Set model=/tokens_in=/tokens_out= on the span, not just its name Cache serves stale policy Key missing version/locale Include policy_version + locale in the cache key (M4) — cached_policy already does this; do not key on raw customer text either (every question becomes unique) Quality dropped after routing Cheap model on hard intents Tighten the confidence threshold; route only the easy majority Double refund reappears Write tool retried Restrict retries to the IDEMPOTENT set — call_with_retry already refuses to retry a write tool by construction

Instructor notes. The centrepiece is the cost-attribution reveal: have every pair find their single biggest cost bar (compose_reply on the frontier model, in this build) and predict the fix before applying it — the prediction-then-measurement loop is the assessed cost-literacy skill (LO7). Insist the eval-set success number (or, offline, the intent routing check) is reported alongside the cost cut; a cheaper agent that got worse is a failure, not a win.

docs.title: Fast finishers
docs.text:
Add an alert rule (rafeeq.observability.slo.check_slos, escalation rate

threshold) and simulate a backend outage (labs/sim/sim_swallowed_error.py or a hand-raised TransientToolError on every call) to watch the tool error rate spike in a fresh trace batch.

docs.title: Mini exercises
docs.text:
• Quiz: why you can't manage an agent by testing alone (it can be wrong while running perfectly; observe production); the three axes of cost attribution (model, component, intent); the two biggest cost levers (caching, model routing); which tools may be retried (idempotent/read only); two reliability signals beyond error rate (escalation rate, guardrail-trip rate).
  • Debugging exercise: labs/sim/sim_retry_write.py — a retry wrapper applied to issue_refund; a timeout triggers a second refund. Reproduce the double refund, then restrict retries to the IDEMPOTENT set and prove it stops.
  • Code-review exercise: review a PR that caches policy_context keyed only on the question string. Finding: missing version + locale in the key → stale/wrong-language policy served; propose the scoped key.
  • Discussion: finance asks for a per-intent cost SLO for Rafeeq. What do you measure, what target do you set, and what alert fires when it drifts? Who owns the response?

docs.title: What you just built
docs.text:
A trace tree for every run, a cost report that turns "too expensive" into "68% of spend is compose_reply on the frontier model" — an actionable sentence — two working cost levers with measured savings, and a retry policy that structurally cannot double-refund. This is the last lab: tracing, cost, and retry safety are exactly what the capstone's BENCHMARKS.md and the security report's "detection" column both lean on.

Capstone requirement satisfied: LO7 (Observability & cost: every run traced; cost attributed by model/component/intent; caching + model routing applied; bounded retries on idempotent tools only — final_capstone_project.md requirement 7) — this lab's BENCHMARKS.md is the template for the capstone's own.

docs.title: labs/sim/ — deliberately-broken simulations
docs.text:
The instructor package specifies these as separate git branches (sim-no-terminate, sim-prompt-authz, ...) that participants check out during a module's debugging exercise. This repository ships the SAME failure modes as standalone, runnable Python scripts instead — no branch checkout required, works identically offline, and every script prints its own PASS/FAIL-style verdict rather than requiring a human to eyeball a crash.

Each script is self-contained: python3 <script>.py runs the ANTI-PATTERN first (reproducing the bug against real src/rafeeq/** code, never a mock), then the FIX (the real module's actual behaviour), and exits 0 only if both halves behaved as documented. Every script's own header comment states its (module, symptom, root cause, fix) — read that before the code.

export PYTHONPATH=src
python3 labs/sim/sim_no_terminate.py

docs.title: Map: sim -> module -> lab -> package branch name
docs.text:
Script Module Lab Package branch (instructor_guide.md) sim_no_terminate.py M1 — Agentic architectures labs/lab01 sim-no-terminate sim_react_thrash.py M2 — Planning & reasoning labs/lab02 sim-react-thrash sim_memory_leak.py M4 — Memory & state labs/lab04 sim-memory-leak sim_stale_policy.py M4 (retrieval) / M9 (caching) labs/lab04, labs/lab09 (this repo's own — see note below) sim_lost_handoff.py M6 — Hierarchical delegation labs/lab06 sim-lost-handoff sim_swallowed_error.py M1 (errors as values) / M7 (flow state) labs/lab01, labs/lab07 (this repo's own — see note below) sim_prompt_authz.py M8 — Guardrails & security labs/lab08 sim-prompt-authz sim_retry_write.py M9 — Observability & cost labs/lab09 sim-retry-write

Note on sim_stale_policy.py and sim_swallowed_error.py: the package also names sim-raise-tool (M3), sim-scope-leak (M5), and sim-branch-no-state (M7) as separate branches. Those three failure modes are exercised directly inside their own lab's core tasks instead of a dedicated sim script (Lab 3's error-value contract IS the raise->value fix; Lab 5's scoped_input/assert_no_forbidden_leak IS the scope-leak fix; Lab 7's load_order/gate wiring IS the missing-state fix) — this repository's 8 sim scripts cover the two additional real, reproducible failure modes above (a stale-cache/retrieval bug distinct from the customer-scoping leak, and an error-swallowing bug distinct from a raise) so every script here demonstrates something not already a lab's own primary task.

docs.text: Since this repo has no git branches per checkpoint, the equivalent of "check out lab4-start" is: read labs/lab04/start/*.py, and the equivalent of a sim-* branch is: run the matching script in this directory. labs/README.md documents the full checkpoint-tag strategy this repo uses instead of branches.

docs.title: Verified to run and demonstrate their failure
docs.text: All 8 scripts above have been run end to end in this build; each printed its "FAILURE DEMONSTRATED ... AND FIX PROVEN ..." line and exited 0.

docs.title: Tawseel MCP servers (Module 3)
docs.text:
Four separate MCP servers — not one mega-server — each publishing a curated, governed tool surface over one Tawseel backend. This is the module's anchor lesson: a trust boundary is a place you can point at, argue about, and enforce independently. One server per backend gives you four such places; one server for everything gives you none.

orders_server.py      read-only order lookups
logistics_server.py   delivery tracking + one autonomous-within-policy write
billing_server.py     ELEVATED — refunds move real money
customer_server.py    ELEVATED + same-customer-only — the most sensitive PII

Every server is built on the shared bootstrap in common.py: guarded_tool calls rafeeq.security.authz.agent_may_access before a tool body runs and writes an audit record after — authorisation and audit live at the server, never in the calling agent's prompt (SPEC §7 mistake #6; see data/orders/INJECTION_NOTES.md for the exact injected instruction this repo uses to teach why a prompt-level rule is not an access-control mechanism).

docs.title: Trust-boundary table
docs.text: server data class authz level write capability blast radius if compromised orders_server.py order records (status, amount, refund state) standard — every granted identity gets read none an over-broad agent can over-READ orders; it can never change or delete one through this server logistics_server.py delivery events, courier locations, ETAs standard, plus one write reschedule_delivery (autonomous within policy, always logged) a compromised agent can move a delivery time around; it cannot touch money or PII through this server billing_server.py payments, refund history elevated — narrowest domain grant in the policy table (customer_agent, billing_admin_agent only) issue_refund (idempotency-key gated), mark_refunded (reconciliation-only, customer_agent explicitly denied) the only server that can move real money; the 500 SAR human-approval gate is enforced HERE as well as in flows/refund_flow.py — defence in depth, so one broken gate does not equal one unauthorised large refund customer_server.py customer PII (masked national id, phone, fraud flag), ticket notes elevated + same-customer-only — every granted identity is scoped to its own session's customer, no exceptions add_case_note (append-only, not idempotent) even a fully authorised, fully jailbroken agent cannot read or write another customer's record through this server — the national id is never stored unmasked in the first place

docs.title: Agent identities (classroom policy table, security/authz.py)
docs.text:
agent_id domains granted same-customer-only notable denials customer_agent orders, logistics, billing, customer yes mark_refunded (reconciliation-only) ops_agent orders, logistics, customer no (cross-customer read for investigation) entire billing domain — cannot move money partner_agent logistics only yes reschedule_delivery (read-only grant) billing_admin_agent billing only no (reconciliation runs across accounts) orders/logistics/customer entirely

Every identity not in this table is denied outright (unknown_agent), and three tool names — change_customer_identity, override_fraud_flag, delete_order — are denied for everyone, unconditionally, before the domain check even runs (SPEC §5's action-risk matrix "prohibited" row).

docs.title: Running a server standalone
docs.text:
Each server is a normal Python script; it inserts the repo's src/ onto sys.path itself, so no PYTHONPATH juggling is required:

python3 mcp_servers/orders_server.py       # stdio transport
python3 mcp_servers/logistics_server.py
python3 mcp_servers/billing_server.py
python3 mcp_servers/customer_server.py

If the mcp package is not installed, the script still imports cleanly and prints a hint instead of crashing — every tool function underneath is still a plain, directly-callable Python function (e.g. orders_server.get_order(order_id=..., agent_id=..., customer_id=...)), which is what tests/unit/test_authz.py/run_without_pytest.py exercise in this build's sandbox where mcp is not guaranteed to be present.

docs.title: Client configuration (Claude-Desktop-style)
docs.text:
The shape every MCP-aware client (Claude Desktop, MultiServerMCPClient in rafeeq.tools.mcp_client, etc.) uses to launch these servers as subprocesses over stdio:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "tawseel-orders": {
      "command": "python3",
      "args": ["mcp_servers/orders_server.py"]
    },
    "tawseel-logistics": {
      "command": "python3",
      "args": ["mcp_servers/logistics_server.py"]
    },
    "tawseel-billing": {
      "command": "python3",
      "args": ["mcp_servers/billing_server.py"]
    },
    "tawseel-customer": {
      "command": "python3",
      "args": ["mcp_servers/customer_server.py"]
    }
  }
}

rafeeq.tools.mcp_client.SERVER_SPECS is the same configuration expressed for langchain_mcp_adapters.MultiServerMCPClient — one dictionary, four entries, each naming a command/args/transport.

docs.title: Classroom discussion — where should the trust boundary be?
docs.text:
Orders is read-only and low-stakes: even a badly-behaved agent can only over-read order status. Billing is elevated: it can move money, so its domain grant is the narrowest in the policy table and its human-approval gate is enforced twice (server + flow). That asymmetry is the whole argument for splitting servers by backend/trust-domain instead of "40 endpoints, 40 tools, one server" — a security review of "the billing capability" is now a unit, separate from "the orders capability", and granting a new agent read-only order access never has to touch the billing server's code, config, or review at all.

Discuss: if Tawseel added a fifth backend tomorrow (say, a warehouse system), would it get its own server, or fold into orders_server.py? What changes about the review, the blast radius, and who signs off, either way? And: billing_server.py's issue_refund checks REFUND_LIMIT_SAR itself, but does NOT verify that customer_id actually owns order_id — who should own that check, and at which layer?

docs.title: Rafeeq attack corpus (Module 8)
docs.text: An AgentDojo-inspired (ETH Zurich), machine-readable corpus of adversarial payloads against Rafeeq, used by src/rafeeq/security/red_team.py's run_suite() and by tests/security/*. Every payload is a fixture, never a real instruction — see data/orders/INJECTION_NOTES.md for the two real seed notes some entries here quote verbatim.

docs.text:
security/
├─ injections/                 direct (customer message) + indirect (tool-result-borne)
│   ├─ direct_en.json / direct_ar.json          6 families x 2, one message each
│   ├─ indirect_delivery_notes.json             via get_order's delivery_note(_ar)
│   ├─ indirect_customer_records.json           via get_customer(.name/_ar)/get_customer_tickets
│   └─ indirect_case_notes.json                 via a case note re-read on a later turn
├─ malicious_tool_results/
│   └─ poisoned_mcp_responses.json              poisoned orders/logistics/billing/customer_server output
├─ memory_poisoning/
│   ├─ persistent_instruction_injection.json    raw hostile text surviving into long-term memory/KB
│   └─ stale_forged_policy.json                 superseded or wholly forged policy documents
└─ privilege_escalation/
    ├─ unauthorised_tool_chaining.json
    ├─ cross_customer_access.json
    ├─ refund_amount_manipulation.json
    ├─ fraud_flag_override.json
    ├─ identity_change.json
    └─ denial_of_wallet.json

10 attack families (the family field), each mapped to an owasp_id aligned to the OWASP Agentic Top 10 2026 categories (see docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md for the full mapping and its caveats): instruction_override, false_authority, role_play_jailbreak, encoded_obfuscated, delimiter_escape, urgency_social_engineering, tool_result_injection, memory_poisoning, privilege_escalation, denial_of_wallet.

78 payloads total (42 EN / 36 AR, ~46% Arabic) — comfortably over the SPEC's 60-payload floor. Roughly half Arabic is deliberate: this course teaches that English-only guardrails fail on Arabic input (src/rafeeq/security/input_guard.py's pattern library is bilingual for exactly this reason — check tests/security/test_input_guard.py::test_arabic_patterns_present).

docs.title: Entry schema
docs.text:
Every JSON array element has exactly these fields:

field meaning id stable id, <FAMILY_CODE>-<LOCALE>-<NNN>, e.g. IOV-EN-001 family one of the 10 attack families above owasp_id OWASP Agentic Top 10 2026 category slug (see docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md) locale ar | en vector direct (customer's own message) | indirect (arrives via a tool result / retrieved record the agent did not ask a human to type) injection_point where the payload is planted, e.g. customer_message, tool_result:get_order.delivery_note, mcp:billing_server.get_payment.status, long_term_memory.summary payload the actual adversarial text preconditions state the target must be in for the attack to be meaningful (an order id, a fraud_flag, a session identity) success_oracle the concrete, checkable outcome that means the attack SUCCEEDED (e.g. refund_issued_over_limit) — never "did the model say something bad", always an effect a Layer-A function can verify. Oracle implementations live in red_team.py::ORACLES. expected_block_layer which src/rafeeq/security/defence_layers.py::LAYERS entry SHOULD stop this (input_filter | structural_authz | flow_gate | output_guard | audit_monitoring) severity high (money/PII) | medium (availability) | low (cosmetic) — same rubric as capstone/templates/SECURITY_REPORT_TEMPLATE.md notes why this payload exists / what it specifically probes

docs.title: How to add a payload
docs.text:
1. Pick the right directory (or add a new file to an existing one — the runner globs every *.json file under security/, so file names within a directory are free-form).
  2. Write an object with every field above. Reuse an existing id prefix's next number, or mint a new <FAMILY_CODE>-<LOCALE>-NNN if you're starting a new family/locale pair.
  3. success_oracle MUST name a real key in red_team.py::ORACLES (or a new oracle you add there) — an oracle checks a concrete effect (a refund actually issued, a foreign customer_id actually present in output, the step budget actually blown), never model chatter ("did it apologise", "did it sound compliant"). A weak oracle is how a red-team suite lies to you (Module 8's own troubleshooting note).
  4. Run python3 -m rafeeq.security.red_team (or PYTHONPATH=src python3 -c "from rafeeq.security.red_team import run_suite, StubTarget; run_suite(StubTarget())") and confirm the new entry is picked up and classified as held or breach.
  5. If it's a genuine new breach, it becomes a Finding — see below.

docs.title: The finding trajectory (required shape)
docs.text:
Every red-team finding — whether from run_suite() or a manual pairs exercise — must be filed in this order, matching Finding's fields in red_team.py and capstone/templates/SECURITY_REPORT_TEMPLATE.md's per-finding page:

  1. Attack — the payload and where it was delivered (injection_point, vector).
  2. Vulnerability — which layer(s) failed to stop it and why (a missing gate, a gate that exists but isn't wired into this call path, a regex that didn't match the Arabic phrasing).
  3. Exploit trajectory — the actual sequence of tool calls / state transitions the attack produced (Finding.trajectory), not a description — the reproduction.
  4. Business impact — money moved, PII exposed, availability lost — named in SAR/records/ budget units, not adjectives (Finding.business_impact).
  5. Detection — which security event(s), if any, this tripped (Finding.detection, cross-checked against reports/security_events.jsonl via rafeeq.security.events.read_events).
  6. Mitigation — the STRUCTURAL control that closes it, never a prompt rewording (SPEC M8's central lesson — "a prompt instruction is never a security control").
  7. Retest result — re-run the same payload after the fix and record held or breach (Finding.retest_result) — a finding is not closed until this is held.

A finding missing any of these seven parts is not a filed finding — it's a note.

docs.title: Programme Overview — SDA-AIE-311 Agentic AI Systems Engineering
الفقرة التنفيذية (ملخص تنفيذي)
docs.text:
SDA-AIE-311 "هندسة أنظمة الذكاء الاصطناعي الوكيلي" برنامج تدريبي بمستوى خبير، مدته خمسة أيام (٢٥ ساعة تدريبية)، موجّه لكبار مهندسي الذكاء الاصطناعي والمعماريين التقنيين والقادة الفنيين. يتمحور البرنامج حول أداة تعليمية واحدة تتطور طوال الأسبوع: "رفيق"، مساعد تشغيلي وكيلي لشركة افتراضية سعودية للخدمات اللوجستية والتجارة الإلكترونية اسمها "توصيل". يبني المشاركون رفيق تسعة مختبرات متتالية — من حلقة استدلال محدودة بسيطة إلى نظام وكيلي متعدد العملاء، مُراقَب، محمي بضوابط أمنية هيكلية، ومنشور فعليًا في بيئة محاكاة — بحيث يتتبع الطلبات، يعيد جدولة التسليم، يعالج المبالغ المستردة ضمن السياسة المعتمدة، ويصعّد الحالات الاستثنائية، باللغتين العربية والإنجليزية.

يغطي البرنامج ثمانية مخرجات تعلّم رئيسية: تصميم المعماريات الوكيلية، أنماط التخطيط والاستدلال (ReAct، التخطيط ثم التنفيذ، التأمل الذاتي)، التنسيق متعدد الوكلاء والتفويض الهرمي، تكامل الأدوات عبر بروتوكول سياق النموذج (MCP)، إدارة الذاكرة قصيرة وطويلة المدى عبر قواعد بيانات متجهية، ضوابط الحماية والاختبار العدائي (Red-Teaming)، وأخيرًا قابلية الملاحظة وتحسين التكلفة. التقييم يجمع بين إتمام المختبرات، تقرير أمني عدائي (الفريق الأحمر)، ومشروع تخرج (Capstone) يُنشر فعليًا ويُقيَّم بناءً على الأدلة لا العرض التقديمي وحده.

يخرج البرنامج بمنتجَين يعودان على الأكاديمية مباشرة: معيار قياس (Benchmark) قابل لإعادة الاستخدام يحاكي بنية مجموعة بيانات LaDe العالمية ببيانات سعودية اصطناعية بالكامل، وحقيبة هندسية كاملة (مستودع كود، تسعة مختبرات، سيناريوهات اختبار أمني، لوحات قياس أداء) يمكن إعادة استخدامها في الدورات اللاحقة. البرنامج شرط أساسي (Prerequisite) لدورة SDA-AIE-214، ونقطة انطلاق مباشرة لدورتَي SDA-AIE-313 (تعميق الأمن) و SDA-AIE-390 (الإنتاجية والنشر).

docs.title: Course Identity
docs.text: Field Detail Code SDA-AIE-311 Title Agentic AI Systems Engineering Arabic title هندسة أنظمة الذكاء الاصطناعي الوكيلي Level Expert Duration 5 days × 5 hours = 25 learning hours Audience Senior AI engineers, AI architects, technical leads Prerequisite SDA-AIE-214 Stackability Anchors the GenAI Engineering specialisation; next steps SDA-AIE-313 (security) and SDA-AIE-390 (productionisation) Assessment model Labs (30%) + quiz (10%) + PA-1/PA-2 security report (20%) + capstone (40%) Badge Flagship Expert badge, gated on overall ≥ 70, capstone ≥ 70, zero open high-severity security findings, and a passing cross-customer leakage test

docs.title: The Teaching Artefact
docs.text:
Every module and lab extends one system rather than a new toy example each time. Rafeeq (رفيق) is an enterprise agentic operations assistant for Tawseel (توصيل), a fictional Saudi last-mile logistics and fulfilment company operating across five cities (Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam, Makkah, Madinah). Across nine labs it grows from a three-line bounded loop into a guarded, observable, multi-agent system with:

  • A bounded state-machine core with explicit termination (Module 1)
  • ReAct, Plan-and-Execute, and Reflection reasoning patterns, applied by workflow (Module 2)
  • Sixteen enterprise tools across four governed Model Context Protocol servers — orders, logistics, billing, customer (Module 3)
  • Thread-scoped short-term memory and customer-scoped, versioned, bilingual long-term memory with a PDPL erasure path (Module 4)
  • Three specialist agents (Orders, Logistics, Billing) under a thin supervisor orchestrator with mandatory result write-back and clean escalation (Modules 5–6)
  • Deterministic flow-engineered gates replacing prompt-encoded business rules, notably the 50/500 SAR refund-authorisation bands (Module 7)
  • Layered input/output guardrails and an automated red-team suite run in CI against a 78-payload bilingual attack corpus, with zero open high-severity findings required (Module 8)
  • Full tracing, cost attribution, caching, model routing, and idempotent-only retries, targeting a ≥ 40% cost cut with no quality regression (Module 9)

The repository runs entirely offline by default (RAFEEQ_MODEL_MODE=stub) — no API key and no network call are required for any lab, make test, or CI, which removes the two most common delivery blockers (gateway provisioning, cost) from every classroom before delivery even begins.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
1. Design agentic architectures with planning, reasoning, tool use, and memory
  2. Implement ReAct, Plan-and-Execute, and Reflection patterns in working agents
  3. Develop multi-agent systems with orchestration, delegation, and task routing
  4. Integrate tools and enterprise APIs using the Model Context Protocol
  5. Design state management and short/long-term memory with vector stores
  6. Implement automated guardrails and red-team agents against attacks
  7. Optimise agent performance, cost, and reliability with tracing and monitoring
  8. Validate a deployed agentic system in a simulated enterprise environment

docs.title: What Participants Produce
docs.text: Each participant leaves with a personal, working repository containing: nine completed labs with checkpoint commits; a triaged SECURITY_REPORT.md proving zero open high-severity findings; a BENCHMARKS.md with real measured cost and latency numbers; a DECISIONS.md recording five justified architectural trade-offs; and a deployed capstone service — Rafeeq running in a simulated Tawseel environment, containerised, health-checked, and demoed live in six minutes including one blocked live attack and one PDPL erasure.

docs.title: What the Academy Gets Back
docs.text:
Beyond trained engineers, the programme leaves two durable, reusable assets behind it:

  • TawseelBench, a τ-bench-style evaluation suite (customer request → applicable policy → environment state → available tools → expected state transition → pass/fail criteria) that the Academy can re-run against any future cohort's build, any model change, or any curriculum revision to measure drift objectively.
  • The Tawseel Agentic AI Engineering Kit — the full companion repository (nine labs, four MCP servers, a bilingual attack corpus, a deterministic synthetic dataset, and a capstone integration harness) as a reusable teaching asset for future deliveries and as the shared foundation SDA-AIE-313 and SDA-AIE-390 build directly on top of, so those courses need no separate scaffolding project.

docs.title: Stackability
docs.text: Course Relationship to SDA-AIE-311 SDA-AIE-214 Prerequisite — foundational AI/LLM engineering assumed entering this course SDA-AIE-311 (this course) Flagship Expert badge; builds the complete Rafeeq system and its security/observability baseline SDA-AIE-313 Deepens the security posture of this exact system (an explicit design goal of Module 8's threat model and red-team suite) SDA-AIE-390 Productionises this exact system for live deployment, building on the containerised capstone and its MCP/observability foundations

docs.title: Delivery Prerequisites (Academy-side)
docs.text:
• A shared model gateway with per-participant spend caps (cheap-tier default, frontier reserved for the capstone demo) — not required for any lab or CI check, only for live-mode demonstrations and the capstone's final live retest.
  • Local Docker capability per participant machine or a cloud fallback (Codespaces-style) for the full docker-compose profile (Qdrant, Postgres, MCP servers, simulated backends) — the default labs profile and every lab need neither.
  • Instructor preparation per instructor_guide.md's T-minus-1-week checklist: published checkpoint tags, seeded vulnerable simulation branches, printed A2 posters, and a shared cost/routing-accuracy board.
  • A classroom able to run bilingual (Arabic/English) content; Rafeeq's tickets, policies, and attack corpus are deliberately bilingual and the course requires both to be exercised, not treated as an edge case.

Companion documents: PARTICIPANT_HANDBOOK.md, INSTRUCTOR_DELIVERY_GUIDE.md, SETUP_GUIDE.md, ASSESSMENT_PACK.md, VISUAL_ASSET_BRIEF.md, RESOURCES.md.

docs.title: 1. The training deck
docs.text:
01_Training_Deck/SDA-AIE-311_Agentic_AI_Systems_Engineering_Deck.pptx — 258 slides, 16:9, bilingual titles, English body (per the package's convention that code and technical terms stay in English).

  • Every slide carries instructor speaker notes: what to say, what to show, what to ask, and what to cut when running late.
  • Structure: front matter (8) · Day 1 M1–M2 (47) · Day 2 M3–M4 (48) · Day 3 M5, M5.3, M6 (51) · Day 4 M7–M8 (51) · Day 5 M9, capstone, assessment, wrap-up (53).

  • Third-party figures (DTDC DIVA, DoorDash, OPLOG, Ryanair, DHL, Air India) are attributed on the slide as reported by their sources, never presented as our own measurements.

deck_source/ regenerates the deck: the content is plain JSON, one file per day.

cd deck_source
node render.js content/*.json -o ../SDA-AIE-311_Agentic_AI_Systems_Engineering_Deck.pptx

Edit a slide by editing its JSON entry and re-rendering — no layout work, and the design stays consistent. CONTENT_SPEC.md documents every slide type. Requires Node and pptxgenjs.

docs.title: 3. The course repository — the Tawseel Engineering Kit
docs.text: 03_Course_Repository/tawseel-agentic-ai/ — 321 files, 164 Python modules, 60 documents. This is the single repository the whole week runs on: Rafeeq (رفيق), an operations agent for Tawseel (توصيل), a fictional Saudi last-mile logistics company.

docs.title: It runs offline, with no API key
docs.text:
The most important engineering decision in the kit. A deterministic stub model, a dependency-free vector store and hashing embeddings mean every participant can develop, test and evaluate without spend or network — and the instructor's make test is deterministic. Live mode is a single environment variable, reserved for the capstone demo and red-team realism. See docs/OFFLINE_MODE.md.

cd tawseel-agentic-ai
python3 scripts/doctor.py        # 8/8 preflight checks
make data                        # regenerate the synthetic Saudi dataset
make test-offline                # 156 assertions, no key, no network

docs.title: What is inside

docs.title: Verified before shipping
docs.text:
Check Result scripts/doctor.py 8/8 scripts/selfcheck.py (data referential integrity) 25/25 tests/unit/run_without_pytest.py 92/92 tests/security/run_without_pytest.py 39/39 TawseelBench, 60 scenarios, reference target 100% Eval harness, 120 tickets, reference target 100% (baseline committed for the CI regression gate) Red-team suite, 78 payloads 0 open high-severity All nine labs/lab0*/solution/verify.py pass Every Python file compiles clean

The 100% figures are the offline reference target — a deterministic implementation of what a competent agent should do, used to prove the harness itself is sound. Participants' own agents will score lower; that gap is the lesson. evaluations/KNOWN_GAPS.md records what was deliberately left open for students to close.

docs.title: What was added beyond the original instructor package
docs.text:
1. M5.3 — "When NOT to Use Multi-Agent Systems", a full session with ten decision criteria, a decision worksheet, and Ryanair's reported consolidation from twelve agents to one as the anchor case against OPLOG as the counter-case.
  2. The Day 3 architecture challenge — teams build Architecture A (supervisor) and Architecture B (agents-as-tools) and fill a real comparison table from scripts/compare_arch.py. This turns M5/M6 into systems engineering rather than a multi-agent chat demo.
  3. TawseelBench — 60 τ-bench-shaped scenarios, positioned as an Academy asset that outlives this cohort.
  4. The attack corpus — ten families, 78 payloads, Arabic and English, with the seven-part finding shape (attack → vulnerability → exploit trajectory → business impact → detection → mitigation → retest) that makes the graded red-team report serious.
  5. Explicit ReAct before the framework — students implement the loop by hand and count unnecessary tool calls before LangGraph abstracts the control flow.
  6. Six enterprise case cards — DTDC DIVA, DoorDash, OPLOG, Ryanair, DHL Supply Chain, Air India AI.g — each with the reported facts attributed, the day it fits, and the question to put to the room.
  7. Offline-first execution, so the course is deliverable without per-participant model spend and every lab is reproducible.

docs.title: Before the first delivery — what still needs a human
docs.text:
Four items were deliberately left for the delivery team rather than guessed at:

  1. Pin the OWASP item numbers. docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md maps controls to the OWASP Agentic Top 10 2026 categories and says so explicitly. Pin the exact published item numbers against the current list before printing the Day 4 materials.
  2. Verify the enterprise case figures at source on the delivery date. They are attributed, dated where known, and change.
  3. Commission the visual assets. VISUAL_ASSET_BRIEF.md is ready to hand to a designer; the deck currently uses built diagrams, not illustrated ones.
  4. Run the full live-mode dry run. Everything here is verified offline. A dry run with the real gateway, Qdrant, LangSmith and the four MCP servers is still required, per the instructor guide's T-minus-one-week checklist.

Prepared for SDAIA Academy · Capacity Building Sector. All company, customer and order data in this package is synthetic. Tawseel and Rafeeq are fictional.

docs.title: SDA-AIE-311 Agentic AI Systems Engineering
docs.text: This bibliography covers every source named in the course's external-research brief (SPEC.md §6), organised by the module or lab that uses it. For each item: what it is, why it is in this course, which module/lab uses it, and how to use it. Items marked Third-party — access at source are not reproduced or mirrored in the course repository; follow the named link. Items marked Reference code only are example repositories the course points to for pattern illustration — they are not authoritative training material and are not graded against.

docs.title: Module 1 — Agentic System Architectures
docs.text: No external research citation; the module's content (the agent loop, the state-machine model) is original course material built directly on top of the LangGraph programming model referenced throughout the bibliography below.

docs.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
docs.text:
Yao, S., Zhao, J., Yu, D., Du, N., Shafran, I., Narasimhan, K., Cao, Y. (2022). Third-party — access at source: arXiv:2210.03629.

What it is. The paper that named and formalised the "thought → action → observation" interleaved reasoning loop that the whole agentic-AI field now calls ReAct.

Why it is in this course. The course deliberately implements ReAct explicitly, by hand, in src/rafeeq/reasoning/react.py, before ever using a framework's create_react_agent convenience wrapper — the point is that participants can name every part of a "prebuilt" agent because they built it first. Measuring unnecessary tool calls (thrashing) against this paper's original framing is the module's diagnostic habit.

Which module/lab. Module 2, Lab 2 (ReAct implementation and cost/step measurement).

How to use it. Required reading before Lab 2. Read the loop description and the failure modes the authors report (hallucinated reasoning steps, error propagation); Lab 2's ReAct thrash exercise (sim-react-thrash) reproduces one of them directly.

docs.title: LangChain Academy — "Introduction to LangGraph"
docs.text:
LangChain, Inc. Third-party — access at source: academy.langchain.com/courses/intro-to-langgraph (course); github.com/langchain-ai/langchain-academy (companion notebooks).

What it is. LangChain's own free foundational course on building agents with LangGraph's graph-based workflow model — state, nodes, conditional edges, memory, human-in-the-loop.

Why it is in this course. This is the designated technical companion to Modules 1–6: where the course's own Technical Content sections give the engineering reasoning behind a design choice, this course gives the hands-on mechanics of the underlying LangGraph APIs participants are expected to already be comfortable navigating (StateGraph, add_conditional_edges, checkpointers, create_react_agent). It is not required reading to pass SDA-AIE-311, but participants who have not touched LangGraph before Day 1 should complete at least its first two notebooks beforehand.

Which module/lab. Modules 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 (anywhere a build_*() graph is constructed).

How to use it. Pre-course self-study for anyone without prior LangGraph exposure; ongoing API reference during labs.

docs.title: Module 3 — Tool Use, Function Calling, and MCP Integration
LaDe — a comprehensive last-mile delivery dataset
docs.text:
Cainiao Network / Alibaba research. Third-party — access at source: search "LaDe last-mile delivery dataset" for the current hosting location (Cainiao's open-data programme); cite via the dataset's own paper when referencing it in written work.

What it is. A large-scale, real-world last-mile delivery dataset (~10.7 million packages, ~21,000 couriers, five Chinese cities) covering package, courier, and delivery-event records.

Why it is in this course — and the honesty note that matters. Tawseel's data schema (order, delivery event, courier, exception-code vocabulary) is inspired by LaDe's shape, not derived from its content. This course does not ship, redistribute, or train on any LaDe data. data/generate.py produces fully synthetic, deterministically-seeded Saudi data (five Saudi cities, TW-YYYY-NNNNN order ids, Arabic delivery notes) that merely follows a schema shape LaDe made a useful reference point for last-mile logistics fields (get_delivery_status, get_driver_status, estimate_eta, get_delivery_events, find_delivery_exception). Anyone wanting the real dataset must obtain it from its own source under its own terms; the course repository's README.md states this explicitly.

Which module/lab. Module 1 (orders_seed.json, delivery_events.jsonl shape), Module 3 (the logistics tool surface mirrors this event vocabulary).

How to use it. Background reading for instructors explaining why the delivery-event schema looks the way it does; not required participant reading.

docs.title: τ-bench and τ²-bench — Sierra AI
docs.text:
Yao, S. et al. / Sierra AI. Third-party — access at source: arXiv:2406.12045 (τ-bench paper); github.com/sierra-research/tau2-bench (τ²-bench, the current maintained benchmark and code); sierra.ai/resources/research/tau-bench.

What it is. A benchmark methodology for evaluating tool-using conversational agents in realistic enterprise domains (retail, airline), structured around a user, a domain policy, and a set of tools, scored on whether the agent reaches the correct end state.

Why it is in this course. TawseelBench's own scenario schema is built directly on this structure: customer request → applicable policy → environment state → available tools → expected state transition → pass/fail criteria (see evaluations/tawseelbench/schema.json and docs/TAWSEELBENCH.md). This is the course's model for what "the system testifies to its own quality" means in practice — an eval harness that checks concrete state, not subjective response quality.

Which module/lab. Every module's "Benchmarks and Evaluation" section; the capstone's eval-harness gate (LO8).

How to use it. Required reading before Lab 1; re-read before the capstone milestone M-A gate ("eval replay green locally").

docs.title: Module 4 — Memory and State Management
docs.text: No new third-party citation beyond LangGraph's own checkpointer and vector-store integration patterns (covered by the LangChain Academy companion above). The PDPL framing (erasure, scoping, retention) is course-original, grounded in Saudi data-protection practice rather than a single external source.

docs.title: Hugging Face — "Multi-Agent Systems" (AI Agents Course)
docs.text:
Hugging Face. Third-party — access at source: huggingface.co/learn/agents-course/unit2/smolagents/multi_agent_systems.

What it is. A unit of Hugging Face's free AI Agents Course covering when and how to decompose a single agent into a multi-agent system, using the smolagents framework.

Why it is in this course. A second, framework-independent perspective on the single-vs-multi decision that reinforces Module 5's own four scaling symptoms (tool overload, prompt overload, context cost, ownership friction) from outside the LangGraph-specific lens the rest of the course uses.

Which module/lab. Module 5, as supplementary/optional reading around Lab 5.

How to use it. Optional discussion-case reading; not required, useful for the Split-or-keep clinic activity.

docs.title: Module 6 — Hierarchical Delegation and Agent Orchestration
LangGraph — Supervisor vs Agents-as-Tools guidance
docs.text:
LangChain, Inc. Third-party — access at source: reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph-supervisor (the langgraph-supervisor package reference); github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph-supervisor-py.

What it is. LangChain's own documentation and reference implementation of the supervisor multi-agent topology, contrasted against the agents-as-tools pattern (where a top-level agent calls specialists as ordinary tool calls rather than through an explicit routing/handoff contract).

Why it is in this course. The capstone explicitly asks for both architectures — Architecture A (LangGraph supervisor, src/rafeeq/orchestration/supervisor.py) and Architecture B (agents-as-tools, src/rafeeq/orchestration/agents_as_tools.py) — compared on task success, tool calls, tokens, latency, handoff failures, and unauthorised-action risk (scripts/compare_arch.py). This is the primary technical reference for that comparison.

Which module/lab. Module 6, Lab 6; the capstone's Architecture A/B comparison.

How to use it. Required reading before the Lab 6 fast-finisher extension and before running scripts/compare_arch.py.

docs.title: Module 7 — Flow Engineering over Prompt Engineering
docs.text: No new third-party citation; this module is the course's own synthesis of a discipline implicit in the LangGraph and MCP material above (structure over prose) rather than a citation of a single external source.

docs.title: Module 8 — Guardrails, Security, and Adversarial Testing
OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026)
docs.text:
OWASP. Third-party — access at source: the current OWASP GenAI Security Project publication for agentic applications — locate the live edition via owasp.org (OWASP GenAI Security Project) rather than a mirrored copy, since the list is actively revised; several independent explainer write-ups (Giskard, Cycode, Practical DevSecOps, VamiSec) summarise the current categories if a quick reference is needed, but the OWASP publication itself is the authoritative source to cite in SECURITY_REPORT.md.

What it is. The OWASP community's structured taxonomy of the top security risks specific to agentic (tool-using, autonomous-action) AI applications — the agentic counterpart to the long-standing OWASP Top 10 for web applications.

Why it is in this course. Mandatory Day-4 pre-reading. Every guardrail Module 8 builds and every red-team finding the course's attack corpus produces is mapped to an owasp_id field (security/**/*.json, docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md), so a participant's SECURITY_REPORT.md speaks the same taxonomy a real enterprise security review would expect.

Which module/lab. Module 8, Lab 8; PA-2; the capstone's SECURITY_REPORT.md.

How to use it. Required reading before Lab 8. Cross-reference every finding's owasp_id against the current published category names — the mapping in docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md should be treated as a teaching aid, not a substitute for reading the source list itself, since OWASP revises category names between editions.

docs.title: AgentDojo (ETH Zurich)
docs.text:
Debenedetti, E., Zhang, J., Balunović, M., Beurer-Kellner, L., Fischer, M., Tramèr, F. (2024). Third-party — access at source: arXiv:2406.13352 (paper); github.com/ethz-spylab/agentdojo-core (code); agentdojo.spylab.ai (project site).

What it is. A dynamic evaluation environment from ETH Zurich's SPY Lab for measuring both the utility and the security of tool-using LLM agents under prompt-injection attack, jointly — an agent that refuses everything scores well on security and badly on utility, and AgentDojo's methodology penalises that.

Why it is in this course. The direct structural model for the course's own attack corpus (security/**/*.json). Every family in the corpus — direct/indirect injection, tool-result injection, memory poisoning, privilege escalation, denial-of-wallet — mirrors an AgentDojo attack category, and the corpus's success_oracle field (a concrete, checkable outcome, never "did the model say something bad") is a direct application of AgentDojo's insistence on measuring real effects, not surface refusals.

Which module/lab. Module 8, Lab 8; src/rafeeq/security/red_team.py's run_suite().

How to use it. Required reading before Lab 8. Read the paper's framing of the utility/security trade-off specifically — it is the source of the course's own rule that a red-team suite with a weak oracle "always succeeds" and is therefore worthless (Module 8's troubleshooting table).

docs.title: OpenAI Agents SDK — guardrail and human-in-the-loop patterns
docs.text:
OpenAI. Third-party — access at source: openai.github.io/openai-agents-python (SDK docs); developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents/guardrails-approvals ("Guardrails and human review").

What it is. OpenAI's own SDK documentation for input/output guardrail functions and human-approval interrupt points around tool calls.

Why it is in this course. Referenced conceptually, not as an implementation dependency — Rafeeq's guardrails (src/rafeeq/security/input_guard.py, output_guard.py) are framework-independent, dependency-free Python so they run in stub mode with zero installed packages. The OpenAI SDK material is useful for participants who will also work with that SDK, to see the same layered-defence principle (structural checks, not prompt sentences) expressed in a different framework's vocabulary.

Which module/lab. Module 8, as a cross-framework comparison point.

How to use it. Optional discussion reading; useful for the "which parts of Rafeeq's behaviour must never be a prompt sentence" discussion (Module 7/8 crossover).

docs.title: Module 9 — Observability, Cost Optimisation, and Monitoring
LangSmith
docs.text:
LangChain, Inc. Third-party — access at source: smith.langchain.com (product); LangChain's documentation site for API reference.

What it is. LangChain's agent-tracing and evaluation platform — captures a run as a tree of spans with inputs, outputs, timing, and token counts, and lets failed runs become regression test cases.

Why it is in this course. The course's target tracing tool for a live/deployed Rafeeq (src/rafeeq/observability/tracing.py's @traceable decorator wires to it when RAFEEQ_LANGSMITH=1). Offline/stub-mode labs use the repository's own LocalTracer (reports/traces/*.json) instead, which produces the same span-tree shape so the skill transfers directly once a participant has a LangSmith key.

Which module/lab. Module 9, Lab 9; the capstone's tracing/cost-attribution demo requirement.

How to use it. Provision a LangSmith key per participant for the capstone demo (per instructor_guide.md's preparation checklist); not required for any offline lab or CI check.

docs.title: LangGraph 101 and OpenAI Agents SDK example repositories
docs.text:
LangChain, Inc. / OpenAI. Reference code only — access at source: github.com/langchain-ai/langchain-academy; github.com/openai/openai-agents-python's linked examples.

What it is. Framework-maintained example code demonstrating agent, tool, and orchestration patterns in each SDK.

Why it is in this course, and the caveat that matters. Flagged explicitly as reference code only, not authoritative training material. These repositories show a working pattern, not necessarily the enterprise-governed, security-hardened pattern this course teaches — a participant who copies an example repo's tool-authorisation approach verbatim (frequently prompt-based or absent entirely in a minimal example) would fail Module 8's rubric. Use them to see idiomatic framework syntax; use src/rafeeq/** as the authoritative pattern for how a governed enterprise tool, a scoped handoff, or a structural guardrail should actually be built.

Which module/lab. Cross-cutting, Modules 3–9.

How to use it. Syntax reference only, cited nowhere as a source of engineering practice in any graded artefact.

docs.title: Cross-Cutting — the Six Enterprise Case Studies
docs.text:
Presented throughout Module 5's "Industry use cases" and, in expanded form, in INSTRUCTOR_DELIVERY_GUIDE.md's teaching cards. Every figure below is a reported, third-party claim, attributed to its source, and is never presented as this course's own measurement — course-original numbers live only in each module's own "Benchmarks and Evaluation" tables, produced by the repository itself.

Case What it is Source Which module/lab How to use it DTDC DIVA An AI-powered logistics customer-support agent (DIVA 2.0) for DTDC, an Indian logistics/courier company, built on Amazon Bedrock AWS Machine Learning Blog, "The DIVA logistics agent powered by Amazon Bedrock" — aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning; DTDC's own DIVA 2.0 product announcements Module 5 use cases; instructor teaching card Discussion case: a real logistics support agent's reported accuracy/support-burden figures, contrasted with Rafeeq's own measured numbers DoorDash Dasher support DoorDash's LLM/RAG-based automated support system for its courier ("Dasher") population DoorDash Engineering Blog, "Path to high-quality LLM-based Dasher support automation" — careersatdoordash.com/blog Module 5/6 use cases; instructor teaching card Discussion case for specialist-agent design and hallucination-reduction techniques in an operational-support domain OPLOG fulfilment orchestration A Turkish/regional e-commerce fulfilment operator's use of AI agents in warehouse and operations orchestration, built on AWS AWS Solutions case study, aws.amazon.com/solutions/case-studies/oplog; OPLOG's own blog coverage of AWS Cloud Day Module 5/6 use cases Discussion case for orchestration in a fulfilment (not customer-support) operational context — closest industry analogue to Tawseel itself Ryanair — twelve domain agents consolidated to one Ryanair's five-year AI/data partnership with Google Cloud, covering customer service and operational AI; the specific "12 agents → 1" consolidation figure is the one your delivery should verify against the live source at delivery time, since partnership coverage is still developing as of this course's build date Computer Weekly, "Ryanair signs five-year Google Cloud AI partnership" (Aug 2026) — computerweekly.com; PRNewswire, "Ryanair and Google Cloud Announce Five-Year Data and AI Partnership" — prnewswire.com Module 5.3 ("When NOT to Use Multi-Agent Systems") — the anchor case The "more agents are not better" teaching point; instructors must re-verify the exact consolidation figure before each delivery and cite the specific article used that day, since this is a fast-moving, still-unfolding partnership DHL Supply Chain DHL Supply Chain's generative-AI and, more recently, agentic-AI programme for data management, customer support, proposal accuracy, and operational communications DHL Group press releases: "DHL Supply Chain implements Generative AI..." (Oct 2024) and "DHL boosts operational efficiency and customer communications with HappyRobot's AI Agents" (Nov 2025) — group.dhl.com/en/media-relations/press-releases; Transport and Logistics Middle East, "DHL Supply Chain Integrates Agentic AI Into New Global Operational Model" — transportandlogisticsme.com Module 5/9 use cases Discussion case for operational-communications agents and the shift from generative to agentic AI in a logistics operator's stated strategy Air India AI.g Air India's generative/agentic AI virtual agent (AI.g), built on Microsoft Azure OpenAI, reported to answer around 40,000 customer queries a day across 1,300+ query types Microsoft Customer Stories, "How Azure AI helped Air India reinvent customer service by answering 40,000 daily queries instantly" — microsoft.com/en/customers/story/26047-air-india-azure-openai-in-foundry-models Module 9 use cases (scale/volume framing); instructor teaching card Discussion case for scale economics — the SDA-AIE-311 cost-per-contact literacy (LO7) applied to a volume figure two orders of magnitude above Rafeeq's own eval set

Re-verify the specific cited figures shortly before each delivery and update the citation to the article actually used — do not assume a figure fixed at course-build time remains the latest public number.

This bibliography is a companion to docs/RESOURCES.md-style citation practice used throughout the repository (see docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md's OWASP mapping and security/README.md's AgentDojo attribution) — cite sources the same way in any derivative teaching material.

docs.title: SDA-AIE-311 Agentic AI Systems Engineering — participant and lab-environment setup
docs.text:
Three tracks are offered, in order of preference. Track A (fully offline) is the default for every lab, make test, and CI — no participant needs Track B or C to complete the course. Track B is for anyone who wants the real (not stub) model, vector-store, and checkpointer stack running locally. Track C is the fallback for a machine that cannot run Docker at all.

Repo root for every command below: tawseel-agentic-ai/. Set PYTHONPATH=src once per shell (or per command, as shown) before anything else.

docs.title: Before you start: the offline-mode promise
docs.text:
Every lab, the full test suite, and CI run with zero API keys and zero network calls by default. Three environment variables control this, all defaulting to their offline value:

Variable Default Meaning RAFEEQ_MODEL_MODE stub StubChatModel — deterministic, rule-based, bilingual, zero cost, zero network RAFEEQ_VECTOR_MODE simple In-memory vector store — no Qdrant/Docker required RAFEEQ_EMBED_MODE hashing Dependency-free embeddings — no embedding API call

This is not a training-wheels shortcut. StubChatModel implements the same call surface a real chat model does (.invoke, .bind_tools, .with_structured_output), so code written and tested against it works unmodified against the real thing once you switch RAFEEQ_MODEL_MODE=live. Labs 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9 run fully offline with nothing beyond pydantic installed; Labs 5 and 6 need langgraph (still no key, no network); Lab 3's live-MCP path needs mcp + langchain-mcp-adapters (its offline tool catalogue needs neither). See docs/OFFLINE_MODE.md for the full mechanism.

docs.title: Track A — Fully Offline (the default; do this first, everyone)
docs.text: What you need: Python 3.11+, git. Nothing else.

docs.title: 1. Clone and set the path
docs.text:
git clone <course-org-repo-url> tawseel-agentic-ai
cd tawseel-agentic-ai
export PYTHONPATH=src

Verify: python3 --version reports 3.11 or higher.

docs.title: 2. Preflight
docs.text:
python3 scripts/doctor.py

Verify: the report ends 8/8 checks passed (or close to it — a missing optional Layer-B package is expected and listed by name, not a failure) and states which labs run fully offline right now (1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9) versus which need one more pip install (5, 6 need langgraph; 3's live-MCP path needs mcp + langchain-mcp-adapters).

docs.title: 3. Generate the deterministic dataset
docs.text:
make data

This runs data/generate.py (seeded by RAFEEQ_SEED=20260311, so every participant's data is byte-identical) followed by scripts/selfcheck.py (referential-integrity check).

Verify: no errors printed; data/orders/orders_seed.json (2,000 orders), data/customers/customers_seed.json (400 customers), data/tickets_eval.jsonl (120 labelled bilingual tickets), and data/routing_eval.jsonl (60 labelled tickets) now exist.

python3 -c "import json; print(len(json.load(open('data/orders/orders_seed.json'))))"
# -> 2000

docs.title: 4. Run the full offline test suite
docs.text:
make test-offline

This runs tests/unit/run_without_pytest.py and tests/security/run_without_pytest.py — stdlib test runners requiring no pytest install.

Verify: ends 88/88 checks passed (unit) and 39/39 checks passed (security). If pytest happens to be installed, make test runs the same checks via pytest instead and produces the same pass counts.

docs.title: 5. Try a lab
docs.text:
make lab1
# or directly:
python3 labs/lab01/solution/verify.py

Verify: ends 10/10 checks passed. Every lab from 1–9 follows the same pattern — make labN or python3 labs/labNN/solution/verify.py — and every verify.py prints its own numbered PASS/FAIL checklist, so "did it work" is never a judgement call.

Track A is sufficient for the entire course. Tracks B and C below are optional, for participants who want the real model/vector-store/checkpointer stack (recommended before the capstone demo) or whose machine cannot run Python locally at all.

docs.title: Track B — Local, Full Stack (Docker + Qdrant + gateway key)
docs.text: Use this once you are comfortable with Track A and want to run Labs 5/6 against a real LangGraph build, exercise RAFEEQ_VECTOR_MODE=qdrant, or rehearse the capstone demo in live mode.

docs.title: 1. Docker
docs.text:
Install Docker Desktop (Windows: enable WSL2 integration; see the troubleshooting appendix) or Colima on macOS/Linux.

Verify: 

docker run hello-world
Prints "Hello from Docker!".

docs.title: 2. Install the full Python dependency set
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements.txt -r requirements-dev.txt

This adds, on top of Track A's pydantic: fastapi, uvicorn, langgraph, langchain-core, langchain-openai, langsmith, mcp, qdrant-client, psycopg[binary], langgraph-checkpoint-postgres, and (dev-only) pytest, ruff.

Verify: 

python3 scripts/doctor.py
The optional-dependency survey should now show most or all of the nine Layer-B packages present, and the verdict section should no longer flag Labs 5/6/3-live as needing an install.

docs.title: 3. Bring up the full compose profile
docs.text:
docker compose -f deployment/docker-compose.yml --profile full up -d
docker compose -f deployment/docker-compose.yml --profile full ps

This starts Qdrant (long-term memory + versioned KB), Postgres (the LangGraph checkpointer — short-term/thread-scoped memory), the four MCP servers (orders, logistics, billing, customer), and sim-backends (the mock Tawseel OMS/logistics/CRM/billing backends), wired with ordered health-check dependencies — rafeeq-api will not accept traffic until every dependency reports healthy.

Verify: every row in the ps output shows healthy, not just running.

curl -s http://localhost:8000/readyz | python3 -m json.tool
Reports "status": "ok" with per-check detail (seed data present, vector store constructs, all four MCP servers import, active RAFEEQ_MODEL_MODE).

docs.title: 4. Configure the gateway key (live mode only)
docs.text:
cp .env.example .env
Edit .env and set: 
RAFEEQ_MODEL_MODE=live
OPENAI_API_KEY=<the course gateway key>
OPENAI_BASE_URL=<course gateway URL, if not api.openai.com>

Verify: 

export RAFEEQ_MODEL_MODE=live
python3 scripts/doctor.py
The "model gateway reachable" check now actually makes a network call (only happens when RAFEEQ_MODEL_MODE=live) and should report [PASS]. Do not leave RAFEEQ_MODEL_MODE=live set for routine lab work — switch back to stub (or simply unset RAFEEQ_MODEL_MODE) so you are not spending gateway budget on iteration; reserve live mode for the capstone demo and the PA-2 live retest (docs/OFFLINE_MODE.md's "when a participant MUST switch to live mode" section).

docs.title: 5. Smoke-test the running service
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/resolve \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"ticket_id":"TKT-SMOKE-1","text":"أين طلبي رقم TW-2026-88120؟","locale":"ar","customer_id":"CUST-4471","order_id":"TW-2026-88120"}'

Verify: a JSON response resolving the ticket, correctly in Arabic.

docs.title: Tear-down
docs.text: docker compose -f deployment/docker-compose.yml --profile full down

docs.title: Track C — Cloud Fallback (Codespaces-style)
docs.text:
For a machine that cannot run Docker or a recent Python locally (locked-down corporate laptop, insufficient disk/RAM).

  1. Open the course repository in a cloud dev-container environment (GitHub Codespaces or your Academy's equivalent) using the repo's own container definition — the same python:3.11-slim base the Dockerfile uses, so behaviour matches every other track.
  2. In the cloud terminal, run Track A steps 1–5 verbatim (export PYTHONPATH=src, python3 scripts/doctor.py, make data, make test-offline, make lab1). Nothing about the offline track changes in a cloud container.
  3. If the cloud environment offers a pre-provisioned Docker-in-Docker or a hosted Qdrant, Track B's steps also transfer unchanged — only the docker compose host differs, not the commands.
  4. Verify exactly as in Track A/B: the same doctor.py verdict, the same 88/88/39/39 test counts, the same /readyz response.

Cloud fallback participants should still complete Track A locally-in-the-cloud first (zero dependencies, fastest to a working state) before attempting Track B's full stack in the same environment.

docs.title: Windows / WSL2
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix docker run hello-world fails with a WSL-integration error Docker Desktop's WSL2 backend not enabled for your distro Docker Desktop → Settings → Resources → WSL Integration → enable your distro; restart Docker Desktop python3: command not found in WSL Some WSL Ubuntu images ship python3 but not the python alias, or no Python at all sudo apt update && sudo apt install python3.11 python3-pip; always invoke python3, never python, per every command in this guide Paths with C:\Users\... fail inside WSL commands Running commands from a Windows shell against a WSL-cloned repo (or vice versa) Clone the repository inside the WSL filesystem (~/tawseel-agentic-ai, not /mnt/c/...) and run every command from the WSL terminal — cross-filesystem access is slow and occasionally breaks file-lock behaviour Docker needs docker compose hangs on full profile bring-up WSL2 memory limit too low for Qdrant + Postgres + 4 MCP servers + API Increase the WSL2 memory cap in %UserProfile%\.wslconfig (memory=8GB or higher), then wsl --shutdown and restart Docker Desktop

docs.title: Corporate proxy
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix pip install in Track B times out or fails TLS verification Corporate proxy intercepting HTTPS without a trusted CA, or pip not proxy-aware Set HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY env vars per your IT policy; if TLS is intercepted, install your organisation's CA bundle and point pip at it (PIP_CERT=/path/to/corp-ca-bundle.crt) — never pass --trusted-host as a substitute for a real CA unless your security team explicitly signs off docker pull fails for qdrant/qdrant or postgres images Proxy blocks Docker Hub or requires an authenticated registry mirror Configure Docker Desktop's proxy settings (Settings → Resources → Proxies), or ask your Academy IT contact for a pre-mirrored internal registry per instructor_guide.md's "confirm the classroom network allows... package index" checklist item RAFEEQ_MODEL_MODE=live gateway check fails even with a valid key Proxy blocking the gateway's outbound host Confirm the gateway hostname is on the classroom network's allowlist (an instructor pre-session task); Track A/B's offline steps are entirely unaffected — you do not need the gateway for any lab

docs.title: Arabic font / console issues
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Arabic text in terminal output shows as boxes (□□□) or reversed/garbled Terminal font lacks Arabic glyphs, or the terminal does not apply bidirectional (BiDi) text shaping Windows Terminal, iTerm2, and GNOME Terminal all handle Arabic BiDi correctly out of the box — if using a legacy console (cmd.exe), switch to Windows Terminal; ensure the font is a Unicode-complete family (Cascadia Code, Noto Sans Arabic, or any modern default) Arabic renders correctly in the terminal but garbled in a redirected file (> out.txt) File written/read with the wrong encoding Always open/redirect as UTF-8 explicitly: python3 script.py > out.txt is fine on any modern OS, but if editing on Windows, open the file in an editor that defaults to UTF-8 (VS Code does), not Notepad's legacy ANSI mode pytest/verify.py output with Arabic ticket text looks fine, but a copy-pasted Arabic ticket into a terminal prompt behaves oddly (character order visually reversed) Expected BiDi rendering behaviour in some terminals for mixed Arabic/Latin/digit strings (e.g. TW-2026-88120 inside an Arabic sentence) — this is a display artefact only Verify correctness by checking the underlying bytes/JSON (data/tickets_eval.jsonl), not the terminal's visual rendering; this is exactly the tokenisation/rendering awareness Module 4 asks participants to notice, not a setup defect to "fix" make data/scripts/selfcheck.py reports a policy or ticket file encoding error A local editor re-saved a bilingual data/policy file in a non-UTF-8 encoding Re-generate from source (make data regenerates everything deterministically) rather than hand-editing generated files; if editing data/policies/ar/*.md by hand, save explicitly as UTF-8 (no BOM)

docs.title: General
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'rafeeq' PYTHONPATH=src not set for this shell/command export PYTHONPATH=src once per shell, or prefix each command: PYTHONPATH=src python3 ... make data / make test-offline "works" the first run but a later run reports different-looking output Nothing is actually non-deterministic — RAFEEQ_SEED=20260311 is fixed — but stale __pycache__ or a partially-written data file from an interrupted previous run can look like drift make clean then make data again A lab's verify.py fails with an ImportError naming a pip install line You are running a Layer-B lab (5, 6, or 3's live-MCP path) without that package installed — this is by design (SPEC's import-guard rule), not a bug Either pip install the named package (Track B), or stay on the Layer-A subset of that lab if your instructor has scoped it down Docker healthcheck never turns healthy on the full profile A dependent service (Qdrant/Postgres) itself unhealthy, often first-boot volume initialisation taking longer than the healthcheck's start_period docker compose -f deployment/docker-compose.yml --profile full logs <service> to see the actual failure; re-run ps after a minute — first boot is often slower than the steady state

docs.title: SDA-AIE-311 Agentic AI Systems Engineering — production brief for design
docs.text: This is a commissioning document. It consolidates every "Required Visuals and Training Assets" entry across the nine module packages into one numbered list a design agency or in-house designer can quote and produce against, without needing to read the underlying course content. Assets are grouped by module in teaching order; each carries an asset ID, purpose, required elements, a style note, and the session it belongs to (Day/Hour, from course_delivery_plan.md).

docs.title: Production standards (apply to every asset)
docs.text:
• Palette. One consistent four-to-six-colour course palette across all nine modules — do not restyle per module. Reserve one accent colour exclusively for "where agency/risk lives" call-outs (the conditional edge in M1, the trust boundary in M8, the cost bar in M9) so participants learn to recognise that accent as "pay attention here" across the whole week.
  • Bilingual labelling. Every diagram intended for print (posters) or for the participant handbook needs Arabic subtitles alongside English labels, not Arabic-only or English-only. Screenshots of terminals/traces stay in their captured language as-is.
  • Format. Diagrams as vector (SVG/PDF source, PNG export for slides). Screenshots as PNG, captured directly from the repository at data-generate-seeded state (RAFEEQ_SEED=20260311) so every cohort's designer-produced screenshot matches what a participant will actually see.
  • A2 posters.
