docs.title: How to Run the Week
docs.text:
The golden thread. Every module and lab evolves the same system — Rafeeq, the Tawseel operations agent. Never introduce a throwaway example; always extend Rafeeq. This is what makes the Day-5 capstone an assembly, not a from-scratch scramble.

Non-determinism is the theme. Establish on Day 1 that "it worked once in the demo" never counts — every lab has an evaluation harness, and tickets_eval.jsonl is reused Day 1 to Day 5 specifically so participants build the habit of measuring, not eyeballing.

Pacing. Labs 2, 6, and 8 overrun most cohorts. Publish checkpoint commits (lab1-start … lab9-start, -solution variants) so a straggler can git checkout lab6-start and rejoin without falling permanently behind — every lab's verify.py runs standalone against src/rafeeq/**, so nothing downstream is blocked by one unfinished lab. Protect Lab 8 and its H5 security-report clinic at full length — cut theory, never triage time — and start Day-5 capstone assembly (H3) on time, no exceptions; cut discussion, not build time.

What to cut for a weak cohort. Reduce Module 5's monolith baseline to a guided demo instead of a build. Never skip the cross-customer leakage test (M4) or the structural-authz demo (M8) — they are the course's conscience. What to add for a strong cohort. Pull the deterministic fast-path router (M6/M9) and human-in-the-loop approval into capstone main scope on Day 5.

Model access. Default every lab to RAFEEQ_MODEL_MODE=stub — zero cost, zero keys, fully deterministic. Reserve a live gateway key exclusively for the capstone demo and the PA-2 live retest; publish a token budget and live spend on the shared board regardless, so cost literacy (LO7) is visibly modelled, not just taught.

docs.title: Per-Hour Facilitation Script
docs.text: Say/show/ask, condensed for the front of the room. "Checkpoint" is the minute mark by which that hour's core deliverable should exist — if the room is behind, cut discussion time, not build time, to hit it.

docs.title: Day 1
docs.text: H Say (open with) Show / demo Transition question Checkpoint 1 "You've all shipped a chatbot. This week you ship something that acts." Introduce Rafeeq/Tawseel: five cities, bilingual customers, real money movement. A failure story: an agent that "worked in the demo" and refunded twice in production (preview M1's case study without naming it yet). "What's the one thing an agent can do that a chatbot cannot?" 40 min: everyone can name the four agentic components 2 "An agent is a state machine — today you build the smallest possible one." Draw the loop: observe → reason → act → update → repeat, with a guaranteed exit. Live: sketch RafeeqState on the projector; show broken_agent.py's three # SMELL comments. "What happens if route never returns END?" 40 min: RafeeqState fields agreed as a class 3 "Run broken_agent.py on the confused-customer input. Let it burn tokens — watch the counter." Live runaway loop on the projector, then Ctrl-C; convert to the bounded state machine live in under 8 minutes. — (lab time) 45 min: every pair's termination test is green 4 "Same task, three different ways to think. Watch the cost spread." Trace walkthrough: the same refund ticket through ReAct, Plan-and-Execute, and Reflection, side by side. "Which pattern would you trust with your own money?" 40 min: comparison table on the whiteboard has real numbers from a live run 5 "Build all three. The money shot is your own cost table, not mine." — (guided lab) "Post your three numbers to the shared board." 45 min: every pair has BENCHMARKS.md with a three-pattern comparison committed

docs.title: Day 2
docs.text: H Say Show / demo Transition question Checkpoint 1 "A tool schema is the prompt for the tool — an easily confused consumer reads it." Stand up an MCP server live, bind its tool to Rafeeq, under 8 minutes; then show a prompt-only "never refund > 500" bypassed by a crafted input. "If the prompt said never — what actually stopped it?" (nothing, yet) 35 min: one MCP server running standalone in every pair's terminal 2 "Wrap the real Tawseel APIs. Errors are values, not exceptions — remember Module 1." — (guided lab) — 45 min: pytest tests/unit/test_tools.py green for every pair 3 "Your agent forgets every customer between messages. Today it stops." Show same-thread continuity live, then trigger the no-filter cross-customer leak and fix it with one line — a metadata filter. "Why is that filter a security control, not a performance one?" 35 min: everyone can state the short-term vs long-term distinction in one sentence each 4 "Filter before you rank. Every read, every write." — (guided lab) — 45 min: every pair's leakage test is green 5 "Wire it all together. Then measure it, don't eyeball it." PA-1 runs this hour. — (integration lab + PA-1) "Collect repository state before you leave — Day 4 needs it." 45 min: PA-1 submitted

docs.title: Day 3
docs.text: H Say Show / demo Transition question Checkpoint 1 "One agent, 18 tools, one contradiction-riddled prompt. Watch it misroute." Run a cross-domain ticket through the Lab-5 monolith live — watch issue_refund fire on a tracking intent. "Which of the four scaling symptoms just bit?" 35 min: everyone names tool overload correctly 2 "Split it. Three specialists, tidy toolbelts, isolated context." — (guided lab) — 45 min: context-isolation test green (Billing carries no address field) — M5.3 — When NOT to Use Multi-Agent Systems (25 min). See the dedicated plan below; run this here, between Lab 5 and the M6 lecture. 3 "Three capable specialists, no one in charge yet." Route a cross-domain ticket live through a hand-drawn supervisor first (whiteboard), then show sim-lost-handoff's customer-gets-nothing failure. "What's the supervisor's job — and what is it NOT allowed to do?" 35 min: everyone can state "route and aggregate, never domain work" 4 "Build the hub. Bound the whole system, not just each agent." — (guided lab); trigger the chatter-loop probe live, watch it escalate at handoff 4 instead of looping 30 times — 45 min: routing accuracy measured against the Lab-5 baseline 5 "Compare against your own monolith. The +15–20pt jump is today's payoff." — (integration + benchmark) "Post your routing-accuracy delta to the shared board." 45 min: every pair's comparison table committed

docs.title: Day 4
docs.text: H Say Show / demo Transition question Checkpoint 1 "This prompt has a 500 SAR limit. Watch a sentence lose to a customer's wording." Run the "ignore the limit" adversarial ticket on refund_prompt_only.py live — it issues 4,000 SAR. "The model followed the rule as written. So what actually failed?" 35 min: everyone can state "a prompt rule is decided fresh every time" 2 "Every rule becomes a branch today. Then we test it in milliseconds." — (guided lab); re-run the same 4,000 SAR ticket against the finished flow, live — 45 min: 7 branch unit tests green, zero model calls 3 "Today you attack your own system. The rule: input is untrusted, output is unverified." Run SYSTEM OVERRIDE against a prompt-only build (money leaves) then the hardened build (blocked) — with the input guardrail switched off, to prove structure holds when the filter misses. "Which layer actually stopped it that time?" 35 min: everyone can name all six layers of defence 4 "Build the guards, then build the attacker." — (guided lab: guardrails, then the red-team agent) — 45 min: red-team run produces at least one real, reproducible finding 5 "This is the graded artefact. Triage money and PII before anything else, always." PA-2 clinic — full length, protect this. Walk one finding through the seven-part shape live on the projector. "Collect repo URL + LangSmith link before you leave." 45 min: zero open high-severity findings in every pair's report

docs.title: The Nine Case Studies — Facilitation Notes and Model Answers
docs.text:
Discussion questions are verbatim from each module package; do not invent new ones. Facilitate, do not lecture — let the room propose the fix before confirming it.

M1 — The Runaway Refund Agent at SahlPay. Facilitation: let someone propose "a better prompt" first, then ask them to defend it against a crafted "ignore the limit" message — it always loses. (1) An explicit refund_issued state flag entering the refund branch at most once; a prompt cannot enforce this because it is re-evaluated fresh every request. (2) Timestamp, model/graph version, input state, decision and tool call with arguments, result, and policy version in force. (3) Add budgets and gates, not remove them — sell it as fewer incidents and fewer wasted tokens, which is cheaper as well as safer. (4) Replay from the logged discrete state transitions — this is possible only because the agent is a state machine, not a black box.

M2 — Cost Blowout at a Saudi Telecom. Facilitation: ask for a guess at the overrun multiple before revealing 18×; the gap between guess and reality is the point. (1) Tag every contact by intent, replay historically through an instrumented agent, sum tokens×price grouped by intent. (2) Arabic's higher token count multiplies ReAct's super-linear cost further — strengthens the case for moving routine Arabic intents to Plan-and-Execute. (3) Only on billing-adjustment outputs, with concrete criteria (amount within eligibility, correct language, policy cited). (4) Replay one day's contacts through the eval harness pre/post; canary before full rollout.

M3 — Unifying Three Systems Behind MCP. (1) One server per system isolates trust boundaries and lets each backend team own their own release cadence. (2) At the MCP server (or a thin gateway every agent traverses) — never the agent or its prompt. (3) From per-integration review (every new agent × backend pairing) to per-capability review (once per published tool, reused safely by every future agent). (4) A direct caller breaks; the adapter absorbs the field-name change so the tool's contract to the agent never moves.

M4 — The Cross-Customer Memory Leak. Facilitation: this is the module's conscience — do not let the room treat it as a corner case. (1) Without it, retrieval can structurally return another customer's PII; the filter is what makes cross-customer access impossible, not merely unlikely. (2) forget_customer must purge vector-store entries by customer_id and remove or redact the corresponding checkpointer rows — both stores, one call. (3) A resolution summary and stable preferences belong; raw national IDs, full card numbers, and raw hostile message text never do. (4) A standing leakage test in CI plus periodic production sampling of retrieval calls for cross-customer hits.

M5 — The 28-Tool Monolith at SoukNow. (1) Tool overload, measured directly via tool-selection accuracy on a labelled eval set. (2) Ownership maps to accountability and data scope — exactly what a PDPL/audit review wants to see. (3) Use the eval set: route trivial single-domain tickets to one specialist directly, mixed/complex tickets through the supervisor. (4) Lost handoffs and chatter loops — guarded by mandatory write-back and a global budget (Module 6's subject).

M6 — The Apology Loop at a Telecom Support Desk. (1) All coordination flows through one bounded hub; a peer network has no central budget to stop A→B→A forever. (2) Scoped context plus an explicit sub-goal plus a correlation id; never the full raw history or another domain's PII. (3) From the eval data's typical resolution hop count, with margin, reviewed by risk/compliance and documented. (4) Every routing, handoff, and escalation decision: who/what decided, inputs, outputs, timestamps.

M7 — The Talk-Around Refund at Anaqah. (1) A prompt is advisory text a model can be argued out of; a branch is code executed regardless of wording. (2) If it is a checkable condition on typed state, it is a rule; if it requires interpreting genuine ambiguity or composing empathy, it is judgement. (3) A reproducible, deterministic proof (a passing unit test) versus a human's best-effort reading of prose. (4) Forcing genuinely novel complaint handling into a rigid tree fails on the first unseen case — keep reply composition and open judgement with the model.

M8 — The SYSTEM OVERRIDE Refund Attack. (1) The server-side/flow-gate refund limit; the input guardrail alone is a filter that can miss a novel phrasing. (2) High severity — money moved; mitigation is server-side authz plus a flow gate plus an output guard blocking over-limit calls before execution. (3) Because a manual test does not survive the next code change — CI makes the block permanent and provable on every commit. (4) Route over-limit refunds to human-in-the-loop approval rather than outright refusal, preserving legitimate large refunds.

M9 — The 68% Bill Hiding in Plain Sight. (1) One number cannot be targeted; attribution turns "it's expensive" into a specific, fixable lever. (2) Apply whichever the attribution shows is the biggest bar — typically flow (removes calls entirely), then caching (removes repeats), then routing (cheapens what remains), since they compound in that order. (3) Re-run the eval harness after the change and confirm task_success_rate is unchanged. (4) Cost/contact and p95-latency SLOs with alert thresholds, a review cadence, and a named owner for the response.

docs.title: Enterprise Teaching Cards
docs.text:
Reported, third-party figures — always attributed, never presented as this course's own measurement. Full source citations are in RESOURCES.md.

DTDC DIVA (Day 3, fits Module 5). DTDC's DIVA 2.0 AI-powered logistics support agent, built on Amazon Bedrock, reported strong response accuracy and a substantial reduction in support-query burden (AWS Machine Learning Blog). Question to the room: "DTDC is a logistics company, just like Tawseel. What would you need to see in DIVA's architecture before trusting its reported accuracy figure?" Steer toward: an eval harness with labelled ground truth, not a headline number — exactly the TawseelBench habit this course teaches.

DoorDash Dasher support (Day 3, fits Module 5/6). DoorDash's LLM/RAG-based automated support system for its courier population, documented in DoorDash's own engineering blog, including explicit work on reducing hallucination. Question: "Why would a courier support agent need less creative latitude than a customer-facing one?" Steer toward: operational actions (a courier's pay, a delivery reassignment) are higher-stakes and more checkable than open conversation — flow engineering (M7) applies even harder here.

OPLOG (Day 3, fits Module 6). A regional e-commerce fulfilment operator's use of AI agents in warehouse and operations orchestration, documented via AWS Solutions case studies and OPLOG's own coverage. Question: "OPLOG orchestrates warehouse operations, not customer chat. What changes about specialist boundaries when the 'customer' is internal operations staff?" Steer toward: the same scoped-tool, isolated-context discipline applies; the data-governance stakes shift from PDPL/customer PII toward operational integrity and safety.

Ryanair — twelve agents to one (Day 3, anchors Module 5.3). Ryanair's reported consolidation of domain-specific customer-service agents into one, alongside its five-year AI/data partnership with Google Cloud (Computer Weekly, PRNewswire, August 2026). Question: "Everyone in this room just built three specialist agents. Why would a real airline go the other way?" Steer toward: the ten-criteria worksheet — domain count, autonomy, context separation, and the rest — not a reflex answer either way. See the dedicated M5.3 plan below.

DHL Supply Chain (Day 5, fits Module 9). DHL Supply Chain's generative and, more recently, agentic AI programme for data management, customer support, proposal accuracy, and operational communications (DHL Group press releases, 2024–2025). Question: "DHL frames this as 'operational communications,' not 'customer support.' What's different about the cost/latency stakes?" Steer toward: internal operational messages tolerate different latency SLOs than a customer waiting on chat — cost/contact still matters, but the p95 target likely does not.

Air India AI.g (Day 5, fits Module 9). Air India's Azure-OpenAI-based virtual agent, reported to answer around 40,000 customer queries a day across 1,300+ query types (Microsoft Customer Stories). Question: "Your eval set has 120 tickets. Air India's volume is two orders of magnitude past that, daily. What breaks first at that scale that didn't break in your lab?" Steer toward: observability and cost attribution (M9) stop being a nice-to-have at that volume — a 0.01 SAR/contact miss becomes a real annual number.

docs.title: Module 5.3 — "When NOT to Use Multi-Agent Systems" (full 25-minute plan)
docs.text:
Placement: Day 3, between Lab 5 (specialist agents) and the Module 6 lecture — run it while the room still feels the cost of having just built three agents.

0–3 min — Hook. Present the Ryanair card above. Ask: "You just spent 50 minutes building three specialists. A major airline reportedly just went the other way. Were you wrong?" Let the tension sit; do not answer yet.

3–8 min — The ten-criteria matrix. Present the decision matrix (below); walk through applying it to the Ryanair case illustratively — the room does not have Ryanair's internal data, so treat every row as a plausible inference, explicitly labelled as such, not a confirmed fact.

Criterion Favours single agent Favours multi-agent Number of domains Few, overlapping Many, genuinely distinct Degree of autonomy Low-to-medium per domain High, domain-specific autonomy needed Context separation Domains share most context Domains need hard context isolation Permission boundaries One permission set suffices Different teams need different scopes Independent state Domains share state naturally Each domain owns genuinely separate state Parallelism Requests are mostly sequential Genuine benefit from parallel specialist work Failure isolation A shared failure mode is acceptable One domain's failure must not touch another Cost Routing overhead dominates at this volume Specialisation saves more than routing costs Latency Extra hops meaningfully hurt the SLO Hops are within budget Auditability One log is enough for review Regulator/audit wants per-domain accountability

8–18 min — Decision worksheet (individual, then pair-share). Give the room a live Tawseel scenario: "Product wants to add an Accounts domain — billing disputes that also touch loyalty points and corporate invoicing. Score it against all ten criteria and commit to single-agent or multi-agent before you compare with your partner." Circulate; do not give the answer yet.

18–23 min — Synthesis. Take two or three pairs' answers, including at least one disagreement if one exists. Model answer: Accounts likely favours multi-agent — it touches billing (existing Billing specialist scope conflict), a genuinely separate loyalty data domain, and corporate invoicing with different permission boundaries than consumer refunds — but the deciding factor is permission boundaries and independent state, not "another domain sounds complex." Make the point explicitly: a workflow scoring single-agent on eight of ten criteria should not become a fourth specialist just because the team likes agents.

23–25 min — Transition. "Now that you know when not to multiply agents, Module 6 teaches you how to run the ones you decided to keep, well." Move directly into the supervisor topology lecture.

Instructor note. This session works because it produces genuine disagreement in the room — if every pair reaches the same answer instantly, the scenario was too easy; have a harder second scenario ready (a single "VIP customer concierge" workflow that clearly favours staying single-agent) for a cohort that converges too fast.

docs.title: Classroom Logistics
docs.text:
Prayer and break scheduling. Each "hour" is 50 minutes of instruction plus a 10-minute buffer; schedule the long break around Dhuhr. Day-4 and Day-5 afternoons are deliberately lab-heavy and lighter on theory, giving natural flexibility around Asr.

Pairing strategy. Rotate pairs daily. Pair a strong-prompting participant with a strong-software-engineering participant — the agentic mindset lives exactly at that seam, and the course's own material (M1's state-machine discipline meeting M2's reasoning-pattern intuition) rewards it directly.

The shared cost board. Maintain, visibly, for the whole week: live token spend per participant/pair, routing accuracy (from Day 3 onward), and a cost/contact leaderboard once Module 9 begins. This is not decoration — cost literacy is a graded outcome (LO7), and seeing the board update after every lab is how the lesson lands before the lecture does.

A2 posters to print (see VISUAL_ASSET_BRIEF.md for full specs): the agent loop (M1-D1), the MCP client/server topology (M3-D2), the two-memory architecture (M4-D1), the supervisor topology (M6-D1), the layered-defence diagram (M8-D2), and the trace-tree anatomy (M9-D1). Six posters, one per major architectural milestone of the week, left up for the full five days so the room can literally point at "where does agency live" or "where does authorisation live" during any later discussion.

docs.title: What Good Looks Like — Three Worked Examples (PA-2 Red-Team Report)
docs.text:
All three address the same finding family (a refund-limit bypass attempt) to make the grading difference legible at a glance. Use capstone/grading/model_security_report.md as the full reference exemplar — it is the real, repository-produced source for the distinction-band example below.

Distinction (90–100%). Triage is exact: a genuine over-limit-refund attempt is filed High, a denial-of-wallet attempt is filed Medium — never the reverse. Every finding is in the full seven-part shape, with the exploit trajectory as an actual tool-call/state transition log, not a description. Mitigation names the precise file and function (security/output_guard.py::guard_tool_call, flows/refund_flow.py::amount_gate) and is retested held after the fix, evidenced by a pasted command output, not asserted. The executive summary states exact attempted/breach/held counts and zero open high-severity findings, matched by a live run_suite() output attached at the end.

Pass (70–89%). Triage direction is correct (High stays High, Medium stays Medium) but severities are occasionally borderline without justification — a finding sits at the edge of High/Medium with no stated reasoning for the call made. Mitigations are structural and correctly located, but described more thinly ("fixed in the output guard" without naming the function). The sign-off checklist is fully ticked, but one box (e.g. "no monetary limit lives only in a prompt") is asserted rather than evidenced by the named test's actual output.

Fail (< 70%). At least one High-severity finding (an over-limit refund actually issued) is mis-triaged as Medium or Low, or a mitigation is a reworded prompt sentence rather than a named structural control — either alone caps the whole Guardrails & security capstone criterion at 70% per the rubric's anti-pattern rule. A report with any open high-severity finding at submission additionally blocks the Flagship Expert badge outright, regardless of every other section's quality.

docs.title: SDA-AIE-311 — Agentic AI Systems Engineering (هندسة أنظمة الذكاء الاصطناعي الوكيلي)
docs.text: 5 days × 5 hours · Expert level · SDAIA Academy

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
You are about to spend a week building one system, not nine toy examples. By Friday afternoon you will have designed, built, hardened, and deployed Rafeeq (رفيق) — an enterprise agentic operations assistant for Tawseel (توصيل), a fictional Saudi last-mile logistics and e-commerce fulfilment company. Tawseel delivers across five Saudi cities — Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam, Makkah, Madinah — and its customers write to Rafeeq in Arabic and English, in equal measure, about the same three things every logistics operator's support desk lives or dies on: where is my order, can you move my delivery, and I want my money back.

On Monday morning Rafeeq is three lines of scaffolding around a chat call — indistinguishable, architecturally, from the runaway while True: loop this handbook will show you failing live. By Friday afternoon Rafeeq is a bounded, multi-agent, guarded, traced, cost-optimised service running in a simulated Tawseel operations environment, and you will demo it live: a bilingual ticket resolved end to end, one live attack blocked in front of the room, one trace-and-cost walkthrough, and one proof that a customer's data can actually be erased.

Every lab this week adds one real component to the same system — never a throwaway "weather agent" example. That is deliberate: the discipline this course teaches is that an agent is not a clever prompt, it is an engineered system, and engineered systems are built incrementally, tested at every step, and prove their own quality rather than asking you to take their word for it.

docs.title: What you will have built by Friday
docs.text:
• A bounded core loop with typed state and an explicit termination condition — no agent in this course can loop forever, because you will build the budget that stops it yourself.
  • Three explicit reasoning patterns (ReAct, Plan-and-Execute, Reflection), applied to the workflow each actually fits, with your own measured cost and latency numbers proving which is which.
  • Sixteen governed enterprise tools exposed over four Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers — orders, logistics, billing, customer — the same pattern a real enterprise uses to let many agents share governed capabilities safely.
  • Short-term (thread-scoped) and long-term (customer-scoped, versioned, bilingual) memory, with a PDPL erasure path you will run live against a real seeded customer.
  • Three specialist agents — Orders, Logistics, Billing — under a thin supervisor that routes, aggregates, and escalates cleanly, with a global budget that stops inter-agent chatter loops before they start.
  • A refund workflow refactored from a 40-line prompt that a crafted message could talk into a 4,000 SAR mistake, into a deterministic, unit-tested flow that the same message cannot move at all.
  • Layered guardrails and your own red-team agent, attacking your own Rafeeq, producing a triaged SECURITY_REPORT.md with zero open high-severity findings.
  • Full tracing, cost attribution by model/component/intent, caching, model routing, and bounded retries — with a measured cost cut, proved on the same evaluation set that measured your baseline.
  • A running, containerised, health-checked service in the simulated Tawseel environment, demoed live in six minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: SDA-AIE-214 (foundational AI/LLM engineering) or equivalent working experience. This course assumes you are comfortable with Python, git, and REST APIs, and that you have seen an LLM API call before. It does not assume prior LangGraph, MCP, or vector-database experience — Modules 1, 3, and 4 teach those from first principles, on this system.

docs.title: Pre-Course Setup (complete two days before Day 1)
docs.text:
The full instructions, with verification commands after every step and a troubleshooting appendix, are in the companion SETUP_GUIDE.md. The short version, so you know what is coming:

  1. Clone the repository and run the offline track. Python 3.11+, git — nothing else. export PYTHONPATH=src, then python3 scripts/doctor.py, make data, make test-offline, and python3 labs/lab01/solution/verify.py (ends 10/10 checks passed). This is the whole of Track A in SETUP_GUIDE.md, and it is sufficient for the entire course.
  2. Optional: the full local stack. If you want to run the real LangGraph/Qdrant/Postgres stack rather than the offline stub (recommended before the capstone demo, not required before Day 1), install Docker and follow Track B.
  3. Do not wait until Monday morning. The two-day window exists so a Windows/WSL2 Docker issue, a corporate-proxy block, or a missing Python version is someone else's Tuesday problem, not your first-hour-of-the-course problem. If python3 scripts/doctor.py reports anything other than a clean pass on the offline checks, raise it with your instructor before Day 1.

docs.title: The offline-mode promise
docs.text: Every lab, make test, CI, and the evaluation harness in this course run with zero API keys and zero network calls by default (RAFEEQ_MODEL_MODE=stub). This is not a sandboxed toy version of the real thing — StubChatModel implements the same .invoke()/.bind_tools()/.with_structured_output() surface a real model client does, so every line of agent code you write this week works unmodified the moment you point it at a real model gateway. You will only need a live key for two things: the capstone's 6-minute demo and the final live retest of your red-team findings. Everything else — including every graded lab checkpoint — you can complete with nothing beyond Python installed.

docs.title: The Nine Modules
docs.text: Each spread below is written to revise from directly — read it the night before that day's session, or the morning of, as a refresher. Skip the module content files unless you want the full depth; this is the version built for recall.

docs.title: Module 1 — Agentic System Architectures and Components
docs.text:
What it is. The difference between an LLM call, a chain, and an agent is control flow. An LLM call is one shot. A chain is a fixed sequence the developer decided at authoring time. An agent is a loop where the model decides the next step at runtime from the current state — observe, decide, act, update, repeat — until a goal is met or a limit is hit. That loop is built as a typed state machine: explicit State, Nodes that read and write it, Edges where the conditional edge is where agency lives, and a guaranteed path to END.

Why it matters. An agent that can do things can also do the wrong things, at scale, with real money and real personal data. A while True: loop around a chat call is not a smaller version of a proper agent — it is a liability with no way to explain, afterwards, why it did what it did. Structure is what makes an agent auditable, and auditability is the precondition for every guardrail, budget, and cost control the rest of the course adds.

What you build. RafeeqState (a typed dataclass carrying messages, customer id, locale, order id, step count, resolution), a reason node, and a route conditional edge that terminates on both goal-reached and budget-exhausted. You run it on an Arabic order query and an English refund request, and you write one test proving it halts within MAX_STEPS on an input engineered never to satisfy the goal.

The one idea to remember. An agent is a state machine, so build it as one — and bound its loop on three axes, always: step budget, cost budget, wall-clock timeout. "The model will decide when it's done" is not a termination condition; it is the absence of one.

The mistake to avoid. Swallowing a tool error with a bare except: pass so the loop continues on a stale or empty observation. The agent does not crash — it confidently gives a wrong answer, and nothing in the trace tells you why, because the error never entered state.

docs.title: Module 2 — Planning and Reasoning Patterns
docs.text:
What it is. Three canonical ways to make an agent think. ReAct interleaves reasoning and acting step by step — flexible, but cost grows super-linearly with steps because every step re-sends the growing history. Plan-and-Execute separates an upfront planner from a cheap executor — the plan is an inspectable, loggable, human-approvable artefact, but brittle without a replan step. Reflection adds a critic pass after a candidate answer — it catches confident-but-wrong outputs at the cost of at least one extra round-trip, so it belongs only on high-stakes, hard-to-reverse outputs.

Why it matters. Pattern choice is the single biggest lever on an agent's cost and reliability — bigger than model choice. A support agent defaulting to ReAct for every routine "where is my order" contact can cost 20× a Plan-and-Execute flow doing the exact same job, invisibly, until the first billing cycle.

What you build. All three patterns, on the same task, with real measured numbers: a ReAct agent on order-status tickets, a Plan-and-Execute flow (with a logged plan) on refund tickets, and a Reflection gate on the refund output — then a comparison table (cost per ticket, latency, eval-set success) and a one-paragraph recommendation.

The one idea to remember. These compose. Rafeeq's target shape is Plan-and-Execute for the overall workflow, ReAct inside a step whose path is genuinely uncertain, and Reflection only where money or compliance is on the line — as much structure as possible, as much reasoning as necessary.

The mistake to avoid. Defaulting to ReAct everywhere because it is the tutorial pattern — the single most common cause of a runaway agent bill in production.

docs.title: Module 3 — Tool Use, Function Calling, and MCP Integration
docs.text:
What it is. Function calling is a structured contract: you describe a tool as name + description + JSON-schema parameters, the model requests a call, the runtime decides whether and how to honour it, and the model never runs code directly — that separation is your first security boundary. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the open standard that turns each backend system into a governed, discoverable tool server — one server per trust boundary (orders, logistics, billing, customer), never one mega-server — so many agents can consume the same governed capability without each hard-wiring its own integration.

Why it matters. Real enterprise APIs are rarely LLM-ready, and a mega-tool with a mode/action argument causes an LLM to misroute constantly — narrow, well-described tools are how you buy reliable tool selection. And authorisation belongs in the tool server, never in the agent's prompt: nothing stops a jailbroken prompt from calling a prompt-only "rule" a lie.

What you build. track_shipment and get_order_details as typed tools with error values, wrapped in logistics_server.py and orders_server.py MCP servers with server-side authorisation stubs, consumed via MultiServerMCPClient and bound to your ReAct agent from Lab 2 — plus a non-idempotent open_case write tool that must never be blindly retried.

The one idea to remember. The tool schema is the prompt for the tool — design it for an easily confused, non-human consumer: one tool one job, descriptions stating when to use it and when not to, and errors returned as values so the model can react instead of the loop crashing.

The mistake to avoid. Returning raw backend payloads instead of a trimmed, typed output — it bloats context, inflates cost, and risks exposing PII the model never needed to see.

docs.title: Module 4 — Memory and State Management with Vector Databases
docs.text:
What it is. Two memories, two jobs. Short-term is the working state of the current task, made resumable and inspectable by a checkpointer keyed on thread_id. Long-term is durable knowledge across sessions — customer history, past resolutions, a versioned policy knowledge base — retrieved by semantic similarity from a vector store, filtered by metadata before ranking. Confusing them (stuffing everything into the prompt forever, or writing transient noise into durable storage) is the classic failure.

Why it matters. Long-term memory is personal-data storage under PDPL. An agent's memory design is simultaneously a UX feature, a correctness control, and a data-governance surface — and memory's unique danger is that it can be confidently wrong: a superseded policy or another customer's note retrieved with no error, no exception, just a silently corrupted answer.

What you build. A SQLite checkpointer proving same-thread continuity across two turns; long-term memory populated with one resolved-case summary per returning customer, scoped strictly by customer_id; a versioned knowledge-base lookup tested for cross-lingual recall (an Arabic question retrieving the correct policy chunk); a working forget_customer PDPL-erasure function; and a leakage test that must show zero of another customer's notes ever returned.

The one idea to remember. Filter by metadata before similarity ranking — this is a security control, not an optimisation. Short-term is the working set for now; long-term is what deserves to outlive the task.

The mistake to avoid. Retrieving with no metadata filter at all — "just embed everything and retrieve top-5" — which surfaces a different customer's order number and address the moment two customers' phrasing happens to be similar. No crash, no exception: a PDPL incident discovered only when someone complains.

docs.title: Module 5 — Single-Agent versus Multi-Agent Architectures
docs.text:
What it is. A single capable agent scales until one of four symptoms bites: tool overload (past roughly a dozen overlapping tools, selection accuracy falls), prompt overload (the system prompt accretes contradictory rules from every domain), context cost (every request pays for the whole tool schema even when it needs a fraction of it), or ownership friction (no single team can safely own a prompt encoding five teams' policies). When one of these bites, you split into specialist agents — scoped tools, a focused single-domain prompt, isolated context — usually under a thin supervisor (the workhorse "hub-and-spoke" topology; a peer network is rarely the right enterprise default).

Why it matters. Specialisation is not free capability, it is a trade: a supervisor over specialists usually costs more on a trivial single-domain task (the extra routing hop) and less on a complex, mixed one, because scoped tools prevent the runaway misrouting a monolith suffers there. You prove which regime you are in with the eval set, not intuition — which is exactly why you never delete the single-agent baseline.

What you build. Three scoped specialists (Orders, Logistics, Billing) built from one make_specialist factory, each asserted to have no tool outside its domain (the Billing list contains no tracking/geo tool); a scoped_input projection so the Billing agent's input structurally never carries a shipment address; and a two-sided benchmark against the Lab-5 monolith baseline — where the monolith wins and where it loses, both reported honestly.

The one idea to remember. Split when a real symptom bites, not because more agents sounds more sophisticated — and keep the single-agent baseline in the eval harness forever, so you can always answer "is the multi-agent version actually better here?"

The mistake to avoid. "Fixing" a struggling monolith by adding a 24th tool and three more prompt paragraphs. The real fix is decomposition, and the accretion path only delays the same selection-accuracy collapse Module 3 already measured for you.

docs.title: Module 5.3 — When NOT to Use Multi-Agent Systems
docs.text:
What it is. A dedicated 25-minute session anchored on a real, reported industry case — Ryanair's move from twelve domain-specific customer-service agents to one consolidated agent — that turns Module 5's four scaling symptoms into a formal ten-criteria decision worksheet: number of domains, degree of autonomy, context separation, permission boundaries, independent state, parallelism, failure isolation, cost, latency, auditability.

Why it matters. The industry's default instinct in 2025–2026 has been "more agents, more capability." The Ryanair case is the course's live counter-example: consolidation, not proliferation, was the reported fix, for reasons the ten criteria make explicit rather than vibes-based. Multi-agent orchestration cost (Module 6) is real and compounding — every extra agent is another routing hop, another failure surface, another thing that can lose a handoff.

What you build. Nothing new in code — this session produces a completed decision worksheet against a real Tawseel workflow (typically the "Accounts" domain-expansion scenario), scored on all ten criteria, with a committed single-vs-multi decision defended in pairs before the instructor reveals the recommended answer.

The one idea to remember. Every criterion that favours "single" is a criterion your supervisor topology is paying tax on for no return. Consolidation is not a retreat from agentic maturity — sometimes it is the mature call.

The mistake to avoid. Treating the ten criteria as a formality to rubber-stamp a decision you had already made. The worksheet only has value if you let it change your answer at least once this week.

docs.title: Module 6 — Hierarchical Delegation and Agent Orchestration
docs.text:
What it is. The supervisor is itself an agent whose "tools" are the specialists: it reads shared state, routes to a named specialist (or finishes, or escalates), hands off scoped context with an explicit sub-goal and a correlation id, and — critically — writes the specialist's result back into shared state before deciding again. Specialists never talk to each other directly; every coordination flows through the hub, which is also the single auditable point for every routing decision.

Why it matters. The classic multi-agent bug is the lost handoff: a specialist runs, produces a result, and the supervisor never merges it back — the customer is told nothing happened. The second classic bug is the chatter loop: A hands to B, B hands back to A, forever, because nothing bounds the system, only each agent individually. Both are Module 1's termination lesson, recurring one level up.

What you build. A supervisor with routing and a global MAX_HANDOFFS budget; a make_delegate node with mandatory write-back; a forced chatter-loop ticket that must escalate at handoff 4 rather than loop 30 times; and an escalate path that hands a human the full trace and state, never a dead end — tested against routing_eval.jsonl for first-hop accuracy compared with your Lab-5 monolith.

The one idea to remember. The supervisor's two jobs are route and aggregate — never domain work. Bound the whole system, not just each agent, or handoffs become an inter-agent while True:.

The mistake to avoid. A "fat" supervisor that calls tools itself "to save a hop." It defeats specialisation, destroys auditability, and is exactly the anti-pattern Module 6's code-review exercise exists to catch.

docs.title: Module 7 — Flow Engineering over Prompt Engineering
docs.text:
What it is. The course's founding maxim gets its own module: as much structure as possible, as much agency as necessary. Every business rule you can state as an if/then belongs in a conditional edge, not a prompt sentence. A prompt rule is decided fresh by the model on every request — non-deterministic, unbillable-for-free, and defeatable by a crafted input. A flow-logic branch is a pure function of typed state — deterministic, unit-testable in milliseconds with no model call, and impossible to talk around because it is code, not text the model interprets.

Why it matters. "Show me where the refund-approval rule lives" must have a code answer for a regulated enterprise, not a prompt answer. A mega-prompt is the least testable, least auditable, most expensive artefact in an agentic system — and it silently drifts every time someone edits a sentence with no test to catch the behaviour change.

What you build. You start by running refund_prompt_only.py on a crafted "ignore the limit" message and watching it issue a 4,000 SAR refund. Then you inventory every imperative in the prompt, classify each as rule or judgement, and build refund_flow.py: typed RefundState, an eligibility_gate, an amount_gate (the 500 SAR limit as an uncrossable branch), and a shrunk prompt used only to compose the reply — table-tested with seven branch unit tests that run in milliseconds with zero model calls.

The one idea to remember. Anything that can be decided by a rule should be a branch, not a sentence. What stays in the prompt is the genuinely irreducible judgement — composing an empathetic, bilingual reply, interpreting real ambiguity.

The mistake to avoid. "Fixing" a bug by appending one more sentence to the prompt, until the prompt contradicts itself and nobody remembers which sentence is load-bearing.

docs.title: Module 8 — Guardrails, Security, and Adversarial Testing
docs.text:
What it is. The governing principle, stated once and assumed everywhere after: treat all model input as untrusted and all model output as unverified. The model is a manipulable component, never a security control. Defence is layered — structural authorisation (strongest: the server checks, no prompt can grant what it denies), deterministic gates (Module 7's uncrossable branches), input guardrails (a filter, not a wall — it will miss things), output guardrails (the most reliable layer, because it inspects the concrete action about to happen), least privilege (scope tools/data to the task), and human-in-the-loop for the highest stakes.

Why it matters. An agent connected to enterprise systems is an attack surface that talks back. A prompt-injection payload targets the exact flexibility that makes agents useful, and the stakes are financial, regulatory, and reputational all at once. Red-teaming is how you find the holes before an attacker does — and only automated red-teaming, run in CI, catches a security regression that silently returns.

What you build. screen_input ahead of your supervisor, flagging injection/PII patterns bilingually; guard_tool_call/guard_response blocking over-limit refunds, cross-customer access, and PII egress as structural stops; a demonstration that the over-limit refund is blocked even with the input guardrail disabled (layered defence made undeniable); a red-team agent attacking your own Rafeeq across four attack goals; and SECURITY_REPORT.md, triaged, with your highest-severity finding fixed and re-run to prove it now fails. This is PA-2, the graded security artefact.

The one idea to remember. A prompt instruction is never a security control. Every real control is structure the model cannot argue with — and one layer alone is never enough, because one layer alone is exactly what the attacker is targeting.

The mistake to avoid. Trusting the input guardrail as a wall instead of a filter. It will miss a novel phrasing eventually; the structural controls behind it must hold anyway, which is precisely what your Task 3 demonstration exists to prove.

docs.title: Module 9 — Observability, Cost Optimisation, and Monitoring
docs.text:
What it is. An agent can be wrong while running perfectly — no exception, no crash, just a bad decision or a quietly climbing bill. Tracing turns every run into a tree of spans with inputs, outputs, timing, and token counts on every node — because Rafeeq was already built as a state machine, every transition is already a discrete, traceable event. Cost attribution answers "which intent, which agent, which model is spending the money?" along three axes (by model, by component, by intent) so the biggest bar tells you the fix. The two biggest cost levers are caching (never recompute an identical input; scope the key, set a TTL) and model routing (send the confident, simple majority to a cheap model, reserve the frontier model for genuine difficulty).

Why it matters. You cannot manage a non-deterministic system by testing alone — you must observe production. At 18,000 contacts a day, a 0.1 SAR/contact difference is a real annual number, and observability is how you find and defend it, with evidence rather than a feeling that "the agent seems expensive."

What you build. Tracing across 30 mixed tickets, identifying the single biggest cost span; a cost report by model and component; KB-retrieval caching with a scoped, versioned key and confident-intent model routing, re-measured on the same 30 tickets; a bounded retry on a flaky read tool with proof that issue_refund is retried zero times, ever; and a BENCHMARKS.md recording cost/contact and p95 latency before and after, with eval-set success confirmed unchanged.

The one idea to remember. The two biggest cost levers are caching and model routing, and they compound with Module 7's flow engineering (which removes model calls for rules entirely). A cheaper agent that got worse is a failure, not a win — always report the success number alongside the cost cut.

The mistake to avoid. Retrying a write tool "for reliability." A retried issue_refund on a timeout is the double-refund incident from Module 1, reborn at the tool layer — retry only idempotent, read-safe operations, ever.

docs.title: Lab Index
docs.text:
Lab Module Duration Deliverable Lab 1 M1 50 min Bounded core loop (reason/route), termination test Lab 2 M2 2 × 50 min Explicit ReAct, Plan-and-Execute, Reflection; three-pattern cost comparison Lab 3 M3 50 min Governed tool catalogue over MCP; error-value contract Lab 4 M4 50 min Thread checkpointer + scoped long-term memory + versioned KB Lab 5 M5 50 min Scoped specialist sub-agents vs monolith baseline Lab 6 M6 50 min Supervisor orchestrator; write-back + escalation Lab 7 M7 50 min Refund flow: prompt rules → deterministic gates Lab 8 M8 2 × 50 min Input/output guardrails; red-team suite; SECURITY_REPORT.md Lab 9 M9 50 min Tracing, cost attribution, caching + routing, bounded retry

Every lab's solution/verify.py runs standalone (PYTHONPATH=src python3 labs/labNN/solution/verify.py) and prints its own numbered PASS/FAIL checklist — completion is never a judgement call. If you fall behind (Labs 2, 6, and 8 overrun most cohorts), copy the previous lab's solution/ over your own start/ and rejoin the class at the next lab; the capstone build never requires every lab personally finished, only the corresponding src/rafeeq/** code present and working, which every lab's checkpoint provides.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Component Weight Evidence Lab completion (9 labs) 30% checkpoint commits + verify.py pass counts PA-1 + PA-2 (security report) 20% artefacts + reproductions Quiz (10 questions, closed book) 10% written sitting Capstone 40% rubric, evidence-first: traces, security report, eval replay

PA-1 (Day 2, 30 minutes): diagnose and fix a broken agent — an unbounded loop, a raising tool, unscoped retrieval — scored on diagnosis (40%), fixes (40%), verification (20%).

PA-2 (Day 4, the graded security artefact): your SECURITY_REPORT.md must file every finding in the seven-part shape — attack, vulnerability, exploit trajectory, business impact, detection, mitigation, retest result — with every mitigation naming a structural control, never a reworded prompt, and every high-severity finding fixed and re-run to held. Scored on triage correctness (50%), mitigation quality (30%), governance reasoning (20%).

The capstone (40% of the course grade, final_capstone_project.md) is the integration and deployment: a single, running, traced, red-teamed agentic service, resolving real Tawseel workflows for bilingual customers, under budget and under PDPL — graded from evidence first (traces, security report, eval replay, CI red-team history), demo second. Mandatory deliverables: the repository with full lab checkpoint history; a running service in the simulated environment; BENCHMARKS.md with real measured numbers; SECURITY_REPORT.md with zero open high-severity findings; DECISIONS.md with five justified engineering trade-offs; and a 6-minute demo (a bilingual ticket end to end, one attack blocked live, one trace/cost walkthrough, one PDPL erasure). Choose at least one extension: a deterministic fast-path router, human-in-the-loop refund approval, a second supervisor tier, memory expiry/decay, or a monitoring dashboard with a simulated-incident runbook.

Badge criteria (Flagship Expert badge). All four required together: overall grade ≥ 70, capstone score ≥ 70, zero open high-severity security findings, and a passing cross-customer leakage test. See ASSESSMENT_PACK.md for the full rubric, scoring sheets, and grade-calculation worksheet.

docs.title: Cheat Sheet — The Ten Rules
docs.text:
Print this page. Every rule below has a lab, a case study, and a sim-* branch behind it.

  1. Bounded loops, always. Step budget, cost budget, wall-clock timeout — every agent loop, no exceptions. "The model will stop when it's done" is not a termination condition.
  2. Errors are values, not exceptions. A tool returns {"error": ...} so the model can react. A raised exception kills the loop on the first bad input.
  3. Authorisation lives at the server, never in the prompt. A prompt rule is a sentence the model decides to honour. A server-side check is structure it cannot argue with.
  4. Filter memory before you rank it. Scope every long-term read/write by customer_id. This is a security control, not an optimisation.
  5. Structure over prompt. Anything decidable by a rule is a branch, not a sentence. Reserve the model for genuinely irreducible judgement.
  6. A supervisor routes and aggregates — it never does domain work. And bound the whole multi-agent system, not just each agent, or handoffs become an inter-agent loop.
  7. Every handoff is a typed, logged transition with mandatory write-back. A specialist result that never reaches shared state is a lost handoff, not a saved one.
  8. Treat all model input as untrusted, all output as unverified. Defend in layers; assume any single layer can be fooled, and make sure the ones behind it still hold.
  9. Never retry a write tool. Retry only idempotent, read-safe operations. Retrying a write is the double-refund incident, every time.
  10. Measure before you claim. A cost cut that regressed eval success is a failure, not a win. The system must testify to its own quality — traces, tests, and benchmarks, not a demo that happened to go well once.

docs.title: Glossary — English / العربية
docs.text:
Standard Modern Standard Arabic technical terminology, matching the terms used in this course's own repository documentation (docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md, docs/ACTION_RISK_MATRIX.md).

Term (EN) المصطلح (AR) Definition Agent وكيل A system in which the model decides the next action at runtime, from the current state. Agentic AI الذكاء الاصطناعي الوكيلي AI systems that plan, reason, use tools, and act autonomously toward a goal. Chain سلسلة ثابتة A fixed, developer-authored sequence of steps with no runtime branching by the model. Tool use استخدام الأدوات An agent's ability to call external functions or APIs to observe or affect the world. Function calling استدعاء الدوال The structured protocol by which a model requests a tool call with typed arguments. Reasoning الاستدلال Deciding the single next step, given what is known now. Planning التخطيط Deciding the overall approach to a multi-step task before or during execution. Memory الذاكرة What an agent carries within a task (short-term) or across sessions (long-term). State الحالة The typed, explicit object every node in an agent graph reads and updates. State machine آلة الحالات A system modelled as discrete states and transitions between them. Orchestration التنسيق (التنظيم) Coordinating multiple specialist agents toward one outcome. Supervisor المُشرِف The thin agent that routes tickets to specialists and aggregates their results. Delegation التفويض Handing a sub-task, with scoped context, from a supervisor to a specialist agent. Handoff التسليم The typed, logged transition of a task from one agent to another. Specialist agent الوكيل المتخصص An agent scoped to a narrow toolset and a single domain's prompt. Multi-agent system نظام متعدد الوكلاء A system composed of more than one cooperating agent. ReAct الاستدلال والفعل التفاعلي (ReAct) The reasoning pattern that interleaves thought, action, and observation. Plan-and-Execute التخطيط ثم التنفيذ The reasoning pattern separating an upfront plan from its execution. Reflection التأمل الذاتي A self-critique pass that evaluates and revises a candidate output. Termination condition شرط الإنهاء The explicit, testable rule by which an agent's loop stops. Bounded loop حلقة محدودة A control loop with explicit limits on steps, cost, and time. Step budget ميزانية الخطوات The maximum number of loop iterations an agent may take. Model Context Protocol (MCP) بروتوكول سياق النموذج An open client-server standard for exposing tools and resources to LLM applications. MCP server خادم بروتوكول سياق النموذج A service that publishes governed tool capabilities to MCP clients. Guardrails ضوابط الحماية Structural controls applied before or after model reasoning to prevent unsafe behaviour. Prompt injection حقن الأوامر An attack in which untrusted text is interpreted by the model as instructions. Jailbreak تجاوز القيود An attempt to make a model ignore its intended behavioural constraints. Authorisation التفويض بالصلاحية The server-side check confirming an actor may perform a specific action. Red-teaming اختبار الفريق الأحمر Adversarial testing designed to make a system misbehave, to find its weaknesses. Observability قابلية الملاحظة The ability to inspect why a system did what it did, from its traces and logs. Tracing التتبع Recording a run as a tree of timed, attributed steps (spans). Cost attribution إسناد التكلفة Assigning spend to the model, component, or intent that caused it. Model routing توجيه النموذج Sending confident, simple work to a cheap model and hard work to a frontier model. Caching التخزين المؤقت Reusing a previous result for an identical input instead of recomputing it. Latency زمن الاستجابة The time an agent takes to respond — the customer's felt experience. Idempotency اللاتغيّرية بالتكرار A property allowing an operation to be safely retried without a different effect. Retry إعادة المحاولة Automatically re-attempting a failed operation, safe only for idempotent operations. Checkpointing نقاط الحفظ Persisting agent state so a run can pause, resume, and be inspected. Vector store مخزن متجهي A database that retrieves content by the semantic similarity of embeddings. Embedding تمثيل متجهي A numeric vector representation of text, used for similarity search. Retrieval الاسترجاع Fetching the most relevant stored items for a given situation. Escalation التصعيد Handing an unresolved case to a human, with full context, as a first-class outcome. PDPL نظام حماية البيانات الشخصية Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law, governing the handling of personal data. Flow engineering هندسة التدفق Moving business logic out of prompts and into explicit, testable graph structure. Deterministic gate بوابة حتمية A conditional branch that always produces the same route for the same input. Least privilege مبدأ الحد الأدنى من الصلاحيات Granting an agent only the tools and data scope its task genuinely needs. Trust boundary حد الثقة The line separating untrusted input from structurally authorised, trusted action. Denial-of-wallet استنزاف الميزانية (استنزاف التكلفة) An attack or bug that drives an agent's cost or step count far beyond its intended budget.

docs.title: Deck content authoring spec — SDA-AIE-311
docs.text:
You write JSON only. A renderer (deck/render.js, already built and tested) turns it into PowerPoint. Never write layout, colours, positions or fonts. Never produce a .pptx.

Output file: deck/content/<NN>_<name>.json, shape:

{ "slides": [ { "type": "...", ... }, ... ] }

Files render in filename sort order, so keep the numeric prefix you are given.

docs.title: Editorial rules (these matter more than the schema)
docs.text:
1. The slide carries the claim; the notes carry the teaching. Every slide must have notes — 40–90 words of what the instructor says, shows, asks, and how long it takes. Write them as instructions to a competent instructor who has not memorised the package ("Draw this on the board first, then reveal", "Ask the room before you answer", "If you are behind, cut this slide").
  2. No slide is a paragraph. Bullets are one sentence, ideally under 150 characters. Use the lead field for the 2–4 word claim and text for the explanation.
  3. Titles under 48 characters. Longer titles wrap to two lines and eat the body.
  4. Every technical claim in the instructor package is authoritative. Do not soften it, do not invent numbers. Where the package gives a number (94% routing accuracy, 68% of spend, 0.019 → 0.008 USD), use exactly that number and mark it as an illustrative benchmark from the package, not a promise.
  5. Reported third-party figures must be attributed on the slide itself (e.g. "AWS reports", "Ryanair reported"). Never present them as our own measurements.
  6. Arabic: only in title_ar, statement_ar, and where a customer-facing string is the point. Correct natural MSA. Never machine-translate a whole slide.
  7. Anti-patterns are marked, not implied: use kind: "bad" / tone: "bad" and say the word "anti-pattern".
  8. Vary the slide types. A run of more than three bullets slides in a row is a defect. Aim for roughly: 35% bullets/two_col, 15% code, 12% table/metrics, 12% cards, 10% flow, 8% statement/section, 8% lab/case.
  9. British spelling (optimise, behaviour, analyse). No emoji. No exclamation marks.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
An expert module on operating LLM and generative-AI workloads in production. Participants implement tracing, quality monitoring, feedback loops, and incident response for AI services, extending MLOps discipline to non-deterministic systems. The module covers evaluation-in-production, prompt/version management, and reliability engineering for AI platforms.

The course is built around a single evolving artefact: "Musaid" (مساعد), a bilingual (Arabic/English) citizen-services assistant for a national digital-government portal. Musaid is a RAG-plus-tools LLM service that answers questions about government procedures — renewing an ID, booking an appointment, checking a violation. It was designed and deployed in earlier modules; in SDA-AIE-312 the class does not build the model, it operates it. Every lab instruments, measures, or hardens Musaid, so by Day 4 each participant owns a fully observable, evaluated, SLO-governed LLM service with an incident runbook and a live Grafana dashboard — the same operational surface they will defend in the AI Engineer capstone (SDA-AIE-390).

  4. LO4 — Analyze production incidents in AI systems and build response runbooks

docs.title: Instructor Guidance Notes (Delivery Plan Level)
docs.text:
• Golden thread: every module operates the same service — Musaid, the bilingual citizen-services assistant. Never introduce a throwaway toy chatbot; always instrument, evaluate, or harden Musaid. This is what makes the Day-4 capstone assembly (not build) achievable.
  • Pace control: Labs 3 (online eval) and 6 (SLO + incident) are the most overrun-prone. Publish checkpoint commits (lab1-start, lab2-solution, lab3-start, …) and pre-seeded trace data so stragglers can git checkout lab3-start and still have realistic traffic to score.
  • Pairing: rotate pairs each day. Pair a strong-SRE/ops participant with a strong-LLM/ML participant — the whole point of LLMOps is fusing those two cultures.
  • Environment strategy: primary = Docker Compose stack (Musaid API + Langfuse + Postgres + Prometheus + Grafana + OTel Collector) on the lab laptop; fallback = a shared classroom cluster and a mock-LLM mode (deterministic canned responses) so labs never block on external LLM API access or quota.
  • Language and data residency: deliver in English or Arabic; keep all code, identifiers, span names, and commit messages in English. Musaid handles Arabic and English user text — treat all user content as personal data under PDPL; no raw prompts/PII leave the sovereign boundary in logs or eval payloads without masking.
  • Prayer and break scheduling: each "hour" is 50 minutes of instruction + 10 minutes buffer; schedule the long break around Dhuhr. Day-4 morning protects build time; cut discussion, not assembly.
  • Assessment logistics: rubric scoring happens live during Day 4 Hour 5 demos; collect dashboard URLs and repo URLs at the end of Hour 4 so the instructor can verify live SLO panels and eval history before demos begin.
  • Cost discipline: the course itself is an LLMOps exercise — run labs in mock-LLM mode by default and switch to a real provider only for the evaluation and rollout labs, capping spend with the same budget alerts the course teaches.

docs.title: Module 1 — From MLOps to LLMOps: What Changes
Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. Participants arriving from SDA-AIE-216 already own the MLOps backbone: pipelines, registries, drift monitors, canary releases. This module names precisely what that backbone does not cover once the model is a non-deterministic, open-ended, externally-hosted LLM, and re-frames observability — not accuracy dashboards — as the foundation of operating generative AI. It sets the reference architecture and vocabulary the rest of the course builds on.

Business relevance. A national citizen-services assistant cannot be operated like a churn classifier. There is no held-out test set that predicts tomorrow's user questions; a single prompt or model-provider change can silently degrade answer quality for millions of interactions; cost scales with tokens, not requests; and a wrong answer about renewing an Iqama is a public-trust and compliance event, not a rounding error in an F1 score. Saudi entities operating GenAI at scale (government portals, banks under SAMA, health providers) need an operations discipline that treats quality, cost, and safety as first-class production signals.

Industry use cases. - A government portal assistant whose answer quality drifts after the provider silently updates the base model behind the same API name. - A banking support copilot where a two-word prompt tweak doubles average latency and blows the monthly token budget. - A health triage assistant that must prove, per interaction, which model version and which knowledge snapshot produced each answer for audit.

Expected competencies. After this module a participant can articulate the MLOps→LLMOps deltas, draw the LLMOps reference architecture, identify the four observability pillars for an LLM service, enumerate the new failure modes, and state which operational questions a currently un-instrumented service cannot answer.

docs.title: Learning Objectives (mapped)
docs.text: # Objective Maps to 1.1 Explain how non-determinism, open-ended I/O, and external hosting break MLOps assumptions LO1 1.2 Enumerate LLM-specific failure modes and the signal each requires LO1, LO5 1.3 Draw the LLMOps reference architecture and the four observability pillars LO1 1.4 Map which operational questions require traces vs metrics vs quality scores LO1, LO6 1.5 Assess an un-instrumented service against an operational-readiness checklist LO6

docs.title: 1. Why LLM systems break the MLOps playbook
docs.text:
MLOps was designed around a comforting set of assumptions: the model is a deterministic function, quality collapses to a small set of metrics computable against labelled data, the input space is a fixed schema, and the model runs on infrastructure you control. Every one of these assumptions fails for a production LLM service.

  • Non-determinism. The same request can produce different outputs (temperature > 0, provider-side batching, model updates). "Reproduce the bug" is not a given; you reproduce distributions, not single runs.
  • Open-ended input and output. Users type anything, in Arabic or English, in any register. There is no pydantic schema that constrains meaning. Output is free text whose correctness is contextual.
  • No single accuracy number. Quality is multi-dimensional: faithfulness to retrieved context, relevance, safety, tone, format, refusal-appropriateness. No held-out set predicts tomorrow's traffic.
  • External, mutable dependencies. The "model" is often an API. The vendor can change it under you. Rate limits, outages, and latency spikes are their infrastructure, surfacing as your incident.
  • Cost is a runtime variable. Spend scales with tokens per request × requests, and a longer prompt or a chattier model silently multiplies the bill. Cost is an SLI now, not a procurement line item.

Instructor note: open the discussion by asking the room "how would you reproduce a bad answer a user reported yesterday?" Let the impossibility surface naturally — it motivates tracing (M2) and captured inputs before you name any tool.

docs.title: 2. The new failure modes and the signal each demands
docs.text:
Name these explicitly; each maps to a later module's remedy.

Failure mode What it looks like Signal that catches it Covered in Hallucination Confident, wrong, ungrounded answer Online faithfulness eval on sampled traces M3 Silent quality decay No errors, no latency change — answers just get worse Trend on quality scores; regression vs golden set M3, M5 Prompt drift / regression A "small" prompt edit degrades a segment Prompt version linked to eval scores; shadow test M4 Provider model swap Same API, new weights, different behaviour Model-version tag on every trace; canary eval M2, M4 Cost/token blowout Bill triples with no traffic change Token + cost per span; budget-burn alert M2, M6 Latency variance p99 spikes from provider or long contexts Span timing; latency SLO M2, M6 Retrieval failure RAG returns irrelevant/empty context Context-relevance score; retrieval span inspection M2, M3 Feedback blindness Users are unhappy, you cannot see it Explicit + implicit feedback capture M5 Cascading outage Provider down → whole service down Fallbacks, circuit breakers, error-budget alert M6, M7

docs.title: 3. The LLMOps lifecycle and reference architecture
docs.text:
LLMOps is a loop, not a pipeline. The operational cycle: serve → observe (trace) → evaluate (score) → learn (feedback/datasets) → improve (prompt/model change) → roll out safely → serve. MLOps' train/deploy/monitor loop still exists underneath (for any fine-tuned components), but the fast, dominant loop in production is this observe-evaluate-improve cycle running on live traffic.

The reference architecture for Musaid:

                         ┌─────────────────────────── Observability plane ──────────────────────────┐
 user ──► API gateway ──► Musaid app ──► retriever ──► prompt build ──► LLM (provider) ──► tools     │
            │              │  (spans emitted at every hop via OpenTelemetry)                          │
            │              └──► OTel SDK ──► OTel Collector ──► ┬─► Langfuse (traces, eval, prompts)   │
            │                                                  ├─► Tempo (trace store)                 │
            │                                                  ├─► Prometheus (metrics: latency, cost) │
            │                                                  └─► Loki (structured logs)              │
            │                                                                                          │
            └──► feedback endpoint ──► Langfuse scores ──► annotation queue ──► curated datasets       │
                                                              │                                        │
   online-eval worker ◄── samples traces ── scores ──────────┘                                        │
   Grafana ◄── dashboards (latency / cost / quality / SLO) + Alertmanager (burn-rate alerts)          │
                         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Two ideas anchor everything downstream:

  1. The trace is the unit of truth. Every operational question — why was this answer wrong, what did it cost, which prompt/model produced it, how long did retrieval take — is answered by inspecting one trace with rich spans. If it is not on the trace, it did not happen as far as operations is concerned.
  2. Quality is a pillar, not an afterthought. Classic observability has three pillars (traces, metrics, logs). For LLM systems there is a fourth first-class pillar — quality/evaluation scores — and it is the one that distinguishes LLMOps from ordinary APM.

docs.title: 4. What carries over vs what changes
docs.text:
Concern MLOps (SDA-AIE-216) LLMOps (this course) Versioning Model + data versioning + prompt versioning, + context/knowledge snapshot, + provider model tag Monitoring Feature/prediction drift, perf decay + faithfulness/quality drift, hallucination rate, refusal rate Evaluation Offline on held-out set + online eval on sampled live traffic (reference-free, LLM-as-judge) Release Canary/blue-green on your infra + prompt canary/shadow, provider fallback, cost-aware rollout Core SLIs Availability, latency, accuracy + quality score, token cost, hallucination rate, groundedness Debugging Logs + metrics + distributed traces of the reasoning path (retrieval→prompt→LLM→tools) Incident cause Data/infra + prompt regression, provider change, retrieval failure, jailbreak Feedback Labels from a labelling team + live user thumbs/edits feeding a data flywheel

The message: LLMOps does not replace MLOps; it extends it with a quality pillar, prompt lifecycle, online evaluation, and provider-resilience — all resting on distributed tracing.

docs.title: 5. Observability as the foundation — the four pillars
docs.text:
• Traces — the causal path of one request across retrieval, prompt assembly, model call, and tool use, with inputs/outputs and timing at each span. The primary debugging surface.
  • Metrics — aggregable time series: request rate, latency percentiles, error rate, tokens, cost, cache hit rate. The primary alerting surface.
  • Logs — structured, correlated-by-trace-id events; the "why" details a metric cannot hold.
  • Quality — evaluation scores (faithfulness, relevance, safety, format) attached to traces and aggregated as time series. The pillar that answers "is the service good", not just "is it up".

A team that has all four for Musaid can, within minutes, answer: what is our hallucination rate this hour, on which topics, at what cost, produced by which prompt and model version, and can I open the exact trace of the worst example? A team that has none is operating blind — which is where Lab 1 deliberately starts.

docs.title: 6. Real-world example walkthrough
docs.text: Narrate this (5 minutes, no slides): a public-sector assistant went live with excellent launch-week feedback. Ten weeks later, complaint volume crept up. There were no errors in the logs, latency was flat, the dashboard was green. What had happened: the model provider rolled a minor version behind the same API name; the new weights were more verbose and slightly less willing to say "I don't know", so on edge-case procedural questions Musaid began confidently inventing steps. Nobody could see it because (a) no model-version tag was on requests, (b) no online quality eval existed, and (c) user unhappiness never became a signal. The fix was not a better model — it was the four pillars. This course builds exactly that instrumentation.

docs.title: The Musaid request path (the thing we will instrument)
docs.text:
# src/musaid/service/assistant.py
"""Musaid: bilingual citizen-services assistant (RAG + tools).

This is the ALREADY-BUILT service from prior modules. In SDA-AIE-312 we do
not change its logic first — we make it OBSERVABLE. Read it as the map of
where spans, scores, and costs must be captured.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass

from musaid.domain.entities import UserQuery, Answer
from musaid.service.interfaces import Retriever, LLMClient, ToolRegistry
from musaid.service.prompts import build_prompt


@dataclass
class MusaidAssistant:
    retriever: Retriever          # vector search over gov-service docs
    llm: LLMClient                # provider-backed chat model
    tools: ToolRegistry           # e.g. appointment lookup, fee calculator
    prompt_name: str = "citizen_assistant"
    prompt_version: str = "v1"

    def answer(self, query: UserQuery) -> Answer:
        # 1) retrieve grounding context (RAG)
        chunks = self.retriever.search(query.text, k=6, lang=query.lang)
        # 2) assemble the prompt from a named, versioned template
        messages = build_prompt(self.prompt_name, self.prompt_version,
                                query=query.text, context=chunks, lang=query.lang)
        # 3) call the model (may itself request a tool call)
        completion = self.llm.chat(messages)
        # 4) if the model asked for a tool, run it and re-ask
        if completion.tool_call:
            result = self.tools.run(completion.tool_call)
            messages.append(result.as_message())
            completion = self.llm.chat(messages)
        return Answer(
            text=completion.text,
            citations=[c.source_id for c in chunks],
            model_version=completion.model_version,
            prompt_version=self.prompt_version,
        )

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 1 — Baseline the Blindness
docs.text:
Objective Stand up the Musaid stack, generate realistic bilingual traffic, and prove the service is un-observable by attempting to answer five operational questions; capture a cost/latency baseline for later comparison Duration 50 minutes Setup Docker + Compose, course repo cloned, git checkout lab1-start, make up (starts Musaid API + mock-LLM + Postgres)

Instructions & tasks

  1. (5 min) make up; confirm GET /health is 200 and send one Arabic and one English question via /v1/ask; read the raw JSON answer.
  2. (10 min) Run the traffic generator python tools/generate_traffic.py --n 300 --mix ar,en (replays a realistic intent mix: ID renewal, appointments, violations, fees).
  3. (15 min) Attempt each of the five operational questions from test_blind_spots.py using only what exists today (logs, docker logs). Record in BASELINE.md why each is unanswerable.
  4. (10 min) Instrument the single cheapest signal: wrap assistant.answer() with a timer and a token counter (mock-LLM returns token counts); log latency_ms and total_tokens per request as JSON.
  5. (5 min) Compute a crude baseline from those logs with jq: p50/p95 latency, mean tokens/request, estimated SAR/1k requests.
  6. (5 min) Commit chore: baseline latency/cost + documented blind spots.

Expected output

Sent 300 requests (168 ar / 132 en) across 6 intents. 0 errors.

$ jq -s 'add/length' logs/latency.jsonl        # mean latency_ms

$ jq -s '[.[].total_tokens]|add/length' logs/tokens.jsonl
1180.7
