docs.title: 6. Known limitations and open items
docs.text: Recorded honestly so that the next instructor inherits the problems along with the material.

docs.title: Licensing and access constraints
docs.text: Item Consequence The FT Visual Vocabulary is not open-licensed — © The Financial Times Limited, all rights reserved It can only be linked, never reproduced in slides or handouts without clearance from FT syndication. Deck slide 59 teaches the nine categories in the course's own words and links to the repository. The EU Publications Office maintains a separately-licensed derivative, which is the one to put in a printed pack The OWID Grapher source code is no longer MIT The current licence permits viewing and studying the code only. Do not tell a class they can fork it. The date the licence changed is unverified — say "the current licence", not a year. Wikipedia and most secondary sources are out of date NYT COVID data is CC BY-NC 4.0 Noncommercial, attribution required. The dataset is archived — it stopped updating 24 March 2023, and the excess-deaths files on 18 January 2021 Several Saudi government sites block automated access dga.gov.sa, sdaia.gov.sa and parts of my.gov.sa return 403 or a WAF block to scripts. All *.data.gov.sa hosts were unreachable from the research environment — an egress restriction, not evidence about the portal. No scraping exercise was written against any of them, by design; the three worked exercises in the sources guide use browser retrieval and direct PDF download only FiveThirtyEight's archive is gone from its URLs ABC redirected the archive on 15 May 2026; every fivethirtyeight.com/features/… URL now 302s to abcnews.com/politics. Every 538 reference in the deck and in the pack routes through web.archive.org. Re-check before each delivery DGA, Vision 2030 and DataSaudi state no reuse licence All three are cite-only in the guide. Absence of a stated licence is not permission

docs.title: Historical claims that are hedged rather than asserted
docs.text:
The research file carries an explicit UNVERIFIED / DISPUTED section, and fifteen items in it shaped what the slides and the pack are allowed to say. The ones that most affect delivery:

Claim How it is handled Snow's "83 deaths in the week ending 2 September", "535 workhouse inmates, 5 deaths", "70 brewery workers" Omitted entirely. Widely repeated, not verified against Snow's own text. The workhouse well and the brewery beer allowance are stated without numbers Whether Snow's walking-distance map appeared in the second edition of his book Not asserted. Sources differ on whether the 1855 vestry report is dated 1854 or 1855 Nightingale's rose causing specific reforms Hedged. The diagram was the persuasive centrepiece of her lobbying; no primary document attributing a reform to it was verified, and Hugh Small argues her Lines diagram was probably more influential Minard's troop figures Cited as "the standard tabulated transcription", not as manuscript figures. The 422,000 → 10,000 arithmetic was verified against that transcription Romano et al. (2020) effect sizes The citation, journal, volume, pages, DOI and verbatim conclusions are used; no sample size or percentage-point difference is quoted — they were not retrievable The FT trajectory chart's 11 March 2020 launch Stated as "on Burn-Murdoch's own account"; not verified against the original FT page or tweet timestamp FiveThirtyEight's 2020 final probability Not stated anywhere. The widely repeated "Biden 89 in 100" could not be verified from a live source A FiveThirtyEight critique of the hurricane cone of uncertainty Does not exist as far as could be verified. The critique is attributed to Broad et al. (BAMS, 2007) and to Alberto Cairo Awards for "How the Virus Got Out" Not claimed. The 2021 Pulitzer went to the Times' pandemic coverage as a whole, and the citation does not name graphics The Trendalyzer sale price Not stated. The March 2007 Google acquisition is confirmed; terms were not disclosed The 10th-anniversary edition of Storytelling with Data ISBN, date, publisher and page count confirmed; its chapter list is unverified. Say "six lessons, ten chapters", which holds for the 2015 edition

docs.title: Deviations from the INSTRUCTOR_PACKAGE, as flagged in the notebooks README
docs.text:
Five, all deliberate, all flagged in the notebooks where they occur.

# Deviation Resolution 1 bad_dashboard_m1.png (Lab 1) and cluttered_m3.png (Lab 3) are not shipped with the data package Both are built in code inside the notebook, which makes the critique target reproducible and lets participants see each violation in the source 2 Several expected-output blocks say three regions are below target The data says nine are below target, five of those are stalled (Tier 1), and three are more than 9 pp below. The notebooks use all three counts and name which is which; the story's ask is about the five stalled regions 3 Module 3's code example annotates a "March 2024 service outage" behind Najran's plateau No such step change exists in tayseer_services.csv. Najran rises smoothly and flattens over the last nine months; Lab 3 annotates the nine-month stall instead 4 Module 2's expected output says national adoption goes 41% → 68% and crosses 65% in month 21 The data says 34.2% → 63.8%, never crossing. The notebooks use the data; the gap to target is the whole point of the story 5 Lab 2 is specified with four questions lab2_questions.csv ships five — Q5 is the thirteen-overlapping-lines / small-multiples question. Lab 2 covers all five

docs.title: Open items for the next instructor
docs.text: # Item What to do 1 Two new activities reference notebook sections that do not yet exist. Slide 69 points at "lab2_chart_selection_starter.ipynb, section 2b" and slide 109 at "lab4_dashboard_starter.ipynb, section 4b-alt". Neither section is present in the shipped starters: Lab 2 contains no per-capita, rank-shift or Lorenz work, and Lab 4 contains no animation-versus-small-multiples build Either add the two sections to the starter and solution notebooks, or run both activities from regional_equity_latest.csv, regional_equity_lorenz.csv and the run sheets in CRITIQUE_ACTIVITY_PACK.md. The data and the facilitator script are complete; only the notebook scaffolding is missing 2 critique_canon.csv's module_used_in column disagrees with the deck's placement for four rows — CAN-02 (Minard: CSV M3, deck M1), CAN-04 (Gapminder: CSV M5, deck M4), CAN-05 (OWID: CSV M4, deck M3) and CAN-08, which the CSV keeps as one row and the deck splits across M3 and M5 The deck is the authority for where a work is taught; the CSV for what is said about it. Reconcile the column, or leave it and note the split — the pack documents it either way 3 Deck slide 20 says "nine traps"; the sources guide carries ten verified gotchas plus one instructor-judgement item The deck's nine are a subset chosen for the slide. The two it omits — several stats.gov.sa deep links 404, and the disputed SDAIA-versus-DGA ownership of the national portal — are in the guide. The "percentages do not travel" bullet on the slide is instructor judgement, not a verified source finding, and is marked as such in the guide 4 The Gapminder figure uses Plotly's bundled Gapminder sample dataset, which ends in 2007 Adequate for the animation-versus-small-multiples argument, which is about form rather than currency. If a participant asks why the frame says 2007, say so plainly. Do not present it as current Gapminder Tools data 5 Three canon figures are reconstructions, not reproductions — the needle, the 538 displays and the Incalculable Loss mock-up Each carries a footnote saying so, and the caption is on the slide. Say it out loud when the slide goes up; a reconstruction presented as a reproduction is the exact failure the course is teaching against 6 Plotly PNG export requires a Chrome binary that is not present in every training environment and cannot always be downloaded The notebooks always write the interactive HTML, which is the real deliverable, and always render a matplotlib mirror as a PNG. Nothing in out/ is missing as a result 7 Arabic rendering depends on an installed font. setup_arabic() looks for Amiri, then Scheherazade, then KacstOne, then FreeSerif, and returns False if none is present or if arabic-reshaper / python-bidi are missing Install with apt-get install -y fonts-hosny-amiri and verify with fc-list :lang=ar. Check this on the room's actual machines the week before. If it fails, fall back to English labels and say so on the slide — shipping tofu boxes or disconnected letters in front of a room that reads Arabic natively costs the instructor the room 8 Whether the Red Team activity runs on Day 2, or is dropped to protect Lab 4b, is left as an explicit instructor-judgement call on the pre-flight slide Red Team is the better predictor of Day 3 performance. Protect it if you can. The compressed-delivery table in CRITIQUE_ACTIVITY_PACK.md gives the cut order if you cannot 9 Every public URL in the front matter and in the sources guide needs re-verification before each delivery Saudi government web estate is consolidating actively — 236 sites closed in 2024. The re-verification checklist at the end of PUBLIC_DATA_SOURCES_GUIDE.md is the list to work through 10 Deck slide 19 states download formats and developer APIs for the national open data portal that the research could not verify first-hand — all *.data.gov.sa hosts were unreachable Either verify on-network and keep the row, or reduce it to what is confirmed: the portal exists, it is linked from the GASTAT footer, and its licence is an attribution-plus-disclosure open licence whose exact name is unverified. The sources guide already takes the reduced position

docs.title: Saudi Public Data Sources — a vetted guide
مصادر البيانات العامة السعودية
docs.text: Verified 14 September 2026 — re-verify before each delivery.

docs.title: Who this is for
docs.text:
The Tayseer dataset is synthetic, deliberately, so that nothing in the training room is sensitive. When a participant takes this course home, the first thing they need is a real source. This guide is the vetted shortlist: four source families, what each actually holds, the exact live URLs, how you get data out, what the licence permits, and — where the licence is not stated at all — what that means in practice.

Everything below was checked on 14 September 2026. Saudi government web estate is being consolidated actively; the DGA closed 236 government websites in 2024 while consolidating toward 581 platforms under a unified design system. Put the date you checked next to every URL you put on a slide, and re-check before each delivery. The gotchas in Part 3 are not hypothetical — each one has bitten somebody.

Confidence levels used throughout: High means verified first-hand against the live source; Medium means verified from a secondary source or from page titles only; Low means not reachable from the research environment and therefore not verified first-hand at all.

docs.title: 1. GASTAT — General Authority for Statistics · الهيئة العامة للإحصاء
docs.text:
The single most useful source in this list, and the only one with a licence permissive enough to build a real deliverable on.

Field Detail Main site https://www.stats.gov.sa/en/ Statistical database https://database.stats.gov.sa/home/landing Census 2022 section https://www.stats.gov.sa/en/statistics?index=119025 — five sub-sections including Administrative Area Information Use policy https://www.stats.gov.sa/en/use-policy Confidence High — licence text read directly from the use-policy page

What it holds. Population by region, demographics, households, labour force, ICT access and usage surveys, CPI and GDP. Census 2022 in full, including the Administrative Area Information tables that carry population by region — the denominators a per-capita analysis needs.

Access mechanism. Per-release PDF plus XLSX on each publication page; a separate statistical database with its own interface; microdata by request. There is no public REST API. The advertised RSS feed at /en/rss/stats returns 404 — do not build anything on it.

Licence for reuse — stated precisely. The use policy permits reuse including commercial reuse, on three conditions: GASTAT is acknowledged as the official source; modifications are clearly indicated; and modified material is not presented as official statistics. Logos are excluded from the grant. In practice this means a participant may build on GASTAT data for a real workplace deliverable with attribution — which is unusual enough among the four sources here to be worth naming out loud in class. It is the only one of the four where redistribution is affirmatively permitted.

Update cadence. Quarterly for GDP and labour; monthly for CPI; annual for the ICT survey and population estimates; the census roughly decennially.

docs.title: 2. DGA — Digital Government Authority · هيئة الحكومة الرقمية
docs.text:
Field Detail Main site https://dga.gov.sa/en Digital transformation indicators https://dga.gov.sa/ar/DT-indicators Digital experience maturity https://dga.gov.sa/en/CX-indicators/digital-experience-maturity-index-2025 Report PDFs Published under https://dga.gov.sa/sites/default/files/YYYY-MM/... Confidence Medium — the site returns 403 to automated fetches, so page content was verified from titles and from secondary announcements

What it holds. Two separate annual indices, and they are routinely confused.

Index Arabic What it measures Scope Qiyas — Digital Transformation Measurement Index مؤشر قياس التحول الرقمي Entity-level digital maturity 240 entities, 95 criteria DXMI — Digital Experience Maturity Index مؤشر نضج التجربة الرقمية User-experience maturity of individual services Service-level

There is no DGA product called a "Digital Government Maturity Index". The World Bank GovTech Maturity Index (GTMI) is a third, non-Saudi index frequently confused with both. Conflating them in a SDAIA room is conspicuous.

Access mechanism. Public web pages and PDF reports. The site blocks automated fetching, so budget for manual screenshotting. A scripted scraping exercise built against dga.gov.sa will fail in the room.

Licence for reuse — not stated. No reuse licence was found, and the block on automated access prevented verification. What that means in practice: cite, do not redistribute. Quote a figure with its source and the date you checked it; do not republish a DGA table, chart or report PDF in a handout or a public deliverable. Absence of a stated licence is not permission — the default is all rights reserved.

Update cadence. Annual, both indices.

docs.title: 3. The Saudi Open Data ecosystem
docs.text: Three things travel under this heading and they are not equivalent. The national portal itself could not be verified first-hand; the two reachable alternatives can be taught with, on stricter terms.

docs.title: 3a. The national open data portal
docs.text:
Field Detail Portal https://open.data.gov.sa — linked from the GASTAT footer Second indexed host https://od.data.gov.sa Confidence Low — all *.data.gov.sa hosts were unreachable from the research environment. This is an egress restriction, not evidence of a dead portal

What it holds. Not first-hand verified. Dataset counts, the category list, the available download formats, the API shape and the exact licence name are all unconfirmed and must not be stated as fact in class. Describe it as the national portal and send participants to read it themselves.

Licence for reuse. Per my.gov.sa, an "Open Data License" permitting sharing and derivative works conditional on attribution and on disclosing the licence type when redistributing. The exact licence name and full text were not verified. In practice: treat it as attribution-plus-licence-disclosure, and read the licence on the portal itself before any participant publishes anything derived from it.

Ownership. Sources disagree on whether the portal is operated by SDAIA or by the DGA. Verify on-network before asserting either in a SDAIA context.

docs.title: 3b. DataSaudi — Ministry of Economy and Planning
docs.text:
Field Detail URL https://datasaudi.sa/en Confidence Medium — reachable and inspected; licence read from the site footer

What it holds. Interactive economic and social visualisations for the Kingdom and all thirteen regions, including density maps. It is the closest public analogue to the Case C regional comparison, which makes it an excellent live demo.

Access mechanism. Browser only in practice — the site is JavaScript-rendered, so a plain HTTP fetch returns metadata and nothing else. Any retrieval exercise against it needs a headless browser.

Licence for reuse — not stated as an open licence. The footer carries "Copyright. All Rights Reserved © 2026". In practice: good for demonstration in a live session, risky to redistribute. Show it on screen; do not paste its charts into a deliverable.

docs.title: 3c. RCRC Open Data
docs.text:
Field Detail URL https://opendata.rcrc.gov.sa Platform An Opendatasoft instance republishing GASTAT census tables, with an explore UI and an API console Confidence Medium — reachable and inspected

Access mechanism. The browser explore UI works normally and exports cleanly. The API path is disallowed by robots.txt — use the UI, not the console, in any exercise you set.

Licence for reuse — not verified. The underlying census tables are GASTAT's and carry the GASTAT terms; RCRC's own terms for the republished instance were not verified. In practice: prefer going back to stats.gov.sa for anything you intend to publish, and use RCRC for convenience of export only.

docs.title: 4. Vision 2030
docs.text:
Field Detail Main site https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/en Annual reports hub https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/en/annual-reports NTP Annual Report 2025 https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/media/uxhfb5if/ntp_en_annual_report_2025.pdf — KPI appendix, pp. 79–86 Vision 2030 Annual Report 2025 https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/media/ecdjfopq/vision2030_annual_report_2025_en.pdf — over 30 MB Annual Report 2024 https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/media/25042025ev1/En-Annual%20Report-Vision2030-2024.pdf Executive summary (2024 ed.) https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/media/jgvb3mrb/executive-summary-vision2030.pdf Confidence High for the URLs, the structure and the cadence; the contents of the 2025 annual report PDF itself are unverified

What it holds. The Vision document and the annual reports of the Vision Realization Programs. The national KPI figures live inside the VRP annual-report PDFs, not on the site as data. The single most useful artefact in this entire guide is the KPI appendix of a VRP report: the NTP Annual Report 2025 carries, on pp. 79–86, a table with columns for baseline value, baseline year, target, target year, actual and actual year. That is a real, published baseline/target/actual table, and it is the exact shape of the scorecard participants are asked to build in the capstone.

Access mechanism. PDF only. The site is JavaScript-rendered, so a plain HTTP fetch returns metadata. Transcribe the appendix by hand or with a PDF table extractor; there is no data endpoint.

Licence for reuse — not stated. No reuse licence was found. In practice: cite with attribution; do not assume redistribution rights. A KPI table transcribed for internal analysis is normal practice; republishing the report's tables or figures is not covered by anything you can point to.

Update cadence. Annual, published in Q2 of the following year — the 2025 report was released on 25 April 2026.

How to use the confidence column in class. A Medium-confidence figure is fine in a discussion and wrong on a printed slide without its hedge. If you put fact 11, 12 or 14 on a slide, put the word "reported" in front of it and the source beside it.

docs.title: Part 3 — Gotchas
docs.text:
Every item here was checked on 14 September 2026 and every one has cost somebody time. Each is paired with what to do instead.

# The trap What to do instead 1 The census portal is dead. saudicensus.sa and portal.saudicensus.sa no longer resolve — DNS failure, not a 404. Old bookmarks and old slides are broken Census 2022 now lives inside stats.gov.sa. Go via https://www.stats.gov.sa/en/statistics?index=119025 and its Administrative Area Information sub-section 2 Several government sites block automated access. dga.gov.sa, sdaia.gov.sa and parts of my.gov.sa return 403 or a WAF block to scripts while working normally in a browser Retrieve by hand and screenshot. Do not set a scraping exercise against any of these — it will fail live in the room 3 Vision 2030 and DataSaudi are JavaScript-rendered. A plain HTTP fetch returns metadata only Use a headless browser if you must automate, or download the PDFs directly by URL. For teaching, prefer the PDF route — it is one step, and it works 4 Stale GASTAT pages outrank current ones. An internet-usage page from 10 May 2018 reporting 2017 data still ranks above the 2025 ICT release Check the publication date on every page before quoting it. Never quote a GASTAT figure from a search-result snippet 5 Several stats.gov.sa deep links 404 Use the /en/statistics?index=… form rather than a deep link copied from an older document 6 No 2025 or 2026 Saudi population estimate has been published The current official figure is the mid-2024 estimate, 35,300,280. Anything more recent is somebody's projection — say so if you use one 7 No 2026 UN E-Government Survey exists The most recent edition is 2024, rank 6 with an EGDI of 0.96022. Do not cite a "2026 EGDI" 8 There is no "Digital Government Maturity Index" DGA runs two indices — Qiyas (transformation, entity-level) and DXMI (experience, service-level). The World Bank GovTech Maturity Index is a third, non-Saudi index. Name the one you mean 9 Ownership of the national open data portal is disputed in sources — SDAIA or DGA Verify on-network before asserting either, particularly in a SDAIA context where the room will know 10 Government website consolidation is ongoing. 236 sites closed in 2024 alone Version-date every link in course materials and re-check the week before delivery

One further trap, flagged as instructor judgement rather than as a research finding. Every index above is a composite with its own weighting. Quoting a change in an index score as if it were a change in a quantity — "digital transformation rose 1.16 points" — is the same class of error as averaging an average. Percentages of composites do not travel. This appears on the deck's gotchas slide and is the instructor's call, not a verified fact about any of these sources.

docs.title: Part 4 — Could not verify
docs.text:
These were investigated and could not be confirmed. They must not be stated as fact in class, on a slide, or in a handout. If a participant asserts one, the correct response is "that is not verified — here is how you would check it", not agreement.

# Claim Status 1 Dataset counts, category lists, API details and the exact licence name on the national open data portal Not verified. All *.data.gov.sa hosts were unreachable from the research environment — an egress restriction, not evidence about the portal 2 Whether the national open data portal is operated by SDAIA or by the DGA Sources disagree. Unresolved 3 Any official GASTAT population-density figure Not published as a headline statistic. It is derivable as population ÷ area, but a derived figure is yours, not GASTAT's, and must be labelled as such 4 The contents of the Vision 2030 Annual Report 2025 PDF itself The URL and the release date are verified; the contents are not. The 93% headline is Medium confidence from trade press 5 Licensing and terms of use for DGA, Vision 2030 and DataSaudi Not stated on any of the three. Treat all three as cite-only 6 The World Bank GovTech Maturity Index 2025 ranking for Saudi Arabia Not verified. Do not quote a GTMI position

docs.title: Part 5 — Three worked exercises with real data
docs.text: Each of these is doable after the course with nothing but a browser and the course's own notebook environment. Each respects the access constraints in Part 3 — none of them scrapes a site that blocks scripts, and none redistributes material whose licence is not stated.

docs.title: Exercise 1 — Rebuild Case C on real population data
docs.text:
Source. GASTAT, Census 2022 Administrative Area Information. Licence: reuse permitted with attribution, including commercially. This is the only one of the three exercises whose output you may publish.

Retrieval steps. 1. Go to https://www.stats.gov.sa/en/statistics?index=119025 and open the Administrative Area Information sub-section. Do not use a deep link from an older document — several 404. 2. Download the population-by-region table as XLSX. Check the publication date on the page before you take the figures; stale pages outrank current ones in search. 3. Verify your transcription by summing: the thirteen regional figures must come to exactly 32,175,224. If they do not, you have taken a Saudi-only or non-Saudi-only column. 4. Take any count you care about for the same thirteen regions from your own organisation's reporting — service volumes, registrations, applications, visits.

The chart it should produce. Two sorted horizontal bars side by side: the raw count, and the same count per 1,000 residents. Compute the rank on each and the rank shift between them. The deliverable is not the pair of charts but the one-sentence subtitle that states the denominator, the period and the comparison, in under fifteen words — and the written answer to the Case C question, what is the raw-count map a map of?

What it teaches. Exactly what Case C teaches on synthetic data, with the participant's own numbers and the real census denominator. A raw-count map is, to a very good approximation, a population map. Expect the rank shift to be large; in the Tayseer data the largest is six places.

docs.title: Exercise 2 — Build a real baseline/target/actual scorecard
docs.text:
Source. Vision 2030, National Transformation Program Annual Report 2025, KPI appendix, pp. 79–86: https://www.vision2030.gov.sa/media/uxhfb5if/ntp_en_annual_report_2025.pdf. Licence: none stated. Cite with attribution; keep the output internal.

Retrieval steps. 1. Download the PDF directly by URL. Do not attempt to scrape the site — it is JavaScript-rendered and will return metadata only. 2. Go to pp. 79–86. The appendix carries six columns: baseline value, baseline year, target, target year, actual, actual year. 3. Transcribe six to ten KPIs by hand, or with a PDF table extractor, into a CSV with exactly those six columns plus the KPI name. Hand transcription of ten rows takes about fifteen minutes and is the honest route. 4. Record the report version and the date you downloaded it in the CSV header. The 2025 report was released 25 April 2026; a 2026 report will supersede it in Q2 2027.

The chart it should produce. A bullet chart per KPI: a bar for the actual, a marker for the target, a light band for the range between baseline and target, sorted by proportion of the gap closed. Annotate each bar with its baseline year and actual year — different KPIs in that appendix have different reference years, and a scorecard that hides that is making a comparison it has not earned.

What it teaches. The shape of a real public-sector scorecard, and the single most common defect in one: rows whose actual and target are measured in different years, presented in one column as though they were contemporaneous. It is also the direct rehearsal for the capstone deliverable.

docs.title: Exercise 3 — Chart a ranking that is not a quantity
docs.text:
Source. UN E-Government Development Index, country page for Saudi Arabia: https://publicadministration.un.org/egovkb/en-us/Data/Country-Information/id/149-Saudi-Arabia. Four editions are on the record: 52nd in 2018, 43rd in 2020, 31st in 2022, and 6th in 2024 with an EGDI of 0.96022. There is no 2026 edition.

Retrieval steps. 1. Open the country page in a browser and read the rank and index value for each edition. Four editions is a small enough series to transcribe by hand, and the page is reachable without any special handling. 2. Record both the rank and the index value for each edition in two separate columns. The exercise depends on having both. 3. Note the edition years explicitly — 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024, biennial. Do not interpolate the missing years, and do not extend the series to 2026.

The chart it should produce. A single line chart of index value over the four editions, with the rank annotated at each point as text rather than plotted. Invert nothing and plot no rank axis. Then write the annotation that explains why: a rank is a position in a field whose composition changes between editions, so the nine-place move between 2018 and 2020 and the twenty-five-place move between 2022 and 2024 are not comparable quantities, while the index value is at least on a stable scale. If the participant wants a rank chart as well, it must be a second panel with its own explicit caveat.

What it teaches. The composite-index trap, on a real series a Saudi analyst will be asked about. It also rehearses the Minard units discipline — read what the number actually is before you encode it — and the honest refusal that Case C teaches: a technically correct chart aimed at the wrong question tells you nothing, and saying so out loud is the analyst's job.

Re-verification checklist before each delivery. Open every URL in Part 1. Confirm the census route through stats.gov.sa still works. Check whether a 2025 or 2026 GASTAT population estimate has appeared, and whether a 2026 UN E-Government Survey exists — if either has, facts 6, 7 and 9 change. Check whether the Vision 2030 2026 annual report has been published. Re-read the GASTAT use policy; it is the only licence in this guide that permits redistribution, and the course's advice to participants depends on it.

docs.title: Data Dictionary — SDA-DSC-112 Tayseer dataset family
docs.text: Programme: Data Visualization and Storytelling (SDA-DSC-112) · SDAIA Academy Golden thread: the Tayseer (تيسير) National Digital Services Programme Coverage: July 2021 – June 2026 (60 months) · 13 administrative regions · 9 service categories · 4 channels All data is synthetic. No real individual, entity or transaction is represented.

docs.title: 1. Grain and joins
docs.text:
dim_calendar (month) ─┐
dim_regions  (region) ─┼─→ tayseer_services  [month × region × service_category × channel]

Every other dataset joins on region, month, service_category, channel or service_id.

docs.title: 2. The three measure rules
docs.text:
Rule Applies to Consequence Additive transactions, complaints Safe to SUM at any grain Semi-additive unique_users Sum within a month, never across months Non-additive digital_adoption_pct, cost_per_txn_sar, csat, avg_completion_min, sla_met_pct Never AVERAGE — recompute from components

The deliberate teaching artefact: for the latest month, AVERAGE(digital_adoption_pct) returns 61.2% while the correct user-weighted recomputation returns 63.8%. The 2.6-point gap is the averages-of-averages bug, and it is reproducible from the shipped data.

71 of 71 extension checks passed.

Three results worth quoting on a slide:

  • The Gini coefficient of digital transactions against population is 0.0372 — deliberately small, because the inequality in this programme sits in the level of adoption (50.0% to 67.8%) rather than in the concentration of volume. A class that expects a dramatic Lorenz curve learns something useful when it does not get one.
  • Jazan ranks 7th of 13 on a raw digital-transaction choropleth and 13th of 13 per capita — a six-place fall, and the whole Case C argument.
  • The truncated-axis bar pair (national adoption, y-axis from 60) carries a Tufte lie factor of 36.8: a 3.50% real change drawn as a 128.71% one.

104 of 104 checks passed across the package (33 core + 71 extension).

docs.title: Hands-on lab notebooks — SDA-DSC-112
docs.text:
Data Visualization and Storytelling · SDAIA Academy · Data Scientist Track

Twelve notebooks: a starter and a solution for each of the six hands-on labs. Every lab runs against the same golden thread — the Tayseer (تيسير) National Digital Services Programme — so the story compounds across the three days instead of restarting every session.

docs.title: 1. Quick start
docs.text:
cd <package root>/notebooks
pip install -r requirements.txt
apt-get install -y fonts-hosny-amiri        # Lab 3 only; see §6
jupyter lab                                  # or: jupyter notebook

Open a starter, Run All, and work through the # TODO blocks. A starter notebook runs clean on a fresh kernel — no cell errors before you have written anything; each TODO prints the shape and the numbers you should end up with.

To re-execute everything headlessly (this is exactly how the shipped solutions were produced):

cd <package root>/notebooks
for nb in lab1_*_solution lab2_*_solution lab3_*_solution \
          lab4_*_solution lab5_*_solution lab6_*_solution; do
  jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --inplace "$nb.ipynb"
done

Order matters once. Lab 6 imports story/tayseer_storyboard.py, which Lab 5 writes. Run Lab 5 before Lab 6. Labs 1–4 are independent of each other.

docs.title: 2. What is in this folder
docs.text:
Path What it is lab1_perception_starter/solution.ipynb Perception audit and five encodings lab2_chart_selection_starter/solution.ipynb Chart chooser and the first honest charts lab3_declutter_redesign_starter/solution.ipynb Before/after redesign, colour, Arabic RTL lab4_dashboard_starter/solution.ipynb The interactive Tayseer dashboard (4a + 4b) lab5_storyboard_starter/solution.ipynb Storyboard the Tayseer narrative lab6_delivery_clinic_starter/solution.ipynb The executive delivery clinic tayseer_viz.py The course library: measures, theme, sorted_bar, Arabic helpers app/dashboard.py The Dash cross-filtering app (written by Lab 4, run from a terminal) story/ The narrative package (written by Labs 5 and 6) out/ Every figure, at dpi = 150, ready to drop into slides out/starter/ Created on a student's first run; their figures land here so they never overwrite out/ requirements.txt Pinned lower bounds

tayseer_viz.py is deliberately thin. It holds the plumbing that every lab shares — the Okabe–Ito palette, the decluttered matplotlib theme, the correctly-implemented non-additive measures, one principle-compliant chart function, and the Arabic reshaping/bidi helpers — so each notebook stays about its teaching point.

docs.title: 3. The labs, the datasets they touch, and runtime
docs.text:
Runtimes are wall-clock for a full headless re-execution on a 2-core container.

Lab Minutes of class time Datasets it loads Runtime Figures produced 1 · Perception 50 tayseer_services.csv, encoding_accuracy_ranking.csv ~10 s 4 2 · Chart selection 50 tayseer_services.csv, tayseer_transactions_sample.csv, lab2_questions.csv, chart_chooser.csv, kpi_targets.csv ~15 s 6 + 1 HTML 3 · Declutter & RTL 50 tayseer_services.csv, brand_palette.csv, dim_regions.csv, dim_calendar.csv ~15 s 7 4 · Dashboard 100 (4a + 4b) tayseer_services.csv, dim_*, kpi_targets.csv, region_directors.csv, dim_services.csv, dashboard_usability_tests.csv ~15 s 4 + 1 HTML + app/dashboard.py + lab4_bi_measures.md 5 · Storyboard 50 regional_scorecard_latest.csv, investment_options.csv, investment_option_region_allocation.csv, support_tickets.csv, csat_survey_responses.csv, branch_monthly.csv, dim_regions.csv, tayseer_services.csv ~10 s 8 + BLUF memo + story/ 6 · Delivery clinic 50 qa_bank.csv, rehearsal_scores.csv, investment_option_region_allocation.csv, participants_roster.csv, story/tayseer_storyboard.py ~10 s 1 + story/

Full set, twelve notebooks, end to end: under two minutes.

docs.title: 4. The measure rules — read this before editing anything
docs.text:
This is the single error the course exists to prevent, and every notebook enforces it.

Class Columns Rule Additive transactions, complaints SUM at any grain Semi-additive unique_users SUM within a month, never across months Non-additive digital_adoption_pct, cost_per_txn_sar, csat, avg_completion_min, sla_met_pct never AVERAGE — recompute from components

The weight is not the same for every non-additive measure. It comes from data/supporting/kpi_targets.csv, which is the programme's semantic layer:

KPI Formula Weight KPI-01 Digital adoption % SUM(adoption/100 × unique_users) / SUM(unique_users) × 100 unique_users KPI-02 Cost per transaction SUM(cost × transactions) / SUM(transactions) transactions KPI-03 CSAT SUM(csat × transactions) / SUM(transactions) transactions KPI-04 Avg completion time SUM(minutes × transactions) / SUM(transactions) transactions KPI-05 SLA met % SUM(sla × transactions) / SUM(transactions) transactions

Adoption is a property of users (did this person go digital?); cost, satisfaction, completion time and SLA are properties of transactions. tayseer_viz implements each one and refuses to roll up a non-additive column without its declared weight:

import tayseer_viz as tv
df = tv.load_facts()
latest = df[df.month == df.month.max()]

tv.adoption(latest)        # 63.84  — correct (KPI-01)
latest.digital_adoption_pct.mean()   # 61.19  — the averages-of-averages bug
tv.by(latest, "region", "cost_per_txn_sar")   # correct at any grain

docs.title: 5. Published figures these notebooks reproduce
docs.text:
Every number below is asserted in a notebook cell, so a change to the data breaks the run rather than silently changing a claim.

Figure Value Where Weighted national adoption vs naive average 63.8% vs 61.2% (2.64 pp gap) Lab 1 task 1, Lab 4 task 3 Cost per transaction across the window 25.66 → 16.94 SAR (−34%) Lab 2 tasks 1 and 6 CSAT across the window 3.71 → 4.16 (+12%) Lab 2 tasks 1 and 6 Regions above the 18 SAR cost target 5 — Jazan, Najran, Al-Baha, Asir, Northern Borders Lab 3 task 2 …and they are the same five that stalled on adoption asserted Lab 3 task 2 Regions below the 65% adoption target 9 (KPI-08) Lab 2 task 4 Severe laggards, more than 9pp below target 3 — Jazan, Najran, Al-Baha Lab 1, Lab 2 Population share of the five stalled regions 15.8% Lab 5 task 1 Their digital transactions per capita vs national −12.1% Lab 5 task 1 Authentication failures as a share of their tickets 27% vs 17% elsewhere Lab 5 task 4 Do-nothing December shortfall in the five 8.7 pp Lab 5 task 4 Dashboard usability: gauge wall → inverted pyramid 72.2 s → 11.2 s, 24% → 86% correct, 31% → 0% gave up Lab 4 task 10 Rehearsal rounds 54% → 86% (+32 points), all 24 improved Lab 6 task 7

docs.title: 6. Arabic and RTL (Lab 3, task 6)
docs.text:
matplotlib will draw Arabic as disconnected letters in left-to-right order unless you reshape and bidi the string first, and it needs a font that actually carries Arabic glyphs. Both are handled by tayseer_viz:

ok, font = tv.setup_arabic()       # registers an Arabic font; returns (True, 'Amiri')
ax.set_title(tv.ar("نسبة التبني الرقمي"), **tv.arabic_kwargs())

setup_arabic() looks for Amiri, then Scheherazade, then KacstOne, then FreeSerif. If none is present, or arabic-reshaper / python-bidi are missing, it returns False and emits a warning — fall back to English labels and say so on the slide. Shipping tofu boxes or disconnected letters is worse than shipping English.

Install a font with apt-get install -y fonts-hosny-amiri (or fonts-sil-scheherazade, fonts-kacst, fonts-noto-naskh-arabic). Verify with fc-list :lang=ar.

The lab also teaches the two RTL rules that are not about glyphs: a ranking axis puts the first/best on the right, and a time axis runs right-to-left (ax.invert_xaxis()). Translating the labels without mirroring the axis produces a chart that reads backwards to an Arabic-first audience.

docs.title: 7. Running the Dash app (Lab 4b)
docs.text:
A Dash app cannot run inside a notebook cell, so Lab 4 writes it and then compiles and imports it to prove it is sound. To actually use it:

cd <package root>/notebooks
python app/dashboard.py            # -> http://127.0.0.1:8050

It demonstrates all four interaction patterns — a channel filter, click-to-cross- filter on the regional bar, a drill path (national → region → service category → channel) with a breadcrumb, and a measure toggle — plus a rls_scope() function that is the code equivalent of the Power BI RegionDirector row-level-security role.

docs.title: 8. Static export of Plotly figures
docs.text:
Plotly's PNG export (kaleido ≥ 1) requires a Chrome binary, which is not present in every training environment and cannot always be downloaded. The notebooks therefore:

  1. always write the interactive HTML, which is the real deliverable, and
  2. always render a matplotlib mirror of the same view as a PNG in out/.

tv.save_plotly(fig, name) attempts the PNG and reports cleanly if it cannot. Nothing in out/ is missing as a result — lab2_q2_trend.png mirrors lab2_q2_interactive.html, and lab4_dashboard_static.png mirrors lab4_dashboard.html.

docs.title: 9. Chart doctrine — what every figure in out/ obeys
docs.text:
The notebooks are themselves an exhibit, so they follow the rules they teach:

  • bars start at zero; only line charts may truncate an axis
  • sorted by value wherever a ranking exists
  • direct labelling instead of legends
  • a reference line (target or national mean) wherever good/bad is the question
  • one accent colour carrying the argument, everything else grey
  • takeaway titles — the conclusion, not the topic
  • Okabe–Ito palette, colour-blind safe, with the message carried redundantly by position, a reference line and text as well as by hue
  • no dual axes, no 3D, no gauges, and no pie charts — except the two built deliberately for critique, in Lab 1 task 2 and Lab 1 task 4

docs.title: 10. Known deviations from the INSTRUCTOR_PACKAGE
docs.text:
Small, deliberate, and flagged in the notebooks where they occur:

  1. Asset substitution. bad_dashboard_m1.png (Lab 1) and cluttered_m3.png (Lab 3) are not shipped with the data package, so both are built in code inside the notebook. That makes the critique target reproducible and lets participants see each violation in the source.
  2. "Three regions" vs "five". Several expected-output blocks in the INSTRUCTOR_PACKAGE say three regions are below target. The data says nine are below target, five of those are stalled (Tier 1), and three are more than 9pp below. The notebooks use all three counts and name which is which; the story's ask is about the five stalled regions, matching README.md and validation_report.md.
  3. No March 2024 outage. Module 3's code example annotates a "March 2024 service outage" behind Najran's plateau. No such step change exists in tayseer_services.csv — Najran rises smoothly and flattens over the last nine months. Lab 3 annotates the nine-month stall, which the data does support.
  4. Adoption never crosses 65%. Module 2's expected output says national adoption goes "41% → 68%, crosses 65% in month 21". The data says 34.2% → 63.8%, never crossing. The notebooks use the data; the gap to target is the whole point of the story.
  5. Five Lab 2 questions, not four. lab2_questions.csv ships Q1–Q5 (Q5 is the thirteen-overlapping-lines / small-multiples question). Lab 2 covers all five.

docs.title: Tayseer semantic layer
docs.text: Grain of the fact table: month x region x service_category x channel (28,080 rows).

docs.title: Additivity, first
docs.text: Class Columns Rule Additive transactions, complaints SUM at any grain Semi-additive unique_users SUM within a month, never across months Non-additive digital_adoption_pct, cost_per_txn_sar, csat, avg_completion_min, sla_met_pct never AVERAGE - recompute from components

docs.title: Power BI (DAX)
docs.text:
Digital Adoption % :=
    DIVIDE(
        SUMX(tayseer, tayseer[digital_adoption_pct] / 100 * tayseer[unique_users]),
        SUM(tayseer[unique_users])) * 100

Cost per Transaction :=
    DIVIDE(
        SUMX(tayseer, tayseer[cost_per_txn_sar] * tayseer[transactions]),
        SUM(tayseer[transactions]))

CSAT :=
    DIVIDE(
        SUMX(tayseer, tayseer[csat] * tayseer[transactions]),
        SUM(tayseer[transactions]))

Delta vs Target := [Digital Adoption %] - 65

Regions Below Target :=
    CALCULATE(
        DISTINCTCOUNT(tayseer[region]),
        FILTER(VALUES(tayseer[region]), [Digital Adoption %] < 65))

Row-level security role RegionDirector on the tayseer table:

[region] = LOOKUPVALUE(
    region_directors[region],
    region_directors[email], USERPRINCIPALNAME())

docs.title: Tableau (calculated fields)
docs.text:
Digital Adoption %:
    SUM([digital_adoption_pct] / 100 * [unique_users]) / SUM([unique_users]) * 100

Cost per Transaction:
    SUM([cost_per_txn_sar] * [transactions]) / SUM([transactions])

Below Target flag:
    IF [Digital Adoption %] < 65 THEN "Below" ELSE "On/above" END

RLS: a user filter on region_directors, USERNAME() mapped to email.

docs.title: Why SUMX and not AVERAGE
docs.text: AVERAGE(tayseer[digital_adoption_pct]) returns 61.2%; the recomputation returns 63.8%. The 2.6-point gap is the averages-of-averages bug, and it moves with the filter context - it is not a constant offset that can be corrected afterwards.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Direct the next SAR 40M to targeted regional activation in Jazan, Najran, Al-Baha, Asir and Northern Borders.

Why now: At the current pace the programme misses its December adoption commitment by about 1 point nationally, and the five regions finish 8.7 points short.

Rationale: These five regions hold the entire national shortfall against the 65% target, and their stall has a scoped, fixable cause.

Evidence (one line each): - National adoption 63.8% vs the 65% target — the gap is concentrated in five regions, not diffuse. - Those five add under 0.08pp per month and are 12.1% below the national digital-transactions-per-capita rate — they are not simply small. - Authentication failures are 27% of their support tickets versus 17% elsewhere — a known and fixable root cause. - OPT-A closes 0.0532 adoption points per SAR million, 1.6x the channel rebuild, and lands in 6 months rather than 14. - Projected December: OPT-A 66.0% national with 4 of 5 stalled regions at target; OPT-B 65.2% with none; OPT-C 65.7% with none.

Risks and how they are managed: - Delivery risk is Medium (regional office capacity) — mitigated by the 90-day checkpoint on adoption slope. - The recommendation holds even at Finance's lower adoption estimate of 61.2%, because the regional concentration is unchanged.

The ask: Approve the reallocation to OPT-A; first checkpoint in 90 days.

In the appendix, on request: measure definitions and the 61.2% vs 63.8% reconciliation; per-region allocation of the SAR 40M; do-nothing December projection by region.

Full analysis and dashboard in appendix; methodology available on request.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A specialist module that deepens modelling skill beyond the foundations. Participants master gradient-boosting frameworks, imbalanced and cost-sensitive learning, model interpretability with SHAP, and rigorous validation design. The emphasis is on winning reliable performance on messy, real-world tabular problems.

Course facts Course code SDA-DSC-211 Level Specialist · متخصص Learning path Data Scientist Track Domain Data Science Duration 4 days × 5 learning hours = 20 hours Delivery mode Remote (live online) Target audience Data scientists progressing to specialist modelling roles Prerequisites SDA-AIE-111 (cross-listed); SDA-DSC-111 Assessment Modelling challenge; interpretability report

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Develop high-performance models with XGBoost and LightGBM
  2. Design validation schemes that respect leakage, grouping, and time order
  3. Apply techniques for imbalanced, noisy, and cost-sensitive problems
  4. Analyze model behaviour using SHAP and permutation importance
  5. Optimize feature pipelines and model ensembles for tabular data
  6. Evaluate models for stability, calibration, and business impact

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
A specialist module that deepens modelling skill beyond the foundations. Participants master gradient-boosting frameworks, imbalanced and cost-sensitive learning, model interpretability with SHAP, and rigorous validation design. The emphasis is on winning reliable performance on messy, real-world tabular problems — the kind that dominate Saudi banking, telecom, health, and government analytics.

The course is built around a single evolving artefact: "Tamweel" (تمويل), a consumer-financing default-risk model for a Saudi lender supervised under SAMA rules. Participants receive a realistic, imbalanced applications dataset and build the model up across every module — first a strong gradient-boosted baseline, then a leakage-proof validation scheme, cost-sensitive thresholds, SHAP explanations fit for a regulator, calibrated probabilities that price expected loss, and a stacked ensemble. By Day 4 each participant owns a documented, calibrated, explainable model and defends it in an applied modelling challenge — the same shape of deliverable expected in SDA-DSC-390 (the Data Science Capstone).

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this course, participants will be able to:

  1. LO1 — Develop high-performance models with XGBoost and LightGBM
  2. LO2 — Design validation schemes that respect leakage, grouping, and time order
  3. LO3 — Apply techniques for imbalanced, noisy, and cost-sensitive problems
  4. LO4 — Analyze model behaviour using SHAP and permutation importance
  5. LO5 — Optimize feature pipelines and model ensembles for tabular data
  6. LO6 — Evaluate models for stability, calibration, and business impact

docs.title: Instructor Guidance Notes (Delivery Plan Level)
docs.text:
• Golden thread: every module operates on the same Tamweel default-risk dataset. Never introduce a throwaway toy dataset (no load_breast_cancer) — always evolve the Tamweel model. This is what makes the Day-4 challenge achievable and the interpretability report coherent.
  • Pace control: Labs 1 and 4 overrun most often (Optuna tuning and SHAP rendering are time sinks). Publish checkpoint notebooks/commits (lab1-start, lab1-solution, lab2-start, …) so stragglers can fast-forward: git checkout lab4-start. Cap Optuna trials in-class (e.g. 40) and hand out a pre-computed study.pkl.
  • Pairing: rotate pairs each day. Pair a strong-statistics participant (from SDA-DSC-111) with a strong-engineering participant; the validation-rigour ↔ tooling transfer is the point.
  • Environment strategy: primary = local Python 3.12 venv with the pinned requirements.txt; fallback = Google Colab (GPU not required — CPU LightGBM is fast on this dataset). Verify both the week before delivery; SHAP + recent NumPy versions are the usual break point.
  • Language: deliver in English or Arabic; keep all code, identifiers, column names, and commit messages in English (production convention in Saudi enterprise/banking environments — mixed-language columns break downstream pipelines and SAMA reporting).
  • Prayer and break scheduling: each "hour" is 50 minutes of instruction + 10 minutes buffer; schedule the long break around Dhuhr. Day-4 sprints are deliberately continuous — protect them from theory creep.
  • Determinism discipline: set and log every random seed from Hour 1. Much of Day 3's stability clinic depends on participants having seeded their earlier work; make it a habit early.
  • Assessment logistics: the private leaderboard scores on a held-out ledger the participants never see, using a business cost metric (SAR), not raw AUC — collect submission files at the end of Day-4 Hour 3 so scoring completes before the Hour-5 reveal.

docs.title: Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. Gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) are the workhorse of applied tabular ML and win the majority of real-world structured-data problems. Yet most practitioners treat XGBoost and LightGBM as black boxes with magic hyperparameters. This module opens the box: participants learn how boosting fits residuals stage by stage, why the histogram algorithm made GBDTs fast, what leaf-wise growth trades against level-wise growth, and — most usefully — which hyperparameters actually move the needle and in which direction.

Business relevance. For Saudi banks, telecoms, and government analytics teams, the dominant modelling substrate is tabular: applications, transactions, subscriber records, service tickets. On these, a well-tuned GBDT typically beats both logistic regression and deep learning while training in seconds on a laptop. Knowing how to extract that last few points of performance — and knowing when you have hit the ceiling — is directly what separates a specialist data scientist from a practitioner who runs fit() with defaults.

Industry use cases. - A consumer lender scores default risk at application time to set approval and pricing (our Tamweel golden thread). - A telecom predicts churn from usage and billing features to target retention offers within budget. - A utility forecasts non-technical loss (meter tampering) from consumption patterns, a highly imbalanced tabular problem.

Expected competencies. After this module a participant can train and early-stop an XGBoost/LightGBM model, read a learning curve, tune the high-leverage hyperparameters deliberately (not by superstition), run an Optuna study with pruning, and explain to a colleague why leaf-wise growth needs num_leaves controlled rather than max_depth alone.

docs.title: 1. From a single tree to an additive ensemble
docs.text:
A single decision tree is high-variance: it memorises. Boosting turns many weak, shallow trees into one strong model by adding them sequentially, each correcting the errors of those before it. Formally, boosting builds an additive model

F_0(x) = base score (e.g. log-odds of the prior)
F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + η · h_m(x)

where each new tree h_m is fit to the negative gradient of the loss at the current predictions (for squared error, that gradient is the residual; for log-loss it is y − p). The learning rate η shrinks each tree's contribution so no single tree dominates — smaller η needs more trees but generalises better. This is gradient descent in function space: instead of nudging parameters, each step adds a function that points down the loss surface.

Teach this with a picture, then a number. Show residuals shrinking over 5 boosting rounds on a 1-D toy, then immediately return to Tamweel — the same mechanism, 40,000 rows and 34 features.

docs.title: 2. Second-order boosting: why XGBoost was a leap
docs.text:
XGBoost popularised using the second-order Taylor expansion of the loss — both the gradient g_i and the Hessian h_i. The optimal leaf weight and the split gain then have closed forms:

optimal leaf weight  w* = − (Σ g_i) / (Σ h_i + λ)
split gain           = ½ [ G_L²/(H_L+λ) + G_R²/(H_R+λ) − (G_L+G_R)²/(H_L+H_R+λ) ] − γ

Two regularisation knobs fall directly out of this maths and are worth naming in class: λ (reg_lambda, L2 on leaf weights) shrinks weights toward zero; γ (min_split_loss) is a minimum gain a split must clear to be kept — it is pruning expressed as a threshold. Understanding that these come from the objective, not from folklore, is what lets participants tune them with intent.

docs.title: 3. The histogram algorithm and why LightGBM is fast
docs.text: Naive split-finding sorts every feature at every node — expensive. The histogram algorithm buckets each feature into a fixed number of bins (default 255) once, then evaluates splits on bin boundaries. This is the single biggest speed idea in modern GBDTs and both libraries use it (tree_method="hist" in XGBoost; native in LightGBM). LightGBM adds two tricks: GOSS (keep high-gradient rows, subsample low-gradient ones) and EFB (bundle mutually-exclusive sparse features). Practical consequence: on Tamweel-scale data LightGBM trains in a few seconds on CPU, which is why we use it as the default lab engine and keep XGBoost for cross-checking.

docs.title: 4. Leaf-wise vs level-wise growth — the hyperparameter that confuses everyone
docs.text:
• XGBoost (level-wise / depth-wise): grows the tree one full level at a time; max_depth is the natural control.
  • LightGBM (leaf-wise / best-first): always splits the leaf with the highest gain, producing deep, asymmetric trees. This is more accurate per split but overfits fast if uncontrolled. Here num_leaves is the primary complexity control, not max_depth.

The classic mistake: setting max_depth=6 in LightGBM and expecting XGBoost-like behaviour. A leaf-wise tree of depth 6 can have up to 2^6 = 64 leaves; if you leave num_leaves=31 (the default), depth is the binding constraint and the model is smaller than you think — or if you raise num_leaves without a depth cap, it explodes. Rule of thumb: keep num_leaves < 2^max_depth, tune num_leaves as the real dial.

docs.title: 5. The hyperparameters that actually matter (and their direction)
docs.text:
Participants leave with this mental table, ordered by leverage:

Parameter (LGBM / XGB) What it controls Increase → Typical range n_estimators + learning_rate model capacity / step size more trees + smaller LR = better, slower LR 0.01–0.1; trees via early stopping num_leaves / max_depth tree complexity more complex, more overfit leaves 15–255; depth 3–10 min_child_samples / min_child_weight leaf minimum evidence more = smoother, less overfit 20–200 subsample (bagging) row sampling per tree <1 adds regularisation + speed 0.6–1.0 colsample_bytree / feature_fraction column sampling per tree <1 adds regularisation + decorrelation 0.6–1.0 reg_lambda, reg_alpha L2 / L1 on weights more = simpler 0–10 min_split_gain / gamma minimum split gain more = more pruning 0–1

Golden pattern: fix a low learning rate, let early stopping choose n_estimators, then tune complexity and regularisation with a search. Never grid-search n_estimators — early stopping does it for free and correctly per configuration.

docs.title: 6. Common mistakes & production considerations
docs.text:
1. No early stopping, or early stopping on the training set — you must pass a genuine held-out validation set (leak-free, per Module 2).
  2. Tuning learning rate and n_estimators independently — they trade off; fix LR, early-stop the count.
  3. Ignoring categorical handling — LightGBM handles categoricals natively (categorical_feature=); one-hot exploding a 400-city column is slower and often worse.
  4. Reading the training-set feature importance as truth — split/gain importance is biased toward high-cardinality features; this motivates Module 4's permutation importance and SHAP.
  5. Chasing 0.001 AUC with 500 Optuna trials while ignoring leakage (Module 2) and calibration (Module 5) — misallocated effort; the business metric rarely moves.
  6. Production drift blindness — the boosted model that wins today degrades as the population shifts; log inputs and monitor (foreshadows Module 5 stability + SDA-DSC-212).

docs.title: A clean, early-stopped LightGBM baseline
docs.text:
# src/tamweel/models/baseline_lgbm.py
"""Tamweel default-risk baseline. One honest validation split here;
Module 2 replaces this with a leakage-proof, time-aware CV harness."""
from __future__ import annotations
import lightgbm as lgb
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

RANDOM_STATE = 42
TARGET = "default_90dpd"

def load_xy(path: str) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.Series]:
    df = pd.read_parquet(path)
    y = df[TARGET].astype(int)
    X = df.drop(columns=[TARGET, "application_id", "decision_date"])
    # LightGBM reads pandas 'category' dtype natively — no one-hot needed
    for col in X.select_dtypes("object"):
        X[col] = X[col].astype("category")
    return X, y

def train_baseline(X: pd.DataFrame, y: pd.Series) -> lgb.LGBMClassifier:
    X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(
        X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

    model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(
        objective="binary",
        learning_rate=0.03,        # low LR; count chosen by early stopping
        n_estimators=5000,         # upper bound — early stopping cuts it down
        num_leaves=63,             # leaf-wise complexity dial (NOT max_depth)
        min_child_samples=80,      # leaf must see >=80 rows -> smoother
        subsample=0.8, subsample_freq=1,
        colsample_bytree=0.8,
        reg_lambda=2.0,
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1, verbose=-1,
    )
    model.fit(
        X_tr, y_tr,
        eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)],
        eval_metric="auc",
        callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(200), lgb.log_evaluation(100)],
    )
    p = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]
    print(f"best_iteration={model.best_iteration_}  "
          f"AUC={roc_auc_score(y_val, p):.4f}  "
          f"PR-AUC={average_precision_score(y_val, p):.4f}")
    return model

docs.title: Optuna tuning with pruning
docs.text:
# src/tamweel/models/tune_lgbm.py
"""Deliberate, validation-driven search. Fix LR low, early-stop the tree
count, and let Optuna prune unpromising trials to save time in class."""
import optuna
import lightgbm as lgb
from optuna.integration import LightGBMPruningCallback
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
import numpy as np

def objective(trial, X, y):
    params = {
        "objective": "binary", "metric": "auc", "verbosity": -1,
        "learning_rate": 0.03,
        "num_leaves": trial.suggest_int("num_leaves", 15, 255, log=True),
        "min_child_samples": trial.suggest_int("min_child_samples", 20, 300),
        "subsample": trial.suggest_float("subsample", 0.6, 1.0),
        "colsample_bytree": trial.suggest_float("colsample_bytree", 0.6, 1.0),
        "reg_lambda": trial.suggest_float("reg_lambda", 1e-3, 10.0, log=True),
        "reg_alpha": trial.suggest_float("reg_alpha", 1e-3, 10.0, log=True),
    }
    cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
    scores = []
    for fold, (tr, va) in enumerate(cv.split(X, y)):
        dtr = lgb.Dataset(X.iloc[tr], y.iloc[tr])
        dva = lgb.Dataset(X.iloc[va], y.iloc[va])
        pruning = LightGBMPruningCallback(trial, "auc", valid_name="valid_0")
        booster = lgb.train(
            params, dtr, num_boost_round=5000, valid_sets=[dva],
            callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(150), pruning])
        p = booster.predict(X.iloc[va], num_iteration=booster.best_iteration)
        scores.append(roc_auc_score(y.iloc[va], p))
    return float(np.mean(scores))

def run_study(X, y, n_trials: int = 40) -> optuna.Study:
    study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize",
                                pruner=optuna.pruners.MedianPruner())
    study.optimize(lambda t: objective(t, X, y), n_trials=n_trials)
    print("best AUC:", round(study.best_value, 4))
    print("best params:", study.best_params)
    return study

docs.title: XGBoost cross-check (same interface, level-wise growth)
docs.text:
# src/tamweel/models/baseline_xgb.py
import xgboost as xgb
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

def train_xgb(X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val):
    model = xgb.XGBClassifier(
        tree_method="hist",           # histogram algorithm, like LightGBM
        learning_rate=0.03, n_estimators=5000,
        max_depth=6,                  # level-wise: depth is the natural dial
        min_child_weight=5.0,         # Hessian-weighted leaf minimum
        subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8,
        reg_lambda=2.0, gamma=0.0,
        eval_metric="auc", early_stopping_rounds=200,
        enable_categorical=True, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1,
    )
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)], verbose=100)
    p = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]
    print(f"XGB best_iteration={model.best_iteration}  "
          f"AUC={roc_auc_score(y_val, p):.4f}")
    return model

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 1 — A Baseline That Beats the Benchmark
docs.text:
Objective Train, early-stop, and tune a LightGBM (and cross-check XGBoost) default-risk model on Tamweel; beat the provided logistic-regression benchmark (AUC 0.741) by a documented margin Duration 50 minutes Setup Python 3.12, pip install lightgbm xgboost optuna scikit-learn pandas pyarrow, course repo, git checkout lab1-start; dataset data/tamweel_train.parquet

Instructions & tasks

  1. (5 min) Load tamweel_train.parquet; confirm the shape (≈40,000 × 35), the base default rate (≈7.4%), and cast object columns to category.
  2. (10 min) Run train_baseline; record best_iteration_, validation AUC and PR-AUC. Note how many trees early stopping actually kept.
  3. (10 min) Deliberately break it to learn: set learning_rate=0.3, re-run, observe worse validation AUC and a much smaller best_iteration_. Restore 0.03. Discuss the LR/tree-count trade-off with your pair.
  4. (15 min) Run run_study(X, y, n_trials=40) (a pre-computed study.pkl is provided as fallback). Retrain with study.best_params; record the new AUC.
  5. (5 min) Cross-check with train_xgb; compare AUC and training time to LightGBM.
  6. (5 min) Write one paragraph in RESULTS.md: your best AUC, the margin over the 0.741 benchmark, and which hyperparameter mattered most (read optuna.importance.get_param_importances(study)).

Expected output 

$ python -m tamweel.models.baseline_lgbm
best_iteration=612  AUC=0.7863  PR-AUC=0.3120
$ python -m tamweel.models.tune_lgbm      # 40 trials, ~90s on a laptop
best AUC: 0.7911
best params: {'num_leaves': 41, 'min_child_samples': 140, ...}
param importance (top): num_leaves 0.38, min_child_samples 0.27, reg_lambda 0.14

Acceptance criteria: tuned validation AUC ≥ 0.785 and strictly greater than the baseline; early stopping used (no hand-set n_estimators); RESULTS.md names the top parameter.

Troubleshooting guidance

Symptom Cause Fix LightGBMError: Do not support special JSON characters in feature name Arabic/space column names Rename columns to English snake_case on load (course loader does this) Categorical columns treated as numeric Left as object/int codes Cast to pandas category; pass categorical_feature="auto" AUC suspiciously high (>0.95) A leaked feature (e.g. days_past_due) slipped in Preview Module 2 — drop post-outcome columns; the loader excludes them, custom code may not Optuna very slow in class Too many trials / no pruning Cap n_trials=40; ensure MedianPruner active; use provided study.pkl

Instructor notes. The deliberate learning_rate=0.3 step in task 3 is the highest-value 5 minutes — participants see early stopping cut the tree count and AUC drop, internalising the LR/count trade-off far better than a slide. Fast finishers: have them set num_leaves=511 with no min_child_samples and watch train-AUC → 0.99 while val-AUC falls (overfitting made visible), a perfect bridge to Module 2.

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz (5 questions) 1. In LightGBM, which parameter is the primary complexity control? (a) max_depth (b) num_leaves (c) n_estimators (d) learning_rate → b 2. You lower learning_rate from 0.1 to 0.03. What should happen to the early-stopped best_iteration_? → it increases (more, smaller steps). 3. Why never grid-search n_estimators? → early stopping selects it optimally per configuration for free. 4. Which importance type is biased toward high-cardinality features? → split/gain importance (motivates permutation/SHAP in M4). 5. True/False: max_depth=6 fully controls a LightGBM tree's size. → False (leaf-wise growth; num_leaves binds).

Coding exercise. Given a fixed dataset, produce a learning curve: plot train vs validation AUC against boosting round using evals_result. Identify the round where validation plateaus and training keeps rising — mark the overfitting onset.

Debugging exercise. A participant's model shows validation AUC below train AUC by 0.15 with num_leaves=255, min_child_samples=5. Diagnose and prescribe two parameter changes; predict their effect on the gap.

Discussion questions. - Your model gains 0.004 AUC from 300 more Optuna trials. Where else could that hour go for more business value? - When would you not reach for a GBDT on tabular data? (tiny n, need for a monotone/linear audit story, hard extrapolation beyond training range).

docs.title: Case Study — The Overfit Champion at a Riyadh Consumer Lender
docs.text:
Scenario. A data scientist at a Riyadh consumer-finance company reports an internal-validation AUC of 0.94 on default prediction — far above the team's usual 0.79 — and requests deployment. Risk is thrilled; the model lead is suspicious.

Business context. A 0.94-AUC default model would be worth tens of millions of SAR in avoided losses if real. It is not: the model was tuned with num_leaves=511, no min_child_samples, and — the real culprit — a feature current_dpd (current days-past-due) that only exists after the loan has started performing.

Technical challenge. Separate genuine boosting skill from overfitting and leakage. Retrain with disciplined complexity control and an application-time-only feature set.

Constraints. SAMA model-risk governance requires a defensible validation story; the model must be explainable (Module 4); the team has one week before a model-risk committee review.

Solution approach (facilitate, don't lecture). (1) Re-run with strong regularisation and early stopping — AUC falls to 0.80, the honest number. (2) Audit features for outcome leakage (full treatment is Module 2) — remove current_dpd and two siblings. (3) Show the learning curve before/after to the committee as evidence of discipline. (4) Frame the 0.80 as trustworthy vs the 0.94 as fictional.

How do you present "the number went down and that's good news" to a risk committee? 3. What repository/process control would have caught current_dpd before it reached tuning? 4. Is 0.80 good enough to ship? What other evidence (calibration, cost, fairness) does the committee need?
