docs.title: Timing Recommendations
docs.text:
• Protect Lab 4 (feature engineering, the leakage lesson) and Lab 6 (backtesting) at full length; compress the M6 theory if behind — it lands through the lab.
  • Day-3 afternoon is deliberately light on new theory so the backtest and capstone get uninterrupted build time; guard that.
  • If a cohort is strong: pull the multi-area global model (Module 4 case study) into the capstone main scope and add a fourth model family (TBATS/Prophet).
  • If a cohort is weak: reduce Lab 7 to two constraint scenarios and demo the third; never drop the backtest report — it is the course's deliverable and thesis made visible.
  • Hard rule: capstone assembly (Day 3 H4) must start on time; cut discussion, not build time. Collect repo URLs at the end of H4 so backtest results can be spot-checked before the H5 demos.

docs.title: Discussion Prompts (use during transitions)
docs.text:
1. "What is the most expensive forecasting error you've seen reach a decision — and would a backtest have caught it?"
  2. "Your model's MAPE is 1.6%. Your interval covers 90% on average but 78% on the hottest afternoons. Which number does the control room feel?"
  3. "When is the free seasonal-naive forecast the right answer, and how would your report prove it?"
  4. "Who owns the reserve-margin quantile — forecasting, operations, or risk? What does your answer imply about which number you publish?"
  5. "If the repository is the audit evidence for an accuracy claim, what does your current backtest testify?"

docs.title: Wrap-up (Day 3 final 15 minutes)
docs.text:
• Map each capstone requirement to the module that taught it (one slide): decomposition→M1, stationarity→M2, classical→M3, features→M4, intervals→M5, backtest→M6, selection→M7.
  • Reinforce the single thesis one last time: respect the arrow of time so every reported accuracy number would survive contact with the future. The leakage-safe features, the time-aware backtest, and the calibrated intervals are three faces of that one discipline.
  • Forward pointer: SDA-DSC-311 builds on this pipeline; SDA-DSC-213 (Experimentation & Causal Inference) is the sibling "what actually works" skill for decisions forecasting alone cannot answer.
  • Collect: repo URLs, BACKTEST_REPORT.md, DECISION_RECORD.md, BENCHMARKS.md; issue Forecasting-badge recommendations within 5 working days.

End of instructor package. All code samples target Python 3.12 with statsmodels ≥ 0.14, pmdarima ≥ 2.0, sktime ≥ 0.30, and LightGBM ≥ 4.0. Verify pinned versions in the course lock file before each delivery. The golden thread — the Tayyar national load-forecasting service on the ksa_grid_demand hourly series — runs unbroken from decomposition (Module 1) to the backtested, calibrated, defensibly-selected production pipeline of the capstone.

docs.title: SDA-DSC-212 — Time Series Analysis and Forecasting
تحليل السلاسل الزمنية والتنبؤ
docs.text:
Instructor-ready training package · SDAIA Academy · Data Scientist Track Specialist level · 3 days × 5 learning hours = 15 hours

Everything in this repository advances one artefact: Tayyar (تيّار), a day-ahead load-forecasting service for the Central Operating Area of the Saudi grid. Three years of hourly demand carry every lesson in the course — from decomposition, through classical and ML models, to probabilistic day-ahead forecasts validated by rolling-origin backtests.

The thesis. Respect the arrow of time, so that every reported accuracy number would survive contact with the future. The leakage-safe features, the time-aware backtest and the calibrated intervals are three faces of that one discipline.

docs.title: What is here
docs.text: Path What it is SDA-DSC-212_Time_Series_Training_Deck.pptx The 46-slide master deck covering all three days, with speaker notes on every slide notebooks/ 14 notebooks — a start and a solution for each of the seven labs src/tayyar/ The reference implementation the labs build against data/ The Tayyar datasets, including the deliberately messy raw file tools/ Generators for the data, the reference run, the figures, the posters and the assessment workbook figures/ Every chart and diagram used in the deck, regenerable from real data assessment/ Capstone brief and the assessment workbook (quiz bank, rubrics, scoring sheets) templates/ DECISION_RECORD.md and BACKTEST_REPORT.md skeletons for participants case_studies/ Four facilitator briefs: electricity load, retail demand, government service demand, traffic flow instructor/ Facilitator run-sheet, A4 posters, the data and resource catalogue, the leakage exercise reference_results.json Every number quoted in the deck and the notebooks, regenerable config.yaml The single committed config the pipeline runs from

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements.txt
make doctor        # verify the environment; prints OK/MISS per package and dataset
make data          # regenerate every dataset (deterministic, seed 212)
make reference     # run the reference pipeline -> reference_results.json + figures/
jupyter lab notebooks/

make all rebuilds the datasets, the reference numbers, the figures, the posters, the deck and the assessment workbook, in that order.

docs.title: Course outline
docs.text: Day Theme Modules End-of-day deliverable 1 Seeing the signal M1 structure & decomposition · M2 stationarity & autocorrelation Clean hourly series + decomposition panel + stationarity report 2 Building forecasts M3 ARIMA & exponential smoothing · M4 feature-based ML · M5 probabilistic (starts) SARIMAX, ETS and a LightGBM forecaster, all producing 24-hour forecasts 3 Trust and selection M5 intervals & calibration · M6 backtesting & evaluation · M7 case study · capstone Rolling-origin backtest report, calibrated intervals, model-selection decision

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. LO1 Analyse trend, seasonality and autocorrelation structure in time series
  2. LO2 Develop classical forecasting models including ARIMA and exponential smoothing
  3. LO3 Implement ML and gradient-boosting approaches with engineered temporal features
  4. LO4 Design backtesting frameworks with proper time-based validation
  5. LO5 Evaluate forecasts using scale-appropriate accuracy and uncertainty metrics
  6. LO6 Compare model families to select the right approach per use case

docs.title: The labs
docs.text:
Lab Title Module The trap it teaches 1 Load, index and decompose the Tayyar series M1 A silent gap is invisible until you declare the frequency 2 The stationarity report M2 ADF and KPSS have opposite null hypotheses 3 Classical baselines: SARIMAX and ETS M3 An exogenous regressor you will not have at forecast time is a leak 4 LightGBM feature-based forecaster M4 Two planted leaks: a shuffle split and a centred rolling window 5 Calibrated day-ahead intervals M5 Two planted bugs: a confidence interval, and coverage measured on the training set 6 The rolling-origin backtest report M6 One planted leak: a "backtest" that fits once and scores in-sample 7 End-to-end selection and the decision record M7 One planted fault: selection by argmin(MASE) alone

Every start notebook is genuinely broken in the way described. Every solution notebook executes end to end and reproduces the numbers in reference_results.json.

docs.title: Reference results
docs.text:
The reference run produces, among others:

Series 26,280 hourly rows, 2021–2023, Asia/Riyadh, peak ≈ 57.9 GW Decomposition daily strength 0.97 · weekly 0.61 · trend 0.97 · multiplicative (level/swing corr 0.94) Stationarity one seasonal difference at m = 24 suffices — D = 1, d = 0 Classical (daily peak, 28-day hold-out) SARIMAX + temperature MASE 0.333 · SARIMA no-exog 0.342 · ETS 0.434 ML (60 rolling origins, 24 h horizon) LightGBM MASE 0.445 · seasonal-naive 0.770 · DM p < 0.001 Intervals raw quantile band coverage 0.786 → 0.902 after CQR, but only 0.845 on peak hours Leakage demonstration a leaked design reports a model 2.3× more accurate than it actually is

The peak-hour coverage shortfall is deliberate and is taught, not hidden: conformal prediction guarantees marginal coverage, not conditional coverage.

docs.title: About the data
docs.text:
data/ksa_grid_demand.csv is synthetic, generated by tools/make_tayyar_data.py with a documented design: a growth trend, three seasonalities, a piecewise weather response with a 21 °C balance point, Ramadan / Eid / National Day calendar effects, a structural break in October 2022, and AR(1) innovations. The qualitative shape follows publicly documented behaviour of hot-arid grid load; UCI's ElectricityLoadDiagrams20112014 (CC BY 4.0) is the reference for the daily cycle and noise scale.

It is synthetic on purpose. Ground truth is known, so grading is objective; the series is reproducible across cohorts; and nothing depends on operational grid data that cannot be distributed. The limit is worth stating to participants: a model that does well here has not been validated against real telemetry. See instructor/DATA_AND_RESOURCE_CATALOG.md for the full design note, the planted defects, and the open datasets to use for a real-data variant.

The raw file ships with deliberate defects — 19 duplicate timestamps, out-of-order rows, 64 missing hours in 34 runs, and 7 sensor zeros. Lab 1 exists to find them.

docs.title: Capstone Project — Tayyar: a backtested day-ahead load-forecasting service
docs.text: SDA-DSC-212 · Time Series Analysis and Forecasting · 40% of the course grade

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are the forecasting lead for Tayyar (تيّار), the national load-forecasting service you have been building since Day 1. The operations-planning unit of the grid operator has asked for a production-ready day-ahead forecasting pipeline for the Central Operating Area, plus a backtest report it can put in front of the regulator and the control room.

Everything you built in Labs 1–7 is a component. The capstone is the integration, plus one extension of your own. The service must forecast the next 24 hours of hourly demand, deliver a calibrated interval for reserve sizing, and — crucially — prove its own accuracy through a rolling-origin backtest that respects the arrow of time.

The repository is the evidence. A stranger should clone it, run one command, and reproduce every number in your report.

docs.title: 1. Clean, reproducible pipeline · LO1
docs.text: A src/tayyar package that runs end to end from a committed config: load → clean/index → decompose → feature-build → fit candidates → backtest → select → report. Fixed splits and seeds; pinned dependencies; a single make run (or python -m tayyar.pipeline.run) reproduces every reported number.

docs.title: 2. Decomposition and diagnostics · LO1
docs.text: A correct tz-aware hourly DatetimeIndex with explicit frequency and a stated gap policy. MSTL decomposition with reported daily and weekly seasonal strengths. A stationarity report (ADF + KPSS, reconciled) with the chosen (d, D) justified.

docs.title: 3. At least three model families · LO2, LO3
docs.text: A seasonal-naive baseline, one classical model (SARIMAX with temperature and calendar, or ETS), and one feature-based ML model (LightGBM). Every model leakage-safe and reproducible.

docs.title: 4. Calibrated probabilistic forecast · LO5
docs.text:
A 90% day-ahead prediction interval with empirical coverage in 0.88–0.92 on the held-out test window, produced by quantile regression plus conformal calibration (CQR) or an equivalently justified method. Coverage reported marginally and by hour-of-day.

This is the requirement most submissions miss, and they miss it for one reason: they calibrate on a window from a different regime. Exchangeability is an assumption, not a formality.

docs.title: 5. Rolling-origin backtest · LO4
docs.text: At least 50 origins, expanding or sliding window, 24-hour horizon, no temporal leakage — the training data at every origin must end at or before that origin. Report MASE (against seasonal-naive), a percentage metric, coverage, and pinball loss per model. Include a per-origin breakdown that flags Eid and heatwave weeks. If your compute budget forces a retrain cadence coarser than "refit at every origin", say so and quantify the effect on a subsample — a stated budget decision is engineering; an unstated one is a defect.

docs.title: 6. Model-selection decision · LO6
docs.text: A DECISION_RECORD.md recommending one production model with evidence: a Diebold-Mariano test against the runner-up, the constraints and weights you applied, your flip-conditions, a fallback for the weeks the champion loses, and a monitoring contract (metrics, thresholds, retrain cadence).

docs.title: 7. Report and communication · LO5, LO6
docs.text: A BACKTEST_REPORT.md an operator would accept — the comparison table, the decision, the known limits — plus a decision-language reserve brief with no unexplained jargon. BENCHMARKS.md filled in with your measured numbers.

docs.title: Choose at least one extension
docs.text:
Extension What it must show Multi-area global model Extend to all four operating areas with a global LightGBM (area_id categorical); backtest per area against per-area baselines Adaptive conformal (ACI / EnbPI) Replace static CQR with an online-updating interval; show improved conditional summer-afternoon coverage Weather-uncertainty propagation Widen the interval to reflect temperature-forecast error; show the coverage impact using temp_forecast_28d.csv Automated retraining trigger A monitor that fires when rolling MASE or coverage breaches threshold, with a test proving it fires on injected drift Champion / challenger harness A scheduled backtest that continuously re-evaluates a challenger against the incumbent and reports promotion eligibility

The extension adds up to +5 bonus, capped at 100, and only if mandatory scope scores ≥ 80.

docs.title: Target architecture
docs.text:
config.yaml ──► tayyar.pipeline.run
   │
   ├─ data.load ─► clean tz-aware hourly series (gaps materialised)
   ├─ analysis  ─► MSTL decomposition + ADF/KPSS stationarity report
   ├─ features  ─► lags · rolling(.shift(1)) · calendar(Fri–Sat, Ramadan/Eid) · Fourier
   ├─ models    ─► seasonal-naive · SARIMAX+temp / ETS · LightGBM · quantile+CQR
   ├─ eval      ─► rolling origins → MASE / MAPE / coverage / pinball
   └─ pipeline  ─► constraint-weighted select → DECISION_RECORD + BACKTEST_REPORT + brief

Serving view:  origin features → champion → {p50, p90, p95} → reserve brief (with Eid fallback)

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
1. A git repository URL (public or instructor-shared) with full history and checkpoint commits.
  2. A one-command reproducible run that regenerates every reported number from the committed config.
  3. BACKTEST_REPORT.md — the model-comparison table, the per-origin breakdown, the calibrated-interval coverage, and the model-selection decision.
  4. DECISION_RECORD.md — recommendation, constraints and weights, DM evidence, flip-conditions, fallback, monitoring contract.
  5. BENCHMARKS.md — the benchmark table filled from your runs.
  6. A 5-minute demo: clone-to-running, one day-ahead forecast with its interval, the backtest table, and the decision defended — including where the model loses.

docs.title: Milestones and gates
docs.text: Milestone Due Gate M-A clean series + decomposition + stationarity report End Day 1 instructor spot-check of index, gaps, strengths M-B classical + ML models producing 24 h forecasts End Day 2 leak check PASS; forecasts vs actuals plotted M-C calibrated 90% interval Day 3 H1 coverage 0.88–0.92 on the held-out window M-D rolling-origin backtest + DM selection Day 3 H3 ≥ 50 origins, no leak, champion chosen M-E decision record + extension + demo Day 3 H5 rubric scoring

docs.title: Anti-pattern flags
docs.text:
Any one of these caps its criterion at 70%:

  • train_test_split(shuffle=True), anywhere
  • a centred rolling feature
  • a "backtest" that scores in-sample
  • MAPE reported without MASE or a named baseline
  • a champion declared on a sub-1% gap with no Diebold-Mariano test
  • a confidence interval where a prediction interval is required

Pass ≥ 70. Distinction ≥ 90.

docs.title: What earns marks that a sharper model does not
docs.text: A report that names where the model loses — the Eid weeks, the summer afternoons where conditional coverage falls short — and ships a documented fallback scores above a silent, marginally sharper submission. Candour is a deliverable.

docs.title: Case Study 1 — Day-Ahead Load Forecasting for the Central Operating Area
docs.text: SDA-DSC-212 · Time Series Analysis and Forecasting · Facilitator brief

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
Primary module fit M7 — Forecasting Case Study (integrates M1–M6) Secondary fit M3 (SARIMAX vs ETS), M5 (interval calibration), M6 (rolling-origin evidence) LOs exercised LO6 primary; LO1–LO5 as integration Suggested slot Day 3, Hour 4 — 50 minutes, immediately before capstone demos Alternative slot Day 1, Hour 1 as a 15-minute framing of the golden thread (scenario + decision question only) Duration 50 minutes Group size 3–4 participants; 5–6 groups in a room of 20 Data source data/ksa_grid_demand.csv, data/ksa_calendar.csv, data/temp_forecast_14d.csv (this repository)

This is the primary case. It is not a detour from Tayyar — it is Tayyar, stated as a business problem rather than a modelling exercise, and it is the last thing participants discuss before they defend their own capstone.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The Central Operating Area covers Riyadh and its industrial belt and is the largest of the four areas the national grid operator dispatches. Its demand in the course dataset runs from about 18,500 MW on a January night to 57,852 MW on the evening of 20 July 2023 — a factor of just over three between the annual trough and the annual peak, almost all of it cooling load. Annual mean demand rose from 31,744 MW in 2021 to 34,630 MW in 2023.

Nouf Al-Harthi is the day-ahead scheduling engineer in the operations-planning unit. Every afternoon at 14:00 she publishes the next day's hourly demand schedule. Generation units are committed against it: which plants run, which are held spinning, which are cold. Units with slow start-up curves cannot be recalled once the schedule is issued, and the interconnector schedule with the neighbouring area is agreed on the same numbers. If Nouf's schedule is too low, the control room buys expensive fast-start capacity inside the day or, in the worst case, sheds feeders. If it is too high, gas is burned turning turbines that nothing needs.

Nouf currently uses a similar-day method: take the same weekday two weeks ago, scale by a temperature ratio, and adjust by hand for Ramadan and holidays. It works, and its weakness is exactly where it costs most — the first hot week of May, the days either side of Eid, and the afternoon of a heatwave. She has asked for a forecasting service. She has also said, plainly, that she will not put a number in front of the control room that she cannot explain, and that a model which is right on average but wrong on the four hardest weeks of the year is worse than the method she has now.

The decision she makes differently depending on the answer is concrete: the reserve margin she carries between 12:00 and 18:00 tomorrow. A tighter, better-calibrated interval lets her carry less spinning reserve for the same risk. A wider or miscalibrated one costs money every day, or costs a feeder once.

docs.title: The decision question
docs.text: At 14:00 today, how much generation capacity should the operator prepare for each hour tomorrow?

docs.title: Business context and the cost of being wrong
docs.text:
The two errors are not symmetric, and the whole design of the service follows from that.

Take the 2023 system peak of 57,852 MW. A 1% error at peak is 579 MW — roughly one mid-size gas turbine. Using illustrative cost figures (participants should be told these are teaching numbers, not the operator's published tariffs):

Over-forecast by 579 MW Under-forecast by 579 MW What happens 579 MW held spinning across a 6-hour afternoon window that nothing dispatches 579 MW of capacity short at the peak hour Illustrative unit cost ~USD 40 / MWh incremental fuel and O&M on idle spinning reserve ~USD 5,000 / MWh value of lost load Cost of the error 579 MW × 6 h × 40 = ~USD 139,000 per day 579 MW × 1 h × 5,000 = ~USD 2.9 million

The ratio is roughly 20:1 per hour of exposure, and that ratio has a direct technical consequence. The newsvendor solution to an asymmetric loss is the quantile q* = c_under / (c_under + c_over). With 5,000 and 40 that is 0.992. This is why an operator schedules to something near the upper tail, not to the median, and why a service that reports only a point forecast is answering a question nobody asked. It is also why a symmetric metric — MAE, RMSE, MAPE — cannot by itself select the production model for this decision.

Nouf's real ask is therefore not "the most accurate model". It is a calibrated upper quantile she can defend, plus an honest statement of where it fails.

docs.title: What makes this series hard
docs.text:
Three seasonal periods at once. Daily (m = 24), weekly (m = 168), annual (m ≈ 8,766). In the course data MSTL puts daily seasonal strength at 0.972 and weekly at 0.610 — the daily cycle is nearly deterministic, the weekly one is real but far weaker. Any single-seasonality SARIMA specification has to choose one and let the others leak into the residuals.

The weekend is Friday and Saturday. In pandas dayofweek (Monday = 0) that is [4, 5]. Every cohort produces at least one model that has quietly assumed Saturday–Sunday.

Weather is not a linear driver. Demand responds to a balance point: above roughly 21 °C cooling load rises steeply with temperature and slightly convexly; below about 14 °C a much milder heating response appears; in between the response is nearly flat. Monthly mean temperature in the dataset runs from 13.8 °C in January to 38.2 °C in July, with an absolute maximum of 49.5 °C. A model given raw temp_c and a linear term will fit the middle of the year and miss both ends. Cooling- and heating-degree features (cdd = max(temp − 21, 0), hdd = max(14 − temp, 0)) encode the physics directly.

Temperature is exogenous, and at serve time it is a forecast, not an observation. This is the single most important operational point in the case. At 14:00 today, tomorrow's temperature is itself a prediction. data/temp_forecast_14d.csv carries 48 weekly origins through 2023 with realistic error growth: mean absolute error 0.79 °C at leads of 1–24 h, rising to 1.08 °C at 24–72 h and 2.05 °C beyond a week. A model validated on realised temperature and served on forecast temperature is optimistic by an amount nobody has measured.

Ramadan is a shape change, not a level change. In the generative design daytime demand (06:00–15:00) falls by about 7% and the post-Iftar window (19:00–01:00) rises by about 7.5%. A single is_ramadan dummy captures none of this — it needs an interaction with hour-of-day. Eid drops the level by roughly 9.5% for four to five days; National Day by about 4.5% for one. The Hijri dates move about eleven days earlier each Gregorian year, so a model that learned "April is a Ramadan month" from 2021–2022 will apply it wrongly to 2023.

A structural break. On 1 October 2022 a large industrial customer connects and the level steps up by about 3.1%. It is not a trend, not seasonality, and not an outlier. It is a permanent regime change in the middle of the training window, and it is why the stationarity report in reference_results.json reads ADF p = 0.026 (stationary) against KPSS p = 0.01 (not stationary) — the classic difference-stationary verdict caused by a level shift.

Data-quality traps in the raw file. ksa_grid_demand.csv has 26,235 rows against a true 26,280 hours: 64 missing hours in 34 runs (the longest is 5 hours), 19 duplicated timestamps, 7 sensor zeros in demand_mw, and rows that are not monotonic in time — 192 positions where the timestamp goes backwards. A read_csv followed straight into a model will train on a series that is silently out of order, and a log transform will fail or produce -inf on the zeros.

docs.title: Technical agenda
docs.text:
What participants actually investigate, in order:

  1. Build a defensible index (M1). Read the raw file, sort, de-duplicate with a stated rule, reindex onto a complete tz-aware hourly DatetimeIndex in Asia/Riyadh so the 64 gaps become explicit NaN, and record a gap policy. Decide what a zero means and defend the decision.
  2. Decompose and choose the transform (M1). MSTL with periods [24, 168]. Report seasonal strengths. Test whether the seasonal swing scales with the level (in the reference run the level–swing correlation is 0.937, which argues for multiplicative structure and therefore a log transform).
  3. Reconcile ADF and KPSS, and locate the break (M2). Run both tests, reconcile the verdicts, choose (d, D) — the reference solution reaches stationarity at (d=0, D=1) on the seasonal difference — and decide separately how to handle the October 2022 step: dummy, split sample, or ignore with justification.
  4. Fit the classical candidates (M3). Seasonal-naive baseline; SARIMAX with temperature and calendar regressors; ETS. Compare like for like on a common held-out window. Read the residual diagnostics honestly — in the reference run SARIMAX beats ETS on every point metric (MAPE 2.05% vs 2.68%) but its Ljung-Box p-value is 0.000, meaning structure remains in the residuals and the model is under-specified.
  5. Reduce the problem to a supervised matrix (M4). Lags, .shift(1)-guarded rolling statistics, Fourier terms for the three periods, calendar flags, degree-day features. Assert no leakage before fitting anything. Interpret feature importance by family — the reference build splits gain roughly 33% rolling, 29% lag, 26% Fourier, 7% calendar, 5% weather.
  6. Produce and calibrate an interval (M5). Quantile LightGBM plus split-conformal calibration. The reference run moves 90% coverage from 0.786 to 0.902 at the cost of widening the mean interval from 2,418 MW to 3,235 MW — and conditional coverage in the 12:00–18:00 peak window is still only 0.845. That gap is the case's most instructive number.
  7. Backtest, then choose (M6, M7). Sixty rolling origins at a 24-hour horizon. Report MASE against seasonal-naive, a percentage metric, coverage and pinball loss. Run Diebold-Mariano against the runner-up. Then apply the constraints below and write a decision record with flip-conditions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: Constraint What it does to model choice Publication deadline The schedule is issued at 14:00. Feature build, fit and forecast must complete inside a short window with room for a failed run. Refitting a large-m seasonal ARIMA at every origin does not fit; a pre-fitted model with a fast forecast step, or a gradient-boosted model with a cached feature store, does. Explainability Nouf must narrate the number to a control-room shift engineer and, eventually, to a regulator. A component story ("trend plus daily cycle plus 3,100 MW of cooling load at 44 °C") is worth real accuracy. Feature importance is not the same thing and must not be presented as causal. Serve-time data availability A SARIMAX with temperature cannot be served without a temperature forecast for every hour of tomorrow. If the weather feed fails at 13:40, what runs? The service needs a degraded-mode fallback that uses no exogenous input. Cost asymmetry Selection must be driven by an asymmetric or quantile loss, not by MAE. A model that wins on MAE and loses on upper-tail pinball loss is the wrong model for this decision. Maintenance A feature pipeline is a standing liability with an owner and an on-call rota. A 0.2 percentage-point MAPE gain that costs a permanent engineering commitment is a bad trade for a unit of this size, and participants should be willing to say so. Known-weak weeks Eid weeks and the first heatwave of the season are where the method being replaced already fails. A replacement that also fails there has not solved the problem, whatever its annual average says.

docs.title: Facilitation plan
docs.text:
Fifty minutes. The facilitator's job is to keep groups on the decision and off the leaderboard.

Minutes Phase What the facilitator does 0–5 Setup Read the decision question aloud. Put the 579 MW arithmetic and the 20:1 ratio on the board. State the constraint list without discussing it. Assign each group a role, not a model: Group 1 argues for SARIMAX, Group 2 for LightGBM+CQR, Group 3 for ETS, Group 4 for seasonal-naive-plus-conformal. Say explicitly that groups are assigned, not choosing — the point is to make the strongest case for a position, including one they disagree with. 5–20 Small-group work Groups build the case for their assigned family using the backtest numbers they generated in Lab 6 and the constraint table. Circulate. Ask one question per group and move on: to the SARIMAX group, "what runs at 13:40 if the weather feed is down?"; to the LightGBM group, "who owns the feature pipeline in year two?"; to the ETS group, "show me the Eid week"; to the naive group, "what is the interval and how did you calibrate it?" Do not answer. Do not correct a wrong number yet — note it for the debrief. 20–34 Plenary — the advocacy round Three minutes per group, strictly timed, standing. Rule: each group must state one condition under which its own recommendation should be abandoned. Hold every group to it; a group that cannot name a flip-condition has not finished thinking. After the last group, ask the room for a show of hands and record the split on the board without comment. 34–44 Plenary — the constraint sweep Take the constraints one at a time and ask which recommendations survive each. Deliberately reorder the weights halfway through: "the regulator has just asked for the model's reasoning in writing" — then ask who changes their vote. The teaching point is that the answer moves with the constraint weights and that the weights must therefore be written down, which is exactly what DECISION_RECORD.md demands. 44–50 Debrief Correct the numbers you noted while circulating, briefly and without naming groups. Then state the one thing to carry into the capstone: the deliverable is a recommendation with evidence and flip-conditions, not a model. Show the conditional coverage figure — 0.902 marginal, 0.845 in the peak window — and let it sit for a moment before closing.

docs.title: Discussion questions
docs.text:
1. Nouf will not publish a number she cannot explain. Does that constraint have a price, and what is it here? A good answer names the accuracy gap between the interpretable candidate and the ML candidate from the group's own backtest, converts it to MW at the peak, and then argues either that the gap is small enough to buy the explainability or that it is large enough to justify investing in an explanation layer instead. An answer that treats explainability as free, or as a soft preference to be overruled by MAPE, has missed the point.

2. The service is validated on realised temperature but served on forecast temperature. How much of the reported accuracy is real? A good answer proposes measuring it rather than estimating it: re-run the backtest substituting temp_forecast_14d.csv at the matching lead, and report the degradation. It should note that the day-ahead lead has only about 0.79 °C mean absolute error, so the effect may be modest at h+24 and severe at h+168, and that the interval — not just the point forecast — must widen to absorb weather uncertainty. The strongest answers observe that this is a form of training–serving skew and belongs in the monitoring contract.

3. Conditional coverage in the 12:00–18:00 window is 0.845 against a marginal 0.902. Is the service fit to publish? A good answer takes a position and pays for it. Either: no, because the hours that miss are exactly the hours the reserve decision is made, and marginal coverage is the wrong guarantee for an hour-specific decision — so calibrate conditionally, by hour block. Or: yes, provisionally, with the shortfall documented and an operational buffer applied to peak hours until conditional calibration ships. Both are defensible; "0.902 is inside 0.88–0.92 so we pass" is not.

4. How should the October 2022 structural break be handled, and what would change your mind? A good answer enumerates the options — a step dummy, discarding pre-break data, a shorter training window, letting the model learn it through recent lags — and evaluates them against the cost of each. Discarding pre-break data removes the only two summers in the record, which matters more for a summer-peaking series than the bias from the step does. A good answer names that trade-off explicitly rather than picking an option by habit.

5. If the asymmetric cost ratio is 20:1, why not simply forecast the 99th percentile every hour? A good answer works through what happens: the interval becomes so wide that the reserve is effectively fixed, the forecast stops informing the decision, and the daily over-forecast cost compounds into a figure comparable with the rare shedding event it is avoiding. It should also question the 5,000 USD/MWh figure itself — the value of lost load is a policy input, not a measurement, and the whole quantile choice hangs off it. The best answers ask who owns that number and observe that it should appear in the decision record as an assumption, not a constant.

6. What single monitoring signal would tell you first that this service has stopped working? A good answer prefers a leading signal to a lagging one, and prefers a decision-relevant signal to a statistical one — rolling conditional coverage in the peak window, or rolling MASE against the seasonal-naive baseline, will move before annual MAPE does. It should name a threshold and what happens when the threshold is breached, because a monitor with no action attached is decoration.

docs.title: Expected outputs
docs.text:
Each group hands in, on one side of paper or one slide:

  1. A named recommendation: one model family, for this decision, at this horizon.
  2. The evidence: three to five numbers from the group's own backtest, including at least one probabilistic metric and one comparison against a named baseline.
  3. The constraint weighting actually applied, written as weights or as an ordering, with the reasoning for the top constraint.
  4. Two flip-conditions — specific, measurable events that would reverse the recommendation.
  5. A degraded-mode fallback: what the service publishes at 14:00 when its primary input is missing.
  6. One sentence naming where the model loses.

Item 6 is not optional and is graded as heavily as item 1.

docs.title: Common failure modes in this case
docs.text: Failure mode What it looks like Facilitator's redirect Leaderboard thinking The group ranks candidates by MAPE and stops. The constraint table is never opened. "Your winner is 0.3 points ahead. Show me the Diebold-Mariano test. Now show me who maintains it in 2027." Force the constraint sweep before any recommendation is spoken aloud. Point forecast only The recommendation is a single hourly number. The reserve margin is never mentioned. "Nouf has your forecast. Tell her how much reserve to carry." The question cannot be answered without a quantile, and groups discover that faster by being asked than by being told. Realised temperature treated as available The service assumes tomorrow's temperature is known because the training data contains it. "It is 14:00. Where does tomorrow's 15:00 temperature come from?" Then point them at temp_forecast_14d.csv and the 0.79 °C day-ahead error. Ramadan as a single dummy One binary flag, no hour interaction; the model under-forecasts every Iftar evening and over-forecasts every Ramadan morning. Ask the group to plot the average hourly profile inside and outside Ramadan on the same axes. The two curves cross, and no additive flag can represent that. Coverage read marginally and declared done 0.902 is inside the 0.88–0.92 band, so the interval is pronounced calibrated. "Which hours miss?" Have them recompute coverage by hour block on the spot. The 0.845 peak-window number ends the discussion faster than any explanation. The break is differenced away without being understood Seasonal differencing removes the level step, the KPSS test passes, and nobody has noticed a permanent +3.1% regime change. "What happened on 1 October 2022?" A model that cannot answer that question will misattribute the step to trend and extrapolate it.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
File Rows Use in this case data/ksa_grid_demand.csv 26,235 The raw series. Hourly, Asia/Riyadh, 2021-01-01 to 2023-12-31, columns timestamp, demand_mw, temp_c. Contains the planted defects — use this file, not the clean one, so the cleaning decisions stay visible. data/ksa_calendar.csv 1,095 Daily calendar flags: is_weekend, is_ramadan, is_eid, is_national_day, is_founding_day. Join on date, not on timestamp. data/temp_forecast_14d.csv 16,128 48 weekly origins through 2023, 336 hours each. Required for question 2. data/ksa_grid_demand_4area.csv 105,120 Optional. Four operating areas in long format, for groups that want to argue the multi-area maintenance case.

Preparation. No preparation is needed beyond the repository itself, and by Day 3 every group already has a cleaned series and a backtest from Labs 1–6. If the case is run cold — with a group that has not done the labs — allow an extra 20 minutes and hand out ksa_grid_demand_clean.csv (26,280 rows, no defects) instead of the raw file, so the session is spent on the decision rather than on data repair.

A word on the data's status. The series is synthetic by design. The structure it contains is planted and therefore known, which is what makes it gradeable. The consequence is that a model which performs well here has been validated against a generative process, not against real grid telemetry, and no participant should claim otherwise in their capstone. See instructor/DATA_AND_RESOURCE_CATALOG.md for the full generative design and its limits.

docs.title: Case Study 2 — Retail Demand and the Replenishment Decision
docs.text: SDA-DSC-212 · Time Series Analysis and Forecasting · Facilitator brief

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
Primary module fit M4 — Feature-Based ML Forecasting (multi-series, rolling features, leakage) Secondary fit M5 (asymmetric loss motivates quantiles), M6 (WAPE, MASE, RMSSE and horizon alignment) LOs exercised LO3 primary; LO5 and LO6 in the debrief Suggested slot Day 2, Hour 5 — the first half of the M5 slot, as the motivation for probabilistic forecasting Alternative slot Day 2, Hour 3, as a contrast case inside M4 theory (drop the plenary to 8 minutes) Duration 40 minutes Group size 3–4 participants Data source Kaggle Store Sales — Time Series Forecasting, or the M5 Forecasting dataset. Runs as a paper case with no data if connectivity is unavailable. See Data below.

This case exists to break one habit the electricity series encourages: that the model with the smallest error is the model you should ship. In retail it usually is not, and the reason is arithmetic rather than opinion.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A grocery chain operates 54 stores across the Kingdom and carries roughly 33 product families per store. Replenishment for the ambient categories runs on a weekly cycle with a lead time of seven days: the order placed on Sunday arrives the following Sunday and has to cover the week after that. Fresh categories run daily with a two-day lead time. Nothing about the forecast horizon is a modelling preference — it is set by the logistics contract.

Reem Al-Dossari is the demand planner for the ambient categories. Every Sunday morning she approves about 1,800 store-family order quantities. She does not approve them individually; a planning system proposes quantities from a forecast and she overrides the ones that look wrong, which in practice means the ones a store manager has complained about. Her performance is measured on two numbers that pull against each other: on-shelf availability, which the commercial team watches, and shrink and markdown, which finance watches.

The analytics team has replaced the incumbent moving-average forecast with a gradient-boosted model. Aggregate MAE across all store-family series improved by 18%. Three months later, Reem's availability has not improved and her markdown has risen. She wants to know why a better forecast made her decision worse.

The decision she makes differently is the order quantity per store-family for the coming week — specifically, how much cover to carry above the expected demand. Today that buffer is a flat percentage applied to every series. What she actually needs is a buffer that differs by series and by week, and a forecast that tells her which weeks are uncertain.

docs.title: The decision question
docs.text: How many units of each store-family should be ordered this Sunday to cover the week after next, given a seven-day lead time?

docs.title: Business context and the cost of being wrong
docs.text:
The two errors have different names, different owners and different sizes, and that asymmetry is the entire case.

Take one ambient store-family, using illustrative figures that should be stated as teaching numbers:

Value Mean weekly demand 60 units Standard deviation of weekly demand 18 units Unit margin on a sale SAR 12 Cost of an unsold unit (holding + eventual markdown) SAR 4

The critical ratio is q* = c_under / (c_under + c_over) = 12 / (12 + 4) = **0.75**. The cost-minimising order is the 75th percentile of the demand distribution, not its mean.

Under a normal approximation that is 60 + 0.674 × 18 ≈ 72 units. Ordering the mean instead — which is exactly what an MAE-optimal point forecast delivers — leaves the shelf short in about half of all weeks rather than a quarter, and costs 12 × E[shortfall] on each of them. Across 1,800 store-families the difference is not a rounding error, and it is invisible to every symmetric accuracy metric on the dashboard.

This is why Reem's MAE improved and her outcome did not. A model tuned to the conditional mean is optimising a loss function that her business does not have. The correction is not a better point model; it is a quantile forecast at the ratio her cost structure implies, and a different ratio for a fresh category where the unsold unit is written off entirely (c_over rises, q* falls, and the optimal buffer shrinks).

docs.title: What makes this series hard
docs.text:
It is not one series, it is thousands. Fifty-four stores times thirty-three families is around 1,780 series, most of them short, many of them sparse. Fitting an individual model per series is neither affordable nor statistically sensible for the sparse ones. This is the multi-series problem: a global model with a series identifier as a categorical feature, learning shared structure across series while retaining series-level level and shape.

Intermittent demand. A meaningful fraction of store-family combinations sell zero units in most periods. On a zero-heavy series MAPE is undefined and MAE is minimised by forecasting zero forever — an all-zeros forecast can be the accuracy winner and is worthless. This is the case for RMSSE or MASE against a seasonal-naive denominator, and for Croston-style methods being mentioned by name even though the course does not teach them.

Promotions are an exogenous driver that is known in the future. Promotional calendars are planned weeks ahead, which makes them one of the rare covariates genuinely available at serve time — unlike weather in CS1, which is itself a forecast. That makes promotions high-value features and high-risk ones: a model trained with an accurate promotional flag and served with a provisional one degrades quietly.

Calendar effects that are not weekly. Pay-cycle effects near month end; Ramadan, where category behaviour diverges sharply (staples and dates rise, prepared foods shift by time of day); Eid, where the pattern is a pre-holiday surge followed by a trough; back-to-school. These are multiplicative and category-specific, and a single global holiday dummy will average them into uselessness.

Lag leakage, in a form specific to panel data. Two variants bite here that do not arise in a single series: a scaler or target encoder fitted on the whole panel, which lets one store's future inform another store's past; and a lag computed after a groupby that has not been sorted within group. Both produce plausible, wrong numbers.

Horizon and lead time must match. The forecast has to cover the lead-time demand — the sum of demand over the seven days between the order arriving and the next order arriving — not the demand on any single day. A daily model evaluated on daily error tells you nothing directly about the quantity that matters; the error of the sum over the lead time is the relevant quantity, and it is not the sum of the daily errors because the errors are correlated.

Structural change from range decisions. A product delisted, a store refitted, a new private-label line introduced. Series start, stop and step for commercial reasons that no time-series diagnostic will explain.

docs.title: Technical agenda
docs.text:
1. Frame the loss before touching a model (M5, M7). Derive the critical ratio from the margin and holding cost. State the quantile the business needs. Write it down before any model is fitted — the whole case turns on this happening first.
  2. Build the panel and the leakage guards (M4). Long format with store_id, family, date. Lags and rolling statistics computed within series, on a sorted index, with .shift(1) before every rolling window. Assert that no feature at time t uses an observation at or after t.
  3. Engineer the calendar and promotional features (M4). Day of week, day of month, pay-cycle proximity, holiday flags with lead and lag windows (the day before Eid matters more than Eid itself), promotion flags, and promotion flags for the following week where they are genuinely known at order time.
  4. Fit a global model against per-series baselines (M4). One LightGBM across the panel with series identifiers as categoricals, versus seasonal-naive per series and a simple per-series ETS. Test whether the global model helps the sparse series or only the dense ones — this is usually the most surprising result of the session.
  5. Choose metrics that survive zeros (M6). WAPE for aggregation across series of different scales; MASE or RMSSE against a seasonal-naive denominator; MAE per series for diagnostics. Demonstrate concretely that MAPE is unusable on the sparse series rather than asserting it.
  6. Re-evaluate at the decision horizon (M6). Aggregate the forecast over the seven-day lead window and score that. Compare the ranking of models under daily error against the ranking under lead-time error, and note whether the champion changes.
  7. Produce the quantile the decision needs (M5). Refit at q = 0.75 with pinball loss, or calibrate an interval and take the upper quantile. Score with pinball loss at that quantile, not with MAE, and compute the resulting inventory outcome — units short and units unsold — for both the mean forecast and the quantile forecast.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: Constraint What it does to model choice Lead time is fixed by contract The horizon is not tunable. A model that is excellent at h+1 and mediocre at h+7 is mediocre for this decision. 1,800 decisions a week, one planner The output must be trustworthy enough to auto-approve most lines. That means the model's uncertainty has to be usable as an exception filter: flag the 5% of lines where the interval is widest, and let Reem spend her morning on those. Explainability at the line level When a store manager challenges an order quantity, the planner needs a reason in one sentence. Global-model feature importance does not answer "why 72 for this store this week". Some form of local attribution, or a simple decomposition, is an operational requirement rather than a nicety. Serve-time promotional data Promotional plans are provisional until locked. If the model is trained on final plans and served on provisional ones, the accuracy reported in the backtest is not the accuracy delivered. Cold-start series New products and new stores have no history. Whatever is chosen must have a defined behaviour for a series with three observations, and that behaviour must be stated rather than discovered in production. Retraining cadence 1,800 series retrained weekly is cheap for one global model and expensive for 1,800 individual ones. This usually decides the case on its own, and groups should say so rather than pretending accuracy decided it.

docs.title: Facilitation plan
docs.text:
Forty minutes.

Minutes Phase What the facilitator does 0–4 Setup Give the scenario in three sentences and stop at the puzzle: MAE improved 18%, availability did not move, markdown rose. Ask the room for one-line hypotheses and write four or five on the board without evaluating any of them. Do not reveal the critical ratio. 4–8 Framing the loss Hand each group the cost card — margin SAR 12, unsold-unit cost SAR 4, mean 60, sd 18 — and ask a single question: "how many units should she order?" Nothing else. Let them argue. Most groups will answer 60 within a minute and then start to doubt it. 8–22 Small-group work Groups compute the critical ratio, the implied order quantity, and the expected cost of ordering the mean instead. Then they extend it: a fresh category where the unsold unit is a total write-off, and a high-margin low-volume line. Circulate with one question per group: "what does your ratio become if the item is fresh?"; "what is the ratio for a series that sells 0.3 units a week?"; "which of your model's metrics would have caught this?" 22–33 Plenary Two minutes per group at the board. Require each group to write its ratio and its order quantity, not describe them. Collect the ratios in a single column — the spread across category types is the lesson, and it is more persuasive on the board than in speech. Then ask the question the case is built on: which accuracy metric, of the ones on the dashboard, would have distinguished the good model from the bad one? The honest answer is none of them, and it is worth letting the room reach that conclusion rather than announcing it. 33–40 Debrief Connect forward, not backward. This is the last thing before M5, so close on the sentence that opens M5: the point forecast answers the wrong question, and the quantile answers the right one. Then name the two retail-specific traps to carry into the lab — intermittency breaking MAPE, and panel leakage through a globally fitted scaler.

If the session runs with data on machines, replace minutes 8–22 with the hands-on variant: groups compute WAPE and MASE on a supplied panel extract, then compute units-short and units-unsold under a mean forecast and a q=0.75 forecast. This is stronger but needs 55 minutes, not 40.

docs.title: Discussion questions
docs.text:
1. Reem's MAE improved by 18% and her outcome got worse. Is the new model worse than the old one? A good answer separates the model from the decision rule. The model may be strictly better as an estimator of the conditional mean while being worse as an input to an order quantity, because the decision rule that consumes it assumes the input is something else. The strongest answers point out that the incumbent moving average was probably biased upward on volatile series, and that its bias was accidentally doing the job of a service-level buffer — which is a common and uncomfortable finding in real replacements.

2. What is the right critical ratio for a fresh category, and what does that do to the forecast you need? A good answer recognises that c_over rises sharply when the unsold unit is written off rather than marked down, which pushes q* below 0.5 — so the cost-minimising order is below the mean. It should notice the uncomfortable implication that the correct policy deliberately runs out of stock some of the time, and that this is a commercial decision the planner cannot make alone.

3. On a series that sells in 15 weeks out of 52, what metric would you report, and what would you refuse to report? A good answer rules out MAPE on the grounds that it is undefined at zero and that percentage errors on tiny denominators dominate any average. It proposes MASE or RMSSE against a seasonal-naive denominator, notes that MAE alone is minimised by an all-zero forecast, and — the mark of a strong answer — questions whether a point forecast is the right output at all for a series like this, as opposed to a probability of a non-zero week and an expected size when non-zero.

4. When should this chain fit one global model, and when should it fit 1,780 individual ones? A good answer argues from data volume per series and from maintenance cost, not from sophistication. Global models help short and sparse series by borrowing structure, and can hurt a long, idiosyncratic, high-volume series that has its own dynamics. A defensible design is often a hybrid: a global model for the tail, individual models for the twenty series that account for most of the revenue. The best answers note that the maintenance argument is doing more work than the accuracy argument, and say so.

5. Promotions are known in advance — until they are not. How would you handle a model whose most important feature is provisional at serve time? A good answer proposes measuring the degradation rather than assuming it: backtest with the provisional plan as it stood at order time, not with the final plan as recorded. It should consider training on provisional data if that is what will be served, and should treat the divergence between provisional and final plans as a monitorable quantity in its own right.

6. The forecast is for a seven-day lead-time total, but the model is fitted daily. Where does that go wrong? A good answer recognises that lead-time demand is a sum of correlated errors, so its variance is not seven times the daily variance, and that an interval built by naively scaling the daily interval will be wrong in a direction that depends on the sign of the error correlation. It should propose either forecasting the aggregate directly or simulating paths and aggregating them, and should note that the model ranking can change between the two evaluations.

docs.title: Expected outputs
docs.text:
1. A one-page cost card: margin, over-stock cost, derived critical ratio, and the implied quantile, for three different category types.
  2. The order quantity each group would place for the worked example, with its arithmetic shown.
  3. A metric recommendation: which metrics the planning dashboard should carry, which it should drop, and one sentence of justification for each.
  4. A statement of the model architecture the group recommends — global, per-series, or hybrid — with the constraint that decided it named explicitly.
  5. One paragraph explaining to Reem, in language with no statistical vocabulary in it, why the number the system proposes is higher than the number it expects to sell.

Item 5 is the hardest and the most valuable. It rehearses LO6 directly.

docs.title: Common failure modes in this case
docs.text: Failure mode What it looks like Facilitator's redirect Ordering the mean The group computes an excellent forecast and orders exactly that many units, without ever asking what the forecast is for. "You have ordered 60. Demand was 78. What did that cost, and what would ordering 72 have cost when demand was 45?" Make them do both arithmetics; the asymmetry appears immediately. Reaching for a bigger model The response to poor outcomes is a neural network, or more features. The loss function is never examined. "Suppose your new model is perfect at estimating the mean. Does Reem's problem go away?" It does not, and that is the fastest route to the actual lesson. MAPE on intermittent series The evaluation script runs, produces a number in the thousands of percent or a divide-by-zero, and the group works around it by dropping the zero rows. Dropping the zeros drops the hardest part of the problem and inflates every metric. Ask what fraction of rows were dropped, then ask what the model's accuracy is on the rows they threw away. Panel leakage through global preprocessing A StandardScaler or target encoder fitted on the entire panel, or lags computed without sorting within group. The backtest looks excellent. Ask them to prove temporal integrity the same way Practical Assessment 2 does: shuffle the future rows and confirm no past feature value changes. It usually fails on the first attempt. Evaluating at the wrong horizon Daily h+1 accuracy is reported and the seven-day lead time is never modelled. "The order arrives next Sunday. What does your h+1 accuracy tell Reem about the week after that?" Nothing, and groups see it at once. One holiday dummy for everything Ramadan, Eid and back-to-school share a single is_holiday flag, and the model learns their average, which describes none of them. Have them plot two categories through the same Ramadan. The curves move in opposite directions, which no shared flag can express.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
This case has no course-provided dataset. Three options, in order of preference:

Option What it is Preparation Kaggle Store Sales — Time Series Forecasting Daily unit sales by store and product family for an Ecuadorian grocery chain, with accompanying oil-price, holiday and promotion tables. Familiar shape: store identifier, product family, date, sales, promotion indicator. Requires a Kaggle account to download; check the competition page for the current licence and redistribution terms before handing it out. Download and stage on the training machines before the session. Take a subset — 5 stores, 8 families, two years — so the panel fits in memory and a LightGBM fit takes seconds rather than minutes. M5 Forecasting (Walmart) dataset Daily unit sales for a large hierarchical retail panel with calendar and price tables, and a substantial fraction of intermittent series. Richer than needed for a 40-minute case, and the better choice if the case is extended into a lab. Check the current licence terms on the competition page. Subset aggressively. The full panel is far too large for a classroom exercise and the intermittency lesson is fully visible in a few hundred series. Paper case Run the session on the cost card alone, with no data. None. This is the default if connectivity is uncertain, and it loses less than instructors expect — the critical-ratio argument is the point of the case, and it is arithmetic, not computation.

A note on substituting the course data. Do not try to run this case on ksa_grid_demand.csv. Electricity demand is dense, smooth and strictly positive; it has none of the intermittency, promotional response or panel structure that this case exists to teach. If a retail panel is genuinely unavailable, run the paper case rather than a bad analogy.

docs.title: Case Study 3 — Government Service Demand and Workforce Planning
docs.text: SDA-DSC-212 · Time Series Analysis and Forecasting · Facilitator brief

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
Primary module fit M2 — Stationarity and Autocorrelation (structural breaks, level shifts, what differencing hides) Secondary fit M5 (uncertainty as a staffing input), M6 (backtesting across a regime change) LOs exercised LO1 primary; LO5 and LO6 in the plenary Suggested slot Day 1, Hour 4 — second half of the M2 theory hour, once ADF and KPSS have been introduced Alternative slot Day 3, Hour 2, as the motivating case for backtest design across a regime change Duration 35 minutes Group size 3–4 participants Data source No course dataset ships for this case. Run as a paper case, or generate a series with the recipe in Data below.

The electricity series has one structural break and it is polite about it. This case has three kinds of discontinuity in two years, and none of them is an outlier to be cleaned away. It is the case that teaches the difference between a series that is non-stationary and a series that has changed.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Manafith is a national digital services platform — a fictional composite, used here so that no real organisation's operational figures are implied. It handles licence renewals, permit applications, document attestations and status enquiries for individuals and businesses. Volume arrives through three channels: the mobile application, the web portal, and a contact centre that handles the cases the self-service channels cannot close. Roughly nine in ten transactions complete without human involvement. The tenth generates a support contact, and every support contact needs an agent.

Faisal Al-Otaibi runs workforce planning for the contact centre. He publishes a staffing plan every Wednesday covering the following seven days, in half-hourly intervals, across three skill groups. The plan is binding: agent shifts are rostered a week ahead under a labour agreement, and changing them inside three days means overtime rates or an outsourced overflow contract at a premium. Faisal's plan is built from a demand forecast, and his forecast today is a four-week moving average of the same weekday and half-hour, adjusted by hand.

It has failed three times in the past year, each time for a different reason. In March a new release moved a high-volume journey into self-service; call volume fell by a third and the moving average took a month to catch up, during which Faisal paid for agents who had nothing to do. In June a regulatory deadline for a mandatory registration produced a fortnight of volume that peaked at four times normal, concentrated in the last three days before the cut-off. In September a five-hour platform outage produced almost no transactions, followed by a compressed catch-up surge — and then his moving average, having ingested the outage as a genuine low, under-staffed the following week.

The decision Faisal makes differently depending on the answer is the number of agents rostered per half-hour interval for each of the next seven days, and — separately and more importantly — how much overflow capacity to pre-contract. The first is a point decision. The second is a decision about uncertainty, and today he makes it by instinct.

docs.title: The decision question
docs.text: How many agents should be rostered in each half-hour of the next seven days, and how much overflow capacity should be pre-contracted against the possibility that demand exceeds the plan?

docs.title: Business context and the cost of being wrong
docs.text:
The asymmetry here is smaller than in CS1 but it runs in the same direction, and it has a second dimension that electricity does not: queues are non-linear.

Illustrative figures, to be stated as teaching numbers:

Value Typical weekday support contacts 12,000 Contacts handled per agent-shift 40 Agents required at plan 300 Fully loaded agent cost per shift SAR 440 Overflow (outsourced) cost per contact SAR 26

Over-forecast by 10%. Thirty agents rostered with nothing to do: 30 × 440 = SAR 13,200 for the day. Unpleasant, linear, and entirely recoverable next week.

Under-forecast by 10%. Twelve hundred contacts arrive with no one to take them. If they go to overflow: 1,200 × 26 = SAR 31,200 — about 2.4 times the over-staffing cost. If overflow capacity was not pre-contracted, they queue, and queueing is where the linearity stops. A service operating at 95% occupancy that receives 10% more arrivals does not see 10% more waiting time; average wait rises by a multiple, abandonment climbs, and a proportion of abandoned contacts return the next day and are counted again. The under-staffing error partially creates its own demand.

The honest summary for participants: the direct cost ratio is modest, roughly 2.4:1, but the under-forecast error has a convex tail that the ratio does not capture, and the correct response is therefore not simply "forecast a higher quantile" but "forecast a quantile and pre-contract the overflow that covers the difference between the plan and the upper quantile". Faisal needs a forecast distribution, not a forecast.

docs.title: What makes this series hard
docs.text:
Three distinct types of discontinuity, which demand three different treatments.

Type Example here Correct treatment What goes wrong if treated as the others Permanent level shift The March release moves a journey to self-service; volume steps down ~30% and stays down Step dummy, or discard pre-break history, or a short training window — a decision that must be argued Treated as an outlier, it is smoothed away and the model over-forecasts for months Transient known event The June regulatory deadline: a two-week ramp with a sharp terminal peak An event feature with a countdown, or an explicit intervention model Treated as a level shift, the model expects the elevated level to persist Anomaly to exclude The September five-hour outage: near-zero transactions, then a catch-up surge Excluded from training as a target, retained as a flag; the catch-up surge is not an anomaly and must stay Ingested as genuine demand, the level estimate collapses and the following week is under-staffed

Participants who do not distinguish these three will apply the same tool to all of them, and that is the single most valuable discovery in this case.

Strong multiple seasonality with a hard operating envelope. Intraday demand is not a smooth sinusoid — it is near-zero overnight, rises steeply from about 08:00, peaks mid-morning, dips around the midday prayer and lunch, and has a distinct evening shoulder. The weekly cycle is Friday–Saturday down. The annual cycle is dominated by administrative and academic deadlines, not by weather. A Fourier basis fitted to a smooth 24-hour period represents the overnight floor badly; a full set of hour-of-day dummies represents it well but costs 23 parameters.

Campaign effects that are known in advance and are not repeatable. Awareness campaigns, ministerial announcements and app-store featuring produce spikes that are known to the communications team and not to the forecaster. A campaign flag is only useful if someone maintains it, which is an organisational constraint rather than a technical one.

Ramadan changes the shape of the working day. Public-sector hours shorten, the intraday peak shifts earlier, and a substantial evening peak appears after Iftar that does not exist for the rest of the year. As in CS1, a single is_ramadan flag cannot express a shape change.

Growth that is not a trend. Adoption of a new digital service is closer to a logistic curve than a line. Fitting a linear or exponential trend to the steep part of an S-curve and extrapolating seven days ahead is survivable; extrapolating a quarter ahead is not.

Data-quality traps particular to service telemetry. Contact records are timestamped at different points in the pipeline — arrival, answer, disposition — and the three do not agree during a queueing episode, which is exactly when accuracy matters. Half-hour buckets recorded in UTC and displayed in local time drift by an hour if daylight-saving logic is inherited from an international platform, even though Asia/Riyadh has no daylight saving. And a suppressed channel (a contact form taken offline for a day) looks identical to genuinely low demand unless someone logs it.

docs.title: Technical agenda
docs.text:
1. Plot before testing (M1). Two years of hourly data on one axis, with the three known events annotated. Most of this case is visible in that one plot, and the discipline of drawing it before running a test is the first thing to enforce.
  2. Run ADF and KPSS and interpret the disagreement (M2). A series with a permanent level shift will typically produce the pattern participants have just been taught to recognise: ADF rejecting its unit-root null while KPSS rejects its stationarity null. Have them reach the verdict and then ask whether differencing is the right response to a known, dated, explainable step.
  3. Distinguish the three discontinuities (M2, M6). Classify each of the three events using the table above, and state the treatment for each with a justification.
  4. Design a backtest that spans the break (M6). Origins placed only after March 2023 make the model look stable and prove nothing. Origins spanning the break reveal how long recovery takes. The recovery time — how many days of degraded accuracy the break causes — is itself the number Faisal cares about, because it tells him how long he is exposed.
  5. Build calendar and event features (M4). Hour-of-day treatment, day-of-week, a deadline countdown feature, holiday flags with lead and lag windows, is_ramadan interacted with hour, and a maintained campaign flag with a named owner.
  6. Produce a distribution, not a number (M5). Quantile forecasts at the roster level and at the overflow level. Two different quantiles for two different decisions, derived from two different cost structures — this is the case's cleanest illustration of LO5.
  7. Translate to a staffing plan (M7). Convert forecast contacts per interval into agents using the handling rate, then state what the plan does when demand exceeds the upper quantile. A forecast that stops before this step has not answered Faisal's question.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: Constraint What it does to model choice Rosters lock seven days ahead The horizon is 168 hours at half-hourly resolution. Errors at the far end of the horizon dominate, and a model whose accuracy decays steeply with lead time is unsuitable regardless of its h+1 performance. Two years of history, one regime change in it There is not enough data to discard the pre-break period casually — doing so removes an entire annual cycle including the previous year's Ramadan. Events are known but not recorded The deadline and campaign features depend on someone maintaining a calendar. If no owner exists, the model must not depend on them, and that limitation belongs in the decision record rather than being wished away. Explainability to a workforce committee The staffing plan is negotiated with an operations committee that will challenge specific intervals. "The model says so" fails in that room. A component story — baseline, weekday effect, deadline effect — survives it. The plan must degrade gracefully If the forecast service fails on a Wednesday morning, the roster still has to be published. A documented fallback (last-four-weeks same-interval median, with a stated uplift) is a deliverable, not a contingency. The forecast changes people's shifts Unlike a load forecast, this one determines when named individuals work. Volatile week-to-week roster changes have a human cost that no accuracy metric records, and a slightly less accurate but more stable forecast may be the better product.

docs.title: Facilitation plan
docs.text:
Thirty-five minutes. This case is best run immediately after ADF and KPSS, while the reconciliation table is still on the board.

Minutes Phase What the facilitator does 0–4 Setup Show a single annotated plot of the two-year series with the three events marked but unlabelled — three arrows, no captions. Give the scenario in three sentences. Ask each group to write down, before any discussion, what they think each of the three arrows is. Collect nothing; the private commitment is what matters. 4–8 The trap Give the ADF and KPSS results for the raw series and ask for the verdict. The room will correctly reach "difference-stationary — difference once". Let them. Then ask a single question and stop talking: "what does differencing do to the March event, and is that what you want?" 8–22 Small-group work Groups fill in the three-discontinuity table for their series: classify each event, choose a treatment, and state what breaks if they choose wrongly. Then they design the backtest: where do the origins go, and what would the backtest report if all origins sat after March? Circulate. Questions to use: "your model has forgotten March by June — how did you check?"; "the outage produced almost no volume; is the following Tuesday's surge an anomaly too?"; "you have used a step dummy — what is its value on a date after the training window ends?" 22–31 Plenary One group presents the classification table; the others amend rather than repeat. Then take the backtest design to the board and place the origins physically, as marks on a timeline. Ask what the reported MASE would be under each placement. Groups that placed origins only in the stable period will see their number is meaningless, and seeing it is worth more than being told. 31–35 Debrief Close on the distinction the case exists to teach: non-stationary and changed are different diagnoses with different treatments, and a statistical test cannot tell them apart. Only knowing what happened on 1 March can. Then connect to Tayyar's own 1 October 2022 break, which participants will meet in Lab 2 within the hour.

docs.title: Discussion questions
docs.text:
1. ADF and KPSS disagree, and the reconciliation rule says "difference once". Should you? A good answer separates the statistical verdict from the causal one. Differencing will make the tests pass, and it will also convert a known, dated, permanent and explainable level shift into an unexplained one-off shock in the differenced series — discarding information rather than using it. A step dummy keeps the explanation. The strongest answers note that the choice depends on whether more shifts of the same kind are expected: if releases like March's happen twice a year, the model should be able to represent them, which argues for the structure rather than the difference.

2. Should the September outage hours be removed from the training data? What about the surge that followed? A good answer treats the two differently and says why. The outage is a supply failure, not a demand observation, so it is not evidence about demand and should be excluded as a target while being retained as a flag. The subsequent surge is demand — deferred demand, genuinely arriving — and removing it would teach the model that outages have no consequence. The best answers observe that this distinction requires operational knowledge no diagnostic can supply, and that the forecaster therefore needs a channel to the operations team.

3. Faisal needs one number for the roster and a different number for the overflow contract. What are they? A good answer derives two quantiles from two cost structures. The roster balances idle agent cost against overflow cost, giving a moderate quantile. The overflow contract balances a small option premium against the queue collapse it prevents, giving a much higher one. It should note that these are the same forecast distribution consumed twice, which is the argument for producing a distribution in the first place, and that reporting only a p50 forces both decisions to be made by instinct.

4. Two years of history and an S-shaped adoption curve. How much of that history should the model see? A good answer refuses to answer in the abstract and proposes measuring it: fit with several training-window lengths and compare backtest performance across origins that span the break. It should recognise the tension — a short window adapts quickly but has seen only one Ramadan, a long window is stable but carries a regime that no longer exists — and should consider weighting recent observations more heavily rather than choosing a hard cut-off.

5. A more accurate forecast that changes rosters more often may be a worse product. Do you agree? A good answer takes the constraint seriously rather than dismissing it as non-technical. It might propose measuring roster churn alongside accuracy, constraining week-to-week changes, or forecasting a smoothed staffing requirement rather than raw demand. The weakest answers assert that accuracy is the objective and stability is someone else's problem; the strongest recognise that the objective was never accuracy, it was a good roster.

6. The June deadline was known months in advance and the model still missed it. Whose failure is that? A good answer resists both easy positions — it was not purely a modelling failure, and not purely an organisational one. It identifies the missing artefact: an event calendar with an owner, a schema, and a service-level expectation for how far ahead entries appear. It should note that this makes the forecast service dependent on a process the forecasting team does not control, and that the dependency belongs in the monitoring contract and in the decision record.

docs.title: Expected outputs
docs.text:
1. The completed three-discontinuity table: each event classified, its treatment chosen, and the failure mode of the wrong treatment named.
  2. A backtest design sketched on a timeline: origin placement, training window policy, and one sentence on what the design would fail to detect.
  3. Two quantiles with their cost derivations — one for the roster, one for the overflow contract.
  4. A feature list for the model, marked to show which features require an external owner to maintain and who that owner is.
  5. A stated fallback: what the roster is built from on a Wednesday when the forecast service is unavailable.

docs.title: Common failure modes in this case
docs.text: Failure mode What it looks like Facilitator's redirect Everything unusual is an outlier All three events are winsorised or removed, the series becomes smooth and stationary, and the model can no longer represent anything that has actually happened to this service. "Your model is now unable to forecast the next regulatory deadline. There is one in November. What does it say?" Differencing used as a reflex The KPSS test fails, so the group differences, the test passes, and the March release is never discussed again. Ask what the differenced series looks like on 1 March. It is a single large spike with no explanation attached — the group has converted knowledge into noise. Backtest origins placed only in the stable period Sixty origins, all after June 2023, an excellent MASE, and no evidence at all about behaviour under change. "Your service exists because of three events. How many of them does your backtest contain?" A step dummy with no serving definition The dummy is 1 after March in training; nobody has defined its value at forecast time, or it is silently 0 because the feature builder only saw historical rows. This is a training–serving skew defect and belongs to the same family as the leakage exercise. Have them trace one serving row through the feature builder by hand. Contacts forecast, agents forgotten The deliverable is a curve of predicted contacts. The conversion to agents, the handling rate, and the roster granularity are never addressed. "Faisal cannot roster 4,312 contacts. How many people, in which half-hour?" Ramadan handled as a holiday A single flag that lowers the level, when the actual effect is a compressed working day and a new evening peak. Same redirect as CS1: plot the mean intraday profile inside and outside Ramadan on one axis and let the crossing curves make the argument.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
No dataset ships with the course for this case. Choose one of three routes.

Route 1 — paper case (default). Run the session on the annotated plot and the scenario alone. The classification exercise, the backtest design and the two-quantile derivation all work on paper and fit the 35 minutes comfortably. This is the recommended route for the Day 1 slot.
