Route 2 — generate a series. The following recipe produces a two-year hourly transaction series containing all three discontinuities, in the same style and timezone as the course's own generator. It runs in under a second and is reproducible from the seed. Verified output: 17,520 rows, mean 555 transactions per hour, median daily volume around 11,900, and a peak deadline day near 54,000.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(212)
idx = pd.date_range("2022-01-01", "2023-12-31 23:00", freq="h", tz="Asia/Riyadh")
h, dow, doy = idx.hour.to_numpy(), idx.dayofweek.to_numpy(), idx.dayofyear.to_numpy()

open_hours = ((h >= 8) & (h <= 22)).astype(float)
daily  = 0.25 + 0.75*np.exp(-((h - 11)**2)/18) + 0.55*np.exp(-((h - 20)**2)/12)
weekly = np.where(np.isin(dow, [4, 5]), 0.55, 1.0)      # KSA weekend: Fri, Sat
annual = 1 + 0.10*np.sin(2*np.pi*(doy - 30)/365.25)
trend  = (1 + 0.22) ** (np.arange(len(idx))/(365.25*24))  # ~22% YoY adoption

lam = 900.0 * trend * annual * weekly * (0.05 + 0.95*open_hours) * daily

# 1. permanent level shift: self-service release, 1 March 2023
lam = np.where(idx >= pd.Timestamp("2023-03-01", tz="Asia/Riyadh"), lam*1.35, lam)

# 2. transient known event: registration deadline, 1 July 2023
window   = (idx >= pd.Timestamp("2023-06-15", tz="Asia/Riyadh")) & \
           (idx <  pd.Timestamp("2023-07-01", tz="Asia/Riyadh"))
days_to  = (pd.Timestamp("2023-07-01", tz="Asia/Riyadh") - idx).total_seconds()/86400
lam = np.where(window, lam*(1 + 2.4*np.exp(-days_to/4.0)), lam)

# 3. anomaly to exclude: five-hour platform outage, 12 September 2023
outage = (idx >= pd.Timestamp("2023-09-12 09:00", tz="Asia/Riyadh")) & \
         (idx <  pd.Timestamp("2023-09-12 14:00", tz="Asia/Riyadh"))
lam = np.where(outage, lam*0.04, lam)

df = pd.DataFrame({"timestamp": idx, "transactions": rng.poisson(lam)})
df.to_csv("data/manafith_transactions.csv", index=False)

Two deliberate omissions in this recipe are worth pointing out to participants. There is no catch-up surge after the outage — add one if you want the full third-discontinuity discussion, and note that having to add it by hand is itself a lesson in how much of a service's behaviour a generative model does not capture. And there is no Ramadan shape change; borrow the treatment from tools/make_tayyar_data.py, which multiplies daytime hours down and post-Iftar hours up rather than shifting the level.

Route 3 — a public substitute. Public hourly contact-centre data is scarce, and most published call-centre datasets are small or synthetic. If a real series is wanted, the practical substitutes are web-traffic and page-request series (for example, the Wikipedia Web Traffic Time Series Forecasting dataset on Kaggle, which is daily page views for a large panel of articles and contains genuine campaign-driven spikes and level shifts). Check the current licence on the source page before distributing. This is a reasonable proxy for the shape of the problem — spikes, shifts, event-driven demand — but it carries no channel or workforce structure, so the staffing half of the case still has to be run on paper.

Whichever route you take, say plainly that Manafith is fictional. The scenario is a composite built to be plausible for a Riyadh audience; no figure in it describes a real platform, and participants should not repeat any of it as fact.

docs.title: Case Study 4 — Short-Horizon Traffic Flow Forecasting
docs.text: SDA-DSC-212 · Time Series Analysis and Forecasting · Facilitator brief

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
Primary module fit M4 — Feature-Based ML Forecasting (temporal features, multiple seasonality in a supervised matrix) Secondary fit M1 (multiple seasonal periods and their strengths), M6 (horizon-dependent evaluation) LOs exercised LO3 primary; LO1 and LO4 in support Suggested slot Day 2, Hour 3 — inside M4 theory, before Lab 4 Alternative slot Day 1, Hour 3, as a second decomposition example alongside the load series Duration 30 minutes Group size 3–4 participants Data source UCI Metro Interstate Traffic Volume, or a local corridor extract. Runs as a paper case without data. See Data.

This is the shortest of the four cases and the one with the widest horizon range. It exists to make two points that the electricity series makes less sharply: that the useful horizon is not a modelling choice but a consequence of what the forecast is for, and that a series can be dominated by a seasonal pattern and still be almost entirely unpredictable in the moments that matter.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A metropolitan traffic management centre monitors a ring-road corridor with loop detectors and gantry cameras at roughly one-kilometre spacing. Each detector reports vehicle counts, occupancy and mean speed in five-minute bins, aggregated to hourly for planning purposes. The corridor carries about 6,500 vehicles per hour per direction at the morning peak and roughly a fifth of that overnight.

Layla Al-Ghamdi is the duty operations manager. She makes three decisions on different clocks and the same data:

  1. Within the hour — where to pre-position the three incident-response units on shift. A unit already near a congestion front reaches an incident far faster than one dispatched from a depot.
  2. Day ahead — which of the variable-message sign campaigns and ramp-metering plans to activate tomorrow, and when to start them. Metering that begins after the queue has formed achieves very little; metering that begins too early irritates drivers and erodes compliance.
  3. Week ahead — whether to authorise a lane closure for maintenance on a given night, and which night.

The same forecasting service is expected to inform all three. It currently does not: the centre uses a historical profile — the average of the same weekday and hour over the past six weeks — which is accurate on a dry Tuesday and useless on the days Layla actually needs help.

The difference the forecast makes is concrete for each decision. For pre-positioning it is the minutes between an incident occurring and a unit arriving. For metering it is the start time of a plan. For maintenance it is which night the closure happens, and therefore how many vehicle-hours of delay it causes.

docs.title: The decision question
docs.text: Where should the three incident-response units be positioned for the next hour, and at what time tomorrow should the ramp-metering plan be activated?

docs.title: Business context and the cost of being wrong
docs.text:
Traffic delay costs are convex in a way that makes the asymmetry sharper than the raw numbers suggest, because a corridor near capacity has almost no headroom.

Illustrative figures, to be stated as teaching numbers:

Value Corridor peak flow 6,500 veh/h Vehicles affected by a one-hour partial blockage ~4,000 Mean additional delay per affected vehicle 7 minutes Value of travel time SAR 45 per vehicle-hour Delay cost of one such hour 4,000 × (7/60) × 45 ≈ **SAR 21,000**

A widely cited traffic-engineering rule of thumb holds that every minute a lane stays blocked generates roughly four minutes of residual congestion after it clears. On that basis, an incident-response unit that arrives five minutes sooner because it was pre-positioned correctly removes something like twenty minutes of downstream congestion — on the illustrative figures above, roughly SAR 7,000 from a single incident. A corridor with two or three incidents a day, several hundred days a year, makes that a serious number.

The asymmetry: over-forecasting flow puts a response unit somewhere it is not needed, which costs the fuel and the opportunity cost of it not being somewhere else — bounded and small. Under-forecasting flow leaves the unit at the depot when the queue forms, which costs the convex delay above. As in the other three cases, the two errors are not the same size, and a symmetric metric will not distinguish a model that fails safely from one that does not.

There is a second and less obvious asymmetry in time. A forecast that is right about the peak's magnitude but half an hour late about its onset is, for a metering decision, almost as bad as no forecast at all. Point-in-time accuracy metrics score onset timing errors weakly, and a group that notices this has understood something most production traffic-forecasting dashboards have not.

docs.title: What makes this series hard
docs.text:
Multiple seasonality, one of which is bimodal. The daily cycle has two peaks, not one, and they are asymmetric: the morning peak is sharper and more predictable (people leave for work in a narrow window), the evening peak is broader and flatter (people leave work across two hours or more). A single-harmonic Fourier term cannot represent a bimodal day; three or four harmonics can, and demonstrating this by fitting increasing numbers of harmonics is an excellent five-minute exercise in the M4 slot.

The weekly cycle is a shape change, not a scale change. Friday and Saturday do not have a smaller version of the weekday profile — they have a different profile entirely, with no morning commuter peak, a later start, and a broad afternoon and evening plateau. A multiplicative weekend factor applied to the weekday shape is wrong at every hour of the day, and it is wrong in compensating directions, which means the average error looks acceptable.

Weather affects flow and speed in opposite directions. Rain typically reduces volume slightly (some trips are deferred or cancelled) while reducing capacity substantially, so congestion rises even though counts fall. A model that treats rain as a demand shifter will get the sign of the congestion effect wrong. In a Riyadh context the equivalents are dust and low-visibility events, and extreme heat, which suppresses discretionary midday trips.

Incidents are the dominant source of variance and are close to unforecastable. A blocked lane produces a sharp drop in downstream flow and a queue upstream. Incidents are approximately random in timing, so the conditional forecast given no incident is highly accurate and the marginal forecast is not. This gives the case its most important structural lesson: the honest output is a distribution with a heavy lower tail on flow (and a heavy upper tail on travel time), and the service's real value at h+1 is less "what will the flow be" than "how likely is it that something has gone wrong".

Detector data is noisy in characteristic ways. Loop detectors drop out, and a dropout reads as zero flow — which is indistinguishable from a fully blocked road unless occupancy is checked at the same time. Detectors drift and under-count. Lane-level counts sum to a link total only when every lane's detector is healthy. A cleaning step that drops zeros without checking occupancy will delete exactly the incident hours the service exists to detect.

The predictable horizon is short and it is asymmetric across the day. At h+1 on a free-flowing overnight corridor, persistence is nearly unbeatable. At h+1 during the onset of the morning peak, persistence is badly beaten by anything that knows the time of day. At h+24, the calendar carries almost all the information and the recent lags carry very little. A single model reported at a single horizon hides all of this; a horizon-by-horizon error curve, split by time of day, reveals it — and that plot is the single most useful artefact the case produces.

docs.title: Technical agenda
docs.text:
1. Decompose and quantify the seasonal periods (M1). MSTL with periods [24, 168]. Report the strengths. Compare the daily and weekly strengths against the load series — in the course data the load series has daily strength 0.972 and weekly 0.610, and a commuter corridor typically has a higher weekly strength because the weekday/weekend difference is a shape change rather than a level change.
  2. Fit Fourier bases of increasing order (M4). One, two, three, four harmonics against the daily period. Plot the fitted daily profile at each order and identify the order at which the second peak appears. This takes five minutes and settles the "how many harmonics" question for the rest of the course.
  3. Build the supervised matrix (M4). Lags at 1, 2, 3, 24, 168; .shift(1)-guarded rolling means and standard deviations; hour, day of week, weekend flag, holiday flag; weather features at the forecast lead, not the realised value.
  4. Model weekday and weekend shape explicitly (M4). Either interact hour-of-day with a weekend flag, or fit separate Fourier bases per day type. Compare with the naive multiplicative factor and show where the multiplicative version fails.
  5. Evaluate horizon by horizon (M6). Direct models at h+1, h+3, h+6, h+12, h+24, each backtested over the same origins. Plot error against horizon, and again split by time of day. Compare each against two baselines: persistence (y_{t}) and the historical profile (same weekday and hour, averaged). Persistence wins at short horizons, the profile wins at long ones, and the crossover point is the interesting number.
  6. Handle incidents honestly (M5, M6). Flag known incident hours. Report accuracy with and without them, and state both. Then discuss whether the service should predict flow, or predict the probability of a disruption — they are different products with different evaluation regimes.
  7. Note the spatial structure without modelling it (extension). Congestion propagates upstream at a roughly constant shockwave speed, so a detector's future is partly written in its neighbour's present. Say this, show it as a lagged cross-correlation between two adjacent detectors, and stop. That single plot is the on-ramp to spatiotemporal forecasting, and it is enough for a 15-hour course.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: Constraint What it does to model choice Sub-minute latency at h+1 The pre-positioning decision is made in real time from a live feed. A model that needs a 40-feature build across 300 detectors before it can score is not a candidate at this horizon, whatever its accuracy. Three horizons, three decisions One model is unlikely to serve h+1, h+24 and h+168 well. A defensible design is different models per horizon, and groups should be willing to recommend that rather than forcing a single artefact. Weather is a forecast at serve time Same constraint as CS1. A model validated on observed rainfall and served on forecast rainfall is optimistic by an unmeasured amount. Detector availability varies Detectors fail. The model must have a defined behaviour when an input is missing, and "impute with the mean" is a choice that has to be defended given that a missing detector and a blocked road look similar. Operator trust is fragile and asymmetric A duty manager who is sent to the wrong place twice stops using the tool. The failure that destroys trust is a confident wrong forecast, not an uncertain one, which is a direct argument for shipping the interval alongside the point. The forecast competes with a human who is very good An experienced duty manager reads this corridor well. The service has to beat the historical profile and be worth the attention it costs. A marginal accuracy gain that requires monitoring a new screen is not obviously a gain.

docs.title: Facilitation plan
docs.text:
Thirty minutes. Keep it tight; this case is a sharpener inside a theory hour, not a full workshop.

Minutes Phase What the facilitator does 0–3 Setup Show two plots side by side with the axes labelled and the series unlabelled: one day of the load series, one day of the traffic series. Ask the room which is which and why. The bimodal shape gives it away instantly, and that is the point — the shape is the information. 3–6 The three decisions State Layla's three decisions and their horizons. Ask a single question: "one model or three?" Take a show of hands, record the split, and move on without resolving it. 6–18 Small-group work Two tasks, both concrete. (a) Design the feature set for h+1 and for h+24 separately, and mark every feature that appears in only one of the two lists. (b) Predict, before running anything, which of persistence and the historical profile wins at each of h+1, h+6 and h+24, and at what horizon they cross. Circulate: "your h+1 model uses lag168 — what is it contributing that lag1 does not?"; "your h+24 model uses lag1 — where does lag1 come from at serve time when the origin is 24 hours back?"; "an incident starts at 07:40. Which of your features sees it?" 18–26 Plenary Collect the feature-list differences on the board in two columns. The columns are strikingly different, and that difference is the case's main technical claim made visible. Then take the persistence-versus-profile predictions and, if data is available, show the actual crossover; if not, ask the groups to defend their predictions against each other. 26–30 Debrief Two closing points, stated once each. First: the horizon is set by the decision, and the feature set follows the horizon, not the other way round. Second: show the lagged cross-correlation between adjacent detectors, say the words "spatiotemporal forecasting", say that this course does not teach it, and name where to read about it. Do not start it.

docs.title: Discussion questions
docs.text:
1. One model for all three horizons, or three models? Defend the choice on grounds other than accuracy. A good answer argues from serving constraints and maintenance rather than from error curves. Three models mean three feature pipelines, three monitoring contracts and three ways to fail, against a single model that is mediocre at two of the three horizons. A strong answer might propose a single feature pipeline serving three lightweight direct models — one build, three heads — which gets most of the accuracy for one maintenance liability.

2. Incidents cause most of the variance and cannot be predicted. What should the service output? A good answer stops trying to predict the unpredictable and reframes the product. Options include: a conditional forecast plus an explicit disruption probability; a lower quantile of flow as an operational planning figure; or a change-detection service that flags departures from the conditional forecast quickly rather than forecasting further ahead. The best answers note that this changes the evaluation entirely — detection latency and false-alarm rate replace MAPE — and that this is a product decision, not a modelling one.

3. Rain reduces volume and reduces capacity. How would you build a feature set that gets both effects right? A good answer recognises that flow and congestion are different targets and that a single weather coefficient cannot serve both. It might propose modelling speed or occupancy alongside volume, or interacting the weather feature with a measure of how close the corridor already is to capacity, so that rain has a small effect on a quiet Sunday and a large one at 08:00 on a Tuesday. Answers that just add is_raining and move on have not engaged with the mechanism.

4. At h+1 overnight, persistence is nearly unbeatable. Is a machine-learning model justified at all? A good answer separates the average case from the useful case. Persistence is excellent when nothing is happening, which is most of the time and none of the times that matter; the model earns its place at peak onset and during recovery from disruption. The right evaluation is therefore conditional — error during transitions, not error overall — and the strongest answers propose reporting exactly that, and being willing to conclude that persistence should serve overnight while the model serves peak hours.

5. A detector reads zero. What does your pipeline do, and what is the risk of each option? A good answer refuses to answer without a second variable. Zero flow with zero occupancy is a dead detector; zero flow with high occupancy is a blocked road, which is the single most important event the corridor can produce. Imputing both cases the same way either deletes real incidents or invents them. A good answer proposes the joint check and states the fallback for each branch.

6. Congestion propagates upstream. You have not been taught spatiotemporal models. What can you do with that fact anyway? A good answer stays inside the course's toolkit and gets real value from it: use lagged values of the downstream detector as exogenous features for the upstream one, choosing the lag from the observed cross-correlation peak. That is a dynamic regression, which the course does teach, and it captures a large part of what a graph model would. The best answers name the limitation — it does not generalise to a whole network without one model per pair — and identify that as the point where a spatiotemporal method starts to earn its complexity.

docs.title: Expected outputs
docs.text:
1. Two feature lists, for h+1 and h+24, with the differences marked and one sentence explaining each difference.
  2. A predicted error-versus-horizon curve for the model, persistence and the historical profile, drawn by hand on one axis, with the crossover points marked and defended.
  3. A one-paragraph product statement: what the service outputs, at what horizon, for which of Layla's three decisions, and what it explicitly does not attempt.
  4. A stated rule for detector zeros, with both branches of the occupancy check.

docs.title: Common failure modes in this case
docs.text: Failure mode What it looks like Facilitator's redirect One feature list for every horizon lag1 appears in the h+24 model. The group has built a recursive forecaster without deciding to. "It is 14:00 and you are forecasting 14:00 tomorrow. What is lag1?" Either it is a prediction, which makes this a recursive model with compounding error, or it does not exist. Both are answers; not having noticed is not. Weekend modelled as a multiplicative factor A single weekend coefficient scales the weekday profile down. The morning peak survives, scaled — on a day when it does not exist. Overlay the mean weekday and mean weekend profile. No single multiplier maps one onto the other, and the plot ends the argument. Incidents cleaned out of the training data Anomalous hours are removed, the model becomes excellent at forecasting uneventful traffic, and it is now blind to the only thing Layla is paid to manage. "You have removed every hour in which your user needed you. What is the model for?" Detector zeros imputed blindly Zeros are forward-filled or interpolated, deleting real blockages along with dead detectors. Ask for the occupancy value at those timestamps. If it was never loaded, that is the finding. Single-harmonic daily seasonality One sine and one cosine at period 24. The fitted daily profile has one peak; the data has two. Have them plot the fit against the mean observed profile. The missing second peak is visible immediately, and the fix is one line. Chasing the spatial model The group decides the real answer is a graph neural network and spends the session designing one they cannot build or evaluate today. Redirect to the lagged cross-correlation. Get one concrete, testable exogenous feature out of the spatial insight, then move on. The ambition is right; the timescale is not.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
No dataset ships with the course for this case. Three routes.

Route 1 — UCI Metro Interstate Traffic Volume. Hourly westbound traffic volume for a single interstate detector station between Minneapolis and Saint Paul, with accompanying hourly weather attributes (temperature, precipitation, cloud cover, a categorical weather description) and a holiday indicator, covering roughly 2012 to 2018 and running to approximately 48,000 hourly rows. It is a single-series dataset, freely downloadable from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, and it carries almost everything this case needs: bimodal daily seasonality, a strong weekday/weekend shape change, holiday effects and weather covariates. Confirm the current licence and citation requirements on the UCI page before redistributing.

Preparation. The series has gaps of several months. Reindex onto a complete hourly index in the local timezone, materialise the gaps as NaN, and either restrict to a continuous span or state a gap policy — the same discipline as Lab 1. Note for the facilitator: this corridor is in a continental climate with snow, so the weather semantics differ from a Riyadh corridor. Say so; do not silently transplant the interpretation.

Route 2 — a local corridor extract. If the delivering institution has access to a Saudi corridor's detector data, use it. It is worth substantial preparation time: a local corridor makes the Friday–Saturday weekend, the Ramadan intraday shift and the summer midday suppression visible in a way no imported dataset can. Aggregate to hourly, keep occupancy alongside volume so that the detector-zero discussion is possible, and check for a campaign or roadworks log.

Route 3 — paper case. The feature-list exercise, the persistence-versus-profile prediction and the product-statement discussion all work with no data at all, using hand-drawn profiles. This is the default for the 30-minute M4 slot, and it loses little.

For the spatiotemporal on-ramp. The standard public benchmarks in the graph-based traffic forecasting literature are METR-LA (loop-detector speeds from a Los Angeles freeway network) and PEMS-BAY (loop-detector speeds from the San Francisco Bay Area), both at five-minute resolution across a few hundred sensors with an accompanying road-network adjacency matrix. They are widely used as the reference datasets for spatiotemporal models. Name them in the debrief as where to read next; do not attempt to use them in this course, which has neither the hours nor the learning outcomes for graph models.

docs.title: Data and Resource Catalogue
docs.text:
SDA-DSC-212 · Time Series Analysis and Forecasting · Instructor reference

This document covers what ships with the course, how it was made and why it is synthetic, what open data is worth reaching for when a cohort wants a real-data variant, which external courses and texts this one is measured against, and the content of the 15–20 minute overview of the modern forecasting landscape that keeps the course current without expanding its scope.

Every figure describing a course-provided file was measured from the file itself. Figures describing external datasets are stated at the level of confidence they deserve; where a detail matters operationally — a licence, a row count, a redistribution term — verify it on the source page before handing anything to a cohort.

docs.title: The temperature forecast files, measured
docs.text:
Forecast error grows with lead time, as it should. Measured against the realised series:

Lead 14-day file: MAE 28-day file: MAE 1–24 h 0.79 °C 0.75 °C 24–72 h 1.08 °C 0.95 °C 72–168 h 1.50 °C 1.19 °C 168–336 h 2.05 °C 1.54 °C 336–672 h — 2.08 °C

The point for participants: the exogenous regressor that makes SARIMAX work is not an observation at serve time. It is another model's output, with its own error, and a service that never measures the effect of substituting it is reporting an accuracy it does not deliver.

docs.title: The planted defects in ksa_grid_demand.csv
docs.text:
The raw file is 45 rows short of the true 26,280 and contains four distinct classes of defect. Every one of them is deliberate, and each teaches a specific step of Lab 1.

Defect Measured extent What it teaches Where Silent gaps 64 missing hours in 34 runs — 14 one-hour, 12 two-hour, 7 three-hour, and 1 five-hour outage A CSV read straight into pandas produces a DatetimeIndex with no frequency and no visible holes. Only reindexing onto a complete hourly range materialises them as NaN. Until then, lag24 silently spans 25 hours. Lab 1, Task "build the index"; feeds the gap-policy requirement in the capstone Duplicated timestamps 19 duplicated rows (26,216 unique timestamps across 26,235 rows) set_index succeeds and reindex fails, or worse, an aggregation silently double-counts. Forces an explicit de-duplication rule — first, last, or mean — and forces it to be written down. Lab 1 Sensor zeros 7 rows with demand_mw == 0.0 A grid never draws zero. These are sensor failures, not observations. They must be caught before the log transform — log(0) is -inf and propagates silently through a decomposition. Lab 1, and again in Lab 2 when the transform is chosen Non-monotonic rows 192 positions where the timestamp decreases; a 400-row block is shuffled Row order is not time order. Every lag, every rolling window and every .diff() is wrong until the frame is sorted, and none of them raise an error. Lab 1

A cohort that fixes all four in Lab 1 gets a series identical to ksa_grid_demand_clean.csv except at the 64 imputed hours. The reference run in reference_results.json records 26,235 raw rows, 26,280 clean rows, 71 missing values after reindexing, a longest gap of 5 hours, and 66 imputed values — the difference between 71 and 64 being the sensor zeros that were converted to NaN before imputation.

docs.title: Structure planted in the demand series
docs.text:
Knowing what is in the series is what makes it gradeable. From tools/make_tayyar_data.py:

Component Design Level and trend Base 27,500 MW, compounding at about 2.9% per year Annual seasonality Two harmonics on day-of-year, peaking around mid-July — the residual summer effect after weather is accounted for separately Daily seasonality Three harmonics on hour-of-day, amplitude about ±15% at the fundamental Weekly seasonality Multiplicative: 0.945 on Friday and Saturday, 1.012 otherwise Weather response Piecewise around a 21 °C balance point: cooling load 1 + 0.0165·CDD + 0.00012·CDD² above it, plus a milder heating response 0.0090·HDD below 14 °C. The quadratic term is why a linear temperature coefficient under-fits the extreme afternoons. Ramadan A shape change, not a level change: daytime hours 06:00–15:00 multiplied by 0.930, post-Iftar hours 19:00–01:00 by 1.075 Eid Level multiplied by 0.905 across the Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha windows National Day Level multiplied by 0.955 on 23 September Structural break 1 October 2022: a permanent +3.1% step, described in the generator as a large industrial customer connecting Heatwaves Three planted multi-day temperature excursions: +3.4 °C for 6 days from 2021-07-28, +4.0 °C for 7 days from 2022-08-04, +3.6 °C for 5 days from 2023-07-17 Innovations AR(1) with coefficient 0.72 on the log scale, so the remainder has genuine memory and the ACF is not white noise after seasonal adjustment Temperature process Annual sinusoid (mean 26 °C, amplitude 12.5 °C) plus a diurnal sinusoid (amplitude 6.5 °C) plus AR(1) weather noise with coefficient 0.93 Seed 212, fixed. Regenerating the data reproduces it exactly.

docs.title: 2. How the course dataset was built, and why it is synthetic
docs.text: tools/make_tayyar_data.py builds every file in data/ from a single seed in a few seconds. The construction is multiplicative — level × trend × annual × daily × weekly × calendar × weather × exp(AR(1)) — with the structural break applied last as a step, and the defects injected afterwards into a copy.

docs.title: Why a controlled synthetic series is the right choice here
docs.text:
Ground truth is known, so the assessment can be graded. When the generator says the seasonal strength is high, the break is on 1 October 2022 and the balance point is 21 °C, an instructor can mark a stationarity report or a feature-importance interpretation against a fact rather than against a plausible-sounding narrative. With real telemetry there is no answer key, and the assessment degrades into rewarding fluency.

It is reproducible across cohorts. Every cohort meets the same 57,851.5 MW peak, the same five-hour outage and the same 19 duplicated timestamps. Benchmarks in the module tables mean something across deliveries. A cohort in March and a cohort in November can be compared. A dataset refreshed from a live feed cannot support that.

Each defect exists to teach one thing. Real data is messy in ways that are correlated, overlapping and often uninteresting — a hundred small artefacts of one ingestion bug. The planted defects here are four clean, separable lessons that map to four steps of Lab 1. That is a teaching property, not a realism property, and it is the right trade for a 15-hour course.

There are no distribution restrictions. Real Saudi hourly grid telemetry is not available for redistribution to a training cohort. A synthetic series can be committed to the repository, handed to participants, pushed to their own public capstone repositories and reused without a licence conversation.

The difficulty is calibrated. The signal-to-noise ratio was chosen so that a competent day-ahead model lands around 2–2.5% MAPE and a seasonal-naive baseline around 4%. That gap is wide enough for model comparison to be meaningful and narrow enough that no model looks miraculous. Real data with this much structure would make the labs trivial; real data with less would make them unfinishable in an hour.

docs.title: What it is not, and what must be said out loud
docs.text:
A model that does well here has not been validated on real telemetry. It has been validated against a generative process whose functional form it can in principle recover. The weather response is a known quadratic; the Ramadan effect is a known pair of multipliers; the innovations are AR(1) by construction. A LightGBM that reaches 2.3% MAPE on this series has learned a structure that was put there on purpose.

Four specific limits are worth naming to a cohort of practising data scientists:

  1. The noise is too well-behaved. Real load series contain measurement artefacts, metering changes, DST-like clock issues, retrospective restatements and periods where a substation's data is simply wrong for a month. None of that is here beyond the four planted defects.
  2. The break is single, clean and dated. Real series drift, break repeatedly, and break for reasons nobody records. The October 2022 step is unusually cooperative.
  3. The weather–demand relationship is stationary. In reality it moves — air-conditioning stock grows, efficiency standards change, behaviour shifts. The balance point is not a constant of nature.
  4. There is no genuine regime the model has never seen. Every heatwave in the test window is drawn from the same process as those in the training window. The extrapolation failure that tree-based models suffer on a genuine record-breaking day is under-represented here, and it is the failure that matters most operationally.

The honest framing for participants, and the one the capstone rubric rewards: this dataset is a flight simulator. It is the right place to learn the instruments and the procedures, and passing in it is not a licence to fly. Any capstone that claims validated real-world performance on the basis of these numbers should lose marks for it.

docs.title: 3. Open-source datasets for extension work and real-data variants
docs.text:
For instructors who want a real-data variant, and for participants continuing after the course. Licences and row counts change; verify on the source page before redistributing anything.

Dataset Source and licence Scale and frequency What it is good for here ElectricityLoadDiagrams20112014 UCI Machine Learning Repository. Published under CC BY 4.0. 370 client consumption series, 15-minute resolution, 2011–2014, in kW The closest real-data substitute for the Tayyar series. Excellent for decomposition and seasonality (M1), for multi-series and global-model work (M4), and for showing what genuinely messy consumption data looks like — several series begin part-way through the period and read zero before they start, which is a better cleaning exercise than anything that can be planted. Aggregate to hourly before use; 15-minute resolution multiplies every runtime by four for no pedagogical gain. Monash Time Series Forecasting Repository — electricity_hourly Monash Time Series Forecasting Archive (Godahewa et al., 2021), distributed via Zenodo; most records are CC BY 4.0 — check the individual record. 321 hourly series, 2012–2014 The archive's hourly electricity set is an aggregation of the UCI data and is the cleanest drop-in replacement if Tayyar cannot be used. Its real value is the archive around it: dozens of datasets in a single consistent .tsf format with published baseline results for classical and ML methods, which makes it the natural home for a "does our model beat the published baseline" exercise. Use the archive's own baselines rather than inventing benchmarks. Open Power System Data — time series package open-power-system-data.org, compiled from ENTSO-E and European TSO publications. Licensing is stated per data package on the platform — check the package page. European country and control-area series at 15, 30 and 60 minutes: load, generation by technology, wind and solar, and day-ahead operational forecasts published by the TSOs themselves The one dataset in this list that supports the exercise nothing else does: comparing a model's forecast against a real operator's own published day-ahead forecast for the same hours. That turns an abstract benchmark into a concrete one — "we beat the TSO's forecast on 43% of hours" is a sentence with meaning. It is the strongest available basis for an advanced or follow-on session on M6 and M7. Kaggle — Store Sales: Time Series Forecasting Kaggle competition dataset; requires an account. Check the competition rules for redistribution terms. Daily unit sales by store and product family for a grocery chain, with holiday, oil-price and promotion tables The default dataset for CS2. Panel structure, promotions, holidays and enough intermittency to break MAPE convincingly, at a size that fits a classroom machine after subsetting. Kaggle — M5 Forecasting (Accuracy / Uncertainty) Kaggle competition dataset; check the competition rules. Daily unit sales for a large hierarchical retail panel, with calendar and price tables; a large fraction of series are intermittent Richer than CS2 needs, and the right choice if the retail case is extended into a full lab. The M5 Uncertainty track is also the best public example of a competition scored on quantiles rather than point accuracy, which makes it a strong companion to M5 of this course. Nixtla example datasets Bundled with the Nixtla open-source libraries (statsforecast, mlforecast, neuralforecast, utilsforecast) and their documentation; the libraries are Apache-2.0, the bundled datasets are small and intended for examples. Small hourly and daily electricity and demand series, plus loaders for the M-competition datasets Lightweight benchmarking. The value is less the data than the uniform API across three paradigms — the same series fitted by a classical model, a gradient-boosted feature model and a neural model with near-identical calling conventions. That makes it the cheapest way to run the modern-landscape overview in section 5 as a live demonstration rather than a slide. UCI — Metro Interstate Traffic Volume UCI Machine Learning Repository; confirm licence and citation on the page. Approximately 48,000 hourly rows, single detector station, roughly 2012–2018, with hourly weather attributes and a holiday flag The default dataset for CS4. Bimodal daily seasonality, a weekday/weekend shape change, holidays and weather covariates in one small file. METR-LA and PEMS-BAY Standard public benchmarks in the spatiotemporal traffic-forecasting literature; distributed with several open research repositories. Loop-detector speeds at 5-minute resolution across a few hundred sensors, with a road-network adjacency matrix Name only. These are where the CS4 debrief points participants who want to continue into graph-based spatiotemporal forecasting. They are out of scope for this course and should not be introduced into it.

docs.title: Choosing between them
docs.text:
If the requirement is "replace Tayyar with real data", use the Monash hourly electricity set: it is clean, hourly, well-documented, has published baselines and needs almost no preparation. Accept that the labs lose the Saudi calendar effects, the Fri–Sat weekend and the planted defects, which means Lab 1 and roughly half of Lab 4 need rewriting.

If the requirement is "add a real-data session on top of Tayyar", use Open Power System Data. The comparison against a published operational forecast is the single most valuable thing on this list and it exists nowhere else.

If the requirement is "give participants somewhere to go afterwards", point at the Monash archive and its baseline tables, and at the M5 Uncertainty track for anyone who took M5 seriously.

docs.title: 4. Reference courses and texts
docs.text: Resource What this course should take from it Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice — the Python edition The primary academic benchmark. Take the conceptual sequencing — structure and decomposition before stationarity, stationarity before ARIMA, point forecasts before intervals, and evaluation as a first-class topic rather than an appendix — and take the statistical rigour, particularly its insistence that a forecast is a distribution and that residual diagnostics are not optional. Where this course diverges (much heavier weight on gradient-boosted models and on the production pipeline), be able to say why. Coursera — Time Series Forecasting with Python: Models to Production Confirms that the classical-plus-ML structure of M3–M4 is the current market expectation rather than a local preference, and reinforces the production emphasis of M7. Take the framing that a model is not finished until it is served; leave the breadth, which is wider than 15 hours can carry. Kaggle Learn — Time Series A source of short feature-engineering exercises for M4: lags, trend and seasonality as features, Fourier terms, and the hybrid pattern of fitting a simple model to the trend and a gradient-boosted model to its residuals. Its exercises are the right length for a 10-minute mini-exercise. Do not take its evaluation practice, which is lighter than this course requires. DataCamp — Designing Forecasting Pipelines for Production The benchmark for turning the Day-3 capstone from a notebook into a believable service: configuration-driven runs, a shared feature module used by both training and serving, and monitoring. It works from hourly electricity data, so its examples transfer directly. Take the pipeline discipline; the capstone's "a stranger should clone it and reproduce every number" requirement is the same standard stated more sharply.

docs.title: 5. The modern forecasting landscape — a 15–20 minute overview slot
docs.text:
Placement. Day 3, at the start of Hour 4, immediately before CS1 and the capstone assembly. Participants have by then built classical models, a feature-based ML model, calibrated intervals and a rolling-origin backtest, so they can place each stage against something they have done themselves.

Purpose, stated to the room in the first thirty seconds. This course does not teach deep learning, and that is deliberate — a 15-hour course that added neural forecasting would have to remove backtesting or calibration to make room, and both matter more. What follows is a map, so that when someone proposes a transformer or a foundation model in a meeting next month, participants can ask the right three questions instead of either deferring or dismissing.

Structure. Four stages, roughly four minutes each. For each: what it is, when it earns its place, and one honest caveat. The through-line is a single question repeated at every stage — what does this buy, and what does it cost to keep running?

docs.title: Stage 1 — Statistical forecasting
docs.text:
What it is. Models with an explicit stochastic structure fitted per series: naive and seasonal-naive baselines, exponential smoothing and the ETS taxonomy, ARIMA and SARIMA, SARIMAX with exogenous regressors, Theta, and multiple-seasonality extensions such as TBATS or MSTL followed by a simple model on the deseasonalised remainder. Everything in M3, plus the decomposition in M1.

When it earns its place. When the series count is small and each series is long. When covariates are few or absent. When a component story is required — a model that can say "trend contributes this much, the daily cycle this much, temperature this much" survives a regulatory conversation that feature importance does not. When intervals must be available immediately: ETS and ARIMA produce analytic prediction intervals from the model's own error variance, with no calibration step. And, practically, when nobody will be available to maintain a feature pipeline.

One honest caveat. The interval is only as good as the distributional assumption behind it. In this course's own reference run, SARIMAX with temperature produces the best classical point forecast (2.05% MAPE against ETS at 2.68%) and a Ljung–Box p-value of 0.000, meaning autocorrelation remains in its residuals and the model is under-specified. Its analytic 90% interval covers 96.4% of observations — wider than advertised, which happens to be the safe direction, but it is miscalibration all the same. A well-fitting classical model that fails its residual diagnostics is reporting an uncertainty it has not earned.

docs.title: Stage 2 — Feature-based machine learning
docs.text:
What it is. Reduce forecasting to supervised regression. Build a design matrix of lags, rolling statistics, calendar variables and Fourier terms; fit a gradient-boosted tree ensemble — LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost. Train one global model across many series with a series identifier as a categorical feature, rather than one model per series. Choose recursive or direct multi-step strategies deliberately. All of M4.

When it earns its place. When there are many series and few of them are individually long — the global model borrows structure across the panel and rescues the short ones. When covariates are rich and their interactions matter: temperature × hour × Ramadan is trivial for a tree ensemble and awkward for a linear specification. When training must be fast and cheap: this course's LightGBM fits in seconds on a laptop. Gradient-boosted models on engineered features have been the dominant approach in recent large-scale forecasting competitions, and they remain the default first serious model for tabular-shaped forecasting problems.

One honest caveat. Trees cannot extrapolate. A tree's prediction is an average of training targets in a leaf, so it is bounded by the range of the target it was trained on — on a record-breaking demand day it will under-forecast the peak, systematically and silently, which is precisely the day the forecast matters most. The mitigations are known (difference the target, model a ratio to a baseline, normalise per series) and none of them is automatic. The second, larger cost is organisational: the feature pipeline is a permanent liability. It must be versioned, shared identically between training and serving, monitored for skew, and owned. A 0.3-point MAPE gain that comes with a standing engineering commitment is often a bad trade, and being able to say so is part of LO6.

docs.title: Stage 3 — Neural forecasting
docs.text:
What it is. Models trained end to end on raw or lightly processed series, learning their own representations. The families worth naming: DeepAR, an autoregressive recurrent model producing probabilistic forecasts across a panel; N-BEATS and N-HiTS, deep stacks of fully connected blocks with interpretable trend and seasonality variants; the Temporal Fusion Transformer, which handles static covariates, known-future covariates and past covariates explicitly and produces quantile outputs; and more recent transformer and patch-based architectures such as PatchTST, with simple linear baselines like DLinear deliberately maintained alongside them as controls. The competition landmark worth mentioning is the M4 winner, a hybrid of exponential smoothing and a recurrent network, which was neither purely statistical nor purely neural.

When it earns its place. When there are very many related series and a great deal of data — the regime where a global neural model can learn shared structure that neither a per-series statistical model nor a hand-built feature set can express. When covariate structure is complex enough that engineering features by hand is the bottleneck. When probabilistic output across many horizons is required natively rather than bolted on. And when there is a team to own it.

One honest caveat. The published gains are frequently smaller than the abstracts suggest, and sometimes disappear under fair comparison. The DLinear result — that a simple linear model matched or beat several transformer architectures on standard long-horizon benchmarks — is worth stating plainly, not because transformers are useless but because it demonstrates how weak the baselines in that literature often were. The practical caveat is cost: tuning, hardware, longer training cycles, and a much larger surface for silent failure. For a single hourly series with three years of history, which is the situation most participants will actually face, a neural model is very unlikely to beat a well-built LightGBM by enough to justify itself.

docs.title: Stage 4 — Foundation models for time series
docs.text:
What it is. Models pre-trained on very large and diverse collections of time series, then applied to a new series zero-shot — a forecast with no fitting on the target series at all. Representative examples: TimeGPT from Nixtla, offered as a commercial API; Chronos from Amazon, which tokenises series values and trains a language-model architecture over them, with open weights; Lag-Llama; Moirai from Salesforce; and TimesFM from Google. The architectural ideas differ, but the proposition is the same one: forecasting as a pre-trained capability rather than a per-series fitting exercise.

When it earns its place. Three situations, and they are genuinely valuable ones. Cold start — a new series with almost no history, where every method in stages 1 to 3 has nothing to fit. Breadth at low cost — thousands of low-value series that do not individually justify a modelling effort. And as a fast baseline: getting a credible zero-shot forecast in minutes tells you the difficulty of a problem before committing to a project, which is a real and underrated use.

One honest caveat. Zero-shot claims on public benchmarks are hard to verify, because the pre-training corpora are large and not always fully disclosed, so it can be impossible to establish that a benchmark series was not seen in training. Treat published zero-shot numbers as a hypothesis about your data, not a result on it — and test it the way this course tests everything else, with a rolling-origin backtest on your own series against your own baselines. Three further practical limits: covariate handling is weaker and less flexible than a SARIMAX or a TFT for a problem where a known-future regressor such as temperature carries most of the signal; a hosted model is an external dependency inside a 14:00 publication deadline, with the latency and availability implications that carries; and explainability is close to nil, which for a regulated operational decision may end the conversation on its own.

docs.title: Closing the slot
docs.text:
Two sentences, and then straight into CS1:

The progression is not a ladder where each rung replaces the one below it. It is a widening set of answers to the question "how much structure do I have to specify myself", and the right answer for a given problem is usually further down that list than the literature implies.

Whichever stage a model comes from, it enters production through the same gate: a rolling-origin backtest, a calibrated interval, a named baseline it beats, and a written record of the decision. That gate is what this course is actually about, and it does not move.

docs.title: The course's own data
docs.text:
Freely redistributable. Every file in data/ is generated by tools/make_tayyar_data.py from a fixed seed. It contains no real operational telemetry, no personal data and no third-party copyrighted content. It may be distributed to participants, committed to participants' own public capstone repositories, and reused in later deliveries without restriction.

Two conditions attach, and both are pedagogical rather than legal:

  1. It must be labelled as synthetic wherever it appears. A capstone repository that presents this series as Saudi grid data, or that reports a MAPE as evidence of real-world performance, is making a claim it cannot support. Data-provenance honesty is part of the assessed work.
  2. ksa_grid_demand_clean.csv is instructor-only until Lab 1 is graded. It is the answer key. It may be released afterwards, and should be — participants comparing their cleaned series against it learn more than the mark tells them.

docs.title: External datasets
docs.text:
Nothing in section 3 may be re-hosted by the Academy without checking its terms first. The safe default for every one of them is to link to the source and have participants download it themselves. That is also better practice, since it makes the provenance visible.

UCI ElectricityLoadDiagrams20112014. Published under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), which permits redistribution and adaptation with attribution. Carry the attribution wherever the data or anything derived from it appears — slides, notebooks and any derived dataset:

ElectricityLoadDiagrams20112014, UCI Machine Learning Repository. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Available at https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/321/electricityloaddiagrams20112014

Confirm the donor name and the current citation format on the dataset page before publishing; UCI has revised its citation guidance over time.

Monash Time Series Forecasting Archive. Datasets are distributed through Zenodo with per-record licensing; most are CC BY 4.0. Cite the archive paper (Godahewa, Bergmeir, Webb, Hyndman and Montero-Manso, 2021) alongside the individual dataset record.

Open Power System Data. Licensing is stated per data package and derives from the underlying TSO and ENTSO-E sources. Check the specific package page and reproduce whatever attribution it specifies.

Kaggle competition datasets (Store Sales, M5, Wikipedia Web Traffic). Governed by the competition rules accepted at download, which commonly restrict redistribution. Do not stage these on a shared Academy drive without checking. Participants download them under their own accounts.

UCI Metro Interstate Traffic Volume, METR-LA, PEMS-BAY. Check terms on the respective source pages before any redistribution.

docs.title: Course materials
docs.text: The notebooks, briefs, case studies and generator scripts in this repository are Academy teaching materials. Distribute them through the Academy's normal channels. If a delivery publishes them publicly, strip ksa_grid_demand_clean.csv and the solution notebooks from the public copy first — they are answer keys, and the assessment depends on them not being available before the labs are graded.

docs.title: Facilitator Run-Sheet — SDA-DSC-212 Time Series Analysis and Forecasting
docs.text: 3 days × 5 learning hours = 15 hours. Each "hour" is 50 minutes of instruction plus a 10-minute buffer. Schedule the long break around Dhuhr. Deliver in Arabic or English; keep all code, column names and commit messages in English — mixed-language identifiers break tooling in Saudi enterprise environments.

docs.title: The one thing to hold on to
docs.text:
Every module advances the same artefact: Tayyar, a day-ahead load-forecasting service for the Central Operating Area. Never introduce a throwaway airline-passengers toy set beyond one warm-up plot. The golden thread is what makes the Day-3 backtest report and the capstone achievable in fifteen hours.

The non-negotiable is temporal leakage. Publish the leakage-smells poster (instructor/posters/P1_leakage_smells.pdf) on the wall and point at it every single time a random split appears on anyone's screen.

docs.title: T-minus one week
docs.text:
• Fork or clone the course repo; push the checkpoint tags lab1-start … lab7-start and lab1-solution … lab7-solution, and the sim-* branches: sim-gap, sim-agg, sim-spurious, sim-overdiff, sim-aic-trap, sim-nodamp, sim-centred-roll, sim-heatwave, sim-hetero, sim-train-coverage, sim-fit-once, sim-lucky-split, sim-leaderboard, sim-asymmetric.
  • Regenerate the datasets: python tools/make_tayyar_data.py. Confirm 26,280 clean rows, peak ≈ 57.9 GW, mean ≈ 33.1 GW.
  • Run python tools/run_reference.py and check every number against reference_results.json. This is your answer key and the source of every figure in the deck.
  • Execute all seven solution notebooks end to end on a clean machine and on the Colab fallback (data pre-loaded to a mounted drive). Budget: Lab 6 takes about 11 minutes.
  • Verify the two fragile installs, pmdarima and Prophet, on both Windows and macOS. Pin working versions in the lock file. Neither is required by the core labs — the course runs on statsmodels, LightGBM and scikit-learn — but participants will try to install them.
  • Time-box Lab 4 (feature engineering) and Lab 6 (backtesting). Confirm git checkout labN-start fast-forwards a straggler cleanly.
  • Print the five A4 posters: instructor/posters/ALL_POSTERS.pdf.
  • Prepare the shared leaderboard for the Day-3 bake-off (MASE, coverage, pinball).

docs.title: T-minus two days — participant email
docs.text:
• Python 3.12, git, a GitHub account.
  • conda/uv environment; pip install pandas numpy matplotlib statsmodels scipy scikit-learn lightgbm jupyter
  • VS Code (or preferred IDE) with the Python extension.
  • Clone the course repo and run make doctor — it prints ✓/✗ per package.
  • Confirm the classroom network allows github.com and PyPI, or configure a mirror. Pre-download the datasets to the shared drive for offline rooms.

docs.title: Day 1 — Seeing the Signal
docs.text:
Hour Session Mode Theory/Lab Facilitator focus 1 Why time series breaks ordinary ML · course kickoff interactive lecture + failure story 80/20 Tell the failure story as a story, not a slide. Ask who has shipped a model whose live accuracy did not match validation. Almost every hand goes up. 2 Decomposition: trend, seasonality, remainder (M1) lecture + live STL demo 65/35 Do the clean-and-decompose live in under 8 minutes. Deliberately skip asfreq once, show the seasonal smear, then fix it. 3 Lab 1 — load, index, resample, decompose guided lab, pairs 15/85 Circulate. Do not warn anyone about the messy timestamps. Let a pair discover the silent row loss. 4 Stationarity and autocorrelation (M2) lecture + ACF/PACF walkthrough 65/35 Run the verdict-reconciliation drill: call p-value pairs, room says the reconciled verdict aloud. Quiz the ADF/KPSS nulls cold. 5 Lab 2 — the stationarity report guided lab, pairs 15/85 Watch for pairs who difference until ADF is happy and stop thinking. Send them to the lag-1 ACF.

End of Day 1 deliverable. A clean hourly Tayyar series with decomposition plots and a stationarity report (ADF/KPSS, ACF/PACF). This is capstone milestone M-A — spot-check the index, the gap policy and the reported strengths before anyone leaves.

Activities available: decomposition read-aloud (15 min) · "component or covariate?" card sort (10 min) · ACF/PACF speed round (15 min) · verdict reconciliation drill (10 min).

docs.title: Day 2 — Building Forecasts
docs.text:
Rotate the pairs. Put a strong-statistics participant with a strong-ML participant — the M3→M4 bridge is exactly where that skill transfer pays off.

Hour Session Mode Theory/Lab Facilitator focus 1 ARIMA and SARIMA (M3) lecture + demo 65/35 Flag the m = 24 wall early and say it is deliberate. Do not hide that the fitted SARIMAX fails its own Ljung-Box test — that honesty is why the ML route exists. 2 ETS (M3) + Lab 3 micro-lecture + guided lab 40/60 Run "explain it to the control room": one sentence each, read aloud, cut any sentence containing the word "parameter". 3 Feature-based ML forecasting (M4) lecture + feature-build demo 60/40 Run "what does this feature see?" — eight candidates, thumbs up/down. Include the ambiguous one (temperature) and let the argument happen. 4 Lab 4 — LightGBM forecaster guided lab, pairs 10/90 Protect the full 50 minutes. Run task 1 as a race: first pair to name both planted leaks precisely wins. 5 Probabilistic forecasting (M5) + Lab 5 start lecture + lab 45/55 End the day after Lab 5 task 3, with the room holding an interval that visibly under-covers. They will think about it overnight.

End of Day 2 deliverable. SARIMAX and ETS baselines plus a LightGBM feature-based forecaster, all producing 24-hour forecasts. Capstone milestone M-B — the leak check must pass.

docs.title: Day 3 — Trust and Selection
docs.text:
Hour Session Mode Theory/Lab Facilitator focus 1 Intervals and calibration (M5) + Lab 5 finish micro-lecture + lab 35/65 The CQR fix lands hard this morning because they slept on a broken interval. Then show the conditional-coverage table — 0.90 marginal hides 0.845 on peak hours. 2 Backtesting and forecast evaluation (M6) lecture + backtest dissection 55/45 Run "baseline first" (10 min): every pair hand-computes the seasonal-naive error for one day. That number is what everything must beat. 3 Lab 6 — rolling-origin backtest guided lab, pairs 10/90 Protect the full 50 minutes. Run the shared leaderboard on the projector. Then the significance debate: class predicts the DM verdict by eye, then runs it. 4 Case study + capstone assembly (M7) case discussion + project work 20/80 Start on time — cut discussion, not build time. Collect repository URLs at the END of this hour so you can spot-check backtests before the demos. 5 Capstone demos + assessment + wrap-up presentations 15/85 Five minutes each. Grade from the repository first: clone, run the one command, check the numbers regenerate.

End of Day 3 deliverable. A rolling-origin backtest report with calibrated intervals, a model-selection decision, and the capstone demo. Milestones M-C, M-D, M-E.

docs.title: Pace control
docs.text:
• If you are behind: compress the M6 theory — it lands through the lab anyway. Reduce Lab 7 to two constraint scenarios and demo the third.
  • Never drop the backtest report. It is the course's deliverable and its thesis made visible.
  • If the cohort is strong: pull the multi-area global model into the capstone main scope and add a fourth model family (TBATS or Prophet) to the bake-off.
  • If the cohort is weak: keep every lab, cut every optional activity, and hold the golden thread.
  • Publish checkpoint tags so stragglers fast-forward: git checkout lab4-start.

docs.title: Common issues and their resolutions
docs.text: Issue Frequency Resolution pmdarima / Prophet install fails on Windows or macOS wheels High Pin known-good versions; fall back to the provided Colab notebooks — no penalty. Neither is required by the core labs. auto_arima or SARIMAX with m=24 runs for minutes High Model the daily series with m=7; leave sub-daily structure to the ML route. This is a deliberate, teachable wall. ADF and KPSS null hypotheses read backwards High The 2×2 poster. Quiz it cold. ADF small p = stationary; KPSS small p = non-stationary. Suspiciously low MAPE (a leak survives) High Re-run assert_no_leakage; check .shift(1) on every rolling feature and that no shuffle split remains. KSA weekend coded as Saturday–Sunday Medium Friday(4) and Saturday(5) in pandas dayofweek, where Monday = 0. Check the calendar join. Backtest scores in-sample (MASE ≈ 0) Medium Training data at every origin must end at or before that origin. Never predict points the model trained on. Confidence versus prediction interval confusion Medium A prediction interval includes the noise, so it is wider. Forecasting always wants it. Rolling backtest with SARIMAX refit is slow Medium Expected. Cache the cheap models, parallelise the folds, shrink the candidate grid, or state a coarser retrain cadence and quantify its effect. Quantile crossing (q95 < q50) Low Sort the per-row quantiles, or use a monotone constraint. Coverage good marginally, fails on hot afternoons Low Report coverage by hour band. Switch to adaptive conformal (ACI/EnbPI). MSTL panels come out blank Low MSTL drops the DatetimeIndex from its components, and STL cannot handle NaN. Interpolate first, then reattach the index before plotting.

docs.title: Discussion prompts (use during transitions)
docs.text:
1. What is the most expensive forecasting error you have seen reach a decision — and would a backtest have caught it?
  2. Your model's MAPE is 2.3%. Your interval covers 90% on average but 85% on the hottest afternoons. Which number does the control room feel?
  3. When is the free seasonal-naive forecast the right answer, and how would your report prove it?
  4. Who owns the reserve-margin quantile — forecasting, operations, or risk? What does your answer imply about which number you publish?
  5. If the repository is the audit evidence for an accuracy claim, what does your current backtest testify?

docs.text:
• One slide mapping each capstone requirement to the module that taught it: decomposition → M1, stationarity → M2, classical → M3, features → M4, intervals → M5, backtest → M6, selection → M7.

docs.title: Practical Assessment 2 — The Leakage Post-Mortem
