docs.title: The core lesson
docs.text:
In forecasting, a model is only as trustworthy as the temporal integrity of its evaluation.

State it once, at the end. Do not state it at the beginning, and do not restate it. The whole design of this exercise is that participants arrive at it themselves, having measured the gap with their own hands, and a sentence they have earned is worth more than a sentence they have been given.

docs.title: Participant-facing scenario
docs.text:
Hand this out, or read it. It is the entire briefing they get.

Eight weeks ago your team shipped a LightGBM day-ahead forecaster for the Central Operating Area. The validation report was excellent: 1.61% MAPE on a 20% held-out sample. That number was in the deck that got the project approved, and it beat the incumbent SARIMAX comfortably.

The service has now been live for six weeks. Operations reports errors between three and five percent — occasionally worse — and the day-ahead scheduling engineer has quietly gone back to her similar-day spreadsheet for the afternoon peak. Nothing in the code has changed since the validation run. The model that produced 1.61% and the model producing 4% are the same model, running on the same data source.

The engineer who built it has left. You have the training script and the feature-building code. The head of the unit wants three things from you by the end of the hour, in this order:

  1. What is the true day-ahead accuracy of this model?
  2. Why did the validation report say otherwise?
  3. What has to change so that this cannot happen again?

You will not be marked on making the model better. You will be marked on establishing what it actually does, on identifying precisely which lines of code broke temporal integrity, and on re-measuring honestly once you have fixed them. A correct diagnosis with a worse-looking number scores higher than a good number with no diagnosis.

docs.title: Your tasks
docs.text:
1. Detect. Establish that the reported 1.61% is not achievable at serve time. Do not argue it from first principles — demonstrate it.
  2. Identify. Name every engineered feature that uses information not available at the forecast origin, and state for each one exactly which future observations it touches. A feature name without that statement does not count.
  3. Redesign. Rebuild the feature pipeline so that every feature at origin t is computable from information available at or before t. Prove it with an automated check, not by inspection.
  4. Re-run. Re-evaluate under a rolling-origin backtest at the 24-hour horizon.
  5. Compare. Report the corrected figure against the original, state the ratio between them, and write one paragraph an executive who approved the project on the original number can read.

docs.title: The rule that governs all of it
docs.text: At forecast origin t, the model may use any observation timestamped at or before t, and nothing else. Every failure in this exercise is a violation of that one sentence.

docs.title: The exact planted defects
docs.text:
Facilitator reference. Do not distribute before the exercise.

There are two independent classes of defect — three leaking features and one broken evaluation design — and participants must find both classes to score full marks on diagnosis. Finding the features and leaving the shuffle split in place is the most common partial answer.

docs.title: Defect class 1 — the leaking features
docs.text:
All three are added in tools/leak_demo.py to a feature matrix that is otherwise clean:

Xleak["roll_mean24_centred"]  = y.rolling(24, center=True, min_periods=1).mean()
Xleak["roll_max24_centred"]   = y.rolling(24, center=True, min_periods=1).max()
Xleak["demand_next_day_mean"] = y.shift(-24).rolling(6, min_periods=1).mean()
Feature What it looks like What it actually contains roll_mean24_centred "the last day's average demand" The mean of y[t-12 … t+11]. Eleven of those twenty-four hours are after the forecast origin. roll_max24_centred "the last day's peak" The maximum over the same window. Worse than the mean, because a maximum is dominated by a single extreme value — so a future spike propagates into the feature almost undiluted. demand_next_day_mean An exogenous input "known" from a planning system mean(y[t+19 … t+24]). It contains the target itself, y[t+24], as one of six terms. This is not a subtle leak; it is the answer written into the question paper.

The first two are the interesting ones. They are the leaks that survive code review, because the variable name is accurate about the window length and silent about its position.

docs.title: Defect class 2 — the broken evaluation design
docs.text:
train_test_split(Xleak[ok], Y24[ok], test_size=.2, random_state=0, shuffle=True)

A random shuffle over an autocorrelated hourly series places the hour before and the hour after most test observations into the training set. The model is not forecasting; it is interpolating between two known neighbours. This leaks even with a perfectly clean feature matrix — which is exactly what design B below is built to prove.

docs.title: What a clean pipeline does instead
docs.text:
src/tayyar/features/build.py is the corrected reference, and it is already in the repository — participants who think to read it will find the fix in four lines:

base = out[col].shift(1)                       # <-- the leakage guard
for w in windows:
    r = base.rolling(w, min_periods=max(2, w // 4), center=False)

.shift(1) before the rolling window, center=False always. The module also ships assert_no_leakage(), which applies two checks: no feature correlates with the target above 0.9999, and — the check worth teaching — shuffling the future rows of the target must not change any past feature value. That second check is a genuine test of temporal integrity rather than a heuristic, and it catches the centred windows immediately.

docs.title: The measured numbers
docs.text:
One model. One dataset. One target: demand 24 hours ahead. Only the evaluation design and one feature block change between the four rows. These are measured values from leak_results.json, reproducible by running python tools/leak_demo.py from the repository root.

Design Split Features Day-ahead MAPE What it is A Random shuffle, 20% held out Leaky (three centred/future features added) 1.61% The number in the approval deck. Both defects present. B Random shuffle, 20% held out Clean 2.00% Isolates the split. Fixing the features alone still leaves a 2.00% figure that cannot be delivered. C Time-ordered, last 20% held out Clean 3.54% An honest single split. The first defensible number. D Rolling-origin backtest, 8 origins Clean 3.66% Decision-grade evidence. Per-origin range 2.31% to 4.89%.

The headline: 3.66 / 1.61 = 2.27. The leaked design reported a model 2.3 times more accurate than it actually is. Operations reported three to five percent; design D says 3.66% with a per-origin range of 2.31% to 4.89%. The field observation and the honest backtest agree. The approval deck and reality do not.

Three things in that table are worth drawing out in the debrief, and they are the reason there are four rows rather than two:

B is the row that surprises people. Fixing the features and keeping the shuffle still yields 2.00% — a number that would still have got the project approved and would still have failed in production. Participants who only find the features have found roughly half the problem, and the half they found is the easier half.

The gap from B to C is larger than the gap from A to B. 2.00 → 3.54 is 1.54 points; 1.61 → 2.00 is 0.39. On an autocorrelated series, the evaluation design leaks more than the features do. This inverts most people's prior, which is that leakage is a feature-engineering problem. It is primarily a validation-design problem.

D is only slightly worse than C, and that is the point of D. The single time-ordered split gives 3.54% and the rolling-origin backtest gives 3.66% — close on average. But C is one number from one arbitrary cut point, and D is eight, with a spread from 2.31% to 4.89%. C cannot tell you that the model has weeks where it doubles its error. D can, and the operations report of "three to five percent" is legible only against D's spread.

docs.title: A second, independent measurement
docs.text:
reference_results.json records the same effect at a different framing, from the main reference run:

Design MAPE Shuffled split with a centred rolling window 1.21% Time-ordered split, 1-step-ahead target 1.40% Honest day-ahead (24-hour horizon) 2.33%

This second table adds a distinct lesson worth thirty seconds in the debrief: even with a clean split and clean features, the horizon matters enormously. A 1-step-ahead evaluation reports 1.40% for a service that must deliver 2.33% at the horizon it actually serves. Reporting h+1 accuracy for an h+24 service is not leakage, but it is the same category of error — measuring something easier than the job.

docs.title: The subtlety worth teaching: where pandas centres an even window
docs.text:
This is the technical heart of the exercise and it should not be asserted from the front. Make participants prove it.

rolling(24, center=True) has to place a 24-element window around a single point, and 24 is even, so it cannot be symmetric. Pandas resolves this by taking [t-12, t+11] — twelve hours before, eleven after, plus the current hour. Not [t-11, t+12]. Most people, asked to guess, guess wrong, and almost nobody has checked.

The consequence is direct: at forecast origin t, this feature has already read eleven hours of the future. For a next-hour target it contains the target itself. For the 24-hour-ahead target used in this exercise it does not literally contain y[t+24], but it contains eleven observations the forecaster cannot possibly have at 14:00 — and the model, quite reasonably, uses them.

docs.title: The proof, in six lines
docs.text:
Have every pair run this and read the output aloud before they touch the model:

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
s = pd.Series(np.arange(50, dtype=float))          # the value at index i IS i
r = s.rolling(24, center=True, min_periods=1)
print(r.min()[30], r.max()[30])       # -> 18.0 41.0   i.e. the window is [t-12, t+11]
print(s.rolling(25, center=True, min_periods=1).min()[30],
      s.rolling(25, center=True, min_periods=1).max()[30])   # -> 18.0 42.0  (odd: symmetric)
print(s.shift(1).rolling(24, min_periods=1).min()[30],
      s.shift(1).rolling(24, min_periods=1).max()[30])       # ->  6.0 29.0  (the clean version)

Because the series holds its own index as its value, min and max over the window report the window's first and last positions directly. At t = 30 the centred 24-window spans 18 to 41 — eleven hours past the origin. The odd-length 25-window spans 18 to 42, genuinely symmetric. The .shift(1).rolling(24) version spans 6 to 29, ending strictly before t, which is the only one of the three that a forecaster may use.

Three points to make once the output is on screen:

  1. The asymmetry is not a bug. It is a documented, arbitrary tie-break for even windows. Any convention would be wrong for forecasting; the problem is center=True at all.
  2. The magnitude of the leak depends on the window's parity in a way nobody expects. A 24-hour centred window leaks 11 hours; a 25-hour centred window leaks 12. Reasoning about this from memory is how the defect gets past review.
  3. The fix is not "use an odd window". The fix is center=False and .shift(1), and it is unconditional. There is no forecasting situation in which a centred window is correct.

Facilitator note. Do not accept "I know how centring works" from a confident participant. Ask them, before they run the code, whether the 24-window is [t-12, t+11] or [t-11, t+12]. In most rooms the split is roughly even, which is itself the argument for running the check.

docs.title: Facilitator timing plan
docs.text:
Thirty minutes of work, five of debrief. Pairs, at machines, with the repository checked out.

Minutes Phase What the facilitator does 0–3 Brief Read the scenario. Put the three questions on the board: what is the true accuracy, why did validation lie, what changes. Say that diagnosis outscores accuracy. Say nothing about leakage, centring, or splits. Resist every attempt to be asked what to look for. 3–6 The window check Everyone runs the six-line snippet, before touching the model. Ask the room for a show of hands on [t-12, t+11] versus [t-11, t+12] first, record the split on the board, then let them run it. Three minutes, no discussion, straight into the next phase. 6–16 Detect and identify Pairs work through tools/leak_demo.py and the feature matrix. Circulate. Give no answers; give questions instead. In escalating order of directness, for a pair that is stuck: "at 14:00 today, which rows of this dataframe exist?"; "pick your most important feature — write down which timestamps it reads"; "what does shuffle=True do to two adjacent hours?"; "there is a function in src/tayyar/features/ whose name tells you what it does." Do not go past the fourth question before minute 13. Note which pairs find the split defect as well as the feature defects — that distinction drives the debrief. 16–25 Redesign and re-run Pairs rebuild the features with .shift(1) and center=False, run assert_no_leakage, then re-evaluate under a time-ordered split and a rolling-origin backtest. Most will reproduce something close to designs C and D; exact reproduction of 3.54 and 3.66 depends on their split and origin choices and should not be required. Watch for the pair that fixes the features, keeps the shuffle, gets ~2.0% and declares victory — that is design B, and it is the most instructive wrong answer in the room. If one appears, hold it for the debrief rather than correcting it in private. 25–30 Write-up Individual, silent, five minutes. Each participant writes the comparison table and the executive paragraph. Enforce the silence — this is the assessed artefact and it must be individual work. 30–35 Debrief Put all four measured designs on the board in order. Ask the room to predict the B row before revealing it; the underestimate is consistent and it makes the point better than any explanation. Then draw the two gaps: A→B is 0.39 points, B→C is 1.54. Say once, and only here: on an autocorrelated series the evaluation design leaks more than the features do. Show the D spread — 2.31% to 4.89% — against the operations report of three to five percent, and let the room notice that the honest backtest predicted the field result. Then, and not before, state the core lesson. Finish by pointing at the capstone anti-pattern list, where shuffle=True and centred rolling features each cap a criterion at 70%.

If the room is ahead of schedule, the extension is: quantify how much of the A→B gap comes from each of the three leaking features by removing them one at a time. roll_max24_centred usually contributes more than roll_mean24_centred, and asking why before measuring is a good thirty seconds.

If the room is behind, cut the redesign phase to fixing the features only, and present designs C and D from leak_results.json rather than having participants generate them. The diagnosis is the assessed skill; the re-run is the confirmation.

docs.title: Scoring rubric
docs.text: Total 100. Marked on the individual write-up, with the pair's working available as evidence.

docs.title: Leak diagnosis notes — 40%
docs.text: Band Description 36–40 Both defect classes identified. All three leaking features named, each with a statement of which future observations it reads — including the correct [t-12, t+11] span for the centred windows. The shuffle split is identified as an independent defect, with the autocorrelation argument stated. The relative size of the two effects is noticed and commented on. 28–35 Both classes identified and all three features named, but the window span is described loosely ("it sees the future") rather than precisely, or the relative magnitude is not addressed. 20–27 All three features found; the shuffle split missed or mentioned only in passing. This is the common ceiling and it should be applied firmly — a fix that leaves the split in place ships a 2.00% number that is still wrong. 10–19 Only the obvious defect (demand_next_day_mean) found. The centred windows, which are the ones that survive code review, were not recognised as leaks. 0–9 Leakage asserted without evidence, or the diagnosis is "the model overfitted".

docs.title: Correct fixes — 40%
docs.text: Band Description 36–40 Feature pipeline rebuilt with .shift(1) and center=False throughout. Temporal integrity proved automatically — assert_no_leakage or an equivalent check, with the future-shuffle test present, not merely a correlation threshold. Evaluation moved to a time-ordered split and then to a rolling-origin backtest with training data at every origin ending at or before that origin. 28–35 Features and split both corrected and the backtest runs, but integrity is argued by inspection rather than demonstrated by a check that would fail if the leak returned. 20–27 Features fixed, evaluation still shuffled; or evaluation fixed, one leaking feature left in. 10–19 Leaking features deleted rather than replaced, so the model loses the legitimate rolling information it should have had. The pipeline is now honest and needlessly weaker, and the write-up does not notice. 0–9 No working fix, or a "fix" that changes the reported number without changing what the features read.

docs.title: Honest re-measurement — 20%
docs.text:
Band Description 18–20 Corrected figure reported at the 24-hour horizon under a rolling-origin backtest, with the per-origin spread, not just the mean. The ratio to the original stated explicitly. The executive paragraph states the model is roughly 2.3 times less accurate than reported, without hedging, and says what it is nonetheless still good for. 14–17 Corrected figure and ratio reported honestly; the spread omitted, so the write-up cannot explain the "three to five percent" field report. 8–13 A corrected figure is reported but framed defensively — the degradation is attributed to drift, to data changes, or to production conditions rather than to the evaluation. 0–7 The corrected figure is presented alongside the original without acknowledging that the original was wrong; or the worse number is quietly not mentioned.

Overriding rule. A write-up that reports a corrected figure worse than the true one, but diagnoses correctly and measures honestly, scores above a write-up that reports a better number with a thinner diagnosis. Say this at the briefing and mean it. The exercise exists to make honest measurement the thing that pays.

docs.title: What this connects to
docs.text:
• Capstone anti-pattern flags. train_test_split(shuffle=True) and centred rolling features each cap a capstone criterion at 70%. This exercise is where participants learn why before it costs them marks.
  • Milestone M-B, end of Day 2, gates on a leak check passing. Any pair that struggles here should be checked against their own Lab 4 output before Day 3 closes.
  • src/tayyar/features/build.py is the reference implementation and its module docstring names the same three traps this exercise plants. Participants who read it during the exercise have not cheated — they have done the correct thing, which is to look for whether the problem is already solved somewhere in the codebase. Say so in the debrief.
  • figures/08_leakage.png is the four-bar chart of designs A–D, generated by tools/leak_demo.py. Show it only in the debrief, after the numbers have been predicted.

docs.title: Lab notebook house style (follow lab1_start.ipynb / lab1_solution.ipynb exactly)
docs.text:
Every lab is TWO notebooks written by tools/make_notebooks.py-style code: labN_start.ipynb and labN_solution.ipynb.

Structure, in order: 1. markdown header: course line, ## Lab N — <Title>, duration, "Work in pairs", git checkout labN-<start|solution>, and the course rule blockquote. 2. markdown "### Tasks" table with the minute allocation per task (from the spec given). 3. a code cell with the standard SETUP block (sys.path, imports, DATA = "../data"). 4. one ### Task k — <short name> markdown heading per task, followed by: - in the start notebook: a code cell of TODO scaffolding — imports that are needed, a comment block stating exactly what to build and in what order, and a HINT line naming the trap the task exists to teach. NO working implementation. - in the solution notebook: the working code, followed where useful by a short markdown paragraph interpreting the result in plain language. 5. a final markdown cell with the commit message and the deliverable file the lab writes. 6. solution only: a final ### Instructor notes markdown cell — the simulation branches to use, what to let participants discover unaided, and a fast-finisher extension.

Rules: - Real, runnable code against the src/tayyar package (see API below). No pseudo-code. - The start notebook must be genuinely incomplete but genuinely runnable up to the TODO. - Labs 4, 5 and 6 must ship the PLANTED BUGS described in their spec in the START notebook, and fix them in the solution. - Keep every printed number consistent with reference_results.json in the repo root. - British/technical prose. No emoji. No bullet padding.

docs.title: MODULE 2 — Stationarity and Autocorrelation
docs.text: Header: Module 2 · "Stationarity and Autocorrelation" · Day 1, Hour 4 (theory, 65/35) + Day 1, Hour 5 = Lab 2 (15/85) · Maps to LO1 (primary), LO2 (differencing)

docs.title: Learning Objectives (verbatim)
docs.text:
# Objective Maps to 2.1 Define weak stationarity and identify sources of non-stationarity LO1 2.2 Apply and reconcile ADF and KPSS tests LO1 2.3 Apply regular and seasonal differencing to achieve stationarity LO1, LO2 2.4 Compute and interpret ACF and PACF LO1 2.5 Translate ACF/PACF signatures into candidate ARIMA orders LO1, LO2

Purpose/framing line for title slide: "Classical models assume stationarity — diagnose it, transform to it, then read autocorrelation to fingerprint the model." Business relevance: a model fit to non-stationary data produces "confidently wrong forecasts" — projects yesterday's level/variance into a future where both moved; mistaking trend for stationary mean is called "the single most expensive analytical error" in demand/economic forecasting.

docs.title: Technical Content
docs.text:
1. Stationarity, precisely - Weak (covariance) stationarity = 3 things constant over time: mean, variance, autocovariance at each lag (depends only on gap k, not position). - Matters because ARIMA-family models estimate ONE parameter set assumed to hold throughout. - Three sources of non-stationarity, each with its remedy: - Trend (mean changes) → differencing or detrend by modeling trend - Seasonality (mean changes periodically) → seasonal differencing or model the season - Changing variance (heteroskedasticity) → variance-stabilizing transform (log, Box-Cox) - Tayyar has all three: growth trend, multi-period seasonality, summer-amplified variance. Fix order: stabilize variance (log, Module 1) → then difference.

2. Testing stationarity: ADF and KPSS — opposite nulls - ADF: null = "has a unit root" = non-stationary. Small p (< 0.05) → reject non-stationarity → evidence of stationarity. - KPSS: null = "is stationary." Small p (< 0.05) → reject stationarity → evidence of non-stationarity. - The 2×2 reconciliation table (verbatim):

KPSS says stationary KPSS says non-stationary ADF says stationary Stationary — proceed Difference-stationary; try differencing ADF says non-stationary Trend-stationary; detrend Non-stationary — difference and re-test
  • Teaching point: using both is best practice because they can disagree — the disagreement itself is informative (trend-stationary vs difference-stationary). Never rely on one test or eyeballing alone.

3. Differencing: regular and seasonal - Regular: ∇y_t = y_t − y_{t−1} removes trend → gives d in ARIMA. - Seasonal: ∇m y_t = y_t − y removes seasonal pattern of period m → gives D in SARIMA. - Discipline: - Difference as little as possible. Over-differencing injects artificial negative autocorrelation at lag 1, inflates variance. Signature: lag-1 ACF strongly negative (< −0.5), noisier-than-needed series. - Order of operations: seasonal differencing first, re-test; regular difference only if still non-stationary. Most series need d ≤ 2, D ≤ 1. - pmdarima.arima.ndiffs / nsdiffs estimate d, D from tests — "automation proposes, the analyst disposes."

4. ACF and PACF: the model fingerprint - ACF(k) = correlation between y_t and y_{t−k}. PACF(k) = correlation at lag k after removing intervening lags' effect. - Fingerprint table (verbatim):

Pattern ACF PACF Suggests AR(p) tails off (decays) cuts off after lag p AR order p MA(q) cuts off after lag q tails off MA order q ARMA(p,q) tails off tails off mixed; use information criteria Seasonal spike at lag m, 2m, … spike at m seasonal terms
  • "Cuts off" = drops inside significance band (±1.96/√n).
  • Tayyar's daily-differenced series: expect spike at lag 24 and multiples.

docs.title: Design Principles / Best Practices / Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Principles - Transform for variance, difference for mean — do them in that order. - Stationarity is a means, not the goal — invert every transform to forecast on the original scale. - Autocorrelation is structure, not noise — strong ACF is exploitable signal; flat ACF ≈ 0 everywhere = already white noise, nothing beats naive.

Common mistakes (each planted in Lab 2 starter) 1. Interpreting ADF's null backwards ("p > 0.05 so it's stationary"). 2. Over-differencing until stationary but the model is worse. 3. Differencing before stabilizing variance — heteroskedasticity survives. 4. Reading the ACF of a non-stationary series (slow, linear decay) and mistaking it for high AR order rather than a trend to difference. 5. Ignoring seasonal spikes at lag m because default lags=20 doesn't reach 24. 6. Running tests on log series but forecasting/evaluating on raw series without back-transforming.

Production considerations: Re-run stationarity diagnostics on a schedule (regime shift risk — tariff change, new industrial load). Persist chosen d, D, transform for reproducibility; drift in these choices is itself a monitored signal.

docs.text:
src/tayyar/analysis/stationarity.py — stationarity_report(series: pd.Series) -> dict 

adf_p = adfuller(s, autolag="AIC")[1]
kpss_p = kpss(s, regression="c", nlags="auto")[1]
adf_stationary = adf_p < 0.05      # reject unit root
kpss_stationary = kpss_p > 0.05    # fail to reject stationarity
if adf_stationary and kpss_stationary: verdict = "stationary"
elif not adf_stationary and not kpss_stationary: verdict = "non-stationary (difference)"
elif adf_stationary and not kpss_stationary: verdict = "difference-stationary"
else: verdict = "trend-stationary (detrend)"

src/tayyar/analysis/differencing.py — suggest_orders(), make_stationary() 

def suggest_orders(series, m=24):
    d = ndiffs(s, test="adf")
    D = nsdiffs(s, m=m, test="ocsb")
    return {"d": int(d), "D": int(D), "m": m}

def make_stationary(series, d, D, m):
    """Seasonal difference FIRST, then regular. Minimal differencing."""
    for _ in range(D): s = s.diff(m)
    for _ in range(d): s = s.diff(1)

src/tayyar/analysis/correlograms.py — correlograms(series, lags=60, path=...) 

plot_acf(series.dropna(), lags=lags, ax=ax[0])   # MA(q): cuts off at q
plot_pacf(series.dropna(), lags=lags, ax=ax[1], method="ywm")  # AR(p): cuts off at p
ax[0].set_title("ACF — look for spikes at 24, 48 (daily seasonality)")

docs.title: Lab 2 — The Stationarity Report
docs.text:
• Objective: produce a defensible stationarity report; test, difference to right order, propose candidate ARIMA orders from ACF/PACF.
  • Duration: 50 min. Setup: git checkout lab2-start; pip install pmdarima
  • Tasks:
  • (8 min) Run stationarity_report on raw log-demand; interpret ADF+KPSS together; record verdict; predict differencing needed.
  • (10 min) suggest_orders (m=24) → make_stationary (seasonal first); re-run report to confirm stationarity.
  • (10 min) Plot before/after differencing; check lag-1 ACF for over-differencing signature; reduce d if seen.
  • (12 min) ACF/PACF with lags=60; annotate seasonal spike at lag 24; read candidate (p,q) and seasonal (P,Q).
  • (5 min) Write STATIONARITY.md: verdict, chosen (d,D), 2–3 candidate SARIMA orders with justification.
  • (5 min) Commit: feat(analysis): stationarity report + candidate SARIMA orders.
  • Expected output (verbatim): 
    $ python -m tayyar.analysis.run_stationarity
Raw log-demand : ADF p=0.42  KPSS p=0.01  -> non-stationary (difference)
Suggested       : d=1, D=1, m=24
After D=1,d=1   : ADF p=0.00  KPSS p=0.10  -> stationary
ACF/PACF        : PACF cuts ~lag 2; ACF spike at 24 -> candidates:
                  SARIMA(2,1,1)(1,1,1)[24], (1,1,2)(0,1,1)[24], (2,1,0)(1,1,0)[24]
Wrote acf_pacf.png, STATIONARITY.md
  • Troubleshooting: ADF+KPSS both "non-stationary" mislabeled → nulls read backwards; lag-1 ACF ≈ −0.6 → over-differenced, reduce d; no seasonal spike → set lags ≥ 2×m; "p-value greater than 0.1" warning → expected, treat as p>0.1.

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz (Q&A verbatim): 1. ADF p=0.01 — stationary or not? → evidence of stationary (reject unit root). 2. KPSS p=0.01 — stationary or not? → evidence of non-stationary (reject stationarity). 3. Which comes first for seasonal data, seasonal or regular differencing? → seasonal, then re-test. 4. ACF tails off, PACF cuts off after lag 2 — model/order? → AR(2). 5. A slowly, linearly decaying ACF indicates what? → a trend (non-stationary); difference before reading further.

Debugging exercise: Branch sim-overdiff differences twice where once suffices; diagnose negative lag-1 ACF and fix. Pattern-matching drill: Six anonymized ACF/PACF pairs (AR, MA, ARMA, seasonal, white noise, non-stationary); label + candidate order.

docs.title: Case Study — Forecasting a Non-Stationary Economic Indicator
docs.text:
• Scenario: planning ministry forecasts monthly economic activity index for quarterly budgeting; analyst regressed index on trending oil-price, reported near-perfect fit that collapsed out of sample.
  • Business context: budget allocations move on these forecasts; spurious relationship → over-commitment.
  • Technical challenge: establish integration order of both series, difference to stationarity, only then assess genuine relationship.
  • Constraints: short monthly history (~120 points); strong annual seasonality; structural break at known policy change (must not blindly difference away).
  • Solution approach: (1) ADF/KPSS each series; (2) determine d for each; (3) seasonal differencing for annual pattern; (4) re-test relationship on stationary series; (5) discuss structural break — dummy vs split sample.
  • Discussion questions: Why does regressing two trending series give spurious high R²? How decide dummy vs model reset for the break? With 120 points, what limits differencing? When is slow ACF decay a sign to difference vs genuine long memory?

docs.title: MODULE 3 — ARIMA and Exponential Smoothing
docs.text: Header: Module 3 · "ARIMA and Exponential Smoothing" · Day 2, Hour 1 (ARIMA/SARIMA, 65/35) + Day 2, Hour 2 (ETS + Lab 3, 40/60) · Maps to LO2 (primary), LO3

docs.title: Learning Objectives (verbatim)
docs.text:
# Objective Maps to 3.1 Specify and fit ARIMA/SARIMA models with justified orders LO2 3.2 Incorporate exogenous regressors with SARIMAX LO2, LO3 3.3 Select an exponential-smoothing/ETS specification from the taxonomy LO2 3.4 Diagnose model adequacy from residuals LO2, LO5 3.5 Compare ARIMA and ETS and choose per situation LO2, LO6

Framing: classical models remain the model to beat in regulated/safety-critical settings — "the forecast rose because the level term updated and the summer seasonal factor kicked in" is accepted by a control-room engineer; "the gradient boosting said so" is not.

docs.title: Technical Content
docs.text:
1. The ARIMA family - AR(p): y_t depends linearly on its own p past values. I(d): d differences to reach stationarity. MA(q): y_t depends on last q forecast errors (shocks). - SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)m adds seasonal AR(P), seasonal diff(D), seasonal MA(Q) at period m. For hourly Tayyar with daily cycle, m=24. - Practical constraint: m=24 (or 168) → state space grows, estimation slows sharply. Practitioners often model a daily-aggregated series with m=7 in SARIMA, leave sub-daily to ML (Module 4) — "where classical methods strain."

2. Order selection - Read correlograms (Module 2): AR from PACF cutoff, MA from ACF cutoff, seasonal terms from spikes at m. - Minimize information criterion (AICc for small samples, BIC for parsimony) across candidate grid. pmdarima.auto_arima automates stepwise search but analyst constrains it (max_p, seasonal=True, m, D) and confirms winner's residuals. - Never compare AIC across different d. Lower is better; differences under ~2 not meaningful.

3. SARIMAX: exogenous regressors - Load driven by temperature (available as forecast at prediction time). SARIMAX = SARIMA + linear function of X_t. - Tayyar adds temperature + calendar dummies (weekend, Ramadan, Eid). - Two cautions: (1) need FUTURE regressor values at forecast time (weather forecast — its error propagates); (2) regressors must be genuinely exogenous/available ahead, or it's a leak.

4. Exponential smoothing and ETS - Forecast as weighted average of past observations with exponentially decaying weights. - Ladder: SES (level only, flat forecast) → Holt (level+trend; damped_trend=True prevents implausible long-horizon extremes — "almost always the safer production choice") → Holt-Winters (level+trend+season, additive or multiplicative). - ETS taxonomy: (Error, Trend, Seasonal), each ∈ {None, Additive, Multiplicative}, e.g. ETS(A,Ad,M) = additive error, additive damped trend, multiplicative season. - statsmodels.ETSModel (or sktime/statsforecast automated selection) picks spec by AICc. ETS handles single seasonal period cleanly; multiple seasonalities need TBATS or ML route.

5. Residual diagnostics - Fitted model trustworthy only if residuals are white noise. Checks: - Residual ACF / Ljung-Box: null = "residuals independent." Small p → autocorrelation remains → raise an order. - Residual mean ≈ 0 (no bias), roughly constant variance (transform worked). - Approximate normality (histogram/Q-Q) — matters for interval validity more than point forecast. - plot_diagnostics() gives all four panels at once. Diagnostics are mandatory, not optional — "an un-diagnosed auto_arima result is a liability."

docs.title: Design Principles / Best Practices / Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Common mistakes 1. Comparing AIC across models with different differencing orders. 2. Trusting auto_arima without checking residual autocorrelation (Ljung-Box). 3. Forgetting exogenous regressors need future values at forecast time (temperature leak/unavailable). 4. Un-damped Holt trend → absurd long-horizon forecasts. 5. Fitting multiplicative seasonality/ETS to a series containing zeros. 6. Reporting forecasts on log scale, or back-transforming a log-mean without bias correction.

Production considerations: Refit on a schedule (parameter drift); persist orders, treat re-selection as monitored event. Classical intervals are cheap and honest — the baseline fancier methods must beat. For thousands of series, prefer automated ETS (statsforecast, vectorized/fast) over per-series hand-tuning.

docs.text:
src/tayyar/models/sarimax.py — fit_sarimax(), forecast_sarimax() 

def fit_sarimax(y, exog, order=(2,1,1), seasonal_order=(1,1,1,7)):
    model = sm.tsa.SARIMAX(y, exog=exog, order=order, seasonal_order=seasonal_order,
        enforce_stationarity=False, enforce_invertibility=False)
    return model.fit(disp=False)

def forecast_sarimax(res, exog_future, steps):
    fc = res.get_forecast(steps=steps, exog=exog_future)
    ci = fc.conf_int(alpha=0.10)   # 90% interval

src/tayyar/models/auto_order.py — select_arima() with mandatory Ljung-Box 

model = pm.auto_arima(y, X=exog, seasonal=True, m=m, d=1, D=1,
    max_p=3, max_q=3, max_P=2, max_Q=2,
    information_criterion="aicc", stepwise=True, suppress_warnings=True)
lb = acorr_ljungbox(model.resid(), lags=[14], return_df=True)
ok = p > 0.05
print(f"... Ljung-Box p={p:.3f} -> {'white noise OK' if ok else 'STRUCTURE LEFT'}")

src/tayyar/models/ets.py — fit_ets(), forecast_ets() 

def fit_ets(y, seasonal_periods=7):
    """Holt-Winters with DAMPED trend and multiplicative season."""
    model = ETSModel(y, error="add", trend="add", damped_trend=True,
        seasonal="mul", seasonal_periods=seasonal_periods)
    return model.fit(disp=False)

docs.title: Lab 3 — Classical Baselines: SARIMAX and ETS
docs.text:
• Objective: fit SARIMAX (temp+calendar) and automated ETS on daily Tayyar; diagnose both; 14-day-ahead forecasts with intervals.
  • Duration: 50 min. Setup: git checkout lab3-start; pip install statsmodels pmdarima
  • Tasks:
  • (5 min) Aggregate to daily-mean; build exog frame (daily mean temp, weekend, Ramadan, Eid flags from ksa_calendar.csv); hold out last 14 days as test.
  • (12 min) Run select_arima (m=7, d/D from Lab 2); confirm Ljung-Box passes; raise order and re-fit if not; record selected orders.
  • (10 min) Fit fit_ets (damped trend, multiplicative season); inspect res.summary() for smoothing params.
  • (10 min) Forecast 14 days both models (SARIMAX needs future exog — provided temp forecast); plot vs held-out actuals with 90% intervals.
  • (8 min) Compute MAE/MAPE on 14-day window each; note winner + hypothesis; run plot_diagnostics() for SARIMAX.
  • (5 min) Commit: feat(models): SARIMAX + ETS baselines with intervals and diagnostics.
  • Expected output (verbatim): 
    $ python -m tayyar.models.run_classical
Selected (2,1,1)x(1,1,1)[7] | Ljung-Box p=0.214 -> white noise OK
ETS(A,Ad,M) chosen | alpha=0.41 beta=0.02 gamma=0.18 phi=0.98
14-day test  SARIMAX: MAE=612 MW  MAPE=1.9%   coverage(90%)=0.93
14-day test  ETS    : MAE=744 MW  MAPE=2.4%   coverage(90%)=0.86
Winner: SARIMAX (temperature regressor pays off in a heatwave week)

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz: 1. What do p,d,q control in ARIMA? → AR order, differencing order, MA order. 2. m for a daily cycle on hourly data? → 24. 3. Why must exogenous regressors be known at forecast time? → need future values to forecast; otherwise leak/unavailable. 4. Ljung-Box p < 0.05 on residuals means? → residual autocorrelation remains; model under-specified. 5. When is damped trend preferable? → almost always for multi-step horizons.

Debugging exercise: sim-aic-trap compares AIC across models with different d; explain invalidity and fix. Specification drill: given three series' ACF/PACF + descriptions, write SARIMA order + ETS(E,T,S) spec, defend choice.

docs.title: Case Study — Day-Ahead Load Forecasting for Reserve Margins
docs.text:
• Scenario: Tayyar must deliver day-ahead daily-peak forecast with trustworthy interval (reserve margin set from upper bound); engineers reject uninterpretable models.
  • Business context: interval, not just point, drives money and reliability; too wide = wasteful reserves; too narrow = load-shedding risk.
  • Technical challenge: choose SARIMAX (interpretable, interval-native, temperature-aware) vs ETS (fast, robust, no exog) for strongly seasonal + weather-driven series; defend to non-statisticians.
  • Constraints: publication deadline (minutes); temperature only as forecast (error must be acknowledged); model must be explainable component-by-component.
  • Solution approach: (1) ETS as no-exog baseline; (2) SARIMAX adding temp+calendar; (3) diagnose both; (4) compare on held-out window with intervals AND coverage; (5) recommend SARIMAX if temperature materially helps and coverage holds, else simpler ETS.
  • Discussion questions: How does temp-forecast error propagate into the load interval, and how would you widen the interval? When ship simpler ETS despite SARIMAX's lower point error? Explain SARIMAX to control-room engineer in one sentence? What monitoring signals orders gone stale?

docs.text:

Metric targets: residual white noise (Ljung-Box p>0.05); day-ahead MAPE ≤2.5%; interval coverage 0.88–0.93; fit+forecast time <30s; exogenous value quantified vs no-exog (MAE delta).

docs.title: MODULE 4 — Feature-Based ML Forecasting
docs.text: Header: Module 4 · "Feature-Based ML Forecasting" · Day 2, Hour 3 (theory, 60/40) + Day 2, Hour 4 = Lab 4 (10/90) · Maps to LO3 (primary), LO4

docs.title: Learning Objectives (verbatim)
docs.text:
# Objective Maps to 4.1 Reduce a forecasting task to a supervised feature matrix without leakage LO3, LO4 4.2 Engineer lag, rolling-window, calendar, and Fourier features LO3 4.3 Train and tune gradient-boosting models (LightGBM) for forecasting LO3 4.4 Choose recursive vs direct multi-step forecasting strategies LO3 4.5 Interpret feature importance and compare against classical baselines LO3, LO6

Framing: "the catch, hammered throughout, is that every convenience of ML forecasting is also a fresh way to leak the future."

docs.title: Technical Content
docs.text:
1. Forecasting as supervised learning (reduction) - Core move: build a feature row for y_t using info strictly before t — lags (y_{t-1}, y_{t-24}, y_{t-168}), rolling stats of the past, calendar attributes of t, exogenous X_t (temperature known at forecast time). - sktime.make_reduction / skforecast automate "reduction to tabular ML." Peril: split, features, validation must all respect time.

2. The feature families - Lag features: y at 1, 2, 3, 24, 48, 168 hours ago — chosen from the ACF (significant lags = useful features). - Rolling-window statistics: mean/min/max/std over past 24h, 168h — smoothed level and volatility. Critical: windows must end BEFORE the target (.shift(1) after rolling) or leakage. - Calendar features: hour-of-day, day-of-week, month, is-weekend (Fri–Sat), is-Ramadan, is-Eid, is-National-Day — cyclic (sin/cos) or categorical. - Fourier terms: pairs of sin(2πkt/m), cos(2πkt/m) compactly encode smooth seasonality of period m with few columns — the ML way to represent multiple seasonalities (daily+weekly+annual) jointly, which MSTL/SARIMA cannot. - Exogenous & interactions: temperature, explicit interactions (temp × is_afternoon) capturing the nonlinear AC-driven peak.

3. Multi-step strategies: recursive vs direct - Recursive: one model per one step; feeds predictions back as lags. Compact, but errors compound; predicted lags differ in distribution from true lags. - Direct: separate model per horizon (h=1..24), predicts directly from origin features. No compounding, but H models, no cross-horizon coherence guarantee. - Hybrid/multi-output (DirRec, or single model with horizon as feature) trades off. - Decision rule: short horizons + strong autocorrelation → recursive; longer horizons/compounding risk → direct. Tayyar's 24h day-ahead: direct-per-horizon (skforecast.ForecasterDirect) is robust default.

4. Gradient boosting for forecasting - Trees CANNOT extrapolate beyond training range — will never forecast demand higher than any seen. Mitigate: (a) model a differenced/detrended target so level trend handled outside trees, or (b) include a trend feature (time index) with care. - Tune with time-series cross-validation (Module 6), never random folds. Key knobs: num_leaves, learning_rate + n_estimators, min_child_samples, regularization. - For many series, train one global model with series ID as categorical — shares strength across series, often beats per-series models.

docs.title: Design Principles / Best Practices / Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Principles - Every feature must be computable at forecast time using only the past — "the module's whole ethic." - Choose lags from the ACF, not a guess. - Prefer differenced/relative targets so trees operate in a stationary, interpolable range.

Common mistakes (planted in Lab 4 starter) 1. train_test_split(shuffle=True) on time series — cardinal leak; test rows precede train rows. 2. Rolling features including the current row (forgot .shift(1)) — target leaks into its own feature. 3. Scaling/encoding fit on the whole dataset before split — future's statistics contaminate the past. 4. Using a future value of an exogenous driver not known at prediction time. 5. Ignoring trees can't extrapolate, then surprised model under-forecasts a record heatwave. 6. Reporting feature importance as causal ("hour_of_day causes demand") rather than associational.

Production considerations: feature pipelines identical in training and serving (shared, versioned feature module — training/serving-skew lesson). Recompute lags from reliable recent-history store at serving time. Retrain on cadence; monitor feature drift; log feature values with prediction for debuggability.

docs.title: Real-World Walkthrough (verbatim numbers)
docs.text: A LightGBM scored MAPE 0.6% in backtest, then failed live: rolling-mean feature used a centred window (pandas default, forgot to shift), so "past 24h average" secretly included the target hour and future neighbours. One .shift(1) fixed it; honest MAPE rose to 2.1% — "worse on paper, real in production."

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
src/tayyar/features/build.py — add_lags(), add_rolling(), add_calendar(), add_fourier() 

def add_rolling(df, col="demand_mw", windows=(24, 168)):
    out = df.copy()
    for w in windows:
        # shift(1) FIRST so the window ends the hour BEFORE the target
        past = out[col].shift(1)
        out[f"roll_mean_{w}"] = past.rolling(w).mean()
        out[f"roll_std_{w}"]  = past.rolling(w).std()
        out[f"roll_max_{w}"]  = past.rolling(w).max()
    return out

def add_fourier(df, periods=(24, 168, 8766), k=3):
    """Compact multi-seasonality encoding: k sin/cos pairs per period."""
    t = np.arange(len(out))
    for m in periods:
        for i in range(1, k + 1):
            out[f"sin_{m}_{i}"] = np.sin(2*np.pi*i*t/m)
            out[f"cos_{m}_{i}"] = np.cos(2*np.pi*i*t/m)

src/tayyar/models/lgbm_forecaster.py — make_direct_targets(), train_direct(), forecast_direct() 

def make_direct_targets(y, H=24):
    """Target for horizon h is y shifted -h (the future we predict)."""
    return pd.DataFrame({f"y_h{h}": y.shift(-h) for h in range(1, H+1)})

def train_direct(X, Y, params):
    for col in Y.columns:
        mask = Y[col].notna() & X.notna().all(axis=1)
        models[col] = lgb.LGBMRegressor(**params).fit(X[mask], Y[col][mask])

docs.title: Case Study — Scaling Load Forecasting Across Operating Areas
docs.text:
• Scenario: Tayyar expands from one area to four (Central, Eastern, Western, Southern); maintaining four hand-tuned SARIMA models is unsustainable; team evaluates a single global LightGBM.
  • Business context: consistency, maintainability, shared learning (a heatwave pattern in one area informs another) matter as much as raw accuracy.
  • Technical challenge: build one feature matrix spanning all areas with area-ID categorical, avoid cross-area leakage, confirm global model matches/beats per-area classical baselines.
  • Constraints: areas differ in level (Central largest) and weather regime; model must not let a large area dominate loss; features identical in training and serving.
  • Solution approach: (1) long-format panel with area_id; (2) per-area target scaling or relative target so levels don't dominate; (3) global LightGBM with area_id categorical + Fourier + temperature; (4) backtest per area (M6); (5) compare to four SARIMAX baselines and maintenance cost.
  • Discussion questions: When does global model beat per-series, when hurt a small idiosyncratic series? Prevent largest area dominating global loss? Leakage risks unique to multi-series panel (e.g., global scaler)? Weigh 0.2% accuracy gain vs four fewer models to maintain?

docs.title: MODULE 5 — Probabilistic Forecasts and Intervals
docs.text: Header: Module 5 · "Probabilistic Forecasts and Intervals" · Day 2, Hour 5 (start, 45/55) → Day 3, Hour 1 (finish Lab 5, 35/65) · Maps to LO5 (primary), LO3, LO4

docs.title: Learning Objectives (verbatim)
docs.text:
# Objective Maps to 5.1 Explain why point forecasts are insufficient and frame decisions as quantile problems LO5 5.2 Produce prediction intervals from classical (analytic) and ML (quantile) models LO5 5.3 Train quantile models with the pinball/quantile loss LO3, LO5 5.4 Apply split-conformal prediction for distribution-free coverage guarantees LO4, LO5 5.5 Evaluate intervals on coverage, sharpness, and pinball loss and diagnose miscalibration LO5, LO6

Framing: "A point forecast is a lie by omission... The interval IS the product." Reserve margin is sized off the UPPER bound of the day-ahead forecast, not the mean.

docs.title: Technical Content
docs.text:
1. Why a point forecast is not enough - Two forecasts can share a mean of 50,000 MW while one is near-certain and the other spans ±8,000 MW — completely different reserve decision. - Reframing: "forecast the distribution, then let the decision pick the quantile it needs." Cost-asymmetric decisions (under-forecasting far more expensive) want a specific quantile, not the mean. - Module ethic: "report uncertainty, and then prove it is honest."

2. Prediction intervals vs confidence intervals - Confidence interval: uncertainty about a parameter (mean level). Prediction interval: uncertainty about a future observation (parameter uncertainty + irreducible noise) — always wider. - Forecasting almost always wants prediction intervals. Classical models produce these analytically (conf_int/summary_frame) but trust distributional assumptions (Gaussian, constant variance) — violated by Tayyar's summer heteroskedasticity, motivating empirical cross-checks.

3. Quantile regression and the pinball loss - Formula: L_τ(y, ŷ) = max( τ·(y − ŷ), (τ − 1)·(y − ŷ) ) - Asymmetric penalty: for τ=0.9, under-prediction costs 0.9/unit, over-prediction costs 0.1/unit — minimizer sits at the 90th percentile. - Fit one model per quantile (τ ∈ {0.05, 0.5, 0.95}); the 0.05/0.95 pair IS a 90% interval. LightGBM: objective="quantile", alpha=τ. Pinball loss is also the evaluation metric for Module 6. - Quantile crossing: independently-fit quantile models can cross (predicted 0.95 < 0.50) — incoherent distribution. Repair: sort predicted quantiles per row (isotonic) or fit monotone-constrained model.

4. Conformal prediction: coverage you can guarantee - Split (inductive) conformal prediction — model-agnostic wrapper guaranteeing marginal coverage under exchangeability assumption: 1. Split history into training set + held-out calibration set. 2. Fit point model on training; on calibration compute nonconformity scores, typically |y − ŷ|. 3. Take the ⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉/n empirical quantile q̂ of those scores. 4. Interval for new point: ŷ ± q̂ — guaranteed ≈(1−α) marginal coverage. - For time series, plain exchangeability is strained (serially correlated, drifting residuals) → use EnbPI or adaptive conformal (ACI), updating q̂ online as coverage errors accumulate. - Conformalised Quantile Regression (CQR): conformalizes the quantile-model interval — sharpness of quantile regression + coverage guarantee of conformal. Taught as the default for Tayyar.

docs.title: Design Principles / Best Practices / Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Principles - Coverage first, sharpness second — an interval missing its coverage target is wrong at any width. - Calibrate on data the model never trained on — conformal/coverage estimates need a held-out window respecting time. - Decisions consume quantiles, not means — elicit cost asymmetry, report the needed quantile.

Common mistakes (planted in Lab 5 starter) 1. Reporting a confidence interval where a prediction interval is required (far too narrow). 2. Trusting an analytic Gaussian interval on a heteroskedastic series — coverage collapses in summer. 3. Estimating coverage on the training set (optimistic) instead of held-out window. 4. Letting quantile models cross and shipping an incoherent distribution. 5. Using vanilla i.i.d. conformal on strongly autocorrelated series, over-trusting the guarantee. 6. Comparing two methods on sharpness alone while one silently under-covers.

Production considerations: monitor rolling empirical coverage as first-class metric (drift 90%→80% signals staleness before point error degrades). Recalibrate conformal quantiles on schedule; persist calibration window and q̂. Expose downstream quantiles (p50, p90, p95) as explicit service outputs.

docs.title: Real-World Walkthrough (verbatim numbers)
docs.text: SARIMAX shipped with analytic 90% interval, "covered 90% in the backtest — averaged over the year." Operations complained: on summer afternoons that mattered, coverage was ~78% — constant-variance assumption under-widened exactly when variance spiked, reserves set too low on hottest days. Fix: CQR widened summer-afternoon interval, tightened calm winter nights, restoring conditional coverage without inflating average width.

QUANTILES = (0.05, 0.50, 0.95)
def train_quantiles(X, y, quantiles=QUANTILES, params=None):
    for q in quantiles:
        models[q] = lgb.LGBMRegressor(objective="quantile", alpha=q, **params).fit(X, y)

def predict_interval(models, X):
    out = pd.DataFrame(preds, index=X.index)
    out.values.sort(axis=1)   # Repair any quantile crossing
    out.columns = [f"q{int(q*100):02d}" for q in sorted(models)]

src/tayyar/eval/pinball.py — pinball_loss(), mean_pinball() 

def pinball_loss(y_true, y_pred, q):
    e = y_true - y_pred
    return float(np.mean(np.maximum(q*e, (q-1.0)*e)))

src/tayyar/models/conformal.py — CQR calibration 

def cqr_calibrate(lo_cal, hi_cal, y_cal, alpha=0.10):
    """Nonconformity = how far the truth fell OUTSIDE the [lo, hi] band."""
    scores = np.maximum(lo_cal - y_cal, y_cal - hi_cal)   # >0 when outside
    n = len(scores)
    k = int(np.ceil((n + 1) * (1 - alpha)))
    q_hat = np.sort(scores)[min(k, n) - 1]
    return float(q_hat)

def cqr_apply(lo, hi, q_hat):
    """Widen the raw quantile interval by the calibrated correction."""
    return lo - q_hat, hi + q_hat

docs.title: Lab 5 — Calibrated Day-Ahead Intervals
docs.text:
• Objective: produce 90% day-ahead intervals for hourly Tayyar demand three ways (analytic SARIMAX, LightGBM quantile, CQR); pick the method whose empirical coverage matches 90% at sharpest width.
  • Duration: 50 min (Day 2 H5 start → Day 3 H1 finish). Setup: git checkout lab5-start; pip install lightgbm statsmodels
  • Tasks:
  • (5 min) Starter reports a confidence interval and estimates coverage on training set — find both bugs, note in INTERVALS.md.
  • (10 min) Reuse Lab 4 feature matrix; split train/calibration/test by time (last 28 days=test; prior 28=calibration); train LightGBM quantile τ∈{0.05,0.50,0.95}; repair crossing.
  • (10 min) Compute empirical coverage + mean width of raw 0.05–0.95 interval on test; expect coverage below 90%.
  • (10 min) Calibrate with cqr_calibrate on calibration window; apply cqr_apply to test interval; recompute — coverage should snap to ≈0.90.
  • (10 min) Add analytic SARIMAX interval (Lab 3) same test window; build comparison table (method × coverage/mean width/mean pinball); plot all three over one hot week.
  • (5 min) Recommend one method with one-paragraph justification in INTERVALS.md. Commit: feat(models): calibrated day-ahead intervals via CQR + coverage report.
  • Expected output (verbatim): 
    $ python -m tayyar.models.run_intervals
Test window: 28 days hourly (672 points)
SARIMAX analytic   : coverage=0.82  width=3100 MW  pinball=210   (under-covers in summer)
LGBM quantile raw  : coverage=0.86  width=2740 MW  pinball=188
LGBM quantile + CQR: coverage=0.91  width=3020 MW  pinball=181   <- hits nominal, sharpest at target
Recommendation: CQR (only method covering >= 0.90; 3% narrower than analytic at equal coverage)
Wrote intervals_hotweek.png, coverage_table.csv, INTERVALS.md

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz: 1. Prediction interval or confidence interval for a future observation? → prediction interval (wider; includes noise). 2. What quantile does minimizing pinball loss at τ=0.9 recover? → the 90th percentile. 3. What does split-conformal guarantee, under what assumption? → marginal (1−α) coverage, under exchangeability of calibration/test scores. 4. Why can independently-fit quantile models be incoherent? → they can cross (q95<q50); fix by sorting/monotone constraint. 5. Two intervals both cover 90% — which do you ship? → the sharper (narrower) one.

Debugging exercise: sim-train-coverage estimates coverage on training set (reports 0.94, delivers 0.83 on test); relocate estimate to held-out window, explain optimism. Elicitation drill: given three decisions (reserve margin, SKU stocking, staff roster) with stated cost asymmetries, name the quantile each decision should consume, justify.

docs.title: Case Study — Sizing the Reserve Margin with Honest Uncertainty
docs.text:
• Scenario: Tayyar must publish 90th- and 95th-percentile load; control room sets spinning reserve to upper bound. Last summer analytic interval under-covered on hottest afternoons, reserves set too low twice.
  • Business context: reserve at 95th percentile = accepting ~5% chance of dipping into emergency reserve on any afternoon — explicit, defensible risk posture. Under-covered upper bound risks load-shedding (headline-grade); over-coverage wastes fuel (merely expensive).
  • Technical challenge: deliver intervals whose coverage holds conditionally on high-demand summer afternoons, not just on average — analytic Gaussian fails exactly here.
  • Constraints: afternoon publication deadline (calibration must be cheap); upper quantile must be explainable; temperature-forecast error inflates true uncertainty, must reflect in width.
  • Solution approach: (1) LightGBM quantile models at 0.5/0.9/0.95; (2) CQR calibration on rolling recent window; (3) report coverage bucketed by hour-of-day and temperature band; (4) if summer-afternoon bucket under-covers, switch to adaptive conformal (ACI) widening online; (5) hand operations the p95 as reserve-sizing input with measured conditional coverage.
  • Discussion questions: Why does analytic Gaussian interval under-cover on high-variance summer afternoons? Marginal vs conditional coverage — perfect on one, dangerous on other? How should temperature-forecast uncertainty widen the load interval? What rolling metric warns interval gone stale before point error degrades?
