docs.title: Quiz Bank — 20 questions
docs.text:
SDA-DSC-213 · Experimentation, A/B Testing and Causal Inference · SDAIA Academy Instructor document — do not distribute to participants.

Format: closed book · 10 questions per cohort · 15 minutes · short written answer (one or two sentences each) · 10% of the course grade.

Each question below gives the question as read to participants, the model answer, and a marking note telling you what earns the mark, what earns half, and what earns nothing. Mark the reasoning, not the vocabulary: a participant who describes the right mechanism in their own words scores full marks; a participant who recites the term without the mechanism does not.

Scoring: 1 mark per question, 10 marks total. Award 0.5 for a half-answer. Pass on the quiz component is 6/10; the quiz is 10% of the overall grade, so it cannot on its own fail a participant.

docs.title: Section 1 — Causal thinking and potential outcomes (Module 1)
Q1. State the fundamental problem of causal inference.
docs.text:
Model answer. For any single unit we can observe only one of its two potential outcomes — Y(1) or Y(0), never both — because the unit either received the treatment or it did not. The individual treatment effect τᵢ = Yᵢ(1) − Yᵢ(0) is therefore never observable; only averages can be identified.

Marking note. Full mark requires both halves: only one potential outcome per unit is observed, and the consequence that individual effects are unobservable. "The counterfactual is missing" alone is half a mark — it names the problem without stating the consequence. Do not require the notation.

docs.title: Q2. Decompose the naive difference of means into its two parts.
docs.text:
Model answer. E[Y | T=1] − E[Y | T=0] = ATT + selection bias, where the selection-bias term is E[Y(0) | T=1] − E[Y(0) | T=0]: the difference in the untreated potential outcome between the two groups. Randomisation forces that term to zero.

Marking note. Full mark for naming both components and stating the bias term in words ("would the treated group have differed anyway, even untreated?"). Half a mark for "effect plus bias" with no definition of the bias term. Zero if the bias term is described as measurement error or as noise.

docs.title: Q3. Why does collecting more data not fix selection bias?
docs.text:
Model answer. More data reduces variance, not bias. A biased estimator converges — with beautiful precision — to the wrong number. In the Module 1 simulator the self-selected estimate converges to +19.3 pp as n grows, while the truth stays at +5.0 pp.

Marking note. Full mark for the variance-versus-bias distinction. Award the mark whether or not they cite the numbers. Zero for "you would need even more data" — that is the misconception the question exists to catch, and it is worth saying so in the debrief.

docs.title: Q4. What is the difference between the ATE and the ATT, and when is the ATT the right estimand?
docs.text:
Model answer. The ATE is E[Y(1) − Y(0)] over the whole population — the effect of giving the treatment to everyone versus no one. The ATT is E[Y(1) − Y(0) | T = 1] — the effect among those who actually received it. The ATT is the right estimand when evaluating a programme that was delivered to a specific or self-selected group, such as the Injaz voluntary training programme: it answers "did it help the people who took it?"

Marking note. Full mark needs the distinction and a correct use case. Half a mark for a correct definition with no use case, or a correct use case with a muddled definition. A participant who says "ATT is for the treated group" and stops has given a tautology — probe once, then award half.

docs.title: Q5. When should you randomise by user rather than by session?
docs.text:
Model answer. When users return and must see a consistent experience across visits (a flip-flopping interface is a different treatment, and it breaks SUTVA's "one version of the treatment"), and when sessions from the same user are not independent — which they are not, so a session-level analysis of a user-randomised test produces standard errors that are far too small.

Marking note. Either reason earns the full mark if it is stated with its mechanism. Both reasons is a strong answer worth flagging for the distinction list. Zero for "because users are more important than sessions."

docs.title: Q6. What does a sample-ratio mismatch (SRM) indicate, and what must you do about it?
docs.text:
Model answer. It indicates a plumbing bug: units were lost or misassigned non-randomly, so the two arms are no longer a randomised comparison. You must not analyse the experiment for effect. Find the cause, fix it, and rerun. An SRM is never something you adjust away.

Marking note. Full mark requires the "do not analyse" half. A participant who says "it means the split is off, so reweight" has given the dangerous answer — zero, and correct it in the debrief. The Day 2 broken dataset makes this concrete: chi-square 16.5, p = 4.8 × 10⁻⁵.

docs.title: Q7. If you halve the minimum detectable effect, what happens to the required sample size?
docs.text:
Model answer. It roughly quadruples: n ∝ 1 / MDE². Detecting an effect half as large costs about four times the sample and, at fixed traffic, about four times the run length.

Marking note. "Four times" or "n ∝ 1/MDE²" earns the full mark. "It goes up a lot" earns half. Anything linear ("it doubles") earns zero — this is the single most common sizing error in practice.

docs.title: Q8. Why is a non-significant result not proof that there is no effect?
docs.text:
Model answer. The test may simply have been under-powered: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. The honest statement is "we could not distinguish the effect from zero at this sample size," accompanied by the confidence interval, which shows which effect sizes remain consistent with the data.

Marking note. Full mark for the power point. Award a bonus flag (not an extra mark) if the participant volunteers that the confidence interval is what tells you what has actually been ruled out — that is capstone-level thinking. Zero for "it means the effect is zero."

docs.title: Q9. Why must CUPED's covariate be measured before treatment?
docs.text:
Model answer. So that the treatment cannot have affected it. If the covariate is post-treatment, part of the treatment effect is subtracted along with the variance, and the adjustment becomes biased. A pre-treatment covariate can only remove noise; it cannot remove signal.

Marking note. Full mark for the "treatment cannot affect it, so the adjustment stays unbiased" mechanism. Half a mark for "because it has to be pre-treatment" — restating the rule is not explaining it. Link in the debrief to the mediator trap in Q19: it is the same error in a different costume.

docs.title: Q10. How does peeking inflate the false-positive rate?
docs.text:
Model answer. Each interim look is another opportunity for the test statistic to cross the α threshold by chance, and the opportunities compound. The false-positive rate rises far above the nominal 5% — in the course simulation, about 25% at 20 looks. Watching continuously requires a sequential or always-valid method, not a fixed-horizon test.

Marking note. Full mark for the compounding-opportunities mechanism. Numbers are not required, but a participant who recalls "roughly 25% at 20 looks" has clearly internalised the simulation. Zero for "peeking changes the data."

docs.title: Q11. Bonferroni and Benjamini–Hochberg — what does each one control?
docs.text:
Model answer. Bonferroni controls the family-wise error rate (FWER): the probability of any false positive in the family. Benjamini–Hochberg controls the false discovery rate (FDR): the expected proportion of discoveries that are false. Bonferroni is the stricter choice, appropriate for a small guardrail family where any single false alarm is costly; BH is appropriate for a large exploratory sweep where you can tolerate some false discoveries among many.

Marking note. Full mark for both definitions. Half a mark for both names with only one correctly defined. A participant who adds when to use each has answered above the bar.

docs.title: Q12. Why can a ratio metric not be t-tested as though it were a mean?
docs.text:
Model answer. Because its denominator is random as well as its numerator — sessions per user, or completions per session, vary across units — so the ordinary variance formula for a mean understates the true variance. Use the delta method (or bootstrap) to get the correct variance.

Marking note. Full mark requires naming the random denominator as the cause. "Use the delta method" alone, with no reason, earns half.

docs.title: Q13. When are clustered standard errors required?
docs.text:
Model answer. When the unit of analysis is finer than the randomisation unit — for example, analysing sessions from a user-randomised experiment. Rows within a cluster are correlated, so unclustered standard errors are too small and the confidence interval is too narrow. In the Injaz session data, clustering on user_id widens the interval from ±0.33 pp to ±0.52 pp on the same point estimate.

Marking note. Full mark for the "analysis unit finer than randomisation unit" rule. Half a mark for "when data are correlated" without connecting it to the design. Zero for "when the sample is large."

docs.title: Q14. State the identifying assumption of difference-in-differences and say how it is supported.
docs.text:
Model answer. Parallel trends: absent the treatment, treated and control units' outcomes would have moved in parallel. It is untestable for the post period by construction. It is supported — never proved — by showing flat pre-treatment coefficients in an event study, and by placebo-timing tests.

Marking note. Full mark requires the assumption and the event-study support. Half a mark for "parallel trends" alone. Award a distinction flag if the participant volunteers that pre-trends support but do not prove the assumption.

docs.title: Q15. Name the three conditions an instrumental variable must satisfy.
docs.text:
Model answer. Relevance (the instrument moves the treatment — testable, first-stage F > 10, and really > 30 for comfort); exclusion (the instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment — not testable, and where most instruments die); independence / exogeneity (the instrument is as-good-as-randomly assigned with respect to unobservables).

Marking note. One third of a mark each, rounded to the nearest half. A participant who marks which conditions are testable and which are not has answered above the bar.

docs.title: Q16. What does an IV estimate identify, and for whom?
docs.text:
Model answer. The LATE — the local average treatment effect — which is the effect among compliers: the units whose treatment status the instrument actually changed. It is not the ATE, and it is not the ATT; the memo must name the population it applies to.

Marking note. Full mark for "LATE" and "compliers". Half a mark for one without the other. A participant who says "the average effect" has missed the whole point of the question.

docs.title: Q17. What happens when you condition on a collider?
docs.text:
Model answer. A spurious association opens up between its causes, even though they are independent in the population. Nothing changed in the world — only which rows you looked at. In the course simulation two independent traits have correlation ≈ 0.00 unconditionally and ≈ −0.20 once you condition on their common effect.

Marking note. Full mark for "creates a spurious association between the causes / induces bias". Half a mark for "it is bad" with no mechanism. Zero for confusing it with confounding — probe the direction of the arrows in the debrief.

docs.title: Q18. State the backdoor criterion.
docs.text:
Model answer. A set of variables is a valid adjustment set if it blocks every backdoor path from treatment to outcome (every path that starts with an arrow into the treatment) and contains no descendant of the treatment. Adjusting for such a set identifies the causal effect.

Marking note. Full mark requires both clauses — blocking backdoor paths and excluding descendants. Half a mark for only the first, which is the usual half-remembered version and is exactly what lets a mediator into the model.

docs.title: Q19. Why should you not control for a mediator when estimating a total effect?
docs.text:
Model answer. A mediator lies on the causal path from treatment to outcome. Conditioning on it blocks part of the effect you are trying to measure, so the estimate shrinks toward zero — you end up reporting only the direct effect while claiming it is the total. Controlling for support_calls in the Injaz analysis shrinks the online-filing estimate from +10.9 pp to +9.8 pp for exactly this reason.

Marking note. Full mark for "it is on the causal path, so blocking it removes part of the effect." Half a mark for "the effect shrinks" with no mechanism. Numbers are not required. This is the highest-frequency real-world error on the list — if more than a third of the cohort misses it, spend five minutes on it before the capstone.

docs.title: Q20. How should an effect be reported to leadership?
docs.text:
Model answer. As an effect size with a confidence interval in business units — percentage points of completion, or completions per month — together with a practical-significance verdict: is the effect large enough to act on, given the decision threshold? Not a p-value, and not "statistically significant" as a synonym for "real and worth doing".

Marking note. Full mark requires effect plus interval plus the practical verdict. Half a mark if the practical-significance half is missing. Zero if the answer centres on a p-value. This question maps directly onto capstone criterion 6; a wrong answer here predicts a weak memo, so use it as an early-warning signal on Day 2 and intervene before Day 4.

docs.title: Which 10 to use
docs.text:
Use one question from each of Q1–Q4 and Q5–Q6, then fill the rest so that every module is represented and at least three questions require a mechanism rather than a definition (Q3, Q9, Q13, Q17, Q19 are the mechanism questions).

Three ready-made sets, all balanced across the six modules:

Set Questions Use it when Set A — standard Q1, Q5, Q6, Q7, Q10, Q11, Q14, Q17, Q19, Q20 Default. One per module family, mixed difficulty, ends on the communication question. Set B — analysis-heavy Q2, Q4, Q6, Q8, Q9, Q12, Q13, Q15, Q18, Q20 A strong, technically confident cohort — more variance and identification, fewer definitions. Set C — foundations Q1, Q3, Q4, Q5, Q7, Q8, Q10, Q14, Q17, Q20 A mixed-background cohort, or one where Day 1 diagnostics showed shaky potential-outcomes intuition.

Rules of thumb when you build your own set:

  • Always include Q20. It is the closest proxy for capstone criterion 6, and a cohort that fails it needs an intervention before Day 4 Hour 3.
  • Always include exactly one of Q6 / Q13. Both test "the design constrains the analysis"; using both wastes a slot.
  • Never use Q9 and Q19 in the same sitting. They are the same lesson (pre-treatment versus post-treatment variables) in two costumes; using both double-counts one concept.
  • Q2, Q15 and Q18 are the hardest; do not use more than two of them in one set or the mean drops below the pass mark for reasons that are about recall rather than understanding.
  • Rotate between cohorts. Sets A, B and C overlap only on Q20, so a participant repeating the course does not sit the same paper.

docs.title: When to run it
docs.text:
Day 4, Hour 5, immediately before the capstone briefings — 15 minutes, closed book, papers collected before the first presentation starts. Running it earlier costs capstone build time; running it after the briefings means marking a cohort that has just heard the answers discussed.

If the cohort is running late on Day 4, the quiz is the first thing to move, not to cut: run it at the start of Day 4 Hour 1 instead, when Modules 1–6 are all complete and only the communication material is outstanding. In that case swap Q20 out for Q16 and assess communication through the memo alone.

docs.title: Run of Show — minute-by-minute facilitator plan
docs.text: SDA-DSC-213 · Experimentation, A/B Testing and Causal Inference · SDAIA Academy 4 days × 5 learning hours · Instructor document · print double-sided

docs.title: How to read this document
docs.text:
Each learning hour is 50 minutes of instruction + a 10-minute buffer. The buffer is not slack you may spend: it absorbs the overrun you will have, covers prayer and comfort breaks, and lets people move between rooms. The long break sits around Dhuhr, between Hours 3 and 4.

Clock Block 08:45 – 09:00 Room open · machines on · instructor smoke-test 09:00 – 09:50 Hour 1 09:50 – 10:00 Break 10:00 – 10:50 Hour 2 10:50 – 11:00 Break 11:00 – 11:50 Hour 3 11:50 – 12:40 Dhuhr and long break (50 min) 12:40 – 13:30 Hour 4 13:30 – 13:40 Break 13:40 – 14:30 Hour 5 14:30 – 14:45 Close-out · collect deliverables · preview tomorrow

Adjust the whole grid, not individual hours, if Dhuhr moves seasonally — keep the long break aligned to it and keep the 50/10 rhythm. Announce the day's grid on the board every morning; a cohort that knows when the next break is stops asking.

Slides. Deck: Experimentation_and_Causal_Inference_P6.1.04_SDAIA_Academy_Enriched.pptx. This document refers to deck sections (M1 … M7) rather than slide numbers, because slide numbering shifts between deck revisions. Figures are named by file, from figures/; they are the same images as in the deck, and they are what you should project during a lab when the deck is closed.

Checkpoint. Every segment ends with a checkpoint: a thing that must be observably true before you move on. Check it by looking at two or three screens, not by asking "everyone good?" — the room will always say yes.

Cut guidance. Every hour has an explicit "if you are running late, cut this". Cut in the order given. Two things are never cut: the freeze step in any lab, and the event-study / parallel-trends observation in Lab 5b.

docs.title: DAY 1 — Causal thinking and honest experiments
docs.text: Modules: M1 Causal Thinking & Potential Outcomes · M2 Experiment Design & Randomisation End-of-day deliverable: a selection-bias simulation + a fully specified, frozen Injaz experiment design doc.

docs.title: Hour 1 · 09:00–09:50 — "What actually works?" + kickoff + the Injaz golden thread
docs.text:
Time Segment Instructor does Slides / assets 09:00 The poll (5 min) Ask, before any introduction: "Injaz completion is 8 points higher for users who received an SMS reminder. Should we send reminders to everyone?" Take a show of hands. Let the room argue for three minutes. Do not resolve it. — 09:05 Name what just happened (5 min) Someone will say "maybe reminders go to people who already engage." Write that sentence on the board verbatim and tell them it is the entire course, made rigorous. m1_confounding_triangle.png 09:10 Course frame (10 min) Outcomes LO1–LO6, the 4-day shape, the assessment split (labs 30 / PA 20 / quiz 10 / capstone 40). State the rule now and repeat it daily: a correct "we cannot conclude" is worth full marks. Deck: cover + delivery plan 09:20 The Injaz golden thread (12 min) Introduce the platform and the four questions (uploader, reminders, training, autofill). Emphasise: no throwaway examples; one notebook grows all week; the toolkit they build is the capstone's toolkit. Deck: M1 opener 09:32 Failure story (8 min) Tell one real-shaped failure: a programme that looked beneficial because healthy people enrolled. Ask the room what evidence would have caught it. m5_ladder_of_evidence.png 09:40 Environment check (10 min) Everyone runs python environment_check.py. Walk the room. Anyone red goes to the Colab fallback now, not at Lab 1. environment_check.py

Checkpoint: every participant's screen shows RESULT: PASS, or is on Colab with the install cell run. Names of anyone still broken go on a list for the break.

If you are running late, cut: the failure story (8 min) — the poll already did its work. Never cut the environment check; a broken machine costs an hour at 11:00 instead of ten minutes at 09:40.

docs.title: Hour 2 · 10:00–10:50 — Potential outcomes and the fundamental problem (M1)
docs.text:
Time Segment Instructor does Slides / assets 10:00 Two worlds (10 min) Define Y(1), Y(0), τᵢ = Yᵢ(1) − Yᵢ(0) on the board. Use one named Injaz user, not a population. m1_two_worlds.png 10:10 The fundamental problem (8 min) Only one potential outcome is ever observed; causal inference is a missing-data problem where exactly half the data is missing by construction. Deck: M1 §3 10:18 Estimands (10 min) ATE, ATT, CATE. Drill the discipline: name the estimand before touching data. "The ATT on completion for triggered users in Q2" is answerable; "the effect" is not. Deck: M1 §2 10:28 The decomposition, derived live (14 min) Whiteboard: E[Y|T=1] − E[Y|T=0] = ATT + (E[Y(0)|T=1] − E[Y(0)|T=0]). Do it slowly, in full. This is the algebraic spine of the week. m1_bias_decomposition.png 10:42 Why randomisation works (8 min) (Y(0), Y(1)) ⊥ T is manufactured, not hoped for. It also balances the confounders you never thought to measure — the property no matching model can buy. Deck: M1 §4

Checkpoint: ask three participants at random to state the selection-bias term in words. If two of three cannot, re-derive it in two minutes before the break — Lab 1 measures this quantity directly and lands flat if the room has not internalised it.

If you are running late, cut: the CATE half of the estimands segment (4 min) — it is re-introduced properly on Day 3. Never cut the live derivation.

docs.title: Hour 3 · 11:00–11:50 — Lab 1: simulate potential outcomes and selection bias
docs.text:
Notebook: notebooks/lab1_start.ipynb · Data: simulated_potential_outcomes.parquet · Pairs

Time Segment Instructor does Checkpoint 11:00 Frame the lab (3 min) This is the only file in the course containing both potential outcomes. That is impossible in reality, and that is exactly why we start here: you can watch an estimator succeed or fail against a truth you can see. — 11:03 Task 1–2 (15 min) Complete the simulator; implement both assignment mechanisms and the naive estimator. Walk the room. Planted ATE prints ≈ +0.050 11:18 Task 3 (10 min) Compute the naive difference under each mechanism; write the markdown cell explaining why they differ although the true effect is identical. Self-selected ≈ +0.193, randomised ≈ +0.050 11:28 Task 4 (8 min) Compute the selection-bias term directly and verify naive ≈ ATT + bias. Bias term ≈ +0.143 11:36 Task 5 — the emotional core (9 min) The n ∈ {1k, 10k, 100k, 1M} sweep. Say nothing; watch faces as the "big data" estimate converges confidently to the wrong answer. Plot shows convergence to 0.193, not 0.050 11:45 Debrief (5 min) One participant reads their three-sentence manager summary aloud. Land the line: more data buys precision, never truth. —

Checkpoint before the long break: every pair's notebook prints the four numbers (0.050 / 0.193 / 0.050 / 0.143) and has the convergence plot.

If you are running late, cut: Task 4's manual bias computation (8 min) — the simulator prints it anyway; assign it as an optional over-lunch exercise. Never cut Task 5. If you must choose, cut the debrief and let the plot speak.

Common stumbles: naive randomised estimate far from 0.050 → n too small or unlucky seed, average over seeds. Self-selection estimate ≈ true ATE → opt-in is not actually correlated with literacy; print the correlation. Bias term ≈ 0 under self-selection → they revealed the wrong potential outcome; check observed = where(T==1, y1, y0).

docs.title: 11:50 – 12:40 · Dhuhr and long break
docs.text: Use ten minutes of this to fix any machine still failing environment_check.py. Do not use it to prepare Hour 4; prepare Hour 4 the night before.

docs.title: Hour 4 · 12:40–13:30 — Experiment design and randomisation (M2)
docs.text:
Time Segment Instructor does Slides / assets 12:40 Anatomy of an experiment (8 min) Unit → assignment → trigger → exposure → outcome. Walk the diagram once, end to end, before any detail. m2_experiment_anatomy.png 12:48 Randomisation unit (10 min) The decision tree: does the user return? do units interact? how coarse can you afford to go? Coarser units cost power; finer units cost validity. m2_randomisation_unit_tree.png 12:58 SUTVA and interference (8 min) No interference, one version of the treatment. Shared devices, household spillover, region-to-region talk. Name the containment design for each: cluster, switchback. m2_interference.png 13:06 OEC and guardrails (10 min) Exactly one OEC. Guardrails are a family and are tested as one. Introduce the trigger and say plainly that the analysis population is triggered users. Deck: M2 §metrics 13:16 Assignment mechanics and SRM (14 min) Why hash rather than draw: deterministic, stateless, reproducible, independent across experiments via the salt. Then SRM: what it detects, and the rule that it is never adjusted away. m2_srm_diagnostic.png

Checkpoint: the room can answer, without notes, "what is the OEC and how many should an experiment have?" and "what do you do when SRM fails?" The second answer must contain the words do not analyse.

If you are running late, cut: the switchback design detail inside the SUTVA segment (4 min) and the balance-check preview (it is done hands-on in Lab 2 anyway).

docs.title: Hour 5 · 13:40–14:30 — Lab 2: design and randomise the uploader experiment
docs.text:
Notebook: notebooks/lab2_start.ipynb · Data: injaz_users_pool.csv, injaz_experiment_results_srm_broken.csv · Pairs

Time Segment Instructor does Checkpoint 13:40 Task 1 — the design doc (10 min) They fill hypothesis, unit + justification, OEC, three guardrails, trigger, unit of analysis. Circulate and read two aloud, one strong and one thin, without naming authors. Every pair has a written unit justification of two sentences 13:50 Task 2 — hash assignment (8 min) hash_assign on the 200k pool with salt="injaz-uploader-2026q2". Split ≈ 50/50 and stable across reruns 13:58 Task 3 — SRM, both ways (7 min) Run SRM on the clean assignment (passes), then on the broken file (fails). Let them see what a real bug looks like. Clean p ≈ 0.61; broken chi² ≈ 16.5, p ≈ 4.8 × 10⁻⁵ → INVALID 14:05 Task 4 — balance table (10 min) Build the balance table over age, literacy, prior sessions, device age, region (one-hot). Watch for the re-randomisation temptation. All |SMD| < 0.1; worst ≈ 0.009 14:15 Task 5 — interference audit (5 min) Two plausible SUTVA violations and the design change each would require. Two written violations per pair 14:20 Task 6 — freeze the plan (10 min) AnalysisPlan(...) → freeze_plan(). The hash is printed and written into the design doc. This is pre-registration in miniature and it is graded on Day 4. Every pair has a plan_hash; lab2_frozen_plan.json written

Stop the room the moment someone proposes re-randomising an imbalanced covariate. Two minutes, standing up: re-rolling until the covariates look nice is choosing your assignment based on the data, and it biases the design. The correct response is adjust in analysis, never re-roll.

Checkpoint before close: every pair has a printed plan_hash and a complete design doc.

If you are running late, cut: Task 5's interference audit (5 min) — set it as a 10-minute homework and review it in Day 2 Hour 1. Never cut Task 6. A cohort that leaves Day 1 without a frozen plan has no Day 4.

14:30–14:45 close-out: collect nothing; remind them the design doc travels with them all week. Preview Day 2: "tomorrow we find out how long this experiment has to run, and all the ways an honest analyst accidentally lies."

docs.title: DAY 2 — Powering and analysing experiments
docs.text: Modules: M3 Power Analysis & Sample Sizing · M4 Analysis Pitfalls End-of-day deliverable: a sample-size calculator + a correct, corrected analysis of the uploader experiment. PA-1 is assessed today.

docs.title: Hour 1 · 09:00–09:50 — Power, MDE and sample size (M3)
docs.text:
Time Segment Instructor does Slides / assets 09:00 Yesterday's homework (5 min) Two pairs read their interference audits. Thirty seconds each, then move. — 09:05 Type I and Type II (10 min) The two errors, α and β, and why teams obsess over the first and ignore the second. Power = 1 − β = the probability of detecting a true effect of a given size. Introduce the Arabic term alongside: power / القوة الإحصائية. m3_type_i_ii.png 09:15 The four-way relationship (10 min) α, power, effect size, n — fix any three and the fourth is determined. Drive this with the slider, not with algebra. m3_four_way_tradeoff.png 09:25 The quadratic (10 min) n ∝ 1/MDE². Halve the MDE, quadruple the sample. Project the curve and leave it on screen. m3_mde_vs_n.png 09:35 Traffic to calendar (10 min) Three things bite teams: n is per arm; not every eligible user triggers; a whole number of weeks is a floor. The KSA working week matters — Fri–Sat traffic is about 58% of a weekday's in the Injaz forecast. m3_run_length_pipeline.png 09:45 CUPED preview (5 min) A pre-treatment covariate removes noise, not signal. Variance falls by ρ². Full treatment in Hour 3. m3_cuped_variance.png

Checkpoint: ask the room "if you halve the MDE, what happens to n?" The answer four times should come back instantly, from several voices.

If you are running late, cut: the CUPED preview (5 min) — Hour 3 covers it properly. Pin the MDE-vs-n curve to the wall; you will point at it for the rest of the course.

docs.title: Hour 2 · 10:00–10:50 — Lab 3: the sample-size calculator and run-length plan
docs.text:
Notebook: notebooks/lab3_start.ipynb · Data: injaz_pre_period.csv, injaz_traffic_forecast.csv

Time Segment Instructor does Checkpoint 10:00 Task 1 (8 min) Implement sample_size_proportions; cross-check against statsmodels at baseline 0.55, MDE 0.02. Both agree; n/arm ≈ 9,670 10:08 Task 2 (8 min) Plot required n vs MDE over [0.005, 0.05]; annotate the blow-up. The curve is on screen and annotated 10:16 Task 3 (8 min) MDE achievable at live traffic in a 4-week window. MDE ≈ 0.006 → a 2-point lift is comfortably detectable 10:24 Task 4 (8 min) Run-length plan for 2 arms, then 3; note the traffic multiplier and the whole-week floor. At MDE 0.02 both round to the 14-day whole-week floor the lab uses (arithmetic: 3 and 4 days) — rerun at MDE 0.005 to make the multiplier bite: 42 → 56 days 10:32 Task 5 (10 min) Estimate CUPED variance reduction from the pre-period file; recompute n and run length. corr ≈ 0.37 → variance reduction ≈ 13.5% 10:42 Task 6 (8 min) Write the one-paragraph sizing recommendation into the design doc. Every pair's design doc §6 is filled

Watch for: a run length that looks impossibly short — they forgot the arm multiplier or the trigger rate. A negative or absurd n — the MDE pushed p₂ outside (0,1).

Note on expected numbers: the CUPED reduction here is ≈13.5%, driven by a pre/post correlation of ≈0.37. If a pair reports 40%, they have used a post-treatment covariate. That is a teaching moment, not an arithmetic slip.

If you are running late, cut: Task 4's three-arm variant (4 min) — state the multiplier verbally instead. Never cut Task 5; CUPED is a mandatory capstone requirement.

docs.title: Hour 3 · 11:00–11:50 — Analysis pitfalls: peeking and multiple testing (M4)
docs.text:
Time Segment Instructor does Slides / assets 11:00 Unit of analysis (10 min) Randomise users, analyse sessions, and your standard errors are fiction. Show the widening: same point estimate, honest interval. m4_unit_of_analysis.png 11:10 Ratio metrics and the delta method (8 min) A random denominator breaks the ordinary variance formula. Deck: M4 §variance 11:18 CUPED, properly (7 min) θ = cov(Y,X)/var(X); the covariate must be pre-treatment or the adjustment is biased. Same lesson as the mediator trap on Day 3, in a different costume. m3_cuped_variance.png 11:25 Peeking, live (13 min) Run the peeking simulation in front of them. Nominal 5% becomes ≈25% at 20 looks. Then the rule: watch continuously only with a sequential method. m4_peeking_staircase.png 11:38 Multiple testing (12 min) Bonferroni controls FWER; BH controls FDR. Which family is which: guardrails → Bonferroni; segment sweep → BH. Finish with Simpson's paradox. m4_correction_family.png, m4_simpsons_paradox.png

Checkpoint: the room can state which correction goes with which family, and why they are different questions.

If you are running late, cut: Simpson's paradox (5 min) — it reappears in the Day 3 DAG material. Never cut the live peeking run; it is the demonstration that changes behaviour.

docs.title: Hour 4 · 12:40–13:30 — Lab 4: analyse the uploader experiment correctly
docs.text:
Notebook: notebooks/lab4_start.ipynb · Data: injaz_experiment_results.csv, injaz_pre_period.csv, injaz_sessions.csv.gz This is one of the two most overrun-prone labs. Protect it at full length.

Time Segment Instructor does Checkpoint 12:40 Task 1 — the effect (8 min) Two-proportion test and OLS+HC3 on triggered users; confirm identical point estimates. +2.2 pp, 95% CI [+1.3, +3.0], both methods agree 12:48 The trap, sprung (4 min) Ask them to rerun on all 80,000 assigned users. The effect falls to +1.3 pp. Ask why before explaining: assigned users who never reached the step cannot have been affected. Both numbers in the notebook, correctly labelled 12:52 Task 2 — CUPED (8 min) Adjust with prior_completion_rate; the interval narrows. +2.1 pp, CI [+1.3, +2.9]; variance reduction ≈ 13.5% 13:00 Task 3 — guardrails (8 min) Four guardrails, Bonferroni across the family. Drop-off falls and survives correction; nothing regresses after correction. Correction applied, m stated 13:08 Task 4 — the segment sweep (10 min) Let a pair announce "it works great for Android users in Riyadh!" Then apply BH and watch it evaporate. Survivors are hypotheses for the next test, not findings. BH applied; survivors labelled as hypotheses 13:18 Task 5 — clustering (7 min) Session-level analysis of a user-randomised test: the interval widens from ±0.33 pp to ±0.52 pp on the same estimate. Clustered SE reported 13:25 Task 6 — the decision paragraph (5 min) Lift, CI, guardrail verdict, and an explicit statistical-vs-practical sentence. Every pair has written it

If you are running late, cut: Task 5 (7 min) — demo it from the solution notebook instead of having them type it; the concept survives, the practice does not. Do not cut Task 4; the BH moment is the highest-value 10 minutes of Day 2.

docs.title: Hour 5 · 13:40–14:30 — Reading results honestly + PA-1
docs.text:
Time Segment Instructor does Assets 13:40 CIs versus p-values (10 min) The interval tells you what has been ruled out; the p-value tells you almost nothing on its own. Practise the sentence: "not distinguishable from zero at this sample size". Deck: M4 close 13:50 Practical significance (10 min) Introduce the decision threshold as a business quantity. Preview the capstone: an interval that excludes zero but straddles the threshold is the capstone's central lesson. m7_uncertainty_to_decision.png 14:00 PA-1 — assessed, 30 min (30 min) Hand out the broken experiment: an SRM failure and a session-level analysis of a user-randomised test. They diagnose both defects and produce a corrected, correctly-powered analysis. Scored: diagnosis 40% · corrected analysis 40% · verification evidence 20%. injaz_experiment_results_srm_broken.csv, injaz_sessions.csv.gz

Checkpoint: PA-1 scripts collected before anyone leaves. A participant who "fixed" the SRM by reweighting has the diagnosis wrong — mark it and address it in Day 3 Hour 1, because the same instinct will reappear in the capstone.

If you are running late, cut: the CI-versus-p-value segment down to 5 minutes. PA-1 is assessed and cannot be shortened below 30 minutes — if you cannot protect 30 minutes, move PA-1 to the start of Day 3 Hour 1 and say so at close-out.

14:30–14:45 close-out: preview Day 3 with one sentence: "tomorrow, everything we did today becomes impossible, and we do it anyway — carefully."

docs.title: DAY 3 — When you cannot randomise
docs.text: Modules: M5 Quasi-Experiments (matching, DiD, IV) · M6 Causal Graphs & Confounding End-of-day deliverable: a DiD estimate of the reminder rollout + a DAG-justified observational analysis with refutation tests.

docs.title: Hour 1 · 09:00–09:50 — Quasi-experiments and matching (M5)
docs.text:
Time Segment Instructor does Slides / assets 09:00 The ladder of evidence (8 min) RCT at the top; everything below buys a weaker guarantee in exchange for being possible. Every method today is an attempt to approximate a coin flip. m5_ladder_of_evidence.png 09:08 Confounding, formally (10 min) Back to the Day 1 decomposition. Observational adjustment can only handle confounders you named and measured — randomisation handles the ones you never knew existed. m1_confounding_triangle.png 09:18 Propensity scores (12 min) P(T=1 | X) as a balancing score; matching, weighting, and what each does with the units it cannot use. m5_propensity_overlap.png 09:30 Overlap and common support (10 min) No comparable control means no counterfactual. Trimming changes the estimand, and the memo must say so. m5_propensity_overlap.png 09:40 The assumption you are spending (10 min) Unconfoundedness given X is assumed and unverifiable. What can be checked: overlap, post-matching balance, and how strong a hidden confounder would have to be (Rosenbaum). Deck: M5 §assumptions

Checkpoint: the room can say what matching can and cannot fix. If anyone says "matching removes bias", correct it on the spot: matching removes bias from the confounders you measured.

If you are running late, cut: the weighting variants inside the propensity segment (4 min); IPW is demonstrated in the lab.

docs.title: Hour 2 · 10:00–10:50 — Lab 5a: match to evaluate the training programme
docs.text:
Notebook: notebooks/lab5a_start.ipynb · Data: injaz_users.csv

Time Segment Instructor does Checkpoint 10:00 Task 1 — propensity and overlap (8 min) Estimate propensity on age, literacy, prior sessions, device age, region; plot overlap and identify common support. Overlap plot produced 10:08 Task 2 — match (10 min) Nearest-neighbour with a caliper; post-matching balance table. Worst |SMD| falls from ≈0.57 to ≈0.03 10:18 Task 3 — estimate (10 min) Matched ATT, cross-checked with IPW, contrasted with the naive difference. Naive +11.5 pp → matched ≈ +6.5 pp, IPW ≈ +6.6 pp 10:28 Task 4 — refute (12 min) Random-common-cause, placebo outcome, and a Rosenbaum-bounds sensitivity statement. Note: the placebo outcome must not be in the adjustment set. Two refutations run; Γ ≈ 1.20–1.25* stated 10:40 Task 5 — write the finding (10 min) "Naive +11.5 points → matched ≈ +6.5 points," with the caveat about unobserved confounders. Make the Day-1 connection explicit: this is the same headline, now defensible. Written finding, with the caveat

Instructor note on Rosenbaum. Γ here is around 1.20–1.25 — the conclusion survives a modest hidden confounder but not a strong one. Do not let the room read that as failure. Say the honest sentence out loud: "this result would be overturned by an unmeasured variable that changed the odds of enrolling by about 20%, and I cannot rule that out."* That sentence is what a top-band capstone contains.

If you are running late, cut: the IPW cross-check in Task 3 (5 min) and one of the two refutations in Task 4. Keep the sensitivity statement — it is a capstone requirement.

docs.title: Hour 3 · 11:00–11:50 — Difference-in-differences and instrumental variables (M5)
docs.text:
Time Segment Instructor does Slides / assets 11:00 Two lines (10 min) DiD as the difference of two before/after differences. Draw it before writing any regression. m5_did_two_lines.png 11:10 Parallel trends (12 min) The identifying assumption, in the exact sentence they will be asked to say on Day 4. Untestable for the post period; supported by flat pre-trends. m5_event_study.png 11:22 Event studies (8 min) How to read one: pre-period coefficients near zero, a jump at activation, and the shape of the ramp-in afterwards. m5_event_study.png 11:30 Staggered rollouts, honestly (8 min) With waves and time-varying effects, TWFE is a weighted average of 2×2 comparisons that can use already-treated units as controls, with some negative weights. Flag the modern estimators; do not teach them here. Deck: M5 §staggered 11:38 Instrumental variables (12 min) The valve metaphor; the three conditions; first-stage F; and the fact that IV identifies the LATE, for compliers only. m5_iv_valve.png

Checkpoint: three participants, at random, state the parallel-trends assumption in one sentence. This is the exact question asked live during capstone briefings, so practise it now.

If you are running late, cut: the staggered-rollout segment to 4 minutes (say it, do not derive it) — the ramp-in evidence appears in Lab 5b anyway.

docs.title: Hour 4 · 12:40–13:30 — Lab 5b: DiD on the regional reminder rollout
docs.text:
Notebook: notebooks/lab5b_start.ipynb · Data: injaz_regions_panel.csv, injaz_regions_panel_pretrend.csv The second overrun-prone lab. Protect it at full length.

Time Segment Instructor does Checkpoint 12:40 Task 1 — the panel (10 min) Inspect 13 regions × 24 months; mark treated_post from the activation waves (periods 10, 13, 16, 19; four regions never treated). Panel shape and wave structure confirmed 12:50 Task 2 — TWFE (12 min) Estimate with region-clustered SEs. +2.6 pp, 95% CI [+2.5, +2.7] 13:02 Task 3 — the event study (12 min) Estimate and plot. Every pair must produce this plot; it is the exhibit most likely to appear in the capstone. Pre-period coefficients within ±0.5 pp of zero, none significant 13:14 Task 4 — the parallel-trends breaker (8 min) Re-run on injaz_regions_panel_pretrend.csv. Pre-period coefficients now run from −1.6 pp upward and are clearly non-zero; the naive DiD reads +4.2 pp. DiD is not identified here — report the failure honestly. Both event-study plots side by side 13:22 Task 5 — write the finding (8 min) Effect, CI, identifying assumption, one threat to validity. Written finding

The number to explain. The planted ATT is +3.0 pp, but TWFE recovers +2.6 pp. That gap is not a bug: the programme ramps in over about two months, and TWFE averages the weak early months in with the mature ones. Say this explicitly — it is the opening for the staggered-DiD capstone extension, and a participant who reports +2.6 pp and explains why it is an underestimate is already writing distinction-band work.

If you are running late, cut: Task 5's written finding (do it as homework). Never cut Task 3 or Task 4. The side-by-side event study is the module's credibility lesson and the single most-reused capstone exhibit.

docs.title: Hour 5 · 13:40–14:30 — Causal graphs and confounding (M6) + Lab 6
docs.text:
Notebook: notebooks/lab6_start.ipynb · Data: injaz_users.csv, collider_sim.parquet

Time Segment Instructor does Assets 13:40 Micro-lecture: three junctions (8 min) Chain, fork, collider — and what conditioning does to each. Eight minutes, no more. m6_three_junctions.png 13:48 The backdoor criterion (7 min) Block all backdoor paths; include no descendant of the treatment. Both clauses, every time. m6_backdoor_dag.png 13:55 Lab 6 Tasks 1–2 (12 min) Draw the Injaz DAG; list backdoor paths by hand; derive the adjustment set and state why support_calls is excluded. Adjustment set = {digital_literacy, device_age} 14:07 Lab 6 Task 3 — the collider (10 min) Two independent traits; condition on their common effect. corr −0.0005 → −0.204 on completed == 1 14:17 Lab 6 Task 4 — identify → estimate (8 min) The DoWhy workflow if installed; the causal_utils path if not. Both give the same adjustment set. Effect estimated with the correct set 14:25 Brief PA-2 (5 min) Hand out PA-2 now; it is completed and assessed in Day 4 Hour 1. Tell them to read it tonight, not to solve it. PA-2 handout

Checkpoint: every participant can name one mediator and one collider in the Injaz DAG and say what happens if each is controlled for.

If you are running late, cut: Lab 6 Task 4 (8 min) — it is repeated at the top of Day 4 Hour 1. Never cut Task 3; the collider demonstration is the module.

Deviation from the catalogue, deliberate. The instructor package schedules PA-2 on Day 3. Hour 5 has 50 minutes and cannot hold both Lab 6 and a 30-minute assessment. PA-2 is therefore briefed at the end of Day 3 Hour 5 and completed and assessed in Day 4 Hour 1, immediately after the mediator-trap segment that it tests. Announce this to the cohort so the change is on the record.

14:30–14:45 close-out: collect nothing; tomorrow is build day. One sentence of preview: "tomorrow you decide, and you sign your name to it."

docs.title: DAY 4 — From evidence to decision
docs.text: Modules: M6 deep-dive · M7 Experimentation Case Study · Capstone End-of-day deliverable: the capstone package + decision memo + a 6-minute briefing. Hard rule: capstone framing (Hour 3) starts on time. Cut discussion, never build time.

docs.title: Hour 1 · 09:00–09:50 — Causal graphs deep-dive, refutation, and PA-2
docs.text:
Time Segment Instructor does Assets 09:00 The mediator trap, made real (12 min) Lab 6 Task 5. They add support_calls to the adjustment set and watch the effect shrink — +10.9 pp → +9.8 pp on the online-filing estimate. This is the emotional payoff of Module 6: the effect they measured all week, quietly erased by a "sensible" control. notebooks/lab6_start.ipynb 09:12 Refutation tests (8 min) Placebo outcome, random common cause, subset stability. What each can and cannot tell you. Warn them: a placebo outcome that is in the adjustment set produces a meaningless result. m6_identification_flow.png 09:20 When identification fails (5 min) Say the honest sentence: "not identifiable from this data; here is the variable that would need to be measured." Remind them this earns full marks. Deck: M6 close 09:25 PA-2 — assessed, 25 min (25 min) Observational dataset plus a proposed kitchen-sink regression. Draw the DAG, identify the mediator and collider being wrongly controlled, produce the correctly-identified estimate with a refutation. Scored: identification 50% · refutation 30% · written verdict 20%. PA-2 handout, injaz_users.csv

Checkpoint: PA-2 scripts collected. Anyone who left support_calls in the model needs a two-minute conversation before the capstone starts.

If you are running late, cut: the "when identification fails" segment (5 min) — it recurs in Hour 2. PA-2 may compress to 25 minutes but not below.

docs.title: Hour 2 · 10:00–10:50 — Lab 7: the autofill decision, end to end (M7)
docs.text:
Notebook: notebooks/lab7_start.ipynb · Data: injaz_autofill_ab.csv, injaz_regions_panel.csv This is the dress rehearsal for the capstone. Everything they build here they reuse in Hour 3.

Time Segment Instructor does Checkpoint 10:00 Method selection (6 min) The first question is always "can we randomise going forward?" Walk the flowchart once. m7_method_selection.png 10:06 Task 1 — frame and freeze (8 min) Estimand, method, OEC, guardrails, MDE, threshold. Freeze the plan before any analysis cell. Every pair has a plan_hash 10:14 Task 2 — analyse the A/B (10 min) CUPED-adjusted, robust SEs, guardrails with correction. +1.6 pp, CI [+0.8, +2.4] CUPED-adjusted; guardrails clean after correction 10:24 Task 3 — the decision plot (8 min) Pull in the reminder DiD; build the combined plot with the +1.0 pp threshold line. Plot shows both intervals and the threshold 10:32 Task 4 — validate and reconcile (7 min) SRM and balance for the A/B; restate the DiD's parallel-trends caveat; name any disagreement. SRM p ≈ 0.90; worst |SMD| ≈ 0.019 10:39 Task 5 — the memo (7 min) Ship/hold recommendation and one sentence of "what would change this." One-page memo drafted 10:46 Task 6 — peer review (4 min) Exchange memos. Each reviewer checks that uncertainty and assumptions are stated, not hidden. Every memo reviewed by another pair

The debrief that matters (do it even if you cut everything else): ask two pairs who chose HOLD and one who chose SHIP to say why. The point estimate clears the threshold; the interval does not. A pair that says "p < 0.05, ship it" has just demonstrated, in front of the room, the exact error the capstone is designed to catch. Handle it generously — it is the most useful mistake of the week.

If you are running late, cut: Task 6 peer review (4 min) and the method-selection walkthrough (down to 3 min). Never cut Task 3; the decision plot is a capstone deliverable.

docs.title: Hour 3 · 11:00–11:50 — Capstone kickoff and build (M-A, M-B)
docs.text:
Notebook: notebooks/capstone_starter.ipynb · Brief: capstone/CAPSTONE_BRIEF.md Starts at 11:00 sharp. This is the hard rule of Day 4.

Time Segment Instructor does Gate 11:00 Brief the capstone (8 min) Two linked decisions; requirements 1–7; one extension minimum; the rubric. Then the sentence, one more time: a correct "we cannot conclude" earns full marks. — 11:08 M-A: frame, freeze, size (22 min) They complete the design doc, freeze the plan, and produce the sizing with the CUPED alternative. Circulate and spot-check plans — this is the M-A gate. M-A · 11:30: every participant has a hashed plan, frozen before results, and a sizing paragraph 11:30 M-B: analyse the A/B (20 min) SRM, balance, effect with robust variance, CUPED, guardrails with the correct correction family. M-B · 11:50: integrity checks pass, or the experiment is declared invalid with evidence

Spot-check script for M-A (30 seconds per participant): What is your estimand? Which users are in your analysis population? What is your threshold, and where did it come from? Show me the hash. Four questions, four sentences. If any answer is missing, they are not through the gate.

If you are running late: cut the brief to 5 minutes and point at CAPSTONE_BRIEF.md. Do not cut build time. If a participant is stuck on the freeze at 11:20, give them the Lab 7 plan as a starting point and have them edit it — a frozen plan they adapted beats no plan.

docs.title: Hour 4 · 12:40–13:30 — Capstone build and decision memo (M-C, M-D)
docs.text:
Time Segment Instructor does Gate 12:40 M-C: evaluate the pilot (25 min) DiD with event study, or matching with sensitivity. DAG and identifying assumption written out. At least two refutations. M-C · 13:05: a refutation or validation check is present and its result is stated 13:05 M-D: memo and extension (20 min) One-page memo from DECISION_MEMO_TEMPLATE.md; decision plot with the threshold; the chosen extension. M-D · 13:25: memo complete 13:25 Self-audit (5 min) SELF_AUDIT_CHECKLIST.md, completed honestly. Every "no" they keep must appear in the memo as a stated limitation. Checklist completed

Circulate looking for exactly four things, in this order of severity:

  1. A plan frozen after the results cell (check the cell numbers, not their word).
  2. support_calls — or any post-treatment variable — sitting in an adjustment set.
  3. The analysis run on all assigned users rather than triggered users.
  4. A memo that recommends SHIP on an interval that crosses +1.0 pp.

Each of these is a rubric anti-pattern. Catching one at 13:00 turns a capped criterion into a teaching moment; catching it at 14:00 is just marking.

If you are running late: cut the extension. It is worth at most +5 bonus and only if the mandatory scope is already ≥ 80. The memo is worth 15 points and is never cut.

docs.title: Hour 5 · 13:40–14:30 — Quiz, briefings, and wrap-up
docs.text:
Time Segment Instructor does Assets 13:40 Quiz (15 min) Ten questions, closed book, papers collected before the first briefing. instructor/QUIZ_BANK.md 13:55 Briefings (25 min) Six minutes per team — or three-minute board briefings if the cohort is large. Score against the rubric live. For each team, the class probes one assumption. Ask every presenter the live question: state your identifying assumption and the one unmeasured variable that would break it. capstone/CAPSTONE_BRIEF.md §6 14:20 Wrap-up (10 min) One slide mapping each mandatory requirement to the module that taught it: design→M2, power→M3, analysis→M4, causal evaluation→M5/M6, communication→M7. Then the through-line: randomisation is the gold standard; every observational method is an assumption-laden attempt to approximate it, and honesty about those assumptions is the graded skill. Forward-point to SDA-DSC-311, which consumes exactly these estimates. Deck: wrap-up

Timing with a large cohort. At 25 minutes you fit four 6-minute briefings. With more teams than that, switch to 3-minute board briefings and score the rest from the submitted memos, or run two parallel briefing rooms with a second assessor. Decide this before Day 4 starts, not at 13:55.

Collect: analysis notebooks, frozen design docs, decision memos, self-audit checklists, quiz papers, PA-1 and PA-2 scripts.

Issue: Causal-badge recommendations within 5 working days. Badge requires ≥ 70 overall, capstone ≥ 70, and zero integrity flags (identical simulated seeds and results across submissions are checked).

docs.title: Appendix — running-late triage, in priority order
docs.text:
If the whole course is behind, cut in this order. Everything above the line is expendable; nothing below it is.

Cut freely 1. Discussion prompts and transitions (any day, any hour). 2. Day 1 Hour 1 failure story. 3. Day 2 Hour 3 Simpson's paradox. 4. Day 3 Hour 3 staggered-rollout derivation (state it instead). 5. Lab cross-checks: IPW in 5a, three-arm sizing in Lab 3, session clustering in Lab 4 (demo from the solution instead). 6. Capstone extensions.

Compress, do not cut 7. Module 7 theory — it lands through Lab 7 anyway. 8. PA-1 and PA-2 to 25 minutes each, floor. 9. Briefings from 6 minutes to 3.

Never cut - The freeze step in Lab 2, Lab 7 and the capstone. - Lab 1 Task 5 (the convergence-to-the-wrong-answer sweep). - Lab 4 Task 4 (the BH segment sweep). - Lab 5b Tasks 3 and 4 (event study and the parallel-trends breaker). - Lab 6 Task 3 (the collider) and Day 4 Hour 1's mediator trap. - Capstone build time in Day 4 Hours 3 and 4. - The sentence, repeated daily: a correct "we cannot conclude" earns full marks.

docs.title: Appendix — cohort adjustments
docs.text:
If the cohort is strong. Bring the staggered-DiD estimator and the EconML CATE forest into main scope on Days 3–4. Add unequal allocation to Lab 3 and an always-valid confidence sequence to Lab 4. Expect the capstone extensions to be genuinely attempted rather than gestured at.

If the cohort is weak. Reduce Lab 5a to a guided demo and keep Lab 5b hands-on. Give the Lab 2 frozen plan out as a starting point for the capstone rather than requiring a plan from scratch. Never cut the parallel-trends / event-study observation — a weak cohort needs the credibility lesson more, not less.

Pairing. Rotate pairs each day. Pair a strong-statistics participant with a strong-Python participant: the A/B intuition and the panel-data wrangling are different skills, and the transfer between them is the point.

docs.title: Setup Guide
docs.text:
SDA-DSC-213 · Experimentation, A/B Testing and Causal Inference · SDAIA Academy Instructor document. Work through this in order. Nothing here takes long; everything here costs an hour of classroom time if it is skipped.

Naming note. The catalogue text refers to a script called check_env.py. In this package the script is environment_check.py, at the root of course_assets/. Use that name in every message you send participants.

docs.title: 1. T-minus 1 week — instructor checklist
docs.text:
Allow 90 minutes. Do it on a clean machine or a fresh virtual environment, not on the laptop where everything already works.

  • Clone / copy the course package and confirm the tree matches §2 of README.md: data/, causal_utils/, notebooks/ (17 notebooks), figures/ (30 PNGs), capstone/, instructor/.
  • Create a clean environment and install the core stack: pip install -r requirements-core.txt.
  • Regenerate the datasets from fixed seeds: cd data && python make_data.py && cd ... This rewrites all 12 data files and GROUND_TRUTH.json.
  • Run python environment_check.py. It must print RESULT: PASS and exit 0. If any of the three ground-truth smoke tests fails, the seeds have moved and ANSWER_KEY.md no longer matches what participants will see — regenerate the answer-key numbers before teaching.
  • Install the optional causal stack in a second environment: pip install -r requirements.txt (adds dowhy, econml, linearmodels, networkx). This is the heaviest dependency chain in the course; test it early, and test it on the Colab fallback too.
  • Dry-run all 7 labs end to end, *_start.ipynb then *_solution.ipynb. Time Labs 4 and 5b specifically — they are the two overrun-prone sessions and you need to know your own pace on them.
  • Confirm the no-DoWhy path. Deliberately run Lab 6 and the capstone starter in the core-only environment and confirm every optional cell is skippable with a causal_utils equivalent immediately below it. You will have at least one participant who cannot install DoWhy.
  • Verify the classroom can reach PyPI. If it cannot, pre-mirror wheels for the causal stack, or plan to teach entirely on the core stack (which is fully supported — see §7).
  • Print the A4 posters: two-worlds counterfactual (m1_two_worlds.png), MDE-vs-n quadratic (m3_mde_vs_n.png), the three DAG junctions (m6_three_junctions.png), the method-selection flowchart (m7_method_selection.png). The MDE curve stays on the wall from Day 2 Hour 1 to the end.
  • Load the simulators and check the sliders work: confounding dial, peeking sandbox, collider generator, parallel-trends breaker.
  • Set up the shared leaderboard (recovered ATE accuracy, sizing plans, DiD estimates). One shared sheet is enough.
  • Print RUN_OF_SHOW.md, ANSWER_KEY.md and QUIZ_BANK.md double-sided. You will not want to be scrolling on Day 4.
  • Prepare PA-1 and PA-2 handouts and decide when PA-2 runs (see the deviation note in RUN_OF_SHOW.md, Day 3 Hour 5).
  • Send the participant setup email (§3) — a full week out, so there is time for a second round with anyone who is stuck.

docs.title: 2. T-minus 2 days — checklist
docs.text:
Allow 45 minutes.

  • Chase every participant who has not replied to the setup email with their environment_check.py output. Assume silence means "not done". This single follow-up is worth more than any other item on this list.
  • Triage the failures. Sort replies into: (a) PASS — nothing to do; (b) core-stack failure — fix over email using §6; (c) optional-stack failure only — reassure them, it is fine; (d) cannot install anything — put them on the Colab path (§7) and confirm they have run the install cell once before Day 1.
  • Prepare 2–3 loaner machines or a shared Colab workspace for the people who will nevertheless arrive broken. There is always at least one.
  • Confirm the classroom has: reliable Wi-Fi, a projector that renders matplotlib legibly from the back row, a whiteboard large enough for the Day 1 derivation, and power at every seat.
  • Confirm room bookings against the prayer schedule for the actual teaching dates, and adjust the whole grid in RUN_OF_SHOW.md if Dhuhr has moved. Do not adjust individual hours.
  • Copy the datasets to a USB drive and to a shared folder. A participant who cannot run make_data.py should be able to copy data/ in 30 seconds.
  • Rerun environment_check.py on the teaching machine — the one you will actually project from.
  • Decide the briefing format for Day 4 Hour 5 (six-minute briefings, or three-minute board briefings for a large cohort). Decide it now, not at 13:55 on Day 4.

docs.title: 3. Participant setup email — ready to send
docs.text:
Send at T-minus 1 week. Copy from the line below; replace the four bracketed fields.

Subject: SDA-DSC-213 — please set up your laptop before [DATE] (about 20 minutes)

Dear participant,

Welcome to Experimentation, A/B Testing and Causal Inference (SDA-DSC-213), running [DATES] at [LOCATION].

This is a hands-on course: you will be writing and running code from the third hour of Day 1. Please complete the setup below before the course starts and reply to this email with the output of the final step. It takes about twenty minutes, and doing it now means we spend Day 1 on causal inference rather than on pip.

1. Install Python 3.12 (3.10 or 3.11 also work) from python.org, or use an existing Anaconda/Miniconda installation.

2. Create a clean environment and install the core packages.

python -m venv sda-dsc-213
source sda-dsc-213/bin/activate        # Windows: sda-dsc-213\Scripts\activate
pip install numpy scipy pandas matplotlib statsmodels scikit-learn pyarrow jupyterlab

3. Install the optional causal packages. These have the heaviest dependency chain in the course, which is why we ask you to try them early:

pip install dowhy econml linearmodels networkx

If this step fails, do not worry and do not spend time on it. Every lab in the course runs without these packages — each notebook provides an equivalent that uses only the packages from step 2. Just tell us in your reply that step 3 did not work.

4. Download the course package from [LINK] and unzip it.

5. Generate the datasets.

cd course_assets/data
python make_data.py
cd ..

6. Verify everything, and send us the result.

python environment_check.py

You should see RESULT: PASS at the end. Please reply to this email with the last ten lines of that output, whether it passed or failed. If it failed, send it anyway — that is exactly what we need to help you before Day 1.

If you cannot install software on your machine (a locked-down work laptop, for example), reply and say so. We will send you a Google Colab link that runs everything in the browser with no installation at all.

Before Day 1, please also refresh hypothesis testing and confidence intervals from SDA-DSC-111 — the linked pre-read takes about 30 minutes.

On the day, please bring: your laptop and charger, and the machine you actually did the setup on.

We look forward to seeing you.

[INSTRUCTOR NAME] SDAIA Academy

docs.title: 4. How to verify an environment
docs.text:
Ask for the output of one command; everything else is guesswork.

python environment_check.py

A passing run ends with:

RESULT: PASS — environment is ready to teach
  required packages : all importable
  datasets          : 12 files, all present with the expected row counts
  ground truth      : 3/3 smoke assertions passed

How to read the sections:

Section What a problem there means 1. Python Below 3.10 — reinstall. This is the only version problem worth fixing. 2. Required packages A blocking failure. The named pip install line in the message is the fix. 3. Optional packages Never blocking. skip lines here are expected and fine. 4. Course toolkit causal_utils is not importable — they are running the script from the wrong directory, or the package did not unzip fully. 5. Datasets Missing or wrong row counts — cd data && python make_data.py. 6. Supporting files An incomplete copy of the package. Re-download. 7. Ground-truth smoke tests The data exists but the planted truths have drifted — the seeds moved. Regenerate; if it persists, the answer key needs regenerating too.

Useful flags: --quiet prints summary lines only; --root /path/to/course_assets runs it against a package elsewhere on disk. The script exits non-zero on failure, so it can be dropped into a CI check.

docs.title: 5. Colab fallback — the standing plan B
docs.text:
Every notebook's first cell is a commented install block. The Colab path is:

  1. Open the notebook in Colab (File → Upload notebook, or from Drive).
  2. Uncomment and run the first cell: 
    !pip install -q numpy scipy pandas matplotlib statsmodels scikit-learn pyarrow
!pip install -q dowhy econml linearmodels networkx   # optional, slow
  3. Get the data into the session — either upload the data/ folder, or run make_data.py in Colab, or mount Google Drive with a shared copy of data/. For a whole class, the Drive-mount route is fastest.
  4. Upload causal_utils/ alongside the notebook, or sys.path.append the folder from Drive.
  5. Run environment_check.py --root <path> in a cell to confirm.

Cost: roughly five minutes per session for the optional packages, and the runtime resets if the tab is idle. Tell Colab users to re-run the install cell after any disconnect, and to download their notebook at every break — a lost runtime on Day 4 costs their capstone.

docs.title: 6. The eight issues you will actually see
docs.text: Ordered by how often they occur.

docs.title: 1. DoWhy / EconML installation fails — frequency: high
docs.text:
Symptom. Long dependency resolution, a compiler error, or a version conflict with an existing numpy/scikit-learn.

Fix. In order: (a) do nothing — say clearly that the course runs without them and point at the fallback table in README.md §4; (b) install into a clean virtual environment rather than the system Python; (c) pin versions from requirements.txt; (d) use Colab for Lab 6 and the capstone extension only; (e) in a restricted network, install from pre-mirrored wheels.

Say this to the room on Day 1: "If DoWhy will not install, you are inconvenienced, not blocked. Every lab has a path that needs only numpy, pandas, scipy, statsmodels and scikit-learn."

docs.title: 2. "No module named causal_utils" — frequency: high
docs.text:
Symptom. The import fails in a notebook that ran fine yesterday.

Fix. They opened the notebook from a different working directory. Either launch Jupyter from the course_assets/ root, or add at the top of the notebook:

import sys, pathlib
sys.path.append(str(pathlib.Path.cwd().parent))   # from notebooks/ -> course_assets/

docs.title: 3. A dataset is missing or has the wrong row count — frequency: high
docs.text:
Symptom. FileNotFoundError, or environment_check.py reports a row-count mismatch.

Fix. cd data && python make_data.py. If the counts still differ, they have an older copy of make_data.py — re-copy the package. Never regenerate data mid-cohort: participants who regenerate on Day 3 get numbers that no longer match their neighbours' or the leaderboard's.

docs.title: 4. pyarrow missing, so the .parquet files will not load — frequency: medium
docs.text:
Symptom. Lab 1 or Lab 6 fails on pd.read_parquet with an engine error.

Fix. pip install pyarrow. It is in the core requirements but is the one package people drop when they hand-type the install line. environment_check.py catches it in section 2.

docs.title: 5. The notebook kernel is not the environment they installed into — frequency: medium
docs.text:
Symptom. Packages install successfully but the notebook still cannot import them.

Fix.

python -m ipykernel install --user --name sda-dsc-213

then select that kernel in the notebook. Confirm with import sys; print(sys.executable) in a cell and compare it to the interpreter: line printed by environment_check.py.

docs.title: 6. Plots do not render, or render illegibly — frequency: medium
docs.text:
Symptom. Blank output cells, or text too small to read from the back row.

Fix. %matplotlib inline at the top of the notebook. For legibility, call causal_utils.use_sdaia_style(base_size=13) when projecting — it matches the deck and enlarges the base font.

docs.title: 7. Results differ between participants — frequency: medium
docs.text:
Symptom. Two people get different ATE estimates from the same lab.

Fix. Three causes, in order of likelihood: (a) the seed was not set, or was set after the first random draw; (b) they regenerated the data at different times with a modified make_data.py; (c) they are analysing different rows — usually all assigned users versus triggered users, which is the Day 2 trap and worth surfacing to the whole room rather than fixing quietly.

docs.title: 8. The machine cannot install anything at all — frequency: low, but always at least one
docs.text:
Symptom. A locked-down corporate laptop: no admin rights, a blocked package index, or a proxy that intercepts TLS.

Fix. Go to Colab (§5) immediately. Do not spend Day 1 fighting the proxy. Give them the Drive-mounted data/ and causal_utils/ folders so they skip the upload step, and pair them with someone on a working local install so that at least one machine in the pair can run everything. Remind them to download their notebook at every break.

docs.title: 7. If a participant cannot install anything — the full Colab path
docs.text:
Prepare this before Day 1, once, and reuse it for every cohort.

  1. Put data/ and causal_utils/ in a shared Google Drive folder with view access for the cohort.
  2. Prepare a header cell that participants paste into any lab notebook:

from google.colab import drive
drive.mount('/content/drive')
import sys
sys.path.append('/content/drive/MyDrive/SDA-DSC-213/course_assets')
DATA = '/content/drive/MyDrive/SDA-DSC-213/course_assets/data/'
import causal_utils as cu
3. Have them change the data paths in each notebook from ../data/ to DATA. One find-and-replace per notebook. 4. Optional packages: !pip install -q dowhy econml linearmodels networkx, run once per session, roughly five minutes. If time is short, skip it — the core-stack path is fully supported. 5. Verify with !python /content/drive/MyDrive/SDA-DSC-213/course_assets/environment_check.py --root /content/drive/MyDrive/SDA-DSC-213/course_assets.

What this costs them. Nothing on Days 1–3. On Day 4, the risk is a runtime disconnect during the capstone build. Mitigate it: tell Colab users at every break to File → Download → Download .ipynb, and check they have done it at the M-B and M-C gates.

docs.title: 8. Post-course
docs.text:
• Collect: analysis notebooks, frozen design docs, decision memos, self-audit checklists, quiz papers, PA-1 and PA-2 scripts.
  • Score the capstone against the rubric in capstone/CAPSTONE_BRIEF.md §6. Grade the reasoning and honesty first, the point estimate second.
  • Check for academic-integrity flags: identical simulated seeds and identical results across submissions.
  • Issue Causal-badge recommendations within 5 working days. The badge requires ≥ 70 overall, capstone ≥ 70, and zero integrity flags.
  • Record which segments overran and by how much; annotate your copy of RUN_OF_SHOW.md for the next cohort. Labs 4 and 5b are the ones worth timing precisely.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
A comprehensive module on building modern, scalable, production-ready data architectures that feed AI and analytics. Participants trace the evolution from warehouses and lakes to the Lakehouse, master Delta Lake with ACID transactions and compute-storage separation, and work with ELT, streaming, data quality, and governance. A hands-on build of a local Mini-Lakehouse with Delta Lake and PySpark anchors the learning.

The course is built around a single evolving artefact: "Masar" (مسار), the national smart-mobility data platform of a Saudi ride-hailing and public-transit operator. Across the five days participants ingest Masar's raw trip records, GPS telemetry, driver and vehicle data, and payments; land them in a medallion (bronze → silver → gold) Lakehouse on Delta Lake; harden them with ELT transformations, streaming ingestion, quality tests, and governance controls; and finally serve them to two consumers — an ETA / demand-forecasting AI feature store and an operations BI dashboard. Every lab produces a component of the Mini-Lakehouse capstone, so by Day 5 each participant owns a working, tested, governed Lakehouse feeding both an AI model and a BI layer — the same shape of platform they will scale in SDA-DSC-215 (Big Data Analytics with Spark) and SDA-DSC-313.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this course, participants will be able to:

  1. LO1 — Compare data warehouses, data lakes, and Lakehouse architectures across use cases
  2. LO2 — Explain compute-storage separation and its impact on cost, elasticity, and scale
  3. LO3 — Design ELT pipelines suited to modern cloud data environments
  4. LO4 — Implement Delta Lake tables with ACID transactions and schema enforcement
  5. LO5 — Develop streaming and event-driven ingestion patterns for real-time data
  6. LO6 — Apply data-quality, observability, and governance controls across pipelines
  7. LO7 — Build a working Mini-Lakehouse with Delta Lake and PySpark
  8. LO8 — Connect Lakehouse components to AI, reporting, and analytics consumers
