docs.title: 13. Capstone linkage
docs.text: The capstone requires a git repository with full history and a one-command make pipeline, plus BENCHMARKS.md filled from your own runs. Both are only possible if your local environment is the pinned one: benchmark numbers from a mismatched Spark or a hosted runtime are not comparable across the cohort, and the academic-integrity check compares benchmark artefacts across repositories. This lab establishes the reproducible substrate that every capstone deliverable is measured on.

docs.title: LAB 01 — Land the Masar Raw Feeds into Bronze
docs.text:
Field Value Lab ID LAB-01 Module M1 — Evolution of Data Architecture: Warehouse, Lake, Lakehouse Day / Hour Day 1, Hour 3 Duration 50 minutes (20% theory / 80% lab), pairs Difficulty Foundational LO mapping LO1 (primary — medallion / Lakehouse layering), LO7 (contributes — first Mini-Lakehouse component), LO6 (touched — lineage metadata as governance) Prerequisites LAB-00 complete (make doctor = 0 fail); M1 lecture (warehouse vs lake vs Lakehouse, medallion, swamp smells) Checkpoint git tag lab1-start (solution: lab1-solution) Deliverable bronze.trips, bronze.gps_events, bronze.drivers as append-only Delta tables under lakehouse/bronze/, each carrying _ingested_at, _source_file, _batch_id; plus LAB1_NOTES.md with ≥ 3 named swamp risks and the filled benchmark table

Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. Grains, ratios and file-count reductions hold at either scale; absolute row counts do not.

docs.title: Why this lab matters
docs.text: Masar's ETA model is retrained weekly from trip and GPS history; the operations dashboard reads the same lineage. If the landing zone fails — or worse, silently succeeds while losing history — the AI system does not crash, it degrades invisibly. A pipeline that overwrites bronze on every run cannot reprocess when a silver transformation is later found to be wrong, so a bug discovered in week six is unfixable for weeks one to five: the raw evidence is gone. A landing zone with no _source_file cannot answer the regulator's question "which file produced this row?", and a landing zone with no profiling lets a 3.1% null dropoff_geohash reach the feature table as a plausible-looking zero. This lab builds the layer that makes every later correction possible, and it deliberately ships with the swamp smells you will spend Days 2–4 cleaning up.

docs.title: Task 2 — Implement land_bronze.py (10 min)
docs.text:
Open src/masar/ingest/land_bronze.py. The starter has the docstring and stubs; fill them in. Bronze rules: append-only, as-received (no casting, no cleaning, no dropping), plus lineage metadata.

# src/masar/ingest/land_bronze.py
"""Land raw Masar source files into the bronze zone.

Bronze rules enforced here:
  - append-only (never overwrite history)
  - keep data AS-RECEIVED (no cleaning, no typing beyond the source)
  - attach ingestion lineage: when, from which file, and under which batch
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import uuid
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F

from masar.spark import get_spark

BRONZE = "./lakehouse/bronze"
RAW = "./data/raw"


def _batch_id(feed: str, business_date: str) -> str:
    """Deterministic-prefix, unique-suffix batch id: traceable AND collision-free."""
    stamp = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ")
    return f"{feed}_{business_date}_{stamp}_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}"


def _with_lineage(df: DataFrame, batch_id: str) -> DataFrame:
    """Every bronze table carries the same three lineage columns (CONVENTIONS.md)."""
    return (
        df.withColumn("_ingested_at", F.current_timestamp())
          .withColumn("_source_file", F.input_file_name())
          .withColumn("_batch_id", F.lit(batch_id))
    )


def _append(df: DataFrame, table: str, path: str) -> int:
    """Append-only write. Registers the table in the catalog at the canonical path."""
    spark = get_spark()
    spark.sql("CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS bronze")
    n = df.count()
    (df.write
        .format("delta")
        .mode("append")               # NEVER overwrite: bronze is an immutable ledger
        .option("mergeSchema", "false")
        .option("path", path)
        .saveAsTable(table))
    total = spark.read.format("delta").load(path).count()
    print(f"Landed {n:,} rows -> {path}  (append, total now {total:,})")
    return total


def land_trips(business_date: str) -> int:
    spark = get_spark("land-trips")
    batch_id = _batch_id("trips", business_date)
    raw = (
        spark.read
        .option("header", True)
        .option("mode", "PERMISSIVE")      # keep malformed rows, do NOT drop them
        .option("inferSchema", False)      # everything lands as STRING: as-received
        .csv(f"{RAW}/trips_{business_date}.csv")
    )
    return _append(_with_lineage(raw, batch_id), "bronze.trips", f"{BRONZE}/trips")


def land_gps(business_date: str) -> int:
    """GPS pings arrive as newline-delimited JSON with a nested `payload` struct."""
    spark = get_spark("land-gps")
    batch_id = _batch_id("gps", business_date)
    raw = spark.read.json(f"{RAW}/gps/gps_{business_date}.ndjson")   # schema-on-read
    return _append(_with_lineage(raw, batch_id),
                   "bronze.gps_events", f"{BRONZE}/gps_events")


def land_drivers() -> int:
    spark = get_spark("land-drivers")
    batch_id = _batch_id("drivers", datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))
    raw = (
        spark.read
        .option("header", True)
        .option("mode", "PERMISSIVE")
        .option("inferSchema", False)      # hire_date has MIXED formats: keep as string
        .csv(f"{RAW}/drivers.csv")
    )
    return _append(_with_lineage(raw, batch_id), "bronze.drivers", f"{BRONZE}/drivers")


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Land a Masar raw feed into bronze")
    p.add_argument("--feed", required=True, choices=["trips", "gps", "drivers", "all"])
    p.add_argument("--date", default="2026-06-01", help="business date YYYY-MM-DD")
    args = p.parse_args()

    if args.feed in ("trips", "all"):
        land_trips(args.date)
    if args.feed in ("gps", "all"):
        land_gps(args.date)
    if args.feed in ("drivers", "all"):
        land_drivers()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The session builder is already written for you — read it, do not re-create Spark ad hoc:

# src/masar/spark.py
"""One place to build the Spark session with Delta Lake enabled.

Every lab imports get_spark() — never reconfigure Spark ad hoc in a notebook.
"""
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession


def get_spark(app_name: str = "masar-lakehouse") -> SparkSession:
    """Spark 3.5 + Delta Lake 3.2 session for the Masar Lakehouse.

    Storage and compute are separate even locally: data lives under
    ./lakehouse (a stand-in for object storage s3://masar-lakehouse),
    compute is this JVM. enableHiveSupport() gives us a persistent
    catalog so `bronze.trips` means the same thing in every process
    (and to dbt in Lab 3).
    """
    return (
        SparkSession.builder
        .appName(app_name)
        .config("spark.sql.extensions",
                "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
        .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog",
                "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
        .config("spark.sql.warehouse.dir", "./lakehouse")
        .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "8")   # small = laptop-friendly
        .config("spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled", "true")
        .enableHiveSupport()
        .getOrCreate()
    )

What to look for: inferSchema=False. Landing everything as STRING is a deliberate bronze decision — inference would guess at the mixed timestamp formats and silently null out the 2% that do not match, destroying evidence before you have looked at it. Typing happens at the silver boundary in Lab 3.

docs.title: Task 3 — Land one day, then land it again (10 min)
docs.text:
python -m masar.ingest.land_bronze --feed trips   --date 2026-06-01
python -m masar.ingest.land_bronze --feed gps     --date 2026-06-01
python -m masar.ingest.land_bronze --feed drivers

# now re-run the SAME day on purpose
python -m masar.ingest.land_bronze --feed trips   --date 2026-06-01

Verify the append semantics and the batch boundary:

python - <<'PY'
from masar.spark import get_spark
spark = get_spark("verify")
df = spark.table("bronze.trips")
print("total rows:", df.count())
df.groupBy("_batch_id").count().orderBy("_batch_id").show(truncate=False)
print("distinct source files:", df.select("_source_file").distinct().count())
PY

Discuss with your pair before moving on (this is the graded teaching moment): bronze now contains 96,400 rows for a day that only had 48,200 trips. That is correct. Bronze is an append-only ledger of what arrived, not a model of what is true. The two batches are distinguishable by _batch_id, so silver can deterministically keep the latest version per trip_id (Lab 3) without ever having lost the earlier one. Overwriting instead would have made the duplication invisible — and the history unrecoverable.

docs.title: Task 4 — Profile bronze for swamp smells (15 min)
docs.text:
Complete src/masar/ingest/profile_bronze.py:

# src/masar/ingest/profile_bronze.py
"""Cheap data-profiling pass to surface 'swamp' smells before we trust bronze."""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

from masar.spark import get_spark

BRONZE = "./lakehouse/bronze"


def profile(table_path: str, key: str | None = None) -> None:
    spark = get_spark("profile-bronze")
    df = spark.read.format("delta").load(table_path)
    n = df.count()
    print(f"\n=== {table_path} ===")
    print(f"rows={n:,}  columns={len(df.columns)}  files={df.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")

    # 1) Null / empty rate per column: a high rate on a key column is a swamp smell.
    #    CSV lands as STRING, so treat '' as missing too.
    exprs = []
    for c in df.columns:
        col = F.col(f"`{c}`")
        missing = F.when(col.isNull() | (col.cast("string") == F.lit("")), 1).otherwise(0)
        exprs.append(F.round(F.sum(missing) / F.lit(n), 4).alias(c))
    print("-- missing rate per column --")
    df.select(exprs).show(truncate=False, vertical=True)

    # 2) Duplicate business keys. Bronze ALLOWS duplicates, but we must SEE them.
    if key and key in df.columns:
        dupes = df.groupBy(key).count().filter("count > 1")
        print(f"duplicate {key} groups: {dupes.count():,}")
        dupes.orderBy(F.desc("count")).show(5, truncate=False)

    # 3) Format drift on timestamp-ish string columns (the 2% defect).
    for c in ("pickup_ts", "dropoff_ts", "hire_date"):
        if c in df.columns:
            iso = df.filter(F.col(c).rlike(r"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}")).count()
            eu = df.filter(F.col(c).rlike(r"^\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{4}")).count()
            print(f"{c}: iso-like={iso:,}  dd/mm/yyyy-like={eu:,}  other={n - iso - eu:,}")

    # 4) Value-domain surprises on low-cardinality columns.
    for c in ("city", "status", "payment_type", "producer_version"):
        if c in df.columns:
            print(f"-- distinct {c} --")
            df.groupBy(c).count().orderBy(F.desc("count")).show(10, truncate=False)


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("table", help="e.g. bronze/trips")
    p.add_argument("--key", default=None, help="business key to check for duplicates")
    args = p.parse_args()
    profile(f"./lakehouse/{args.table}", key=args.key)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• bronze.trips, bronze.gps_events, bronze.drivers all exist as Delta tables at lakehouse/bronze/<table> and are queryable by name (spark.table("bronze.trips"))
  • Every bronze table carries _ingested_at, _source_file and _batch_id
  • Landing is append-only: re-running trips for 2026-06-01 produced 96,400 rows, not 48,200
  • No cleaning, casting, filtering or de-duplication happened at this layer (all source columns still STRING for CSV feeds; GPS payload still a nested struct)
  • The two landings are separable by _batch_id

  • LAB1_NOTES.md names ≥ 3 swamp risks, each with the evidence line and the layer that will fix it

docs.title: Self-check questions
docs.text:
Q1. Bronze now holds 96,400 rows for a day with 48,200 trips. Is this a bug? Justify in medallion terms.

Answer No. Bronze is an append-only ledger of what *arrived*, not a model of what is *true*. Duplication at bronze is expected and is resolved deterministically at the silver boundary by keeping the latest row per `trip_id` (Lab 3's incremental MERGE). Preventing the duplication by overwriting would destroy the ability to reprocess history, which is the whole reason bronze exists. The duplication is visible and attributable because of `_batch_id`.

Q2. Why does land_trips set inferSchema=False and land every column as STRING?

Answer Schema inference would guess types from a sample and silently coerce or null out values that do not fit — precisely the ~2% of rows with `DD/MM/YYYY HH:MM` timestamps and any oddly formatted `fare_sar`. That is data loss disguised as convenience, and it happens *before* anyone has profiled the file. Bronze keeps data as-received; typing is a deliberate, tested transformation at silver where a failure is visible and a quarantine path exists.

Q3. A colleague proposes "just fix that one bad row" directly in bronze.trips. What do you tell them?

Answer Bronze is immutable. Editing it breaks reproducibility: the silver table can no longer be rebuilt from raw and the audit chain from a curated value back to its source row is severed. The correction belongs in silver as reproducible logic (a MERGE from a corrections fixture, as in Lab 4), so that the fix is reviewable, re-runnable and visible in the Delta history. If the source itself was wrong, the corrected file is *landed as a new batch*, not swapped in place.

Q4. What would break downstream if _source_file were not captured?

Answer Three things. (1) Incident forensics: when a bad batch is discovered you cannot select the rows it produced, so you cannot scope the blast radius or reprocess only the affected window. (2) Audit: you cannot answer "which delivered file produced this number in the regulatory report". (3) Late-arrival analysis: you lose the ability to correlate arrival file with business date, which is exactly the diagnosis path for the Module 3 undercount bug.

Q5. bronze.gps_events keeps payload as a nested struct rather than flattening lat/lon/speed_kmh into top-level columns. Why is that the right call at bronze — and what future incident does it help you diagnose?

Answer Flattening is a transformation and belongs at silver; keeping the struct preserves the source document shape exactly as delivered, including any new keys a producer adds. It also keeps `producer_version` next to the payload it describes — which is what lets you diagnose the semantic-drift incident where `producer_version` 2.5.0 emits `speed_kmh` in m/s while 2.4.0 emits km/h. The key and type are unchanged, so schema validation passes; only the version-to-payload correlation reveals it.

Q6. You need to reprocess six months of trips because a silver derivation was wrong. What in this lab makes that possible, and what would have made it impossible?

Answer Possible because bronze retained every landed row, untyped and unfiltered, with lineage — so silver can simply be rebuilt from bronze with corrected logic (ELT's core payoff, Module 3). Impossible if landing had used `mode("overwrite")`, dropped malformed rows with `mode("DROPMALFORMED")`, or cleaned at the landing step: in each case the raw evidence no longer exists and only a re-extraction from the source system — which retention policy may forbid — could recover it.

docs.title: LAB 02 — Cost and Elasticity Model for Masar
docs.text:
Field Value Lab ID LAB-02 Module M2 — Compute–Storage Separation and Cloud Economics Day / Hour Day 1, Hour 5 Duration 50 minutes (20% theory / 80% lab), pairs Difficulty Foundational–Intermediate (analysis-heavy, light coding) LO mapping LO2 (primary — compute–storage separation, cost, elasticity, scale), LO1 (reinforced — why the Lakehouse is economically viable), LO7 (contributes — BENCHMARKS.md seed) Prerequisites LAB-01 complete (bronze.trips, bronze.gps_events landed); M2 lecture (object storage, Parquet, elasticity spectrum, cost model) Checkpoint git tag lab2-start (solution: lab2-solution) Deliverable A runnable src/masar/econ/cost_model.py producing a storage-vs-compute split with a stated dominant driver; measured data-skipping evidence from src/masar/econ/scan_cost.py; LAB2_NOTES.md containing the coupled-vs-decoupled comparison table, the break-even statement, cited price sources, and the elasticity-guardrail rationale

Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. Grains, ratios and file-count reductions hold at either scale; absolute row counts do not.

docs.title: Why this lab matters
docs.text: Masar's ETA model is only retrained if someone approves the compute budget, and the operations dashboard only refreshes every 15 minutes if that refresh is affordable. When the economics of the platform fail, the AI system fails quietly through starvation: history gets truncated to save storage (so the model loses seasonality), retrains are cut from weekly to monthly (so the model drifts), and features are sampled instead of computed (so training and serving diverge). The counter-failure is just as real — an unbounded autoscaling cluster with no idle termination produces a bill that gets the whole platform cancelled in month two. This lab teaches you to defend a Lakehouse in an architecture review with numbers you measured yourself, and to name the layout decisions that turn decoupling from a possibility of savings into realised savings.

docs.title: Task 1 — Fill in real prices and cite them (10 min)
docs.text:
Open src/masar/econ/cost_model.py. Replace the placeholder prices with the current published list prices of one cloud region you choose (KSA-relevant options: me-central-1 / me-south-1 / a European region if the ME price is not published). Record the URL and the date you read it in LAB2_NOTES.md — an uncited price is an unusable model.

# src/masar/econ/cost_model.py
"""Transparent storage-vs-compute cost model for the Masar platform.

All prices are INPUTS; the point is to SEE which axis dominates, and to be
able to defend every number in an architecture review.

Sources (fill in and keep current):
  storage_gb_month : <provider> standard object storage, <region>, list price, read <date>
  core_hour        : <provider> general-purpose 4-core node, <region>, on-demand, read <date>
  spot_discount    : <provider> published spot/preemptible discount range, read <date>
"""
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Prices:
    storage_gb_month: float = 0.023      # object storage $/GB-month
    core_hour: float = 0.06              # decoupled compute $/core-hour (on-demand)
    spot_multiplier: float = 0.35        # spot ≈ 65% cheaper than on-demand
    warehouse_core_hour: float = 0.18    # coupled MPP warehouse: node runs 24/7
    warehouse_storage_gb_month: float = 0.21   # storage inside the warehouse node


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Job:
    """One scheduled workload on the decoupled platform."""
    name: str
    cores: int
    runtime_hours: float
    runs_per_month: int
    spot: bool = False

    def monthly_core_hours(self) -> float:
        return self.cores * self.runtime_hours * self.runs_per_month

    def monthly_compute(self, p: Prices) -> float:
        rate = p.core_hour * (p.spot_multiplier if self.spot else 1.0)
        return self.monthly_core_hours() * rate


def lakehouse_monthly_cost(total_gb: float, jobs: list[Job],
                           p: Prices = Prices()) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Decoupled: pay per byte KEPT and per second of compute that RUNS."""
    storage = total_gb * p.storage_gb_month
    compute = sum(j.monthly_compute(p) for j in jobs)
    total = storage + compute
    return {"storage": round(storage, 2),
            "compute": round(compute, 2),
            "total": round(total, 2),
            "compute_share": round(compute / total, 3)}


def warehouse_monthly_cost(total_gb: float, nodes: int, cores_per_node: int,
                           p: Prices = Prices()) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Coupled: the cluster must be sized for the DATA and runs 24/7.

    Storage and compute cannot be scaled independently, so idle hours are
    billed and retaining history forces you to add compute you do not need.
    """
    hours = 730.0
    compute = nodes * cores_per_node * hours * p.warehouse_core_hour
    storage = total_gb * p.warehouse_storage_gb_month
    total = storage + compute
    return {"storage": round(storage, 2),
            "compute": round(compute, 2),
            "total": round(total, 2),
            "compute_share": round(compute / total, 3),
            "idle_share": round(1 - (0.9 * 30) / hours, 3)}   # ~0.9h of real work/day


def break_even_utilisation(total_gb: float, nodes: int, cores_per_node: int,
                           p: Prices = Prices()) -> float:
    """Monthly decoupled core-hours at which the Lakehouse stops being cheaper.

    Above this many core-hours per month, an always-on coupled cluster of the
    same shape would cost less than paying per second — i.e. the workload is
    steady 24/7 and elasticity buys you nothing.
    """
    wh = warehouse_monthly_cost(total_gb, nodes, cores_per_node, p)
    lakehouse_storage = total_gb * p.storage_gb_month
    budget_for_compute = wh["total"] - lakehouse_storage
    return round(budget_for_compute / p.core_hour, 1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    prices = Prices()

    # Masar's three scheduled workloads (sizes from the M2 lecture)
    jobs = [
        Job("nightly_elt",           cores=16, runtime_hours=0.33, runs_per_month=30),
        Job("hourly_stream_compact", cores=4,  runtime_hours=0.10, runs_per_month=720),
        Job("weekly_feature_build",  cores=32, runtime_hours=0.50, runs_per_month=4,
            spot=True),
    ]

    TOTAL_GB = 12_000        # 36 months of raw GPS + trips + curated layers

    lh = lakehouse_monthly_cost(TOTAL_GB, jobs, prices)
    wh = warehouse_monthly_cost(TOTAL_GB, nodes=8, cores_per_node=16, p=prices)

    print("lakehouse :", lh)
    print("warehouse :", wh)
    print("saving    : %.1f%%" % (100 * (1 - lh["total"] / wh["total"])))
    print("break-even core-hours/month:",
          break_even_utilisation(TOTAL_GB, 8, 16, prices))
    print("actual core-hours/month    :",
          round(sum(j.monthly_core_hours() for j in jobs), 1))

    # Sensitivity: what if GPS volume doubles (new city)?
    doubled = replace(prices)                       # same prices, more data
    print("2x data   :", lakehouse_monthly_cost(TOTAL_GB * 2, jobs, doubled))

What to look for: the model has no hidden constants. Every number is either a cited price, a stated data volume, or a job shape you can defend. That property is what lets it survive a review.

docs.title: Task 3 — Measure data skipping, do not assume it (10 min)
docs.text:
Complete src/masar/econ/scan_cost.py. The point is to measure bytes and files read, not to trust the physical plan's appearance.

# src/masar/econ/scan_cost.py
"""Demonstrate that columnar + partitioned reads scan far less data.

The cost of decoupled compute is dominated by BYTES SCANNED, so we
measure it directly rather than trusting intuition.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse

from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F

from masar.spark import get_spark

SILVER = "./lakehouse/silver/trips"


def scan_metrics(df: DataFrame) -> dict[str, int]:
    """Execute the plan and read the scan metrics Spark recorded.

    'number of files read' and 'size of files read' come from the file-scan
    node; they are the honest measure of what decoupled compute paid for.
    """
    df.count()                                   # force execution
    plan = df._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan()
    out: dict[str, int] = {}

    def walk(node) -> None:
        it = node.metrics().iterator()
        while it.hasNext():
            entry = it.next()
            name, metric = entry._1(), entry._2()
            if name in ("numFiles", "filesSize", "numOutputRows"):
                out[name] = out.get(name, 0) + metric.value()
            if "files read" in metric.name().get() or "file" in metric.name().get():
                out[metric.name().get()] = out.get(metric.name().get(), 0) + metric.value()
        kids = node.children().iterator()
        while kids.hasNext():
            walk(kids.next())

    walk(plan)
    return out


def compare_scans(silver_path: str = SILVER) -> None:
    spark = get_spark("scan-cost")
    df_all = spark.read.format("delta").load(silver_path)
    total_cols = len(df_all.columns)

    # A. Naive: every column, filter applied after the scan is planned wide.
    naive = df_all.filter(F.col("city") == "Riyadh")

    # B. Column-pruned: only the 3 columns the question needs.
    pruned = (df_all
              .select("trip_id", "city", "fare_sar")
              .filter(F.col("city") == "Riyadh"))

    # C. Pruned + partition filter + a stats-friendly range predicate.
    #    `city` is the partition column => whole directories are skipped.
    pruned_part = (df_all
                   .select("trip_id", "city", "pickup_ts", "fare_sar")
                   .filter((F.col("city") == "Riyadh")
                           & (F.col("pickup_ts") >= F.lit("2026-06-01"))
                           & (F.col("pickup_ts") <  F.lit("2026-06-02"))))

    for label, q, cols in (("naive full read", naive, total_cols),
                           ("column-pruned", pruned, 3),
                           ("pruned + partition filter", pruned_part, 4)):
        m = scan_metrics(q)
        files = m.get("number of files read", m.get("numFiles", 0))
        size = m.get("size of files read", m.get("filesSize", 0))
        print(f"{label:28s} rows={m.get('numOutputRows', 0):>9,} "
              f"cols={cols:>2}/{total_cols} files={files:>4} "
              f"bytes={size:>12,}")

    print("\n--- physical plan of the pruned query ---")
    pruned.explain("formatted")
    print("\n--- physical plan of the pruned + partition-filtered query ---")
    pruned_part.explain("formatted")


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("path", nargs="?", default=SILVER)
    args = p.parse_args()
    compare_scans(args.path)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it and capture the output:

python -m masar.econ.scan_cost lakehouse/silver/trips | tee -a LAB2_NOTES.md

What to look for in the plan (this is what you paste into your notes as evidence):

  • PartitionFilters: [isnotnull(city#123), (city#123 = Riyadh)] — whole directories skipped, the cheapest possible saving.
  • PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(pickup_ts), GreaterThanOrEqual(pickup_ts,...)] — the predicate reached the Parquet reader, so row groups whose min/max cannot match are never decompressed.
  • ReadSchema: struct<trip_id:string,city:string,fare_sar:double> — three columns, not twenty-six. This is column pruning and it is where most of the byte saving comes from.
  • All three queries return the same Riyadh trip count. Same answer, a fraction of the bytes: that is the entire economic argument for Parquet under a decoupled engine.

If your Spark build does not expose scan metrics through executedPlan().metrics(), open the Spark UI (http://localhost:4040 while the job runs) → SQL/DataFrame tab → click the query → read number of files read and size of files read from the scan node. Record those numbers instead; the lesson is identical.

Fill the benchmark table in LAB2_NOTES.md:

Query Columns read Files read Bytes read Filter pushdown Relative bytes scanned naive full read no 1.00 column-pruned no pruned + partition filter yes (city, pickup_ts)

  2. Break-even: the Lakehouse stops being cheaper above ≈ <N> core-hours/month of sustained compute — i.e. if Masar's workload became a steady 24/7 load at this cluster size, a coupled system would win. Masar's actual demand is <M> core-hours/month, so we are at <M/N> of break-even.

docs.title: Task 5 — Write the elasticity guardrails and justify them (5 min)
docs.text:
Inspect infra/cluster/masar-elt-cluster.yaml and justify each guardrail in LAB2_NOTES.md:

# infra/cluster/masar-elt-cluster.yaml
# Ephemeral job cluster: exists only for the ELT run, then dies.
cluster:
  name: masar-elt
  spark_version: "3.5"
  autoscale:
    min_workers: 2
    max_workers: 8          # bounded elasticity: no runaway bill
  autotermination_minutes: 10   # MANDATORY: kill idle compute
  node_type: general-4core
  spot:
    enabled: true           # restartable ELT tolerates preemption
    on_demand_driver: true  # keep the driver stable
  tags:
    cost_center: masar-data-platform
    workload: elt-nightly

Your rationale must answer, in one line each:

  • Why autotermination_minutes: 10 and not 60 or 0? (What does each extreme cost?)
  • Why max_workers: 8 and not unbounded? (Elasticity without a bound is an unbounded bill; also, past a point the ELT is shuffle-bound, not core-bound.)
  • Why spot for the weekly feature build but on_demand_driver: true? (Losing an executor costs a retried task; losing the driver costs the whole job.)
  • What do the tags buy you? (Unattributed compute is unmanageable; per-workload attribution is how you find the one dashboard costing 40% of the bill.)

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• python -m masar.econ.cost_model runs and prints a storage / compute / total / compute_share split for the Lakehouse and a comparable figure for the coupled warehouse
  • Every price in Prices is a real published list price with a cited URL and read-date in LAB2_NOTES.md
  • The 36-month storage estimate is derived from measured daily volumes, with the extrapolation factor stated explicitly
  • The dominant cost driver is stated with its compute_share and a one-line reason
  • scan_cost.py produced three measured rows (files and bytes read) and the plans show PartitionFilters, PushedFilters and a reduced ReadSchema
  • The pruned query reads ≤ 25% of the naive query's columns and returns an identical count
  • The coupled-vs-decoupled comparison table is complete in LAB2_NOTES.md
  • A break-even figure is stated with its assumptions, and Masar's actual utilisation is compared against it
  • autotermination_minutes and the spot/on-demand-driver split are each justified in one line
  • At least one sensitivity result recorded (retention change, spot off, or uncompacted-silver runtime)
  • Commit feat(econ): cost model + data-skipping benchmark for Masar exists

docs.title: Self-check questions
docs.text:
Q1. You predicted storage would dominate the bill and the model says compute is 30% of a small total while the warehouse's compute is 87% of a large one. Reconcile the two.

Answer They measure different things. In the decoupled model you pay for compute *only while jobs run* — Masar's three jobs total ~2,100 core-hours/month, so compute is a modest line and storage is the steady floor. In the coupled model the cluster is sized for the **data** and billed 24/7 whether or not work happens, so ~96% of its compute hours are idle and compute swamps everything. The lesson is not "compute is big" or "storage is big" — it is that decoupling converts a fixed cost into a variable one, which is why *elasticity* is the lever.

Q2. Decoupling moved data to cheap object storage, yet a team's bill went up after migration. Give the two most likely causes and the fix for each.

Answer (1) Every query full-scans an unpartitioned, uncompacted table, so compute pays to read data a filter could have skipped — fix with partitioning on a low-cardinality column, ZORDER on the common filter columns, and scheduled OPTIMIZE. (2) Autoscaling clusters never idle-terminate, so "elastic" compute is running 24/7 anyway — fix with `autotermination_minutes` and bounded `max_workers`, plus spot for restartable jobs. Decoupling *enables* savings; layout and elasticity discipline *realise* them.

Q3. Why does partitioning by city help the scan benchmark, and why would partitioning by trip_id hurt it catastrophically?

Answer `city` has ~5 distinct values, so each partition is a directory containing large files; a `city = 'Riyadh'` filter eliminates whole directories before any file is opened (`PartitionFilters`). `trip_id` is a unique key: partitioning by it produces one tiny file per trip — millions of objects. Listing dominates the job, per-file overhead dwarfs the data, and no filter can skip anything useful. That is the small-files problem, and it makes object storage both slow *and* expensive (Module 4 fixes it with OPTIMIZE).

Q4. Masar adds a new city and daily GPS volume doubles. Which line item grows, by how much, and does the compute/storage balance shift?

Answer Storage roughly doubles (it is linear in bytes kept): in the model, $276 → $552/month. Compute does **not** double automatically — it grows only with the additional runtime needed to process the extra rows, which is sublinear if the cluster is already parallel and the layout supports skipping. So `compute_share` falls (0.30 → 0.18 in the shipped example), and the platform gets relatively *more* storage-weighted as it scales. This is the argument for retaining raw history: the marginal cost of keeping more is small compared with the option value of reprocessing.

Q5. When is a coupled warehouse still the right architectural call for Masar?

Answer When the workload is small, structured, steady and latency-critical with high concurrency — e.g. a sub-second, hundreds-of-concurrent-users operational dashboard over a few GB. There, the always-on cost is small in absolute terms, the elasticity has nothing to exploit (utilisation is near break-even), and the warehouse's coupled storage gives lower latency than fetching objects over the network. The honest position in a review is: decoupling wins for the AI/analytics estate; a small serving-tier warehouse or cache in front of gold can still be justified — provided it is a *cache*, not a second source of truth (that would recreate the M1 two-tier problem).

Q6. Your break-even calculation says the Lakehouse loses above ~318,000 core-hours/month. A colleague says "then we should just make our jobs bigger to get closer to break-even." What is wrong with that reasoning?

Answer Break-even is a *comparison point*, not a target. Consuming more core-hours does not create value; it just raises the bill until the alternative architecture would have been equally bad. The correct reading is a risk statement: Masar operates at under 1% of break-even utilisation, so there is enormous headroom to add workloads (more retrains, more backfills, more ad-hoc analysis) before the economics would favour a coupled system. That headroom is precisely what lets the AI team retrain weekly instead of monthly.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Pruned and naive plans look identical Filter applied after collect()/toPandas(), so Spark planned a full scan Keep the filter on the DataFrame before any action; never filter in Python No PushedFilters in the plan Predicate is on a derived/casted expression, or the column has no Parquet statistics Filter on a native stored column (city, pickup_ts), not on year(pickup_ts) or a cast(...) compute_share ≈ 1.0 unexpectedly Storage GB under-estimated (usually retention months forgotten) Recount: daily volume × 365 × retention years × extrapolation factor, across all layers, not just raw Prices "feel wrong" by 1000× Mixed per-GB and per-TB units, or per-node vs per-core rates Normalise everything to $/GB-month and $/core-hour before it enters Prices scan_metrics returns an empty dict This Spark build does not surface scan metrics through the Py4J plan walk Read number of files read / size of files read from the Spark UI SQL tab (localhost:4040) and record those All three queries read the same number of files The table has only one file per partition (sample too small), so pruning has nothing to skip Land 3 days of trips (Lab 1 stretch goal 1) before benchmarking, or accept the column-pruning result and note the limitation PartitionFilters empty though you filtered on city The benchmark table was written without .partitionBy("city") Rebuild with python -m masar.econ.prepare_benchmark_input; confirm lakehouse/silver/trips/city=Riyadh/ directories exist Bytes read increase after adding a filter Delta statistics are stale, or the added predicate forced a wider column set Run OPTIMIZE (Lab 4) to refresh file statistics; check the ReadSchema line — you may have selected more columns Timings vary by 3× run to run JVM warm-up, OS page cache, and other laptop load Report relative bytes/files scanned, not wall-clock seconds; run each query twice and use the second Savings claim of 98% challenged as unrealistic The coupled baseline was sized for peak, and list prices ignore committed-use discounts State the caveat explicitly: apply a 30–50% enterprise discount to the warehouse baseline and re-report. A model that survives its own caveats wins the review FileNotFoundException: lakehouse/silver/trips On lab2-start without the shipped sample python -m masar.econ.prepare_benchmark_input to build it from your Lab 1 bronze

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
1. Spot-vs-on-demand for the weekly feature build. Compute the saving from spot=True and pair it with an interruption-risk statement: what is the expected retry cost if the job is preempted at 80% completion, and does that change the recommendation?
  2. Cost per consumer. Split the compute line by consumer — AI feature build vs BI mart refresh — and produce a per-consumer monthly figure. This is the number a platform team actually gets asked for, and it is the seed of the capstone's cost attribution.
  3. Serverless / per-TB-scanned model. Add a third pricing model ($ per TB scanned) and show how the measured bytes from Task 3 translate into a query bill. Which of the three scan variants would you allow a BI tool to run against gold?
  4. Layout sensitivity. Rewrite the benchmark table unpartitioned and re-run scan_cost.py. Quantify the extra bytes an unpartitioned layout costs per dashboard refresh, then multiply by 40 dashboards × 96 refreshes/day — the "Tabadul" case study in one number.
  5. Egress trap. Extend Prices with a cross-region egress rate and model the cost of running compute in a different region from storage. State the architectural rule this implies.

docs.title: Capstone linkage
docs.text: This lab delivers capstone mandatory requirement 2 (Compute–storage discipline, LO2): the object-storage-style layout is already in place from Lab 1, and this lab produces the cost/scan analysis section of BENCHMARKS.md — capstone deliverable 3 — with your own measured columns-read, files-read and bytes-read figures. The break-even statement and the guardrail rationale are two of the five entries required in DECISIONS.md (capstone deliverable 6): partition-key choice and elastic-compute guardrails. The measurement technique you built here is reused twice more: to quantify the small-files reduction after OPTIMIZE in Lab 4 (requirement 2's "measured file-count reduction") and to benchmark direct-serve versus materialised marts in Lab 8.

docs.title: LAB 03 — Build the ELT Pipeline to silver.trips
docs.text:
Field Value Lab ID LAB-03 (delivered as 3a + 3b) Module M3 — ETL versus ELT in Modern Stacks Day / Hour Day 2, Hour 3 (Lab 3a) and Day 2, Hour 5 (Lab 3b) Duration 90 minutes total — 3a: 35 min, 3b: 55 min (10–15% theory / 85–90% lab), pairs Difficulty Intermediate LO mapping LO3 (primary — ELT pipeline design for cloud data environments), LO6 (secondary — tests, freshness, governance-as-code), LO7 (contributes — the silver node of the Mini-Lakehouse) Prerequisites LAB-01 complete (bronze.trips, bronze.drivers landed, append-only, with lineage); M3 lecture (ETL vs ELT, dbt layering, idempotency, incremental models, late-arriving data) Checkpoint git tags lab3-start (3a), lab3b-start (3b) · solutions: lab3a-solution, lab3-solution Deliverable A dbt project building stg_trips, stg_drivers and an incremental, merge-on-trip_id silver.trips with a 3-day lookback; ≥ 6 passing tests plus a source-freshness SLA; a demonstrated late-arrival backfill; LAB3_NOTES.md with the filled benchmark table

Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. Grains, ratios and file-count reductions hold at either scale; absolute row counts do not.

docs.title: Why this lab matters
docs.text: silver.trips is the single conformed definition of "a Masar trip" — the ETA model trains on it, the demand forecast aggregates it, and the operations dashboard counts it. If this transformation fails, nothing crashes: the numbers merely become wrong, consistently and confidently. The specific failure this lab inoculates against is the most common bug in production data engineering: a WHERE trip_date = current_date() filter that silently drops trips settling after midnight, undercounting by ~2% forever. Downstream, that undercount underpays drivers, skews the demand model's training labels, and makes the dashboard disagree with the data-science notebook — the exact two-tier divergence Module 1 diagnosed, now reproduced inside one platform by a three-word filter. You will build the fix (lookback window + idempotent MERGE + a unique test) and then prove it works by landing a late trip and watching it merge exactly once.

docs.title: Part 3a — Sources, freshness and staging models (35 min)
Task 1 — Declare bronze as dbt sources with a freshness SLA (15 min)
docs.text:
Create models/staging/masar/_masar__sources.yml. Note that _ingested_at (the lineage column Lab 1 wrote) is what makes freshness measurable — this is the payoff for that discipline.

# dbt/masar/models/staging/masar/_masar__sources.yml
# Declares bronze Delta tables as dbt sources + a freshness SLA.
version: 2

sources:
  - name: bronze
    schema: bronze
    description: "Append-only landing zone. Never mutated. Lab 1 output."
    tables:
      - name: trips
        identifier: trips
        loaded_at_field: _ingested_at
        freshness:                       # fail the build if bronze is stale
          warn_after:  {count: 6,  period: hour}
          error_after: {count: 24, period: hour}
        columns:
          - name: trip_id
            description: "Business key as received. May be duplicated at bronze."
          - name: _batch_id
            description: "Landing batch. Distinguishes re-runs of the same day."

      - name: drivers
        identifier: drivers
        loaded_at_field: _ingested_at
        freshness:
          warn_after:  {count: 24, period: hour}
          error_after: {count: 72, period: hour}

      - name: gps_events
        identifier: gps_events
        loaded_at_field: _ingested_at
        freshness:
          warn_after:  {count: 1, period: hour}
          error_after: {count: 6, period: hour}

dbt source freshness

What to look for: the trips source is fresh if you landed it today. Deliberately prove the check works — it is a guard, not decoration:

# temporarily tighten the SLA to 1 minute and re-run
sed -i.bak 's/{count: 6,  period: hour}/{count: 1, period: minute}/' \
    models/staging/masar/_masar__sources.yml
dbt source freshness            # expect WARN on bronze.trips
mv models/staging/masar/_masar__sources.yml.bak \
   models/staging/masar/_masar__sources.yml

Record in LAB3_NOTES.md: what upstream failure does a 6h warn / 24h error SLA on bronze.trips actually catch, and what does it miss? (It catches a stopped landing job. It misses a landing job that runs on time and lands empty or wrong data — that is a volume/quality check, Module 6.)

docs.title: Task 2 — Write stg_trips and stg_drivers (20 min)
docs.text:
Staging is 1:1 with the source: rename, cast, normalise. No joins, no business rules, no aggregation. Every source quirk is isolated here so that a source rename touches exactly one model.

Three quirks from CONVENTIONS.md must be handled at this boundary:

Quirk Where it comes from Staging treatment Mixed timestamp formats (~2% DD/MM/YYYY HH:MM) pickup_ts, dropoff_ts parse both formats with coalesce, flag unparseable Timestamps are Asia/Riyadh wall clock; the Lakehouse stores UTC all timestamps to_utc_timestamp(..., 'Asia/Riyadh') — once, here Everything landed as STRING (Lab 1's inferSchema=False) all columns explicit cast per column 
-- dbt/masar/models/staging/masar/stg_trips.sql
-- Staging: 1:1 with source. Rename, cast, normalise. NO joins, NO business logic.
{{ config(materialized='view') }}

with source as (

    select * from {{ source('bronze', 'trips') }}

),

parsed as (

    select
        cast(trip_id          as string)  as trip_id,
        cast(rider_id         as string)  as rider_id,
        cast(driver_id        as string)  as driver_id,
        cast(vehicle_id       as string)  as vehicle_id,
        initcap(trim(city))               as city,
        cast(pickup_zone_id   as string)  as pickup_zone_id,
        cast(dropoff_zone_id  as string)  as dropoff_zone_id,

        -- The source ships TWO timestamp formats (~2% of rows use dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm).
        -- Parse both, coalesce, then normalise Asia/Riyadh wall clock -> UTC ONCE.
        to_utc_timestamp(
            coalesce(
                to_timestamp(pickup_ts,  'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'),
                to_timestamp(pickup_ts,  'dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm')
            ), 'Asia/Riyadh')             as pickup_ts,
        to_utc_timestamp(
            coalesce(
                to_timestamp(dropoff_ts, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'),
                to_timestamp(dropoff_ts, 'dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm')
            ), 'Asia/Riyadh')             as dropoff_ts,

        cast(distance_km      as double)  as distance_km,
        cast(duration_min     as double)  as reported_duration_min,  -- source value; may be negative
        cast(fare_sar         as double)  as fare_sar,
        cast(surge_multiplier as double)  as surge_multiplier,
        lower(trim(payment_type))         as payment_type,
        lower(trim(status))               as status,
        nullif(trim(dropoff_geohash), '') as dropoff_geohash,        -- '' is missing, not a value

        -- lineage carried forward from bronze (Lab 1)
        _batch_id,
        _ingested_at

    from source
    where trip_id is not null            -- drop unkeyed garbage at the boundary

)

select * from parsed

-- dbt/masar/models/staging/masar/stg_drivers.sql
-- Staging: 1:1 with bronze.drivers. hire_date arrives in MIXED formats on purpose.
{{ config(materialized='view') }}

with source as (

    select * from {{ source('bronze', 'drivers') }}

),

parsed as (

    select
        cast(driver_id  as string)   as driver_id,
        cast(full_name_en as string) as full_name_en,
        initcap(trim(city))          as driver_city,

        -- three observed formats; add a branch only for a format you have SEEN
        coalesce(
            to_date(hire_date, 'yyyy-MM-dd'),
            to_date(hire_date, 'dd/MM/yyyy'),
            to_date(hire_date, 'MMM d, yyyy')
        )                            as hire_date,

        cast(rating as double)       as driver_rating,
        lower(trim(status))          as driver_status,
        cast(national_id_hash as string) as national_id_hash,   -- PDPL: pseudonymised, never re-identify
        cast(phone_hash as string)       as phone_hash,         -- PDPL: pseudonymised
        _batch_id,
        _ingested_at

    from source
    where driver_id is not null

)

select * from parsed

Build and inspect:

dbt run --select staging
dbt show --select stg_trips --limit 5

# how many timestamps failed BOTH formats? (must be 0 — otherwise add a branch)
dbt show --inline "select count(*) as unparseable from {{ ref('stg_trips') }} where pickup_ts is null"
# how many hire_date values failed all three formats?
dbt show --inline "select count(*) as unparseable from {{ ref('stg_drivers') }} where hire_date is null"

What to look for: unparseable = 0 for both. A non-zero count means the source ships a format you have not seen — go back to Lab 1's profiling output, find it, and add exactly that branch. Never "fix" it with a blanket try_cast that turns every parse failure into a silent null: that is how a 2% defect becomes a 2% invisible data loss.

Commit 3a:

git add dbt/masar/models/staging LAB3_NOTES.md
git commit -m "feat(staging): dbt sources with freshness SLA + typed stg_trips/stg_drivers"

docs.title: Part 3b — Incremental silver.trips, tests, and the backfill drill (55 min)
Task 3 — Write silver.trips as an incremental merge with a lookback window (20 min)
docs.text:
This is the model the whole course depends on. Four properties must hold simultaneously:

  1. Deduplicated — bronze legitimately holds two batches of the same day (Lab 1); silver keeps the latest landed version of each trip_id, not DISTINCT and not the first.
  2. Incremental with a lookback — reprocess a 3-day window, not just today, so late-arriving trips are picked up.
  3. Idempotent — MERGE on trip_id, so re-running changes nothing.
  4. Conformed — one row per real-world completed trip, typed, with derived features computed once, here.
-- dbt/masar/models/marts/silver/silver_trips.sql
-- silver.trips: the conformed contract. One row per completed, valid trip.
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    incremental_strategy='merge',
    unique_key='trip_id',
    file_format='delta',
    schema='silver',
    alias='trips',
    partition_by=['city'],
    on_schema_change='append_new_columns'
) }}

with trips as (

    select * from {{ ref('stg_trips') }}

    {% if is_incremental() %}
      -- LOOKBACK: reprocess a 3-day window so late-arriving trips are
      -- corrected (merged), not missed. Merge-on-trip_id => idempotent.
      -- NOTE: the window is on pickup_ts (event time), NOT on _ingested_at:
      -- a trip that ENDED yesterday but ARRIVED today must be inside it.
      where pickup_ts >= (
          select date_sub(max(pickup_ts), {{ var('lookback_days', 3) }})
          from {{ this }}
      )
    {% endif %}

),

-- Bronze is append-only, so the same trip_id can appear in several batches.
-- Keep the LATEST landed version per key: DISTINCT would keep a stale row.
deduped as (

    select * from (
        select
            *,
            row_number() over (
                partition by trip_id
                order by _ingested_at desc, _batch_id desc
            ) as _rn
        from trips
    )
    where _rn = 1

),

drivers as (

    select
        driver_id,
        driver_rating,
        driver_status
    from {{ ref('stg_drivers') }}

),

joined as (

    select
        d.trip_id,
        d.rider_id,                                   -- PDPL: personal data, never leaves silver un-masked
        d.driver_id,
        d.vehicle_id,
        d.city,
        d.pickup_zone_id,
        d.dropoff_zone_id,
        d.pickup_ts,                                  -- UTC (normalised in staging)
        d.dropoff_ts,                                 -- UTC
        to_date(from_utc_timestamp(d.pickup_ts, 'Asia/Riyadh')) as trip_date,  -- business date, +03
        d.distance_km,
        d.reported_duration_min,                      -- as delivered; may disagree with the truth
        round((unix_timestamp(d.dropoff_ts)
               - unix_timestamp(d.pickup_ts)) / 60.0, 2) as duration_min,      -- derived truth
        d.fare_sar,
        d.surge_multiplier,
        d.payment_type,
        d.status,
        d.dropoff_geohash,
        dr.driver_rating,
        dr.driver_status,
        round(d.fare_sar / nullif(d.distance_km, 0), 3)          as fare_per_km,
        hour(from_utc_timestamp(d.pickup_ts, 'Asia/Riyadh'))     as pickup_hour,
        dayofweek(from_utc_timestamp(d.pickup_ts, 'Asia/Riyadh')) as day_of_week,
        case when hour(from_utc_timestamp(d.pickup_ts, 'Asia/Riyadh')) < 6
             then 1 else 0 end                                    as is_night,
        d._batch_id,
        d._ingested_at,
        current_timestamp()                                       as _loaded_at

    from deduped d
    left join drivers dr on d.driver_id = dr.driver_id

    where d.status = 'completed'          -- silver = conformed, valid, completed trips
      and d.dropoff_ts > d.pickup_ts      -- reject impossible durations (source has negatives)
      and d.fare_sar > 0                  -- reject non-positive fares
      and d.distance_km > 0

)

select * from joined

Build it:

dbt run --select silver_trips

Then immediately run it again and compare. On the second run the lookback selects the same window, the MERGE matches every row, and nothing changes — that is idempotency, visible.

dbt run --select silver_trips
python - <<'PY'
from masar.spark import get_spark
spark = get_spark("lab3-verify")
df = spark.table("silver.trips")
print("silver.trips rows:", df.count(), "cols:", len(df.columns))
print("distinct trip_id :", df.select("trip_id").distinct().count())
spark.sql("DESCRIBE HISTORY delta.`./lakehouse/silver/trips`") \
     .select("version", "operation", "operationMetrics").show(5, truncate=False)
PY

What to look for: rows == distinct trip_id (the dedup worked), 27 columns, and a MERGE operation in the Delta history whose numTargetRowsUpdated on the second run reflects an unchanged table.

docs.title: Task 4 — Declare the tests (15 min)
docs.text:
Tests are the contract of silver.trips, checked on every build. Add them next to the model.

# dbt/masar/models/marts/silver/_silver__models.yml
version: 2

models:
  - name: silver_trips
    description: >
      Conformed, completed Masar trips. GRAIN: one row per trip_id.
      Timestamps are UTC; trip_date is the Asia/Riyadh business date.
      Contract for all downstream AI and BI consumers.
    columns:
      - name: trip_id
        description: "Business key. Unique, non-null."
        tests: [unique, not_null]

      - name: city
        tests:
          - not_null
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['Riyadh', 'Jeddah', 'Dammam', 'Mecca', 'Medina']

      - name: status
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['completed']         # silver holds completed trips only

      - name: fare_sar
        tests:
          - not_null
          - dbt_utils.accepted_range:
              min_value: 0
              inclusive: false

      - name: duration_min
        tests:
          - not_null
          - dbt_utils.accepted_range:
              min_value: 0
              max_value: 480                # 8h: longer is a data problem, not a trip
              inclusive: false

      - name: driver_id
        tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              to: ref('stg_drivers')
              field: driver_id

      - name: pickup_ts
        tests: [not_null]

      - name: rider_id
        description: "PDPL: personal data. Never propagated raw to gold/BI/online store."
        tests: [not_null]

Add one custom data test — SQL that must return zero rows:

-- dbt/masar/tests/assert_no_future_trips.sql
-- A trip cannot end in the future. Catches timezone drift and bad source clocks.
select
    trip_id,
    dropoff_ts
from {{ ref('silver_trips') }}
where dropoff_ts > current_timestamp() + interval 1 hour

Install dbt_utils (needed for accepted_range) and run the suite:

cat > packages.yml <<'YML'
packages:
  - package: dbt-labs/dbt_utils
    version: [">=1.1.0", "<2.0.0"]
YML
dbt deps
dbt test --select silver_trips

What to look for: every failure is a logic bug to fix, never a test to delete. The two you are most likely to hit:

Failing test What it is telling you Correct fix unique_silver_trips_trip_id Dedup window is wrong — DISTINCT used, or row_number() partitioned by the wrong key Restore the row_number() over (partition by trip_id order by _ingested_at desc) filter relationships_silver_trips_driver_id Trips reference a driver_id absent from stg_drivers (orphan) Do not switch to an inner join (that silently deletes trips). Quantify the orphans, decide with the business whether they are quarantined (silver.trips_quarantine, Lab 6) or admitted with a null-rated driver, and record the decision

docs.title: Task 5 — The backfill drill: prove late-arriving data is handled (15 min)
docs.text:
This is the point of the entire module. Do not skip it.

# 1. Baseline: how many trips does silver hold, and how many for the target date?
python - <<'PY'
from masar.spark import get_spark
spark = get_spark("drill-before")
spark.table("silver.trips").groupBy("trip_date").count().orderBy("trip_date").show()
PY

# 2. Land the late-arrival fixture into BRONZE (a trip that ENDED yesterday,
#    ARRIVING today, in its own batch — exactly the production failure mode)
python -m masar.ingest.land_bronze --feed trips --date 2026-06-01 \
       --source data/fixtures/late_trips/trips_late_2026-06-02.csv

# 3. Run the incremental model
cd dbt/masar && dbt run --select silver_trips

Verify the three properties that matter:

python - <<'PY'
from masar.spark import get_spark
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
spark = get_spark("drill-after")

t = spark.table("silver.trips")
late_ids = [r.trip_id for r in spark.read.option("header", True)
            .csv("data/fixtures/late_trips/trips_late_2026-06-02.csv")
            .select("trip_id").collect()]

print("late trip ids:", late_ids)
print("present in silver:", t.filter(F.col("trip_id").isin(late_ids)).count())
print("counted ONCE    :", t.filter(F.col("trip_id").isin(late_ids))
                            .groupBy("trip_id").count()
                            .filter("count > 1").count() == 0)
t.groupBy("trip_date").count().orderBy("trip_date").show()
spark.sql("DESCRIBE HISTORY delta.`./lakehouse/silver/trips`") \
     .select("version", "operation", "operationMetrics").show(3, truncate=False)
PY

What to look for: the late trip is present, appears exactly once, and the Delta history's last MERGE shows numTargetRowsInserted = 1 with numTargetRowsUpdated = 0. Now run dbt run --select silver_trips again and confirm the next MERGE inserts 0 and updates 0 rows — re-running a backfill is a no-op. That is what makes a six-month backfill safe to run twice.

The counter-experiment (2 min, do it — it is what makes the lesson stick). Temporarily replace the lookback block with the naive filter and re-run:

{% if is_incremental() %}
  where to_date(pickup_ts) = current_date()     -- THE BUG
{% endif %}

Rebuild from scratch (dbt run --select silver_trips --full-refresh, then land the late fixture, then dbt run). The late trip is now missing. Record both counts side by side in LAB3_NOTES.md, then restore the correct model.

dbt docs generate
dbt docs serve --port 8081      # open the DAG: sources -> stg_* -> silver.trips

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• dbt debug passes and the project runs with method: session against the local Delta Lakehouse
  • bronze.trips, bronze.drivers, bronze.gps_events are declared as dbt sources with a freshness SLA, and dbt source freshness runs
  • stg_trips and stg_drivers are views, are 1:1 with their sources, contain no joins, and parse both timestamp formats (0 unparseable rows)
  • All timestamps are normalised to UTC exactly once, in staging; trip_date is the Asia/Riyadh business date
  • silver.trips is materialized='incremental', incremental_strategy='merge', unique_key='trip_id', file_format='delta', and lands at lakehouse/silver/trips
  • The lookback window filters on event time (pickup_ts), not ingest time, and its length is a parameter (var('lookback_days', 3))
  • Duplicate bronze batches are resolved by latest row per key, not DISTINCT: count(*) == count(distinct trip_id)
  • ≥ 6 declared tests plus 1 custom data test, all passing (PASS=12 WARN=0 ERROR=0)
  • The backfill drill shows the late trip merged exactly once, and a repeat run inserts and updates 0 rows
  • The naive-filter counter-experiment is recorded in LAB3_NOTES.md with both counts
  • dbt docs generate produces the lineage graph
  • The benchmark table is filled from your own runs
  • Commit feat(silver): incremental conformed trips with tests + freshness exists

docs.title: Self-check questions
docs.text:
Q1. Why does the lookback window filter on pickup_ts rather than on _ingested_at?

Answer Because the bug being fixed is a mismatch between *event time* and *arrival time*. A trip that happened yesterday and arrived today has an old `pickup_ts` and a new `_ingested_at`. Filtering on `_ingested_at` would select the newly arrived rows but leave the window anchored to arrival, so any correction to a row that arrived *earlier* would never be reprocessed. Filtering on `pickup_ts >= max(pickup_ts) - 3 days` reprocesses a window of *business* time, which is what the incentive calculation and the model labels are keyed on. (A production refinement is to bound both: event-time window for correctness, ingest-time for efficiency.)

Q2. Why is DISTINCT the wrong way to remove the duplicate trip_id rows Lab 1 created?

Answer `DISTINCT` deduplicates identical *rows*, not keys. If the second batch corrected a fare, the two rows differ, so `DISTINCT` keeps **both** — the `unique` test then fails. Worse, if you then applied `DISTINCT trip_id` semantics via a `GROUP BY`, you would get an arbitrary (often the stale) version. The correct pattern is "latest row per key": `row_number() over (partition by trip_id order by _ingested_at desc, _batch_id desc) = 1`. Deterministic, and it makes corrections win over originals.

Q3. MERGE is idempotent and INSERT is not. Explain precisely why, in terms of what happens on a retry.

Answer A MERGE keyed on `trip_id` matches the incoming row against the existing one and updates it in place; re-applying the identical row sets the same values, so the table state after two runs equals the state after one. An INSERT has no key semantics: the second run appends a second copy, so the table state diverges with every retry, breaking every downstream count. Retries are not an edge case — orchestrators retry on transient failure by design — so a non-idempotent transform is a duplicate generator waiting for a network blip.

Q4. The relationships test on driver_id fails: 14 trips reference drivers absent from stg_drivers. Give two defensible responses and one indefensible one.

Answer Defensible: (a) quarantine the orphans to `silver.trips_quarantine` with a reason code, keep silver clean, and raise the count as a source-data incident with the driver-master owner; (b) admit them with null driver attributes, document that `driver_rating` is nullable in the silver contract, and add a volume alert so a jump from 14 to 14,000 is caught. Indefensible: switching the `left join` to an `inner join`, which makes the test pass by silently deleting 14 real trips — the fare revenue disappears from BI and the trips disappear from the model's training set, with no record that anything happened.

Q5. silver.trips keeps reported_duration_min alongside a derived duration_min. Why keep both?

Answer `duration_min` derived from `dropoff_ts - pickup_ts` is the value downstream consumers should trust (the source column contains negatives). Keeping the source value lets you *measure the disagreement*: a rising delta between reported and derived duration is an early signal that a source system's clock, timezone, or app version has changed — exactly the class of silent semantic drift the GPS `producer_version` incident represents. Discarding the source value would make that drift undetectable. It costs one column and buys an observability signal.

Q6. ELT is the default in this course. Name a Masar case where ETL — transforming before the data lands — is still correct.

Answer Masking or tokenising direct identifiers before they ever reach the platform. If raw rider phone numbers or national IDs must not be stored even in bronze under PDPL data-minimisation, hashing them at the edge (as `drivers.csv` already does with `national_id_hash` and `phone_hash`) is a transform-before-load. The second case is a low-latency operational sink — a pre-aggregated dispatch feed where the transformation must happen in flight because there is no time to land and re-read. Neither undermines ELT for the analytics estate; both are narrow, justified exceptions.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
1. Intermediate model. Add int_trip_payments joining stg_trips to a new stg_payments (source data/raw/payments_YYYY-MM-DD.csv: payment_id, trip_id, amount_sar, method, status, settled_ts) and refactor the settlement logic out of the mart. Then answer: how many completed trips have no settled payment, and which layer should own that discrepancy?
  2. Parameterised six-month backfill. Add a backfill_start / backfill_end var pair and prove that running the same range twice produces identical row counts and zero MERGE updates.
  3. Source rename drill. Rename fare_sar to fare_amount_sar in a copy of the bronze table and demonstrate that only stg_trips needs editing. Time it. This is the concrete payoff of the staging layer.
  4. Snapshot the contract. Add a dbt snapshot on stg_drivers (SCD-2 on driver_rating) and discuss which downstream features would change if driver rating were treated as slowly changing rather than current-state.
  5. Quarantine preview. Instead of dropping the 58 invalid rows, route them to silver.trips_quarantine with a reject_reason column. You will formalise this in Lab 6 — building it now makes that lab a 10-minute exercise.

docs.title: Capstone linkage
docs.text: This lab delivers capstone mandatory requirement 3 (ELT pipeline, LO3) in full: dbt staging → silver, incremental merge on trip_id with a lookback window, source-freshness plus ≥ 6 data tests, and a demonstrated late-arrival backfill. It also produces the silver layer contract required by capstone requirement 1 — one row per trip_id; enforced schema; conformed timezone and units; completed valid trips only — which Lab 4 hardens with Delta CHECK constraints and Lab 6 gates with Great Expectations. silver.trips is the single upstream of every gold table in requirement 8, so its grain and its tests are what make the BI star schema and the AI feature table reconcile. The backfill drill is a required element of the 6-minute capstone demo, and the naive-filter counter-experiment is a ready-made entry for DECISIONS.md (capstone deliverable 6): why the lookback window is 3 days and what it costs.

docs.title: LAB 04 — Delta Lake: ACID, MERGE, Time Travel, Maintenance
docs.text:
Field Value Lab ID LAB-04 (delivered as 4a + 4b) Module M4 — Delta Lake and ACID Transactions Day / Hour Day 3, Hour 2 (Lab 4a) and Day 3, Hour 4 (Lab 4b), wrapped in Hour 5 Duration 90 minutes total — 4a: 25 min, 4b: 65 min (10–15% theory / 85–90% lab), pairs Difficulty Intermediate–Advanced LO mapping LO4 (primary — Delta tables, ACID, schema enforcement), LO6 (secondary — audit trail, PDPL erasure, retention governance), LO2 (reinforced — small-files cost), LO7 (contributes — the hardened silver node) Prerequisites LAB-03 complete (silver.trips built by dbt, 42,038 rows, all tests passing); M4 lecture (transaction log, OCC, MERGE, time travel, OPTIMIZE/ZORDER/VACUUM) Checkpoint git tags lab4-start (4a), lab4b-start (4b) · solutions: lab4a-solution, lab4-solution Deliverable silver.trips as a constrained Delta table with positive_fare and valid_duration CHECK constraints; an idempotent MERGE proven twice; a time-travel audit diff; a demonstrated PDPL erasure; OPTIMIZE/ZORDER/VACUUM run with before/after numFiles; LAB4_NOTES.md with the retention justification and the filled benchmark table

Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. Grains, ratios and file-count reductions hold at either scale; absolute row counts do not.

docs.title: Why this lab matters
docs.text: silver.trips is written by a nightly dbt job, corrected by ad-hoc upserts, read by the ETA model's training run and by the operations dashboard — sometimes at the same moment. Without a transaction layer, a reader that arrives mid-write sees a half-written table, and the AI system trains on a state that never existed. Delta's log makes that impossible, and it buys three more things Masar cannot operate without: schema enforcement, so a source that starts sending fare_sar as a string fails loudly instead of poisoning the feature table; time travel, so a disputed report can be recomputed from the exact table state it was filed from; and MERGE, so a PDPL erasure request is an atomic, auditable commit rather than a rewrite-and-pray. This lab also confronts the tension you will actually have to defend in a governance review: aggressive VACUUM saves storage but destroys the audit trail, while conservative VACUUM preserves history and can retain data an erasure was supposed to remove. There is no universal right answer — only a documented, defensible one, and you will write yours.

cd ~/masar-lakehouse

docs.title: Part 4a — Enforcement and the transaction log (25 min)
Task 1 — Add constraints and read the log aloud (15 min)
docs.text:
Complete src/masar/delta/create_silver.py:

# src/masar/delta/create_silver.py
"""Harden silver.trips into a self-validating Delta table.

Partitioning is chosen to AVOID the small-files trap: `city` has 5 values,
not 42,038. Constraints are checked on EVERY future write, so the table
defends its own contract without a downstream job having to remember to.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

from masar.spark import get_spark

SILVER = "./lakehouse/silver/trips"

CONSTRAINTS = {
    "positive_fare":  "fare_sar > 0",
    "valid_duration": "dropoff_ts > pickup_ts",
    "known_city":     "city IN ('Riyadh','Jeddah','Dammam','Mecca','Medina')",
}


def create_silver_trips(staged_df) -> None:
    """Only needed if silver.trips does not already exist (dbt normally builds it)."""
    (staged_df.write
        .format("delta")
        .partitionBy("city")            # low-cardinality: 5 cities, not trip_id
        .mode("overwrite")
        .option("overwriteSchema", "true")
        .save(SILVER))


def add_constraints() -> None:
    """Constraints apply to FUTURE writes; existing rows must already comply."""
    spark = get_spark("delta-constraints")
    for name, expr in CONSTRAINTS.items():
        # violating rows must be cleaned first, or the ALTER is rejected
        bad = spark.sql(
            f"SELECT count(*) AS n FROM delta.`{SILVER}` WHERE NOT ({expr})"
        ).first()["n"]
        if bad:
            print(f"[skip] {name}: {bad:,} existing rows violate `{expr}` — clean first")
            continue
        spark.sql(
            f"ALTER TABLE delta.`{SILVER}` ADD CONSTRAINT {name} CHECK ({expr})"
        )
        print(f"[ok]   {name}: CHECK ({expr})")


def show_properties() -> None:
    spark = get_spark("delta-constraints")
    spark.sql(f"SHOW TBLPROPERTIES delta.`{SILVER}`").show(truncate=False)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    add_constraints()
    show_properties()

python -m masar.delta.create_silver

Now open the log. This is the single most valuable five minutes of Module 4 — do not read about it, read it.

ls -1 lakehouse/silver/trips/_delta_log/
python -m json.tool < lakehouse/silver/trips/_delta_log/00000000000000000000.json | head -60

Read aloud to your pair, naming each action:

  • {"protocol": {...}} — the reader/writer versions required to understand this table.
  • {"metaData": {..., "schemaString": "...", "partitionColumns": ["city"], "configuration": {"delta.constraints.positive_fare": "fare_sar > 0"}}} — the schema is metadata in the log; so are your constraints.
  • {"add": {"path": "city=Riyadh/part-00000-....snappy.parquet", "size": 984213, "stats": "{\"numRecords\":18418,\"minValues\":{...},\"maxValues\":{...}}"}} — a file added by this commit, with its min/max statistics. Those statistics are exactly what powered the data skipping you measured in Lab 2.
  • {"remove": {...}} in a later commit — a file logically deleted (tombstoned). The bytes are still on disk until VACUUM.
  • {"commitInfo": {"operation": "MERGE", "operationMetrics": {...}}} — the audit record.

The insight to state out loud: the current table state is not a directory listing — it is the replay of the log. That is why a half-written set of Parquet files is invisible (atomicity), why a reader is pinned to one version (snapshot isolation), and why hand-copying a Parquet file into the directory corrupts nothing except your own understanding — Delta will simply ignore it, because it is not in the log.

# how many commits so far, and what did each one do?
python -m masar.delta.time_travel --history

docs.title: Task 2 — Prove enforcement rejects bad writes (10 min)
docs.text:
Two negative tests. Both must fail; capture the exact error text in LAB4_NOTES.md.

# run as: python - <<'PY' ... PY
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from masar.spark import get_spark

spark = get_spark("negative-tests")
SILVER = "./lakehouse/silver/trips"
good = spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER).limit(1)

# --- Test A: CHECK constraint violation (negative fare) ---
bad_fare = good.withColumn("trip_id", F.lit("trp_BADFARE")) \
               .withColumn("fare_sar", F.lit(-5.0))
try:
    bad_fare.write.format("delta").mode("append").save(SILVER)
    print("FAIL: the constraint did not fire")
except Exception as e:
    print("PASS (constraint):", str(e).splitlines()[0])

# --- Test B: schema enforcement (wrong type) ---
bad_type = good.withColumn("trip_id", F.lit("trp_BADTYPE")) \
               .withColumn("fare_sar", F.lit("forty-two"))     # string, not double
try:
    bad_type.write.format("delta").mode("append").save(SILVER)
    print("FAIL: schema enforcement did not fire")
except Exception as e:
    print("PASS (schema):", str(e).splitlines()[0])

# --- Test C: what mergeSchema would have done (DO NOT leave this enabled) ---
extra = good.withColumn("trip_id", F.lit("trp_NEWCOL")) \
            .withColumn("driver_mood", F.lit("cheerful"))
try:
    extra.write.format("delta").mode("append").save(SILVER)
    print("FAIL: a new column was accepted without mergeSchema")
except Exception as e:
    print("PASS (new column rejected):", str(e).splitlines()[0])
print("row count unchanged:", spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER).count())

What to look for: all three rejected, and the row count is unchanged — the rejected writes left no partial data behind. That is atomicity: there is no such thing as a half-applied Delta write.

Discuss with your pair: enforcement is the default and evolution is opt-in. mergeSchema / on_schema_change='append_new_columns' exists for changes you decide; the log records them as metadata commits so an auditor can see when the contract changed and who changed it. A schema surprise is a bug; a schema change is a reviewed event.

docs.title: Part 4b — MERGE, time travel, PDPL, maintenance (65 min)
Task 3 — Idempotent MERGE upserts (20 min)
docs.text:
Complete src/masar/delta/merge_ops.py:

# src/masar/delta/merge_ops.py
"""Upsert corrected trips and apply a PDPL right-to-erasure delete.

Both are atomic Delta commits: auditable, retryable, isolated from readers.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json

from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F

from masar.spark import get_spark

SILVER = "./lakehouse/silver/trips"


def load_corrections(path: str) -> DataFrame:
    """Corrections arrive with the silver grain: one row per corrected trip_id."""
    spark = get_spark("merge-ops")
    target_schema = spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER).schema
    return (spark.read
            .option("header", True)
            .schema(target_schema)          # enforce the contract on the SOURCE too
            .csv(path))


def upsert_corrections(corrections_df: DataFrame) -> None:
    """MERGE keyed on trip_id => re-running is a no-op (idempotent).

    whenMatchedUpdateAll is safe here ONLY because the source has exactly the
    target schema and exactly one row per key. Both are checked above.
    """
    spark = get_spark("merge-ops")
    dupes = (corrections_df.groupBy("trip_id").count()
             .filter("count > 1").count())
    if dupes:
        raise ValueError(f"{dupes} duplicate trip_id in corrections: MERGE would be ambiguous")

    target = DeltaTable.forPath(spark, SILVER)
    (target.alias("t")
        .merge(corrections_df.alias("s"), "t.trip_id = s.trip_id")
        .whenMatchedUpdateAll()
        .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
        .execute())

    metrics = (spark.sql(f"DESCRIBE HISTORY delta.`{SILVER}` LIMIT 1")
               .select("version", "operation", "operationMetrics").first())
    m = metrics["operationMetrics"]
    print(f"v{metrics['version']} {metrics['operation']}  "
          f"matched={m.get('numTargetRowsMatchedUpdated', m.get('numTargetRowsUpdated'))} "
          f"inserted={m.get('numTargetRowsInserted')} "
          f"updated={m.get('numTargetRowsUpdated')}")


def erase_rider(rider_id: str) -> None:
    """PDPL right to erasure: remove a data subject's rows. Atomic, logged commit.

    Physical removal from history completes at the next VACUUM past retention.
    """
    spark = get_spark("merge-ops")
    target = DeltaTable.forPath(spark, SILVER)
    before = spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER) \
                  .filter(F.col("rider_id") == rider_id).count()
    target.delete(F.col("rider_id") == rider_id)
    after = spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER) \
                 .filter(F.col("rider_id") == rider_id).count()
    print(f"erasure committed for {rider_id}: {before} rows removed, {after} remain "
          f"in the CURRENT version; run VACUUM past retention to purge history")


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--corrections", help="path to a corrections CSV")
    p.add_argument("--erase-request", help="path to a PDPL erasure request JSON")
    args = p.parse_args()

    if args.corrections:
        upsert_corrections(load_corrections(args.corrections))
    if args.erase_request:
        with open(args.erase_request) as fh:
            req = json.load(fh)
        erase_rider(req["rider_id"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
