spark = get_spark("before")
ids = [r.trip_id for r in spark.read.option("header",True)
       .csv("data/fixtures/corrections/trips_corrections_2026-06-03.csv")
       .select("trip_id").collect()]
spark.read.format("delta").load("./lakehouse/silver/trips") \
     .filter(f"trip_id in ({','.join(repr(i) for i in ids)})") \
     .select("trip_id","fare_sar","surge_multiplier","duration_min").show()
PY

python -m masar.delta.merge_ops --corrections data/fixtures/corrections/trips_corrections_2026-06-03.csv
python -m masar.delta.merge_ops --corrections data/fixtures/corrections/trips_corrections_2026-06-03.csv   # again

What to look for: run 1 reports updated=5; run 2 reports updated=0 — the source rows are already the target rows, so the MERGE has nothing to change. Note that a commit is still written on run 2 (a MERGE that changes nothing is still a transaction); idempotency is about the table state, not about the commit count. Record both operationMetrics blocks in LAB4_NOTES.md.

docs.title: Task 4 — Time travel: audit and recovery (10 min)
docs.text:
# src/masar/delta/time_travel.py
"""Read a past table state for audit or to reproduce a model's training set."""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse

from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F

from masar.spark import get_spark

SILVER = "./lakehouse/silver/trips"


def history(limit: int = 20) -> None:
    spark = get_spark("time-travel")
    (spark.sql(f"DESCRIBE HISTORY delta.`{SILVER}` LIMIT {limit}")
          .select("version", "timestamp", "operation", "operationMetrics")
          .show(truncate=False))


def as_of_version(v: int) -> DataFrame:
    spark = get_spark("time-travel")
    return (spark.read.format("delta").option("versionAsOf", v).load(SILVER))


def as_of_date(ts: str) -> DataFrame:
    spark = get_spark("time-travel")
    return (spark.read.format("delta").option("timestampAsOf", ts).load(SILVER))


def diff_versions(v_old: int, v_new: int, key: str = "trip_id",
                  col: str = "fare_sar") -> None:
    """Which rows changed between two versions, and by how much?"""
    old = as_of_version(v_old).select(key, F.col(col).alias(f"{col}_old"))
    new = as_of_version(v_new).select(key, F.col(col).alias(f"{col}_new"))
    (old.join(new, key)
        .filter(F.col(f"{col}_old") != F.col(f"{col}_new"))
        .withColumn("delta", F.round(F.col(f"{col}_new") - F.col(f"{col}_old"), 2))
        .show(truncate=False))


def restore(v: int) -> None:
    spark = get_spark("time-travel")
    spark.sql(f"RESTORE TABLE delta.`{SILVER}` TO VERSION AS OF {v}")
    print(f"restored to v{v}; note this creates a NEW version, it does not erase history")


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--history", action="store_true")
    p.add_argument("--version", type=int)
    p.add_argument("--timestamp")
    p.add_argument("--diff", nargs=2, type=int, metavar=("OLD", "NEW"))
    p.add_argument("--restore", type=int)
    a = p.parse_args()

    if a.history:
        history()
    if a.version is not None:
        print("rows at v%d: %d" % (a.version, as_of_version(a.version).count()))
    if a.timestamp:
        print("rows at %s: %d" % (a.timestamp, as_of_date(a.timestamp).count()))
    if a.diff:
        diff_versions(*a.diff)
    if a.restore is not None:
        restore(a.restore)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

python -m masar.delta.time_travel --history
python -m masar.delta.time_travel --diff 2 3          # pre-merge vs post-merge versions
python -m masar.delta.time_travel --version 2
python -m masar.delta.time_travel --restore 2         # recovery drill
python -m masar.delta.time_travel --history           # RESTORE appears as a NEW version
python -m masar.delta.time_travel --restore 3         # and back again

Or in SQL, which is the form an auditor will ask for:

SELECT count(*) FROM delta.`./lakehouse/silver/trips` VERSION AS OF 2;
SELECT count(*) FROM delta.`./lakehouse/silver/trips` TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-06-15 00:00:00';

What to look for: RESTORE does not rewind history — it appends a new commit whose state equals the old one. The audit trail is append-only, which is precisely what makes it trustworthy: you cannot quietly un-happen a bad MERGE, you can only record the correction.

Then prove the two-part truth that governance reviews turn on:

python - <<'PY'
from masar.spark import get_spark
spark = get_spark("pdpl-drill")
P = "./lakehouse/silver/trips"
cur = spark.sql(f"DESCRIBE HISTORY delta.`{P}` LIMIT 1").first()["version"]
rid = "rid_0000042"
print("current version:", cur)
print("rows in CURRENT version :",
      spark.read.format("delta").load(P).filter(f"rider_id = '{rid}'").count())
print("rows in PREVIOUS version:",
      spark.read.format("delta").option("versionAsOf", cur - 1).load(P)
           .filter(f"rider_id = '{rid}'").count())
PY

Expected: 0 rows in the current version, > 0 in the previous one. The erasure is committed but not yet complete. The rider's data survives in time-travel history — and on disk in tombstoned Parquet files — until a VACUUM past the retention window removes it. Write in LAB4_NOTES.md:

  1. The date by which VACUUM must run for this request to be fully satisfied, given your retention setting.
  2. How you reconcile "reproduce the past for the regulator" with "erase this rider": the honest answer is that the retention window is the reconciliation — history is preserved only for as long as the documented policy allows, and any audit older than that window is answered from an immutable report artefact, not from the live table.
  3. Which other tables hold this rider's data (bronze.trips — immutable — and any gold/feature tables), and what your erasure runbook does about each. An erasure applied to silver alone is not an erasure.

docs.title: Task 6 — OPTIMIZE, ZORDER, VACUUM (15 min)
docs.text:
-- src/masar/delta/maintain.sql  (run on a schedule, e.g. nightly)

-- 0) Baseline: record numFiles and sizeInBytes BEFORE anything.
DESCRIBE DETAIL delta.`./lakehouse/silver/trips`;

-- 1) Compact small files and cluster by the columns queries filter on.
--    ZORDER co-locates related rows so min/max stats prune more aggressively.
OPTIMIZE delta.`./lakehouse/silver/trips`
  ZORDER BY (city, pickup_ts);

-- 2) Verify: file count should drop sharply, average file size should rise.
DESCRIBE DETAIL delta.`./lakehouse/silver/trips`;

-- 3) Reclaim storage older than the retention window.
--    RETENTION IS A GOVERNANCE DECISION: 168h keeps 7 days of time travel.
--    Do NOT set 0 hours: it destroys audit history and can break concurrent readers.
VACUUM delta.`./lakehouse/silver/trips` RETAIN 168 HOURS;

-- 4) What WOULD be deleted, without deleting it (always run this first in prod):
VACUUM delta.`./lakehouse/silver/trips` RETAIN 168 HOURS DRY RUN;

Run it with measurement on both sides:

python - <<'PY'
import time
from masar.spark import get_spark
spark = get_spark("maintenance")
P = "./lakehouse/silver/trips"

def detail(tag):
    d = spark.sql(f"DESCRIBE DETAIL delta.`{P}`").first()
    print(f"{tag:8s} numFiles={d['numFiles']:>4}  sizeMB={d['sizeInBytes']/1048576:7.1f}"
          f"  avgFileKB={d['sizeInBytes']/max(d['numFiles'],1)/1024:8.1f}")

def timed_query(tag):
    t = time.time()
    n = spark.sql(f"""SELECT count(*) FROM delta.`{P}`
                      WHERE city = 'Riyadh'
                        AND pickup_ts >= '2026-06-01' AND pickup_ts < '2026-06-02'""").first()[0]
    print(f"{tag:8s} filtered read: {n:,} rows in {time.time()-t:.2f}s")

detail("before"); timed_query("before")
spark.sql(f"OPTIMIZE delta.`{P}` ZORDER BY (city, pickup_ts)").show(truncate=False)
detail("after");  timed_query("after")

spark.sql(f"VACUUM delta.`{P}` RETAIN 168 HOURS DRY RUN").show(5, truncate=False)
spark.sql(f"VACUUM delta.`{P}` RETAIN 168 HOURS").show(truncate=False)
detail("vacuum")
PY

Now try the mistake, so you have seen the guardrail fire:

python - <<'PY'
from masar.spark import get_spark
spark = get_spark("vacuum0")
try:
    spark.sql("VACUUM delta.`./lakehouse/silver/trips` RETAIN 0 HOURS").show()
except Exception as e:
    print("BLOCKED:", str(e).splitlines()[0])
PY

What to look for: Delta refuses RETAIN 0 HOURS unless spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled is disabled. Leave that check enabled. Zero retention destroys time travel and can break a reader or a concurrent writer that is still holding an older snapshot — it deletes files a running query is about to open.

Write the retention decision in LAB4_NOTES.md. A defensible answer names three inputs: (a) the longest audit or dispute window you must serve from the live table, (b) the PDPL erasure SLA — data must not persist past its documented purpose, and (c) the storage cost of the tombstoned files. State your chosen number and what would change it.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• silver.trips carries positive_fare and valid_duration CHECK constraints (visible in SHOW TBLPROPERTIES)
  • A negative-fare write is rejected by the constraint, and the error text is captured
  • A wrong-type write is rejected by schema enforcement, and an unexpected new column is rejected without mergeSchema
  • The row count is unchanged after all rejected writes (atomicity — no partial data)
  • The first commit JSON was opened and its protocol / metaData / add (with stats) actions identified
  • MERGE run 1 updated 5 rows; MERGE run 2 updated 0 rows; both operationMetrics recorded
  • DESCRIBE HISTORY shows the full commit timeline with operation types
  • A version diff shows the 5 corrected fares old vs new
  • RESTORE was demonstrated and it is understood that restore appends a version rather than erasing history
  • The erasure removes the rider from the current version while the pre-erasure version still contains them
  • LAB4_NOTES.md names every other table holding that rider's data and what the runbook does about each
  • OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (city, pickup_ts) reduced numFiles by ≥ 10× with before/after DESCRIBE DETAIL recorded
  • VACUUM ... RETAIN 168 HOURS ran (with a DRY RUN first), and RETAIN 0 HOURS was blocked
  • LAB4_NOTES.md justifies the retention window against audit needs, PDPL, and storage cost
  • The benchmark table is filled from your own runs
  • Commit feat(delta): constrained silver + merge/erasure + optimize/vacuum exists

docs.title: Self-check questions
docs.text:
Q1. A concurrent reader starts a query at version 5 while a MERGE commits version 6. What does the reader see, and what mechanism guarantees it?

Answer The reader sees the complete, consistent state of version 5 for the whole query — snapshot isolation. Delta resolves the file list once, from the log up to version 5, and reads exactly those Parquet files. Version 6's commit adds new files and tombstones old ones in the log, but does not delete bytes, so the reader's files remain readable. The danger is VACUUM: if it physically removes those tombstoned files while the query is still running, the reader fails with a `FileNotFoundException`. That is the concurrency half of why `RETAIN 0 HOURS` is blocked.

Q2. Your second MERGE run reported updated = 0 but still created a new version in the history. Is idempotency broken?

Answer No. Idempotency is a property of the resulting **table state**, not of the commit count. The second MERGE evaluated the same source against the same target, found every row already equal, and wrote a commit that changed no data. A consumer reading version *n* and version *n+1* gets identical results. If you need commit-level idempotency too (for example to avoid triggering a downstream change-data-feed), guard the operation with a source-batch marker so a repeated batch is skipped entirely.

Q3. Why is partitioning by city right here, and partitioning by trip_id catastrophic?

Answer `city` has five values, so each partition holds thousands of rows in a handful of large files, and a `city = 'Riyadh'` predicate eliminates whole directories before any file is opened. `trip_id` is unique, so partitioning by it creates one directory and one tiny file per trip — 42,038 objects here, hundreds of millions in production. Listing dominates every job, per-file metadata dwarfs the data, no filter can skip usefully, and OPTIMIZE cannot merge across partition boundaries. It converts a cheap decoupled read into an expensive one — the exact failure Module 2 warned about, self-inflicted at the table layer.

Q4. A regulator asks what silver.trips contained on 1 June. Under what conditions can Delta answer, and what would make the answer impossible?

Answer Delta answers with `TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-06-01'` provided (a) the commits from that date are still in `_delta_log` (log retention, default 30 days, `delta.logRetentionDuration`) and (b) the Parquet files those commits reference have not been physically removed by VACUUM (`delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration`, default 7 days). A short VACUUM retention, or a log cleanup shorter than the audit window, makes the answer impossible — the query fails rather than returning wrong data, which is the correct failure mode but no help to the regulator. The operational habit that prevents the problem is pinning and recording the table version used for every filing.

Q5. You erased a rider from silver.trips. Name at least three places their data still exists and what your runbook must do about each.

Answer (1) Delta time-travel history and tombstoned files under `lakehouse/silver/trips` — removed by VACUUM once past retention; the erasure is only complete after that runs. (2) `bronze.trips`, which is immutable and append-only — the runbook must either apply a documented exception (bronze is the ledger, protected by access control and its own retention policy) or run a scoped delete against bronze as a deliberate, logged exception to immutability. (3) Downstream gold and feature tables (`gold.trip_features`, `gold.eta_features`) and the Redis online store, which must be rebuilt or key-deleted. Plus any exported reports and dbt test artefacts. An erasure that touches one table is not an erasure — this is why the classification and retention job in Module 6 is a platform-level control, not a per-table script.

Q6. OPTIMIZE cut numFiles from 214 to 9 and the filtered read from 1.9 s to 0.4 s. Which part of that improvement is compaction and which is ZORDER, and how would you separate them?

Answer Compaction removes per-file overhead: 214 file opens, 214 footer reads and 214 task launches collapse into 9. ZORDER changes *which* files a predicate can skip, by co-locating rows with similar `city` and `pickup_ts` so each file's min/max range is narrow. Separate them by running `OPTIMIZE` with no `ZORDER BY` on a copy of the table, measuring, then running `OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (city, pickup_ts)` and measuring again. On a small single-day sample most of the win is compaction; at production scale, with months of data and selective predicates, ZORDER is usually the larger term because it multiplies the effect of the file statistics you saw in the log's `add` actions.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix ConcurrentModificationException / ConcurrentAppendException Two writers hit optimistic-concurrency conflict on the same files Retry the commit; narrow each writer to disjoint partitions (city) so their file sets do not overlap; discuss OCC — no corruption occurred VACUUM removes nothing All tombstoned files are still inside the retention window Expected. Explain the default 7-day safety; use DRY RUN to see what would go, and re-run after the window passes VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS blocked Delta's retentionDurationCheck safety Keep the check enabled. If a demo needs it, disable it on a throwaway copy only, never on silver.trips and never in production Constraint not enforced / ALTER TABLE fails Rows violating the predicate already exist Constraints validate future writes and are rejected if current data violates them — clean or quarantine the offending rows first (create_silver.py reports the count) Millions of tiny files Partitioned by a high-cardinality column, or a streaming sink with no maintenance Repartition by city; schedule OPTIMIZE as a nightly task, not as an incident response MERGE fails: Cannot perform Merge as multiple source rows matched ... the same target row The corrections source has duplicate trip_ids Deduplicate the source first (merge_ops.py raises on this deliberately); decide which version wins by an explicit ordering, never arbitrarily Time travel fails: Cannot time travel Delta table to version 2 The log was cleaned (delta.logRetentionDuration) or the files were vacuumed Nothing recovers it. Set delta.logRetentionDuration ≥ your audit window and delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration to match, before you need them RESTORE appears to do nothing You restored to the version you are already on, or read the table by a stale cached snapshot Check DESCRIBE HISTORY — RESTORE writes a new version; call spark.catalog.refreshTable("silver.trips") if you cached it Erasure "succeeded" but the rider still appears in a dashboard Gold/feature tables and the online store were not rebuilt Erasure is a platform operation: re-run the gold models and purge the Redis keys; this is exactly why the runbook in GOVERNANCE.md is a capstone deliverable numFiles did not drop after OPTIMIZE Files were already at target size, or the table is tiny Check the metrics map returned by OPTIMIZE (numFilesAdded / numFilesRemoved); on a sample table run several MERGE cycles first to create the small files Filtered read got slower after ZORDER ZORDER on columns nobody filters on, or the sample is too small for clustering to matter ZORDER only the columns that appear in real predicates (city, pickup_ts); measure with the Lab 2 scan-metrics helper, not by intuition DESCRIBE DETAIL shows format: parquet, not delta Someone wrote raw Parquet into the table directory, or the path is wrong Never write non-Delta files under a Delta path — the log will not see them and the table's view of reality diverges. Rebuild from Lab 3 Every write is rejected after adding known_city The data contains a city outside the constraint list (e.g. trailing whitespace, riyadh lowercase) This is the constraint doing its job — fix the staging normalisation (initcap(trim(city))) rather than dropping the constraint

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
1. Concurrency drill. Open two terminals with two Spark sessions and start a MERGE in each against different cities. Observe both succeed (disjoint files). Then run both against the same city and observe the optimistic-concurrency retry or conflict. Record which exception you got and explain why no corruption is possible either way.
  2. Change Data Feed. Enable delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true, run a MERGE, and read the change feed (readChangeFeed, startingVersion). Discuss how this would let a downstream gold table update incrementally instead of rebuilding.
  3. Generated column for the partition key. Add a generated trip_date column derived from pickup_ts and partition a copy of the table by (city, trip_date). Measure the effect on a single-day query and on the file count — is the extra partition level worth it at this data volume? At 100× the volume?
  4. Retention policy as code. Set delta.logRetentionDuration and delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration as table properties to match the retention you justified, and write the one-paragraph policy that a governance reviewer would sign.
  5. VACUUM-0 disaster simulation. On a copy of the table, disable the retention check, run VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS, then attempt a time-travel read and a concurrent query. Document both failures. Delete the copy afterwards.

docs.title: Capstone linkage
docs.text: This lab delivers capstone mandatory requirement 4 (Delta Lake, LO4) in full: silver as constrained Delta with schema and CHECK enforcement, idempotent MERGE upserts, a time-travel audit, OPTIMIZE/VACUUM with a justified retention, and one demonstrated PDPL erasure. The before/after numFiles measurement is the "measured file-count reduction" required by capstone requirement 2, and it belongs in BENCHMARKS.md (deliverable 3) next to the Lab 2 scan analysis. The erasure drill and the retention justification are the core of GOVERNANCE.md (deliverable 4): PII classification, access levels, retention policy with PDPL justification, and a demonstrated erasure. Two of the five required DECISIONS.md entries (deliverable 6) come straight from here — VACUUM retention and partition-key choice. The time-travel audit and the idempotent second MERGE are both required beats of the 6-minute capstone demo, and the constrained silver.trips is the table that the Lab 6 quality gate, the Lab 7 orchestrated DAG, and the Lab 8 feature and BI layers all build on.

docs.title: LAB 05 — Stream GPS Into The Lakehouse
docs.text:
Field Value Lab ID LAB-05 Module M5 — Streaming Data and Event-Driven Architectures Day / Hour Day 4 · Hour 2 Duration 60 minutes (7 timed tasks) Difficulty Advanced (highest overrun risk in the course — watch the clock) LO mapping LO5 (primary) · LO4 (Delta atomic commit) · LO7 (bronze/silver contracts) · LO6 (duplicate + late-data quality) Prerequisites LAB-01 (bronze landing), LAB-04a/04b (Delta, MERGE, OPTIMIZE), Docker Desktop running, Java 17, Python 3.11 venv active Checkpoint git tag lab5-start (fast-forward) · lab5-solution (reference) Deliverable bronze.gps_events + silver.vehicle_positions Delta tables, a dedicated checkpoint per query, LAB5_NOTES.md with the kill/restart proof table, and two fan-out sinks (ETA feature input + operations alerts)

Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. Grains, ratios and file-count reductions hold at either scale; absolute row counts do not.

docs.title: 1. Why this lab matters
docs.text:
The course question: "What happens to Masar's AI system if THIS part of the data platform fails?"

The ETA model that riders see in the Masar app does not consume trips. It consumes vehicle positions — a continuous stream of GPS pings from ~14,000 vehicles across Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam, Mecca and Medina. Everything downstream of this lab is fed by the pipeline you are about to build:

Vehicles ──► Kafka ──► Spark Structured Streaming ──► bronze.gps_events ──► silver.vehicle_positions ──┬──► gold.eta_features   (AI)
 (GPS SDK)   masar.      exactly-once, checkpointed    (raw, append-only,      (deduped, unit-normalised,│
             gps.pings                                  _ingested_at,           watermarked)             └──► operations alerts (Ops)
                                                        _source_file,
                                                        _batch_id)

Four concrete failure modes, and what each does to the AI system:

If this fails… The AI system experiences… No checkpoint on the streaming query Restart replays committed offsets. bronze.gps_events gains ~7,000 duplicate pings. rolling_zone_demand_15m inflates, the ETA model predicts a phantom rush hour, surge fires in an empty district. Duplicate event_id not deduplicated at silver Same physical vehicle counted twice in rolling_avg_speed_10m. Speed averages are unaffected but demand counts are not — the model's most important feature drifts by +0.4% permanently. Out-of-order / late ts aggregated on processing time A ping that happened at 07:58 but arrived at 08:04 (tunnel, dead zone, phone buffering) is counted in the 08:00–08:05 window. Demand is misattributed to the wrong five minutes; dispatch rebalances drivers into a spike that already ended. Watermark too aggressive Pings past tolerance are silently dropped. The zone with the worst cellular coverage — reliably the one with the highest surge — systematically under-reports demand. The model learns that coverage holes are quiet places.

Streaming failures are rarely loud. They do not raise exceptions; they produce plausible wrong numbers. Task 3 of this lab is the drill that turns "exactly-once" from a slogan into a number you counted yourself.

docs.title: Task 1 — Produce Masar GPS pings into Kafka (8 min)
docs.text:
Open src/masar/stream/gps_producer.py. The starter file emits pings without a key, which is deliberate mistake #4 from the module. Fix it and add the fixture replay modes.

# src/masar/stream/gps_producer.py
"""Replay Masar GPS pings into Kafka.

Key = trip_id  =>  all pings for one trip land in ONE partition  =>  strictly
ordered per trip. Without a key Kafka round-robins and per-trip order is lost.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import argparse, json, sys, time
from pathlib import Path
from kafka import KafkaProducer

TOPIC = "masar.gps.pings"
BOOTSTRAP = "localhost:9092"


def make_producer() -> KafkaProducer:
    return KafkaProducer(
        bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP,
        key_serializer=lambda k: k.encode("utf-8"),
        value_serializer=lambda v: json.dumps(v).encode("utf-8"),
        acks="all",            # durability: leader + replicas acknowledge
        linger_ms=20,          # small batching window; do NOT set this to 0
        retries=5,
    )


def emit(producer: KafkaProducer, ping: dict) -> None:
    # ping shape (data/raw/gps/gps_YYYY-MM-DD.ndjson):
    # {"event_id","vehicle_id","driver_id","trip_id","ts",
    #  "payload":{"lat","lon","speed_kmh","heading_deg","accuracy_m"},
    #  "producer_version"}
    producer.send(TOPIC, key=ping["trip_id"], value=ping)


def replay(path: Path, rate_hz: float, limit: int | None) -> int:
    producer = make_producer()
    sent = 0
    delay = 0.0 if rate_hz <= 0 else 1.0 / rate_hz
    with path.open() as fh:
        for line in fh:
            line = line.strip()
            if not line:
                continue
            emit(producer, json.loads(line))
            sent += 1
            if sent % 1000 == 0:
                print(f"  … {sent:>7,} pings sent", flush=True)
            if limit and sent >= limit:
                break
            if delay:
                time.sleep(delay)
    producer.flush()
    print(f"[producer] {sent:,} pings -> {TOPIC} from {path.name}")
    return sent


if __name__ == "__main__":
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--source", default="data/raw/gps/gps_2026-06-01.ndjson*")
    ap.add_argument("--rate", type=float, default=2000.0, help="pings/sec; 0 = as fast as possible")
    ap.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=50000)
    a = ap.parse_args()
    sys.exit(0 if replay(Path(a.source), a.rate, a.limit) else 1)

Run it, then confirm with a console consumer in a second terminal:

# terminal A
python -m masar.stream.gps_producer --limit 50000 --rate 2000

# terminal B — confirm bytes actually landed
docker compose exec kafka kafka-console-consumer.sh \
  --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --topic masar.gps.pings --from-beginning --max-messages 2 \
  --property print.key=true --property key.separator=' | '

# terminal B — confirm the keyed partitioning worked
docker compose exec kafka kafka-run-class.sh kafka.tools.GetOffsetShell \
  --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic masar.gps.pings

Checkpoint: all three partitions have a non-zero offset, and the two consumed messages print a trip_id as the key.

docs.title: Task 2 — Stream Kafka → bronze.gps_events exactly-once (14 min)
docs.text:
bronze.gps_events must satisfy the bronze contract from CONVENTIONS: append-only, never mutated, carries _ingested_at, _source_file, _batch_id. Implement src/masar/stream/ingest_gps_stream.py.

# src/masar/stream/ingest_gps_stream.py
"""Kafka masar.gps.pings -> bronze.gps_events, exactly-once.

Exactly-once is NOT a single feature. It is the composition of two things:
  (1) Kafka offsets recorded durably in the query CHECKPOINT, and
  (2) Delta's ATOMIC per-micro-batch commit, made idempotent with
      txnAppId/txnVersion so a replayed batch_id is a no-op.
Kill the job mid-batch and the batch either committed fully or not at all;
the restart resumes from the last committed offset. No loss, no duplication.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, DataFrame
from pyspark.sql.types import (StructType, StructField, StringType,
                               DoubleType, TimestampType)
from masar.spark import get_spark

TOPIC        = "masar.gps.pings"
BOOTSTRAP    = "localhost:9092"
BRONZE_PATH  = "./lakehouse/bronze/gps_events"
CHECKPOINT   = "./lakehouse/_checkpoints/gps_events_bronze"   # ONE per query. Sacred.
TXN_APP_ID   = "masar_gps_events_bronze"

# The wire schema is EXACTLY data/raw/gps/gps_YYYY-MM-DD.ndjson. Do not invent columns.
PAYLOAD_SCHEMA = StructType([
    StructField("lat",         DoubleType()),
    StructField("lon",         DoubleType()),
    StructField("speed_kmh",   DoubleType()),
    StructField("heading_deg", DoubleType()),
    StructField("accuracy_m",  DoubleType()),
])

PING_SCHEMA = StructType([
    StructField("event_id",         StringType()),
    StructField("vehicle_id",       StringType()),
    StructField("driver_id",        StringType()),
    StructField("trip_id",          StringType()),
    StructField("ts",               TimestampType()),   # EVENT time, from the device
    StructField("payload",          PAYLOAD_SCHEMA),
    StructField("producer_version", StringType()),
])


def parse(raw: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
    return (raw
        .select(
            F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"), PING_SCHEMA).alias("p"),
            F.col("topic"),
            F.col("partition"),
            F.col("offset"),
            F.col("timestamp").alias("_kafka_ts"))     # PROCESSING time — keep both clocks
        .select(
            F.col("p.event_id").alias("event_id"),
            F.col("p.vehicle_id").alias("vehicle_id"),
            F.col("p.driver_id").alias("driver_id"),
            F.col("p.trip_id").alias("trip_id"),
            F.col("p.ts").alias("ts"),                 # keep the raw event time verbatim
            F.col("p.payload").alias("payload"),       # bronze keeps the struct AS RECEIVED
            F.col("p.producer_version").alias("producer_version"),
            F.col("_kafka_ts"),
            F.concat_ws("/", F.lit("kafka:/"), F.col("topic"),
                        F.col("partition").cast("string")).alias("_source_file"),
            F.col("offset").alias("_kafka_offset")))


def write_batch(batch_df: DataFrame, batch_id: int) -> None:
    """foreachBatch gives us the batch_id, which we use twice:
       - as the bronze lineage column `_batch_id`
       - as Delta's txnVersion, making a replayed batch an idempotent no-op."""
    out = (batch_df
           .withColumn("_batch_id", F.lit(batch_id).cast("long"))
           .withColumn("_ingested_at", F.current_timestamp())
           .withColumn("ingest_date", F.to_date(F.col("_kafka_ts"))))
    (out.write
        .format("delta")
        .mode("append")
        .partitionBy("ingest_date")
        .option("txnAppId", TXN_APP_ID)      # idempotent-write guard
        .option("txnVersion", batch_id)      # replay of this batch_id is dropped
        .option("mergeSchema", "false")      # bronze schema is fixed; drift must be visible
        .save(BRONZE_PATH))
    print(f"Batch {batch_id}: appended {out.count():,} pings", flush=True)


def run(starting_offsets: str = "earliest", trigger_seconds: int = 30) -> None:
    spark = get_spark("masar-gps-events-bronze")
    raw = (spark.readStream
           .format("kafka")
           .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP)
           .option("subscribe", TOPIC)
           .option("startingOffsets", starting_offsets)
           .option("maxOffsetsPerTrigger", 20000)     # bounded batch => predictable latency
           .option("failOnDataLoss", "true")          # surface retention gaps loudly
           .load())

    (parse(raw).writeStream
        .queryName("gps_events_bronze")
        .foreachBatch(write_batch)
        .outputMode("append")
        .option("checkpointLocation", CHECKPOINT)
        .trigger(processingTime=f"{trigger_seconds} seconds")
        .start()
        .awaitTermination())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

Start it and watch bronze grow. In a third terminal, poll the row count:

Expected console transcript (terminal C)

docs.title: Task 3 — The kill / restart exactly-once proof (10 min — do not skip)
docs.text:
This is the module's thesis. Every pair kills the job and counts.

# 3a. Record the pre-kill state
python -m masar.tools.count --table bronze.gps_events --distinct event_id
#   rows=50,000  distinct_event_id=49,801  (the 0.4% seeded dup rate — expected, from source)

# 3b. Re-arm the producer so there is in-flight work to interrupt
python -m masar.stream.gps_producer --limit 60000 --rate 3000 &
PRODUCER_PID=$!

# 3c. Start the stream, then KILL IT MID-BATCH.
#     Wait until you see "Batch N: appended …" scroll past, then Ctrl-C
#     WITHIN the next few seconds — you want to interrupt a batch in flight,
#     not between batches.
python -m masar.stream.ingest_gps_stream
# ^C

# 3d. Count immediately after the kill
python -m masar.tools.count --table bronze.gps_events --distinct event_id

# 3e. Restart. Change NOTHING. The checkpoint does the work.
python -m masar.stream.ingest_gps_stream

# 3f. Final count once batches drain to 0
wait $PRODUCER_PID
python -m masar.tools.count --table bronze.gps_events --distinct event_id

Record the numbers in LAB5_NOTES.md using this exact table:

Stage Pings produced (cumulative) Rows in bronze.gps_events Distinct event_id Duplicates introduced by the pipeline Clean run (Task 2) 50,000 Immediately after kill 110,000 After restart, drained 110,000

The number that matters is the last column, and it must be 0. Source-level duplicates (the seeded 0.4% event_id collisions) are a data problem you fix in Task 5 at silver. Pipeline-introduced duplicates are an engineering problem, and the checkpoint is why you have none.

Expected transcript

docs.title: Task 4 — Late, duplicate and out-of-order events (12 min)
docs.text:
Now inject the defect classes from data/fixtures/late_pings/. One fixture carries all three — late arrival, duplicate event_id and shuffled ts — because that is how they actually arrive: one reconnecting device flushes a backlog and every class is in it. Keep the bronze stream running throughout; bronze accepts everything, correctness is silver's job.

# 4a. Produce the whole fixture: 520 pings, back-dated 2–47 minutes, 20 duplicate
#     event_ids, deliberately unsorted.
python -m masar.stream.gps_producer \
  --source data/fixtures/late_pings/gps_late_2026-06-04.ndjson --rate 0

# 4b. Isolate the duplicate-event_id class from what you just produced.
python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
  SELECT event_id, COUNT(*) AS copies
  FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/bronze/gps_events\`
  GROUP BY event_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY copies DESC LIMIT 10"

# 4c. Isolate the out-of-order class: pings whose ts goes backwards within a trip.
python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
  SELECT trip_id, COUNT(*) AS backwards_steps FROM (
    SELECT trip_id, ts,
           LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY trip_id ORDER BY _ingested_at, ts) AS prev_ts
    FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/bronze/gps_events\`)
  WHERE prev_ts IS NOT NULL AND ts < prev_ts
  GROUP BY trip_id ORDER BY backwards_steps DESC LIMIT 10"

# 4d. Inspect what bronze actually received
python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
  SELECT
    COUNT(*)                                            AS rows,
    COUNT(DISTINCT event_id)                            AS distinct_events,
    COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT event_id)                 AS duplicate_rows,
    MIN(ts)                                             AS min_event_ts,
    MAX(ts)                                             AS max_event_ts,
    MAX(_kafka_ts)                                      AS max_processing_ts,
    ROUND(AVG(UNIX_TIMESTAMP(_kafka_ts) - UNIX_TIMESTAMP(ts)), 1) AS avg_lag_seconds,
    ROUND(MAX(UNIX_TIMESTAMP(_kafka_ts) - UNIX_TIMESTAMP(ts)), 1) AS max_lag_seconds
  FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/bronze/gps_events\`
"

Expected output

rows      distinct_events  duplicate_rows  min_event_ts          max_event_ts          max_processing_ts     avg_lag_seconds  max_lag_seconds
110,999   110,237          762             2026-06-30 07:34:02   2026-06-30 08:21:55   2026-06-30 08:22:03   6.4              1798.0

Read that last column out loud: 1,798 seconds — nearly 30 minutes of event-time lag. A processing-time aggregation would have filed all of it under 08:20.

Now answer, in LAB5_NOTES.md, before you write any code:

  1. Which of the three defects can a watermark fix? Which can it not?
  2. Which can dropDuplicates fix, and what state does that cost?
  3. Which is invisible to both and only appears in the downstream metric?

docs.title: Task 5 — silver.vehicle_positions: dedupe, watermark, normalise (10 min)
docs.text:
Silver's contract: one row per event_id, event-time ordered, units normalised, only positions accurate enough to trust.

# src/masar/stream/build_vehicle_positions.py
"""bronze.gps_events -> silver.vehicle_positions (streaming).

Silver contract:
  * exactly one row per event_id                (dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark)
  * event-time semantics with 5-minute lateness (withWatermark on event_ts)
  * speed_kmh ALWAYS in km/h                    (producer_version 2.5.0 emits m/s)
  * accuracy_m <= 50                            (worse fixes are not positions, they are noise)
"""
from __future__ import annotations
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from masar.spark import get_spark

BRONZE_PATH = "./lakehouse/bronze/gps_events"
SILVER_PATH = "./lakehouse/silver/vehicle_positions"
CHECKPOINT  = "./lakehouse/_checkpoints/vehicle_positions_silver"   # its OWN checkpoint
WATERMARK   = "5 minutes"
MAX_ACCURACY_M = 50.0

def run() -> None:
    spark = get_spark("masar-vehicle-positions")

    bronze = spark.readStream.format("delta").load(BRONZE_PATH)

    flat = (bronze
        .select(
            "event_id", "vehicle_id", "driver_id", "trip_id",
            F.col("ts").alias("event_ts"),
            F.col("payload.lat").alias("lat"),
            F.col("payload.lon").alias("lon"),
            F.col("payload.speed_kmh").alias("_speed_raw"),
            F.col("payload.heading_deg").alias("heading_deg"),
            F.col("payload.accuracy_m").alias("accuracy_m"),
            "producer_version", "_kafka_ts", "_ingested_at", "_batch_id")
        # THE SIGNATURE INCIDENT: 2.5.0 emits the SAME KEY speed_kmh but in m/s.
        # Type-compatible => schema validation passes => silent semantic drift.
        .withColumn("speed_kmh",
            F.when(F.col("producer_version") == F.lit("2.5.0"),
                   F.col("_speed_raw") * F.lit(3.6))
             .otherwise(F.col("_speed_raw")))
        .drop("_speed_raw")
        .withColumn("event_lag_s",
            F.unix_timestamp("_kafka_ts") - F.unix_timestamp("event_ts"))
        .withColumn("is_late", F.col("event_lag_s") > F.lit(120))
        .filter(F.col("accuracy_m") <= F.lit(MAX_ACCURACY_M))
        .filter(F.col("lat").between(16.0, 33.0) & F.col("lon").between(34.0, 56.0)))

    deduped = (flat
        .withWatermark("event_ts", WATERMARK)
        # Watermark-bounded dedup: keeps state only for the lateness window,
        # instead of remembering every event_id ever seen.
        .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"]))

    (deduped.writeStream
        .format("delta")
        .queryName("vehicle_positions_silver")
        .outputMode("append")
        .partitionBy("event_date")  if False else deduped.writeStream  # see note below
        .format("delta")
        .queryName("vehicle_positions_silver")
        .outputMode("append")
        .option("checkpointLocation", CHECKPOINT)
        .trigger(processingTime="30 seconds")
        .start(SILVER_PATH)
        .awaitTermination())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

Deliberate defect in the starter. The writeStream chain above is malformed — the starter file ships this way on purpose (mistake #5's cousin: copy-paste stream wiring). Rewrite it as a single clean chain, and decide for yourself whether silver.vehicle_positions should be partitioned. Justify your choice in notes; a hint lives in the Task 6 file-count numbers.

Run it alongside the bronze stream, then verify all three defects are handled:

python -m masar.stream.build_vehicle_positions &

python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
  SELECT
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/bronze/gps_events\`)          AS bronze_rows,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/vehicle_positions\`)   AS silver_rows,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT event_id)
       FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/vehicle_positions\`)                 AS silver_dupes,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/vehicle_positions\`
       WHERE is_late)                                                        AS late_rows,
    (SELECT ROUND(MAX(speed_kmh),1) FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/vehicle_positions\`
       WHERE producer_version = '2.5.0')                                     AS max_speed_250,
    (SELECT ROUND(MAX(speed_kmh),1) FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/vehicle_positions\`
       WHERE producer_version = '2.4.0')                                     AS max_speed_240
"

Expected output

bronze_rows  silver_rows  silver_dupes  late_rows  max_speed_250  max_speed_240
110,999      108,914      0             487        118.8          121.4

Three things to read here: silver_dupes = 0 (dedup works), late_rows = 487 of the ~500 fixture pings (13 fell outside the 5-minute watermark — that is the trade-off, not a bug), and the two max_speed values now agree (before the unit fix, max_speed_250 reads 33.0 — a plausible-looking number that would have taught the ETA model that 2.5.0 vehicles crawl).

docs.title: Task 6 — Fan out: ETA features and operations alerts (8 min)
docs.text:
One silver stream, two independent consumers — the point of event-driven architecture.

# src/masar/stream/fanout.py
"""Two consumers of silver.vehicle_positions. Neither knows the other exists.

  A) ETA feature input  -> gold.eta_features' rolling inputs (event-time windowed)
  B) Operations alerts  -> ops console (processing-time is CORRECT here: an alert
                            is about NOW, not about when the event happened)
"""
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from masar.spark import get_spark

SILVER_PATH = "./lakehouse/silver/vehicle_positions"

def eta_feature_input() -> None:
    """Event-time 15-min zone demand + 10-min avg speed: the two rolling inputs
    consumed by gold.eta_features (rolling_zone_demand_15m, rolling_avg_speed_10m)."""
    spark = get_spark("masar-eta-feature-input")
    positions = spark.readStream.format("delta").load(SILVER_PATH)

    rolling = (positions
        .withWatermark("event_ts", "5 minutes")
        .groupBy(F.window("event_ts", "15 minutes", "5 minutes").alias("w"),
                 F.col("trip_id"))
        .agg(F.countDistinct("vehicle_id").alias("rolling_zone_demand_15m"),
             F.avg("speed_kmh").alias("rolling_avg_speed_10m"))
        .select(F.col("w.start").alias("window_start"),
                F.col("w.end").alias("window_end"),
                "trip_id", "rolling_zone_demand_15m", "rolling_avg_speed_10m"))

    (rolling.writeStream.format("delta").outputMode("append")
        .option("checkpointLocation", "./lakehouse/_checkpoints/eta_feature_input")
        .trigger(processingTime="60 seconds")
        .start("./lakehouse/gold/_streaming/eta_feature_input")
        .awaitTermination())


def operations_alerts() -> None:
    """Ops cares about the last 2 minutes of wall-clock reality."""
    spark = get_spark("masar-ops-alerts")
    positions = spark.readStream.format("delta").load(SILVER_PATH)

    alerts = (positions
        .withColumn("alert_type",
            F.when(F.col("speed_kmh") > 140, F.lit("SPEEDING"))
             .when(F.col("accuracy_m") > 35, F.lit("DEGRADED_FIX"))
             .when(F.col("event_lag_s") > 600, F.lit("STALE_TELEMETRY")))
        .filter(F.col("alert_type").isNotNull())
        .select("event_ts", "_kafka_ts", "vehicle_id", "driver_id", "trip_id",
                "alert_type", "speed_kmh", "accuracy_m", "event_lag_s"))

    (alerts.writeStream.format("console")
        .outputMode("append").option("truncate", False).option("numRows", 10)
        .option("checkpointLocation", "./lakehouse/_checkpoints/ops_alerts")
        .trigger(processingTime="30 seconds")
        .start()
        .awaitTermination())

python -c "from masar.stream.fanout import operations_alerts as f; f()"

docs.title: 4. Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• Kafka topic masar.gps.pings exists with 3 partitions and messages keyed by trip_id; all three partitions carry offsets.
  • bronze.gps_events is a Delta table carrying _ingested_at, _source_file, _batch_id, written in append mode only.
  • Each streaming query has its own checkpointLocation under ./lakehouse/_checkpoints/; no two queries share one.
  • Kill/restart drill executed, counted, and recorded: pipeline-introduced duplicates = 0.
  • silver.vehicle_positions has zero duplicate event_id (COUNT(*) = COUNT(DISTINCT event_id)).
  • Late pings from data/fixtures/late_pings/gps_late_2026-06-04.ndjson are attributed to their event-time window, and the drop count beyond the watermark is recorded (not zero, and explained).
  • Out-of-order ts handled without a sort — order is not a prerequisite for correctness when you use event time.
  • producer_version = "2.5.0" rows have speed_kmh in km/h; max speed for 2.4.0 and 2.5.0 are within ~10% of each other.
  • Both fan-out consumers run simultaneously off the same silver table with independent checkpoints.
  • OPTIMIZE run on bronze.gps_events with numFiles before/after recorded.
  • LAB5_NOTES.md committed with all five required answers.

docs.title: 5. Self-check questions
docs.text:
Q1. Exactly-once is often described as a Kafka feature. Precisely which component in your pipeline provides it, and what would break if you moved the checkpoint into the same directory as another query's?

Answer Neither Kafka nor Delta provides exactly-once alone. Kafka gives **at-least-once with replay** (durable offsets you can rewind to). Delta gives an **atomic, idempotent sink** (a micro-batch commit is all-or-nothing, and `txnAppId`/`txnVersion` makes a replayed `batch_id` a no-op). Exactly-once is the *composition*: `./lakehouse/_checkpoints/gps_events_bronze` records which Kafka offsets were included in each committed Delta transaction, so after a crash the restart resumes at the last committed offset and cannot re-append what already committed. Sharing a checkpoint directory between two queries corrupts both: the second query reads the first's offset log and state, believes it has already processed data it never saw (silent data loss) or replays state that does not belong to it (corruption). Spark does not always fail loudly on this — which is why "one checkpoint per query" is a rule, not a preference.

Q2. data/fixtures/late_pings/gps_late_2026-06-04.ndjson delivers a trip's pings shuffled. Your silver job does not sort. Why is the result still correct?

Answer Because every downstream computation is keyed on **event time** (`event_ts`), not on arrival order. `withWatermark("event_ts", "5 minutes")` plus `F.window("event_ts", …)` assigns each ping to the window it belongs to regardless of when it arrived, and Spark holds the window open until the watermark passes. Sorting an unbounded stream is not merely expensive — it is undefined, because there is no "last" record. Ordering is what Kafka's `trip_id` partition key gives you *within* a partition; correctness across arrival delay is what the watermark gives you. They solve different problems.

Q3. Your dedup uses dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"]) rather than dropDuplicates(["event_id"]). What does the plain version cost, and what does the watermarked version give up in exchange?

Answer Plain `dropDuplicates` on a stream keeps **every `event_id` ever seen** in state, forever. At Masar's 1.2M pings/day the state store grows unbounded and the job OOMs within days — this is module mistake #3 wearing a different hat. `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark` bounds state to the watermark window: only `event_id`s seen within the last 5 minutes of event time are remembered. The trade-off is real — a duplicate that arrives **more than 5 minutes after its twin** will pass through. You accept that because Masar's observed duplicate mechanism is producer-side retry within seconds, so the 5-minute window covers essentially all of it. Document that assumption; if the duplicate mechanism changes, so must the window.

Q4. Bronze accepted the producer_version = "2.5.0" pings with no error at all. Why did schema enforcement not catch the m/s incident, and where is the correct place to catch it?

Answer Schema enforcement checks **names and types**. Version 2.5.0 emits the same key `speed_kmh` with the same type `double` — it is structurally identical and semantically wrong. This is *semantic drift*, and no schema check will ever see it. The correct place to catch it is twofold: (1) a **transform** at the bronze→silver boundary that normalises on `producer_version`, which is exactly what you wrote in Task 5 — this is why bronze must preserve `producer_version` verbatim; and (2) a **distribution check** (M6) on the silver `speed_kmh` mean per `producer_version`. A hard rule like `speed_kmh BETWEEN 0 AND 200` passes happily on m/s values; only a distribution comparison against a known-good baseline flags "2.5.0 vehicles average 8.7 km/h and 2.4.0 vehicles average 31.4 km/h." Fixing it in bronze would be wrong: bronze is append-only and as-received, and destroying the raw evidence removes your ability to prove what the device sent.

Q5. Ops alerts aggregate on processing time; ETA features aggregate on event time. Both read the same silver table. Is one of them wrong?

Answer No — the clock you choose follows the **question you are answering**. *"Is anything wrong right now?"* is a processing-time question. An alert about a vehicle whose last fix was 30 minutes ago is urgent **now**, at 08:22, regardless of the event's timestamp. Filing it under the 07:52 window would file it into the past and nobody would see it. *"How busy was zone Z between 07:45 and 08:00?"* is an event-time question. A ping that happened at 07:58 belongs in that window whether it arrives at 07:58 or 08:04, or the ETA model learns a demand curve shifted by network latency. The mistake is not using one clock or the other; it is using processing time for an event-time question, which is module mistake #2 and the reason `_kafka_ts` and `ts` are both preserved all the way through bronze and silver.

Q6. The 30-second trigger produced 248 files for ~15 minutes of data. A participant proposes a 1-second trigger for lower latency. Cost this out.

Answer A 1-second trigger produces roughly 30× the files: ~7,400 files for the same 15 minutes, ~1.7M files/year for the GPS feed alone. Consequences: (a) every downstream read pays per-file open cost — the small-files problem from M4, and a `silver.vehicle_positions` rebuild goes from seconds to minutes; (b) the `_delta_log` accumulates a commit per second, so listing and checkpointing the log itself becomes the bottleneck; (c) object-storage request charges scale with file count, so this is a direct M2 cost regression. The latency you bought is also mostly illusory: end-to-end latency is trigger interval + processing + commit, and at 1 second the fixed commit overhead dominates. The production answer is a trigger sized to the downstream SLA (30–60 s for Masar's ETA refresh) plus a **scheduled OPTIMIZE** on the sink. If a genuine sub-second requirement exists, it is served by reading Kafka directly in the inference service, not by shredding the Lakehouse.

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Rows 1–5 are from the module package. Rows 6–11 are additions from delivery experience — expect at least two of them per cohort.

# Symptom Cause Fix 1 Duplicates after restart No checkpoint, or one shared between queries One dedicated checkpointLocation per query under ./lakehouse/_checkpoints/<query_name> 2 Failed to construct kafka consumer Kafka SQL connector jar missing from the session Add org.apache.spark:spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.12:3.5.1 to spark.jars.packages in src/masar/spark.py 3 Late events dropped unexpectedly Watermark too short for observed lateness Widen withWatermark; measure MAX(_kafka_ts - ts) first and size to p99, not to max 4 Demand attributed to the wrong window Aggregating on _kafka_ts Aggregate on event_ts; _kafka_ts is for lag measurement and ops alerts only 5 Thousands of tiny files in bronze Trigger interval too small Larger trigger + scheduled OPTIMIZE as a DAG task (LAB-07) 6 Batch 0: appended 0 pings forever, no error startingOffsets=latest and the producer already finished before the query started Use startingOffsets=earliest for the lab, or start the stream first and the producer second. Deleting the checkpoint also resets this — but never do that on a table you care about 7 java.net.ConnectException: localhost:9092 from Spark but kafka-console-consumer works The console consumer runs inside the container; Spark runs on the host and needs the advertised listener Confirm KAFKA_CFG_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS=PLAINTEXT://localhost:9092 in docker-compose.yml, then docker compose restart kafka 8 Cannot start query with id … as another query with same id is already running A previous run is still alive in a background shell, holding the checkpoint lock ps aux \| grep ingest_gps_stream then kill it. Do not delete _delta_log/ or the checkpoint to "unstick" it — that is how you manufacture the duplicates this lab is proving you avoid 9 silver.vehicle_positions row count stuck while bronze grows Silver's watermark has not advanced because the fixture replay finished and no new event time is arriving; append-mode output waits for the watermark to close windows Emit a few live pings (--limit 100) to advance event time, or switch the drill to trigger(availableNow=True) for a deterministic drain 10 Detected deleted data from streaming source / failOnDataLoss error Kafka retention expired offsets the checkpoint still points at (common after a long break or a docker compose down) Restore from bronze.gps_events — it is append-only and complete. Reset the topic and re-run from earliest. Note in LAB5_NOTES.md that this is exactly why bronze exists 11 max_speed_250 reads ~33 while max_speed_240 reads ~121, and nothing failed The m/s semantic drift is unhandled — no error is possible because the type is correct Apply the producer_version normalisation in the bronze→silver transform (Task 5), and add the per-version distribution check in LAB-06 12 Ops-alert console query floods with DEGRADED_FIX The accuracy_m <= 50 silver filter and the accuracy_m > 35 alert threshold overlap by design This is correct behaviour, not a bug: silver drops unusable fixes, ops is warned about marginal ones. Tune the alert threshold and record the reasoning

docs.title: 7. Stretch goals
docs.text:
1. Second consumer group. Start a third consumer on masar.gps.pings in its own consumer group that prints a live per-city ping rate. Prove with kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --all-groups that both groups hold independent offsets and neither slows the other. This is producer/consumer decoupling made visible.
  2. Watermark tuning clinic. Re-run Task 4 with watermarks of 30 s, 5 min and 30 min. Record for each: rows admitted, rows dropped, and peak state-store size from the stateOperators block of the query progress JSON. Plot the three points and defend your production choice.
  3. Backfill with availableNow. Replace the 30 s trigger with .trigger(availableNow=True) and reprocess a full day of data/raw/gps/gps_2026-06-01.ndjson.gz from earliest. Confirm the row count matches the batch-read count of the same file exactly. This is the replay path you will reach for when a downstream bug forces reprocessing.
  4. Kafka lag SLO. Instrument the streaming query listener (spark.streams.addListener) to emit numInputRows, processedRowsPerSecond and end-offset lag per batch to a Delta table. Define a lag SLO and write the alert rule. Lag is the single headline health metric for any stream.
  5. Break it deliberately. On a branch, remove the txnAppId/txnVersion options and keep the checkpoint. Kill mid-batch and restart. Explain precisely why exactly-once still holds (checkpoint alone is sufficient for the Delta sink) and what the idempotent-write options actually protect against (a foreachBatch body that writes to more than one sink, or that is retried by Spark's task-level retry).

docs.title: LAB 06 — Quality Gate And Governance
docs.text:
Field Value Lab ID LAB-06 Module M6 — Data Quality, Observability, and Governance Day / Hour Day 4 · Hour 4 Duration 50 minutes (6 timed tasks) Difficulty Intermediate (conceptually demanding, technically moderate) LO mapping LO6 (primary) · LO4 (MERGE DELETE + VACUUM for erasure) · LO3 (gate sits at the ELT promotion boundary) Prerequisites LAB-03b (silver.trips incremental model), LAB-04b (Delta MERGE, time travel, VACUUM), LAB-05 (silver.vehicle_positions for the producer_version drift check) Checkpoint git tag lab6-start (fast-forward) · lab6-solution (reference) Deliverable quality/suites/silver_trips_suite.py + gps_events_suite.py, a gate that acts, silver.trips_quarantine with real rows in it, rendered GX data docs, GOVERNANCE.md classification table, and a demonstrated PDPL erasure

Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. Grains, ratios and file-count reductions hold at either scale; absolute row counts do not.

docs.title: 1. Why this lab matters
docs.text:
The course question: "What happens to Masar's AI system if THIS part of the data platform fails?"

Lab 5 proved the pipeline moves data without losing or duplicating it. That guarantees delivery, not truth. A pipeline can be flawlessly exactly-once and still deliver 48,200 rows of nonsense on time, every time.

The ETA model is trained on silver.trips and silver.vehicle_positions. It has no way to know whether a duration_min of -14 is a bug or a fact; it will fit a curve through it. It has no way to know that on 12 June the fare_sar column silently changed units. It will learn whatever you promote.

If this fails… The AI system experiences… No gate at promotion 40 rows with null trip_id reach silver.trips. The MERGE key is null, so the incremental model's WHEN MATCHED never matches and every subsequent run re-inserts them. By Friday the fact table has 280 phantom trips and the driver-daily mart under-reports utilisation. Alert-only gate ("we emailed someone") 120 negative fares reach gold.eta_features via silver.trips. historical_route_duration is computed from trips including the corrupt ones. Nobody reads the email. The model degrades by 6% and the investigation starts three weeks later. Fail-fast applied too broadly The whole 48,200-row batch is blocked because 120 fares are negative. silver.trips goes stale. The morning BI dashboard shows yesterday. The ETA model retrains on a gap. You have converted a 0.25% data problem into a 100% availability outage. No distribution monitoring The producer_version = "2.5.0" m/s incident from Lab 5 passes every schema check and every range check, because m/s values are valid doubles inside a plausible range. rolling_avg_speed_10m drops silently. Only a drift check on the mean sees it. No PDPL retention Precise lat/lon for identifiable riders accumulates in bronze indefinitely. There is no lawful basis for keeping it past its purpose, no mechanism to honour an erasure request, and the platform is one audit away from a finding.

The line to hold in this lab: a quality gate is a decision, not an alarm. An alarm that fires while bad data still flows past it is worse than no alarm, because it manufactures the belief that someone is watching.

docs.title: Task 1 — The suite: silver.trips as executable contract (10 min)
docs.text:
Every expectation below maps to one level of the quality pyramid and carries a response class — FAIL_FAST or QUARANTINE. Writing the response class into the suite metadata is what makes the gate in Task 2 a decision rather than a print statement.

# quality/suites/silver_trips_suite.py
"""The silver.trips data contract, expressed as executable expectations.

Column set is EXACTLY data/raw/trips_YYYY-MM-DD.csv conformed to silver:
  trip_id, rider_id, driver_id, vehicle_id, city, pickup_zone_id,
  dropoff_zone_id, pickup_ts, dropoff_ts, distance_km, duration_min,
  fare_sar, surge_multiplier, payment_type, status, dropoff_geohash

Every expectation carries meta.response_class, consumed by masar.quality.gate:
  FAIL_FAST  -> integrity. Promoting anything is worse than promoting nothing.
  QUARANTINE -> partial. Isolate the bad rows, promote the good ones, alert.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import great_expectations as gx

SUITE_NAME = "silver_trips.contract"
KSA_CITIES = ["Riyadh", "Jeddah", "Dammam", "Mecca", "Medina"]
TRIP_STATUS = ["completed", "cancelled_rider", "cancelled_driver", "no_show"]
PAYMENT_TYPES = ["mada", "credit_card", "apple_pay", "cash", "wallet"]

FAIL_FAST = {"response_class": "FAIL_FAST"}
QUARANTINE = {"response_class": "QUARANTINE"}


def build_suite(context) -> None:
    suite = context.add_or_update_expectation_suite(SUITE_NAME)
    validator = context.get_validator(
        batch_request=(context.get_datasource("masar_lakehouse")
                       .get_asset("silver_trips")
                       .build_batch_request()),
        expectation_suite=suite,
    )

    # ---- Level 1: schema -------------------------------------------- FAIL_FAST
    validator.expect_table_columns_to_match_set(
        column_set=["trip_id", "rider_id", "driver_id", "vehicle_id", "city",
                    "pickup_zone_id", "dropoff_zone_id", "pickup_ts", "dropoff_ts",
                    "distance_km", "duration_min", "fare_sar", "surge_multiplier",
                    "payment_type", "status", "dropoff_geohash"],
        exact_match=False, meta=FAIL_FAST)
    validator.expect_column_values_to_be_of_type("fare_sar", "DoubleType", meta=FAIL_FAST)
    validator.expect_column_values_to_be_of_type("pickup_ts", "TimestampType", meta=FAIL_FAST)

    # ---- Level 2: key integrity ------------------------------------- FAIL_FAST
    validator.expect_column_values_to_not_be_null("trip_id", meta=FAIL_FAST)
    validator.expect_column_values_to_be_unique("trip_id", meta=FAIL_FAST)
    validator.expect_column_values_to_not_be_null("pickup_ts", meta=FAIL_FAST)

    # ---- Level 3: value constraints --------------------------------- QUARANTINE
    validator.expect_column_values_to_be_between(
        "fare_sar", min_value=0, strict_min=True, max_value=5000, meta=QUARANTINE)
    validator.expect_column_values_to_be_between(
        "duration_min", min_value=0, strict_min=True, max_value=600, meta=QUARANTINE)
    validator.expect_column_values_to_be_between(
        "distance_km", min_value=0, strict_min=True, max_value=400, meta=QUARANTINE)
    validator.expect_column_values_to_be_between(
        "surge_multiplier", min_value=1.0, max_value=5.0, meta=QUARANTINE)
    validator.expect_column_values_to_be_in_set("city", KSA_CITIES, meta=QUARANTINE)
    validator.expect_column_values_to_be_in_set("status", TRIP_STATUS, meta=QUARANTINE)
    validator.expect_column_values_to_be_in_set("payment_type", PAYMENT_TYPES, meta=QUARANTINE)
    validator.expect_column_pair_values_A_to_be_greater_than_B(
        "dropoff_ts", "pickup_ts", or_equal=False, meta=QUARANTINE)

    # Known 3.1% null rate: tolerated, monitored, NOT silently accepted.
    validator.expect_column_values_to_not_be_null(
        "dropoff_geohash", mostly=0.95, meta=QUARANTINE)

    # ---- Level 4: distribution -------------------------- QUARANTINE (scheduled)
    # Baseline FROZEN from a known-good period (2026-05-01..2026-05-31).
    # Never recompute a baseline from the batch you are validating.
    validator.expect_column_mean_to_be_between(
        "fare_sar", min_value=28.0, max_value=52.0, meta=QUARANTINE)
    validator.expect_column_median_to_be_between(
        "duration_min", min_value=9.0, max_value=26.0, meta=QUARANTINE)

    validator.save_expectation_suite(discard_failed_expectations=False)
    print(f"[gx] saved suite {SUITE_NAME} with "
          f"{len(suite.expectations)} expectations")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    build_suite(gx.get_context(context_root_dir="./quality/gx"))

Now write the companion suite for the streaming table from Lab 5. It is shorter but carries the check that a schema validator can never make:

# quality/suites/gps_events_suite.py
"""Contract for bronze.gps_events / silver.vehicle_positions.

The point of interest is the LAST expectation. producer_version 2.5.0 emits
speed_kmh in m/s: same key, same type, wrong unit. No schema or range rule can
see it. Only a per-version distribution comparison can.
"""
import great_expectations as gx

SUITE_NAME = "gps_events.contract"
FAIL_FAST = {"response_class": "FAIL_FAST"}
QUARANTINE = {"response_class": "QUARANTINE"}


def build_suite(context) -> None:
    suite = context.add_or_update_expectation_suite(SUITE_NAME)
    v = context.get_validator(
        batch_request=(context.get_datasource("masar_lakehouse")
                       .get_asset("silver_vehicle_positions").build_batch_request()),
        expectation_suite=suite)

    v.expect_column_values_to_not_be_null("event_id", meta=FAIL_FAST)
    v.expect_column_values_to_be_unique("event_id", meta=FAIL_FAST)
    v.expect_column_values_to_not_be_null("event_ts", meta=FAIL_FAST)
    v.expect_column_values_to_be_between("lat", 16.0, 33.0, meta=QUARANTINE)   # KSA bounds
    v.expect_column_values_to_be_between("lon", 34.0, 56.0, meta=QUARANTINE)
    v.expect_column_values_to_be_between("accuracy_m", 0, 50, meta=QUARANTINE)
    v.expect_column_values_to_be_between("heading_deg", 0, 360, meta=QUARANTINE)
    v.expect_column_values_to_be_in_set("producer_version", ["2.4.0", "2.5.0"], meta=QUARANTINE)

    # A hard range rule passes on m/s values (8.7 is a valid "km/h").
    # This mean check is the ONLY rule that catches the semantic drift.
    v.expect_column_mean_to_be_between("speed_kmh", 24.0, 46.0, meta=QUARANTINE)

    v.save_expectation_suite(discard_failed_expectations=False)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    build_suite(gx.get_context(context_root_dir="./quality/gx"))

docs.title: Task 2 — The gate that acts: fail-fast and quarantine (14 min)
docs.text:
The starter src/masar/quality/gate.py ships with deliberate mistake #1 — it alerts and promotes anyway. Replace it.

# src/masar/quality/gate.py
"""Quality gate at the bronze -> silver promotion boundary.

Three outcomes, decided by the response_class in each expectation's meta:

  FAIL_FAST  failed  -> raise. Nothing is promoted. The batch is blocked.
  QUARANTINE failed  -> split. Bad rows -> silver.trips_quarantine (with the
                        reason), good rows -> silver.trips. Alert either way.
  all passed         -> promote everything. Alert nothing.

The gate never promotes a row it could not justify, and never blocks a batch
for a fault it could isolate.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F
from masar.spark import get_spark

SILVER = "./lakehouse/silver/trips"
QUARANTINE = "./lakehouse/silver/trips_quarantine"

KSA_CITIES = ["Riyadh", "Jeddah", "Dammam", "Mecca", "Medina"]
TRIP_STATUS = ["completed", "cancelled_rider", "cancelled_driver", "no_show"]


class GateBlocked(RuntimeError):
    """Raised on FAIL_FAST. The DAG task fails; nothing is promoted."""


@dataclass
class GateResult:
    promoted: int
    quarantined: int
    blocked: bool
    reasons: dict


def _failed_by_class(gx_result, response_class: str) -> list[str]:
    """Return expectation ids that FAILED and carry this response_class."""
    return [
        r["expectation_config"]["kwargs"].get("column", "<table>")
        + ":" + r["expectation_config"]["expectation_type"]
        for r in gx_result["results"]
        if not r["success"]
        and r["expectation_config"]["meta"].get("response_class") == response_class
    ]


# One predicate per QUARANTINE expectation. Keeping these beside the suite is a
# duplication you accept knowingly: GX tells you WHICH rule failed; Spark tells
# you WHICH ROWS failed it. Both are needed to quarantine with a reason.
QUARANTINE_RULES = {
    "fare_non_positive":     F.col("fare_sar") <= 0,
    "fare_implausible":      F.col("fare_sar") > 5000,
    "duration_non_positive": F.col("duration_min") <= 0,
    "duration_implausible":  F.col("duration_min") > 600,
    "distance_non_positive": F.col("distance_km") <= 0,
    "city_not_in_ksa_set":   ~F.col("city").isin(*KSA_CITIES),
    "status_unknown":        ~F.col("status").isin(*TRIP_STATUS),
    "dropoff_before_pickup": F.col("dropoff_ts") <= F.col("pickup_ts"),
    "surge_out_of_range":    ~F.col("surge_multiplier").between(1.0, 5.0),
}


def gate_and_promote(candidate: DataFrame, gx_result, batch_id: str) -> GateResult:
    spark = get_spark()

    # ---- 1. FAIL FAST on integrity ------------------------------------------
    integrity_failures = _failed_by_class(gx_result, "FAIL_FAST")
    if integrity_failures:
        alert(f"FAIL-FAST: batch {batch_id} blocked. "
              f"Integrity expectations failed: {integrity_failures}")
        raise GateBlocked(
            f"FAIL-FAST: integrity expectations failed {integrity_failures}; "
            f"batch {batch_id} blocked, nothing promoted")

    # ---- 2. QUARANTINE partial value failures -------------------------------
    reason = F.array_remove(F.array(*[
        F.when(pred, F.lit(name)).otherwise(F.lit(None))
        for name, pred in QUARANTINE_RULES.items()
    ]), None)

    tagged = candidate.withColumn("_quarantine_reasons", reason)
    bad = tagged.filter(F.size("_quarantine_reasons") > 0)
    good = tagged.filter(F.size("_quarantine_reasons") == 0).drop("_quarantine_reasons")

    bad.cache(); good.cache()
    n_bad, n_good = bad.count(), good.count()

    if n_bad:
        (bad.withColumn("_quarantined_at", F.current_timestamp())
            .withColumn("_batch_id", F.lit(batch_id))
            .write.format("delta").mode("append")
            .option("mergeSchema", "true")
            .save(QUARANTINE))
        by_reason = (bad.select(F.explode("_quarantine_reasons").alias("r"))
                       .groupBy("r").count().collect())
        detail = {row["r"]: row["count"] for row in by_reason}
        alert(f"QUARANTINED {n_bad} rows to silver.trips_quarantine -> {detail}")
    else:
        detail = {}

    # ---- 3. Promote the good rows (idempotent MERGE on trip_id, from LAB-04b)
    from delta.tables import DeltaTable
    tgt = DeltaTable.forPath(spark, SILVER)
    (tgt.alias("t").merge(good.alias("s"), "t.trip_id = s.trip_id")
        .whenMatchedUpdateAll().whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute())

    print(f"[gate] batch {batch_id}: promoted {n_good:,}, quarantined {n_bad:,}")
    return GateResult(promoted=n_good, quarantined=n_bad, blocked=False, reasons=detail)


def alert(msg: str) -> None:
    print(f"[DATA-ALERT] {msg}", flush=True)   # wire to Slack/PagerDuty in production

Run both drills. Predict the outcome of each before you press enter, and write your prediction in LAB6_NOTES.md.

# Drill A — the fixture as shipped. The 40 null-key rows trip a FAIL_FAST rule
# before any quarantine logic runs. Expect: BLOCKED, nothing promoted, zero quarantined.
python -m masar.quality.gate --batch data/fixtures/dirty_batch/trips_2026-06-05_dirty.csv

# Drill B — the SAME batch with its integrity faults repaired upstream, which is what
# the source team would send you after Drill A blocked. Strip the unkeyed rows, then
# re-gate. Expect: 120 quarantined, 41,976 promoted, no block.
python - <<'PY'
import csv, pathlib
src = "data/fixtures/dirty_batch/trips_2026-06-05_dirty.csv"
dst = pathlib.Path("logs/dirty_batch_keys_repaired.csv"); dst.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
with open(src, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh, dst.open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as out:
    r = csv.DictReader(fh)
    w = csv.DictWriter(out, fieldnames=r.fieldnames); w.writeheader()
    seen = set()
    for row in r:
        if not row["trip_id"] or not row["rider_id"] or not row["pickup_ts"]:
            continue                       # the fail-fast class: unkeyed, untimed
        if row["trip_id"] in seen:
            continue                       # the duplicate trip_ids, also fail-fast
        seen.add(row["trip_id"])
        w.writerow(row)
print(f"wrote {dst} with the integrity faults removed")
PY
python -m masar.quality.gate --batch logs/dirty_batch_keys_repaired.csv

# Verify the quarantine actually caught them, with reasons
python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
  SELECT _quarantine_reasons[0] AS reason, COUNT(*) AS rows
  FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/trips_quarantine\`
  GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC"

# Verify NOTHING from drill A reached silver
python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS null_keys_in_silver
  FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/trips\` WHERE trip_id IS NULL"

docs.title: Task 3 — Observability: freshness, volume, drift (10 min)
docs.text:
Row-level rules validate content. These three validate the pipeline's health, and they catch what no row rule can.

# src/masar/quality/observe.py
"""The four data-SRE signals. Freshness, volume, schema drift, distribution drift.

Every one of these can fire while EVERY ROW passes EVERY expectation.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from masar.spark import get_spark
from masar.quality.gate import alert

BASELINE_WINDOW = ("2026-05-01", "2026-05-31")   # FROZEN known-good period


def check_freshness(path: str, table: str, sla_hours: int = 6) -> None:
    spark = get_spark()
    last = (spark.read.format("delta").load(path)
            .agg(F.max("_ingested_at").alias("m")).collect()[0]["m"])
    age_h = None if last is None else (datetime.now() - last).total_seconds() / 3600
    if last is None or age_h > sla_hours:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"FRESHNESS breach: {table} last updated {last} "
            f"({age_h:.1f}h ago, SLA {sla_hours}h)")
    print(f"[obs] freshness {table}: {age_h:.2f}h old, SLA {sla_hours}h  OK")


def check_volume(path: str, table: str, expected: int, tol: float = 0.30) -> None:
    spark = get_spark()
    n = spark.read.format("delta").load(path).count()
    dev = abs(n - expected) / expected
    if dev > tol:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"VOLUME anomaly: {table} has {n:,} rows vs expected ~{expected:,} "
            f"({dev:+.1%}, tolerance {tol:.0%})")
    print(f"[obs] volume {table}: {n:,} rows ({dev:+.1%} of baseline)  OK")


def check_schema_drift(path: str, table: str, expected_columns: set[str]) -> None:
    spark = get_spark()
    actual = set(spark.read.format("delta").load(path).columns)
    added, removed = actual - expected_columns, expected_columns - actual
    if added or removed:
        alert(f"SCHEMA drift in {table}: added={sorted(added)} removed={sorted(removed)}")
    else:
        print(f"[obs] schema {table}: {len(actual)} columns, no drift  OK")


def check_distribution_drift(path: str, table: str, column: str,
                             baseline_mean: float, tol: float = 0.20,
                             group_by: str | None = None) -> None:
    """The signal that catches semantic drift. Baseline is FROZEN, never recomputed
    from the batch under test — that is the 'baseline-the-bug' failure mode."""
    spark = get_spark()
    df = spark.read.format("delta").load(path)
    if group_by:
        rows = df.groupBy(group_by).agg(F.mean(column).alias("m")).collect()
        for r in rows:
            dev = abs(r["m"] - baseline_mean) / baseline_mean
            flag = "DRIFT" if dev > tol else "ok   "
            print(f"[{flag}] {table}.{column} [{group_by}={r[group_by]}]: "
                  f"{r['m']:.2f} vs baseline {baseline_mean:.2f} ({dev:+.1%})")
            if dev > tol:
                alert(f"DISTRIBUTION drift: {table}.{column} for "
                      f"{group_by}={r[group_by]} is {dev:+.1%} off frozen baseline")
    else:
        m = df.agg(F.mean(column).alias("m")).collect()[0]["m"]
        dev = abs(m - baseline_mean) / baseline_mean
        if dev > tol:
            alert(f"DISTRIBUTION drift: {table}.{column} mean {m:.2f} "
                  f"vs baseline {baseline_mean:.2f} ({dev:+.1%})")
        else:
            print(f"[obs] drift {table}.{column}: {m:.2f} vs {baseline_mean:.2f}  OK")

Fire each one against its injected fault:

# Freshness — simulate a stalled upstream by validating against a 1-hour SLA
python -m masar.quality.observe --check freshness --table silver.trips --sla-hours 1

# Volume — the feed dropped half its rows
python -m masar.quality.observe --check volume --table silver.trips --expected 84000

# Schema drift — a source added a column nobody announced
python -m masar.quality.observe --check schema --table silver.trips

# Distribution drift — THE CURRENCY SHIFT. Load the fixture first.
python -m masar.quality.gate --batch data/fixtures/currency_shift/trips_2026-06-05_currency_shift.csv
python -m masar.quality.observe --check drift --table silver.trips \
       --column fare_sar --baseline 38.4 --group-by city

# Distribution drift — THE m/s INCIDENT from LAB-05
python -m masar.quality.observe --check drift --table silver.vehicle_positions \
