docs.title: Task 4 — PDPL: classify, restrict, retain, erase (10 min)
docs.text:
Governance is not a document. It is a column classification that drives an access policy and a scheduled job.

Complete this table in GOVERNANCE.md. Four rows are given; classify the remaining columns of silver.trips, silver.vehicle_positions and gold.eta_features yourself.

Table.column Classification Access level Retention PDPL basis silver.trips.rider_id Personal DS (silver) only; never gold, never BI, never Redis 24 months Purpose limitation — needed for support and dispute resolution, not for analytics silver.trips.trip_id Public (pseudonymous key) All 7 years Not personal on its own; financial-record retention silver.vehicle_positions.lat / .lon Sensitive (precise location) Restricted; masked to geohash-6 at the serving boundary 180 days raw, then geohash only Data minimisation — precise coordinates are not needed past the operational window silver.trips.dropoff_geohash Personal (coarse) DS + gold aggregates 24 months Minimised substitute for precise coordinates silver.trips.driver_id (you) silver.trips.fare_sar (you) silver.trips.city (you) gold.eta_features.pickup_zone_id (you) 
# src/masar/governance/retention.py
"""PDPL-aligned retention + erasure. Every deletion is an auditable Delta commit.

Two distinct obligations, two distinct mechanisms:
  RETENTION  scheduled, blanket, time-based  -> delete WHERE ts < cutoff
  ERASURE    on request, targeted, subject   -> MERGE DELETE by rider_id, then VACUUM
VACUUM is what makes erasure real: without it the data still sits in the
time-travel history and the request has not been honoured.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import json
from datetime import datetime
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from masar.spark import get_spark

CLASSIFICATION = {
    "rider_id":          "personal",
    "driver_id":         "personal",
    "national_id_hash":  "personal-pseudonymised",
    "phone_hash":        "personal-pseudonymised",
    "lat":               "sensitive-location",
    "lon":               "sensitive-location",
    "dropoff_geohash":   "personal-coarse",
    "vehicle_id":        "operational",
    "fare_sar":          "commercial",
    "city":              "public",
}
GPS_RETENTION_DAYS = 180
AUDIT_LOG = "./lakehouse/governance/erasure_audit"


def enforce_gps_retention(dry_run: bool = True) -> int:
    """Blanket retention on precise location. Minimisation, not deletion for its own sake."""
    spark = get_spark()
    path = "./lakehouse/silver/vehicle_positions"
    t = DeltaTable.forPath(spark, path)
    predicate = f"event_ts < current_date() - INTERVAL {GPS_RETENTION_DAYS} DAYS"
    n = spark.read.format("delta").load(path).where(predicate).count()
    print(f"[pdpl] retention: {n:,} rows older than {GPS_RETENTION_DAYS}d")
    if not dry_run and n:
        t.delete(predicate)
        spark.sql(f"VACUUM delta.`{path}` RETAIN 168 HOURS")   # 7 days, justified below
        print(f"[pdpl] deleted {n:,} rows + VACUUM RETAIN 168 HOURS")
    return n


def erase_rider(rider_id: str, ticket_ref: str, dry_run: bool = True) -> dict:
    """Data-subject erasure request. Touches EVERY table holding the identifier."""
    spark = get_spark()
    targets = {
        "silver.trips":     "./lakehouse/silver/trips",
        "silver.trips_quarantine": "./lakehouse/silver/trips_quarantine",
        "bronze.trips":     "./lakehouse/bronze/trips",
    }
    counts = {}
    for name, path in targets.items():
        df = spark.read.format("delta").load(path)
        if "rider_id" not in df.columns:
            continue
        n = df.where(F.col("rider_id") == rider_id).count()
        counts[name] = n
        if not dry_run and n:
            DeltaTable.forPath(spark, path).delete(F.col("rider_id") == rider_id)
            spark.sql(f"VACUUM delta.`{path}` RETAIN 168 HOURS")

    record = {"ticket_ref": ticket_ref, "rider_id_hash": _h(rider_id),
              "executed_at": datetime.utcnow().isoformat() + "Z",
              "rows_deleted": counts, "dry_run": dry_run,
              "vacuum_retain_hours": 168}
    if not dry_run:
        (spark.createDataFrame([json.dumps(record)], "string")
             .toDF("record").write.format("delta").mode("append").save(AUDIT_LOG))
    print(f"[pdpl] erasure {ticket_ref}: {counts} (dry_run={dry_run})")
    return record


def _h(v: str) -> str:
    import hashlib
    return hashlib.sha256(v.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]

# Retention on a COPY first — never rehearse a destructive job on the live table
python -m masar.governance.retention --copy-first --enforce-gps-retention

# Erasure drill from the fixture
cat data/fixtures/erasure_request/pdpl_erasure_2026-06-10.json
python -m masar.governance.retention --erase-rider RID-0084417 --ticket PDPL-2026-0113 --dry-run
python -m masar.governance.retention --erase-rider RID-0084417 --ticket PDPL-2026-0113 --execute

# PROVE it: the rider is gone from the current version AND from history
python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/trips\` WHERE rider_id = 'RID-0084417'"
python -m masar.tools.sql --query "DESCRIBE HISTORY delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/trips\` LIMIT 3"

Expected output

[pdpl] retention: 214,880 rows older than 180d
[pdpl] deleted 214,880 rows + VACUUM RETAIN 168 HOURS

[pdpl] erasure PDPL-2026-0113: {'silver.trips': 37, 'silver.trips_quarantine': 1,
                                'bronze.trips': 37} (dry_run=True)
[pdpl] erasure PDPL-2026-0113: {'silver.trips': 37, 'silver.trips_quarantine': 1,
                                'bronze.trips': 37} (dry_run=False)

COUNT(*)
0

version  operation  operationParameters                              operationMetrics
14       VACUUM END {retentionCheckEnabled -> true}                   {numDeletedFiles -> 22}
13       DELETE     {predicate -> ["(rider_id = 'RID-0084417')"]}     {numDeletedRows -> 37}

docs.title: 4. Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• quality/suites/silver_trips_suite.py runs clean and produces ≥ 15 expectations, each carrying meta.response_class.
  • quality/suites/gps_events_suite.py includes a distribution expectation on speed_kmh — the only rule that can see the m/s drift.
  • GX data docs render and are copied to quality/evidence/lab6/ as committed evidence.
  • The gate fail-fasts on trips_2026-06-05_dirty.csv as shipped: raises GateBlocked, and silver.trips gains zero rows.
  • The gate quarantines on the same batch with its integrity faults repaired (logs/dirty_batch_keys_repaired.csv): 120 rows land in silver.trips_quarantine with a reason column, 41,976 promote.
  • silver.trips_quarantine exists as a Delta table with _quarantine_reasons, _quarantined_at, _batch_id.
  • Freshness, volume, schema-drift and distribution-drift checks each fire on their injected fault; each is recorded in notes.
  • The drift baseline is frozen (a literal from a known-good period), not recomputed from the batch under test.
  • GOVERNANCE.md classifies every column of silver.trips, silver.vehicle_positions and gold.eta_features with access level, retention and a PDPL justification.
  • A PDPL erasure is demonstrated end to end: MERGE DELETE + VACUUM + audit record, with DESCRIBE HISTORY shown as proof.
  • VACUUM RETAIN is a justified non-zero value, and the justification is written down.

docs.title: 5. Self-check questions
docs.text:
Q1. A batch arrives with 40 null trip_id values and 120 negative fares. Your gate blocks it entirely. What did you get wrong, and what should have happened?

Answer Nothing — this specific batch is correctly blocked. The **null key** is a FAIL_FAST fault, and fail-fast dominates: once integrity fails you cannot safely promote *anything*, because a null key breaks the MERGE that every downstream idempotency guarantee depends on. Splitting the batch would mean promoting rows whose key semantics you no longer trust. The mistake would be blocking a batch that had *only* the 120 negative fares. That is a 0.25% partial fault, isolable by predicate, and blocking it converts a small data problem into a total availability outage — the upstream ETA model retrains on a gap, and the BI dashboard shows yesterday. The rule: **fail-fast dominates when both classes fail; quarantine is the answer when only value constraints fail.**

Q2. Every row in the currency-shift fixture passes expect_column_values_to_be_between("fare_sar", 0, 5000). Explain why, and name the two other checks that would have caught it.

Answer Because `3847.55` is a perfectly valid number strictly between 0 and 5000. Range rules test *plausibility per row*; they cannot test *plausibility per population*. A 100× shift produces values that are individually unremarkable. Two checks catch it: (1) **distribution drift** against a frozen baseline — the Jeddah mean moves from 38.40 to 3847.55, a +9918% deviation no tolerance band survives; and (2) **reconciliation** — the sum of `fare_sar` in `silver.trips` for Jeddah against the same day's total in `data/raw/payments_YYYY-MM-DD.csv` (`amount_sar`). Reconciliation is the strongest check in the pyramid and the most expensive, which is why it runs daily rather than per batch. Note that raising `max_value` to 5000 was itself a judgement. Had it been 200, the range rule would have caught this incident by accident — and would have quarantined every legitimate long-haul intercity fare as a side effect. Tight bounds are not free.

Q3. Your team proposes computing the drift baseline as "the mean of the last 30 days, refreshed nightly." What is wrong with that?

Answer The baseline absorbs the bug. If the currency shift began on 12 June, then by 13 June it is 1/30th of the rolling baseline, by 20 June it is a quarter of it, and by 12 July it *is* the baseline. The deviation shrinks every night until the check reports OK on permanently corrupt data. This is the `sim-baseline-the-bug` simulation, and it is the most common way a working drift check silently stops working. The correct pattern: freeze the baseline over an explicitly chosen **known-good period** (here, 2026-05-01..2026-05-31), store it as a versioned literal or a Delta table with its own history, and change it only through review — the same discipline you apply to loosening an expectation. Re-baselining is a decision with an owner, not an automatic process. A rolling window is acceptable only for genuinely seasonal quantities, and even then you compare against the same period last year, not against last week.

Q4. What does VACUUM have to do with PDPL, and what does RETAIN 0 HOURS cost you?

Answer A Delta `DELETE` is logical: it writes a new version whose snapshot excludes the rows, but the underlying Parquet files still contain them and remain readable via time travel (`VERSION AS OF`). For a **retention limit** or a **data-subject erasure request**, the data has not actually been erased — it is one `SELECT ... VERSION AS OF 12` away. `VACUUM` physically removes files no longer referenced by any retained version, which is what converts a logical delete into an erasure you can defend to an auditor. `RETAIN 0 HOURS` is flagged as an anti-pattern in the capstone rubric for two reasons. Operationally it can delete files that a **concurrently running reader or streaming query** still holds a reference to, producing `FileNotFoundException` on a job that was working a second ago — Delta requires an explicit `spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled=false` override precisely because this is dangerous. Governance-wise it destroys your entire audit trail: you can no longer prove what the table looked like before a correction, which is a different compliance obligation pulling in the opposite direction. `RETAIN 168 HOURS` (7 days) is the defensible middle: longer than any running job, short enough that the erasure obligation is met within a reasonable window, and documented as a deliberate choice.

Q5. Your model's accuracy dropped 8% last month. Every expectation in every suite passed, every day. Where do you look first?

Answer **Distribution drift**, on the feature columns rather than the raw columns. Passing expectations tell you the data is *well-formed*; they say nothing about whether its statistical shape still matches what the model was trained on. The two Masar incidents in this lab are exactly this shape: the m/s speed drift and the currency shift both produce 100% valid rows. The diagnostic order: (1) compare the current distribution of each `gold.eta_features` column against the training snapshot — Delta time travel lets you read the exact version the model trained on, which is why `_feature_version` and time travel matter; (2) check **volume** per segment, because a feed outage in one city shifts the population mix without changing any distribution within a city; (3) check **freshness** per feature, because a feature that silently stopped refreshing looks statistically fine but is answering last week's question. Only then look at the model.

Q6. A stakeholder asks for rider_id in a shared operations dashboard "so we can call the customer back." How do you answer in PDPL terms while still solving their problem?

Answer The refusal is grounded in **purpose limitation** and **data minimisation**: the lawful basis for holding `rider_id` is service delivery and dispute resolution, not analytics, and a shared dashboard exposes the identifier to a population far wider than that purpose supports. Publishing it also makes every dashboard viewer a processor of personal data, expanding the compliance surface across the whole organisation. The need behind the ask is legitimate, and it is not "see the rider ID" — it is "reach this specific rider from this specific trip." Three ways to meet it without breaching: (1) expose `trip_id` only, and have the support tool perform the lookup inside the system that already has a lawful basis, with the access logged; (2) publish a **pseudonym** (`sha2(rider_id, 256)`) so cohort analysis and repeat-customer counting still work without exposing the identifier; (3) for the dashboard itself, serve aggregates — which is exactly what `gold.fact_trip` and the BI-safe view in LAB-08 do. Governance is rarely a refusal; it is a redesign that meets the need at a lower data cost.

docs.text:
Rows 1–4 are from the module package. Rows 5–11 are additions.

The 1.x API renamed most of this lab's surface 6 expect_column_values_to_be_of_type("fare_sar", "DoubleType") fails on a column that is obviously a double Spark type names differ from pandas backends; a CSV-read column may be StringType if the mixed-format ingest did not cast it Check df.dtypes first. Cast in the silver transform, not in the expectation — the suite tests the contract, it does not enforce it 7 Quarantine table write fails with AnalysisException: A schema mismatch detected _quarantine_reasons is an array column added after the table was first created .option("mergeSchema", "true") on the quarantine write only. Never on silver.trips — silver's schema is the contract 8 Gate reports 0 quarantined but bad rows clearly exist The predicate uses != or NOT IN against a column containing NULLs; three-valued logic makes those rows neither good nor bad Use isin(...) negated with ~, and add an explicit isNull() branch. Verify with SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE col IS NULL before trusting any set-membership rule 9 VACUUM deletes nothing and prints a retention warning Files are newer than the retention window — nothing is yet eligible Expected on a freshly built table. To rehearse the full erasure path, set spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled=false on a copy only, and note in GOVERNANCE.md that this override never runs in production 10 Erasure "succeeds" but the rider is still queryable DELETE ran without VACUUM, or VACUUM ran with a retention window that still covers the pre-delete version Run both; then prove it with DESCRIBE HISTORY and a failed VERSION AS OF read. A deletion you cannot prove is not a deletion 11 Freshness check passes on a table nobody has written to in days _ingested_at is set by the transform, and the transform re-ran over unchanged data Freshness must measure the source watermark (MAX(pickup_ts) or the Kafka offset lag), not the write timestamp. A pipeline that re-processes stale data on schedule looks perfectly fresh 12 Data docs render but show an old run GX writes docs to uncommitted/; the browser cached the previous index.html Re-run with --build-docs and hard-refresh. Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. docs.title: 1. Why this lab matters
docs.text:
The course question: "What happens to Masar's AI system if THIS part of the data platform fails?"

Every component you need already exists. You have exactly-once streaming ingest (LAB-05), a quality gate that acts (LAB-06), an incremental silver model (LAB-03b) and a constrained Delta table with MERGE and time travel (LAB-04). Nothing in this lab is new logic.

What does not exist yet is the guarantee that they run in the right order, exactly, and recoverably. That is what orchestration is. It is not a scheduler.

If this fails… The AI system experiences… No declared dependency silver >> gold build_trip_features runs at 02:07 while build_silver_trips is still merging at 02:09. Gold builds from a half-written silver snapshot — Delta gives you a consistent snapshot, so no error is raised. The feature table is simply missing the last two hours of trips. Every night. Non-idempotent gold (INSERT instead of replaceWhere/MERGE) The DAG retries a transient S3 timeout. gold.zone_hourly_demand now contains two rows for the same (city, date, hour). The BI dashboard double-counts demand, the ETA model's rolling_zone_demand_15m doubles, and surge pricing fires at 2× on a normal Tuesday. Gold built directly from bronze The quality gate is bypassed. The 120 negative fares and the null keys that LAB-06 blocked flow straight into the feature table. Every control you built is decorative. No recovery path build_silver fails at 02:30. Someone re-runs "the parts that failed" by hand at 09:00, in a remembered order, having skipped the gate because "it passed yesterday." This is the twelve-notebooks failure, and it produces wrong numbers with no error and no alert. Over-partitioned gold gold.driver_daily partitioned by (city, date, driver_id) produces 14,000 directories per day. The dashboard query that used to take 800 ms now takes 40 s, and the M2 object-storage request bill triples.

The thesis of this lab is Task 5: break the pipeline on purpose, then recover it with a full re-run and prove the end state is identical. If a full re-run is safe, every operational problem becomes tractable. If it is not, every operational problem becomes an archaeology project.

docs.title: Task 1 — Wire the DAG (15 min)
docs.text:
# orchestration/dags/masar_medallion.py
"""The Masar Mini-Lakehouse as one dependency-ordered, idempotent DAG.

    land_bronze ─► quality_gate ─► build_silver ─┬─► gold_zone_hourly_demand ─┐
                                                 ├─► gold_driver_daily        ├─► optimize_vacuum
                                                 └─► gold_trip_features ──────┘

Three properties make this production-grade, and all three were built in
earlier modules:
  * dependency ordering  — gold cannot start until silver's task SUCCEEDS
  * idempotency          — every task is safe to re-run; retries cannot corrupt
  * atomicity per task   — a failed task leaves no half-written Delta table
Together they mean a full re-run recovers from ANY failure with no duplicates.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
import pendulum

from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator

from masar.ingest.land_bronze import land_trips, land_drivers, land_vehicles, land_zones
from masar.quality.gate import gate_and_promote_task
from masar.quality.observe import observability_task
from masar.transform.build_silver import build_silver_trips
from masar.transform.build_gold import (build_zone_hourly_demand,
                                        build_driver_daily,
                                        build_trip_features)
from masar.delta.maintain import optimize_and_vacuum

RIYADH = pendulum.timezone("Asia/Riyadh")

default_args = {
    "owner": "masar-data-platform",
    "retries": 2,
    "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=2),
    "retry_exponential_backoff": True,
    "execution_timeout": timedelta(minutes=45),
    "depends_on_past": False,     # each run is independent BECAUSE tasks are idempotent
}

with DAG(
    dag_id="masar_medallion",
    description="Masar Mini-Lakehouse: bronze -> gate -> silver -> gold -> maintain",
    schedule="0 2 * * *",                    # nightly 02:00 Asia/Riyadh
    start_date=datetime(2026, 6, 1, tzinfo=RIYADH),
    catchup=False,                           # backfills are explicit and parameterised
    max_active_runs=1,                       # no two runs mutating silver concurrently
    default_args=default_args,
    tags=["masar", "lakehouse", "medallion"],
    params={"run_date": "{{ ds }}", "lookback_days": 3},
) as dag:

    t_land = PythonOperator(
        task_id="land_bronze",
        python_callable=lambda **ctx: (land_trips(**ctx), land_drivers(**ctx),
                                       land_vehicles(**ctx), land_zones(**ctx)),
    )

    # LAB-06's gate. On FAIL_FAST it raises GateBlocked -> this task fails ->
    # every downstream task is skipped. That is the dependency doing its job.
    t_gate = PythonOperator(task_id="quality_gate",
                            python_callable=gate_and_promote_task)

    t_silver = PythonOperator(task_id="build_silver",
                              python_callable=build_silver_trips)

    t_obs = PythonOperator(task_id="observability",
                           python_callable=observability_task)

    t_demand = PythonOperator(task_id="gold_zone_hourly_demand",
                              python_callable=build_zone_hourly_demand)
    t_driver = PythonOperator(task_id="gold_driver_daily",
                              python_callable=build_driver_daily)
    t_feats = PythonOperator(task_id="gold_trip_features",
                             python_callable=build_trip_features)

    t_maint = PythonOperator(task_id="optimize_vacuum",
                             python_callable=optimize_and_vacuum)

    # The single most important line in this file.
    t_land >> t_gate >> t_silver >> t_obs >> [t_demand, t_driver, t_feats] >> t_maint

Verify the graph before running anything:

airflow dags list | grep masar
airflow tasks list masar_medallion --tree
airflow dags test masar_medallion 2026-06-30       # parse + dry structure check

docs.title: Task 2 — Idempotent BI marts with documented grain (20 min)
docs.text:
Grain is a contract. Write it in the docstring, enforce it in the write, and assert it in a test. All three, every time.

# src/masar/transform/build_gold.py
"""Gold marts and the feature table. Pure, idempotent transforms from silver.

Grain is DOCUMENTED in each docstring and ENFORCED by the write strategy:
  * partition overwrite (replaceWhere) for date-partitioned rebuilds
  * MERGE on the grain key where a partition boundary does not align
Either way, running a task twice must produce byte-identical row counts.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from masar.spark import get_spark

SILVER_TRIPS     = "./lakehouse/silver/trips"
SILVER_POSITIONS = "./lakehouse/silver/vehicle_positions"
SILVER_DRIVERS   = "./lakehouse/silver/drivers"
GOLD             = "./lakehouse/gold"
LOOKBACK_DAYS    = 3          # covers late-arriving trips (LAB-03b's lookback)


def build_zone_hourly_demand(**_) -> None:
    """gold.zone_hourly_demand
    GRAIN : exactly one row per (city, pickup_zone_id, date, hour)
    SOURCE: silver.trips  (never bronze — the gate is upstream of silver)
    WRITE : replaceWhere on the last LOOKBACK_DAYS days => idempotent rebuild
    """
    spark = get_spark()
    trips = spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER_TRIPS)

    demand = (trips
        .filter(F.col("status") == "completed")
        .withColumn("date", F.to_date("pickup_ts"))
        .withColumn("hour", F.hour("pickup_ts"))
        .filter(F.col("date") >= F.date_sub(F.current_date(), LOOKBACK_DAYS))
        .groupBy("city", "pickup_zone_id", "date", "hour")
        .agg(F.count("*").alias("trips"),
             F.countDistinct("driver_id").alias("active_drivers"),
             F.avg("fare_sar").alias("avg_fare_sar"),
             F.avg("duration_min").alias("avg_duration_min"),
             F.avg("distance_km").alias("avg_distance_km"),
             F.avg("surge_multiplier").alias("avg_surge"))
        .withColumn("_built_at", F.current_timestamp()))

    (demand.write.format("delta")
        .mode("overwrite")
        .partitionBy("date")                     # date ONLY. Not city. Not zone.
        .option("replaceWhere",
                f"date >= current_date() - INTERVAL {LOOKBACK_DAYS} DAYS")
        .option("overwriteSchema", "false")
        .save(f"{GOLD}/zone_hourly_demand"))
    _assert_grain(f"{GOLD}/zone_hourly_demand",
                  ["city", "pickup_zone_id", "date", "hour"])


def build_driver_daily(**_) -> None:
    """gold.driver_daily
    GRAIN : exactly one row per (driver_id, date)
    SOURCE: silver.trips joined to silver.drivers
    WRITE : MERGE on the grain key — the grain does not align to a single
            partition column pair cleanly across the lookback, and MERGE is
            idempotent by construction (LAB-04b).
    """
    spark = get_spark()
    trips = spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER_TRIPS)
    drivers = spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER_DRIVERS)

    daily = (trips
        .withColumn("date", F.to_date("pickup_ts"))
        .filter(F.col("date") >= F.date_sub(F.current_date(), LOOKBACK_DAYS))
        .groupBy("driver_id", "date")
        .agg(F.count("*").alias("trips"),
             F.sum(F.when(F.col("status") == "completed", 1).otherwise(0))
              .alias("trips_completed"),
             F.sum(F.when(F.col("status").startswith("cancelled"), 1).otherwise(0))
              .alias("trips_cancelled"),
             F.sum("fare_sar").alias("gross_earnings_sar"),
             F.sum("distance_km").alias("distance_km"),
             F.sum("duration_min").alias("on_trip_minutes"),
             F.avg("surge_multiplier").alias("avg_surge"))
        .join(drivers.select("driver_id", "city", "rating", "status"), "driver_id", "left")
        .withColumn("completion_rate",
                    F.round(F.col("trips_completed") / F.col("trips"), 4))
        .withColumn("_built_at", F.current_timestamp()))

    path = f"{GOLD}/driver_daily"
    if not DeltaTable.isDeltaTable(spark, path):
        daily.write.format("delta").partitionBy("date").save(path)
    else:
        (DeltaTable.forPath(spark, path).alias("t")
            .merge(daily.alias("s"), "t.driver_id = s.driver_id AND t.date = s.date")
            .whenMatchedUpdateAll()
            .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
            .execute())
    _assert_grain(path, ["driver_id", "date"])


def _assert_grain(path: str, keys: list[str]) -> None:
    """A grain assertion is a data-contract test. Failing it fails the DAG task."""
    spark = get_spark()
    df = spark.read.format("delta").load(path)
    total = df.count()
    distinct = df.select(*keys).distinct().count()
    if total != distinct:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"GRAIN VIOLATION in {path}: {total:,} rows but only {distinct:,} "
            f"distinct {keys}. The write strategy is not idempotent.")
    print(f"[gold] {path.split('/')[-1]}: {total:,} rows, grain {keys} verified")

Now prove idempotency. This is the acceptance test, not an optional extra.

python -c "from masar.transform.build_gold import build_zone_hourly_demand as f; f()"
python -m masar.tools.count --table gold.zone_hourly_demand

python -c "from masar.transform.build_gold import build_zone_hourly_demand as f; f()"
python -m masar.tools.count --table gold.zone_hourly_demand      # MUST be identical

python -c "from masar.transform.build_gold import build_driver_daily as f; f()"
python -c "from masar.transform.build_gold import build_driver_daily as f; f()"
python -m masar.tools.count --table gold.driver_daily

Expected output

[gold] zone_hourly_demand: 8,640 rows, grain ['city', 'pickup_zone_id', 'date', 'hour'] verified
table=gold.zone_hourly_demand  rows=8,640
[gold] zone_hourly_demand: 8,640 rows, grain ['city', 'pickup_zone_id', 'date', 'hour'] verified
table=gold.zone_hourly_demand  rows=8,640      <- identical. idempotent.

[gold] driver_daily: 42,612 rows, grain ['driver_id', 'date'] verified
[gold] driver_daily: 42,612 rows, grain ['driver_id', 'date'] verified
table=gold.driver_daily  rows=42,612

See the failure yourself (2 minutes). Change .mode("overwrite") to .mode("append") in build_zone_hourly_demand, run it twice, and watch _assert_grain raise GRAIN VIOLATION: 17,280 rows but only 8,640 distinct. Then revert. This is module mistake #3, and the assertion is what turns it from a silent BI bug into a failed DAG task.

docs.title: Task 3 — Point-in-time-correct gold.trip_features (15 min)
docs.text:
gold.trip_features is the platform-scale rehearsal for gold.eta_features, which you build in LAB-08. The single non-negotiable property is that no feature value may depend on information that did not exist at pickup_ts.

# src/masar/transform/build_gold.py  (continued)

def build_trip_features(**_) -> None:
    """gold.trip_features
    GRAIN : exactly one row per trip_id
    SOURCE: silver.trips + silver.vehicle_positions
    RULE  : POINT-IN-TIME CORRECT. Every window is strictly BEFORE pickup_ts.
            rangeBetween(-3600, -1) — the -1 is not cosmetic. rangeBetween(-3600, 0)
            includes the current row's own timestamp, which on ties admits trips
            that started in the same second, i.e. information from the future.
    """
    spark = get_spark()
    trips = spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER_TRIPS)
    positions = spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER_POSITIONS)

    t = (trips.filter(F.col("status") == "completed")
              .withColumn("pickup_epoch", F.col("pickup_ts").cast("long")))

    # ---- prior-hour demand in the pickup zone, strictly before this trip -----
    w_zone = (Window.partitionBy("city", "pickup_zone_id")
                    .orderBy(F.col("pickup_epoch"))
                    .rangeBetween(-3600, -1))

    # ---- the driver's completed trips in the prior 24h, strictly before ------
    w_driver = (Window.partitionBy("driver_id")
                      .orderBy(F.col("pickup_epoch"))
                      .rangeBetween(-86400, -1))

    feats = (t
        .withColumn("zone_demand_prev_hr", F.count("*").over(w_zone))
        .withColumn("zone_avg_fare_prev_hr", F.avg("fare_sar").over(w_zone))
        .withColumn("driver_trips_prev_24h", F.count("*").over(w_driver))
        .withColumn("start_hour", F.hour("pickup_ts"))
        .withColumn("day_of_week", F.dayofweek("pickup_ts"))
        .withColumn("is_night", (F.hour("pickup_ts") < 6) |
                                (F.hour("pickup_ts") >= 22))
        .select("trip_id", "city", "pickup_zone_id", "dropoff_zone_id",
                "driver_id", "vehicle_id",
                F.col("pickup_ts").alias("feature_ts"),
                "start_hour", "day_of_week", "is_night",
                "surge_multiplier",
                "zone_demand_prev_hr", "zone_avg_fare_prev_hr",
                "driver_trips_prev_24h")
        .withColumn("_feature_version", F.lit("v1"))
        .withColumn("_built_at", F.current_timestamp()))

    (feats.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite")
        .option("overwriteSchema", "false")
        .save(f"{GOLD}/trip_features"))
    _assert_grain(f"{GOLD}/trip_features", ["trip_id"])
    _assert_point_in_time()


def _assert_point_in_time() -> None:
    """Structural leakage lint: recompute one feature with an inclusive window and
    require it to DIFFER. If prior-hour and through-now agree, the window is not
    actually excluding the present."""
    spark = get_spark()
    trips = (spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER_TRIPS)
             .filter(F.col("status") == "completed")
             .withColumn("pickup_epoch", F.col("pickup_ts").cast("long")))
    strict = Window.partitionBy("city", "pickup_zone_id").orderBy("pickup_epoch").rangeBetween(-3600, -1)
    leaky = Window.partitionBy("city", "pickup_zone_id").orderBy("pickup_epoch").rangeBetween(-3600, 3600)
    cmp = (trips.withColumn("strict", F.count("*").over(strict))
                .withColumn("leaky", F.count("*").over(leaky))
                .filter(F.col("leaky") <= F.col("strict")))
    n = cmp.count()
    print(f"[lint] point-in-time: {n:,} trips where an inclusive window would not "
          f"add rows (expected: only sparse-zone edge cases)")

Spot-check one trip by hand. Do not accept the assertion as proof — verify it yourself:

python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
WITH probe AS (
  SELECT trip_id, city, pickup_zone_id, feature_ts, zone_demand_prev_hr
  FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/gold/trip_features\`
  WHERE zone_demand_prev_hr BETWEEN 8 AND 40
  ORDER BY feature_ts LIMIT 1
)
SELECT
  p.trip_id, p.feature_ts, p.zone_demand_prev_hr AS feature_value,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/trips\` s
     WHERE s.city = p.city AND s.pickup_zone_id = p.pickup_zone_id
       AND s.status = 'completed'
       AND s.pickup_ts >= p.feature_ts - INTERVAL 60 MINUTES
       AND s.pickup_ts <  p.feature_ts)                       AS recount_strictly_prior,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/trips\` s
     WHERE s.city = p.city AND s.pickup_zone_id = p.pickup_zone_id
       AND s.status = 'completed'
       AND s.pickup_ts >= p.feature_ts - INTERVAL 60 MINUTES
       AND s.pickup_ts <= p.feature_ts + INTERVAL 60 MINUTES) AS recount_if_leaking
FROM probe p"

Expected output

trip_id      feature_ts           feature_value  recount_strictly_prior  recount_if_leaking
TRP-770118   2026-06-28 07:14:33  17             17                      44

feature_value == recount_strictly_prior proves the window is correct. recount_if_leaking = 44 is what a careless rangeBetween(-3600, 3600) would have handed the model — 2.6× the true value, and 27 of those 44 trips had not happened yet. Record both numbers in MINI_LAKEHOUSE.md; you will meet this exact arithmetic again in LAB-08's leakage drill.

docs.title: Task 6 — Maintenance as a task, and document the contracts (10 min)
docs.text:
# src/masar/delta/maintain.py
"""OPTIMIZE and VACUUM as a DAG task, not a manual afterthought."""
from masar.spark import get_spark

TABLES = {
    "./lakehouse/bronze/gps_events":       ["vehicle_id", "trip_id"],
    "./lakehouse/silver/trips":            ["city", "pickup_zone_id"],
    "./lakehouse/silver/vehicle_positions":["vehicle_id"],
    "./lakehouse/gold/zone_hourly_demand": ["city", "pickup_zone_id"],
    "./lakehouse/gold/driver_daily":       ["driver_id"],
    "./lakehouse/gold/trip_features":      ["city", "pickup_zone_id"],
}
RETAIN_HOURS = 168      # 7 days. Justified in GOVERNANCE.md. Never 0.

def optimize_and_vacuum(**_) -> None:
    spark = get_spark()
    for path, zorder in TABLES.items():
        before = spark.sql(f"DESCRIBE DETAIL delta.`{path}`").collect()[0]["numFiles"]
        spark.sql(f"OPTIMIZE delta.`{path}` ZORDER BY ({', '.join(zorder)})")
        spark.sql(f"VACUUM delta.`{path}` RETAIN {RETAIN_HOURS} HOURS")
        after = spark.sql(f"DESCRIBE DETAIL delta.`{path}`").collect()[0]["numFiles"]
        print(f"[maintain] {path}: numFiles {before} -> {after}")

docs.title: 4. Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
• masar_medallion parses, and airflow tasks list --tree shows land >> gate >> silver >> observability >> [3 gold tasks] >> maintain.
  • No gold task reads from bronze. Every gold source is silver.*.
  • gold.zone_hourly_demand at grain (city, pickup_zone_id, date, hour), gold.driver_daily at (driver_id, date), gold.trip_features at (trip_id) — each documented and asserted by _assert_grain.
  • Every gold task run twice produces identical row counts and checksums.
  • gold.trip_features uses rangeBetween(-3600, -1) (strictly prior) and the manual spot-check confirms feature_value == recount_strictly_prior.
  • make pipeline runs the entire medallion with one command and writes a timestamped log.
  • Injected failure in build_silver causes all downstream tasks to be skipped (UPSTREAM_FAILED), and gold is provably unchanged.
  • A full re-run after the fix reproduces the exact pre-failure state (diff of the snapshots is empty).
  • optimize_and_vacuum runs as the terminal DAG task, with numFiles before/after recorded and RETAIN 168 HOURS.
  • MINI_LAKEHOUSE.md documents every table's layer, grain, source, write strategy and contract enforcement point.
  • max_active_runs=1 is set, and you can explain why.

docs.title: 5. Self-check questions
docs.text:
Q1. Your gold tasks are siblings running in parallel. build_driver_daily takes 24 s and build_trip_features takes 34 s. Could optimize_vacuum start at 25 s?

Answer No. `[t_demand, t_driver, t_feats] >> t_maint` creates an edge from *each* gold task to `t_maint`, and Airflow's default trigger rule is `all_success` — every upstream task must have succeeded. `t_maint` starts when the slowest sibling finishes, at 34 s. This matters beyond scheduling. If `build_trip_features` fails, `optimize_vacuum` is skipped, so the maintenance job never runs against a table that is mid-rebuild. Had you used `trigger_rule="all_done"` to "make sure maintenance always runs," you would be compacting and vacuuming a table whose build just failed — potentially removing files a retry needs. The default trigger rule is a safety property, not a convenience.

Q2. Why is catchup=False combined with an explicit pipeline-backfill target better than catchup=True?

Answer `catchup=True` means that if the DAG is paused for a week and then unpaused, Airflow immediately schedules seven runs. They may execute concurrently (bounded only by `max_active_runs`), all mutating the same `silver.trips` and gold tables, in an order determined by the scheduler rather than by you. On a laptop this is an OOM; in production it is a stampede against shared storage. `catchup=False` plus a parameterised backfill makes reprocessing an **explicit decision with a stated range**, run serially, observable, and reviewable. It also forces you to prove idempotency across the window — which is what the stretch goal asks for. The general principle: a pipeline should never do something expensive and destructive because of a scheduling side effect. Backfills are operations, and operations should be commands.

Q3. build_zone_hourly_demand uses replaceWhere on a 3-day window. What happens to a trip that arrives 5 days late?

Answer It lands in `silver.trips` correctly — the MERGE is keyed on `trip_id` and has no date restriction — but it is **silently absent from `gold.zone_hourly_demand`**, because the aggregate only rebuilds the last 3 days and that trip's date falls outside the rebuild window. The gold mart is now permanently wrong for that date, and nothing raises. Three responses, in order of increasing cost: (1) size the lookback to your observed late-arrival p99 rather than to a round number — measure `pickup_ts` vs `_ingested_at` in `bronze.trips` and pick from data; (2) emit a **volume reconciliation** check (LAB-06) comparing `SUM(trips)` in the mart against `COUNT(*)` in silver per date, which turns a silent gap into an alert; (3) trigger a targeted backfill for any date whose silver row count changed since the last mart build. Note that the same lookback trade-off applies to the streaming watermark from LAB-05 — this is the same decision at a different time scale.

Q4. A colleague says "re-running land_bronze appends the same file again, so a full re-run must duplicate bronze." Are they right?

Answer They are right about the mechanism and wrong about the consequence — and the distinction is the whole point of Task 5. `land_bronze` does append. Bronze may well grow on a re-run, and that is acceptable by design: bronze is append-only, immutable, and carries `_batch_id` and `_source_file` precisely so that a duplicate landing is *identifiable*. Bronze's contract is "everything we ever received," not "one row per real-world event." The guarantee lives one layer down. The gate promotes into `silver.trips` with a **MERGE on `trip_id`**, and re-applying a matched row updates it to the same values — a no-op. So no matter how many times bronze receives the same trip, silver holds exactly one row for it, and every gold table derives from silver. The duplication stops at the first keyed write. Two caveats worth stating: the streaming bronze table additionally uses `txnAppId`/`txnVersion`, which makes even bronze idempotent per batch id; and if bronze growth is operationally undesirable, the fix is a landing-manifest check, not making the task non-re-runnable. A task you are afraid to re-run is a task you cannot recover.

Q5. Which single line in the DAG file would you defend hardest in code review, and why?

Answer `t_land >> t_gate >> t_silver >> t_obs >> [t_demand, t_driver, t_feats] >> t_maint`. Every other line configures something; this line *is* the platform's correctness guarantee. It encodes three things simultaneously: gold cannot build from unrefreshed silver (the twelve-notebooks failure), the quality gate cannot be bypassed (LAB-06's controls become structural rather than advisory), and observability runs before promotion to consumers rather than after. The specific edge to defend hardest is `t_gate >> t_silver`. Any proposal to run them in parallel "for speed," or to move the gate downstream of silver "so we can inspect what failed," destroys the guarantee that nothing unvalidated is ever readable by a consumer. The gate is upstream of the promotion or it is decoration. A close second is `max_active_runs=1`: without it, two DAG runs can MERGE into `silver.trips` concurrently, and while Delta's optimistic concurrency will keep the table *consistent*, it may fail one run with a concurrent-modification exception at 02:00 with nobody watching.

Q6. gold.trip_features uses rangeBetween(-3600, -1). Why not -3600, 0?

Answer `rangeBetween` on an ordered window is inclusive of both bounds, and the bound is a *value range over the ordering column*, not a row offset. With `orderBy(pickup_epoch)` and an upper bound of `0`, the frame includes every row whose `pickup_epoch` equals the current row's — that is, every trip that started **in the same second** in the same zone. At Masar's volumes that is not hypothetical: a busy Riyadh zone at 07:45 starts several trips per second. Those trips are, from the perspective of the trip being predicted, the future. Including them inflates `zone_demand_prev_hr` by a small amount that correlates strongly with exactly the congestion the model is trying to predict — which is the worst possible kind of leakage, because it is small enough to look like a real signal and large enough to move the metric. `-1` makes the frame end one second before the current row's timestamp, so the current second is excluded entirely. The general rule: for any point-in-time feature, the upper bound must be strictly less than the event time, and you should be able to point at the character in the code that makes it so.

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Rows 1–5 are from the module package. Rows 6–12 are additions.

# Symptom Cause Fix 1 Gold double-counts on re-run INSERT/append aggregate replaceWhere overwrite, or MERGE on the grain key; add _assert_grain 2 Gold built from stale silver Missing dependency edge Declare t_silver >> t_gold* explicitly 3 Feature leakage detected Window includes current or future rows rangeBetween(-3600, -1) — strictly prior 4 DAG import error Task callable signatures mismatch Every callable accepts **context / **_ 5 Small files on gold Over-partitioned Partition by date only; OPTIMIZE with ZORDER on the filter columns 6 Broken DAG: No module named 'masar' Airflow's DAG parser runs in a process that does not have the project on PYTHONPATH export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/src:$PYTHONPATH before airflow db migrate, or pip install -e .. Do not sys.path.append inside the DAG file — DAG files are parsed constantly and should stay side-effect-free 7 replaceWhere fails: Data written out does not match replaceWhere The DataFrame contains rows outside the replaceWhere predicate — typically because the aggregate was not filtered to the same lookback window Filter the source to the same predicate you pass to replaceWhere. The two must agree exactly; Delta is protecting you from a partial overwrite 8 ConcurrentAppendException on silver.trips Two DAG runs, or a DAG run and the LAB-05 streaming job, writing the same table Set max_active_runs=1; keep streaming writes to bronze.* and silver.vehicle_positions only. Never MERGE into a table a stream is appending to without partition-level isolation 9 airflow dags test succeeds but make pipeline writes nothing airflow dags test runs tasks in-process with the DAG's environment; the Makefile shell lacks AIRFLOW_HOME or the venv Export AIRFLOW_HOME inside the Makefile recipe (as shown) — each recipe line is a fresh shell 10 optimize_vacuum errors Cannot vacuum with retention less than 168 hours Someone lowered RETAIN_HOURS below the configured safety threshold Do not disable retentionDurationCheck. Raise the value, and if a shorter window is genuinely required, document the justification in GOVERNANCE.md — the rubric flags RETAIN 0 as an anti-pattern 11 _assert_grain passes locally, fails in the DAG The DAG runs with a different run_date, so the lookback window covers a date with duplicate source rows that your manual run did not touch Good — the assertion is doing its job. Investigate the duplicate at source rather than relaxing the assertion. This is exactly the class of bug a grain contract exists to catch 12 Pipeline takes 20+ minutes on a laptop Every task starts its own SparkSession, paying ~15 s JVM startup each, and the default shuffle partitions (200) are absurd for this data size Reuse one session via masar.spark.get_spark()'s singleton; set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=8 for local runs. Teach the concept at cloud scale, run it at laptop scale (M2) 13 gold.driver_daily MERGE is slower each night The MERGE scans the whole target because the join condition has no partition predicate Add AND t.date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 3 DAYS to the merge condition so Delta can prune partitions. Measure with DESCRIBE HISTORY's operationMetrics.numTargetFilesScanned

docs.title: 7. Stretch goals
docs.text:
1. Seven-day backfill. Run make pipeline-backfill FROM=2026-06-24 TO=2026-06-30, then prove the result is byte-identical to seven consecutive incremental runs. Any divergence is a latent non-idempotency you have not found yet.
  2. Data-contract test that fails the DAG. Promote _assert_grain into a first-class Airflow task using trigger_rule="all_success" after each gold build, and add contract assertions for freshness (MAX(date) = run_date) and non-emptiness. A contract that is not tested is a comment.
  3. Run metadata table. Emit per-task {dag_run_id, task_id, rows_in, rows_out, duration_s, task_started_at} into ./lakehouse/governance/pipeline_runs. You now have cost attribution and a performance baseline — and the raw material for the M2 benchmark table.
  4. Sensor instead of schedule. Replace the land_bronze schedule trigger with a file sensor on data/raw/trips_{{ ds }}.csv. Discuss what this buys (no run on a day the feed is late, instead of a run that silently processes nothing) and what it costs (a DAG that can hang forever without a timeout).
  5. Convert the gold tasks to a TaskGroup and parameterise them over cities, so gold_zone_hourly_demand fans out to five parallel tasks. Measure whether it is faster; on a laptop it will not be, and understanding why — the shuffle is not the bottleneck, JVM startup is — is the M2 lesson applied to your own pipeline.

Everything LAB-08 serves is built here. gold.zone_hourly_demand is the mart against which the BI star schema must reconcile — if SUM(fare_sar) over gold.fact_trip does not equal the mart's revenue for the same day, one of the two is wrong and LAB-08 will make you find out which. gold.trip_features is the rehearsal for gold.eta_features, and the rangeBetween(-3600, -1) decision you made in Task 3 is the same decision you will be graded on in LAB-08's leakage drill — where two of the thirteen columns leak in exactly this way.

docs.title: 1. Why this lab matters
docs.text:
The course question: "What happens to Masar's AI system if THIS part of the data platform fails?"

Five days of work arrive here. Every table you built exists to be consumed by exactly two things: the ETA model that quotes a rider's arrival time, and the operations dashboard the leadership reviews at 08:00. This is the layer where a data platform either pays for itself or quietly poisons the thing it was built to serve.

The failure mode of this layer is unique in the course: it does not look like a failure. Streaming failures produce duplicate counts you can see. Quality failures produce quarantine rows you can count. Serving failures produce a model that scores 0.94 R² in the notebook and misses the ETA by four minutes in the app.

If this fails… The AI system experiences… Feature leakage The model trains on distance_km — the metered distance, known only when the trip ends. Offline R² 0.94. At inference the value does not exist, so the serving code substitutes the planned route distance, or a zero, or the mean. Live MAE is 4× the offline number and nobody can explain why. Offline ≠ online The training pipeline computes rolling_zone_demand_15m from silver.vehicle_positions; the inference service recomputes it from a Kafka consumer with a different window. The model was trained on one distribution and scored on another. This is training/serving skew, and it degrades silently and permanently. Stale online features driver_recent_trip_count is refreshed nightly into Redis. At 19:00 on a Thursday the value is 19 hours old. A driver who has completed 11 trips today reads as having completed 0. The model treats an exhausted driver as a fresh one. Non-conformed dimensions Two dim_date tables exist because someone needed a fiscal calendar. The revenue dashboard and the demand dashboard disagree by 3%, and the M1 two-tier divergence you spent Day 1 diagnosing has been rebuilt inside your own gold layer. PII at the boundary rider_id reaches a shared dashboard and the Redis keyspace. Every dashboard viewer becomes a processor of personal data. This is a PDPL finding, and unlike the others it has a legal consequence rather than a metric one.

The lab has two halves that must both be delivered: the BI star and the AI product, derived from the same governed silver so that the analyst's "trips per zone" and the model's demand feature cannot silently disagree. Between them sits Task 3, the leakage drill, which is mandatory.

docs.title: Task 1 — Build the BI star schema (12 min)
docs.text:
Five tables, exactly as named in CONVENTIONS. Conformed means one dim_date and one dim_driver serve every fact in the platform — that is what makes numbers reconcile across dashboards.

-- dbt/masar/models/marts/gold/dim_date.sql
{{ config(materialized='table', file_format='delta') }}
-- GRAIN: one row per calendar date. THE conformed date dimension. There is
-- exactly one of these in the platform, forever.
with spine as (
  select explode(sequence(date('2026-01-01'), date('2026-12-31'), interval 1 day)) as date
)
select
    cast(date_format(date, 'yyyyMMdd') as int)          as date_key,
    date                                                as full_date,
    year(date)                                          as year,
    quarter(date)                                       as quarter,
    month(date)                                         as month,
    date_format(date, 'MMMM')                           as month_name_en,
    day(date)                                           as day_of_month,
    dayofweek(date)                                     as day_of_week,
    date_format(date, 'EEEE')                           as day_name_en,
    -- KSA working week: Sunday..Thursday. Getting this wrong silently
    -- shifts every "weekend demand" analysis by two days.
    case when dayofweek(date) in (6, 7) then true else false end as is_weekend,
    weekofyear(date)                                    as week_of_year
from spine

-- dbt/masar/models/marts/gold/dim_driver.sql
{{ config(materialized='table', file_format='delta') }}
-- GRAIN: one row per driver_id (type-1; current attributes only).
-- PDPL: national_id_hash and phone_hash are NOT exposed. Classification from
-- GOVERNANCE.md drives this select list, not convenience.
select
    d.driver_id                                         as driver_key,
    d.driver_id,
    d.full_name_en,
    d.city,
    d.hire_date,
    d.rating,
    d.status,
    datediff(current_date(), d.hire_date)               as tenure_days,
    case when datediff(current_date(), d.hire_date) < 90 then 'new'
         when datediff(current_date(), d.hire_date) < 365 then 'established'
         else 'veteran' end                             as tenure_band
from {{ ref('silver_drivers') }} d

-- dbt/masar/models/marts/gold/dim_vehicle.sql
{{ config(materialized='table', file_format='delta') }}
-- GRAIN: one row per vehicle_id.
select
    v.vehicle_id                                        as vehicle_key,
    v.vehicle_id,
    v.plate_hash,                       -- already pseudonymised at source
    v.make, v.model, v.model_year, v.capacity, v.fuel_type, v.city,
    year(current_date()) - v.model_year                 as vehicle_age_years
from {{ ref('stg_vehicles') }} v

-- dbt/masar/models/marts/gold/dim_zone.sql
{{ config(materialized='table', file_format='delta') }}
-- GRAIN: one row per zone_id. Bilingual labels; centroid at zone resolution
-- (never per-trip coordinates — that is the PDPL minimisation line).
select
    z.zone_id                                           as zone_key,
    z.zone_id, z.zone_name_en, z.zone_name_ar,
    z.city, z.district, z.centroid_lat, z.centroid_lon
from {{ ref('stg_zones') }} z

-- dbt/masar/models/marts/gold/fact_trip.sql
{{ config(materialized='incremental', file_format='delta',
          unique_key='trip_id',
          incremental_strategy='merge',
          partition_by=['pickup_date']) }}
-- GRAIN: exactly one row per trip_id.
-- PDPL: rider_id is NOT selected. It never crosses the serving boundary.
--       A pseudonym is provided for cohort analysis instead.
select
    t.trip_id,
    cast(date_format(t.pickup_ts, 'yyyyMMdd') as int)   as date_key,
    t.driver_id                                         as driver_key,
    t.vehicle_id                                        as vehicle_key,
    t.pickup_zone_id                                    as pickup_zone_key,
    t.dropoff_zone_id                                   as dropoff_zone_key,
    sha2(t.rider_id, 256)                               as rider_pseudonym,
    to_date(t.pickup_ts)                                as pickup_date,
    t.pickup_ts, t.dropoff_ts, t.city, t.payment_type, t.status,
    -- measures
    t.fare_sar, t.distance_km, t.duration_min, t.surge_multiplier,
    round(t.fare_sar / nullif(t.distance_km, 0), 3)     as fare_per_km_sar
from {{ ref('silver_trips') }} t
where t.status = 'completed'
{% if is_incremental() %}
  and to_date(t.pickup_ts) >= current_date() - interval 3 days
{% endif %}

cd dbt/masar && dbt run --select marts.gold && dbt test --select marts.gold && cd -

Now the check that matters — reconciliation against LAB-07's mart:

python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
WITH star AS (
  SELECT d.full_date AS date, f.city,
         ROUND(SUM(f.fare_sar), 2) AS revenue_sar, COUNT(*) AS trips
  FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/gold/fact_trip\` f
  JOIN delta.\`./lakehouse/gold/dim_date\`  d ON f.date_key = d.date_key
  GROUP BY 1, 2),
mart AS (
  SELECT date, city,
         ROUND(SUM(trips * avg_fare_sar), 2) AS revenue_sar, SUM(trips) AS trips
  FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/gold/zone_hourly_demand\`
  GROUP BY 1, 2)
SELECT s.date, s.city, s.trips AS star_trips, m.trips AS mart_trips,
       s.revenue_sar AS star_rev, m.revenue_sar AS mart_rev,
       ROUND(ABS(s.revenue_sar - m.revenue_sar) / m.revenue_sar, 5) AS rel_diff
FROM star s JOIN mart m ON s.date = m.date AND s.city = m.city
ORDER BY rel_diff DESC LIMIT 5"

2026-06-30  Jeddah  11,880      11,880      455,109.60  455,109.60  0.00000
2026-06-30  Dammam   6,412       6,412      238,201.44  238,201.44  0.00000
2026-06-29  Riyadh  17,996      17,996      722,110.05  722,110.10  0.00000
2026-06-28  Mecca    4,118       4,118      160,988.22  160,988.22  0.00000

rel_diff = 0 across the board. Both numbers descend from the same silver.trips through the same gate. If yours does not reconcile, do not adjust a number — find which of the two paths filtered differently (status = 'completed' is the usual culprit).

docs.title: Task 2 — Build gold.eta_features (10 min)
docs.text:
The AI product. Thirteen columns, exactly as specified in CONVENTIONS — no additions, no omissions.

# src/masar/transform/build_eta_features.py
"""gold.eta_features — the AI product.

GRAIN : exactly one row per trip_id
COLUMNS (CONVENTIONS.md, exact): trip_id, pickup_zone_id, dropoff_zone_id,
  hour_of_day, day_of_week, rolling_zone_demand_15m, rolling_avg_speed_10m,
  driver_recent_trip_count, weather_condition, distance_km,
  historical_route_duration, feature_ts, label_actual_duration_min

WARNING — THIS FILE SHIPS WITH DELIBERATE DEFECTS.
Four of these columns are computed in a way that leaks, is stale, or does not
exist at inference time. Task 3 is where you find them. Do not read the
solution guide first; the drill only works if you classify before you are told.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window
from masar.spark import get_spark

SILVER_TRIPS     = "./lakehouse/silver/trips"
SILVER_POSITIONS = "./lakehouse/silver/vehicle_positions"
WEATHER          = "data/raw/weather_hourly.csv"
OUT              = "./lakehouse/gold/eta_features"


def build(**_) -> None:
    spark = get_spark("masar-eta-features")
    trips = (spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER_TRIPS)
             .filter(F.col("status") == "completed")
             .withColumn("pickup_epoch", F.col("pickup_ts").cast("long")))
    pos = spark.read.format("delta").load(SILVER_POSITIONS)
    weather = (spark.read.option("header", True).option("inferSchema", True).csv(WEATHER)
               .withColumn("hour_ts", F.to_timestamp("hour_ts")))

    # --- (A) rolling zone demand, 15 minutes -------------------------------
    w_demand = (Window.partitionBy("city", "pickup_zone_id")
                      .orderBy("pickup_epoch")
                      .rangeBetween(-450, 450))          # <-- inspect this
    # --- (B) driver recent trip count ---------------------------------------
    w_driver = (Window.partitionBy("driver_id")
                      .orderBy("pickup_epoch")
                      .rangeBetween(-86400, 0))          # <-- and this
    # --- (C) historical route duration --------------------------------------
    w_route = (Window.partitionBy("pickup_zone_id", "dropoff_zone_id")
                     .orderBy("pickup_epoch")
                     .rangeBetween(-2592000, -1))        # prior 30 days, strictly before

    # --- (D) rolling average speed, 10 minutes ------------------------------
    speed = (pos.groupBy("trip_id")
                .agg(F.avg("speed_kmh").alias("rolling_avg_speed_10m")))  # <-- and this

    feats = (trips
        .withColumn("rolling_zone_demand_15m", F.count("*").over(w_demand))
        .withColumn("driver_recent_trip_count", F.count("*").over(w_driver))
        .withColumn("historical_route_duration", F.avg("duration_min").over(w_route))
        .withColumn("hour_of_day", F.hour("pickup_ts"))
        .withColumn("day_of_week", F.dayofweek("pickup_ts"))
        .withColumn("feature_ts", F.col("pickup_ts"))
        .join(speed, "trip_id", "left")
        .join(weather.select(F.col("city").alias("w_city"), "hour_ts",
                             F.col("condition").alias("weather_condition")),
              (F.col("city") == F.col("w_city")) &
              (F.date_trunc("hour", F.col("pickup_ts")) == F.col("hour_ts")),
              "left")                                     # <-- and this join key
        .select(
            "trip_id", "pickup_zone_id", "dropoff_zone_id",
            "hour_of_day", "day_of_week",
            "rolling_zone_demand_15m", "rolling_avg_speed_10m",
            "driver_recent_trip_count", "weather_condition",
            "distance_km",                                 # <-- and this column
            "historical_route_duration", "feature_ts",
            F.col("duration_min").alias("label_actual_duration_min")))

    feats.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save(OUT)
    print(f"[gold] eta_features: {feats.count():,} rows, 13 columns")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    build()

python -m masar.transform.build_eta_features
python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
  SELECT * FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/gold/eta_features\` ORDER BY feature_ts LIMIT 3"

Train the baseline. Write the number down; you will need it in 20 minutes.

          driver_recent_trip_count    0.021

An R² of 0.943 on trip-duration prediction. Take thirty seconds and ask whether you believe it.

docs.title: Task 3 — THE FEATURE LEAKAGE DRILL (mandatory, 15 min)
docs.text:
Do not skip this task. Do not shorten it. If you are behind schedule, cut Task 6.

You will classify every one of the 13 columns of gold.eta_features into exactly one of four categories. Ambiguity is not permitted; if a column could be two, pick the one that would cause the worse production failure and say so in your justification.

Code Meaning The test to apply VALID The value is knowable at feature_ts, from data that existed at feature_ts, and the same value can be produced at inference time. "At the exact moment a rider taps Request, could I compute this from data already written?" STALE Computable in principle, but the value the online path will actually serve is materially older than feature_ts. The feature is right offline and out of date online. "How old is the value Redis holds at 19:00 on a Thursday?" LEAKAGE The value depends on information that did not exist at feature_ts — the current instant, the future, or the outcome itself. "Does computing this require knowing anything that happened at or after feature_ts?" UNAVAILABLE ONLINE Legitimately point-in-time correct offline, but no online path can supply it at inference latency, or the source has not landed yet. "Is there a Redis key or an API that returns this in under 20 ms, right now?"

Fill this in before reading anything else. Use LAB8_LEAKAGE.md.

# Column Classification Justification (one sentence: what is known at feature_ts, and what the code actually used) Fix 1 trip_id 2 pickup_zone_id 3 dropoff_zone_id 4 hour_of_day 5 day_of_week 6 rolling_zone_demand_15m 7 rolling_avg_speed_10m 8 driver_recent_trip_count 9 weather_condition 10 distance_km 11 historical_route_duration 12 feature_ts 13 label_actual_duration_min

Three diagnostics to run while you classify. Each one is evidence for at least one row.

# D1 — does the demand window admit trips that had not started yet?
python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
WITH probe AS (SELECT trip_id, pickup_zone_id, feature_ts, rolling_zone_demand_15m
               FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/gold/eta_features\`
               WHERE rolling_zone_demand_15m BETWEEN 10 AND 60
               ORDER BY feature_ts LIMIT 1)
SELECT p.trip_id, p.feature_ts, p.rolling_zone_demand_15m AS as_built,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/trips\` s
    WHERE s.pickup_zone_id = p.pickup_zone_id AND s.status='completed'
      AND s.pickup_ts >= p.feature_ts - INTERVAL 15 MINUTES
      AND s.pickup_ts <  p.feature_ts)                       AS strictly_prior,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/trips\` s
    WHERE s.pickup_zone_id = p.pickup_zone_id AND s.status='completed'
      AND s.pickup_ts >  p.feature_ts
      AND s.pickup_ts <= p.feature_ts + INTERVAL 7.5 MINUTES) AS from_the_future
FROM probe p"

# D2 — when were the GPS pings behind rolling_avg_speed_10m actually recorded?
python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
SELECT t.trip_id, t.pickup_ts, t.dropoff_ts,
       MIN(p.event_ts) AS first_ping, MAX(p.event_ts) AS last_ping,
       ROUND((UNIX_TIMESTAMP(MAX(p.event_ts)) - UNIX_TIMESTAMP(t.pickup_ts))/60.0, 1)
         AS minutes_after_pickup
FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/trips\` t
JOIN delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/vehicle_positions\` p ON p.trip_id = t.trip_id
GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY t.pickup_ts LIMIT 3"

# D3 — correlation of each feature with the label. A near-perfect one is a confession.
python -m masar.serve.train_eta --corr-only --features gold.eta_features

Expected diagnostic output

D1:
trip_id     feature_ts           as_built  strictly_prior  from_the_future
TRP-770118  2026-06-28 07:14:33  31        14              17

D2:
trip_id     pickup_ts            dropoff_ts           first_ping           last_ping            minutes_after_pickup
TRP-770118  2026-06-28 07:14:33  2026-06-28 07:36:10  2026-06-28 07:14:41  2026-06-28 07:36:02  21.5
TRP-770119  2026-06-28 07:14:51  2026-06-28 07:29:04  2026-06-28 07:15:02  2026-06-28 07:28:58  14.1
TRP-770120  2026-06-28 07:15:02  2026-06-28 07:52:47  2026-06-28 07:15:12  2026-06-28 07:52:39  37.7

D3: pearson r with label_actual_duration_min
  distance_km                 0.9471
  rolling_avg_speed_10m      -0.7218
  historical_route_duration   0.5140
  rolling_zone_demand_15m     0.2883
  driver_recent_trip_count    0.0412
  hour_of_day                 0.1109

Read D1 out loud: 17 of the 31 trips counted in that feature had not started yet. Read D2: the last ping feeding rolling_avg_speed_10m was recorded 21.5 minutes after pickup — that is, after the trip ended. Read D3: a feature correlating 0.947 with the label is not a feature.

Now fix them. For each column you marked LEAKAGE, STALE or UNAVAILABLE ONLINE, apply a fix that keeps the column name (the contract is fixed) and changes only how it is computed. Then retrain:

python -m masar.transform.build_eta_features --fixed
python -m masar.serve.train_eta --features gold.eta_features --split time --test-days 2

Expected output after the fix

[train] rows=42,038  train=31,522  test=10,516
[train] R2  = 0.712     (was 0.943)
[train] MAE = 4.58 min  (was 1.81 min)
[train] top features by gain:
          historical_route_duration   0.381
          planned_distance_km         0.244   # distance_km, recomputed from the route
          rolling_zone_demand_15m     0.171
          rolling_avg_speed_10m       0.118

R² fell from 0.943 to 0.712. MAE more than doubled. This is the correct outcome and you should be pleased. The first number was never real; it was the model reading the answer. The second number is what the platform can actually deliver at 07:14:33 with the data that exists at 07:14:33 — and it is the number that will hold up live. Record both, and the delta, in LAB8_NOTES.md.

docs.title: Task 4 — Materialise online and prove offline == online (10 min)
docs.text:
The rule: copy the value, never recompute it. Any online path that re-derives a feature is skew by construction.

# src/masar/serve/materialize_online.py
"""Materialise the latest zone-level feature slice into Redis.

Keyspace (CONVENTIONS.md):  masar:features:zone:{zone_id}

Values are COPIED from gold.eta_features. There is no feature logic in this
file and there must never be any — the moment this file computes something,
offline and online can disagree.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import json, redis
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window
from masar.spark import get_spark

GOLD = "./lakehouse/gold/eta_features"
KEY  = "masar:features:zone:{zone_id}"

# Only columns that are (a) zone-grained and (b) safe to serve. The label and
# every trip-grained column are excluded — see GOVERNANCE.md and LAB8_LEAKAGE.md.
ONLINE_COLUMNS = ["rolling_zone_demand_15m", "rolling_avg_speed_10m",
                  "historical_route_duration", "weather_condition"]


def materialize(feature_version: str = "v2") -> int:
    spark = get_spark("masar-materialize-online")
    feats = spark.read.format("delta").load(GOLD)

    w = Window.partitionBy("pickup_zone_id").orderBy(F.col("feature_ts").desc())
    latest = (feats.withColumn("_rn", F.row_number().over(w))
                   .filter("_rn = 1")
                   .select("pickup_zone_id", "feature_ts", *ONLINE_COLUMNS))

    r = redis.Redis(host="localhost", port=6379, decode_responses=True)
    pipe, n = r.pipeline(), 0
    for row in latest.collect():
        payload = {c: row[c] for c in ONLINE_COLUMNS}
        payload["feature_ts"] = row["feature_ts"].isoformat()
        payload["_feature_version"] = feature_version
        pipe.set(KEY.format(zone_id=row["pickup_zone_id"]), json.dumps(payload))
        n += 1
    pipe.execute()
    print(f"[serve] materialised {n} zone keys to redis under masar:features:zone:*")
    return n

# src/masar/serve/consistency_check.py
"""Offline == online. Compare EVERY key, not a spot check.

This is the test the capstone extension asks you to wire into CI. A serving
layer that is not continuously proven consistent is not consistent; it is
merely untested.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import json, redis
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window
from masar.spark import get_spark
from masar.serve.materialize_online import GOLD, KEY, ONLINE_COLUMNS

TOL = 1e-6

def check() -> int:
    spark = get_spark("masar-consistency-check")
    w = Window.partitionBy("pickup_zone_id").orderBy(F.col("feature_ts").desc())
    offline = {r["pickup_zone_id"]: r for r in
               (spark.read.format("delta").load(GOLD)
                .withColumn("_rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("_rn = 1")
                .select("pickup_zone_id", "feature_ts", *ONLINE_COLUMNS).collect())}

    r = redis.Redis(host="localhost", port=6379, decode_responses=True)
    mismatches = []
    for zone_id, off in offline.items():
        raw = r.get(KEY.format(zone_id=zone_id))
        if raw is None:
            mismatches.append((zone_id, "MISSING_ONLINE", None, None)); continue
        on = json.loads(raw)
        for c in ONLINE_COLUMNS:
            ov, nv = off[c], on.get(c)
            same = (ov == nv) if isinstance(ov, str) else (
                ov is not None and nv is not None and abs(float(ov) - float(nv)) <= TOL)
            if not same:
                mismatches.append((zone_id, c, ov, nv))

    print(f"[consistency] zones checked : {len(offline)}")
    print(f"[consistency] columns/zone  : {len(ONLINE_COLUMNS)}")
    print(f"[consistency] mismatches    : {len(mismatches)}")
    for m in mismatches[:10]:
        print(f"[consistency]   MISMATCH zone={m[0]} col={m[1]} offline={m[2]} online={m[3]}")
    if mismatches:
        raise SystemExit(1)
    print("[consistency] PASS — offline == online for every zone and every column")
    return 0

python -m masar.serve.materialize_online
docker compose exec redis redis-cli GET "masar:features:zone:ZN-RUH-014"
python -m masar.serve.consistency_check

Expected output

$ python -m masar.serve.materialize_online
[serve] materialised 412 zone keys to redis under masar:features:zone:*

$ redis-cli GET "masar:features:zone:ZN-RUH-014"
{"rolling_zone_demand_15m": 14, "rolling_avg_speed_10m": 28.4,
 "historical_route_duration": 17.62, "weather_condition": "clear",
 "feature_ts": "2026-06-30T23:51:08", "_feature_version": "v2"}

$ python -m masar.serve.consistency_check
[consistency] zones checked : 412
[consistency] columns/zone  : 4
[consistency] mismatches    : 0
[consistency] PASS — offline == online for every zone and every column

Now break it deliberately and confirm the check catches it:

docker compose exec redis redis-cli SET "masar:features:zone:ZN-RUH-014" \
  '{"rolling_zone_demand_15m": 99, "rolling_avg_speed_10m": 28.4, "historical_route_duration": 17.62, "weather_condition": "clear", "feature_ts": "2026-06-30T23:51:08", "_feature_version": "v2"}'
python -m masar.serve.consistency_check ; echo "exit=$?"
python -m masar.serve.materialize_online   # restore

[consistency] mismatches    : 1
[consistency]   MISMATCH zone=ZN-RUH-014 col=rolling_zone_demand_15m offline=14 online=99
exit=1

A consistency check that has never failed is a check you have not tested.
