docs.title: 4. Acceptance criteria
docs.text:
BI product - [ ] All five star tables exist with the exact CONVENTIONS names: gold.fact_trip, gold.dim_driver, gold.dim_vehicle, gold.dim_zone, gold.dim_date. - [ ] gold.fact_trip is at grain one row per trip_id, built incrementally with merge on trip_id. - [ ] Exactly one dim_date and one dim_driver exist in the platform — conformed, shared, no fiscal variant. - [ ] Star revenue reconciles with gold.zone_hourly_demand at rel_diff = 0. - [ ] dim_date.is_weekend uses the KSA working week (Friday–Saturday weekend).

AI product - [ ] gold.eta_features has exactly the 13 CONVENTIONS columns — no more, no fewer, correctly named. - [ ] Grain is one row per trip_id. - [ ] Every column classified in LAB8_LEAKAGE.md into exactly one of VALID / STALE / LEAKAGE / UNAVAILABLE ONLINE, each with a written justification and a fix. - [ ] Every LEAKAGE, STALE and UNAVAILABLE ONLINE column is fixed, keeping the column name. - [ ] Both metrics recorded: pre-fix (inflated) and post-fix (honest), with the delta and a one-paragraph explanation of why the drop is the correct result.

Serving - [ ] Redis populated under the exact keyspace masar:features:zone:{zone_id}. - [ ] consistency_check passes across all zones and all online columns, and has been shown to fail on an injected divergence (exit code 1). - [ ] No feature is recomputed in the online path — materialize_online.py contains zero feature logic. - [ ] pdpl_boundary_check passes: no rider_id, no raw lat/lon, no national_id_hash or phone_hash in any gold product or Redis key.

docs.title: 5. Self-check questions
docs.text:
Q1. Your fixed model scores R² 0.712. A stakeholder says the old 0.943 model was better and asks you to revert. What do you say?

Answer The 0.943 model was not better; it was measured wrong. It scored highly because `distance_km` — the *metered* distance recorded when the trip ended — correlates 0.947 with trip duration, and `rolling_avg_speed_10m` was averaged over GPS pings emitted during and after the trip. Both are outcomes of the journey, not inputs to a prediction made before it starts. Offline, the model had access to them; at 07:14:33 when a rider taps Request, neither exists. Reverting does not restore 0.943 in production — it produces 0.943 on a report and roughly the same live error as the fixed model, or worse, because the serving code must invent substitute values for the missing columns and the model was trained to trust them heavily. The concrete framing for the stakeholder: *the honest model tells you it will miss by about 4.6 minutes; the leaking model tells you it will miss by 1.8 and then misses by 5.* The second is more expensive precisely because you believed it. The right response to a disappointing honest number is better features, not a restored fiction.

Q2. Why is dropoff_zone_id VALID while distance_km is LEAKAGE? Both describe the destination.

Answer Because of *when the value is fixed*, not what it describes. In Masar's booking flow the rider states a destination before requesting, so `dropoff_zone_id` is an **input** the platform holds at `feature_ts`. `distance_km` in `silver.trips` is the **metered** distance the vehicle actually travelled, written at `dropoff_ts` — a different quantity that happens to share a name with something knowable. The fix keeps the contract column name and changes the source: compute `distance_km` from the routing engine's planned route at booking (or, offline, as a great-circle/route estimate between zone centroids from `gold.dim_zone`). That value exists at `feature_ts`, is reproducible online, and is genuinely predictive — it just is not clairvoyant. The general lesson: this dependency is invisible in the schema. Both columns are typed and populated identically. Only knowing *when each value is written* separates them, which is why point-in-time correctness is a property of the pipeline, not of the table. Worth noting the counterfactual: if Masar allowed destination-less requests, `dropoff_zone_id` would move to UNAVAILABLE ONLINE for that segment. The classification depends on the product, not only the data.

Q3. weather_condition is point-in-time correct offline. Why is it still a problem?

Answer `data/raw/weather_hourly.csv` lands after the hour it describes. Offline, joining a 07:14 trip to the 07:00 weather row is legitimate — that hour's observation existed by the time the feature table was built. Online, at 07:14, the 07:00 row has not arrived yet. The feature is correct and unobtainable, which is the definition of UNAVAILABLE ONLINE. The distinction from LEAKAGE matters operationally. A leaking feature must be *changed*; an unavailable one must be *re-sourced*. Here the fix is to shift the join to the **last observed hour** (`hour_ts <= date_trunc('hour', feature_ts) - INTERVAL 1 HOUR`), apply the same shift in training and in materialisation, and serve it from the Redis zone key so inference reads a value rather than waiting on a file. The cost is one hour of weather staleness, which for a condition category changing on the scale of hours is acceptable — and it is now the *same* one hour offline and online, which is the property that actually matters. The failure to avoid is fixing it only in the serving path. That produces a model trained on current-hour weather and served last-hour weather: textbook training/serving skew, and invisible to every check except the consistency test.

Q4. materialize_online.py deliberately contains no feature logic. Why is that a rule rather than a style preference?

Answer Because the alternative cannot be kept correct. The moment the online path computes anything, there are two implementations of one definition, and they will diverge — not through negligence, but through ordinary maintenance. Someone widens the offline demand window from 15 to 20 minutes and does not know the online service has its own copy; someone fixes a null-handling bug in one and not the other; the two are written in different languages by different teams on different release cycles. Divergence is the default state of duplicated logic. When it diverges, the model is trained on one distribution and scored on another. This degrades accuracy continuously and silently: no error, no alert, no row-level check fires, because both values are individually valid. It is the exact failure the M8 case study describes. Copying makes divergence structurally impossible — the online value *is* the offline value, byte for byte, and `consistency_check` proves it for every key on every run. The cost is that online features are only as fresh as the last materialisation, which is a real constraint you manage with refresh cadence (a DAG task, with freshness monitoring) and by accepting STALE classification where the cadence is not enough. That is a bounded, measurable, monitorable cost. Skew is none of those things.

Q5. Both gold.fact_trip and gold.eta_features count trips. What structurally prevents them from disagreeing?

Answer They both derive from `silver.trips`, which is downstream of a single quality gate and holds exactly one row per `trip_id`. Neither reads bronze; neither applies its own cleaning. The BI aggregate and the model's demand feature are two projections of one conformed table, so a trip that the gate quarantined is absent from both, and a correction MERGEd into silver reaches both on the next DAG run. This is the answer to the Day-1 two-tier problem, and it is why the medallion contract matters more than any individual transform. In the two-tier world the warehouse had one trip count and the lake had another, and reconciling them was a permanent quarterly ritual. Here it is not a process — it is a property of the topology. Two things can still break it, and both are worth naming. First, **filter divergence**: `fact_trip` selects `status = 'completed'` and so does `build_eta_features`, but if one of them changes and the other does not, the counts drift with no error. Task 1's reconciliation query is the guard, and it belongs in CI. Second, **timing**: if the star is rebuilt at 02:30 and the feature table at 04:00, they reflect different silver snapshots. The DAG's sibling-task structure from LAB-07 is what keeps them on the same run — which is a real argument for building both gold products in one DAG rather than two.

Q6. A colleague adds driver_rating_at_trip_time from silver.drivers. Classify it before it ships.

Answer **STALE at best, LEAKAGE at worst, depending on how `silver.drivers` is modelled — and as described it is LEAKAGE.** `silver.drivers` is a type-1 dimension: it holds the driver's *current* rating, overwritten on each load. Joining it to a trip from three weeks ago attaches today's rating to that trip. If the driver's rating fell because of incidents that happened after the trip, the feature encodes future information about that driver's behaviour — and since rating changes correlate with the very service quality that affects trip duration, this leaks in a way that will look like genuine signal. The name is itself the tell: `_at_trip_time` claims a point-in-time semantic the source cannot supply. Three responses. (1) Make the dimension type-2 (`valid_from`/`valid_to`) and join as-of `feature_ts` — correct, and the reason SCD2 exists. (2) Derive the rating from `gold.driver_daily` restricted to dates strictly before `feature_ts` — cheaper, and already point-in-time by construction. (3) Drop it; `driver_recent_trip_count` already carries much of the driver-quality signal without the modelling burden. Whichever you choose, this is the drill generalising: **every join to a mutable dimension is a point-in-time question**, and the schema will never ask it for you.

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Rows 1–5 are from the module package. Rows 6–13 are additions.

# Symptom Cause Fix 1 Offline metric suspiciously high Feature leakage (current or future window) Restrict every window to strictly prior; run the D1/D2/D3 diagnostics on each feature 2 Online ≠ offline value Feature recomputed in the online path Materialise/copy from gold; delete the computation from the serving code 3 Dashboards disagree Non-conformed dimension One dim_date, one dim_driver, shared by every fact 4 Raw rider_id in BI output PII not masked at the boundary sha2(rider_id, 256) as rider_pseudonym; drop the raw column from the select list 5 Slow dashboard Unoptimised gold OPTIMIZE + ZORDER on the star's filter columns (LAB-07's maintenance task) 6 consistency_check reports MISSING_ONLINE for a handful of zones Those zones had no trips in the current window, so gold.eta_features has no latest row and no Redis key was written Decide the contract: either serve a documented default with an explicit is_default flag, or let the inference service fall back and log it. Silently serving a stale key from last week is the worst of the three 7 R² rises after your "fix" A fix reintroduced leakage through a different column — commonly recomputing historical_route_duration with rangeBetween(-2592000, 0) Re-run D3. Any feature whose correlation with the label exceeds ~0.85 deserves an explicit written defence before it ships 8 redis.exceptions.ConnectionError: Connection refused from Spark but redis-cli PING works redis-cli runs inside the container; the Python client runs on the host and needs the published port Check ports: ["6379:6379"] in docker-compose.yml; use host="localhost", not the compose service name, from host code 9 fact_trip row count exceeds silver.trips completed count The incremental merge lost its unique_key, or a dimension join fanned out because a dimension has duplicate keys Assert grain on fact_trip (COUNT(*) = COUNT(DISTINCT trip_id)) and on every dim_*. A dimension with a duplicate key silently multiplies your fact table and your revenue 10 Star reconciliation shows a consistent small gap against zone_hourly_demand One side filters status = 'completed' and the other does not, or the mart's 3-day replaceWhere lookback does not cover the star's full range Align the filters explicitly and compare over the intersection of date ranges. Never "adjust" one number to match the other 11 Redis keys written but values are "NaN" or "null" historical_route_duration is null for zone pairs with no prior trips in the 30-day window, and json.dumps happily serialises None Decide and document the null contract: impute the city median with an is_imputed flag, or omit the key. The inference service must not have to guess 12 pdpl_boundary_check fails on gold.dim_zone centroid coordinates The check is matching any lat/lon column name Coordinates at zone grain are aggregate reference data, not personal data; coordinates at trip or ping grain are. Scope the assertion to grain, and record the reasoning in GOVERNANCE.md — this distinction is the whole of data minimisation 13 Time-based train/test split gives a wildly different R² than a random split Correct and expected: a random split lets the model see future trips from the same zone-hour in training Always split by time for a temporal prediction problem. A random split is itself a form of leakage, and it is the second most common way an offline metric lies

docs.title: 7. Stretch goals
docs.text:
1. Consistency check in CI. Wire consistency_check into a GitHub Action that runs after every pipeline run and fails the build on any mismatch. This is a named capstone extension and the highest-value one — it converts a one-time proof into a standing guarantee.
  2. Leakage lint. Write a static check that parses build_eta_features.py, finds every rangeBetween(a, b), and fails if b >= 0 for any window ordered by a timestamp. Add it to CI. A structural rule catches the class of bug; a drill catches one instance.
  3. Point-in-time training snapshot. Use Delta time travel to reproduce the exact gold.eta_features version a given model trained on (VERSION AS OF n), and record the version alongside _feature_version in the model registry. Retrain and confirm you get the identical metric — reproducibility is what makes a model auditable.
  4. Freshness SLO on the online store. Add feature_ts age monitoring per Redis key and alert when p99 exceeds the refresh cadence. This is the direct fix for the STALE classification, and it turns a known weakness into a measured one.
  5. Direct-serve benchmark. Query gold.fact_trip directly with Trino or Spark SQL and benchmark p95 latency against the pre-aggregated gold.zone_hourly_demand at 1, 10 and 50 concurrent users. Then argue, with your own numbers, whether the materialised mart is justified — the M8 "do not reintroduce the two-tier problem casually" judgement, made with evidence.

docs.title: 8. Capstone linkage
docs.text:
This lab delivers Capstone mandatory requirement 8 (Serving, LO8) in full:

Capstone requirement Produced here Point-in-time-correct feature table served offline gold.eta_features, all 13 columns, leakage-drill-verified Materialised online with consistency proven masar:features:zone:{zone_id} + consistency_check passing across all zones Conformed star schema BI mart that reconciles gold.fact_trip + four dim_*, rel_diff = 0 against gold.zone_hourly_demand PDPL-safe serving view rider_pseudonym, zone-grain coordinates only, pdpl_boundary_check

LAB8_LEAKAGE.md is the single most defensible artefact you will bring to the demo. The rubric caps the Serving criterion at 70% for feature leakage, and the assessment notes instruct instructors to "ask the participant to run the leakage drill and explain the inflated metric" as a live verification. Your two-number answer — 0.943 before, 0.712 after — with a per-column classification behind it, is what a distinction-band response looks like.

For DECISIONS.md (capstone deliverable #6), two of your five required engineering decisions come from this lab: the feature window (why strictly prior, and why 15 minutes rather than 5 or 60) and online store yes/no (why Redis is justified by a measured latency requirement rather than adopted by default, and why it is a derived copy rather than a second pipeline).

For the 6-minute demo, this lab supplies the closing beat: both consumers reading the same governed gold — the dashboard query and the Redis lookup, side by side, returning numbers that agree because they descend from one silver table through one gate. That is the whole course in one screen.

docs.title: ACT-01 — Architecture Card-Sort
docs.text: Field Value Activity ID ACT-01 Module M1 — Evolution of Data Architecture Day / Hour Day 1 · Hour 2 (after the warehouse → lake → lakehouse timeline, before CS-01) Duration 15 minutes (20 with the extended debrief) Format Team card-sort against two independent axes Group size 3–4 per team Deliverable 12 cards placed on a 2-axis grid, each with a one-word justification

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
By the end participants can, for any workload put in front of them:

  1. Say whether it belongs on a warehouse, a lake, or a Lakehouse, and why that is a statement about the workload's requirements, not about fashion; and
  2. Say which medallion layer it should read — bronze, silver, or gold — and why reading the wrong layer is a governance failure rather than a performance choice.

The activity's real purpose is to establish that these are two independent questions. Teams that collapse them ("gold means warehouse") have the wrong model, and the sort is designed to expose that within four minutes.

docs.title: 2. Materials (printable)
docs.text:
• Card deck: §7, 12 cards, printed on A5 and cut. One deck per team.
  • Grid mat: one A2 sheet per team, drawn as below (or two rows of sticky-note headers on the table).
  • Markers, one per team.
                  BRONZE          SILVER          GOLD
              ┌──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
   WAREHOUSE  │              │              │              │
              ├──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤
   LAKE       │              │              │              │
              ├──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤
   LAKEHOUSE  │              │              │              │
              └──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘

docs.title: 3. Setup (2 minutes before the session)
docs.text: Cut one deck per team and shuffle it. Place a grid mat and a deck face-down on each table. Do not explain the grid in advance — the first instruction reveals it.

docs.title: 4. Run of show
docs.text: Min What happens Facilitator 0–1 Instruction. "Twelve workloads. Two questions per card: which architecture serves it, and which medallion layer does it read? Place every card. You have eight minutes." Do not define the axes further. Ambiguity is productive here. 1–9 Sort. Teams place all 12. Every card gets a one-word justification written on it. Circulate. One question per table only: "Card 4 — who is harmed if that reads bronze?" 9–12 Gallery walk. Each team moves one table right and marks, in a second colour, any card it would move. Silent. Enforce silence. Disputes are for minute 12. 12–16 Resolve the contested cards. Cards 3, 7, 9 and 11 attract the most movement; work those four publicly. Build the master grid on the board as you go. 16–20 Debrief. §5. Land the "two independent axes" point explicitly.

docs.title: 5. Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. Which cards did every team place identically, and which split the room? (The splits are where the judgement lives. Cards 1, 2, 5 are near-unanimous; 3, 7, 9, 11 are not.)
  2. Did any card belong on a warehouse? (Push hard. Almost none require one; several are conventionally served by one. The distinction between "requires" and "is usually" is the whole M1 argument.)
  3. Which cards read bronze — and would you let a business user run them? (Bronze access is a governance decision. Only cards 3 and 9 justify it, and only for named roles.)
  4. Did anyone place a card in "warehouse + bronze"? (Nobody should. Warehouses do not hold raw immutable feeds. That empty cell is itself a finding about what a warehouse is.)
  5. What happens if the fraud investigator (card 3) is given gold instead of bronze? (The investigation fails: gold has been deduplicated, filtered, conformed and aggregated. The evidence of the fraud may be exactly the row that silver dropped.)

docs.title: 6. Answer key
docs.text:
# Card Architecture Layer Rationale 1 Executive daily KPI dashboard Lakehouse (warehouse acceptable as a logic-free cache) Gold Conformed, aggregated, fast, stable grain. This is what gold is for. A warehouse copy is defensible only if it computes nothing (CS-01's cache invariant) 2 ETA-model training on raw GPS Lakehouse (lake acceptable) Silver + Gold Reads silver.vehicle_positions for validated positions and gold.eta_features for the point-in-time feature set. Never bronze — training on unvalidated duplicates poisons the model 3 Ad-hoc fraud investigation Lakehouse (lake acceptable) Bronze Contested. The fraud may live in exactly what silver removed — a duplicate, an outlier, a quarantined row. Investigation needs the unmodified record. Restricted access, named role, audited 4 Real-time surge pricing Lakehouse Gold (fed by a stream) Reads gold.zone_hourly_demand / the online store. Never bronze — a duplicate ping inflates surge (CS-05) 5 Monthly regulatory submission Lakehouse Gold, version-pinned Needs conformance and reproducibility. The pin is the point (CS-04) 6 Data-scientist exploratory notebook Lakehouse or Lake Silver Needs breadth and trustworthiness, not a pre-modelled grain. Gold is too narrow; bronze is too raw for exploration to be meaningful 7 Nightly ML feature build Lakehouse Silver → Gold Contested. It reads silver and writes gold. Teams that place it in one cell have missed that a pipeline spans layers — a good discovery 8 PDPL erasure request execution Lakehouse Bronze + Silver + Gold (all) Erasure must reach every layer holding the subject's data. Requires ACID delete + VACUUM — this is the card that only a Lakehouse can serve; a plain lake cannot delete a row transactionally 9 Debugging "why is yesterday's count wrong?" Lakehouse Bronze Contested. You are reconciling gold against the raw record; you need what actually arrived, including late and duplicate rows (CS-03) 10 Driver-facing weekly earnings statement Lakehouse Gold Conformed, reproducible, and legally consequential. Must match the number that paid them 11 Streaming operations alerting (speeding, geofence) Lakehouse Silver (streaming) Contested. Needs unit-normalised, deduplicated positions — bronze would alert on duplicates and on m/s values (CS-11) — but cannot wait for a gold batch build 12 Historical trend analysis over 3 years Lakehouse (warehouse conventionally) Gold Stable grain, wide time range, well-served by a partitioned/ZORDERed mart. The classic warehouse workload, and the one where a Lakehouse must prove itself on cost and speed

Grid summary: every card lands on Lakehouse; no card lands on warehouse+bronze; the medallion axis spreads 3 bronze / 3 silver / 6 gold (with card 7 spanning and card 8 spanning all three).

The finding to land: the architecture axis is nearly degenerate — a Lakehouse serves everything — while the medallion axis discriminates sharply. That is the design claim of M1 made visible on a table, and it is why the rest of the course is about layers rather than about platforms.

docs.title: 8. Cohort variants
docs.text:
Small cohort (< 8 participants). Run as one table, facilitator-led, with each participant placing two cards and defending them to the room before placement. Total 12 defences at ~40 seconds each. Add a rule: any other participant may challenge a placement once, and the challenge must cite a consumer who would be harmed. This converts the activity from a sort into a seminar and works better than splitting six people into two thin teams. Duration unchanged.

Large cohort (> 20 participants). Run as a two-round tournament. Round 1: teams of 4 sort only the six odd-numbered cards (5 min). Round 2: teams pair up (now 8 people) and merge their grids for the full 12, resolving disagreements (7 min). Then a single plenary resolution of the four contested cards. The merge step is where the learning happens at scale — two teams that placed card 3 differently must now argue it. Use a wall-sized shared grid for the plenary so the whole room sees one master answer. Duration 20 minutes.

docs.title: ACT-02 — "Spot the Swamp" Gallery Walk
docs.text: Field Value Activity ID ACT-02 Module M1 — Evolution of Data Architecture Day / Hour Day 1 · Hour 2 (immediately after ACT-01) Duration 10 minutes (15 with the extended debrief) Format Gallery walk — four folder listings posted around the room Group size 3–4 per team; teams rotate Deliverable A scored card per listing: swamp / at-risk / healthy, with the single worst symptom named

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Participants learn to read a storage layout as a diagnosis. A data lake becomes a data swamp through a small number of specific, recognisable, individually-reasonable decisions — and every one of them is visible in a directory listing before a single query is run.

By the end, participants can name the four swamp symptoms — no schema contract, no partition discipline, no lineage, no ownership — and can spot which of the four is present from a listing alone.

docs.title: 2. Materials (printable)
docs.text:
• Four listings (§7), each printed A3 and posted on a wall with space beneath for cards.
  • Scoring cards: 4 per team, printed from §6.
  • Blu-tack, markers.

docs.title: 3. Setup (5 minutes before the session)
docs.text: Post listings A, B, C, D at four separated points in the room — far enough apart that teams cannot overhear each other. Place a small stack of blank scoring cards under each. Do not label which is which; teams score all four.

docs.title: 4. Run of show
docs.text: Min What happens Facilitator 0–1 Instruction. "Four storage layouts from four real platforms. For each: swamp, at-risk, or healthy — and name the single worst symptom. Two minutes per station. You will not have time to be thorough; that is deliberate." The time pressure is the point. Diagnosis is a first-glance skill. 1–9 Rotate. Teams spend 2 minutes at each station, post a card, and move on the signal. Call the rotation loudly every 2 minutes. Do not let teams linger. 9–13 Read the cards. At each station, read the room's verdicts aloud and note the spread. Where teams disagree, that listing is doing its job. B and D split rooms most often. 13–15 Debrief. §5. Land the four symptoms as a checklist.

docs.title: 5. Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. Which listing did you diagnose fastest, and what did you look at first? (Almost everyone looks at filenames first. Filenames encode schema, partitioning and time — three of the four symptoms — which is why a listing is diagnostic at all.)
  2. Listing B has no obvious mess. Why is it still at-risk? (Because it has no _delta_log, so no transactions, no schema enforcement and no time travel; and because v2/ next to final/ means two definitions of the same data with no way to know which is authoritative. It is CS-01's two-tier problem inside one folder.)
  3. What single addition would improve every one of the four listings? (A _delta_log — i.e. a transaction layer. Then: a partition convention, and an owner recorded somewhere machine-readable.)
  4. Which symptom is the most expensive to fix later? (Missing lineage. Partitioning can be rewritten and schemas can be inferred, but you cannot retroactively learn where a file came from — that information was never captured.)
  5. Which of these four is Masar's bronze layer allowed to look like? (Only D. And note why D looks boring — CS-09's ADR made it boring on purpose.)

docs.title: 8. Answer key
docs.text:
Station Verdict Worst symptom Which of the four is missing Who gets hurt first A SWAMP No schema contract, no ownership, no convention of any kind. trips_final_v2_USE_THIS.csv is a filename doing the job an architecture should do All four. Schema, partitioning, lineage and ownership are each absent Everyone, immediately. Nobody can answer "which file is the trips table" without asking Ahmed, and Ahmed left B AT RISK (the most instructive station) No transaction layer — no _delta_log, so no ACID, no schema enforcement, no time travel — plus v1/v2/final as three coexisting definitions Schema contract and lineage. Partitioning is partly present; ownership is unknowable The next person to compute a metric. Which of v1, v2, final is authoritative? Two analysts will pick differently — CS-01 inside one bucket C AT RISK (healthy design, failing operations) Small-file decay: 2,880 files/day averaging 11 KB, no OPTIMIZE, and no _delta_log checkpoint since commit 10, so every read replays 11,440 commit files Partition discipline — specifically the maintenance half of it. Schema, lineage and ownership are fine Query latency, then cost. This is CS-02's full-scan tax arriving through a streaming sink (CS-05, decision 12) D HEALTHY None. Contracts with units, ownership, retention by PDPL class, checkpointed log, sensible file sizes, producer_version retained None Nobody — and note that D is deliberately boring. Boring is the goal

The four symptoms, as the takeaway checklist:

Symptom Question it answers Visible in a listing as No schema contract "What is in this file, and what does it mean?" Bare CSV/Parquet with no _delta_log, no contract file, meaningful filenames No partition discipline "Can I read a slice without reading everything?" No key=value directories, or thousands of tiny files, or no maintenance No lineage "Where did this row come from and when?" No _ingested_at / _source_file / _batch_id, no manifest No ownership "Who do I call when it is wrong?" No OWNERS file, personal-name folders, DO_NOT_DELETE

Station C is the one to spend time on: it has three of the four and still fails. Good design decays without scheduled maintenance, and decay is not a defect anyone introduced — it is a rate, so the counter-measure must also be a rate (a DAG task, not a runbook).

docs.title: 9. Cohort variants
docs.text:
Small cohort (< 8 participants). Do not rotate — bring all four listings to the table as A3 sheets and run it as a diagnosis race: 90 seconds per listing, individually written verdicts, then reveal all four at once and compare. With few people the rotation costs more time than it generates discussion. Add the extension question: "Rank the four by how expensive they would be to fix" (answer: A hardest, because nothing is recoverable; then B; C is a scheduled job away from healthy).

Large cohort (> 20 participants). Use eight stations — two copies of each listing — posted on opposite sides of the room, so no more than three teams queue at any one. Add a second scoring round: after the rotation, each team is assigned one station and must write, on a flipchart, the three-step remediation plan for that listing. Read the four remediation plans aloud in the debrief; they are more valuable than the verdicts and they turn a 10-minute activity into a 20-minute one that carries its own weight before LAB-01.

docs.title: ACT-03 — Cost-Model Auction / Cloud-Bill Autopsy
docs.text: Field Value Activity ID ACT-03 Module M2 — Compute–Storage Separation and Cloud Economics Day / Hour Day 1 · Hour 6 (after LAB-02's cost model, before or after CS-02) Duration 20 minutes Format Two-phase: a silent sealed-bid auction on cost drivers, then a bill autopsy against the truth Group size 3–4 per team; 3–6 teams Deliverable A bid sheet per team, then a ranked remediation list scored by SAR saved per engineering day

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Two skills, in this order:

  1. Estimate before you measure. Participants commit a number to each cost driver before seeing the bill. Committing publicly to a wrong number is the fastest way to dislodge appliance-era intuitions — chiefly the belief that storage is expensive.
  2. Rank by return, not by size. The most valuable fix in a cloud bill is almost always the least interesting one. Forcing a ranking by SAR saved per engineering day produces a different order than every team's instinct.

docs.title: 2. Materials (printable)
docs.text:
• Bid sheet (§6), one per team.
  • The bill (§7), one per team, kept face-down until phase 2.
  • Remediation menu (§8), one per team, distributed with the bill.
  • Calculators or a laptop per team. A visible scoreboard on a flipchart.

docs.title: 3. Setup (2 minutes)
docs.text:
Place a bid sheet face-up and the bill face-down on each table. Draw the scoreboard:

          | idle | scan | spot | storage | API | TOTAL | rank error
  Team A  |      |      |      |         |     |       |
  Team B  |      |      |      |         |     |       |

docs.title: 4. Run of show
docs.text: Min What happens Facilitator 0–2 Frame. "A Lakehouse platform costs SAR 462,000 a month. Before you see a single line of the bill, you will bid: how much of it is each of these five things? Sealed bids. No talking between teams." Give the context in §6's header only. No hints. 2–8 Phase 1 — the auction. Teams fill the bid sheet: a SAR figure for each of five drivers, summing to ≤ 462,000. Circulate to confirm every cell has a number. "Wrong is fine; blank is not." 8–10 Post the bids. Write every team's five numbers on the scoreboard. Do not reveal the truth yet. Note publicly where the spread is widest. It is always storage (teams over-bid it 5–10×) and idle (teams under-bid it). 10–11 Reveal. Turn the bills over. Score: 1 point per driver within ±20% of truth; 3 bonus points for the correct rank order of the five. The reveal is loud. Let it be. 11–18 Phase 2 — the autopsy. Using the remediation menu, teams rank fixes by SAR saved per engineering day and commit to what they would do with only 3 engineering days. Push: "You have 3 days, not 12. Which three fixes?" 18–20 Debrief. §5. Land the ratio table and the storage revelation.

docs.title: 5. Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. Who over-bid storage, and by how much? (Most teams bid SAR 80,000–150,000. The truth is 27,000 — 5.8% of the bill. This is the appliance-era intuition dying in public, which is why the auction is worth the six minutes.)
  2. Who under-bid idle compute? (Idle is SAR 121,000 — the single largest recoverable line — and it is invisible on a bill, because a cloud invoice charges you for a running cluster identically whether or not anything ran on it.)
  3. Did your rank order match? (Rank matters more than magnitude. A team with the right order and wrong magnitudes will make correct decisions; the reverse will not.)
  4. What did you buy with your 3 days? (Correct: idle termination + right-sizing (0.5 d), spot for the nightly build (0.5 d), and start on compaction (2 d). That is SAR ~180,000/month for 3 days.)
  5. Why does every team's instinct rank compaction first? (Because it is the interesting problem. Name the bias out loud: engineers optimise for intellectual return, and FinOps pays for financial return. The gap between those two is where cloud bills go to die.)
  6. What would you have bid if the platform were on-premises? (Storage would genuinely have been a large share. The intuition is not stupid — it is stale. Decoupling inverted the ratio.)

On-demand premium 42,000 9.1% 20,000–50,000 Roughly right 4. Storage at rest 27,000 5.8% 80,000–150,000 Over by 3–6× 5. Storage API requests 31,000 6.7% 5,000–15,000 Under by 2–5×

The two systematic errors are the lesson: storage at rest is over-estimated and the cost of reading is under-estimated. In a decoupled architecture, data is nearly free to keep and expensive to read badly. Rows 4 and 5 together say it precisely: keeping 340 TB costs less than the API calls to open its files.

• 1 point per driver bid within ±20% of truth (max 5).
  • 3 bonus points for the exactly correct rank order of the five.
  • 5 points for a remediation ranking whose top 3 match A, B, C in that order.

docs.title: 10. Cohort variants
docs.text:
Small cohort (< 8 participants). Run as individual sealed bids rather than team bids, then a single group autopsy. With 6 people you get 6 independent estimates, which makes the spread — and therefore the shared misconception — far more visible than 2 team bids would. Add a closing question with the extra time: "Your bill grows 8% a month. Which of these fixes survives that, and which is a one-off?" (Answer: A and F survive because they are policies; C survives only if optimizeWrite/autoCompact make it continuous; D and E are one-offs consumed within a year.)

Large cohort (> 20 participants). Run the auction as a live open outcry rather than sealed bids, one driver at a time, with teams calling numbers and the facilitator recording the range on the scoreboard. It is faster (4 minutes for all five) and the anchoring effect becomes visible and discussable — early loud bids drag later ones, which is exactly how cost estimates converge on wrong numbers in real organisations. Then split phase 2: half the teams rank the menu, half write the one-page CFO memo from CS-02 §8.4, and pair them for a 3-minute exchange. Duration 25 minutes.

docs.title: ACT-04 — ELT Idempotency Relay
docs.text: Field Value Activity ID ACT-04 Module M3 — ETL vs ELT and the Transformation Layer Day / Hour Day 2 · Hour 3 (during or immediately after LAB-03) Duration 20 minutes Format Physical relay — teams execute a pipeline by hand, with the facilitator injecting failures Group size 4 per team (one per relay station); 3–6 teams racing Deliverable A correct final table after four rounds including two injected failures, plus a per-station write-mode ruling

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Participants feel idempotency rather than define it. Each team executes a four-stage pipeline by physically moving row cards between trays. The facilitator then kills a stage mid-run and orders a restart. Teams whose stations use INSERT end with duplicated rows; teams whose stations use MERGE or replaceWhere end correct.

By the end, participants can state which write mode belongs at which stage, and — the harder point — can articulate why idempotency's real value is that it makes re-running free, and free re-runs are what make investigation free.

docs.title: 2. Materials (printable)
docs.text:
• Row cards (§7): 24 trip cards per team, printed on card stock and cut. Six carry duplicate trip_ids; four are late arrivals; two are corrections.
  • Station mats (§7): four A4 sheets per team, labelled BRONZE / SILVER / GOLD-DAILY / GOLD-DRIVER, each with its write mode blank.
  • Round cards (§8): four sealed cards per team, opened on the facilitator's call.
  • Four trays or marked areas per team. A stopwatch.

docs.title: 3. Setup (5 minutes)
docs.text: Per team: four station mats in a row, a tray at each, the 24 row cards face-down in a "source" pile at the head of the line, and the four round cards sealed. Assign one person per station. The person at station 1 is the only one who may draw from the source.

docs.title: 4. Run of show
docs.text: Min What happens Facilitator 0–2 Frame. "You are a pipeline. Cards are rows. Each station has a write mode, and you choose it now — before you know what is coming." Teams write a mode on each mat: INSERT / MERGE on <key> / replaceWhere <predicate> / overwrite. Do not advise. The wrong choice is the lesson. 2–5 Round 1 — clean run. Open round card 1. Station 1 draws 12 cards (day 1), applies its mode, passes on. Each station applies its own mode. Time it. Note the elapsed time on the board. 5–6 Checkpoint. Every team counts rows at each station and writes the count on the mat. Correct: bronze 12, silver 12, gold-daily 1 row per (date), gold-driver 1 row per driver. 6–9 Round 2 — day 2 with late arrivals. Open round card 2: 12 more cards, of which 4 belong to day 1 and 2 are corrections to day-1 rows already processed. Watch the gold stations. INSERT teams now have two rows for day 1. 9–11 Round 3 — THE KILL. Mid-round, shout "STOP — station 3 has crashed." That person turns away from the table. After 20 seconds: "Recovered. Re-run the whole pipeline from the source." This is the moment the activity exists for. Say nothing else. 11–15 Re-run. Teams re-run all 24 cards from the source through all four stations. INSERT teams end with 48 bronze rows and doubled gold aggregates. MERGE teams end identical to before. 15–17 Count and score. §9's scoring. Read the counts aloud, team by team. The spread is dramatic and does the teaching for you. 17–20 Debrief. §5. Land the "free investigation" point, not just the arithmetic.

docs.title: 5. Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. Which stations broke, and which survived? (Bronze append is correct — bronze grows on re-run by design and downstream dedups. The gold aggregate stations are where INSERT is fatal, because a doubled aggregate is both invisible and consequential.)
  2. Why is append right for bronze but wrong for gold? (Bronze's grain is "an arrival"; a re-arrival is a real fact and should be recorded. Gold's grain is "one row per date" or "one row per driver per day"; a second row at that grain is not a fact, it is a corruption.)
  3. What did the late arrivals do to a team using replaceWhere date = today? (They were lost — a day-1 row arriving on day 2 falls outside date = today. This is CS-03's exact undercount, produced by hand in nine minutes.)
  4. After the kill, how did you decide whether it was safe to re-run? (Idempotent teams did not decide — they just re-ran. INSERT teams had to reason about what had already happened, under time pressure, with incomplete information. That is the 03:00 on-call experience in miniature.)
  5. What does that mean for how often you would investigate a suspicion? (This is the real answer. If re-running is free, you investigate on a hunch. If re-running is dangerous, you wait until you are sure — and in CS-03 that wait was four months.)
  6. Where does the 3-day lookback come from, and what does it cost? (From the arrival-lag distribution. It costs re-processing three days of rows on every run — seconds — and it buys absorbing 99.98% of late arrivals.)

docs.title: 6. Answer key — write mode per station
docs.text:
Station Grain Correct mode Why What INSERT does 1. BRONZE one row per arrival append An arrival is a fact; a re-arrival is also a fact. Immutable, append-only. Re-run grows history on purpose Nothing wrong — append is the correct behaviour here. The row count doubling on re-run is expected and downstream dedup handles it 2. SILVER one row per trip_id MERGE on trip_id, 3-day lookback Corrections update in place; late arrivals land in the day they belong to; re-run is a no-op Duplicate trip_ids; corrections coexist with the values they were meant to replace 3. GOLD-DAILY one row per date replaceWhere date IN (lookback window) The whole window is deterministically rebuilt from silver, so a re-run reproduces it exactly Two rows per date. The dashboard SUM() doubles and looks like a demand spike 4. GOLD-DRIVER one row per (driver_id, date) MERGE on (driver_id, date) Late trips update prior days, so a merge beats a partition replace here Two rows per driver per day; the incentive payment doubles

The nuance worth ten seconds: stations 3 and 4 both hold aggregates and take different modes. replaceWhere is right when a whole partition can be deterministically rebuilt; MERGE is right when rows for old periods keep changing. Teams that use one mode everywhere get one of the two wrong.

docs.title: Expected counts
docs.text: After R1 After R2 After the kill + full re-run Bronze (append) 12 24 48 — correct and expected Silver (MERGE) 12 20 (24 minus 6 dup ids, plus 2 corrections applied in place) 20 — unchanged Gold-daily (replaceWhere) 1 2 2 — unchanged Gold-driver (MERGE) 5 8 8 — unchanged Gold-daily if INSERT 1 2 4 — doubled, silently Gold-driver if INSERT 5 13 21 — tripled, silently

docs.title: Row cards (24 per team; print on card stock, cut, shuffle within their round)
8. Round cards (sealed; open on the facilitator's call)
docs.text:
ROUND 1  "Normal day. Process the 12 cards in the source pile."

ROUND 2  "Day two. Twelve more cards. Four of them belong to yesterday.
          Two are corrections to rows you already processed.
          Four are duplicates of ids you have already seen."

ROUND 3  "*** STOP. STATION 3 HAS CRASHED. ***
          Station 3: turn away from the table. Do nothing for 20 seconds.
          ... Recovered. RE-RUN THE ENTIRE PIPELINE FROM THE SOURCE.
          You do not know which rows station 3 had finished."

ROUND 4  "Count every station. Write the counts on your mats.
          Then answer, in one sentence: was it SAFE to re-run?"

docs.title: 9. Scoring
docs.text: Criterion Points Silver holds exactly 20 rows, one per trip_id, corrections applied 5 Gold-daily holds exactly 2 rows 5 Gold-driver holds exactly 8 rows 5 Late arrivals landed on 2026-06-01, not 06-02 5 Bronze holds 48 rows and the team can explain why that is correct 3 Team wrote correct write modes on all four mats before round 1 3 Fastest correct team 2 bonus Penalty: any station where a human had to reason about "what had already happened" −5

docs.title: 10. Cohort variants
docs.text:
Small cohort (< 8 participants). Run one shared pipeline with the facilitator as station 1, and give every participant a written prediction sheet before each round: "how many rows will each station hold after this round?" Reveal after each round. With few people the race disappears, so the prediction-and-reveal loop supplies the tension. Add the extension: after round 4, ask each participant to change one station's mode and predict the effect, then test it.

Large cohort (> 20 participants). Run 5–6 teams in parallel as a race, with a visible scoreboard and a strict 90-second limit per round to force errors. Then add a round 5: teams swap tables and must audit another team's final state against the source pile and write a one-line defect report. Auditing someone else's pipeline is closer to the real job than running your own, and it surfaces the doubled-aggregate defect much more vividly than counting your own cards. Duration 28 minutes. If space is tight, run in two waves of three teams with the second wave observing the first's round 3 — watching another team's kill-and-restart is nearly as instructive as suffering it.

docs.title: ACT-05 — The Human Delta Transaction Log
docs.text: Field Value Activity ID ACT-05 Module M4 — Delta Lake, ACID and the Transaction Log Day / Hour Day 3 · Hour 3 (between LAB-04a and LAB-04b, before CS-04) Duration 20 minutes Format Embodied simulation — participants physically enact commits, concurrent writers, time travel and VACUUM Group size Whole room, with assigned roles; 8–24 works ideally Deliverable A correct reconstruction of the table at three different versions, and a written statement of what VACUUM destroyed

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Participants stop thinking of Delta as "Parquet with features" and start thinking of it as an ordered log of add/remove actions over an immutable file set, from which any version of the table is derived rather than stored.

By the end they can: replay a log by hand to produce the current file set; explain why two concurrent writers do not corrupt each other; explain exactly what time travel reads; and state precisely what VACUUM makes impossible.

docs.title: 2. Materials (printable)
docs.text:
• File cards (§7): ~20 blue A5 cards, each representing one Parquet data file, with a filename and its row contents.
  • Commit cards (§7): ~12 white A5 cards, each a _delta_log entry with a version number and its add / remove actions.
  • Role badges (§7): READER, WRITER-A, WRITER-B, VACUUM, LOG-KEEPER.
  • Two long tables or floor areas: one marked _delta_log (ordered, left to right), one marked object storage (unordered heap).

docs.title: 3. Setup (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Lay out the two areas. Place file cards part-0000 through part-0004 in object storage and commit cards for versions 0–2 in the log area, in order. Distribute role badges: one LOG-KEEPER, one READER, two WRITERS, one VACUUM. Everyone else is an auditor and scores the READER's reconstructions.

Write the rule on the board and enforce it all session:

Object storage is a heap. It has no order and no idea what a table is. The log is the only thing that knows which files are the table.

docs.title: 4. Run of show
docs.text: Min Phase What happens Facilitator 0–2 Frame. "This table is not a folder. It is a list of instructions for which files are currently in the table. You are going to be the reader that follows them." Point at the heap. "How many rows are in the table right now?" Nobody can answer without the log. That is the point. 2–5 Replay 1. READER walks the log from version 0 to version 2, physically picking up files that are added and putting down files that are removed. Announces the resulting file set and row count. Auditors check. Expected: part-0000, part-0002, part-0003 (see §6). 5–9 Concurrent writers. WRITER-A and WRITER-B each prepare a commit at the same time, both having read version 2. Both write their new data files into the heap. Both then try to hand LOG-KEEPER a card numbered version 3. LOG-KEEPER accepts only the first. The second must retry: re-read the log (now at v3), check whether the conflict is real, renumber to v4, and re-submit. Do not explain this — let LOG-KEEPER discover the collision. 9–11 Discuss the collision. What just happened, and why is the loser's data file still fine in the heap? Land: the data write is not the transaction. The commit is the transaction, and the log is the serialisation point. 11–14 Time travel. READER reconstructs the table VERSION AS OF 2 while the current version is 4. Then VERSION AS OF 0. Auditors check both. Note aloud that the reader is holding a past table while writers continue — no locks, no blocking. 14–17 VACUUM. VACUUM takes a retention parameter called out by the facilitator (RETAIN 0 HOURS) and physically removes from the heap every file not referenced by the current version. Then READER is asked to reconstruct VERSION AS OF 2 again. It fails. Files are gone. Let the READER physically search the heap and not find them. This is the most memorable ten seconds of M4. 17–20 Debrief. §5. Land the three-line summary.

docs.title: 5. Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. Before the replay, could anyone say how many rows were in the table? (No. The heap is meaningless without the log. The log is the table; the files are just bytes.)
  2. Why did the losing writer not corrupt anything? (Its data file was written to a new path in the heap, unreferenced by any commit. An unreferenced file is invisible — it is not "bad data in the table", it is not in the table at all. This is why writes can be optimistic: the expensive part is safe to do in parallel and only the cheap part is serialised.)
  3. What did the losing writer have to do? (Re-read the log, determine whether its change actually conflicts — two writers touching different partitions usually do not — and retry at the next version. Optimistic concurrency: assume no conflict, verify at commit, retry if wrong.)
  4. While READER held version 2, did any writer have to wait? (No. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers, because a reader is holding a fixed list of files that nothing will delete — until VACUUM.)
  5. What exactly did VACUUM destroy? (Not data in the current table — that is untouched. It destroyed every past version, i.e. the audit trail, the ability to reproduce a filing (CS-04), and the ability to roll back a corrupted feature (CS-11 R1).)
  6. What would RETAIN 0 HOURS have done to the READER mid-query? (Deleted files the READER was actively reading. This is the sim-vacuum0 failure and it breaks concurrent readers, not just history.)
  7. So what is the right retention? (A governance number set by the longest window over which someone may credibly ask "what did it say then" — the regulatory dispute window, not a storage convenience. And for fixed points like a filing, pin the version rather than relying on a sliding window.)

docs.title: Replay 1 — the file set at each version
docs.text:
Version Commit actions File set after Rows 0 add part-0000 (200), add part-0001 (200) 0000, 0001 400 1 add part-0002 (150) 0000, 0001, 0002 550 2 remove part-0001, add part-0003 (180) 0000, 0002, 0003 530 3 (WRITER-A wins) add part-0004 (120) 0000, 0002, 0003, 0004 650 4 (WRITER-B retries) remove part-0000, add part-0005 (210) 0002, 0003, 0004, 0005 660

Key observations to draw out: - part-0001 still physically exists in the heap after version 2. It was removed from the table, not deleted from storage. That distinction is what makes time travel possible and what VACUUM later erases. - Version 2's file set (0000, 0002, 0003) is fully reconstructible as long as 0000 and 0001's successors survive in the heap. - After VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS, only files referenced by version 4 survive: 0002, 0003, 0004, 0005. part-0000 and part-0001 are gone, so versions 0, 1, 2 and 3 are all unreadable — a single command destroyed four versions of history.

docs.title: The concurrent-write resolution
docs.text:
WRITER-A WRITER-B Read version 2 2 Data files written to heap part-0004 part-0005 Commit attempted v3 v3 Outcome Accepted Rejected — v3 exists Retry — Re-read log (now v4 is next). Check conflict: B removes part-0000, A did not touch it → no real conflict. Commit as v4. Final Both changes present Both changes present

If B's change had conflicted — say both removed part-0000 — the retry must fail rather than silently proceed, and the writer's application logic decides what to do. Make this explicit: optimistic concurrency does not mean "everyone wins"; it means "conflicts are detected at commit rather than prevented by a lock."

docs.title: The three-line summary (write on the board at the end)
docs.text:
1. The log is the table.        Files are bytes; the log says which bytes count.
2. The commit is the transaction.  Data can be written in parallel; only the
                                   log entry is serialised. That is ACID on a heap.
3. VACUUM is a governance decision. It does not free space from your table;
                                    it deletes your past.

docs.title: 8. Cohort variants
docs.text:
Small cohort (< 8 participants). Everyone holds a role and the facilitator is LOG-KEEPER (which lets you control the collision timing precisely). Drop the auditor role and instead have each participant, after every phase, write the current file set on a shared sheet — the discipline of writing it down is what the auditors would otherwise provide. Add an extension with the spare time: introduce OPTIMIZE as a sixth role, who removes four small files and adds one large one in a single commit, then ask the READER whether the table's contents changed (they did not — only its layout, which is the exact point of compaction).

Large cohort (> 20 participants). Run two identical tables in parallel (two logs, two heaps, two full role sets) and give them different VACUUM retentions: table 1 RETAIN 0 HOURS, table 2 RETAIN 168 HOURS. Everyone else audits. At minute 14, ask both READERs to reconstruct version 2 simultaneously — one succeeds, one cannot. The side-by-side failure is far more persuasive than a single demonstration and it makes the retention debate concrete without a single slide. Then run a 4-minute plenary on "what retention would you set for gold.fact_trip, and what for bronze.gps_events, and why are they different?" Duration 26 minutes.

docs.title: ACT-06 — Human Kafka
docs.text: Field Value Activity ID ACT-06 Module M5 — Streaming Data and Event-Driven Architectures Day / Hour Day 4 · Hour 1 (before LAB-05; pairs naturally with CS-05) Duration 20 minutes Format Embodied simulation — partitions, offsets, consumer groups, rebalance and replay, acted out with keyed cards Group size Whole room; needs at least 9 people (1 producer, 4 partitions, 4 consumers). Scales to 30 Deliverable Each consumer's offset ledger, reconciled at the end; plus the room's answer to "what did the replay cost us?"

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Participants physically experience the four properties that make a log different from a queue:

  1. Ordering is per partition, not per topic — and the partition key decides what is ordered.
  2. An offset is a reader's position, not a property of the message — messages are not consumed and destroyed.
  3. Consumer groups are independent — two groups read the same events at different speeds without interfering.
  4. Replay is a normal operation — resetting an offset is a routine act, not a recovery project.

docs.title: 2. Materials (printable)
docs.text:
• Event cards (§7): 40 cards, each a GPS ping with vehicle_id, ts, speed_kmh. Printed and shuffled.
  • Partition mats (§7): 4 A3 sheets labelled PARTITION 0–3, each with an offset ruler printed down the side (0, 1, 2, …).
  • Offset ledgers (§7): one per consumer.
  • Role badges: PRODUCER, PARTITION 0–3, CONSUMER-GROUP-AI (2 people), CONSUMER-GROUP-OPS (2 people), OBSERVER (everyone else).
  • A hash rule posted visibly: partition = (last digit of vehicle_id) mod 4.

docs.title: 3. Setup (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Lay the four partition mats in a row on a long table or the floor. The PRODUCER stands at one end with the shuffled deck. The two consumer groups stand on the far side, each with its own ledger. Post the hash rule and the layout:

              PRODUCER  (keys by vehicle_id)
                  │
      ┌───────────┼───────────┬───────────┐
      ▼           ▼           ▼           ▼
  ┌───────┐   ┌───────┐   ┌───────┐   ┌───────┐
  │ PART 0│   │ PART 1│   │ PART 2│   │ PART 3│    cards laid LEFT TO RIGHT
  │ 0 1 2 │   │ 0 1 2 │   │ 0 1 2 │   │ 0 1 2 │    in arrival order = OFFSETS
  └───────┘   └───────┘   └───────┘   └───────┘
      ▲           ▲           ▲           ▲
      └───────────┴─────┬─────┴───────────┘
                        │
         GROUP: ai-features        GROUP: ops-alerts
         (2 consumers)             (2 consumers)
         own offsets               own offsets

docs.title: 4. Run of show
docs.text: Min Phase What happens Facilitator 0–2 Frame. "This is not a queue. Nothing is consumed and destroyed. Each of you is a position in a log that everyone can read." Post the hash rule. 2–5 Produce. PRODUCER deals all 40 cards, one at a time, applying the hash rule aloud. Each partition lays its cards left to right — that ordering is the offsets. Enforce "aloud". The room must hear the key deciding the partition. 5–8 Consume, both groups. Each group's two consumers split the partitions (2 each) and read forward, recording partition:offset in their ledger. AI group reads slowly (every card). OPS group reads fast (skims). Both groups read the same cards. Ask an observer: "Did the AI group's reading remove anything from the OPS group's view?" 8–10 Ordering check. Ask: "Vehicle VEH-00884 appears 5 times. Are its pings in order?" Then: "Are ping 3 of VEH-00884 and ping 3 of VEH-00459 in order relative to each other?" Answers: yes and no, and it does not matter. This is the ordering guarantee, discovered rather than told. 10–13 Rebalance. Tap one OPS consumer and say "you have crashed." They step away. The remaining OPS consumer must take over all 4 partitions, starting from the committed offsets in the ledger, not from the beginning. Watch for a consumer restarting from offset 0 — that is the reprocessing bug from CS-05's INC-2025-0412, produced live. 13–16 Replay. "The OPS alerting rule was wrong all morning. Reset the ops-alerts group to offset 0 on every partition and re-read." Then the key question: "What happened to the AI group's offsets?" (Nothing. That independence is the whole architecture.) 16–18 The poisoned card. Slip in one prepared card with ts 11 hours in the future (§7). Ask both groups: "Your watermark is now driven by the highest timestamp you have seen. What happens to every card after this one?" They are all classified as late. One card silenced the pipeline. This is CS-10's Round 3, felt rather than read. 18–20 Debrief. §5. Land the four properties.

docs.title: 5. Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. Did reading remove anything? (No. A log is read at a position; messages persist for the retention period. This is the single largest difference from a traditional queue and it is what makes everything else possible.)
  2. Whose ordering is guaranteed? (One vehicle's pings, because vehicle_id was the key. Two different vehicles have no ordering guarantee relative to each other — and no consumer needs one. You choose the key by asking what must not be reordered.)
  3. What would have happened if the key had been city? (Three keys, four partitions: one partition idle, one holding a third of all events. Total lag would look flat while one partition grew without bound. Ask the room to physically re-deal 10 cards by city and look at the mats.)
  4. When the OPS consumer crashed, why did the survivor not start from zero? (Because offsets are committed by the group, not held by the individual. Restarting from zero would reprocess everything — surge inflated on phantom demand, exactly CS-05's incident.)
  5. The replay reset OPS to zero. What did the AI group have to do? (Nothing. Two groups, two offset ledgers, zero coordination. This is why a new consumer costs nothing and needs no producer change.)
  6. The future-dated card. (One bad clock advanced the watermark past every subsequent legitimate event. Lag reads zero. Throughput reads normal. Output stops. In streaming, the dangerous failures are the quiet ones.)
  7. What did the replay cost? (Compute to re-process, and duplicate side effects if the consumer's sink is not idempotent — OPS would re-fire every alert. This is why replay strategy and sink idempotency are one decision, not two.)

docs.title: Partition assignment (hash rule: last digit of vehicle_id mod 4)
docs.text:
vehicle_id last digit partition VEH-00884 4 0 VEH-00459 9 1 VEH-02210 0 0 VEH-03427 7 3 VEH-01922 2 2 VEH-00787 7 3 VEH-00698 8 0 VEH-00001 1 1

Every ping from one vehicle lands on one partition, always. That is the ordering guarantee, and it is a consequence of the key, not of the broker.

docs.title: Expected end state
docs.text: ai-features group ops-alerts group After the initial read p0:10, p1:9, p2:11, p3:10 p0:10, p1:9, p2:11, p3:10 After the OPS crash + rebalance unchanged one consumer now owns all 4, resuming from committed offsets After the OPS replay unchanged reset to p0:0, p1:0, p2:0, p3:0, then re-read to the end Side effects of the replay none every alert re-fired, unless the sink is idempotent

docs.title: The four properties (write on the board at the end)
docs.text:
1. ORDER IS PER PARTITION.   The key decides what is ordered. Choose it by
                             asking: what must not be reordered?
2. AN OFFSET IS A POSITION.  Not a property of the message. Reading destroys
                             nothing. Two readers, two positions, no conflict.
3. GROUPS ARE INDEPENDENT.   A new consumer is a new group and a starting
                             offset. No producer change. No coordination.
4. REPLAY IS ROUTINE.        Reset an offset and re-read. The cost is compute
                             plus any non-idempotent side effect.

docs.title: 8. Cohort variants
docs.text:
Small cohort (< 8 participants). Reduce to 2 partitions and 2 consumer groups of one person each; the facilitator is the PRODUCER and also plays the second member of a group when the rebalance is needed. Deal 20 cards rather than 40. Keep every phase — the rebalance and the replay are the two that must survive a cut, and the poisoned card is worth more than the volume. Add an extension: give one participant a second, different hash rule (partition = hash(trip_id) mod 2) and re-deal 8 cards, then ask what broke (a vehicle's pings now scatter across partitions; per-vehicle ordering is gone).

Large cohort (> 20 participants). Use 6 partitions, 3 consumer groups (ai-features, ops-alerts, and a new fraud-investigation group introduced at minute 13 starting from offset 0). The third group is the payoff: it joins mid-session, reads the entire history from the beginning, and requires no change from the producer and no coordination with the other two groups. Stop the room and say so explicitly — that moment is LinkedIn's insight, physically demonstrated, and it is the bridge into CS-10. Everyone not holding a role is an OBSERVER with a specific assignment: half track total events processed across all groups (it exceeds 40, which surprises people), half track whether any group ever waited for another (none did). Duration 26 minutes.

docs.title: ACT-07 — Watermark Clinic
docs.text: Field Value Activity ID ACT-07 Module M5 — Streaming Data and Event-Driven Architectures Day / Hour Day 4 · Hour 2 (immediately after LAB-05's late-data task, or between CS-05 and CS-10) Duration 15 minutes Format Triage clinic — teams commit to a watermark, then triage 12 late events against it Group size 3–4 per team Deliverable A committed watermark per consumer with its residual stated, and a ruling on all 12 late events

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Participants stop treating the watermark as a safety setting where longer is safer, and start treating it as a two-sided trade with a cost in both directions, made with a number drawn from an arrival distribution.

Three specific outcomes: 1. Choose a watermark from data, and state the residual it drops. 2. Understand that a watermark bounds latency and state, never retention — the dropped events are still in bronze. 3. Recognise that different consumers need different watermarks off the same stream.

docs.title: 2. Materials (printable)
docs.text:
• Commitment card (§6), one per team — filled in before the triage cards are handed out.
  • Late-event cards (§7), 12 per team, printed and cut.
  • Triage sheet (§7), one per team.
  • The arrival-lag distribution (§5 P1) projected or printed.

docs.title: 3. Setup (2 minutes)
docs.text: Distribute the commitment card and project the arrival-lag distribution. Keep the 12 event cards face-down until every team has committed a number. The commitment must precede the evidence — that is what makes the triage honest.

docs.title: 4. Run of show
docs.text: Min What happens Facilitator 0–2 Frame. Project the distribution. "Devices in tunnels and basements flush late. You must choose how long to wait. Choose now, before you see what arrives." State both costs explicitly: too short loses data, too long grows state until the job dies. 2–5 Commit. Teams fill the commitment card: a watermark for the Ops path, one for the AI path, and the residual each accepts. Circulate. Reject any answer without a residual percentage. "You dropped 1.7% of what? Give me events per day." 5–6 Read the commitments aloud. Write every team's two numbers on the board. The spread is the discussion. Expect Ops 10 s–5 min, AI 5–30 min. 6–11 Triage. Deal the 12 late-event cards. For each: PROCESSED / DROPPED / STILL IN BRONZE? against the team's own committed watermark. Circulate with one question: "Card 9 — is that event lost?" The answer is no, and most teams have not internalised it. 11–13 Score. Read the answer key. Teams score their own triage. The score depends on their own watermark, so two teams can both be fully correct with different rulings — say this out loud. 13–15 Debrief. §5. Land the three outcomes.

docs.title: 5. Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. Did anyone choose the same watermark for Ops and for AI? (If so, ask what a 4-minute-old harsh-braking alert is worth. Then ask what a 0.8% incomplete feature is worth. They are different questions and they take different answers off the same stream.)
  2. Card 9 arrived 22 minutes late and your watermark is 10 minutes. Is that event lost? (No. It is in bronze.gps_events, which is append-only and complete. It is excluded from the streaming aggregate, and it will be included by the next batch rebuild of gold.eta_features. The watermark bounds latency and state, never retention.)
  3. What is the cost of a 60-minute watermark? (State ≈ events/s × watermark × per-key state. At 620 ev/s peak that is 6× the state of a 10-minute window — and it is exactly how CS-05's INC-2025-0517 reached 41 GB, OOMed, and froze the demand map for 4.5 hours during the morning peak. The long watermark caused a worse outage than any amount of late data would have.)
  4. Card 12 arrives with a timestamp in the future. What does your watermark do? (It advances to that timestamp, and every subsequent legitimate event is then classified as late and dropped. One device with a broken clock can silence the pipeline for the whole fleet, and lag will read zero throughout.)
  5. How would you know your watermark is wrong? (Monitor the drop rate as a first-class metric — count events discarded as late, segmented by producer_version and by vehicle. A rising drop rate means the arrival distribution has moved, and the watermark must be re-derived. A watermark set once and never revisited is a guess that used to be a decision.)
  6. When would you re-derive it? (Quarterly, and immediately after any producer, network or device-fleet change. Same discipline as CS-03's batch lookback window — they are the same decision at different timescales.)

docs.title: The 12 cards (cut; deal all 12 to each team)
8. Answer key
docs.text:
Rulings below use the reference watermarks: Ops 30 s, AI 10 min. A team with different committed numbers is scored against its own numbers — say this clearly, because it is the difference between a rule and a decision.

Card Lag OPS (30 s) AI (10 min) In bronze? Note 1 3 s P P yes The 96.2% normal case 2 24 s P P yes Inside 30 s, just 3 1m42 D P yes The first divergence between the two consumers 4 4m13 D P yes — 5 7m45 D P yes Still inside the AI window 6 13m45 D D yes Beyond both. Absorbed by the next batch rebuild 7 16m42 D D yes Tunnel flush 8 16m37 D D yes Same burst. Arrives in the same micro-batch as card 7 — a burst is not 480 batches 9 22m10 D D yes The key card. Dropped from both streams, not lost. Batch rebuild includes it 10 1h32 D D yes The 0.01% tail. A device offline for a shift 11 4m23, DUP D D as late; also a DUPLICATE of card 2 yes Two independent reasons to exclude it. Dedup on event_id catches it if the watermark does not 12 −11h30 BREAKS THE PIPELINE BREAKS THE PIPELINE yes Advances the watermark 11 h; every later legitimate event is then late and dropped. Lag reads zero throughout

Lost forever: zero of twelve. Every card is in bronze.gps_events. This is the answer teams most often get wrong and the one that changes how they think.

The card that breaks everything: 12. The defence is a plausibility check on event time before it can influence the watermark:

.withColumn("_clock_skew_s", unix_timestamp("_ingested_at") - unix_timestamp("ts"))
trusted   = df.filter(col("_clock_skew_s") > -60)     # only these drive the watermark
untrusted = df.filter(col("_clock_skew_s") <= -60)    # -> quarantine, counted, alerted

Never clamp ts to now() — that is a silent repair, which CS-09 classifies as never-before-Bronze and CS-11 prices at SAR 2.4M.

docs.title: Reference watermarks, with the reasoning
docs.text:
Path Watermark Admits Drops/day (of 15M) Why Ops alerts 30 s 98.3% ~255,000 An alert about a 4-minute-old event is worthless; latency dominates AI / silver→gold 10 min 99.93% ~10,500 Feature correctness dominates; 10 min is within the 5-min freshness budget at a 30 s trigger Training none (batch from bronze) 100% 0 Bronze is append-only and complete

The accepted failure mode, as a sentence: "Under a 30-second watermark the Ops path misses ~1.7% of events, all of which are late enough that an alert would no longer be actionable; under a 10-minute watermark the AI streaming path misses ~0.07%, all of which are retained in bronze.gps_events and absorbed by the next batch rebuild. Neither path loses data; both trade latency for completeness in the direction their consumer requires."

docs.title: 9. Cohort variants
docs.text:
Small cohort (< 8 participants). Run as individual commitments, then a single group triage in which each participant owns two cards and must rule on them aloud against their own watermark. With few people the divergence between individuals' watermarks becomes the discussion — two people ruling card 5 differently, both correctly, is the clearest possible demonstration that the watermark is a decision rather than a fact. Add the extension: give one participant a 60-minute watermark and ask them to compute the state cost at 620 events/s.

Large cohort (> 20 participants). Run as a two-role clinic: half the teams are the Ops consumer, half are the AI consumer, and neither knows the other's committed watermark. Deal the same 12 cards to both. At minute 11, pair one Ops team with one AI team and have them reconcile their rulings card by card — they will disagree on cards 3, 4 and 5, and the reconciliation forces the "one stream, two consumers, two watermarks" insight to be argued for rather than told. Then run a 3-minute plenary on card 12 only. Duration 22 minutes.

docs.title: ACT-08 — Quality-Gate Tribunal
docs.text: Field Value Activity ID ACT-08 Module M6 — Data Quality, Observability and Governance Day / Hour Day 4 · Hour 5 (during or immediately after LAB-06's gate task; pairs with CS-06) Duration 20 minutes Format Tribunal — teams are the gate and must rule on 10 real defects from the shipped fixtures Group size 3–4 per team; one member is the presiding judge who must announce and defend each ruling Deliverable A signed ruling sheet: for all 10 scenarios, a verdict (BLOCK / QUARANTINE / ALERT-ONLY), a scope, and the one-line justification

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Participants learn that a quality gate makes three different decisions, not one, and that choosing between them is a judgement about integrity versus meaning versus noise — not about severity.

Three outcomes: 1. BLOCK when partial promotion would produce silent corruption (integrity defects: keys, referential integrity, schema). 2. QUARANTINE when a bounded subset is untrustworthy and the rest is fine (the default for almost everything). 3. ALERT-ONLY rarely, and never for anything that would reach a model.

And the scoping rule: the scope of the ruling matters as much as the ruling. Blocking a whole batch because one city drifted converts a quality incident into an availability incident.

docs.title: 2. Materials (printable)
docs.text:
• Case cards (§7): 10 scenarios, each on A5, all drawn from the shipped fixtures in data/fixtures/.
  • Ruling sheet (§6), one per team.
  • The gate's three options posted large on the wall (§3).
  • Optional: a gavel. It is not a joke — it materially raises the seriousness of the rulings.

docs.title: 3. Setup (3 minutes)
docs.text:
Post on the wall:

   BLOCK          the whole batch is rejected. Nothing is promoted.
                  Use when partial promotion produces SILENT CORRUPTION.

   QUARANTINE     the failing rows/segment go to a quarantine table with the
                  failing expectation and batch id. Everything else promotes.
                  Use when the defect is BOUNDED and the rest is trustworthy.

   ALERT-ONLY     everything promotes; a human is notified.
                  Use when the signal is INFORMATIONAL and nothing downstream
                  will act on the data before a human does.

Then write the tribunal's standing rule beneath it:

A gate that only notifies is not a gate. If corrupt data reaches silver while an email sits unread, you have built an alarm, not a control.

docs.title: 4. Run of show
docs.text: Min What happens Facilitator 0–3 Frame. "You are the quality gate for Masar. Ten batches are in front of you this morning. For each: block, quarantine, or alert — and scope it." Read the standing rule aloud. Emphasise scope. Half the learning is in scope. 3–12 Deliberate. Teams rule on all 10 cards, writing verdict + scope + justification. Circulate. One question per team: "You blocked case 6. Four cities are fine. What did you just cost the business?" 12–18 The tribunal. Take cases in this order: 1, 4, 6, 9, 10 (the five that split rooms). The presiding judge of a randomly chosen team announces the ruling; the room may challenge; the judge defends. You play the operations manager under challenge: "You just stopped 19% of my platform because a statistic looked odd." Make them earn it. 18–20 Debrief. §5. Read the answer key for the five cases not argued. Land the integrity/meaning/noise distinction.

docs.title: 5. Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. Which cases did the room agree on instantly? (Cases 2 and 3 — null keys and a referential break. Integrity defects are unambiguous, and they are the only ones that justify a whole-batch block.)
  2. What made cases 6 and 9 hard? (Both are semantic: the data is individually valid and collectively wrong. Neither has a row-level rule. And in both, only part of the platform is affected — so scope is the whole decision.)
  3. Did anybody rule ALERT-ONLY on anything that feeds a model? (If so, walk them through the consequence: the model trains on it before a human reads the email. The sim-alertonly failure — the alarm rings and the corrupt data flows anyway.)
  4. Why is "no data" better than "wrong data"? (A gap in a dashboard prompts a question; plausible wrong numbers prompt a decision. Quarantine converts an invisible semantic corruption into a visible, bounded, operational gap — that conversion is the entire purpose of a gate.)
  5. Case 10 — you blocked it. What is now broken? (Nothing yet, and that is the point: an unknown producer_version is not a defect you can see, it is a defect you cannot rule out. Gating on it is how CS-11 becomes a one-day incident instead of a four-day one.)
  6. What is the cost of over-blocking? (Availability. A gate that blocks too readily gets disabled by an operations team under pressure, and a disabled gate protects nothing. Calibration is a safety feature.)
