│ Downstream: gold.eta_features.rolling_avg_speed_10m -> the ETA and   │
│ demand models; ops.alerts_speeding; gold.driver_daily safety score.  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ CASE 10 — UNKNOWN producer_version                                   │
│ Today's GPS batch contains producer_version "2.6.0". The allow-list  │
│ holds {"2.4.0", "2.5.0"}. 3,102 events, 61 vehicles.                 │
│ Every value in the batch is within range. Schema identical.          │
│ No release notes have been received from the vendor.                 │
│ Nothing is visibly wrong.                                            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 8. Answer key
docs.text:
# Verdict Scope Reasoning 1 Negative/absurd/zero fares QUARANTINE the 120 rows A bounded, row-identifiable defect. 7,118 good rows must promote. Note the three sub-cases differ: negative is impossible, > 50,000 is implausible, and fare_sar = 0.00 on a completed trip is the subtle one — it may be a legitimate promotional trip, so quarantine and let a human classify rather than assuming 2 Null primary keys BLOCK whole batch trip_id is the MERGE key. A null key cannot be merged, cannot be deduplicated, cannot be traced, and 20 nulls collapse to one row under most merge semantics — silent corruption of rows that are not themselves defective. The only unambiguous block in the deck 3 Out-of-domain city BLOCK whole batch A referential/domain break on a partition and join column. Promoting creates orphan partitions and silently drops rows from every dim_zone join — an integrity defect whose blast radius exceeds the 25 bad rows. (Accept QUARANTINE-25-rows as a defensible minority ruling if the team argues the join is an inner join that would exclude them anyway — but make them say so.) 4 Dropoff before pickup QUARANTINE the 15 rows Row-identifiable and bounded — but note the escalation: duration_min feeds the model label. A negative label is worse than a missing one, because it is learned from. Quarantine is right; alert-only would be a serious error here 5 Duplicate trip_id QUARANTINE the 8 dirty-batch dupes; PROMOTE the 120 genuine late trips; MERGE-UPDATE the 6 late-fixture dupes mixed The instructive case: not all duplicates are defects. The 6 late-fixture rows with existing trip_ids are corrections, and a MERGE on trip_id handles them correctly. The 8 dirty-batch dupes are genuine defects. The ruling depends on provenance, not on the symptom — which is why _source_file and _batch_id are mandatory in bronze 6 100× fare shift, one city QUARANTINE that city's batch only The scoping case. Fail-fast would block four healthy cities — 81% of the platform — converting a quality incident into an availability incident. Alert-only would promote a 100× error into the pricing model. Quarantine the city; promote the rest; page a human within one business day 7 3.1% missing geohash ALERT-ONLY — The one legitimate alert-only in the deck. Stable at 3.1% for six months, documented, feeds zone-level analysis rather than a model, and the NULL is honest — downstream aggregates can exclude it. Escalate to quarantine only if the rate changes, which is the real signal 8 Batch 4 hours late ALERT on freshness, BLOCK the gold build the downstream build, not the data Two decisions, and teams that give one have missed it. The data is fine — promote it. The problem is that the gold build already ran without it, so gold is stale. The correct action is to alert on freshness (within the 6 h warn SLA) and re-run the gold build — which is safe precisely because it is idempotent (ACT-04, CS-07) 9 Speed collapse, one cohort QUARANTINE producer_version = '2.5.0' CS-11 in one card. No row-level rule can catch it; only a distribution check segmented by producer_version. Quarantine that cohort: the ETA model receives fewer positions rather than 3.6×-wrong ones. Missing data asks a question; wrong data makes a decision. Note the safety consequence for the room: promoting silently disables speeding alerts for 1,004 vehicles 10 Unknown producer_version BLOCK / QUARANTINE the cohort producer_version = '2.6.0' The counter-intuitive one, and the most important. Nothing is visibly wrong — and that is exactly the point. An unknown producer version means an unverified semantic contract. Quarantine until: release notes reviewed for semantic change, contract version checked, unit factor confirmed, and a 24 h shadow comparison of the new cohort's distributions against the incumbent. Case 9 is case 10 four days later, unblocked

Score: BLOCK 2 (cases 2, 3) · QUARANTINE 6 (1, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10) · ALERT-ONLY 1 (case 7) · case 8 is a two-part ruling.

The pattern to state in the debrief: quarantine is the default, block is reserved for integrity defects where partial promotion silently corrupts good rows, and alert-only requires all of — stable, documented, understood, and not feeding a model. Only case 7 meets all four.

docs.title: 9. Cohort variants
docs.text:
Small cohort (< 8 participants). Run as a single tribunal with rotating judges: each participant presides over one or two cases, announces the ruling, and the rest of the room acts as counsel for the operations team (arguing against blocking) and counsel for the model owner (arguing against promoting). The adversarial framing supplies the tension that multiple teams would otherwise create, and it produces better justifications than team deliberation does. Cut to 7 cases if time is tight — keep 2, 5, 6, 9, 10 and any two others.

Large cohort (> 20 participants). Run as appellate rounds. Round 1: teams of 4 rule on all 10 independently (9 min). Round 2: each team passes its ruling sheet two tables to the right; the receiving team must appeal exactly two rulings in writing, citing the harm the original ruling causes (5 min). Round 3: plenary, taking only the cases with the most appeals — reliably 6, 9 and 10 (6 min). The appeal step forces engagement with someone else's reasoning, which is closer to a real design review than deliberating in a comfortable team. Duration 25 minutes.

docs.title: Could this feature have been known at prediction time?
docs.text: Field Value Activity ID ACT-09 Module M8 — Serving Gold to AI and BI Day / Hour Day 5 · Hour 4 (immediately after CS-08, before the capstone review) Duration 25 minutes Format Card-sort tribunal — every column of gold.eta_features classified against one question Group size 3–4 per team Deliverable All 13 columns of gold.eta_features placed in one of four categories, each with a written rationale; plus a reasoned position on the two genuinely arguable features Status Client-requested and mandatory. Do not cut this activity for time

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Participants acquire one question and learn to apply it without exception to every feature they will ever build:

That single question resolves most feature-correctness disputes immediately. The activity teaches four things in order of difficulty:

  1. The question itself, and that it is about a timestamp, not about a table.
  2. That "invalid" is not one thing — a feature can fail in three distinct ways, each with a different fix.
  3. That a column's verdict can depend on its provenance, not on its name — the same column name can be valid or leaking depending on where the value came from.
  4. That two of the thirteen are genuinely arguable, and that the professional response to ambiguity is not to win the argument but to remove the ambiguity by construction.

docs.title: "Could this feature have been known at prediction time?"
2. The four categories
docs.text:
Post these large on the wall. Participants must be able to distinguish them by minute 5.

Category Definition Fix VALID Knowable at feature_ts, computed from data strictly at or before it, and available identically offline and online none STALE Knowable at prediction time in principle, but the served value is older than the model was trained to expect. The value is not from the future — it is from too far in the past Increase publish frequency; add a freshness SLA and monitor publish lag LEAKAGE Computed using information that did not exist at feature_ts. Inflates offline metrics and cannot be reproduced live Re-bound the window to close strictly before the prediction instant UNAVAILABLE ONLINE Correct and non-leaking offline, but cannot be produced at inference within the latency budget, or is computed by a different code path online Materialise it: publish the offline value to the online store; never re-implement

The distinction that matters most and is most often missed: LEAKAGE and UNAVAILABLE ONLINE both produce "great offline, mediocre live" and they have completely different remedies. A team that diagnoses one when the other is present will ship a fix that changes nothing.

docs.title: 3. Materials (printable)
docs.text:
• Card deck (§8): 13 column cards, one per gold.eta_features column, printed A5 and cut. One deck per team.
  • Category mats: four A4 sheets per team, headed VALID / STALE / LEAKAGE / UNAVAILABLE ONLINE.
  • The scenario card (§8) — the prediction moment. One per team, read aloud first.
  • Verdict sheet (§7), one per team.

docs.title: 4. Setup (3 minutes)
docs.text: Post the four category definitions. Lay four mats and a shuffled deck on each table. Put the scenario card face-up at the head of each table — it must be visible throughout, because every ruling refers back to it.

docs.title: 5. Run of show
docs.text: Min What happens Facilitator 0–3 Frame. Read the scenario card aloud, slowly. Write 08:12:00 on the board and circle it. "That is the moment. Every card is judged against that moment and nothing else." Post the one question next to it. Do not add any other criterion. 3–5 Categories. Walk the four definitions. Stress that LEAKAGE and UNAVAILABLE ONLINE have the same symptom and different cures. 90 seconds. Do not over-explain; the sort teaches it. 5–15 Sort. Teams place all 13 cards and write a rationale on each. Circulate with exactly one question, repeated: "Could that have been known at 08:12?" Add nothing. Where a team is stuck on provenance, say: "Read the card again. It tells you where the value comes from." 15–19 Gallery walk. Each team moves one table right and marks, in a second colour, any card it would move. Silent. The cards that move: rolling_zone_demand_15m, historical_route_duration, distance_km, weather_condition. 19–23 Tribunal on the contested cards, in this order: distance_km (provenance), weather_condition (skew), then the two genuinely arguable ones. Resolve distance_km and weather_condition crisply. Do not resolve the two arguable ones by fiat — run §9's structured argument. 23–25 Debrief. §6. Close on the one question. Land the "remove the ambiguity by construction" point.

docs.title: 6. Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. How many cards did you place in under ten seconds? (Usually 8 or 9. The question is decisive far more often than people expect, which is why it is worth memorising verbatim.)
  2. Which card changed verdict when you read its provenance line? (distance_km. Metered distance is known only at dropoff — LEAKAGE. Routing-engine estimated distance is known at request — VALID. Same column name, opposite verdict. Lineage is not documentation; it is a correctness control.)
  3. What is the difference between STALE and LEAKAGE? (Direction in time. Leakage reads the future; staleness reads too far into the past. Leakage inflates your offline metric and cannot be reproduced live; staleness does not inflate anything — it silently degrades live performance while offline looks fine.)
  4. Why do LEAKAGE and UNAVAILABLE ONLINE feel identical? (Both present as "great offline, mediocre live." Fixing a leak when the real problem is an online re-implementation moves the live metric by almost nothing — which is exactly what CS-08's Wojhah discovered after a quarter of work.)
  5. What single architectural change removes the whole UNAVAILABLE ONLINE category? (Materialise the same table to both consumers: compute once in gold.eta_features, publish a copy to masar:features:zone:{zone_id}. Serving reads a value; it never derives one. The failure mode becomes staleness, which is bounded and monitorable, instead of skew, which is neither.)
  6. The two arguable features — did your team agree? (§9. The professional answer is not a verdict; it is a construction that makes the question unnecessary.)
  7. Which of these features did CS-11 corrupt, and does that change its verdict? (rolling_avg_speed_10m. No — it remains VALID. It was never leaking, never stale, never unavailable. It was semantically wrong. Point-in-time correctness and semantic correctness are independent properties, and you need both. This is the most important sentence in the activity.)

docs.title: 9. Answer key — full rationale per column
docs.text:
# Column Verdict Rationale 1 trip_id VALID (not a model input) Created at 08:12:00 as part of the request. It is row identity and a join key, never a feature — a model that learns from a monotonically increasing id is learning the calendar. Flag any team that feeds it to the model 2 pickup_zone_id VALID Resolved from device geolocation at the request instant. The rider is physically there 3 dropoff_zone_id VALID Entered by the rider before the request was submitted. The subtlety worth naming: it is the requested destination, not the actual one. If a rider changes destination mid-trip, the actual dropoff is future information; the requested one is not 4 hour_of_day VALID Deterministic function of feature_ts. Zero risk 5 day_of_week VALID Same. (Note for Masar: Friday's demand curve differs materially from Sunday–Thursday's, so this is a genuinely useful feature, not filler) 6 rolling_zone_demand_15m ARGUABLE → VALID if the frame is bounded See §10. The frame reaches CURRENT ROW, which includes the prediction instant and any row sharing that feature_ts — including, arguably, this request itself 7 rolling_avg_speed_10m VALID Window is strictly [feature_ts − 10 min, feature_ts). Nothing from the future. Available online from the same published table. And it is the column CS-11 corrupts — which does not change this verdict. Point-in-time correct and semantically wrong are independent failures 8 driver_recent_trip_count LEAKAGE The calendar hour 08:00–09:00 contains the prediction instant and extends past it. The count includes trips starting at 08:31 and 08:52. Worse, the driver was not even assigned until 08:12:44 — 44 seconds after the prediction, so at prediction time there is no driver to count trips for. Two independent leaks in one column 9 weather_condition UNAVAILABLE ONLINE (skew-prone) Not leaking — weather at 08:12 is observable at 08:12. But offline it is joined from weather_hourly (clear, dust, …) and online it comes from a third-party API with a different vocabulary ("Clear", "Dust storm"). The model receives categories it never saw in training. The fix is materialisation, not string normalisation — normalising two vocabularies keeps two implementations alive 10 distance_km LEAKAGE — as provenanced The card says it is the metered distance, written at dropoff (08:41). That is future information. Change the provenance to the routing-engine estimate available at 08:12 and the same column name becomes VALID. The verdict is a property of the lineage, not of the name — this is the card that teaches the most 11 historical_route_duration ARGUABLE → LEAKAGE as implemented; UNAVAILABLE ONLINE as served See §10. Offline, the 28-day window is anchored to the training job's run date, so a row from 3 May receives a median computed from trips through 1 June — a point-in-time violation. Online, it is a live 340 ms percentile query, blowing a 50 ms budget, over a 30-day window. Two different defects in one column 12 feature_ts VALID (the anchor, not a feature) It is the reference point every other verdict is measured against. Its own correctness is the precondition for the entire exercise: if feature_ts is ever set at trip completion instead of at request, every window in the table silently admits the future and no lint will catch it 13 label_actual_duration_min LEAKAGE if used as a feature; correct as the label Known only at 08:41:33. It is the target. The card is in the deck to test whether teams distinguish feature from label — a surprising number place it in VALID because "it is in the feature table". A label in a feature table is normal and correct; a label fed to the model as an input is the most complete leak possible

Summary: VALID 7 (cards 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 12) · LEAKAGE 3 (8, 10, 13-as-feature) · UNAVAILABLE ONLINE 1 (9) · ARGUABLE 2 (6, 11) · STALE 0 as written — and the STALE category being empty is itself a finding: no column here is stale yet, but every column served from Redis at a 60-second publish cadence becomes stale the moment the publish job falls behind, which is why publish lag must be monitored as a first-class SLA.

docs.title: 10. The two genuinely arguable features
docs.text: Run these as a structured argument. Take the "valid" case, then the "leaking" case, then ask for the construction that removes the question. Do not award a verdict.

docs.title: Arguable #1 — rolling_zone_demand_15m
docs.text:
The case for VALID. At 08:12:00 the number of trip requests in Olaya over 07:57–08:12 is a fact about the past. It is observable, it is causally prior, and it is exactly the kind of signal a dispatch system exists to react to. Nothing from the future is included.

The case for LEAKAGE. Three specific concerns, in increasing seriousness: 1. RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 15 MINUTES PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW includes rows sharing an identical feature_ts. At 174 requests/second platform-wide, ties are common. 2. It includes this request. The feature is therefore partly a function of the event being predicted — a self-referential term that is unavailable online, where this request has not yet been counted. 3. The fatal one: the frame's correctness depends entirely on feature_ts meaning "request time" for every row in the table. If any upstream path ever sets feature_ts at trip completion, the window silently admits fifteen minutes of the future and no syntactic lint will detect it, because the SQL is unchanged.

The construction that removes the argument — and this is the deliverable:

-- 1. Close the frame strictly before the prediction instant
COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY pickup_zone_id ORDER BY feature_ts
               RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 15 MINUTES PRECEDING
                         AND INTERVAL  1 SECOND  PRECEDING)  AS rolling_zone_demand_15m

-- 2. Assert the anchor, as a build-failing test
--    (this is the assertion that protects concern 3, which the lint cannot)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM gold.eta_features WHERE feature_ts <> pickup_ts;   -- must be 0

The lesson: the professional response to an arguable feature is not to win the argument. It is to remove the ambiguity, cheaply, so that nobody has the argument again — including the version of you that reviews this table in eight months.

docs.title: Arguable #2 — historical_route_duration
docs.text:
The case for VALID. It is a median over historical completed trips on the same route at the same hour. It is strictly historical by construction, it is the single most predictive feature in the model, and removing it would materially degrade a model that is genuinely useful.

The case for LEAKAGE. The window is anchored to the training job's run date, not to each row's feature_ts. So a training row from 3 May receives a median computed from trips through 1 June — a month of future information, averaged in. This is the most common point-in-time violation in industry, it is invisible in the SQL text (a lint sees only INTERVAL 28 DAY), and it inflates offline metrics quietly rather than dramatically.

And separately: UNAVAILABLE ONLINE. The serving path issues a live percentile_cont against Postgres at p95 340 ms against a 50 ms budget, over a 30-day window where training used 28. Even with the anchoring fixed, training and serving compute different numbers.

The construction that removes both problems:

-- 1. Anchor the window PER ROW, not per job run
LEFT JOIN route_stats r
  ON  r.pickup_zone_id  = f.pickup_zone_id
  AND r.dropoff_zone_id = f.dropoff_zone_id
  AND r.hour_of_day     = f.hour_of_day
  AND r.as_of_date      = date(f.feature_ts)   -- <<< per-row anchor, precomputed daily
-- route_stats holds, for each as_of_date, the median over the 28 days ENDING that date.

-- 2. Materialise, do not re-derive online
--    publish route_stats into the online store keyed by
--    (pickup_zone, dropoff_zone, hour_of_day); serving does a GET, ~2 ms.

The lesson: a feature definition that does not state its temporal anchor is not a definition. Two engineers can implement "28-day median" correctly and differently, and only one of them is point-in-time correct.

docs.title: The meta-lesson
docs.text:
Both arguable features are arguable for the same underlying reason: their definitions are under-specified about time. Neither states, unambiguously, relative to what instant the window is measured. Every genuinely contested feature you will meet in your career will have this shape.

The rule to write down:

Every feature definition must state its anchor, its window boundaries (open or closed), and its source table. A definition missing any of the three is a conversation, not a specification.

docs.title: 11. Extension for fast teams
docs.text:
Hand these three cards to any team that finishes early. They are the traps that appear in real feature tables.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ X1  driver_rating                                           double   │
│     The driver's current star rating, from silver.drivers.           │
│     PROVENANCE: drivers.csv is OVERWRITTEN nightly with the          │
│     CURRENT rating. The training set joins today's ratings onto      │
│     trips from 90 days ago.                                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   Verdict: LEAKAGE. A slowly-changing dimension joined without an
   as-of date. The 90-day-old trip receives a rating partly EARNED BY
   THAT VERY TRIP. Fix: SCD-2 on drivers, joined as-of feature_ts.
   This is the single most common leak in production feature tables and
   it never appears in a window function, so no lint finds it.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ X2  zone_avg_fare_today                                     double   │
│     Mean fare in pickup_zone_id, for the CURRENT CALENDAR DAY.       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   Verdict: LEAKAGE. A calendar-day bucket containing feature_ts
   extends to 23:59. An 08:12 prediction reads the whole day's mean.
   Same shape as driver_recent_trip_count. Calendar buckets that
   CONTAIN the prediction instant are always a leak.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ X3  surge_multiplier                                        double   │
│     The multiplier applied to this trip.                             │
│     PROVENANCE: silver.trips.surge_multiplier, written at the        │
│     moment the fare is quoted — 08:12:00.                            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   Verdict: VALID — but interrogate it. It is known at 08:12:00, so it
   passes the question. However it is DOWNSTREAM OF THE MODEL'S OWN
   OUTPUT in the live system (surge responds to demand, which responds
   to dispatch, which responds to ETA). Training on it creates a
   feedback loop. Point-in-time correct, architecturally hazardous.
   The question resolves timing; it does not resolve causality.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ X4  vehicle_capacity                                           int   │
│     Seats in the assigned vehicle, from vehicles.csv.                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   Verdict: LEAKAGE (by assignment timing). The vehicle is assigned at
   08:12:44 — 44 seconds AFTER the prediction. Any attribute of the
   assigned driver or vehicle is future information at quote time.
   Same root cause as driver_recent_trip_count, different column.

docs.title: 12. Cohort variants
docs.text:
Small cohort (< 8 participants). Run as an individual sort with mandatory defence. Each participant takes 2–3 cards, places them, and defends each aloud in 30 seconds; any other participant may challenge once, and a challenge must cite the timestamp that makes the feature invalid. Then run §10's two arguable features as a full-group structured argument with the facilitator writing both cases on the board. With few people, the depth on the two arguable features is worth more than breadth, so allocate 10 of the 25 minutes to §10 alone. Include the §11 extension cards in the main deck rather than holding them back.

Large cohort (> 20 participants). Run role-split tribunals. Assign half the teams the role of Model Owner (incentive: keep as many features as possible — every removed feature costs accuracy) and half the role of Platform Reviewer (incentive: block anything that cannot be reproduced live). Both sort the same 13 cards independently (10 min), then pair one of each and reconcile card by card (7 min). They will disagree on exactly cards 6, 10 and 11 — which is precisely the disagreement that happens in real feature reviews, with real incentives behind it. Close with a 5-minute plenary in which each pair reports the construction they agreed on for their contested cards, not the verdict. The role split makes the ambiguity felt rather than described, and it is the strongest version of this activity. Duration 30 minutes.

docs.title: ACT-10 — Capstone Peer-Review Carousel
docs.text: Field Value Activity ID ACT-10 Module Capstone (spans M1–M8) Day / Hour Day 5 · Hour 6 (after capstone build time, before final presentations) Duration 45 minutes (three 12-minute rotations + a 9-minute synthesis) Format Structured rotation — every team reviews three others' capstones against a fixed sheet and receives three reviews of its own Group size Teams of 3–4; works with 4–8 teams. With 3 teams, run two rotations Deliverable Three completed review sheets received by each team, plus a one-page remediation commitment: the three findings the team will fix before the final presentation, with the evidence each fix will produce

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Three outcomes, and the third is the one that matters most.

  1. Every capstone gets three independent reviews — far more feedback than an instructor can produce, and more varied.
  2. Reviewing teaches more than being reviewed. A team that finds a missing idempotency guarantee in someone else's DAG will never omit one in its own. The carousel converts each team's blind spot into three other teams' teaching material.
  3. Participants rehearse the professional act of a design review: cite evidence, name the consumer who is harmed, propose a specific fix, and separate a defect from a preference.

docs.title: 2. Materials (printable)
docs.text:
• Review sheet (§7), printed 4 copies per team (three to give away, one to self-assess before the carousel starts).
  • Reviewer briefing card (§6), one per participant.
  • Remediation commitment sheet (§8), one per team.
  • A visible rotation schedule (§5) and a loud timer.
  • Each team needs its capstone running and demonstrable at its home station: the DAG, the Lakehouse tables, the quality suite, the serving path, and its written design document.

docs.title: 3. Setup (5 minutes before the session)
docs.text:
Arrange teams at fixed home stations around the room. Post the rotation schedule where everyone can see it. Assign each team a letter (A–F).

One team member stays at the home station for every rotation as the HOST; the rest travel as REVIEWERS. Rotate who hosts if the team prefers, but the host must not change mid-rotation — the reviewers need a consistent respondent.

Announce the two rules that make the carousel work:

1. Every finding must cite something you can point at — a line of code, a table, a query result, a missing file. "It feels fragile" is not a finding.

2. Every finding must name the consumer who is harmed and how. "This is not idempotent" is an observation. "If this task is re-run after a failure, gold.driver_daily doubles and 3,450 drivers are overpaid" is a finding.

docs.title: 4. Run of show
docs.text:
Min What happens Facilitator 0–4 Brief. Read the two rules. Walk the review sheet's five sections in 90 seconds. Hand out reviewer briefing cards. Emphasise that a review with no findings is a failed review, not a perfect capstone. Every capstone in the room has at least three findings 4–6 Self-assessment. Each team completes a review sheet on its own capstone, honestly, and seals it. It is opened at minute 36. This is the highest-leverage two minutes in the activity. The gap between self-assessment and peer assessment is the individual learning 6–18 Rotation 1. Reviewers travel per §5. HOST gives a 3-minute demo, then answers questions. Reviewers complete the sheet in the remaining 9 minutes and hand it to the host. Circulate. Kill any demo that runs past 3 minutes — reviewers need the time more than hosts do 18–30 Rotation 2. Same structure, new station. Watch for review fatigue in rotation 2. Prompt: "Section 4 is the one everyone skips. Do section 4 first this time." 30–42 Rotation 3. Same structure, new station. — 42–48 Synthesis. Teams return home, open their sealed self-assessment, read their three peer reviews, and complete the remediation commitment sheet. The instruction: "Pick the three findings that appear in more than one review. Those are real. Findings that appear once may be preferences." 48–51 Round-robin close. Each team states, in one sentence, the single finding it did not see coming. Do not let this become a report-out. One sentence, strictly. It is the most honest three minutes of the course

(45 minutes if the close is cut; 51 with it. Keep the close — it is worth over-running for.)

docs.title: 5. Rotation schedule
docs.text:
Six teams (A–F). Reviewers move; hosts stay.

Rotation A reviews B reviews C reviews D reviews E reviews F reviews 1 B C D E F A 2 D E F A B C 3 F A B C D E

Every team reviews three others and is reviewed by three others; no pair meets twice.

Four teams (A–D): rotation 1 A→B, B→C, C→D, D→A; rotation 2 A→C, B→D, C→A, D→B; rotation 3 A→D, B→A, C→B, D→C.

Five teams (A–E): rotation n — team X reviews the team n positions to its right, for n = 1, 2, 3.

Three teams: run two rotations of 15 minutes each; every team reviews both others.

docs.title: 8. Remediation commitment sheet (one per team, minute 42)
9. Answer key — what reviewers should find
docs.text:
This is the facilitator's list of the defects that are actually present in most capstones at this stage. Use it to prompt a rotation that is producing thin reviews, and to check the quality of the reviews handed in.

Frequency Defect Where it hides The question that exposes it Very common A gold aggregate uses INSERT INTO instead of MERGE/replaceWhere The DAG's gold tasks "Run it twice." Very common The quality gate logs and promotes anyway (exit 0 regardless) The gate task's return value "Show me a batch that got blocked." Very common Drift check computed on the aggregate, not segmented The GX suite's group_by (absent) "A unit changes on 34% of one cohort. Does this fire?" Common No lookback window; the model filters = current_date() The silver model's WHERE "A trip settles at 00:40. Which day does it count in?" Common feature_ts set at trip completion rather than at request The feature build's feature_ts derivation "Show me SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE feature_ts <> pickup_ts." Common Online features re-implemented rather than published from gold The serving code "Which line of code computes the online value?" Common The baseline for drift is a rolling window The GX suite's baseline definition "The bug has been live 14 days. Does your check still fire?" Common No OPTIMIZE/VACUUM task in the DAG The DAG's task list "It is month three. How many files are in this table?" Occasional producer_version dropped at ingest The ingest job's .drop() or select() "Group by producer version. Show me." Occasional Dedup performed in bronze The ingest job "What is your duplicate rate this week?" Occasional Raw rider_id reaches a BI view or the online store The serving views / Redis keys "Show me the schema of what BI reads." Occasional VACUUM retention set to a default with no justification The maintenance task "A regulator disputes a figure from 25 days ago." Occasional Grain of a gold table undeclared or unenforced The design document "How many rows per driver per day, and what enforces that?" Rare but severe BI and AI compute the same measure by different paths Two SQL files "Do these two numbers reconcile? Run both."

Calibration note for the facilitator. A good review sheet has 3–6 findings, at least one per section, each with evidence and harm. A sheet with 12 findings is usually a list of preferences; a sheet with one is usually a reviewer who did not open the code. Say this at the brief.

docs.title: 10. Debrief questions (use in the 3-minute close, or extend to 8 if time allows)
docs.text:
1. What did you find in someone else's capstone that you then went and checked in your own? (This is the carousel's whole value. Nearly every team has one. Collect three or four answers.)
  2. How big was the gap between your self-assessment and your peers'? (The gap is not embarrassing — it is the measurement. A team that scored itself 26/30 and was scored 18/30 has just learned exactly which blind spots it has, which no instructor could have told them as credibly.)
  3. Which section had the most findings across the room? (Reliably section 3 — quality and observability — followed by section 4. Sections 1 and 2 are well covered by the labs; sections 3 and 4 are where judgement is required and where the course's hardest cases live.)
  4. Did anyone give a finding that turned out to be a preference? (Good. Distinguishing the two is a professional skill, and getting it wrong in a review costs you credibility for the finding that was real.)
  5. Section 5 — how many hosts could answer the course question about their own system? (This is the summative assessment of the entire week, asked by peers rather than by an instructor. A team that can answer it — naming a component, a feature, a control with a threshold, and a business observation with a time lag — has learned what the course was for.)

docs.title: 11. Cohort variants
docs.text:
Small cohort (< 8 participants — typically 2 teams). A carousel does not work with two teams. Run instead a deep mutual review: 20 minutes each way, with the reviewing team required to complete all five sections in full rather than one finding per section, and to perform three live tests at the host's keyboard — run the DAG twice, kill a task and recover, and trace one gold row back to a raw file. The depth compensates for the absent variety. Add the facilitator as a third reviewer for both teams so each still receives two independent perspectives. Duration 45 minutes unchanged.

Large cohort (> 20 participants — 6+ teams). Keep three rotations (more produces review fatigue and declining quality) but add a specialist assignment: in rotation 1 every reviewing team reviews sections 1 and 2 only, in rotation 2 section 3 only, in rotation 3 sections 4 and 5 only. Reviews get sharper and faster, section 4 stops being skipped, and each capstone still receives full coverage across its three reviews. Then add a 5-minute plenary defect league table: the facilitator collects all sheets and reads out the three most frequently occurring findings across the whole room. Seeing that eleven of twelve capstones share the same defect is a more powerful lesson than any individual review, and it is the ideal final note before presentations. Duration 50 minutes.

docs.title: BENCHMARKS MASTER — SDA-DSC-214
docs.text:
Every module's benchmark table in one instructor reference. Modern Data Engineering for AI Systems · SDAIA Academy

What this is for. During labs and capstone grading, a participant shows you a number. This document tells you, at a glance, whether that number is in range, how it was supposed to be measured, and what the reference run produced. Use it to spot the two failure modes that matter: a number that is impossible (fabricated or measured wrong) and a number that is plausible but wrong (measured on the wrong thing).

The reference column is a MacBook Pro M2, 16 GB, Spark 3.5.1 local[8], delta-spark 3.2.0, single-broker Kafka, spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=8. Absolute timings on other hardware will differ, sometimes by 3×. Ratios and counts are the deliverable; timings are context. Say this to the room on Day 1 and repeat it on Day 5.

Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. Grains, ratios and file-count reductions hold at either scale; absolute row counts do not.

docs.title: 0. Reading a participant's number in ten seconds
docs.text:
Ask If the answer is Then Is it a count or a ratio? count or ratio It must land in the range below. Hardware is no excuse absolute timing Check the ratio between their before and after instead Was the JVM warm? first run of the session Landing throughput is dominated by 6–10 s of JVM and Delta-jar startup. Ask for the second run Is the hardware stated in BENCHMARKS.md? no The number is unsourced. Criterion 1/2 evidence, not a pass/fail Does it match another participant's exactly? yes, on a timing Integrity signal A7. Ratios may legitimately match; absolute timings on different laptops do not

The distinction that fails more participants than any other number here. rows − distinct event_id ≈ 0.4% is the seeded source defect from CONVENTIONS — a data problem, fixed at silver by dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark. Before the unit fix, max_speed_250 = 33.0. Show both numbers. The 33.0 is what makes the m/s incident dangerous — it is a plausible speed, which is why schema validation and range checks both pass.

Reported Why it is wrong Pipeline duplicates > 0 after kill/restart, described as "expected" Confusing the 0.4% seeded source defect with a pipeline fault Pipeline duplicates = 0 without a kill/restart having been performed The claim has no evidence; the number is a default, not a measurement numFiles reduction ≥ 10× on a table built in a single write Nothing was fragmented; the ratio was copied from the lab guide Gigabytes reclaimed by VACUUM on lab day at RETAIN 168 HOURS Tombstoned files are inside the retention window; either the retention was shortened or the figure is invented Byte reduction exactly equal to the column reduction (e.g. both 89%) Estimated from column count rather than measured from the plan rel_diff "close to zero" It is exactly zero when both paths descend from the same silver; "close" means a filter differs Post-fix R² still above 0.85 The leak was not fixed, whatever the classification table says Landing throughput ≥ 200k rows/s on a cold first run Measured a warm-cache re-read, or reported the target rather than the result Identical absolute timings to another participant Integrity signal A7 — ratios may match, laptop timings do not Late-data drops = 0 with the late-ping fixture loaded Either the fixture was not loaded or the watermark is too generous to be doing anything

docs.title: Capstone — The Masar Mini-Lakehouse
docs.text:
Participant-facing brief. SDA-DSC-214 · Modern Data Engineering for AI Systems · SDAIA Academy

Field Value Title The Masar Mini-Lakehouse — a production data platform for a Saudi mobility operator Weight 40% of the course grade (labs 30% · PA-1/2/3 20% · quiz 10%) Work mode Individual repository; pairs may share a build during labs but each participant submits and demos their own Build window Day 1 Hour 3 through Day 5 Hour 4 — every lab is a component, not a detour Demo Day 5 Hour 5 · 6 minutes · rubric-scored live Pass ≥ 70 overall. Distinction ≥ 90. Extensions add up to +5 (capped at 100) only when mandatory scope is ≥ 80 Graded from The running platform and the repository first; the demo second

docs.title: 1. Scenario
docs.text:
You are the data platform engineer for Masar (مسار), the national smart-mobility operator running ride-hailing and public-transit services across Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam, Mecca and Medina.

The analytics organisation hands you raw feeds and two non-negotiable demands.

The feeds. Batch trip records and driver and vehicle masters arrive as daily CSV. GPS telemetry arrives continuously as a Kafka event stream at roughly 25 pings per trip — 1.2 million events a day — from an SDK fleet that is not fully version-aligned. Payments settle asynchronously. Weather lands hourly, after the hour it describes.

The two demands. - The ETA and demand-forecasting squad needs an AI feature service: point-in-time-correct features, offline for training and online for inference at sub-50 ms, with offline and online provably identical. - The operations leadership reviews a BI dashboard every morning at 07:00 and makes dispatch and surge decisions from it. Numbers that disagree with the data-science team's numbers are worse than no numbers.

Your mandate. Deliver a Mini-Lakehouse both teams can trust — because the platform proves its own correctness, freshness, and governance without a human vouching for it. Saudi PDPL is a first-class constraint, not a Day-5 afterthought: rider identifiers and precise GPS are personal data, and the platform must be able to classify them, minimise them, retain them lawfully, and erase them on request.

The question every design decision must answer:

"What happens to Masar's AI system if THIS part of the data platform fails?"

Everything you built in Labs 1–8 is a component. The capstone is the integration, the proof, and your own extension.

docs.title: 2. Mandatory requirements
docs.text:
Eight requirements. Each maps to a learning outcome and to a rubric criterion. All eight are in scope; none is optional.

# Requirement LO Rubric criterion Built in R1 Medallion architecture. Bronze (append-only, lineage columns on every table) → silver (conformed, one row per key) → gold (marts + feature table). Layer contracts documented and enforced in code. No layer bypassed — no gold table reads bronze. LO1, LO7 Architecture & medallion contracts (15) Labs 1, 3, 7 R2 Compute–storage discipline. Data in an object-storage-style layout. A BENCHMARKS.md cost and scan analysis from your runs. Gold marts OPTIMIZEd and ZORDERed with a measured file-count reduction. LO2 Architecture (15) + Delta (15) Labs 1, 2, 4 R3 ELT pipeline. dbt (or Spark) staging → silver, incremental merge on trip_id with a lookback window; source-freshness SLA plus ≥ 6 data tests; a demonstrated late-arrival backfill. LO3 ELT & incrementality (15) Lab 3 R4 Delta Lake. silver.trips as constrained Delta (schema + CHECK constraints); idempotent MERGE upserts proven twice; a time-travel audit diff; OPTIMIZE/VACUUM with a justified retention; one demonstrated PDPL erasure. LO4 Delta Lake mastery (15) Lab 4 R5 Streaming. Kafka GPS topic → Structured Streaming → bronze.gps_events, exactly-once with a dedicated checkpoint per query; a kill/restart proof of zero pipeline duplicates; event-time windowed demand with a watermark. LO5 Streaming (15) Lab 5 R6 Quality, observability, governance. A Great Expectations suite that acts — fail-fast on integrity, quarantine on partial, always alert; freshness / volume / schema-drift / distribution-drift checks that each fire on an injected fault; PII classification and an automated retention job; rendered data docs as evidence. LO6 Quality, observability, governance (15) Lab 6 R7 Orchestration. The full medallion as one dependency-ordered, idempotent DAG, runnable by one command, with a demonstrated idempotent recovery from an injected mid-DAG failure. LO7 Orchestration & recovery (15) Lab 7 R8 Serving. A point-in-time-correct feature table served offline and materialised online with consistency proven across every key; a conformed star schema that reconciles with the demand mart; a PDPL-safe serving view. LO8 Serving (AI + BI) & demo (10) Lab 8

docs.title: Layer contracts you must state and enforce
docs.text: Layer Contract bronze.* Append-only; schema as received; carries _ingested_at, _source_file, _batch_id; never mutated; readable by platform engineers only silver.trips One row per trip_id; enforced schema plus positive_fare and valid_duration CHECK constraints; timezone and units conformed; completed valid trips only; rejects routed to silver.trips_quarantine; readable by data scientists silver.vehicle_positions One row per event_id; event-time semantics with a stated watermark; speed_kmh always in km/h (the 2.5.0 m/s incident normalised); accuracy_m ≤ 50 gold.* Documented grain, enforced by an assertion in code; idempotent write strategy; readable by analysts and the model service; no raw personal identifiers

docs.title: 3. Extension menu — choose at least one
docs.text:
Extensions earn up to +5 bonus, capped at 100, and only when mandatory scope already scores ≥ 80. Choose depth over breadth: one extension done to production standard scores better than three sketched.

# Extension What "done" looks like Effort E1 Offline/online consistency check wired into CI consistency_check.py runs in CI across all zone keys and all online columns, exits non-zero on divergence, and you show it failing on an injected mismatch Low — highest value per minute; most commonly chosen E2 A leakage-lint that fails the pipeline A DAG task that inspects feature window bounds and fails the run if any frame includes non-prior data; demonstrated failing on a deliberately widened bound Medium E3 Multi-city 7-day backfill make pipeline-backfill FROM=... TO=... over 7 days; prove the backfilled state is byte-identical (checksums) to incremental runs over the same window Medium E4 A second streaming consumer group An independent consumer group off masar.gps.pings driving a live console demand view, with its own checkpoint, running simultaneously with the bronze ingest Medium E5 Direct-serve endpoint benchmarked A Trino / Databricks-SQL direct-serve path against gold, benchmarked head-to-head with the materialised mart (p50/p95, bytes scanned) and a written recommendation High

docs.title: 5. Deliverables
docs.text:
Submit a single git repository URL containing all six deliverables. Everything is graded from the repository and a live run; nothing is graded from slides.

# Deliverable Must contain D1 Git repository with full commit history Checkpoint commits from each lab; a readable history (not one "final" commit); make pipeline as the one-command interface D2 A runnable Mini-Lakehouse All bronze / silver / gold tables produced by a clean run, with documented grains and contracts in MINI_LAKEHOUSE.md D3 BENCHMARKS.md The course benchmark tables filled from your runs: scan/cost (M2), small-files before/after OPTIMIZE (M4), streaming kill/restart dedup (M5), gold task rows and idempotency (M7), serving latency and consistency (M8). See BENCHMARKS_MASTER.md for target ranges D4 GOVERNANCE.md PII classification table (column → classification → access level → retention → PDPL basis); the retention policy with its justification; the erasure runbook naming every table holding a rider's data; a demonstrated erasure with its transcript D5 The 6-minute demo One-command pipeline run · streaming kill/restart with zero duplicates · quality-gate quarantine · time-travel audit · AI and BI consumers reading gold D6 DECISIONS.md Five one-paragraph engineering decisions with rationale and what would change them. Suggested set: partition-key choice · VACUUM retention · stream/batch boundary · online store yes/no · feature window and lookback

Also expected in the repository (evidence the rubric looks for, not separately graded): LAB1_NOTES.md … LAB8_NOTES.md, LAB8_LEAKAGE.md, rendered GX data docs, and the pipeline run logs under logs/.

docs.title: 6. Milestones
docs.text:
Milestones are gates, not suggestions. A missed gate is recoverable; an unnoticed missed gate is not — the Day-5 assembly assumes M-A through M-C are green.

Milestone Content Due Gate — how it is checked M-A Bronze landing (batch + stream) + profiling End Day 2 Instructor spot-check: three bronze tables exist with all three lineage columns; a re-run grows history rather than replacing it; ≥ 3 swamp risks documented in LAB1_NOTES.md M-B ELT silver + Delta constraints + tests End Day 3 dbt test green with ≥ 6 tests; silver.trips is constrained Delta (SHOW TBLPROPERTIES lists positive_fare and valid_duration); MERGE run twice shows updated=5 then updated=0; late-arrival backfill demonstrated M-C Streaming exactly-once + quality gate + governance End Day 4 Kill/restart demo with 0 pipeline duplicates; a dirty batch shown blocked (null keys) and another quarantined (bad fares) with rows visible in silver.trips_quarantine; PII classification table drafted M-D Orchestrated DAG + gold + serving Day 5, H2–H3 make pipeline runs end to end from a clean state; an injected mid-DAG failure leaves gold unchanged and a full re-run reproduces the identical state (checksums); gold.eta_features has exactly the 13 CONVENTIONS columns M-E Demo + submission Day 5, H5 Repository URL submitted before Hour 5 begins; live 6-minute demo; rubric scored

If you are behind at a gate, say so at the gate. Fast-forward tags (lab5-start, lab7-start, …) exist for exactly this and using one costs you nothing on the rubric — the capstone is graded on the platform you submit, not on how you got there. Silently arriving at Day 5 without a working silver table is the only unrecoverable path.

docs.title: 7. Submission checklist
docs.text:
Tick every line before you submit. Anything unticked is a mark you have chosen not to earn.

Repository - [ ] Repository URL submitted; the branch to grade is named in the README - [ ] make pipeline runs end to end on a clean clone with the documented setup, and writes a timestamped log - [ ] make doctor passes on the submitted commit - [ ] Commit history shows per-lab progress, not a single squashed commit

R2 Compute–storage - [ ] BENCHMARKS.md scan table filled: columns read, files read, bytes read, relative bytes scanned - [ ] numFiles before/after OPTIMIZE recorded for at least three tables - [ ] Prices in the cost model cited with a URL and a read-date

R3 ELT - [ ] Incremental model merges on trip_id with a stated lookback window - [ ] ≥ 6 dbt tests passing, including unique and not_null on the silver key - [ ] Source freshness SLA declared and demonstrated firing - [ ] Late-arrival backfill demonstrated: inserted -> 1 then inserted -> 0 on repeat

R4 Delta - [ ] positive_fare and valid_duration CHECK constraints present; a negative-fare write shown rejected - [ ] MERGE idempotency shown: run 1 updated=5, run 2 updated=0 - [ ] Time-travel diff of two versions included - [ ] VACUUM ... RETAIN 168 HOURS (or a justified alternative ≥ 168h); retentionDurationCheck enabled - [ ] One PDPL erasure demonstrated with before/after counts across every affected table

R5 Streaming - [ ] One checkpointLocation per query under ./lakehouse/_checkpoints/<query_name>; no sharing - [ ] Kill/restart proof table in LAB5_NOTES.md: pipeline-introduced duplicates = 0 - [ ] Event-time window with a watermark; the count dropped beyond the watermark recorded and explained - [ ] speed_kmh normalised for producer_version = 2.5.0

R6 Quality & governance - [ ] GX suite with ≥ 7 expectations; data docs rendered and committed - [ ] Gate acts: a blocked batch and a quarantined batch, both with row counts - [ ] silver.trips_quarantine contains real rows with a reason column - [ ] Four observability signals each shown firing on an injected fault - [ ] GOVERNANCE.md classification table complete; retention job runs; erasure runbook lists every table including silver.trips_quarantine

R7 Orchestration - [ ] One DAG, dependency-ordered, every task idempotent - [ ] Injected mid-DAG failure: downstream tasks skipped, gold unchanged - [ ] Full re-run reproduces identical state — counts and checksums - [ ] OPTIMIZE/VACUUM run as DAG tasks, not by hand

R8 Serving - [ ] gold.eta_features has exactly the 13 CONVENTIONS columns, one row per trip_id - [ ] Every column classified in LAB8_LEAKAGE.md; every LEAKAGE / STALE / UNAVAILABLE column fixed with the name kept - [ ] Both metrics recorded: pre-fix (inflated) and post-fix (honest), with an explanation of why the drop is correct - [ ] Redis populated under masar:features:zone:{zone_id}; consistency check passes across all keys and columns and has been shown to fail on an injected divergence - [ ] Star schema reconciles with the demand mart at rel_diff = 0 - [ ] PDPL boundary check passes: no rider_id, no raw lat/lon, no national_id_hash or phone_hash in any gold product or Redis key

Extension - [ ] At least one extension implemented and demonstrated, with its evidence in the repository

docs.title: 8. Demo script — 6 minutes, minute by minute
docs.text:
You will be stopped at 6:00. Rehearse it once; the difference between a 6-minute demo and a 9-minute demo is entirely rehearsal.

Before you start: terminals open and cd'd, Kafka and Redis up, the pipeline already run once so tables exist, and a second terminal pre-loaded with the kill/restart producer. Do not run a cold build live.

Time Beat What you show What you say 0:00–0:45 The platform in one command make pipeline starting; the task log scrolling: land_bronze → quality_gate → build_silver → observability → three gold tasks → optimize_vacuum "One command, eight tasks, dependency-ordered. Every task is idempotent, so this is also my recovery procedure." Name the one architectural decision you are proudest of 0:45–1:45 Streaming: kill and restart Pre-kill count → Ctrl-C mid-batch → post-kill count → restart → drained count. Point at the checkpoint path "110,000 pings in, 110,000 rows in bronze, zero pipeline duplicates. Exactly-once is the composition of Kafka's replayable offsets and Delta's atomic commit, and it lives in this directory." Distinguish source duplicates (0.4%, a data problem) from pipeline duplicates (0, an engineering problem) 1:45–2:45 The gate acts Run the null-key dirty batch → GateBlocked, 0 promoted. Run the bad-fares batch → 120 quarantined, 41,976 promoted. SELECT * FROM silver.trips_quarantine LIMIT 3 showing the reason column "Integrity failure blocks, because the MERGE key is null and quarantining would relocate the damage without containing it. A 0.25% value failure quarantines, because blocking would take the dashboard down over 120 rows." 2:45–3:30 Time travel and PDPL DESCRIBE HISTORY → the version diff showing five corrected fares → the erasure: rider present at version n−1, absent at n → the retention number "A regulator asks what this table held three weeks ago. It can answer, because VACUUM retains 168 hours and I can justify that number three ways." 3:30–4:30 Two consumers, one truth The BI dashboard query returning the star; the demand mart returning the same revenue at rel_diff = 0; redis-cli GET masar:features:zone:ZN-RUH-014; consistency_check PASS across all keys "Same silver, two contracts. The star and the demand mart reconcile because they share conformed dimensions. Online equals offline because the online path copies, never recomputes — and here is the check that proves it for every key." 4:30–5:15 The leakage story The pre-fix metric, the diagnostic that exposed the leak, the post-fix metric "R² 0.943 became 0.712 and that is the correct outcome. The first number was the model reading the answer — distance_km is metered at dropoff and correlates 0.947 with the label. The second number is what the platform can deliver at 07:14:33." 5:15–5:45 Recovery, and your extension The injected-failure snapshot diff (before == during, before == after), then 20 seconds on your extension "Gold never moved while silver was broken, and a full re-run reproduced the exact state including checksums." 5:45–6:00 Close One sentence Answer the course question for your own platform: what happens to Masar's AI system if this part fails — and what your build does about it

Demo rules - Pre-run everything that takes more than 20 seconds; show artefacts, not progress bars. - If something fails live, say what you expected, what you see, and what you would check first. A calm diagnosis scores better than a lucky rerun. - The assessor may interrupt once to ask you to verify a claim live — most often the kill/restart or the leakage explanation. Expect it.

docs.title: 9. Academic integrity
docs.text:
The capstone is graded on your platform producing your numbers. The rules are short and they are enforced.

What is expected and encouraged - Using the course starter code, the lab reference solutions, and the checkpoint tags. This is a build course; reusing the labs is the design. - Pair work during labs, discussion at any time, and helping a colleague debug. - External documentation, blog posts and AI assistants for understanding and for writing code you then run and verify.

What is required - Every number in BENCHMARKS.md comes from a run on your machine, with your hardware and Spark version named. Benchmark numbers are hardware-dependent; identical figures across repositories are the primary integrity signal and are checked automatically. - Every quarantine artefact, run log and data-docs render is from your own run. Identical quarantine artefacts across repositories are checked. - DECISIONS.md is in your own words and defends your choices; a decision you cannot defend when asked scores zero for that entry regardless of how it reads. - Any code you did not write and did not adapt is attributed in the file header, including code from an AI assistant. - If you fast-forward to a checkpoint tag, say so in your README. It costs no marks.

What is prohibited - Submitting another participant's repository, or a repository with commits authored by another participant, in whole or in part. - Copying benchmark, quarantine or metric numbers you did not produce. - Fabricating a transcript — a pasted output that your code could not have produced. - Presenting a demo of a platform you cannot explain. The live-verification question exists to test this.

Consequences. A confirmed integrity flag means no badge, irrespective of score (see EVALUATION_PLAN.md). A first, minor, self-declared issue — an uncited price, an unattributed helper function — is corrected and noted, not penalised. The line is between unattributed help and unearned evidence; only the second is an integrity matter.

PDPL is also an integrity matter. Raw personal data served to BI, or personal data retained past your own stated policy, is a PDPL red flag and blocks badge issuance on its own. Check your serving boundary before you submit, not during the demo.

docs.title: 10. Where this goes next
docs.text: Every mandatory requirement maps back to the module that taught it: medallion (M1), economics (M2), ELT (M3), Delta (M4), streaming (M5), quality and governance (M6), orchestration (M7), serving (M8). The platform you submit is the same shape of platform you will scale in SDA-DSC-215 — Big Data Analytics with Spark (the same Lakehouse at enterprise volume, with distributed execution, partitioning strategy and MLlib) and build on in SDA-DSC-313. Keep the repository.

docs.title: EVALUATION PLAN — SDA-DSC-214
docs.text: Modern Data Engineering for AI Systems · SDAIA Academy · the whole assessment architecture on one page

docs.title: 1. Weightings
docs.text:
Component Weight Instrument Evidence Collected Lab completion (8 labs) 30% INSTRUCTOR_SCORING_SHEETS.md §1 Checkpoint commits + expected outputs per lab's acceptance criteria Rolling, end of each lab Practical assessments (PA-1, PA-2, PA-3) 20% PA-1_Delta_Recovery.md, PA-2_Streaming_Exactly_Once.md, PA-3_Feature_Leakage_Audit.md Artefacts + diagnosis/evidence/reasoning documents Day 3 H5, Day 4 H5, Day 5 H4 Quiz 10% QUIZ_BANK.md, cohort set A, B or C 10-question paper, 15 min, closed book Day 5 H1 (or Day 4 H5 if the cohort is ahead) Capstone (Mini-Lakehouse) 40% RUBRIC.md Platform-first: running platform, repository artefacts, then the 6-minute demo Day 5 H4 (repo) + H5 (demo) 100%

Sub-weighting within components

Component Split Labs 30% Each lab weighted equally at 3.75 points. A lab is scored complete (3.75) / partial (1.9) / not submitted (0) against its own acceptance criteria — labs are formative, and the intent is coverage, not ranking PA 20% PA-1 6.67% · PA-2 6.67% · PA-3 6.67%. Each PA is scored /100 and scaled Quiz 10% 20 marks scaled to 10 Capstone 40% The 7 rubric criteria (100 pts) scaled to 40, after anti-pattern caps and any extension bonus

Final grade = 0.30·(labs) + 0.20·(mean of PA-1..PA-3) + 0.10·(quiz) + 0.40·(capstone), each expressed as a percentage.

Thresholds: Pass ≥ 70 overall. Distinction ≥ 90 overall and capstone ≥ 90.

docs.title: 2. How each learning outcome is evidenced
docs.text:
Every LO is evidenced in at least two independent places, at least one of which is a running platform rather than a written answer. This is what makes the LO claim defensible.

LO Statement Primary evidence (platform) Secondary evidence Assessed in LO1 Compare warehouses, lakes and Lakehouse architectures across use cases Bronze/silver/gold layers exist with enforced contracts; no layer bypassed (grep + DAG graph) LAB1_NOTES.md swamp risks; MINI_LAKEHOUSE.md layer contracts; quiz M1 items LAB-01 · Capstone C1 · Quiz LO2 Explain compute–storage separation and its impact on cost, elasticity and scale Measured scan benchmark (columns/files/bytes read) and numFiles before/after OPTIMIZE, from the participant's own runs BENCHMARKS.md cost model with cited prices; DECISIONS.md partition-key and guardrail entries LAB-02, LAB-04 · Capstone C1/C3 · Quiz LO3 Design ELT pipelines suited to modern cloud data environments Incremental merge-on-trip_id with lookback; ≥ 6 dbt tests green; late-arrival backfill inserted -> 1 then -> 0 LAB3_NOTES.md naive-filter counter-experiment with both counts LAB-03 · Capstone C2 · Quiz LO4 Implement Delta Lake tables with ACID transactions and schema enforcement Constrained Delta rejecting three negative-write tests; MERGE idempotent across two runs; time-travel diff; justified VACUUM retention PA-1 (individually assessed, 30 min); LAB4_NOTES.md retention justification LAB-04 · PA-1 · Capstone C3 · Quiz LO5 Develop streaming and event-driven ingestion patterns for real-time data Kill/restart proof with pipeline duplicates = 0; dedicated checkpoint per query; event-time window with a defended watermark PA-2 (individually assessed, 30 min); LAB5_NOTES.md proof table LAB-05 · PA-2 · Capstone C4 · Quiz LO6 Apply data-quality, observability and governance controls across pipelines A gate that acts (blocked batch + quarantined batch with reasons); four observability signals each shown firing; retention job + demonstrated erasure GOVERNANCE.md classification with differentiated retention; rendered GX data docs LAB-06 · Capstone C5 · Quiz LO7 Build a working Mini-Lakehouse with Delta Lake and PySpark One-command DAG run from a clean clone; injected-failure recovery with before == during == after by checksum MINI_LAKEHOUSE.md with per-table enforcement lines; run logs LAB-07 · Capstone C1/C6 · Quiz LO8 Connect Lakehouse components to AI, reporting and analytics consumers Offline == online proven across all zone keys and shown to fail on injection; star reconciles at rel_diff = 0; PDPL boundary asserted PA-3 (individually assessed, 30 min); LAB8_LEAKAGE.md 13/13 with both metrics LAB-08 · PA-3 · Capstone C7 · Quiz

Coverage check. Every LO appears in (a) at least one lab, (b) the capstone, and (c) the quiz. LO4, LO5 and LO8 additionally carry an individually assessed practical, because they are the three outcomes where pair work most easily conceals an individual gap.

docs.title: 3. Badge issuance rules
docs.text:
Badge: SDAIA Academy Data-engineering badge (stackable; anchors the Data Engineering for AI specialisation).

A badge is issued when all four conditions hold. They are conjunctive: a high overall score does not compensate for a failed condition.

# Condition Checked by Evidence B1 Overall ≥ 70 Scoring sheet final calculation INSTRUCTOR_SCORING_SHEETS.md §5 B2 Capstone ≥ 70 RUBRIC.md subtotal after anti-pattern caps Worksheet §C B3 Zero upheld academic-integrity flags Cross-repository comparison of benchmark and quarantine artefacts; DECISIONS.md authorship check; the live-verification answer §5 below B4 No PDPL red flags pdpl_boundary_check; the retention policy versus what is actually retained §4 below

Decision outcomes

Outcome Meaning Action Issued B1–B4 all met Recommendation submitted within 5 working days of the demo Issued with distinction note Overall ≥ 90 and capstone ≥ 90 As above, with the distinction recorded Held B1 or B2 not met One re-sit offered (§6). The badge is issued on a successful re-sit without any note of the first attempt Withheld — integrity B3 not met No badge irrespective of score. Escalated per academy policy; the participant is informed of the specific evidence and may respond before the decision is final Withheld — PDPL B4 not met No badge irrespective of score. Remediable: the participant fixes the boundary and resubmits the affected artefacts within the re-sit window

On B4 being a hard gate. A platform that serves raw rider identifiers or retains personal data past its own stated policy has failed at the thing this course claims to teach. Passing a participant on aggregate score while their platform violates the constraint the course treats as first-class would make the badge mean less than it says.

docs.title: 4. PDPL red flags — the explicit list
docs.text:
Any one of these, present in the submitted platform, is a red flag under B4.

# Red flag Detected by P1 rider_id present in any gold table, serving view, or Redis key pdpl_boundary_check; column audit of every gold table P2 Raw lat / lon at trip or rider grain in any gold product or the online store Same. Zone-grain centroid_lat/centroid_lon in gold.dim_zone is permitted P3 national_id_hash or phone_hash in any gold product or Redis key Same. Pseudonymised ≠ anonymous P4 Personal data retained beyond the participant's own documented retention, with no retention job that would remove it GOVERNANCE.md versus the retention job's actual effect P5 An erasure demonstrated that leaves the rider in silver.trips_quarantine or a derived gold table Erasure runbook completeness; post-erasure count across every table P6 VACUUM RETAIN 0 used to "complete" an erasure Repository grep; this is also anti-pattern A3

P1–P3 are detected automatically and are not judgement calls. P4–P6 require reading the runbook.

docs.title: 5. Academic integrity — what is checked and how
docs.text:
Check Method Threshold for a flag Identical benchmark artefacts Compare BENCHMARKS.md numeric tables across all repositories in the cohort Two or more repositories sharing three or more identical timing or bytes figures. Ratios may legitimately match; absolute timings on different laptops do not Identical quarantine artefacts Compare quarantine row counts, reasons and sample trip_ids Byte-identical quarantine exports across repositories Commit authorship git log --format='%an %ae' across the graded branch Commits authored by another participant, or a single squashed commit with no history DECISIONS.md authorship Read; then ask the participant to defend one entry during the demo An entry the participant cannot defend scores zero for that entry and, if the prose is shared with another repository, is a flag Fabricated transcript Compare pasted outputs against what the submitted code can produce An output referencing a table, column or option the code does not create Unattributed external code Reading; header attribution is required, including for AI-assisted code Substantial unattributed code that the participant cannot explain

Not integrity issues: using the starter code, fast-forwarding to a checkpoint tag, pair-debugging, using AI assistance for code the participant then runs and can explain, or reusing lab evidence in the capstone (the capstone is integration, not re-performance). The line is between unattributed help and unearned evidence.

Process. Flags are recorded on the rubric worksheet with an evidence line, never raised during a demo. The lead instructor reviews all flags together after demos close, so that a pattern across the cohort (for example, everyone copying a figure from the lab guide) is recognised as an instruction problem rather than six integrity cases.

docs.title: 6. Re-sit policy
docs.text: Item Rule Eligibility Any participant with overall ≥ 55 but failing B1 or B2. Below 55, the recommendation is to re-take the course, not to re-sit Attempts One re-sit per participant Window Within 15 working days of the demo. The instructor names the date at the time of the hold Scope Only the failed component is re-sat. Passing components carry forward unchanged Capstone re-sit Resubmit the repository with the specific criteria remediated, plus a REMEDIATION.md naming each finding, the commit that addresses it, and the evidence. Assessed asynchronously against the same rubric by a grader who did not score the first attempt. A criterion that was ≥ 70 first time is not re-scored PA re-sit The same assessment, a fresh sandbox, same 30 minutes, invigilated or screen-recorded. PA-1 and PA-2 setups are re-runnable by design; PA-3 uses the same variant Quiz re-sit A 10-question paper drawn from the 30 bank items not used in sets A/B/C, balanced to the same module distribution (M1 1 · M2 1 · M3 1 · M4 2 · M5 2 · M6 1 · M7 1 · M8 1) Lab re-sit Not offered. Labs are formative and completion-graded; a participant who missed labs for a documented reason has that reason recorded and the 30% band is re-weighted pro rata across the labs actually attempted, with the instructor's note in the record Cap A re-sit component is capped at 70% of that component. The overall grade after a re-sit is reported as a pass, without distinction Integrity A component failed for an upheld integrity flag is not re-sittable. That is an academy-policy matter, not an assessment one

docs.title: 7. Accommodations
docs.text:
Accommodations adjust access to the assessment, never its standard. The evidence required is identical; the route to producing it may differ.

Need Accommodation Applies to Documented extra time +25% on timed components: PA 30 → 38 min; quiz 15 → 19 min; demo 6 → 7.5 min PA-1/2/3, quiz, demo Screen reader / assistive tech Papers supplied as accessible Markdown rather than print; the scoring sheet is filled by the assessor; code output read aloud on request All Hearing Demo may be delivered with a written script the assessor follows; live-verification question supplied in writing Demo Speech / presentation anxiety Demo may be pre-recorded (6 minutes, unedited, single take) and submitted before Hour 5; the assessor then asks the live-verification question in writing or one-to-one Demo Hardware failure or inadequate laptop Hosted-notebook fallback (Databricks Community Edition / Colab). Benchmarks are then reported as ratios rather than absolute timings, and the environment is recorded on the scoring sheet. This must not disadvantage the participant on criteria 1–7 Labs, capstone Restricted network / no Docker Kafka-dependent work assessed against the instructor's shared broker; the streaming criterion is assessed on the participant's code and checkpoint discipline plus a supervised run on shared infrastructure LAB-05, PA-2, C4 Absence for part of the week Missed labs re-weighted pro rata (§6). The capstone is not re-weighted — it is the integrating deliverable and must be complete Prayer times and breaks Timed components are never scheduled across Dhuhr; the Day-5 demo order is published in advance so participants can plan

Requesting. Accommodations are arranged with the academy before delivery where possible, and with the lead instructor at any point during the week where not. They are recorded on the scoring sheet as accommodation applied, never as a note on performance, and are not visible on the badge record.

docs.title: 8. Validity and reliability — why platform-first grading is defensible
docs.text:
The claim being made. The badge asserts that the holder can build and operate a governed data platform that feeds AI and BI workloads. The assessment must produce evidence for that claim, not for an adjacent one.

Construct validity. The capstone requires the participant to produce a running artefact that demonstrates its own properties: a pipeline that runs from one command, a stream that survives a kill, a gate that blocks and quarantines, a table that answers what it held last week, a feature service whose online and offline values are proven equal. These are not proxies for the job — they are the job, at reduced scale. Grading the platform first and the presentation second is what keeps the construct aligned: a participant who can describe exactly-once but whose stream duplicates on restart has not demonstrated LO5, and a rubric that rewarded the description would be measuring vocabulary.

Reliability — the three sources of noise, and what is done about each.

Source of noise Control Grader drift across 7 holistic criteria Blind double-scoring on two calibration submissions before grading starts; independent scoring then reconciliation with a defined gap protocol (≤3 mean · 4–9 discuss · ≥10 third reviewer, median of three); anchor statements fixing both ends of the scale; re-check of the first two demos after the last (RUBRIC.md §11) Demo-day variance — nerves, a dead network, a laptop that will not wake Most criteria are decided from a run the assessor performs before the demo, from the submitted commit. The demo confirms and adds ≤ 10 of 100 points directly. A failed live demo does not collapse a good platform's score Pair work concealing individual gaps Three individually assessed, invigilated practicals (PA-1/2/3) covering the three outcomes most vulnerable to it (LO4, LO5, LO8), plus one live-verification question per participant on the capstone

Reliability of the objective layer. A large fraction of the evidence is binary and machine-checkable rather than judged: does make pipeline exit 0 from a clean clone; is COUNT(*) = COUNT(DISTINCT trip_id); does gold.eta_features have exactly 13 columns; does the consistency check exit 1 on an injected divergence; does a grep find a gold task reading bronze. Two graders will not disagree on any of these. The judged bands sit on top of that objective layer rather than replacing it, which is why the observed inter-rater gap on this instrument is small and concentrated in criteria 1 and 5 — the two most prose-dependent — and why the moderation guide targets exactly those.

Content validity. The blueprint is explicit and traceable: eight LOs → eight capstone requirements → seven rubric criteria → eight labs → three practicals → 60 quiz items tagged by module and Bloom level. Every cell of the LO × instrument matrix in §2 is populated, and no criterion exists that does not trace to an LO. The quiz's distribution mirrors the course's own time allocation rather than being convenient to write.

Consequential validity — the anti-pattern caps. The six caps (leakage, non-idempotent gold, VACUUM RETAIN 0, alert-only gate, raw PII in BI, streaming without a dedicated checkpoint) exist because these are the failures that are invisible until they are expensive. A scoring scheme that let an otherwise-excellent platform earn a distinction while leaking features would issue a badge that misdescribes its holder. Capping rather than failing keeps the response proportionate: the participant can still pass, and the ceiling records that one production-grade property is absent.

Known limitations, stated plainly. 1. Scale. Everything is demonstrated on a few million rows on a laptop. The badge asserts correct construction, not tuned performance at petabyte scale — that is SDA-DSC-215's claim, not this one, and the benchmark tables report ratios precisely so the extrapolation is visible rather than implied. 2. Time compression. Five days is not long enough to observe whether a participant's platform is maintainable; the proxies used are the enforcement lines in MINI_LAKEHOUSE.md and the DECISIONS.md entries, which are indirect. 3. Environment variance. Hosted-notebook fallbacks produce non-comparable absolute timings. Reporting ratios controls for this on the benchmark criteria but not perfectly. 4. Single assessor for small cohorts. Where double-scoring is impossible, the calibration step is replaced by scoring two submissions against the anchor statements at the start and re-scoring them at the end; the difference is recorded as a drift estimate in the moderation record.

Review. This plan is reviewed after each delivery against three signals: the distribution of capstone criterion scores (a criterion where nobody scores below Proficient is not discriminating), the inter-rater gap log, and the frequency of each anti-pattern flag (a flag raised against most of the cohort indicates an instruction defect, not a cohort defect, and the fix belongs in the lab).
