docs.title: 3. Participant brief (hand this page out)
docs.text:
PA-3 — Feature Leakage Audit · 30 minutes · individual

The ETA squad has submitted masar-eta-duration v3.1 for production approval. The model card claims R² 0.941 and MAE 1.87 minutes on trip-duration prediction. Your signature is required on the platform side before rollout.

You have:

  • The feature table ./lakehouse/_assessments/pa3/eta_features — the 13 CONVENTIONS columns of gold.eta_features, one row per trip_id.
  • The builder that produced it: scripts/assessments/pa3_setup.py.
  • The model card above.
  • silver.trips, silver.vehicle_positions, gold.dim_zone and data/raw/weather_hourly.csv.

The single test you apply to every column:

Could this value have been known at prediction time — that is, at feature_ts, the instant the rider taps Request — from data that had already been written?

Your task, in order:

  1. Classify all 13 columns into exactly one of four classes. Ambiguity is not permitted; if a column could be two, choose the one that would cause the worse production failure and say so.
Code Meaning The question to ask VALID Knowable at feature_ts from data that existed then, and reproducible online "At the moment of Request, could I compute this from data already written?" STALE Computable in principle, but the value the online path actually serves is materially older than feature_ts "How old is the value Redis holds at 19:00 on a Thursday?" LEAKAGE Depends on information that did not exist at feature_ts — the current instant, the future, or the outcome "Does computing this require knowing anything at or after feature_ts?" UNAVAILABLE ONLINE Point-in-time correct offline, but no online path can supply it at inference latency "Is there a key or an API returning this in under 20 ms, right now?"
  1. Name the leaking features and prove each with a query or a computed number, not an assertion.
  2. Fix the training join to be point-in-time correct. Keep every column name — the contract is fixed — and change only how each value is computed and how the training set is assembled. Include the split.
  3. Report the honest metric and write the paragraph you would send the ETA squad.

Constraints - The output must still have exactly the 13 CONVENTIONS columns, correctly named, at one row per trip_id. - You may not drop a column to "fix" it; a contract column is fixed and must be re-sourced or re-computed. - Do not read the Lab-8 answer key. Two columns are not what they were in the lab.

Deliverable artefacts (all three required):

Artefact Content PA3_CLASSIFICATION.md The 13-row table: column, class, one-sentence justification naming what the code actually used, and the fix src/masar/transform/build_eta_features_pa3.py The corrected builder, plus the corrected training split PA3_REPORT.md Both metrics (claimed and honest), the delta, the evidence for each leak, and the paragraph to the ETA squad

Time budget suggestion: 12 min classify and probe · 10 min fix · 6 min retrain and report · 2 min commit.

docs.title: 4. Marking scheme
docs.text: Total 100. Pass ≥ 70 for badge contribution.

docs.title: 4a. Classification — 40 marks
docs.text:
3 marks per correctly classified column (13 × 3 = 39), rounded to 40 with one discretionary mark for a justification that names the exact window bound or join key responsible.

A column scores its 3 marks only when the class and the justification are right. A right class with a wrong reason scores 1.

Partial-credit rule Marks Correct class, justification names the mechanism (the bound, the join key, the source column) 3 Correct class, justification generic ("it leaks", "not available") 1 driver_recent_trip_count marked LEAKAGE and the staleness also named 3 (see key) weather_condition marked LEAKAGE with a correct explanation of the arrival lag 2 (the remediation differs; see key) label_actual_duration_min marked "N/A" or "not a feature" 0 Any column left unclassified or given two classes 0

Band descriptors — Classification

Band Marks Descriptor Distinction 36–40 12 or 13 correct with mechanism-level justifications; the two Lab-8 reversals (rolling_avg_speed_10m, historical_route_duration) are both correct; the participant states the product assumption dropoff_zone_id rests on Proficient 28–35 10–11 correct; typically one of weather_condition / driver_recent_trip_count is misclassified, or one reversal is answered from memory of the lab Developing 18–27 7–9 correct; distance_km is found but the subtler window bounds are not; justifications assert rather than name Insufficient 0–17 distance_km marked VALID, or fewer than 7 correct

docs.title: 4b. Fixes and the point-in-time join — 35 marks
docs.text:
Sub-criterion Marks What earns it P1. rolling_zone_demand_15m bound corrected 6 rangeBetween(-900, -1) — strictly prior; participant notes the feature's mean falls P2. historical_route_duration bound corrected 6 rangeBetween(-2592000, -1); the current trip is excluded from its own route average; null contract for unseen zone pairs stated (impute city median with an is_imputed flag, or omit) P3. distance_km re-sourced 8 Replaced with the planned/route distance at booking — routing-engine estimate, or the route/great-circle distance between gold.dim_zone centroids. Column name unchanged P4. weather_condition shifted on both sides 5 hour_ts <= date_trunc('hour', feature_ts) - INTERVAL 1 HOUR, applied identically in training and in materialisation P5. driver_recent_trip_count remediated as staleness 4 Online refresh cadence matched to volatility (hourly, not nightly) with feature_ts age monitoring; the offline bound is already correct and the participant says so P6. Split corrected to a time split 6 Random 75/25 replaced with a temporal split (train < cut-off, test ≥ cut-off), because a random split over a temporally ordered table trains on the future of its own test set

Band descriptors — Fixes

Band Marks Descriptor Distinction 32–35 All six; the label is also stripped from ONLINE_COLUMNS; the fixed builder still emits exactly 13 correctly named columns and the participant verifies that assertion Proficient 25–31 Four or five; typically the split or the weather_condition symmetry is missed Developing 15–24 The obvious leak (distance_km) fixed, the window bounds left alone Insufficient 0–14 A column dropped instead of re-sourced, the contract broken, or nothing rebuilt

docs.title: 4c. Honest metric and reporting — 25 marks
docs.text:
Sub-criterion Marks What earns it M1. Both metrics reported with the delta 8 Claimed R² 0.941 / MAE 1.87 → honest R² ≈ 0.71 / MAE ≈ 4.7, with the delta stated M2. Evidence for each leak, computed not asserted 8 E.g. the correlation of distance_km with the label; the count of same-second trips admitted by the 0 bound; a row showing the trip's own duration inside its route average M3. The paragraph to the ETA squad 6 Explains why the drop is the correct outcome in operational terms, not statistical ones; makes the cost argument (a model promising ±1.9 that delivers ±5 is more expensive than one that promises ±4.7) M4. Governance callout 3 Flags the label in ONLINE_COLUMNS as serving the answer, and notes that the card's "Known limitations: none material" is itself the finding

Band descriptors — Reporting

Band Marks Descriptor Distinction 22–25 All four; the report would survive being forwarded unedited to the squad lead; it names what the honest model still cannot do and what feature work would legitimately raise the number Proficient 17–21 Both metrics and most evidence; the paragraph argues statistically rather than operationally Developing 10–16 Metrics reported without evidence, or the drop framed as a regression Insufficient 0–9 No retrain, or the honest metric asserted without running it

docs.title: Automatic caps
docs.text: Condition Cap A contract column dropped rather than re-sourced Fixes capped at 40% Output does not have exactly the 13 CONVENTIONS columns Overall capped at 60% label_actual_duration_min retained in ONLINE_COLUMNS after the fix Reporting capped at 60% Honest metric quoted without a retrain transcript M1 scores 0

docs.title: 5a. Per-column classification — the complete key
docs.text:
# Column Class Justification (what is known at feature_ts vs what the code used) Required fix 1 trip_id VALID The entity key, assigned at request time. An identifier, not a model input — it must be excluded from the feature vector, but it is knowable at feature_ts and reproducible online, so VALID rather than LEAKAGE. Accept a participant who argues it should be out of scope entirely, provided they say why None. Exclude from the feature vector; keep for joins and traceability 2 pickup_zone_id VALID The rider's current location resolved to a zone at request time; available online as a direct request parameter None 3 dropoff_zone_id VALID Masar's booking flow requires a stated destination before request, so this is an input, not an outcome. Product-dependent — if destination-less requests existed it would be UNAVAILABLE ONLINE for that segment None. Document the product assumption 4 hour_of_day VALID Derived purely from feature_ts, which at inference is the request timestamp. Deterministic, zero-latency, no source dependency None 5 day_of_week VALID As #4. Interpret against the KSA working week (Fri–Sat weekend), consistent with gold.dim_date.is_weekend None 6 rolling_zone_demand_15m LEAKAGE rangeBetween(-900, 0). rangeBetween bounds are inclusive and operate on the ordering column's value range, so an upper bound of 0 admits every trip whose pickup_epoch equals this one's — every trip starting in the same second, in the same zone. At Riyadh rush-hour density that is several trips, and they are the future rangeBetween(-900, -1). Expect the feature's mean to fall by a few percent — small, correlated with congestion, and therefore the dangerous kind 7 rolling_avg_speed_10m VALID Reversed from the Lab-8 starter. Here it averages speed_kmh from other vehicles in the pickup zone over the 10 minutes strictly before feature_ts, with this trip_id excluded by the join predicate. Zone-grained, so it is materialisable to Redis. Verify the two guards explicitly: z.src_trip != f.trip_id and z.ping_ts < f.feature_ts None. Verify both guards; document the null contract for zones with no recent pings 8 driver_recent_trip_count STALE rangeBetween(-86400, -1) is point-in-time correct offline. The failure is online: the model card says the online store is refreshed by the nightly DAG, so at 19:00 on a Thursday the value is 19 hours old — a driver who has completed 11 trips today reads as 0 and the model treats an exhausted driver as a fresh one. Accept LEAKAGE as a defensible second answer only if the participant also names the staleness, because that is the failure that actually bites Two-part: refresh the driver slice on a cadence matched to the feature's volatility (hourly), and monitor feature_ts age as a serving SLA 9 weather_condition UNAVAILABLE ONLINE data/raw/weather_hourly.csv lands after the hour it describes. Joining a 07:14 trip to the 07:00 row is legitimate offline — that observation existed when the table was built — but at 07:14 live the 07:00 row has not arrived. Point-in-time correct and unobtainable. The distinction from LEAKAGE is operational: a leaking feature must be changed, an unavailable one must be re-sourced Join to the last observed hour: hour_ts <= date_trunc('hour', feature_ts) - INTERVAL 1 HOUR, applied identically in training and in materialisation, and served from the Redis zone key. One hour of staleness — but the same hour on both sides 10 distance_km LEAKAGE The metered distance the vehicle actually travelled, written at dropoff_ts in silver.trips. Pearson r with the label ≈ 0.95 and it carries 0.601 of the card's stated gain — the model is reading the answer. At inference the value does not exist, so serving must substitute something the model was trained to trust heavily. The single largest contributor to the inflated metric Recompute as the planned route distance at booking: the routing engine's estimate, or offline the route/great-circle distance between gold.dim_zone centroids. Keep the column name; change only the source. May be internally aliased planned_distance_km for clarity 11 historical_route_duration LEAKAGE Reversed from the Lab-8 starter. rangeBetween(-2592000, 0) includes the current row, so each trip's own duration_min — the label itself — is one term inside its own 30-day route average. On a sparse zone pair with two prior trips that is a third of the feature; on an unseen pair it is the label. Subtle, plausible, and it survives every schema and range check rangeBetween(-2592000, -1). Define and document the null contract for zone pairs with no prior trips (impute the city median with an is_imputed flag, or omit) 12 feature_ts VALID The as-of timestamp itself — the anchor every other column's correctness is defined against. Metadata, not a model input; knowable by definition, because it is the request time None. Exclude from the feature vector; retain for point-in-time joins, materialisation and freshness monitoring 13 label_actual_duration_min LEAKAGE The target. Trivially leaking if it enters the feature vector, and — as the model card in fact specifies — a serving hazard, because it appears in ONLINE_COLUMNS, so the online store would be publishing the answer. Do not accept "N/A": classifying the label as LEAKAGE is the discipline that catches the non-obvious label proxies, which is exactly what #10 and #11 are Strip from the feature vector and from ONLINE_COLUMNS. Keep in the offline table — that is what a training set is

Tally: VALID 7 · STALE 1 · LEAKAGE 4 · UNAVAILABLE ONLINE 1.

docs.title: 5b. The two defects that live in the model card, not the table
docs.text: Defect Why it matters Fix Random 75/25 split on a temporally ordered table Every test row has training rows from after it. Even with all four leaking features repaired, a random split inflates the metric, because the model has seen the same evening's traffic conditions from both sides. A time split is the only honest estimator for a forecasting task --split time --test-days 2: train on 2026-06-01..28, test on 29–30 label_actual_duration_min in ONLINE_COLUMNS The online store would serve the answer to anyone who can read a zone key, and a downstream consumer would eventually "use the feature that correlates best". It is also a governance finding: the label is trip-grained and therefore should never be materialised at zone grain Remove it, and every trip-grained column, from ONLINE_COLUMNS; the online payload is zone-grained only "Known limitations: none material" Not a defect in itself but the finding that frames the report. A card claiming R² 0.94 on trip duration with no stated limitation has not been reviewed Rewrite the section with the honest metric, the point-in-time contract, and the serving staleness bound

docs.title: 5c. Evidence a distinction answer produces
docs.text:
# The blunt one: correlation with the label.
$ python -m masar.serve.train_eta --corr-only --features _assessments/pa3/eta_features
pearson r with label_actual_duration_min
  distance_km                 0.9483        <- a feature does not do this
  historical_route_duration   0.7742        <- suspiciously high for a 30-day mean
  rolling_avg_speed_10m      -0.3106
  rolling_zone_demand_15m     0.2914
  driver_recent_trip_count    0.0407

# The precise one: how many trips does the demand bound admit from the same second?
$ python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
WITH probe AS (SELECT trip_id, city, pickup_zone_id, feature_ts, rolling_zone_demand_15m
               FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/_assessments/pa3/eta_features\`
               WHERE rolling_zone_demand_15m BETWEEN 10 AND 60 ORDER BY feature_ts LIMIT 1)
SELECT p.trip_id, p.feature_ts, p.rolling_zone_demand_15m AS as_built,
 (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/trips\` s
   WHERE s.pickup_zone_id=p.pickup_zone_id AND s.city=p.city AND s.status='completed'
     AND s.pickup_ts >= p.feature_ts - INTERVAL 15 MINUTES
     AND s.pickup_ts <  p.feature_ts)                    AS strictly_prior,
 (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/trips\` s
   WHERE s.pickup_zone_id=p.pickup_zone_id AND s.city=p.city AND s.status='completed'
     AND s.pickup_ts =  p.feature_ts)                    AS same_second
FROM probe p"
trip_id     feature_ts           as_built  strictly_prior  same_second
TRP-770118  2026-06-28 07:14:33  17        14              3

# The one that finds defect 2: is the trip inside its own route average?
$ python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
SELECT f.trip_id, t.duration_min AS own_duration, f.historical_route_duration AS as_built,
  ROUND((SELECT AVG(s.duration_min) FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/trips\` s
     WHERE s.pickup_zone_id=t.pickup_zone_id AND s.dropoff_zone_id=t.dropoff_zone_id
       AND s.status='completed' AND s.pickup_ts < t.pickup_ts
       AND s.pickup_ts >= t.pickup_ts - INTERVAL 30 DAYS), 2) AS strictly_prior
FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/_assessments/pa3/eta_features\` f
JOIN delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/trips\` t USING (trip_id)
ORDER BY f.feature_ts LIMIT 3"
trip_id     own_duration  as_built  strictly_prior
TRP-770118  21.6          19.44     18.36
TRP-770119  14.2          14.20     NULL          <- first trip on this pair: the feature IS the label
TRP-770120  37.7          29.83     26.90

# The one that clears rolling_avg_speed_10m (the Lab-8 reversal):
$ python -m masar.tools.sql --query "
SELECT COUNT(*) AS pings_from_this_trip_or_later
FROM delta.\`./lakehouse/_assessments/pa3/eta_features\` f
JOIN delta.\`./lakehouse/silver/vehicle_positions\` p ON p.trip_id = f.trip_id
WHERE p.event_ts >= f.feature_ts"
pings_from_this_trip_or_later
0                              <- the trip's own pings are excluded; the feature is clean

Row 2 of the third query is the sentence to put in the report: on a zone pair with no prior trips, historical_route_duration equals the trip's own duration exactly. That is not a leak, it is the label wearing a different column name.

docs.title: 5d. Reference metrics
docs.text:
Claimed (card) Honest (fixed features + time split) Δ R² 0.941 0.706 −0.235 MAE (min) 1.87 4.71 +2.84 (×2.52) Top feature distance_km 0.601 historical_route_duration 0.352 — Split random 75/25 time, train < 2026-06-29 — 
$ python -m masar.transform.build_eta_features_pa3 --fixed
[gold] eta_features (pa3, fixed): 42,038 rows, 13 columns

$ python -m masar.serve.train_eta --features _assessments/pa3/eta_features \
      --split time --test-days 2
[train] rows=42,038  train=31,528  test=10,510  (time split at 2026-06-29 00:00)
[train] R2  = 0.706     (card claimed 0.941)
[train] MAE = 4.71 min  (card claimed 1.87)
[train] top features by gain:
          historical_route_duration   0.352
          distance_km                 0.259   # planned route distance, from dim_zone centroids
          rolling_zone_demand_15m     0.166
          rolling_avg_speed_10m       0.129
          hour_of_day                 0.048

These are PA-3's numbers, not Lab 8's. The canonical Lab-8 leakage drill runs R² 0.943 → 0.712 and MAE 1.81 → 4.58 min on a different defect mix (masar.transform.build_eta_features). PA-3's variant claims 0.941 / 1.87 and lands at 0.706 / 4.71. Both sets are correct for their own artefact; do not "reconcile" them.

Accept ±0.03 on R² and ±0.4 min on MAE — the exact numbers depend on the participant's imputation choice for unseen zone pairs and on their planned-distance estimator. What must be true: R² falls into the 0.66–0.76 band and distance_km is no longer the dominant feature. A submission still reporting R² > 0.85 has not fixed the leak, whatever the classification table says.

docs.title: 5e. The reference paragraph to the ETA squad
docs.text:
Recommendation: do not ship v3.1 as measured. The offline numbers are not wrong arithmetic; they are the right arithmetic on the wrong table.

Four of the thirteen features in gold.eta_features used information that did not exist when a prediction would be made. distance_km is the metered distance written at dropoff_ts, and it correlates 0.948 with the label — the model was reading the answer, and it carried 60% of the reported gain. historical_route_duration included the current trip inside its own 30-day route average; on a zone pair with no prior trips the feature equals the label exactly. rolling_zone_demand_15m counted every trip starting in the same second, which at rush hour in Riyadh is several trips that had not happened yet. And the label itself is listed in ONLINE_COLUMNS, so the online store is configured to publish the answer to anything that can read a zone key. Separately, the random 75/25 split trains on the future of its own test set, which inflates the number again even after the features are repaired.

Rebuilt point-in-time correctly — planned route distance at booking instead of metered distance, both rolling windows made strictly prior, weather shifted to the last observed hour on both the training and the serving side, and a temporal split — the model scores R² 0.706, MAE 4.71 minutes. That is not a regression. It is the first honest measurement of this model, and it is the number that will hold up live.

The operational case for the honest number is a cost argument, not a statistical one. The leaking model tells the dispatcher it will miss by 1.9 minutes and then misses by about 5; the honest model tells the dispatcher it will miss by 4.7 and misses by about 4.7. The second is cheaper precisely because you can plan against it. Two things would legitimately raise it: a live traffic-speed feed at zone grain served from Redis at under 20 ms, and a routing-engine ETA as a feature rather than a distance. Both are feature work. Neither is a metric change.

One governance item, separate from accuracy: driver_recent_trip_count is point-in-time correct offline but refreshed nightly online, so at 19:00 it is 19 hours stale and an exhausted driver reads as fresh. Move that slice to an hourly refresh and monitor feature_ts age as a serving SLA. And the card's "Known limitations: none material" should be rewritten — a model card that claims R² 0.94 on trip duration with no stated limitation has not been reviewed, and that is the finding that should have caught this before I did.

docs.title: 6. Instructor delivery notes
docs.text:
Do not release this brief before every participant has submitted LAB8_LEAKAGE.md. The classification key overlaps the lab's on eleven rows.

Timing. At T+12 announce "you should be fixing, not still classifying" — participants over-invest in the table. At T+24 announce "retrain now, even if a fix is incomplete; an honest number on a partial fix scores; no number scores nothing."

What separates the bands in practice.

Observation Frequency What it signals Marks distance_km VALID Very high in a cohort that has not done Lab 8; rare after The anchor lesson. Ask: "when is that number written?" Marks rolling_avg_speed_10m LEAKAGE from memory of the lab High — this is the trap Recall substituting for reasoning. Ask them to show the join predicate that would prove it, and let them find the two guards themselves Marks historical_route_duration VALID from memory of the lab High — the other trap Same intervention: "read the upper bound aloud" Misses the random split High Treats leakage as a property of columns rather than of the whole training procedure Misses the label in ONLINE_COLUMNS Medium Read the table, not the card. The card is part of the evidence Marks weather_condition LEAKAGE Medium Reasonable confusion; 2 of 3 marks. Draw the line: leaking = must change; unavailable = must re-source. The category exists to force different remediation Fixes only the serving side of weather_condition Medium Textbook skew, manufactured while fixing skew. Say so plainly Notices that the tally matches the lab's while two rows differ Low Distinction signal — flag in moderation

Live verification (60 seconds, during marking). Point at one column the participant marked VALID and ask for the query that would prove it. A distinction answer names the predicate without opening a file.

Capstone linkage. PA-3 assesses capstone requirement 8 (Serving, LO8) and the point-in-time property of requirement 7. Feature leakage is a capstone anti-pattern flag capping a criterion at 70%, and the capstone's live verification explicitly authorises asking a participant to "run the leakage drill and explain the inflated metric" — PA-3 is the rehearsal for that question, marked.

docs.title: Peer Review Form — Masar Mini-Lakehouse
docs.text:
SDA-DSC-214 · Day 5, Hour 4 (capstone assembly) · 10 minutes per review

Field Value When Day 5, Hour 4, after M-D is green and before demos Duration 10 minutes per review, strictly timed. Each participant gives two reviews and receives two Pairing Assigned by the instructor across pairs that did not work together during labs Counts toward the grade? No. Peer review is formative. It does not contribute to the capstone score Why it is here Two hours before the demo is the last moment a finding is still cheap to fix. Reviewing someone else's platform is also the fastest way to see your own

docs.title: Ground rules — read these aloud before the round starts
docs.text:
1. Evidence, not opinion. Every line on this form asks you to point at a file, a command output, or a table. "The architecture looks clean" is not a finding. "build_gold.py:64 reads ./lakehouse/bronze/trips" is.
  2. Run it, do not read it. You have ten minutes. Spend seven of them running the author's commands and three writing. A platform that reads well and does not run has a finding you will only get by running it.
  3. The author is silent for the first five minutes. No tour, no explanation, no "let me just show you". You are testing whether the repository speaks for itself, which is exactly what the assessor will test.
  4. One question per section, maximum. If you need more than that to understand a section, that is the finding.
  5. No scores, no comparisons, no rankings. You are not grading. Never say "mine does X" — it is not information the author can use.
  6. Every finding gets a location. A finding without a file path or a command is a feeling.
  7. Hand the form to the author, not to the instructor. The instructor sees it only if the author chooses to attach it.

docs.title: Timing — hold to it
docs.text:
Minutes Activity 0:00–0:30 Author states one sentence: which branch and which command runs the platform. Then silence 0:30–5:00 Reviewer works alone: clone or cd, run the commands in §1, open the four documents in §2 5:00–7:00 Reviewer runs the two probes in §3 7:00–9:00 Reviewer writes findings. Author may answer direct questions only 9:00–10:00 Reviewer reads the three findings aloud and states the single highest-value fix. Author writes it down and does not defend it

The author does not defend anything during this round. Explanation is the assessor's job to elicit, not the reviewer's time to spend. If a finding is wrong, the author discovers that when they check it.

docs.title: Section 1 — Does it run? (4 minutes, run every line)
docs.text:
Run these against the author's repository. Record what you observed, not what you expected.

# Command Observed Verdict 1.1 make doctor ______ PASS / FAIL / ABSENT 1.2 make pipeline (or the DAG trigger named in the README) runtime __ · last task ______ PASS / FAIL / ABSENT 1.3 Re-run the same command immediately row counts identical? YES / NO — which table differed: ____ IDEMPOTENT / NOT 1.4 python -m masar.tools.sql --query "SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT trip_id) FROM delta.\./lakehouse/silver/trips`"` __ / ____ GRAIN HELD / BROKEN 1.5 Column count of gold.eta_features ______ / 13 CONTRACT MET / NOT

1.6 — The cold-start question. You had only the README. Did you have to ask the author anything to get 1.2 to run? NO — the README was sufficient / YES — I had to ask: ______________________________________

This single line is the most useful thing on the form. An assessor grading from a clean clone hits exactly this wall.

docs.title: Section 2 — Do the documents match the platform? (3 minutes)
docs.text:
Open each document and check one specific claim against the running platform. Do not read the whole file.

# Document Pick one claim and verify it Claim checked Matches? 2.1 MINI_LAKEHOUSE.md Choose any gold table. Does the stated grain hold in the data, and is the enforcement line (file + line) real? ______ YES / NO / NO ENFORCEMENT LINE 2.2 BENCHMARKS.md Pick one number. Could it have come from this machine? Is the hardware and Spark version stated? ______ PLAUSIBLE / UNSOURCED 2.3 GOVERNANCE.md Take the erasure runbook. Does it list silver.trips_quarantine? ______ YES / NO 2.4 DECISIONS.md Read one decision. Does it state what would change the decision? ______ YES / NO 2.5 LAB8_LEAKAGE.md Count the classified columns and the fixes. _ / 13 classified · _ fixes COMPLETE / PARTIAL

docs.title: Section 3 — Two probes (2 minutes — pick the two the author has not already demonstrated to you)
docs.text:
Run two. These are the checks an assessor will make, and finding them here is worth more than finding them at 16:45.

  • P1 — Layer bypass. grep -rn "lakehouse/bronze" src/masar/transform/ dbt/ orchestration/ Result: no gold code reads bronze / found at: ______

  • P2 — Checkpoint discipline. ls -d ./lakehouse/_checkpoints/*/ and grep every checkpointLocation in the repo. Result: one per query / shared or missing: ______

  • P3 — Retention. grep -rn "RETAIN\|retentionDurationCheck" . Result: >= 168 HOURS, check enabled / found: ______

  • P4 — Serving boundary. Print the columns of every gold table and the JSON of one Redis key. Result: no rider_id / lat / lon / *_hash / found: ______

  • P5 — Window bounds. grep -rn "rangeBetween" src/ Result: all upper bounds are -1 / found an inclusive 0 at: ______

  • P6 — Gate acts. Open the quarantine table: SELECT * FROM delta. + the quarantine path + LIMIT 5 Result: rows present with a reason column / empty or no reason: ____

docs.title: Section 4 — Three findings (write these; they are the deliverable)
Section 5 — One thing to keep
docs.text:
Name one thing this platform does that you would change your own build to match. Be specific enough that the author knows what you mean, and specific enough that you could actually do it in the next hour.

____________________________________________________________________________
____________________________________________________________________________

This is not a courtesy. Half the value of the round is transfer between builds, and a vague compliment transfers nothing.

docs.title: Section 6 — The single highest-value fix
docs.text:
If the author has time for exactly one change before the demo, it is:

____________________________________________________________________________

Estimated time to make it: ______ minutes
Why this one rather than the others: ________________________________________
____________________________________________________________________________

Read this aloud at 9:00. It is the last thing the author hears from you.

docs.title: Section 7 — Author's response (filled by the author, after the round)
docs.text:
Finding 1  ACTED [ ]  DEFERRED [ ]  DISAGREE [ ]   note: _____________________
Finding 2  ACTED [ ]  DEFERRED [ ]  DISAGREE [ ]   note: _____________________
Finding 3  ACTED [ ]  DEFERRED [ ]  DISAGREE [ ]   note: _____________________

Highest-value fix: MADE [ ]  NOT MADE [ ]   because: _________________________

One thing this review changed about how I will present the demo:
____________________________________________________________________________

Disagreeing is a legitimate outcome and does not need to be justified to the reviewer. Ignoring a finding without deciding is not.

docs.title: Instructor notes
docs.text:
Running the round. Two reviews per participant, 10 minutes each, back to back, with a 2-minute rotation — 22 minutes of Hour 4 total. Assign pairings on a card before the hour starts; do not let the room self-organise, or strong builds will review strong builds.

Enforce the silence. The first five minutes of author silence is the single mechanic that makes this instrument work, and it is the one participants break. Announce it, then police it once — after that the room self-polices.

Watch for these and intervene.

Observation Intervention Reviewer reads code instead of running it "Ten minutes. Run 1.2 first, read after." Findings without locations Hand the form back. One sentence: "Where?" Author narrating over the reviewer Restate the silence rule once; after that, move the author to the other side of the room Reviewer scoring or ranking "No scores. What would you fix, and where?" Both reviewers give the same author the same finding That is a real signal. Tell the author it came from two independent reviews

What to collect. Nothing, unless the author volunteers it. If you want a cohort-level read, ask for a show of hands on 1.6 — how many of you could run the other person's platform without asking a question? In a strong cohort that number is above half; below a third, spend the next five minutes on READMEs rather than on features, because the assessor grades from a clean clone.

Peer review does not feed the rubric. If a reviewer surfaces something that would be an anti-pattern flag, the author is expected to fix it. You will find it yourself in Hour 5 if they do not — and finding it fixed is the outcome this round exists to produce.

docs.title: SDA-DSC-214 — Quiz Bank
docs.text:
Course: Modern Data Engineering for AI Systems (SDA-DSC-214), SDAIA Academy Golden thread: Masar (مسار) — every item is set in the Masar Lakehouse the cohort built. Weight: 10% of the course grade. Closed book, 15 minutes, 10 questions per cohort.

Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. Grains, ratios and file-count reductions hold at either scale; absolute row counts do not.

docs.title: How to use this bank
docs.text:
Field Value Items 60, tagged M1–M8 Bloom levels recall (state it) · apply (use it on a Masar case) · analyse (diagnose evidence and justify) Difficulty easy (≥ 85% expected correct) · medium (60–85%) · hard (< 60%; discriminates the distinction band) Formats MCQ (four options; every non-key option is a misconception observed in delivery) · T/F+J (true/false plus a one-sentence justification — the justification carries the mark) · SHORT (one to three sentences) · DEBUG (read code or output and state what is wrong) Marking MCQ 1 mark. T/F+J 2 marks (0.5 verdict + 1.5 justification). SHORT 2 marks. DEBUG 3 marks (1 identify, 1 consequence, 1 fix). Ready sets Three balanced 10-question papers (A/B/C) at the end, each with a separate printable answer key

Rules of thumb for the marker. A correct verdict with a wrong reason scores the verdict only. On DEBUG items, "it will break" scores nothing; the participant must name the mechanism. Numbers quoted from the reference runs are accepted within ±10% unless the item says otherwise.

Item distribution: M1 7 · M2 7 · M3 8 · M4 9 · M5 9 · M6 8 · M7 6 · M8 6.

docs.title: Q1 · MCQ · recall · easy
docs.text:
Which architecture combines lake storage economics with warehouse transactional reliability?

A. A two-tier lake-plus-warehouse estate B. Lakehouse C. An MPP data warehouse with external tables D. An operational data store fed by CDC

Answer: B. Rationale: Only the Lakehouse puts a transaction layer directly over open files; A is the two-tier problem, not its solution.

docs.title: Q2 · MCQ · recall · easy
docs.text:
What single property turns a directory of Parquet files into a Delta table?

A. A Hive metastore entry pointing at the directory B. A _SUCCESS marker written by the last job C. The _delta_log transaction log D. Consistent partition directories

Answer: C. Rationale: ACID, time travel and schema enforcement all derive from replaying _delta_log; the Parquet files alone are just files.

docs.title: Q3 · T/F+J · apply · medium
docs.text:
"When a single bad row is found in bronze.trips, the correct action is to edit that row in place."

Answer: False. Rationale: Bronze is append-only and immutable; corrections belong in silver as reproducible logic, because an in-place edit destroys the raw record the late-arrival backfill and the time-travel audit both depend on.

docs.title: Q4 · SHORT · analyse · medium
docs.text:
A data-science notebook reports 91% on-time deliveries; the executive dashboard reports 87%. Name the architectural cause and the architectural fix.

Answer: Two copies of the same data with two different late-arrival rules — the two-tier problem. Fix: consolidate onto one governed silver table with a single late-arrival rule, read by both BI and DS. Rationale: The defect is not a bad ETL job but the existence of a second pipeline; only consolidation removes the class of bug.

docs.title: Q5 · MCQ · apply · medium
docs.text:
Which bronze layout choice is the fastest route to a data swamp?

A. partitionBy("ingest_date") B. partitionBy("trip_id") C. Writing one Delta table per source feed D. Carrying _source_file on every row

Answer: B. Rationale: A high-cardinality partition key produces millions of one-row files — the small-files problem, self-inflicted at landing time.

docs.title: Q6 · SHORT · recall · easy
docs.text:
Name the three lineage columns every Masar bronze table carries, and say what each answers.

Answer: _ingested_at (when we received it), _source_file (which file or Kafka partition it came from), _batch_id (which run wrote it). Rationale: Together they let any bronze row be traced to a run and a source without consulting an external log.

docs.title: Q7 · DEBUG · analyse · hard
docs.text:
(df.write.format("delta")
   .mode("overwrite")                 # land_bronze.py
   .partitionBy("ingest_date")
   .save("./lakehouse/bronze/trips"))
The landing job is re-run for the same day. State what is wrong, the consequence, and the fix.

Answer: mode("overwrite") violates the bronze append-only contract. Consequence: the previous landing of that partition is destroyed, so a re-ingest of a corrected file silently erases the original record and the late-arrival backfill and time-travel audit lose their source of truth. Fix: mode("append"), and rely on the keyed MERGE at silver to make re-runs harmless. Rationale: Bronze's contract is "everything we ever received", not "one row per real-world event" — de-duplication is silver's job.

docs.title: Module 2 — Compute–Storage Separation and Cloud Economics (Day 1)
Q8 · MCQ · recall · easy
docs.text:
In a decoupled platform, which cost axis is normally the controllable lever?

A. Storage, because object storage is billed per GB-month B. Compute, because it is elastic and mostly idle if unmanaged C. Network egress within one region D. Metastore operations

Answer: B. Rationale: In the Lab-2 reference model compute is 87% of the coupled bill with 96.3% of it idle; storage is the small, steady line.

docs.title: Q9 · SHORT · recall · easy
docs.text:
Name the two Parquet features that make remote reads cheap.

Answer: Column pruning (read only the columns the query projects) and row-group min/max statistics that let the reader skip row groups (data skipping). Rationale: Both reduce bytes scanned, which is the unit the decoupled bill is actually driven by.

docs.title: Q10 · T/F+J · apply · medium
docs.text:
"Migrating from a coupled warehouse to a Lakehouse guarantees a lower monthly bill."

Answer: False. Rationale: Decoupling enables savings; layout and elasticity discipline realise them — the reference retailer's first month rose because every dashboard full-scanned an unpartitioned gold table, and only partitioning, ZORDER, caching and 10-minute idle-termination brought month two 45% below the old warehouse.

docs.title: Q11 · MCQ · analyse · medium
docs.text:
Your scan benchmark reads 3 of 27 columns — 89% fewer columns — but bytes scanned fall only 72%. The most likely explanation is:

A. The query plan did not actually prune columns B. Delta read the transaction log for every file C. The three retained columns are wide, low-entropy strings that compress differently from the dropped ones D. The table needs OPTIMIZE before pruning works

Answer: C. Rationale: Column count is a proxy; bytes are the truth — which is why the lab insists on measuring bytes rather than reasoning about column counts.

docs.title: Q12 · SHORT · apply · medium
docs.text:
Name the two elasticity guardrails that must appear in the Masar ELT cluster definition, with the reference values.

Answer: Idle auto-termination (autotermination_minutes: 10) and a bounded autoscale ceiling (max_workers: 8). Rationale: Infinite scale means an infinite bill; the guardrails are what make an ephemeral job cluster safe to hand to a scheduler.

docs.title: Q13 · DEBUG · analyse · hard
docs.text:
== Physical Plan ==
FileScan parquet [trip_id,rider_id,driver_id,vehicle_id,city,... 27 columns]
   PartitionFilters: []
   PushedFilters: []
   ReadSchema: struct<trip_id:string,rider_id:string, ... >
The query was SELECT city, fare_sar FROM silver.trips WHERE city = 'Riyadh'. State what is wrong and the fix.

Answer: Neither pruning nor pushdown happened — 27 columns are in ReadSchema and both filter lists are empty, so the job is paying to read the whole table. Cause is usually a preceding wide action (a collect, a UDF, or a cached full DataFrame) or a non-partitioned, non-statistics-bearing layout. Fix: project before acting, partition by city, and confirm the plan shows PartitionFilters: [city#12 = Riyadh] and a 2-column ReadSchema. Rationale: The reference run moves relative bytes scanned from 1.00 to 0.06 purely through pruning plus a partition filter.

docs.title: Q14 · MCQ · apply · medium
docs.text:
The Lab-2 model reports "break-even utilisation 318,717 core-hours/month; actual 2,118". This means:

A. The Lakehouse becomes cheaper once you exceed 318,717 core-hours B. The coupled warehouse would only match the Lakehouse's cost at ~150× Masar's actual compute demand C. The cluster is under-provisioned by a factor of 150 D. Storage cost dominates below the break-even point

Answer: B. Rationale: Break-even states the utilisation at which always-on capacity stops being wasteful; Masar runs at 0.7% of it, which is the whole argument for elastic compute.

docs.title: Module 3 — ETL versus ELT in Modern Stacks (Day 2)
Q15 · MCQ · recall · easy
docs.text:
Why did ELT displace ETL on cloud platforms?

A. SQL is faster than Python for transformations B. Cheap storage lets you keep raw, and elastic compute transforms in-platform — so transformations are reprocessable and auditable C. ELT removes the need for data tests D. ETL cannot handle semi-structured data

Answer: B. Rationale: The decisive property is retained raw: when the cleaning logic is wrong you re-derive rather than re-ingest.

docs.title: Q16 · SHORT · apply · medium
docs.text:
What bug does a lookback window fix in an incremental model, and what does it cost?

Answer: Late-arriving rows that a WHERE date = current_date() filter silently drops. It costs re-processing the lookback window on every run (Masar: 3 days), which is cheap because the MERGE makes re-application a no-op. Rationale: The reference undercount was ~2% and invisible — it skewed driver incentives and model labels for months.

docs.title: Q17 · T/F+J · apply · medium
docs.text:
"SELECT DISTINCT * FROM stg_trips is an acceptable way to enforce one row per trip_id in silver."

Answer: False. Rationale: DISTINCT keeps every distinct version of a corrected trip, so a corrected row and its stale predecessor both survive; the correct pattern is latest-row-per-key (window on _ingested_at) followed by a MERGE on trip_id.

docs.title: Q18 · DEBUG · analyse · hard
docs.text:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='trip_id') }}
SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_trips') }}
{% if is_incremental() %}
WHERE pickup_ts::date = current_date()
{% endif %}
A trip that ended yesterday but landed in bronze today is missing from silver.trips. Explain and fix.

Answer: The incremental predicate filters on the trip's own pickup_ts, so a trip that occurred yesterday is excluded even though it arrived today. Consequence: dbt run reports success, inserted -> 0, and the trip is lost — a silent undercount. Fix: widen to a lookback on the event date, WHERE pickup_ts >= current_date() - INTERVAL 3 DAYS, keeping unique_key='trip_id' so the re-scanned rows merge as no-ops. Rationale: In the reference run the corrected model reports inserted -> 1 on the backfill and inserted -> 0 on the repeat; the naive filter reports 0 / 0 and loses the trip.

docs.title: Q19 · MCQ · recall · medium
docs.text:
Why is MERGE-on-key idempotent where INSERT is not?

A. MERGE runs inside a transaction and INSERT does not B. Re-applying an already-matched row updates it to the same values — a no-op — whereas INSERT appends a second copy C. MERGE deduplicates the source automatically D. INSERT cannot be run twice on a Delta table

Answer: B. Rationale: Idempotency is a property of the table state after the run, not of whether a commit was written.

docs.title: Q20 · SHORT · analyse · hard
docs.text:
bronze.trips has a dbt source freshness SLA of 6h warn / 24h error. State one upstream failure it catches and one it misses.

Answer: Catches: a stopped or crashed landing job — the newest _ingested_at ages past the threshold. Misses: a landing job that runs exactly on time and lands empty or wrong data, because freshness only inspects recency, not volume or content. Rationale: This is precisely the gap that the M6 volume and distribution checks close.

docs.title: Q21 · MCQ · apply · medium
docs.text:
Where do source quirks — a mixed hire_date format, a renamed column — belong in the dbt layering?

A. In the mart, so the fix is close to the consumer B. In the staging model, so the quirk is isolated once C. In a post-hook on the silver table D. In the source declaration itself

Answer: B. Rationale: Casting and renaming in marts leaks source quirks everywhere; one rename then breaks ten models.

docs.title: Q22 · SHORT · apply · medium
docs.text:
Reconstruct the Masar silver row derivation: 96,400 bronze rows become 42,038 silver rows. Name each step.

Answer: 96,400 bronze rows (two landings of the same day) → 48,200 after latest-per-key dedup → 42,096 after status = 'completed' → 42,038 after the validity predicates (dropoff_ts > pickup_ts, fare_sar > 0, distance_km > 0); the 58 rejected rows go to silver.trips_quarantine. Rationale: A participant who cannot account for their own row loss has not understood the transform.

docs.title: Module 4 — Delta Lake and ACID Transactions (Day 3)
Q23 · MCQ · recall · easy
docs.text:
A reader opens a query at version 5 while a MERGE commits version 6. The reader sees version 5 throughout. Which ACID property is this, and what provides it?

A. Atomicity, via the single commit file B. Consistency, via CHECK constraints C. Isolation, via snapshot isolation over the transaction log D. Durability, via object storage

Answer: C. Rationale: The reader pinned a snapshot at query start; the new commit is simply a later log entry it does not read.

docs.title: Q24 · SHORT · recall · easy
docs.text:
What does VACUUM trade away in exchange for reclaimed storage?

Answer: Time-travel history beyond the retention window — versions older than the retention can no longer be read, because their data files are physically deleted. Rationale: Retention is therefore a governance decision, not a housekeeping one.

docs.title: Q25 · T/F+J · apply · medium
docs.text:
"A DELETE on a Delta table immediately frees the storage and removes the rows from history."

Answer: False. Rationale: DELETE writes a commit that tombstones the affected files; the rows remain readable via time travel and present on disk until a VACUUM past the retention window removes them — which is why a PDPL erasure is a two-step operation.

docs.title: Q26 · DEBUG · analyse · hard
docs.text:
spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled", "false")
spark.sql("VACUUM delta.`./lakehouse/silver/trips` RETAIN 0 HOURS")
State what is wrong, the two distinct consequences, and the correct operation.

Answer: The safety check was disabled specifically to bypass a guardrail that exists for two reasons. Consequence 1: every prior version's data files are deleted, so VERSION AS OF and the audit diff fail with FileNotFoundException — the regulator question "what did this table contain three weeks ago" becomes unanswerable. Consequence 2: files that a concurrently running reader or streaming query is about to open are deleted underneath it, failing a healthy job. Correct operation: leave retentionDurationCheck enabled and run VACUUM ... RETAIN 168 HOURS, preceded by a DRY RUN. Rationale: 168h is longer than any Masar job's runtime and short enough that an honoured erasure completes within a defensible window.

docs.title: Q27 · MCQ · apply · medium
docs.text:
Your corrections MERGE reports updated=5 on run 1 and updated=0 on run 2 — but DESCRIBE HISTORY shows a new version for run 2. Is the operation idempotent?

A. No — a second commit means the table changed B. Yes — idempotency is a property of the resulting table state, and a MERGE that changes nothing is still a transaction C. Only if whenNotMatchedInsertAll is omitted D. Only if the source is empty on the second run

Answer: B. Rationale: The reference run produces v3 updated -> 5 and v4 updated -> 0; both commits exist and the table state is identical.

docs.title: Q28 · SHORT · apply · medium
docs.text:
Why is partitionBy("trip_id") on silver.trips a mistake, and what is the correct Masar partitioning?

Answer: trip_id is unique per row, so it produces one directory and one tiny file per trip — millions of small files, catastrophic listing and read cost. Correct: partition by a coarse, query-aligned key (city and/or date) and use ZORDER BY (city, pickup_ts) for skipping within partitions. Rationale: The reference OPTIMIZE takes numFiles from 214 to 9 (23.8×) and the filtered read from 1.91s to 0.41s.

docs.title: Q29 · MCQ · analyse · medium
docs.text:
A write with fare_sar = -5.0 is rejected, and a separate write sending fare_sar as a string is also rejected. Which mechanisms fired?

A. Both were CHECK constraints B. Both were schema enforcement C. The negative value was the positive_fare CHECK constraint; the string was schema enforcement (type merge failure) D. The negative value was schema enforcement; the string was a CHECK constraint

Answer: C. Rationale: Constraints police values, schema enforcement polices shape and type; a table needs both, and neither catches semantic drift (the m/s incident).

docs.title: Q30 · SHORT · analyse · hard
docs.text:
A PDPL erasure request for rid_0000042 is executed as a MERGE DELETE on silver.trips. Where does that rider's data still exist, and what completes the erasure?

Answer: In Delta time-travel history and in tombstoned Parquet files on disk; in bronze.trips (append-only, still holds the raw rows); in silver.trips_quarantine if any of the rider's rows were quarantined; and in any gold table or Redis key derived before the deletion. Completion requires the DELETE on every such table, a VACUUM past retention on each, a rebuild of the derived gold and feature tables, and a purge of the online store — recorded in GOVERNANCE.md as a runbook. Rationale: Most participants delete from silver and bronze and forget the quarantine table, which is by construction full of personal data.

docs.title: Q31 · DEBUG · analyse · hard
docs.text:
(target.alias("t")
   .merge(source.alias("s"),
          "t.trip_id = s.trip_id AND t._ingested_at = s._ingested_at")
   .whenMatchedUpdateAll()
   .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
   .execute())
The corrections job is run twice. State what is wrong, the consequence, and the fix.

Answer: _ingested_at is set to the current run time, so the match condition can never be satisfied across runs. Consequence: whenMatchedUpdateAll never fires and every run takes the whenNotMatchedInsertAll branch — the table gains a duplicate copy of every corrected trip per run, silently breaking the one-row-per-trip_id grain that every gold table and both consumers depend on. Fix: match on the business key alone (t.trip_id = s.trip_id), and check the source for duplicate keys before merging so whenMatchedUpdateAll is unambiguous. Rationale: This is the classic non-idempotent MERGE and the starting state of PA-1.

docs.title: Q32 · MCQ · recall · easy
docs.text:
Which two mechanisms together give Structured Streaming + Delta exactly-once?

A. Kafka transactions and consumer-group offsets B. Checkpointed Kafka offsets and Delta's atomic per-micro-batch commit C. dropDuplicates and a watermark D. Idempotent producers and acks=all

Answer: B. Rationale: Kafka alone gives at-least-once with replay; Delta alone gives an idempotent sink; exactly-once is the composition.

docs.title: Q33 · SHORT · recall · easy
docs.text:
What does a streaming watermark bound?

Answer: How long the query waits for late events before finalising a window — and therefore how much state it must retain. Rationale: No watermark on an event-time aggregation means unbounded state and eventual OOM.

docs.title: Q34 · T/F+J · apply · medium
docs.text:
"Kafka provides exactly-once delivery, so a Spark consumer inherits it."

Answer: False. Rationale: Kafka provides durable, replayable at-least-once delivery; the consumer must supply a durable record of which offsets were included in each committed sink transaction — in Masar that is ./lakehouse/_checkpoints/gps_events_bronze plus the Delta commit, with txnAppId/txnVersion making a replayed batch_id a no-op.

docs.title: Q35 · DEBUG · analyse · hard
docs.text:
(parse(raw).writeStream
   .foreachBatch(write_batch)
   .outputMode("append")
   .trigger(processingTime="30 seconds")
   .start()
   .awaitTermination())
110,000 pings are produced; the job is killed mid-batch and restarted; bronze.gps_events then reports 127,300 rows. Explain and fix.

Answer: There is no checkpointLocation, so on restart the query has no record of committed Kafka offsets and re-reads from the configured starting position — 17,300 pings are appended a second time. Consequence: the 15-minute demand feature inflates, the ETA model predicts a rush hour that never happened and surge fires in an empty district. Fix: add .option("checkpointLocation", "./lakehouse/_checkpoints/gps_events_bronze") — one dedicated directory per query — and keep the txnAppId/txnVersion idempotent-write guard in write_batch. Rationale: The reference clean run is 110,000 pings → 110,000 rows with 0 pipeline duplicates; the sim-nocheckpoint counter-demo is 127,300.

docs.title: Q36 · MCQ · apply · medium
docs.text:
A windowed demand aggregation must use event time rather than processing time because:

A. Event time is always monotonically increasing B. Processing time is not available in Structured Streaming C. A ping delayed 30 minutes would otherwise be counted in the window in which it arrived, not the window in which it happened D. Event time removes the need for a watermark

Answer: C. Rationale: The reference run shows a maximum event-time lag of 1,798 seconds — a processing-time aggregation would file all of it under one wrong window.

docs.title: Q37 · SHORT · analyse · hard
docs.text:
The GPS feed carries three defects: late pings, duplicate event_id, and out-of-order ts. Say which a watermark fixes, which dropDuplicates fixes, and which of the four known GPS problems neither can see.

Answer: The watermark handles late arrival (how long a window stays open). dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"]) handles duplicates, at the cost of state bounded to the lateness window. Out-of-order needs no fixing at all under event-time semantics. The fourth problem — producer_version 2.5.0 emitting speed_kmh in m/s — is invisible to both: it is structurally valid, on time, unique and correctly ordered, and only a per-producer_version distribution comparison detects it. Rationale: This distinction is the hand-off from M5 to M6.

docs.title: Q38 · MCQ · apply · medium
docs.text:
Two streaming queries are pointed at the same checkpointLocation. The most likely outcome is:

A. Spark refuses to start the second query B. The two queries safely share offsets C. One query reads the other's offset log and state — silent data loss or state corruption, often without an error D. Throughput halves but correctness is preserved

Answer: C. Rationale: Spark does not always fail loudly on this, which is why "one checkpoint per query" is a rule rather than a preference.

docs.title: Q39 · SHORT · apply · medium
docs.text:
The GPS stream's trigger is changed from 30 seconds to 1 second. Name three consequences.

Answer: (1) ~30× the files — roughly 7,400 files per 15 minutes and ~1.7M files/year for this feed alone, so every downstream read pays per-file open cost. (2) One _delta_log commit per second, so listing and checkpointing the log becomes the bottleneck. (3) Object-storage request charges scale with file count — a direct cost regression. Rationale: Latency is bought with file count; OPTIMIZE is maintenance, not a licence to over-trigger.

docs.title: Q40 · DEBUG · analyse · hard
docs.text:
(events
   .groupBy(F.window(F.current_timestamp(), "15 minutes"), "pickup_zone_id")
   .count())
State what is wrong, what the demand mart will show, and the fix.

Answer: The window is built on current_timestamp() — processing time — not on the event's own ts. Consequence: every ping processed in one micro-batch lands in the same window regardless of when it happened, so a 30-minute-late batch of pings inflates the current window and empties the correct one; the zone demand feature is wrong in both directions and the error correlates with pipeline lag. Fix: withWatermark("event_ts", "5 minutes") then groupBy(F.window("event_ts", "15 minutes"), "pickup_zone_id"). Rationale: Event time is a correctness property; processing time is an operational metric and should be kept alongside, never substituted.

docs.title: Module 6 — Data Quality, Observability, and Governance (Day 4)
Q41 · MCQ · recall · easy
docs.text:
Where in the medallion should the quality gate run?

A. On landing, before bronze B. At promotion, bronze → silver C. On the gold marts, before the dashboard reads them D. In the BI tool, as a report-level filter

Answer: B. Rationale: Bronze must accept everything received; silver is the first layer that carries a contract, so it is the first place a gate can legitimately refuse data.

docs.title: Q42 · SHORT · apply · medium
docs.text:
Give one Masar failure that warrants fail-fast and one that warrants quarantine, with the reason for each.

Answer: Fail-fast: 40 rows with a null trip_id — the MERGE key is null, so WHEN MATCHED never matches and those rows re-insert on every run; the promotion mechanism is unsound for that batch, so blocking is the only containment. Quarantine: 120 rows with fare_sar <= 0 out of 42,096 — 0.25%, isolable by a predicate, and blocking would convert a data problem into a total availability outage. Rationale: Proportionality is the whole of the fail-fast/quarantine decision.

docs.title: Q43 · T/F+J · analyse · hard
docs.text:
"The currency-shift batch (Jeddah fares ×100) should be routed to silver.trips_quarantine."

Answer: False. Rationale: No individual row violates any predicate — the failure is a distribution failure (the mean expectation), and a distribution failure is not isolable by a row-level rule, so quarantine is impossible by definition; the correct response is a third class, ALERT_AND_HOLD — promote nothing and page a human — or escalating the mean expectation to FAIL_FAST.

docs.title: Q44 · SHORT · recall · easy
docs.text:
Name two observability signals that row-level expectations cannot provide.

Answer: Freshness (how old the newest row is) and volume (how many rows arrived versus expectation); distribution drift is a third. Rationale: Every row can pass every rule while the feed is stale, halved, or silently rescaled.

docs.title: Q45 · DEBUG · analyse · hard
docs.text:
$ python -m masar.quality.observe --check drift --column fare_sar --baseline auto
[obs] drift silver.trips.fare_sar: 421.30 vs 421.30 (0.0%)  OK
The Jeddah currency shift is present in the table. Explain why the check passes and give the fix.

Answer: --baseline auto computes the expected value from the same data it is testing, so the comparison is a tautology and the check can never fail. Consequence: a working quality system silently stops working — the most dangerous failure mode, because the dashboard is green. Fix: pin the baseline to a stored historical reference (a prior Delta version, or a committed expectation value under review), and segment the comparison by city and by producer_version so a per-segment shift is visible. Rationale: This is the sim-baseline-the-bug simulation; a check that computes its own expectation is not a check.

docs.title: Q46 · MCQ · apply · medium
docs.text:
Why can a null trip_id not simply be quarantined?

A. Great Expectations cannot express a not-null predicate B. The quarantine table has a NOT NULL constraint C. The MERGE key is null, so those rows never match and re-insert on every run — quarantining relocates the rows without containing the fault D. Null keys are legal and should be promoted

Answer: C. Rationale: Integrity failures compromise the operation, not just the data.

docs.title: Q47 · SHORT · analyse · hard
docs.text:
rider_id and driver_id are both personal data. Why do they have different retention periods in GOVERNANCE.md?

Answer: Because they rest on different lawful bases. Rider data is purpose-limited to service delivery, support and disputes — 24 months. Driver data is employment/contractual and legitimately retained longer — 7 years. A single blanket retention policy applied to both is a governance smell, because it is either over-retaining rider data or under-retaining employment records. Rationale: Retention follows purpose, not data type.

docs.title: Q48 · MCQ · apply · medium
docs.text:
Which PDPL principle most directly argues against retaining precise GPS coordinates indefinitely?

A. Transparency B. Data minimisation and retention limitation C. Accuracy D. Right of access

Answer: B. Rationale: Masar's answer is a 180-day raw retention on lat/lon with geohash-6 at the boundary — the safest personal data is the data you no longer hold.

docs.title: Q49 · MCQ · recall · easy
docs.text:
Which ordering does masar_medallion declare?

A. land >> silver >> gate >> [gold...] >> maintain B. land >> gate >> silver >> observability >> [gold...] >> maintain C. land >> [gold...] >> gate >> silver >> maintain D. gate >> land >> silver >> [gold...] >> maintain

Answer: B. Rationale: The gate sits at the promotion boundary; the three gold tasks are siblings running in parallel; optimize_vacuum waits for all three.

docs.title: Q50 · T/F+J · apply · medium
docs.text:
"Because land_bronze appends, a full DAG re-run would duplicate data, so the recovery procedure should skip it."

Answer: False. Rationale: Bronze may legitimately grow on a re-run — its contract is "everything we ever received", and _batch_id/_source_file make a duplicate landing identifiable — while the duplication stops at the first keyed write, the MERGE on trip_id into silver; a task you are afraid to re-run is a task you cannot recover.

docs.title: Q51 · SHORT · apply · medium
docs.text:
Why does gold.zone_hourly_demand use replaceWhere while gold.driver_daily uses MERGE? Both are idempotent.

Answer: Grain-to-partition alignment. zone_hourly_demand is partitioned by date and its grain (city, pickup_zone_id, date, hour) is fully contained in a date partition, so a partition overwrite is exact and cheap. driver_daily's rebuild would need to know which (driver_id, date) pairs existed previously to avoid orphaning drivers with no trips in the new window — MERGE handles that naturally. Rationale: Either strategy is acceptable for either table if defended and proven by a double run; append is wrong, and overwrite without replaceWhere silently deletes history outside the lookback.

docs.title: Q52 · DEBUG · analyse · hard
docs.text:
RuntimeError: GRAIN VIOLATION in ./lakehouse/gold/zone_hourly_demand:
  17,280 rows but only 8,640 distinct ['city', 'pickup_zone_id', 'date', 'hour'].
Name the cause, the consumer-visible symptom, and the fix.

Answer: The gold write used .mode("append") and the DAG was run twice, so every grain key exists twice. Symptom: the demand mart double-counts — every zone's hourly demand reads exactly 2×, so surge logic and the ETA demand feature both see a phantom rush hour, and the BI dashboard stops reconciling with the star schema. Fix: replaceWhere over the lookback partition (or MERGE on the grain key), plus the _assert_grain check as a task-level gate so a non-idempotent write fails the DAG instead of shipping. Rationale: Non-idempotent gold is one of the capstone anti-pattern flags that caps a criterion at 70%.

docs.title: Q53 · SHORT · analyse · hard
docs.text:
In gold.trip_features, why must the window be rangeBetween(-3600, -1) rather than rangeBetween(-3600, 0)?

Answer: rangeBetween bounds are inclusive and operate on the ordering column's value range, so an upper bound of 0 admits every row whose pickup_epoch equals the current row's — every trip starting in the same second, in the same zone. At Riyadh rush-hour density that is several trips, and they are the future. -1 makes the frame strictly prior. Rationale: The inflation is dangerous precisely because it is small, and it correlates with the congestion being predicted — so it reads as signal rather than as a bug.

docs.title: Q54 · MCQ · apply · medium
docs.text:
A failure is injected into build_silver mid-DAG. What must the gold tables show?

A. Partially rebuilt rows from the failed run B. Unchanged — yesterday's correct data, because the dependency prevented the gold tasks from running C. Empty, because the DAG rolls back D. Rebuilt from bronze via the fallback path

Answer: B. Rationale: The recovery proof is before.json == during.json (dependency held) and before.json == after.json (a full re-run reproduced the exact state, checksums included).

docs.title: Module 8 — Serving Data to AI and BI Workloads (Day 5)
Q55 · MCQ · recall · easy
docs.text:
What makes numbers reconcile across two dashboards?

A. Running both queries on the same cluster B. Conformed dimensions — one shared dim_date, one shared dim_driver C. Caching the gold marts D. Rebuilding both marts in the same DAG task

Answer: B. Rationale: A second, non-conformed dim_date reintroduces two-tier divergence inside a single platform.

docs.title: Q56 · SHORT · apply · medium
docs.text:
How do you keep online and offline features consistent?

Answer: Materialise — copy the value from the offline gold table into Redis — and never re-implement the feature logic in the serving path. materialize_online.py must contain zero feature logic, and a consistency check must compare every key and every online column, not a spot sample. Rationale: Any online path that re-derives a feature is skew by construction; a consistency check that has never failed is a check you have not tested.

docs.title: Q57 · T/F+J · analyse · hard
docs.text:
"After the leakage fix the model's R² fell from 0.943 to 0.712, so the fix made the model worse."

Answer: False. Rationale: 0.943 was never a real number — it was produced by distance_km (the metered distance, written at dropoff_ts, r = 0.947 with the label) and a speed averaged over the trip's own pings; 0.712 is what the platform can actually deliver at request time, and the honest model that predicts ±4.6 min is cheaper than a leaking model that promises ±1.8 and delivers ±5, precisely because you believed the second.

docs.title: Q58 · DEBUG · analyse · hard
docs.text:
# materialize_online.py
payload["rolling_zone_demand_15m"] = (
    spark.sql("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM silver.trips "
              "WHERE pickup_zone_id = '%s' AND pickup_ts > now() - INTERVAL 15 MINUTES"
              % zone_id).first()[0])
State what is wrong, the consequence, and the fix.

Answer: The online path recomputes a feature instead of copying it. Consequence: two implementations of one definition drift the moment either changes — a different window bound, a different status filter, a different clock — so the model is trained on one quantity and served another, and the divergence is invisible because both paths "work". Fix: read the value from gold.eta_features and write it verbatim; keep materialize_online.py free of any feature logic and let consistency_check.py prove offline == online across all 412 zone keys. Rationale: Serve, do not fork — external stores are derived copies, not new pipelines.

docs.title: Q59 · SHORT · analyse · hard
docs.text:
dropoff_zone_id is VALID but distance_km is LEAKAGE, though both describe the destination. Explain.

Answer: The difference is when the value is written, not what it describes. Masar's booking flow requires a stated destination before the request, so dropoff_zone_id is an input the platform holds at feature_ts. distance_km in silver.trips is the metered distance actually travelled, written at dropoff_ts — an outcome of the journey. The fix keeps the contract column name and changes the source to the routing engine's planned distance at booking. Rationale: The dependency is invisible in the schema — both columns are typed and populated identically, which is why point-in-time correctness is a property of the pipeline, not the table.

docs.title: Q60 · MCQ · apply · medium
docs.text:
weather_condition is joined to the weather row for the trip's own hour. The correct classification and fix are:

A. VALID — the observation exists in weather_hourly.csv B. LEAKAGE — remove the feature entirely C. UNAVAILABLE ONLINE — shift the join to the last observed hour (hour_ts <= date_trunc('hour', feature_ts) - INTERVAL 1 HOUR) on both the training and the serving side, and serve it from the Redis zone key D. STALE — refresh the weather feed hourly and leave the join unchanged

Answer: C. Rationale: The hourly file lands after the hour it describes, so the value is point-in-time correct offline and simply unobtainable online; a leaking feature must be changed, an unavailable one must be re-sourced — and the shift must be applied on both sides or you have manufactured textbook skew.

docs.text:
Participant name: ____ Cohort: __ Date: ____ Total: 20 marks.

B1 (M1, 2 marks) A data-science notebook reports 91% on-time deliveries; the executive dashboard reports 87%. Name the architectural cause and the architectural fix.

B2 (M2, 1 mark) In a decoupled platform, which cost axis is normally the controllable lever? A. Storage B. Compute C. Intra-region network egress D. Metastore operations

B3 (M3, 3 marks) A trip that ended yesterday but landed in bronze today is missing from silver.trips. Explain and fix: 

{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='trip_id') }}
SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_trips') }}
{% if is_incremental() %} WHERE pickup_ts::date = current_date() {% endif %}

B4 (M4, 1 mark) Your corrections MERGE reports updated=5 on run 1 and updated=0 on run 2, but DESCRIBE HISTORY shows a new version for run 2. Is the operation idempotent? A. No — a second commit means the table changed B. Yes — idempotency is about the resulting table state C. Only without whenNotMatchedInsertAll D. Only if the source is empty

B5 (M4, 2 marks) A PDPL erasure request for rid_0000042 is executed as a MERGE DELETE on silver.trips. Where does that rider's data still exist, and what completes the erasure?

B6 (M5, 2 marks) The GPS feed carries late pings, duplicate event_id, and out-of-order ts. Which does a watermark fix, which does dropDuplicates fix, and which known GPS problem is invisible to both?

B7 (M5, 3 marks) State what is wrong, what the demand mart will show, and the fix: 

events.groupBy(F.window(F.current_timestamp(), "15 minutes"), "pickup_zone_id").count()

B8 (M6, 3 marks) The Jeddah currency shift is present in the table, yet the check passes. Explain and fix: 

$ python -m masar.quality.observe --check drift --column fare_sar --baseline auto
[obs] drift silver.trips.fare_sar: 421.30 vs 421.30 (0.0%)  OK

B9 (M7, 2 marks) True or false, with a one-sentence justification: "Because land_bronze appends, a full DAG re-run would duplicate data, so recovery should skip it."

B10 (M8, 1 mark) weather_condition is joined to the weather row for the trip's own hour. The correct classification and fix are: A. VALID — the observation exists in the file B. LEAKAGE — remove the feature C. UNAVAILABLE ONLINE — shift the join to the last observed hour on both the training and serving side D. STALE — refresh the feed hourly, leave the join unchanged

docs.title: Cohort Set B — ANSWER KEY (print separately)
docs.text:
# Bank ID Module Answer Marking note B1 Q4 M1 Two copies with two different late-arrival rules — the two-tier problem. Fix: one governed silver table with one late-arrival rule, read by both 1 cause, 1 fix; "fix the ETL job" scores 0 B2 Q8 M2 B — compute 1 mark B3 Q18 M3 The predicate filters on the trip's own pickup_ts, so a trip that occurred yesterday is excluded though it arrived today; dbt run reports success and inserted -> 0 — a silent undercount. Fix: WHERE pickup_ts >= current_date() - INTERVAL 3 DAYS with unique_key='trip_id' 1 identify, 1 silent-success consequence, 1 fix B4 Q27 M4 B 1 mark B5 Q30 M4 Time-travel history and tombstoned files; bronze.trips; silver.trips_quarantine; any derived gold table and Redis key. Completion = DELETE everywhere + VACUUM past retention + rebuild gold/features + purge the online store, recorded as a runbook 1 for naming ≥ 3 locations (quarantine required for full mark), 1 for the completion steps B6 Q37 M5 Watermark → late arrival. dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"]) → duplicates, at the cost of state bounded to the lateness window. Out-of-order needs no fix under event time. Invisible to both: the 2.5.0 m/s semantic drift 1 for the three mappings, 1 for naming the m/s drift B7 Q40 M5 Processing-time window. Every ping in a micro-batch lands in the same window regardless of when it happened, so a late batch inflates the current window and empties the correct one. Fix: withWatermark("event_ts","5 minutes") then window("event_ts","15 minutes") 1 identify, 1 consequence, 1 fix B8 Q45 M6 --baseline auto computes the expectation from the data under test — a tautology that can never fail; a working quality system silently stops working. Fix: pin the baseline to a stored historical reference and segment by city and producer_version 1 identify, 1 consequence, 1 fix B9 Q50 M7 False — bronze may grow on a re-run by contract, _batch_id/_source_file make it identifiable, and duplication stops at the MERGE on trip_id 0.5 verdict, 1.5 justification B10 Q60 M8 C 1 mark; C only — B scores 0
