docs.title: RUBRIC — Masar Mini-Lakehouse Capstone (100 points)
docs.text:
SDA-DSC-214 · Instructor instrument. Not distributed to participants in this form — participants receive CAPSTONE_BRIEF.md, which states the criteria and weights.

Field Value Total 100 points across 7 criteria Pass ≥ 70 · Distinction ≥ 90 Bonus Extensions +5 max, capped at 100, only if mandatory scope ≥ 80 Grading order Platform and repository first, demo second. The point of the course is that the platform speaks Scoring moment Repository and run evidence reviewed in Day 5 Hour 4 (collected at the end of the hour); demo scored live in Hour 5

Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. Grains, ratios and file-count reductions hold at either scale; absolute row counts do not.

docs.title: 0. How to use this instrument
docs.text:
1. Before demos, run the participant's make pipeline from their submitted commit and open their BENCHMARKS.md, GOVERNANCE.md, MINI_LAKEHOUSE.md, DECISIONS.md and LAB8_LEAKAGE.md. Fill the worksheet in §9 as far as the artefacts allow. Most criteria are decidable here.
  2. During the demo, confirm the beats you could not verify statically and ask one live-verification question (§10).
  3. Score each criterion into a band, then pick a point within the band. Do not average sub-criteria arithmetically — the bands are holistic and the sub-criteria are evidence prompts, not a checklist to tally.
  4. Apply anti-pattern caps last (§8). A cap overrides the band.
  5. Moderate against §11 before releasing marks.

Evidence hierarchy. When two sources disagree, trust in this order: (1) a run you executed, (2) a committed transcript with a matching commit SHA, (3) the demo, (4) the participant's prose. A claim that exists only at level 4 is unevidenced and scores at the Developing band for that sub-criterion however well written.

docs.title: 1. Architecture & medallion contracts — 15 points
docs.text:
What is being assessed: whether the layers are real boundaries with enforced contracts, or three folders with data in them.

Band Points Observable evidence Distinction 14–15 Bronze / silver / gold cleanly separated; no gold table reads a bronze path (verifiable by grep and by the DAG graph). MINI_LAKEHOUSE.md states for every table: grain · source · write strategy · the file and line where the contract is enforced · who may read it · what breaks if it breaks. Enforcement is in code — _assert_grain, CHECK constraints, unique/not_null tests — not prose. Lineage columns present on every bronze table and used at least once in an investigation the participant can describe Proficient 11–13 Layers separated and contracts documented, with one gap: a table whose grain is stated but not enforced, or one enforcement location undocumented, or a single defensible bypass (e.g. an observability task reading bronze) that the participant identifies and justifies Developing 8–10 Layers exist but contracts are prose only; grain is asserted nowhere in code; one gold table derives from bronze; or MINI_LAKEHOUSE.md documents grain and source but omits enforcement for most tables Insufficient 0–7 Layers muddled; gold built from bronze as the normal path; no documented contracts; bronze mutated in place

Prompts for the marker: Which file enforces silver.trips grain? Show me a gold table's grain assertion. What is in bronze that is not in silver, and why?

docs.title: 2. ELT & incrementality — 15 points
docs.text:
What is being assessed: whether a re-run is safe and a late-arriving trip is counted exactly once.

Band Points Observable evidence Distinction 14–15 Incremental model merges on trip_id with a stated, justified lookback (3 days) — the justification appears in DECISIONS.md. ≥ 6 tests passing including unique and not_null on the silver key plus a relationships test. Source freshness declared and shown firing. Backfill proven with both runs: inserted -> 1 then inserted -> 0. The naive-filter counter-experiment is recorded with both counts side by side. Row derivation (96,400 → 42,038) accounted for step by step Proficient 11–13 Incremental merge works and the backfill is demonstrated, but the test suite is thin (6 tests, all generic), or the freshness SLA is declared but never shown firing, or the counter-experiment is described rather than run Developing 8–10 Incremental configured but the lookback is absent or arbitrary; the backfill is asserted, not shown; fewer than 6 tests; the participant cannot account for their own row loss Insufficient 0–7 Full-refresh only; a late-arrival bug present (date = current_date()); no tests on the silver key

Prompts: Run dbt test in front of me. Why 3 days and not 1 or 7? Where did 6,162 rows go between bronze dedup and silver?

docs.title: 3. Delta Lake mastery — 15 points
docs.text:
What is being assessed: whether the table defends itself, whether re-running is a no-op, and whether retention is a decision rather than a default.

Band Points Observable evidence Distinction 14–15 positive_fare and valid_duration CHECK constraints visible in SHOW TBLPROPERTIES; three negative-write tests captured with their exact error text and the row count shown unchanged. MERGE idempotency shown as updated=5 / updated=0, with the participant volunteering that a commit is still written on the second run. Time-travel diff of two versions included. VACUUM ... RETAIN 168 HOURS with a DRY RUN first; retentionDurationCheck enabled; the retention justified against all three inputs (audit window · PDPL erasure SLA · storage cost) with a stated trigger for changing it. PDPL erasure demonstrated across every affected table, silver.trips_quarantine included. OPTIMIZE/ZORDER with numFiles before/after ≥ 10× and a measured read-time improvement Proficient 11–13 Constraints, idempotent MERGE, time travel and OPTIMIZE all present; retention stated but justified on one input only, or the erasure omits the quarantine table, or the negative-write errors are summarised rather than captured Developing 8–10 Delta used as a file format: constraints absent or only one present; MERGE works but idempotency shown by a single run; VACUUM run with an unexamined default; no time-travel evidence Insufficient 0–7 No constraints; non-idempotent writes; VACUUM RETAIN 0; _delta_log manipulated by hand

Prompts: Run your corrections MERGE twice, now. Why 168 hours? What else holds this rider's data?

docs.title: 4. Streaming — 15 points
docs.text:
What is being assessed: whether exactly-once is engineered or hoped for, and whether the window is about when things happened.

Band Points Observable evidence Distinction 14–15 One dedicated checkpointLocation per query under ./lakehouse/_checkpoints/<query_name>, no sharing; txnAppId/txnVersion idempotent-write guard present. Kill/restart proof table with three counts (before, immediately after a mid-batch kill, after drain) and pipeline-introduced duplicates = 0, with source duplicates (~0.4%) explicitly distinguished. Event-time window with a stated watermark, the beyond-watermark drop count recorded and non-zero, and the watermark value defended at both ends. The 2.5.0 m/s normalisation applied and its detection explained. OPTIMIZE run on the streaming sink with numFiles before/after Proficient 11–13 Streams reliably with a dedicated checkpoint and event-time windowing, but the dedup story is thin (watermark chosen without defence, or the drop count is zero and unexplained), or the kill was taken between batches, or the source/pipeline duplicate distinction is stated without evidence Developing 8–10 Stream runs and lands data; checkpoint present but a watermark is missing (unbounded state), or the kill/restart is asserted rather than shown Insufficient 0–7 Duplicates on restart; processing-time aggregation; no checkpoint or a shared one; the sink deleted to make counts look right

Prompts: Kill it now and restart it — read me the count. Which of your two queries owns that checkpoint directory? Why five minutes and not thirty?

docs.title: 5. Quality, observability, governance — 15 points
docs.text:
What is being assessed: whether the gate acts, whether the signals fire, and whether governance is enforced by code rather than described in a document.

Band Points Observable evidence Distinction 14–15 GX suite with ≥ 7 expectations, versioned and reviewed; data docs rendered and committed. The gate acts on both paths: a null-key batch blocked (0 promoted, 0 quarantined) and a bad-fares batch quarantined (120 isolated, 41,976 promoted), with silver.trips_quarantine holding real rows and a reason column. All four observability signals shown firing on injected faults, including the distribution drift on fare_sar by city and on speed_kmh by producer_version. The participant identifies the currency-shift case as not quarantinable and proposes a third response class. PII classification complete with differentiated retention by lawful basis; retention job runs; erasure runbook names every table Proficient 11–13 Gate acts on both paths and the suite is adequate, but one observability signal is described rather than demonstrated, or the quarantine has no reason column, or the classification applies one blanket retention to all personal data Developing 8–10 Suite exists and runs; the gate alerts but promotes anyway, or blocks everything indiscriminately; observability is row-level only; governance is a document with no enforcement Insufficient 0–7 Alerts only, no action; no quarantine table or an empty one; raw PII retained with no policy; --baseline auto drift checks presented as working monitoring

Prompts: Show me a row in quarantine and tell me why it is there. Make a signal fire. Why do rider and driver retention differ?

docs.title: 6. Orchestration & recovery — 15 points
docs.text:
What is being assessed: whether the platform can be run and recovered by someone who is not the author.

Band Points Observable evidence Distinction 14–15 One DAG, dependency-ordered land >> gate >> silver >> observability >> [3 gold] >> maintain, every task idempotent and retryable. make pipeline runs from a clean clone and writes a timestamped log. Injected mid-DAG failure: downstream tasks UPSTREAM_FAILED, gold unchanged (before == during by checksum). Full re-run reproduces the identical end state (before == after, checksums included) — and the participant re-runs the whole DAG, not the failed task. They can explain why re-running land_bronze is safe in three parts (bronze contract · duplication stops at the keyed MERGE · txnAppId on the stream). Maintenance is a DAG task Proficient 11–13 DAG runs end to end with correct dependencies and one-command execution; recovery demonstrated but partial — the failed task is re-run rather than the DAG, or idempotency is proven by row counts without checksums Developing 8–10 Tasks orchestrated but some steps still run by hand; the failure drill is described rather than performed; maintenance run manually Insufficient 0–7 Hand-run sequence of notebooks or scripts; non-idempotent gold (append aggregates); no recovery path

Prompts: Delete a gold table and recover it with one command. Why is re-running land_bronze safe? Show me the during snapshot.

docs.title: 7. Serving (AI + BI) & demo — 10 points
docs.text:
What is being assessed: whether the two consumers read one truth, and whether the participant can defend the honest number.

Band Points Observable evidence Distinction 9–10 gold.eta_features has exactly the 13 CONVENTIONS columns at one row per trip_id; all 13 classified in LAB8_LEAKAGE.md with written justifications; every LEAKAGE/STALE/UNAVAILABLE column fixed at the computation, not by renaming or dropping. Both metrics recorded (pre-fix inflated, post-fix honest) with a paragraph on why the drop is correct. Offline == online proven across all zone keys and columns, and shown to exit 1 on an injected divergence. Star reconciles with the demand mart at rel_diff = 0. PDPL boundary asserted (no rider_id, no raw lat/lon, no hashes). Demo is crisp, rehearsed, and finishes inside 6 minutes Proficient 7–8 Both consumers work; the classification misses one or two columns (typically weather_condition or driver_recent_trip_count), or reconciliation is asserted rather than shown, or consistency is spot-checked on one key rather than all; demo runs slightly long or needs a retry Developing 5–6 Serving works mechanically but a leak remains, or the online path recomputes a feature, or the star does not reconcile and the participant adjusts a number rather than finding the divergent filter Insufficient 0–4 Leakage present and undetected; online ≠ offline; raw personal identifiers served; no demo or a demo of someone else's platform

Prompts: Which column leaked, which bound caused it, and which diagnostic showed you? Break Redis and run your consistency check.

docs.title: 8. Anti-pattern flags — automatic caps
docs.text:
Any one of these caps the named criterion at 70% of its points, regardless of the band the evidence would otherwise support. Caps are not negotiable and are not averaged away. Record every flag on the worksheet with its evidence line; a flag with no evidence line is not a flag.

# Anti-pattern How it presents Caps A1 Feature leakage A feature computed from data at or after feature_ts; an inclusive window upper bound (0); a metered/outcome column used as an input; a metric > 0.85 correlated feature undefended Criterion 7 → max 7.0 A2 Non-idempotent gold .mode("append") on an aggregate; overwrite without replaceWhere; a double run changing row counts; a grain assertion absent or failing Criterion 6 → max 10.5 A3 VACUUM RETAIN 0 Zero or sub-168h retention; retentionDurationCheck disabled anywhere in the repository Criterion 3 → max 10.5 A4 Alert-only quality gate Validation failures logged or emailed while the batch promotes regardless; no quarantine table, or one that is empty Criterion 5 → max 10.5 A5 Raw rider IDs in BI outputs rider_id, raw lat/lon, national_id_hash or phone_hash present in any gold product, serving view, or Redis key Criterion 7 → max 7.0 and triggers the PDPL badge check (see EVALUATION_PLAN.md) A6 Streaming without a dedicated checkpoint No checkpointLocation; two queries sharing one; a checkpoint under /tmp or inside the sink table Criterion 4 → max 10.5

Two additional caps specific to this instrument:

# Condition Caps A7 Benchmark, quarantine or metric artefacts identical to another participant's Overall score withheld pending integrity review (see §12) A8 A demo of a platform the participant cannot explain when asked one live-verification question Criterion 7 → max 7.0, and re-verify criteria 3, 4 and 6 from the repository rather than the demo

docs.title: 10. Live-verification questions — pick exactly one
docs.text:
The assessment notes authorise one live check per participant. Choose the one that targets the criterion you were least able to decide from the repository. Say up front: "I am going to ask you to verify one claim live."

Target Question Distinction answer Streaming (4) "Kill the stream and restart it. Read me the count before and after." Kills mid-batch, reads three numbers, distinguishes source from pipeline duplicates unprompted Serving (7) "Run the leakage drill and explain the inflated metric." Names the specific column, the specific window bound, the specific diagnostic, and both numbers — without opening a file Delta (3) "Run your corrections MERGE twice and read the metrics." updated=5 then updated=0, and notes that a commit is still written on the second run Orchestration (6) "Delete a gold table and bring it back with one command." make pipeline; explains why a full re-run is the recovery procedure rather than a targeted repair Quality (5) "Make an observability signal fire." Injects the fault, shows the alert, and names what the signal would not have caught Architecture (1) "Which file and line enforces the grain of gold.driver_daily?" Names it from memory; opens it to confirm rather than to search

docs.title: 11. Moderation guide — keeping two graders consistent
docs.text: Why this section exists. Seven holistic criteria and two graders will drift. The observed drift on this rubric is systematic and predictable, and these five practices remove most of it.

docs.title: 11a. Calibrate before you grade
docs.text: Before the first demo, both graders independently score the same two submissions — one expected mid-band, one expected strong — and compare. Discuss every criterion where you differ by more than 2 points. Do not proceed until you agree on what "enforced in code" and "proven" mean for this cohort. Twenty minutes here saves an appeal later.

docs.title: 11b. The four disagreements that actually happen
docs.text: Disagreement The rule to apply "Documented" vs "enforced" — one grader accepts a stated grain in MINI_LAKEHOUSE.md, the other demands an assertion in code Enforcement means a failing path exists: an assertion, a constraint, or a test that would fail if the contract broke. Prose is documentation and belongs in the Proficient band, not Distinction "Shown" vs "asserted" — a participant writes that the backfill worked A claim needs a transcript with numbers, or you ran it. "It works on my machine" is level-4 evidence (§0) and scores Developing for that sub-criterion Partial evidence across labs — the kill/restart is in LAB5_NOTES.md but not repeated for the capstone Lab evidence counts, provided the commit SHA is in the same repository and the code has not changed since. The capstone is integration, not re-performance. Check git log on the streaming file Effort vs outcome — a participant who clearly worked hard but whose platform does not run Score the platform. Note the effort in §E for the badge conversation. The rubric measures a deliverable, and saying so kindly is part of the job

docs.title: 11c. Anchor statements
docs.text:
Read these before scoring. They fix the ends of the scale.

A 15/15 on any criterion means: an engineer who has never seen this repository could reproduce the claim from the repository alone, in under ten minutes, without asking the author a question.

A 70% score means: the platform works and would survive a normal week, but a specific named failure mode would take it down and the participant has not defended against it.

A sub-70 score means: a failure mode is present in the submitted platform right now, not merely undefended.

docs.title: 11d. Score independently, then reconcile
docs.text:
Both graders score all seven criteria without seeing each other's sheet. Then compare.

Gap Action ≤ 3 points total Take the mean. No discussion needed 4–9 points total Discuss only the criteria differing by ≥ 2. Each grader names the evidence line, not the impression. Re-score together ≥ 10 points total, or a disagreement about a band on any criterion A third reviewer reads the repository blind (no scores shown) and scores the disputed criteria. Take the median of three Disagreement about an anti-pattern flag The flag stands or falls on the evidence line. If neither grader can write the line, there is no flag

docs.title: 11e. Order effects and fatigue
docs.text:
• Demos are scored in the order they are given; graders reliably score the first two submissions harshly and the last two generously. Re-check the first two after the last one.
  • Do not score more than five demos without a break.
  • Never score a participant you paired with during labs on criterion 7 alone; swap with the co-grader.
  • Record the score before discussing the participant with anyone, including them.

docs.title: 11f. Feedback that is worth reading
docs.text:
For each criterion below Distinction, write one sentence in this shape:

"[What you observed] — [what would have moved it a band] — [where in your repo that would live]."

Example: "Your backfill is described in LAB3_NOTES.md but the second run's inserted -> 0 is not captured — one more paste of the repeat run would have moved ELT to Distinction — it belongs beside the first transcript in the same file."

Participants act on that. They do not act on "good work, thin evidence".

docs.title: 12. Integrity handling within this instrument
docs.text: Do not confront a suspected integrity issue during a demo. Score the criteria from the repository, tick A7, write the evidence line (which artefacts, which other repository, which identical values), mark Integrity flag in §E, and hand the sheet to the lead instructor. The badge decision is made in EVALUATION_PLAN.md, not here. A participant whose flag is not upheld receives their uncapped score with no note in the record.

docs.title: 13. Criterion-to-requirement-to-lab map
docs.text:
Use this when a participant asks why a criterion scored where it did, or when deciding which lab to point a re-sit at.

Criterion Pts Capstone req. LO Primary lab PA that pre-tests it 1 Architecture & medallion contracts 15 R1, R2 LO1, LO7 LAB-01, LAB-07 — 2 ELT & incrementality 15 R3 LO3 LAB-03 — 3 Delta Lake mastery 15 R4, R2 LO4 LAB-04 PA-1 4 Streaming 15 R5 LO5 LAB-05 PA-2 5 Quality, observability, governance 15 R6 LO6 LAB-06 — 6 Orchestration & recovery 15 R7 LO7 LAB-07 — 7 Serving (AI + BI) & demo 10 R8 LO8 LAB-08 PA-3

A participant who failed PA-1, PA-2 or PA-3 is at elevated risk on the corresponding criterion. Tell them so before Day 5, not after.

docs.title: CS-01 — The Reporting Divergence at "Naql" Logistics
docs.text: Field Value Case ID CS-01 Module M1 — Evolution of Data Architecture Day / Hour Day 1 · Hour 3 (after the warehouse → lake → lakehouse timeline, before LAB-01) Duration 45 minutes Format Table discussion Group size 4–5 per table; 3–6 tables Deliverable One flipchart per table: the single conformed definition of "on-time", the layer it lives in, and a three-step cutover plan with the reconciliation evidence the CFO will be shown Materials Evidence pack §5 printed one copy per table (5 pages); flipchart + markers; the medallion diagram on the wall Facilitator prep 10 min. Read §7 model answers. Decide in advance which table you will push on Q3 — that is where the case earns its time

docs.title: 1. Scenario
docs.text:
"Naql" (نقل) is a Saudi last-mile logistics firm operating in Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam. Over six years it accumulated two data platforms:

  • a data lake — Spark on object storage, owned by the data-science group, used to train the delivery on-time model and to run ad-hoc analysis;
  • a cloud data warehouse — owned by the BI group, loaded nightly by a copy job from the lake plus two direct source extracts.

For the week of 1–7 June 2026 the CEO dashboard shows 87.0% on-time deliveries. The data-science on-time model's evaluation report, for the same week and the same fleet, shows 91.2%.

Neither team can explain the other's number. The COO has stopped quoting either one in the weekly operations review. An executive has asked, in writing, "which of our two data teams should we keep?"

docs.title: 2. Business context
docs.text:
Item Figure Deliveries in the disputed week 1,184,000 Contractual SLA threshold with the three largest B2B customers 90.0% on-time Driver incentive scheme under review, annualised SAR 4,000,000 Time the incentive decision has been frozen 1 month (and counting) SLA penalty exposure if the true figure is below 90% SAR 1,150,000 per quarter across three contracts Cost of the nightly warehouse copy job (compute + egress) SAR 46,000 / month

The 4.2-point gap is not academic. At 87.0% Naql is in breach of all three SLAs and owes penalties; at 91.2% it is compliant and the incentive scheme is justified. The same week of the same business is simultaneously a breach and a success, depending on which system you query. That is the two-tier problem stated in money.

docs.title: 3. Technical challenge
docs.text:
Two independently maintained pipelines compute the same business metric from the same underlying events and disagree. The divergence is not a bug in either system — each is internally consistent and each passes its own tests. It is a definitional divergence that has hardened into two codebases.

Three specific mechanisms are in play, and the teams must find all three from the evidence:

  1. Late-arriving proof-of-delivery events. The warehouse pipeline computes on-time at 02:00 for the previous calendar day and never revisits it. The lake pipeline recomputes a rolling 7-day window every run, so it absorbs POD events that arrive up to 72 hours late.
  2. Timezone handling. Source events are UTC. The warehouse load applies +03 at ingest and stores local timestamps; the lake stores UTC and converts at presentation. Deliveries between 21:00 and 24:00 UTC fall on different calendar days in the two systems.
  3. Cancellation semantics. The warehouse counts cancelled_by_customer deliveries in the denominator; the lake excludes them.

docs.title: 4. Constraints
docs.text:
• Neither system can be frozen. BI runs the daily operations review; the lake runs three production models.
  • The regulator (and the three B2B contracts) require a single auditable definition of on-time, with the ability to reproduce any historical figure on demand.
  • Arabic and English address fields (district_name_ar, district_name_en) must survive any consolidation byte-exact — a previous migration mangled Arabic to ???? and cost the firm a customer.
  • Migration budget: one quarter, two engineers.
  • No new licence spend approved.

docs.title: 5. Evidence pack
docs.text: Hand out all five pages at minute 4. Do not narrate them — let teams find the divergence themselves. Page 5 is the trap.

docs.title: P1 — Executive dashboard tile (warehouse), week 2026-06-01 → 2026-06-07
docs.text:
ON-TIME DELIVERY RATE                       Source: dw.fact_delivery_daily
                                            Refreshed: 2026-06-08 02:14 +03
        87.0%                               Deliveries: 1,184,003
        ▼ 1.4 pts vs prior week             On-time:    1,030,083
                                            SLA floor:  90.0%   ✖ BREACH

docs.title: P2 — Data-science model evaluation report (lake), same week
docs.text:
on_time_rate.......... 0.9118
n_deliveries.......... 1,127,455
n_on_time............. 1,027,993
window................ 2026-06-01T00:00:00Z .. 2026-06-07T23:59:59Z (UTC)
computed_at........... 2026-06-10T04:00:11Z
source................ s3://naql-lake/curated/deliveries/  (rolling 7d rebuild)

Note the row counts: 1,184,003 vs 1,127,455 — a difference of 56,548 deliveries. The teams that spot this in the first five minutes are the teams that solve the case.

docs.title: P3 — The two SQL definitions, side by side
docs.text:
Warehouse (dw_load_delivery_daily.sql, last modified 2023-11-02):

SELECT
  delivery_date,
  COUNT(*)                                              AS deliveries,
  SUM(CASE WHEN pod_ts <= promised_ts THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS on_time
FROM stg_delivery
WHERE delivery_date = DATEADD(day, -1, CURRENT_DATE)      -- yesterday, once, forever
GROUP BY delivery_date;
-- stg_delivery.pod_ts was written as CONVERT_TZ(src.pod_ts_utc,'UTC','Asia/Riyadh')
-- status filter: none

Lake (ontime_features.py, last modified 2026-04-19):

w = spark.read.format("delta").load("s3://naql-lake/curated/deliveries")
w = (w.filter(F.col("pod_ts_utc").between(start_utc, end_utc))
       .filter(~F.col("status").isin("cancelled_by_customer", "cancelled_by_merchant")))
rate = w.agg(F.avg((F.col("pod_ts_utc") <= F.col("promised_ts_utc")).cast("int"))).first()[0]
# rolling rebuild: the last 7 days are recomputed on every run

docs.title: P4 — Late POD arrival profile (from the lake's ingestion log)
docs.text:
Lag between physical delivery and POD event landing Share of deliveries < 1 hour 94.1% 1–6 hours 3.6% 6–24 hours 1.5% 24–72 hours 0.7% > 72 hours 0.1%

At 1,184,003 deliveries/week, the 2.3% arriving after 6 hours is 27,232 deliveries the warehouse's 02:00 job never sees for the day it belongs to. Their on-time rate is materially worse than the fleet average (they are late partly because something went wrong), which is why the warehouse number is not simply noisier — it is biased.

docs.title: P5 — Row-count reconciliation, prepared by an intern the day before the session
docs.text:
Filter applied Row count All delivery rows, week of 2026-06-01, UTC boundaries 1,127,455 All delivery rows, week of 2026-06-01, +03 boundaries 1,131,090 ... plus cancelled_by_customer and cancelled_by_merchant 1,187,638 Warehouse dw.fact_delivery_daily sum for the week 1,184,003

The residual 3,635 rows between the third line and the warehouse figure are the late PODs that arrived after each nightly job ran. Every part of the 4.2-point gap is explained by this table. Teams that build this table themselves have solved the case; do not hand them the interpretation.

docs.title: 6. Facilitation script (minute-by-minute)
docs.text: Min Activity Facilitator does Watch for 0–3 Frame. Read the scenario aloud. Put the two numbers on the board: 87.0% and 91.2%. Ask only: "Which one do we send to the regulator?" Do not answer. Let the silence sit. Someone will say "average them." Write it on the board. You will return to it in the debrief. 3–5 Distribute the evidence pack, one per table. State the deliverable and the clock. Circulate; make sure every table has all 5 pages. Tables that start reading P1 first and never reach P5. Nudge: "P5 was made by an intern. Is it useful?" 5–17 Round 1 — Find the gap. Tables work to enumerate every mechanism producing divergence. Visit each table once. Ask one question and leave: "You have three mechanisms — are you sure there isn't a fourth?" Teams that stop at timezone. Timezone is the smallest of the three effects (3,635 rows); late arrivals and the cancellation filter are much larger. 17–20 Fast round-robin. Each table names one mechanism, no repeats. Build the master list on the board. Enforce "no repeats" strictly — it forces later tables to find the subtle ones. Aim to have the board read: late arrivals · timezone · cancellation semantics · (bonus) no reconciliation ever run · (bonus) two owners of one definition. 20–33 Round 2 — Design the fix. Tables produce the flipchart deliverable: the one conformed definition, the layer it lives in, the three-step cutover, and the CFO evidence. Push hard on layer. If a table writes the definition into a BI tool's semantic layer, ask: "Who computes it for the model, then?" The most common wrong turn is "put the definition in the BI tool." That recreates the divergence with extra steps. 33–41 Present. Two tables present for 3 minutes each; the rest add deltas only. Pick one strong table and one that made an instructive mistake. Present the mistake second and repair it live. Keep to time. Cut the third presenter. 41–45 Debrief. Deliver §10. Close on §11 verbatim. Erase "average them" from the board deliberately, out loud. —

docs.title: 7. Discussion questions with model answers
docs.text:
Q1. Why does having two pipelines almost guarantee eventual divergence?

Model answer. Because a business definition is not a constant — it is a series of decisions ("do cancellations count?", "how late is too late?", "which day does a 23:40 UTC delivery belong to?"), and each pipeline makes those decisions independently, at a different time, under a different owner, in response to a different request. Divergence is not caused by a defect; it is caused by two independent decision-making processes applied to the same question. The rate of divergence is the rate at which the business changes its mind, which is never zero. A second pipeline is therefore not a redundancy — it is a guarantee of eventual disagreement, with the disagreement discovered at the worst possible moment (an SLA dispute, an audit, a board meeting).

Push further: ask whether tests would have prevented it. They would not — each pipeline passes its own tests. Only a reconciliation between the two, run continuously, would have caught it, and nobody owns that because it belongs to neither team.

Q2. Which of the four two-tier costs — duplication, staleness, skew, governance — is most expensive here, and why?

Model answer. Skew, by a wide margin, and the money proves it: the SAR 4M incentive decision and SAR 1.15M/quarter of SLA exposure both hinge on which number is true. Duplication costs SAR 46k/month for the copy job (real, but an order of magnitude smaller). Staleness costs a day of decision latency (annoying, survivable). Governance is the latent worst: Naql cannot presently answer "what was our on-time rate on 3 June, and prove it" for a regulator, which is an unbounded liability — but it has not yet been called.

The pedagogical point: the cheap-to-measure cost (duplication, SAR 46k) is the one organisations optimise, and the expensive one (skew) is the one they discover in a crisis. Accept "governance" as an answer if the team argues the unbounded-liability case well.

Q3. How would you prove the consolidated number is correct to a sceptical CFO?

Model answer. Not by asserting it. By producing three artefacts:

  1. A reconciliation report that starts from each of the two legacy numbers and walks, line by line, to the new one — exactly the shape of evidence page P5, but signed and repeatable. 87.0% → +2.6 pts (late PODs now absorbed) → +1.9 pts (cancellations excluded per contract wording) → −0.3 pts (UTC day boundary) → 91.2%. A CFO does not need to understand Spark; a CFO needs to see that every point of the gap is accounted for and each step cites the contract clause or engineering rule that justifies it.
  2. One reviewed definition in one place — silver.deliveries plus a single is_on_time derivation, code-reviewed, with the contract clause quoted in the model's description, versioned in git.
  3. Reproducibility on demand — time travel to the version of the table as of any filing date (this foreshadows M4 and CS-04), so that "what did we report on 8 June and why" is a query, not an archaeology project.

Add the human step: run both old pipelines and the new one in parallel for four weeks and publish the daily delta before cutover. Trust is rebuilt by a boring, unbroken sequence of matching numbers, not by a convincing architecture diagram.

Q4. What would you keep the warehouse for, if anything, after consolidation?

Model answer. Legitimate residual reasons: (a) an existing BI tool with a deep licence commitment and hundreds of built reports, where the migration cost exceeds the benefit this quarter; (b) very high-concurrency, low-latency serving of a small curated mart where a specialised engine genuinely outperforms; (c) a regulatory requirement for a specific certified platform.

The illegitimate reason — and the one Naql actually has — is "the BI team is used to it." The test to apply: does anything downstream of the warehouse compute a business definition, or does it only render one computed upstream? If it computes, the two-tier problem is intact and the divergence will return. If it only renders — a thin, scheduled, column-for-column copy of gold.fact_trip-equivalent marts with no logic — the warehouse is a cache, and caches are fine. Make teams state the cache invariant: no transformation, no filter, no CASE statement in the copy job. Anything else is a second pipeline wearing a disguise.

Q5 (reserve, use if a table finishes early). The lake team's number is the more correct one. Should the data-science team therefore own the consolidated definition?

Model answer. No — and this is the trap. Being right this time is not the same as being the right owner. The definition of "on-time" is a commercial definition, written in a customer contract; its owner is the commercial/operations function, with engineering as the implementer and both BI and DS as consumers. Ownership by either consumer reproduces the original failure with a different winner. The architecture must make the definition ownable by a non-engineer: one named table, one named column, one description field quoting the contract clause, one review process.

docs.title: 8. Solution approach
docs.text:
Target state. A single Lakehouse; both consumers read the same conformed layer.

Sources ──► bronze.deliveries        (immutable, append-only, _ingested_at/_source_file/_batch_id)
   POD     bronze.pod_events          raw, no logic, nothing dropped, Arabic preserved byte-exact
   WMS         │
               ▼
          silver.deliveries          ONE conformed table. UTC storage. ONE is_on_time rule.
               │                     3-day lookback MERGE on delivery_id absorbs late PODs.
               ▼
          gold.delivery_daily  ──┬──► BI dashboard   (renders; computes nothing)
                                 └──► on-time model  (trains; computes nothing)

Migration sequence (the deliverable teams should produce).

  1. Land both feeds into bronze, unchanged. Do not fix anything here. This is the step that makes every later step provable, because bronze is what both legacy pipelines also read from. Arabic fields land as-is; a byte-comparison test against source is part of the definition of done.
  2. Write one silver.deliveries with one reviewed rule set. UTC storage; is_on_time = pod_ts_utc <= promised_ts_utc; exclusion of cancelled_by_customer and cancelled_by_merchant (justified by quoting the contract clause in the model description); incremental MERGE on delivery_id with a 3-day lookback so the 2.3% of late PODs land in the day they belong to.
  3. Run the reconciliation in parallel for four weeks. Publish the daily three-way delta (warehouse, lake, silver). Expect the silver number to sit at ~91.2% and the deltas to be stable and explainable. Do not cut over on a good week; cut over on four boring weeks.
  4. Repoint both consumers at gold. The dashboard reads gold.delivery_daily. The model reads the same table. Neither contains a CASE WHEN.
  5. Retire the copy job. Only after step 4 has run for two weeks. Save the SAR 46k/month and, more importantly, remove the second decision-making process.
  6. Institutionalise. Every regulatory or contractual filing pins the table version used (foreshadow M4). A reconciliation test runs nightly and pages someone if BI and model inputs ever differ by more than zero.

Why the ordering matters. Teams often want to start at step 2. Starting at step 1 is what makes step 3 possible — you cannot reconcile three numbers if only two of them are derived from a common, immutable record.

docs.title: 9. What good looks like vs common wrong turns
docs.text: What good looks like Common wrong turn Finds all three divergence mechanisms and quantifies each against P5 Finds timezone, declares victory. Timezone is 3,635 rows of a 56,548-row gap Puts the definition in silver and treats BI + model as equal downstream consumers Puts the definition in the BI semantic layer, leaving the model to re-implement it — the original bug, relocated Proposes a parallel-run reconciliation before cutover Proposes a big-bang cutover with a "validation script" run once Names a business owner for the definition, not an engineering owner Assigns ownership to whichever team was right this time Keeps the warehouse only as a logic-free cache, with the cache invariant written down Keeps the warehouse "for performance" with no invariant, and the copy job quietly regrows logic Treats immutable bronze as the precondition for provability Fixes data on the way into bronze, destroying the ability to reconcile against the legacy numbers States what happens to the model when the definition changes (retrain, re-baseline) Discusses only the dashboard; forgets the model was trained on the other definition and its labels are now stale Handles Arabic explicitly (byte-exact test in the definition of done) Never mentions the Arabic constraint, which is how the previous migration failed Averages nothing "Report 89% while we investigate"

docs.title: 10. Debrief (4 minutes)
docs.text:
Deliver these four beats in order.

  1. Nothing was broken. Point at P3. Both queries are correct implementations of a defensible definition. Every test in both systems is green. The failure is architectural, not defective — which is why no amount of testing inside either pipeline would have found it.
  2. The gap was entirely explainable, and nobody had explained it. P5 took an intern one afternoon. It had never been run in six years, because reconciliation between two platforms belongs to neither platform's owner. Work that belongs to no one does not get done.
  3. This is the two-tier problem, and it is why the Lakehouse exists. Not because object storage is cheap or because open formats are pleasant — but because a single copy of conformed data with a single place to encode a business rule is the only architecture in which a company can answer "what is our on-time rate" with one number.
  4. Connect to Masar and to the course question. For the next five days you build one Lakehouse for Masar, in which gold.fact_trip serves BI and gold.eta_features serves AI, and both descend from one silver.trips. Ask the room the unifying question with this case's specifics: "What happens to Masar's ETA model if the definition of a completed trip diverges between BI and the feature pipeline?" Answer: the model trains on labels the business does not recognise, and no dashboard will ever show it.

Then erase "average them" from the board, out loud, and say why: averaging two numbers you cannot explain produces a third number you cannot explain.

docs.title: 11. The one sentence participants should leave with
docs.text: Two pipelines computing the same business metric is not redundancy — it is a guarantee of eventual disagreement, discovered at the worst possible moment; the Lakehouse exists so that a definition lives in exactly one place and every consumer reads it, rather than recomputing it.

docs.title: CS-02 — The Surprise Cloud Bill at "Tabadul" Analytics
docs.text: Field Value Case ID CS-02 Module M2 — Compute–Storage Separation and Cloud Economics Day / Hour Day 1 · Hour 6 (after the cost-model walkthrough, before or immediately after LAB-02) Duration 50 minutes Format Investigation (cost autopsy) with a written recommendation Group size 3–4 per team; each team is "the FinOps tiger team" Deliverable A one-page memo to the CFO: the four largest cost drivers ranked by SAR, the fix for each, the SAR/month saved, the engineering days required, and the guardrail that stops recurrence Materials Evidence pack §5 printed per team (6 pages); calculators or laptops; blank memo template (§8.4) Facilitator prep 15 min. Work the arithmetic in §7 yourself once — participants will challenge your numbers and you must be able to derive them live

docs.title: 1. Scenario
docs.text:
"Tabadul" (تبادل) is the analytics unit of a Saudi holding company. In April 2026 it completed a migration from an on-premises appliance warehouse to a cloud Lakehouse. The business case, approved by the board, promised 40% cost savings within two quarters.

The first full month on the new platform is May 2026. The bill arrived on 3 June. It is 20% higher than the on-premises run-rate it replaced.

The CFO has scheduled a review for Thursday. The platform lead has asked your team to find out what happened and what to do about it, in that order.

docs.title: 2. Business context
docs.text:
Item Figure On-premises run-rate being replaced (amortised appliance + support + DC) SAR 385,000 / month Business case target after migration SAR 231,000 / month (−40%) Actual May 2026 cloud bill SAR 462,000 / month (+20% vs on-prem, +100% vs target) Gap to business case SAR 231,000 / month BI dashboards in production 40, refreshing every 15 minutes, 06:00–22:00 +03 Nightly ML feature build 1 job, ~90 minutes Data growth 8% / month Analyst headcount served 55 Deadline to show savings 60 days

Two things are true simultaneously and teams must hold both: the migration was not a mistake, and the current bill is not defensible. Decoupling compute from storage bought elasticity — the option to pay only for what you use. Tabadul exercised none of it.

docs.title: 3. Technical challenge
docs.text:
The platform is architecturally correct and economically catastrophic. Specifically:

  • The gold marts are one unpartitioned Delta table per subject area, written by an append job that produces thousands of small files and has never been compacted. Every dashboard query full-scans.
  • Autoscaling is enabled, minimum worker count is set to the peak requirement, and idle termination is disabled because an engineer disabled it in March to stop a demo cluster dying mid-presentation.
  • All jobs run on on-demand instances. The nightly feature build is fully restartable and idempotent — a textbook spot workload — and pays on-demand rates.
  • There is no cost attribution: no tags, no per-dashboard or per-team chargeback. Nobody can name the most expensive dashboard.

docs.title: 4. Constraints
docs.text:
• Dashboard refresh cadence cannot change. The business has refused; treat it as fixed. (This is deliberate: it removes the easy answer and forces teams to attack cost-per-query instead of query count.)
  • Savings must be demonstrable within 60 days — so fixes with a long lead time score poorly.
  • Data volume grows 8% / month; any fix that does not scale is a deferral, not a solution.
  • No reduction in analyst headcount or dashboard count.
  • The team has two engineers, part-time: budget roughly 12 engineering days for the whole programme.

docs.title: P1 — May 2026 bill, decomposed
docs.text:
Line item SAR / month Share Interactive/BI compute (the dashboard cluster) 268,000 58.0% Job compute (nightly feature build + 6 small ETL jobs) 121,000 26.2% Object storage (data at rest, 340 TB) 27,000 5.8% Storage API requests (GET/LIST) 31,000 6.7% Egress + networking 9,000 1.9% Other (logging, metastore, monitoring) 6,000 1.3% Total 462,000 100%

The headline for the debrief: storage is 5.8% of the bill. Every instinct from the on-premises era says "data is expensive." In a decoupled architecture, data at rest is nearly free and reading it badly is what costs money.

docs.title: P2 — Dashboard cluster utilisation, one representative week (hours)
docs.text:
Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat Sun Cluster running (h) 24 24 24 24 24 24 24 Hours with ≥1 query 16 16 16 15 7 6 16 Hours fully idle 8 8 8 9 17 18 8

Idle hours per week: 76 of 168 = 45.2%. Applied to the interactive line: 268,000 × 0.452 ≈ SAR 121,000 / month spent on a cluster with zero queries running.

Note the Friday/Saturday shape — the Saudi weekend. A naive "9-to-5 weekday" schedule imported from a foreign template would be wrong here; the Sunday column is a full working day.

docs.title: P3 — Query plan for the single most-run dashboard query (explain("formatted"), abridged)
docs.text:
== Physical Plan ==
* HashAggregate (5)
  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(city#12, hour_ts#19, 200)
     +- * HashAggregate (3)
        +- * Project [city#12, hour_ts#19, fare_sar#21]
           +- * ColumnarToRow (1)
              +- FileScan parquet gold.trip_revenue_hourly[
                   trip_id#10, rider_id#11, city#12, pickup_zone_id#13, dropoff_zone_id#14,
                   pickup_ts#15, dropoff_ts#16, distance_km#17, duration_min#18, hour_ts#19,
                   surge_multiplier#20, fare_sar#21, payment_type#22, status#23]
                 Batched: true
                 DataFilters: []
                 PartitionFilters: []
                 PushedFilters: []
                 ReadSchema: struct<trip_id:string,rider_id:string,city:string, ... 11 more fields>
                 Location: InMemoryFileIndex(1 path)
                 numFiles: 41,882
                 sizeInBytes: 96.4 GB

Read the four decisive lines aloud in the debrief: PartitionFilters: [], PushedFilters: [], numFiles: 41,882, sizeInBytes: 96.4 GB. The query needs three columns and returns 720 rows. It reads fourteen columns and 96.4 GB, in 41,882 file opens.

docs.title: P4 — Dashboard query volume
docs.text:
Value Dashboards 40 Refresh interval 15 min Serving window 06:00–22:00 +03 = 16 h/day Refreshes per dashboard per day 64 Queries per dashboard refresh (avg tiles) 6 Queries / day 15,360 Queries / month (30 d) 460,800 Mean bytes scanned per query 74 GB Bytes scanned / month ≈ 34 PB

34 petabytes scanned per month to render 40 dashboards from 340 TB of data. Each byte is read, on average, 100 times a month.

docs.title: P5 — Cluster configuration (as deployed)
docs.text:
name: bi-interactive
node_type: r5.4xlarge          # 16 vCPU, 128 GB
autoscale:
  min_workers: 12              # set to peak, "so dashboards are never slow"
  max_workers: 12

docs.title: 6. Facilitation script (minute-by-minute)
docs.text: Min Activity Facilitator does Watch for 0–3 Frame. "The migration promised 40% savings. Month one is 20% over the old bill. The CFO meets you Thursday. What do you tell her?" Deliberately do not allow an answer yet. Write SAR 385k → 462k (target 231k) on the board and leave it there all session. Teams that immediately say "the migration failed." Note who; you will use them in the debrief. 3–6 Distribute the pack. State the memo deliverable and the 12-engineering-day budget. Emphasise the budget aloud — it is what turns this from a list of ideas into a ranked plan. — 6–14 Round 1 — Where does the money go? Teams decompose P1 and must produce a SAR figure for each of: idle compute, over-scanning, on-demand premium, small-file overhead. Circulate. To any team without a number: "Give me a number. Wrong is fine; absent is not." Teams that discuss without arithmetic. FinOps is arithmetic. 14–17 Anchor round. Each team calls out its estimate for idle compute only. Write all estimates on the board. Do not correct yet. Spread of estimates is itself the lesson: nobody at Tabadul had a number either. Estimates should cluster near SAR 120k. 17–33 Round 2 — Build the memo. Rank the four drivers, name a fix each, estimate SAR saved and days spent, and specify one guardrail. Push on savings per engineering day — that is the ranking criterion, not absolute savings. Ask each team: "If you only get 3 of your 12 days, which fix do you do?" Teams that put "migrate back on-prem" in the memo. Take it seriously for 30 seconds, then price it. 33–43 CFO panel. You play the CFO. Two teams present their memo in 3 minutes. Interrupt with §7 Q3-style challenges. Be a sceptical but fair CFO: "You're telling me the same team that promised 40% now promises 55%. Why should I believe the second number?" Teams that promise savings without a measurement plan. That is the exact failure that got Tabadul here. 43–50 Debrief. §10. Show the reference answer table in §8.2. Close on §11. Reveal that the four fixes total ~SAR 267k/month for ~9 engineering days, i.e. the business case was achievable all along. —

docs.title: 7. Discussion questions with model answers
docs.text:
Q1. Why did decoupling alone not deliver savings?

Model answer. Because decoupling does not reduce cost — it converts cost from fixed to variable and hands you the controls. On the appliance, storage and compute were fused and pre-paid: reading a table badly was already paid for, so nobody optimised it. In the cloud, every bad read is a fresh invoice line. Tabadul migrated the architecture and kept the appliance-era operating habits: a permanently-on cluster sized for peak (the appliance was always on and sized for peak, and that was correct there), unpartitioned tables (the appliance's own indexes hid this), and no attribution (there was nothing to attribute — the appliance was one number).

The precise formulation to write on the board: elasticity is an option, and an unexercised option has a cost but no benefit. Tabadul is paying the premium for elasticity (cloud unit prices exceed amortised appliance unit prices) while consuming a fixed-capacity workload profile. That is the worst square of the matrix, and it is exactly where naive migrations land.

Q2. Which fix yields the most savings per engineering hour — compaction, caching, or idle-termination?

Model answer. Rank by SAR saved ÷ engineering days:

Fix SAR/month saved Eng. days SAR per eng. day Idle termination + right-sized min_workers + weekend schedule ~121,000 0.5 242,000 Spot for the nightly feature build ~42,000 0.5 84,000 OPTIMIZE + ZORDER + partitioning of the four gold marts ~76,000 3 25,300 Result caching / hot-mart materialisation for BI ~28,000 5 5,600

Idle termination wins by two orders of magnitude and it is a configuration change: autotermination_minutes: 20, min_workers: 3, plus a schedule that respects the Saudi weekend. It is also the least intellectually interesting fix, which is precisely why engineers under-propose it and why you must make the class rank by ratio rather than by absolute saving.

Compaction is second on absolute savings and third on ratio, but it is the only fix that scales with the 8%/month growth, so it must not be dropped — frame it as "do the config change this week, the layout change this month."

Caching is last: highest effort, most new moving parts, and it optimises a cost that partitioning has already largely removed. A team that proposes caching first has optimised the interesting problem rather than the expensive one.

Q3. How would you present month-two numbers to rebuild leadership trust?

Model answer. Trust was destroyed by a single unfalsifiable promise ("40% savings"). It is rebuilt by many small falsifiable ones. The memo must contain:

  • A baseline stated before the fix, in the same units as the bill (SAR/month by line item), so the claim can be checked against the invoice rather than against a dashboard the team controls.
  • Per-fix attribution: after tagging, the CFO sees bi-interactive fall from 268k to 147k as a line item, not a slide. Attribution is the deliverable; savings is the consequence.
  • A committed cadence: a weekly one-page cost report with forecast vs actual, published whether the news is good or bad. Publishing a bad week on time buys more credibility than a good week published on request.
  • Unit economics, not totals: SAR per dashboard-refresh and SAR per TB scanned. Totals will rise again with 8%/month growth and a growing business should cost more; unit cost falling while totals rise is the honest story, and it survives growth.
  • An explicit statement of what would falsify the plan and what happens then.

Q4. What guardrail prevents this recurring as data grows 8%/month?

Model answer. Guardrails must be automatic and preventive, not a policy document. Four, in order of value:

  1. Mandatory cost tags enforced at cluster/job creation — an untagged resource cannot be created. Without attribution, no other guardrail can be targeted.
  2. A budget alert with a unit-cost trigger, not only a total — page when SAR per TB scanned rises, because the total is supposed to rise at 8%/month and a total-only alert will be either permanently firing or permanently muted.
  3. OPTIMIZE/VACUUM as scheduled DAG tasks, not a runbook step (this is exactly what LAB-07 builds — say so). Small-file decay is not an event, it is a rate; the counter-measure must also be a rate.
  4. Idle termination and bounded autoscale as policy defaults in the cluster template, so that the only way to get an always-on cluster is an explicit, reviewed exception with a name attached to it.

Note the 8% figure explicitly: at 8%/month, volume doubles in 9 months. A one-off cleanup delivers a saving that is fully consumed within a year. Only the scheduled, automatic fixes survive.

Q5 (reserve). Should Tabadul migrate back to the appliance?

Model answer. Price it, do not dismiss it. Migrating back costs the migration budget again (sunk cost already spent, plus new spend), reinstates a fixed peak-sized capital commitment against a workload growing 8%/month (the appliance must be sized for month 24, and paid for from month 1), and forfeits the elasticity option permanently. Meanwhile the four fixes above reach ~SAR 195,000/month for ~9 engineering days — below the business-case target of 231k. The correct answer is that the cloud architecture is fine and the operating model is not, and operating models are cheap to change.

docs.title: 8.1 The four fixes, in execution order
docs.text:
Week 1 — configuration (0.5 days, ~SAR 121,000/month). 

autotermination_minutes: 20     # was 0
autoscale: {min_workers: 3, max_workers: 12}   # was min=max=12
# plus: scheduled scale-to-zero outside 06:00-22:00 +03, with Friday/Saturday reduced
Right-sizing the floor and terminating on idle recovers essentially all of the 45.2% idle. Keep max at 12 so peak behaviour is unchanged — the business constraint (refresh cadence, dashboard responsiveness) is respected.

Week 1 — spot for the nightly build (0.5 days, ~SAR 42,000/month). The feature build is idempotent and restartable, which is the only precondition for spot. State this explicitly to the class: idempotency is a cost lever, not just a correctness property. It is the same design decision M3, M4 and M7 keep making, cashed out in SAR.

Weeks 2–3 — layout (3 days, ~SAR 76,000/month, and it scales). 

-- one-off remediation
OPTIMIZE gold.trip_revenue_hourly ZORDER BY (city, hour_ts);
OPTIMIZE gold.fact_trip           ZORDER BY (city, pickup_ts);
-- and, going forward, partition on the two universal dashboard filters
ALTER TABLE gold.fact_trip SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite = true,
  delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact   = true
);
Plus partitioning the marts by city and date, and rewriting the dashboard queries to select only the columns they use. Expected effect on P3's query: numFiles 41,882 → ~300; bytes scanned 74 GB → ~4 GB; PartitionFilters and PushedFilters populated.

Week 4+ — attribution and guardrails (2 days, savings enabling). Tags on every cluster and job; a weekly unit-cost report; OPTIMIZE/VACUUM promoted to DAG tasks; cluster-policy defaults.

docs.title: 9. What good looks like vs common wrong turns
docs.text: What good looks like Common wrong turn Every claim carries a SAR figure derived from the pack Qualitative list of "best practices" with no arithmetic Ranks fixes by savings per engineering day Ranks by absolute savings, so compaction beats a 30-minute config change Notices storage is only 5.8% and stops trying to delete data Proposes an aggressive retention cut, saving ~SAR 8k and destroying the audit trail Ties spot eligibility to the job being idempotent Proposes spot for the interactive BI cluster, then discovers dashboards die mid-refresh Reads P2's Friday/Saturday columns and schedules to the Saudi week Imports a Mon–Fri schedule and turns off the cluster on Sunday, a full working day Proposes attribution first because nothing else can be targeted without it Leaves tagging as a "phase 3 nice-to-have" Distinguishes total cost (which must rise with growth) from unit cost (which must fall) Promises the total bill will fall forever at 8%/month growth Respects the fixed refresh cadence and attacks cost-per-query Recommends "refresh hourly instead of every 15 minutes" — the one thing the business excluded Says out loud that the architecture is fine and the operating model is not Concludes the migration was a mistake

docs.title: 10. Debrief (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Read P1 line 3 aloud: storage is 5.8%. In the appliance era, data volume was the cost. In a decoupled architecture, data at rest is nearly free and reading it badly is the entire bill. Every participant carries the old intuition; this line is where it dies.
  2. Read P3's four lines aloud. PartitionFilters: [], PushedFilters: [], numFiles: 41,882, 96.4 GB scanned to return 720 rows. Then say: nobody wrote a bad query. They wrote a reasonable query against a badly laid-out table. Physical layout is a cost control, and it is set by the writer, not the reader.
  3. The ratio table (§7 Q2). The most valuable fix in the case is a two-line YAML change worth SAR 242,000 per engineering day, and it is the one every engineer proposes last. Name the bias: we optimise the interesting problem, not the expensive one.
  4. Elasticity is an option. Tabadul paid the premium and never exercised it. Say the sentence: you do not save money by moving to the cloud; you gain the ability to stop paying for what you are not using, and you must then actually stop.
  5. Bridge to LAB-02 and to the course question. In the lab, participants will run the naive / pruned / partition-filtered query on Masar's own silver.trips and watch ReadSchema and bytes-scanned collapse. Then ask: "What happens to Masar's AI system if the feature build's cost is not controlled?" Answer: it gets run less often. Feature freshness is a budget decision before it is an engineering one, and a stale feature is a degraded model — which is exactly the failure CS-11 will show you on Day 5.

docs.title: 11. The one sentence participants should leave with
docs.text: Separating compute from storage does not make anything cheaper; it converts a fixed bill into a variable one and hands you the controls — and until you set idle termination, lay the data out for the queries you actually run, and attribute every riyal to something a person owns, you are paying a premium for an elasticity you never exercise.

docs.title: CS-03 — The Silent Undercount at "Wusool" Mobility
docs.text: Field Value Case ID CS-03 Module M3 — ETL vs ELT and the Transformation Layer Day / Hour Day 2 · Hour 4 (immediately after LAB-03's incremental MERGE task) Duration 45 minutes Format Investigation → design exercise Group size 3–4 per team Deliverable (a) The exact SQL/dbt config that fixes the daily model; (b) a backfill runbook for six months that is safe to run twice; (c) the two tests that would have caught this in week one, written as dbt test YAML Materials Evidence pack §5 per team (5 pages); the Masar late_trips fixture open on the projector (data/fixtures/late_trips/trips_late_2026-06-02.csv, 126 rows / 120 new trip_id) Facilitator prep 10 min. Have data/fixtures/late_trips/README.md and the LAB-03 solution's incremental model open in tabs — you will demo the fix live in the debrief

docs.title: 1. Scenario
docs.text:
"Wusool" (وصول) is a Saudi mobility operator. Every morning at 06:00 a pipeline computes the previous day's completed trips per driver, and that figure pays the driver incentive.

For four months, drivers have complained the count is low. Each complaint is investigated individually; each time, finance re-runs the query and gets the same number, and the complaint is closed as unfounded. A driver representative has now escalated to a labour-relations review, with a sample of 40 drivers who each have app screenshots showing more completed trips than they were paid for.

Finance is confident. The count is reproducible. The query is correct.

The count is also wrong.

docs.title: 2. Business context
docs.text:
Item Figure Incentive pool paid from the daily completed-trip count SAR 2,000,000 / month Period under review 6 months Estimated systematic undercount (to be derived by the teams) ~1.9% of completed trips Estimated underpayment over 6 months ≈ SAR 228,000 Drivers in the escalated sample 40 Drivers affected at all (any month) ~2,900 of 3,450 Second-order exposure The same daily table is the label source for the zone demand-forecasting model

The financial exposure is recoverable — Wusool can pay the difference. The harder exposures are the two that money does not fix: a labour-relations finding of systematic underpayment, and a demand model trained for six months on labels that are biased, not merely noisy.

docs.title: 3. Technical challenge
docs.text:
The daily model reads:

WHERE trip_date = current_date() - INTERVAL 1 DAY

and materialises with INSERT INTO ... SELECT. It runs once per day, at 06:00 +03, and never revisits a day it has already written.

Trips whose payment settles after midnight — airport runs, long inter-city trips, trips where the driver's device was offline, and every trip flowing through the delayed settlement path — land in bronze.trips after the 06:00 job for the day they belong to has already run. They are then never counted, because tomorrow's run filters on tomorrow's date.

Nothing errors. The row exists in bronze. It simply never enters the aggregate. The query is a correct implementation of a wrong assumption: that a day's data is complete at the moment you choose to look at it.

docs.title: 4. Constraints
docs.text:
• Source cannot be re-ingested. The upstream vendor retains 14 days; bronze is the only copy of anything older. (Frame this as a good property: immutable bronze is the reason the six-month correction is possible at all.)
  • Six months of history must be corrected and every corrected figure must be traceable back to raw for the labour review.
  • The fix must be auditable: a reviewer with no Spark knowledge must be able to follow the chain from a driver's payment to a trip_id in bronze.trips.
  • The backfill will be run by an on-call engineer, possibly twice, possibly interrupted. It must be safe under both.
  • The correction must not disturb the current daily run.

docs.title: P1 — Driver complaint, verbatim (translated)
docs.text:
"On Thursday 4 June I completed 19 trips. The app shows 19. The incentive statement shows 17. On Sunday I completed 22, the statement shows 22. It is not every day. It is the busy days."

"It is not every day. It is the busy days." — this single observation is the case. Late settlement correlates with load; the undercount is therefore not uniform, which is what makes it both hard to spot in aggregate and legally serious.

docs.title: P2 — The model as written (models/marts/driver_daily_trips.sql)
docs.text:
{{ config(materialized='incremental') }}

SELECT
    trip_date,
    driver_id,
    COUNT(*) AS completed_trips,
    SUM(fare_sar) AS gross_fare_sar
FROM {{ ref('silver_trips') }}
WHERE status = 'completed'
  AND trip_date = current_date() - INTERVAL 1 DAY   -- <<<< the bug
GROUP BY trip_date, driver_id

There is no unique_key. There is no incremental_strategy. is_incremental() is never called. The incremental materialisation is therefore an append, and re-running it duplicates rows — which is why nobody re-runs it, which is why nobody ever noticed the late trips.

docs.title: P3 — Ingestion lag distribution for bronze.trips (30-day sample, from _ingested_at minus dropoff_ts)
docs.text:
Lag from trip completion to landing in bronze.trips Share of completed trips < 1 hour 91.4% 1–6 hours 6.7% 6–24 hours (still lands before the 06:00 job for its own day) 1.2% 24–48 hours (lands AFTER its day's job has run) 1.6% 48–72 hours 0.3% > 72 hours 0.02%

1.9% of completed trips land after their day's aggregate was written and are never counted. Cross-check the arithmetic with the class: SAR 2,000,000 × 1.9% × 6 months ≈ SAR 228,000.

docs.title: P4 — Reconciliation, one day, run today for 4 June 2026
docs.text:
-- what the incentive was paid from
SELECT SUM(completed_trips) FROM gold.driver_daily WHERE trip_date = '2026-06-04';
-- 6,681

-- what bronze actually holds for that day, as of now
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bronze.trips
WHERE status='completed' AND DATE(dropoff_ts) = '2026-06-04';
-- 6,809

-- difference: 128 completed trips, 1.88%

And the smoking gun — the same query grouped by landing time:

SELECT DATE(_ingested_at) AS landed_on, COUNT(*)
FROM bronze.trips
WHERE status='completed' AND DATE(dropoff_ts)='2026-06-04'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

landed_on   | count
2026-06-04  |  6,203
2026-06-05  |    478      <- 6,681 counted by the 06:00 job on 06-05
2026-06-06  |    112      <- never counted
2026-06-07  |     16      <- never counted

docs.title: P5 — The Masar fixture, for the live drill
docs.text:
data/fixtures/late_trips/trips_late_2026-06-02.csv — 126 rows, 120 of them new trip_id values for 2026-06-02, plus 6 rows that duplicate trip_ids already present in data/raw/trips_2026-06-02.csv.

That fixture is Wusool's bug in miniature, and it is the fixture LAB-03 already made participants handle. The 120 new rows are the undercount. The 6 duplicates are the reason the fix must be a MERGE and not a re-insert — a lookback window that re-reads three days and appends would double-count every trip in those three days. State this explicitly: the naive fix for the undercount creates an overcount.

docs.title: 6. Facilitation script (minute-by-minute)
docs.text: Min Activity Facilitator does Watch for 0–3 Frame. Read P1 aloud, including the last sentence. Ask: "Finance re-ran the query and got the same number. Does that make the number right?" Write "reproducible ≠ correct" on the board. Leave it up. The room will split. Good. 3–5 Distribute the pack; state the three deliverables. — — 5–14 Round 1 — Find it. Teams locate the mechanism from P2–P4. Circulate silently for the first 4 minutes. Then to any stuck team: "P4 has two queries. Why did I give you the second one?" Most teams find it in 6–8 minutes. If a team finds it in 2, give them the extension in §7 Q5 immediately. 14–17 Board the mechanism. One team explains; the rest confirm or correct. Draw the timeline: trip completes 23:40 Thu → lands 02:10 Sat → Friday's 06:00 job already ran → nothing ever looks again. Teams that describe it as "a timezone bug." It is not; it is a completeness bug. Correct this firmly — the distinction matters for the fix. 17–32 Round 2 — Design the fix. All three deliverables. Emphasise deliverable (b): safe to run twice. Hand out P5 physically at minute 20, mid-round: "here is your test fixture — 126 rows, 120 new, 6 duplicates." Watch teams that had proposed a lookback + append visibly rewrite. The 6 duplicates are the pedagogical payload. Do not reveal them before minute 20. 32–40 Present & stress-test. Each team hands its runbook to another team, which tries to break it: "I ran it, it failed at hour 3, I ran it again from the start." Score survival, not elegance. A runbook that survives a double-run wins. Teams that add "check whether it already ran" as a manual step — that is a human idempotency guarantee, i.e. none. 40–45 Debrief + live demo. Run the LAB-03 solution's incremental model twice with the fixture landed in between; show MERGE counts 120 inserted / 6 updated, then 0 / 0. Close on §11. The second run showing zeros is the whole module in one screen. —

docs.title: 7. Discussion questions with model answers
docs.text:
Q1. Why did the original filter feel correct yet undercount?

Model answer. Because it encodes an assumption that is invisible until stated: "a day's data is complete by the time I process it." In batch systems fed by well-behaved sources, that assumption holds often enough to survive review. It fails whenever the arrival time of a fact is decoupled from the occurrence time of the fact — which is always true in mobility, payments, IoT and anything involving a device that can be offline.

The bug is the confusion of two different timestamps that both look like "when": - event time (dropoff_ts) — when the trip finished; a property of the world; - processing/arrival time (_ingested_at) — when we learned about it; a property of our infrastructure.

The query filtered on event time but the job schedule implicitly filtered on arrival time, and the intersection of the two silently dropped everything that arrived late. Once a day is written, the pipeline has no mechanism to ever revisit it — there is no reopening of a closed period.

Say the general form: a filter on event time combined with a single-pass schedule is a silent completeness bug in every batch pipeline that has ever been written.

Q2. How does idempotency make the six-month backfill safe to run (even twice)?

Model answer. Idempotency means f(f(x)) = f(x): applying the operation twice leaves the same state as applying it once. Concretely, replace INSERT INTO with a MERGE keyed on the natural grain:

{{ config(
     materialized='incremental',
     incremental_strategy='merge',
     unique_key=['trip_date','driver_id']
) }}

Now a re-run overwrites the affected (trip_date, driver_id) rows rather than adding to them. The consequences are all operational, and they are what actually matter at 03:00:

  • The on-call engineer does not need to know whether the previous attempt succeeded, partially succeeded, or died between the write and the log line. They just run it again.
  • The backfill can be chunked by month and each chunk retried independently, with no coordination and no state file.
  • A failure halfway through leaves a partially correct table rather than a corrupted one, and completing the run repairs it.
  • The same code path serves the daily run and the six-month backfill, so the backfill is executing exactly the logic that will run tomorrow — which is what makes the corrected figures defensible to the labour review.

Contrast this with a non-idempotent backfill: it requires a runbook step that says "check whether this month already ran," i.e. it requires a human to hold correctness in their head at 03:00 during an incident. That is not a guarantee; that is a hope.

Q3. What downstream AI harm did the label skew cause, and how would you detect it?

Model answer. This is the question that connects M3 to the whole course, and it is worth over-running on.

The daily completed-trip table feeds the zone demand-forecasting model's labels. The undercount is not random — P1's driver said it: "it is the busy days." Late settlement correlates with load, with airport and inter-city trips, with peak hours, and with poor connectivity. So the model has been trained for six months on labels that are systematically low exactly where demand is highest.

The consequence is not "the model is slightly noisier." It is that the model has learned a flattened demand curve: it under-predicts peaks. Downstream, that under-allocates drivers precisely at the peaks, which increases rider wait times and cancellations at peak — which then reduces completed trips at peak in the next period, which confirms the model's under-prediction. The bias is self-reinforcing through the dispatch feedback loop. Retraining on more of the same data makes it worse, not better.

Detection, in the order they would fire: 1. Reconciliation between gold.driver_daily and a fresh recount from bronze.trips for a closed period — the P4 query, run nightly for T−7. This is the cheapest and it catches it in one day. 2. Residual analysis segmented by hour and zone: if the model's errors were random, residuals would be centred at zero across every segment. Here they are negative at peak hours and near zero off-peak. A residual plot by hour-of-day would have shown a clear shape from week one. 3. A freshness/completeness monitor on the source: bronze.trips continues to receive rows for trip_date = T on T+1 and T+2. That is a signal, sitting in plain view in the ingestion log, that the period is not closed.

The general lesson to land: BI shows you a number; a model learns the shape of the error. A 1.9% undercount is invisible on a dashboard tile and structural in a model's weights. This is the same asymmetry that CS-11 will make the centrepiece of the whole course.

Q4. What test, added earlier, would have caught this in week one?

Model answer. Two, and teams should write both as dbt YAML:

# 1. Reconciliation: the mart must equal a fresh recount of a CLOSED period.
#    This is the test that actually catches the bug.
- name: driver_daily_reconciles_to_bronze
  description: >
    For a period 7 days old (assumed closed), the sum of completed_trips in the mart
    must equal the count of completed trips in bronze for the same trip_date.
    Fails if late-arriving rows were never absorbed.
  test: assert_equal_counts
  config:
    where: "trip_date = current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAY"

# 2. Source freshness / late-arrival surveillance: rows must stop arriving for a
#    closed day. If they don't, the lookback window is too short.
- name: no_arrivals_for_closed_days
  description: >
    Fails if bronze.trips receives any row whose dropoff_ts is older than the
    lookback window (3 days). Directly measures whether the chosen window is adequate.
  test: assert_no_rows
  config:
    where: "_ingested_at::date - dropoff_ts::date > 3"

Plus the two hygiene tests that should have existed anyway and would have made the bug loud rather than silent:

models:
  - name: driver_daily
    tests:
      - dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns:
          combination_of_columns: [trip_date, driver_id]   # would fail loudly on any re-run
    columns:
      - name: completed_trips
        tests: [not_null, dbt_utils.accepted_range: {min_value: 0}]

Make the point explicitly: unique_combination_of_columns does not detect the undercount, but it removes the fear of re-running, and the fear of re-running is what let the undercount survive four months. Tests that make an operation safe are worth as much as tests that detect a fault.

The second test is the subtle one and the one to spend time on: it does not check the mart at all. It measures the assumption the mart depends on. Most data tests check outputs; the tests that prevent silent bugs check assumptions.

Q5 (extension for fast teams). What lookback window should Wusool choose, and how do you defend the number?

Model answer. From P3: a 3-day lookback captures 99.98% of arrivals; a 2-day window captures 99.68%; a 1-day window captures 98.1% (the status quo plus one day). The residual beyond 3 days is 0.02%, roughly 1 trip in 5,000.

Defend it as a cost/completeness trade-off with a stated residual, never as "3 days feels right": each extra lookback day re-MERGEs ~48,200 rows, costing seconds; 3 days is cheap. But the number must be re-derived from the arrival distribution quarterly, because a vendor change or a settlement-process change moves the tail — and the no_arrivals_for_closed_days test above is precisely the automatic alarm for that.

This is the same conversation as the streaming watermark in M5 (ACT-07): how long do you keep a period open, given that keeping it open costs state and closing it early costs correctness? Point forward to it explicitly — the batch lookback and the streaming watermark are the same decision at different timescales.

docs.title: 8.1 The fixed model
docs.text:
{{ config(
     materialized       = 'incremental',
     incremental_strategy = 'merge',
     unique_key         = ['trip_date','driver_id'],
     on_schema_change   = 'fail'
) }}

WITH scoped AS (
    SELECT *
    FROM {{ ref('silver_trips') }}
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    {% if is_incremental() %}
      -- reprocess a 3-day window so late arrivals land in the day they belong to
      AND trip_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL {{ var('lookback_days', 3) }} DAY
    {% endif %}
)
SELECT
    trip_date,
    driver_id,
    COUNT(*)        AS completed_trips,
    SUM(fare_sar)   AS gross_fare_sar,
    MAX(_ingested_at) AS _last_recomputed_at   -- audit column for the labour review
FROM scoped
GROUP BY trip_date, driver_id

Three changes carry the whole fix: merge (safe re-run), unique_key at the true grain (defines what "the same row" means), and a lookback window instead of a single day (reopens recently-closed periods).

docs.title: 8.2 The backfill runbook (deliverable b)
docs.text:
# Backfill 2026-01-01 .. 2026-06-30, one month at a time.
# Safe to run twice, safe to resume, requires no memory of prior attempts.
for m in 2026-01 2026-02 2026-03 2026-04 2026-05 2026-06; do
  dbt run --select driver_daily \
          --vars "{'backfill_month': '${m}', 'lookback_days': 400}" \
          --target prod
  dbt test --select driver_daily --vars "{'backfill_month': '${m}'}"
done
