Runbook properties to make participants state explicitly: - Resumable — a failure at month 4 is fixed by re-running the whole loop. - Idempotent — a completed month re-run produces 0 rows updated. - Verifiable — dbt test after each month runs the reconciliation test on that month. - Auditable — every corrected row carries _last_recomputed_at, and dbt docs regenerates lineage from the corrected figure back to bronze.trips and to _source_file, which is exactly the chain the labour review needs. - Non-disruptive — it writes the same table by the same code path as the daily run, so there is no "backfill version" of the logic that could differ from production.

docs.title: 8.3 The correction communication
docs.text: The labour review will not read SQL. Produce for it: the per-driver delta table (old count, new count, difference, SAR owed), the arrival-lag distribution P3 as the explanation of why it happened, and the lineage graph as the proof that the new figure derives from raw. Wusool should pay the difference before being asked to. State to the class that the engineering fix is 20 lines and the institutional repair is everything else.

docs.title: 9. What good looks like vs common wrong turns
docs.text: What good looks like Common wrong turn Distinguishes event time (dropoff_ts) from arrival time (_ingested_at) explicitly Calls it a timezone bug and adds a CONVERT_TZ, which changes the number without fixing completeness Fixes with MERGE on (trip_date, driver_id) Adds a 3-day lookback and keeps INSERT INTO — turning an undercount into a 3× overcount, which the 6 duplicate rows in the fixture will demonstrate Derives the lookback window from P3's arrival distribution and states the residual Picks 7 days because "7 is safe", with no cost or residual analysis Writes a reconciliation test against a closed period Writes only not_null and unique tests, neither of which detects an undercount Writes a test on the assumption (do rows still arrive for closed days?) Tests only the output table Traces the label skew into the demand model and names the feedback loop Treats it purely as a payroll error Backfill runbook survives being run twice by a stranger at 03:00 Runbook contains "first check whether this month has already been processed" Notes that unique_key removes the fear of re-running, which is what let the bug survive Treats the uniqueness test as unrelated to the incident Pays the drivers before the review demands it Focuses entirely on the technical remediation

docs.title: 10. Debrief (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Point at "reproducible ≠ correct" on the board. Finance re-ran the query dozens of times and got the same answer every time. Reproducibility is a property of the computation; correctness is a property of the relationship between the computation and the world. Wusool had perfect reproducibility of a wrong number for four months.
  2. The driver was the best monitoring system Wusool had. "It is not every day, it is the busy days" is a precise, correct, actionable bug report from someone with no access to the pipeline. It was closed as unfounded four times because the system of record agreed with itself. When a human with ground truth disagrees with your platform, the platform is on trial, not the human.
  3. Run the live demo. Land data/fixtures/late_trips/trips_late_2026-06-02.csv between two dbt run invocations of the fixed model. First run: 120 inserted, 6 updated. Second run, unchanged input: 0 inserted, 0 updated. That pair of lines is M3 in its entirety — processes only what changed, corrects late data, never duplicates.
  4. Name the general class. Every batch pipeline in the world contains a filter on event time and a schedule that decides when to look. Where those two meet without a lookback and a merge, there is a silent undercount waiting. It will not raise an error, it will not fail a test, and it will bias a model before it embarrasses a dashboard.
  5. The course question. "What happens to Masar's AI system if late-arriving trips are silently dropped?" The demand model learns a flattened peak, under-allocates drivers at exactly the busiest hours, and the resulting cancellations confirm its own under-prediction. The data engineering defect became a self-fulfilling operational failure — and no dashboard anywhere showed a red number.

docs.title: 11. The one sentence participants should leave with
docs.text: A filter on event time plus a schedule that only ever looks once is a silent undercount, not a bug report — fix it with a lookback window and a MERGE on the true grain, and remember that a model does not merely inherit the error, it learns its shape.

docs.title: CS-04 — Reproducing a Disputed Report at "Aman" Payments
docs.text: Field Value Case ID CS-04 Module M4 — Delta Lake, ACID and the Transaction Log Day / Hour Day 3 · Hour 5 (after LAB-04's DESCRIBE HISTORY / VERSION AS OF task) Duration 50 minutes Format Investigation (forensic reconstruction) with a written regulator response Group size 3–4 per team; one team member nominated as "the person who signs the response" Deliverable (a) The exact query sequence that reconstructs the filed figure; (b) a one-page response to the regulator; (c) a filing-versioning policy that prevents recurrence, including the VACUUM retention number and its justification Materials Evidence pack §5 per team (6 pages); a printed DESCRIBE HISTORY output (P3) large enough to annotate Facilitator prep 15 min. Be able to explain the difference between VERSION AS OF and TIMESTAMP AS OF without notes, and the exact interaction between VACUUM retention and time travel — teams will find the edge case in §7 Q2

docs.title: 1. Scenario
docs.text:
"Aman" (أمان) is a Saudi payments processor. On 14 May 2026 it filed its monthly regulatory settlement report for April 2026, generated from gold.settlement_monthly in its Lakehouse.

On 4 June 2026 — three weeks later — the regulator disputes one figure: total settled value for the city of Jeddah. The regulator's own reconciliation, built from the acquirer side, gives SAR 41,882,340. Aman filed SAR 41,714,905. The difference is SAR 167,435.

Aman's engineers re-run the report today. It produces a third number: SAR 41,903,118.

The table has been written to 61 times since the filing. Nobody took a snapshot. The person who ran the filing job has left the company.

The regulator's letter asks one question: "State the value of the table from which the filed figure was derived, as it stood on 14 May 2026, and demonstrate that the filed figure follows from it."

docs.title: 2. Business context
docs.text:
Item Figure Disputed figure — Aman filed SAR 41,714,905 Regulator's independent figure SAR 41,882,340 Difference in dispute SAR 167,435 Figure if the report is re-run today SAR 41,903,118 Maximum administrative penalty for an unreproducible regulatory filing SAR 5,000,000 Days to respond 10 business days Filings per year subject to the same exposure 12

The SAR 167,435 discrepancy is small and is very likely explainable. The unreproducibility is the actual exposure. A processor that cannot state what it filed, or reproduce it, has a control failure — and a control failure is priced far above any single month's discrepancy. Teams that spend the session chasing the SAR 167,435 have misread the case; the regulator asked a question about evidence, not about arithmetic.

docs.title: 3. Technical challenge
docs.text:
Reconstruct the exact state of gold.settlement_monthly (and everything it derives from) as of 14 May 2026, recompute the filed figure from it, demonstrate the match, and explain the two subsequent deltas — without a backup, a snapshot, or the engineer who ran it.

Complicating the reconstruction: a PDPL erasure request was executed on 22 May 2026 for seven rider identities, deleting 29 rows from silver. Those rows contributed to the April settlement. Current data must not contain them; the historical explanation must nonetheless account for them. Teams must resolve the apparent contradiction between "reproduce the past exactly" and "the past must no longer exist."

docs.title: 4. Constraints
docs.text:
• No separate snapshot exists. Do not let a team's answer be "we should have taken one" — that is the policy fix, not the response to the regulator.
  • VACUUM runs weekly, RETAIN 720 HOURS (30 days). 14 May to 4 June is 21 days. Time travel is available — barely. This margin is the case's central tension and the source of §7 Q2.
  • A PDPL erasure ran on 22 May and must be honoured in current data.
  • 10 business days to respond.
  • The response must be intelligible to a regulator's auditor, not only to an engineer.

docs.title: P1 — The regulator's letter (extract)
docs.text:
"... the Authority's reconciliation of settled value for Jeddah for the period 2026-04-01 to 2026-04-30 yields SAR 41,882,340 against the SAR 41,714,905 reported in your filing of 14 May 2026. You are directed to state the value of the source table as at the date of filing and to demonstrate that the reported figure follows from it. A response that cannot evidence the state of the data at the time of filing will be treated as a deficiency in record-keeping controls irrespective of the arithmetic difference."

Read the bolded sentence aloud twice. The regulator is not asking Aman to be right; it is asking Aman to be evidenced.

docs.title: P2 — The filing job's log line (the only surviving artefact of the filing run)
docs.text:
2026-05-14 03:11:47 UTC  INFO  settlement_report v1.4.2
2026-05-14 03:11:47 UTC  INFO  reading gold.settlement_monthly period=2026-04
2026-05-14 03:12:09 UTC  INFO  rows=3,412  cities=5
2026-05-14 03:12:09 UTC  INFO  wrote /reports/settlement_2026-04_filed.pdf  sha256=8f3c...a91d

Note what is absent: no table version, no commit timestamp, no input checksum. The job recorded what it produced and nothing about what it read. This absence is the control failure, and it is the thing the policy deliverable must fix.

docs.title: P3 — DESCRIBE HISTORY gold.settlement_monthly (abridged, 61 commits; the decisive rows)
docs.text:
version timestamp (UTC) operation operationParameters operationMetrics 118 2026-06-04 02:00:11 MERGE predicate: period='2026-04' numTargetRowsUpdated: 41 117 2026-06-02 02:00:09 OPTIMIZE zOrderBy: [city, period] numFilesAdded: 6, numFilesRemoved: 214 ... ... ... ... ... 96 2026-05-22 14:33:52 DELETE predicate: rider_id IN (...) numDeletedRows: 29 95 2026-05-21 02:00:14 MERGE predicate: period='2026-04' numTargetRowsUpdated: 188 ... ... ... ... ... 88 2026-05-15 02:00:07 MERGE predicate: period='2026-04' numTargetRowsUpdated: 121 87 2026-05-14 02:07:33 MERGE predicate: period='2026-04' numTargetRowsUpdated: 64 86 2026-05-13 02:00:11 MERGE predicate: period='2026-04' numTargetRowsUpdated: 203

Version 87, committed 02:07:33 on 14 May, is the last commit before the filing job read the table at 03:11:47. That is the answer to the regulator's first question, and it is derivable from the log alone with no snapshot, no backup, and no surviving engineer. Let teams find it; do not point at it.

docs.title: P4 — VACUUM history on the same table
docs.text:
2026-06-01 04:00:00  VACUUM gold.settlement_monthly RETAIN 720 HOURS
                     -> deleted 1,144 files no longer referenced and older than 2026-05-02 04:00:00
2026-05-25 04:00:00  VACUUM gold.settlement_monthly RETAIN 720 HOURS
2026-05-18 04:00:00  VACUUM gold.settlement_monthly RETAIN 720 HOURS

Today is 2026-06-04. The most recent VACUUM removed files unreferenced since 2026-05-02. Version 87 (14 May) is still readable — with 12 days of margin. The next VACUUM, on 2026-06-08, will move the horizon to 2026-05-09 and the margin becomes 5 days. If the dispute had arrived five weeks later instead of three, the answer would have been "we cannot."

Ask the room, at exactly this moment: what should you do before lunch? (Answer: pin version 87 — see §8.1 step 0.)

docs.title: P5 — The PDPL erasure record
docs.text:
data/fixtures/erasure_request/pdpl_erasure_2026-06-10.json is the course's equivalent fixture; Aman's is the same shape.

{"request_id":"PDPL-2026-0417","received":"2026-05-20","executed":"2026-05-22T14:33:52Z",
 "legal_basis":"PDPL Art. 18 - right to erasure","subjects":7,
 "rows_deleted":{"silver.payments":29,"gold.settlement_monthly":29},
 "delta_versions":{"silver.payments":73,"gold.settlement_monthly":96},
 "value_removed_sar":{"JED":0.00,"note":"erased rows were rider-identifying; monetary aggregates were preserved by design"}}

The design decision recorded in that last field is the resolution of the whole PDPL/audit tension, and teams should be made to find it: Aman's gold settlement table stores monetary aggregates keyed by city and period, with rider identity carried only for lineage. Erasure removed the identifying rows without changing the settled totals. Whether the class believes that is an acceptable design is §7 Q3.

docs.title: P6 — The three numbers, and where they come from
docs.text:
Number Source SAR 41,714,905 Filed 14 May. Derived from table version 87. SAR 41,882,340 The regulator's figure, built from acquirer-side records that include late settlements through end of May. SAR 41,903,118 Re-run today from version 118, which includes 61 subsequent commits of late-settlement MERGEs.

The pattern is now visible: 41,714,905 < 41,882,340 < 41,903,118. All three are increasing. This is not a discrepancy; it is a period that was still absorbing late settlements when it was filed, seen at three different moments. This is CS-03's late-arrival problem, wearing a regulator's letterhead — say so explicitly in the debrief.

docs.title: 6. Facilitation script (minute-by-minute)
docs.text: Min Activity Facilitator does Watch for 0–4 Frame. Read P1's bolded sentence twice. State the three numbers. Ask: "Which one is right?" then immediately: "Wrong question. What did the regulator actually ask for?" Write on the board: "The regulator asked for evidence, not for arithmetic." Teams that start reconciling SAR 167,435. That is the trap and roughly half the room falls into it. 4–6 Distribute the pack; state the three deliverables and nominate the signer at each table. The "who signs" device raises the seriousness noticeably. Use it. — 6–16 Round 1 — Reconstruct. Find the version, prove it, produce the query sequence. Circulate. Prompt any stuck team with: "P2 tells you when the job read the table. P3 tells you when every commit happened. That is enough." Teams using TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-05-14' — a plausible answer that resolves to midnight and lands on version 86, the wrong version. This error is gold; save it for the debrief. 16–20 Board it. One team walks through version 87 and the timestamp argument. Draw the timeline: v86 (13 May 02:00) → v87 (14 May 02:07) → filing job reads (14 May 03:11) → v88 (15 May 02:00). Confirm the class understands why VERSION AS OF 87 is defensible and a date-only TIMESTAMP AS OF is not. 20–24 Interrupt with P4. Read the VACUUM history aloud. Ask: "How much margin do you have, and what do you do before lunch?" This is the highest-energy moment in the case. Let the realisation land. The answer is: pin version 87 now — CLONE it or extend retention — before the 8 June VACUUM. 24–36 Round 2 — Respond and prevent. Write the regulator response and the versioning policy. Push on PDPL: "You just told the regulator you can reproduce May. You also told a rider their data is erased. Both are true. Explain how." Teams that promise the regulator a full historical dataset including erased personal data. That is a PDPL breach committed in a compliance letter. 36–45 Read-aloud. Two nominated signers read their response verbatim. The room plays the regulator's auditor. Challenge with: "You say version 87. How do I know you did not choose the version that flatters you?" (Answer: the log timestamp bounds it independently of the figure; the choice was made by the clock, not by the result.) Responses that read as engineering documentation. Rewrite one live, in plain language. 45–50 Debrief. §10. Close on §11. Reveal P6's monotonic pattern last — the "discrepancy" was a late-arrival profile all along. —

docs.title: 7. Discussion questions with model answers
docs.text:
Q1. Why is time travel superior to manual snapshot backups for audit?

Model answer. Five reasons, in ascending order of importance:

  1. It is not optional. A snapshot exists only if someone remembered. The transaction log is written by every commit, unconditionally, as a byproduct of writing at all. Aman's engineers took no snapshot and still have the evidence.
  2. It is complete. A snapshot captures the state someone thought to capture. The log captures every state, plus who/what/when for each transition — DESCRIBE HISTORY gives operation, predicate, and metrics per commit. That transforms "here is a copy" into "here is the causal history."
  3. It is cheap. Delta versions share unmodified files; a version costs the delta, not the table. Aman has 118 recoverable versions of a multi-terabyte table for a fraction of one full copy. Snapshot economics force a retention trade-off that log economics largely dissolve.
  4. It is queryable in place. SELECT ... VERSION AS OF 87 runs against the production table with the production code path. A restored backup runs against a restored copy, which is a different object in a different location, and every difference is a fresh source of doubt.
  5. It resists the credibility attack. The auditor's real question is "did you pick the version that flatters you?" With time travel, the version is selected by an independently recorded clock — the job log at 03:11:47 against the commit log at 02:07:33 — before anyone knows what figure it produces. With a manual backup, the selection is a human decision made by an interested party.

State the limitation honestly too: time travel is bounded by retention, and retention is a policy choice that can be set to zero. Which is Q2.

Q2. What VACUUM retention would have made this impossible, and why?

Model answer. Anything shorter than the elapsed time from filing to dispute — here 21 days. Concretely:

Retention Outcome for this dispute RETAIN 168 HOURS (7 d, the common default) Version 87's files deleted on ~21 May. Reconstruction impossible. Deficiency finding. RETAIN 720 HOURS (30 d, Aman's setting) Readable on 4 June with 12 days' margin. Readable, barely. RETAIN 0 HOURS Time travel destroyed immediately; also breaks concurrent readers mid-query.

The general rule participants should write down: VACUUM retention is a governance decision, not a storage optimisation. The floor is set by the longest interval over which someone may credibly ask "what did it say then" — for regulatory filings that is the dispute window in the regulation, not an engineer's estimate of convenience.

And the deeper point: retention alone is the wrong instrument for this. Retention is a window that slides; a filing is a fixed point. Relying on a sliding window to protect a fixed point means the protection expires at a date nobody has diarised. The correct control is to pin the filing version — CREATE TABLE ... CLONE gold.settlement_monthly VERSION AS OF 87 (a shallow clone costs almost nothing and freezes the file references) or a retained tag — so that reproducibility is independent of retention entirely. Aman's 12-day margin is not a system that works; it is a system that has not failed yet.

Push the counter-argument for balance: PDPL and storage cost both push retention down. The resolution is not a single retention number but differentiated retention — short on raw personal data, long on financial aggregates, and pinned on filed artefacts.

Q3. How do you reconcile "reproduce the past" with "honour a PDPL erasure"?

Model answer. They conflict only if you assume reproducing the past requires re-materialising personal data. It does not. Three moves resolve it:

  1. Separate the identifying columns from the reportable aggregate. P5 shows Aman did this by design: the settlement figures are aggregates by city and period; rider identity was present for lineage only. Erasure removed the identity rows and did not change any monetary total. The filed figure is therefore fully reproducible without reproducing any erased personal data. This is the architectural answer and it must be made before the erasure request arrives.
  2. Where an aggregate genuinely depends on erased rows, reproduce the aggregate, not the rows, and disclose the erasure as an annotation on the historical view: "version 87 contained 29 rows relating to 7 data subjects subsequently erased under PDPL Art. 18 on 2026-05-22 (request PDPL-2026-0417); their contribution to the reported total was SAR 0.00 / SAR X." The regulator gets the number and the explanation; the data subject gets the erasure. A documented, quantified gap is an acceptable audit artefact; an undocumented one is not.
  3. Never resolve it by refusing the erasure. PDPL erasure is a legal obligation, not an option to be traded against audit convenience. Where a genuine legal-retention obligation conflicts (financial records under a 7-year retention), the correct response is a documented lawful-basis exemption applied to the specific columns required, not a blanket refusal, and it is a legal determination — engineering's job is to make both outcomes technically possible and evidenced.

The one-line formulation: erasure removes the person, not the accounting. Design your gold layer so that this is true by construction, and the conflict never arises.

Q4. What operational habit prevents future disputes?

Model answer. Version-pinning every filing, automatically, in the filing job itself. Compare P2's log line with what it should have been:

2026-05-14 03:11:47 UTC  INFO  settlement_report v1.4.2
2026-05-14 03:11:47 UTC  INFO  reading gold.settlement_monthly  DELTA_VERSION=87  commit_ts=2026-05-14T02:07:33Z
2026-05-14 03:11:47 UTC  INFO  input_checksum=e7b1...44ac  rows=3,412
2026-05-14 03:12:09 UTC  INFO  pinned  gold.settlement_monthly_filed_2026_04  (SHALLOW CLONE VERSION AS OF 87)
2026-05-14 03:12:09 UTC  INFO  wrote /reports/settlement_2026-04_filed.pdf  sha256=8f3c...a91d

Four additions, each cheap: record the version read, record the input checksum, pin a shallow clone, and store all of it with the artefact. The whole 10-day fire drill collapses into one query against a table that already exists.

Then generalise: the filing job should not merely read a version, it should declare one. spark.read.option("versionAsOf", pinned).table(...) makes the report a function of an explicit input, so re-running the filing job a year later reproduces the filed PDF byte-for-byte. A report that is a function of "whatever the table says now" is not a report; it is an observation.

Add the governance wrapper: a filing register — one row per filing, holding period, table, version, checksum, clone name, report hash, and the name of the person who signed. That register is what turns a 10-day forensic exercise into a 10-minute lookup, and it is the only part of the response the regulator will actually keep.

Q5 (reserve). The three numbers are all different. Which one should Aman now tell the regulator is correct?

Model answer. None of them, phrased that way — the question is malformed and saying so is the right answer. April's settled value is not a scalar; it is a quantity that converges as late settlements arrive. Aman should state: the figure filed on 14 May was correct as of version 87 (evidenced); the regulator's figure reflects acquirer records through end of May; today's figure reflects 61 further commits; the three differ by late settlements, which are enumerable trip-by-trip from the commit history. Then propose the actual fix: agree with the regulator a cut-off convention — either file at T+45 when the period has demonstrably closed, or file at T+14 and submit a defined restatement at T+45. The dispute exists because two parties measured a converging quantity at two different times and both called it "April".

This is CS-03 with a regulator attached. Say that out loud.

docs.title: 8.1 The reconstruction (deliverable a)
docs.text:
Step 0 — before anything else, protect the evidence. The 8 June VACUUM will cut the margin to 5 days.

CREATE TABLE gold.settlement_monthly_filed_2026_04
SHALLOW CLONE gold.settlement_monthly VERSION AS OF 87;

Step 1 — establish the version by the clock, not by the figure. Filing job read the table at 2026-05-14 03:11:47 UTC (P2). The latest commit at or before that instant is version 87, committed 02:07:33 (P3). Version 88 lands 2026-05-15 02:00:07, after the read. The version is bounded by two independent logs.

DESCRIBE HISTORY gold.settlement_monthly;   -- the evidence, unaltered

Step 2 — recompute the filed figure from that version.

SELECT SUM(settled_value_sar) AS filed_total
FROM   gold.settlement_monthly VERSION AS OF 87
WHERE  period = '2026-04' AND city = 'JED';
-- 41,714,905.00   == the filed figure. Reproduced.

Step 3 — explain each subsequent delta, quantified.

SELECT 87 AS version, SUM(settled_value_sar) FROM gold.settlement_monthly VERSION AS OF 87
  WHERE period='2026-04' AND city='JED'
UNION ALL SELECT 96,  SUM(settled_value_sar) FROM gold.settlement_monthly VERSION AS OF 96
  WHERE period='2026-04' AND city='JED'   -- immediately after the PDPL DELETE
UNION ALL SELECT 118, SUM(settled_value_sar) FROM gold.settlement_monthly VERSION AS OF 118
  WHERE period='2026-04' AND city='JED';  -- today

Then attribute the movement to specific commits:

-- every commit that touched the April period after the filing, with its row impact
SELECT version, timestamp, operation,
       operationMetrics['numTargetRowsUpdated'] AS updated,
       operationMetrics['numTargetRowsInserted'] AS inserted,
       operationMetrics['numDeletedRows']        AS deleted
FROM   (DESCRIBE HISTORY gold.settlement_monthly)
WHERE  version > 87
  AND  operationParameters['predicate'] LIKE '%2026-04%'
ORDER  BY version;

Step 4 — annotate the PDPL erasure. Version 96 is the DELETE. Per P5, value_removed_sar.JED = 0.00: the erasure removed identifying rows and did not move the settled total. State this in the response with the request ID and legal basis.

Step 5 — reconcile to the regulator's figure. The gap SAR 41,714,905 → 41,882,340 is late settlements landing between 14 May and end of May, enumerable from the commits in step 3.

docs.title: 8.2 The regulator response (deliverable b) — reference text
docs.text:
RE: Settlement filing 2026-04, Jeddah — response to query of 4 June 2026

1. The filing of 14 May 2026 was derived from gold.settlement_monthly at
   Delta table version 87, committed 2026-05-14 02:07:33 UTC. The filing job
   read the table at 03:11:47 UTC the same day; version 88 was not committed
   until 2026-05-15 02:00:07 UTC. The version is therefore bounded by two
   independently recorded logs and was not selected after the fact.

2. Recomputing the reported measure against version 87 reproduces the filed
   figure exactly: SAR 41,714,905.00. The query and the immutable commit
   history are attached (Appendix A) and the version has been pinned as
   gold.settlement_monthly_filed_2026_04.

3. The difference of SAR 167,435 against the Authority's figure is accounted
   for in full by late settlements recorded between 15 and 31 May 2026,
   itemised by commit in Appendix B (31 commits, 1,204 settlements).

4. On 2026-05-22 Aman executed erasure request PDPL-2026-0417 under PDPL
   Art. 18 for seven data subjects (29 rows, table version 96). The erased
   records were rider-identifying; they carried no settled value for Jeddah
   in the period and the reported total is unaffected. Personal data has not
   been re-materialised to answer this query, and will not be.

5. Control improvement, effective for the 2026-05 filing: every filing now
   records the source table version and input checksum, pins that version as
   an immutable clone, and is entered in a filing register. Reproduction of
   any filing is a single query and does not depend on retention windows.

docs.title: 8.3 The policy (deliverable c)
docs.text: Control Setting Justification Filing job records source DELTA_VERSION + input checksum Mandatory, job fails without it P2's absence is the root control failure Every filing pinned via SHALLOW CLONE VERSION AS OF Mandatory, at filing time Makes reproducibility independent of retention Filing register table period · table · version · checksum · clone · report hash · signer Turns forensics into a lookup VACUUM retention, financial gold tables RETAIN 2160 HOURS (90 d) ≥ the regulatory dispute window with margin; pinned clones cover beyond it VACUUM retention, raw personal data Per DATA_DICTIONARY (24 months rider, 90 d geohash p7) PDPL minimisation; not aligned to the financial number Erasure log with per-table version and value impact Mandatory Lets audit and PDPL coexist, evidenced Filing cut-off convention agreed with the regulator T+14 file, T+45 restate Removes the converging-quantity dispute at source

docs.title: 9. What good looks like vs common wrong turns
docs.text: What good looks like Common wrong turn Answers the question asked — evidences the version — before touching the arithmetic Spends the session reconciling SAR 167,435 and never states a version Uses VERSION AS OF 87, justified by the job log timestamp against the commit log Uses TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-05-14', which resolves to midnight and returns version 86 — a wrong number, confidently produced Pins the version immediately, before the next VACUUM Notes the 12-day margin and does nothing about it Treats VACUUM retention as governance with a stated floor Treats retention as a storage setting, or proposes RETAIN 0 to save cost Separates erasure of identity from preservation of aggregates Promises the regulator the full historical dataset, re-materialising erased personal data in a compliance letter Recognises the three numbers as one converging quantity measured at three times Declares one of the three "the true number" Fixes the job so the next filing is self-evidencing Fixes only this filing, manually Writes a response a non-engineer can act on Sends the auditor a notebook Names the control failure plainly (the job logged its output and not its input) Blames the departed engineer

docs.title: 10. Debrief (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. The evidence existed the whole time. Nobody took a snapshot, the engineer left, 61 commits landed on top — and the answer was still recoverable, precisely because the transaction log is written unconditionally by every write. Auditability you have to remember to switch on is auditability you will not have.
  2. The TIMESTAMP AS OF error. If any team used a date-only timestamp, put version 86 and version 87 side by side and show the different total. A plausible query, a confident answer, a wrong number, delivered to a regulator. Time travel gives you the power to be precisely wrong about the past; the discipline is to bound the version by an independent clock.
  3. Retention is governance. At RETAIN 168 HOURS — a very common default — this case ends with a deficiency finding and up to SAR 5,000,000 of exposure. The margin Aman had was 12 days and shrinking on a schedule nobody had diarised. A control that expires silently is not a control.
  4. PDPL and audit are not opponents if gold is designed so that erasure removes the person and not the accounting. That design decision is made months before the erasure request arrives, or not at all.
  5. Reveal P6's pattern. All three numbers increase. This was never a discrepancy — it was a period still absorbing late settlements, observed at three moments and called "April" three times. It is CS-03's undercount with a regulator's letterhead. The fix is a cut-off convention, i.e. an agreement about when a period is closed, which is the same conversation as the lookback window in M3 and the watermark in M5.
  6. The course question. "What happens to Masar's AI system if we cannot reproduce the state of a table on a past date?" You cannot reproduce a training run; you cannot explain a model's behaviour; you cannot answer "what did the model see" after an incident. On Day 5, CS-11 will require exactly this capability to roll a corrupted feature back to its last trusted version — reproducibility is not only an audit control, it is the remediation mechanism.

docs.title: 11. The one sentence participants should leave with
docs.text: A regulator does not ask whether your number was right; it asks you to evidence what your data said at the moment you filed — so record the table version with every filing, pin it, and treat VACUUM retention as a governance floor set by your dispute window rather than a storage setting set by convenience.

docs.title: CS-05 — Live Dispatch at "Sareea" Ride-Hailing
docs.text: Field Value Case ID CS-05 Module M5 — Streaming Data and Event-Driven Architectures Day / Hour Day 4 · Hour 1 (before LAB-05, as the design brief that LAB-05 then implements) Duration 45 minutes Format Design exercise Group size 4 per team Deliverable A one-page streaming design: topic + partition key, delivery semantics, watermark with a defended number, what stays batch, the single metric that tells you the stream is healthy, and the failure mode you accept Materials Evidence pack §5 per team (5 pages); A3 blank sheets for the pipeline drawing; the LAB-05 ASCII architecture on the projector Facilitator prep 15 min. Have data/fixtures/late_pings/README.md open (520 rows: 284 within, 216 beyond, 20 duplicates) — the beyond/within split is the watermark argument in real numbers

docs.title: 1. Scenario
docs.text:
"Sareea" (سريع) operates ride-hailing in Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam. Dispatch decides, minute by minute, where to send idle drivers. Today that decision is made from a demand map built overnight: a batch job ingests the day's GPS and trip events at 01:00 and produces a zone-demand table used by dispatch for the following day.

Dispatch is therefore always reacting to yesterday's demand. When a concert, a match at the stadium, a flight bank at the airport, or a sandstorm shifts demand within the hour, drivers arrive where demand was.

The COO wants zone demand within one minute of the events that create it. The head of engineering has one non-negotiable condition: "whatever you build must not double-count. If it double-counts, surge goes up, riders are charged more for demand that does not exist, and we are on the news."

docs.title: 2. Business context
docs.text:
Item Figure Vehicles emitting GPS 14,000 GPS ping interval 5 seconds GPS events per day ~15,000,000 Trips per day 48,200 Current demand-map latency ~26 hours Target demand-map latency ≤ 60 seconds Mean rider wait, current 6.4 min Mean rider wait, modelled with 60-second rebalancing 4.9 min Modelled uplift in trip acceptance +3.1 pts Modelled annual revenue impact SAR 18,600,000 Cost ceiling for the streaming platform SAR 65,000 / month Cost of a 10% spurious surge event (refunds + regulatory attention + churn) SAR 400,000+, plus unquantified reputational cost

The asymmetry is the whole case: the upside of speed is large and modelled; the downside of double-counting is smaller in expectation but unbounded in consequence. A design that is fast and occasionally wrong is worse than a design that is slightly slower and always right.

docs.title: 3. Technical challenge
docs.text:
Move from a nightly batch demand map to a streaming pipeline computing zone demand within a minute, at 15M events/day, without losing or double-counting events, in a system that is restarted for deploys twice a week.

The specific hard parts: - Duplicates inflate surge. At-least-once delivery is the default of every message broker. Left uncorrected, a redelivery after a restart counts the same vehicle twice in the same zone and the surge multiplier rises on phantom demand. - Late pings are structural, not exceptional. Riyadh has tunnels, multi-storey car parks and underground malls. A device buffers and flushes; pings arrive minutes after the moment they describe. - Restart safety. Deploys, autoscaling events and broker rebalances all restart consumers. Correctness must survive all three without human intervention. - Bounded cost. Unbounded state is the classic streaming cost failure: a window kept open too long grows state until the job dies at the worst moment.

docs.title: 4. Constraints
docs.text:
• Devices in tunnels/basements deliver pings minutes late (P3 quantifies it).
  • The platform is redeployed twice a week; it must be restart-safe with no manual reconciliation.
  • SAR 65,000/month ceiling.
  • Cannot change the device firmware or the 5-second emission interval this year.
  • The historical feature build for the ETA model stays as it is — do not propose rewriting everything as a stream.
  • Ops needs an alert path off the same data; it must not compete with the AI path for the same consumer offsets.

docs.title: P1 — The event, as it arrives (one line of gps_YYYY-MM-DD.ndjson)
docs.text:
{"event_id":"ev_00009f025f480001","vehicle_id":"VEH-00884","driver_id":"DRV-02492",
 "trip_id":"TRP-20260601-0000000","ts":"2026-06-01T19:38:56Z",
 "payload":{"lat":26.41803,"lon":50.10770,"speed_kmh":15.3,"heading_deg":211,"accuracy_m":17.3},
 "producer_version":"2.4.0"}

Five fields carry the entire design: event_id (the dedup key), vehicle_id and trip_id (candidate partition keys), ts (event time, not arrival time), and producer_version (which will matter more than anyone expects — see CS-11).

docs.title: P2 — Volume and shape
docs.text:
Value Events/day 15,000,000 Mean events/second 174 Peak events/second (17:00–19:00 +03) 620 Peak/mean ratio 3.6× Mean event size 268 bytes Peak ingress ~166 KB/s (~14 GB/day) Duplicate event_id rate at source 0.4% (~60,000/day) Out-of-order ts rate ~1% Vehicles 14,000 Zones 63

Note 0.4% duplicates arrive from the producer itself, before any broker redelivery. Deduplication is required by the data, not only by the delivery semantics. Teams that plan to rely on exactly-once delivery to avoid a dedup step have already failed.

docs.title: P3 — Ping arrival-lag distribution (measured over 7 days)
docs.text:
Lag (event time → arrival at the broker) Share Cumulative ≤ 5 s 96.20% 96.20% 5–30 s 2.10% 98.30% 30 s – 2 min 0.90% 99.20% 2–5 min 0.55% 99.75% 5–10 min 0.18% 99.93% 10–30 min 0.06% 99.99% > 30 min (device offline for a shift) 0.01% 100.00%

This table is the watermark argument. Teams must select a watermark from this distribution and state the residual they are accepting. Do not let anyone answer "10 minutes because that seems safe."

The Masar fixture makes it concrete: data/fixtures/late_pings/gps_late_2026-06-04.ndjson holds 520 late pings — 284 arriving within a 5-minute watermark and 216 beyond it, plus 20 duplicates. That is a 45% drop rate for events that were late by more than five minutes; whether that is acceptable depends entirely on what the number is used for, which is §7 Q2.

docs.title: P4 — Two failure post-mortems from Sareea's first streaming attempt (2025, abandoned)
docs.text:
INC-2025-0412  "Surge spike, Olaya, 18:40-19:05"
  Consumer restarted during a deploy. Offsets were committed BEFORE the sink write.
  7,300 pings reprocessed and re-counted. Zone Z-RUH-01 demand read 1.41x actual.
  Surge rose to 2.3x on demand that did not exist. 412 rider complaints, SAR 61,000
  in goodwill refunds. Root cause recorded as "restart timing".

INC-2025-0517  "Demand map frozen, all cities, 03:12-07:40"
  Windowed aggregation used a 60-minute watermark to 'be safe about tunnels'.
  State store grew to 41 GB, executor OOM, job died, no alert until the morning
  standup. Demand map served stale data for 4.5 hours during the morning peak.

These two incidents are the two failure modes of the same decision, in opposite directions. Give them to the teams together; the design must survive both.

docs.title: P5 — Target architecture (from LAB-05, which teams will build next hour)
docs.text:
Vehicles ──► Kafka ──► Spark Structured Streaming ──► bronze.gps_events ──► silver.vehicle_positions ──┬──► gold.eta_features   (AI)
 (GPS SDK)   masar.      exactly-once, checkpointed    (raw, append-only,      (deduped, unit-normalised,│
             gps.pings                                  _ingested_at,           watermarked)             └──► operations alerts (Ops)
                                                        _source_file,
                                                        _batch_id)

Hand this out at minute 25, not before. Teams design first, then compare against it. A team whose design differs is not necessarily wrong — make them defend the difference.

docs.title: 6. Facilitation script (minute-by-minute)
docs.text: Min Activity Facilitator does Watch for 0–4 Frame. Give the COO's requirement and the head of engineering's condition, verbatim. Put the two numbers on the board: SAR 18.6M upside, unbounded downside. Ask: "Which of those two numbers should drive your design?" Teams that optimise for the 60 seconds. The condition, not the target, is the binding constraint. 4–6 Distribute P1–P4 (hold P5 back). State the one-page deliverable. — — 6–18 Round 1 — Draw the pipeline. A3 sheet: sources → broker → processing → storage → consumers. Every arrow must be labelled with its delivery guarantee. Circulate. One question per table: "Draw me the arrow where a duplicate can be created." Most teams have not thought about where. Teams that draw one consumer serving both AI and Ops. Ask what happens when the alerting consumer falls behind. 18–25 Round 2 — The five decisions. Partition key · delivery semantics · watermark (with a number from P3) · what stays batch · the health metric. Hand out P4's two post-mortems now, if you have not already, to any team whose watermark is either 30 seconds or an hour. "Exactly-once" asserted without a mechanism. Ask: "exactly-once between which two points?" 25–28 Reveal P5. Teams compare their design against the reference and mark the differences. Be explicit: differences are for defending, not for correcting. — 28–38 Design review. Two teams present in 4 minutes; the room asks one question each. You ask the killer question of §7 Q2 and Q4. Play the head of engineering: "Convince me this cannot double-count during Thursday's deploy." Teams whose answer to restart safety is "we'll be careful during deploys." 38–45 Debrief. §10. Show the exactly-once equation. Close on §11 and hand straight into LAB-05. The bridge line: "You have one hour to build what you just designed." —

docs.title: 7. Discussion questions with model answers
docs.text:
Q1. Why would at-least-once (duplicates) directly harm the business here?

Model answer. Because the downstream consumer of a ping count is a pricing decision. Zone demand is a count of distinct vehicles and requests in a window; the surge multiplier is a monotonic function of that count. A duplicate does not add noise to a report — it adds a rider that does not exist to a market that then prices itself accordingly.

The harm chain, which teams should be able to recite: duplicate ping → inflated zone demand → surge multiplier rises → riders charged more for demand that is not there → complaints, refunds (SAR 61,000 in INC-2025-0412 alone), regulatory attention on pricing fairness, and a rebalancing decision that sends drivers to an empty zone, which reduces supply where demand actually is. The duplicate causes a real physical misallocation of 14,000 vehicles.

Contrast with a domain where at-least-once is fine: a page-view counter, a log aggregation, an ML training set of 15M rows where 0.4% duplicates barely move a gradient. The lesson is not that duplicates are always fatal; it is that the acceptable delivery semantic is a property of the consumer, not of the pipeline, and here one consumer sets prices.

Then close the loop on P2: even with perfect exactly-once delivery, the producer emits 0.4% duplicate event_ids. Exactly-once transport does not give you exactly-once data. You need a dedup on event_id regardless.

Q2. How do you pick the watermark given tunnel-delayed pings vs the cost of state?

Model answer. Derive it from P3, state the residual, and — crucially — recognise that different consumers need different watermarks off the same stream.

From P3: a 2-minute watermark admits 99.20% of events; 5 minutes admits 99.75%; 10 minutes admits 99.93%. Each additional minute of watermark holds more window state open: state ≈ (events/second) × (watermark seconds) × (per-key state size), so at 620 events/s peak, going from 5 to 60 minutes is a 12× state increase — which is exactly how INC-2025-0517 reached 41 GB and died.

The correct design is two watermarks, not one:

Consumer Watermark Residual dropped Why Dispatch / surge (real-time) 2 minutes 0.80% A demand map is a decision aid with a 60-second SLA. An event 5 minutes late describes a world that no longer exists; admitting it late is worth less than emitting the window on time. Under-counting by 0.8% is safe (it under-surges, never over-surges). silver.vehicle_positions → gold.eta_features (AI) 10 minutes 0.07% Feature correctness matters more than latency; the batch feature build tolerates minutes. Historical / training none — batch reprocess from bronze.gps_events 0% Bronze is append-only and complete. Anything dropped by any watermark is still in bronze and can be recomputed.

That last row is the key insight and most teams miss it: the watermark only decides what the streaming aggregate sees. It never loses data, because bronze is append-only and holds every event including the very late ones. A watermark is a latency/completeness trade on a derived view, not a retention policy. Once teams see that, the anxiety about dropping 0.8% evaporates and the decision becomes tractable.

Defend the number, never the feeling: "2 minutes, admitting 99.2% of events, dropping ~120,000 of 15M per day from the real-time view only, all of which remain in bronze and are absorbed by the next batch rebuild."

Q3. What single metric tells you the stream is keeping up?

Model answer. Consumer lag — the difference between the latest offset produced to a partition and the latest offset committed by the consumer group, measured per partition.

Why it beats the alternatives: - Throughput looks healthy right up until it does not; a consumer processing 174 events/s looks fine while 620/s arrive, and only lag reveals the deficit. - Latency of the last processed record is a lagging indicator; it tells you about the record you finished, not the queue you have not started. - CPU / memory tells you the machine is busy, not that the work is being completed.

Lag is the integral of the deficit: it is zero when you are keeping up, and it grows monotonically the moment you are not, long before anything fails. The alert condition should be on the derivative as well as the level — "lag increasing for 5 consecutive minutes" fires earlier than any absolute threshold and is robust to a legitimate burst.

Watch for the per-partition subtlety: total lag can look flat while one partition — the one holding the hot key — grows without bound. Sareea's vehicle_id partitioning avoids the hottest-key problem, but a design keyed by city would put a third of 15M events on one partition and total lag would hide it. Alert per partition.

Second-place answers worth acknowledging: watermark progression (if the watermark stops advancing, a partition has gone silent and windows will never close — INC-2025-0517's silent precursor) and checkpoint commit interval. A mature design alerts on all three, but if you get one number on a wall, it is lag.

Q4. What stays batch, and why not stream everything?

Model answer. Stay batch for anything that is (a) not latency-sensitive, (b) needs a wide historical window, or (c) needs to be reprocessed when logic changes.

Workload Stream or batch Reason Ping → bronze.gps_events Stream It is the ingestion path; it must be continuous and exactly-once Dedup + unit normalisation → silver.vehicle_positions Stream Cheap, stateless-ish, needed by both consumers 1-minute zone demand for dispatch Stream This is the 60-second business requirement gold.eta_features historical build (rolling windows, joins to weather and zones) Batch Needs days of history, joins several dimensions, and is rebuilt whenever feature logic changes Model training sets Batch Point-in-time correctness over months Daily/monthly BI marts Batch Nobody dispatches from a monthly mart Backfills and corrections Batch By definition

The architectural name for this is Kappa-lite: stream into the lakehouse once, exactly once, and refine downstream in whichever mode fits each consumer. It beats a full Lambda architecture (two parallel implementations of the same logic, batch and streaming, kept in sync by hope) because it has one ingestion path and one copy of the raw truth — which is CS-01's lesson arriving from a different direction.

The cost argument matters too and lands well with a COO: streaming everything means every historical recomputation becomes a replay of 15M events/day across the retention window, at streaming infrastructure prices, inside the SAR 65,000/month ceiling. Batch reprocessing from bronze is dramatically cheaper for exactly the workloads that need reprocessing most often.

Q5. Exactly-once is often called impossible. What exactly are you claiming when you claim it?

Model answer. The claim is not that a message is delivered exactly once — over an unreliable network that is genuinely impossible. The claim is about the observable end state:

exactly-once effect = at-least-once delivery + idempotent, transactional sink + checkpointed offsets committed atomically with the write

Each term does specific work: - At-least-once delivery — Kafka retains events and replays from an offset; nothing is lost. - Checkpointed offsets — Structured Streaming records which offsets a micro-batch covers, in the checkpoint, as part of committing the batch. - Atomic sink — the Delta commit for that micro-batch either lands entirely or not at all. - Committed together — the offset advance and the data commit are one atomic fact. This is precisely what INC-2025-0412 got wrong: offsets were committed before the sink write, so a restart in between skipped nothing but replayed a batch that had already partly landed.

The order is the whole thing. Write, then commit offsets, atomically. And place the checkpoint next to its sink — one checkpoint per streaming query, never shared, never inside the table directory.

docs.title: 8.1 The five decisions, with justification
docs.text: Decision Choice Justification Topic + partitioning masar.gps.pings, keyed by vehicle_id, 24 partitions Ordering is only required per vehicle (a vehicle's position sequence must not reorder). 14,000 vehicles across 24 partitions gives even distribution and no hot key. Keying by city would create a 3-way skew; keying by trip_id orders per-trip but fragments a vehicle's idle-time pings across partitions. Choose the key by asking: what must not be reordered? Retention 7 days on the topic Long enough to replay a full week after a bad deploy or a logic bug; bronze is the permanent record so the topic does not need to be one. Delivery semantics Exactly-once effect, per §7 Q5 The business condition. Achieved by construction, not by care. Consumer groups Separate groups for the AI path and the Ops alert path Independent offsets mean a slow or crashed alerting consumer cannot delay ingestion, and a replay of one does not replay the other. This is the fan-out in P5 and the reason it is drawn as a fan-out. Watermark 2 min for the dispatch aggregate; 10 min for the silver→gold feature path; batch rebuild from bronze for training Derived from P3, with stated residuals; bronze retains everything regardless. Dedup dropDuplicates(["event_id"]) within the watermark, in silver — not in bronze Bronze is the immutable record and must keep the duplicates (they are evidence). Silver is where the data becomes trustworthy. Checkpoint One per query, on durable object storage, outside the table path Shared checkpoints are the second-most-common streaming outage after unbounded state. Trigger 30 seconds Meets the 60-second end-to-end SLA with margin; larger micro-batches are far more file-efficient than a continuous trigger. Health metric Consumer lag per partition; alert on 5 minutes of monotonic increase §7 Q3 Maintenance Scheduled OPTIMIZE on bronze.gps_events and silver.vehicle_positions A 30-second trigger writes 2,880 commits/day; without compaction, read latency degrades within weeks (this is CS-02's small-file tax arriving in a streaming sink)

docs.title: 8.2 The accepted failure mode (make every team write this line)
docs.text:
"Under a 2-minute watermark, approximately 0.8% of pings (~120,000/day) arrive too late to be counted in the real-time dispatch view. They are retained in full in bronze.gps_events and are absorbed by the next batch rebuild of gold.eta_features. The real-time view therefore under-counts demand slightly and never over-counts it, which is the safe direction for surge."

A design that does not name its accepted failure mode has not been designed; it has been hoped for. The direction of the error — under, never over — is the part that makes it acceptable to the head of engineering.

docs.title: 8.3 Cost sanity check against the SAR 65,000 ceiling
docs.text:
Component Sizing SAR/month Kafka (3 brokers, 14 GB/day ingress, 7-day retention ≈ 100 GB + replication) modest 14,000 Structured Streaming cluster (2–6 workers, 30 s trigger, 620 ev/s peak) autoscaled 31,000 Object storage (bronze GPS, ~14 GB/day compressed) 5 TB/year 4,000 OPTIMIZE/VACUUM maintenance job (nightly, spot) 20 min/night 3,000 Monitoring, lag metrics, alerting — 4,000 Total 56,000

Within ceiling with ~14% headroom. Note for the class: the 60-minute-watermark design from INC-2025-0517 does not fit — its state store alone forces a larger cluster class. The watermark decision is a cost decision as well as a correctness one.

docs.title: 9. What good looks like vs common wrong turns
docs.text: What good looks like Common wrong turn Picks the partition key by asking "what must not be reordered?" and answers vehicle_id Partitions by city, creating a 3-way hot-key skew that per-partition lag will expose in week one Derives the watermark from P3 and states the residual and its direction "10 minutes, to be safe" — the exact reasoning that produced INC-2025-0517 Uses different watermarks for different consumers off one stream One watermark for the whole platform, forcing dispatch latency and AI completeness to trade against each other Understands the watermark never loses data because bronze is append-only Treats watermark drop as permanent data loss and inflates it to compensate Separate consumer groups for AI and Ops One consumer serving both, so a stuck alerting sink stalls feature ingestion States exactly-once as at-least-once + idempotent sink + atomically committed offsets Asserts "we'll use exactly-once" as a configuration flag Dedups on event_id in silver, keeping duplicates in bronze as evidence Dedups at ingest, destroying the ability to measure the 0.4% producer duplicate rate Keeps the historical feature build in batch (Kappa-lite) Proposes streaming everything, then cannot reprocess when feature logic changes Names consumer lag per partition as the health metric, alerting on the derivative Monitors CPU and throughput, both of which look fine while falling behind Schedules OPTIMIZE on the streaming sinks from day one Ignores small files; read latency degrades over weeks and is diagnosed as "Delta is slow" Writes the accepted failure mode as a sentence Claims no data is ever lost, which is either false or expensive

docs.title: 10. Debrief (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. The condition beat the target. The COO asked for 60 seconds; the head of engineering said "must not double-count." Every good design in the room was shaped by the second sentence. Latency targets are negotiable; correctness conditions are the architecture.
  2. Put the equation on the board and leave it there for the rest of the day: exactly-once effect = at-least-once delivery + idempotent transactional sink + offsets committed atomically with the write INC-2025-0412 had all three components and got the ordering wrong. Streaming correctness is mostly about what is committed together with what.
  3. The two post-mortems are the same decision in opposite directions. Watermark too short: lose late data. Watermark too long: unbounded state, OOM, and a frozen demand map during the morning peak — a worse outcome than losing 0.8% of pings. The watermark is not a safety setting where more is safer; it is a trade with a cost on both sides.
  4. The insight most teams miss: a watermark decides what the stream sees, not what you keep. Bronze is append-only and holds everything. This is why the medallion architecture and streaming fit together so well — you can be aggressive about latency in the derived view precisely because the raw layer forgives you.
  5. Hand into LAB-05. "You have one hour to build this: Kafka → Structured Streaming → bronze.gps_events → silver.vehicle_positions → two sinks. You will kill the job mid-batch and restart it, and you will prove zero duplicates."
  6. The course question. "What happens to Masar's AI system if the GPS stream duplicates or drops events?" Duplicates inflate rolling_zone_demand_15m and the model learns phantom peaks; drops deflate it and the model learns a flattened curve. And — foreshadow CS-11 deliberately — "a stream that is perfectly exactly-once can still deliver perfectly corrupted data; on Day 5 you will meet the incident where every event arrived exactly once and the model still broke."

docs.title: 11. The one sentence participants should leave with
docs.text: Exactly-once is not a delivery guarantee you switch on, it is an end state you construct — at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent sink plus offsets committed atomically with the write — and every remaining design choice, above all the watermark, is a trade between latency, completeness and state that you must make with a number and name as an accepted failure mode.

docs.title: CS-06 — The Silent Currency Bug at "Muqeem" Analytics
docs.text: Field Value Case ID CS-06 Module M6 — Data Quality, Observability and Governance Day / Hour Day 4 · Hour 5 (after the data-quality pyramid, before or alongside LAB-06's gate) Duration 45 minutes Format Investigation → design exercise Group size 3–4 per team Deliverable (a) The one check that would have caught this, written as a Great Expectations expectation with its baseline definition; (b) the gate ruling — fail-fast, quarantine, or alert-only — scoped precisely; (c) a correction plan; (d) the answer to "how do you avoid baselining the bug?" Materials Evidence pack §5 per team (6 pages); data/fixtures/currency_shift/trips_2026-06-05_currency_shift.csv open on the projector (7,230 rows, 2,125 shifted, mean 37.40 → 3,739.86) Facilitator prep 15 min. Be ready to compute a PSI by hand on the projector — teams will ask "how do you actually measure drift?" and the answer must be arithmetic, not a library call

docs.title: 1. Scenario
docs.text:
"Muqeem" (مقيم) runs analytics for a mobility operator. It ingests trip records from a third-party vendor that operates one city's fleet under a franchise agreement.

On 12 June 2026, the vendor deployed a change to its export job. A fare field that had always been sent in halalas (1/100 SAR) began being sent in riyals — a 100× reduction in the numeric value — for that one city only. The vendor's release notes described it as "align currency units with the platform standard." Nobody at Muqeem read them; nobody at Muqeem had been told they existed.

Every ingested row is individually valid. The schema is unchanged. The type is unchanged. The values are plausible. No pipeline errored, no test failed, no alert fired.

Over the following two weeks, the demand-pricing model — which uses mean fare per zone as a demand-intensity proxy — degraded. It was noticed on 26 June when a regional manager asked why the city's surge had not risen during a sandstorm.

docs.title: 2. Business context
docs.text:
Item Figure Cities on the platform 5 Cities affected 1 (the vendor's franchise city) Share of platform trips affected ~19% Detection lag 14 days Mean fare, affected city, before the change SAR 3,741 (halalas, i.e. SAR 37.41) Mean fare, affected city, after the change SAR 37.41 (riyals) Mispricing exposure — under-surged trips, 14 days SAR 1,340,000 in foregone revenue Revenue forecast error for the quarter SAR 8,700,000 overstated (the forecast used pre-change fares for the whole city) Cost of retraining and re-baselining the pricing model ~SAR 190,000 Rows to correct 214,000

Note the scale relationship the class should see: the data defect cost SAR 1.34M in two weeks, and one distribution check — perhaps two hours of engineering — would have caught it on day one. Data quality is the highest-return engineering work in a platform, and it is the first thing cut.

docs.title: 3. Technical challenge
docs.text:
No row-level rule can catch a 100× shift that stays inside a plausible range. Every row passes:

  • schema check — passes (same field, same double);
  • not-null — passes;
  • range check fare_sar BETWEEN 0 AND 20000 — passes (37.41 is further inside the range than 3,741 was);
  • referential integrity — passes;
  • freshness, volume, row count — all normal.

Only a check that looks at the shape of a population rather than the validity of a row can see it. That is the top two tiers of the data-quality pyramid — distribution and reconciliation — and it is exactly the tier most teams never build.

docs.title: 4. Constraints
docs.text:
• Cannot re-ingest. Bronze is immutable and the vendor retains 7 days. (Again, frame immutability as the enabler: bronze holds both the pre- and post-change values, which is what makes the correction provable.)
  • The other four cities are unaffected and must not be blocked while the affected city is corrected.
  • The correction must be auditable — the franchise agreement has a revenue-share clause, so corrected figures are contractually consequential.
  • Detection must be reduced from 14 days to ≤ 1 day for the next occurrence.
  • The vendor cannot be compelled to change process this quarter; the control must sit on Muqeem's side of the boundary.

Seven expectations, all green, on the day the data broke. Read the result line aloud. A green test suite is evidence that the checks you wrote passed; it is not evidence that the data is correct.

docs.title: P4 — Distribution check, computed after the fact (what would have fired)
docs.text:
Population Stability Index for fare_sar, JED, 10 deciles, baseline 2026-05-01 → 2026-05-31:

Date PSI vs baseline Verdict at threshold 0.20 2026-06-10 0.014 stable 2026-06-11 0.011 stable 2026-06-12 6.81 breach — every decile boundary crossed 2026-06-13 6.79 breach

And the simpler check that also fires, computable in one query:

SELECT city, DATE(pickup_ts) AS d, AVG(fare_sar) AS mean_fare
FROM   silver.trips
WHERE  status='completed' AND DATE(pickup_ts) >= current_date() - 30
GROUP  BY city, d;
-- alert when mean_fare deviates > 25% from the trailing 28-day median for the SAME city

PSI of 6.81 against a threshold of 0.20. This is not a subtle statistical signal requiring a sophisticated detector — it is a 34× threshold breach. It went undetected for 14 days because nobody was computing it at all.

docs.title: P5 — The vendor's release note (retrieved on 27 June, after the fact)
docs.text:
vendor-export v3.7.0 — 2026-06-12
* Align currency units with platform standard (halalas -> SAR) in trip export.
* Fix pagination bug in incremental extract.
* Bump dependency: jackson 2.15.2 -> 2.16.1

One bullet, second-hand, in a changelog nobody at Muqeem subscribed to, describing a semantic change to a financial field as an "alignment". Every element of this is realistic and every element is a control failure: there was no data contract, so a unit change was a routine release note rather than a breaking change.
