Run the LAB-06 gate against it during the debrief.

docs.title: 6. Facilitation script (minute-by-minute)
docs.text: Min Activity Facilitator does Watch for 0–4 Frame. Project P1's two rows. Say nothing for fifteen seconds. Then: "Which of these two rows is invalid?" The answer is neither. Let someone say it. Teams that immediately spot the 100×. Ask them: "now write me the row-level rule that catches it." They cannot. 4–6 Distribute P2, P3, P5 (hold P4 back). State the four deliverables. — — 6–15 Round 1 — Why did nothing fire? Teams audit the P3 suite expectation by expectation and state, for each, why it passed. Circulate. Demand a per-expectation answer, not a summary. Teams that say "the range was too wide." Push: what range would have caught it and not produced false alarms? (Answer: none — 37.41 is a more plausible fare than 3,741.) 15–18 Board the pyramid. Build schema → constraint → referential → distribution → reconciliation on the board and mark where the P3 suite stops. The visual — a suite that stops two tiers below the defect — is the module in one image. — 18–20 Reveal P4. PSI 6.81 against a 0.20 threshold. Ask: "how long would this check have taken to write?" The answer is roughly two hours, against SAR 1.34M. Let the room do that arithmetic. 20–33 Round 2 — Design. All four deliverables. Push hardest on the baseline question. Ask every table: "Your baseline is a trailing 28-day window. The bug has now been live for 14 of those days. What does your check say tomorrow?" This is the "baseline-the-bug" trap and it is the highest-value moment of the case. 33–41 Tribunal. Each team states its gate ruling — block, quarantine, or alert — and is challenged by the room. Play the operations manager: "You just blocked 19% of my platform's trips because a statistic looked odd. Justify that." Teams that block all five cities. Scope matters as much as the ruling. 41–45 Debrief + live drill. Run the LAB-06 gate against currency_shift. Close on §11. Show the gate quarantining the affected city while promoting the rest. —

docs.title: 7. Discussion questions with model answers
docs.text:
Q1. Why did every schema and range check pass while the data was wrong?

Model answer. Because those checks answer the question "is this row well-formed?", and the row was perfectly well-formed. They cannot answer "does this population mean what it used to mean?", which is a different question requiring a different kind of evidence: a comparison against history rather than against a rule.

Work through P3 expectation by expectation — this is worth doing explicitly:

Expectation Why it passed column exists The vendor renamed nothing type is Double 34.11 and 3402.0 are both doubles not null Values are present between 0 and 20000 34.11 is deeper inside the range than 3402.0 was — the corrupted data is more conformant status in set Untouched trip_id unique Untouched row count 40k–60k Volume unchanged; the vendor's job ran normally

The fourth row is the one to dwell on. A widened range does not help; a narrowed range would have to be narrow enough to exclude 34.11, which would then reject every legitimate fare in the other four cities. There is no row-level rule that separates these two populations, because the defect is not in any row — it is in the relationship between the rows and their history.

The generalisation: schema and constraint checks validate syntax and bounds; they are blind to semantics. Semantic defects — unit changes, currency changes, encoding changes, a field's meaning being redefined — are always type-compatible, because the type was never the thing that changed. (Point forward: CS-11 is the same class of defect on speed_kmh, and it is the signature incident of the course precisely because this class is the one that platforms are structurally blind to.)

Q2. What baseline period do you freeze, and how do you avoid "baselining the bug"?

Model answer. The trap: a rolling baseline computed over the trailing N days will, after N days of corrupted data, treat the corruption as normal and go quiet. Muqeem's 14-day detection lag is roughly half the width of a typical 28-day rolling window — a rolling baseline would have started losing sensitivity from day one and been fully desensitised by day 28. Worse, it would then flag the correction as an anomaly.

The defence is layered, and teams should propose at least three of these five:

  1. A frozen, human-approved baseline. Pick a period certified as known-good (Muqeem: May 2026, before the vendor release), freeze it, version it in git, and change it only through review. The baseline becomes an artefact with an owner, not a side effect of a window function.
  2. Never let a baseline auto-refresh across an unexplained breach. If drift fired and was resolved as a true positive, the baseline must be re-cut deliberately. If it fired and was dismissed, the dismissal must be recorded with a reason. A baseline that silently absorbs whatever it sees is not a baseline.
  3. Anchor to something outside the data feed. A drift check compares data to data and can be fooled by data. A reconciliation check compares two independent measurements of the same physical fact and cannot: here, fare_sar / distance_km should sit near a stable SAR-per-km for a given city and surge, and that ratio is anchored by the tariff, which is a published business fact. When the ratio moves 100× and the tariff did not change, the data is wrong — regardless of what any baseline says.
  4. Multiple time horizons. Compare against yesterday, against the trailing 28 days, and against the frozen baseline. A step change breaks all three simultaneously; a gradual real trend breaks only the long one. The pattern of which horizons fire tells you what kind of change you are looking at.
  5. Segment by producer. Compute drift per city, per vendor, per producer_version. An aggregate over all five cities dilutes a 100× shift in one city into a ~19% platform-wide move that may fall under a naive threshold. Always segment drift by the dimension along which change is deployed — this is the single most transferable lesson in the case and it is exactly what CS-11 will require for producer_version.

Q3. Fail-fast or quarantine here, and scoped to what?

Model answer. Quarantine, scoped to the affected city's batch. Not fail-fast, and not alert-only.

The reasoning teams must produce:

  • Not fail-fast, because fail-fast blocks the whole batch, and 81% of the platform's trips are unaffected. Blocking four healthy cities to stop one broken feed converts a data-quality incident into an availability incident. Fail-fast is right when the defect threatens integrity — a null primary key, a broken referential relationship, a schema violation that would corrupt every downstream join — because then partial promotion produces silent corruption. A distribution shift in one segment does not threaten integrity; it threatens meaning in a bounded scope.
  • Not alert-only, because alert-only promotes the bad rows into silver while sending an email. That is the sim-alertonly failure: the alarm rings and the corrupt data flows anyway, and by the time a human reads the email the model has trained on it. A gate that only notifies is not a gate.
  • Quarantine, scoped to city = 'JED' AND pickup_ts >= '2026-06-12': the affected rows go to silver.trips_quarantine with the failing expectation and the batch id recorded; the other four cities promote normally; downstream consumers of JED see no new data rather than wrong data; and a human decides within one business day.

Then the point that separates a good answer from an excellent one: "no data" is a visible, honest failure state and "wrong data" is an invisible one. A dashboard with a gap prompts a question; a dashboard with plausible wrong numbers prompts a decision. Quarantine converts a silent semantic corruption into a loud, bounded operational gap. That conversion is the entire purpose of a quality gate.

The gate ruling table for the deliverable:

Signal Ruling Scope Null trip_id / rider_id Block (fail-fast) Whole batch — keys are integrity Referential break (driver_id not in drivers) Block Whole batch Schema change (new/removed/retyped column) Block Whole batch Distribution drift, one segment, PSI > 0.20 Quarantine The segment only Distribution drift, all segments simultaneously Block Whole batch — a platform-wide shift is more likely a pipeline bug than a data event Range violation, < 0.5% of rows Quarantine The rows Freshness late by < 2 h Alert —

Q4. What lineage would have shortened detection from two weeks to one day?

Model answer. Two distinct things, and teams often conflate them:

Column-level lineage answers "what does this feed?". When fare_sar drifts, lineage names every consumer within seconds: silver.trips → gold.fact_trip (revenue dashboard) → gold.zone_hourly_demand (pricing model input) → the demand-pricing model → the surge multiplier → the quarterly forecast. Without it, the 26 June question "why did surge not rise in the sandstorm" takes days to trace back to a fare field. With it, the drift alert on 12 June arrives pre-annotated with its blast radius, which is what makes an on-call engineer act on it rather than triage it.

Source-and-version lineage answers "what changed?". Every bronze row carries _source_file, _batch_id, _ingested_at (the CONVENTIONS.md requirement), and — where the source declares one — the producer's version. Then the first query after any alert is:

SELECT vendor_export_version, city, COUNT(*), AVG(fare_sar)
FROM   bronze.trips
WHERE  DATE(_ingested_at) >= current_date() - 3
GROUP  BY 1, 2;

which lays the release boundary directly against the metric shift and turns a two-week investigation into a two-minute one. Muqeem could not run this query because the vendor's export version was never captured. Retrieving P5's release note on 27 June required a human to think to ask the vendor for it.

The organisational half of the answer matters as much: subscribe to the producer's release notes and treat a semantic change as a breaking change by contract. A data contract that specifies fare_sar: double permits everything that happened. A contract that specifies fare_sar: double, unit: SAR, monotonic_with: distance_km, expected_mean_range: [25, 55] makes the vendor's release a contract violation detectable at the boundary, on the first row of the first batch.

Q5 (reserve). The vendor's change made the data more correct — SAR is the platform standard. Was the vendor wrong?

Model answer. The vendor's destination was right and its process was wrong, and separating these two is the point. Moving to SAR aligns with the platform standard; doing it in a patch release, announced in one changelog bullet, on a live financial field, with no contract, no version signal in the data, and no coordination window, is the failure. The correct process: a new field (fare_sar_v2) or an explicit unit field carried in the payload, dual-emission for an overlap period, a contract version bump, and a coordinated cutover.

The transferable rule: there is no such thing as a safe silent semantic change. If the meaning of a value changes, the name or the contract version must change with it, so that consumers break loudly at the boundary instead of degrading quietly downstream.

docs.title: 8.1 The check that catches it (deliverable a)
docs.text:
# quality/suites/silver_trips_suite.py — the distribution tier
expect_column_mean_to_be_between(
    column="fare_sar",
    min_value=lambda ctx: ctx.baseline["fare_sar_mean"] * 0.75,
    max_value=lambda ctx: ctx.baseline["fare_sar_mean"] * 1.25,
    # CRITICAL: evaluated per city. An aggregate over 5 cities dilutes a 100x
    # shift in one city to a ~19% platform move and may not breach at all.
    group_by="city",
    meta={
        "tier": "distribution",
        "baseline": "frozen 2026-05-01..2026-05-31, approved by data-platform lead, git-versioned",
        "on_failure": "quarantine the failing city's batch; promote all other cities",
    },
)

# the reconciliation tier - anchored outside the feed, cannot be fooled by the feed
expect_column_pair_ratio_to_be_between(
    numerator="fare_sar", denominator="distance_km",
    min_value=1.8, max_value=6.5,           # SAR per km, from the published tariff
    group_by=["city", "surge_multiplier"],
    meta={"tier": "reconciliation",
          "why": "the tariff is a business fact independent of the data feed"},
)

Both are needed. The first detects the change; the second is immune to a poisoned baseline because its reference point is a published tariff rather than the data's own history.

docs.title: 8.2 The correction plan (deliverable c)
docs.text:
1. Do not modify bronze. It holds the vendor's actual output and is the evidence for the franchise revenue-share discussion.
  2. Quarantine forward from the detection moment — the gate stops further JED rows entering silver.
  3. Determine the boundary exactly, from bronze rather than by assumption: 
    SELECT DATE(_ingested_at) AS d, MIN(_batch_id), AVG(fare_sar)
FROM bronze.trips WHERE city='JED' AND status='completed'
  AND DATE(_ingested_at) BETWEEN '2026-06-09' AND '2026-06-15'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;   -- the step is between two adjacent batch ids
  4. Correct in silver by MERGE (the M4 skill), normalising the affected window and stamping provenance: 
    MERGE INTO silver.trips t
USING (SELECT trip_id, fare_sar * 100 AS fare_sar_corrected FROM bronze.trips
       WHERE city='JED' AND _batch_id >= :first_affected_batch) s
ON t.trip_id = s.trip_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.fare_sar = s.fare_sar_corrected,
                             t._corrected_by = 'INC-2026-0626',
                             t._corrected_at = current_timestamp();
    Idempotent: re-running updates the same rows to the same values. Auditable: DESCRIBE HISTORY shows the commit; _corrected_by names the incident.
  5. Rebuild the affected gold partitions and re-baseline the pricing model on corrected data. Record the honest metric before and after — do not quietly ship the better number.
  6. Restate the quarterly forecast with the correction disclosed. The SAR 8.7M overstatement was reported to leadership and must be unreported to them.
  7. Close the loop at the boundary: a data contract with the vendor specifying unit and expected distribution, a subscription to their release notes, and the vendor's export version carried as a column in every batch.

docs.title: 8.3 Observability that would have made this a one-day incident
docs.text:
Signal Implementation Detection time Per-city mean-fare drift vs frozen baseline GX expectation, nightly + per-batch < 24 h PSI on fare_sar per city, 10 deciles Nightly job vs frozen baseline, threshold 0.20 < 24 h fare_sar / distance_km reconciliation vs tariff Per-batch expectation < 1 h Vendor export version carried into bronze Contract + ingest change Enables 2-minute root cause Column-level lineage from fare_sar to the pricing model Catalog Turns an alert into an actionable blast radius Model input-distribution monitor on zone_hourly_demand Drift monitor on features, not just on sources Catches it even if the source check is missed

The last row is the defence in depth that CS-11 will make mandatory: monitor the features the model consumes, not only the sources you ingest.

docs.title: 9. What good looks like vs common wrong turns
docs.text: What good looks like Common wrong turn Explains per-expectation why all 7 checks passed Concludes "the tests were bad" without saying which and why Recognises no row-level rule can separate the populations Proposes a tighter range, which then rejects legitimate fares in the other four cities Computes drift per city, and says why aggregation would hide it Computes a platform-wide mean, dilutes 100× in one city to ~19%, and misses it again Freezes and versions a known-good baseline with a named owner Uses a trailing 28-day rolling baseline that absorbs the bug within a fortnight Adds a reconciliation check anchored to the published tariff Relies solely on drift, which can be fooled by a poisoned baseline Quarantines the affected city and promotes the other four Fails the whole batch, converting a quality incident into an availability incident Rejects alert-only explicitly, naming the sim-alertonly failure "Alert the team and let them decide" — corrupt data reaches silver while the email is unread Corrects with MERGE in silver, leaves bronze untouched, stamps _corrected_by Edits bronze to "fix the data", destroying the evidence for the revenue-share discussion Restates the SAR 8.7M forecast and re-baselines the model honestly Fixes the pipeline and lets the old forecast stand Fixes the boundary — data contract with unit and distribution, plus version-in-data Fixes only Muqeem's side, so the next vendor semantic change is equally invisible States the general rule: semantic changes are always type-compatible Treats this as a one-off currency mistake

docs.title: 10. Debrief (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Project P3's last line: 7/7 PASSED. Every test green on the day the data broke. A green suite tells you the checks you wrote passed. It tells you nothing whatsoever about the checks you did not write. Test coverage is a map of your imagination, not of your risk.
  2. Walk the pyramid. Schema → constraint → referential → distribution → reconciliation. Muqeem built the bottom three and stopped. The defect lived in the top two. The bottom three are cheap, fast and reflexively built; the top two require a baseline and a business anchor, which means they require a decision and an owner — which is why they are the ones that do not get built.
  3. PSI 6.81 against a threshold of 0.20. Not a marginal signal. A 34× breach, invisible for two weeks because nobody was computing it. The check is about two hours of work. The incident cost SAR 1.34M plus an SAR 8.7M forecast restatement. Let the class do the ratio out loud.
  4. Segment by the dimension along which change is deployed. Muqeem needed to segment by city because that is how the vendor's change landed. Tomorrow's incident segments by producer_version — and you will meet it on Day 5.
  5. Gates must act, not notify. Quarantine converts an invisible semantic corruption into a visible, bounded operational gap. "No data" asks a question; "wrong data" makes a decision.
  6. Run the fixture live. data/fixtures/currency_shift/trips_2026-06-05_currency_shift.csv — 2,125 of 7,230 rows shifted, mean 37.40 → 3,739.86, in the opposite direction. Show the gate quarantining and the other cities promoting. Then note: your check must be symmetric, because the next one will go the other way.
  7. The course question. "What happens to Masar's AI system if a source silently changes the meaning of a field?" The model degrades over weeks while every operational signal stays green, and the business notices only when a human asks why reality and the dashboard disagree. This is the exact shape of CS-11, which you will investigate tomorrow — with speed_kmh instead of fare_sar, and with the AI, not BI, as the only casualty.

docs.title: 11. The one sentence participants should leave with
docs.text: Row-level validity is not correctness: a 100× unit change passes every schema, null and range check ever written, so a platform that stops at the bottom of the data-quality pyramid is structurally blind to exactly the class of defect that damages AI systems most — and the only cures are a frozen, segmented distribution baseline and a reconciliation anchored to a fact outside the data feed.

docs.title: CS-07 — From Twelve Notebooks to One DAG at "Rakeez" Data
docs.text: Field Value Case ID CS-07 Module M7 — Building the Mini-Lakehouse (Orchestration) Day / Hour Day 5 · Hour 1 (before LAB-07, as the design brief LAB-07 implements) Duration 45 minutes Format Design exercise (wall-based DAG construction + migration plan) Group size 4 per team Deliverable (a) The DAG on the wall — 12 task cards arranged with dependencies drawn; (b) an idempotency ruling for each task (append / merge / replaceWhere / overwrite) with the write mode named; (c) a four-phase incremental migration plan with a reconciliation gate between phases Materials Twelve task cards per team (text in §5 P1, print and cut); large wall space or A1 paper; markers; sticky arrows Facilitator prep 15 min. Print and cut the card decks (12 cards × number of teams). Have the LAB-07 orchestration/dags/masar_medallion.py open but not projected

docs.title: 1. Scenario
docs.text:
"Rakeez" (ركيز) runs the analytics platform for a mobility operator. The platform is twelve notebooks, executed by hand every morning by whoever is available, in an order that lives in one senior engineer's head and, partially, in a wiki page last edited fourteen months ago.

On Sunday 7 June a new hire ran them. She ran them in the order they appear in the folder listing, which is alphabetical. Notebook 08_gold_zone_demand therefore ran before 11_silver_trips_refresh.

No error occurred. Every notebook completed successfully. The gold table was rebuilt from Saturday's silver data.

The 08:00 operations review allocated Sunday's drivers from Saturday's demand map. Nobody noticed until Tuesday.

docs.title: 2. Business context
docs.text:
Item Figure Notebooks executed daily by hand 12 Time to run them, when nothing goes wrong 55 min of an engineer's morning Mornings per year ~250 Engineer-days consumed annually by manual execution ~29 Drivers allocated from the stale demand map on 7 June 3,180 Estimated misallocation cost, one day SAR 340,000 in lost trips and elevated rider wait Days before anyone noticed 2 Engineers on the team 3 People who know the correct execution order 1 (on annual leave in August) Prior incidents of the same class in 12 months (from the wiki's edit history) 4

The SAR 340,000 is the visible cost. The structural cost is the bus factor of one, and the fact that the platform's correctness depends on a human remembering a sequence at 07:00 — which is a control that degrades with fatigue, holidays, turnover, and the alphabet.

docs.title: 3. Technical challenge
docs.text:
Convert an implicit, human-ordered, non-idempotent sequence into an explicit, ordered, idempotent, recoverable pipeline — without a rewrite. The logic in the twelve notebooks is correct and battle-tested; it is the execution model that is broken.

Four properties are missing and must be added:

  1. Explicit ordering — dependencies declared in code, not remembered.
  2. Idempotency — every task safe to re-run, so recovery is "run it again" rather than "reason about what already happened."
  3. Observability — a failed or skipped step must be visible; today a stale table looks identical to a fresh one.
  4. Recoverability — a failure at step 9 must not require manual reconstruction of steps 1–8.

docs.title: 4. Constraints
docs.text:
• The logic must be preserved, and preservation must be proved by reconciliation, not asserted. The business will not accept "we rewrote it and it looks right."
  • The team is three engineers with a full backlog; no capacity for a big-bang rewrite.
  • Runs must be reproducible by anyone, including someone hired next month.
  • Must be recoverable after a mid-pipeline failure without a senior engineer's intervention.
  • The migration must not stop the daily platform for a single day.

docs.title: P1 — The twelve notebooks (print one set of cards per team; cut on the lines)
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 01_ingest_trips_csv                                                          │
│ Reads data/raw/trips_YYYY-MM-DD.csv  ->  bronze.trips                        │
│ Write: df.write.mode("append")                                               │
│ Reads nothing else. Adds _ingested_at, _source_file, _batch_id.              │

docs.title: P2 — The wiki page (last edited 2025-04-19)
docs.text:
Morning run order 1. Run the four ingest notebooks (01–04). 03 can be skipped on weekends. 2. Run 11 and 12 (silver). Note: 11 must come after 05 or the quarantine table is stale. 3. Run 06 and 07. 4. Then the gold ones (08, 09, 10). Order between them does not matter 10 must be last, see incident 2024-11-02. 5. If anything fails, ask Faisal.

Three failure signatures in one page: a conditional ("can be skipped on weekends") that a tired human will get wrong; a struck-through correction encoding an incident nobody documented properly; and a named person as the recovery procedure.

12/12 OK. Twelve green checkmarks on a run that produced a stale demand map, a stale driver-daily mart, and stale ETA features. Read this line aloud in the debrief and pause. A pipeline with no dependency model cannot distinguish success from disaster, because it has no concept of what a task was supposed to read.

docs.title: P4 — What happened when they tried to fix it by re-running
docs.text:
At 09:40 on 7 June, once the staleness was suspected, an engineer re-ran 08_gold_zone_demand:

09:41  08_gold_zone_demand  OK  720 rows inserted
-- gold.zone_hourly_demand now contains 1,440 rows for 2026-06-07
-- every hour of every city appears TWICE, with different values
-- the dashboard's SUM() doubles; demand appears to have spiked 100%

INSERT INTO is not idempotent. The attempted fix made it worse, and the second failure was louder than the first — a doubled demand map is at least visible. Note for the class: three of the twelve notebooks use INSERT INTO at an aggregate grain, so this trap is armed in three places.

docs.title: P5 — Cost of an outage under the current model
docs.text: Value Mean time to detect a stale/incorrect run 2 days Mean time to repair (identify affected tables, rebuild in order, verify) 3.5 hours Requires the senior engineer Yes, in 4 of 4 past incidents Incidents in 12 months 4 Annual cost of incidents (misallocation + repair) ~SAR 1,100,000 Annual cost of manual execution (29 engineer-days) ~SAR 190,000

docs.title: 6. Facilitation script (minute-by-minute)
docs.text: Min Activity Facilitator does Watch for 0–4 Frame. Read the scenario. Project P3 and read 12/12 OK aloud. Ask: "This run destroyed a day of dispatch. What in this log tells you that?" The answer: nothing does. Write "green is not correct" on the board. Teams that blame the new hire. Redirect immediately and firmly: she followed the only ordering visible to her. 4–7 Distribute card decks (P1) and P2. Give each team wall space. Physically hand over the cut cards — the tactile step matters for engagement. — 7–20 Round 1 — Build the DAG. Arrange all 12 cards; draw every dependency arrow. Circulate. One question: "Point at the edge that would have prevented 7 June." Teams that arrange in numeric order without reading the card bodies. Teams that forget 05 → 11. 20–24 Cross-check. Each team walks to the next team's wall and marks, in a different colour, any edge they believe is missing or wrong. Enforce silence during the walk; disputes are resolved at minute 24, not during. The most-disputed edge is 05_quality_gate → 11_silver_trips, which is exactly the right thing to argue about. 24–34 Round 2 — Idempotency ruling per task. For each of the 12 cards write the correct write mode: append / merge / replaceWhere / overwrite. Then reveal P4. Hand out P4 at minute 28, mid-round. Teams that had left INSERT INTO on the gold tasks will visibly react. Teams that answer "overwrite" for everything. Ask what that does to bronze.trips history. 34–41 Round 3 — Migration plan. Four phases, with a reconciliation gate between each. Constraint: the platform runs every day throughout. Ask each team: "Which phase delivers value first, and what would you cut if you had two weeks instead of eight?" Big-bang plans. Also plans that begin with a rewrite of the notebook logic. 41–45 Debrief. §10. Hand into LAB-07. Close on §11. The bridge: "In the next hour you build this DAG for Masar, then you break it and watch gold get held back." —

docs.title: 7. Discussion questions with model answers
docs.text:
Q1. Why is "run these in order" a latent production incident?

Model answer. Because it stores a correctness-critical invariant in the least durable medium available: human memory, and then relies on that memory being accessed correctly under the worst conditions — early morning, time pressure, staff turnover, holidays, and an incident already in progress.

Four properties make it a latent incident rather than merely a risk:

  • The failure is silent. Running gold before silver produces no error, because the gold job reads a table that exists and contains data. It is yesterday's data, and no component in the system has any way to know that was not the intention.
  • The failure is delayed. Two days elapsed. The blast radius (drivers allocated, trips lost, riders waiting) had fully materialised before anyone knew.
  • It degrades rather than breaks. Four incidents in twelve months, each survived, each reinforcing the belief that the system works. Systems that fail loudly get fixed; systems that fail quietly get normalised.
  • It is anti-correlated with capability. The senior engineer's competence is what makes the arrangement viable, which is precisely what removes the pressure to fix it. The wiki page's step 5 — "ask Faisal" — is a single point of failure written down as a procedure.

The sharp formulation for the board: an implicit dependency is a dependency that the computer cannot check. The moment the ordering exists only in a person, the system has no ability to distinguish a correct run from an incorrect one — which is exactly what 12/12 OK in P3 proves.

Q2. Which property — ordering, idempotency, or observability — would have prevented the stale dashboard, and how?

Model answer. Prevention, detection, and recovery are three different jobs and each property does one:

  • Ordering prevents it. A declared dependency 11_silver_trips_refresh >> 08_gold_zone_demand makes the 7 June run impossible. The scheduler will not start 08 until 11 has succeeded. This is the direct answer.
  • Observability would have detected it. Even with the wrong order, a freshness assertion on the gold task's input ("silver.trips must contain rows with trip_date = {{ ds }}") fails the task loudly at 07:14 instead of producing a green tick. Detection time falls from 2 days to 2 minutes.
  • Idempotency would have made the repair safe. P4 shows what happened without it: the attempted fix doubled the mart. With replaceWhere on the date partition, re-running 08 after 11 is a complete, correct, one-command repair.

The answer teams should converge on: ordering is necessary but not sufficient. Orchestration guarantees a task runs after its declared upstream succeeded; it cannot guarantee the upstream produced today's data — a task can succeed while writing nothing. That gap is closed by data-aware assertions on inputs, not by the DAG topology. Teams that say "ordering, and that is enough" should be asked: "What if 11_silver_trips_refresh succeeds but the source file was missing, so it merged zero rows?" The DAG is green; gold is stale again.

So: ordering + input freshness assertions + idempotent writes — the three together, each doing a different job.

Q3. How do you migrate incrementally without a big-bang rewrite?

Model answer. The principle: change the execution model first, the code last, and prove equivalence at every step. The twelve notebooks contain correct logic; the value is in orchestrating them, not in rewriting them.

Phase Duration What changes Risk Reconciliation gate before proceeding 1. Wrap, do not rewrite 1 week Each notebook becomes a parameterised, callable task (papermill, a %run, or a thin main(ds)). Zero logic changes. The DAG runs them in the wiki's order. Very low DAG output must be byte-identical to a manual run on the same day. Run both for 5 days. 2. Declare real dependencies 1 week Replace the wiki's linear order with the true dependency graph. Tasks that can run in parallel now do. Add input freshness assertions. Low Same outputs; wall-clock time drops (~55 min → ~18 min). The 7 June failure mode is now impossible. 3. Make every task idempotent 2–3 weeks Convert INSERT INTO → MERGE / replaceWhere per §8.2, one task at a time, each with its own reconciliation. Make the quality gate exit non-zero on integrity failures. Medium — this is the only phase touching write behaviour Per task: run twice, assert row counts identical and numTargetRowsUpdated = 0 on the second run. 4. Operationalise 1 week Retries with backoff, SLA alerting, OPTIMIZE/VACUUM as DAG tasks, backfill by date parameter, on-call runbook that says "re-run the DAG" and nothing else. Low A deliberate kill-and-restart drill: fail a task mid-run, re-run the whole DAG, assert a clean identical state.

Two rules to state explicitly: - Never change orchestration and logic in the same commit. If output changes, you must know which of the two caused it. - Phase 1 delivers most of the value. After one week, the run is one command, reproducible by anyone, with a log. The bus factor of one is already gone. Teams proposing an eight-week plan whose first value lands in week six have mis-sequenced it.

Q4. What does "one command runs the platform" buy the team culturally, not just technically?

Model answer. This question is not soft; it is where the durable value is, and it is worth protecting time for.

  • It removes fear. Today nobody re-runs anything, because re-running might double a mart (P4). Fear of re-running is why the 7 June error sat for two days: investigating meant touching production. When every task is idempotent, investigation becomes free, and free investigation is the precondition for a team that fixes things early.
  • It distributes competence. The new hire's failure was an onboarding failure, not a personal one. A DAG is executable documentation: the dependency graph is the wiki page, and it cannot go fourteen months out of date because the platform runs from it.
  • It converts heroism into engineering. "Ask Faisal" is a procedure that fails in August. On-call becomes a role a junior can hold, which is what makes on-call sustainable and what lets the senior engineer work on something new.
  • It changes what the team argues about. Time currently spent reconstructing what ran, in what order, from which data, becomes time spent on the actual questions — grain, feature correctness, cost. The 29 engineer-days per year are the smaller half of that gain.
  • It makes incidents blameless by construction. After the migration there is no ordering for a human to get wrong, so an incident cannot be attributed to a person's memory. Systems that make individual error impossible are the only systems in which blameless post-mortems are honest rather than polite. (Point forward: CS-11's post-incident review depends on exactly this.)

docs.title: 8.1 The correct DAG
docs.text:
┌── 01_ingest_trips ──┐
                 │                      │

                 │                      │  │
                 ├── 03_ingest_drivers ─┤  │
                 │                      │  │
                 └── 04_ingest_payments ┘  │
                          │               │
                          ▼               │
                 05_quality_gate_trips     │      (must FAIL the run on integrity defects)
                          │               │
            ┌─────────────┼───────────────┘
            ▼             ▼               ▼
   11_silver_trips  12_silver_vehicle  06_silver_drivers   07_silver_payments
            │        _positions │              │                   │
            │             │     │              │                   │
            ├─────────────┴─────┼──────────────┤                   │
            ▼                   ▼              ▼                   │
   08_gold_zone_demand   10_gold_eta_features  09_gold_driver_daily│
            │                   │              │                   │
            └───────────────────┴──────────────┴───────────────────┘
                                ▼
