Dependency edges that matter and are commonly missed: - 05_quality_gate → 11_silver_trips — silver must not be built from a batch that failed integrity checks. This is the edge teams argue about; the argument is the lesson. - 12_silver_vehicle_positions → 08_gold_zone_demand and → 10_gold_eta_features — both gold marts consume vehicle positions, not just trips. - 06_silver_drivers → 09_gold_driver_daily — the driver dimension must be current before the daily mart joins it. - The four ingests are mutually independent and should run in parallel; the wiki's linear order was never required. - 13_maintenance is a new task, not one of the twelve. Compaction and vacuum belong in the pipeline (CS-02's lesson), not in a runbook.

docs.title: 8.2 Idempotency ruling per task (deliverable b)
docs.text:
# Task Current Correct Why 01 ingest_trips append append Bronze is append-only and immutable. Re-run grows history; downstream dedups. Correct as is. 02 ingest_gps append append Same. 03 ingest_drivers overwrite overwrite (or SCD-2 merge) A full daily dimension snapshot; overwrite is idempotent. Note the trade-off: overwrite loses driver history — acceptable only because Delta time travel retains it. 04 ingest_payments append append Same as 01. 05 quality_gate exit 0 always exit non-zero on integrity failures Not a write-mode issue; a gate issue. A gate that always exits 0 is a log line. 06 silver_drivers overwrite overwrite Full rebuild of a 3,450-row dimension; idempotent and cheap. 07 silver_payments INSERT INTO MERGE on payment_id Re-run currently doubles rows. 08 gold_zone_demand INSERT INTO replaceWhere date = {{ ds }} Grain is city × date × hour; the whole date partition is deterministically rebuilt. This is the task that broke on 7 June and again in P4. 09 gold_driver_daily INSERT INTO MERGE on (driver_id, date) Grain is driver × day; late trips update prior days, so merge beats replaceWhere here. 10 gold_eta_features overwrite (whole table) replaceWhere date = {{ ds }} Whole-table overwrite is idempotent but rebuilds all history nightly — correct and wasteful. Partition-scoped replace is both. 11 silver_trips MERGE on trip_id MERGE on trip_id, 3-day lookback Already correct — this is CS-03's pattern. 12 silver_vehicle_positions MERGE on event_id MERGE on event_id Already correct. 13 maintenance (does not exist) OPTIMIZE + VACUUM, idempotent by nature New task.

Summary for the board: three tasks (07, 08, 09) are actively unsafe to re-run, and they are all at aggregate grain — which is exactly where a doubled row is least visible and most damaging.

docs.title: 8.3 The reconciliation gate (how equivalence is proved)
docs.text:
Between every phase, and before cutover:

-- for each table, for the same business date, old pipeline vs new
SELECT 'gold.zone_hourly_demand' AS tbl, COUNT(*) AS rows,
       SUM(demand_count) AS total, MIN(hour_ts), MAX(hour_ts)
FROM   gold.zone_hourly_demand_NEW WHERE date = '2026-06-07'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'gold.zone_hourly_demand', COUNT(*), SUM(demand_count), MIN(hour_ts), MAX(hour_ts)
FROM   gold.zone_hourly_demand_OLD WHERE date = '2026-06-07';
-- assert: identical on every column. Any difference is investigated, never explained away.

Run in parallel for five business days including a Friday — Friday's demand curve differs materially from Sunday–Thursday's, so a Friday in the parallel run is a genuine test rather than a repetition.

docs.title: 9. What good looks like vs common wrong turns
docs.text: What good looks like Common wrong turn Builds the DAG from the card bodies (what each reads and writes) Arranges cards in numeric order, reproducing the 7 June bug on the wall Includes the 05_quality_gate → 11_silver_trips edge and defends it Treats the quality gate as a side-branch that reports rather than blocks Runs the four ingests in parallel Keeps the wiki's linear order, which was never a dependency Adds a maintenance task to the DAG Leaves OPTIMIZE/VACUUM in a runbook, so it happens until it does not Names a specific write mode per task and can say why "Make everything idempotent" with no per-task mode Distinguishes replaceWhere (deterministic partition rebuild) from MERGE (late-arriving updates) Uses MERGE everywhere, including where a partition rebuild is simpler and cheaper Adds input freshness assertions, recognising ordering alone is insufficient Assumes a green DAG means fresh data — a task can succeed writing zero rows Phases the migration so phase 1 delivers value in week one, with zero logic change Big-bang rewrite, or "first we modernise the code" Separates orchestration changes from logic changes in different commits Changes both at once, then cannot attribute an output difference Runs a parallel reconciliation including a Friday Validates once on a quiet Tuesday Treats the new hire's error as an onboarding/system failure Adds "read the wiki carefully" to onboarding Makes on-call recovery "re-run the DAG" Writes a longer runbook

docs.title: 10. Debrief (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Read 12/12 OK from P3 aloud. Every task succeeded and the day was destroyed. A system with no dependency model has no concept of what a task was supposed to read, so it cannot distinguish success from disaster. Green is a statement about exit codes, not about data.
  2. P4 is the second lesson and the more expensive one. The attempt to fix it doubled the mart. Without idempotency, your recovery procedure is itself a risk, which is why nobody re-runs anything, which is why problems sit for two days. Idempotency does not merely enable recovery — it makes investigation free, and free investigation is what makes a team fast.
  3. The wiki page is the artefact to remember. A conditional, a struck-through correction encoding an undocumented incident, and a named person as the recovery procedure. Every mature platform has this page. A DAG is that page, made executable and unable to go stale.
  4. Do not blame the new hire. She followed the only ordering the system exposed. The alphabet was the most authoritative source of truth available to her, and it was wrong. When a system's correctness depends on a person not making an obvious mistake, the system is the defect.
  5. Hand into LAB-07. "You will build this DAG for Masar, trigger it once, inject a silver failure, watch gold get held back rather than build stale, then re-run the whole DAG and get a clean identical state."
  6. The course question. "What happens to Masar's AI system if the pipeline runs out of order?" gold.eta_features is built from yesterday's silver.trips, so feature_ts claims today while the values describe yesterday. The model serves confidently wrong predictions, offline evaluation looks fine because the same stale features are used for both, and — as on Day 5 — nothing in BI shows a thing.

docs.title: 11. The one sentence participants should leave with
docs.text: An execution order that lives in a person's head is an invariant the computer cannot check, so a run can report 12/12 OK while producing a stale platform — declare the dependencies in code, assert freshness on every input, and make every task safe to re-run, because the point of idempotency is not elegance but that it makes investigation free.

docs.title: CS-08 — The ETA Model That Won Offline and Lost Live at "Wojhah"
docs.text: Field Value Case ID CS-08 Module M8 — Serving Gold to AI and BI Day / Hour Day 5 · Hour 4 (after LAB-08's leakage drill; immediately before CS-11) Duration 45 minutes Format Investigation → design exercise Group size 3–4 per team Deliverable (a) A per-feature verdict on the eight features in P3 (valid / leaking / unavailable online) with the reason; (b) the corrected definition of the leaking feature; (c) the CI check that would block the whole class of bug; (d) three sentences to the stakeholder who was told R²=0.93 and must now be told 0.78 Materials Evidence pack §5 per team (6 pages); ACT-09 card deck available as an extension for fast teams Facilitator prep 15 min. Rehearse the "why does leakage inflate the offline metric" explanation with a concrete row — the mechanism must be shown, not asserted

docs.title: 1. Scenario
docs.text:
"Wojhah" (وجهة) built a new ETA model for its ride-hailing app. In offline evaluation on a held-out month it scored R² = 0.93, against the incumbent rule-based heuristic's 0.61. The review was celebratory. The model shipped in a 20% A/B test.

After three weeks live, the A/B readout is in. The new model's mean absolute ETA error is 4.9 minutes. The heuristic's is 4.8 minutes. The model is, within noise, no better than the thing it replaced — and it cost a quarter of a data-science team's capacity.

The product director has asked, in a written message that has been forwarded widely: "Why should I believe any offline number your team ever produces again?"

docs.title: 2. Business context
docs.text:
Item Figure Offline R² claimed at review 0.93 Offline R² after the leak is removed 0.78 Incumbent heuristic R² 0.61 Live MAE, new model 4.9 min Live MAE, heuristic 4.8 min Data-science capacity spent 1 quarter, 3 people Rider cancellations attributable to ETA error > 5 min 8.4% of quoted trips Modelled annual value of a 1-minute MAE improvement SAR 12,400,000 Value actually delivered SAR 0 Online feature-lookup latency budget p99 ≤ 50 ms

The honest model at R² = 0.78 is genuinely better than the heuristic's 0.61 and would deliver real value. The tragedy is not that the model was bad; it is that the inflated number destroyed the credibility needed to ship the good one. Make sure the room reaches this — it changes what "the fix" means.

docs.title: 3. Technical challenge
docs.text:
Diagnose why offline and live diverge and fix it structurally, so the entire class of bug cannot recur — not with a patch to one feature.

Two distinct defects are present and teams must separate them:

  1. Temporal leakage — at least one feature is computed with information that would not exist at prediction time.
  2. Offline/online skew — the online serving path re-implements feature logic independently, so the value the model sees in production differs from the value it was trained on, even for non-leaking features.

Both produce "great offline, mediocre live," and the remedies are different. A team that finds only the first will fix the metric and still ship a model that behaves differently in production.

docs.title: 4. Constraints
docs.text:
• Cannot retrain endlessly — one retrain cycle is budgeted.
  • The fix must generalise: prevent the class, not the instance. A code review comment is not a fix.
  • The online path must stay under p99 ≤ 50 ms.
  • PDPL applies: no raw rider_id may reach the online store or BI (CONVENTIONS.md).
  • The corrected metric must be published downward, honestly, to the same audience that heard 0.93.

docs.title: P1 — The offline evaluation, as presented at review
docs.text:
model: eta_gbm_v3     trained 2026-05-02   eval window 2026-05-03 .. 2026-06-01
                      split: random 80/20 on rows
R2 ......... 0.9312
MAE ........ 1.41 min
p90 abs err. 2.9 min
baseline (heuristic): R2 0.6104, MAE 4.77 min

Two defects are visible in the header alone before any feature is examined. split: random 80/20 on rows — a random split on a temporal problem puts trips from 30 May in the training set and trips from 3 May in the test set, so the model is evaluated partly on its own future. And eval window overlaps the training window entirely. Ask the room to find these before handing out P3; roughly a third of teams will.

docs.title: P2 — The live A/B readout
docs.text:
experiment: eta_gbm_v3 @ 20%    2026-06-08 .. 2026-06-28    n = 411,882 quoted trips
                       control (heuristic)   treatment (eta_gbm_v3)
MAE (min)              4.81                  4.93
p90 abs err (min)      9.2                   9.4
rider cancel rate      8.3%                  8.6%

Offline MAE 1.41 min; live MAE 4.93 min. A 3.5× degradation between the evaluation and the world. That ratio is the signature of leakage — not of overfitting, which degrades gently and symmetrically.

docs.title: P3 — The feature table (gold.eta_features) as built for training
docs.text:
# Column Definition as implemented Team verdict 1 pickup_zone_id Zone of pickup, known at request 2 dropoff_zone_id Requested destination, known at request 3 hour_of_day hour(feature_ts) in Asia/Riyadh 4 day_of_week dayofweek(feature_ts) 5 rolling_zone_demand_15m COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY pickup_zone_id ORDER BY feature_ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 15 MINUTES PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) 6 rolling_avg_speed_10m AVG(payload.speed_kmh) over the last 10 min in the pickup zone, from silver.vehicle_positions 7 driver_recent_trip_count COUNT(*) of that driver's trips in the current hour 8 historical_route_duration Median duration_min for (pickup_zone, dropoff_zone, hour_of_day) over the preceding 28 days — weather_condition Weather at feature_ts, joined from weather_hourly — distance_km Metered distance — label_actual_duration_min The label

Hand this out with the verdict column blank. It is the case's core exercise.

docs.title: P4 — The single query that exposes the leak
docs.text:
-- for one trip, what does each feature "see" relative to prediction time?
SELECT trip_id,
       feature_ts,                             -- when the prediction is made
       pickup_ts,
       dropoff_ts,                             -- when the trip ENDED
       driver_recent_trip_count,
       rolling_zone_demand_15m
FROM   gold.eta_features
WHERE  trip_id = 'TRP-20260605-0004417';

trip_id                | feature_ts          | pickup_ts           | dropoff_ts          | driver_recent_trip_count | rolling_zone_demand_15m
TRP-20260605-0004417   | 2026-06-05 08:12:00 | 2026-06-05 08:12:00 | 2026-06-05 08:41:33 | 6                        | 84

The prediction is made at 08:12. driver_recent_trip_count = 6 counts the driver's trips in the hour 08:00–09:00, which includes trips that started at 08:31 and 08:52 — after the prediction. A driver who goes on to complete many trips in an hour is a driver working a fast, dense zone, and the model has learned to read the future from the count. The feature is a partial answer to the question being asked.

Make participants notice the second-order subtlety: rolling_zone_demand_15m uses CURRENT ROW, which is arguably correct (the current row is the prediction moment) but silently includes any row with an identical feature_ts — and, more importantly, its online implementation may not respect the same boundary. This is one of the two genuinely arguable features and it deserves discussion, not a verdict.

docs.title: P5 — The online serving path
docs.text:
# services/eta_online/features.py   (written by the platform team, February 2026)
def get_features(trip_request):
    z = trip_request.pickup_zone_id
    return {
      "rolling_zone_demand_15m": redis.get(f"masar:features:zone:{z}:demand_15m"),
      "rolling_avg_speed_10m":   redis.get(f"masar:features:zone:{z}:speed_10m"),
      "driver_recent_trip_count": pg.query(                       # <-- different source
          "SELECT count(*) FROM trips WHERE driver_id=%s AND started_at > now() - interval '1 hour'",
          trip_request.driver_id),
      "historical_route_duration": pg.query(                      # <-- different logic
          "SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY duration_min) FROM trips "
          "WHERE pickup_zone_id=%s AND dropoff_zone_id=%s AND started_at > now() - interval '30 days'", z, d),
      "weather_condition": weather_api.current(z),                # <-- third source
    }

Three different sources for five features, none of them the table the model was trained from. Note the specific mismatches: - driver_recent_trip_count online is a trailing hour (correct!); offline it was the calendar hour (leaking). The online value is systematically lower than the training value — the model receives a feature whose distribution it has never seen. - historical_route_duration online uses 30 days; offline 28 days. Small, but a silent, permanent, unmonitored difference. - weather_condition online comes from a live API; offline from weather_hourly. Different vocabularies are possible ("Clear" vs clear).

docs.title: P6 — Offline/online consistency check, run after the fact
docs.text:
keys compared: 10,000 recent trips
feature                      | match | mismatch | mean abs delta
rolling_zone_demand_15m      | 9,942 |       58 | 0.4
rolling_avg_speed_10m        | 9,988 |       12 | 0.1
driver_recent_trip_count     | 1,204 |    8,796 | 2.7      <-- 88% mismatch
historical_route_duration    | 6,610 |    3,390 | 1.9
weather_condition            | 9,301 |      699 | n/a

88% of production requests received a driver_recent_trip_count the model had never been trained on. This check took twenty minutes to write and did not exist.

docs.title: 6. Facilitation script (minute-by-minute)
docs.text: Min Activity Facilitator does Watch for 0–3 Frame. Project P1 and P2 side by side: offline MAE 1.41, live MAE 4.93. Read the product director's message aloud. Write "offline 1.41 → live 4.93" on the board. Teams that say "overfitting." Ask: does overfitting produce a 3.5× gap? (No — it degrades gently. This gap has a mechanism.) 3–6 P1 only. "Two defects are visible in this header before you see a single feature. Find them." 90 seconds, no discussion. Random split on temporal data; train/eval window overlap. 6–8 Distribute P3–P6. State the four deliverables. — — 8–20 Round 1 — Per-feature verdict. Every one of the eight rows gets valid / leaking / unavailable-online, plus a reason. Circulate with the single question: "Could this feature have been known at 08:12?" Say nothing else. Teams that mark features valid because "it's in the historical table." The table is not the question; the timestamp is. 20–25 Board it. Build the verdict table publicly. Argue features 5 and 8 properly — they are genuinely arguable. Do not resolve 5 and 8 quickly. Ambiguity here is the real skill. Teams that want a rule that decides every case mechanically. There isn't one; there is a question. 25–30 Reveal P6. The 88% mismatch. Ask: "You fixed the leak. Would the live number improve?" (No — the online path still sends a different feature.) This is the moment the second defect lands. Let it land hard. 30–38 Round 2 — Structural fix + CI check + the three sentences. Push on CI: "Your check must fail a pull request. Write the assertion." Fixes phrased as process ("we'll review features more carefully"). Reject firmly: a process is not a check. 38–43 Read the three sentences aloud. Two teams. The room plays the product director. Challenge the weakest one live and rewrite it together. Sentences that hide the correction in passive voice. 43–45 Debrief. §10. Close on §11 and hand into CS-11. The bridge line: "Every feature you just certified as valid assumed the data was correct. Next case: what if it isn't?" —

docs.title: 7. Discussion questions with model answers
docs.text:
Q1. Why did the leaking feature score so well offline?

Model answer. Because driver_recent_trip_count computed over the calendar hour contains a compressed answer to the question being asked.

The mechanism, concretely, using P4's row: the prediction is made at 08:12 and the feature counts the driver's trips in 08:00–09:00 — six of them, several starting after 08:12. What makes a driver complete six trips in one hour? Short trips, in a dense zone, with fast traffic. Exactly the conditions that make this trip short. The feature therefore correlates strongly with the label, not because it predicts duration but because it is partially computed from the same future that produced the label.

The model, quite correctly, weights it heavily. Offline it is rewarded for doing so, because the evaluation rows also carry future-contaminated features. Live, at 08:12, that future does not exist: the online path can only count trips up to 08:12, which for this driver is two, not six. The model receives a value from a distribution it never saw, applies a large learned weight to it, and produces a confidently wrong number.

Two amplifiers made it worse: - The random 80/20 split put 30 May trips in training and 3 May trips in test. With a temporal problem, the model gets to see the future in the most literal sense. A temporal split (train ≤ date T, test > T) is mandatory, and it alone would have dropped the reported R² substantially. - Train/eval window overlap (P1: trained 2026-05-02, eval 2026-05-03..06-01) means the evaluation is not held out in time at all.

The general rule to write down: a feature that is suspiciously predictive is suspicious. A jump from 0.61 to 0.93 on a problem where the dominant term is traffic — which nobody can observe in advance — should have triggered an investigation at review, not applause. Treat an unexpectedly good offline metric as a bug report until proven otherwise.

Q2. How does serving the same feature table offline and online prevent recurrence?

Model answer. Because it removes the possibility of divergence rather than the occurrence of it.

Today there are two implementations of every feature (P5): one in SQL for training, one in Python/SQL for serving, written by different teams at different times against different sources. Two implementations of one definition is CS-01's two-tier problem, arriving in the feature layer. They will diverge, and P6 shows they already have — 88% on one feature, 34% on another, silently, for months.

The fix is materialise, do not re-implement:

gold.eta_features  (computed ONCE, in the batch pipeline, point-in-time correct)
        ├──► training set        (read directly)
        └──► publish job ──► Redis  masar:features:zone:{zone_id}   (a COPY of the same values)

The online store becomes a cache of computed values, not a second computation. Serving reads a value; it never derives one. Consequences:

  • Correctness by construction — there is only one definition, so there is nothing to keep in sync.
  • The p99 ≤ 50 ms budget becomes easy — a Redis GET is ~1–3 ms, versus P5's live Postgres percentile query, which is both slow and a different answer.
  • Feature changes propagate atomically — change the definition, the next publish updates both consumers.
  • PDPL is enforceable at one boundary — the publish job is the single place where rider_id can be dropped and zone-level aggregates emitted, satisfying "never emit raw rider_id into BI or the online store."

The residual risk is staleness, not skew: the online copy is as fresh as the last publish. That is a monitorable, bounded, honest failure mode — publish lag — and it replaces an unmonitorable one. Make teams state the publish cadence and the staleness SLA explicitly.

Q3. What automated check catches leakage before a model ships?

Model answer. Three checks, all runnable in CI, in increasing order of power:

(1) A point-in-time assertion on the feature table. Every feature row must be derivable from data whose timestamp is <= feature_ts. Implemented as a leakage lint over the feature SQL: any window function whose frame extends to CURRENT ROW or FOLLOWING, any join to a table on a key without a <= feature_ts predicate, any aggregate over a calendar bucket containing feature_ts, fails the build.

# ci/leakage_lint.py — fails the PR
FORBIDDEN = [
  r"RANGE BETWEEN .* AND CURRENT ROW",       # includes the prediction instant
  r"(UNBOUNDED|\d+\s+\w+)\s+FOLLOWING",       # explicit future
  r"date_trunc\('hour',\s*feature_ts\)",      # calendar bucket containing the prediction
]
# every feature must instead be bounded: ... PRECEDING AND INTERVAL '1' SECOND PRECEDING

(2) A label-shuffle / future-ablation test. Recompute each feature using only data strictly before feature_ts and compare the value to what the pipeline produced. Any feature whose value changes is reading the future. This is stronger than the lint because it tests behaviour rather than syntax, and it catches leakage that arrives through a join three models deep.

(3) The offline/online consistency check (P6), run continuously in production. For a sample of served requests, log the feature vector actually used and compare it to the offline table for the same key and timestamp. Alert on any mismatch rate above a threshold. This is the check that would have caught the second defect, which the leakage lint cannot see at all.

State the principle: (1) and (2) protect against leakage; (3) protects against skew. They are different bugs with the same symptom, and you need all three. Add the process check that costs nothing: a temporal train/test split enforced in the training harness, not chosen per project.

Q4. How do you rebuild stakeholder trust after an inflated metric is corrected downward?

Model answer. The correction is the easy part; the credibility is the deliverable. Four moves:

  1. Say the number first, plainly, in the active voice. "Our reported R² of 0.93 was wrong. The correct figure is 0.78. We found the cause." Not "the metric has been revised" and not a paragraph of context before the number. Burying the correction is what makes the next number unbelievable.
  2. Explain the mechanism in one sentence a non-specialist can repeat. "One input counted trips the driver had not yet taken, so the model was partly reading the answer." A stakeholder who can re-explain your bug to their own boss is a stakeholder who has forgiven it.
  3. Publish what changes so it cannot recur, and make it checkable. "Every feature is now checked in CI against 'could this have been known at prediction time'; the build fails otherwise. Training and serving now read the same table." An automated gate is a promise a stakeholder can audit; a commitment to be more careful is not.
  4. Re-anchor on the honest comparison and the real decision. 0.78 against the heuristic's 0.61 is a material improvement worth an estimated SAR 12.4M/yr if it holds live. Ask for a re-run of the A/B with the corrected model, with the success criterion agreed in advance, in live MAE — never again in offline R².

And the institutional point, which is the one worth the most: the offline metric is not the deliverable; the live outcome is. Wojhah's review celebrated an offline number as if it were a result. The fix is to make the A/B, not the evaluation notebook, the gate for the celebration.

Q5 (reserve, or use ACT-09 as the extension). Which features in P3 are genuinely arguable?

Model answer. Two.

Feature 5, rolling_zone_demand_15m. The frame RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 15 MINUTES PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW includes the prediction instant itself. Argument for valid: at 08:12 the zone's demand over 07:57–08:12 is observable; nothing from the future is included. Argument for leaking: rows sharing an identical feature_ts are included, and — the practical concern — the count includes this very request, so the feature is partly a function of the event being predicted; and if any upstream row has a feature_ts assigned at completion rather than request, the frame silently admits the future. Verdict: valid in principle, fragile in practice. Make it robust by bounding the frame to INTERVAL 1 SECOND PRECEDING and by asserting that feature_ts = pickup_ts for every row. The discipline is to remove the ambiguity, not to win the argument.

Feature 8, historical_route_duration. A 28-day median over prior trips on the same route. Argument for valid: it is strictly historical, and it is the single most useful feature in the model. Argument for leaking: if the 28-day window is computed relative to the training run date rather than each row's feature_ts, then a trip on 3 May receives a median computed from trips through 1 June — a classic and very common point-in-time violation that a lint on the SQL text will not catch. Verdict: valid if and only if the window is anchored per row to feature_ts; leaking if anchored to the job's run date. You cannot tell from the definition as written in P3, which is the lesson: a feature definition that does not state its anchor is not a definition.

Note also that feature 8 is the one most likely to be unavailable online at acceptable latency if computed live (P5 does exactly this, with a live percentile query) — which is why it must be materialised, not re-derived.

docs.title: 8.1 Per-feature verdicts (deliverable a) — facilitator key
docs.text:
# Column Verdict Reason 1 pickup_zone_id Valid Present in the request itself 2 dropoff_zone_id Valid Requested destination, stated at request time 3 hour_of_day Valid Derived from feature_ts; deterministic and known 4 day_of_week Valid Same 5 rolling_zone_demand_15m Arguable → valid if bounded Frame must exclude the current instant; feature_ts must equal pickup_ts. See §7 Q5 6 rolling_avg_speed_10m Valid Strictly trailing 10 minutes of vehicle positions. (And the feature CS-11 will corrupt — flag this for tomorrow.) 7 driver_recent_trip_count LEAKING Calendar-hour bucket containing feature_ts; includes trips that start after the prediction 8 historical_route_duration Arguable → valid if per-row anchored Must be a 28-day window ending at each row's feature_ts, not at the job's run date — weather_condition Valid, but skew-prone Offline from weather_hourly, online from a live API — different vocabularies, must be materialised — distance_km Valid Estimated route distance is known at request. (Note: metered distance is NOT — if the pipeline uses metered distance_km from the completed trip, this becomes LEAKING. Ask the room.)

The distance_km note is the best trap in the pack. gold.eta_features.distance_km sourced from silver.trips.distance_km is the metered distance, known only at dropoff. Sourced from the routing engine's estimate at request time, it is valid. Same column name, opposite verdict, depending on provenance — which is the whole point of lineage.

docs.title: 8.2 The corrected feature (deliverable b)
docs.text:
-- WRONG (leaking): calendar hour containing the prediction
COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY driver_id, date_trunc('hour', feature_ts))  AS driver_recent_trip_count

-- RIGHT: strictly trailing window, closed before the prediction instant
COUNT(*) OVER (
    PARTITION BY driver_id
    ORDER BY feature_ts
    RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 60 MINUTES PRECEDING
              AND INTERVAL  1 SECOND  PRECEDING
) AS driver_recent_trip_count

Both are one line. One is a quarter of wasted capacity and a credibility crisis; the other is not. That is the module in a diff.

docs.title: 8.3 The structural fix
docs.text:
silver.trips ┐
        silver.vehicle_positions├──► gold.eta_features ─┬──► training  (read directly)
              weather_hourly    │   ONE definition,     │
                    zones      ─┘   point-in-time       └──► publish_features job
                                    correct                        │
                                                                   ▼
                                              Redis  masar:features:zone:{zone_id}
                                              (a COPY; no logic; PDPL filter applied here)
                                                                   │
                                                                   ▼
                                                          eta_online service
                                                          (GET only, p99 ~3 ms)

Four properties: one definition, publish-not-recompute, PDPL enforced at the single boundary, latency budget met by construction.

docs.title: 8.4 CI gates (deliverable c)
docs.text: Gate Runs Fails the build when Leakage lint on feature SQL every PR A window frame reaches CURRENT ROW/FOLLOWING, or a calendar bucket contains feature_ts, or a join lacks a <= feature_ts predicate Future-ablation test every PR Recomputing any feature with only pre-feature_ts data changes its value Temporal split enforcement training harness The train/test split is not strictly temporal, or windows overlap Offline/online consistency hourly, production Mismatch rate on any feature exceeds 1% of sampled requests PDPL boundary audit every publish Any rider_id, raw lat/lon, or national_id_hash appears in a BI view or an online-store key

docs.title: 8.5 The three sentences (deliverable d) — reference
docs.text: "Our reported offline R² of 0.93 was wrong; the correct figure is 0.78, and we found the cause: one input counted trips a driver had not yet taken, so the model was partly reading the answer. We have removed it, moved training and serving onto the same feature table so they can no longer disagree, and added a build check that fails any future feature which uses information unavailable at prediction time. At an honest 0.78 against the heuristic's 0.61 we still expect a material improvement, and we would like to prove it in a live A/B with the success criterion agreed in advance and measured in live error, not offline score."

docs.title: 9. What good looks like vs common wrong turns
docs.text: What good looks like Common wrong turn Applies one question to every feature: could this have been known at prediction time? Applies intuition per feature and gets the arguable ones wrong in both directions Spots the random split and the train/eval overlap from P1's header alone Goes straight to the features and never questions the evaluation design Finds both defects — leakage and offline/online skew Fixes the leak, ships, and is surprised the live number barely moves Notices distance_km provenance changes its verdict Marks distance_km valid because "distance is obviously known" Treats features 5 and 8 as genuinely arguable and removes the ambiguity by construction Demands a mechanical rule that classifies every feature Fixes by materialising one table to both consumers Fixes by rewriting the online code to match the offline code — two implementations again, briefly aligned Writes CI assertions that fail a build Proposes "a feature review checklist" Reads the 3.5× offline/live gap as a mechanism, not as overfitting Diagnoses overfitting and proposes regularisation Publishes the corrected number first, in the active voice Presents context, then buries the correction in paragraph three Re-anchors the decision on live MAE agreed in advance Promises a better offline number next time Treats an unexpectedly good metric as a bug report Celebrates it

docs.title: 10. Debrief (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Offline 1.41 min → live 4.93 min. That 3.5× is not overfitting, which degrades gently. It is the signature of a feature that does not exist at prediction time. Learn the shape: a large, abrupt offline/live gap means leakage; a small, gradual one means overfitting.
  2. One question, applied without exception. Could this feature have been known at prediction time? That single question resolves eight of ten features immediately and identifies the two that need a design decision rather than a verdict. You will use it again in fifteen minutes in ACT-09 against every column of gold.eta_features.
  3. P6 is the second, quieter lesson. 88% of live requests received a driver_recent_trip_count from a distribution the model had never seen. Fixing the leak alone would have moved the live number by almost nothing. Two implementations of one definition always diverge — you saw it at Naql in BI on Day 1, and here it is again in the feature layer. Materialise, do not re-implement.
  4. The tragedy is the credibility, not the model. R² = 0.78 beats the heuristic's 0.61 and is worth an estimated SAR 12.4M/yr. That model may now never ship, because the number that preceded it was not true. Your offline metric is a claim about the future; treat an unexpectedly good one as a bug report.
  5. Hand into CS-11. "Everything you have just certified as a valid, non-leaking, consistently-served feature assumed one thing: that the underlying data means what it says. Tomorrow's incident is the case where every feature is valid, every pipeline is green, and the model degrades anyway — because a source silently changed what a number means. In particular, look again at feature 6."
  6. The course question. "What happens to Masar's AI system if features are computed differently for training and serving?" The model is evaluated in one world and deployed into another, and the only place the difference is visible is the live metric — which arrives three weeks and one quarter of capacity too late.

docs.title: 11. The one sentence participants should leave with
docs.text: Ask one question of every feature — could this have been known at prediction time? — and then serve training and inference from the same materialised table, because leakage inflates the number you present and offline/online skew destroys the model you actually ship, and both wear the identical disguise of "great offline, mediocre live".

docs.title: CS-09 — The Medallion Architecture as an Industry Benchmark (Databricks)
docs.text: Field Value Case ID CS-09 Module M1 — Evolution of Data Architecture Day / Hour Day 1 · Hour 4 (immediately after CS-01, before LAB-01) Duration 60 minutes Format Design exercise (classification + written architecture decision) Group size 3–4 per team Deliverable A one-page Architecture Decision Record (ADR) answering: which transformations belong in Bronze, Silver and Gold for Masar's 15M daily GPS events — and which must NEVER occur before Bronze persistence Materials Blank ADR template (§8.4) one per participant; the transformation deck (§5 P3) printed and cut, one set per team; the exemplar ADR (§8.3) held back until minute 45 Facilitator prep 20 min. Read §8.2's classification table until you can defend any single row unprompted. Participants will challenge rows 3, 9, 13 and 18 — those four are where the learning is

docs.title: 1. Scenario
docs.text:
The medallion architecture — Bronze → Silver → Gold — is the reference pattern Databricks popularised for Lakehouse design, and it is now the de facto industry benchmark. Almost every team can recite the three names. Far fewer can answer the only question that matters in practice: for a specific transformation, which layer does it belong in, and why?

Masar is about to land its first production feed: 15,000,000 GPS events per day from 14,000 vehicles, at one ping per vehicle every 5 seconds. The platform team has drafted a design in which the ingestion job performs deduplication, drops pings with poor GPS accuracy, converts speed to a canonical unit, hashes the driver identifier, and writes the result to bronze.gps_events.

The design is efficient. It is also irreversible, and it will make the next twelve months of the platform's failures undiagnosable.

Your teams must decide, transformation by transformation, what Bronze is for.

docs.title: 2. Business context
docs.text:
Item Figure GPS events per day 15,000,000 Vehicles 14,000 Emission interval 5 seconds Raw event size ~268 bytes Raw daily volume (uncompressed / compressed) ~4.0 GB / ~0.9 GB Annual bronze storage at full retention ~330 GB compressed Annual object-storage cost of retaining every raw event ≈ SAR 1,100 Cost of the drafted "efficient" design's savings (dedup + accuracy filter at ingest) ~1.4% of events dropped → ≈ SAR 15/year saved Cost of one undiagnosable data incident (CS-11's actual cost) SAR 2,400,000

Put those last two lines next to each other and the entire architectural argument is settled by arithmetic: the drafted design saves roughly fifteen riyals a year and forfeits the ability to investigate a multi-million-riyal incident. Bronze retention is not a cost decision. It is an insurance decision priced at approximately nothing.

docs.title: 3. Technical challenge
docs.text:
Classify every transformation in Masar's GPS pipeline into one of four buckets:

Bucket Meaning Bronze Applied at landing. Must be additive and lossless: it may add metadata, never remove or reinterpret a source value Silver Applied when raw becomes trustworthy: validated, deduplicated, conformed, typed, unit-normalised, joined to reference data Gold Applied when trustworthy becomes useful: aggregated, windowed, modelled to a grain, shaped for one named consumer NEVER before Bronze Destroys information the raw record carried. Must not happen upstream of Bronze persistence under any circumstances

The fourth bucket is the point of the case. Bronze/Silver/Gold is a progressive refinement; the boundary that actually protects the platform is the one before Bronze.

docs.title: 4. Constraints
docs.text:
• Bronze must satisfy CONVENTIONS.md: every bronze table carries _ingested_at, _source_file, _batch_id.
  • Bronze must be append-only. A re-run grows history; it never replaces it.
  • PDPL applies. Precise GPS (payload.lat, payload.lon) is sensitive-personal; driver_id is personal. Retention for raw GPS is 30 days (see data/DATA_DICTIONARY.md).
  • The AI consumer (gold.eta_features) and the BI consumer (gold.fact_trip) must both descend from the same Silver.
  • The design must survive a producer changing behaviour without telling anyone — this is not hypothetical; it is CS-11.

docs.title: P1 — The raw event, exactly as the producer emits it
docs.text:
{"event_id":"ev_00009f025f480001","vehicle_id":"VEH-00884","driver_id":"DRV-02492",
 "trip_id":"TRP-20260601-0000000","ts":"2026-06-01T19:38:56Z",
 "payload":{"lat":26.41803,"lon":50.10770,"speed_kmh":15.3,"heading_deg":211,"accuracy_m":17.3},
 "producer_version":"2.4.0"}

Every field on this line is a fact about the world as the device reported it. Bronze's job is to record that report faithfully, including the parts that are wrong.

docs.title: P2 — The drafted "efficient" ingestion design (the proposal under review)
docs.text:
# ingest/land_gps.py  -- AS DRAFTED. Four of these five steps are architectural errors.
(spark.readStream.format("kafka").load()
   .select(from_json(col("value"), GPS_SCHEMA).alias("e")).select("e.*")
   .dropDuplicates(["event_id"])                                  # (1) dedup at ingest
   .filter(col("payload.accuracy_m") < 20)                        # (2) drop imprecise pings
   .withColumn("speed_mps", col("payload.speed_kmh") / 3.6)       # (3) unit conversion
   .drop("payload.speed_kmh")                                     #     ... and drop the original
   .withColumn("driver_id", sha2(col("driver_id"), 256))          # (4) hash the driver id
   .drop("producer_version")                                      # (5) "not needed downstream"
   .writeStream.format("delta").outputMode("append")
   .option("checkpointLocation", CKPT).table("bronze.gps_events"))

Have teams mark each of the five steps before they see the classification table. Then, in the debrief, walk through what each one costs:

Step What it destroys Which incident it makes undiagnosable (1) dedup at ingest The 0.4% duplicate rate — a producer health metric A firmware regression that triples duplicates becomes invisible (2) accuracy filter ~1% of pings and, with them, the accuracy distribution Tunnel/urban-canyon coverage analysis; a device fleet with degrading GPS (3) unit conversion + drop The value the producer actually sent CS-11 entirely. The 3.6× ratio is the evidence; converting by 3.6 at ingest silently corrects v2.5.0 and silently corrupts v2.4.0, and there is no way to tell them apart afterwards (4) hash driver_id Nothing, if done consistently — but at the wrong layer It couples ingestion to a key-management lifecycle; a rotated salt breaks bronze history irreversibly (5) drop producer_version The only column that correlates a data change with a deployment CS-11's root cause is found by GROUP BY producer_version. Without it, there is no investigation

Step (3) plus step (5) together are precisely the configuration in which the course's signature incident is permanently unsolvable. That is the sentence to leave hanging in the room.

docs.title: P3 — The transformation deck (print and cut; one set per team)
docs.text:
Twenty cards. Each team sorts all twenty into four piles labelled BRONZE / SILVER / GOLD / NEVER-BEFORE-BRONZE.

 1. Add _ingested_at, _source_file, _batch_id
 2. Parse the JSON string into typed columns
 3. Deduplicate on event_id
 4. Convert speed from m/s to km/h (unit normalisation)
 5. Hash driver_id / rider_id (PII pseudonymisation)
 6. Derive a precision-7 geohash from lat/lon
 7. Drop lat/lon after deriving the geohash
 8. Normalise ts from device-local time to UTC
 9. Cast speed_kmh from string to double
10. Filter out pings with accuracy_m > 20
11. Join to zones.csv to attach zone_id
12. Remove statistical outliers (speed > 200 km/h)
13. Compute rolling_avg_speed_10m
14. Assign a surrogate key to the vehicle dimension
15. Repair a malformed record by inferring the missing field
16. Enrich with weather via a late-arriving join
17. Aggregate to zone x hour demand counts
18. Reject a row that fails the schema contract
19. Compute label_actual_duration_min for training
20. Apply the PDPL retention delete + VACUUM

docs.title: P4 — The reference picture
docs.text:
SOURCES                BRONZE                    SILVER                      GOLD
  ───────                ──────                    ──────                      ────
  Kafka       ─┐    append-only, immutable    validated, deduped,       modelled to a grain,
  GPS SDK      ├──►  EXACTLY as received  ──►  conformed, unit-      ──►  shaped per consumer
  CSV drops    │     + lineage metadata        normalised, joined         ┌── BI: fact/dim star

docs.title: 7. Discussion questions with model answers
docs.text:
Q1 — the centrepiece. Masar receives 15 million GPS events daily. Which transformations belong in Bronze, Silver and Gold, and which must NEVER occur before Bronze persistence?

Model answer. The full classification is §8.2. The principle behind it, which is what participants must be able to apply to a card that was not in the deck:

  • Bronze answers "what did the source actually say?" Therefore the only admissible transformations at Bronze are additive: attaching lineage metadata (_ingested_at, _source_file, _batch_id), and parsing the wire format into typed columns without changing any value. Bronze may add columns. It may never remove a row, remove a column, or reinterpret a value. Bronze is an evidence store before it is a data store.
  • Silver answers "what is true about the world?" Therefore Silver is where judgement is applied: dedup, unit normalisation, timezone normalisation, validation, quarantine, conforming joins to reference data. Every Silver decision is reversible by re-running from Bronze, which is exactly what makes it safe to be opinionated there.
  • Gold answers "what does this specific consumer need?" Therefore Gold is aggregation, windowing, grain selection, feature engineering, star-schema modelling — and there are legitimately several Golds, one per consumer, because BI's needs and the ETA model's needs genuinely differ. gold.fact_trip and gold.eta_features are siblings, not layers.
  • NEVER-before-Bronze is any transformation that destroys information the source provided: dropping rows for any reason, dropping columns, converting units in place, repairing values, filtering outliers, or discarding provenance such as producer_version.

The test to apply to any card, and the sentence worth memorising: "If this transformation is wrong, can I fix it by re-running?" If yes, it belongs in Silver or Gold. If no — if being wrong means the information is gone forever — it must not happen before Bronze.

Then the economics, because the objection is always cost: at 15M events/day, retaining every raw event costs roughly SAR 1,100/year. The drafted "efficient" design saves about SAR 15/year and forfeits the investigation of an incident that cost SAR 2.4M. Bronze is the cheapest insurance in the entire platform.

Q2. Card 3 — deduplication. Everyone agrees duplicates are bad. Why is dedup at Bronze wrong?

Model answer. Because the duplicate rate is a signal about the producer, not noise in the data. Masar's GPS feed carries ~0.4% duplicate event_ids (~60,000/day). That number is a health metric: if it triples after a firmware rollout, something is wrong with the device fleet, and that is worth knowing.

Dedup at Bronze destroys the metric permanently and silently. Nobody notices, because the deduplicated data looks fine — which is exactly why it is dangerous.

The correct design: Bronze keeps duplicates; Silver removes them. silver.vehicle_positions deduplicates on event_id; bronze.gps_events retains everything and a monitor computes the duplicate rate per producer_version per day. If Silver's dedup logic is later found to be wrong (wrong key, wrong window), Silver is rebuilt from Bronze in an afternoon. If Bronze deduplicated, there is nothing to rebuild from.

There is one narrow, legitimate exception worth naming so teams do not over-apply the rule: transport-level idempotency — an exactly-once sink that prevents the same micro-batch being written twice on restart — is not "dedup", it is correct write semantics, and it belongs at Bronze. The distinction: preventing your pipeline from writing a record twice is correctness; removing records the producer sent twice is interpretation.

Q3. Card 9 — casting speed_kmh from string to double. Is that Bronze?

Model answer. This is the subtlest card in the deck and it deserves the time.

Parsing the wire format is Bronze; changing a value is not. JSON arrives as bytes; turning those bytes into a typed column so the data is queryable at all is part of reading the source, not of interpreting it. So a cast is admissible at Bronze — on one condition: the cast must be total and lossless.

The failure mode is what happens to a value that does not cast. If speed_kmh is the string "n/a" and the pipeline casts to double, Spark yields null, and an unparseable value has silently become a missing value. The information "the producer sent us the literal string n/a" is destroyed at the one layer that was supposed to preserve it. That is a NEVER-before-Bronze act wearing the costume of a cast.

The correct pattern, and the one to put on the board:

# Bronze: parse permissively, keep the original, never lose a row
.withColumn("_raw", col("value").cast("string"))            # the bytes, always retained
.withColumn("e", from_json(col("_raw"), GPS_SCHEMA, {"mode": "PERMISSIVE",
                                        "columnNameOfCorruptRecord": "_corrupt_record"}))
# rows that fail to parse land WITH their _corrupt_record, they are not dropped

So: cast at Bronze only with a permissive mode and a corrupt-record column, so that failure is recorded rather than erased. A strict cast that nulls or drops belongs in Silver, where it can quarantine.

Note the connection to CS-11: the incident is invisible to type checks precisely because the type never changed. Casting is not validation. A double is a double whether it means km/h or m/s.

Q4. Card 13 — rolling_avg_speed_10m. Silver or Gold?

Model answer. Gold, and the reasoning generalises to every windowed computation.

The distinguishing question is not "is it a calculation?" but "is it a fact about a record, or a fact about a consumer's question?" rolling_avg_speed_10m is not a property of any GPS ping — it is a 10-minute window chosen because the ETA model's feature engineering wanted 10 minutes. A different consumer wants 5, or 30. The window length is a modelling decision, not a truth about the world, and modelling decisions live in Gold.

Silver's job on speed is different and more fundamental: make speed_kmh actually mean km/h for every row (unit normalisation, card 4), so that any Gold consumer computing any window gets a defensible answer. Silver produces a trustworthy quantity; Gold produces an aggregate for a purpose.

Sharpen it with the test from §8.1: if two consumers would legitimately want different versions of this transformation, it is Gold. If both consumers need it done the same way or neither can be trusted, it is Silver. Nobody wants speed in m/s for some purposes and km/h for others — that is Silver. Everybody wants their own window length — that is Gold.

Flag the forward reference explicitly: rolling_avg_speed_10m is the exact column CS-11 corrupts, and the reason the corruption is fatal is that Silver failed to normalise the unit, so Gold's window faithfully averaged two incompatible quantities.

Q5. Card 18 — rejecting a row that fails the schema contract. Surely rejecting bad data is good?

Model answer. Rejecting is good. Rejecting before Bronze is not, and the distinction is the same one as Q2.

A row that violates the schema contract is evidence that the producer sent something unexpected. It is often the single most valuable row in the batch — it is the first sign of a producer change, a firmware bug, an encoding problem, an upstream outage. Discarding it at ingest destroys the earliest available warning, and destroys it most reliably in exactly the situations that matter most.

The correct pattern: Bronze lands everything, including malformed records, with a _corrupt_record column and its lineage metadata. Silver applies the contract and routes failures to silver.trips_quarantine. The gate then has three properties Bronze-side rejection cannot have: the bad rows are counted (so a spike is detectable), inspectable (so a human can diagnose), and recoverable (so a contract fixed on Tuesday can reprocess Monday's quarantine).

The one-line rule: quarantine, never delete. A rejected row is a measurement; deleting it is choosing not to measure.

Q6. Card 5 — hashing PII. Doesn't PDPL require this as early as possible?

Model answer. PDPL requires minimisation and appropriate protection, and it is satisfied by access control on Bronze plus hashing at the Silver boundary — not by destroying identifiers at ingest.

Three reasons hashing at Bronze is the wrong layer: 1. Bronze is where the erasure obligation is discharged. PDPL Art. 18 erasure requires deleting a specific data subject's rows (MERGE DELETE + VACUUM, per CONVENTIONS.md). If Bronze holds only irreversible hashes with no key mapping, you cannot reliably identify a subject's rows to erase them — a privacy control has obstructed a privacy right. 2. Salt rotation breaks history irreversibly. Key management is an operational lifecycle. Rotate the salt and Bronze's historical hashes no longer join to anything, forever. 3. The protection Bronze needs is access, not transformation. Column-level access control, short retention (30 days for raw GPS), and audit logging protect the data while keeping it usable for erasure and investigation.

The correct boundary: hash and minimise at the Silver→Gold boundary, where CONVENTIONS.md's rule bites — never emit raw rider_id into BI or the online store. That is one enforceable checkpoint, in one publish job, auditable in one place. Which is also, note, exactly the boundary CS-08 identified for offline/online serving.

Card 7 (drop lat/lon after deriving the geohash) is the same argument at higher stakes: precise location is sensitive-personal, the geohash is the minimised form, and the minimisation happens on the way into Silver/Gold — with raw coordinates retained in Bronze under a 30-day retention and strict access, then aged out by the retention job (card 20), not by the ingest job.

docs.title: 8.1 The four questions that decide any card
docs.text:
Apply in order; the first that answers decides the layer.

  1. "If this is wrong, can I fix it by re-running?" — No → it must not happen before Bronze.
  2. "Does this remove or reinterpret anything the source sent?" — Yes → not Bronze.
  3. "Would two legitimate consumers want it done differently?" — Yes → Gold. No → Silver.
  4. "Is this a fact about the record, or a fact about somebody's question?" — Record → Silver. Question → Gold.

docs.title: 8.2 The classification (facilitator key)
docs.text:
# Transformation Layer Rationale (one line) 1 Add _ingested_at, _source_file, _batch_id BRONZE Purely additive lineage metadata; mandated by CONVENTIONS.md and the basis of every later investigation 2 Parse JSON into typed columns BRONZE Reading the wire format is not interpreting it — provided parsing is permissive and corrupt records are retained, not dropped 3 Deduplicate on event_id SILVER The 0.4% duplicate rate is a producer health metric; Bronze must retain it so a firmware regression is visible 4 Convert speed m/s → km/h (unit normalisation) SILVER Makes the column mean one thing for every row; must be applied per producer_version and is reversible by rebuild 5 Hash driver_id / rider_id SILVER (boundary to Gold) Bronze needs the raw key to discharge PDPL erasure; protect Bronze with access control and 30-day retention instead 6 Derive a precision-7 geohash from lat/lon SILVER Additive derivation and the PDPL-minimised form; it is a fact about the record, so it belongs to Silver, not to a consumer 7 Drop lat/lon after deriving the geohash NEVER before Bronze Precise coordinates are the source's actual measurement; minimise on the way out of Bronze, and age raw coordinates out with the retention job (card 20) 8 Normalise ts device-local → UTC SILVER Storage is UTC by convention; but the original offset must survive in Bronze, since a wrong-timezone producer is only diagnosable from what it sent 9 Cast speed_kmh string → double BRONZE, conditionally Admissible only in permissive mode with a _corrupt_record column; a strict cast that nulls unparseable values is a silent deletion and belongs in Silver 10 Filter pings with accuracy_m > 20 NEVER before Bronze Drops ~1% of rows and the entire accuracy distribution; degrading GPS across a device fleet becomes undetectable 11 Join to zones.csv to attach zone_id SILVER Conforming join to reference data; a fact about the record, needed identically by every consumer 12 Remove outliers (speed > 200 km/h) NEVER before Bronze (then SILVER as quarantine) 210 km/h may be a real fact about a real vehicle, or a sensor fault, or a unit change — you cannot know at ingest, and after deletion you can never know 13 Compute rolling_avg_speed_10m GOLD The 10-minute window is a modelling choice made by one consumer; a different consumer wants a different window 14 Assign a surrogate key to the vehicle dimension GOLD Surrogate keys serve dimensional modelling for BI; they are an artefact of the star schema, not of the world 15 Repair a malformed record by inferring the missing field NEVER before Bronze Replaces what the source said with what we guessed; the guess is unmarked, unversioned and unfalsifiable afterwards 16 Enrich with weather via a late-arriving join GOLD Late-arriving enrichment is consumer-specific and point-in-time sensitive (see CS-08); doing it early bakes in an as-of assumption 17 Aggregate to zone × hour demand counts GOLD Aggregation to a grain is by definition consumer-shaped — this is gold.zone_hourly_demand 18 Reject a row failing the schema contract SILVER (quarantine, never delete) A contract violation is the earliest warning of a producer change; Bronze must land it, Silver must quarantine it, nobody may delete it 19 Compute label_actual_duration_min for training GOLD A label exists only for a model; it is a fact about a training question, not about a GPS ping 20 Apply the PDPL retention delete + VACUUM BRONZE (as a governed lifecycle job, never as part of ingest) The one legitimate deletion from Bronze — executed by a separate, audited retention job under a documented legal basis, not silently by an ingestion pipeline

Summary counts: BRONZE 4 (of which one conditional, one lifecycle) · SILVER 8 · GOLD 5 · NEVER-before-Bronze 4 (cards 7, 10, 12, 15).

Note for the facilitator: cards 7, 10, 12 and 15 are precisely the four steps the drafted design in P2 wanted to do at ingest (plus dropping producer_version, which is card 1's inverse). The deck and the draft are the same argument seen twice.

docs.title: 8.3 Exemplar ADR (hand out at minute 54, not before)
docs.text:
# ADR-001 — Transformation placement for the Masar GPS pipeline

Status:   Accepted
Date:     2026-06-01
Deciders: Data Platform Lead, ML Platform Lead, Data Protection Officer
Context module: M1 — Evolution of Data Architecture

## Context

Masar ingests 15,000,000 GPS events per day from 14,000 vehicles (one ping per
vehicle per 5 s), landing via Kafka into the Lakehouse. Two consumers depend on
this feed: gold.eta_features (ETA and demand models) and gold.fact_trip (BI).

The drafted ingestion job performed deduplication, an accuracy filter, a unit
conversion, PII hashing and dropped producer_version before persisting to
bronze.gps_events. Each step reduced downstream work. Together they made the
landed data an interpretation of the source rather than a record of it.

Raw retention for this feed costs approximately SAR 1,100 per year. The steps
the draft proposed would save approximately SAR 15 per year.

## Decision

We adopt a medallion architecture as progressive refinement, with an explicit
fourth category of transformations that are prohibited before Bronze.

BRONZE — "what did the source actually say?"  Append-only, immutable.
  Permitted, and only these:
    - attach _ingested_at, _source_file, _batch_id
    - parse the wire format into typed columns in PERMISSIVE mode, retaining a
      _corrupt_record column so unparseable rows are landed, never dropped
    - the governed PDPL retention job (separate, audited, documented legal basis)

SILVER — "what is true about the world?"  Rebuildable from Bronze at any time.
    - deduplicate on event_id
    - normalise speed units to km/h, applied PER producer_version
    - normalise ts to UTC, retaining the original offset from Bronze
    - derive precision-7 geohash; conform-join to zones
    - validate against the data contract; route failures to quarantine
    - hash driver_id / rider_id at the boundary out of Silver

GOLD — "what does this consumer need?"  One Gold per consumer.
    - rolling_avg_speed_10m, rolling_zone_demand_15m and other windowed features
    - zone x hour demand aggregates
    - dimensional surrogate keys and the BI star schema
    - point-in-time weather enrichment; training labels

NEVER BEFORE BRONZE — prohibited upstream of Bronze persistence:
    - dropping rows for ANY reason (accuracy filters, outlier removal, contract
      violations, deduplication)
    - dropping or replacing columns (lat/lon after geohash; speed_kmh after
      conversion; producer_version)
    - repairing or inferring values
    - any strict cast that converts an unparseable value to null

producer_version is mandatory in Bronze and is never dropped. It is the only
column that correlates a change in the data with a change in a deployment.

## Consequences

Positive
  + Any Silver or Gold defect is repaired by re-running from Bronze. Bronze
    defects would be unrecoverable, so Bronze is kept minimal and additive.
  + Producer health is measurable: duplicate rate, accuracy distribution,
    parse-failure rate and unit distribution are all computable per
    producer_version because none of them were filtered away at ingest.
  + A semantic producer change (a unit change with an unchanged type) remains
    diagnosable, because both the original values and the producer version
    survive in Bronze.
  + PDPL erasure is executable, because Bronze retains the subject keys needed
    to identify a subject's rows.

Negative — accepted costs
  - Bronze stores ~1.4% of rows that will never be used downstream, and every
    duplicate. Cost: ~SAR 15/year. Accepted.
  - Silver carries more work per run (dedup, unit normalisation, validation),
    increasing Silver compute by an estimated 20%. Accepted.
  - Bronze holds raw lat/lon and raw driver_id, i.e. sensitive-personal and
    personal data. This is mitigated by column-level access control, a 30-day
    retention on raw GPS, audit logging, and the governed retention job — NOT
    by transformation at ingest. This is a real, ongoing obligation and it is
    the price of retaining erasure capability and diagnosability.
  - Consumers must not read Bronze directly. Enforced by access policy; a
    consumer reading Bronze bypasses every quality guarantee in the platform.

## Alternatives considered

A. Filter and normalise at ingest (the drafted design). Rejected: saves ~SAR 15
   per year and forfeits investigation of incidents costing millions. The
   asymmetry is not close.
B. Two Bronze tables — raw and cleaned. Rejected: a second copy is a second
   pipeline, and consumers will read whichever they find first (see CS-01).
C. Retain raw only for 7 days. Rejected: shorter than the observed detection
   lag for semantic defects (14 days at Muqeem, 5 days at Masar), so the
   evidence would expire before the incident is noticed.

docs.title: 9. What good looks like vs common wrong turns
docs.text: What good looks like Common wrong turn Defines each layer by the question it answers Defines layers by technology or by "clean vs dirty" Applies "if this is wrong, can I re-run?" as the decisive test Decides card by card on intuition and is inconsistent by card 10 Puts dedup in Silver and can explain the duplicate rate as a producer metric Puts dedup in Bronze for efficiency, destroying a health signal to save SAR 15/year Treats cards 7, 10, 12, 15 as NEVER and can say what each destroys Treats "removing bad data early" as obviously good Allows casting at Bronze only in permissive mode with a corrupt-record column Allows any cast at Bronze, so unparseable values silently become nulls Keeps producer_version in Bronze and says why Drops it as "not needed downstream" — and makes CS-11 unsolvable Puts PII hashing at the Silver→Gold boundary, protecting Bronze with access control and retention Hashes at ingest, breaking PDPL erasure and coupling Bronze to salt rotation Quarantines contract failures rather than deleting them Rejects at ingest and loses the earliest warning of every producer change Distinguishes transport idempotency (Bronze, correct) from producer dedup (Silver) Conflates the two and concludes exactly-once sinks are "dedup at Bronze" ADR names a real negative consequence, including the PDPL obligation Bronze retention creates ADR lists only benefits Prices the decision: SAR 1,100/yr retention vs SAR 2.4M incident Argues architecture on aesthetics

docs.title: 10. Debrief (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Re-run the P2 hand count. Compare with the minute-9 counts. The room will have moved from marking one or two of the five steps to marking four or five. Say what changed: not their knowledge of the medallion names, but their possession of a test they can apply — if this is wrong, can I re-run?
  2. The asymmetry is the architecture. Silver and Gold mistakes are a re-run. Bronze mistakes are permanent. Every rule about Bronze follows from that one sentence, and none of them are about cleanliness.
  3. Price it out loud. SAR 1,100/year to retain everything. SAR 15/year saved by the "efficient" design. SAR 2.4M for the incident it would have made undiagnosable. Bronze is the cheapest insurance in the platform and it is the first thing an efficiency review proposes to cut.
  4. Name the four NEVER cards — drop rows, drop columns, repair values, filter outliers — and note that the drafted job in P2 did all four. Efficient, sensible-looking, and it would have quietly removed the platform's ability to explain itself.
  5. Forward reference, stated plainly. "On Day 5 you will investigate an incident in which a producer changed speed_kmh from km/h to m/s while keeping the same field name and the same type. You will solve it with two columns: the original speed_kmh values and producer_version. The design on this slide (P2) deletes one and converts the other. Whether you can solve that incident was decided here, on Day 1, in the ingestion job."
  6. The course question. "What happens to Masar's AI system if Bronze is not immutable?" Every downstream layer becomes unrebuildable, every incident becomes unfalsifiable, and every model degradation becomes a matter of opinion rather than of evidence.

docs.title: 11. The one sentence participants should leave with
docs.text: Bronze answers "what did the source actually say", Silver answers "what is true about the world", and Gold answers "what does this consumer need" — so the only transformations permitted before Bronze are additive ones, because a Silver or Gold mistake costs a re-run while a Bronze mistake costs the truth, permanently, for about fifteen riyals a year.

docs.title: CS-10 — LinkedIn and Kafka: Designing a Central Messaging Backbone
docs.text:
Field Value Case ID CS-10 Module M5 — Streaming Data and Event-Driven Architectures Day / Hour Day 4 · Hour 3 (after CS-05 and LAB-05; this is the design exercise that generalises both) Duration 75 minutes (three escalating rounds of 15 min + reviews) Format Design exercise, scored Group size 4 per team; 3–6 teams Deliverable A completed design sheet (§8.5) with a value and a justification for all twelve decisions, plus the team's answer to "what breaks first at 15M events/day and how do you know before it does" Materials Design sheet §8.5 printed per team; the escalation cards §5 P4–P6 in three sealed envelopes per team, opened on the facilitator's signal; the scoring sheet §8.6 for cross-team review; A1 paper for the architecture drawing Facilitator prep 25 min. This is the longest and most demanding case in the course. Rehearse the round transitions — the escalations must arrive after teams have committed to a design, never before

This is a design exercise, not a Kafka tutorial. No team should spend a minute on broker installation, CLI syntax or configuration files. Every deliverable is a decision with a justification. If a team asks "which flag sets that", the answer is: "name the behaviour you want and why; the flag is a footnote."

docs.title: 1.1 Where the pattern comes from
docs.text:
Kafka originated at LinkedIn around 2010, to solve an organisational problem rather than a technical one. LinkedIn had many systems that each needed data from many other systems: profile updates, connection graphs, activity feeds, search indexing, monitoring, offline analytics, and a growing set of recommendation models. The result was a dense mesh of point-to-point integrations — each producer knowing each consumer, each new consumer requiring a change to every producer, each pipeline built and operated independently.

The reframing was to stop treating data movement as integration and start treating it as publication. Producers publish facts to a durable, ordered, replayable log. Consumers subscribe independently, at their own pace, and read from their own position. Adding a consumer becomes a decision the consumer makes alone; the producer neither knows nor cares.

Two properties made this more than a message queue and they are the two properties that matter for this case:

  • The log is durable and replayable. A message is not consumed and destroyed; it is read at an offset. A new consumer can start from the beginning. A broken consumer can rewind and reprocess. Reprocessing becomes a routine operation instead of a data-recovery project.
  • Consumers are decoupled in time and in failure. A slow, crashed or newly-deployed consumer does not slow the producer and does not affect other consumers, because each group holds its own offsets.

LinkedIn ran this at a scale measured in trillions of messages per day. Masar's 15 million events per day is four to five orders of magnitude smaller — which is exactly why the architecture, not the scale, is what transfers.

docs.title: 1.2 What Masar must build
docs.text:
Masar's 14,000 vehicles emit, every 5 seconds:

vehicle_id, latitude, longitude, speed, heading, timestamp, trip_id

Two consumers exist today and both are business-critical, with genuinely different requirements:

Consumer Needs Tolerance ETA features (AI) Complete, correct, unit-normalised positions feeding gold.eta_features Minutes of latency acceptable; incompleteness is not Operations alerts (Ops) Speeding, harsh braking, vehicle-stopped-in-traffic, geofence breach Seconds of latency required; a missed late event is acceptable

More consumers are coming: a fraud investigation team, a regulator reporting feed, and a driver-safety scoring model. The design must make adding the fourth consumer a decision the fourth consumer makes alone.

docs.title: 2. Business context
docs.text: Item Figure Vehicles 14,000 Emission interval 5 s Events per day 15,000,000 Mean events/second 174 Peak events/second (17:00–19:00 +03) 620 Mean event size 268 bytes Daily volume (raw / compressed) ~4.0 GB / ~0.9 GB Duplicate event_id rate at source 0.4% (~60,000/day) Out-of-order ts rate ~1% Ops alerting latency requirement < 5 s end to end ETA feature freshness requirement < 5 min Streaming platform budget SAR 65,000 / month Planned new consumers in 12 months 3

docs.title: 3. Technical challenge
docs.text: Design the pipeline from vehicle to both consumers, then defend it against three escalating realities that arrive after the design is committed.

docs.title: 4. Constraints
docs.text:
• Device firmware cannot change this year: the 5-second interval, the field names and the transport are fixed.
  • The platform is redeployed twice a week; correctness must survive restarts without human intervention.
  • Bronze must be append-only and immutable (CS-09's ADR is binding).
  • PDPL: precise lat/lon is sensitive-personal; retention on raw GPS is 30 days.
  • SAR 65,000/month ceiling.
  • No design may require a producer change to add a consumer.
