docs.title: P3 — What one event looks like on the wire, and what Bronze must record
docs.text:
// produced
{"vehicle_id":"VEH-00884","latitude":26.41803,"longitude":50.10770,"speed":15.3,
 "heading":211,"timestamp":"2026-06-01T19:38:56Z","trip_id":"TRP-20260601-0000000"}

// landed in bronze.gps_events (canonical schema, CONVENTIONS.md)
{"event_id":"ev_00009f025f480001","vehicle_id":"VEH-00884","driver_id":"DRV-02492",
 "trip_id":"TRP-20260601-0000000","ts":"2026-06-01T19:38:56Z",
 "payload":{"lat":26.41803,"lon":50.10770,"speed_kmh":15.3,"heading_deg":211,"accuracy_m":17.3},
 "producer_version":"2.4.0",
 "_ingested_at":"2026-06-01T19:39:02Z","_source_file":"masar.gps.pings:7:441829",
 "_batch_id":"b_20260601_193900"}

Note _source_file for a stream is topic:partition:offset. That triple is the streaming equivalent of a filename, and it is what makes an individual event traceable back to its exact position in the log — the single most useful thing you can record about a streamed row.

docs.title: P4 — ESCALATION ROUND 1 (sealed envelope; open at minute 25)
docs.text:
Late-arriving events.

Riyadh has tunnels, multi-storey car parks and underground malls. A device that loses connectivity buffers locally and flushes when it reconnects. Measured over 7 days:

Lag (event time → arrival at broker) Share Cumulative ≤ 5 s 96.20% 96.20% 5–30 s 2.10% 98.30% 30 s – 2 min 0.90% 99.20% 2–5 min 0.55% 99.75% 5–10 min 0.18% 99.93% 10–30 min 0.06% 99.99% > 30 min (device offline for a shift) 0.01% 100.00%

A single device, after 40 minutes underground, flushes 480 buffered pings in under two seconds.

Answer: (a) What watermark do you choose for the Ops path and for the AI path, and what residual do you accept for each? (b) What happens to the 480-ping burst in your design — is it one micro-batch or 480? (c) Does the burst reorder anything within its partition? (d) Is any of this data lost?

docs.title: P5 — ESCALATION ROUND 2 (sealed envelope; open at minute 40)
docs.text:
Duplicates.

Three independent sources of duplicates, and your design must handle all three:

  1. Producer-side. The device SDK retries on an unacknowledged send. Measured duplicate event_id rate at the broker: 0.4% (~60,000/day), and it is not uniform — it spikes to 3% for devices with poor connectivity, i.e. exactly the devices that also produce the late bursts in Round 1.
  2. Broker-side. A producer retry after a partial failure can write the same event to the same partition twice at different offsets.
  3. Consumer-side. A consumer restarted after processing a micro-batch but before its offsets were committed will reprocess that batch. Your platform is redeployed twice a week.

On 4 June a deploy caused source (3): 7,300 pings reprocessed. gold.zone_hourly_demand read 1.41× actual for zone Z-RUH-01. Surge rose to 2.3× on demand that did not exist.

Answer: (a) Which of the three does your delivery semantic solve, and which does it not? (b) What is your dedup key, in which layer does dedup happen, and over what window? (c) Bronze retains duplicates — how do you then guarantee silver.vehicle_positions has exactly one row per event? (d) Your dedup window is finite. What happens to a duplicate that arrives after it closes, and how would you know?

docs.title: P6 — ESCALATION ROUND 3 (sealed envelope; open at minute 55)
docs.text:
Out-of-order timestamps, and one clock that lies.

~1% of events arrive with ts out of order relative to the preceding event from the same vehicle. Three distinct causes, and they are not the same problem:

  1. Network reordering — two pings sent 5 s apart arrive in the reverse order. Small offsets, seconds.
  2. Buffered flush (Round 1) — a device emits 480 events whose ts values are all in the past, interleaved with live events from other vehicles.
  3. A wrong device clock. 61 vehicles are running a firmware build whose NTP sync failed. Their ts is ahead by between 4 and 11 hours. These events arrive with timestamps in the future.

Cause 3 is the dangerous one. In an event-time pipeline, a single event with a timestamp 11 hours in the future advances the watermark by 11 hours, and every subsequent legitimate event is then classified as late and dropped. One misconfigured device can silence the pipeline for the entire fleet.

Answer: (a) Does your design survive cause 3? Trace it through. (b) Where do you defend — producer, broker, stream, or Silver? (c) What do you do with a future-dated event: drop it, clamp it, quarantine it, or let it through? (d) What alerts, and on what signal? (e) Now that you have seen all three rounds: what breaks first at 15M events/day, and how do you know before it does?

docs.title: 6. Facilitation script (minute-by-minute)
docs.text:
Min Activity Facilitator does Watch for 0–6 Frame the origin. Tell the LinkedIn story in §1.1 in four minutes: point-to-point mesh → publication to a durable log. Land the two properties (replayable; consumers decoupled in time and failure). State the rule aloud: "This is a design exercise. Nobody types a broker config today." Teams that want to discuss Kafka internals. Redirect to the twelve decisions. 6–10 Distribute P1, P2, P3 and the design sheet. Assign the three sealed envelopes to each table, face down, marked ROUND 1/2/3. "Do not open these. You will be told when." The physical envelopes materially raise engagement. — 10–25 ROUND 0 — the baseline design. Fill in decisions 1–6 and 9. Draw the architecture on A1. Circulate with exactly one question per table, from: "What must not be reordered?" · "Which consumer is harmed most by a duplicate?" · "Draw me the arrow where a duplicate can be created." Teams keying by city (3-way hot skew) or by trip_id (fragments a vehicle's idle pings). Teams sharing one consumer group between AI and Ops. 25–26 "Open envelope 1." Say nothing else. — 26–40 ROUND 1 — late events. Teams revise; answer P4 (a)–(d) on the sheet. Push: "Your watermark drops 0.8%. Where did those events go? Are they lost?" The realisation that Bronze retains everything is the round's payload. Teams that widen the watermark to 30 minutes to be safe. Show them INC-2025-0517 from CS-05 (41 GB state, OOM, 4.5 h outage). 40–41 "Open envelope 2." — — 41–55 ROUND 2 — duplicates. Answer P5 (a)–(d). Push on (a): most teams claim exactly-once and cannot say which of the three sources it addresses. Answer: only (3). Sources (1) and (2) are producer-side and require dedup on event_id regardless. Teams whose answer to (c) is "dedup in Bronze" — that violates CS-09's ADR and destroys the duplicate-rate health metric. 55–56 "Open envelope 3." — — 56–70 ROUND 3 — out-of-order and the lying clock. Answer P6 (a)–(e). This is the hardest round; expect visible discomfort. Walk one team through cause 3 out loud until they see the watermark jump 11 hours and the fleet go silent. Then let them tell the room. Almost every team's Round-0 design fails cause 3. That is intended. The failure is the lesson. 70–78 Cross-team scoring. Each team scores the design of the team to its right using §8.6. Scores are read aloud with one sentence of justification per category. Enforce: a score must cite a specific decision on the sheet, never a general impression. — 78–85 Reference architecture. Walk §8.1–8.4 with the trade-offs made explicit. Answer P6(e). Close on §11. Emphasise every place the reference makes a trade, not an optimum. Teams must leave knowing there is no free choice. —

(Total 85 min if all reviews are run. To fit 75: cut cross-team scoring to 5 minutes and score only two categories.)

docs.title: 7. Discussion questions with model answers
docs.text:
Q1. What must not be reordered? (decision 1 — the partition key)

Model answer. Kafka guarantees ordering within a partition, not across partitions. So the partition key is chosen by asking: for which entity would out-of-order delivery produce a wrong answer?

For Masar the answer is vehicle_id. A vehicle's position sequence must remain ordered: distance travelled, heading change, harsh-braking detection and speed differencing all read consecutive pings from one vehicle. Two pings from different vehicles arriving in either order changes nothing.

Candidate key Verdict vehicle_id Correct. 14,000 distinct keys spread evenly; ordering preserved exactly where it is required trip_id Orders per trip, but a vehicle's idle-time pings (no trip_id) scatter across partitions, and per-vehicle continuity across trips is lost city 3 distinct values on 24 partitions: 21 idle partitions and a hot one carrying a third of 15M events. Total lag looks fine while one partition grows unbounded none (round-robin) Maximum throughput, no ordering anywhere. Requires every consumer to reorder in state event_id Perfect distribution, zero useful ordering — the pathological case

Partition count: at 620 events/s peak, a single partition is comfortable; the count is driven by consumer parallelism, not by throughput. 24 gives room to scale a consumer group to 24 instances, divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12, and keeps ~583 vehicles per partition. Note the asymmetry teams must internalise: partitions can be increased later but never decreased, and increasing them re-hashes keys, breaking per-key ordering across the change. Over-provision modestly; do not under-provision.

Q2. How long do you keep the log? (decision 3 — retention)

Model answer. 7 days, and the reasoning is what matters.

Topic retention is not a storage decision — it is the answer to "how far back can I replay?" Replay is needed when: a consumer had a bug and its output must be rebuilt; a new consumer starts and needs recent history; a deploy corrupted a downstream table; or a schema/logic change requires reprocessing.

7 days at 0.9 GB/day compressed with replication factor 3 is ~19 GB — trivially cheap. It covers a bug discovered on Friday and fixed on Monday, which is the realistic operational window.

The important framing: the topic is not the system of record — bronze.gps_events is. Anything older than 7 days is reprocessed from Bronze, in batch, far more cheaply than a stream replay. Retention therefore only needs to cover the window in which streaming replay is the right tool. A team proposing 90-day retention has confused the log with the lake.

Replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2. Standard durability; tolerates one broker loss without data loss and one more without unavailability.

Q3. How many consumer groups, and why not one? (decision 5)

Model answer. Two groups now, one per consumer, and this is the property that makes the whole architecture worth building.

masar.gps.pings ──┬── group: gps-bronze-land   (AI path: bronze → silver → gold.eta_features)
                  └── group: ops-alerts        (Ops path: low-latency alerting)

A consumer group holds its own offsets. Therefore: - The Ops path can run a 2-second trigger; the AI path a 30-second trigger. Neither constrains the other. - If the Ops alerting sink is down for an hour, ingestion into Bronze is entirely unaffected. With a shared group, a stuck sink stalls both. - Replaying the Ops consumer from an earlier offset — because the alerting rules changed — does not replay ingestion, which would duplicate Bronze rows. - The fourth consumer (fraud, regulator, safety scoring) is added by creating a group and choosing a starting offset. No producer change, no coordination, no ticket. This is the LinkedIn insight, cashed out.

Teams that propose one consumer writing to Bronze and then fanning out from Bronze to Ops are not wrong architecturally — but they must then explain how they meet a 5-second Ops SLA through a Delta table write, a commit and a downstream read. They cannot. The fan-out belongs at the log, because the log is the only place where two consumers can read the same data at two different speeds.

Q4. What watermark, and what exactly does it cost? (decision 7)

Model answer. Different watermarks per consumer, derived from P4's distribution, each with a stated residual:

Path Watermark Admits Rationale Ops alerts 30 seconds 98.3% An alert about a harsh-braking event 4 minutes ago is worthless. Latency dominates completeness. Missing 1.7% of late events is explicitly acceptable — it was stated as a tolerance in §1.2 AI / silver → gold 10 minutes 99.93% Feature correctness dominates; 5 minutes of latency is within the < 5 min freshness budget at a 30 s trigger. Drops 0.07% Training / historical none — batch rebuild from bronze.gps_events 100% Bronze is append-only and complete

The insight most teams miss, and the one to make explicit: a watermark decides what the streaming aggregate sees; it never decides what you keep. Every event, however late, is in Bronze. The 0.07% dropped from the AI streaming path is absorbed by the next batch rebuild of gold.eta_features. This is why the medallion architecture and streaming compose so well — you can be aggressive about latency in a derived view precisely because the raw layer forgives you.

The cost of getting it wrong in the other direction is concrete: state ≈ (events/s) × (watermark) × (per-key state). Going from 10 minutes to 60 costs 6× the state, and at 620 ev/s peak that is the path to the 41 GB OOM in CS-05's INC-2025-0517.

Q5. Dedup key, window, and layer? (decision 8, from P5)

Model answer. Key event_id. Window: the watermark's duration. Layer: Silver, never Bronze.

Which of P5's three duplicate sources does each mechanism address?

Source Addressed by Notes (1) Producer SDK retry Dedup on event_id in Silver Exactly-once delivery does not help — the producer genuinely sent two distinct messages (2) Broker-side producer retry Idempotent producer + dedup on event_id Belt and braces (3) Consumer reprocess on restart Exactly-once effect: checkpointed offsets committed atomically with the Delta write This is the only one delivery semantics solves

Teams that answer "exactly-once handles duplicates" have answered one third of the question. Exactly-once transport does not give you exactly-once data — the 0.4% producer duplicates arrive as legitimately distinct messages.

Bronze retains duplicates (CS-09's ADR): the duplicate rate is a producer health metric, spiking to 3% on poorly-connected devices, and destroying it saves nothing. Silver deduplicates:

(spark.readStream.table("bronze.gps_events")
   .withWatermark("ts", "10 minutes")
   .dropDuplicates(["event_id", "ts"])       # bounded by the watermark
   .writeStream.option("checkpointLocation", SILVER_CKPT)
   .toTable("silver.vehicle_positions"))

P5(d) is the question that separates a good answer from an excellent one: a duplicate arriving after the dedup window closes will pass through. With a 10-minute window and P4's distribution, that is ~0.07% of duplicates — roughly 40 events/day. Detect it, do not pretend it cannot happen:

-- daily audit: duplicates that escaped the streaming dedup window
SELECT event_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM silver.vehicle_positions
WHERE DATE(ts) = current_date() - 1 GROUP BY event_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

and repair with a batch MERGE. Every streaming dedup is bounded; the mature design pairs it with an unbounded batch audit.

Q6. The lying clock. Does your design survive it? (P6)

Model answer. Almost no Round-0 design does, and this is the most valuable failure in the case.

Trace it: 61 vehicles emit ts 4–11 hours in the future. Spark's watermark is max(event_time_seen) − watermark_delay. One event at T+11h drives the watermark to T+11h−10min. Every subsequent legitimate event, at real time T, is now more than 10 minutes behind the watermark and is dropped as late. The pipeline goes silent for the entire fleet. Nothing errors. Throughput is normal. Consumer lag is zero — the consumer is happily reading and discarding everything.

Where to defend, in order of preference:

  1. At the stream, before the watermark is computed — the essential defence. Route future-dated events out before they can influence event time: 
    .withColumn("_clock_skew_s",
            unix_timestamp("_ingested_at") - unix_timestamp("ts"))
# a negative skew means the device claims the future
.withColumn("_ts_trusted", col("_clock_skew_s") > -60)   # 60 s of tolerable skew
# only trusted rows drive the watermark; untrusted rows are branched to quarantine
    This is a plausibility check on event time itself, and it is the streaming analogue of CS-06's reconciliation tier: it compares the device's claim against an independent clock (the broker's / ingest's).
  2. In Silver, as quarantine. Future-dated events land in Bronze (they are what the device said — CS-09 forbids dropping them) and are routed to quarantine in Silver with the measured skew recorded.
  3. At the producer. Correct, but the firmware cannot change this year — and, more generally, you cannot rely on a defence that lives in the system that is broken.

Do not clamp. Rewriting ts to now() produces a plausible, wrong, unmarked value — a silent repair, which CS-09 classifies as NEVER-before-Bronze and CS-11 will show you the cost of.

Alert on the skew distribution per producer_version: 

SELECT producer_version, COUNT(*) AS n,
       AVG(unix_timestamp(_ingested_at) - unix_timestamp(ts)) AS mean_skew_s
FROM   bronze.gps_events WHERE DATE(_ingested_at) = current_date()
GROUP  BY producer_version;
The 61 bad devices appear immediately as a distinct producer_version cohort with a negative mean skew. Segment by producer version — the same instruction as CS-06, and the exact query CS-11 will require tomorrow.

Q7. What breaks first at 15M events/day, and how do you know before it does? (P6(e))

Model answer. Ranked by how soon it bites, with the leading indicator for each:

Rank What breaks Why Leading indicator Alert 1 Small files in the Delta sinks A 30 s trigger writes 2,880 commits/day per sink. Within weeks numFiles reaches six figures and read latency climbs DESCRIBE DETAIL numFiles, and mean file size numFiles > 5000 or mean file size < 32 MB → scheduled OPTIMIZE 2 Streaming state growth Watermark × event rate × per-key state. Grows silently until an executor OOMs, usually at peak State-store rows and bytes per micro-batch Any monotonic growth over 30 min at steady input rate 3 Per-partition consumer lag on a skewed key If the key is ever changed to something skewed, one partition grows while the total looks flat Per-partition lag, never the sum Lag increasing for 5 consecutive minutes on any single partition 4 Watermark stall A silent partition (all its vehicles offline) stops advancing event time; windows never close and output silently stops Watermark timestamp per query Watermark not advancing for 3× the trigger interval 5 Checkpoint contention / accidental sharing Two queries sharing a checkpoint path corrupt each other's offsets on restart Checkpoint path uniqueness assertion at deploy Deploy-time check, not a runtime alert 6 Cost Autoscaling upward under sustained load, quietly, against the SAR 65,000 ceiling SAR per million events (unit cost) Unit cost rising while volume is flat

The primary metric on the wall is per-partition consumer lag, alerting on the derivative. The secondary is watermark progression — because a stalled watermark is the failure mode where lag is zero and nothing is being produced, which is invisible to every throughput-based monitor.

Say the general lesson: in streaming, the dangerous failures are the quiet ones. A crashed consumer pages someone. A consumer that reads everything and drops it because a device from the future poisoned the watermark does not.

docs.title: 8. Solution approach — reference architecture
docs.text: Present this as one defensible set of trade-offs, not as the answer. Every line below gives something up.

docs.title: 8.1 The twelve decisions
docs.text: # Decision Value Trade-off explicitly accepted 1 Partition key vehicle_id Per-trip ordering is not guaranteed across a vehicle's trips; acceptable because no consumer needs it 2 Partitions 24 Over-provisioned for today's 620 ev/s. Chosen because partitions cannot be reduced and increasing them breaks per-key ordering across the change 3 Retention 7 days Cannot stream-replay beyond a week; anything older is batch-reprocessed from bronze.gps_events, which is cheaper anyway 4 Replication RF 3, min.insync.replicas=2 3× storage (~19 GB — negligible) for single-broker-loss durability 5 Consumer groups Two: gps-bronze-land, ops-alerts Two pipelines to operate instead of one, in exchange for independent latency, independent failure and free consumer addition 6 Delivery semantics Exactly-once effect: at-least-once delivery + idempotent Delta sink + offsets committed atomically with the write Slightly higher latency than fire-and-forget; solves only consumer-side duplicates, so producer dedup is still required 7 Watermark Ops 30 s · AI 10 min · training none (batch from Bronze) Ops drops 1.7% of late events (accepted, stated); AI drops 0.07% from the streaming view only — all retained in Bronze 8 Dedup Key event_id; window = watermark; in Silver Bronze carries ~60,000 duplicate rows/day (retained deliberately as a health metric); ~40 late duplicates/day escape the window and are caught by a daily batch audit 9 Checkpoint One per query, on durable object storage, outside the table path Operational discipline required at deploy; a shared checkpoint is a top-two cause of streaming outages 10 Replay Ops: new consumer group from a chosen offset. AI: never replay the stream — rebuild silver/gold in batch from Bronze Batch rebuild is slower than a replay but cannot duplicate Bronze rows, which a stream replay into an append-only sink would 11 Backpressure Bounded maxOffsetsPerTrigger; autoscale 2–6 workers; lag alert on the derivative Under a sustained burst the AI path falls behind rather than failing — a deliberate choice of late over lost. Ops path is never throttled 12 Health metric Per-partition consumer lag (alert: increasing 5 min) + watermark progression (alert: stalled 3× trigger) Two metrics rather than one, because lag alone cannot see a poisoned watermark

docs.title: 8.2 Round 1 — late events, resolved
docs.text:
• 480-ping burst arrives as one or two micro-batches, not 480 — micro-batch boundaries are time-based, not event-based. Throughput impact is negligible (480 events against 620/s peak).
  • Within its partition the burst is ordered by arrival, so its event times are all in the past relative to neighbouring live events: it is out-of-order by construction.
  • Ops path (30 s watermark): the whole burst is late and dropped. Correct — a 40-minute-old harsh-braking alert is worthless.
  • AI path (10 min watermark): the burst is late and dropped from the streaming aggregate.
  • Nothing is lost. All 480 events are in bronze.gps_events. The next batch rebuild of gold.eta_features includes them. The watermark bounded latency and state; it did not bound retention.

docs.title: 8.3 Round 2 — duplicates, resolved
docs.text: Bronze: retain. Silver: dropDuplicates(["event_id","ts"]) under the 10-minute watermark. Daily batch audit for escapees, repaired by MERGE. Producer-side idempotence enabled where the SDK supports it. Monitor duplicate_rate per producer_version per day as a producer health metric — a rate that triples after a firmware rollout is a device-fleet defect worth knowing about, and it is only visible because Bronze kept the duplicates.

docs.title: 8.4 Round 3 — out-of-order and the lying clock, resolved
docs.text:
gps = (spark.readStream.format("kafka").option("subscribe","masar.gps.pings").load()
  .select(from_json(col("value").cast("string"), GPS_SCHEMA).alias("e"),
          col("topic"), col("partition"), col("offset"), col("timestamp").alias("_broker_ts"))
  .select("e.*", "topic", "partition", "offset", "_broker_ts")
  .withColumn("_ingested_at", current_timestamp())
  .withColumn("_source_file", concat_ws(":", col("topic"), col("partition"), col("offset")))
  .withColumn("_clock_skew_s", unix_timestamp("_ingested_at") - unix_timestamp("ts")))

# 1. BRONZE lands EVERYTHING, including future-dated events. Nothing is dropped.
(gps.writeStream.option("checkpointLocation", BRONZE_CKPT)
    .outputMode("append").toTable("bronze.gps_events"))

# 2. SILVER: only clock-plausible rows drive the watermark; the rest are quarantined.
trusted   = gps.filter(col("_clock_skew_s") > -60)
untrusted = gps.filter(col("_clock_skew_s") <= -60)      # device claims the future

(trusted.withWatermark("ts", "10 minutes")
        .dropDuplicates(["event_id", "ts"])
        .transform(normalise_speed_by_producer_version)   # <-- CS-11's missing step
        .writeStream.option("checkpointLocation", SILVER_CKPT)
        .toTable("silver.vehicle_positions"))

(untrusted.writeStream.option("checkpointLocation", QUAR_CKPT)
          .toTable("silver.vehicle_positions_quarantine"))

Three properties: Bronze is complete, the watermark cannot be poisoned by one device, and the 61 bad devices are counted in quarantine rather than silently discarded — so the alert on _clock_skew_s per producer_version fires within a day.

docs.title: 8.6 Scoring sheet (cross-team review; 5 points each, 40 total)
docs.text:
# Category 0–1 2–3 4–5 1 Partition key Chosen for throughput or arbitrarily Reasonable key, weak justification vehicle_id (or equivalent), justified by "what must not be reordered" 2 Consumer topology One group for both consumers Two groups, no reasoning Two groups, justified by independent latency + failure + free consumer addition 3 Delivery semantics "Exactly-once" asserted as a setting Correct mechanism stated Mechanism stated and correctly scoped to consumer-side duplicates only 4 Watermark One watermark for everything, or a round number with no source Derived from the distribution Per-consumer watermarks, residual stated per path, and "nothing is lost, Bronze retains it" 5 Dedup In Bronze, or absent On event_id in Silver In Silver, windowed, plus the batch audit for escapees and the duplicate rate as a producer health metric 6 Clock skew (Round 3) Design fails; watermark poisoned Detected, but clamped or dropped pre-Bronze Bronze lands it, quarantined in Silver, watermark protected, alert per producer_version 7 Failure prediction No answer, or "it will scale" One failure mode named Ranked failure modes, each with a leading indicator and an alert condition 8 Trade-off honesty Design presented as optimal Some costs acknowledged Every major decision names what it gives up, including an accepted failure mode

32–40 production-ready · 24–31 sound, gaps in observability · 16–23 works until it does not · < 16 re-run Round 0.

docs.title: 9. What good looks like vs common wrong turns
docs.text: What good looks like Common wrong turn Picks the key by asking "what must not be reordered?" Picks city (3 keys, hot partition) or round-robin (no ordering anywhere) Two consumer groups; can state what each buys One consumer writing Bronze then fanning out from Bronze, missing the 5 s Ops SLA by design Retention 7 days, because the log is not the system of record 90-day retention, confusing the log with the lake Scopes exactly-once to consumer-side duplicates only Claims exactly-once solves all three duplicate sources Dedups in Silver, keeps duplicates in Bronze as a health metric Dedups at ingest, violating CS-09's ADR and destroying the signal Pairs the bounded streaming dedup with an unbounded batch audit Treats the dedup window as absolute Per-consumer watermarks with stated residuals One watermark; or 30 minutes "to be safe", reproducing the 41 GB OOM Knows the watermark bounds latency and state, never retention Believes a watermark drop is permanent data loss Survives the lying clock by protecting the watermark before it is computed Design silently drops the entire fleet's data and reports zero lag Quarantines future-dated events with the skew recorded Clamps ts to now() — a silent repair Names per-partition lag and watermark progression Monitors throughput and CPU, both healthy while output has stopped Schedules OPTIMIZE on streaming sinks from day one Discovers small files in month three and concludes "Delta is slow" Every decision names what it gives up Presents the design as optimal

docs.title: 10. Debrief (7 minutes)
docs.text:
1. The origin insight, restated as a test. LinkedIn's move was from integration to publication: producers publish, consumers subscribe at their own offsets. The test of whether you have built that, rather than a message queue with extra steps: can a new consumer be added without any producer knowing? If yes, you have a backbone. If no, you have point-to-point integration with a broker in the middle.
  2. Replayability changes what is possible operationally. Because the log is durable and positional, reprocessing is a routine operation, not a recovery project. That single property is why a bad deploy on Friday is fixed on Monday by resetting an offset, instead of by a data-restoration ticket.
  3. The three escalations were one lesson. Late events, duplicates and out-of-order timestamps are all the same problem: event time and processing time are different things, and every streaming decision is a trade about how long you are willing to wait for the world to finish telling you what happened. The watermark is that trade, made explicit and given a number.
  4. Round 3 broke almost every design in the room, and it broke them silently. One device with a wrong clock, and the pipeline reads everything and produces nothing, with zero lag and normal throughput. In streaming, the dangerous failures are the quiet ones, which is why watermark progression must be monitored alongside lag.
  5. What survives contact with 15M events/day is not throughput — 620 events/s is unremarkable. It is file hygiene, bounded state, per-partition observability, and a design that fails late rather than lost. Scale did not break anything in this case; unbounded things did.
  6. The course question. "What happens to Masar's AI system if the streaming backbone is designed for one consumer?" The second consumer is bolted on, they share offsets, and the first outage of one becomes an outage of both — and the third consumer, the one that has not been imagined yet, requires a producer change and therefore never gets built. Architecture is mostly about what you make cheap for the person who comes after you.
  7. Hand forward to CS-11, deliberately. "Every design in this room now handles late events, duplicates, out-of-order timestamps and a lying clock. Tomorrow you will investigate an incident in which all of that worked perfectly. Every event arrived exactly once, in order, with a correct timestamp and a valid schema — and the AI model degraded by 18% anyway."

docs.title: 11. The one sentence participants should leave with
docs.text: Kafka's contribution was not speed but decoupling: a durable, ordered, replayable log lets every consumer read at its own position and its own pace, so the real design work is not the broker but the twelve decisions around it — partition key, watermark, dedup key and layer, checkpoint, replay and the health metric — and every one of them is a trade you must name, including the failure you agree to accept.

docs.title: CS-11 — The Masar National Mobility Data Incident
The signature case study of SDA-DSC-214
docs.text: Field Value Case ID CS-11 Modules M5 (streaming ingest) · M6 (quality, observability, governance) · M8 (serving AI and BI) — the course's integrating case Day / Hour Day 4 evening brief (10 min) → Day 5 · Hours 2–3 (90 minutes) Duration 90 minutes Format Staged incident investigation → remediation exercise → blameless post-incident review Group size 4–5 per team, each team is an incident response squad; assign roles (Incident Lead · Data Detective · Model Owner · Scribe) Deliverable (a) A completed investigation worksheet naming the causal chain; (b) the five conclusions; (c) a remediation plan with four executable controls; (d) a completed blameless post-incident review Materials Evidence pack released in six timed stages (P1–P6), printed and held by the facilitator; investigation worksheet §7 one per team; post-incident review template §11 one per team; a laptop per team with the Masar Lakehouse and the fixture available Fixture data/fixtures/incident_speed_unit/gps_2026-06-05_v250.ndjson.gz (shipped gzipped as .ndjson.gz) — 47,583 events, 1,004 vehicles, mean speed_kmh 35.45 → 9.85, a ratio of 3.60× Facilitator prep 45 minutes, mandatory. Read data/fixtures/incident_speed_unit/README.md end to end. Run every query in §10 once against the shipped data so you know what the output looks like. Pre-print and separate the six evidence stages into six physical stacks — the staging is the pedagogy

docs.title: Facilitator note — why this case exists
docs.text:
Every previous case in this course had a component that failed. Here nothing fails. The producer works. The stream is exactly-once. The schema validates. Great Expectations is green. The DAG is green. The dashboards are correct. Freshness, volume and row counts are all normal. Every engineer did their job correctly.

And the AI system degrades by 18%.

This is the gap between "everything is healthy" and "the system is working", and closing that gap is what separates a data engineer from a data engineer who can be trusted with an AI platform. Do not let teams find the answer quickly. The value of this case is in the forty minutes where they cannot see it.

docs.title: 1. Scenario
docs.text:
Masar (مسار) is the national smart-mobility platform of a Saudi ride-hailing and public-transit operator. It serves 14,000 vehicles across Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam, Mecca and Medina, and its Lakehouse feeds two consumer families:

  • BI — gold.fact_trip and its conformed dimensions, driving the executive dashboard, city-level operations reporting and the monthly regulatory submission.
  • AI — gold.eta_features and gold.zone_hourly_demand, driving the rider-facing ETA quote and the demand-forecasting model that positions vehicles ahead of demand.

It is 08:00 on Thursday 9 June 2026. The model-monitoring job has raised its first alert in four months:

ALERT  demand_forecast_v4  |  severity: HIGH  |  fired 2026-06-09 08:00:04 +03
  7-day rolling MAPE:  11.4%  ->  13.5%   (target <= 12.0%)
  accuracy deterioration vs 30-day baseline:  -18.2%
  affected: all zones, RUH/JED/DMM;  MAK/MED within tolerance
  last model deploy: 2026-04-19 (51 days ago)
  last feature-pipeline change: none in 30 days

The on-call data engineer opens the executive dashboard first, as everyone does.

It looks completely normal. Trip counts are on trend. Revenue is on trend. Completion rate, cancellation rate, mean fare, driver utilisation, city mix — every tile is within its usual band. There is no red anywhere in the platform.

The Chief Data Officer will ask, in ninety minutes, one question: "Is our data broken, or is our model broken?"

Your teams must answer it, and prove it.

docs.title: 2. Business context
docs.text:
Item Figure Vehicles on the platform 14,000 Vehicles affected by the firmware rollout 1,004 (34% of the fleet cohort; 7.2% of all vehicles) GPS events/day ~15,000,000 Events in the incident batch 47,583 Demand-forecast MAPE before 11.4% Demand-forecast MAPE after 13.5% Accuracy deterioration −18.2% ETA quotes affected per day ~412,000 Mean ETA over-prediction on affected zones +3.8 minutes Rider cancellations attributable to ETA drift, per day ~5,900 Revenue impact, 4 days undetected SAR 1,180,000 Vehicle-positioning misallocation cost, 4 days SAR 740,000 Model re-baselining and retraining SAR 190,000 Incident response, investigation, remediation SAR 290,000 Total incident cost SAR 2,400,000 Cost of the control that would have prevented it ≈ SAR 12,000 (one distribution monitor, two engineer-days)

The final two rows are the case. A control costing about two engineer-days would have prevented a SAR 2.4M incident, and it was not built because nothing in the platform was ever red.

docs.title: 3. Technical challenge
docs.text:
Teams must uncover, from evidence alone, a seven-link causal chain in which every link behaved correctly:

1. GPS producer firmware rolled from producer_version 2.4.0 -> 2.5.0 on 34% of the fleet
                                  |
2. speed_kmh values silently became METRES PER SECOND -- same field name, same double type
                                  |
3. Schema validation ACCEPTED it, because the TYPE was unchanged and the values were plausible
                                  |
4. Silver transformations continued normally: dedup passed, ranges passed, joins passed
                                  |
5. gold.eta_features.rolling_avg_speed_10m was corrupted -- averaging km/h and m/s together
                                  |
6. The ETA feature distribution shifted; the model read "this zone is crawling" for a third
   of the fleet and began over-predicting journey times
                                  |
7. AI predictions degraded by 18%, while BI -- which reports counts, revenue and completion,
   not speed -- showed absolutely nothing

The intellectual difficulty is link 3. Everyone accepts that a schema check catches a renamed or retyped field. Almost nobody has internalised that a schema is a statement about structure and says nothing whatsoever about meaning — and that a unit is meaning, not structure.

docs.title: 4. Constraints
docs.text:
• Bronze is immutable. Do not permit a team to "fix the data at source" — the raw record is what the device sent and it is the evidence.
  • The firmware cannot be rolled back within the incident window. 1,004 vehicles are in the field; an OTA rollback takes 6 days. The fix must be on the platform side.
  • The CDO's question must be answered in 90 minutes, with evidence.
  • Riders are being quoted wrong ETAs right now. There is a live-mitigation decision to make before the root cause is fully proven — teams must handle acting under uncertainty.
  • PDPL applies throughout: raw lat/lon is sensitive-personal; nothing in the response may re-materialise personal data into BI or the online store.

docs.title: 5. The incident timeline
docs.text:
Give teams the left two columns only at the start (as "what we know so far"). The right column is the facilitator's key and is revealed during the debrief. The asymmetry between what was happening and what was observed is the entire case.

When What was observed at the time What was actually happening Day 1 — Sun 2026-06-05, 09:00 UTC (12:00 +03) Nothing. No alert, no ticket, no anomaly. Device firmware 2.5.0 begins rolling to 1,004 vehicles. It keeps the field name speed_kmh and its double type, and starts writing metres per second. Day 1, 09:00–23:59 Ingest normal: 15.02M events. Consumer lag flat. Zero parse errors. GX suite 7/7 PASSED. 47,583 events land in bronze.gps_events with speed_kmh values 3.6× too small. Bronze faithfully records exactly what the device sent — including producer_version = "2.5.0". Day 2 — Mon 2026-06-06 DAG green. dbt test green. Freshness green. Volume green. Dashboard normal. silver.vehicle_positions promotes every affected row. Dedup passes. Range check 0 <= speed_kmh <= 200 passes — 9.85 is deeper inside the range than 35.45 was. gold.eta_features.rolling_avg_speed_10m begins averaging km/h and m/s in the same window. Day 3 — Tue 2026-06-07 ETA quotes drift long on some routes. 3 rider complaints reach support; all closed as "traffic". The model, reading a collapsed speed feature, infers heavy congestion in affected zones and over-predicts durations by ~3.8 min. Demand forecasting begins under-serving those zones. Day 4 — Wed 2026-06-08 Cancellation rate up 0.3 pts — within its normal daily band. Nobody investigates. ~5,900 additional cancellations. Vehicles positioned away from zones the model believes are congested. Revenue impact accumulating at ~SAR 295k/day. Day 5 — Thu 2026-06-09, 08:00 +03 Model-monitoring alert: 7-day MAPE 11.4% → 13.5%, −18.2%. BI dashboard entirely normal. Every platform health signal green. Four days of corrupted features have moved the rolling metric past its threshold. The first and only signal the platform ever produced came from the model, not from the data platform. Day 5, 08:00–09:30 (this session) Teams investigate.

Note for the debrief: the platform never detected this. The model did. And the model detected it on a 7-day rolling metric, which is why it took four days. Nothing in the data platform — not schema validation, not Great Expectations, not freshness, not volume, not lineage, not the DAG — produced a single signal at any point.

docs.title: 6. Evidence pack — released in six stages
docs.text:
How to run the staging. Six physical stacks. Release one at a time on the clock in §8. Never release early, even if a team asks. Never hint. A team that reaches the answer at P3 has been given the case by the facilitator, not by the evidence.

After each release, require every team to write one sentence in the worksheet's "What this rules in / rules out" box before they discuss. This forces evidence to be interpreted rather than accumulated.

What this rules in / rules out. Rules out: a missing batch, a partial write, a schema change large enough to appear in the log, a manual edit. Rules in: the volume of data is right and the content of data is wrong. This is the moment to say to a stuck team: "you have been looking for a missing row. Start looking for a wrong value."

Note the last useful line: version 808/809 is the boundary, and gold.eta_features VERSION AS OF 808 will be the rollback target in §9.

Read the RESULT block aloud. Then read the fourth-from-last row aloud again: payload.speed_kmh double → double —.

What this rules in / rules out. Rules out: any structural change. Rules in the entire lesson of the case — the schema is identical and the data is wrong. If teams have not yet framed the question as "what changed in the values", P4 forces it.

At this point, hold the room and ask one question: "If the schema is identical, what is the smallest thing that could have changed?" Take answers. The one you want is: the meaning.

docs.title: P5 — Producer release notes (released at minute 46)
docs.text:
Retrieved from the device vendor's firmware portal, on request, after the investigation reached the producer:

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Masar Telematics SDK — release 2.5.0                        2026-06-05
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Rollout: staged, cohort A (1,004 vehicles), from 09:00 UTC
 Rollback: OTA, estimated 6 days for full fleet

 CHANGES
  * Reduced GPS fix interval jitter (median -180 ms)
  * Battery: sleep-state tuning, ~4% improvement on idle
  * Harmonised telemetry units to SI across the payload for consistency
    with the vehicle CAN-bus integration.
  * Fixed a rare crash in the offline buffer flush path
  * Dependency bump: openssl 3.0.13 -> 3.0.14

 BREAKING CHANGES
  none
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Bullet three. "Harmonised telemetry units to SI across the payload." Ten words. Filed under CHANGES, not under BREAKING CHANGES, because the field name did not change and the type did not change — and by the vendor's definition of "breaking", which is a structural definition, that is entirely defensible.

SI unit for speed is metres per second. The field is still called speed_kmh.

What this rules in / rules out. This is the root cause. But do not let the room stop here — the causal chain is not "a vendor made a mistake". It is: the vendor made a change that was breaking in every sense except the one anybody was checking.

docs.title: Day 4, end of session — the 10-minute brief
docs.text:
Do not describe the incident. Set the scene and stop:

"Tomorrow morning you are the on-call incident squad for a national mobility platform. At 08:00 the demand-forecasting model's accuracy has fallen 18%. The BI dashboard is completely normal. Every quality check is green. Every pipeline succeeded. Nothing has failed. Read nothing tonight. Come with the question you would ask first."

Assign roles now so no time is lost in the morning: Incident Lead (runs the clock and the hypothesis list), Data Detective (runs the queries), Model Owner (holds the AI perspective and asks "what does this do to the feature?"), Scribe (owns the worksheet and the post-incident review).

docs.title: Day 5 — the 90 minutes
docs.text: Min Stage Facilitator does Watch for 0–5 Alert. Read the P1 alert block aloud verbatim. Hand out the worksheet and P1. Start a visible countdown clock to 09:30. The clock matters. Time pressure produces the premature hypotheses that make the debrief valuable. Teams that open a laptop immediately. Make them write H1–H3 first. 5–12 Round 1 — hypotheses, no evidence. Every team writes at least four hypotheses on the worksheet before any further evidence. Circulate and read them. Say nothing. Typical H1: "the model drifted." H2: "training data is stale." H3: "a pipeline failed." All three will be killed by P2/P3. 12–14 Release P2 (BI dashboard). One sentence in the log, then discuss. Ask one table: "Is this dashboard wrong?" The answer is no, and the room needs to hear it. Teams that assume BI is lying. It is not. It is measuring something else. 14–24 Round 2. Teams kill hypotheses against P2. Prompt: "What does this dashboard never look at?" Teams that get stuck asserting "the data must be fine, everything is green." Good. Let them sit in it. 24–26 Release P3 (_delta_log). "Row counts are correct to within 0.3%. What does that tell you?" The intended shift: stop looking for missing rows, start looking for wrong values. 26–36 Round 3 — laptops open. Teams query the Lakehouse. This is the first point at which running a query is more useful than thinking. Circulate with exactly one question: "What columns does your dashboard use, and what columns does your model use?" Do not elaborate. Teams that query trips instead of GPS. The dashboard's world and the model's world barely intersect — that is the finding. 36–38 Release P4 (schema diff). Read RESULT: SCHEMAS ARE IDENTICAL aloud. Then: "If the schema is identical, what is the smallest thing that could have changed?" Take answers until someone says the meaning. This is the pivot of the case. Do not rush it. 38–46 Round 4 — the cracking query. Teams must find the GROUP BY producer_version. To a team within reach: "You have a column in Bronze that nobody has grouped by yet." Nothing more. Most teams reach it here. A team that reaches it at minute 30 without P4 has done excellent work — say so publicly. 46–48 Release P5 (release notes). Read bullet three aloud, then the "BREAKING CHANGES: none" line. Pause. The reaction to those two lines together is the emotional centre of the case. 48–54 Round 5 — quantify. Teams compute the ratio (expect ~3.6) and the drift statistic. Push for a statistic: "3.6× is a number. Give me the one you would put in an alert threshold." Teams that stop at "it looks wrong." PSI/KS is the deliverable. 54–56 Release P6 (histograms). Point at the bimodality. "What does two humps in one column always mean?" Answer: two populations — two producers, two units, or two definitions. 56–68 Round 6 — remediation. All four controls (R1–R4), each with an owner and a done-test. Plus the live-mitigation decision (worksheet Q6). Force the live decision to be made before they feel certain: "Riders are being quoted wrong ETAs while you write this. What do you do at 08:40, not at 09:30?" Teams that only plan long-term fixes. Incident response has two clocks. 68–78 The CDO briefing. Each team gives a 90-second briefing answering "is our data broken or our model broken?" You play the CDO. Interrupt with: "You are telling me a firmware update on 7% of vehicles cost us 2.4 million riyals and no alarm went off anywhere?" Let them answer. Briefings that lead with technical detail. The answer is one sentence, then the evidence. 78–86 Post-incident review. Teams complete §11's template. Enforce the blameless framing explicitly. Any team that writes "the vendor should have..." is redirected: "The vendor is not on your team and will do this again. What control do you own?" This is the most transferable ten minutes of the course. Protect it. 86–90 Debrief. §12. Reveal the timeline's right-hand column. Close on §13 verbatim. Deliver the two headline numbers last: SAR 2.4M against SAR 12k. —

docs.title: 9. The five conclusions teams must reach
docs.text: These are the assessable outcomes. A team has not completed CS-11 until it can state all five in its own words. Take them in order in the debrief; each one sets up the next.

docs.title: Conclusion 1 — Why schema validation missed a semantic change
docs.text:
A schema is a contract about structure: field names, types, nullability, nesting. It says nothing about meaning: units, scale, currency, timezone, encoding, coordinate reference system, or the definition of an enum value.

speed_kmh was a non-null double before the change and a non-null double after it. Every structural validator — a Spark StructType check, an Avro or Protobuf compatibility check, Delta's mergeSchema, a JSON Schema validator, a dbt contract on types — reports FULL_COMPATIBLE, and each is correct in reporting so.

The general form: semantic changes are always type-compatible, because the type is not what changed. This makes them structurally invisible to the entire class of validation most platforms rely on. The same defect class produced CS-06's currency change (halalas → riyals, double → double) and would produce identical results for a timezone change (timestamp → timestamp), a coordinate-system change (double → double) or a redefinition of status = 'completed' (string → string).

The corollary teams must state: a green schema check is evidence of nothing except that the shape is unchanged. Validation that stops at structure is validating the envelope and not the letter.

docs.title: Conclusion 2 — Why BI did not expose the failure
docs.text:
BI measures what the business transacts: trips completed, revenue earned, fares charged, cancellations, driver utilisation, city mix. Every one of those is derived from silver.trips and gold.fact_trip. speed_kmh appears in none of them. The dashboard was not fooled and did not fail — it was measuring a different part of the world, correctly, the entire time.

The deeper structural point, and the one that transfers: BI aggregates are counts and sums of discrete business events. Corrupting a continuous physical measurement does not move a count. Meanwhile AI features are transformations of continuous measurements, and a scale error passes through them directly and proportionally.

Say the consequence plainly: a healthy BI layer is not evidence of a healthy data platform. For four days, a BI-centric view of platform health was not merely unhelpful — it was actively reassuring, and that reassurance is what allowed a 0.3-point cancellation rise on Day 4 to be dismissed. Most organisations' entire data-observability practice is BI-shaped, which means it is blind to precisely the failures that damage AI systems.

docs.title: Conclusion 3 — Why AI was disproportionately affected
docs.text:
Four mechanisms compound, and teams should name at least three:

  1. Direct functional dependence. rolling_avg_speed_10m is computed from payload.speed_kmh. A 3.6× scale error propagates into the feature at full strength. No aggregation dilutes it; averaging km/h and m/s together produces a value that is neither.
  2. Models weight features, they do not sanity-check them. A dashboard is read by a human with priors — an analyst seeing a mean speed of 9 km/h across Riyadh would question it. A gradient-boosted model has no priors and no concept of "km/h". It has a learned weight, and it applies it faithfully to a number from a distribution it has never seen.
  3. Feature semantics amplify the error into a decision. Low average speed means congestion to this model. The corrupted feature did not merely add noise; it delivered a confident, coherent, entirely false narrative — "a third of the fleet is crawling" — that the model acted on correctly given its inputs. Corrupted features do not make models uncertain; they make models confidently wrong.
  4. The feedback loop closes. The demand model, believing affected zones congested, positioned vehicles away from them. Fewer vehicles produced longer waits and more cancellations, which the model then observed as reduced demand — confirming its own error. The data defect became a self-reinforcing operational failure, which is why the cost grew each day rather than staying constant.

The transferable statement: BI degrades gracefully and visibly; AI degrades silently and compounds. A wrong number on a dashboard is a wrong number. A wrong number in a feature is a wrong decision, repeated 412,000 times a day, that changes the world the next batch of data describes.

docs.title: Conclusion 4 — Why observability must include feature distributions
docs.text:
Masar's observability, before the incident, covered: freshness, volume, row counts, schema conformance, null rates, referential integrity, range checks, pipeline success, and consumer lag. Every one of them was green throughout. They are the standard, respectable set, and they are all operational signals — they answer "did the pipeline run?" rather than "does the data mean what it meant yesterday?"

What was missing is a distribution monitor on the features the model actually consumes, segmented by the dimension along which change is deployed:

monitor: gold.eta_features.rolling_avg_speed_10m
  statistic: PSI (10 deciles) vs frozen baseline 2026-05-01..2026-05-31
  segment by: producer_version, city, hour_of_day
  threshold: PSI > 0.20 warn, > 0.30 page
  observed on 2026-06-06: PSI 1.87   -> would have paged on DAY 2

Four properties make this the right control, and each is a design decision teams should articulate:

  • It monitors the feature, not the source. A source monitor on speed_kmh also fires here, but the feature is what the model consumes and is where every upstream defect eventually converges. Monitoring the last mile catches defects you did not anticipate.
  • It uses a frozen, versioned baseline with a named owner. A rolling baseline would have absorbed the corruption within a fortnight (CS-06's "baseline-the-bug" trap) and then flagged the correction as the anomaly.
  • It segments by producer_version. Aggregated over the whole fleet the mean moved 25.7% — large, but a 34%-of-a-cohort effect is exactly the kind that a global threshold can be tuned to ignore. Segmented, the v2.5.0 cohort's mean is 9.85 against 35.45, a 3.6× separation that no threshold survives. Always segment drift by the dimension along which change is deployed.
  • It watches for bimodality, not only for mean shift. Two humps in one column means two populations — which is the signature of a semantic split rather than a real-world change, and it is the fastest thing to eyeball once a monitor exists to look at.

State the principle: "the pipeline ran" and "the data is still what it was" are different questions, and only the second one protects a model.

docs.title: Conclusion 5 — Why data contracts must specify semantics and units, not merely types
docs.text:
The contract in force on 5 June:

# contracts/gps_events.yml  (v1.2 — the contract that PASSED on the day of the incident)
fields:
  - name: payload.speed_kmh
    type: double
    nullable: false

That contract was fully satisfied by the corrupted data. It is a type declaration wearing the word "contract", and it cannot express the thing that changed.

The contract that makes this class impossible:

# contracts/gps_events.yml  (v2.0 — unit-aware, semantic)
fields:
  - name: payload.speed_kmh
    type: double
    nullable: false
    unit: "km/h"                     # SEMANTIC. A change here is a BREAKING change.
    unit_field: "payload.speed_unit" # producer MUST declare its unit in the payload
    valid_range: [0, 200]
    expected_distribution:
      mean:   {min: 25.0, max: 45.0}   # a scale error breaks this; a traffic change does not
      p05:    {min:  8.0, max: 20.0}
      p95:    {min: 40.0, max: 60.0}
    reconciles_with:
      expression: "silver.trips.distance_km / (silver.trips.duration_min / 60)"
      tolerance_pct: 25                # independent measurement of the same physical fact
    segment_monitoring_by: ["producer_version"]

producer_contract:
  version_field: producer_version
  breaking_change_policy: |
    ANY change to a field's unit, scale, currency, timezone, coordinate reference
    system, or enum meaning is a BREAKING change, EVEN IF the name and the type
    are unchanged. A breaking change REQUIRES a new field name or a major
    contract version bump, and dual emission for one overlap period.
  allowed_producer_versions: ["2.4.0"]   # new versions are GATED, not auto-accepted

Four clauses do the work: unit makes the meaning explicit and therefore checkable; expected_distribution makes a scale error a contract violation on the first batch; reconciles_with anchors the field to an independent measurement (distance_km / duration_min from silver.trips) so that no baseline poisoning can hide it; and allowed_producer_versions turns an unannounced producer change into a hard failure at the boundary rather than a silent acceptance.

And the organisational half, which is the harder half: the vendor's release note said "BREAKING CHANGES: none", and by a structural definition of "breaking" that was true. The contract must therefore define what breaking means, in writing, jointly, and that definition must include semantics. Otherwise two parties will each act correctly under two different definitions, which is exactly what happened.

The sentence to write down: a type is a promise about shape; a unit is a promise about meaning; and models consume meaning.

docs.title: 10. Facilitator answer key — the exact detection queries
docs.text: Have all four of these run and their output printed before the session. Teams will produce approximations; you must be able to show the canonical form.

docs.title: Q1 — Delta time-travel diff: prove the data changed at a point in time
docs.text:
-- Compare the feature table across the boundary commit (P3: versions 808 -> 809)
SELECT 'v808 (2026-06-05)' AS version,
       COUNT(*)                          AS n,
       ROUND(AVG(rolling_avg_speed_10m), 2) AS mean_speed,
       ROUND(PERCENTILE(rolling_avg_speed_10m, 0.05), 2) AS p05,
       ROUND(PERCENTILE(rolling_avg_speed_10m, 0.95), 2) AS p95
FROM   gold.eta_features VERSION AS OF 808
UNION ALL
SELECT 'v809 (2026-06-06)',
       COUNT(*), ROUND(AVG(rolling_avg_speed_10m),2),
       ROUND(PERCENTILE(rolling_avg_speed_10m,0.05),2),
       ROUND(PERCENTILE(rolling_avg_speed_10m,0.95),2)
FROM   gold.eta_features VERSION AS OF 809;

-- version              n       mean_speed   p05    p95
-- v808 (2026-06-05)   47,884      30.4      14.2   48.8
-- v809 (2026-06-06)   47,930      22.6       4.1   42.7
--
-- Row counts identical to within 0.1%. Values collapsed. This is the moment.

Same query shape against the source, to locate the change one layer earlier:

SELECT DATE(ts) AS d, ROUND(AVG(payload.speed_kmh), 2) AS mean_kmh, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM   bronze.gps_events
WHERE  ts BETWEEN '2026-06-01' AND '2026-06-09'
GROUP  BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
-- the step appears on 2026-06-05, partway through the day (09:00 UTC)

docs.title: Q2 — The query that cracks it: per-producer_version mean speed
docs.text:
SELECT producer_version,
       COUNT(*)                                  AS events,
       COUNT(DISTINCT vehicle_id)                AS vehicles,
       ROUND(AVG(payload.speed_kmh), 2)          AS mean_speed_kmh,
       ROUND(PERCENTILE(payload.speed_kmh, 0.50), 2) AS p50,
       ROUND(PERCENTILE(payload.speed_kmh, 0.95), 2) AS p95,
       ROUND(MAX(payload.speed_kmh), 2)          AS max_speed
FROM   bronze.gps_events
WHERE  DATE(ts) = '2026-06-05'
GROUP  BY producer_version
ORDER  BY producer_version;

-- producer_version  events      vehicles  mean_speed_kmh  p50    p95    max_speed
-- 2.4.0             14,972,300    12,996        35.45     33.9   61.2     118.4
-- 2.5.0                 47,583     1,004         9.85      9.4   17.0      32.9
--
-- ratio of means: 35.45 / 9.85 = 3.60      <-- exactly the m/s -> km/h factor
-- max speed for v2.5.0 is 32.9. As km/h that is a fleet that never exceeds 33 km/h.
-- As m/s it is 118 km/h. The second reading is the plausible one.

This single query is the case. One GROUP BY on a column that a careless Bronze design would have dropped (CS-09, card 1 vs P2 step 5). Show it and let the room sit with how small it is.

The confirming cross-check, and the strongest evidence for the CDO because it uses an independent measurement:

-- Reconciliation: ping speed vs metered speed from silver.trips.
-- These are two independent measurements of the same physical fact.
WITH ping AS (
  SELECT trip_id, producer_version, AVG(payload.speed_kmh) AS ping_speed
  FROM   bronze.gps_events WHERE DATE(ts) = '2026-06-05'
  GROUP  BY trip_id, producer_version),
metered AS (
  SELECT trip_id, distance_km / NULLIF(duration_min,0) * 60 AS metered_speed
  FROM   silver.trips WHERE status = 'completed' AND DATE(pickup_ts) = '2026-06-05')
SELECT p.producer_version,
       COUNT(*)                                            AS trips,
       ROUND(AVG(p.ping_speed), 2)                         AS mean_ping_speed,
       ROUND(AVG(m.metered_speed), 2)                      AS mean_metered_speed,
       ROUND(AVG(m.metered_speed) / AVG(p.ping_speed), 2)  AS ratio
FROM   ping p JOIN metered m USING (trip_id)
GROUP  BY p.producer_version;

-- producer_version  trips   mean_ping_speed  mean_metered_speed  ratio
-- 2.4.0             43,120        35.45             36.02         1.02   <- agree
-- 2.5.0              4,764         9.85             35.71         3.63   <- disagree by 3.6x
--
-- The metered speed comes from the trip meter, NOT from the GPS SDK.
-- It did not change. Therefore the GPS SDK did.

docs.title: Q3 — Drift statistics: PSI and KS on the feature
docs.text:
# quality/drift/psi.py — the check that would have paged on Day 2
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import ks_2samp

def psi(expected, actual, buckets=10):
    """Population Stability Index. <0.10 stable, 0.10-0.20 moderate, >0.20 breach."""
    edges = np.percentile(expected, np.linspace(0, 100, buckets + 1))
    edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    e = np.histogram(expected, bins=edges)[0] / len(expected)
    a = np.histogram(actual,   bins=edges)[0] / len(actual)
    e, a = np.clip(e, 1e-6, None), np.clip(a, 1e-6, None)
    return float(np.sum((a - e) * np.log(a / e)))

baseline = spark.sql("""
    SELECT rolling_avg_speed_10m FROM gold.eta_features
    WHERE feature_ts BETWEEN '2026-05-01' AND '2026-05-31'
""").toPandas()["rolling_avg_speed_10m"].values          # FROZEN, versioned, owned

current = spark.sql("""
    SELECT rolling_avg_speed_10m FROM gold.eta_features
    WHERE DATE(feature_ts) = '2026-06-06'
""").toPandas()["rolling_avg_speed_10m"].values

print("PSI :", round(psi(baseline, current), 3))        # 1.870   (threshold 0.20)
ks = ks_2samp(baseline, current)
print("KS  :", round(ks.statistic, 3), "p =", ks.pvalue) # 0.310   p < 1e-300

# AND — the segmentation that makes it unmissable:
for pv in ("2.4.0", "2.5.0"):
    cur = spark.sql(f"""
        SELECT f.rolling_avg_speed_10m
        FROM   gold.eta_features f
        JOIN   (SELECT DISTINCT trip_id, producer_version FROM bronze.gps_events
                WHERE DATE(ts)='2026-06-06') g USING (trip_id)
        WHERE  g.producer_version = '{pv}'
    """).toPandas()["rolling_avg_speed_10m"].values
    print(pv, "PSI =", round(psi(baseline, cur), 3))
# 2.4.0 PSI = 0.021    <- stable, as expected
# 2.5.0 PSI = 6.940    <- catastrophic, unmissable at ANY threshold

Point out the contrast for the class: aggregated PSI 1.87 (a breach that a lenient threshold might survive); segmented PSI 6.94 (a breach nothing survives). Segmentation is not a refinement — it is the difference between a signal that can be argued with and one that cannot.

docs.title: Q4 — Blast radius: what else consumes speed_kmh?
docs.text:
-- run at the moment the root cause is confirmed, before writing the CDO briefing
SELECT downstream_table, downstream_column, consumer, last_refreshed
FROM   governance.column_lineage
WHERE  upstream_table  = 'bronze.gps_events'
  AND  upstream_column = 'payload.speed_kmh';

-- downstream_table          downstream_column         consumer            last_refreshed
-- silver.vehicle_positions  speed_kmh                 (intermediate)      2026-06-09 02:11
-- gold.eta_features         rolling_avg_speed_10m     demand_forecast_v4  2026-06-09 02:44
-- gold.eta_features         rolling_avg_speed_10m     eta_gbm_v3          2026-06-09 02:44
-- gold.driver_daily         mean_speed_kmh            driver_safety_score 2026-06-09 02:44
-- ops.alerts_speeding       speed_kmh                 ops_alerting        2026-06-09 (live)

Two findings the teams should surface from this and that nobody expects:

  1. driver_safety_score is also corrupted. Drivers on v2.5.0 vehicles have had four days of artificially low mean speeds, which flatters their safety score. This is an HR and fairness issue, not just a modelling one, and it must be disclosed and corrected.
  2. ops.alerts_speeding silently stopped firing for 1,004 vehicles — every reported speed is 3.6× too low, so no vehicle in the affected cohort has triggered a speeding alert since Day 1. A safety control was silently disabled for four days. For a national mobility platform under a regulator, this is arguably the most serious consequence in the entire incident, and it is invisible in every number on the executive dashboard.

Deliver finding 2 last in the debrief. It is the point at which the room understands that "the dashboard looked fine" is not a mitigating fact.

docs.title: 11. Remediation exercise
docs.text: Four controls. Each needs an owner, an implementation, and a done-test — something you can run that proves the control works.

docs.title: R1 — Immediate: roll back the corrupted feature via Delta time travel
docs.text:
-- 1. Confirm the last trusted version (P3: v808 is 2026-06-05, before the corruption)
DESCRIBE HISTORY gold.eta_features;

-- 2. Verify before restoring — never restore a version you have not inspected
SELECT COUNT(*), ROUND(AVG(rolling_avg_speed_10m),2)
FROM   gold.eta_features VERSION AS OF 808;      -- 47,884 rows, mean 30.4  OK

-- 3. Pin the corrupted state FIRST. It is the evidence for the post-incident review
--    and for the vendor conversation. Restoring without pinning destroys it.
CREATE TABLE incident.eta_features_corrupted_2026_06_09
SHALLOW CLONE gold.eta_features VERSION AS OF 812;

-- 4. Restore
RESTORE TABLE gold.eta_features TO VERSION AS OF 808;

-- 5. Rebuild forward with the unit normalisation applied (R2 below), then re-score.

Done-test: SELECT AVG(rolling_avg_speed_10m) FROM gold.eta_features WHERE DATE(feature_ts) = '2026-06-08' returns a value in [25, 45], and the model's MAPE on a re-scored backtest returns to ≤ 12.0%.

Note the sequencing and make teams justify it: pin before you restore. Restoring first and pinning second is a race against the next VACUUM (CS-04's lesson arriving as an operational habit). And restore before the vendor conversation, not after — the SAR 295k/day is still accruing.

The live-mitigation decision (worksheet Q6), made at 08:40 and not at 09:30: exclude v2.5.0 vehicles from feature computation immediately — a one-line filter — accepting a 7.2% reduction in feature coverage rather than a 3.6× error on 34% of a cohort. Cost: slightly noisier features for four days. Benefit: correct ETAs restored within the hour. Acting on a well-founded hypothesis before proof is complete is correct incident response, provided the action is reversible and its cost is bounded. Teams that wait for certainty lose another SAR 295k.

docs.title: R2 — Contract: a unit-aware data contract
docs.text:
Implement contracts/gps_events.yml v2.0 as specified in Conclusion 5. Plus the normalisation that should have existed in Silver from day one:

# src/masar/transform/normalise.py
UNIT_FACTOR = {"2.4.0": 1.0, "2.5.0": 3.6}   # v2.5.0 emits m/s; multiply to reach km/h

def normalise_speed_by_producer_version(df):
    """Make speed_kmh actually mean km/h for every row, whatever the producer sent.
    An UNKNOWN producer_version FAILS. It is never silently passed through."""
    known = F.create_map([F.lit(x) for kv in UNIT_FACTOR.items() for x in kv])
    return (df
        .withColumn("_speed_factor", known[F.col("producer_version")])
        .withColumn("_unit_known",   F.col("_speed_factor").isNotNull())
        .withColumn("speed_kmh_raw", F.col("payload.speed_kmh"))        # keep the original
        .withColumn("speed_kmh",     F.col("payload.speed_kmh") * F.col("_speed_factor")))
    # rows where _unit_known is false are routed to quarantine by the caller, never promoted

Done-test: inject a synthetic batch with producer_version = "2.6.0". The pipeline must quarantine it and fail the gate, not promote it. A contract that passes unknown versions has learned nothing from the incident.

docs.title: R3 — Monitoring: a distribution-drift monitor on rolling_avg_speed_10m
docs.text:
# quality/monitors/feature_drift.py — runs after every gold build, before serving
MONITORS = [{
    "feature":   "gold.eta_features.rolling_avg_speed_10m",
    "baseline":  "frozen:2026-05-01..2026-05-31",   # versioned in git, owner: ML Platform Lead
    "statistic": "psi", "buckets": 10,
    "segment_by": ["producer_version", "city"],      # <<< the clause that makes it unmissable
    "thresholds": {"warn": 0.20, "page": 0.30},
    "on_page":   "block_serving",                    # a monitor that only notifies is a log line
}]

Apply the same monitor to every column of gold.eta_features, not only to speed — the next incident will be in a different column.

Done-test: replay data/fixtures/incident_speed_unit/gps_2026-06-05_v250.ndjson.gz through the pipeline. The monitor must page within one build cycle with segmented PSI ≈ 6.9 and must block serving. This is the single most important regression test in the platform, and it belongs in CI.

docs.title: R4 — Gate: a producer-version gate
docs.text:
# quality/gates/producer_version_gate.py — runs at the Bronze -> Silver boundary
ALLOWED = {"2.4.0"}    # explicit allow-list; new versions are ADMITTED, never assumed

def gate(batch_df, batch_id):
    seen = {r.producer_version for r in
            batch_df.select("producer_version").distinct().collect()}
    unknown = seen - ALLOWED
    if unknown:
        quarantine(batch_df.filter(F.col("producer_version").isin(list(unknown))), batch_id)
        alert(severity="HIGH",
              title=f"Unknown producer_version in {batch_id}: {sorted(unknown)}",
              body=("Rows quarantined, NOT promoted to silver. A new producer version "
                    "requires: (1) vendor release notes reviewed for semantic changes, "
                    "(2) contract v-bump if any unit/scale/timezone/enum meaning changed, "
                    "(3) UNIT_FACTOR entry added, (4) 24h shadow comparison of the new "
                    "cohort's distributions against the incumbent, (5) explicit "
                    "allow-list addition by a named approver."))
        return "QUARANTINE"
    return "PROMOTE"

Done-test: the same fixture replay must quarantine all 47,583 v2.5.0 events at the Bronze→Silver boundary on Day 1, and must page. Nothing reaches silver.vehicle_positions until a human adds "2.5.0" to the allow-list with a UNIT_FACTOR entry.

Make the room notice what R4 costs: it converts an unannounced producer change from a silent semantic corruption into a loud, bounded, visible operational gap — 34% of a cohort's positions missing until someone acts. That is exactly the conversion CS-06 argued for, and it is the trade the platform should always make. Missing data asks a question; wrong data makes a decision.

docs.title: Remediation summary
docs.text:
# Control Prevents Detects Owner Effort R1 Time-travel rollback + live filter — — Data Platform on-call 1 hour R2 Unit-aware contract + Silver normalisation Yes — the class — Data Platform Lead 3 days R3 Segmented feature-drift monitor — Yes — within one build ML Platform Lead 2 days R4 Producer-version gate Yes — at the boundary Yes — Day 1 Data Platform Lead 1 day

Total: ~6 engineer-days, ≈ SAR 12,000, against an incident that cost SAR 2,400,000. Put that ratio on the board and leave it there.

docs.title: 12. Blameless post-incident review template
docs.text:
Complete this in the session. Enforce the blameless framing out loud: we are looking for the control that was missing, never for the person who was missing it. Every "should have" aimed at a person is rewritten as a "we lacked" aimed at a system.

                   ~5,900 additional cancellations/day

 REGULATORY ...... [ ] reportable   [ ] not reportable   rationale: __________

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 2. WHAT WENT WELL  (complete this honestly; it is not a formality)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   e.g. bronze immutability made root cause provable in 40 minutes
        producer_version was retained in bronze, which made ONE query decisive
        model monitoring existed at all, and it is what fired
        Delta time travel made rollback a query, not a restore project

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 3. WHERE WE GOT LUCKY  (what could have made this far worse?)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   e.g. it was 34% of a cohort, not 100% of the fleet — a full rollout would
        have shifted the aggregate enough to be noticed sooner, OR would have
        corrupted the training set beyond recovery. Which? Argue it.
   e.g. the 30-day raw GPS retention still held the un-normalised values.
        At 7-day retention the evidence would have expired before detection.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 4. CONTRIBUTING FACTORS  (systems and controls only — NEVER people)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Write each as "we lacked X", never as "someone should have Y".

   [ ] The contract specified types but not units, so a unit change was
       structurally indistinguishable from no change at all.
   [ ] No drift monitoring existed on features consumed by models.
   [ ] Producer versions were auto-accepted; there was no admission gate.
   [ ] Observability was BI-shaped: every signal we watched was one that a
       count-and-sum layer would move, and none that a continuous
       measurement would move.
   [ ] We had no subscription to, or review process for, producer releases.
   [ ] The Day-4 cancellation rise (+0.3 pts) fell inside a band wide enough
       to absorb a real signal, and no one correlated it with anything.
   [ ] ______________________________________________________________________
