docs.title: 13. What good looks like vs common wrong turns
docs.text: What good looks like Common wrong turn Reaches GROUP BY producer_version and can say why that column Groups by city, hour, zone and driver, never by the producer Reads "row counts normal, values wrong" from P3 and pivots the search Keeps hunting for a missing batch or a failed job Accepts the BI dashboard as correct and asks what it does not measure Assumes BI is lying or lagging States that a schema is structure and a unit is meaning Concludes "our schema validation is broken" and proposes stricter types Confirms with the independent metered-speed reconciliation Relies solely on the drift statistic, which a poisoned baseline could hide Segments the drift statistic and shows PSI 0.02 vs 6.94 Reports an aggregate PSI of 1.87 and argues about thresholds Names the bimodality as the signature of two populations Describes it only as "the mean went down" Makes the live-mitigation decision at 08:40 on a hypothesis Waits for proof and loses another SAR 295k Pins the corrupted version before restoring Restores immediately and destroys the evidence Finds the blast radius beyond ETA — driver_safety_score and the disabled speeding alerts Stops at the demand model Proposes all four controls, each with a done-test Proposes "better monitoring" with no statistic, segment, threshold or action Builds the drift monitor on the feature, with a frozen segmented baseline Monitors the source only, on a rolling baseline that would absorb the bug Writes a contract clause defining what "breaking" means Blames the vendor's release note Post-incident review says "we lacked a control" Post-incident review says "the vendor should have told us" Answers the CDO in one sentence, then evidence Opens the briefing with the _delta_log

docs.title: 14. Debrief (4 minutes — deliver exactly these six beats)
docs.text:
1. Nothing failed. Reveal the timeline's right-hand column. The producer worked. The stream was exactly-once. The schema validated. GX was 12/12 and 8/8. The DAG was 14/14. Freshness, volume, lag, nulls, referential integrity — all green, every day, throughout. Every component did precisely what it was told, and the AI system degraded by 18%. Type-compatibility is not semantic compatibility, and no amount of operational health tells you the data still means what it meant.

  2. The platform never detected it. The model did. For four days the only signal Masar produced came from a 7-day rolling model metric — the slowest, furthest-downstream, most lagging indicator in the entire stack. Everything designed to detect data problems was watching the wrong kind of thing. Observability that is BI-shaped is blind to the failures that damage AI, and worse than blind: it is reassuring, which is what allowed a real Day-4 signal (cancellations +0.3 pts) to be dismissed as normal.

  3. One GROUP BY cracked it — and a Day-1 design decision decided whether that was possible. Show Q2 again. GROUP BY producer_version, two rows, ratio 3.60. On Day 1 of this course, in CS-09, a perfectly sensible "efficient" ingestion design proposed dropping producer_version as "not needed downstream" and converting units at ingest. That design makes this incident permanently unsolvable. Whether you could solve today's problem was decided on Monday morning, in a job nobody thought was interesting.

  4. BI and AI fail differently, and the difference is structural. BI aggregates counts and sums of discrete business events; a corrupted continuous measurement does not move them. AI transforms continuous measurements; a scale error passes straight through, and the model does not become uncertain — it becomes confidently wrong, and then acts, and its actions change the world that the next batch of data describes. BI degrades visibly and stops. AI degrades silently and compounds.

  5. Deliver the two findings from the blast radius last. driver_safety_score has been flattering 1,004 vehicles' drivers for four days — an HR and fairness problem. And ops.alerts_speeding has fired for none of them since Day 1, because every reported speed was 3.6× too low. A safety control was silently disabled for four days on a national mobility platform, and the executive dashboard was green the entire time. Let that sit before you move on.

  6. The ratio. SAR 2,400,000 for the incident. Approximately SAR 12,000 — six engineer-days — for the four controls that would have prevented and detected it. The controls were not built because nothing was ever red. The whole discipline of this course is the practice of building controls for failures that will never announce themselves, and the course question in its final form:

"What happens to Masar's AI system if THIS part of the data platform fails?"

Here, nothing failed. And that is the most dangerous case of all.

docs.title: 15. The one sentence participants should leave with
docs.text: A data platform can be entirely healthy — exactly-once, schema-valid, tests green, dashboards correct — while silently feeding an AI system data that no longer means what it used to mean; so contracts must specify units and semantics rather than only types, observability must watch the distributions of the features models actually consume, segmented by the dimension along which change is deployed, and the raw layer must retain the producer version that makes the one decisive query possible.

"""One place to build the Spark session with Delta Lake enabled."""
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession


def get_spark(app_name: str = "masar-lakehouse") -> SparkSession:
    return (
        SparkSession.builder
        .appName(app_name)
        .config("spark.sql.extensions",
                "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
        .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog",
                "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
        .config("spark.sql.warehouse.dir", "./lakehouse")
        .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "8")
        .config("spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled", "true")
        .enableHiveSupport()
        .getOrCreate()
    )

docs.title: 1.2 src/masar/ingest/land_bronze.py — complete
docs.text:
"""Land raw Masar source files into the bronze zone.

Bronze rules enforced here:
  - append-only (never overwrite history)
  - keep data AS-RECEIVED (no cleaning, no typing beyond the source)
  - attach ingestion lineage: when, from which file, and under which batch
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import uuid
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F

from masar.spark import get_spark

BRONZE = "./lakehouse/bronze"
RAW = "./data/raw"


def _batch_id(feed: str, business_date: str) -> str:
    stamp = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ")
    return f"{feed}_{business_date}_{stamp}_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}"


def _with_lineage(df: DataFrame, batch_id: str) -> DataFrame:
    return (
        df.withColumn("_ingested_at", F.current_timestamp())
          .withColumn("_source_file", F.input_file_name())
          .withColumn("_batch_id", F.lit(batch_id))
    )


def _append(df: DataFrame, table: str, path: str) -> int:
    spark = get_spark()
    spark.sql("CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS bronze")
    n = df.count()
    (df.write
        .format("delta")
        .mode("append")
        .option("mergeSchema", "false")
        .option("path", path)
        .saveAsTable(table))
    total = spark.read.format("delta").load(path).count()
    print(f"Landed {n:,} rows -> {path}  (append, total now {total:,})")
    return total


def land_trips(business_date: str, source: str | None = None) -> int:
    spark = get_spark("land-trips")
    raw = (spark.read
           .option("header", True)
           .option("mode", "PERMISSIVE")
           .option("inferSchema", False)
           .csv(source or f"{RAW}/trips_{business_date}.csv"))
    return _append(_with_lineage(raw, _batch_id("trips", business_date)),
                   "bronze.trips", f"{BRONZE}/trips")


def land_gps(business_date: str, source: str | None = None) -> int:
    spark = get_spark("land-gps")
    raw = spark.read.json(source or f"{RAW}/gps/gps_{business_date}.ndjson")
    return _append(_with_lineage(raw, _batch_id("gps", business_date)),
                   "bronze.gps_events", f"{BRONZE}/gps_events")


def land_drivers(source: str | None = None) -> int:
    spark = get_spark("land-drivers")
    today = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    raw = (spark.read
           .option("header", True)
           .option("mode", "PERMISSIVE")
           .option("inferSchema", False)
           .csv(source or f"{RAW}/drivers.csv"))
    return _append(_with_lineage(raw, _batch_id("drivers", today)),
                   "bronze.drivers", f"{BRONZE}/drivers")


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Land a Masar raw feed into bronze")
    p.add_argument("--feed", required=True, choices=["trips", "gps", "drivers", "all"])
    p.add_argument("--date", default="2026-06-01")
    p.add_argument("--source", default=None, help="override the source path (fixtures)")
    a = p.parse_args()
    if a.feed in ("trips", "all"):
        land_trips(a.date, a.source)
    if a.feed in ("gps", "all"):
        land_gps(a.date, a.source)
    if a.feed in ("drivers", "all"):
        land_drivers(a.source)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: 2. Teaching moments — what to say and exactly when
docs.text:
When Trigger The moment Say this Min 5, after Task 1 Pairs have grepped the raw files The defects are the curriculum "Everything you just found — the 3.1% empty geohash, the two date formats, the negative durations — is in this file on purpose. Write them down. You will fix each one at a specific layer, and I will ask you which layer." Min 12, during Task 2 Someone asks "shouldn't we clean this first?" Bronze is a ledger, not a model "Cleaning at landing means the only copy you have is the cleaned one. When your cleaning rule turns out to be wrong in week six, what do you re-run it against?" Min 14 A pair sets inferSchema=True Inference is silent data loss Run it live: inference nulls the 2% dd/MM/yyyy timestamps. "Your pipeline just deleted 1,928 timestamps and told you nothing." Min 22, Task 3 — the headline moment Second landing completes, totals hit 96,400 Bronze should allow duplication Stop the room. "Who thinks 96,400 rows for a 48,200-trip day is a bug?" Take a show of hands, then: "It is correct. Bronze records what arrived. Silver decides what is true — and it can, because _batch_id tells it which arrival is later. If we had overwritten, the duplication would be invisible and the history gone." Min 30, Task 4 Null-rate table on screen A null rate is a downstream design decision "3.1% missing dropoff_geohash. Who owns what happens next — engineering, data science, or operations? Your answer determines which layer encodes the rule." Min 38, Task 5 GPS file counts on screen File count is a cost, not an aesthetic "Remember this number. Module 2 will price it and Module 4 will fix it. Object storage bills you for listing, not just for bytes." Min 45, wrap — The unifying question "What happens to Masar's AI system if the landing zone fails? Not a crash. A model retrained on a table you can no longer rebuild."

Rehearse: the inferSchema=True demo (30 seconds) and the 96,400 reveal. Those two carry the hour.

docs.title: 3. Common wrong answers and how to redirect
docs.text: What you will see Why it happens Redirect (do not just correct) mode("overwrite") in land_trips Habit from ETL/warehouse work; "I don't want duplicates" Ask: "Run it twice. Now show me yesterday's data." Let them discover it is gone. Then: "Which layer removes duplicates, and why is that better?" .dropDuplicates("trip_id") at landing Conflating bronze with silver "You just made a business decision — which copy wins? — inside an ingestion job, with no test and no record. Move it to silver where it is reviewable" inferSchema=True Convenience Live demo (above). Then: "Bronze's job is to be a faithful copy. Typing is a transformation and transformations belong where they can fail loudly" mode("DROPMALFORMED") Sounds hygienic "How many rows did you just drop? You cannot answer, because they are gone. PERMISSIVE keeps them and lets you count them" Lineage columns added after a groupBy/distinct Copy-paste ordering Show _source_file is null: input_file_name() is only meaningful on a direct file scan "Swamp risks" listed as vague adjectives ("data is messy") Not enough rigour Require the evidence line: risk + the number that proves it + the layer that fixes it. Reject anything without all three Partitioning bronze by trip_id "for fast lookups" Warehouse index intuition Let them do it in the stretch goal and measure. The file count argues better than you can Committing lakehouse/ to git No .gitignore awareness Catch it early — it is a capstone hand-in failure. git rm -r --cached lakehouse Landing GPS with spark.read.json(..., multiLine=True) Copied from a JSON-array example Works but reads the whole file as one document — show the partition count collapse to 1 and the memory spike

docs.text:
Reference prices used for the numbers in §5 (state to the room that these are illustrative list prices and that participants must cite their own):

Input Reference value Note storage_gb_month 0.023 standard object storage, $/GB-month core_hour 0.06 decoupled general-purpose compute, on-demand spot_multiplier 0.35 ≈ 65% discount warehouse_core_hour 0.18 coupled MPP node, always on warehouse_storage_gb_month 0.21 storage inside the warehouse 
"""Transparent storage-vs-compute cost model for the Masar platform."""
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Prices:
    storage_gb_month: float = 0.023
    core_hour: float = 0.06
    spot_multiplier: float = 0.35
    warehouse_core_hour: float = 0.18
    warehouse_storage_gb_month: float = 0.21


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Job:
    name: str
    cores: int
    runtime_hours: float
    runs_per_month: int
    spot: bool = False

    def monthly_core_hours(self) -> float:
        return self.cores * self.runtime_hours * self.runs_per_month

    def monthly_compute(self, p: Prices) -> float:
        rate = p.core_hour * (p.spot_multiplier if self.spot else 1.0)
        return self.monthly_core_hours() * rate


def lakehouse_monthly_cost(total_gb, jobs, p: Prices = Prices()):
    storage = total_gb * p.storage_gb_month
    compute = sum(j.monthly_compute(p) for j in jobs)
    total = storage + compute
    return {"storage": round(storage, 2), "compute": round(compute, 2),
            "total": round(total, 2), "compute_share": round(compute / total, 3)}


def warehouse_monthly_cost(total_gb, nodes, cores_per_node, p: Prices = Prices()):
    hours = 730.0
    compute = nodes * cores_per_node * hours * p.warehouse_core_hour
    storage = total_gb * p.warehouse_storage_gb_month
    total = storage + compute
    return {"storage": round(storage, 2), "compute": round(compute, 2),
            "total": round(total, 2), "compute_share": round(compute / total, 3),
            "idle_share": round(1 - (0.9 * 30) / hours, 3)}


def break_even_utilisation(total_gb, nodes, cores_per_node, p: Prices = Prices()):
    wh = warehouse_monthly_cost(total_gb, nodes, cores_per_node, p)
    budget_for_compute = wh["total"] - total_gb * p.storage_gb_month
    return round(budget_for_compute / p.core_hour, 1)

"""Build a benchmark-shaped silver.trips from the participant's own bronze."""
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from masar.spark import get_spark


def main() -> None:
    spark = get_spark("prepare-benchmark-input")
    b = spark.table("bronze.trips")
    df = (b.dropDuplicates(["trip_id"])
           .withColumn("fare_sar", F.col("fare_sar").cast("double"))
           .withColumn("distance_km", F.col("distance_km").cast("double"))
           .withColumn("pickup_ts", F.coalesce(
               F.to_timestamp("pickup_ts", "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"),
               F.to_timestamp("pickup_ts", "dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm")))
           .filter("status = 'completed'"))
    (df.repartition(12, "city")
       .write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("overwriteSchema", "true")
       .partitionBy("city").save("./lakehouse/silver/trips"))
    print("benchmark input rows:", df.count())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: 2. Teaching moments — what to say and exactly when
docs.text:
When Trigger The moment Say this Min 2, before Task 1 — Force the prediction "Before you touch the model: write down, now, whether storage or compute will be the bigger line for Masar. Fold the paper. We open it at minute 25." Min 8, Task 1 A pair uses the default prices An uncited price is an unusable model "In a review, the first question is 'where did $0.023 come from?' If the answer is 'the lab file', the model dies in that sentence." Min 25, Task 2 — the headline moment compute_share prints Open the folded papers Poll the room. Most predicted storage. "Compute is 30% of a $394 bill on the decoupled side — and 87% of a $19,000 bill on the coupled side. Decoupling did not make compute cheaper per hour. It made you stop paying for the hours you do not use: 96% of the warehouse's compute hours are idle." Min 30, Task 3 First ReadSchema with 3 columns This is why decoupling works at all "Compute is on the far side of a network. The only reason that is affordable is that Parquet lets it read 3 columns of 27 and skip row groups that cannot match. Format choice is an economic decision." Min 35, Task 3 Partition-filter row shows a 4× file drop Layout is a cost control "Same question, same answer, 6% of the bytes. Nobody bought a bigger cluster." Min 40, Task 4 Break-even number appears Reframe break-even as headroom "Masar runs at 0.7% of break-even utilisation. That is not a warning — it is the budget to retrain weekly instead of monthly. Elasticity is what buys the AI team its cadence." Min 45, Task 5 — The unifying question "What happens to Masar's AI system if the economics fail? Nothing dramatic. History gets truncated to save money, retrains get cut to monthly, and the model drifts. Cost failures starve AI; they do not crash it."

Rehearse: the folded-prediction reveal. It is the entire emotional arc of this lab.

docs.title: 3. Common wrong answers and how to redirect
docs.text: What you will see Why it happens Redirect compute_share ≈ 1.0 Storage GB estimated from the sample (172 GB) with no extrapolation, or retention months forgotten "How many months are you keeping, and is that the whole platform or just raw?" Make them state the extrapolation factor out loud Storage estimate off by 1000× Mixed GB/TB, or per-TB prices used per-GB Force normalisation into Prices before any arithmetic "Lakehouse saves 98%, done" Comparing list-price always-on warehouse against elastic Lakehouse with no caveats "Your CFO has a 40% committed-use discount. Re-run with the warehouse at 0.6×. Is the story still true?" (It is — ~96% — but they must show they anticipated the challenge) Naive and pruned plans identical Filter applied after collect()/toPandas() Have them print the plan for both; the ReadSchema line settles it Using wall-clock seconds as the benchmark Familiar from application performance work "Run it three times." The variance makes the argument. Bytes and files are stable; seconds are not PushedFilters: [] on the partition-filtered query and a claim of failure city moved to PartitionFilters, which is better than pushdown Teach the distinction: partition filters skip directories before any file is opened; pushed filters skip row groups inside files Modelling the warehouse as also elastic Not internalising coupling "If the warehouse can scale compute to zero overnight, what happens to the data stored on those nodes?" Guardrail rationale written as "best practice" No cost reasoning Require a number: "10 minutes of idle × how many days × the cluster rate = what?" Concluding "storage is free, keep everything forever" Over-correcting from the compute reveal Point at PDPL: retention is also a legal constraint, not only a cost one. Bridges to M4/M6

docs.title: 4. Timing checkpoints
docs.text:
Clock Participants should be… If behind If ahead Min 5 Predictions folded; lab2-start checked out; benchmark table present Run prepare_benchmark_input for them Start pricing research Min 15 Real prices in Prices with URL + date cited in LAB2_NOTES.md Give them the reference prices and require the citation as homework Add a second cloud's prices for a sensitivity column Min 25 cost_model.py run; compute_share recorded; prediction reveal done Hand them the reference __main__ block; the lesson is reading the number, not typing it Run the three sensitivity variants Min 35 scan_cost.py run; three measured rows; plans captured Switch them to the Spark UI fallback immediately — do not debug Py4J in lab time Stretch goal 4 (unpartitioned rewrite) Min 42 Comparison table filled; dominant driver and break-even written Give them the table skeleton and require only the two sentences Stretch goal 1 (spot risk quantification) Min 48 Guardrail rationale written; committed Commit partial work —

Overrun policy. Task 5 can be assigned as homework. Task 3 cannot be cut — the measured scan is the only evidence in this lab, and it is a capstone deliverable.

docs.title: 5. Filled benchmark tables (reference run)
docs.text:
Cost model (12 TB, three jobs, reference prices):

Line Coupled warehouse (8×16 cores, always on) Decoupled Lakehouse Delta Storage / month $2,520.00 $276.00 −89% Compute / month $16,819.20 $118.40 −99% Total / month $19,339.20 $394.40 −98% compute_share 0.87 0.30 — Idle share of paid compute 0.963 ≈ 0 — Break-even utilisation — 318,717 core-h/month actual 2,118 (0.7%) 2× data (new city) +$2,520 storage + new nodes +$276 storage, compute ~flat compute_share 0.30 → 0.18

Scan benchmark (7-day sample, 294k rows, 27 columns, partitioned by city):

Query Columns read Files read Bytes read Filter pushdown Relative bytes scanned naive full read 27 / 27 12 11,943,208 no 1.00 column-pruned 3 / 27 12 3,344,098 no (column pruning only) 0.28 pruned + partition filter 4 / 27 4 716,592 yes (city partition, pickup_ts pushdown) 0.06 Metric Category Target after M2 Reference result Cost model completeness Analysis separates storage vs compute, states driver pass Data-skipping proven Performance pruned plan shows PushedFilters + fewer cols pass Bytes scanned reduction Performance pruned ≤ 25% of naive columns 3/27 = 11% of columns, 28% of bytes Elasticity guardrails Governance idle-termination + bounded autoscale specified autotermination_minutes: 10, max_workers: 8 Break-even identified Analysis stated with assumptions 318,717 core-h/month at 8×16 coupled baseline

Interpretation to give the room: columns dropped from 27 to 3 (89% fewer) but bytes only dropped 72%. Why? Because trip_id and city are wide, low-entropy strings and the remaining columns compress well — column count is a proxy, bytes are the truth. This is exactly why the lab insists on measuring.

docs.title: 6. Grading notes
docs.text:
Criterion Weight Full marks Partial Zero Prices real and cited 15% Every price has a URL + read-date Cited but stale/regional mismatch Lab defaults left in place Storage estimate derived, not assumed 15% Daily volume × retention × stated extrapolation factor, all shown Number given, derivation missing Copied from the slide Model output correct and interpreted 20% Storage/compute/total/compute_share for both architectures, dominant driver stated with a reason Numbers without interpretation Model does not run Measured scan evidence 25% Three rows with files and bytes read; plans show PartitionFilters, PushedFilters, reduced ReadSchema; identical counts across variants Plans only, no measured bytes No evidence, or counts differ between variants (a correctness bug) Break-even + comparison table 15% Break-even stated with assumptions and compared to actual utilisation Break-even without assumptions Missing Guardrails justified 10% Each of autotermination / max_workers / spot-with-on-demand-driver / tags justified in cost terms Restates the YAML Missing

Red flags - Identical LAB2_NOTES.md numbers across pairs when prices were supposed to be independently sourced → flag for the Day-5 integrity check. - A saving claim > 95% presented with no caveat → not wrong, but coach it: an un-caveated model loses reviews. Require the discount sensitivity. - Bytes-read column left empty with "the plan shows pushdown" → this is the single most common shortfall; it fails the capstone's BENCHMARKS.md requirement, so mark it down now while it is cheap.

Carry into Module 3. Put the class's median compute_share and the median relative-bytes-scanned figure on the board. Open M3 with: "ELT is only affordable because of these two numbers. Now let us spend that compute correctly."

docs.title: Build the ELT Pipeline to silver.trips
docs.text:
Field Value Lab LAB-03 (3a + 3b) · Module 3 · Day 2 Hours 3 and 5 · 90 minutes total · pairs Tags lab3-start (3a) → lab3a-solution; lab3b-start (3b) → lab3-solution Room setup Projector on a terminal running dbt run --select silver_trips with the Delta history query aliased; whiteboard timeline for the late-arrival drill (event time vs arrival time on two parallel axes) Pre-flight On a clean clone: dbt debug green, dbt deps resolves dbt_utils, the late-arrival fixture exists at data/fixtures/late_trips/trips_late_2026-06-02.csv and contains 1 trip whose pickup_ts is on 2026-06-01 Pairing Deliberately pair a strong-SQL participant with a strong-Python/Spark participant; 3a rewards SQL, 3b rewards pipeline thinking

Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. Grains, ratios and file-count reductions hold at either scale; absolute row counts do not.

docs.title: 1.1 dbt/masar/profiles.yml and dbt_project.yml
docs.text:
As printed in the participant guide. Two things to verify in every pair's terminal:

echo $DBT_PROFILES_DIR          # must be .../dbt/masar
grep -A2 'method' dbt/masar/profiles.yml    # must read: method: session

docs.title: 1.2 Sources — models/staging/masar/_masar__sources.yml
docs.text: As printed in the participant guide. The teaching point is that loaded_at_field: _ingested_at only works because Lab 1 wrote that column. Say it out loud: the governance control in Module 3 is paid for by the discipline in Module 1.

docs.title: 1.3 models/staging/masar/stg_trips.sql — complete
docs.text:
The participant version is the reference. The three graded behaviours:

-- (1) BOTH timestamp formats parsed, then normalised ONCE to UTC
to_utc_timestamp(
    coalesce(
        to_timestamp(pickup_ts,  'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'),
        to_timestamp(pickup_ts,  'dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm')
    ), 'Asia/Riyadh')             as pickup_ts,

-- (2) '' is missing, not a value
nullif(trim(dropoff_geohash), '') as dropoff_geohash,

-- (3) source duration is kept under a name that says it is unverified
cast(duration_min as double)      as reported_duration_min,

docs.title: 1.4 models/marts/silver/silver_trips.sql — complete
docs.text:
The participant version is the reference. The four graded properties, each with the line that delivers it:

Property Delivered by Incremental + idempotent materialized='incremental', incremental_strategy='merge', unique_key='trip_id' Late-arrival safe where pickup_ts >= (select date_sub(max(pickup_ts), {{ var('lookback_days', 3) }}) from {{ this }}) — event time, parameterised Deduplicated correctly row_number() over (partition by trip_id order by _ingested_at desc, _batch_id desc) = 1 Conformed status = 'completed', dropoff_ts > pickup_ts, fare_sar > 0, distance_km > 0; derived features computed once

Note for the instructor on alias/schema. schema='silver' + alias='trips' is what makes the dbt model resolve to the canonical silver.trips from CONVENTIONS.md. Pairs who leave the default get silver.silver_trips, which breaks every later lab's table reference. Catch this at the min-20 checkpoint of 3b, not at the end.

docs.title: 1.5 Tests
docs.text: _silver__models.yml as printed (12 tests total: 2 on trip_id, 2 on city, 1 on status, 2 on fare_sar, 2 on duration_min, 2 on driver_id, 1 on pickup_ts, 1 on rider_id) plus the custom assert_no_future_trips.sql. Reference run: PASS=12 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0.

docs.title: 1.6 The backfill drill — reference commands and outcomes
docs.text:
python -m masar.ingest.land_bronze --feed trips --date 2026-06-01 \
       --source data/fixtures/late_trips/trips_late_2026-06-02.csv
cd dbt/masar && dbt run --select silver_trips
Run Delta operationMetrics Meaning before drill WRITE numOutputRows -> 42038 full build no new data MERGE inserted -> 0, updated -> 0 idempotent after late fixture MERGE inserted -> 1, updated -> 0 late trip caught once repeat of the same backfill MERGE inserted -> 0, updated -> 0 backfills are safe to re-run

The counter-experiment. Keep a branch sim-naive-filter with the where to_date(pickup_ts) = current_date() variant pre-baked so pairs can switch in 30 seconds rather than editing and rebuilding. Result: the late trip is absent, count stays 42,038.

docs.title: 2. Teaching moments — what to say and exactly when
Lab 3a (35 min)
docs.text: When Trigger The moment Say this Min 3 dbt debug green ELT in one sentence "dbt is not moving any data. It is issuing SQL to the engine that already holds the data. That is the L-then-T in ELT, and it is only affordable because of the cost model you built yesterday." Min 10 Freshness SLA tightened to 1 minute and WARNs A guard you never fired is not a guard "You have now seen the check fail. Every alert you add should be tested by making it fire once, deliberately, on the day you add it." Min 12 — What freshness misses "Freshness catches a stopped job. It does not catch a job that runs on time and lands an empty file. Which check catches that?" (volume — Module 6) Min 25 Both timestamp formats parsed Isolate quirks at the boundary "That coalesce exists in exactly one model. When the source adds a third format, you edit one file. Put it in the mart instead and you edit ten." Min 30 A pair reports non-zero unparseable rows Never mask a parse failure "A blanket cast turns 1,928 timestamps into nulls and tells you nothing. Find the format, add the branch."

docs.title: Lab 3b (55 min)
docs.text:
When Trigger The moment Say this Min 10 Someone writes DISTINCT for dedup DISTINCT is the wrong tool "Your second batch corrected a fare. The rows now differ. DISTINCT keeps both — and your unique test fails. You do not want distinct rows, you want the latest row per key." Min 20 First dbt run --select silver_trips completes Check the alias Walk the room: spark.table("silver.trips").count() must work. If it is silver.silver_trips, fix it now Min 30 Second run shows updated -> 0 Idempotency, visible "You just ran the transformation twice and the table did not change. That is why your orchestrator is allowed to retry, why a backfill is safe, and why disaster recovery is a re-run instead of a project." Min 35 A relationships test fails Never delete a failing test "The test is correct and the data is wrong. You have three options: quarantine, admit-with-nulls, or fix the source. Deleting the test is not one of them." Min 42 — the headline moment Late trip merged, inserted -> 1 The whole module in one number Stop the room. "This trip ended yesterday and arrived today. With WHERE trip_date = current_date() it is invisible forever — a 2% silent undercount that underpays drivers and skews your model's labels. With a lookback window and a merge on the key, it is counted exactly once. Three lines of SQL. That is Module 3." Min 46 Counter-experiment run See the bug, not just the fix Require every pair to see the missing trip. The fix means nothing without the failure Min 52 dbt docs lineage graph on screen Docs generated from the work itself "This graph cannot drift from the pipeline, because it is the pipeline. That is the audit artefact PDPL governance needs, and you got it for free."

Rehearse: the min-42 reveal, and have sim-naive-filter pre-baked so the counter-experiment costs 2 minutes, not 10.

docs.title: 3. Common wrong answers and how to redirect
docs.text: What you will see Why it happens Redirect Lookback on _ingested_at Sounds like "process what just arrived" Draw the two timelines. Ask: "Which axis does the incentive payment use?" (event time) where pickup_ts >= current_date() - 3 Absolute rather than relative to the table Works today, breaks on any backfill or after an outage. Anchor on max(pickup_ts) from {{ this }} No lookback at all, just is_incremental() with a _ingested_at > max() filter Copied from a generic dbt example Run the drill; the late trip is caught (it arrived late) but a correction to an older trip is not. Both matter DISTINCT or group by trip_id for dedup Familiar SQL reflex See min-10 teaching moment Dedup applied after the join Order-of-operations slip Symptom: Cannot perform MERGE as multiple source rows matched. Fix the CTE order inner join drivers to make relationships pass Wants a green test "You just deleted 14 real trips and their revenue. Show me where that is recorded." Deleting a failing test Time pressure Non-negotiable. Mark it down; it is the difference between a pipeline and a hobby Casting/renaming in the mart Skipped staging discipline Set the stretch-goal rename drill as a live challenge: "Rename fare_sar upstream. Time how long your version takes to fix." to_timestamp(pickup_ts) with no format Assumes Spark guesses It does — for one format. Run the null count Timezone applied twice (to_utc_timestamp in staging and in the mart) Copy-paste Symptom: times 6 hours off. Normalise once, present with from_utc_timestamp status IN ('completed','cancelled_rider') in silver "We might need cancellations" Legitimate design question — but then the accepted_values test and the silver contract must change together, and every downstream count changes. Make them state the contract Model named silver_trips with default schema Missed the alias/schema config Fix immediately; Labs 4, 6, 7, 8 all reference silver.trips

docs.title: Lab 3a — 35 minutes
docs.text: Clock Participants should be… If behind If ahead Min 5 dbt debug green, DBT_PROFILES_DIR exported Hand them the working profiles.yml; do not debug profiles in lab time Start sources Min 15 Sources declared; dbt source freshness run; the deliberate WARN seen Give them the sources YAML; require only that they run it and see the WARN Add payments as a fourth source Min 28 stg_trips + stg_drivers built as views; unparseable counts = 0 Give them stg_drivers; stg_trips is the one they must write Classify hire_date patterns (Lab 1 stretch goal 2) Min 33 3a committed Commit partial —

docs.title: Lab 3b — 55 minutes
docs.text:
Clock Participants should be… If behind If ahead Min 15 silver_trips.sql written; first dbt run in flight Give them the deduped CTE — the lookback is the part they must own — Min 20 Table resolves as silver.trips; row count 42,038 = distinct trip_id Fix the alias now Add the int_trip_payments stretch model Min 30 Second run shows updated -> 0; tests written Give them the tests YAML; the drill matters more Write the custom "no future trips" test Min 35 dbt test green (PASS=12) Let one test fail and move on; record it Add an accepted_range on distance_km Min 45 Backfill drill complete: late trip merged once, repeat run is a no-op Do not skip. Fast-forward everything else to get here Run the counter-experiment Min 50 Counter-experiment recorded; docs generated Assign the counter-experiment as homework with a screenshot Parameterised 6-month backfill Min 55 Benchmark table filled; committed — —

Overrun policy. 3b routinely runs long. Compressible: dbt docs (Task 6), the custom data test, the benchmark table. Not compressible: Task 5. Walk the room during it and confirm each pair sees numTargetRowsInserted -> 1. If you cut anything else to protect it, that is the right trade.

Run Rows processed Strategy Duration Duplicate keys MERGE inserted / updated initial full build 42,038 (from 96,400 bronze rows) create 21.6 s 0 — incremental (no new data) 42,038 scanned, 0 changed merge 4.1 s 0 0 / 0 incremental (1 late trip) 42,039 source rows merge 3.8 s 0 1 / 0 incremental (repeat of same backfill) 42,039 source rows merge 3.6 s 0 0 / 0 counter-experiment (= current_date()) 0 merge 2.9 s 0 0 / 0 — late trip LOST

Metric Category Target after M3 Reference result Silver conformance Correctness 1 row per trip_id, key tests pass 42,038 rows = 42,038 distinct trip_id Incrementality Performance rerun processes only the lookback window 21.6 s → 4.1 s (5.3×) Backfill correctness Correctness late trip counted exactly once inserted -> 1, repeat inserted -> 0 Test coverage Quality ≥ 6 tests incl. unique/not_null/relationships 12 declared + 1 custom = 13 Freshness SLA Observability 6h warn / 24h error enforced on bronze enforced; WARN demonstrated

docs.title: 6. Grading notes
docs.text:
Lab 3 is the heaviest formative lab and it is a direct capstone component (requirement 3). Grade it against the contract, not the SQL style.

Criterion Weight Full marks Partial Zero Sources + freshness 10% 3 sources declared with SLAs; freshness run; WARN demonstrated Declared, never run Missing Staging discipline 15% Views, 1:1 with source, no joins, both timestamp formats parsed, UTC normalised once, 0 unparseable Casting present but a quirk unhandled Joins/business logic in staging Incremental config 15% incremental + merge + unique_key='trip_id' + file_format='delta', resolving to silver.trips Correct strategy, wrong table name Append strategy or table materialisation Lookback window 15% On event time, parameterised, anchored on max(pickup_ts) from {{ this }} Present but on ingest time or hard-coded Absent Dedup correctness 10% Latest row per key via row_number(); count(*) == count(distinct trip_id) DISTINCT used but test passes by luck Duplicates present Tests 15% ≥ 6 declared + 1 custom, all passing, no test deleted to go green 6 tests, one failing and documented Tests deleted/weakened to pass Backfill drill 15% Late trip merged exactly once and repeat run is a no-op, both evidenced from operationMetrics Late trip merged, repeat not shown Not attempted Notes + benchmark + commit 5% Counter-experiment recorded with both counts; benchmark filled; conventional commit Partial Missing

Red flags - A green dbt test with fewer tests than the model started with → a test was deleted. Check git diff on the YAML. This is the single most important integrity signal in this lab. - silver.trips row count equal to bronze (96,400) → dedup absent; every downstream count in Labs 4, 7 and 8 will be double. - Identical LAB3_NOTES.md backfill metrics across pairs → the operationMetrics timestamps and version numbers differ per run; identical blocks mean copied output.

Fast-forward path. git checkout lab3-solution && cd dbt/masar && dbt deps && dbt run && dbt test. Record who used it; a pair that fast-forwards Lab 3 will struggle in Lab 4's MERGE work, so pair them with a strong finisher on Day 3.

Carry into Module 4. Ask three pairs for their second-run operationMetrics and put them on the board. Open M4 with: "dbt just did a MERGE for you. Today you find out what a MERGE actually is, why it is atomic, and what the log recorded while it happened."

docs.title: Delta Lake: ACID, MERGE, Time Travel, Maintenance
docs.text:
Field Value Lab LAB-04 (4a + 4b) · Module 4 · Day 3 Hours 2 and 4, wrapped in Hour 5 · 90 minutes total · pairs Tags lab4-start (4a) → lab4a-solution; lab4b-start (4b) → lab4-solution Room setup Projector with a text editor open on lakehouse/silver/trips/_delta_log/00000000000000000000.json (pretty-printed, large font) and a second terminal aliased to DESCRIBE HISTORY. Print the A4 "Delta transaction log" and "Optimistic concurrency" posters Pre-flight On a clean clone: run Lab 3 to completion, then verify SHOW TBLPROPERTIES is empty of constraints (participants must add them), the corrections fixture has exactly 5 unique trip_ids that exist in silver, and pdpl_erasure_2026-06-10.json names a rider_id with > 0 rows Overrun risk Highest of the course alongside Lab 5. Protect Task 1 (log reading) and Task 3 (second MERGE). Everything else is compressible

Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. Grains, ratios and file-count reductions hold at either scale; absolute row counts do not.

docs.title: 1.1 src/masar/delta/create_silver.py
docs.text:
Participant version is the reference. Instructor notes:

  • The bad = ... WHERE NOT (expr) pre-check exists so the ALTER TABLE never fails opaquely. If a pair's Lab 3 filters were weaker than the reference, positive_fare may report skipped rows — that is a good outcome to surface: constraints and upstream filters are the same contract expressed twice, and a mismatch is a real finding.
  • known_city is a third, optional constraint. Add it if the room is fast; it produces the most instructive failure (whitespace / casing from a sloppy staging model).

docs.title: 1.2 src/masar/delta/merge_ops.py
docs.text:
Participant version is the reference. Two design choices to defend if asked:

Choice Why .schema(target_schema) when reading the corrections CSV Enforces the contract on the source, so a malformed correction file fails at read time with a clear error rather than inside the MERGE Explicit duplicate check before whenMatchedUpdateAll() whenMatchedUpdateAll is only safe with exactly one source row per key. Delta would raise Cannot perform Merge as multiple source rows matched...; raising our own error first makes the cause obvious

docs.title: 1.3 src/masar/delta/time_travel.py and maintain.sql
docs.text: Participant versions are the reference. The diff_versions helper is what turns "time travel exists" into "time travel answers a question" — make sure every pair runs it, not just --history.

docs.title: 1.4 Reference command sequence (the instructor demo, 8 minutes)
docs.text:
# 1. the log (2 min)
python -m json.tool < lakehouse/silver/trips/_delta_log/00000000000000000000.json | head -60

# 2. enforcement (1 min) — three rejections, row count unchanged
python -m masar.delta.create_silver
python - < scripts/demo_negative_writes.py

# 3. idempotent MERGE (2 min) — the reveal
python -m masar.delta.merge_ops --corrections data/fixtures/corrections/trips_corrections_2026-06-03.csv
python -m masar.delta.merge_ops --corrections data/fixtures/corrections/trips_corrections_2026-06-03.csv

# 4. audit (1.5 min)
python -m masar.delta.time_travel --history
python -m masar.delta.time_travel --diff 2 3

# 5. erasure + maintenance (1.5 min)
python -m masar.delta.merge_ops --erase-request data/fixtures/erasure_request/pdpl_erasure_2026-06-10.json
python - < scripts/demo_maintenance.py

Rehearse this end to end the evening before. The log-opening and the updated=0 reveal are the two beats that carry Module 4.

docs.title: 2. Teaching moments — what to say and exactly when
Lab 4a (25 min)
docs.text: When Trigger The moment Say this Min 8 — the headline moment of 4a First commit JSON on the projector Read the log aloud Point at each action: "protocol — what a reader must understand. metaData — the schema is a log entry, and so is your CHECK constraint. add — one Parquet file, with its min/max stats: those are the statistics that made your Lab 2 query skip 8 of 12 files. remove — a tombstone; the bytes are still on disk. commitInfo — the audit record." Then: "The current state of this table is not what is in the directory. It is what you get by replaying this log. Everything else in Module 4 follows from that one sentence." Min 12 Someone asks about half-written files Atomicity, concretely "If Spark dies mid-write, the Parquet files exist but no commit references them. A reader replaying the log never sees them. There is no such thing as a half-applied Delta write." Min 18 Negative-fare write rejected Schema enforcement is the anti-swamp "This is the property a raw lake lacks. Module 1's swamp is exactly a directory of Parquet with nobody checking. One line of metadata is the difference." Min 22 New-column write rejected Enforce by default, evolve on purpose "mergeSchema exists. It is opt-in and it writes a metadata commit — so a schema change is a reviewed event with an audit trail, not a surprise you find in a dashboard."

docs.title: Lab 4b (65 min)
docs.text: When Trigger The moment Say this Min 18 — the headline moment of 4b Second MERGE prints updated=0 Idempotency at the storage layer "dbt gave you this in Lab 3. Now you have seen what it actually is: a keyed, atomic, retryable operation. This is why your orchestrator may retry a failed task, why a six-month backfill is safe to run twice, and why recovery is a re-run rather than a project." Min 20 Someone notices a commit was still written State, not commits "Idempotency is about the table's state, not the commit count. Two runs, one result. If you also need commit-level idempotency — say, to avoid triggering a change feed — guard on a batch marker." Min 28 --diff 2 3 output on screen Audit made real "Five fares changed. You can show a regulator the before, the after, and the commit that did it, without having taken a backup." Min 32 RESTORE creates a new version History is append-only "You cannot un-happen a bad MERGE. You can only record the correction. That is what makes the trail trustworthy." Min 40 — the governance moment Rider absent from current, present in v(n−1) An erasure that touches one table is not an erasure "Legally, is this rider erased? No. They are in the time-travel history, in tombstoned files, in bronze, in your gold features, and in Redis. Erasure is a platform operation. Write the runbook." Min 52 numFiles 214 → 9 Maintenance is scheduled, not heroic "Nobody bought a bigger cluster. Read time fell 4.6× because you stopped opening 214 files. OPTIMIZE belongs in the DAG next to backups." Min 58 RETAIN 0 HOURS blocked Retention is governance, not a space hack "Two failures at once: your audit trail dies, and any query holding an older snapshot gets a FileNotFoundException mid-flight. Leave the check on." Min 62 Retention justification written The unifying question "What happens to Masar's AI system if this table layer fails? A training run reads a half-written table, or a disputed number can never be reproduced, or an erasure request cannot be honoured. None of those show up as a red pipeline."

docs.title: 3. Common wrong answers and how to redirect
docs.text: What you will see Why it happens Redirect "The table is already Delta, so 4a is done" Lab 3 wrote Delta "Delta the format is not Delta the contract. Show me what happens when a negative fare arrives." Then run the negative test ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT fails and they drop the constraint Existing rows violate it The constraint is right and the data is wrong. Find the rows, decide (quarantine vs fix upstream), then add it. This is the same lesson as "never delete a failing test" Disabling retentionDurationCheck to make VACUUM 0 work Wants to see storage reclaimed now "You just deleted your audit trail to save 4 MB on a laptop." If they want the demo, do it on a throwaway copy — never on silver.trips Expecting updated=0 to mean "no commit" Conflating state with log See the min-20 moment Expecting VACUUM to reclaim space immediately Default 7-day retention Use DRY RUN to show what would be removed and when. Expected behaviour, not a bug Claiming the erasure is complete after DELETE Only looked at the current version Have them query versionAsOf n-1. Then ask about bronze, gold and Redis whenMatchedUpdateAll() with a partial-column corrections file Copied the pattern Missing columns become null and silently wipe good data. Either supply the full target schema (reference solution) or use an explicit whenMatchedUpdate(set={...}) ZORDER on trip_id "because it is the key" Index intuition again ZORDER helps range and equality predicates that queries actually use. Nobody filters silver by a single trip_id in analytics. ZORDER what the dashboards filter on Partitioning by (city, trip_date) on a one-day sample and reporting no gain Over-partitioning at small scale Correct observation — reward it. Then ask what changes at 36 months and 5 cities Reading numFiles from ls instead of DESCRIBE DETAIL Habit ls counts tombstoned files too; only the log knows the live set. Good bridge back to the min-8 moment Hand-copying a Parquet file into the table directory to "add data" Curiosity Excellent teachable accident: Delta ignores it entirely. "The directory is not the table. The log is the table."

docs.title: 6. Grading notes
docs.text:
Lab 4 is a direct capstone component (requirement 4) and is also the subject of PA-1, the 30-minute Day-3 practical assessment. Grade strictly; a weak Lab 4 predicts a failed PA-1.

Criterion Weight Full marks Partial Zero Constraints present and enforced 20% positive_fare + valid_duration in SHOW TBLPROPERTIES; negative write rejected with the error captured Constraints added, negative test not run Constraints dropped to make writes pass Schema enforcement understood 10% Wrong-type and new-column writes rejected; row count unchanged afterwards One of two mergeSchema left enabled on the table Log literacy 10% Can name protocol / metaData / add (with stats) / remove / commitInfo and say what replaying the log means Opened the file, cannot explain it Not attempted MERGE idempotency 20% Run 1 = 5 updated, run 2 = 0, both operationMetrics captured; explains state-vs-commit Both runs done, no metrics captured Only one run, or non-keyed upsert Time-travel audit 15% DESCRIBE HISTORY plus a version diff showing the 5 changed fares; RESTORE understood as append-only History shown, no diff Not attempted PDPL erasure 15% Current/previous version contrast proven and the multi-table runbook written (bronze, gold, Redis, history) Delete demonstrated, runbook missing Claims erasure is complete after DELETE Maintenance + retention 10% Before/after numFiles recorded; VACUUM DRY RUN then 168h; RETAIN 0 blocked and left blocked; three-input retention justification Numbers recorded, justification thin retentionDurationCheck disabled

Red flags — act immediately - spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled = false anywhere in a participant's code → this is a production-safety failure and a capstone red flag. Have them revert it and write two sentences on why. - A "demonstrated erasure" with no mention of bronze, gold or the online store → PDPL red flag. Badge issuance requires no PDPL red flags; catch it here, on Day 3, where it is cheap to fix. - Identical benchmark tables across repositories → version numbers and timestamps are per-run; identical DESCRIBE HISTORY blocks mean copied output. Flag for the Day-5 integrity check. - A pair whose silver.trips holds 96,400 rows → Lab 3 dedup never worked. Fix before Day 4; every gold aggregate will be double.

Fast-forward path. git checkout lab4-solution then re-run the four drills against their own table. A pair that fast-forwards Lab 4 must still personally run the second MERGE and the erasure drill — those two are assessed in PA-1 and demoed in the capstone.

Carry into Module 5. Ask the room for their numFiles before/after. Open M5 with: "A streaming sink writes a file every trigger. At a 30-second trigger that is 2,880 files a day. You now know exactly what that costs and exactly which scheduled job fixes it."

docs.text:

Have lab5-solution's file ready to paste for anyone past 16 min 3 Kill/restart proof 10 min 10 min Protect this absolutely. Every pair must kill and count 4 Fixtures 12 min 12 min Discussion-heavy; the three questions matter more than the code 5 Silver 10 min 14 min The malformed writeStream chain trips people; give the hint at 6 min 6 Fan-out + OPTIMIZE 8 min 6 min First thing to cut. Demo it instead 7 Notes/commit 8 min 5 min

If you are 15 minutes behind at Task 4: skip Task 6 entirely, demo the OPTIMIZE numbers from your own run, and preserve full time for Tasks 3 and 5. Task 3 is the module's proof and Task 5 contains the m/s incident that LAB-06 depends on.

docs.title: Task 1 — gps_producer.py
docs.text:
The participant file is complete as printed in the lab. The only deliberate defect is in lab5-start, where emit() reads:

producer.send(TOPIC, value=ping)          # STARTER (wrong) — no key
producer.send(TOPIC, key=ping["trip_id"], value=ping)   # SOLUTION

Diagnostic to show the room why it matters:

docker compose exec kafka kafka-console-consumer.sh \
  --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic masar.gps.pings \
  --partition 0 --from-beginning --max-messages 20 \
  --property print.key=true --property key.separator=' | ' | cut -d'|' -f1 | sort -u | wc -l

Unkeyed: ~20 distinct trip_ids in partition 0 (round-robin, per-trip order destroyed across partitions). Keyed: pings for one trip are contiguous within a single partition.

docs.title: Task 2 — ingest_gps_stream.py
docs.text:
As printed in the participant guide. Three points to draw out at the whiteboard:

  1. foreachBatch is a choice, not a requirement. A plain writeStream ... .start(path) to a Delta sink is already exactly-once. foreachBatch is used here to obtain the batch_id for the bronze _batch_id lineage column and to demonstrate txnAppId/txnVersion. Say this out loud — participants otherwise conclude that exactly-once requires foreachBatch.
  2. _source_file for a stream is kafka://topic/partition, not a path. The bronze contract says the column must exist and identify provenance; it does not say the provenance must be a file.
  3. mergeSchema=false on bronze is deliberate. If the producer adds a field, you want the job to fail loudly, not to silently widen the raw table. Schema drift must be a decision.

docs.title: Task 3 — Reference numbers
docs.text:
Stage Pings produced Rows in bronze.gps_events Distinct event_id Pipeline-introduced dupes Clean run 50,000 50,000 49,801 0 After kill 110,000 90,000 89,642 0 After restart, drained 110,000 110,000 109,562 0

sim-nocheckpoint branch for the counter-demo: 127,300 rows for 110,000 pings → 17,300 phantom positions.

Rows minus distinct event_id is always ~0.4% — that is the seeded source defect from CONVENTIONS, not a pipeline fault. Participants confuse these constantly. Write both columns on the board and label them "data problem — fixed at silver" and "engineering problem — prevented by the checkpoint."

docs.title: Task 4 — Answers to the three questions
docs.text: Question Answer Which defect can a watermark fix? Late arrival. The watermark decides how long a window stays open for stragglers. It does not fix duplicates and does not fix out-of-order — out-of-order needs no fixing at all under event-time semantics Which can dropDuplicates fix, and at what cost? Duplicate event_id. Unbounded dropDuplicates retains every key ever seen → unbounded state → OOM. dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark bounds it to the lateness window, at the cost of missing a duplicate that arrives more than 5 minutes after its twin Which is invisible to both? The m/s semantic drift. It is not late, not duplicated, not out of order, and structurally valid. Only a per-producer_version distribution comparison sees it — which is LAB-06

docs.title: Task 5 — build_vehicle_positions.py, corrected write chain
docs.text:
(deduped.writeStream
        .format("delta")
        .queryName("vehicle_positions_silver")
        .outputMode("append")
        .option("checkpointLocation", CHECKPOINT)
        .trigger(processingTime="30 seconds")
        .start(SILVER_PATH)
        .awaitTermination())

On partitioning silver.vehicle_positions: the defensible answer at lab scale is do not partition. 1.2M rows/day with a 30-second trigger already produces ~2,900 files/day; adding a partition column multiplies directory count without improving any query in this course. At production scale, partition by event_date only, and ZORDER by vehicle_id. Accept either answer if the participant measured; reject "partition by vehicle_id" (14,000 directories/day) in every case.

Reference verification numbers:

bronze_rows  silver_rows  silver_dupes  late_rows  max_speed_250  max_speed_240
110,999      108,914      0             487        118.8          121.4

Before the unit fix, max_speed_250 = 33.0. Show both. The 33.0 is what makes the incident dangerous — it is a plausible speed.

The 2,085-row gap (110,999 → 108,914) decomposes as: ~762 duplicate event_id removed, ~13 late pings beyond the watermark, ~1,310 rows filtered by accuracy_m > 50 and the KSA bounding box. Have participants account for the gap; a participant who cannot explain their own row loss has not understood the transform.

docs.title: 3. Answer key — self-check questions
docs.text: Q One-line grading criterion Q1 Must name both mechanisms (checkpointed offsets + atomic Delta commit) and identify the checkpoint path. Naming only Kafka, or only Delta, is a partial answer Q2 Must say event-time windows make arrival order irrelevant. Bonus: notes that sorting an unbounded stream is undefined, not merely expensive Q3 Must identify unbounded state growth as the cost, and name the trade-off (a duplicate arriving after the watermark passes through) Q4 Must distinguish structural validation from semantic correctness, and place the fix at the bronze→silver transform, not in bronze Q5 Must say neither is wrong and tie the clock to the question being asked. A participant who says "always use event time" has memorised the slide, not the reasoning Q6 Must quantify file growth (~30×) and name at least one of: per-file read cost, _delta_log growth, object-storage request charges

docs.title: 4. Common participant errors and the intervention
docs.text: # Error Frequency Intervention 1 Deletes the checkpoint to "reset" after a failure Very high Stop the room. This is the exact action that manufactures the duplicates the lab is proving you avoid. Make the offender demonstrate the duplication, then restore 2 Two queries pointing at one checkpoint directory High Show the state-store corruption. Establish the rule: checkpoint path = query name, always 3 Confuses source duplicates (0.4% seeded) with pipeline duplicates Very high Two-column board diagram. Ask "who introduced this row?" 4 startingOffsets=latest with a producer that already finished High Explains the "Batch 0: 0 pings forever" symptom. Ties to troubleshooting row 6 5 Filters accuracy_m in bronze Medium Bronze is append-only and as-received. Filtering there destroys the evidence needed to prove what the device sent 6 Fixes the m/s drift by clamping speed_kmh to a range Medium The clamped values are wrong, not missing. Normalise on producer_version 7 Sorts the stream to handle out-of-order Medium Ask what "sorted" means for an unbounded input. Usually resolves itself 8 1-second trigger "for lower latency" Low–medium Let them run it for two minutes, then DESCRIBE DETAIL. The file count teaches faster than the explanation

docs.title: 5. Facilitation script for Task 3 (the module's thesis)
docs.text:
Run this as a synchronised room activity, not as independent work.

  1. "Everyone stop. Hands off keyboards." (30 s)
  2. "Run the count. Write the number on your sheet." Collect three numbers verbally from around the room. (1 min)
  3. "Start the producer. Start the stream. When you see a batch line, count to three and hit Ctrl-C." (2 min)
  4. "Run the count again. Write it down." (1 min)
  5. "Restart. Change nothing. No flags. No deleted directories." (2 min)
  6. "Final count." Then ask one pair: "How many pings did you produce? How many rows are in bronze? Are those the same number?" (2 min)
  7. Counter-demo on the projector: sim-nocheckpoint, same drill, 17,300 extra rows. (1.5 min)

Close with the question that carries to the capstone: "Which two mechanisms did that, and where do they live in your repo?" Do not accept a conceptual answer — make them name lakehouse/_checkpoints/gps_events_bronze and the Delta commit.

docs.title: Task 1 — suites
docs.text:
Both files are complete as printed in the participant guide. Three instructor notes:

  1. meta.response_class is the load-bearing idea. GX has no built-in notion of severity; encoding it in meta is what makes the gate a decision engine rather than a boolean. Participants who put the severity logic in the gate instead of the suite have a working lab and a worse design — accept it, but make them articulate the difference.
  2. mostly=0.95 on dropoff_geohash encodes the known 3.1% null rate from CONVENTIONS. This teaches that a tolerated defect must still be bounded and monitored, not silently accepted. If the null rate rises to 8%, this expectation fires.
  3. The frozen baseline in the mean expectations (fare_sar 28–52, from 2026-05-01..05-31) is the setup for Task 3's discussion. Point at the literal and say "this number came from a decision, not from a computation."

Clean-batch validation reference:

[gx] validating silver_trips.contract against silver.trips (42,038 rows)
[gx]   20 expectations : 20 passed, 0 failed

docs.title: Task 2 — gate.py, and the reference outcomes
docs.text:
Fixture FAIL_FAST failures QUARANTINE failures Outcome Promoted Quarantined baseline day batch (42,096 completed) 0 1 (duration_min between) quarantine + promote 42,038 58 dirty batch, as shipped 2 (not_null, unique) 1 BLOCKED — GateBlocked raised 0 0 dirty batch, integrity repaired 0 1 (fare_sar between) quarantine + promote 41,976 120 trips_2026-06-05_currency_shift.csv 0 1 (mean between) promote all — see below 42,096 0

The currency-shift row is the one to dwell on. No row violates any predicate, so QUARANTINE_RULES matches nothing and all 42,096 completed rows promote. The GX mean expectation fails, but there is no row-level predicate to split on — a distribution failure is not isolable by definition. This is the correct moment to ask the room:

"The suite says this batch failed. The gate promoted all of it. Is that a bug?"

The answer is that a distribution failure demands a third response class the lab has not built: ALERT_AND_HOLD — promote nothing, page a human, because you cannot identify which rows are wrong. Strong cohorts arrive here unprompted; it is the best five minutes in the module. Accept either "add a third class" or "escalate the mean expectation to FAIL_FAST" as a valid answer, provided the participant explains why quarantine is impossible here.

The two defences to demand in Task 2:

Why a null trip_id cannot be quarantined. Because the MERGE key is null, so WHEN MATCHED never matches and the row re-inserts on every run — quarantining it does not contain the damage, it just relocates 40 rows while the promotion mechanism itself is unsound for that batch. Integrity failures compromise the operation, not just the data.

Why 120 negative fares must not block 41,976 good trips. Because the fault is 0.25%, isolable by a predicate, and blocking converts a data problem into a total availability outage: silver goes stale, the BI dashboard shows yesterday, and the ETA model retrains on a gap. Proportionality is the whole of the fail-fast/quarantine decision.

Push back hard on any team that gets these backwards. The instructor notes in the package call for exactly this.

docs.title: Task 3 — reference outputs
docs.text:
All four are printed in the participant guide. The reference numbers:

Check Fault Output freshness SLA 1h vs 6.3h age RuntimeError: FRESHNESS breach … (6.3h ago, SLA 1h) volume expected 84,000, actual 42,038 VOLUME anomaly … (-49.96%, tolerance 30%) schema loyalty_tier added upstream [DATA-ALERT] SCHEMA drift … added=['loyalty_tier'] drift fare_sar by city Jeddah ×100 Jeddah 3847.55 vs 38.40 (+9918.6%), four other cities OK drift speed_kmh by producer_version 2.5.0 in m/s 2.5.0 9.62 vs 34.60 (-72.2%), 2.4.0 OK

The --baseline auto trap. Run it on the projector after participants have seen the real drift:

$ python -m masar.quality.observe --check drift --column fare_sar --baseline auto
[obs] drift silver.trips.fare_sar: 421.30 vs 421.30 (0.0%)  OK

Let the room sit with it for a moment. A check that computes its own expectation always passes. This is the sim-baseline-the-bug simulation and it is the most common way a working quality system silently stops working.

docs.title: Task 4 — PDPL classification answer key
docs.text:
Column Classification Access Retention PDPL basis silver.trips.trip_id Public (pseudonymous key) All 7 years Financial-record retention; not personal alone silver.trips.rider_id Personal DS on silver only 24 months Purpose limitation — support and disputes, not analytics silver.trips.driver_id Personal (also employment data) DS + ops; pseudonymised in BI 7 years Contractual/employment basis; longer than rider data and for a different reason silver.trips.vehicle_id Operational All 7 years Not personal — but linkable to a driver via silver.drivers, so linkage risk must be assessed silver.trips.fare_sar Commercial All 7 years Financial record; not personal silver.trips.city Public All 7 years Not personal silver.trips.pickup_zone_id / dropoff_zone_id Personal (coarse location) DS + gold aggregates 24 months Minimised location; zone grain, not coordinates silver.trips.dropoff_geohash Personal (coarse) DS + gold 24 months Minimised substitute for precise coordinates silver.vehicle_positions.lat / .lon Sensitive (precise location) Restricted; geohash-6 at the boundary 180 days raw Data minimisation + retention limit silver.drivers.national_id_hash Personal-pseudonymised Restricted (HR/compliance) Employment + 7 years Pseudonymised ≠ anonymous; still personal data under PDPL silver.drivers.phone_hash Personal-pseudonymised Restricted 24 months post-termination Same gold.eta_features.pickup_zone_id Personal (coarse) Model service + DS 24 months Zone grain is the minimisation choice; the model does not need coordinates gold.eta_features.trip_id Public key All 24 months Joins to nothing personal at gold

The point participants most often miss: driver_id and rider_id are both personal but have different lawful bases and therefore different retention. Rider data is purpose-limited to service delivery; driver data is employment/contractual and legitimately retained longer. A single blanket retention policy is a governance smell.

RETAIN 168 HOURS justification (reference answer). Not 0, because (a) it can delete files a concurrently running reader or streaming query still references, producing FileNotFoundException on a healthy job — Delta requires an explicit safety override for exactly this reason; and (b) it destroys the audit trail needed to prove what a table looked like before a correction, which is a competing compliance obligation. Not 30 days, because that leaves erased personal data physically recoverable for a month after the request was honoured. Seven days is longer than any Masar job's runtime and short enough that erasure completes within a defensible window.

13       DELETE     {predicate -> ["(rider_id = 'RID-0084417')"]}   {numDeletedRows -> 37}

The quarantine row is the detail that separates a good answer from a complete one. Most participants erase from silver.trips and bronze.trips and forget silver.trips_quarantine — which is a table full of personal data by construction. docs.title: Task 1 — the DAG
docs.text:
Complete as printed. Three teaching points:

  1. t_land >> t_gate >> t_silver >> t_obs >> [t_demand, t_driver, t_feats] >> t_maint is the only line that matters. Everything else is configuration. Ask the room which line they would defend hardest in review before revealing the answer.
  2. max_active_runs=1 is not obvious and is usually omitted. Without it, two runs can MERGE into silver.trips concurrently; Delta's optimistic concurrency keeps the table consistent but fails one run with ConcurrentAppendException at 02:00 with nobody watching. Surface this.
  3. The default trigger rule (all_success) is a safety property. If a participant "fixes" a skipped maintenance task with trigger_rule="all_done", they have just arranged to compact and vacuum a table whose build failed. Catch this.

Reference tree output is in the participant guide.

docs.title: Task 2 — reference numbers
docs.text:
Table Grain Rows (run 1) Rows (run 2) Write strategy gold.zone_hourly_demand (city, pickup_zone_id, date, hour) 8,640 8,640 replaceWhere 3-day partition overwrite gold.driver_daily (driver_id, date) 42,612 42,612 MERGE on grain key gold.trip_features (trip_id) 42,038 42,038 full overwrite

The append counter-demo (.mode("append") run twice) produces:

RuntimeError: GRAIN VIOLATION in ./lakehouse/gold/zone_hourly_demand:
  17,280 rows but only 8,640 distinct ['city', 'pickup_zone_id', 'date', 'hour'].
  The write strategy is not idempotent.

Run this on the projector. It converts module mistake #3 from a bullet point into a stack trace.

Why zone_hourly_demand uses replaceWhere and driver_daily uses MERGE. Both are idempotent; the choice is about grain-to-partition alignment. zone_hourly_demand is partitioned by date and its grain is fully contained within a date partition, so a partition overwrite is exact and cheap. driver_daily's grain is also date-scoped, but the lookback window rebuild would need to know which driver/date pairs existed previously to avoid orphaning rows for drivers who had no trips in the new window — MERGE handles that naturally. Accept either strategy for either table if the participant can defend it and the double-run proof passes. The wrong answer is append, and the sophisticated-looking wrong answer is overwrite without replaceWhere (which silently deletes history outside the lookback).

On partitioning. partitionBy("date") only. Reject partitionBy("city", "date", "driver_id") — 14,000 directories per day, module mistake #5. If a participant proposes it, have them run DESCRIBE DETAIL and count files.

docs.title: Task 3 — point-in-time correctness
docs.text:
Reference spot-check:

trip_id      feature_ts           feature_value  recount_strictly_prior  recount_if_leaking
TRP-770118   2026-06-28 07:14:33  17             17                      44

The -1 in rangeBetween(-3600, -1) is the exam question. rangeBetween bounds are inclusive and operate on the ordering column's value range, not on row offsets. With an upper bound of 0, the frame includes every row whose pickup_epoch equals the current row's — every trip starting in the same second, in the same zone. At Riyadh rush-hour density that is several trips, and they are the future.

Make participants say why the inflation is especially dangerous: it is small (a few percent), it correlates with congestion (exactly the thing being predicted), and it therefore looks like signal rather than like a bug. Large leakage gets caught; small leakage gets shipped.

_assert_point_in_time is a weak lint by design — it only detects the degenerate case where a wider window adds nothing. Say so. The real defence is the code review of the window bound, plus LAB-08's leakage drill. A lint that participants believe is complete is worse than no lint.

docs.title: Task 4 — reference full-run output
docs.text: As printed in the participant guide. Total ~3m 40s on a 16 GB laptop with spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=8. If a cohort is seeing 20+ minutes, check for per-task SparkSession creation (JVM startup ×8) and the default 200 shuffle partitions.

docs.title: Task 5 — the recovery proof
docs.text:
Reference snapshots:

before.json = during.json    (dependency held: gold untouched)
before.json = after.json     (full re-run reproduced the exact state, checksums included)

The question participants must answer: why is re-running land_bronze safe?

Reference answer, in three parts:

  1. Bronze may grow on a re-run, and that is within contract. Bronze is append-only and immutable, and carries _batch_id and _source_file precisely so a duplicate landing is identifiable. Bronze's contract is "everything we ever received," not "one row per real-world event."
  2. The duplication stops at the first keyed write. The gate promotes into silver.trips with a MERGE on trip_id; re-applying a matched row updates it to the same values — a no-op. Every gold table derives from silver.
  3. The streaming bronze table (bronze.gps_events) is additionally idempotent per batch via txnAppId/txnVersion from LAB-05.

Reject the answer "we should skip land_bronze on a re-run." A task you are afraid to re-run is a task you cannot recover, and the whole thesis of the lab collapses. If a participant's land_bronze genuinely is not re-runnable, that is a real defect and Task 5 is the correct moment to find it.

docs.title: 5. Facilitation script for Task 5
docs.text:
Run synchronised, whole room, 15 minutes:

  1. "Snapshot. Read me your gold.driver_daily count." Collect three. (2 min)
  2. "Set the failure variable. Run the pipeline. Do not touch anything when it fails." (4 min)
  3. "Diff before and during. Read me the output." Expect silence — the diff is empty. Ask: "Why is gold unchanged? Nobody told it not to build." Answer: the dependency edge. (3 min)
  4. "Unset the variable. Run the WHOLE pipeline. Not the failed task. The whole thing." (4 min)
  5. "Diff before and after." Empty again. (2 min)

Close with: "You just recovered a production data platform from a mid-pipeline failure without knowing what failed, without running anything by hand, and without inspecting a single table. That is what orchestration buys. Everything else is a scheduler."

This is the capstone rehearsal — the rubric's Orchestration & recovery criterion is decided entirely by whether diff before.json after.json comes back empty.
