docs.title: 2. THE LEAKAGE DRILL — COMPLETE ANSWER KEY
docs.text: Do not distribute this section until every pair has submitted their classification.

docs.title: 2.1 Per-column answer key
docs.text: # Column Classification Rationale — what is knowable at feature_ts, and what the starter code actually used Fix 1 trip_id VALID The entity key, assigned at request time. It is an identifier, not a model input, and must be excluded from the feature vector — but it is knowable at feature_ts and reproducible online, so it is VALID rather than LEAKAGE. Accept a participant who argues it should be excluded from the drill entirely, provided they say why None. Exclude from the feature vector; keep for joins and traceability 2 pickup_zone_id VALID The rider's current location, resolved to a zone at request time. Available online as a direct request parameter None 3 dropoff_zone_id VALID Masar's booking flow requires a stated destination before request, so this is an input, not an outcome. Contrast with distance_km (#10), which describes the same journey but is written at dropoff_ts. Product-dependent: if destination-less requests existed, this would be UNAVAILABLE ONLINE for that segment None. Document the product assumption it rests on 4 hour_of_day VALID Derived purely from feature_ts, which at inference is the request timestamp. Deterministic, zero-latency, no source dependency None 5 day_of_week VALID Same as #4. Note the KSA working week (Fri–Sat weekend) when interpreting it, consistent with gold.dim_date.is_weekend None 6 rolling_zone_demand_15m LEAKAGE rangeBetween(-450, 450) is a centred ±7.5-minute window. Diagnostic D1 shows 17 of 31 counted trips started after feature_ts. Those trips had not happened. Worse, the leaked half correlates with exactly the congestion the model is predicting, so it reads as strong genuine signal rangeBetween(-900, -1) — the prior 15 minutes, strictly before. Recompute; expect the feature's mean to roughly halve 7 rolling_avg_speed_10m LEAKAGE The starter averages speed_kmh over the trip's own GPS pings, grouped by trip_id. Diagnostic D2 shows the last such ping was recorded 21.5 minutes after pickup — i.e. after the trip ended. This is not a feature, it is a compressed encoding of the label: a slow trip is a long trip. Pearson r with the label is −0.72 Average the speed of other vehicles in the pickup zone over the 10 minutes strictly before feature_ts, from silver.vehicle_positions, excluding this trip_id. Zone-grained, so it is also materialisable to Redis 8 driver_recent_trip_count STALE rangeBetween(-86400, 0) is point-in-time correct offline except for the inclusive upper bound (a minor same-second leak). The dominant problem is online: the value is refreshed by a nightly batch, so at 19:00 on a Thursday it is 19 hours old. A driver who has completed 11 trips today reads as 0, and the model treats an exhausted driver as a fresh one. Accept LEAKAGE as a defensible second answer if the participant identifies the 0 bound — but require them to also name the staleness, because that is the failure that will actually bite Two-part: change the bound to -1; and refresh the driver slice into the online store on a cadence matched to the feature's volatility (hourly, not nightly), with feature_ts age monitoring 9 weather_condition UNAVAILABLE ONLINE data/raw/weather_hourly.csv lands after the hour it describes. Joining a 07:14 trip to the 07:00 row is legitimate offline — that observation existed when the feature table was built — but at 07:14 live, the 07:00 row has not arrived. Point-in-time correct and unobtainable. The distinction from LEAKAGE is operational: a leaking feature must be changed, an unavailable one must be re-sourced Join to the last observed hour: hour_ts <= date_trunc('hour', feature_ts) - INTERVAL 1 HOUR. Apply the identical shift in training and in materialisation, and serve from the Redis zone key. One hour of staleness, but the same hour on both sides 10 distance_km LEAKAGE In silver.trips this is the metered distance the vehicle actually travelled, written at dropoff_ts. Pearson r with the label is 0.947 and it carries 0.612 of the model's gain — the model is essentially reading the answer. At inference the value does not exist, so the serving code must substitute something, and the model was trained to trust it heavily. This is the single largest contributor to the inflated metric Recompute as the planned route distance at booking: the routing engine's estimate, or offline the route/great-circle distance between gold.dim_zone centroids. Keep the column name (the contract is fixed); change only the source. Participants may internally alias it planned_distance_km for clarity 11 historical_route_duration VALID rangeBetween(-2592000, -1) — the mean duration_min of completed trips on the same (pickup_zone_id, dropoff_zone_id) pair over the prior 30 days, strictly before feature_ts. Correctly excludes the current trip. Zone-pair grained, so it is materialisable to Redis. After the fix it becomes the model's top feature at 0.381 gain — which is the right outcome: historical route behaviour should be the strongest honest signal None. Verify the -1 bound explicitly. Define and document the null contract for zone pairs with no prior trips (impute city median with an is_imputed flag, or omit) 12 feature_ts VALID The as-of timestamp itself — the anchor every other column's correctness is defined against. Metadata, not a model input. It is knowable by definition (it is the request time) None. Exclude from the feature vector; retain for point-in-time joins, materialisation and freshness monitoring 13 label_actual_duration_min LEAKAGE The target. Trivially leaking if it ever enters the feature vector, and a PDPL/operational hazard if it is materialised to Redis — the online store would then be serving the answer. Participants sometimes want to mark this "N/A"; do not accept that. Classifying the label as LEAKAGE is the discipline that catches the non-obvious label proxies, which is what #7 and #10 are Strip from the serving payload and from ONLINE_COLUMNS. Keep in the offline table (that is what a training set is)

docs.title: 2.3 The four deliberate defects in build_eta_features.py
docs.text:
Each is marked with # <-- inspect this in the starter:

Marker Line Defect Fixed form (A) w_demand .rangeBetween(-450, 450) — centred window .rangeBetween(-900, -1) (B) w_driver .rangeBetween(-86400, 0) — inclusive upper bound .rangeBetween(-86400, -1) + hourly online refresh (D) speed pos.groupBy("trip_id").agg(avg(speed_kmh)) — the trip's own pings Zone-grained, prior 10 min, excluding this trip join weather join date_trunc('hour', pickup_ts) == hour_ts — current hour hour_ts == date_trunc('hour', feature_ts) - INTERVAL 1 HOUR select distance_km metered distance passed straight through planned route distance from dim_zone centroids / routing estimate

docs.title: 2.4 Reference metrics
docs.text:
Pre-fix (leaking) Post-fix (honest) Δ R² 0.943 0.712 −0.231 MAE (min) 1.81 4.58 +2.77 (×2.53) Top feature distance_km (0.612) historical_route_duration (0.381) —

Pearson r with the label, pre-fix: distance_km 0.947 · rolling_avg_speed_10m −0.722 · historical_route_duration 0.514 · rolling_zone_demand_15m 0.288 · driver_recent_trip_count 0.041 · hour_of_day 0.111.

The rule of thumb to give the room: any feature correlating above ~0.85 with the label deserves a written defence before it ships. It is occasionally legitimate; it is usually a confession.

docs.title: 2.5 Facilitation script for Task 3
docs.text:
1. Pens down, terminals closed. Five minutes, pairs, no code. Classify all 13 columns from the column names and the CONVENTIONS schema alone. (5 min)
  2. Collect votes on three columns only — distance_km, rolling_avg_speed_10m, weather_condition — by show of hands per class. Record the split on the board. Most rooms mark distance_km VALID. (2 min)
  3. Run D1, D2, D3 together. Read the numbers aloud: "seventeen of thirty-one had not started"; "the last ping was twenty-one and a half minutes after pickup"; "nought point nine four seven." (4 min)
  4. Re-vote the same three columns. The shift is the lesson. (1 min)
  5. Fix and retrain. (5 min)
  6. The close. Put 0.943 and 0.712 side by side and ask: "Which of these two models would you rather deploy, and which would you rather present?" Then: "The honest one tells you it will miss by four and a half minutes. The other tells you one point eight, and then misses by five. The second is more expensive precisely because you believed it." (3 min)

Do not tell them the answer before step 3. The re-vote is what makes it stick.

docs.title: Task 1 — the BI star
docs.text:
All five models are complete as printed. Grading notes:

  • Exactly one dim_date and one dim_driver. If a participant adds a fiscal-calendar variant, they have rebuilt the M1 two-tier divergence inside their own gold layer. This is a named common mistake (#4) and should be caught.
  • dim_date.is_weekend must use the KSA working week (Fri–Sat). Getting this wrong shifts every weekend-demand analysis by two days and is invisible in testing.
  • fact_trip must not select rider_id. sha2(rider_id, 256) as rider_pseudonym is the correct treatment. Check the select list, not the docstring.
  • Reconciliation must be exact (rel_diff = 0). Both descend from one silver.trips through one gate. A non-zero diff is almost always a status = 'completed' filter mismatch or a lookback-window range mismatch — never "adjust" one side.

Reference reconciliation output is in the participant guide.

docs.title: Task 4 — online materialisation and consistency
docs.text:
Reference: 412 zone keys, 4 columns each, 0 mismatches.

materialize_online.py must contain zero feature logic. This is the acceptance criterion that matters most and the easiest to fudge. Read the file. Any F.avg, F.count, Window, or arithmetic on a feature value is a fail — the only permitted operations are select-latest-per-key, serialise, and write.

The injected-divergence test is mandatory. A consistency check that has never failed is a check that has not been tested. Reference:

[consistency] mismatches    : 1
[consistency]   MISMATCH zone=ZN-RUH-014 col=rolling_zone_demand_15m offline=14 online=99
exit=1

The MISSING_ONLINE discussion (troubleshooting row 6) is worth two minutes if time allows: zones with no recent trips have no latest row and therefore no key. Three options — documented default with an is_default flag, service-side fallback with logging, or omission — and the worst option is the one that happens by accident: silently serving last week's key. Ask which of the three a participant's inference service would actually do.

docs.title: Task 5 — PDPL boundary
docs.text:
Reference output is in the participant guide. The dim_zone centroid question (troubleshooting row 12) is the substantive one: coordinates at zone grain are aggregate reference data; coordinates at trip or ping grain are personal data. That distinction is data minimisation, and it should appear in GOVERNANCE.md.

Required in LAB8_NOTES.md: three PDPL principles implemented (minimisation, purpose limitation, and either retention limits or access control), and one thing an analyst genuinely cannot do. Reference answer for the second: an analyst cannot compute per-rider lifetime value or repeat-rider cohorts by identity — only by pseudonym, which breaks if the pseudonym salt rotates, and cannot be joined to any external customer system. That is a real cost. A participant who claims the governance costs nothing has not thought about it.

docs.title: 4. Answer key — self-check questions
docs.text: Q Grading criterion Q1 Must explain that 0.943 was measured wrong, not better, and that reverting does not restore it in production. Bonus: the "tells you 1.8 and misses by 5" framing, or notes that serving must invent substitutes for missing columns Q2 Must locate the difference in when the value is written (feature_ts vs dropoff_ts), not in what it describes. Bonus: the destination-less-request counterfactual Q3 Must distinguish UNAVAILABLE ONLINE from LEAKAGE and propose the last-observed-hour shift applied on both sides. A participant who fixes only the serving path has created textbook skew and should be told so Q4 Must argue that duplicated logic diverges through ordinary maintenance, not negligence. Bonus: names the bounded cost (staleness, managed by refresh cadence + monitoring) against the unbounded one (skew, unmonitorable) Q5 Must name the shared silver.trips and the single gate. Bonus: names both residual risks — filter divergence and build-timing divergence — and the guards for each Q6 Must identify the type-1 dimension problem: today's rating attached to a three-week-old trip. Bonus: proposes SCD2 as-of join, or derivation from gold.driver_daily restricted to prior dates. Best answers note the column name is the tell

docs.title: 5. Common participant errors
docs.text: # Error Frequency Intervention 1 Marks distance_km VALID Very high — most rooms The D3 correlation (0.947). Then ask: "when is that number written?" 2 Marks rolling_avg_speed_10m VALID because "speed is an input" High D2: the last ping is 21.5 min after pickup. The trip was over 3 Marks label_actual_duration_min "N/A" High Refuse. Classifying the label is the discipline that catches label proxies — which is what #1 and #2 are 4 Marks weather_condition LEAKAGE Medium Reasonable confusion. Draw the distinction: leaking = must change; unavailable = must re-source. The category exists precisely to force different remediation 5 Disappointed by the metric drop; asks whether they broke it Very high This is the emotional peak. Say plainly: this is the correct outcome and it is what the lab is for 6 Fixes leakage, R² rises Medium A fix reintroduced leakage elsewhere — usually historical_route_duration rebuilt with a 0 upper bound. Re-run D3 7 Recomputes features in materialize_online.py High Skew by construction. Read their file; delete the computation 8 Random train/test split High Itself a form of leakage — the model sees future trips from the same zone-hour. Always split by time 9 Two dim_date variants Medium The M1 two-tier divergence, rebuilt in their own gold layer 10 rider_id in fact_trip Medium PDPL boundary violation and a rubric anti-pattern flag 11 Adds columns to gold.eta_features Medium The 13-column contract is fixed by CONVENTIONS. Fixes change the computation, never the column set 12 Redis connection refused from Spark, works in redis-cli Medium Container vs host. Published port + host="localhost"

docs.title: 7. Grading guidance (capstone criterion Serving (AI + BI) & demo, 10 pts)
docs.text:
Band Evidence 90–100 All 13 columns classified correctly with written rationale, all four defects found and fixed at the computation (not the contract), both metrics recorded with an explanation of why the drop is correct, offline == online proven across all keys and shown to fail on injection, conformed star reconciling at 0, PDPL boundary asserted 70–89 Works, but the classification misses one or two columns (typically weather_condition or driver_recent_trip_count), or reconciliation is asserted rather than shown, or consistency is spot-checked on one key rather than all < 70 Leakage remains · online ≠ offline · raw PII served · star does not reconcile

Automatic caps at 70% (capstone anti-pattern flags): feature leakage, raw rider IDs in BI outputs.

Live verification the assessment notes authorise: ask the participant to run the leakage drill and explain the inflated metric. A distinction-band answer names the specific column, the specific window bound, the specific diagnostic that revealed it, and both numbers — without opening a file.

docs.title: 8. Capstone handoff
docs.text:
This is the last lab. What each participant should now hold:

Capstone artefact Source Requirement 8 (Serving) complete This lab DECISIONS.md entries: feature window; online store yes/no Task 3 and Task 4 Demo closing beat: both consumers reading the same gold Task 6 dashboard query + Redis lookup, side by side Extension candidate #1 (consistency check in CI) Stretch goal 1 — the highest-value extension and the one most often chosen Extension candidate #2 (leakage lint) Stretch goal 2 — a structural rule that catches the class, not the instance

The sentence to close the course on, after the dashboard query and the Redis lookup return agreeing numbers on the same screen:

"Those two numbers agree because they descend from one silver table, through one gate, built by one DAG, from one stream you can kill and restart. Every day of this course is in that agreement. When it stops being true, you now know which layer to look at."

docs.title: Masar Lakehouse (مسار)
docs.text:
Starter repository for SDA-DSC-214 — Modern Data Engineering for AI Systems (هندسة البيانات الحديثة لأنظمة الذكاء الاصطناعي), SDAIA Academy.

You clone this on Day 1 and grow it into your capstone. Every lab writes into the same lakehouse: Lab 1 lands bronze, Lab 3 transforms it to silver, Lab 4 makes silver ACID, Labs 5–8 stream, test, orchestrate and serve it. There are no throwaway datasets and no restarts.

The question the whole course keeps asking: "What happens to Masar's AI system if THIS part of the data platform fails?"

Masar is a national smart-mobility platform — ride-hailing plus public transit, operating in Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam. Two consumers depend on the same data: an ETA model retrained weekly, and an operations dashboard read hourly. The architecture exists so they read the same numbers.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Do the full setup in labs/LAB_00_Environment_Setup.md two days before Day 1. The short version:

git clone <your-fork-url> masar-lakehouse
cd masar-lakehouse
git checkout lab1-start

python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows/WSL2: source .venv/bin/activate
make install                       # pinned stack + `pip install -e .`

make doctor                        # must report 0 fail
make data                          # generate the Masar dataset (pinned seed)
docker compose up -d               # Kafka + Redis (needed from Day 4)

make pipeline                      # build the entire medallion, end to end

make doctor is the single source of truth for setup. Any [fail] must be fixed before Day 1. Kafka/Redis [warn] is fine until Day 4.

docs.title: The one command
docs.text:
make pipeline

Land bronze → quality gate → build silver → observability → three gold marts → OPTIMIZE + VACUUM. Dependency-ordered, idempotent, and safe to run twice.

It routes through orchestration/run_local.py, which needs no Airflow. Once you have Airflow installed, USE_AIRFLOW=1 make pipeline runs the same graph through it — the task definitions are shared, so the two cannot drift.

docs.title: How the starter marks your work
docs.text:
Everything in src/masar/** is real, working code. The parts you implement are delimited:

# ── TODO(lab-3): keep the LATEST landed version per trip_id ───────────
#   What : ...
#   Why  : ...
#   Ref  : solutions/lab3_elt.py :: dedupe_latest_per_key
deduped = typed.dropDuplicates(["trip_id"])      # naive starter version
# ── end TODO(lab-3) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────

The code inside the block runs — make pipeline works on Day 1. It is deliberately the naive version, the one a competent engineer writes before they have met the failure mode. The lab's own acceptance test is what exposes the gap. You are not filling in blanks; you are finding and fixing a plausible bug, which is the part that transfers.

solutions/README.md lists every block and what its starter version gets wrong. Opening it before you attempt the task costs you the lesson.

docs.title: Two things that are unusual, and why
docs.text:
Heavy imports are function-local. import masar never imports PySpark. So scripts/doctor.py can report a MISSING dependency instead of dying on an ImportError while trying to tell you about it, and the unit tests run in about a second on a machine with no Spark at all.

lakehouse/ and data/raw/ are git-ignored. Data is regenerated from a pinned seed (make data), never committed. Committing Delta tables makes the repo unclonable and the _delta_log meaningless — its commits would be somebody else's.

docs.title: Everyday commands
docs.text:
Command Does make List every target make doctor Check Java 17, Python 3.11, Spark, Delta, dbt, GX, Kafka, Redis make data Generate the Masar dataset from the pinned seed make land Land every raw feed into bronze make gate Run the quality gate: fail-fast, quarantine, promote make silver / make gold Build the conformed and served layers make stream Replay GPS → Kafka → bronze → silver make serve Materialise online features, prove offline == online, check PDPL make pipeline The one command. The whole medallion make dbt-run / make dbt-test The ELT models and their tests make gx Build the GX suites and render the data docs make optimize / make vacuum Compact files; reclaim storage (dry run) make test The unit tests make clean Remove caches and logs — keeps the lakehouse

Useful overrides: DATE=2026-06-02, USE_AIRFLOW=1, FROM=… TO=…, LAB=7.

docs.title: The recovery drill (Lab 7's thesis)
docs.text:
python -m masar.tools.snapshot --out /tmp/before.json
python orchestration/run_local.py --run --inject-failure build_silver
python -m masar.tools.snapshot --out /tmp/during.json
diff <(jq -S . /tmp/before.json) <(jq -S . /tmp/during.json)   # empty: the dependency held

python orchestration/run_local.py --run                        # full re-run
python -m masar.tools.snapshot --out /tmp/after.json
diff <(jq -S . /tmp/before.json) <(jq -S . /tmp/after.json)    # empty: idempotent recovery

Both diffs empty is the capstone's central claim, demonstrated rather than asserted. If a full re-run is safe, every operational problem is tractable.

docs.title: Checkpoint tags
docs.text:
Each lab starts from a tag. If you fall behind, check out the next -start tag and you are caught up — no lab depends on you having finished the previous one perfectly.

Tag What you get lab0-setup Empty scaffold. make doctor should be green. lab1-start Stubs for landing and profiling. lab2-start Bronze landed; silver.trips sample for the scan benchmark. lab3-start dbt project scaffolded; sources declared. lab4-start silver.trips from Lab 3, unconstrained. lab5-start Kafka compose file; producer and stream stubs. lab6-start GX scaffold; the dirty-batch fixtures. lab7-start All prior modules importable; DAG stub. lab8-start gold/* from Lab 7; Redis running; dbt configured. lab1-solution … lab8-solution Each lab's completed state.

docs.title: Simulation and incident tags
docs.text:
Tag Simulates Used in bad-batch The dirty batch mid-pipeline: 40 null keys, 120 bad fares, 25 bad city codes, 15 reversed timestamps. Fail-fast fires, then quarantine. M6 / Lab 6 sim-swamp Bronze landed with no profiling, no lineage and overwrite-on-rerun. The data lake as swamp — the thing Lab 1 exists to prevent. M1 sim-two-tier A separate warehouse copy that has drifted from the lake: two "revenue" numbers, neither reconcilable. The two-tier problem this course solves. M1 / M3

Instructors also keep incident-speed-unit, which lands the producer 2.5.0 GPS batch (speed_kmh in m/s) so the Module 6 detection drill has a real incident to find.

docs.title: For instructors: publishing the tags
docs.text:
Tags are cut from a single linear history so that a participant who checks out lab5-start gets everything Labs 1–4 produced, in the state Lab 5 assumes.

# from a clean main, at the commit that ends each lab's setup
git tag -a lab3-start -m "LAB-03 start: dbt scaffolded, bronze landed"

# solution branches carry the completed TODO blocks
git checkout -b lab3-solution lab3-start
#   apply solutions/lab3_elt.py's blocks into src/ and dbt/
git commit -am "solution(lab3): incremental idempotent silver.trips"
git tag -a lab3-solution -m "LAB-03 solution"

# simulation tags branch off and are never merged back
git checkout -b sim-swamp lab1-start
#   remove lineage columns, switch bronze writes to overwrite, delete profiling
git commit -am "sim(swamp): unprofiled, unlineaged, overwriting bronze"
git tag -a sim-swamp -m "M1 simulation: the data swamp"

git push origin --tags

Checklist before a cohort starts. Every -start tag must:

  1. pass make doctor with 0 fail on a clean machine;
  2. pass make test;
  3. run make pipeline to completion (the naive TODO blocks are working code — that is the point);
  4. contain the LAB_N_NOTES.md template the lab asks participants to fill in;
  5. be reachable by git fetch --tags from the fork participants cloned.

Run steps 1–3 from a fresh clone, not from your working tree. The most common failure is a tag that works only because of an untracked file.

docs.title: Capstone deliverables
docs.text:
Fill these from your own runs. The templates tell you what "filled in" means.

  • docs/ARCHITECTURE.md — the design and its failure modes
  • docs/DATA_CONTRACTS.md — grain, keys, SLAs, owners, per layer
  • GOVERNANCE.md — from docs/GOVERNANCE_TEMPLATE.md
  • DECISIONS.md — from docs/DECISIONS_TEMPLATE.md

Benchmark figures are compared across the cohort. Numbers copied from the slides, from a classmate, or from the template are an academic integrity issue.

docs.title: Masar Lakehouse — Architecture
docs.text:
The question this architecture exists to answer: "What happens to Masar's AI system if THIS part of the data platform fails?" Every component below is documented with its failure mode, because a design that only describes the happy path is a design nobody can operate.

Masar (مسار) is a national smart-mobility platform: ride-hailing plus public transit, operating in Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam. Two consumers depend on the same data — an ETA model retrained weekly, and an operations dashboard read hourly — and the whole point of the architecture is that they read the same numbers.

Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. Grains, ratios and file-count reductions hold at either scale; absolute row counts do not.

docs.title: 1. The shape
docs.text:
SOURCES                LANDING            CONFORMED           SERVED
 ─────────              ───────            ─────────           ──────
 trips CSV      ─┐                                          ┌─ gold.fact_trip ─────┐
 drivers CSV     │                                          │  gold.dim_* ─────────┤─► BI

Storage is ./lakehouse/ locally and an object-storage bucket (s3://masar-lakehouse/) in production. The directory layout is identical — zone/table/partition=.../part-*.parquet — so the move is a configuration change, not a rewrite. That is compute-storage separation made physical: kill the JVM and the data is still there.

docs.title: 2. The layers, and what each one promises
Bronze — an append-only ledger of what ARRIVED
docs.text:
Property Decision Failure mode if you get it wrong Write mode append, never overwrite A bug found in week six is unfixable for weeks one to five: the evidence is gone. Typing Everything lands as STRING (inferSchema=False) Inference guesses at the two timestamp formats and silently nulls the 2% that do not match — destroying evidence before anyone looked. Schema mergeSchema=false An upstream schema change is absorbed silently, and the drift Module 6 exists to catch never surfaces. Lineage _ingested_at, _source_file, _batch_id on every row "Which file produced this row?" is the first question a regulator asks, and landing time is the only cheap moment to answer it.

Landing the same day twice doubles the rows, and that is correct. The two batches are distinguishable by _batch_id, so silver can deterministically keep the latest version per key without ever having lost the earlier one. Overwriting would have made the duplication invisible and the history unrecoverable.

docs.title: The gate — the only door into silver
docs.text:
Three outcomes, decided by each expectation's meta.response_class (quality/gate_config.yml is the policy; masar.quality.gate is the engine):

  • FAIL_FAST — integrity. Null or duplicate business key, missing event time, schema change, type change. Promoting anything from such a batch is worse than promoting nothing. The task raises; every downstream task is skipped.
  • QUARANTINE — partial. Bad fares, impossible durations, unknown cities. Bad rows go to silver.trips_quarantine with their reason; good rows are promoted. Alert either way.
  • All pass — promote, alert nothing.

Getting this split wrong fails in two directions, and the second is worse: too much fail-fast and someone adds a bypass flag until the gate is decoration; too much quarantine and a batch with duplicate keys reaches silver, where MERGE becomes ambiguous and the result is undefined.

docs.title: Silver — the conformed contract
docs.text:
One row per business key. Completed, valid trips only. Timestamps stored UTC, presented Asia/Riyadh (+03). City codes mapped to names exactly once. speed_kmh always in km/h, whatever the producer version claimed.

Enforced in three independent places, on purpose:

  1. Delta CHECK constraints on the table — every future write, every writer.
  2. dbt tests on the model — every build, in CI.
  3. The gate at promotion — every batch, before it lands.

Anything filtered out still exists in bronze. Nothing is destroyed; it is excluded from the contract downstream consumers may rely on.

docs.title: Gold — two products, one truth
docs.text:
• BI: a conformed star (fact_trip + dim_date, dim_driver, dim_vehicle, dim_zone) plus two marts (zone_hourly_demand, driver_daily). Conformed dimensions are what make numbers reconcile across dashboards; two dim_dates is how "last week" comes to mean two different things.
  • AI: eta_features and trip_features, point-in-time correct, plus a Redis slice at masar:features:zone:{zone_id} copied from gold — never recomputed.

docs.title: 3. The five decisions that carry the design
3.1 Partition on cardinality, not on the key
docs.text: silver.trips is partitioned by city: five values. Partitioning by trip_id would create 42,038 directories — a metadata storm, a tripled object-storage request bill, and a dashboard query that goes from 800 ms to 40 s. gold.driver_daily is partitioned by date only, not by (city, date, driver_id), for the same reason.

docs.title: 3.2 Idempotency is what makes recovery possible
docs.text:
Every task is safe to re-run. That is not tidiness; it is the property that turns "re-run the whole thing" into a safe instruction. Without it, a 02:30 failure becomes a 09:00 archaeology project in which somebody re-runs "the parts that failed", in a remembered order, having skipped the gate because "it passed yesterday".

Table Strategy Why this one bronze.* append + txnAppId/txnVersion The ledger grows; replayed batches are dropped by Delta. silver.trips MERGE on trip_id Keyed upsert: re-running updates the same rows to the same values. gold.zone_hourly_demand replaceWhere on the date window Replaces exactly the partitions recomputed; O(lookback), not O(history). gold.driver_daily MERGE on (driver_id, date) The grain does not align to one partition column cleanly. gold.*_features full overwrite Small, derived, cheap to rebuild; simplest correct thing.

docs.title: 3.3 Event time everywhere it matters
docs.text:
Late data is the norm, not the exception. Three mechanisms, one principle:

  • Silver lookback — a 3-day window on pickup_ts (event time), not on _ingested_at. A trip that ended Monday but arrived Wednesday must stay inside the window for the full lookback, so every re-run re-merges it.
  • Streaming watermark — 5 minutes on event_ts. Bounds both the lateness tolerated and the state kept.
  • Feature windows — strictly prior, rangeBetween(..., -1).

The one place processing time is correct is the operations alerter: an alert is about NOW, not about when the event happened.

docs.title: 3.4 Point-in-time correctness is structural, not a review item
docs.text:
Every rolling feature is declared as a FeatureWindow in masar.transform.feature_spec and asserted at build time. A window whose upper bound is not strictly negative fails the build.

rangeBetween(-3600, 0) reads as "the last hour" and is not: rangeBetween is inclusive of both bounds, so it admits every other trip that started in the same second. In a busy zone at 07:14 that is several trips which had not happened yet. One character; a metric that lies. A lint that runs beats a rule everyone agrees with.

docs.title: 3.5 PDPL is a constraint on the design, not a review at the end
docs.text:
Classification (masar.governance.classification) is the root of everything else: access control, retention windows, what may cross the serving boundary, and what an erasure request has to touch.

Two rules that are routinely got wrong:

  1. A hash is not anonymisation. national_id_hash is pseudonymised personal data. It still belongs to a person, is still in scope for erasure, and still must not reach a dashboard.
  2. Precise location is its own class. Metre-resolution lat/lon reveals homes and routines. A zone centroid does not — the resolution is the control.

masar.serve.pdpl_boundary_check asserts all of this and exits non-zero, so it belongs in CI. Governance that lives in a PDF is checked when someone remembers; governance that lives in a build step is checked every time.

docs.title: 4. Failure modes, and what holds
docs.text: If this fails The AI system… What contains it Landing overwrites instead of appending degrades invisibly — no reprocessing is possible after any later bug append-only bronze; _batch_id makes re-lands visible The gate is bypassed trains on negative fares and unkeyed rows gold builds from silver only; the DAG edge enforces it Silver dedup keeps an arbitrary row silently loses ~half of all corrections row_number() over _ingested_at desc A gold task appends instead of merging double-counts demand → surge fires at 2× on a normal Tuesday replaceWhere / MERGE + a grain assertion on every write A feature window includes the present offline R² rises, live performance does not FeatureWindow.assert_point_in_time() fails the build A producer changes a field's meaning learns a fleet that never speeds up per-producer_version distribution check vs a frozen baseline The streaming job is killed mid-batch (nothing) checkpointed offsets + Delta's atomic commit with txnVersion Online features are recomputed rather than copied training/serving skew appears weeks later consistency_check compares every key, exits non-zero VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS is run loses the audit trail and the erasure evidence retention is config (MASAR_VACUUM_RETAIN_HOURS), never 0; the Delta retention check stays enabled

docs.title: 5. Orchestration
docs.text:
land_bronze ─► quality_gate ─► build_silver ──┐
                               build_drivers ─┴─► observability ─┬─► gold_zone_hourly_demand ─┐
                                                                 ├─► gold_driver_daily        ├─► optimize_vacuum
                                                                 └─► gold_trip_features ──────┘

The graph is declared once, in masar.orchestration.runner, and imported by both orchestration/dags/masar_medallion.py (Airflow 2.9 TaskFlow) and orchestration/run_local.py (no Airflow at all). They cannot disagree about what the pipeline is, and no lab ever blocks on an orchestrator install.

quality_gate has retries=0 on purpose: retrying a deterministic integrity rejection is a slower way of ignoring it.

docs.title: 6. Where to go next
docs.text:
• docs/DATA_CONTRACTS.md — the per-layer contracts: grain, keys, SLAs, owners
  • docs/GOVERNANCE_TEMPLATE.md — PDPL classification, retention, erasure
  • docs/DECISIONS_TEMPLATE.md — the ADR log for your capstone
  • docs/BENCHMARKS_TEMPLATE.md — the measurements that back every claim above

docs.title: Masar Lakehouse — Data Contracts
docs.text:
A data contract is a promise one team makes to another about the shape, quality and timeliness of a dataset — plus the place that promise is enforced. A contract with no enforcement point is a wish.

Every table below states: grain, keys, freshness SLA, owner, what breaks a consumer, and where the contract is enforced.

Fill in the Owner column with a real person or rota before the capstone review. "The data team" is not an owner; it is an absence of one.

docs.title: How to read the enforcement column
docs.text:
Enforcement Means Delta CHECK The table rejects the write. Every writer, forever. dbt test The build fails in CI before anything is published. GX + gate The batch is blocked or split at promotion time. Grain assert The build task raises if row count ≠ distinct key count. Lint A build-time assertion on the code, not the data.

Layered on purpose. Any single one of these can be bypassed by someone in a hurry; three cannot be bypassed by accident.

docs.title: Bronze — the landing zone
docs.text:
Promise: everything that arrived, exactly as it arrived, with lineage. Non-promise: uniqueness, typing, validity, or completeness of any kind.

Table Grain Keys Freshness SLA Owner Enforcement bronze.trips one row per delivered record (duplicates expected) none warn 6h / error 24h TBD source freshness (dbt), _batch_id lineage bronze.gps_events one row per delivered ping none warn 1h / error 6h TBD source freshness, txnAppId/txnVersion idempotency bronze.drivers one row per delivered roster record none warn 24h / error 72h TBD source freshness bronze.vehicles one row per delivered record none warn 24h / error 72h TBD source freshness bronze.zones one row per delivered record none warn 72h / error 168h TBD source freshness bronze.payments one row per delivered record none warn 6h / error 24h TBD source freshness

Universal bronze columns. Every table carries _ingested_at (when the platform saw it), _source_file (which file or Kafka partition it came from) and _batch_id (which landing run produced it).

What breaks a consumer: treating bronze as if it had a grain. It does not. Counting bronze.trips and reporting it as "trips yesterday" will be wrong the first time a day is re-landed — which is a normal, correct operation.

Retention: indefinite for trips (the reprocessing substrate); 180 days for bronze.gps_events (precise location, purpose-bound — see GOVERNANCE_TEMPLATE.md).

docs.title: Silver — the conformed contract
docs.text: Promise: one row per business key; conformed, typed, valid. This is THE contract. Changing a column here is a breaking change and goes through review as one.

docs.title: silver.trips
docs.text:
Field Value Grain Exactly one row per trip_id Primary key trip_id (unique, not null) Foreign keys driver_id → silver.drivers, pickup_zone_id/dropoff_zone_id → dim_zone Partitioned by city (5 values — never by trip_id) Freshness SLA ≤ 6 hours behind bronze Volume ~42,000 rows/day, ±30% tolerance Owner TBD

Guarantees:

  • status = 'completed' only. Cancellations and no-shows stay in bronze.
  • pickup_ts, dropoff_ts in UTC; trip_date is the Asia/Riyadh business date. Both source timestamp formats are parsed.
  • city is a conformed NAME (Riyadh), never a raw code (RUH).
  • fare_sar > 0, distance_km > 0, dropoff_ts > pickup_ts.
  • duration_min is DERIVED from the timestamps, not the reported value. reported_duration_min is kept alongside it and may disagree — that disagreement is itself a data-quality signal.
  • dropoff_geohash is ~3.1% null. Known, tolerated, monitored at a 95% threshold so a degradation is an event.

Enforcement: Delta CHECK (positive_fare, valid_duration, known_city) · dbt tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values, accepted_range, relationships) · GX + gate at promotion.

What breaks a consumer: a duplicated trip_id. Every downstream MERGE becomes ambiguous, which is undefined behaviour rather than a wrong number.

docs.title: silver.vehicle_positions
docs.text:
Field Value Grain Exactly one row per event_id Primary key event_id Partitioned by event_date Freshness SLA ≤ 15 minutes behind the stream Volume ~1.2M rows/day Owner TBD

Guarantees:

  • Deduplicated within a 5-minute watermark.
  • speed_kmh is ALWAYS km/h, whatever producer_version claimed. Producer 2.5.0 emits m/s under the same key and type; the conversion happens here, once, so no consumer has to know it ever happened.
  • accuracy_m ≤ 50. A worse fix is noise, not a position.
  • lat/lon inside the Saudi bounding box.
  • event_lag_s and is_late are retained so lateness stays measurable.

Enforcement: GX gps_events.contract (including the per-version mean check) · streaming filters in build_vehicle_positions.

What breaks a consumer: the speed unit. Every value stays individually plausible, so nothing errors; the ETA model simply learns that a third of the fleet crawls, and ETAs for those vehicles inflate for weeks.

docs.title: silver.drivers · silver.payments · silver.trips_quarantine
docs.text:
Table Grain Keys SLA Owner silver.drivers one row per driver_id, type-1 driver_id ≤ 24h TBD silver.payments one row per payment_id payment_id ≤ 6h TBD silver.trips_quarantine one row per rejected row per batch none n/a TBD

silver.trips_quarantine carries _quarantine_reasons (an array — a row can be wrong in more than one way), _quarantined_at and _batch_id. A quarantine table without reasons is a landfill: "120 rows rejected" starts an investigation, "120 rows: fare_non_positive" ends one.

docs.title: Gold — the served products
docs.text: Promise: stable, documented, consumer-facing. Two consumers, one truth.

docs.title: BI: the conformed star
docs.text:
Table Grain Key SLA Owner Notes gold.fact_trip one row per trip_id trip_id ≤ 6h TBD FKs to all four dimensions; no rider_id — a pseudonym only gold.dim_date one row per calendar date date_key static TBD THE conformed date dimension. Exactly one exists. is_weekend = Fri+Sat (KSA) gold.dim_driver one row per driver_id (type-1) driver_key ≤ 24h TBD national_id_hash/phone_hash excluded by classification gold.dim_vehicle one row per vehicle_id vehicle_key ≤ 24h TBD gold.dim_zone one row per zone_id zone_key ≤ 168h TBD Centroid at ZONE resolution, never per-trip gold.zone_hourly_demand one row per (city, zone, date, hour) composite ≤ 6h TBD Also an input to surge pricing gold.driver_daily one row per (driver_id, date) composite ≤ 6h TBD gold.bi_trips_safe one row per trip_id trip_id ≤ 6h TBD PDPL-safe analyst view

Conformed dimensions are the contract. One dim_date, one dim_zone, shared by every fact and mart. Two of either is how the revenue dashboard and the demand dashboard start disagreeing about what "last week" means, and the disagreement is discovered in a steering committee.

gold.zone_hourly_demand is special. Surge pricing reads it. A double-counted row here is not a reporting error — it is a price. That is why its write is MERGE on the full grain key and why _assert_grain runs on every build.

docs.title: AI: the feature products
docs.text:
Table Grain Key SLA Owner gold.eta_features one row per trip_id trip_id ≤ 6h TBD gold.trip_features one row per trip_id trip_id ≤ 6h TBD Redis masar:features:zone:{zone_id} one key per zone zone_id ≤ 15 min TBD

gold.eta_features columns are fixed by CONVENTIONS.md and are not negotiable — the training join, the online store and the model all agree on them:

trip_id, pickup_zone_id, dropoff_zone_id, hour_of_day, day_of_week,
rolling_zone_demand_15m, rolling_avg_speed_10m, driver_recent_trip_count,
weather_condition, distance_km, historical_route_duration, feature_ts,
label_actual_duration_min

Guarantees:

  • Point-in-time correct. Every rolling window is strictly prior: rangeBetween(..., -1). Declared in masar.transform.feature_spec and asserted at build time.
  • Available at inference. No column may depend on data that does not exist at prediction time. distance_km is the ROUTED distance, not the actual — the column name is the contract, the provenance is the implementation.
  • _feature_version on every row and every Redis payload. Without it, "which features produced this prediction?" is unanswerable at exactly the moment somebody needs the answer.
  • Online == offline. The Redis slice is COPIED from gold, never recomputed. masar.serve.consistency_check compares every key and every column and exits non-zero on any mismatch.

What breaks a consumer: a feature computed differently online and offline. It will not disagree at first. It will disagree after someone fixes a rounding bug in one of the two implementations, and the model will get quietly worse with nothing in any log.

docs.title: Contract change process
docs.text:
1. Propose — open a PR against the model, its _*__models.yml, and this file. A schema change with no contract update is not reviewable.
  2. Classify — new columns get a PDPL classification in masar.governance.classification. classify() fails closed, so an unclassified column is treated as personal until somebody has looked.
  3. Test — add the dbt test that makes the new guarantee enforceable. A guarantee with no test is a comment.
  4. Announce — additive changes need notice; removals and renames need agreement from every named owner.
  5. Version — bump _feature_version for any change to a feature's MEANING, even if its name and type are unchanged. Especially then: that is exactly the change nothing else detects.

docs.title: Masar — Architecture Decision Record
docs.text:
Capstone deliverable. Rename to DECISIONS.md. One entry per decision that was genuinely contested. Ten thorough ADRs beat forty thin ones.

An ADR records a decision and the alternative you rejected. If you cannot name a real alternative and a real cost, you did not make a decision — you followed a default, and that needs no record.

Two entries are worked through below as examples of the depth expected. The rest are stubs.

Scale note. Figures quoted in this document assume the full-scale generator run (--scale 1.0); the shipped sample is --scale 0.15 — 7,230 trips/day over 5 days (36,150 trips), 873,763 GPS pings, 3,450 drivers, 3,864 vehicles, 48 zones. Grains, ratios and file-count reductions hold at either scale; absolute row counts do not.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
## ADR-00N — <decision, stated as an outcome>

**Status:** proposed | accepted | superseded by ADR-00M
**Date:** YYYY-MM-DD
**Deciders:** <names>
**Module:** M1–M8

### Context
What forced a choice? What constraint, incident or requirement?

### Options considered
| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A (chosen) | | |
| B | | |

### Decision
What we do, in one sentence, in the present tense.

### Consequences
What this costs, what it forecloses, what now needs monitoring.

### How we would know we were wrong
The observation that would make us revisit this. An ADR with no falsifier is
a statement of preference.

docs.title: ADR-001 — Partition silver.trips by city, not by trip_id
docs.text: Status: accepted · Date: 2026-06-02 · Module: M2, M4

docs.title: Context
docs.text: silver.trips grows by ~42,000 rows/day. Queries filter overwhelmingly by city and date range. Partitioning determines both scan cost and file count, and file count determines object-storage request cost — which at Masar's read volume is not a rounding error.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text: Option Pros Cons city (chosen) 5 partitions; matches the dominant filter; large files Riyadh is ~55% of volume — skew trip_id Perfectly even 42,038 directories/day. Metadata storm, 3× request bill, 800 ms → 40 s dashboards (city, date) Finer pruning ~15 partitions/day; small files within a day at this volume none Simplest Every query scans everything

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Partition by city. ZORDER by (city, pickup_ts) in the nightly OPTIMIZE to recover the intra-partition pruning that a date partition would have given.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Riyadh partitions are ~3× the others; acceptable at this scale, and it is the first thing to revisit if a single-city query becomes the hot path. ZORDER must actually run — without it the pruning argument does not hold.

docs.title: How we would know we were wrong
docs.text: DESCRIBE DETAIL shows average file size dropping below ~64 MB, or the p95 dashboard query exceeds 3 s with numFiles climbing between OPTIMIZE runs.

docs.title: ADR-002 — Materialise online features by copying from gold, never recomputing
docs.text: Status: accepted · Date: 2026-06-04 · Module: M8

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The ETA model needs zone features in under 50 ms at inference. The Lakehouse cannot serve that latency directly, so a derived copy in Redis is required. The question is what writes it.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text: Option Pros Cons Copy from gold.eta_features (chosen) Consistent by construction; one feature implementation Freshness bounded by the batch cadence (~15 min) Recompute in the serving path Always fresh Two implementations of one feature = skew, guaranteed eventually Serve from the Lakehouse directly One store Cannot meet 50 ms

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: masar.serve.materialize_online copies values from gold.eta_features verbatim. There is no arithmetic in that module and there must never be any. masar.serve.consistency_check compares every key and every column against the offline table and exits non-zero on any mismatch; it runs in CI.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Online features are up to one batch stale, which is acceptable for zone-demand features and would not be for a per-second signal. The consistency check is now load-bearing: if it is disabled, the guarantee is gone and nothing else would notice.

docs.title: How we would know we were wrong
docs.text: The consistency check fails, or a product requirement appears that needs sub-batch freshness — at which point the answer is a streaming write into Redis from the same feature job, still without a second implementation.

docs.title: ADR-003 — TBD
docs.text:
Status: proposed · Module: M__

Candidate decisions worth a real ADR (each has a genuine alternative):

  • Silver lookback of 3 days — why not 1, why not 7? What does each cost?
  • MERGE vs replaceWhere per gold table — the grain decides, but say why.
  • Watermark of 5 minutes on positions — the lateness/state trade-off.
  • Failing fast on integrity but quarantining value failures — where is the line?
  • Retention of 168 hours — auditability against minimisation.
  • Airflow vs the shipped runner — what you gained and what you gave up.
  • Storing UTC and presenting +03 — versus storing local time.
  • Keeping bronze indefinitely — reprocessing value against PDPL exposure.

docs.title: Decision log
docs.text: ADR Decision Status Module Date 001 Partition silver.trips by city accepted M2, M4 2026-06-02 002 Copy online features from gold, never recompute accepted M8 2026-06-04 003 TBD proposed

docs.title: What makes an ADR worth reading
docs.text:
• A real alternative. "We considered doing it badly" is not an option.
  • A stated cost. Every decision forecloses something. Name it.
  • A falsifier. What would change your mind, expressed as an observation.
  • A date and a person. Decisions age; anonymous ones age worst.

The test: hand the ADR to an engineer who joins in six months. Can they tell whether the decision still applies, without asking you?

docs.title: Masar — Governance and PDPL Register
docs.text:
Capstone deliverable. Rename to GOVERNANCE.md, fill every TBD, and commit it alongside the code it describes. A governance document that is not in the repository is a governance document that is not maintained.

Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) is treated here as an engineering constraint, not a policy appendix. Every section below should be answerable by pointing at code or config, not at intent.

Field Value Controller Masar (مسار) — TBD legal entity Data Protection Officer TBD Register last reviewed TBD (date) Review cadence TBD (quarterly recommended)

docs.title: 1. Data classification
docs.text:
Classification is the ROOT of every other control: access, retention, what may cross the serving boundary, and what an erasure request must touch.

The machine-readable source of truth is src/masar/governance/classification.py. This table must agree with it — if they diverge, the code wins and this document is out of date.

Class Meaning Retention Readable by Example columns public No restriction no PDPL limit analyst, DS, engineer, DPO city, zone_name_en, distance_km operational Internal identifiers, no data subject no PDPL limit analyst, DS, engineer, DPO trip_id, vehicle_id, event_id commercial Financial values 7 years (tax law, not PDPL) analyst, DS, engineer, DPO fare_sar, amount_sar personal-coarse Indirectly identifying at low resolution 730 days DS, engineer, DPO dropoff_geohash personal-pseudonymised Hashed at source — still personal data 730 days engineer, DPO national_id_hash, phone_hash personal Directly identifies a data subject 730 days engineer, DPO rider_id, driver_id, full_name_en sensitive-location Precise coordinates 180 days DPO only lat, lon

docs.title: Two rules that are routinely got wrong
docs.text:
A hash is not anonymisation. national_id_hash is pseudonymised personal data. It still belongs to a person, it is still in scope for an erasure request, and it still must not reach a dashboard. Treating a hash as anonymous is the most common PDPL mistake in a data platform, and it is usually made in good faith by someone who thinks "we hashed it" is the end of the sentence.

Precise location is its own class. Metre-resolution lat/lon reveals homes, workplaces and routines. A zone centroid does not — the RESOLUTION is the control, which is why centroid_lat is public and lat is not.

Unclassified means restricted. classify() returns personal for any column it does not know. An unclassified column is an unreviewed column, and the safe default for unreviewed data is the strict one. Adding a feature should require a one-line classification decision; that friction is intentional.

docs.title: 2. Lawful basis and purpose
docs.text:
Processing purpose Data used Lawful basis Retention justification Trip fulfilment and billing trips, payments, driver, vehicle TBD (contract) TBD ETA prediction trip history, GPS, weather TBD (legitimate interest / consent) TBD Operations monitoring GPS, positions TBD TBD Financial reporting payments, fares TBD (legal obligation) 7 years, tax law Product analytics aggregated gold marts TBD TBD

State the basis for each purpose separately. "We use the data to run the business" is not a lawful basis; it is a description of a business.

docs.title: 3. Retention and minimisation
docs.text: Dataset Window Mechanism Justification bronze.gps_events 180 days enforce_gps_retention() → DELETE + VACUUM Precise location, purpose-bound. Masar does not need metre-resolution traces from eight months ago to run a network. silver.vehicle_positions 180 days as above as above bronze.trips TBD TBD Reprocessing substrate; balance against personal-data minimisation. silver.trips TBD TBD TBD Delta time travel 168 hours (7 days) VACUUM ... RETAIN 168 HOURS See below.

docs.title: Why RETAIN 168 HOURS, and never RETAIN 0
docs.text:
The retention window is a genuine trade-off with two real sides:

  • Shorter — less storage, less audit history, and an erasure request is satisfied sooner (VACUUM is what makes a delete physical).
  • Longer — more storage, more ability to answer "what did the model see last Tuesday?", and personal data lingers in history longer.

Seven days is chosen because it spans a full weekly retraining cycle: any model can be reproduced against the exact data it was trained on.

RETAIN 0 HOURS is not the aggressive end of that trade-off. It ends the audit trail entirely and can break a reader mid-query against a version you just removed. Delta refuses it unless the retention check is disabled — treat having to disable a safety check as the answer to whether you should.

The tension worth naming: the time travel that makes the platform auditable is the same feature that makes erasure slow. You cannot have one without accepting the other; you can only decide the window and document why.

docs.title: 4. Right to erasure (PDPL Article 18)
docs.text: SLA: TBD (30 days is the usual statutory window) Runbook: python -m masar.governance.retention --erase-request <path> --execute

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Receive — the DPO logs the request with a ticket reference. An erasure with no ticket is an unexplained deletion, which is its own compliance problem.
  2. Scope — enumerate EVERY table holding a joinable identifier, not just the ones with a rider_id column.
  3. Dry run — --dry-run first. Confirm the row counts against the requester's expectation before anything is destroyed.
  4. Execute — MERGE DELETE across every table in scope.
  5. VACUUM — past the retention window. This is the step that makes the erasure real. Until it runs, the request has been recorded, not honoured.
  6. Audit — an immutable record in lakehouse/governance/erasure_audit: ticket reference, hashed subject id, timestamp, per-table row counts. The audit log must prove which request was executed without itself becoming a register of the people who asked to be forgotten — hence the hash.

docs.title: The trap this procedure exists to close
docs.text:
GPS pings are keyed by trip_id and vehicle_id. They have no rider_id.

A rider-keyed erasure across silver.trips therefore does not touch silver.vehicle_positions, and the data subject's metre-resolution location trace survives an erasure that reported success. The fix is to resolve the subject's trip_ids first and delete positions by trip_id (erase_rider_positions).

Any erasure procedure that does not enumerate every table holding a JOINABLE identifier is incomplete, and "we deleted the rider table" is the most common form of that mistake.

Table Holds rider_id? Reached how bronze.trips yes direct silver.trips yes direct silver.trips_quarantine yes direct gold.fact_trip pseudonym only recompute after silver delete silver.vehicle_positions no via trip_id join Redis online store no (zone grain) n/a — no per-subject key exists

docs.title: 5. The serving boundary
docs.text:
Rule: raw rider_id and precise GPS never cross into a BI product or the online store.

Enforced by python -m masar.serve.pdpl_boundary_check, which exits non-zero. It belongs in CI: governance that lives in a PDF is checked when someone remembers; governance that lives in a build step is checked every time.

docs.title: Three controls, applied in order, each doing a different job
docs.text:
1. Pseudonymise — sha2(rider_id, 256). Keeps cohort analysis possible without exposing the identifier.
  2. Minimise — DROP the raw column. Keeping it beside its own hash protects nothing; a column you did not publish cannot leak and does not have to be found again during an erasure.
  3. Reduce resolution — zone ids, not coordinates. The analyst question is about districts.

docs.title: Documented exceptions
docs.text:
Every allow-list entry in masar.serve.pdpl_boundary_check.BOUNDARY_TARGETS must be justified here. An exception with no justification recorded is a leak with a comment in front of it.

Dataset Column allowed Justification gold.fact_trip rider_pseudonym Cohort analysis without the identifier; still in scope for erasure. gold.fact_trip driver_key Driver-level BI is a stated business purpose; exposure is to a named analyst role, never to the online store. gold.dim_driver driver_id, full_name_en Driver-level reporting requires a label. national_id_hash and phone_hash are excluded. TBD TBD TBD

docs.title: What this costs — be honest
docs.text:
An analyst can no longer join a rider to a support ticket, or map a dropoff to a building. Both are real capabilities and both are gone.

State at least one thing your organisation genuinely cannot do as a result. Governance that costs nothing usually protects nothing — if you cannot name a cost, you have probably not applied a control.

docs.title: 6. Access control
docs.text:
Role Bronze Silver Gold Precise GPS Online store Analyst ✗ ✗ ✓ ✗ ✗ Data scientist read-only ✓ ✓ ✗ read-only Data engineer ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ ✓ DPO ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Service account (serving) ✗ ✗ read-only ✗ write

Access to sensitive-location requires a named role and a logged purpose. "The engineer needed to debug something" is not a purpose; it is an absence of one. Record how the log is produced and who reviews it: TBD.

docs.title: 7. Incident register
docs.text:
Date Incident Personal data affected Notified? Remediation Control added TBD TBD TBD TBD TBD TBD

Include near-misses. A control that fired and prevented an incident is the best evidence you have that the register is being maintained rather than back-filled before an audit.

docs.title: 8. Review checklist
docs.text:
• Every column in silver.* and gold.* has a classification
  • Every classification has a retention window and an access rule
  • Every retention window has a stated justification, not just a number
  • pdpl_boundary_check runs in CI and blocks the build on failure
  • Every allow-list exception is justified in §5
  • The erasure runbook has been rehearsed end to end, including VACUUM
  • The erasure scope includes silver.vehicle_positions via the trip join
  • VACUUM retention is documented and is never 0
  • The audit log records ticket refs and hashed subject ids, not raw ids
  • At least one capability genuinely lost to governance is named in §5

docs.title: Solutions — the completed # TODO(lab-N): blocks
docs.text: One file per lab. Each file contains the reference implementation of every # TODO(lab-N): block in src/masar/**, quality/** and dbt/masar/**, with the same function names the starter uses, so a block can be pasted straight back into place.

docs.title: How the starter marks work
docs.text:
Every block a participant implements looks like this:

# ── TODO(lab-3): keep the LATEST landed version per trip_id ───────────
#   What : ...
#   Why  : ...
#   Ref  : solutions/lab3_elt.py :: dedupe_latest_per_key
deduped = typed.dropDuplicates(["trip_id"])      # naive starter version
# ── end TODO(lab-3) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────

The starter code inside the block runs. It is deliberately the naive version — the one a competent engineer writes before they have met the failure mode. make pipeline therefore works on Day 1, and the lab's own acceptance test is what exposes the gap:

Lab Starter behaviour What the lab's check reveals 3 dropDuplicates keeps an arbitrary row corrections silently lose ~50% of the time 5 write without txnAppId a replayed batch duplicates 6 speed passed through unconverted producer 2.5.0 vehicles look becalmed 7 full-table overwrite correct, but O(all history) every night 7 rangeBetween(-3600, 0) same-second trips leak into the feature 8 four defective ETA windows R² 0.943 — the metric is reading the label

That is the pedagogy: participants do not fill in blanks, they find and fix a plausible bug. Handing them the answer first removes the only part that transfers.

docs.title: For instructors
docs.text:
# publish the solution for one lab
git checkout -b lab3-solution lab3-start
python solutions/apply.py --lab 3        # applies lab3_elt.py's blocks
git commit -am "solution(lab3): incremental idempotent silver"
git tag lab3-solution && git push origin lab3-solution

Tell participants at the start of each lab that solutions/ exists and that opening it before attempting the task costs them the lesson, not the marks. The leakage drill in Lab 8 in particular only works if they classify the four columns themselves and are then shown the arithmetic.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
A specialist module on analysing datasets too large for a single machine. Participants master distributed computing concepts, write performant Spark transformations and SQL, and tune jobs through partitioning and caching. The module scales every prior analytics skill to enterprise data volumes.

The course is built around a single evolving artefact: "Masar" (مسار), a national mobility and logistics analytics platform. Participants work against a Saudi-scale ride-hailing and delivery dataset — roughly 2.1 billion trip events per year (~180 GB of Delta-formatted data), plus driver, rider, weather, and city dimension tables. Every lab processes this same golden dataset: Day 1 reads and queries it, Day 2 makes those queries fast, Day 3 trains a distributed ML model on it and packages an end-to-end batch analytics workflow. By the final capstone each participant owns a tuned, query-plan-optimised, MLlib-powered analytics job on Lakehouse storage — the same shape of workload they will extend into streaming in SDA-DSC-313.

  1. LO1 — Explain distributed execution: partitions, shuffles, and lazy evaluation
  2. LO2 — Develop analytical workloads with Spark DataFrames and Spark SQL
  3. LO3 — Optimize job performance through partitioning, caching, and join strategies
  4. LO4 — Implement scalable feature-engineering and ML pipelines with Spark MLlib
  5. LO5 — Analyze query plans to diagnose and resolve performance bottlenecks
  6. LO6 — Design batch analytics workflows on Lakehouse storage

docs.title: Instructor Guidance Notes (Delivery Plan Level)
docs.text:
• Golden thread: every module runs against the same Masar mobility dataset. Never introduce a throwaway range(100) toy example except for a 60-second concept demo — always return to trips, drivers, riders, weather. This is what makes the Day-3 capstone achievable: the data, schema, and helper functions are already familiar by then.
  • Two data scales. The narrative uses the full dataset (2.1 B rows / 180 GB) for realism; the classroom runs a sampled 50 M-row / ~4.2 GB Delta subset that fits a 16 GB laptop or a small 3-node cluster. Always state which scale a number refers to. Publish both masar_sample (laptop) and masar_full (cluster, optional) so numbers are reproducible.
  • Environment strategy: primary = local PySpark 3.5 in a uv/conda env with Delta Lake 3.x (--packages io.delta:delta-spark_2.12:3.2.0); fallback = a managed Spark notebook (Databricks Community / Google Dataproc / a shared 3-node cluster). Verify both the week before delivery; the Spark UI must be reachable (port 4040) in whichever environment wins.
  • Pace control: Labs 3 and 4 are the most overrun-prone because plan-reading is new. Publish checkpoint notebooks (lab3_start, lab3_solution, lab4_start, ...) so stragglers can fast-forward. Keep every lab's dataset path in one config.py so a path change is one edit.
  • Pairing: rotate pairs each day; pair a strong-SQL participant with a strong-Python/ML participant. Reading a physical plan together out loud is the single highest-value activity of Day 2.
  • Language: deliver in English or Arabic; keep all code, column names, and table identifiers in English (production convention in Saudi enterprise data platforms — mixed-language column names break Spark SQL and downstream BI).
  • Prayer and break scheduling: each "hour" is 50 minutes of instruction + 10 minutes buffer; schedule the long break around Dhuhr. Kick off any full-dataset cluster job before a break so the run completes while people are away — big-data waits are a teaching reality, use them deliberately.
  • Assessment logistics: collect notebook/repo URLs and the BENCHMARKS.md table at the end of Day 3 Hour 4; verify each capstone job actually runs against the sample lake before demos begin in Hour 5.

docs.title: Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. Before writing a single fast Spark query, participants must hold an accurate mental model of what happens when they call .count() on two billion rows. This module builds that model: how Spark splits data into partitions, distributes work across executors as tasks, defers computation until an action forces it, and assembles the whole job as a DAG of stages separated by shuffles. Every optimisation later in the course is an application of this one mental model.

Business relevance. Saudi organisations — a national mobility platform, a telecom operator's CDR lake, a bank's transaction history, a ministry's service-usage records — routinely hold datasets that no single server can process. The difference between an analyst who "runs pandas until it OOMs" and one who reasons in partitions and stages is the difference between a query that never finishes and one that returns in seconds against the same data. Distributed literacy is the price of admission to enterprise-scale analytics under Vision 2030 data programmes.

Industry use cases. - A mobility platform computes daily completed-trip revenue per city across 2.1 billion yearly trips — impossible in memory on one machine, trivial as a partitioned Spark aggregation. - A telecom fraud team scans a year of call-detail records to flag SIM-box patterns; the scan only finishes because it is parallelised across dozens of executors reading independent partitions. - A government analytics unit joins service-usage logs to a citizen dimension table nightly; understanding the shuffle that join triggers is what keeps the nightly window under two hours.

Expected competencies. After this module a participant can describe the driver/executor architecture, explain why read then filter then count runs nothing until count, count and reason about partitions, read a job's stages in the Spark UI, and identify where a shuffle boundary falls.
