docs.title: Module 2 — How Machine Learning Works: Data, Models, Predictions
Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. Professionals do not need to build models, but they must understand the machine they are commissioning: what training actually does, what a model actually is, what a prediction actually means, and — above all — how to read a model's outputs without being misled by them. This module opens the black box exactly wide enough for sound judgment: the data → training → model → prediction loop, the difference between learning types, and the plain-language mathematics of "how good is good?"

Business relevance. The most expensive misreadings of AI in organisations are output misreadings: a 95%-accurate model deployed on a 2%-frequency event (useless), a precision-heavy model used where recall mattered (fraud slips through), a confident score treated as a fact (loan wrongly denied, patient wrongly deprioritised). Every one of these failures happens after the technical work is done, in the decision layer — which is staffed by this course's audience. Reading model outputs correctly is a decision-quality skill, not an engineering skill, and regulators of Saudi banking and health increasingly expect decision-makers to evidence it.

Industry use cases. - A telecom retention manager receives a weekly churn-risk list and must decide how far down the ranking to spend the retention budget — a precision/recall trade-off she makes whether she knows the words or not. - A hospital operations head pilots a no-show predictor and must set the threshold that balances wasted reminder calls against empty clinic slots. - A procurement committee must interrogate a vendor's "99.2% accurate" defect-detection claim for a Jubail plant where defects occur in 1 of 400 units.

Expected competencies. After this module a participant can narrate the ML loop end-to-end in plain language; distinguish supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning by the kind of data each consumes; read a confusion matrix and explain precision vs recall with a business example; explain why accuracy misleads on rare events; and recognise overfitting and drift as stories, not equations.

docs.title: Learning Objectives (mapped)
docs.text: # Objective Maps to 2.1 Narrate the data → training → model → prediction loop for a concrete business case LO1, LO2 2.2 Distinguish supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning by their data requirements LO2 2.3 Read a confusion matrix; explain precision, recall, and the accuracy trap in plain language LO6 2.4 Set and justify a decision threshold for a business trade-off LO6, LO4 2.5 Recognise overfitting, data leakage, and drift as failure stories LO5 2.6 Train and interrogate a model in a no-code tool, documenting its outputs LO6, LO1

docs.title: 1. The loop: data → training → model → prediction
docs.text:
Machine learning is one loop, and every ML system a participant will ever meet is an instance of it:

  1. Data. Historical examples, each with the inputs that were known at the time (features) and — for supervised learning — the outcome that eventually happened (label). For the hospital no-show case: appointment records (specialty, lead time, patient age band, prior no-shows, weekday) each labelled showed / did not show.
  2. Training. An algorithm searches for the pattern that best connects features to labels across thousands of examples. Nothing mystical happens: it is systematic trial-and-error at machine speed, scored against the known answers.
  3. Model. The found pattern, frozen and packaged. It is a thing — a file — that can be copied, versioned, tested, and (importantly for governance) audited and retired.
  4. Prediction. The model applied to one new case produces an output — typically a score (0.87) — plus nothing else. It does not know whether it is right. Someone, or some rule, must convert that score into an action.

Two plain-language consequences carry the whole course. First, a model can only learn patterns present in its data — no examples of Ramadan demand means no Ramadan pattern; historical hiring biases in, historical hiring biases out. Second, the model's world stops at training day: reality keeps moving (new fraud tactics, new customer behaviour, a pandemic), so a model is milk, not honey — it expires. That expiry is drift, and mature organisations monitor for it (a forward pointer participants will meet again in later modules and their engineering colleagues live with daily).

docs.title: 2. Three ways machines learn
docs.text:
Learning type Data it needs Question it answers Business examples Supervised Historical examples with known outcomes (labels) "Given what we knew, what will happen?" Churn, fraud, no-shows, demand forecasts, CV screening Unsupervised Examples without labels "What natural groups or oddities exist here?" Customer segmentation, anomaly detection in transactions, grouping similar complaints Reinforcement An environment with feedback (reward/penalty) "What sequence of actions works best?" Dynamic pricing, energy-grid balancing, game-playing systems

Supervised learning dominates enterprise AI (roughly the first two of every three use cases participants will evaluate), and its appetite for labels is the hidden cost centre: someone must have recorded the outcome, consistently, for a long time. "Do we have labels?" is question one of the Module 5 feasibility check — and the most common honest answer, "sort of, in three systems, inconsistently," is where AI budgets actually go.

docs.title: 3. How good is good? Reading model quality like a professional
docs.text:
The single most valuable table of the course. A hospital no-show model evaluated on 1,000 appointments it never saw during training:

Predicted: no-show Predicted: will show Actually no-show (180) 135 caught (true positives) 45 missed (false negatives) Actually showed (820) 90 falsely flagged (false positives) 730 correctly cleared (true negatives)

From this one grid, every headline number a vendor will ever quote:

  • Accuracy = (135 + 730) / 1000 = 86.5% — "how often right overall."
  • Precision = 135 / (135 + 90) = 60% — "when it flags a no-show, how often is it right?" Low precision = wasted reminder calls and annoyed patients.
  • Recall = 135 / 180 = 75% — "of the real no-shows, how many did it catch?" Low recall = empty clinic slots continue.

The accuracy trap, taught as a story: a model that predicts "will show" for everyone achieves 82% accuracy on this data (820/1000) while catching zero no-shows. On rare events — fraud at 0.5%, serious defects at 0.25% — "do nothing" models score in the high 90s. Whenever the event is rare, accuracy is marketing; precision and recall are management. Participants practise the reflex question: "What is the base rate, and what are precision and recall at the threshold you propose?"

Thresholds are business decisions. The model outputs a score; someone chooses the cut-off that turns scores into actions. Lowering the threshold catches more no-shows (recall ↑) at the cost of more false alarms (precision ↓). That trade-off belongs to whoever owns the costs — reminder-call budget vs empty-slot cost — which is precisely why this audience, not the data team alone, must understand it. This is the module's bridge to LO4: an "AI decision" is usually a human policy wrapped around a model score.

docs.title: 4. Why models fail: three stories every professional should recognise
docs.text:
• Overfitting — the student who memorised the textbook. The model learns the training examples too specifically (including their noise) and fails on new cases. Symptom: dazzling performance in the pilot report, disappointment in production. Literate question: "what was performance on data the model never saw?" (the holdout — if the vendor cannot answer, the meeting is over).
  • Data leakage — the exam with the answers printed on it. A feature accidentally contains the outcome (e.g., "reminder call made" as a feature for predicting no-shows, when calls were only made to likely no-shows). Symptom: performance too good to be true. Literate question: "was every feature genuinely knowable before the outcome?"
  • Drift — the world moved on. Customer behaviour, fraud tactics, or referral patterns change; the model's frozen picture decays quietly. Symptom: performance that erodes month by month with no code change. Literate question: "how is performance monitored after launch, and who is alerted when it slips?"

Each story maps to a governance behaviour, not an engineering one: demand holdout evidence, interrogate feature timing, require post-launch monitoring in every AI proposal (all three become scored items on the Module 5 risk side).

docs.title: 5. What no-code tools reveal — and what they hide
docs.text: Lab 2 uses a browser-based no-code tool (Teachable-Machine-class for perception, or a no-code AutoML table trainer) deliberately: watching a model train on your own examples in four minutes demystifies the loop better than any slide. But the debrief must also name what the toy hides: real projects spend most of their effort before training (collecting, cleaning, labelling — Module 3's value chain) and after it (integration, monitoring, retraining). The no-code demo is the visible 20% of an iceberg, and executives who have only seen demos systematically underestimate the other 80%. The module closes by connecting the toy to the profession: the same loop, the same confusion matrix, the same threshold decision — at organisational scale and consequence.

docs.title: 6. Common mistakes and decision-layer considerations
docs.text:
1. Treating the score as a verdict. 0.87 is an input to a policy, not a decision. The policy (threshold + exception path + human review) is where accountability lives.
  2. Quoting accuracy on rare events. The signature of an unexamined claim; retrain the reflex to ask for the base rate.
  3. Judging the model without a baseline. 75% recall means little until compared with the current process ("coordinators guess no-shows at ~40% recall today"). Always ask: better than what we do now, by how much, at what cost?
  4. Confusing the pilot's data with production's data. A model piloted on Riyadh clinics may not transfer to Jazan clinics; population match is a literate question, not a technical nicety.
  5. One-time evaluation. Model quality is a time series, not a certificate. Approval processes that end at launch institutionalise drift.
  6. Skipping the "so what" arithmetic. 90 false positives per 1,000 appointments = 90 unnecessary calls/day at scale; whether that is trivial or ruinous is a business calculation only this audience can do.

docs.title: Worked Example 1 — Training a model on paper (the 10-row exercise)
docs.text:
Before touching software, participants "become the algorithm" with ten historical loan applications:

# Monthly income (SAR) Existing loans Employment years Defaulted? 1 6,000 3 1 Yes 2 22,000 0 8 No 3 9,000 2 2 Yes 4 15,000 1 5 No 5 7,500 3 3 Yes 6 30,000 1 12 No 7 8,000 0 1 No 8 11,000 2 2 Yes 9 18,000 0 6 No 10 6,500 2 1 Yes

Task: find the rule that best separates Yes from No. Most groups converge on something like "income below ~12,000 AND existing loans ≥ 2 → default risk." Debrief points, in order: (1) you just did what training does — searched for the pattern that fits the labels; (2) your rule is a model; (3) apply it to a new applicant (income 10,000, loans 1, years 4 — the rule is uncertain: welcome to confidence scores); (4) note what your rule absorbed — if this bank historically lent less to certain groups, the data would encode it, and so would you (Module 5's bias, discovered by the participants themselves); (5) ten rows made a fragile rule — imagine what 100,000 rows makes (and why data volume/quality is Module 3).

docs.title: Worked Example 2 — Confusion-matrix reading protocol (the four questions)
docs.text:
A laminated card participants keep. For any classification model claim:

  1. What is the base rate? How common is the event actually? (180/1,000 = 18% here; fraud might be 0.5%.)
  2. Show me the grid. Insist on all four cells, not one headline number.
  3. Price the two mistakes. False positive costs what? False negative costs what? In SAR, minutes, or trust.
  4. Who chose the threshold, and on what trade-off? If nobody chose it, the tool's default is silently making policy.

Applied live to the vendor claim from Module 1 ("99.2% accurate defect detection" at 1-in-400 defect rate): a do-nothing model scores 99.75% — the vendor's number is worse than doing nothing until precision/recall are on the table. The room audibly enjoys this arithmetic; let them do it themselves.

docs.title: Worked Example 3 — Dossier §2: Model Sketch (template)
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  AI USE-CASE DOSSIER — §2 MODEL SKETCH                                │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. Learning type: supervised / unsupervised / reinforcement — why?   │
│ 2. Label: what outcome would training need, and is it recorded       │
│    today? (where, by whom, how consistently?)                        │
│ 3. Five candidate features knowable BEFORE the outcome:              │
│ 4. The two mistakes and their business cost:                         │
│    False positive = ______ costing ______                            │
│    False negative = ______ costing ______                            │
│ 5. Which matters more here: precision or recall — and who should own │
│    the threshold?                                                    │
│ 6. Today's baseline: how well does the current process perform?      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Box 3 enforces the leakage lesson ("knowable BEFORE"); box 6 enforces the baseline lesson. A dossier with an empty box 6 is returned: "better than nothing" is not a business case.

docs.title: Worked Example 4 — Reading a model output panel (annotated)
docs.text:
The exhibit every participant will actually face at work: a single prediction card from a deployed system, as a decision-support screen would show it. Annotated for the reading order a literate professional applies:

┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  APPOINTMENT NO-SHOW RISK                    Patient #A-4471  │
│                                                               │
│  RISK SCORE: 0.78  ██████████████░░░░   [HIGH]                │
│                                                               │
│  Top contributing factors:                                    │
│   • 2 prior no-shows in last 6 months          (+ strong)     │
│   • Appointment lead time: 34 days             (+ moderate)   │
│   • Specialty: dermatology                     (+ mild)       │
│  Model: noshow-v2 · trained 2025-11 · threshold 0.65          │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
READING ORDER (taught as a five-step habit):
1. The score is 0.78 — a rank on a scale, NOT "78% certain."
2. The band [HIGH] is a threshold someone set at 0.65 — who, and
   on what cost trade-off? (If the panel doesn't say, ask.)
3. The factors are the model's stated reasons — plausible, useful
   for the conversation with the patient, but correlates, not causes.
4. The model version and training date: 8 months old — has the
   clinic's booking behaviour changed since? (drift question)
5. The action is NOT on the panel: what the coordinator does with
   HIGH is policy — call? double-book? — and policy has an owner.

The debrief point that lands hardest: the panel contains everything except the decision — by design. Systems that print the decision ("DENY SLOT") have quietly moved a human policy into software, and the literate professional notices.

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 2 — Train and Interrogate a No-Code Model
docs.text:
Objective Train a working model in a browser-based no-code tool, deliberately degrade it, read its outputs and confusion matrix, and complete Dossier §2 Duration 50 minutes Setup Browser-based no-code trainer (image classes prepared: e.g., "hard hat / no hard hat" site-safety images, 40 per class, plus a curated unfair variant); tabular fallback (no-show CSV in a no-code AutoML tool); Dossier workbook

Instructions & tasks

  1. (10 min) Train v1. In pairs, train the two-class safety classifier on the provided balanced image set. Test with the 10 held-out images; record how many are correct and each prediction's confidence score.
  2. (10 min) Break it, honestly. Retrain as v2 using the skewed set (all "hard hat" images taken indoors, all "no hard hat" outdoors). Test on the same 10 held-outs. Watch it fail on outdoor hard-hat images — then articulate what it actually learned (lighting, not hats). This is bias-from-data, experienced first-hand.
  3. (10 min) Read the grid. Using the provided 1,000-appointment no-show results sheet (the module's worked matrix), each pair computes accuracy, precision, and recall, then answers: "the do-nothing model scores 82% — is our 86.5% model worth deploying?" Justify with the two mistake costs from the sheet.
  4. (5 min) Move the threshold. Using the threshold slider sheet (three pre-computed operating points: 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.7), pick the threshold you would set as clinic manager and write the one-sentence justification.
  5. (10 min) Dossier §2. Complete the Model Sketch canvas for your own use case. Partner challenge: for each of your five features — "was that truly knowable before the outcome?"
  6. (5 min) Evidence capture. Screenshot v1 and v2 test results with confidences — the second tool-exploration exhibit for the capstone dossier.

Expected output 

v1 model: ≥ 8/10 held-out images correct, confidences recorded
v2 model: visible failure on outdoor hard-hat images + one-sentence diagnosis ("it learned the background")
Grid worksheet: accuracy 86.5%, precision 60%, recall 75% — all three computed by hand
Threshold choice: one operating point selected with cost-based justification
Dossier §2: 6/6 boxes complete, features leakage-checked by partner

Troubleshooting guidance

Symptom Cause Fix Uploads slow / tool blocked on venue network Bandwidth or filtering Pre-loaded instructor accounts; fallback to tabular AutoML path; worst case, instructor-projected training with the room calling the shots v2 fails to fail (still classifies well) Skewed set not skewed enough Use the provided v2-strong-skew image folder; the effect must be unmistakable Pair computes precision with the wrong denominator Row/column confusion Teach the phrase "precision reads DOWN the predicted column"; recheck with the card Participant anxious ("I'm not a maths person") Three-fraction arithmetic framed as maths Reframe: it is counting, division, and pricing mistakes — manager arithmetic, not calculus Confidence scores treated as percentages-of-truth Natural misreading Return to the loop: confidence is the model's self-estimate on training-like data; show v2's high-confidence wrong answers as proof

Instructor notes. Task 2 is the emotional centre of Day 1: participants watch a model learn the wrong thing from honestly collected but badly composed data. Do not shortcut it. Collect two v2 screenshots for the Module 5 bias discussion — referring back to "your own model on Tuesday" is worth ten slides. Fast finishers: retrain v3 with a corrected image set and verify recovery, or run the tabular no-show trainer and compare its reported metrics to their hand-computed ones.

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz (5 questions) 1. Put in order: prediction, data, model, training. → data → training → model → prediction. 2. A fraud model shows 99.4% accuracy; fraud occurs in 0.5% of transactions. What is your first question? → What are precision and recall? (A do-nothing model scores 99.5%.) 3. "Of the real no-shows, how many did we catch?" — precision or recall? → Recall. 4. A feature "final invoice paid late" is proposed to predict "customer will pay late." What is wrong? → Leakage — the feature contains the outcome. 5. Who should set the decision threshold for the reminder-call model? → Whoever owns the costs of both mistakes (the clinic/business owner, informed by the data team).

The base-rate reflex drill. Instructor calls out five claims ("97% accurate churn model", "99.9% accurate airport-security screening"…); participants must respond with the base-rate question and estimate the do-nothing score.

Threshold role-play. Three participants argue the 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.7 operating points as (a) patient-experience lead, (b) finance controller, (c) clinic coordinator; the room votes; instructor reveals there is no "right" answer — only an owned one.

Storytelling exercise. Each participant retells one failure story (overfitting, leakage, drift) in their own industry's terms in under 60 seconds — the test of plain-language mastery.

Discussion questions. - Your current process for the use case in your dossier has never been measured. What does that do to any AI business case, and how would you get a baseline cheaply? - If confidence scores are not probabilities of truth, why do systems show them at all? What should a decision-maker do with them?

docs.title: Case Study — The Churn Model That Wasted the Retention Budget at Tawasul Telecom
docs.text:
Scenario. Tawasul Telecom (regional operator, 6M subscribers) deploys a churn-prediction model. The data-science team reports "89% accuracy"; marketing receives a weekly list of the 20,000 highest-risk subscribers and spends the full retention budget (discount offers averaging SAR 90 each) on them.

Business context. After two quarters, churn is unchanged and the CFO wants the programme cancelled. A post-review finds two compounding misreadings — neither of them a modelling error.

Technical challenge. First, the list was ranked by raw score but the threshold was never costed: at the operating point marketing used, precision was 31% — 7 of 10 discounts went to subscribers who were never leaving (SAR ~1.2M/month in giveaways to loyal customers, some of whom learned to expect discounts). Second, recall at that threshold was 22% — the model caught barely a fifth of true churners, but the "89% accuracy" headline (on a 6% churn base rate) had convinced leadership the problem was solved, so no complementary programme ran.

Constraints. The model itself was adequate; retraining is not the fix. Marketing owns the budget but not the model; data science owns the model but not the offer economics; nobody owned the threshold. The CFO's cancellation review is in three weeks.

Solution approach (facilitate, don't lecture). Participants, in the marketing director's chair, apply the four-question protocol: base rate (6%), full grid (demanded, finally produced), both mistakes priced (wasted discount SAR 90 vs lost subscriber lifetime value SAR 2,400), threshold re-derived from those costs (a much smaller, higher-precision list plus a cheaper bulk touch — an SMS — for the mid-band). The saved programme is presented to the CFO not as "the model works" but as "the decision policy now matches the economics"; a monthly grid review with named threshold ownership is instituted.

Discussion questions. 1. Whose failure was this — data science's, marketing's, or a missing role between them? What is that role called in your organisation? (Bridge to Module 6.) 2. Reconstruct the CFO memo in four sentences using only plain-language terms from this module. 3. The mid-band SMS idea changes the action, not the model. What does that suggest about where AI value actually gets decided? 4. What would you monitor monthly to detect drift in this system, and who should see it?

docs.title: Benchmarks and Evaluation
docs.text: Metric Category Target after M2 How measured Loop narration (data→training→model→prediction) Concept mastery Complete, plain-language, ≤ 90 seconds Cold-call warm-up Day 2 Hour 1 Hand-computed grid metrics Applied numeracy 3/3 correct (accuracy, precision, recall) Lab 2 task 3 worksheet v2 failure diagnosis Bias literacy Correct one-sentence diagnosis ("learned the background") Lab 2 task 2 debrief Threshold justification Decision quality Cost-based, one sentence, owned Lab 2 task 4 sheet Dossier §2 completeness Golden thread 6/6 boxes; features leakage-checked Partner initial + spot-check Quiz 1 items on M2 (3 of 10) Retention ≥ 2/3 cohort median Quiz 1, Day 2 Hour 1

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
1. The ML loop — Purpose: module anchor. Elements: circular flow data → training → model → prediction → (decision → new data), with the "world changes → drift" arrow entering from outside and a padlock icon on "model = frozen file". Style: course palette, bilingual labels. Designer description: "A five-node loop with a clock icon outside pushing a wedge labelled Drift between World and Model."
  2. Confusion-matrix explainer — Elements: the 2×2 grid with the four cells named in business words ("caught", "missed", "false alarm", "correctly cleared"); precision arrow reading down the predicted column, recall arrow reading across the actual row. Style: the exact layout participants use in Lab 2; printable A4.
  3. Threshold slider strip — Elements: one horizontal score axis 0–1 with three flags (0.3/0.5/0.7), each flag showing its grid, its call volume, and its cost line. Style: triptych comparison.
  4. Iceberg of an ML project — Elements: the no-code demo above the waterline; data collection, cleaning, labelling, integration, monitoring, retraining below; % effort annotations. Style: single striking image for the Hour 4 debrief.

docs.title: Images (screenshots)
docs.text:
1. No-code tool mid-training — why: Lab 2 reference; content: two classes with example counts, training progress, and the test pane with a confidence score visible.
  2. v2's confident wrong answer — why: the module's money shot; content: an outdoor hard-hat image classified "no hard hat" at 0.94 confidence.
  3. The filled grid worksheet — why: answer key; content: the 1,000-appointment matrix with the three computations worked in the margin.
  4. Tabular AutoML results page — why: fallback path reference and metric-vocabulary transfer; content: the tool's own precision/recall readout circled, matching the hand computation.

docs.title: Simulations
docs.text:
1. The biased trainer (Lab 2 task 2) — Setup: curated skewed image folders shipped with the course. Expected behaviour: v2 fails systematically on out-of-pattern images with high confidence. Learning objective: models learn what is in the data, which is not always what you meant — bias experienced, not described.
  2. The drifting dashboard — Setup: a three-month model-performance chart handout where recall decays 75% → 61% while accuracy barely moves. Expected behaviour: participants must spot which line matters and draft the two-line alert email. Learning objective: quality is a time series; accuracy can mask decay.

docs.title: Interactive Activities
docs.text:
• Be-the-algorithm (15 min): the 10-row paper training exercise (Worked Example 1), run in groups of three, rules posted and compared.
  • Human confusion matrix (10 min): the room physically sorts 20 prediction cards into the four corners of a floor grid; miscounts are debugged collectively.

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text: Dataset Source Format Size Purpose Safety-image set (balanced + skewed + held-out) Course-authored, synthetic/consented imagery Image folders 2×40 train, 10 test, skewed variant Lab 2 training and bias simulation No-show appointments table Synthetic, KSA-plausible fields (specialty, lead time, weekday) CSV 3,000 rows Tabular fallback + grid worksheet source Grid worksheet (1,000-appointment results) Course-authored Printed sheet 1 page Hand computation of metrics Threshold slider sheets Course-authored (3 operating points, costed) Printed sheet 1 page Task 4 threshold decision

docs.title: Demo Requirements
docs.text:
• Instructor demo: train the balanced classifier live in under five minutes, narrating each loop stage as it happens on screen; then re-run one held-out image and ask the room to act on the confidence score before revealing the answer.
  • Student demo: two pairs present their v2 diagnosis sentence; the room votes on the sharpest phrasing.
  • Expected outputs: every participant has hand-computed the three metrics once and captured v1/v2 screenshots before Day 1 Hour 5.

docs.title: Module 3 — The Data Value Chain and Data-Driven Decision-Making
Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. Models are the visible tip of a long chain: data is collected somewhere, by someone, for some original purpose; it is stored, moved, cleaned, combined, summarised — and only then does it reach a dashboard or a model, and only after that does a human decide anything. Every link can silently corrupt the decision at the end. This module teaches participants to see, map, and interrogate that chain in their own organisation, and to practise the last mile — reading dashboards and turning evidence into decisions — as a discipline rather than a glance.

Business relevance. "Data-driven" fails in two characteristic ways in organisations: garbage travels up the chain and gets laundered into confident-looking charts, or good data arrives and decision-makers misread, cherry-pick, or ignore it. Both failure modes are governance-and-literacy problems in exactly this audience's hands. In the Saudi context the stakes are codified: the Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) regulates what may be collected and why, and NDMO data-management standards make data quality and stewardship formal organisational obligations — the chain this module maps is the chain regulators now audit.

Industry use cases. - A hospital's bed-occupancy dashboard shows 84% while ward staff swear they are full — a discharge-entry lag three links upstream is making an executive number fictional. - A retailer's "top-selling product" ranking silently excludes cash sales from two legacy stores, steering purchasing decisions with a biased denominator. - A ministry KPI review discovers two departments define "case resolved" differently, so the flagship metric compares apples to dates.

Expected competencies. After this module a participant can map the six links of the data value chain for a real process; identify the weakest link and its decision impact; apply the five-question dashboard interrogation protocol; distinguish correlation from causation in a business argument; write a one-paragraph decision memo that cites evidence honestly (including its limits); and name where PDPL/NDMO obligations attach to their chain.

docs.title: Learning Objectives (mapped)
docs.text: # Objective Maps to 3.1 Map the six-link data value chain (collection → storage → processing → analysis → decision → action) for a real organisational process LO3 3.2 Diagnose data-quality failure at each link and trace its impact to the decision LO3, LO5 3.3 Interrogate a BI dashboard using the five-question protocol LO6 3.4 Distinguish correlation from causation in dashboard-based arguments LO6, LO5 3.5 Write a decision memo that states evidence, uncertainty, and the decision taken LO3, LO6 3.6 Locate PDPL/NDMO obligations on the mapped chain LO3

docs.title: 1. The six links, walked slowly
docs.text:
The chain is taught on one running example (hospital bed management) and immediately re-applied to each participant's dossier case:

  1. Collection. Data is born: a nurse discharges a patient in the ward system, a POS terminal logs a sale, a sensor reads a temperature. The literacy question at this link: who records it, when, with what incentive to be accurate? (A discharge entered "when the shift calms down" is data born late; a sales rep's forecast entered to hit a quota is data born biased.)
  2. Storage. Data lands in systems — often several, often disagreeing. The question: which system is the source of truth, and does everyone agree? Duplicate customer records and mismatched IDs live here.
  3. Processing. Data is cleaned, joined, transformed, aggregated. Invisible decisions accumulate: excluded rows, filled-in blanks, currency conversions, timezone handling. The question: what was removed, filled, or assumed on the way — and is it documented?
  4. Analysis. Dashboards, reports, models (Module 2 lives at this link). The question: does the metric definition match what the decision needs? ("Resolved cases" counted at first reply vs at confirmed fix are different businesses.)
  5. Decision. A human (or a policy) chooses. The question: did the decision actually use the evidence, or decorate a decision already made?
  6. Action & feedback. The decision changes the world — and, crucially, changes future data. Reminder calls change no-show rates; the next model trains on the changed world. Mature organisations close the loop deliberately; immature ones are confused by it.

The central teaching image: decisions inherit the weakest link. An impeccable dashboard on top of a lagging collection process is a beautiful picture of a fiction. Participants learn to state chain quality the way engineers state system quality — by its weakest component, not its prettiest.

docs.title: 2. Data quality in six words: complete, correct, current, consistent, relevant, permitted
docs.text:
Six tests, one per finger and thumb-plus:

Test Question Bed-management failure example Complete Are all the cases there? Two wards paper-based; their beds invisible Correct Are values true? Transfers double-counted as discharges Current Fresh enough for this decision? Discharges entered 4 hours late — fatal for hourly bed decisions, harmless for monthly stats Consistent Same definitions everywhere? "Occupied" includes reserved beds in one ward system, excludes them in another Relevant Does it measure what the decision needs? Occupancy % doesn't show bottleneck specialty Permitted May we collect/use it for this purpose? Patient-level dashboards viewed by non-clinical staff — a PDPL question, not a technical one

The sixth test carries the compliance content lightly but firmly: under PDPL, personal data has a lawful purpose at collection, and re-purposing it (say, marketing on clinical data) is a legal event, not a lunchtime decision; NDMO standards oblige entities to know their data (cataloguing), own it (stewardship), and quality-manage it. Participants do not need the statute text — they need the reflex: "Are we permitted, and who is the data steward I should ask?" (SDA-FND-105 takes governance further; this module plants the question.)

docs.title: 3. Reading dashboards like an examiner: the five-question protocol
docs.text:
Dashboards are rhetorical objects: someone chose these metrics, these colours, these scales. The protocol turns passive viewing into examination:

  1. What question is this dashboard answering — and is that my question? (A revenue dashboard cannot answer a margin question, however beautiful.)
  2. Where does each number come from? (Which links of the chain, how fresh, which exclusions? If nobody can say, the number is decoration.)
  3. What is the comparison? A number without a baseline, target, or trend is a fact without meaning. 84% occupancy — versus what plan, what season, what peer?
  4. What would change my mind? Decide before looking harder what evidence would reverse your current instinct — the discipline that defeats cherry-picking.
  5. What is not shown? Absent metrics, truncated axes, cherry-picked date ranges, averages hiding distributions (the average wait of 20 minutes that hides a 3-hour tail).

Add the two classic distortions every professional must spot on sight: truncated y-axes that turn a 2% wiggle into a cliff, and correlation dressed as causation ("stores with more staff have higher sales — hire more staff!" — or do busy stores get more staff?). The causation test in plain language: could a third factor drive both? did the cause precede the effect? what happens when we intervene? — and the honest answer that only a controlled change (pilot, A/B test) settles it.

docs.title: 4. The last mile: from evidence to decision memo
docs.text:
Data-driven decision-making fails most often at the handover from analysis to authority. The module installs a lightweight artefact — the decision memo — as the professional's standard closing move:

  • One paragraph, four sentences: (1) the decision taken; (2) the key evidence, with source and freshness; (3) the main uncertainty or data limit, stated plainly; (4) the review point ("revisit when X or by date Y").
  • Writing the limit sentence is the cultural innovation: it makes honest uncertainty normal paperwork instead of weakness, and it creates the audit trail regulators and post-mortems wish existed.
  • The memo also disciplines the meeting before it: if the dashboard cannot fill sentence 2, the decision is being made on instinct — which is sometimes fine, but should be said.

docs.title: 5. Common breakdowns and organisational considerations
docs.text:
1. The laundering effect. Bad data acquires false authority as it moves up the chain — by the time it is a boardroom chart, nobody present can see link 1. Antidote: chain maps attached to key dashboards ("this number is born where?").
  2. Metric drift. Definitions change (a system migration redefines "active customer") and trend lines silently break. Antidote: definition change-log owned by a named steward.
  3. Dashboard sprawl. 40 dashboards, no decisions. Every dashboard should name its decision and its owner or be retired.
  4. The HiPPO override. Highest-paid person's opinion beats the data with no record that it did. The decision memo makes overrides visible and legitimate — leaders may override evidence, but on the record.
  5. Feedback blindness. Actions change the data (link 6); teams read the change as organic. Classic: reminder calls cut no-shows, and the next quarter's "no-show model performance drop" is actually the programme working.
  6. Permission debt. Data collected for purpose A quietly powering purpose B until an audit or a complaint surfaces it — the PDPL failure mode that turns a data project into a legal event.

docs.title: Worked Example 1 — Value-chain map, filled (hospital bed management)
docs.text:
LINK            WHAT HAPPENS                       WEAKNESS FOUND               DECISION IMPACT
1 Collection    Nurses log admits/discharges       Discharges entered up to     Dashboard overstates occupancy
                in ward system                     4h late on busy shifts       by 6–9 beds at peak
2 Storage       Ward system + ED system +          Reserved beds counted        Two systems disagree by ward;
                surgery scheduler                  differently                  staff distrust the number
3 Processing    Nightly + hourly feeds merged      Hourly feed silently         "Live" view is partially
                to the BI layer                    drops ED boarding patients   yesterday's truth
4 Analysis      Occupancy dashboard, exec view     % only; no specialty         Bottleneck (medicine ward)
                                                   breakdown                    invisible in the average
5 Decision      07:30 bed huddle                   Huddle uses printed 06:00    Decisions made on stale
                                                   snapshot                     data during the fastest hour
6 Action        Transfers, early-discharge         No feedback tag on           Cannot tell which actions
                rounds, elective rescheduling      actions taken                actually relieved pressure
WEAKEST LINK: 1 (late discharge entry) — every downstream improvement inherits it.
CHEAPEST FIX: discharge entry at bedside (workflow change), not a new dashboard.

The punchline participants must reach themselves: the organisation was about to buy a "better dashboard" (link 4) when the failure was at link 1 and the fix was a workflow, not software.

docs.title: Worked Example 2 — Dashboard interrogation, worked live
docs.text: A sample retail dashboard (provided in the media pack) is examined with the protocol on the projector: Q1 reveals it answers "what sold?" while the meeting's question is "what earned?"; Q2 uncovers the two cash-only legacy stores missing from the feed (completeness); Q3 exposes a y-axis starting at 88%, inflating a 3-point dip into a plunge; Q4 is asked aloud ("what would make us not discontinue this line?" — a seasonality check nobody had run); Q5 finds returns are not shown at all — and the "top seller" is also the top-returned item. Fifteen minutes of protocol reverses the meeting's likely decision. This walkthrough is scripted in the instructor pack and rehearsed; it is the module's set-piece.

docs.title: Worked Example 4 — Correlation on trial (worked mini-case)
docs.text:
The causation test applied end-to-end to a claim participants will recognise:

The claim (as presented to a leadership meeting): "Branches that completed the new customer-service training have 14% higher satisfaction scores. Roll the training out everywhere — the data proves it works."

The three-question cross-examination: 1. Could a third factor drive both? Yes, plausibly: training was piloted in volunteer branches — branch managers who volunteer for training are likely the same managers who drive satisfaction by other means. Enthusiasm is the confound. 2. Did the cause precede the effect? Partially checkable: pull the satisfaction trend before the training. In the worked data (provided), the volunteer branches were already 9 points ahead pre-training — most of the gap predates the "cause." 3. What happens when we intervene? The only decisive evidence: assign the next training wave to a random half of the remaining branches and compare after one quarter. In the worked continuation, the randomised effect is +4% — real, worth rolling out, and one-third of the claimed size.

The literate conclusion, written as the meeting's decision memo: "Decision: proceed with a randomised second wave, not a full rollout. Evidence: observed +14% is confounded by volunteer selection; pre-trend explains ~9 points. Limit: true effect unknown until the randomised comparison reads out. Review: end of next quarter." The lesson participants quote back for the rest of the course: the data was accurate; the claim was not — and the fix cost one sentence of humility plus one quarter of patience.

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 3 — Map the Chain, Interrogate the Dashboard
docs.text:
Objective Map the data value chain for the participant's own use case, interrogate a live BI dashboard with the five-question protocol, and write the first decision memo (Dossier §3) Duration Part A 25 min (Day 1 Hour 5) + Part B 35 min (Day 2 Hour 1, before Quiz 1) Setup Chain-map canvas (A3 printed + digital), sample BI dashboard (browser-based, seeded with five deliberate defects), quality-test scoring strips, memo cards

Part A tasks — the chain (25 min, Day 1 Hour 5)

  1. (15 min) Map all six links for your dossier use case on the A3 canvas: one line per link — what happens, who owns it. Unknown owners are written as "?" — a finding, not a failure.
  2. (5 min) Mark the weakest link with the red sticker and write the one-line evidence you would check first.
  3. (5 min) Run the six quality tests (✓/✗/?) down the strip; count the "?" marks — each is a question for a named person back at work.

Part B tasks — the dashboard and the memo (35 min, Day 2 Hour 1)

  1. (15 min) In pairs, interrogate the sample dashboard with the five-question protocol. It contains five seeded defects (missing segment, truncated axis, stale feed date, apples-to-dates definition mix, absent returns metric); log every defect found on the hunt sheet.
  2. (10 min) Write the four-sentence decision memo for the dashboard's headline decision ("discontinue product line D?") — including the limit sentence and review point.
  3. (5 min) Complete Dossier §3 boxes 4–5 for your own use case (permission check + your own memo).
  4. (5 min) Pair exchange: your partner reads your memo cold and must be able to state the decision, the evidence, and the limit without asking you anything.

Expected output 

Part A: 6/6 links mapped, weakest link flagged with evidence line, quality strip scored (typical: 2–3 "?" marks)
Part B: ≥ 4/5 seeded defects found; memo passes the cold-read test; Dossier §3 complete incl. PDPL box

Troubleshooting guidance

Symptom Cause Fix Participant cannot name where their data is born Genuinely doesn't know (common, revealing) "?" is the correct answer — capture it as the first question for the data steward; this is the learning Chain map becomes an IT-systems inventory Confusing systems with links Re-anchor on verbs: born, kept, changed, summarised, decided, acted Pair finds only the visual defects (axis) Stopping at Q3 of the protocol Prompt Q2 aloud: "where does each number come from?" — the stale feed date is on the info tooltip Memo is eight sentences of hedging Limit sentence anxiety Enforce the four-sentence form; one limit, stated plainly, beats five disclaimers PDPL box triggers legal anxiety Overreading the obligation The deliverable is a question for the steward, not a legal opinion; name the steward and move on

Instructor notes. Part A's most common and most valuable outcome is discovering how much nobody in the room knows about link 1 of their own processes — treat "?" density as a success metric and say so. In Part B, the fifth defect (absent returns) is found by fewer than half of pairs; reveal it last and let the "top seller = top returned" twist land. The memo cold-read (task 7) is the quality gate: memos that fail it get 5 minutes of rework before Quiz 1.

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz (5 questions) 1. Name the six links in order. → collection, storage, processing, analysis, decision, action(+feedback). 2. A dashboard is flawless but the decision is still wrong. Name two links that could be responsible. → e.g., collection (data born wrong/late) or decision (evidence ignored/HiPPO). 3. Which quality test does "two departments define 'resolved' differently" fail? → Consistent. 4. "Ice-cream sales and drownings rise together." What is the third factor, and what is this fallacy? → Summer/heat; correlation read as causation. 5. What are the four sentences of a decision memo? → decision, evidence (+source/freshness), limit/uncertainty, review point.

Axis forensics. Five chart pairs (honest vs distorted rendering of the same data); participants identify the distortion in each within 30 seconds per pair.

Correlation courtroom. Prosecution and defence argue "more training hours cause fewer safety incidents at plant sites" from a scatter chart; the room is the jury; the verdict must name the third-factor candidates and the intervention that would settle it.

Definition hunt. Participants write their organisation's definition of one everyday metric ("active customer", "resolved case", "occupied bed") from memory, then compare with a neighbour from a different unit — divergence is the point.

Discussion questions. - Which dashboard in your organisation would fail Q2 ("where does each number come from?") most spectacularly — and who could answer it? - When is deciding against the data legitimate, and what does the decision memo do for that case?

docs.title: Case Study — The Phantom Beds of Al-Shifa Medical City
docs.text:
Scenario. Al-Shifa Medical City (Dammam, 600 beds) runs a celebrated executive dashboard: live occupancy, ED wait times, discharge forecasts. Occupancy reads 84%; ward managers swear they are turning away transfers daily. The COO orders an expensive "AI bed-prediction" procurement to fix a problem the dashboard says is moderate.

Business context. Winter surge is eight weeks away. The AI procurement (SAR 3.2M) is queued for sign-off. A newly literate operations analyst — this course's target profile — asks to walk the chain before the signature.

Technical challenge. The walk finds: discharges entered up to four hours late on busy shifts (link 1); reserved-for-surgery beds counted "available" in one feeder system and "occupied" in another (link 2/consistency); the "live" view built on an hourly feed that silently drops ED boarding patients (link 3/completeness); and an executive average that hides the medicine ward running at 103% while day-surgery sits at 61% (link 4/relevance). True effective occupancy at peak: ~97% in the bottleneck ward. The dashboard was not lying; it was faithfully summarising a broken chain.

Constraints. No budget for new systems before winter; nursing workflow changes require union-style consultation with head nurses; the COO is publicly committed to "an AI solution"; patient-level data on any new screen raises PDPL review.

Solution approach (facilitate, don't lecture). The analyst's memo (four sentences, exhibit in the course pack) reframes the decision: pause the AI procurement; fix link 1 with bedside discharge entry piloted in two wards (workflow, near-zero cost); reconcile the reserved-bed definition (one meeting, one steward decision); add a specialty breakdown to the existing dashboard (one BI change); re-measure in four weeks. Result in the scenario: peak-hour data freshness from 4 hours to 20 minutes, the "phantom beds" gone, and the AI procurement re-scoped — a forecasting model now justified on top of a chain that can feed it honestly (the Module 5 lesson in miniature: feasibility depends on the chain, and the same SAR 3.2M buys far more after the chain is fixed).

Discussion questions. 1. Why did the dashboard's polish make the problem harder to see? Name the laundering effect in your own words. 2. The COO is publicly committed to "AI". Craft the two sentences that redirect the commitment without embarrassing the sponsor. 3. Which of the six quality tests did each finding violate? (Map all four findings.) 4. What changes in this story if the discharge data includes patient identifiers on the new bedside screens? (PDPL reflex check.) 5. After the chain is fixed, write the framing-canvas box 1 (Module 1 style) for the re-scoped forecasting use case.

docs.title: Module 4 — Generative AI and Large Language Models in the Workplace
Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. Generative AI is the first AI generation that non-technical professionals operate directly, every day, with no engineer in between — which makes GenAI literacy an occupational skill, not a technology briefing. This module explains what large language models actually do (and therefore why they hallucinate), builds a practical prompting discipline, installs verification as a habit, and gives participants a defensible answer to the workplace question: which of my tasks should this thing touch, and under what rules?

Business relevance. GenAI adoption in Saudi organisations is running ahead of GenAI governance: staff already paste text into public assistants, and the productivity upside is real — drafting, summarising, translating between Arabic and English, meeting notes, first-pass analysis. The twin risks are equally real: confidential or personal data leaving the organisation through a prompt (a PDPL event), and fluent falsehoods entering documents that decisions rely on. Organisations that train the habits — task-fit judgment, data discipline, verification — capture the upside; organisations that only issue bans push usage into the shadows and keep the risk.

Industry use cases. - A ministry correspondence unit cuts first-draft time for citizen replies from 25 minutes to 6 — with a mandatory verification pass because one hallucinated regulation citation reached a citizen in the pilot. - A Jeddah professional-services firm uses an assistant for bilingual proposal drafting, with a red-line rule: client names and figures never enter external tools. - An operations team turns 40-page shift reports into one-page structured summaries and finds the model quietly smooths over the anomalies that mattered — fixed by prompting for exceptions explicitly.

Expected competencies. After this module a participant can explain next-word prediction and its consequences (fluency without truth) in plain language; state the difference between generative and predictive AI on the family tree; write task-appropriate prompts using the four-part pattern; classify their own tasks on the delegate/draft/verify/never matrix; and apply the confidentiality and verification rules before and after every consequential use.

docs.title: Learning Objectives (mapped)
docs.text: # Objective Maps to 4.1 Explain how an LLM produces text and why hallucination is a design property, not a bug LO1, LO5 4.2 Position generative AI against predictive ML on the family tree, with task examples LO2 4.3 Write effective prompts using the role–task–context–format pattern LO1 4.4 Classify workplace tasks on the delegate / draft / verify / never matrix LO4 4.5 Apply data-confidentiality rules (incl. PDPL reflexes) to assistant use LO5 4.6 Verify AI-generated content before it enters a decision or document LO5, LO6

docs.title: 1. What an LLM actually does — and what follows from it
docs.text:
A large language model is a deep-learning system trained on enormous quantities of text to do one thing extraordinarily well: predict what text plausibly comes next. Every capability participants see — answering, summarising, translating, drafting — is that one skill, steered. Three plain-language consequences follow directly, and together they explain nearly every GenAI behaviour a professional will meet:

  • Fluency is guaranteed; truth is not. The model produces what plausible text looks like. Most of the time, plausible and true coincide — that is what makes the failure mode dangerous. When they diverge, the model states falsehoods with the same polished confidence, because confidence is a property of its prose, not of its knowledge. This is hallucination, and it is not a bug being patched away next release: it is the shadow of the design. (Modern systems reduce it with retrieval and citations — participants should prefer tools that show sources — but reduction is not elimination.)
  • It has a training cut-off and no native access to your facts. Yesterday's org chart, this morning's policy change, your customer's file — absent unless provided in the prompt or connected by the organisation's own systems. The literate reflex: "does the model actually have what it needs to answer this, or will it improvise?"
  • It does not remember or 'know' you — but your prompt goes somewhere. What participants type may be processed outside the organisation depending on the tool and contract. The governance question ("which tool tier is this data allowed in?") is settled before typing, not after.

The single most useful mental model for this audience: an eloquent, endlessly willing junior colleague with encyclopaedic reading, no accountability, and no shame. You would happily let that colleague draft; you would never let them sign.

docs.title: 2. Generative vs predictive: two different contracts
docs.text:
Predictive ML (Modules 2–3) Generative AI Output A score or category about a defined question Open-ended content (text, images, code) Evaluated by Confusion matrix, precision/recall, against labels Human judgment; usefulness; factual verification Wrong looks like A measurable error rate you can monitor A fluent falsehood you must catch Best at Repetitive decisions at scale on structured data Language work: drafting, summarising, translating, transforming Governance handle Threshold, monitoring, retraining Usage policy, data rules, verification workflow

The table earns its place in the dossier: participants whose use case is really a language task (summarise complaints, draft responses) discover in this hour that they may need GenAI, not a trained predictive model — or vice versa. Both routes flow into the same Module 5 scorecard, but the risk profiles differ and the scorecard's risk column knows it.

docs.title: 3. Prompting as professional communication
docs.text:
Prompt quality is not magic; it is the same skill as briefing a junior colleague well. The course pattern — Role, Task, Context, Format (RTCF) — with an upgrade shown live:

  • Weak: "Write about our customer service."
  • Strong: "You are an operations analyst at a Saudi utilities company (role). Draft a one-page summary of the attached 30 complaint excerpts for the head of customer care (task). Context: the audience has 5 minutes and cares about systemic causes, not individual cases; Ramadan operating hours changed on the 10th and may explain some patterns. Format: three themes with counts, one 'exceptions and anomalies' section listing anything that fits no theme, and three recommended next checks — not recommendations, checks."

Four teaching points ride on the example: specificity is free performance; the exceptions section defends against the model's tendency to smooth anomalies into tidy themes; asking for "next checks, not recommendations" keeps the human in the decision seat; and iteration is normal — the second prompt ("now challenge your own summary: what would a sceptic say is missing?") is often worth more than the first. Participants also meet the critique pattern (paste your own draft, ask for weaknesses), which sidesteps hallucination risk almost entirely because the facts are supplied, not generated.

docs.title: 4. The task-fit matrix: delegate, draft, verify, never
docs.text:
The module's decision tool. Two questions position any task: How costly is an undetected error? and How easily can I verify the output?

Easy to verify Hard to verify Low error cost DELEGATE — meeting-note first pass, reformatting, tone adjustment, internal brainstorms DRAFT — idea generation, outline drafts; treat output as raw material High error cost VERIFY — client/citizen-facing text, policy summaries, translations for signature: use freely, verify line-by-line before release NEVER (unassisted) — legal positions, regulatory citations, numbers you cannot check, personal-data judgments; use only with expert review and source-grounded tools

Plus the overriding data gate applied before the matrix: no personal data, no confidential business data, no client identifiers into tools not approved for them — under PDPL, pasting citizen data into a public assistant is a data transfer, with everything that implies. The organisational tiering (public tools / enterprise tools / no tools) is presented as the pattern participants should expect and demand from their employers; SDA-FND-105 covers the governance side in depth.

docs.title: 5. Verification as a workflow, not a virtue
docs.text:
"Always verify" fails as advice because it is unbounded. The course installs a bounded, teachable pass — the three-check verification:

  1. Facts: every checkable claim — names, numbers, dates, citations, quotes — gets checked against a source outside the model. In source-grounded tools, follow the citation; a citation that does not support the sentence is treated as a miss.
  2. Omissions: what did it leave out? (Re-prompt: "list anything in the source you did not include and why." The complaint-summary anomaly problem is caught here.)
  3. Fit: would I sign this? Tone, audience, implications — the uniquely human check.

Time-boxed honestly: the pass costs 20–30% of the drafting time saved — the productivity gain survives, and the hallucination risk largely does not. The cultural rule that makes it stick, stated as policy language participants can take home: "AI drafts, humans sign — and the signer verifies." Accountability never transfers to the tool.

docs.title: 6. Common mistakes and workplace considerations
docs.text:
1. The copy-paste career risk. Sending unverified AI text under your own name; the signature rule exists because the first hallucinated citation that reaches a regulator or citizen is remembered for years.
  2. Confidential data in public tools. The most common real-world violation; the data gate comes before every other consideration, and "it was faster" is not a defence under PDPL.
  3. Prompt laziness. One vague prompt, disappointing output, "the tool is useless." The RTCF pattern plus one iteration resolves the majority of quality complaints.
  4. Anchoring. The first draft frames all subsequent thinking — including wrong framings. Antidote for consequential work: sketch your own position first, then invoke the assistant.
  5. Uniform trust or uniform distrust. Both are literacy failures; the matrix exists to make trust task-shaped.
  6. Skill atrophy and the training pipeline. If juniors delegate all first drafts, where do seniors come from? Teams need deliberate practice policies — an organisational design question this audience owns (Module 6 picks up the workforce thread).
  7. Believing the model's self-reports. Asking "are you sure?" produces confident text about confidence — verification happens outside the model, full stop.

docs.title: Worked Example 1 — The prompt upgrade ladder (before/after, annotated)
docs.text:
Provided as a handout with real outputs side by side:

Rung Prompt Output quality (observed) 1 "Summarise this report." Generic; drops the anomaly; 40% too long 2 + role & audience: "…for the head of customer care, 5-minute read" Correct altitude; still smooths anomalies 3 + format & exceptions clause: "…three themes with counts + an exceptions section" Anomaly (the complaint spike from one district) surfaces 4 + critique iteration: "What would a sceptic say your summary missed?" The annotation column teaches the meta-lesson: each rung is the same request, better briefed — the model did not get smarter; the professional did.

docs.title: Worked Example 3 — Hallucination anatomy (annotated exhibit)

docs.title: Worked Example 5 — A team GenAI usage policy on one page (model text)
docs.text:
The module's outputs, assembled into the artefact most participants will be asked for within a month of returning to work. Presented as a model text to adapt, not adopt:

TEAM AI-ASSISTANT USAGE POLICY (one page — if it needs two, it won't be read)

1. TOOLS. Approved: [enterprise-tier assistant, named]. Not approved for
   work content: personal accounts on public tools. Questions → [named owner].
2. DATA GATE (before every use). Never enter: citizen/customer personal
   data, unpublished figures, contract terms, anything marked confidential.
   Unsure = don't, and ask. (PDPL applies to prompts like any processing.)
3. TASK RULES (the matrix, condensed).
   DELEGATE: internal notes, reformatting, brainstorms — skim before filing.
   DRAFT: outlines and first passes — treat as raw material.
   VERIFY: anything leaving the team under a name — facts, citations,
   numbers checked against sources before release.
   NEVER unassisted: legal/regulatory positions, decisions about people.
4. THE SIGNATURE RULE. AI drafts, humans sign — and the signer verifies.
   Accountability never transfers to the tool.
5. HONESTY. AI-assisted external documents are verified to the same
   standard as human-written ones — which is the point of rules 3 and 4.
6. LEARNING. One shared channel for prompt patterns that worked; juniors
   still write first drafts unassisted on [defined tasks] — skills are
   a team asset we do not automate away by accident.
Review: quarterly, or when tools change. Owner: [name]. Version: 1.0.

The facilitation note attached: rule 6 is the one teams forget and the one this audience — as managers — uniquely owns. A policy without a named owner (footer) fails its own Module 5 lesson.

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 4 — The GenAI Working Session
docs.text:
Objective Run a realistic assisted-work cycle: brief well (RTCF), iterate, catch a planted hallucination with the three-check pass, classify own tasks on the matrix, and complete Dossier §4 Duration 50 minutes (embedded across Day 2 Hour 2 with micro-lectures between tasks) Setup AI assistant in browser (enterprise or public-tier per venue policy — no real personal/confidential data used at any point); complaint-excerpt pack (30 synthetic excerpts, seeded anomaly); hallucination-hunt question set; matrix worksheet

Instructions & tasks

  1. (10 min) The upgrade ladder, live. Run rungs 1 and 3 of the prompt ladder yourself on the complaint pack. Compare outputs: did the anomaly (the one-district spike) survive into your rung-3 summary? Screenshot both.
  2. (10 min) The critique iteration. Ask the sceptic question ("what would a critic say this summary missed?") and then verify one of the model's self-identified gaps against the source excerpts. Note which gaps were real and which were the model performing humility.
  3. (10 min) Hallucination hunt. Ask the two provided questions engineered to sit at the edge of the model's reliable knowledge (sector-specific figures and a niche regulation). Run the three-check pass; document what was checkable, what was not, and what was wrong. At least one planted question reliably produces an unverifiable or false specific — capture it.
  4. (10 min) Matrix your job. List your six most time-consuming regular tasks; place each on the delegate/draft/verify/never matrix; apply the data gate; mark the two with the highest safe upside.
  5. (10 min) Dossier §4. Complete the GenAI applicability check for your use case, including the written-out RTCF prompt (box 4) and the session screenshots (box 5).

Expected output 

Ladder: rung-1 vs rung-3 screenshots; anomaly present in rung 3, absent in rung 1 (typical)
Critique pass: ≥ 1 real gap verified, ≥ 1 performed-humility gap identified as such
Hunt: ≥ 1 unverifiable/false specific documented with the check that caught it
Matrix: 6 tasks placed, data gate applied, top-2 upside tasks marked
Dossier §4: 5/5 boxes complete with evidence attached

Troubleshooting guidance

Symptom Cause Fix The planted questions produce cautious refusals instead of hallucinations Model/tool updated since course prep Use the backup question set (three alternates provided); if all refuse, teach that — refusal behaviour is a tool-selection criterion — and switch to the canned exhibit Participant pastes what looks like real workplace data Habit outrunning the data gate Stop, reset, and use the moment: this is exactly the violation the gate exists for; synthetic packs only Outputs differ across the room for identical prompts Normal model variability Name it explicitly: non-determinism is a property; it is why verification attaches to outputs, not tools "My whole job is in the NEVER box" (legal/finance participants) Over-broad reading of the matrix Decompose the job: the judgment is NEVER-unassisted; the formatting, first-pass reading, and drafting around it rarely are Rung-3 summary still misses the anomaly Exceptions clause omitted or vague Compare against the worked prompt; the clause must demand a section for non-fitting items

Instructor notes. Task 3 is the behavioural payoff of the module — a hallucination the participant caught personally is worth every slide about hallucinations ever shown; make sure each pair gets one, using the backup set if needed. Task 4 routinely produces the day's best discussion when two people with the same job title place the same task in different quadrants: surface it, and let them argue error cost vs verifiability. Fast finishers: run the bilingual test — same RTCF prompt in Arabic and English — and compare quality, an evaluation their organisations will need.

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz (5 questions) 1. In one sentence: what does an LLM fundamentally do? → Predicts plausible next text, steered by the prompt. 2. Why is "it sounded confident" worthless as evidence? → Confidence is a property of the prose, not the knowledge; fluency is uniform across true and false outputs. 3. Name the four parts of the prompt pattern. → Role, Task, Context, Format. 4. A task has high error cost and is hard to verify. Quadrant? → NEVER (unassisted) — expert review and source-grounded tools only. 5. What comes before the matrix for every task? → The data gate: what data would enter the prompt, and which tool tier permits it?

The signature test. Five outputs shown (an email, a policy summary, a translated clause, meeting notes, a statistics claim); for each, participants answer in 15 seconds: "sign, verify, or refuse?" — with the rule that justifies it.

Prompt surgery. Pairs receive a genuinely bad prompt ("make a report about safety") and 3 minutes to rebuild it with RTCF for a stated audience; best rebuild wins the whiteboard point.

Omission drill. Given a 10-line source and a 3-line model summary, list what was dropped and rank which omission is most dangerous — 4 minutes, solo.

Discussion questions. - Your team member produces double the output since adopting an assistant, and you suspect no verification pass. What do you say — and what policy fixes what the conversation cannot? - Which tasks in your unit would you ban from unassisted GenAI today, and what tooling (source-grounded, enterprise-tier) would move them back into VERIFY?

docs.title: Case Study — The Citation That Never Existed: GenAI at the Diwan Correspondence Unit
docs.text:
Scenario. A ministry's correspondence unit (14 officers, ~500 citizen letters/week) pilots an AI assistant for first drafts. Productivity jumps: average drafting time falls from 25 to 6 minutes, backlog clears, officer satisfaction rises. In week seven, a citizen's lawyer replies to a ministry letter pointing out that the regulation article it cites does not exist.

Business context. The letter carried an officer's signature and the ministry's letterhead. The incident escalates to the deputy minister; the easy institutional reflex — ban the tool — would also surrender a 4× productivity gain the unit now depends on and push usage underground (two officers admit to using personal accounts "before the pilot anyway").

Technical challenge. Reconstruct how the fabricated citation survived to signature, and design the workflow that keeps the productivity while making the failure class structurally unlikely.

Constraints. Officers are not lawyers; legal review of all 500 letters/week is impossible; citizen personal data is involved (PDPL applies to what may enter prompts — the pilot tool's tier must be verified); the deputy minister wants an answer in ten days, not a study.

Solution approach (facilitate, don't lecture). The post-incident review maps cleanly onto the module: the officer trusted fluency (no fact-check on the citation — check 1 skipped); the unit had no matrix (citizen-facing legal-adjacent text was implicitly DELEGATE when it is VERIFY-at-minimum); and the tool was not source-grounded (citations generated, not retrieved). The redesign participants should converge on: (1) tier the letters — routine acknowledgements stay VERIFY-light, anything citing regulation requires the officer to open the cited article (a 90-second check) with a checkbox in the workflow; (2) procure/configure a source-grounded tool that links citations to the actual regulation database, converting check 1 from research into a click; (3) the signature rule enters the unit's standing procedure verbatim — "AI drafts, humans sign, the signer verifies"; (4) the two shadow-users are folded into the sanctioned pilot (amnesty + training beats prohibition); (5) a one-page incident memo (Module 3 format) goes to the deputy minister: decision, evidence, limit, review point. Net result in the scenario: drafting time settles at 9 minutes — the verification pass costs 3 — and the failure class has not recurred at scale because it now requires two independent misses.

Discussion questions. 1. Why was "ban the tool" the wrong fix even from a pure-risk perspective? (Shadow usage, and the counterfactual of manual-drafting error rates nobody ever measured.) 2. The officer signed it. The tool generated it. The unit head approved the pilot. Distribute the accountability — and defend your distribution. 3. What changes when the tool becomes source-grounded? Which of the three checks does it absorb, and which does it never absorb? 4. Draft the two-sentence note to all officers announcing the new rule without shaming the officer involved. 5. PDPL angle: what had to be true about the pilot tool for citizen names to lawfully appear in prompts at all?

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
1. How an LLM works (next-word river) — Purpose: module anchor; hallucination made visible. Elements: a sentence flowing left to right with branching candidate next-words and probabilities; one branch leading to a true completion, one to a fluent-false completion, both drawn equally smooth. Style: course palette; the two branches identical in polish, different in a small truth badge. Designer description: "A river of text splitting into two equally wide channels; only a tiny fact-check flag distinguishes them."
  2. Task-fit matrix poster — Elements: the 2×2 with quadrant names, example tasks per quadrant, and the data-gate turnstile drawn in front of the whole matrix. Style: A2 poster + A5 desk card; bilingual.
  3. Three-check verification loop — Elements: facts → omissions → fit as a stamped-pass sequence ending at a signature icon; time-cost annotation (20–30% of time saved). Style: compact workflow strip.
  4. Generative vs predictive split-panel — Elements: the Module 4 §2 table rendered as two machine silhouettes with their contracts written on them. Style: side-by-side comparison, reused in Module 5 risk scoring.

docs.title: Images (screenshots)
docs.text:
1. Rung-1 vs rung-3 outputs side by side — why: the prompt-quality proof; content: same source, generic summary vs themed summary with exceptions section, anomaly highlighted.
  2. The annotated hallucination exhibit — why: Worked Example 3 as a projectable; content: five sentences with check-annotations, the false citation circled.
  3. A source-grounded answer with citations — why: shows the tool class participants should prefer; content: answer with inline citation links, one followed to its source.
  4. Enterprise-tier vs public-tier tool banner — why: makes the data gate concrete; content: the visual cues that identify which tier a participant is typing into.

docs.title: Simulations
docs.text:
1. The planted hallucination (Lab 4 task 3) — Setup: curated question set at the edge of reliable knowledge, with backup alternates. Expected behaviour: ≥ 1 confident unverifiable/false specific per pair. Learning objective: catching a hallucination personally, with the named check that caught it.
  2. The anchoring experiment — Setup: half the room drafts a position on a scenario before seeing an AI draft; half reads the AI draft first, then writes. Expected behaviour: the draft-first half produces visibly more diverse positions. Learning objective: anchoring is real and measurable in your own cohort — sketch first for consequential work.

docs.title: Interactive Activities
docs.text:
• Matrix walk (10 min): the 2×2 taped on the floor; instructor reads tasks; participants stand in their quadrant and defend against neighbours before the reveal discussion.
  • "Sign or refuse" lightning round (5 min): the signature test run as a whole-room card vote (green/yellow/red cards).
