docs.text:
• Instructor demo: the full upgrade ladder run live (rungs 1→4) on the projector with running commentary, ending with the critique iteration surfacing a real caveat — rehearsed, with the canned exhibit as network-failure fallback.
  • Student demo: one pair presents their caught hallucination — the question, the fluent answer, and the check that killed it.
  • Expected outputs: every participant leaves Hour 2 with a personal caught-hallucination screenshot and a six-task matrix of their own job.

docs.title: Module 5 — AI Opportunity and Risk Assessment Frameworks
Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. Everything so far — vocabulary, the ML loop, the data chain, GenAI task-fit — converges here into the course's central professional act: evaluating an AI use case before money and reputation are committed. This module delivers a structured, repeatable framework (the Feasibility–Value–Risk scorecard), trains participants to apply it honestly against evidence rather than enthusiasm, and equips them with a working knowledge of how AI systems fail — bias, drift, brittleness, misuse — so that risk scoring is informed, not ritual.

Business relevance. Industry surveys have consistently found that a large majority of AI initiatives stall before production or fail to return value — and the post-mortems repeat the same causes: no real business owner, data that was never available at the claimed quality, value that was never quantified, risks discovered after deployment instead of before funding. A one-page structured evaluation, applied at the idea stage by business-side professionals, is the cheapest risk control in the entire AI lifecycle. In the Saudi context, where NSDAI momentum creates strong incentive to start AI projects, the differentiating organisational skill is knowing which ones not to start — and being able to defend that judgment to sponsors.

Industry use cases. - A Jeddah bank's innovation committee triages 40 staff-submitted AI ideas into fund / fix-data-first / decline, with the scorecard as the shared language between business, data, and risk teams. - A logistics firm discovers at scoring stage — not month nine — that its "predict delivery delays" idea has no recorded delay-reason labels, converting a doomed project into a six-month data-collection fix. - A government entity scores a citizen-facing eligibility-screening idea and stops it on the risk column: an error denies a citizen a service, which demands human review by design — reshaping, not killing, the use case.

Expected competencies. After this module a participant can score any AI use case on the nine-item FVR scorecard with anchored 1–5 ratings; identify the eight failure modes and attach the relevant ones to a given use case; distinguish reshaping mitigations (human-in-the-loop, narrowed scope, staged rollout) from rejection; and present a fund / fix-first / decline recommendation with evidence-backed reasoning.

docs.title: Learning Objectives (mapped)
docs.text: # Objective Maps to 5.1 Score an AI use case on the Feasibility–Value–Risk scorecard using the scoring anchors LO4 5.2 Identify the eight common AI failure modes and match them to use cases LO5 5.3 Recognise bias sources across the lifecycle (data, labels, deployment context) LO5 5.4 Propose reshaping mitigations (human-in-the-loop, scope narrowing, staged rollout) that change a score LO4, LO5 5.5 Deliver a fund / fix-first / decline recommendation with evidence LO4, LO6 5.6 Withstand and conduct a structured peer challenge (red-team) of a scored use case LO4

docs.title: 1. Why structured evaluation beats enthusiasm
docs.text: Unstructured AI decisions follow predictable pathologies: the demo effect (a polished vendor demo substitutes for evidence about your data), the CEO's-favourite effect (seniority substitutes for feasibility), the pilot trap (a pilot succeeds on curated data and scale-up dies on the real chain), and risk asymmetry (upside is presented, downside is discovered). A structured scorecard defeats these not because the numbers are precise — they are judgments — but because it forces every use case to answer the same nine questions in front of the same audience. Comparability is the product; the score is just the receipt. Two rules make it honest: every score cites its evidence (a Module 3 chain map, a labelled-data check, a baseline measurement — not adjectives), and the scorer is not the sponsor for any use case above a spending threshold.

docs.title: 2. The Feasibility–Value–Risk (FVR) scorecard
docs.text:
Nine items, three per column, each scored 1–5 against written anchors. The course's canonical instrument, used in Lab 5 and the capstone:

Feasibility — can we actually build and run this? - F1 Data readiness. Do the data and labels exist, at quality, accessibly, permitted for this use? (Scored from the Dossier §3 chain map — 1 = data doesn't exist or isn't permitted; 3 = exists but needs significant collection/cleaning work; 5 = exists, quality-tested, permitted, owned.) - F2 Task clarity. Is the prediction/generation task crisply defined with a measurable outcome? (1 = "make us smarter"; 5 = Dossier §1 box 5 quality: named metric, named baseline.) - F3 Integration & operability. Can the output reach the decision point, and can someone own the system after launch? (1 = no path from score to action; 5 = decision workflow identified, owner named, monitoring plausible.)

Value — is it worth it? - V1 Financial impact. Quantified benefit vs baseline (cost saved, revenue gained, loss avoided), in SAR/year, with the arithmetic shown. (1 = unquantified adjectives; 5 = costed against the measured baseline from Dossier §2 box 6.) - V2 Strategic fit. Alignment with organisational strategy and — where relevant — NSDAI priorities (Module 6). (1 = orphan idea; 5 = advances a named strategic objective with an executive sponsor.) - V3 Scale & reuse. Does the value repeat and grow (many decisions, many units), or is it one-off? (1 = single team, single event; 5 = organisation-wide decision made thousands of times.)

Risk — what can go wrong, to whom? (higher score = LOWER risk) - R1 Error consequence. What does a wrong output do to a person, the business, or the public — and is there a human checkpoint before harm? (1 = automated harm to individuals with no review; 5 = errors cheap and self-correcting.) - R2 Bias & fairness exposure. Could performance differ across groups (nationality, gender, region, age)? Do the training data encode past unfairness? (1 = high-stakes decisions about people with known-skewed history; 5 = no people-affecting decisions.) - R3 Compliance & reputation. Personal data (PDPL), sector regulation, explainability requirements, public sensitivity. (1 = personal data + regulated decision + no explainability plan; 5 = no personal data, no regulated surface.)

Reading the totals: column sums (max 15 each), never a single grand total — a use case scoring F14/V13/R4 is not "31/45, decent"; it is a valuable, buildable thing that should not be built as designed. The decision grammar taught: strong F and V with weak R → reshape (add human review, narrow scope, stage the rollout) and re-score; strong V with weak F → fix-first (usually data work — often the honest first project); weak V → decline politely, whatever the demo looked like. Scores of 1 or 2 on R1 or R3 are gates, not weights: no value total overrides them.

docs.title: 3. The eight failure modes (the risk column's field guide)
docs.text:
1. Data bias → decision bias. The Lab 2 hard-hat model at organisational scale: a hiring screener trained on a decade of skewed hiring replicates the skew with mechanical consistency. Bias enters through data composition, label meaning ("good employee" = whoever thrived under old conditions), and deployment mismatch (trained on one population, applied to another).
  2. Drift. The Module 2 expiry story: behaviour, fraud tactics, and demand patterns move; frozen models decay silently. Risk question: who monitors, how often, alerted how?
  3. Brittleness at the edges. Models excel on typical cases and fail strangely on rare ones — which in citizen-facing services are exactly the cases that matter (unusual names, rare circumstances, edge eligibility).
  4. Feedback loops. The system's own actions reshape its future data (Module 3 link 6): a policing-style allocation model over-samples where it over-predicted; a recommender narrows what it learns from.
  5. Hallucination & automation of plausibility. Module 4's failure mode entering documents, decisions, and citizen communications at scale.
  6. Goodhart's law. When the model's metric becomes the target, the metric detaches from the goal: optimising "calls closed per hour" produces fast, bad calls.
  7. Misuse & scope creep. A model built for one purpose quietly applied to another (attendance data → performance scoring), voiding both its validity and its PDPL basis.
  8. Accountability vacuum. "The algorithm decided" — the failure mode that contains all others: no named owner for the threshold, the monitoring, the appeal path. Antidote: every deployed model has a human owner whose name is written down; every automated decision affecting a person has an explanation and an appeal route.

Participants practise attachment, not memorisation: given a use case, name the two or three failure modes with the strongest claim on it, and let those drive the R-column scoring and the mitigation design.

docs.title: 4. Mitigations that change scores (reshaping, not decorating)
docs.text:
The framework is generative, not just evaluative: a poor risk score plus the right mitigation is often a fundable redesign.

  • Human-in-the-loop: the model recommends, a human decides — mandatory where R1 ≤ 2 and often converting it to 4. Cost: throughput; the design question is which cases route to humans (low-confidence bands, high-stakes categories — the Module 2 threshold logic reappearing as governance).
  • Scope narrowing: launch on the sub-population or decision slice where data is strongest and errors are cheapest; expand with evidence.
  • Staged rollout with a shadow phase: run the model alongside the current process, compare before it touches anyone — the organisational version of the holdout principle.
  • Explainability & appeal by design: reasons attached to outputs; an appeal path with a human on the end. Not decoration — in citizen-facing use, the licence to operate.
  • Monitoring with named ownership: the drift antidote written into the proposal (what metric, what cadence, who is paged).

The rule participants internalise: a mitigation that does not change who does what, on which cases, with what evidence — is a paragraph, not a mitigation. Re-score only for the former.

docs.title: 5. Common mistakes and portfolio considerations
docs.text:
1. Scoring the demo, not the chain. F1 comes from the Dossier §3 map, not the vendor's slide. If the chain map has three "?" marks, F1 cannot be a 4.
  2. Value by adjective. "Significant efficiency gains" scores V1 = 1 until arithmetic appears. The baseline requirement (Module 2, box 6) exists precisely for this row.
  3. Risk theatre. Listing generic risks ("data privacy is important to us") without attaching failure modes to this use case's specifics.
  4. Averaging away a gate. The single most dangerous spreadsheet habit: a 14/13/4 use case hidden inside "31/45". Columns are reported separately, gates are absolute.
  5. One-time scoring. Scores are revisited at each stage gate — after the data fix, after the shadow phase — or the framework becomes an approval ritual.
  6. Portfolio blindness. Individual scoring is necessary but not sufficient: a healthy portfolio mixes quick automation wins (Module 1's reclassified items), one or two high-F ML builds, and a GenAI productivity layer — not five moonshots. The Al-Manar case (Module 1) supplies the running portfolio for this discussion.

docs.title: Worked Example 1 — Full FVR scoring: Ramadan demand forecasting at a Riyadh grocery chain
docs.text:
The set-piece walkthrough, scored live with the room challenging each rating:

Item Score Evidence cited (not adjectives) F1 Data readiness 4 3 years of POS sales by SKU/store in one warehouse; promotions log incomplete for year 1; no personal data involved F2 Task clarity 5 "Predict next-week demand per SKU per store; baseline = current buyer guesses, measured at ±38% error" F3 Integration 4 Output feeds the existing weekly ordering screen; supply-chain manager named as owner; monitoring = weekly error report Feasibility 13/15 V1 Financial 4 Waste (perishables) SAR 11M/yr + stockout losses est. SAR 6M/yr; 20% error reduction ≈ SAR 3.4M/yr — arithmetic attached V2 Strategic 3 Fits cost programme; no executive sponsor yet — flagged as the fix V3 Scale 5 4,200 SKU-store combinations, decided weekly, forever Value 12/15 R1 Error consequence 4 Wrong forecast = waste or stockout, costly but self-correcting weekly; no harm to individuals R2 Bias exposure 5 No decisions about people R3 Compliance 5 No personal data; no regulated decision surface Risk 14/15 (low risk) Recommendation FUND Condition: secure the executive sponsor (V2); start with top-200 SKUs in 50 stores (staged rollout by choice, not necessity)

The contrast case is then scored rapid-fire by the room: CV-screening for graduate hiring — F ~11 (data exists), V ~10 (real time savings), R: R1 = 2 (life-affecting decisions), R2 = 1 (decade of skewed hiring history as labels), R3 = 2 (personal data + explainability demands). Gate triggered → reshape: model ranks for human review with mandatory diverse-slate rules, bias audit pre-launch, appeal path — re-scored R = 9 and still funded smaller. The lesson lands: the framework didn't kill the idea; it killed the dangerous version of the idea.

docs.title: Worked Example 2 — The risk register (one-page template)
docs.text:
Failure mode attached How it shows up here Early signal to watch Mitigation (who does what) Owner Drift Ramadan/season shifts; new store formats Weekly error report worsens 3 weeks running Retrain quarterly; alert at error > 25% Supply-chain analytics lead Brittleness New SKUs with no history Error concentrated in items < 8 weeks old Rule-based fallback for new SKUs Buying team Goodhart Buyers "game" the forecast to protect budgets Manual overrides > 30% of orders Override reason codes, monthly review Supply-chain manager

Three rows, filled, with named owners — the standard the capstone dossier must meet. A risk register without names in the owner column is returned.

docs.title: Worked Example 3 — Dossier §5: the scored card (template)
Worked Example 4 — The verdict letters (fix-first and decline, model texts)
docs.text:
Because the scorecard's verdicts must eventually be delivered to people, the course supplies two model letters. Both are four sentences; both cite the scorecard; neither apologises for the framework.

The fix-first letter (to the CEO's war-room sponsor, Bunyan case):

"The churn war-room scored strongly on ambition and weakly on foundations: we have never systematically recorded why customers leave (F1 = 2), and the current retention process has no measured baseline to beat (V1 = 2 — the arithmetic cannot be done yet). We recommend funding the foundation now: six months of exit-reason capture and a baseline measurement, owned by the retention team, at a fraction of the war-room budget. On that evidence, the war-room re-enters scoring next cycle with F and V it can actually earn. This is not a 'no' — it is the version of 'yes' that survives contact with our data."

The decline letter (to a submitter whose idea scored V1 = 1, F1 = 2):

"Thank you for submitting the meeting-transcription analytics idea — the scoring sheet is attached so you can see exactly how the committee read it. It declined on value: no decision we could identify changes based on the output (V1 = 1), and the audio data is neither centrally stored nor cleared for this use (F1 = 2, permission unresolved). If a concrete decision-owner emerges who would act on this weekly, resubmit with that name and the permission answer — those two lines alone would re-open the case. The committee funds evidence, and this letter tells you precisely which evidence."

The teaching point rides in the last sentence of each: a framework-literate organisation tells people how to succeed next time — which is why the Bunyan campaign gets better submissions every year, and why declined submitters keep submitting.

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 5 — Score Your Use Case, Survive the Red Team
docs.text:
Objective Score the participant's own use case on the FVR scorecard with evidence from Dossier §§1–4, attach failure modes and owned mitigations, and defend the recommendation in a structured peer red-team round Duration 50 minutes (Day 2 Hour 4, followed by the M6 express session) Setup FVR scorecard sheets with printed scoring anchors; failure-mode field guide card; risk-register strip; red-team question cards; participants' dossiers §§1–4 open on the table

Instructions & tasks

  1. (20 min) Score, with receipts. Complete the nine ratings using the anchors. Rule enforced by the sheet layout: the evidence line must be filled before the score box — and the evidence must point at a dossier page (§1 box 5 for F2, §3 chain map for F1, §2 box 6 for V1…). Unquantified V1 is capped at 2; chain maps with ≥ 3 "?" cap F1 at 3.
  2. (5 min) Attach failure modes. Pick the 2–3 with the strongest claim on your case from the field guide; write one line each on how it shows up here.
  3. (5 min) Design one real mitigation. Who does what, on which cases, with what evidence — then re-score the one rating it changes. Decoration doesn't re-score.
  4. (15 min) Red-team rounds (2 × 7 min). Pairs swap dossiers. The red-teamer draws three question cards ("What is the baseline number, exactly?", "Which chain link breaks this?", "Who is harmed by a false positive, and what is their appeal path?", "What would make you decline your own idea?"…) and attacks; the owner defends or amends scores live. Amended scores are marked in a second colour — visible honesty is the deliverable.
  5. (5 min) Commit. Write the recommendation line and the two-sentence sponsor justification. This freezes Dossier §5 for the capstone.

Expected output 

Scorecard: 9/9 rated with evidence lines pointing at dossier pages; column totals + gate check done
Failure modes: 2–3 attached with case-specific one-liners; ≥ 1 mitigation with a named owner and a re-scored rating
Red team: ≥ 1 score amended in second colour per participant (cohorts average 2.4 amendments — this is the honesty metric)
Recommendation: committed, with two-sentence sponsor justification

Troubleshooting guidance

Symptom Cause Fix All nines and tens of self-scored optimism (F14 V15 R15) Sponsor scoring own idea Point at the caps: where is the V1 arithmetic? How many "?" on the chain map? The red team will do this anyway — better now Participant gates their own case on R and deflates Reading gates as verdicts Teach the reshape move explicitly: what human checkpoint converts R1 from 2 to 4? Re-score and watch the case revive Evidence lines cite opinions ("our data is good") Adjective habit Evidence must be checkable: a page, a number, a named system, a named person Red team turns hostile or personal Question cards abandoned Cards are the protocol: attacks address the card question, owners answer the question, timekeeper enforces "My use case is GenAI — does FVR even apply?" Perceived predictive bias in the card Yes: F1 becomes source-data/tool-tier readiness, R risks lean on modes 5 and 7; the §4 matrix placement is the evidence

Instructor notes. The amendment count is your live measure of whether the module worked — a room with zero amended scores is a room that performed the scorecard rather than used it; say this out loud at the start of the red-team round. Keep the Al-Manar 6-item ML portfolio on the wall: fast finishers score a second use case from it and experience how much faster the second scoring goes (the framework becoming reflex). The CV-screening contrast case must be scored by the room, not presented — the gate discovery has to be theirs.

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz (5 questions) 1. Why are column totals never merged into one grand total? → A gate-level risk hides inside a healthy-looking sum; columns answer different questions. 2. A use case scores F13 V12 R5. What is the move? → Reshape: design mitigations (human-in-the-loop, scope, staging) that change specific R ratings, then re-score — not average, not decline by reflex. 3. Name the failure mode: "the call-centre model's 'resolution rate' target produced fast, bad calls." → Goodhart's law. 4. What does a mitigation need before it can change a score? → Changed behaviour: who does what, on which cases, with what evidence — plus an owner. 5. Which dossier page is the evidence for F1, and why? → §3 chain map — data readiness is a property of the chain, not of enthusiasm.

Gate hunt. Five one-line use cases read aloud; participants raise a red card the moment they hear a probable R1/R3 gate and name it (citizen eligibility automation, minor-targeted marketing, cross-purpose attendance data…).

Failure-mode bingo. Each participant gets a card with 8 modes; instructor reads six news-style AI incident vignettes; first correct full attachment wins. (Vignettes provided in the media pack, anonymised.)

The decline note. Write the three-sentence decline of a colleague's beloved low-V use case — honest, specific, and relationship-preserving. Peers score for all three properties.

Discussion questions. - Who in your organisation could run this scorecard credibly today — and who would need to accept its verdicts for it to matter? (Bridge to Module 6 roles.) - What is the counter-argument to gates ("we'll never innovate if R1 ≤ 2 always blocks")? Construct and then answer it.

docs.title: Case Study — Forty Ideas, One Committee: the Bunyan Bank Portfolio Triage
docs.text:
Scenario. Bunyan Bank (Jeddah, retail and SME banking) runs an internal "AI ideas" campaign, netting 40 submissions — from "predict SME loan default earlier" to "GenAI assistant for relationship managers" to "AI to write our board reports." An innovation committee (head of digital, head of risk, two business heads, one data-science lead — three of five non-technical) has one month and budget for four initiatives.

Business context. The CEO's favourite — a customer-churn "AI war room" with a vendor demo everyone loved — is submission #7. SAMA-supervised model governance applies to anything touching credit decisions. Last year's single AI project (a chatbot) quietly died after launch for lack of an owner; the committee knows it and the room knows they know it.

Technical challenge. Triage 40 ideas fairly, fast, and defensibly — including telling the CEO that #7 scores badly.

Constraints. One month; three of five committee members non-technical (the point of the exercise: the scorecard is their instrument); data-science lead available 20%; any credit-adjacent model triggers governance review (R3 anchor); the campaign promised every submitter a written response.

Solution approach (facilitate, don't lecture). Round one: all 40 scored on F and V only (30 minutes/idea is too slow — the committee uses a rapid two-anchor screen, F1 and V1, killing 19 ideas at "no data / no number" with respectful fix-first letters, many of them routed to automation/BI teams per the Module 1 classification). Round two: full FVR on the surviving 21. Outcomes participants should reproduce from the provided pack: the SME early-default idea scores F12 V13 R6 → reshape (human credit-officer checkpoint, shadow phase, explainability plan for SAMA-style review) → funded first; the RM GenAI assistant scores high with a VERIFY-workflow condition (Module 4's matrix written into the funding letter); the CEO's war room scores F7 (no labelled churn history — the bank never systematically recorded why customers left) V8 (baseline never measured) → fix-first, presented to the CEO as "fund the data foundation now, the war room in two quarters on real rails"; the board-report writer gates on R3 (confidential financials into an unapproved tool tier) pending enterprise tooling. Four funded, sixteen fix-first or rerouted, twenty declined with reasons — every submitter answered in scorecard language.

Discussion questions. 1. Rehearse the CEO conversation about #7: two minutes, scorecard in hand, career intact. What makes "fix-first" land differently from "no"? 2. The rapid two-anchor screen risks false negatives (good ideas killed at round one). What cheap safeguard fixes that? (Appeal path; resubmission with evidence.) 3. Why did the committee's non-technical majority turn out to be a strength rather than a weakness — and what did the scorecard have to provide for that to be true? 4. The chatbot that died for lack of an owner: which scorecard item now blocks that history from repeating, and is an item enough? 5. Draft the one-paragraph written response to a declined submitter (V1 = 1, F1 = 2) that keeps them submitting next year.

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
1. The FVR scorecard poster — Purpose: the course's central instrument at wall size. Elements: nine items in three columns with 1/3/5 anchor phrases printed under each; the gate rule in a red band across the bottom; "evidence before score" as the header motto. Style: A1 poster + the working A4 sheet, bilingual. Designer description: "Three columns F/V/R, each a ladder of three rungs with anchor text; a red horizontal gate bar under R1 and R3."
  2. Failure-mode field guide — Elements: the eight modes as icon + name + one-line signature + one question to ask; wallet-card format. Style: two-sided laminated card.
  3. The decision grammar map — Elements: flow from column patterns to moves: high-F/high-V/low-R → fund; high-V/low-F → fix-first; gate → reshape or decline; low-V → decline. Style: compact decision tree, six leaves.
  4. Mitigation levers strip — Elements: human-in-the-loop, scope narrowing, shadow phase, explainability+appeal, owned monitoring — each drawn as a lever with "which rating it moves" labelled. Style: horizontal strip, reused in the capstone brief.

docs.title: Simulations
docs.text:
1. The demo-effect ambush — Setup: instructor plays a 90-second slick fake vendor video for a use case the room then scores; the pack's evidence documents contradict three of the demo's implicit claims. Expected behaviour: first-pass scores anchor high, evidence pass drags F down two points; the room feels the demo effect. Learning objective: score the chain, not the demo.
  2. The gate under pressure — Setup: role-play — the "CEO" (instructor) pushes a gated use case ("competitors are doing it"); a volunteer committee must hold or reshape the gate in real time. Expected behaviour: the reshape move (human checkpoint + shadow phase) emerges as the face-saving, risk-honest answer. Learning objective: gates survive contact with power only if reshaping is on the table.

docs.title: Module 6 — National AI Strategy Context (NSDAI) and Workforce Roles
Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. AI literacy in Saudi Arabia is not a private skill; it is participation in a national project. This module places everything the course has built inside its strategic frame: the National Strategy for Data & AI (NSDAI), the institutions that carry it (SDAIA and its ecosystem), the data-and-AI workforce roles organisations actually need, and — most personally — where each participant stands in that landscape and which SDAIA Academy pathway takes them forward. It is deliberately the shortest module and the most personal one: delivered as an express session woven through Day 2 Hours 4–5, it converts two days of literacy into a situated professional identity and a next step.

Business relevance. Vision 2030 positions data and AI as a national economic engine, and NSDAI translates that ambition into pillars every Saudi organisation feels directly: skilled workforce at scale, a regulatory and data ecosystem (PDPL, NDMO standards), sector adoption programmes, and international positioning. For organisations, alignment is practical, not ceremonial — national priorities shape funding, regulation, talent supply, and procurement expectations. For individuals, the workforce pillar is this course: national capability targets are met one literate professional at a time, and the stackable pathway participants are standing in is a designed instrument of that strategy.

Industry use cases. - A government entity writing its data-and-AI plan maps each initiative to NSDAI pillars because that mapping is the language of its oversight reviews. - A utilities company builds an AI team and must decide, before hiring a single data scientist, which of six roles it actually lacks — and discovers the scarcest one is the business-side translator this course trains. - An HR directorate redesigns job families to add data-literacy expectations to every professional role, using the national skills taxonomy as its reference.

Expected competencies. After this module a participant can outline NSDAI's ambition and pillars in plain language; name SDAIA's role and its relationship to NDMO and PDPL enforcement; describe the six workforce roles of a working AI initiative and identify which their organisation lacks; position themselves on the role map; and commit to a concrete next step on the SDAIA Academy pathway (SDA-FND-102 or SDA-FND-103, per profile).

docs.title: Learning Objectives (mapped)
docs.text: # Objective Maps to 6.1 Outline NSDAI's ambition and pillars in plain language, with one organisational implication each LO1 6.2 Describe SDAIA's mandate and the institutional ecosystem (NDMO, PDPL context) LO1, LO3 6.3 Map the six workforce roles of an AI initiative and diagnose gaps in a given organisation LO4 6.4 Position their own role and use case within the national and organisational picture LO4 6.5 Select and justify their next module on the SDAIA Academy pathway LO1

docs.title: 1. NSDAI in plain language: the ambition and the pillars
docs.text:
The National Strategy for Data & AI, launched in 2020 under SDAIA's stewardship, states an ambition participants should be able to repeat without notes: to place Saudi Arabia among the world's leading data-and-AI nations — measured in talent, investment, adoption, and regulation — as an engine of Vision 2030's economic diversification. Taught as five plain-language pillars, each with its "so what" for the participant's organisation:

Pillar (plain form) What it means What it implies inside an organisation Skilled people at scale Training tens of thousands of specialists and raising baseline literacy across the professional workforce Literacy expectations entering ordinary job descriptions; this course and its pathway exist because of this pillar Data as national infrastructure Trusted, governed, shareable data across government and economy — NDMO standards, national platforms, open-data initiatives The Module 3 chain is not optional hygiene; it is the unit of national data quality An AI-friendly regulatory ecosystem PDPL, data-management standards, AI ethics principles — protection that enables adoption rather than merely restricting it "Permitted" (the sixth quality test) has an institutional address; governance questions have owners Adoption in priority sectors Government services, health, energy, mobility, smart cities among the visible fronts Sector programmes shape funding and expectations; a use case aligned with a sector priority carries V2 weight in the Module 5 scorecard International presence Summits, partnerships, standards participation — the Kingdom as a venue and voice in global AI Talent inflows, vendor attention, and benchmark pressure all reach the participant's procurement table

The framing discipline: participants do not memorise strategy prose; they carry the implication column. When Module 5's V2 anchor says "alignment with NSDAI priorities," this table is what scoring it honestly looks like.

docs.title: 2. The institutional map: who does what nationally
docs.text:
Kept deliberately compact — four institutions, one sentence each, and the reflex of knowing whom a question belongs to:

  • SDAIA (Saudi Data & AI Authority): the national steward of the data-and-AI agenda — strategy, national platforms, regulation of data and AI, and the analytics and AI capabilities serving government.
  • NDMO (National Data Management Office): the standard-setter for how public-sector data is managed, classified, quality-controlled, and shared — the institutional home of Module 3's discipline.
  • PDPL (Personal Data Protection Law): the Kingdom's personal-data statute — the legal floor under every "permitted?" question this course has raised, from chain mapping to prompt hygiene.
  • The National Centre for AI and sector regulators: applied AI capability and sector-specific supervision (e.g., SAMA's model-governance expectations in banking) — the reason Module 5's R3 anchor asks about sector regulation, not just PDPL.

The module does not turn professionals into lawyers; it installs the routing table. A use case touching citizen data routes its "may we?" to the data steward and PDPL basis; a credit model routes its explainability question to the sector regulator's expectations; a data-sharing idea routes to NDMO-aligned classification. Knowing the address is the literacy; SDA-FND-105 (unlocked by this module's badge) teaches the law and governance in depth.

docs.title: 3. The six roles of a working AI initiative
docs.text:
Organisations chronically over-hire the famous role and under-hire the connective ones. The working taxonomy, taught through the question each role answers:

Role Question they own Typical background Course participants' likely fit Business owner / sponsor "Is this worth doing, and do I accept the risks?" Line leadership ★ Many participants are or will be this AI translator / product owner "What exactly should it do, and how do we know it works for the business?" Business + this course's skills — framing canvases, FVR scoring, threshold trade-offs ★★ The course's signature destination role Data steward / owner "Is the data known, owned, quality-managed, permitted?" Operations, records, compliance ★ Natural fit for records/compliance professionals Data scientist / analyst "What pattern is in the data, and how good is the model?" Statistics, computing (SDA-DSC track) Pathway option via FND-103/104 AI/ML engineer "How does it run reliably in production?" Software engineering (SDA-AIE track) Pathway option via FND-103/104 Governance / risk reviewer "Should it run at all, under what controls, answerable to whom?" Risk, audit, legal (deepened in FND-105) ★ Natural fit for risk/audit professionals

Three teaching points carry the section. First, every Module 5 mitigation had a name attached — those names are these roles; a mitigation without a role is unstaffed. Second, the translator role is the national bottleneck: models and engineers can be hired or contracted; a person who can frame the problem (M1), read the outputs (M2), interrogate the chain (M3), set the GenAI rules (M4), and score the case (M5) inside their own domain cannot — they must be grown, and this course is deliberately the first step of growing them. Third, roles are hats, not headcount: in a small unit one person wears three hats — the failure is not merging them but leaving one unworn (the chatbot that died ownerless in the Bunyan case was a role-gap incident, not a technology incident).

docs.title: 4. Placing yourself: the personal pathway
docs.text:
The course closes its teaching arc where stackable design intends: each participant leaves with a chosen next step, justified by their role fit —

  • SDA-FND-102 (Data Governance, Ethics & PDPL essentials path) — for participants whose energy peaked at Module 3's "permitted?" test, the chain map, and Module 5's risk column: the governance, stewardship, and compliance-facing professionals. (SDA-FND-101 unlocks FND-102 directly; FND-105, the security-facing module, is also unlocked by this badge.)
  • SDA-FND-103 (Programming & computational foundations path) — for participants — often fresh graduates — who want the builder track: FND-103 opens the doors to FND-104 (Python for data/AI) and onward to the AI Engineer (SDA-AIE-1xx) and Data Scientist (SDA-DSC-1xx) practitioner modules.
  • Staying business-side is also a pathway: the translator/sponsor roles deepen through the Foundations Certificate (SDA-FND-101→105 complete, 17 days), which is itself the prerequisite backbone of both role-track practitioner certificates — the participant who completes it holds the entry credential of the entire academy.

The instrument is the one-page pathway plan (Worked Example 3): role today, role in two years, next module, and the first workplace act of literacy ("the Monday action") — because a course that ends without a Monday action was a lecture, not training.

docs.title: 5. Common mistakes and organisational considerations
docs.text:
1. Strategy tourism. Quoting NSDAI in slide decks without the implication column — alignment claimed, never operationalised. Antidote: V2 scoring discipline; name the pillar and the changed behaviour.
  2. Hiring the famous role first. Five data scientists, no data steward, no translator: expensive people cleaning data they don't own for problems nobody framed. Diagnose gaps with the six-role map before the first requisition.
  3. Literacy as a one-off event. A single course (even this one) decays without practice structures — communities of practice, dossier reviews at idea stage, the scorecard in the funding workflow. The organisational ask participants take home: institutionalise the artefacts, not the memory.
  4. Treating national alignment as government-only. Private-sector participants sometimes bench this module; the correction: PDPL binds them, NDMO patterns reach them through partners and procurement, sector programmes fund them, and the talent market is shaped by the workforce pillar either way.
  5. The unworn hat. Small teams merging roles is fine; the audit question is whether every question in the role table has a name that answers it — for the participant's dossier use case, literally, in writing (Dossier §6 asks).
  6. Pathway drift. Choosing the next module by fashion ("everyone says Python") rather than role fit; the pathway plan's two-year role line exists to anchor the choice.

Gap severity Consequence if unfilled First move Business owner ✓ Operations director — — Confirm risk acceptance in writing Translator / product owner ✗ (nobody) Critical Requirements drift; model answers the wrong question well Develop internally — send two ops analysts through this pathway Data steward Partial (IT "owns databases") High "Permitted?" and quality questions have no answerer Formal stewardship per NDMO-aligned policy Data scientist Contracted Low (for now) Vendor dependence — acceptable at pilot stage Revisit at scale-up ML engineer ✗ Medium Pilot cannot become production Hire after fix-first phase, not before Governance reviewer ✓ Risk dept (untrained in AI) Medium Reviews rubber-stamp or reflex-block FND-102/105 pathway for one risk officer

docs.title: Worked Example 4 — Institutionalising the literacy (the 90-day checklist for unit heads)
docs.text:
For the many participants who lead teams, the module's mistake #3 ("literacy as a one-off event") gets its antidote as a checklist — which course artefact becomes which standing practice, in what order:

Days Move Artefact institutionalised Cost Evidence it took hold 1–14 Decision memos attached to the unit's two most consequential recurring decisions Module 3 memo (4 sentences) Minutes per decision Memos exist and get read back in the next meeting 1–30 The framing canvas required before any "we should use AI for…" conversation proceeds Module 1 canvas, box-1 technology ban One page per idea Solution-first ideas arrive pre-converted into problems 15–45 Five-question protocol run once on every standing dashboard; findings logged Module 3 protocol card One meeting per dashboard At least one metric definition corrected or one feed freshness flagged 30–60 Team GenAI policy adopted (Module 4 model text), owner named, signature rule in effect Task-fit matrix + data gate One page + one briefing Verification passes visible; zero personal data in prompts on spot-check 45–90 FVR screening inserted where AI/automation ideas meet money (however informal the current process) Module 5 scorecard + verdict letters One hour per idea First fix-first or decline letter sent — and received without damage 90 Role-map review of the unit against the six hats Module 6 role strip One session The unworn hat has a name against it, or a development plan

The sequencing logic is deliberate and worth stating: the cheap, personal artefacts (memo, canvas) go first because they build the habit and the credibility; the political artefacts (scorecard at the money gate, role map) go last because they spend that credibility. A unit head who attempts the sequence in reverse — leading with the scorecard — is asking colleagues to accept a gate from someone who has not yet demonstrated the discipline personally. Ninety days, six moves, zero budget: the course's answer to "but will any of this survive contact with the office?"

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 6 — Situate the Use Case, Choose the Path
docs.text:
Objective Complete the six-role map and NSDAI one-pager for the dossier use case, position oneself on the role landscape, and commit to a justified next module and a Monday action (Dossier §6) Duration 20 minutes (Day 2 Hour 4 express, immediately after Lab 5) + 5 minutes inside the capstone hour for the pathway commitment wall Setup Role-map strips, NSDAI pillar cards (bilingual), pathway map poster (the SDAIA Academy stackability diagram), commitment wall with three lanes (FND-102 / FND-103 / Foundations-Certificate-complete)

Instructions & tasks

  1. (7 min) Role map. Fill the six-role strip for your use case: a name, a hat-wearer, or "GAP" against each role. Mark the two most consequential gaps and write the first move for each (hire / develop / assign / formalise).
  2. (6 min) NSDAI one-pager. Using the pillar cards, complete the alignment table — pillars touched, how concretely, and the dossier page that evidences each row. Rows without evidence stay blank; blank is honest.
  3. (4 min) Position yourself. One line: role today → role in two years. Then select your next module and write the role-fit justification sentence.
  4. (3 min) Monday action. Write it to the standard: specific, dated, artefact-producing. Your partner applies the test: "Will I be able to see that you did it?"
  5. (In capstone hour) Commitment wall. Place your named card in your pathway lane during capstone assembly; the wall is photographed and shared with the cohort as the course's closing image.

Expected output 

Role strip: 6/6 rows filled (names or explicit GAPs), 2 gaps prioritised with first moves
One-pager: ≥ 2 pillar rows with dossier-page evidence (typical: 3), no evidence-free rows
Position + pathway: role line + next module + one-sentence role-fit justification
Monday action: passes the partner visibility test
Commitment wall: 100% of cohort carded into a lane

Troubleshooting guidance

Symptom Cause Fix Every role marked GAP (small-team despair) Headcount reading of the role table Hats, not headcount: whose name answers each question, even part-time? GAP means unworn, not unhired One-pager fills all five pillars enthusiastically Strategy tourism reflex Apply the evidence rule; two honest rows beat five hollow ones — say it exactly that way Participant torn between FND-102 and FND-103 Genuine dual fit (common in fresh graduates) The two-year role line decides: govern-and-translate → 102; build → 103. Both remain open — stackability means no wrong door Monday action is a resolution ("be more data-driven") Abstraction habit Enforce the standard: which dashboard, which date, which artefact? Rework until visible Private-sector participant disengages ("NSDAI is government") Scope misreading PDPL binds them; the talent market and sector programmes reach them; have them fill the regulatory + skills rows first

Instructor notes. This lab runs hot on time — the strips and cards are designed for speed, and the discipline is protecting task 4: the Monday action is the single highest-transfer artefact of the entire course, and it deserves its full three minutes plus the partner test. The commitment wall is deliberately public and photographed: cohort-visible commitments survive contact with the office at roughly twice the rate of private ones. Fast finishers: run the role-gap diagnosis (Worked Example 2 format) for their organisation as a whole, not just their use case.

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz (5 questions) 1. State NSDAI's ambition in one sentence of your own words. → (Model answer) Make Saudi Arabia one of the world's leading data-and-AI nations — in talent, investment, adoption, and regulation — as an engine of Vision 2030. 2. A question about whether patient data may feed a new dashboard routes to whom, under what law? → The data steward/owner, under PDPL (with NDMO-aligned classification for public entities). 3. Which role owns "what exactly should it do, and how do we know it works for the business?" → The AI translator / product owner. 4. Why is the translator called the national bottleneck? → Models and engineers can be hired or contracted; domain-embedded translators must be grown from within — which takes exactly this kind of training at scale. 5. What makes a Monday action valid in this course? → Specific, dated, artefact-producing — visible to a colleague.

Pillar snap. Instructor reads eight organisational actions ("we published our datasets in the national open-data portal", "we added data-literacy to all job descriptions"…); participants snap the matching pillar card. 90 seconds.

The unworn hat hunt. Given three one-paragraph mini-scenarios of troubled AI initiatives, name the unworn role hat in each. (Answers: steward, translator, governance reviewer.)

Pathway pitch. Sixty seconds, to a partner: "my next module, and why it fits my two-year role line." Partner may veto fashion-based reasoning once.

Discussion questions. - Your organisation's next requisition can fund one role. Using your own role map: which, and what evidence from your dossier justifies it? - What would it take for the FVR scorecard and the decision memo to become standing procedure in your unit — and who has to say yes?

docs.title: Case Study — Six Hires, No Team: Building AI Capability at Kahraba Utilities
docs.text:
Scenario. Kahraba Utilities (regional power distribution, 4,500 staff) commits to an AI programme after a successful predictive-maintenance vendor pilot on substation transformers. Leadership approves six technical hires. Twelve months later: five data scientists and one ML engineer are on payroll, three proofs-of-concept are "95% done," nothing is in production, the maintenance department has quietly stopped attending project meetings, and the board asks where the value went.

Business context. The Kingdom's utility sector sits squarely in NSDAI's priority-adoption lane; the board's original enthusiasm was strategy-aligned and sincere. The new hires are genuinely skilled. The failure is structural, and its diagnosis is this module's role map.

Technical challenge. Diagnose the capability gap without blaming the people hired, and re-sequence the programme: which roles, which order, which development-versus-hire decisions.

Constraints. No additional headcount this year — gaps must close by assignment and development; the maintenance department's trust must be rebuilt (they experienced the PoCs as "data people asking us to label failures for free"); transformer telemetry includes no personal data, but workforce-scheduling data (a proposed second use case) does — a PDPL boundary the programme crossed casually in a workshop, which legal flagged; the board wants a credible plan in 30 days.

Solution approach (facilitate, don't lecture). The role-map diagnosis participants should produce: business owner — nominally the CTO, actually nobody who owned maintenance outcomes (the maintenance director was never made sponsor); translator — GAP, the central finding: nobody converted "transformer health" into a framed problem with a baseline, a threshold owner, and an integration path into the existing work-order system, so five data scientists optimised models against a question no one had costed; data steward — GAP: telemetry ownership split across OT and IT, quality unknown, the §3 chain never mapped; governance reviewer — assigned late, reflex-blocked the scheduling use case instead of reshaping it (the PDPL flag becomes a routing lesson, not a stop sign). The 30-day plan the case builds toward: make the maintenance director the sponsor with written risk acceptance; develop two senior maintenance engineers as translators (this exact course as step one — the strategy's workforce pillar applied to itself); formalise telemetry stewardship; freeze two of three PoCs (FVR fix-first verdicts on the evidence in the pack) and drive the strongest one through a shadow phase into the work-order system; re-score the scheduling use case with a human checkpoint and a proper PDPL basis before any retry. The closing observation the room should reach unprompted: the SAR-expensive part of the programme was healthy — the missing parts were the two roles that cannot be hired, only grown.

Discussion questions. 1. Rank the six roles by how much their absence explains the twelve lost months. Defend the top two. 2. Why did the maintenance department disengage, and which artefacts from this course (canvas, chain map, threshold sheet) would have kept them at the table? 3. The governance reviewer's reflex-block on the scheduling use case: right instinct, wrong move? Redesign it as a reshape using Module 5's levers. 4. Map Kahraba's recovery plan to NSDAI pillars with the evidence rule enforced — which rows can it honestly fill today? 5. Draft the board's one-paragraph summary in decision-memo form: decision, evidence, limit, review point.

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
1. NSDAI pillars with implication lane — Purpose: module anchor. Elements: five pillar columns, each with its plain-language name (EN/AR) above and its "inside your organisation" implication below; Vision 2030 as the roofline. Style: temple/roofline motif, course palette. Designer description: "Five columns holding a roof labelled Vision 2030; under each column a drawer slides out showing the workplace implication."
  2. Institutional routing map — Elements: SDAIA, NDMO, PDPL, sector regulators as address plates; three example questions travelling dotted routes to the right address. Style: metro-map simplicity, four stations.
  3. The six-role wheel — Elements: six roles around a use case at the hub, each with its owned question; hat icons to reinforce hats-not-headcount; the translator segment highlighted as the bottleneck. Style: wheel diagram, reused in the capstone brief.
  4. SDAIA Academy pathway map — Elements: SDA-FND-101 (highlighted, "you are here") → FND-102/FND-103 arrows → FND-104/105 → Foundations Certificate → both role tracks (AIE / DSC practitioner entry); badge icons at each node. Style: the course's closing slide and the commitment wall's backdrop.

docs.title: Simulations
docs.text:
1. The routing drill — Setup: nine question cards (data-sharing request, citizen-data reuse, credit-model explainability, open-data publication…) and four address mats on the floor. Expected behaviour: participants route cards to institutions in 60 seconds; two cards are deliberately ambiguous (route to two addresses) and spark the debrief. Learning objective: governance questions have addresses; ambiguity is normal and is itself information.
  2. The hiring committee — Setup: groups receive Kahraba's situation pre-diagnosis plus six CVs (one per role, all strong). They may "hire" only two. Expected behaviour: groups that hire the famous roles re-create the case's failure in discussion; groups that hire translator + steward must defend the unglamorous choice. Learning objective: capability is a system; sequence beats star power.

docs.title: Title: The AI Use-Case Evaluation Dossier and Pitch
Project Scenario
docs.text: You are the newly appointed AI translator for your own organisation (or for your chosen scenario-pack organisation). Leadership has heard about your training and hands you the assignment every literate professional eventually receives: "We keep hearing we should be doing AI. Take one real opportunity, evaluate it properly, and tell us — should we fund it?" Your answer is the AI Use-Case Evaluation Dossier: the six-section case file you have been building across both days, completed, evidenced, and defended in a three-minute pitch to a funding committee played by your peers and instructor. The capstone also absorbs the course's hands-on strand (catalog topic 7): your dossier must contain the evidence of your own tool exploration — assistant sessions, the no-code model you trained and broke, the model outputs and confusion matrix you read — because an evaluator who has never touched the tools is an evaluator by hearsay.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Mandatory (maps to grading rubric):

  1. Framing (LO1, LO2): Dossier §1 complete — technology-free problem statement, decision and actor identified, AI job number and generation tagged with justification, success defined in business numbers.
  2. Model sketch and output literacy (LO1, LO2, LO6): Dossier §2 complete — learning type, label source, five leakage-checked features, both mistakes priced, precision-vs-recall position with a named threshold owner, measured (or honestly estimated) baseline.
  3. Data value chain (LO3): Dossier §3 complete — six-link map with owners (or explicit "?"), weakest link flagged with checkable evidence, six quality tests scored, PDPL/permission box answered, one four-sentence decision memo.
  4. Generative-AI check (LO1, LO5): Dossier §4 complete — language-task vs prediction-task verdict, matrix placement with verification step, data-gate answer, one written RTCF prompt.
  5. FVR evaluation (LO4, LO5): Dossier §5 complete — nine anchored scores with dossier-page evidence lines, column totals with gate check, 2–3 attached failure modes, ≥ 1 mitigation with named owner and a re-scored rating, red-team amendments visible in second colour, committed recommendation (fund / fix-first / decline / reshape+fund).
  6. Roles and national context (LO4): Dossier §6 complete — six-role map with gaps and first moves, NSDAI one-pager obeying the evidence rule, personal pathway line and next module, Monday action passing the visibility test.
  7. Hands-on evidence (topic 7, LO6): appended exhibits — Lab 1 assistant screenshots, Lab 2 v1/v2 model screenshots with the one-sentence bias diagnosis, the hand-computed confusion-matrix worksheet, Lab 4 caught-hallucination capture with the check that caught it.
  8. The pitch (all LOs): three minutes to the committee — problem, evidence highlights, recommendation, and one risk you are not able to retire — followed by two minutes of committee questions.

One extension (choose at least one): - Second-opinion scoring: score one additional use case from the Bunyan or Al-Manar packs and compare verdicts in a half-page note - The counter-dossier: a half-page honest case against your own recommendation (the strongest opposing argument, steel-manned) - Bilingual executive summary: the dossier's one-page summary produced in both Arabic and English - The 90-day plan: if funded, the first 90 days — milestones, roles activated, and the two metrics reviewed at day 90 - Tool comparison note: run your §4 RTCF prompt through two different assistants and compare outputs against the three-check pass

docs.title: Architecture (target state)
docs.text:
THE DOSSIER (one evolving artefact, six sections + exhibits)

M1 Framing ──► M2 Model Sketch ──► M3 Chain Map ──► M4 GenAI Check ──► M5 FVR Score ──► M6 Roles/NSDAI
  §1 canvas       §2 canvas +         §3 map + six      §4 matrix +        §5 scorecard      §6 role map +
  job # + gen     grid reading        tests + memo      data gate          + red team        pathway plan
      │                │                  │                 │                  │                  │
      └────────────────┴────────┬─────────┴─────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────┘
                                ▼
              EXHIBITS: assistant sessions · no-code model v1/v2 · confusion-matrix
                        worksheet · caught hallucination · (extension artefact)
                                ▼
              3-MINUTE PITCH ──► committee Q&A ──► verdict recorded on portfolio wall

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
1. The complete six-section dossier (paper workbook or digital file), red-team amendments visible
  2. The exhibits appendix (screenshots and worksheets listed in requirement 7)
  3. The three-minute pitch, delivered live, with the committee Q&A survived
  4. The chosen extension artefact
  5. The pathway card placed on the commitment wall (Dossier §6 commitment made public)

docs.title: Milestones
docs.text: Milestone Due Gate M-A: §§1–2 complete with model exhibits End Day 1 Hour 4 Partner initials on leakage check M-B: §3 complete with memo passing cold read Day 2 Hour 1 Memo exchange test M-C: §4 complete with caught hallucination End Day 2 Hour 2 Screenshot evidence M-D: §5 frozen after red team End Day 2 Hour 4 ≥ 9/9 scores with evidence lines; amendments in second colour M-E: §6 + assembly + pitch Day 2 Hour 5 Rubric scoring live

docs.title: Grading Rubric (100 points)
docs.text:
Criterion Weight 90–100% band 70–89% band < 70% band Framing quality (§1) 10 Technology-free problem, crisp decision/actor, success in numbers Minor solution-first traces; success partly qualitative "We need AI/a chatbot"; no measurable success Model sketch & output literacy (§2 + grid exhibits) 15 Leakage-checked features, both mistakes priced, threshold position owned, baseline present; grid metrics computed correctly One thin element (e.g., estimated baseline unlabelled as estimate) Leaky features unexamined, no baseline, grid misread Data value chain (§3) 15 Six links with owners, credible weakest link, tests scored, PDPL box answered, memo passes cold read Map complete but weakest-link evidence vague Systems inventory instead of chain; permission ignored GenAI check (§4) 10 Correct task-type verdict, defensible matrix placement, data gate applied, usable RTCF prompt Placement defensible but verification step vague Matrix misapplied; data gate skipped FVR evaluation (§5) 25 Anchored scores with page-cited evidence, gates respected, case-specific failure modes, mitigation with owner that re-scores a rating, honest amendments Mostly anchored; 1–2 evidence lines weak; generic failure mode Adjective scoring, averaged gates, decoration mitigations, zero amendments Roles & national context (§6) 10 Honest role gaps with first moves, evidence-ruled NSDAI rows, valid Monday action Role map complete but first moves vague Strategy tourism; resolution-style Monday action Pitch & defence 15 Clear, timed, evidence-led; names the unretired risk; survives Q&A without contradicting the dossier Delivered but reads from dossier; Q&A partially deflected Overtime, evidence-free advocacy, contradicts own scorecard

Pass ≥ 70. Distinction ≥ 90. Extensions add up to +5 bonus (capped at 100) only if mandatory scope scores ≥ 80. The dossier (criteria 1–6) is scored from the frozen artefact collected before pitches begin; the pitch cannot repair a hollow dossier, by design.

docs.title: Assessment Criteria Notes for Instructors
docs.text:
• Grade from the artefact first, pitch second — the course's thesis is that evaluation quality lives in evidence, not eloquence. A charming pitch on an adjective-scored dossier caps at 69.
  • The honesty signals are gradeable: red-team amendments in second colour, explicit "?" marks on the chain map, the blank NSDAI row, the "estimated" label on an unmeasured baseline. Their absence under time pressure usually means performance, not perfection — probe one item live in Q&A.
  • A decline or fix-first recommendation, well evidenced, scores as highly as a fund — say this on Day 1 and repeat it before Lab 5, or the room will optimise for optimism.
  • Committee Q&A discipline: two questions per pitch, drawn from the red-team card deck, at least one aimed at the weakest evidence line you spotted in the frozen dossier.
  • Anti-pattern flags that cap criterion 5 at 70%: gates averaged into totals; a mitigation with no named owner; evidence lines citing opinions; scores unchanged through red team and Q&A.

docs.title: Bonus Tasks (for early finishers / distinction seekers)
docs.text:
1. Score the same use case twice — once as sponsor, once as risk reviewer — and write three sentences on where the two honest readings diverged
  2. Convert the dossier's §3 memo + §5 recommendation into a single one-page executive brief for a board member with five minutes
  3. Design the intake form your organisation would use to collect AI ideas so that they arrive pre-evidenced for FVR screening
  4. Run the Lab 2 no-code experiment on a second dataset class pair and write the one-line bias diagnosis for what v2 learned this time

docs.title: Quiz Bank (20 questions — use 10 per cohort, 15 min, closed book)
docs.text:
(Delivery: Quiz 1 on Day 2 Hour 1 draws from Q1–Q10 (M1–M3); Quiz 2 in Day 2 Hour 5 draws from Q11–Q20 (M4–M6). Swap items across cohorts.)

Q1. A system flags invoices above SAR 50,000 using a rule the finance team wrote. AI or automation, and what is the test? → Automation; "did a human write the rule, or did the system learn the pattern?" Q2. Order the nesting: generative AI, AI, deep learning, machine learning. → AI ⊃ machine learning ⊃ deep learning ⊃ generative AI. Q3. Give plain-language definitions of "model" and "training." → Model: the learned pattern packaged for reuse on new cases; training: showing the algorithm historical examples until it finds the pattern. Q4. Name three of the seven business jobs of AI with one example each. → e.g., forecast a number (Ramadan demand), predict a category (fraud), rank options (retention call list) — any three of the seven. Q5. Why does "95% accuracy" mean little for an event occurring 2% of the time? → A do-nothing model scores 98%; on rare events demand precision and recall, not accuracy. Q6. In the confusion matrix, which number answers "of the real no-shows, how many did we catch?" and what is it called? → True positives over all actual positives; recall. Q7. Who should set a model's decision threshold, and why? → The owner of both mistakes' costs (business side, informed by the data team) — the threshold is a business policy, not a technical constant. Q8. Name the six links of the data value chain in order. → Collection, storage, processing, analysis, decision, action (+feedback). Q9. A flawless dashboard shows a number born four hours late at link 1. What is this effect called and why is it dangerous? → Laundering — bad data gains false authority as it travels; the polish hides the flaw. Q10. State the four sentences of a decision memo. → Decision; evidence with source and freshness; the main limit/uncertainty; the review point. Q11. What single thing does an LLM fundamentally do, and which failure mode follows directly from it? → Predicts plausible next text; hallucination — fluency without guaranteed truth. Q12. Name the four parts of the RTCF prompt pattern. → Role, task, context, format. Q13. A task is high error cost and hard to verify. What quadrant, and what must happen before any GenAI task regardless of quadrant? → NEVER (unassisted); the data gate — what data enters the prompt and which tool tier permits it. Q14. State the signature rule. → AI drafts, humans sign — and the signer verifies. Q15. Why are FVR column totals never merged into one grand total? → A gate-level risk (R1/R3 ≤ 2) hides inside a healthy sum; columns answer different questions and gates are absolute. Q16. A use case scores F13/V12/R5. Name the move and one lever. → Reshape: e.g., human-in-the-loop on high-stakes cases, scope narrowing, or shadow-phase rollout — then re-score the changed rating. Q17. Name four of the eight failure modes. → Any four: data bias, drift, brittleness at the edges, feedback loops, hallucination, Goodhart's law, misuse/scope creep, accountability vacuum. Q18. What must a mitigation contain before it may change a score? → Changed behaviour — who does what, on which cases, with what evidence — plus a named owner. Q19. Name three of the six workforce roles and the question each owns. → e.g., translator ("what exactly should it do and how do we know it works?"), data steward ("is the data known, owned, quality-managed, permitted?"), governance reviewer ("should it run at all, under what controls?"). Q20. Your colleague wants to paste a citizen's complaint (with name and ID) into a public AI assistant "to draft a reply faster." What do you say, citing which law and which course rule? → Stop — personal data may not enter an unapproved tool tier; PDPL governs the processing/transfer, and the data gate precedes the task-fit matrix.

docs.title: Practical Assessments
docs.text:
PA-1 — Use-case evaluation exercise, milestone strand (across both days): the dossier milestones M-A through M-D (partner-verified leakage check, cold-read memo, caught hallucination, red-teamed frozen scorecard). Scored on: artefact completeness (40%), evidence quality — pages cited, "?" marks honest, amendments visible (40%), verification behaviours performed (20%).

PA-2 — Use-case evaluation exercise, final strand (Day 2 Hour 5): the frozen dossier scored on the capstone rubric (criteria 1–6) plus the pitch and committee defence (criterion 7). This is the catalog's named assessment; the two strands together constitute it.

Scheduling note: there is no separate written exam beyond the two quizzes; the course's assessment weight rides on the use-case evaluation exercise, as specified in the catalog.

Pitch quick-score sheet (for live use during Day 2 Hour 5 — full rubric applied to the frozen dossier afterward):

Live signal ✓ / ✗ Notes Problem stated technology-free in the first 30 seconds At least two evidence points cited by dossier page, not memory Recommendation matches the frozen scorecard verdict The unretired risk named honestly (not a humble-brag) Q&A answered from evidence; "I don't know — I'd check §_" accepted as a strong answer Time: within 3:00 ± 15 s

Six checks, scored live in the margin while the committee questions run; any pitch with ≥ 5 checks and a rubric-clean dossier is distinction-track. The sheet exists so instructors never trade eye contact for note-taking during the course's closing minutes.

docs.title: Evaluation Criteria Summary
docs.text:
Component Weight Evidence Quiz 1 (M1–M3, 10 questions) 20% Closed-book sheet, Day 2 Hour 1 Quiz 2 (M4–M6, 10 questions) 20% Closed-book sheet, Day 2 Hour 5 Use-case evaluation exercise — milestone strand (PA-1) 20% Dossier milestones M-A…M-D with partner/instructor gates Use-case evaluation exercise — final dossier & pitch (PA-2) 40% Capstone rubric, artefact-first scoring

Entry badge issuance requires ≥ 70 overall and ≥ 70 on the use-case evaluation exercise (PA-1 + PA-2 combined). The badge counts toward all certificates and both role tracks; record each participant's declared next module (SDA-FND-102 / SDA-FND-103) with the badge recommendation.

docs.title: Preparation Checklist (T-minus 1 week)
docs.text:
• Verify browser access at the venue to: the no-code training tool, the sample BI dashboard workbook, and the approved AI assistant tier — from the participant network, not the presenter network
  • Re-run the hallucination-hunt question set against the current assistant version; refresh with backup questions if the model now refuses or answers correctly (this decays between deliveries — always check)
  • Re-train the v1/v2 no-code models yourself end-to-end; confirm the skewed set still produces the unmistakable v2 failure
  • Print (bilingual): dossier workbooks, framing/model/chain canvases, FVR scorecards with anchors, quality strips, memo cards, protocol cards, role strips, pillar/routing/red-team/task cards, glossary wallet cards
  • Print posters: AI family tree, seven jobs, ML loop, value chain, task-fit matrix, FVR scorecard, six-role wheel, pathway map; hang the portfolio wall and commitment wall lanes
  • Load the media pack: card-deck PDFs, seeded dashboard + answer key, chart-pairs, fake vendor video, annotated hallucination exhibit, case packs (Al-Manar, Tawasul, Al-Shifa, Diwan, Bunyan, Kahraba)
  • Rehearse the four set-pieces to time: the cold-open poll, the live no-code training, the 15-minute dashboard interrogation, the 20-minute Ramadan scoring
  • Prepare both quizzes (10 items each from the bank, swapped from the previous cohort) and the pitch-order draw cards
  • Confirm the scenario pack covers the expected cohort mix (government / banking / health / retail / industrial)

docs.title: Software Installation Checklist (participants, T-minus 2 days email)
docs.text:
• Nothing to install — the course is fully browser-based; bring a laptop or tablet with a modern browser
  • Test the three links in the welcome email (no-code tool, sample dashboard, assistant) and report any corporate-network block before Day 1
  • Create the free account for the no-code tool if the venue tier requires one (step-by-step with screenshots in the email)
  • Optional but encouraged: bring one real use-case idea from your workplace and, if easily available, one screenshot of a dashboard your team actually uses
  • Reminder: no real personal or confidential data will be used at any point — all course data is synthetic; do not bring exports of production systems

docs.title: Common Student Issues & Troubleshooting
docs.text: Issue Frequency Resolution Corporate device blocks the AI assistant or no-code tool High Test links T-2 days; venue Wi-Fi as fallback; instructor-projected shared session as last resort — every lab has a paper path "I'm not technical" anxiety, especially before Lab 2 High Reframe from Hour 1: this is a judgment course, not a maths course; the grid is counting and pricing; pair anxious participants with confident ones Solution-first use cases ("we want a chatbot") High The three-why drill at the framing canvas; box 1's technology ban is the standing fix Senior participants reluctant to have their idea red-teamed Medium Card protocol depersonalises the challenge; instructor red-teams their own worked example first, amending scores publicly Mixed Arabic/English cohort drifting into one language Medium Bilingual materials; let pairs work in either; require the pitch in the language of the participant's real workplace audience Assistant model behaves differently than the rehearsed script Medium Backup question sets + the canned annotated exhibit; teach the variability as content Participants without any workplace use case Medium Scenario pack assignment in Hour 1; pair them with someone from a similar sector Hour 4 Day 2 congestion (Lab 5 + M6 express) Medium Protect the Lab 5 scoring timebox with a visible timer; the M6 strips are designed for 20 minutes — do not let the role map become a discussion circle Phone use during theory blocks Low The interactivity density is the defence; if it persists, convert the next concept into a cold-call round

docs.title: Timing Recommendations
docs.text:
• Protect the four set-pieces and Lab 5 at full length; they carry the course's evidence-over-enthusiasm thesis.
  • If a cohort is strong: add the CV-screening room-scoring as a full exercise in Hour 3 Day 2, and pull bonus task 1 (sponsor-vs-reviewer double scoring) into the capstone hour.
  • If a cohort is weak: shorten Module 4's theory (the lab teaches it), and pre-fill the FVR evidence lines' page references (not the scores) on the sheets to reduce mechanical load — never pre-fill scores.
  • Hard rule: the capstone hour (Day 2 Hour 5) starts on time with dossiers frozen; cut discussion anywhere else, never pitch time. Three-minute pitches are enforced with a visible timer and a friendly bell.
  • Quiz 1 must end by minute 50 of Day 2 Hour 1 — running it last in the hour, after Lab 3 Part B, protects the lab from quiz spillover.

docs.title: Discussion Prompts (use during transitions)
docs.text:
1. "What is the most expensive decision your organisation made last year on a number nobody could trace to its source?"
  2. "Which meeting you attended this month would have gone differently if everyone in the room shared this course's vocabulary?"
  3. "Your organisation will adopt AI with or without literate professionals in the room. What changes about the outcome in each case?"
  4. "Who currently says 'no' to AI ideas in your organisation — and do they say it with evidence or with reflex? Which is more dangerous?"
  5. "If the dossier is the standard, what does last year's biggest technology decision look like in hindsight — which section would have caught the problem?"
  6. "The translator can't be hired, only grown. Who in your team would you grow, and what would it cost you not to?"

docs.title: Wrap-up (final day, last 15 minutes)
docs.text:
• Map each dossier section to its module on one slide — the course compressed to one image; participants photograph it.
  • The commitment wall reading: cohort totals per lane (FND-102 / FND-103 / Foundations Certificate track), photographed and shared to the cohort channel.
  • Three Monday actions read aloud by volunteers; the room applies the visibility test one last time.
  • Forward pointers, concretely: SDA-FND-102 for the governance-and-data path and SDA-FND-105 for security literacy (both build directly on §3's "permitted?" reflex and §5's risk column); SDA-FND-103 → FND-104 for the builder path into both role tracks; the Foundations Certificate (all five FND modules, 17 days) as the entry credential of the entire academy.
  • Collect: frozen dossiers (photograph or file), quiz sheets, and the pathway declarations; issue entry-badge recommendations within 5 working days.

End of instructor package. All activities are browser-based or paper-based by design; verify tool links, the hallucination question set, and the v2 skewed-set behaviour before each delivery — assistant and no-code tool behaviour changes between deliveries, and the course's set-pieces depend on rehearsed outcomes.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
A practical module on working productively and safely with generative-AI tools. Participants master prompt design patterns, output evaluation, and workflow integration for text, code, and data tasks. It equips every professional to use LLM-based assistants responsibly and effectively.

The course is built around a single evolving artefact: a personal Prompt Portfolio — a structured, evaluated, versioned collection of the participant's own working prompts. Every lab adds entries to the portfolio: limitation notes from probing the model, before/after pattern comparisons, refinement histories with rubric scores, workflow prompts for documents, analysis, and code, verification checklists, and a personal safe-use decision record. By the end of Day 2, each participant owns a portfolio they can take back to their desk and use on Sunday morning — and that portfolio is the capstone assessment. Nothing in this course is hypothetical: every prompt is written against realistic Saudi workplace tasks, tested live against a real assistant, evaluated against an explicit rubric, and improved at least once.

docs.text:
By the end of this course, participants will be able to:

  1. LO1 — Explain how large language models generate output and why they hallucinate
  2. LO2 — Design effective prompts using role, context, format, and few-shot patterns
  3. LO3 — Apply iterative prompt refinement to improve output quality and reliability
  4. LO4 — Evaluate generative-AI outputs for accuracy, bias, and appropriateness
  5. LO5 — Integrate generative-AI assistants into document, analysis, and coding workflows
  6. LO6 — Assess data-privacy and confidentiality risks when using AI tools
