Pass ≥ 70. Distinction ≥ 90. Extensions add up to +5 bonus (capped at 100) only if mandatory scope is ≥ 80.

docs.title: Assessment Criteria Notes for Instructors
docs.text:
• Grade from the artefacts first (re-run the pipeline, read the decision log and match rates, spot-run the notebook), the briefing second — the course's thesis is that the work should testify for itself.
  • Anti-pattern flags that cap a criterion at 70%: any merge without validate=; outliers trimmed without a verdict; a finding whose stratified check was skipped; satisfaction claims without coverage disclosure; group rankings without n.
  • Verify one claim live in the challenge round: pick a number from the executive summary and ask the team to trace it to the cell that produced it, within two minutes.
  • Panel composition: instructor + one guest playing the non-technical director; the director asks only plain-language questions — teams must answer without jargon (a graded communication behaviour).
  • The planted structures (Simpson's reversal, June 2024 outage, coverage break, non-random inspections) form the reference finding set; strong teams find 3–4 of them plus something the course team didn't plant — reward the latter explicitly.

docs.title: Bonus Tasks (for early finishers / distinction seekers)
docs.text:
1. Replicate the trailing-90-day municipality breach rate in pure SQL (window frame RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '90 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW minus current row) and reconcile against the pandas version
  2. Quantify the June 2024 outage's displaced demand with a counterfactual dow-expectation estimate and a stated uncertainty range
  3. Build the quality scorecard diff tool (extension 3) and run it against a provided "next quarter" extract with two new planted defects
  4. Draft the one-page NDMO-style data-quality disclosure that would accompany public release of the municipal rankings

docs.title: Quiz Bank (20 questions — use 10 per cohort, 15 min, closed book)
docs.text: Q1. WHERE satisfaction_score != 5 excludes which rows? → score = 5 and all NULL scores (three-valued logic). Q2. COUNT(*) vs COUNT(closed_at) — the difference means what? → total vs closed; the gap is the open backlog (and a completeness metric). Q3. Correct predicate for "all of March 2025"? → half-open range: >= '2025-03-01' AND < '2025-04-01'. Q4. LEFT JOIN then WHERE on a right-side column does what? → silently becomes INNER; move the condition to ON or accept INNER. Q5. Your 1:1 join returned more rows than the left table — first diagnostic? → group the right side by key, HAVING count(*) > 1. Q6. Why can't WHERE filter a window function? → windows evaluate after WHERE; wrap in a CTE and filter outside. Q7. LAG without PARTITION BY across regions causes what? → boundary bleed: each region's first row sees the previous region's last value. Q8. Name the three missingness mechanisms with one example each. → MCAR (flaky export), MAR (paper forms lack GPS), MNAR (angry citizens skip the survey). Q9. Why load a messy CSV with keep_default_na=False first? → to observe disguised missingness (sentinels, empty strings) before declaring it. Q10. Why is one permissive pd.to_datetime pass on mixed formats dangerous? → per-row day/month guessing corrupts silently; parse each format explicitly on its matched subset. Q11. Exact duplicate vs key conflict — the operational difference? → exact rows drop safely; same key + different values needs a stated resolution rule. Q12. Which merge argument catches unexpected cardinality, and what does it cost? → validate=; nothing. Q13. agg vs transform output shapes, and transform's SQL cousin? → per-group vs per-row; window functions. Q14. When is merge_asof correct where an exact-key merge is wrong? → effective-dated reference data ("what was in force at that time"). Q15. An int key column shows 1024.0 after a merge — cause and fix? → NaN forced float64; nullable Int64. Q16. Why is satisfaction_score banned as an SLA-breach feature? → collected after resolution — target-side leakage; violates decision-time availability. Q17. What does shift(1) do in a trailing history feature and what breaks without it? → excludes the current row's own outcome; without it each row leaks into itself. Q18. Naive full-data target encoding fails how? → the answer is smuggled into the question: inflated offline metrics, no production value. Q19. Mean 68h vs median 26h — what do you report for an operational SLA claim and why? → median (+ distribution/ECDF); the tail makes the mean unrepresentative. Q20. A group comparison flips direction after stratification — name the effect and the course rule that catches it. → Simpson's reversal; every aggregate group comparison gets a stratified counterpart before becoming a finding.

docs.title: Practical Assessments
docs.text:
PA-1 — SQL practical (30 min, Day 2 H5, individual): against a fresh scratch schema (same shape, different values), produce: one three-table aggregation with a grain comment, one top-N-per-group, one LAG-based change query, and one fan-out proof-and-fix. Scored: correctness of results (50%), grain/verification discipline (30%), readability (20%). Auto-checked against golden results; discipline scored by rubric.

PA-2 — Wrangling practical (30 min, Day 4 H5, individual): given a small messy CSV (6 planted defects) and a spine table, deliver a cleaning function with counts logged and a validated merge with match-rate report. Scored: defects found and treated (40%), pipeline reproducibility (30%), merge discipline (30%).

PA-3 — Capstone (rubric above): the EDA project with report — 40% of course grade. SQL labs + PA-1/PA-2 and lab completion — 60%.

docs.text:
Component Weight Evidence Lab completion (6 labs) 25% committed artefacts + checkpoint outputs PA-1 (SQL practical) 15% golden-result check + rubric PA-2 (wrangling practical) 10% rubric Quiz 10% 10-question selection Capstone: EDA project with report 40% rubric, artefact-first

Badge issuance (Foundation badge) requires ≥ 70 overall and capstone ≥ 70 and zero academic-integrity flags (identical decision logs or identical "original" findings across teams are checked). docs.title: Timing Recommendations
docs.text:
• Protect Lab 3 and Lab 6 at full length — quality discipline and the EDA loop are the module's soul; compress Module 4's reshaping drills (Section 2) if behind, never its merge discipline (Section 3).
  • If a cohort is strong: pull the SQL-only replication bonus into Day 2, and let Day 5 H3 start capstone drafting early.
  • If a cohort is weak: convert Lab 5's history-feature block to guided live-coding; never drop the leakage demo or the as-of audit — they are the course's thesis for the ML-bound.
  • Hard rule: capstone assembly (Day 5 H4) starts on time; cut discussion, not drafting time. Reports beat rehearsals — a rough briefing of solid findings outscores a polished briefing of thin ones, and the rubric reflects that.
  • The planted discoveries must be found, not announced. If by mid-Lab-6 no pair has the Simpson's reversal, nudge with the stratification-check rule, not the answer.

docs.title: Discussion Prompts (use during transitions)
docs.text:
1. "What is the most expensive wrong number you have seen survive into a leadership deck — and at which of this week's stages would it have died?"
  2. "Your database enforces types and keys; your CSV enforces nothing. What else in your organisation is a CSV pretending to be a database?"
  3. "The mean says 68 hours, the median says 26. Which number does the citizen feel — and which one goes in the press release?"
  4. "Who should own the master table once three teams depend on it — and what does your answer imply about whether analysts are engineers?"
  5. "A feature that predicts brilliantly offline and fails in production — whose failure is it: the model's, the feature's, or the process that let it through?"
  6. "If your EDA can only be trusted because you did it, what have you actually built?"

docs.title: Wrap-up (final day, last 15 minutes)
docs.text:
• Map each capstone requirement to the module that taught it (one slide: SQL → M1/M2, scorecard → M3, master table → M4, features → M5, findings & report → M6).
  • Forward pointers: SDA-FND-105 completes the Foundations Certificate; the Data Scientist track (SDA-DSC-111/112) assumes this module's EDA and wrangling discipline as its floor; the AI Engineer track (SDA-AIE-111) consumes the leakage and train/serve-consistency lessons directly; SDA-DSC-214 industrialises the pipeline thinking into Lakehouse-scale data engineering.
  • Collect: repository links, REPORT.pdf, DECISIONS.md; issue badge recommendations within 5 working days.
  • Close on the golden thread: the same 487,000 rows were, across five days, a database, a mess, a table, a feature source, and finally a brief on a decision-maker's desk — the journey is the job.

End of instructor package. All code samples target Python 3.12, pandas ≥ 2.2, PostgreSQL 16, SQLAlchemy ≥ 2.0, Matplotlib ≥ 3.8, Seaborn ≥ 0.13. Verify pinned versions in the course lock file before each delivery.

A governance-focused module aligning practice with Saudi national frameworks including PDPL, NDMO data standards, and SDAIA AI-ethics principles. Participants learn to assess fairness, transparency, privacy, and accountability across the AI lifecycle. The module prepares professionals to build and operate AI systems that are compliant and trustworthy by design.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
A governance-focused module aligning practice with Saudi national frameworks including PDPL, NDMO data standards, and SDAIA AI-ethics principles. Participants learn to assess fairness, transparency, privacy, and accountability across the AI lifecycle. The module prepares professionals to build and operate AI systems that are compliant and trustworthy by design.

The course is built around a single evolving artefact: the AI Governance File for "Ameen" (أمين) — a fictional benefit-eligibility scoring system operated by a fictional government body, the Social Support Authority (SSA). Every lab produces one section of that file: an ethics self-assessment and risk-tier record (Day 1), a PDPL/NDMO compliance checklist with a gap register (Day 1), a bias-audit report (Day 2), a privacy risk assessment and anonymisation plan (Day 2), a model card and audit-trail design (Day 3), and a risk register with a third-party AI assessment (Day 3). By the final afternoon each participant owns a complete, defensible governance file — the same dossier a real governance office would put in front of a review committee — and defends it in a panel-style capstone that doubles as the module's governance case analysis.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this course, participants will be able to:

  1. LO1 — Explain Saudi data-protection requirements (PDPL) and NDMO governance standards
  2. LO2 — Apply SDAIA AI-ethics principles across the AI system lifecycle
  3. LO3 — Analyze AI systems for bias, fairness, and disparate impact
  4. LO4 — Evaluate privacy risks and apply data-minimisation and anonymisation techniques
  5. LO5 — Design documentation, model cards, and audit trails for accountable AI
  6. LO6 — Assess third-party AI services for compliance and risk

docs.title: Day 1 — Principles and the Regulatory Baseline
docs.text: Hour Session Learning Objectives Delivery Mode Theory/Lab 1 Why AI systems fail governance review + course kickoff + meet "Ameen" Recognise how technically sound AI systems fail on fairness, privacy, and accountability grounds; tour the six governance artefacts of the course Interactive lecture + incident-story discussion 80/20 2 SDAIA AI-ethics principles and risk tiers (M1) The seven principles as practitioner obligations; risk-based classification of AI systems; lifecycle phases Lecture + classification walkthrough 70/30 3 Lab 1 — Ethics baseline for Ameen Classify Ameen's risk tier; score it against the seven principles; open the gap register Guided workshop (pairs) 10/90 4 PDPL essentials and NDMO standards (M2) Legal bases, data-subject rights, controller obligations, breach duties; NDMO domains and data classification Lecture + checklist walkthrough 70/30 5 Lab 2a — PDPL compliance checklist for Ameen Complete the PDPL checklist against the Ameen data-flow pack; draft the RoPA entry Guided workshop (pairs) 10/90

docs.title: Day 2 — Fairness and Privacy in Practice
docs.text: Hour Session Learning Objectives Delivery Mode Theory/Lab 1 Lab 2b — NDMO classification and gap register Classify Ameen's data assets to NDMO levels; consolidate Day-1 findings into the gap register; PA-1 compliance-assessment exercise (30 min) Workshop + timed assessment 20/80 2 Bias, fairness, and disparate impact (M3) Bias sources across the lifecycle; group fairness metrics; the 80% rule; impossibility trade-offs Lecture + worked metric walkthrough 70/30 3 Lab 3 — Bias audit of the Ameen model Compute approval rates, disparate-impact ratio, and error-rate gaps by group; write the bias-audit report Guided workshop (pairs, toolkit + spreadsheet) 10/90 4 Privacy-preserving data handling (M4) Minimisation, pseudonymisation vs anonymisation, k-anonymity, differential privacy in one slide, re-identification risk Lecture + anonymisation walkthrough 70/30 5 Lab 4 — Privacy risk assessment and anonymisation Score re-identification risk on the SSA research extract; apply generalisation/suppression to reach k ≥ 5; record utility loss Guided workshop (pairs) 10/90

docs.title: Day 3 — Accountability, Assurance, and the Governance File
docs.text: Hour Session Learning Objectives Delivery Mode Theory/Lab 1 Transparency, explainability, documentation (M5) + Lab 5 — Model card Documentation as accountability infrastructure; model cards; audit trails; complete the Ameen model card Micro-lecture + workshop 40/60 2 AI risk management and compliance workflows (M6) Risk registers; governance gates in the delivery workflow; assessing third-party AI services Lecture + vendor-pack dissection 60/40 3 Lab 6 — Risk register + third-party assessment Score Ameen's top risks; assess the "Bayan CX" LLM vendor pack against the third-party checklist; PA-2 governance case triage (30 min) Guided workshop + timed assessment 10/90 4 Capstone assembly — the Ameen Governance File Integrate all six sections; complete the self-audit checklist; prepare the committee briefing Project work 0/100 5 Capstone committee panels + assessment + wrap-up 7-minute governance-committee defenses; rubric-based peer + instructor scoring; path to role-track modules Panel presentations 20/80

docs.title: Instructor Guidance Notes (Delivery Plan Level)
docs.text:
• Golden thread: every module works the same system — Ameen at the SSA. Never introduce a throwaway example system for a lab; always evolve the Ameen Governance File. This is what makes the capstone achievable in Day 3 Hour 4: assembly, not creation.
  • Pace control: Labs 2a and 3 are the most overrun-prone (checklists invite rabbit-holes; metric arithmetic invites debugging). Publish checkpoint versions of every artefact (lab2-start.xlsx, lab2-solution.xlsx, …) on the shared drive so stragglers can fast-forward.
  • Pairing: rotate pairs each day. Pair a compliance/governance participant with a hands-on practitioner; the vocabulary transfer in both directions is the point of the mixed audience.
  • Environment strategy: primary = printed/spreadsheet templates plus a hosted notebook (bias-audit toolkit pre-installed) for Lab 3; fallback = pure-spreadsheet versions of every exercise (provided) so the course survives a no-Python cohort or a network outage. Verify both the week before delivery.
  • Language: deliver in English or Arabic; keep all governance artefacts (checklists, registers, model cards) in English for cross-review consistency, and note explicitly that real citizen-facing notices in the Kingdom must be published in Arabic (bilingual is best practice) — flag this wherever notices appear.
  • Prayer and break scheduling: each "hour" is 50 minutes of instruction + 10 minutes buffer; schedule the long break around Dhuhr. Day-3 afternoon is deliberately lighter on theory.
  • Assessment logistics: the compliance-assessment exercise (PA-1) is timed inside Day 2 Hour 1 and the case-triage (PA-2) inside Day 3 Hour 3 — collect artefacts immediately. Committee scoring happens live during Day 3 Hour 5; collect each pair's assembled governance file at the end of Hour 4 so panels can be sequenced and files spot-checked before presentations begin.
  • Sensitivity note: all datasets are synthetic and all organisations fictional. Say this on Day 1 Hour 1 and print it on every dataset — participants from government entities must never be put in the position of discussing their employer's real compliance posture in class.

docs.title: Module 1 — The Responsible-AI Landscape and SDAIA Ethics Principles
Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. Most AI governance failures are not caused by malicious teams but by teams that treated ethics as a poster on the wall rather than a set of testable obligations. This module gives participants the map: the global responsible-AI landscape, the SDAIA AI-ethics principles as the Kingdom's operative framework, risk-based classification of AI systems, and the discipline of turning each principle into concrete controls at specific lifecycle phases. Everything later in the course — PDPL checklists, bias audits, model cards, risk registers — is a mechanism for one of these principles.

Business relevance. The National Strategy for Data & AI positions the Kingdom as a global AI leader, and that ambition is conditional on trust: government entities adopting AI at scale, citizens consenting to data-driven services, and international partners recognising Saudi governance standards. Organisations that can demonstrate principled AI practice win government contracts, pass procurement reviews, and avoid the reputational incidents that have set peer programs back years elsewhere. For practitioners, principle literacy is now interview material and review-gate material in every serious Saudi AI employer.

Industry use cases. - A ministry's AI-procurement committee requires every proposal to state which SDAIA risk tier the system falls into and how each of the seven principles is addressed — vendors who cannot answer are disqualified before technical evaluation. - A bank's model-risk function maps the SDAIA principles onto its existing SAMA model-governance framework so one evidence pack serves two reviewers. - A health-tech startup classifies its triage-assist tool as high-risk early, budgets for human-oversight features from the first sprint, and passes its hospital client's ethics review on the first attempt.

Expected competencies. After this module a participant can name and explain the seven SDAIA AI-ethics principles, classify an AI system into a risk tier and defend the classification, map principles to lifecycle phases and concrete controls, run a structured ethics self-assessment, and open a governance gap register that survives audit.

docs.title: Learning Objectives (mapped)
docs.text: # Objective Maps to 1.1 Describe the responsible-AI landscape: why governance failures happen and what frameworks exist globally and in the Kingdom LO2 1.2 Explain each of the seven SDAIA AI-ethics principles as a practitioner obligation with an example control LO2 1.3 Classify an AI system into a risk tier using a documented, reviewable decision record LO2 1.4 Map principles to AI lifecycle phases and identify which controls belong to which phase LO2, LO5 1.5 Conduct an ethics self-assessment and open a prioritised gap register LO2, LO5

docs.title: 1. Why technically sound AI systems fail governance review
docs.text:
An AI system can be accurate, fast, and profitable — and still be ungovernable. The failure modes worth naming in class, because every one of them recurs in the labs:

  • Unexamined training data: a benefit-eligibility model trained on historical decisions inherits every historical inequity in those decisions; accuracy against biased labels is bias, formalised.
  • Silent scope creep: a model built to prioritise inspection visits gets reused to deny licences — same scores, different consequences, no re-assessment. Purpose limitation is an AI problem, not just a data problem.
  • Accountability vacuum: when a citizen asks "why was I rejected?", no one can answer — the vendor points at the ministry, the ministry points at the model, and the model has no documentation. The absence of a named accountable owner is itself a finding.
  • Privacy debt: features were added because they lifted AUC by 0.4%, not because they were necessary; three years later the retention review finds sensitive attributes nobody can justify holding.
  • Un-monitorable deployment: the system works at launch, drifts for two years, and nobody notices because "monitoring" meant uptime, not fairness or accuracy over subgroups.

Instructor note: open with 5 minutes of participant-sourced examples ("what's the worst AI decision you've heard of?") before showing the canonical international incidents (recruitment screening bias, exam-grading algorithms, welfare-fraud scoring scandals — describe them generically). Participants will supply 80% of the failure taxonomy unprompted; your job is to name the categories.

docs.title: 2. The global landscape in one map
docs.text:
Participants need just enough of the global picture to place the Saudi framework in context:

Framework Type One-line practitioner takeaway OECD AI Principles (2019) Intergovernmental principles The common ancestor: human-centred values, transparency, robustness, accountability — most national frameworks, including the Kingdom's, are interoperable with it NIST AI RMF 1.0 (2023) Voluntary risk framework Four functions — Govern, Map, Measure, Manage — a useful verb set for structuring an AI risk program EU AI Act Binding regulation (phased application) Risk-tiered obligations: prohibited / high-risk / limited / minimal; the reference point for vendors selling into Europe ISO/IEC 42001 (2023) Certifiable management-system standard "ISO 9001 for AI" — an AI management system (AIMS) that auditors can certify; increasingly requested in procurement SDAIA AI Ethics Principles National framework (KSA) The operative framework for this course: seven principles, risk-based, lifecycle-mapped

The convergence matters more than the differences: every serious framework demands risk-proportionate controls, documented accountability, fairness evidence, privacy protection, and human oversight. Teams that build these once can answer to any of the frameworks.

docs.title: 3. The seven SDAIA AI-ethics principles as practitioner obligations
docs.text:
The SDAIA AI Ethics Principles are the Kingdom's reference framework for anyone developing, procuring, or operating AI systems. Teach each principle in three parts: what it demands, what artefact evidences it, and where in this course it is operationalised.

# Principle What it demands of a practitioner Evidence artefact Where in this course 1 Fairness Identify protected/affected groups; measure and mitigate unjustified disparate outcomes across them Bias-audit report M3, Lab 3 2 Privacy & Security Process only necessary personal data, protect it across the lifecycle, honour data-subject rights Privacy risk assessment; PDPL checklist M2, M4, Labs 2 & 4 3 Humanity Keep meaningful human agency: human oversight for consequential decisions, no manipulation, human dignity preserved Human-oversight design record M1, M5 4 Social & Environmental Benefits Justify the system by net benefit; consider societal and environmental externalities, not only sponsor KPIs Benefit/impact statement in the governance file M1, Capstone 5 Reliability & Safety The system performs as intended under expected and reasonably foreseeable conditions; failure modes are known and bounded Evaluation results; monitoring plan M5, M6 6 Transparency & Explainability Affected people know AI is involved; decisions can be explained at the level the audience needs Model card; decision notices M5, Lab 5 7 Accountability & Responsibility A named human/role answers for the system at every lifecycle stage; audit trails make reconstruction possible RACI; audit-trail design; risk register M5, M6

Three teaching emphases:

  1. Principles conflict, and governance is the discipline of resolving conflicts explicitly. Transparency can tension with privacy (explaining a decision may reveal another person's data); fairness interventions can tension with reliability (constraining a model changes its error profile). Mature teams write the trade-off down and have the accountable owner sign it — that written record is the difference between a defensible judgement and negligence.
  2. Every principle needs an artefact. "We care about fairness" is not evidence; a dated bias-audit report with named reviewers is. The course's governance file is precisely the artefact set for the seven principles.
  3. Principles apply to bought systems as much as built ones. Procuring a third-party service does not outsource the obligation (M6 makes this concrete).

docs.title: 4. Risk-based classification of AI systems
docs.text:
Both the SDAIA framework and international practice scale obligations to risk. Teach a four-tier working model:

Tier Description Examples Governance consequence Unacceptable Systems whose intended use violates rights or law Social scoring of citizens' general behaviour; manipulative targeting of vulnerable groups Do not build or buy; escalate if requested High risk Consequential effects on individuals' rights, safety, access to essential services Benefit eligibility (Ameen), hiring screening, credit scoring, medical triage, law-enforcement uses Full governance file: impact assessment, bias audit, human oversight, documentation, monitoring, periodic review Limited risk Meaningful interaction or influence, limited individual consequence Citizen-facing chatbots, recommendation systems, productivity assistants on internal data Transparency obligations (disclose AI involvement), baseline documentation, proportionate review Minimal risk Negligible effect on individuals Spam filtering, predictive maintenance on equipment, internal document search Inventory entry + standard engineering hygiene

The classification decision itself must be documented and reviewable: a one-page decision record stating the system's purpose, affected population, decision consequence, autonomy level (decides / recommends / informs), and the resulting tier with rationale. Classification is revisited whenever purpose, population, data, or autonomy changes — scope creep re-opens the question (failure mode #2 above).

The classification heuristic that survives contact with reality: ask what happens to a specific person when the system is wrong in each direction. A false rejection in Ameen means an eligible family loses support — that single sentence justifies the high-risk tier faster than any scoring matrix.

docs.title: 5. Principles across the AI lifecycle
docs.text:
The SDAIA framework expects principles to be applied across the AI lifecycle, not bolted on at the end. Use a four-phase working lifecycle and make participants place controls in phases:

Lifecycle phase Key governance questions Example controls Plan & design Is the purpose legitimate and proportionate? Which tier? Who is accountable? What data is truly necessary? Risk-tier decision record; benefit statement; data-minimisation review; DPIA trigger check Prepare data Is the data lawfully sourced, representative, classified, and minimised? RoPA entry; NDMO classification; representativeness analysis; datasheet for the dataset Build & validate Does the model meet accuracy and fairness targets? Are limits documented? Bias audit; evaluation on subgroups; model card drafted; human-oversight design Deploy & monitor Do real-world outcomes stay within tolerances? Can decisions be reconstructed? When do we retire? Audit trail; drift and fairness monitoring; incident and appeal channels; periodic re-assessment; decommissioning plan

Two consequences matter most:

  1. Governance effort front-loads. The cheapest place to fix a fairness problem is the purpose statement; the most expensive is production. Teams that skip Plan & Design controls pay for them later with interest.
  2. Every phase leaves evidence. The governance file is not written at the end — it accretes phase by phase. This is exactly how the course's labs are sequenced.

docs.title: 6. Common mistakes & operational considerations
docs.text:
Mistakes to name explicitly (each is seeded somewhere in the course materials): 1. Ethics-washing: publishing principles without artefacts, owners, or gates. Detectable in one question: "show me the last decision this framework changed." 2. Classification by convenience: rating a system limited-risk because high-risk is expensive. The decision record and its reviewability are the antidote. 3. One-time assessment: running the ethics review at launch and never again, while data, population, and purpose drift. 4. Principle-to-slide mapping instead of principle-to-control mapping: a deck that quotes all seven principles but a delivery workflow with zero gates. 5. Accountability diffusion: "the committee is responsible" — committees advise; named roles answer. Every artefact in this course carries an owner field for this reason. 6. Copying foreign frameworks wholesale: importing an EU-shaped process that ignores PDPL specifics, NDMO classification levels, and Saudi institutional structures — locally non-compliant and organisationally alien.

Operational considerations. Position the governance function as an enabler with teeth: it should make the right path the fast path (templates, checklists, pre-approved patterns) while holding real veto power at defined gates. Budget governance effort proportionate to tier — a minimal-risk system should clear review in minutes with an inventory entry; reserving human attention for high-risk systems is itself a governance design decision.

docs.title: Worked Example 1 — Risk-tier decision record for Ameen (filled)
docs.text:
AI SYSTEM RISK-TIER DECISION RECORD                    SSA-GOV-001 v1.0
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
System name:        Ameen — benefit-eligibility scoring
Owner (accountable): Director, Benefits Operations (named individual in the real file)
Purpose:            Score applications to the SSA family-support programme to
                    prioritise caseworker review and recommend eligibility
Affected population: All applicant households (~1.2M applications/year)
Decision consequence: Recommendation feeds caseworker decision on monthly
                    financial support; false rejection delays or denies
                    support to an eligible family
Autonomy level:     RECOMMENDS (caseworker decides; >92% of recommendations
                    accepted unchanged — treat as de-facto deciding)
Special categories: Household income, family composition, disability status
                    (sensitive), region, nationality
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
TIER: HIGH RISK
Rationale: consequential effect on access to essential support; sensitive
data; scale; high de-facto autonomy given caseworker acceptance rates.
Consequences: full governance file required (impact assessment, bias audit,
model card, human-oversight design, audit trail, annual re-assessment).
Review triggers: any change to purpose, data sources, model family,
population, or autonomy level; else annual.
Reviewed by: AI Governance Office        Date: (course date)    Next: +12m

Teaching point: the parenthetical on autonomy is the record's most important line. A "recommendation" system with a 92% acceptance rate is a decision system wearing a disclaimer — governance classifies by effect, not by label.

docs.title: Worked Example 2 — Ethics self-assessment scorecard (template + filled excerpt)
docs.text:
Scoring scale: 0 = absent · 1 = ad-hoc/undocumented · 2 = documented but unevidenced or unowned · 3 = documented, evidenced, owned, and reviewed.

Principle Probe question (one of 3–5 per principle) Score Evidence / gap Fairness Has disparate impact been measured across defined groups within the last 12 months? 0 Never measured → GAP-01 (critical) Privacy & Security Is there a current RoPA entry and a completed privacy impact assessment? 1 Data flows known informally; no RoPA entry → GAP-02 (critical) Humanity Can a caseworker override the recommendation, and is override friction measured? 2 Override exists; acceptance rate not monitored → GAP-03 (major) Social & Env. Benefits Is there a written benefit statement weighing societal cost/benefit? 1 Business case exists; no societal analysis → GAP-04 (minor) Reliability & Safety Are accuracy tolerances defined, with action thresholds, per subgroup? 1 Global AUC tracked; no subgroup tolerances → GAP-05 (major) Transparency & Explainability Are applicants informed that scoring is algorithm-assisted? 0 No disclosure in application journey → GAP-06 (critical) Accountability & Responsibility Is there a named owner and a reconstructable decision trail? 1 Owner named; logs insufficient to reconstruct decisions → GAP-07 (major)

Reading the scorecard: the profile (three criticals concentrated in Fairness, Privacy, Transparency) is typical of systems built model-first. The gap register, not the scores, is the deliverable — scores prioritise; gaps get owners and dates.

docs.title: Worked Example 3 — Principle-to-control mapping (excerpt used as the Lab 1 answer key)
docs.text: Lifecycle phase Fairness Transparency & Explainability Accountability & Responsibility Plan & design Define protected groups + fairness metric before modelling Plan disclosure text in the application journey Name the accountable owner; define appeal path Prepare data Representativeness check vs applicant population Datasheet documenting sources and known skews Data-source sign-off recorded Build & validate Bias audit vs thresholds (M3) Model card with subgroup results (M5) Validation sign-off by someone who did not build it Deploy & monitor Quarterly fairness re-measurement on live decisions Notice + explanation on every adverse decision Immutable audit trail; override analytics (M5/M6)

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 1 — Ethics Baseline for Ameen
docs.text:
Objective Produce the first two sections of the Ameen Governance File: a defensible risk-tier decision record and a seven-principle self-assessment with a prioritised gap register Duration 50 minutes Setup Ameen system brief (4-page handout: purpose, data flows, screenshots, ops facts), scorecard template (spreadsheet + printed), decision-record template

Instructions & tasks

  1. (10 min) Read the Ameen system brief in pairs; independently note the three facts you consider most governance-relevant, then compare — the deltas seed discussion.
  2. (10 min) Complete the risk-tier decision record: purpose, population, consequence, autonomy (the brief contains the 92% acceptance-rate fact — see who finds it), tier + rationale, review triggers.
  3. (20 min) Score all seven principles using the probe-question sheet (three probes per principle); every score of 0–1 must generate a gap-register row with severity (critical/major/minor) and a one-line rationale.
  4. (5 min) Prioritise: mark the three gaps you would fix first and note why (severity × feasibility, not severity alone).
  5. (5 min) File both artefacts into the governance-file folder structure (provided) — section 1 of the Ameen file is now open.

Expected output 

Risk tier: HIGH (with autonomy rationale citing the 92% acceptance rate)
Scorecard: 7 principles scored, ≥ 8 gaps registered
Gap register excerpt:
GAP-01  Fairness      No disparate-impact measurement ever   CRITICAL
GAP-02  Privacy       No RoPA entry / PIA                    CRITICAL
GAP-06  Transparency  No AI-involvement disclosure           CRITICAL
Top-3 priorities marked with feasibility rationale

Troubleshooting guidance

Symptom Cause Fix Pair classifies Ameen as limited-risk Anchored on "it only recommends" Point them to the acceptance-rate fact; ask the "wrong in each direction" question Scores cluster at 2 everywhere Politeness bias / vague probes Enforce the evidence rule: score 2 requires naming a document; score 3 requires naming a reviewer and date Gap register has 25+ rows Probes treated as an audit of everything Scope discipline: one row per failed probe, merge duplicates Pairs argue about severity ratings No shared definition Severity anchors on the handout: critical = legal/rights exposure now; major = exposure under foreseeable change; minor = maturity issue

Instructor notes. The 92% acceptance-rate fact is planted mid-paragraph on page 3 of the brief precisely so some pairs miss it — reveal it during the debrief and let the room re-argue the tier. That moment ("one operational fact changed the classification") is the lab's core lesson. Fast finishers: draft the one-sentence disclosure text that would close GAP-06 and critique it against principle 6.

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz (5 questions) 1. Name the seven SDAIA AI-ethics principles. → Fairness; Privacy & Security; Humanity; Social & Environmental Benefits; Reliability & Safety; Transparency & Explainability; Accountability & Responsibility. 2. What single question most efficiently tests a system's risk tier? → What happens to a specific person when the system is wrong in each direction? 3. Why does a high recommendation-acceptance rate change governance analysis? → De-facto autonomy: the system effectively decides, so oversight must be designed and measured, not assumed. 4. Give one example of two principles in tension and how the tension is resolved. → Transparency vs privacy in explanations; resolved by a documented trade-off signed by the accountable owner. 5. True/False: procuring an AI system transfers the ethics obligations to the vendor. → False — obligations follow the deployer; the vendor assessment (M6) is how they are discharged.

Classification drill. Eight one-line system descriptions (mosque-capacity forecaster, CV-screening tool, chatbot for visa FAQs, exam-proctoring vision system, traffic-signal optimiser, credit-limit adjuster, news recommender, general-behaviour citizen scoring). Individually tier them, then reconcile in pairs. Answer key marks the citizen-scoring item unacceptable and forces the "who is affected" argument for exam proctoring.

Gap-hunting exercise. Given a glossy (fictional) "AI Ethics Charter" one-pager, find the five governance smells (no owners, no gates, no metrics, no review cadence, no scope statement).

Discussion questions. - Your sponsor says governance review adds three weeks and "the model is ready now." What proportionate fast-path do you offer for limited-risk systems, and what do you refuse to fast-path? - Should the ethics self-assessment be done by the building team, an independent office, or both? What does each answer cost?

docs.title: Case Study — Complaint-Triage AI at a Major Municipality
docs.text:
Scenario. A large Saudi municipality deploys "Murshid", an AI triage system that reads citizen complaints (potholes, waste, lighting, safety hazards) from its service app and assigns priority and department routing. Eighteen months in, a journalist's data request shows that average resolution time in three lower-income districts is 2.4× the city average, and that complaints written in informal Arabic or by non-native speakers are systematically classified as lower priority.

Business context. The municipality's leadership had celebrated Murshid publicly (40% faster average triage). The disparity story lands during a national push on municipal service equity. The mayor's office asks the digital team for a response within two weeks: is the system fair, can we prove it either way, and what changes?

Technical challenge. No fairness measurement was ever defined; "priority" labels came from historical dispatcher decisions (which themselves under-prioritised the same districts); the NLP component was trained mostly on formal Arabic; district identifiers were never treated as a governance-relevant attribute.

Constraints. The team cannot take the system offline (complaint volume doubled since launch and manual triage can't absorb it); the response must be publishable, not just internal; the vendor's contract has no fairness or audit clauses (M6 foreshadowing).

Solution approach (facilitate, don't lecture). (1) Emergency measurement first: resolution time, priority distribution, and misrouting rate by district and language register — you cannot manage what you never measured. (2) Classify Murshid properly: consequential access to public services → high risk → full file. (3) Short-term mitigation: human review for the affected districts' complaints while the model is corrected. (4) Root-cause the label problem: historical dispatcher behaviour is the bias source — relabeling a stratified sample with explicit criteria is the fix, not a bigger model. (5) Publish a plain-language note: what was found, what changed, when it will be re-measured — transparency as trust repair.

Discussion questions. 1. Which SDAIA principles were violated, and at which lifecycle phase did each violation enter? (Fairness at Prepare-data via labels; Transparency at Deploy; Accountability throughout.) 2. The 40% average improvement is real. How do you talk about a system that is better on average and worse for specific groups? 3. What three clauses should the renewal contract add? (Audit rights, fairness SLAs, data access for measurement — bridge to M6.) 4. Draft the first sentence of the public note.

Artefact Novice profile Target profile Decision record Tier stated, 1-line rationale, no triggers Tier + autonomy analysis + review triggers Scorecard Scores only Scores + evidence names + gap rows Gap register Unprioritised list Severity + feasibility-ranked top 3

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
1. Seven-principles wheel — Purpose: anchor image for the whole course. Elements: seven segments (one per SDAIA principle) around a hub labelled "Trustworthy AI"; each segment annotated with its evidence artefact and the module that produces it; Arabic principle names as subtitles. Style: flat vector wheel, seven-colour palette reused consistently across all course visuals. Designer description: "Circular wheel diagram, 7 segments with icons (scales = fairness, shield = privacy & security, person = humanity, leaf/community = social & environmental benefits, gauge = reliability & safety, magnifier = transparency, gavel = accountability), outer ring showing artefact names."
  2. Risk-tier pyramid — Purpose: memorisable classification reference. Elements: four tiers (unacceptable at top, minimal at base) with example systems per tier and the governance consequence stated on the right edge; Ameen pinned at high-risk. Style: pyramid with callouts, printable A4.
  3. Lifecycle × principles matrix — Purpose: show that governance is phase-work. Elements: 4 lifecycle phases × 7 principles grid with a control icon in each populated cell; the course's six labs overlaid as coloured pins on the cells they evidence. Style: matrix heat-grid.
  4. "Poster vs practice" split panel (case study) — Purpose: ethics-washing made visible. Elements: left panel: framed principles poster; right panel: delivery pipeline with gates, owners, artefacts. Style: before/after split.

1. Ameen application-journey screenshot (mock): the citizen-facing application form with no AI disclosure; why: participants must spot the missing notice in Lab 1; content: realistic government-portal styling, fictional branding.

docs.title: Simulations
docs.text:
1. Scope-creep tabletop — Setup: mid-lab, hand each pair a one-line memo: "Leadership wants to reuse Ameen scores to prioritise housing-support waitlists next quarter." Expected behaviour: pairs must state whether their tier/assessment still holds (it does not — new consequence, new population) and list what must be redone. Learning objective: classification is event-driven, not annual paperwork.
  2. Committee cold-call — Setup: instructor role-plays a sceptical committee chair and cold-calls two pairs: "Defend your tier in 60 seconds." Expected behaviour: rationale from the decision record, not improvisation. Learning objective: artefacts exist to be defended from.

docs.title: Interactive Activities
docs.text:
• Principles card-sort (15 min): 21 control cards (e.g., "override button", "subgroup AUC report", "retention schedule", "adverse-decision notice") physically sorted onto the seven-principles wheel; pairs justify the three hardest placements.
  • "One fact changes everything" round (10 min): instructor reveals operational facts one at a time (acceptance rate, appeal volume, data source change); class votes after each on whether the risk tier moves.

docs.text:
• Instructor demo: live completion of one principle's scorecard row on the projector — probe, evidence hunt in the brief, score, gap row — in under 4 minutes; the discipline is the message.

docs.title: Module 2 — PDPL and NDMO Data-Governance Frameworks
Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. AI governance stands on data governance: no model is compliant if the data feeding it is unlawfully collected, over-retained, unclassified, or shared without basis. This module makes participants operationally literate in the Kingdom's two foundational instruments — the Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) and the NDMO data-management and personal-data-protection standards — and teaches the working artefacts that evidence compliance: the PDPL obligations checklist, the record of processing activities (RoPA), the data-classification record, and the gap register.

Business relevance. PDPL is enforceable law with real administrative penalties, and SDAIA is the competent authority supervising it; NDMO standards structure how government and government-linked entities must manage data. For any organisation building AI in the Kingdom, these are not optional reference material — they are procurement gate, audit scope, and licence to operate. Practitioners who can complete a compliance assessment correctly save their organisations from the two most expensive outcomes: a regulator finding, and an AI programme frozen mid-flight because nobody can evidence the lawful basis of its training data.

Industry use cases. - A retail group building a recommendation engine must establish the lawful basis for each data source, publish an adequate privacy notice, and honour deletion requests — including inside already-trained models' training sets. - A government entity preparing data for a national AI platform must classify every dataset to NDMO levels before it can be shared, and document the sharing decision. - A hospital group's research arm needs a defensible position on whether its "de-identified" patient extract is still personal data under PDPL (M4 completes this question).

Expected competencies. Participants can state PDPL's scope, legal bases, data-subject rights, and controller obligations; complete a PDPL compliance checklist and RoPA entry for a real data flow; classify data assets to national classification levels; and consolidate findings into a prioritised, owned gap register.

docs.title: Learning Objectives (mapped)
docs.text: # Objective Maps to 2.1 Explain PDPL's scope, legal bases for processing, and the rights it grants data subjects LO1 2.2 Identify controller obligations relevant to an AI system: notices, RoPA, impact assessment, breach duties, cross-border rules LO1 2.3 Describe the NDMO standards' domain structure and apply national data-classification levels LO1 2.4 Complete a PDPL/NDMO compliance checklist and RoPA entry for an AI data flow LO1, LO5 2.5 Consolidate compliance findings into a gap register with owners and severities LO1, LO5

docs.title: 1. PDPL orientation: what it is and who it reaches
docs.text:
The Personal Data Protection Law (issued by Royal Decree M/19 of 1443H / September 2021, amended by Royal Decree M/148 in March 2023) is the Kingdom's comprehensive data-protection law. It came into force in September 2023, with a transition period for entities to reach compliance, and is supported by Implementing Regulations and separate Personal Data Transfer Regulations. SDAIA is the competent authority supervising its application.

Scope points practitioners must hold precisely:

  • Personal data is any data — in any form — that identifies an individual or renders them identifiable, directly or indirectly: name, ID numbers, addresses, phone numbers, photos, and combinations of attributes that single a person out. The "indirectly" clause is why M4's re-identification analysis is a legal exercise, not just a technical one.
  • Sensitive data is a stricter category, including data revealing racial or ethnic origin, religious, intellectual or political belief, criminal and security data, biometric data, genetic data, health data, credit data, and data indicating that a person's parents are unknown. Sensitive data attracts tighter rules (e.g., legitimate interest is not an available basis).
  • Territorial reach: the law applies to processing of personal data of individuals residing in the Kingdom, including processing by entities outside the Kingdom. Cloud location does not opt anyone out.
  • Roles: the controller determines purpose and means; the processor processes on the controller's behalf. AI vendors are typically processors — until they reuse your data for their own model improvement, at which point they have become controllers of that processing and the contract must say what is allowed (M6 returns here).

docs.title: 2. Legal bases, rights, and the consent question in AI
docs.text:
Processing requires a legal basis. Consent is the default basis, and PDPL recognises alternatives including: processing that serves the actual interest of the data subject where contacting them is impossible or difficult; processing under another law or to implement an agreement to which the data subject is party; processing by a public entity for security or judicial purposes; and — since the 2023 amendment — legitimate interest of the controller for non-sensitive data, provided it does not prejudice the data subject's rights and expectations.

Data subjects hold rights that AI systems must be able to honour in practice, not just in policy: the right to be informed of the legal basis and purpose; the right to access their data; the right to obtain a copy in readable format; the right to correction; and the right to destruction of data no longer needed. Consent, where relied on, must be withdrawable as easily as it was given.

The AI-specific teaching points:

  • Purpose limitation bites hardest in AI. Data collected to administer benefits was not thereby collected to train an eligibility model — teams must verify the original purpose covers model training or establish a new basis. "We already have the data" is an infrastructure statement, not a legal one.
  • Rights reach into pipelines. A destruction request must propagate to feature stores, training extracts, backups within policy, and — the hard question — models trained on the data. Teach the practical position: maintain training-set lineage so you can state which model versions a subject's data influenced, and have a documented, defensible retraining/refresh policy.
  • Consent quality: bundled, coerced, or buried consent fails its function. For a government benefit service, consent is often the wrong basis anyway (the power imbalance undermines voluntariness) — a statutory basis is usually the honest one. This nuance separates practitioners from checkbox-fillers.

docs.title: 3. Controller obligations that shape AI delivery
docs.text:
The obligations most relevant to AI teams, each with its artefact:

Obligation Practical meaning for an AI team Artefact Privacy notice Individuals know what is collected, why, on what basis, and that algorithmic scoring is involved Notice text in the application journey Records of processing (RoPA) Every processing activity is inventoried: purposes, categories, recipients, retention, safeguards RoPA entry (Worked Example 2) Data minimisation & retention Collect only what the purpose needs; keep only as long as needed; justify every feature Minimisation review (M4); retention schedule Accuracy Wrong inputs produce wrong decisions about people; correction rights are an accuracy control Data-quality rules; correction workflow Security Organisational and technical measures proportionate to sensitivity; align with NCA controls where applicable Security assessment reference Impact assessment Assess privacy impact for processing likely to pose high risk to data subjects — AI scoring of individuals is the canonical trigger DPIA (M4 completes it) Breach notification Notify SDAIA of personal-data breaches per the Implementing Regulations' timeline (72 hours), and affected individuals where the breach may cause them harm Incident procedure + register Processor contracts Binding terms on processors: purpose limits, security, sub-processing, audit DPA clauses (M6 checklist) Cross-border transfers Transfers outside the Kingdom only under the Transfer Regulations' conditions: adequacy, appropriate safeguards (e.g., standard contractual clauses, binding common rules), or listed exceptions — with minimisation of what is transferred Transfer assessment record

Non-compliance carries administrative fines (up to SAR 5 million per violation, subject to doubling for repeat violations) and, for unlawful disclosure of sensitive data with intent to harm, criminal penalties including imprisonment. Use penalties to motivate, not to teach — the durable motivation is that every obligation above is also simply good AI engineering.

docs.title: 4. NDMO standards: the national data-management spine
docs.text:
The National Data Management Office (NDMO), within SDAIA, issued the National Data Management and Personal Data Protection Standards that government entities (and entities handling government data) implement. Teach the structure, not a clause-by-clause reading: the standards organise data management into fifteen domains, spanning data governance; data catalog and metadata; data quality; data operations; document and content management; data architecture and modelling; reference and master data; business intelligence and analytics; data sharing and interoperability; data value realization; open data; freedom of information; data classification; personal data protection; and data security and protection.

For AI work, four domains do most of the daily lifting:

  1. Data classification. National practice classifies data by the impact of unauthorised disclosure into four levels — Top Secret, Secret, Restricted, Public (with Arabic labels used in official contexts). Classification drives everything downstream: storage controls, sharing decisions, cloud eligibility, anonymisation requirements. An unclassified dataset is an unmanaged risk.
  2. Data catalog & metadata. You cannot govern data you cannot find. AI teams inherit this domain as feature/dataset documentation — the datasheets and lineage that M5's documentation practice extends.
  3. Data quality. Completeness, accuracy, timeliness rules with owners — for AI, quality defects become decision defects about people (the accuracy obligation made operational).
  4. Data sharing & interoperability. Sharing between entities follows documented request/approval flows with classification-appropriate safeguards. "Send me the CSV" is replaced by a sharing record that audit can reconstruct.

How the two instruments interlock: PDPL states what the law requires for personal data; NDMO standards provide the management system in which those requirements are executed and evidenced. In the compliance checklist (Worked Example 1) the two appear as one instrument with two sections — which is exactly how a practitioner should experience them.

docs.title: 5. Running a compliance assessment (the craft)
docs.text:
A compliance assessment is a structured comparison of what is actually happening against what the framework requires, producing findings with evidence. The method taught (and used in Lab 2 and PA-1):

  1. Fix the scope in one sentence. "The Ameen application-scoring data flow, from application submission to score storage" — not "the SSA".
  2. Draw the data flow first. Sources → processing → stores → recipients. Every arrow is a question: basis? classification? retention? Most findings live on arrows, not boxes.
  3. Walk the checklist against evidence, not intentions. The answer to "is there a privacy notice?" is a link or a NO — "the team is aware" scores as absent.
  4. Write findings as: requirement → observed state → gap → severity → owner. A finding without an owner is a complaint.
  5. Resist solutioning during assessment. Fixes come after the full picture; premature fixing biases the assessment toward easy findings.

docs.title: 6. Common mistakes & operational considerations
docs.text:
1. Consent-collecting reflex: demanding consent where another basis is proper (statutory duty, contract), creating both friction and a false impression that withdrawal stops the processing.
  2. RoPA rot: an inventory built once for a compliance push, never updated as pipelines change — detectable by comparing RoPA recipients against actual egress.
  3. Classification inflation: rating everything Secret "to be safe", which paralyses legitimate sharing and pushes teams into shadow channels — the opposite of control.
  4. Notice–reality divergence: the privacy notice describes the system as designed in 2023; the pipeline as built in 2026 does more. The notice is a contract with the public; drift is a finding.
  5. Treating anonymisation claims as exit doors: labelling an extract "anonymised" without analysis (M4 tests these claims and most fail).
  6. Cross-border blindness: a vendor's support engineers in another jurisdiction accessing production data is a transfer; SaaS telemetry can be a transfer. Map access, not just storage.

Operational considerations. Keep the checklist versioned and dated — assessments are snapshots. Schedule reassessment on triggers (new data source, new recipient, purpose change) rather than calendar-only. In government contexts, align evidence formats with what national audit and SDAIA supervision expect: dated documents, named owners, decision records.

docs.title: Worked Example 1 — PDPL/NDMO compliance checklist (excerpt, filled for Ameen)
docs.text:
Status legend: ✔ compliant · ✖ gap · ◐ partial · N/A with rationale.

# Requirement Evidence expected Status Finding P-01 Legal basis identified & documented for each processing purpose Basis register naming statute/consent per purpose ✖ Application processing has statutory footing; model training has no documented basis → GAP-08 (critical) P-02 Privacy notice covers purposes incl. algorithmic scoring Published notice text ✖ Notice predates Ameen; no mention of scoring → merges with GAP-06 P-03 RoPA entry current for this flow RoPA record ≤ 12 months old ✖ No entry → GAP-02 confirmed P-04 Data-subject rights operable (access/copy/correct/destroy) Procedure + fulfilment log ◐ Access/correction via portal; destruction not propagated to training extracts → GAP-09 (major) P-05 Retention schedule defined & enforced Schedule + deletion evidence ✖ Raw applications retained indefinitely "for retraining" → GAP-10 (major) P-06 Impact assessment for high-risk processing Completed DPIA ✖ None → scheduled as Lab 4 output P-07 Breach procedure meets notification timeline Tested incident runbook ◐ Corporate procedure exists; AI-pipeline breaches not in scope → GAP-11 (minor) P-08 Processor contract terms for vendors touching the flow DPA with model vendor ✖ Vendor MSA silent on data protection → GAP-12 (critical, feeds M6) P-09 Cross-border transfer conditions met for any external flow Transfer assessment ◐ Vendor support access from abroad unassessed → GAP-13 (major) N-01 All datasets in flow classified to national levels Classification records ✖ Unclassified → Lab 2b task N-02 Datasets catalogued with owner + metadata Catalog entries ◐ Core register catalogued; training extracts are not → GAP-14 (major) N-03 Data-quality rules defined for decision-critical fields Quality rulebook ◐ Income field validated; disability status free-text → GAP-15 (major) N-04 Sharing with other entities via documented agreements Sharing records ✔ MoU with civil-registry source on file

Teaching point: the checklist's power is the evidence expected column — it converts legal text into inspectable objects. P-01's finding is the classic AI finding: lawful operations, unlawful (undocumented) training reuse.

docs.title: Worked Example 3 — Data-classification decision record (Lab 2b answer-key excerpt)
docs.text:
Data asset Contents Disclosure impact reasoning Level Application register Full identity + income + disability status Serious harm to individuals (discrimination, fraud targeting); large scale Secret Training extract v3 Pseudonymised applications, quasi-identifiers intact Re-identification plausible (M4 proves it) → treat at source level until anonymisation is demonstrated Secret Model artefact + weights Learned parameters Membership-inference risk exists but indirect; operational sensitivity Restricted Aggregate dashboard (region-level counts ≥ 1,000) Statistical aggregates No individual impact; policy sensitivity low Public (after aggregation review)

Teaching point: the training extract inherits the source's level until anonymisation is demonstrated, not asserted — this single rule prevents the most common data-lake violation, and it sets up Module 4.

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 2 — PDPL/NDMO Compliance Assessment of Ameen
docs.text:
Objective Complete the compliance checklist and RoPA entry for the Ameen scoring flow (Part A), classify its data assets and consolidate the course gap register (Part B) Duration 2 × 50 min (Day 1 H5 + Day 2 H1; Part B includes the 30-min PA-1) Setup Ameen data-flow pack (flow diagram, vendor MSA excerpt, current privacy notice, retention memo — with 12 seeded findings), checklist + RoPA + classification templates

Part A tasks (50 min) 1. (10 min) Draw the data flow from the pack: sources, stores, processors, recipients, external arrows. Mark every arrow with basis?/classification?/retention? tags. 2. (25 min) Walk the 13-item checklist against the pack's documents; every ✖/◐ becomes a finding row (requirement → observed → gap → severity → owner). 3. (15 min) Complete the RoPA entry from your findings; flag every UNDOCUMENTED cell rather than leaving blanks.

Part B tasks (50 min) 1. (15 min) Classify the six data assets in the pack using the decision-record format; justify each level in one sentence of impact reasoning. 2. (30 min) PA-1 — Compliance-assessment exercise (individually, timed, collected): a fresh one-page scenario (a telecom launching an AI churn-prediction pilot on subscriber data with an overseas analytics vendor); complete the short-form checklist and name the five most material gaps. 3. (5 min) Merge Lab 1 + Lab 2 findings into the single course gap register; de-duplicate; file section 02 of the governance file.

Expected outputs 

Checklist: 13 items assessed, ≥ 10 of 12 seeded findings caught
RoPA entry: complete, with 3 UNDOCUMENTED flags (basis for training,
            retention, transfer assessment)
Classification: 6 assets levelled; training extract inherits Secret
Gap register: consolidated, deduplicated, every row owned
PA-1 submitted: 5 material gaps named (answer key: no basis for pilot reuse,
            no transfer assessment, notice silent, no RoPA, no DPA terms)

Troubleshooting

Symptom Cause Fix Checklist done in 10 minutes, all ✖ Scoring from vibes, not documents Enforce the evidence column: each status must cite a pack document or its absence Pairs debate legal interpretations at length Treating the lab as a bar exam The lab tests method, not counsel: record the question, flag "legal review needed", move on Training extract classified Public "because pseudonymised" Anonymisation assumed Preview M4 in one line: pseudonymised = still personal data; inherit source level RoPA purposes copied from the notice Notice–reality divergence missed Compare notice date vs Ameen launch date in the pack — the divergence is seeded PA-1 answers list 12 gaps unranked No materiality judgement Require exactly five, ranked — the ranking is what is graded

Instructor notes. The pack's vendor MSA excerpt contains a quietly disastrous clause ("Provider may use anonymized service data to improve its offerings") — pairs who catch it should be asked what "anonymized" means there (nothing, contractually). This clause returns as the centrepiece of M6's vendor assessment. During PA-1 enforce silence and timing; it is the module's formal assessment component.

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz (5 questions) 1. Name four legal bases PDPL recognises besides consent. → Actual interest of the data subject; processing under another law / implementing an agreement; public-entity security/judicial purposes; legitimate interest (non-sensitive data, post-amendment). 2. Which category does health and disability data fall into, and what follows? → Sensitive data; stricter rules — e.g., legitimate interest unavailable, tighter security and access expectations. 3. Within what timeframe must SDAIA be notified of a personal-data breach under the Implementing Regulations? → 72 hours. 4. What are the four national data-classification levels? → Top Secret, Secret, Restricted, Public. 5. A vendor's overseas engineer views production data during a support session. Transfer or not? → Transfer — access from abroad counts; it needs a basis under the Transfer Regulations.

Data-flow drill. Given a one-paragraph description of a smart-parking app, draw the flow and mark three arrows that need a transfer or sharing assessment.

Notice-reality diff. Given a privacy notice and a pipeline diagram that quietly adds a data broker feed, list every sentence of the notice that is now false.

Discussion questions. - The benefits programme is statutory — so why offer applicants any privacy notice choices at all? What is the honest notice for processing people cannot refuse? - Your team wants to keep raw applications forever "because future models." Construct the retention argument that survives both the DPO and the data-science lead.

docs.title: Case Study — Marketing Personalisation at a Gulf Retail Bank
docs.text:
Scenario. "Bank AlKhaleej" (fictional), headquartered in Riyadh, builds a personalisation engine that scores customers for product offers using transaction history, app behaviour, and — via a data-enrichment vendor — inferred lifestyle segments. The engine works; conversion doubles. Then a customer complaint escalates: a customer received a personal-finance offer that could only be explained by the bank knowing about his recent medical spending pattern. The complaint reaches SDAIA as a data-protection query and internal audit opens a file.

Business context. The bank must answer the regulator, decide whether the enrichment vendor relationship is lawful, and keep a revenue-critical system running. SAMA supervision adds a second regulator watching the same facts.

Technical challenge. Reconstruct: what data categories feed the engine (transaction categories that reveal health-adjacent patterns behave like sensitive data even if not labelled "health"); what the notice actually told customers; what basis covers enrichment; whether the vendor's "publicly sourced" segments were lawfully compiled at all.

Constraints. Marketing owns the vendor contract and resists change mid-campaign; the notice was last updated before the engine existed; the enrichment data cannot be verified for source legality; the regulator's questions have deadlines.

Solution approach (facilitate). (1) Freeze enrichment-derived features immediately — reversible, defensible, keeps the core engine running on first-party data. (2) Data-inventory sprint: rebuild the RoPA entry for the engine; categorise transaction-derived features by revealed sensitivity, not by column name. (3) Basis analysis: first-party personalisation may stand on legitimate interest with opt-out; health-adjacent inference cannot. (4) Vendor interrogation with M6's checklist: source legality, consent chain, contract terms — expect failure and plan exit. (5) Notice rewrite + a customer response that admits the inference issue plainly.

Discussion questions. 1. Column names said "merchant category"; the pattern revealed health. Where should sensitivity be assessed — schema or effect? What process implements the answer? 2. Was there any notice text that could have made the enrichment lawful? Or is this a basis problem no notice fixes? 3. Sequence the regulator response: what do you send first, and what do you not volunteer prematurely while investigation is ongoing? 4. What single checklist item, done at design time, would have prevented the entire incident? (P-01 basis-per-purpose, applied to the enrichment feed.)

docs.title: Benchmarks and Evaluation
docs.text:
Metric Category Target after M2 How measured Seeded-finding recall (Lab 2 pack) Assessment quality ≥ 10 of 12 Answer key RoPA completeness Rigor 0 blank cells (UNDOCUMENTED flags allowed) Template check Classification accuracy Knowledge 6/6 assets within one level of key, with impact reasoning Answer key PA-1 material-gap identification Assessment (graded) ≥ 4 of 5 key gaps, correctly ranked PA-1 rubric Checklist evidence discipline Rigor 100% of statuses cite a document or its absence Spot check Data-flow completeness Method All 4 external arrows found (incl. vendor support access) Flow review

Example benchmark table:

Artefact Weak profile Target profile Data flow Boxes only, no arrow annotations Every arrow tagged basis/classification/retention Findings "Not compliant" statements Requirement → observed → gap → severity → owner Classification Levels asserted Levels + impact reasoning + inheritance rule applied

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
1. PDPL obligations map — Purpose: one-page anchor for the law. Elements: centre: "personal data of individuals in KSA"; ring 1: legal bases; ring 2: data-subject rights; ring 3: controller obligations each tagged with its artefact; SDAIA supervision arc over the top. Style: concentric map, course palette. Designer note: sensitive-data categories in a distinct flagged box.
  2. Ameen data-flow diagram (annotated answer key) — Elements: portal, civil-registry interface, income service, scoring pipeline, case-management, vendor support arrow crossing a border line; every arrow tagged with basis/classification/retention status colours. Style: swim-lane with a national-border dashed line.
  3. NDMO fifteen-domain wheel with four highlighted — Elements: all fifteen domains as segments; classification, catalog, quality, sharing enlarged with AI-relevance captions. Style: wheel + callouts.
  4. Classification decision tree — Elements: impact-of-disclosure questions branching to the four levels; inheritance rule for derived datasets as a highlighted side rule. Style: compact flowchart, printable A4.

docs.title: Images (screenshots)
docs.text:
1. Completed checklist spreadsheet matching Worked Example 1 — why: expected-output reference; content: status column colours, findings column, severity tags.
  2. RoPA entry screenshot — why: participants mirror the UNDOCUMENTED-flag discipline; content: the three flagged cells visible.
  3. Vendor MSA excerpt (mock) with the "improve its offerings" clause highlighted — why: trains contract-reading reflex; content: one page, realistic legal formatting.
  4. Privacy notice vs pipeline diff (mock) — why: notice–reality divergence made visual; content: notice paragraph and pipeline element side-by-side with a red delta marker.

docs.title: Simulations
docs.text:
1. Regulator query drill — Setup: mid-Part-B, deliver a mock SDAIA query letter: "Provide the legal basis and RoPA entry for algorithmic scoring of applicants within 5 business days." Expected behaviour: pairs assemble the answer from artefacts already built — or discover what missing artefacts feel like under deadline. Learning objective: compliance artefacts are pre-positioned answers.
  2. Deletion-request trace — Setup: a data subject requests destruction; pairs trace the request across the data-flow diagram marking every store it must reach. Expected behaviour: someone asks "what about the trained model?" — hold the question visibly for M4/M5. Learning objective: rights are pipeline requirements.

docs.title: Interactive Activities
docs.text:
• Basis-matching game (10 min): nine processing scenarios on cards matched to legal bases; two are deliberately arguable to force the "record the question, flag for legal" behaviour.
  • Classification stand-up (10 min): corners of the room labelled with the four levels; instructor reads data assets; participants walk to their answer and defend against the room.

docs.text:
• Instructor demo: assess two checklist items live on the projector — including one where the pack has the evidence (model the ✔ discipline, not just gap-hunting) — in under 6 minutes.
