docs.title: Module 3 — Bias, Fairness, and Impact Assessment
Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. "The model is accurate" and "the model is fair" are different claims, measured differently, and a system can hold the first while badly failing the second. This module gives participants the working machinery of fairness analysis: where bias enters the lifecycle, the core group-fairness metrics and their inescapable trade-offs, the disparate-impact test, and the craft of running and writing a bias audit that stands up to committee scrutiny. It is the evidence engine behind the SDAIA Fairness principle.

Business relevance. Fairness failures are the most publicly explosive AI failures: they turn a technical system into a front-page equity story overnight (Module 1's Murshid case is the pattern). For government AI — eligibility, licensing, enforcement — disparate impact across regions, genders, or nationalities is a political and legal event, not a model metric. Organisations that audit before deployment control the narrative and the remediation cost; organisations audited by others control neither. The bias audit is also fast becoming a procurement deliverable: buyers of AI systems increasingly demand subgroup performance evidence before contract award.

Industry use cases. - An HR platform screening thousands of applications must demonstrate that its shortlisting rates satisfy the four-fifths rule across gender and that error rates are balanced before a large employer will deploy it. - A bank's credit model is audited for disparate impact across regions and age bands as part of model-risk review; the audit's remediation (removing a proxy feature) costs 0.3 AUC points and is approved as a documented trade-off. - A hospital readmission-risk model is found to under-predict risk for patients from remote regions (sparser historical data); clinical oversight rules are tightened for that subgroup while data collection improves.

Expected competencies. Participants can identify bias sources by lifecycle phase, choose and justify fairness metrics for a given decision context, compute approval-rate and error-rate disparities from a scored dataset, apply the 80% rule, reason about metric trade-offs, propose remediations at the correct point in the pipeline, and write a bias-audit report with findings and recommendations.

docs.title: Learning Objectives (mapped)
docs.text: # Objective Maps to 3.1 Identify and name bias sources at each lifecycle phase (historical, representation, measurement, aggregation, evaluation, deployment) LO3 3.2 Define and compute demographic parity, disparate-impact ratio, equal opportunity, and equalized odds from group confusion matrices LO3 3.3 Apply the four-fifths (80%) rule and interpret results with base-rate awareness LO3 3.4 Explain why key fairness metrics cannot all hold simultaneously and manage the trade-off explicitly LO3 3.5 Propose remediations (data, model, threshold, process) matched to the diagnosed bias source LO3, LO2 3.6 Write a bias-audit report suitable for governance-committee review LO3, LO5

docs.title: 1. Where bias enters: a lifecycle taxonomy
docs.text:
Bias is not one thing; it is a family of mechanisms, each entering at a specific phase — which matters because remediation must target the mechanism, not the symptom:

Bias type Enters at Mechanism Ameen example Historical Before the data Past decisions encoded past inequities; the label is the bias Historical caseworker decisions under-approved remote-region applicants; the model learns it as ground truth Representation Prepare data Groups under-sampled → model underfits them Few training examples from newly added application channels Measurement Prepare data Features/labels measured with different fidelity across groups Income verified via employer records for salaried applicants, self-reported for informal workers Aggregation Build One model for populations with different feature–outcome relationships Household-size effects differ across regions; a single global coefficient misfits both Evaluation Validate Benchmarks unrepresentative; only global metrics checked Validation on last year's applicants after eligibility rules changed Deployment Operate Usage context shifts; humans interact with outputs unevenly Caseworkers override low scores for familiar districts more often than remote ones

Proxy features deserve their own emphasis: removing the protected attribute does not remove the bias when other features encode it (district encodes income and origin; employment sector encodes gender in segmented labour markets). "We don't use gender" is the beginning of the analysis, never the conclusion — and removing the protected attribute also removes your ability to measure disparity, which is why governance practice retains protected attributes for audit while excluding them from features.

docs.title: 2. Group fairness metrics from confusion matrices
docs.text:
All core group metrics fall out of per-group confusion matrices. Fix notation: for each group, from predicted-positive/negative × actually-positive/negative counts we get the selection rate (share predicted positive), TPR (true positive rate — of the truly eligible, how many the model approves), and FPR (false positive rate — of the truly ineligible, how many it approves).

  • Demographic parity: selection rates equal across groups. Blind to qualification differences; right when the "positive" is an opportunity to be distributed (outreach, screening-in), misleading when base rates legitimately differ.
  • Disparate-impact ratio (DIR): selection rate of the disadvantaged group ÷ selection rate of the advantaged group. The four-fifths (80%) rule — DIR below 0.8 signals adverse impact — originates in US employment practice but functions worldwide, including in Saudi practice, as a useful screening threshold: a tripwire that triggers investigation, not a verdict.
  • Equal opportunity: TPR equal across groups — among the truly eligible, each group has the same chance of approval. Usually the primary fairness claim for benefit eligibility: the harm that matters most is the eligible family wrongly rejected.
  • Equalized odds: TPR and FPR equal across groups — stricter, and often the committee's expectation once stated in plain language ("errors of both kinds shouldn't concentrate in one group").
  • Calibration within groups: among applicants scored 0.8, about 80% should be truly eligible — in every group. Decision-makers consume scores as probabilities; group-dependent meaning misleads them silently.

The impossibility result, taught in one breath: when base rates differ between groups, a (non-trivial) model cannot simultaneously satisfy calibration and equalized odds — this is a mathematical fact, not an engineering shortfall. Consequence: fairness-metric choice is a policy judgement about which harms matter most, made explicitly, recorded in the governance file, and owned by the accountable owner — exactly the M1 discipline. The practitioner's job is to compute all of them, explain the tension, and force the explicit choice.

Individual vs group fairness: group metrics can all pass while similar individuals are treated differently (and vice versa). Consistency checks — near-identical applications scored very differently — belong in the audit's exploratory section.

docs.title: 3. The bias-audit procedure
docs.text:
The audit method used in Lab 3 and expected in the capstone:

  1. Scope & stakes. System, decision, affected groups, and the harm direction that matters (for Ameen: false rejections of eligible families).
  2. Define groups & justify. Protected/affected attributes chosen with policy input (gender of head-of-household, region, nationality, disability) — including intersections where volume permits (region × gender); small intersections get flagged, not silently dropped.
  3. Choose primary metric(s) before computing. Pre-registration discipline: deciding the metric after seeing results invites motivated selection.
  4. Compute: per-group selection rates, DIR against the most-selected group, TPR/FPR gaps, calibration by score band. Minimum cell sizes noted; confidence intervals or at least n's on everything.
  5. Diagnose: map each disparity to a lifecycle bias source (Section 1's taxonomy) using targeted checks — label re-review samples for historical bias, per-group feature missingness for measurement bias, per-group learning curves for representation bias.
  6. Recommend: remediations matched to sources (Section 4), each with expected effect, cost, and residual risk.
  7. Report: findings with evidence, written for a mixed audience (Worked Example 2's structure).

docs.title: 4. Remediation: match the fix to the mechanism
docs.text:
Intervention point Techniques When right Cautions Data Relabel with explicit criteria; collect/oversample under-represented groups; fix measurement asymmetries; remove/repair proxy features Historical, representation, measurement bias Slowest but only fix that addresses cause; relabeling needs governance of the new criteria Training Reweighing samples; fairness-constrained optimisation Residual disparity after data fixes Constraint choice = metric choice = policy judgement; document it Post-processing / thresholds Group-specific thresholds; score recalibration per group Fast mitigation while causes are fixed Explicitly treats groups differently — needs legal/policy sign-off and transparency; treat as bridge, not destination Process Human review bands; override monitoring; appeal channels; tightened oversight for affected subgroups Deployment bias; interim protection Costs caseworker capacity; override behaviour itself needs monitoring (deployment bias again)

The governance framing: remediation decisions trade fairness, accuracy, cost, and speed. The audit's job is to make the trade-offs explicit and priced; the accountable owner's job is to choose and sign. An audit that ends in "the team will look into it" has failed its purpose.

docs.title: 5. Impact assessment beyond metrics
docs.text: Metrics measure the model; impact assessment considers the system in the world: Who is affected who never appears in the data (non-applicants deterred by the process)? Does the appeal channel function equally across groups (language, digital access, literacy)? What does an error cost a family in time and dignity, not just money? A short structured section in the audit — affected-stakeholder table with harms, severity, likelihood, and existing safeguards — connects fairness analysis to the M1 benefit statement and the M6 risk register. For high-risk government systems this section is what committee members actually read first.

docs.title: 6. Common mistakes & production considerations
docs.text:
1. Fairness through blindness: deleting protected attributes and declaring victory — proxies remain, and measurement becomes impossible.
  2. Metric shopping: computing five metrics, reporting the one that passes.
  3. Ignoring base rates: declaring bias from selection-rate gaps alone when qualification rates genuinely differ — or, conversely, using base-rate differences to excuse gaps among the qualified (the equal-opportunity gap survives that excuse).
  4. Small-cell theatre: headline claims from subgroups of 40 people; report n's, aggregate responsibly, flag what cannot be concluded.
  5. One-time audits: fairness at launch drifts like accuracy drifts; live-decision re-measurement on a schedule (quarterly for Ameen) with tolerance thresholds wired to the M6 risk register.
  6. Auditing the model, ignoring the humans: override patterns can reintroduce every disparity the model fixed; deployment-phase audits must include the human layer.
  7. Publishing raw audit tables without narrative: numbers without harm framing get misread in both directions; the report structure exists for a reason.

Production considerations. Keep an immutable snapshot of the scored dataset behind every audit (reproducibility = credibility); version audit code with the model version audited; require an independent reviewer who did not build the model (M1's validation sign-off pattern); pre-agree publication policy — internal, committee, or public summary — before results exist, so the decision is not contaminated by them.

docs.title: Worked Example 1 — Bias-audit walkthrough on Ameen scores (complete arithmetic)
docs.text:
Scored validation extract: 10,000 applications, ground-truth eligibility from a caseworker re-review panel. Groups: head-of-household gender (A = male, N=6,000; B = female, N=4,000). Threshold: score ≥ 0.60 → recommend approve.

Per-group confusion matrices:

Group A (N=6,000) Group B (N=4,000) Truly eligible 3,000 2,000 Recommended approve 3,720 1,920 True positives (TP) 2,730 1,560 False positives (FP) 990 360 False negatives (FN) 270 440 True negatives (TN) 2,010 1,640

Metric computation:

Metric Group A Group B Gap / ratio Reading Selection rate 3,720/6,000 = 0.62 1,920/4,000 = 0.48 DIR = 0.48/0.62 = 0.774 Below 0.8 → four-fifths tripwire fires TPR (equal opportunity) 2,730/3,000 = 0.91 1,560/2,000 = 0.78 gap = 0.13 Eligible women-headed households are rejected at 22% vs 9% — the primary harm FPR 990/3,000 = 0.33 360/2,000 = 0.18 gap = 0.15 Errors in the favourable direction also concentrate in group A Precision 2,730/3,720 = 0.73 1,560/1,920 = 0.81 −0.08 A approved-recommendation means more in group B — calibration asymmetry signal Accuracy 0.79 0.80 ≈ 0 Global accuracy is identical — and hides everything above

Diagnosis (from the seeded course data): feature-missingness analysis shows income verification succeeds for 88% of group A but 61% of group B (measurement bias — informal-sector employment concentrates in group B's applications); label re-review of 300 stratified cases shows historical under-approval of group B at equal documented need (historical bias in labels).

Recommendation set (as priced options for the owner): (1) fix verification asymmetry via the income-service integration for informal workers — addresses cause, ~2 quarters; (2) relabel a 5,000-case stratified sample with explicit criteria and retrain — addresses label bias, ~1 quarter; (3) interim process control now: mandatory caseworker review of all group-B rejections in score band 0.45–0.60 (the band where the TPR gap concentrates); (4) re-audit quarterly with tolerance TPR-gap ≤ 0.05, DIR ≥ 0.85.

Teaching point: the identical accuracy row is the slide to leave on screen. Every governance failure in this module hides behind a healthy global metric.

docs.title: Worked Example 2 — Bias-audit report structure (the Lab 3 deliverable template)
docs.text:
BIAS-AUDIT REPORT — <system, model version, date>            SSA-AUD-<n>
1. Executive summary          — 5 sentences max: scope, headline finding,
                                primary harm, recommendation, decision needed
2. System & decision context  — what is decided, for whom, at what stakes
3. Groups & metrics           — groups analysed (with n's), metrics chosen
                                and WHY, pre-registered before computation
4. Results                    — the metric table; per-group matrices in annex;
                                intersections; small-cell flags
5. Diagnosis                  — disparity → lifecycle source, with the evidence
                                (missingness tables, relabel sample results)
6. Recommendations            — priced options table: effect, cost, timeline,
                                residual risk; interim controls separated from
                                structural fixes
7. Decision record            — what the accountable owner chose, signed, dated
8. Re-audit plan              — schedule, tolerances, trigger conditions
Annexes                       — data snapshot hash, code version, reviewer
                                independence statement

docs.title: Worked Example 3 — Toolkit snippet (the audit computation, for cohorts using the notebook)
docs.text:
# bias_audit/compute_metrics.py — Lab 3 notebook core (pre-installed environment)
# Works on the synthetic ameen_scored.csv; spreadsheet version provided too.
import pandas as pd
from fairlearn.metrics import MetricFrame, selection_rate, true_positive_rate, false_positive_rate

df = pd.read_csv("data/ameen_scored.csv")        # synthetic; no real persons
df["approved"] = (df["score"] >= 0.60).astype(int)

mf = MetricFrame(
    metrics={
        "selection_rate": selection_rate,
        "tpr": true_positive_rate,               # equal-opportunity view
        "fpr": false_positive_rate,
        "n": lambda y_true, y_pred: len(y_true),
    },
    y_true=df["eligible_truth"],
    y_pred=df["approved"],
    sensitive_features=df["hoh_gender"],         # kept for AUDIT, never a model feature
)
print(mf.by_group.round(3))

rates = mf.by_group["selection_rate"]
print("Disparate-impact ratio:", round(rates.min() / rates.max(), 3))
# Expected on course data: DIR ≈ 0.774, TPR gap ≈ 0.13 — matches Worked Example 1

Teaching point: ten lines of code, and none of them are the hard part — group definition, metric choice, diagnosis, and the decision record are. Keep the toolkit in its place.

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 3 — Bias Audit of the Ameen Model
docs.text:
Objective Execute the full audit procedure on the synthetic Ameen scored dataset and deliver a committee-ready bias-audit report — section 03 of the governance file Duration 50 minutes Setup ameen_scored.csv (10,000 synthetic rows: score, eligibility ground truth, gender, region, nationality, verification-status fields); hosted notebook with fairlearn or the spreadsheet workbook (pivot tables pre-scaffolded); report template

Instructions & tasks

  1. (5 min) Pre-register: write down groups and primary metric with one-line justification before touching the data (collect these — they are graded for the discipline, not the choice).
  2. (15 min) Compute per-group selection rates, DIR, TPR, FPR for gender and region; compute one intersection (region × gender) and flag any cell with n < 100.
  3. (10 min) Diagnose: run the missingness pivot (verification status × group) and read the provided label re-review summary; assign each disparity a lifecycle source.
  4. (15 min) Write the report: executive summary, results table, diagnosis, and a priced three-option recommendation set with an interim control.
  5. (5 min) File section 03; add the residual fairness risk to the course gap register (it will feed M6's risk register).

Expected outputs 

DIR (gender)        ≈ 0.77   → four-fifths tripwire documented
TPR gap (gender)    ≈ 0.13   → primary finding (eligible rejections)
Region analysis     → remote regions: TPR gap ≈ 0.09, small-cell flags on 2 regions
Diagnosis           → measurement bias (verification asymmetry) + historical label bias
Report              → complete template incl. interim control and re-audit tolerances

Troubleshooting guidance

Symptom Cause Fix DIR computed as advantaged ÷ disadvantaged (>1) Ratio direction confusion Convention: min rate ÷ max rate; the ratio ≤ 1 by construction TPR computed over all applicants, not the eligible Denominator error — the classic TPR conditions on truth: TP/(TP+FN); re-derive from the matrix on the board Pair reports 14 metrics, no finding Metric shopping in reverse (drowning) Force the pre-registered primary metric to lead the executive summary Intersection cells of n=23 driving headlines Small-cell theatre Flag-and-aggregate rule: report the flag, not a conclusion Notebook cohort stuck on environment Setup friction Switch pair to the spreadsheet workbook — parity of outcome is by design

Instructor notes. The dataset is generated so the verification-asymmetry diagnosis is findable but not shouted — the missingness pivot must actually be run. Pairs who skip diagnosis and jump to "retrain with fairness constraints" should be asked what mechanism their fix addresses; watch them discover it addresses none. The pre-registration slips make excellent debrief material: read two contrasting metric choices aloud and let the room argue the policy judgement.

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz (5 questions) 1. Selection rates: group A 0.55, group B 0.40. DIR and reading? → 0.727; below 0.8, adverse-impact tripwire — investigate, not verdict. 2. Which metric asks "among the truly eligible, does each group have the same approval chance"? → Equal opportunity (TPR parity). 3. Why can't calibration and equalized odds both hold when base rates differ? → Mathematical impossibility (non-trivial classifier); metric choice becomes a recorded policy judgement. 4. Give one proxy feature for gender in a segmented labour market and the test you'd run. → Employment sector; association test between feature and protected attribute + disparity re-check with feature removed/repaired. 5. Group thresholds as remediation: name the governance requirements. → Explicit differential treatment → legal/policy sign-off, transparency, documented as interim with an exit plan.

Matrix drill. Two fresh confusion matrices (provided); compute all five metrics by hand in 10 minutes. Answer key in the solutions pack.

Debugging exercise. A colleague's audit concludes "no bias: accuracy is 0.79 for both groups." Write the three-sentence rebuttal using Worked Example 1's table.

Label interrogation. Given five historical Ameen decisions (one-paragraph vignettes), identify which would be re-labelled under explicit criteria and what that implies about the training labels.

Discussion questions. - The 80% rule is an imported convention. What should a Saudi government entity use as its tripwire, and who should set it? - Interim group-specific review bands protect one group with extra scrutiny of rejections. A colleague objects this is itself unequal treatment. Resolve it in writing.

docs.title: Case Study — Hiring-Screening AI at a National Employer
docs.text:
Scenario. "Tawteen Talent" (fictional), a Saudi conglomerate hiring at scale, deploys a CV-screening model trained on ten years of its own hiring decisions to shortlist for engineering and operations roles. A year in, the recruitment analytics team notices women's shortlisting rate for technical roles is 31% versus 52% for men with similar qualification profiles; separately, applicants who list only non-Saudi universities show a shortlisting penalty even at equal experience.

Business context. The employer is a flagship participant in national workforce-development programmes: women's participation targets are strategic commitments with board visibility. HR asks whether to switch the model off; the talent-acquisition lead notes screening volume (400k applications/year) makes manual triage impossible.

Technical challenge. The training labels are the company's own historical shortlisting decisions — the model learned the past. CV text features encode gender through activity words, dates of study, and institution names even with the name/gender fields removed. The qualification ground truth needed for a proper equal-opportunity analysis does not exist and must be constructed via structured re-review.

Constraints. Hiring cannot pause; the audit must not become a discovery risk (privileged handling of interim results); the fix must survive next year's hiring-pattern changes; works councils/HR policy require any differential process treatment to be documented and approved.

Solution approach (facilitate). (1) Immediate: human review of all auto-rejected female-candidate CVs for technical roles (interim process control). (2) Construct ground truth: blind structured re-review of a 2,000-CV stratified sample by trained assessors scoring against published criteria. (3) Audit against the constructed truth: selection rates, TPR gaps, proxy analysis on text features. (4) Structural fix: retrain on re-reviewed labels + criteria-based features (skills, certifications) instead of raw CV text; validate that institution-name signal is gone. (5) Governance: quarterly re-audit wired to HR's diversity reporting; model card documents the historical-label decision (M5 tie-in).

Discussion questions. 1. The model reproduced the firm's own history. Whose bias is the finding — the model's or the organisation's — and what does the answer change about remediation ownership? 2. Constructing ground truth by re-review imports the re-reviewers' judgement. How do you govern that? (Criteria publication, inter-rater agreement stats, panel diversity.) 3. Volume makes "switch it off" unrealistic. Construct the interim risk position you would sign. 4. Which parts of this audit belong in the public diversity report, and which in privileged review? Defend the line.

docs.title: Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. Between "we need the data for the model" and "the law protects the person" sits a set of engineering disciplines this module teaches: data minimisation as a design habit, the sharp legal and technical line between pseudonymisation and anonymisation, re-identification risk and how to actually measure it (k-anonymity and its refinements), the modern toolbox (differential privacy, synthetic data) at working-knowledge depth, and the privacy impact assessment (DPIA) that binds it all into a decision document. It converts Module 2's obligations into Module 4's techniques.

Business relevance. Privacy engineering is what lets data be used at all. Organisations that master anonymisation and minimisation unlock analytics, research partnerships, and open-data publication that timid or reckless competitors cannot touch: the timid share nothing and starve their models; the reckless share "de-identified" data that re-identifies, and inherit a breach. In the Kingdom, where the national data agenda pushes simultaneously for data sharing (open data, interoperability) and data protection (PDPL), the practitioners who can hold both are the ones who make national-platform projects possible.

Industry use cases. - A health authority wants hospital data released to university researchers; the release goes ahead only after quasi-identifier generalisation demonstrates k ≥ 5 and the utility loss is documented as acceptable for the research questions. - A telecom builds mobility analytics for urban planning from location traces — the canonical hard case (location data is uniquely re-identifying) — and ships aggregate-only products after a documented re-identification analysis. - The SSA (our golden thread) wants to give its data-science team a training extract without exposing applicant identities, and to publish region-level statistics openly.

Expected competencies. Participants can run a data-minimisation review on a feature list, distinguish pseudonymisation from anonymisation and state the legal consequence of each, compute k for a dataset and apply generalisation/suppression to raise it, articulate l-diversity and the homogeneity attack, explain differential privacy and synthetic data at decision-maker depth, and complete a DPIA for an AI system.

docs.title: Learning Objectives (mapped)
docs.text: # Objective Maps to 4.1 Apply data-minimisation review to an AI feature set: necessity, proportionality, retention LO4 4.2 Distinguish pseudonymisation from anonymisation and state the PDPL consequence of each LO4, LO1 4.3 Assess re-identification risk via quasi-identifiers; compute and raise k-anonymity; recognise the homogeneity attack (l-diversity) LO4 4.4 Position differential privacy and synthetic data correctly: what they guarantee, what they cost, when to reach for them LO4 4.5 Complete a DPIA for a high-risk AI processing activity LO4, LO5

docs.title: 1. Data minimisation as an engineering discipline
docs.text:
Minimisation is the most underrated privacy control because it is the only one with zero residual risk: data you never collected cannot leak, cannot be misused, and never appears in a breach notification. Operationally it is three recurring reviews:

  • Collection review — "necessity per feature": for every field, the team must state the purpose it serves and what breaks without it. The honest test: would we pay SAR 10,000/year to keep this field? — because in risk terms, you do. AUC-lift alone is not necessity; a 0.2% lift from a sensitive field fails proportionality.
  • Access review — "who sees what grain": the data scientist needs distributions, not names; the caseworker needs one applicant, not the register; the dashboard needs aggregates. Grain-matching access to role is minimisation applied to people.
  • Retention review — "necessity over time": every dataset gets a review date and a default-delete posture. "Keep for future models" is a purpose without a limit and fails the test (Ameen's GAP-10).

For AI specifically, minimisation lands at four points: feature selection (fewest personal attributes that meet the documented performance bar), training extracts (sampled and stripped, not full-register copies), logging (M6 of the software-practice module's lesson recurs — no raw personal attributes in logs), and model outputs (return the decision and reasons, not input echoes).

docs.title: 2. Pseudonymisation vs anonymisation: the line that decides everything
docs.text:
• Pseudonymisation replaces direct identifiers (name, national ID) with tokens, keeping a re-linking key or a deterministic mapping. It is a valuable security measure — and the data remains personal data under PDPL, with every obligation intact, because identification is still reasonably possible (by the key holder or by anyone who links quasi-identifiers).
  • Anonymisation severs identifiability such that the individual is no longer identifiable, directly or indirectly, by any means reasonably likely to be used. Genuinely anonymous data exits data-protection obligations — which is exactly why the claim must be demonstrated, and why every governance regime treats the word "anonymised" on a file name as a claim awaiting evidence, not a property.

The practical consequence taught as a rule: a dataset is treated at its source classification until an anonymisation analysis says otherwise (Module 2's inheritance rule). The analysis has a name and a method — re-identification risk assessment — and it is the next section.

docs.title: 3. Re-identification risk and k-anonymity
docs.text:
Direct identifiers are easy; quasi-identifiers are the problem: attribute combinations that single people out. The famous pattern — date of birth + gender + postal area identifying most of a population — generalises: in the Ameen extract, {age, district, nationality, household size} nearly fingerprints many applicants even with IDs removed.

k-anonymity: every record is indistinguishable from at least k−1 others on the quasi-identifier set. Computed by grouping on the quasi-identifiers and finding the minimum group size. Raised by:

  • Generalisation: age 34 → band 30–39; district → region; exact income → income band.
  • Suppression: delete records in groups that stay small after reasonable generalisation (rare nationality × remote district cells), or blank the offending cells.

k is necessary, not sufficient. Two refinements participants must know by attack, not by formula:

  • Homogeneity attack → l-diversity: if all k records in a group share the sensitive value (all five applicants in the cell have the same disability status), the attacker learns it without singling anyone out. l-diversity demands diversity of sensitive values within each group.
  • Background-knowledge and composition attacks: overlapping releases (this year's and last year's extracts) can be differenced; auxiliary public data (social media, leaked datasets) links what each release alone would not. This is why anonymisation decisions consider the release environment, not the file in isolation — and why "publish once, assess every time" is the rule for recurring open-data releases.

The utility ledger: every generalisation costs analytical resolution. A privacy decision without a utility statement is half a decision; Lab 4 requires recording both (k achieved and what analyses the generalisation forecloses).

docs.title: 4. The modern toolbox at decision depth: differential privacy and synthetic data
docs.text:
Participants need working fluency, not implementation skill:

  • Differential privacy (DP) gives a mathematical guarantee about queries/outputs, not datasets: calibrated noise ensures any single individual's presence changes results by at most a bounded amount (the privacy budget ε; smaller = stronger). Right tool for published statistics and aggregate releases (national statistics offices use it for census products) and increasingly for training (DP-SGD) where membership inference is a real threat. Costs: accuracy loss concentrated on small subgroups — which collides directly with M3's need for small-group fairness measurement; naming that collision is the mark of a governance-literate practitioner. Budget management (ε accumulates across queries) is an operational discipline, not a one-time setting.
  • Synthetic data — generated records mimicking the statistical structure of real data — is useful for development environments, demos, and sharing shape without people (this course's own datasets are the demonstration). It is not automatically anonymous: a generator overfitted to its training data can memorise and emit near-copies of real records. A synthetic release needs the same re-identification scrutiny, plus generator-specific checks (nearest-neighbour distance to real records, membership-inference testing). "It's synthetic" is a starting claim with the same standing as "it's anonymised."
  • Choosing: aggregates for the public → DP; record-level research release → generalisation/suppression to k with l-diversity checks + contractual controls; dev/test environments → synthetic; and often the best answer is don't release records at all — bring the analysis to the data (secure research environments, federated queries) rather than the data to the analyst.

docs.title: 5. The privacy impact assessment (DPIA)
docs.text:
The DPIA is where Module 2's legal trigger ("high-risk processing must be assessed") meets this module's techniques. Structure taught (and used in Lab 4):

  1. Description: processing, purposes, data categories, flows (imported from the RoPA — artefacts compose).
  2. Necessity & proportionality: the minimisation review's output; alternatives considered ("could aggregates suffice?").
  3. Risk identification: to data subjects, not to the organisation — unauthorised access, re-identification, function creep, discriminatory effect (cross-reference the M3 audit), chilling effects.
  4. Risk evaluation: likelihood × severity, before controls.
  5. Mitigations: the techniques of this module, mapped risk-by-risk, with residual risk stated honestly.
  6. Consultation & sign-off: DPO consulted; accountable owner accepts residual risk in writing; review triggers defined.

The DPIA's quality marker is the honesty of its residual-risk statement. "All risks mitigated" is the signature of an assessment written to be filed, not used.

docs.title: 6. Common mistakes & production considerations
docs.text:
1. The redaction reflex: removing names/IDs and calling it anonymised — quasi-identifiers untouched. The single most common privacy failure in analytics.
  2. Anonymising the extract, keeping the pipeline: the "anonymised" dataset is regenerated weekly by a job that reads the identified source — the system is identified even if one file is not; assess the pipeline.
  3. Hash-and-hope pseudonymisation: hashing national IDs without salt/pepper — enumerable input spaces make unsalted hashes reversible by brute force; and even done well, it is still pseudonymisation, not anonymisation.
  4. Utility silence: shipping a k=10 dataset nobody can use, discovering it three months later; the utility ledger exists to force the conversation at decision time.
  5. One-release thinking: each quarterly extract safe alone, the sequence linkable — composition is assessed at the programme level.
  6. DP theatre: quoting "we use differential privacy" with ε=15 (weak) or without budget tracking — the guarantee is the parameters, not the phrase.
  7. Synthetic-data laundering: using synthetic generation to dodge review entirely; the generator's training data was real and the output needs testing.

Production considerations. Version anonymisation configurations like code (the generalisation hierarchy is a policy artefact); log releases in a register (who received what, under which analysis, when — composition tracking depends on it); pre-agree the re-identification testing protocol with the receiving party in sharing agreements; and keep the identified source's controls unchanged — anonymisation of outputs never weakens obligations on inputs.

docs.text:
Feature Purpose claimed Necessity test result Decision Household income (banded) Core eligibility signal Required by eligibility criteria Keep (banded at source) Disability status Statutory priority categories Required, sensitive → tightened access, band to category level Keep, restrict Exact birth date "Age is predictive" Age band 5y suffices; exact DOB is a top quasi-identifier Replace with band Applicant phone number In extract "by join accident" No modelling purpose Drop from extract District (fine-grained) Regional cost-of-living signal Region level captures the signal (validated: AUC −0.001) Generalise to region Free-text case notes "Might be useful later" No defined purpose; PII-dense Drop; revisit only with purpose + basis

Teaching point: two of six fields survive unchanged. That ratio is typical of first-pass minimisation on organically grown extracts — and the AUC-validation column shows the review is an empirical exercise, not an act of renunciation.

docs.title: Worked Example 2 — k-anonymity walkthrough on the SSA research extract
docs.text:
Quasi-identifier set: {age, district, nationality, household size}. Extract: 8,000 records.

Before generalisation (grouping on raw QIs): minimum group size k = 1 — 214 records are unique; the "de-identified" extract is a re-identification kit.

Sample of exposed records:

Age District Nationality HH size Group size 67 Al-Aziziyah (rare nationality) 9 1 23 (remote district) Saudi 11 1 41 Al-Rawdah (rare nationality) 2 2

Generalisation pass 1 — age → 10-year bands, district → governorate: k rises to 3 (38 groups below 5). Generalisation pass 2 — nationality → {Saudi, GCC, Other}, household size → {1–3, 4–6, 7+}: k = 5 for 7,912 records; 88 records in stubborn small groups → suppressed.

Result: k ≥ 5 on 98.9% of records, 1.1% suppressed. Utility ledger: governorate-level analysis preserved; district-level programme targeting foreclosed (flagged to the research team — they accepted); age effects now resolvable only to decade.

l-diversity check: 3 of the k≥5 groups are homogeneous on disability status → within-group learning of the sensitive value. Fix: merge those groups one level up on age band. Final release: k ≥ 5, sensitive-attribute diversity verified, release logged in the register.

# privacy_lab/k_check.py — the 6-line k-anonymity check used in Lab 4
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("data/ssa_research_extract.csv")     # synthetic
QI = ["age_band", "governorate", "nationality_group", "hh_size_band"]
k = df.groupby(QI).size().min()
small = df.groupby(QI).size().pipe(lambda s: s[s < 5])
print(f"k = {k}; groups below 5: {len(small)}")

docs.title: Worked Example 3 — DPIA excerpt for the Ameen training pipeline (risk table)

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 4 — Privacy Risk Assessment and Anonymisation
docs.text:
Objective Assess and remediate the SSA research extract: minimisation review, re-identification analysis to k ≥ 5 with l-diversity check, utility ledger, and the DPIA risk table — section 04 of the governance file Duration 50 minutes Setup ssa_research_extract.csv (8,000 synthetic rows, raw quasi-identifiers, 214 seeded unique records); notebook with the k-check script or spreadsheet pivot workbook; generalisation-hierarchy sheet; DPIA template

Instructions & tasks

  1. (8 min) Minimisation first: apply the necessity test to the extract's 14 columns; drop/band before any k analysis (order matters — assess what you should hold, not what you happen to hold).
  2. (7 min) Compute k on the raw quasi-identifier set; count unique records; screenshot the number — it goes in the report as the "before" state.
  3. (15 min) Apply generalisation passes from the hierarchy sheet, recomputing k after each; suppress stubborn residual groups; stop when k ≥ 5 on ≥ 98% of records.
  4. (8 min) Run the l-diversity check on disability status; fix homogeneous groups; record the fix.
  5. (7 min) Write the utility ledger: three analyses preserved, two foreclosed, receiving-team acknowledgment line.
  6. (5 min) Complete the DPIA risk table (5 rows minimum, honest residuals); file section 04; add residual privacy risks to the gap register.

Expected outputs 

Before:  k = 1, 214 unique records on {age, district, nationality, hh_size}
Pass 1:  k = 3 (age bands + governorate)
Pass 2:  k = 5 on 98.9%; 88 records suppressed
l-diversity: 3 homogeneous groups found and merged
Utility ledger: district-level targeting foreclosed (acknowledged)
DPIA: ≥ 5 risks, ≥ 1 residual honestly Medium with acceptance conditions

Troubleshooting guidance

Symptom Cause Fix k computed per-column, not per-combination Conceptual miss — the central one Re-derive on the board: uniqueness lives in combinations; group on the full QI set k = 5 achieved by suppressing 15% of records Generalisation skipped, suppression overused Rule of thumb: generalise first, suppress last, suppression budget ≤ 2% Pair anonymises before minimising Habit of treating all columns as given Re-order: dropping the phone-number column is better than generalising it l-diversity check skipped ("k=5, we're done") k-sufficiency assumption Show the homogeneous-group rows: what does an attacker learn without singling anyone out? DPIA residuals all "Low" Filing instinct Require one residual ≥ Medium with acceptance conditions — the honesty marker

Instructor notes. The before-state moment (k=1, 214 uniques on a file the brief calls "de-identified") is the module's money shot — have every pair post their unique-record count to the shared board before generalising. The utility-ledger step meets resistance ("not our job"); insist: privacy engineering that ignores utility gets routed around, and routed-around controls protect no one. Fast finishers: run the composition thought-experiment (diff two quarterly releases) and write the register rule that prevents it.

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz (5 questions) 1. Pseudonymised data under PDPL: in scope or out? → In scope — still personal data; anonymisation (demonstrated) is what exits scope. 2. Define k-anonymity in one sentence and name its two raising tools. → Every record indistinguishable from ≥ k−1 others on the quasi-identifiers; generalisation and suppression. 3. What does the homogeneity attack exploit and which property answers it? → All k records sharing the sensitive value; l-diversity. 4. What does differential privacy's ε control? → The privacy budget: the maximum influence any individual has on outputs; smaller = stronger guarantee, more noise. 5. Name two checks a synthetic dataset needs before release. → Nearest-neighbour distance to real records (memorisation) and membership-inference testing — plus the standard re-identification lens.

Quasi-identifier hunt. Given a 20-column schema, mark the QI set and rank the top three by re-identification power; justify against public auxiliary data available in practice.

Hash critique. A team proposes SHA-256(national ID) as "anonymisation." Write the two-paragraph rejection: enumerable input space, and category error (pseudonymisation at best).

Release triage. Four requests (public dashboard, university research, vendor debugging, internal BI) — match each to the right technique from Section 4 and state the one control you would attach.

Discussion questions. - The research team says suppressing 88 records "biases the sample against rare groups" — and they are right (it does, and those are often M3's groups of concern). Resolve the privacy–fairness tension explicitly. - Who should hold the authority to approve a record-level release: the data owner, the DPO, or a committee? What does each answer optimise for?

docs.title: Case Study — Hospital Research Extract at a Regional Health Cluster
docs.text:
Scenario. A health cluster in the Eastern Province prepares a research extract for a university partnership on diabetes outcomes: 60,000 patient episodes, "de-identified" by removing names and medical record numbers. A pre-release review (prompted by a new research-office hire) finds the extract contains admission dates, exact ages, district, nationality, occupation, and rare-diagnosis codes. A test linkage against publicly available information re-identifies several individuals in under an hour — including a public figure whose hospitalisation was reported in the press.

Business context. The partnership is signed, the university team is waiting, and the cluster's leadership wants research output for its academic-status ambitions. A breach here would be a sensitive-data incident under PDPL with mandatory notification analysis — health data is squarely in the sensitive category.

Technical challenge. Longitudinal episodes make anonymisation genuinely hard: the sequence of admissions is itself a fingerprint; rare diagnoses defeat generalisation; dates enable linkage to press reports and social media. Aggregation destroys the survival-analysis utility the researchers need.

Constraints. The research questions genuinely need episode-level data; the university's environment is outside the cluster's control; the data-sharing agreement predates the review and specifies "de-identified data" without defining it; publication pressure is real and the researchers are not adversaries — but their laptops travel.

Solution approach (facilitate). (1) Stop the release; the agreement's undefined "de-identified" is the cluster's problem, not its protection. (2) Reframe the sharing model: instead of exporting records, stand up a secure research environment — analysts come to the data, no record-level egress, output checked against small-cell rules before leaving. (3) Where export is unavoidable, apply the full discipline: date shifting (consistent per patient), age/geography generalisation, rare-diagnosis handling (suppress or coarsen), sequence-length capping — then measure k on the episode-level QI set and test-linkage again. (4) Rewrite the agreement: define anonymisation by test outcome, not adjective; specify the re-identification protocol, output rules, and incident duties. (5) Notification analysis for the test re-identifications: reviewed internally under privilege — the review found the risk before an external party did, and the record of that finding and fix is the defensible position.

Discussion questions. 1. The extract was "de-identified" under any casual reading. Write the one-sentence contractual definition of anonymisation that would have prevented this. 2. Secure research environments cost more and slow research. Construct the proportionality argument for when export is acceptable anyway. 3. The public figure's episode was re-identified via press coverage — background knowledge no generalisation of the dataset controls. What does this imply about anonymisation of famous individuals' data, and who else shares that exposure profile? 4. Health data is sensitive under PDPL. Walk the breach-analysis: was there a notifiable breach here, and what turns on the answer?

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
1. Identifiability spectrum — Purpose: the module's anchor. Elements: horizontal spectrum from identified → pseudonymised → k-anonymised → aggregate/DP; a bold legal line between pseudonymised and anonymised labelled "PDPL obligations apply left of here"; technique icons beneath each zone. Style: spectrum bar with the legal line as the dominant visual element.
  2. Quasi-identifier linkage diagram — Elements: "de-identified" extract table and a public auxiliary source with matching QI columns highlighted, converging arrows to a re-identified individual icon. Style: two-table linkage graphic, red match highlighting.
  3. Generalisation hierarchy tree — Elements: age/district/nationality hierarchies as trees (exact → band → coarse), with the Lab 4 pass-1/pass-2 cut lines drawn. Style: three small trees, printable A4 (participants mark their cuts on it).
  4. Sharing-model decision flow — Elements: request type branching to DP-aggregates / k-anonymised export / secure environment / synthetic dev-data / refuse; one control attached per leaf. Style: compact flowchart (mirrors M3's metric tree for visual consistency).

docs.text:
1. k-check output before/after — why: the before/after anchor; content: k = 1; groups below 5: 641 vs k = 5; groups below 5: 0 side by side.
  2. Pivot of a homogeneous group — why: the homogeneity attack made concrete; content: five rows, same age band/governorate, same disability status highlighted.

docs.title: Simulations
docs.text:
1. Live re-identification demo — Setup: instructor projects the raw extract and a mock "public" auxiliary file (fictional social-media-style profile lines); links one record in under two minutes. Expected behaviour: audible discomfort; the point lands. Learning objective: re-identification is a lookup, not a heist. All data fictional — state this before and after.
  2. Composition attack tabletop — Setup: hand out Q1 and Q2 "releases" of the same extract with slightly different suppression; pairs diff them. Expected behaviour: suppressed records in one release recovered from the other. Learning objective: assess programmes, not files.

docs.title: Interactive Activities
docs.text:
• "Keep, band, or drop" auction (12 min): feature cards debated one at a time; teams must fund retention of each field from a fixed risk budget — makes the SAR-10k test visceral.
  • Technique-matching relay (8 min): the four release-triage scenarios on the wall; pairs post technique + control sticky notes and defend.

docs.title: Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. Accountability has a paper trail or it does not exist. This module teaches the documentation infrastructure of trustworthy AI: model cards that tell the truth about capability and limits, datasheets that make datasets interrogable, decision notices that respect the person on the receiving end, explanation methods positioned honestly (what they can and cannot tell you), and audit trails that let a specific decision be reconstructed months later. These artefacts are how the SDAIA principles of Transparency & Explainability and Accountability & Responsibility become inspectable objects.

Business relevance. Documentation is the cheapest control with the highest audit yield: when the regulator query arrives (M2's drill), when the committee convenes (this course's capstone), when the vendor relationship sours (M6), or when a decision is appealed, the organisation with current model cards and reconstructable audit trails answers in hours; the organisation without them convenes a war room. Documentation is also a handover technology — AI systems outlive their builders, and the model card is what makes the successor team's first month survivable. In procurement, buyers increasingly require model cards and evaluation documentation as deliverables; teams fluent in producing them win work.

Industry use cases. - A bank must give declined credit applicants meaningful reasons; reason codes generated from the model's top factors feed a notice template reviewed by legal and consumer-protection functions — explanation as a product feature with governance behind it. - A ministry's AI platform requires a completed model card before any model enters its registry; the card's "out-of-scope uses" section is contractually binding on consuming departments. - During an audit of Ameen, the review team reconstructs a contested decision from 14 months earlier — inputs, model version, score, threshold, caseworker override and its recorded reason — in twenty minutes, because the audit trail was designed, not accreted.

Expected competencies. Participants can write a complete, honest model card; produce a datasheet for a training dataset; design a decision notice that meets transparency obligations without leaking sensitive information; position global vs local explanation methods and their failure modes; and specify an audit-trail event schema that makes decisions reconstructable.

docs.title: Learning Objectives (mapped)
docs.text: # Objective Maps to 5.1 Write a model card covering intended use, out-of-scope uses, data, subgroup evaluation, and limitations LO5 5.2 Produce a datasheet documenting a dataset's provenance, composition, and known skews LO5, LO1 5.3 Design decision notices and explanation content appropriate to the audience and the stakes LO5, LO2 5.4 Position explanation methods (global vs local) honestly, including their failure modes LO5, LO3 5.5 Specify an audit-trail event schema enabling full decision reconstruction LO5

docs.title: 1. Transparency has audiences: one system, four documents
docs.text:
The most common transparency failure is writing one document for four audiences. Teach the audience matrix first, then the artefacts:

Audience Question they ask Artefact Register Affected person "Why was my application rejected, and what can I do?" Decision notice + appeal path Plain language (Arabic for citizens — flag the language note) Operator (caseworker) "How should I use — and when should I distrust — this score?" Operating guide + model card §use Practical, procedural Governance/audit "Was this system validated, for whom does it fail, who owns it?" Model card + datasheet + audit trail Structured, evidenced Technical successor "How do I maintain, retrain, or retire this?" Model card + pipeline docs + decision log Technical

The model card is the hub document; notices and guides are derived views. Getting this dependency right means one source of truth and no divergence between what the committee reads and what the citizen is told.

docs.title: 2. Model cards: structure and the honesty disciplines
docs.text:
The model card (popularised by Mitchell et al., 2019, and now industry-standard from major labs to procurement checklists) is a short structured document answering: what is this model, what is it for, what is it not for, on what was it trained and evaluated, how does it perform — for whom — and what are its limits. The course structure (used in Lab 5 and Worked Example 1):

  1. Model details — name, version, type, owner, dates, contact.
  2. Intended use — the decision it supports, the users, the operating context.
  3. Out-of-scope uses — explicitly named misuses (the section that prevents M1's scope creep; make it specific: "not validated for housing-support prioritisation").
  4. Training & evaluation data — sources, period, size, known skews (links to the datasheet).
  5. Performance — headline metrics and the subgroup table from the M3 audit; a card without subgroup results is pre-2020 practice.
  6. Fairness & limitations — known disparities, small-cell caveats, conditions of degraded performance.
  7. Ethical considerations & mitigations — the trade-offs made and controls attached (imported from the governance file).
  8. Maintenance — retraining cadence, monitoring thresholds, review triggers, decommissioning criteria.
  9. Version history — what changed and why, including threshold changes (M3's simulation lesson).

The honesty disciplines: (a) every claim cites its evidence artefact — the card is an index, not an essay; (b) the limitations section is written by the builders, reviewed by a non-builder — self-reported limitations are systematically flattering; (c) the card versions with the model — a card describing v2 while v3 serves is worse than no card, because it manufactures false confidence.

Datasheets for datasets (Gebru et al.) apply the same discipline upstream: motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing, known skews, recommended and discouraged uses. For Ameen, the datasheet is where the verification asymmetry (M3's diagnosis) gets permanently recorded so no future team rediscovers it the hard way.

docs.title: 3. Explainability: methods, honestly positioned
docs.text:
Participants need decision-maker fluency in the explanation toolbox, including its failure modes:

  • Global explanations — what drives the model overall: feature importance, partial-dependence summaries. Right for governance review and the model card's performance narrative. Failure mode: importance rankings differ across methods and can be unstable under correlated features; treat as descriptive, not causal.
  • Local explanations — why this prediction: SHAP-style attributions, counterfactual statements ("had verified income been X, the recommendation would differ"). Counterfactuals are usually the most honest citizen-facing form because they state what would change the outcome — which is what the person actually needs. Failure modes: attributions on proxy features "explain" with the proxy (an explanation of a biased model is a well-explained biased decision — explanation is not exculpation); counterfactuals must be actionable (do not tell a family to change household size).
  • Inherently interpretable models — scorecards, small rule sets, monotonic GBMs: for high-stakes decisions the governance question "could an interpretable model do this job?" must be asked and its answer recorded before accepting black-box + post-hoc explanation. Post-hoc explanation of an unnecessary black box is complexity chosen, then apologised for.
  • The explanation ≠ transparency point: a perfect SHAP plot does not tell an applicant that AI was involved, what data was used, or how to appeal — those are notice obligations (Section 4), not explanation methods. Systems need both.

docs.title: 4. Decision notices: transparency at the person
docs.text:
The notice is where the whole course faces a human being. Design rules taught through the Ameen adverse-decision notice (Worked Example 2):

  1. Disclose the mechanism: the person is told that an automated scoring system contributed to the decision — plainly, not in clause 14(b).
  2. Give reasons that are true and useful: the top decision factors, stated in the person's terms ("reported income above the programme threshold"), not model jargon ("feature x7 SHAP −0.34").
  3. State the action path: what to correct, how to appeal, to whom, by when — an appeal path that requires digital literacy the affected population lacks fails M3's impact-assessment test.
  4. Do not leak: reasons must not expose other people's data, fraud-detection logic that enables gaming (a real tension — resolve it explicitly and record the resolution), or sensitive inferences.
  5. Language and access: citizen-facing notices in Arabic (bilingual best practice), reading-level checked, available through non-digital channels for the populations that need them.

docs.title: 5. Audit trails: reconstructability as a design requirement
docs.text:
The governance test of an audit trail is one question: can we reconstruct this specific decision, as it was made, with what was known then? Working backwards from that test gives the event schema:

  • Decision event: timestamp, application ID (pseudonymous key), input snapshot reference (not inline PII — M4/M6 log discipline), feature-pipeline version, model version, score, threshold in force, recommendation.
  • Human-action event: caseworker ID, action (accept/override), recorded override reason (from a structured reason list plus free text policy), timestamp.
  • Change events: model deployments, threshold changes (with approver), pipeline changes, policy changes — the M3 threshold simulation showed why these are fairness events; here they become logged events.
  • Access events: who viewed which case — audit trails are themselves personal-data processing; retention, access control, and PDPL obligations apply to them too (the recursive point participants forget).

Integrity properties: append-only storage, clock discipline, retention aligned with the appeals/audit window, and separation of duties (the team operating the model does not administer the trail). The trail's analytics close the loop: override-rate by caseworker and by group is the deployment-bias monitor M3 called for.

docs.title: 6. Common mistakes & operational considerations
docs.text:
1. The aspirational model card: describing the system the team meant to build; every unevidenced claim is a future audit finding.
  2. Card rot: v3 serving, v2 card published — versioning the card with the model is a release-gate rule, not a good intention.
  3. Explanation theatre: shipping SHAP plots to citizens who need "what can I do?" — audience mismatch (Section 1's matrix exists for this).
  4. Gaming-proof secrecy as a blanket excuse: refusing all reason-giving because "people will game it." Some factors are game-proof (verified income), some are not (free-text patterns); the analysis must be factor-by-factor and recorded.
  5. Logs that log everything except the decision: infrastructure logs galore, but no threshold history, no override reasons — reconstruct the server, not the decision.
  6. Free-text-only override reasons: unanalysable; the structured reason list is what turns overrides into monitorable data.
  7. PII-rich audit trails: inlining full applications into logs recreates M4's problem in the compliance layer itself.

Operational considerations. Make card completion a release gate (no card, no deploy — enforced in the M6 workflow); assign each card an owner and a review date; store cards in the same registry as models so drift is structurally impossible; and treat notice text changes as governed changes (legal + DPO review) with their own version history.

docs.title: Worked Example 1 — Model card for Ameen v3 (complete)
docs.text:
MODEL CARD — Ameen Eligibility Scoring v3.2               SSA-MC-003 · v3.2 · (course date)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. MODEL DETAILS
   Gradient-boosted classifier; monthly batch scoring + on-demand rescore.
   Owner: Director, Benefits Operations. Technical steward: SSA Analytics.
   Developed with processor TahleelTech LLC under DPA (SSA-DPA-011).

2. INTENDED USE
   Prioritise caseworker review and recommend eligibility for the family-
   support programme. Users: trained SSA caseworkers. The score RECOMMENDS;
   caseworker decision is required for every adverse outcome.

3. OUT-OF-SCOPE USES (binding)
   × Housing-support or any other programme's prioritisation (not validated)
   × Fraud detection or investigation targeting
   × Fully automated decisions without caseworker action
   × Scoring of non-applicant individuals

4. TRAINING & EVALUATION DATA
   Training: 214,000 historical applications (4 years) with caseworker
   outcomes as labels — KNOWN LIMITATION: labels inherit historical decision
   patterns; see datasheet SSA-DS-007 §known-skews and audit SSA-AUD-002.
   Evaluation: 10,000-case holdout re-reviewed by a criteria-based panel.

5. PERFORMANCE (panel-reviewed holdout, threshold 0.60)
   Global: AUC 0.86 · accuracy 0.79 · recall (eligible) 0.86
   Subgroups (from bias audit SSA-AUD-002):
     TPR — male HoH 0.91 / female HoH 0.78  (gap 0.13 — above tolerance)
     Selection-rate DIR (gender): 0.77 — below 0.8 tripwire
     Regional TPR gap: 0.09 (remote regions); 2 small-cell flags (n<100)

6. FAIRNESS & LIMITATIONS
   Verification asymmetry: income verification succeeds 88% (salaried) vs
   61% (informal sector) — degraded accuracy where verification fails.
   Not validated for: applications via the new mobile channel (< 3 months
   of data); households > 12 members (n=61 in training).

7. ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS & MITIGATIONS
   Interim control: mandatory caseworker review of female-HoH rejections
   in score band 0.45–0.60 (per SSA-AUD-002 recommendation 3, accepted).
   Disability status: category-level only; excluded from notice reasons.

8. MAINTENANCE
   Quarterly fairness re-measurement (tolerances: TPR gap ≤ 0.05, DIR ≥ 0.85);
   annual full re-audit; retraining on relabelled data planned (2 quarters).
   Review triggers: data-source change, threshold change, channel mix shift
   > 10 points. Decommission if tolerances breached 2 consecutive quarters
   without remediation.

9. VERSION HISTORY
   v3.2 (current): threshold 0.60 (was 0.55) — approved SSA-GOV-DEC-041;
   fairness impact assessed in SSA-AUD-002 annex C.
   v3.1: added income-verification status feature. v3.0: model family change.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Evidence index: SSA-AUD-002 (bias audit) · SSA-DS-007 (datasheet) ·
SSA-DPIA-004 (privacy) · SSA-GOV-001 (risk tier) · appeal stats dashboard

Teaching point: section 5 contains unflattering numbers. That is the card doing its job — a card that only reports AUC is marketing. Note also that every hard claim points at an evidence artefact built in an earlier lab: the governance file is composing itself.

docs.title: Worked Example 2 — Adverse-decision notice (annotated)
docs.text:
Subject: Outcome of your family-support application — <reference>

Dear applicant,
Your application has not been approved at this time.            [decision first]

How this decision was made: your application was assessed by an SSA
caseworker, assisted by an automated scoring system that compares
application information against programme criteria.              [mechanism disclosed]

The main factors in this outcome were:
 • Reported household income above the programme threshold for a
   household of your size                                        [true, useful, actionable]
 • Employment income could not be verified with your employer     [actionable]

What you can do:
 • If any information above is incorrect, you can correct it and request
   reassessment at <portal>, any SSA service centre, or by phone <number>.
 • You may appeal within 30 days at <appeal channel>. An appeal is
   reviewed by a caseworker not involved in the original decision.
                                                                  [action path, non-digital channel]
This notice is available in Arabic and English. [language note — Arabic
version is the primary legal text for citizens]

Annotations to teach: no scores or model jargon; both reasons are correctable facts, not immutable traits; the appeal reviewer independence line is a governance control surfacing as citizen-facing text; and what is absent — the fraud-signal factors, deliberately excluded after a factor-by-factor gaming analysis (decision recorded in SSA-GOV-DEC-043).

docs.title: Worked Example 3 — Audit-trail event schema (excerpt)
docs.text:
// decision event — one per scoring
{"event": "eligibility_scored", "ts": "2026-07-05T09:14:02Z",
 "case_ref": "PSD-88213",                    // pseudonymous key, not national ID
 "input_snapshot": "s3://ssa-audit/snap/88213-v7",   // reference, not inline PII
 "pipeline_version": "feat-2.4.1", "model_version": "ameen-3.2",
 "score": 0.57, "threshold": 0.60, "recommendation": "reject"}

// human action — one per caseworker decision
{"event": "caseworker_action", "ts": "2026-07-05T11:40:19Z",
 "case_ref": "PSD-88213", "actor": "CW-0412",
 "action": "override_approve",
 "reason_code": "R04_VERIFICATION_GAP",       // structured list — analysable
 "reason_text_ref": "s3://ssa-audit/notes/88213-a"}

// change event — thresholds are governance events
{"event": "threshold_changed", "ts": "2026-06-01T08:00:00Z",
 "from": 0.55, "to": 0.60, "approved_by": "GOV-DEC-041",
 "fairness_impact_ref": "SSA-AUD-002-annexC"}

Teaching point: run the reconstruction test aloud — with these three events plus the snapshot reference, the contested decision of case PSD-88213 is fully reconstructable, including the fact that a human overrode the model and why. Then run the M4 test: no national IDs, no inline application data — the trail passes its own privacy review.

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 5 — Model Card and Audit-Trail Design for Ameen
docs.text:
Objective Produce the Ameen v3 model card (drawing every evidence claim from sections 01–04 of the governance file), the adverse-decision notice, and the audit-trail event schema — section 05 of the file Duration 50 minutes (Day 3 Hour 1, after the micro-lecture) Setup Model-card template; the pair's own governance file sections 01–04; notice template; event-schema worksheet; the "committee red-team" question cards

Instructions & tasks

  1. (20 min) Complete the nine-section model card. Hard rule: every claim in sections 4–7 must cite an artefact that exists in your file (your audit, your DPIA, your classification records). Claims without citations get struck in review.
  2. (10 min) Write the adverse-decision notice for a rejection driven by the income-threshold and verification factors; run it against the five design rules; mark which factors you excluded and why (one line each).
  3. (10 min) Specify the audit-trail schema: the three event types with field lists; apply the reconstruction test and the PII test to your own schema.
  4. (5 min) Peer red-team: swap cards with another pair; each asks two committee questions from the card deck ("what happens for households above 12 members?"); the card either answers or gains a limitations line.
  5. (5 min) File section 05; update the gap register (documentation gaps now have artefacts closing them — mark GAP-06 and GAP-07 as remediated-by-design, pending deployment).

Expected outputs 

Model card: 9/9 sections, subgroup table present, ≥ 6 evidence citations,
            ≥ 3 honest limitations (incl. the mobile-channel gap)
Notice: passes all 5 design rules; ≥ 1 factor exclusion documented
Schema: 3 event types; reconstruction test passes; 0 PII fields inline
Red-team: ≥ 1 limitations line added from peer questioning

Troubleshooting guidance

Symptom Cause Fix Card reads like a brochure Aspirational-card failure Apply the citation rule ruthlessly; uncited claims get struck on the projector once, publicly Performance section shows global AUC only Subgroup table forgotten It is sitting in their own section 03 — the point of the golden thread; send them to their audit Notice includes "your score was 0.57" Audience mismatch Ask: what does the applicant do with 0.57? Reasons must be actionable facts Schema logs full application JSON inline PII-rich trail Run the M4 test on their own schema; snapshot-by-reference pattern Override reason is free text only Unanalysable design Require the structured code list; free text as supplementary reference

Instructor notes. This lab is where the golden thread pays off visibly — every citation the card needs already exists in the pair's file, and pairs who did thin work in Labs 1–4 now feel it (a productive discomfort; let it happen, then point to the capstone's Hour-4 assembly as recovery time). The red-team step is the best 5 minutes of Day 3 morning: committee questions from peers land harder than from the instructor.

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz (5 questions) 1. Name the model-card section that prevents scope creep and what makes it effective. → Out-of-scope uses; specificity + binding status in procurement/registry. 2. Why must subgroup results appear on the card? → The card is the governance interface; global metrics hide exactly what governance needs to see (M3's identical-accuracy lesson). 3. Counterfactual vs attribution explanation for a citizen — which and why? → Counterfactual: states what would change the outcome; actionable and jargon-free. 4. What single question validates an audit-trail design? → Can we reconstruct this specific decision as it was made, with what was known then? 5. Why do audit trails need their own privacy review? → They are personal-data processing themselves; retention/access/PDPL obligations apply recursively.

Card-critique exercise. A one-page (deliberately flawed) model card is distributed: no version, global metrics only, "no known limitations", out-of-scope section empty. Find five findings in ten minutes; compare against the instructor's model critique.

Notice rewrite. A hostile notice ("Your application was rejected by our AI system. Score: 0.57. Decision final.") — rewrite to pass the five rules in under ten minutes.

Reconstruction drill. Given six mock audit-trail events, answer three questions: what did the model recommend, what did the human do and why, and what threshold was in force? One of the three is deliberately unanswerable — the schema is missing the change event; participants must say so, not guess.

Discussion questions. - The fraud team argues reason-giving enables gaming. The transparency principle demands reasons. Draft the factor-by-factor compromise and who signs it. - Should model cards for government systems be public? Argue both directions, then find the publishable-summary middle.

docs.title: Case Study — Credit-Decision Explanations at a Saudi Retail Bank
docs.text:
Scenario. "Bank AlJisr" (fictional) automates consumer-credit decisions with a gradient-boosted model. Declined customers receive a generic SMS ("application declined per bank policy"). Complaints to the bank's consumer-protection function rise; a sample review finds three systemic problems: customers cannot learn what to fix, front-line staff improvise explanations (sometimes wrong, occasionally leaking model logic), and two declined customers were given different explanations for near-identical profiles by different branches.

Business context. SAMA-supervised consumer-protection expectations require clear communication of decline reasons; the bank also wants fewer repeat applications with unchanged profiles (cost) and fewer escalations (reputation). The model itself audits acceptably on fairness — this is a pure transparency failure on a compliant model.

Technical challenge. Generate decline reasons that are: derived from the actual model factors (not a parallel fiction), stable across channels, actionable, gaming-analysed, and deliverable in Arabic at scale through SMS, app, and branch scripts — with an audit trail proving which reasons each customer was given.

Constraints. Reason codes must survive model retraining (codes map to factor families, not raw features); branch staff need scripts, not SHAP dashboards; legal insists on identical wording across channels; the fraud-adjacent factors are excluded from reasons and that exclusion must be a signed decision.

Solution approach (facilitate). (1) Build the reason-code layer: top model factors mapped to ~12 stable, plain-language reason families, reviewed by legal + consumer protection. (2) Every decision logs its reason codes (audit-trail event) — the "different explanations" problem dies by design. (3) Channel views generated from one source: SMS (short), app (full + what-to-do), branch script (verbatim + FAQ). (4) Gaming analysis per factor family, documented, signed; excluded families listed in the internal card. (5) Measure the fix: repeat-application-with-no-change rate and explanation-related complaints as the KPIs; report both to the consumer-protection committee quarterly.

Discussion questions. 1. The reason-code layer is a translation between model truth and human language. What governs drift between them across retrains? (Card version history + a mapping test in the release gate.) 2. Two customers, near-identical profiles, different outcomes — explanation consistency exposed it. Is that a transparency bug or a fairness bug? Trace the M3 connection. 3. Write the branch-staff one-paragraph script for the "income could not be verified" family. 4. What does the audit trail need to prove which explanation each customer received, and why might that matter in a dispute two years later?

1. The unanswerable question — Setup: during red-team, one planted card question ("what is performance for the new mobile channel?") has no answer in any artefact. Expected behaviour: the honest card gains a limitations line; the dishonest one gains an invented claim — catch it publicly and gently. Learning objective: "we don't know yet" is a valid, auditable card entry; invention is not.
