docs.title: Module 6 — AI Risk Management and Compliance Workflows
Module Overview
docs.text:
Purpose. Everything the course has built — principles, checklists, audits, privacy assessments, documentation — becomes durable only when wired into an operating system: a risk register that stays current, governance gates embedded in the delivery workflow, monitoring that closes the loop from production back to the register, and a disciplined method for the hardest modern case — third-party AI services, where you govern what you did not build and cannot fully inspect. This module supplies that operating system and completes the Ameen Governance File.

Business relevance. The centre of gravity of AI risk has moved to procurement: most organisations now consume more AI than they build — LLM APIs, embedded vendor models, "AI-powered" SaaS features that appear in products overnight. An organisation that can only govern in-house models governs a shrinking fraction of its exposure. Meanwhile, regulators and auditors evaluate systems of control, not heroic individual documents: the question is never "do you have a bias audit?" but "what makes a bias audit happen every time, and what happens when it fails?" Compliance workflows are the answer to that question, and they are what distinguish an AI governance program from an AI governance binder.

Industry use cases. - A ministry procuring a citizen-service chatbot built on a third-party LLM must assess data residency, training-data reuse rights, sub-processors, and exit terms before award — and reject the vendor whose standard contract sends prompt logs abroad for "service improvement". - A bank embeds AI-risk gates into its existing model-risk workflow: no model reaches production without a completed card, audit, and DPIA — enforced by the deployment platform, not by memory (the same gate philosophy as CI/CD quality gates, applied to governance). - An insurer's risk register review catches a silent vendor model update that shifted claim-triage behaviour — because the third-party monitoring control required the vendor to notify version changes, and the register review checked.

Expected competencies. Participants can build and score an AI risk register; design governance gates into a delivery workflow with a RACI that names accountable roles; run a third-party AI assessment across data, model, operational, and contractual dimensions; specify contract clauses that make vendor assurances enforceable; and design the monitoring loop that keeps the whole system live.

docs.title: Learning Objectives (mapped)
docs.text: # Objective Maps to 6.1 Build an AI risk register: identification, likelihood × impact scoring, controls, residual risk, ownership LO6, LO2 6.2 Design governance gates into the AI delivery workflow with a RACI naming accountable roles LO6, LO5 6.3 Assess a third-party AI service across data, model, operational, and contractual dimensions LO6 6.4 Specify the contract clauses that convert vendor assurances into enforceable obligations LO6, LO1 6.5 Design monitoring and incident workflows that keep the register and controls current LO6, LO5

docs.title: 1. The AI risk register: structure and scoring
docs.text:
The register is the memory of the governance program. Structure per entry: ID · risk statement · lifecycle phase · category (fairness / privacy / reliability / transparency / third-party / security) · likelihood (1–5) · impact (1–5) · inherent score (L×I) · existing controls · residual score · owner · review date · status.

Craft rules that separate working registers from theatre:

  • Risk statements name a mechanism and a harm: "verification asymmetry causes higher false rejections for informal-sector applicants" — not "model may be biased." A register row you cannot design a control against is a category, not a risk.
  • Impact is scored on affected people first, organisation second. A risk matrix that only scores reputational damage inverts the SDAIA accountability lens; score both, decide on the max.
  • Residual risk is a claim about control effectiveness — it requires the control to be operating, not designed. A quarterly fairness re-measurement that has never run provides zero residual reduction; registers mark controls as designed/implemented/verified.
  • The register is fed by everything else: M1's gap register seeds it; M3's audit findings and M4's DPIA risks flow in with their artefact references. The Lab 6 exercise is largely a consolidation — the course has been building the register all along, which is the lesson.

docs.title: 2. Governance gates in the delivery workflow
docs.text:
Controls that depend on memory fail; controls embedded in the workflow fire every time. The gate pattern taught (deliberately parallel to CI/CD quality gates, which many practitioners already trust):

Gate When Cannot pass without Who signs G0 — Intake Idea approved for exploration Risk-tier decision record (M1); inventory entry Governance office G1 — Data Before data acquisition/extract Basis-per-purpose check (M2); minimisation review + classification (M2/M4); DPIA trigger check Data owner + DPO consult G2 — Pre-deployment Before production exposure Bias audit vs tolerances (M3); DPIA complete (M4); model card + notices + audit trail verified (M5); third-party assessment if applicable Accountable owner G3 — In-production Quarterly / on triggers Fairness + drift re-measurement vs tolerances; override analytics; register review Governance office G4 — Change Any model/threshold/data/purpose change Change-scaled reassessment (a threshold change ≠ a purpose change); card + notice propagation (M5's rot lesson) Owner per change class G5 — Retirement Decommissioning Data disposition per retention schedule; audit-trail preservation for the appeal window; dependent-system notice Owner + records authority

Proportionality is designed in: high-risk systems traverse all gates with full evidence; limited-risk systems get a fast path (G0 + lightweight G2); minimal-risk systems get G0 only. The fast path is what buys the governance office the political capital to hold the slow path — M1's "right path = fast path" principle, operationalised.

The RACI that makes gates real (excerpt): Accountable = the named business owner (never the committee, never the vendor); Responsible = the delivery team producing evidence; Consulted = DPO, legal, security; Informed = the governance office (who also audits gate compliance). One RACI rule prevents most failures: the person who builds cannot be the person who signs G2.

docs.title: 3. Third-party AI: the assessment discipline
docs.text:
The structural problem: obligations follow the deployer (M1), but visibility stops at the vendor's API. The assessment compensates with four dimensions of structured interrogation (the Lab 6 checklist):

A. Data dimension — Where is our data stored and processed (regions, sub-processors)? Is it used to train or improve the vendor's models — opt-out or absent by contract? Retention of prompts/payloads/logs? Cross-border access paths incl. support staff (M2's transfer lesson)? Deletion on exit — demonstrated how?

B. Model dimension — Provenance: what is this model, what was it trained on (at whatever grain the vendor will state), and what documentation exists (vendor model card — its absence is itself a finding)? Evaluation: will the vendor share evaluation results relevant to our population and language (Arabic performance is a first-class question in the Kingdom, not a footnote)? Version stability: are we notified of model updates, can we pin versions, can we regression-test before switchover?

C. Operational dimension — SLAs and their remedies; incident notification duties and timelines (aligned to our 72-hour PDPL clock — the vendor's duty must be shorter); audit rights (questionnaire? third-party attestation? on-site?); certifications as evidence-not-conclusion (ISO 27001, SOC 2, national frameworks; and NCA cloud requirements where government data is involved); business continuity and our exit path (data export format, transition support, contractual notice periods).

D. Contractual dimension — the clause set that converts answers into obligations (Worked Example 2). The one-line rule participants must retain: an assurance that is not in the contract is a conversation, not a control.

Scoring and decision: each dimension scores red/amber/green with findings; the output is not a grade but a decision recommendation — approve / approve-with-conditions (named conditions, owners, dates) / reject — plus register entries for every accepted amber. Conditions without owners and dates are ambers laundered into greens.

docs.title: 4. Monitoring, incidents, and the closed loop
docs.text:
The register decays without inputs. Wire four feedback channels:

  1. Scheduled re-measurement: the G3 quarterly fairness/drift checks write results into the register (tolerance breach → risk status escalates automatically, not when someone remembers).
  2. Operational signals: override-rate shifts (M5's trail analytics), appeal volumes and outcomes by group, complaint themes — leading indicators that metrics lag.
  3. Change notifications: internal (G4) and vendor (contractual duty) — every change event triggers a scaled reassessment decision, recorded even when the decision is "no reassessment needed, rationale: …".
  4. Incidents: an AI-incident procedure that extends (not duplicates) the corporate incident process, with AI-specific triage questions — is this a data breach (PDPL clock starts), a fairness event (affected-group analysis), a safety event (suspend?), or a transparency event (were people told wrongly)? Every incident closes with a register update and, where warranted, a gate-hardening change: the register is how organisations learn.

docs.title: 5. The compliance workflow as evidence system
docs.text: Reframe for the capstone: every gate produces dated, signed, versioned artefacts filed in a predictable structure — which means the governance file assembles itself as a by-product of delivery. When the M2 regulator drill arrives in real life, the answer is a file path, not a war room. Participants have lived this all course: their Ameen file is the gate-evidence trail of a well-governed system, produced in the order a real delivery would produce it. Say this explicitly on Day 3 — it converts the course from six techniques into one system.

docs.title: 6. Common mistakes & operational considerations
docs.text:
1. Register as annual ritual: built for the audit, untouched between audits — detectable by comparing register review dates against model deployment dates.
  2. Likelihood×impact theatre: precise-looking 4.2×3.8 scores hiding unexamined assumptions; the scoring conversation matters more than the arithmetic — record the rationale, not just the number.
  3. Gates without teeth: a "mandatory" review the deployment platform does not enforce becomes optional under deadline; enforce technically where possible (no registry entry → no deploy).
  4. Certification outsourcing: "the vendor is ISO-certified" ending the analysis — certifications scope their management system, not your use case, your data categories, or your Arabic-language performance.
  5. The silent-update blind spot: vendor model changes shifting behaviour with no internal trigger — the contract clause (notification + version pinning) plus a lightweight behavioural regression suite is the only defence.
  6. Shadow AI: teams adopting AI SaaS features outside any gate — countered by an easy G0 intake (make registration trivial), periodic discovery scans, and procurement-channel controls, in that order of effectiveness.
  7. Conditions that evaporate: approve-with-conditions where nobody tracks the conditions — the register owns them, with dates, like any other risk.

Operational considerations. Right-size to the organisation: a 40-person agency does not need a bank's three-lines-of-defence apparatus — it needs G0/G2 gates, one register, one accountable owner per system, and a quarterly review that actually happens. Maturity grows by adding rigor to a working loop, never by designing the full apparatus first. Budget register review into someone's actual job description; unowned recurring work is how every register dies.

docs.title: Worked Example 2 — Third-party AI contract clause checklist (the enforceability layer)
docs.text: # Clause What it must say Red flag it counters C1 Data use limitation Customer data (incl. prompts/payloads) used solely to provide the service; no training/improvement use without separate written consent "…may use anonymized service data to improve its offerings" (M2's seeded clause) C2 Residency & transfer Named storage/processing regions; support-access paths disclosed; changes require consent; PDPL Transfer-Regulations compliance warranted Silent residency; "global infrastructure" language C3 Sub-processors Current list appended; advance notice + objection right for changes Unlisted fourth parties C4 Retention & deletion Defined retention per data type; deletion on request and at exit, with certification Indefinite log retention C5 Model change notification Advance notice of model/version changes; version pinning or parallel-run option for regression testing Silent updates C6 Documentation & evaluation Vendor model card / system documentation provided and updated; evaluation results relevant to customer's population and language on request "Proprietary — cannot share" as a blanket answer C7 Incident notification Notification within a defined period shorter than the customer's 72-hour regulatory clock, with required content "Prompt notification" undefined C8 Audit & assurance Right to questionnaire annually + third-party attestation; escalation to deeper audit on incident Certification-only assurance C9 Liability & remedies Data-protection breaches outside standard liability caps or under a specific super-cap Breach damages inside a 3-month-fees cap C10 Exit & portability Data export in usable format, transition assistance period, deletion certification Lock-in by data gravity

docs.title: Worked Example 3 — Third-party assessment summary (the Lab 6 vendor, "Bayan CX")
docs.text:
THIRD-PARTY AI ASSESSMENT — Bayan CX (citizen-inquiry LLM assistant)   SSA-TPA-002
Proposed use: draft responses to citizen inquiries for SSA agent review
Data exposed: inquiry text (free text — WILL contain personal & sensitive data
              regardless of policy; assess as if it does)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A. DATA          AMBER-RED  Prompts retained 18 months for "quality"; regional
                            hosting available but support access from 2 foreign
                            sites; improvement-use clause present (C1 fails)
B. MODEL         AMBER      No vendor model card; Arabic evaluation "internal
                            only"; silent model updates (C5/C6 fail); dialect
                            performance unknown for informal Arabic inquiries
C. OPERATIONAL   GREEN-AMBER ISO 27001 + SOC 2; incident notice "prompt"
                            (undefined — C7 fails); exit export supported
D. CONTRACT      RED        4 of 10 clauses absent or failed as above
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
RECOMMENDATION: APPROVE WITH CONDITIONS (register entries RR-07..RR-10):
 1. C1 fixed: no improvement use — contractual, before pilot     (Procurement, +30d)
 2. Regional hosting + support-access restriction or transfer
    assessment completed                                          (DPO, +30d)
 3. Pilot scope: no sensitive-category inquiry routing; agent
    review mandatory on 100% of drafts                            (Ops, at pilot)
 4. Arabic/dialect evaluation on SSA's own 500-inquiry test set
    before scale-up; version pinning for the pilot                (Analytics, +45d)
IF CONDITIONS UNMET IN 60 DAYS → REJECT. Owner: Governance Office.

Teaching point: the free-text line is the assessment's sharpest thought — policy cannot stop citizens typing their national ID and health details into an inquiry box, so the assessment treats inquiry text as personal-and-sensitive by construction. Assessing what people will actually do, not what the policy says, is third-party governance done honestly.

docs.title: Hands-on Lab 6 — Risk Register and Third-Party Assessment
docs.text:
Objective Consolidate the course-long findings into the Ameen risk register, and complete the four-dimension assessment of the Bayan CX vendor pack — section 06, completing the governance file Duration 50 minutes (Day 3 Hour 3; includes the 30-min PA-2 case triage) Setup Register template; the pair's gap register + audit + DPIA outputs; Bayan CX vendor pack (marketing deck, security whitepaper, MSA draft — 9 seeded findings); clause checklist; PA-2 case sheet

Instructions & tasks

  1. (10 min) Consolidate the register: convert the course gap register, audit findings, and DPIA risks into ≥ 6 scored register rows; every row gets mechanism-and-harm phrasing, control status (designed/implemented/verified), and an owner.
  2. (10 min) Assess Bayan CX: walk the four dimensions against the vendor pack; score R/A/G per dimension; catch the seeded findings (the retention period and the improvement-use clause are in the MSA draft's definitions section — where nobody reads).
  3. (30 min) PA-2 — Governance case analysis (individually, timed, collected): one-page case — a ministry has been piloting a third-party CV-screening service for 6 months without any gate; a complaint alleges disparate outcomes; the vendor contract is silent on audit rights. Produce: (a) the five most material findings ranked, (b) immediate/30-day/90-day action plan, (c) the one contract clause you would demand first. Graded against the PA-2 rubric.

Expected outputs 

Register: ≥ 6 rows; RR-03-style honest "open" residual present;
          every control carries a status; every row an owner
Bayan CX: A=AMBER-RED, B=AMBER, C=GREEN-AMBER, D=RED;
          ≥ 7 of 9 seeded findings caught; approve-with-conditions
          recommendation with owned, dated conditions
PA-2 submitted: findings ranked, plan time-phased, clause = audit rights
          (or data-use limitation with argued rationale)

Troubleshooting guidance

Symptom Cause Fix Register rows read "bias risk", "privacy risk" Category-as-risk failure Mechanism-and-harm rule: rewrite one row on the projector as the pattern Residuals scored down for designed-but-unimplemented controls Control-status blindness Status column check: designed controls reduce nothing yet Vendor pack skimmed, marketing deck trusted Assessment by brochure Route them to the MSA definitions section; the findings live where reading is boring Everything scored RED, recommendation = reject Zeal without proportionality The use case (agent-reviewed drafts) tolerates conditions; rejection has costs too — force the conditions exercise PA-2 plans start with "form a committee" Process reflex Immediate actions must change exposure now (suspend, restrict, measure) — committees are 30-day items

Instructor notes. The consolidation step is deliberately easy for pairs with good files and painful for the rest — a preview of the capstone hour, name it as such. During Bayan CX, the pair that catches the free-text insight ("citizens will type sensitive data no matter what") should present it; if nobody does, plant it as a question. PA-2 is the second formal assessment component: enforce timing and silence; the ranked-findings discipline from PA-1 recurs and is graded the same way.

docs.title: Mini Exercises
docs.text:
Quiz (5 questions) 1. What three elements must a register risk statement contain? → Mechanism, harm, affected party — plus scoring, control status, owner in the row. 2. Why does a designed-but-unrun control not reduce residual risk? → Residual risk claims control effectiveness; unoperated controls have none — status must be implemented/verified. 3. Name the two contract clauses that counter silent vendor model updates. → Model-change notification (C5) and version pinning/parallel-run; C6 documentation supports both. 4. A vendor is ISO 27001 certified. What does that not tell you? → Anything about your use case: fairness, Arabic performance, data-use rights, your transfer paths — certification scopes their ISMS, not your risk. 5. Who signs the pre-deployment gate, and who must not? → The accountable business owner; not the builder (separation), not the committee (diffusion), not the vendor (obligations don't transfer).

Gate-design drill. Given the SSA's current delivery flow (5-box diagram), place the six gates and mark which artefacts each consumes from the governance file — the answer key is the file's own table of contents.

Clause hunt. The Bayan CX MSA (2 pages) against the C1–C10 checklist in 10 minutes; score which clauses are present/absent/failed.

Register triage. Twelve one-line risks; score any three and rank all twelve by gut, then compare gut-rank against L×I rank — discuss where they diverge and why the rationale column exists.

Discussion questions. - Shadow AI: a department has been using a consumer LLM for citizen correspondence for months. What is the first action — and defend why it is not "ban it"? - The fast path for limited-risk systems will be abused by optimistic self-classification. Design the countermeasure without destroying the fast path. (Spot-audit of G0 self-classifications; misclassification consequences.)

docs.title: Case Study — Ministry Procurement of a Third-Party LLM Service
docs.text:
Scenario. A service ministry plans "Mujeeb", a citizen-facing assistant answering service questions and drafting case responses, built on a global provider's LLM via a regional integrator. Procurement has a preferred bidder; the governance office is brought in two weeks before award — late, as usual. Review finds: prompt logs retained abroad for 24 months; the integrator's demo used real citizen inquiries harvested from a previous project; Arabic evaluation consists of a marketing benchmark on formal MSA while the inquiry base is heavily dialectal; and the provider reserves the right to update the underlying model without notice.

Business context. The minister's office has announced the assistant publicly with a launch quarter. The integrator is politically well-connected. The governance office's leverage is real but spendable: it can delay award, attach conditions, or escalate — each at a cost.

Technical challenge. Distinguish the fixable from the structural: retention and residency are contract-fixable; the harvested-demo-data issue is an incident requiring its own response (the integrator processed personal data without basis — M2 obligations); dialect performance is an evaluation gap fixable with a proper test set; silent updates are fixable only if the provider offers version pinning — a capability question, not a negotiation question.

Constraints. The launch date is political; the provider's standard terms resist edits below a spend threshold; the integrator relationship will outlive this procurement; citizens will type sensitive data into the box regardless of any disclaimer (the Bayan CX insight at national scale).

Solution approach (facilitate). (1) Separate the incident from the procurement: the harvested-data issue gets an immediate M2-track response (basis analysis, notification assessment) regardless of award. (2) Convert findings into award conditions with the C1–C10 checklist — conditions in the contract, not the meeting minutes. (3) Commission the dialect evaluation on a ministry-built 1,000-inquiry test set as a pre-launch gate with published tolerances. (4) Scope the launch to match residual risk: agent-reviewed drafting first, direct citizen answers only after G3 evidence accumulates — the phased launch protects the announced date and the citizens. (5) Register everything, including the political-pressure risk itself (owner: governance office head; control: this documented decision trail).

Discussion questions. 1. Governance arrived two weeks before award. What structural change makes it arrive at G0 next time, and who has to want that change? 2. The phased-launch compromise trades scope for date. Construct the one-slide version the minister's office actually reads. 3. The integrator harvested real inquiries for a demo. Walk the M2 analysis: basis, breach question, notification clock, and what it means for their fitness as a processor. 4. Write the tolerance sentence for the dialect evaluation gate ("launch proceeds if …") — precise enough that nobody can argue about it in launch week.

docs.title: Simulations
docs.text:
1. Silent-update drill — Setup: mid-lab announcement: "Bayan CX has updated its underlying model, effective last Tuesday. You were not notified." Expected behaviour: pairs identify which conditions/clauses this violates, what evidence they need (regression run on the 500-inquiry set), and what the register does (RR status escalation). Learning objective: the monitoring loop is what makes contracts more than paper.
  2. Escalation role-play — Setup: instructor plays a procurement lead pushing to waive condition 2 ("the vendor says regional hosting is coming next year"). Expected behaviour: participants distinguish waiving (register the accepted risk, owner signs) from ignoring (nothing recorded) — either can be legitimate governance; only one is defensible later. Learning objective: governance permits risk acceptance; it forbids silent risk acceptance.

docs.title: Title: Government AI Deployment — Governance Case Analysis and Compliance Assessment
Project Scenario
docs.text: You are the AI governance office of the Social Support Authority (SSA). Two things are on the committee's agenda this quarter. First, Ameen v3 — the eligibility-scoring system you have assessed all course — needs its complete governance file approved before the annual programme review. Second, the SSA intends two expansions that arrive as a single briefing memo on the morning of Day 3: (a) adopting Bayan CX, the third-party LLM assistant for citizen inquiries, and (b) a request from another agency to reuse Ameen scores for housing-support waitlist prioritisation. Your task is the work of a real governance office: assemble the evidence, analyse the case, take defensible positions on both expansions, and defend the whole file before the SSA Governance Committee — played by your instructor and peer panel. Topic 7 of the syllabus — governance in government AI deployments — is not a lecture; it is this exercise.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Mandatory (maps to grading rubric):

  1. Complete governance file (LO2, LO5): all six sections assembled, internally consistent, cross-referenced (the model card cites the audit; the register cites the DPIA; no orphan claims), with a two-page executive summary written for committee members who will read nothing else.
  2. Regulatory position (LO1): the PDPL/NDMO compliance assessment finalised: checklist, RoPA entry, classification records, and a remediation plan for every open critical gap with owners and dates — including a definitive position on the training-reuse basis question (GAP-08/RR-03).
  3. Fairness position (LO3): the bias-audit report with a signed decision record: which remediation options are adopted, the interim control's monitoring plan, and re-audit tolerances the committee can hold you to.
  4. Privacy position (LO4): the DPIA and anonymisation evidence for the research extract, plus a privacy analysis of the Bayan CX inquiry flow (the free-text problem addressed explicitly).
  5. Accountability infrastructure (LO5): model card, adverse-decision notice, and audit-trail schema, versioned and consistent with every number elsewhere in the file.
  6. Third-party and expansion analysis (LO6): the Bayan CX assessment with an approve-with-conditions/reject recommendation (conditions owned and dated), and a governance analysis of the score-reuse request — tier reassessment, what the out-of-scope card section implies, and what a lawful path to reuse would require.
  7. Committee defense: a 7-minute presentation (3 slides maximum plus the file) followed by 5 minutes of panel questions drawn from the committee question deck and the panel's own reading of your file.

One extension (choose at least one): - A quarterly G3 review pack template: the recurring one-pager that keeps the file alive after approval - A public transparency summary of Ameen (what the SSA would publish), with the internal-vs-public line argued - An AI incident runbook for the SSA extending the corporate incident process with AI-specific triage - A gate-enforcement specification: which gates get technical enforcement and how - An Arabic-dialect evaluation protocol for the Bayan CX pilot (test-set design, tolerances, gate sentence)

docs.text:
Criterion Weight 90–100% band 70–89% band < 70% band File completeness & internal consistency 20 All six sections present, cross-referenced; numbers agree everywhere; executive summary committee-ready Complete but with consistency slips (card vs audit numbers drift) Missing sections, orphan claims, no executive summary PDPL/NDMO compliance assessment 15 Checklist evidence-disciplined; RoPA complete; every critical gap owned and dated; reuse-basis position defensible Assessment sound; remediation plan thin or partially unowned Checklist theatre; basis question dodged Bias & fairness analysis 15 Correct metrics, sound diagnosis, priced remediations, signed decision record, tolerances stated Metrics correct; diagnosis or decision record weak Computation errors; no diagnosis; no decision Privacy risk & data handling 15 Anonymisation demonstrated with utility ledger; DPIA honest residuals; free-text problem addressed Techniques applied; residuals cosmetic or Bayan CX privacy thin Redaction-reflex thinking; no DPIA Documentation & audit trail 10 Card evidence-indexed with subgroup results; notice passes all rules; trail passes reconstruction + PII tests Artefacts present with audience or versioning slips Brochure card; score-leaking notice; unreconstructable trail Risk register & third-party assessment 15 Mechanism-phrased register, honest residuals; vendor conditions owned/dated; reuse analysis correctly forces G0 re-entry Register sound; conditions or reuse analysis underspecified Category-risks; brochure-based vendor assessment Committee defense & decisions doc 10 Answers from evidence; concedes unknowns honestly; DECISIONS.md shows trade-off literacy Defends adequately; some improvisation beyond the file Cannot locate own evidence; invents answers under pressure

Pass ≥ 70. Distinction ≥ 90. Extensions add up to +5 bonus (capped at 100) only if mandatory scope is ≥ 80.

docs.title: Assessment Criteria Notes for Instructors
docs.text:
• Grade from the file first, the presentation second — the course's thesis is that governance lives in evidence, not eloquence. A polished presentation over a thin file scores below a plain presentation over a rigorous file.
  • The score-reuse request is the discriminator between bands: strong pairs recognise it re-opens classification (new purpose, new population, new consequence → G0), cite their own out-of-scope card section, and describe the lawful path; weak pairs treat it as a feature request.
  • Anti-pattern flags that cap a criterion at 70%: residual risks all "Low"; conditions without owners/dates; invented answers in panel Q&A (test once per panel: ask one question whose answer is not in any artefact — the correct response names the gap and the process to close it, not a guess).
  • Panels: 3–4 pairs per panel; peers score with the short rubric card; instructor score prevails on disputes. Keep the committee question deck visibly in play — participants met it in Lab 5, and recognising returning questions rewards preparation.

docs.title: Bonus Tasks (for early finishers / distinction seekers)
docs.text:
1. Run the full governance file against a second system profile (provided: a predictive-maintenance system, deliberately minimal-risk) and produce the proportionate two-page fast-path file — demonstrating right-sizing, the rarest governance skill
  2. Draft the SSA's response to the mock SDAIA regulator query (M2's drill) using only file references — timed at 30 minutes
  3. Produce the committee's rejection letter for Bayan CX assuming conditions fail at 60 days — the exit decision written before it is needed
  4. Map the complete Ameen file against an international framework (NIST AI RMF functions or ISO/IEC 42001 clauses) in a two-column table — the interoperability argument made concrete

docs.title: Quiz Bank (20 questions — use 10 per cohort, 15 min, closed book)
docs.text: Q1. Name the seven SDAIA AI-ethics principles. → Fairness; Privacy & Security; Humanity; Social & Environmental Benefits; Reliability & Safety; Transparency & Explainability; Accountability & Responsibility. Q2. A system "only recommends" but 92% of recommendations are accepted unchanged. Governance implication? → De-facto autonomy: classify and control it as a deciding system; oversight must be designed and measured. Q3. The single question that most efficiently tests risk tier? → What happens to a specific person when the system is wrong in each direction? Q4. Four legal bases PDPL recognises besides consent? → Actual interest of the data subject; processing under another law / implementing an agreement; public-entity security/judicial purposes; legitimate interest (non-sensitive data, post-amendment). Q5. Five data-subject rights under PDPL? → To be informed; access; obtain a copy; correction; destruction (plus withdrawal of consent where consent is the basis). Q6. Breach notification to SDAIA — the timeline under the Implementing Regulations? → 72 hours. Q7. The four national data-classification levels? → Top Secret, Secret, Restricted, Public. Q8. Why does a training extract inherit its source's classification? → Until anonymisation is demonstrated by analysis, identifiability — and therefore impact of disclosure — is presumed unchanged. Q9. Selection rates 0.48 vs 0.62 — compute DIR and interpret. → 0.774; below the 0.8 four-fifths tripwire → investigate (tripwire, not verdict). Q10. Equal opportunity vs demographic parity in one sentence each. → EO: equal TPR among the truly eligible across groups; DP: equal selection rates across groups regardless of eligibility. Q11. Why can identical global accuracy hide serious unfairness? → Accuracy aggregates over error types and groups; opposite error patterns (high FN for one group, high FP for another) can produce equal accuracy — Worked Example 1's exact construction. Q12. Removing the protected attribute from features: sufficient, and what does it break? → Not sufficient (proxies remain); it also breaks disparity measurement — keep protected attributes for audit, exclude from features. Q13. Pseudonymised data under PDPL — in scope or out, and why? → In scope: re-identification remains reasonably possible; only demonstrated anonymisation exits obligations. Q14. Define k-anonymity and name the attack l-diversity answers. → Each record indistinguishable from ≥ k−1 others on the quasi-identifiers; the homogeneity attack (all k share the sensitive value). Q15. Generalise first, suppress last — why? → Generalisation preserves records at lower resolution; suppression deletes information entirely and biases the sample against rare (often fairness-relevant) groups. Q16. Which model-card section prevents scope creep, and what makes it work? → Out-of-scope uses; specificity plus binding status in registry/procurement. Q17. The one-question validation of an audit-trail design? → Can this specific decision be reconstructed as it was made, with what was known then? Q18. Why does a designed-but-unimplemented control not reduce residual risk? → Residual risk is a claim about operating effectiveness; a control that has never run has none — hence the designed/implemented/verified status column. Q19. "The vendor is ISO 27001 certified" — what does this not establish? → Anything about your use case: data-use rights, fairness, Arabic performance, transfer paths; certification scopes the vendor's management system, not your risk. Q20. An assurance the vendor gave in a meeting but not in the contract is…? → A conversation, not a control — convert it to a clause (C1–C10) or register the gap.

docs.title: Practical Assessments
docs.text:
PA-1 — Compliance-assessment exercise (30 min, Day 2 Hour 1, individual): Given a one-page scenario (telecom churn-prediction pilot with an overseas analytics vendor), complete the short-form PDPL/NDMO checklist and name the five most material gaps, ranked. Scored on: gap identification vs key (50%), materiality ranking (30%), evidence discipline — every status cites the scenario text (20%). This is the catalog's compliance-assessment component in its standalone form; the capstone's Requirement 2 is its integrated form.

PA-2 — Governance case analysis (30 min, Day 3 Hour 3, individual): Given a one-page case (ungated ministry pilot of a third-party CV-screening service with a disparate-outcome complaint and an audit-silent contract), produce ranked findings, an immediate/30-day/90-day action plan, and the first contract clause to demand. Scored on: findings vs key (40%), plan quality — immediate actions change exposure now (40%), clause choice with rationale (20%). This is the catalog's governance case analysis component in miniature; the capstone panel is its full form.

PA-3: Capstone (rubric above) — 40% of course grade. Labs completion + PA-1/PA-2 — 60%.

docs.title: Evaluation Criteria Summary
docs.text:
Component Weight Evidence Lab completion (6 governance-file sections) 30% Filed artefacts vs per-lab expected outputs and seeded-finding recall targets PA-1 (compliance-assessment exercise) + PA-2 (governance case analysis) 20% Collected timed artefacts vs rubrics Quiz 10% 10-question selection from the bank Capstone (governance case analysis + compliance assessment, integrated) 40% 100-point rubric, file-first grading

Badge issuance (Foundation badge) requires ≥ 70 overall and capstone ≥ 70 and zero academic-integrity flags (identical register rows, audit numbers, or DECISIONS.md text across pairs are checked — the synthetic datasets make copied numbers detectable).

docs.title: Common Student Issues & Troubleshooting
docs.text: Issue Frequency Resolution Mixed audience: practitioners bored by law, compliance staff anxious about metrics High The pairing strategy is the fix — enforce mixed pairs Day 1 and rotate; each half teaches the other Participants treat checklists as tick-boxes, not evidence instruments High The evidence rule, enforced publicly and early (Lab 1); strike one uncited claim on the projector once Legal-interpretation rabbit-holes ("but what does the regulation really mean…") High The lab rule: record the question, flag "legal review needed", move on — method is the syllabus, counsel is not Denominator errors in fairness metrics (TPR over all applicants) Medium Whiteboard re-derivation from the confusion matrix; the matrix drill exists for this "Anonymised = names removed" instinct persisting past M4 Medium The live re-identification demo; repeat the inheritance rule at every mention Pairs with thin Day 1–2 artefacts hitting the wall in Lab 5/capstone Medium Checkpoint solutions let them fast-forward; grade their own-work sections accordingly Participants wanting to discuss their employer's real systems Medium Redirect firmly to fictional materials (sensitivity note); offer the framework, never the forum Notebook environment friction for non-programmers Low Spreadsheet parity is by design — switch them without ceremony Panel anxiety (Day 3 presentations) Low The Lab 5 red-team is the rehearsal; question deck familiarity lowers stakes

docs.title: Timing Recommendations
docs.text:
• Protect Lab 3 and Lab 6 at full length; compress M4 theory (the lab teaches it) and M5's lecture (the artefacts teach it) if behind.
  • If a cohort is strong: pull the composition-attack tabletop and the second Bayan CX condition-negotiation into main scope; add the NIST/ISO mapping bonus as a group exercise.
  • If a cohort is weak: drop the intersection analysis from Lab 3 and the l-diversity fix to a demonstration; never drop PA-1, PA-2, or the committee panels — they are the catalog's assessment components.
  • Hard rule: capstone assembly (Day 3 Hour 4) starts on time; cut discussion, not assembly time. Files must be collected at end of Hour 4 for panel sequencing.

docs.title: Discussion Prompts (use during transitions)
docs.text:
1. "Whose AI decision has affected you or your family — and could anyone have explained it to you?"
  2. "Your model is 94% accurate. For whom is it 78% accurate — and how would you currently find out?"
  3. "If SDAIA's query letter arrived this morning, is your organisation's answer a file path or a war room?"
  4. "Which costs more: three weeks of governance review, or the Murshid headline? Who in your organisation gets to make that trade?"
  5. "What is the most personal data you've typed into a third-party AI tool this month — and where do you think it is now?"

docs.title: Wrap-up (final day, last 15 minutes)
docs.text:
• One slide: map each capstone rubric criterion to the module that taught it and the artefact that evidences it — the course as one system, shown once more.
  • Forward pointers: this module completes the AI & Data Foundations Certificate (SDA-FND-101→105) and is required for Expert-level certificates in both tracks; it also anchors the AI Security micro-specialization (with SDA-AIE-313 and SDA-AIE-311). Next step: role-track modules — and note to engineers that the audit trail, gates, and evidence discipline built here reappear as CI/CD gates and MLOps controls in the AI Engineer track.
  • Collect: assembled governance files, DECISIONS.md, peer rubric cards; issue badge recommendations within 5 working days.
  • Close with the course's thesis, stated plainly: trustworthy AI is not a property of models — it is a property of the evidence system around them, and each participant just built one.

End of instructor package. Regulatory references (PDPL, Implementing and Transfer Regulations, NDMO standards, SDAIA AI Ethics Principles) reflect published guidance as of authoring; instructors must verify current versions before each delivery. All organisations, systems, persons, and datasets in this package are fictional and synthetic.

docs.title: Internal hosting — nginx + oauth2-proxy
docs.text:
Recommended hosting for the Trainer Portal (see HOSTING.md, Option A).

File Purpose docker-compose.yml Two containers: oauth2-proxy (SSO gate, the only published port) and nginx (static files) oauth2-proxy.cfg Entra ID tenant, allowed groups, cookie and TLS settings — replace every <…> nginx.conf Serves MkDocs directory URLs; forces downloads for binaries; no-index headers 
export ENTRA_CLIENT_ID=… ENTRA_CLIENT_SECRET=… COOKIE_SECRET=$(openssl rand -base64 32 | head -c 32)
export DEPLOY_PATH=/srv/trainer-portal/site
docker compose up -d

The GitHub Actions self-hosted runner (label sdaia-internal) copies each new build into $DEPLOY_PATH — see the deploy-internal job in .github/workflows/publish.yml. Nothing in this folder contains a secret; keep it that way.

docs.title: Administrator guide
docs.text: For Academy Admins who run the Hub. Content owners: see CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
• Create a private repository sdaia-academy-training in the Academy's GitHub organisation (Internal visibility is also fine on GitHub Enterprise). Disable forking.
  • Install Git and Git LFS, unzip the bootstrap into a working folder, then pull the binaries from Drive (every file is verified against the SHA-256 recorded in the migration mapping): 
    python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python scripts/migration/migrate_from_drive.py --source "G:/My Drive/SDAIA/CB/Academy/Catalog/New Catalog" --repo . --binaries-only
  • Create the first commit with scripts/migration/init_git_repo.py — not plain git add -A. Several migrated lab repositories contain their own .gitignore files that would silently drop 179 shipped assets; the script force-adds every mapped file and verifies the index: 
    python scripts/migration/init_git_repo.py
git remote add origin git@github.com:<org>/sdaia-academy-training.git
git push -u origin main          # pushes Git LFS objects too
  • Set github_repo (and later portal_url) in hub-config.yml, then python scripts/refresh_generated.py so "Report a problem" links point at the right repository.
  • Replace SDAIA-Academy in .github/CODEOWNERS with the real organisation / team slugs.

docs.title: People
docs.text:
• Create the teams in PERMISSIONS.md and add members.
  • For each course, set content_owner and reviewer in metadata.yml (one PR per learning path is fine). The validator refuses Approved/Published status until both are set.
  • Apply the main branch ruleset from PERMISSIONS.md.
  • Enable secret scanning, push protection and Dependabot alerts.

docs.title: Portal
docs.text:
• Choose hosting with SDAIA IT — HOSTING.md (recommended: internal hosting behind SSO).
  • Set repository variables: DEPLOY_TARGET (internal · azure-swa · github-pages · none), and for internal hosting DEPLOY_PATH.
  • Set repository secrets if needed: AZURE_STATIC_WEB_APPS_API_TOKEN (Option B only).
  • Run Actions → Publish Trainer Portal → Run workflow and verify sign-in is required.
  • Announce the portal URL to trainers; update the announcement on portal/index.md.

docs.title: 2. Day-to-day
docs.text: Task How Merge content Only after required approvals and green checks; squash-merge with the PR title CODE: summary Publish a course version After merge: git tag SDA-AIE-311/v1.1 <sha> && git push origin SDA-AIE-311/v1.1 → Release workflow Add a course python scripts/new_course.py … (see CONTRIBUTING.md) — starts as Draft Archive a course Move to archive/…, add a README with the reason and replacement, set status: Archived Change the taxonomy Edit taxonomy.yml via PR; run make check — the validator catches values no longer allowed Feature a course on the home page featured: list in hub-config.yml Post an announcement Edit the Trainer announcements section of portal/index.md Triage feedback Issues arrive labelled feedback + type; assign the course owner, label urgent if a delivery is affected

docs.title: 3. Scheduled care
docs.text: When What Weekly Check the portal's Content health page and open issues labelled urgent Monthly The Review reminders workflow opens an issue listing courses whose next_review is within 30 days Quarterly Review LFS storage/bandwidth usage; update pinned tool versions in requirements.txt; review team membership Yearly Review this governance model with Academy leadership

docs.title: 4. When a check fails
docs.text: Check Typical cause Fix validate › metadata Missing field, value not in taxonomy.yml, bad date Correct metadata.yml; schema is schemas/course-metadata.schema.json validate › structure Required file or folder missing Restore it (templates in shared/templates/course-template/) validate › links Renamed/moved file Update the relative link validate › generated AUTO blocks stale Warning only — the publish workflow regenerates them security › secret Credential pattern found Remove it; if it was ever pushed, follow SECURITY.md security › personal data Phone/ID/IBAN/e-mail patterns in data Confirm synthetic and add to .security-allowlist.yml with a reason, or remove security › size File > 5 MB not in LFS / > 50 MB Track with LFS / move to release asset publish › build MkDocs error Run make portal locally; the previous portal stays online

docs.title: 5. Migration follow-up (from the audit)
docs.text: The migration audit lists every open item. Priorities: P0 owners + hosting + 6 security items → P1 approve the complete courses → P2 recover the missing SDA-AIE-214 package, complete DSC-211/DSC-112 packages, decide L0-FDV → P3/P4 build missing materials. Each course's open items are also listed on its page under Ownership and version.

docs.title: 6. Local commands
docs.text:
make check      # validate + links + security + generated-content check
make refresh    # regenerate AUTO blocks and portal pages
make portal     # assemble and build the portal into site/
make serve      # live preview on http://127.0.0.1:8000

docs.title: 7. Portal engine lifecycle (important)
docs.text:
The portal is built with MkDocs 1.6 + Material for MkDocs 9.7, pinned in requirements.txt. The Material team has announced that MkDocs 2.0 is backward-incompatible (plugins and theme overrides stop working, no migration path) and that future MkDocs 1.x updates are unlikely. Material 9.7.5+ already restricts MkDocs to <2. Actions:

  • Never upgrade to MkDocs 2.x; review Dependabot PRs for mkdocs / mkdocs-material carefully.
  • The content is plain Markdown + YAML metadata; the only engine-specific parts are mkdocs.yml, scripts/build_portal.py (nav generation) and portal/assets/. Migrating engines is therefore a contained task.
  • Re-evaluate annually. The Material team's successor, Zensical, aims to build existing mkdocs.yml projects without changes (not fully there as of early 2026); other options include staying pinned on MkDocs 1.6 while it is secure.

docs.title: Hosting the private Trainer Portal
docs.text: The portal is a static site built from this repository (make portal → site/, ~300 MB including slides, PDFs and datasets). It must only be reachable by authenticated SDAIA staff. Ordinary public GitHub Pages does not meet that requirement and must not be used.

docs.title: Requirements (in priority order)
docs.text:
1. Security — no anonymous access; data stays in an approved environment; TLS; audit trail.
  2. SDAIA identity — sign in with the SDAIA account (Microsoft Entra ID / SDAIA IdP), access by group.
  3. Simple for trainers — one URL, single sign-on, no GitHub account.
  4. Low operational overhead — static files, no database, no application server to patch.
  5. Automated deployment — every merge to main that passes validation publishes; failures publish nothing.

docs.title: Options evaluated
docs.text:
A. SDAIA internal hosting + SSO proxy (recommended) B. Azure Static Web Apps (Standard) + Entra ID C. GitHub Enterprise Cloud private Pages Public GitHub Pages Access control Entra ID / SDAIA IdP via oauth2-proxy, restricted to an Academy Trainers group Entra ID custom provider pinned to the SDAIA tenant; route rules require an trainer role Only people with read access to the repository None — anyone with the URL Trainer experience SDAIA SSO, no GitHub account SDAIA SSO, no GitHub account Every trainer needs a GitHub Enterprise seat and repo access — Data location SDAIA-controlled environment Azure region chosen at creation — confirm against SDAIA cloud/data-classification policy GitHub's cloud Public internet Size limits None practical 500 MB per environment on Standard (Free: 250 MB — too small) 1 GB site limit — Operations One small container/VM + reverse proxy; self-hosted runner inside the network Fully managed Fully managed — Deployment publish.yml → build → copy site/ to the internal web root (self-hosted runner) publish.yml → Azure/static-web-apps-deploy action publish.yml → actions/deploy-pages Not permitted Fit ✅ Best balance of security, sovereignty and trainer experience ✅ Good if SDAIA approves Azure for this data ⚠️ Only if trainers are already enterprise members ❌

References: GitHub — private Pages require GitHub Enterprise Cloud and are visible only to people with read access to the repository; Azure — custom (Entra ID) authentication requires the Standard plan; storage quotas as above. Verify current plan terms before procurement.

docs.title: Recommended architecture (Option A)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph GitHub[GitHub — private repository]
      PR[Merged pull request] --> CI[publish.yml<br/>validate · generate · build · link-check]
    end
    CI -- site artefact --> R[Self-hosted runner<br/>inside SDAIA network]
    R -- rsync / image push --> W[(Static web root<br/>nginx)]
    T[Trainer browser] -- HTTPS --> P[oauth2-proxy<br/>Entra ID / SDAIA IdP<br/>group = Academy-Trainers]
    P --> W

Sample configuration: deploy/internal-nginx/ (nginx + oauth2-proxy, Docker Compose). The workflow step is already present in .github/workflows/publish.yml (DEPLOY_TARGET=internal).

docs.title: Setup checklist
docs.text:
• SDAIA IT provides a host (VM or Kubernetes namespace) with TLS certificate and internal DNS, e.g. trainers.academy.sdaia.gov.sa (TODO: confirm name).
  • Register an Entra ID application (redirect https://<host>/oauth2/callback), restrict it to the SDAIA tenant and assign the Academy Trainers + Academy Content groups.
  • Deploy deploy/internal-nginx/docker-compose.yml; store the client secret and cookie secret in the host's secret store (never in this repository).
  • Register a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner on a host that can reach the web root; label it sdaia-internal.
  • Set repository variables: DEPLOY_TARGET=internal, DEPLOY_PATH=/srv/trainer-portal/site.
  • Merge to main and confirm the portal loads only after SSO sign-in (test with an account outside the group — it must be refused).

docs.title: Option B quick start (Azure Static Web Apps)
docs.text:
1. Create a Static Web App on the Standard plan in the approved region.
  2. Register an Entra ID app for the SDAIA tenant; store AZURE_CLIENT_ID / AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET as Static Web App application settings.
  3. Copy deploy/azure-static-web-apps/staticwebapp.config.json into the built site (the publish workflow does this) and replace <TENANT_ID>.
  4. Assign the trainer role to users/groups (role invitations or an Entra-group role function).
  5. Set DEPLOY_TARGET=azure-swa and the secret AZURE_STATIC_WEB_APPS_API_TOKEN.

docs.title: Option C quick start (GitHub Enterprise Cloud)
docs.text: Settings → Pages → Source: GitHub Actions; Visibility: Private. Set DEPLOY_TARGET=github-pages. Every portal user must have read access to this repository.

docs.title: What is not acceptable
docs.text:
• Public GitHub Pages or any host without authentication.
  • Copying site/ to shared drives or file shares (breaks the single source of truth and access control).
  • Embedding secrets in mkdocs.yml, workflows or the site.

docs.title: Large files
docs.text: Training repositories hold decks, PDFs, spreadsheets, datasets and notebooks. Git stores every version of every file forever, so binaries are kept out of normal Git history.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text: File Storage Enforced by Binary formats — pptx pdf docx xlsx parquet png jpg gif npz npy zip gz tar pkl pt onnx mp4 sqlite db Git LFS .gitattributes Any other file larger than 5 MB (large CSV / JSONL / NDJSON) Git LFS — add its path to .gitattributes scripts/security_scan.py fails the PR otherwise Any file larger than 50 MB Admin approval required; prefer a GitHub Release asset or approved SDAIA storage and link to it scripts/security_scan.py Files larger than 100 MB Never in the repository (GitHub hard limit) GitHub Model weights, VM images, software installers Not stored — document where to download from in setup.md review Derived data (CSV exports of Parquet, generated renders) Not stored — keep the generator script review

docs.title: Current footprint (migration, 2026-09-27)
docs.text: See the migration audit §4: 324 files / ≈194 MB in LFS; the largest migrated file is 13.5 MB. GitHub LFS storage and bandwidth are billed per organisation — monitor Settings → Billing → Git LFS, and use actions/cache for LFS in CI (the publish workflow does).

docs.title: Working with LFS
docs.text:
git lfs install                 # once per machine
git lfs track "path/to/big.csv" # adds a line to .gitattributes — commit it
git lfs ls-files                # what is in LFS
GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1 git clone <url>   # clone without downloading binaries (text-only work)
git lfs pull --include="catalog/ai-engineer/SDA-AIE-311-*"   # fetch binaries for one course

docs.title: GitHub teams and permissions
docs.text: Least privilege: people get the lowest role that lets them do their job, and every change to main passes review and automated checks.

docs.title: Teams
docs.text:
Team Members Repository role Why academy-admins 2–3 Hub administrators Admin Settings, branch protection, secrets, releases, emergency fixes content-foundation-core Owners of SDA-FND-* and Level-0 courses Maintain Merge approved changes in their path; manage labels/issues content-ai-engineer Owners of SDA-AIE-* courses Maintain 〃 content-data-scientist Owners of SDA-DSC-* courses Maintain 〃 reviewers-technical Subject-matter reviewers Write Push branches, review and approve PRs reviewers-instructional Instructional designers / QA Write 〃 trainers Trainers who want repository access (optional) Read Browse and download; raise issues. Most trainers only need the portal

Portal access is managed separately through the SDAIA identity group (Academy Trainers) — see HOSTING.md. A trainer does not need a GitHub account.

docs.title: CODEOWNERS
docs.text:
.github/CODEOWNERS routes every pull request to the right team automatically:

/catalog/ai-engineer/      @SDAIA-Academy/content-ai-engineer
/catalog/data-scientist/   @SDAIA-Academy/content-data-scientist
/catalog/foundation-core/  @SDAIA-Academy/content-foundation-core
/catalog/beginner/         @SDAIA-Academy/content-foundation-core
/.github/ /scripts/ /taxonomy.yml /hub-config.yml /mkdocs.yml   @SDAIA-Academy/academy-admins

When individual owners are assigned, add per-course lines (more specific lines win), e.g. /catalog/ai-engineer/SDA-AIE-311-*/ @owner-handle.

docs.title: Branch protection for main (Settings → Rules → Rulesets)
docs.text:
• Require a pull request before merging — 2 approvals, dismiss stale approvals on new commits
  • Require review from Code Owners
  • Require status checks: validate, security (and portal-build once hosting is live)
  • Require conversation resolution
  • Require linear history
  • Block force pushes and deletions
  • Apply to administrators (emergency fixes still go through a PR — CONTENT_GOVERNANCE.md §10)

docs.title: Organisation settings
docs.text:
• SAML SSO with Microsoft Entra ID, SCIM provisioning of team membership from Entra groups if available
  • 2FA required; base permission No access; members cannot create public repositories or fork private ones
  • Secret scanning + push protection, Dependabot alerts
  • Audit-log streaming to the SDAIA SIEM (if available)

docs.title: Migration audit — Google Drive → Trainer Knowledge Hub
docs.text: Scope: G:/My Drive/SDAIA/CB/Academy/Catalog/New Catalog · Audit date: 2026-09-27 · Method: every file and every archive member was hashed (SHA-256) and classified by scripts/migration/build_mapping.py; this report is generated by scripts/migration/audit_report.py from the resulting migration mapping. Nothing on Drive was modified or deleted.

docs.title: 1. Summary
docs.text: Measure Value Files on Drive (Phase 1 inventory) 590 (99 are Google Drive desktop.ini system files) Archives opened (.zip / .tar.gz) 14, containing 1555 files (one further archive was kept unopened in archive/) Items analysed in total 2145 (Drive files + archive members) Courses identified 37 — 31 in Module Catalog v2 + 6 Level-0 programmes Courses with a materials folder on Drive 30 · 7 exist only as catalog/platform entries Storage on Drive 242.6 MB (archives expand to a further 276.5 MB) Migrated into the repository 1444 files, 273.1 MB — 324 files / 194.1 MB in Git LFS Exact duplicates not migrated 389 files, 105.5 MB Excluded system/derived artefacts 298 (listed individually in the mapping) Items needing review 23 Needs Review · 6 Security Concern Courses with material in every standard component (guide, slides, labs, activities, assessments, datasets, solutions, setup) 0 of 37

docs.title: Headline findings
docs.text:
1. The catalog is well defined; the materials are not. All 37 courses have authoritative catalog data (Module Catalog v2 or the AthkaX workbooks), but only 30 have a materials folder, and only a handful have slides, labs, datasets and assessments.
  2. Instructor packages are AI-assisted drafts. The 26 instructor packages share the structure defined in _agent_build/AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS.md, which instructs an AI agent to copy catalog facts and author the pedagogical content (labs, code, quizzes). They are strong starting points but must be technically reviewed before approval.
  3. One package is missing, two are incomplete. The file named INSTRUCTOR_PACKAGE.md for SDA-AIE-214 is actually the Addendum v1.0, which itself says the full package is authoritative — the full package is not on Drive. SDA-DSC-211 and SDA-DSC-112 packages stop after the modules (no capstone, assessment package or instructor-guide sections).
  4. Titles disagree across documents for 21 courses (§6). The Hub uses Module Catalog v2 as the single source; the other names are recorded as aliases so searches still find them.
  5. No credentials or secrets were found. Six dataset files contain Saudi-format phone / national-ID / e-mail patterns; all come from packs documented as synthetic and are flagged for confirmation (§8).

docs.title: 11. Repository taxonomy
docs.text:
The proposed catalog/<domain>/ layout was adjusted: the source material, the Module Catalog and the certification rules are all organised by delivery track, so catalog/ is organised by track and the domain is a metadata field (with its own portal view). This keeps course codes and folders aligned (SDA-AIE-* ⇒ catalog/ai-engineer/).

catalog/
├── beginner/          L0-FAE … L0-FDV          (6)
├── foundation-core/   SDA-FND-101 … 105        (5)
├── ai-engineer/       SDA-AIE-111 … 390        (15)
└── data-scientist/    SDA-DSC-111 … 390        (11)

Lab repositories that shipped as runnable projects (Tawseel, Tayyar, Injaz, Masar, Dalil, Tayseer, Manafeth) are kept intact under labs/<repo>/ so they still run; they are not split across folders.

docs.title: What was populated (all 37 workbooks)
docs.text:
نموذج التأهيل (Qualification Form): bilingual title (row 4) + 7 multiple-choice questions per program testing prerequisite knowledge appropriate to each course level (based on each instructor package's Prerequisites chain; general workforce readiness for Level-0 and Foundation programs). Each question: Arabic + English text, 2 minutes, 1 mark, 4 options, exactly one correct answer (marked TRUE in columns أ–د).

الاختبار القبلي / الاختبار البعدي (Pre-Test / Post-Test): bilingual title + 7 multiple-choice questions per program on core course content. Pre- and post-test use identical items (standard practice for measuring learning gain).

Question evidence sources: - 27 programs (all AIE, DSC-111→215, all FND): converted from the 20-item Quiz Banks in each course's INSTRUCTOR_PACKAGE.md, with the bank's answer as the correct option. - 10 programs (DSC-311, 312, 313, 390 + all 6 Level-0): no instructor package exists — questions generated from each workbook's own bilingual description/objectives/topics. Review these first.

Metadata updates (تفاصيل الحدث / معلومات الحدث): - العدد المستهدف = 25 (propagated from SDA-AIE-311, the only workbook that had it). - الدورات → «يوجد» and نموذج التأهيل → «يوجد» (tabs now contain content to be reflected on the platform).

docs.title: Report a problem or suggest an improvement
docs.text:
Your feedback goes straight to the course owner as a tracked GitHub issue. Choose the form that fits; each takes about a minute. Include the course code and, where possible, the file or slide number.

I want to report… Form A mistake in slides, guides, labs or assessments Content error A lab or notebook that does not run Broken lab A file that is referenced but missing Missing file Installation / environment / network trouble Setup problem Content that is out of date (tools, versions, regulations) Outdated material An idea to make a course better Suggested improvement

Every course page has the same links pre-filled with the course code (Report a problem, and on the troubleshooting page, report a broken lab / setup problem / content error).

Note

These forms need a GitHub account with access to the Hub repository. Trainers without one can send the same information to Academy support — see When something fails on the course's troubleshooting page — and an Academy Admin will log it.

Urgent, during a live delivery? Contact Academy support immediately (troubleshooting page of the course), then log the issue so it is fixed for everyone.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: A five-minute tour for trainers. You do not need a GitHub account — everything is here in the portal.

docs.title: 1. Find your course
docs.text: Use the search box (top of every page, or press S / /) and type a course code, a title word, a tool or a topic — for example SDA-DSC-212, forecasting, PySpark, LangGraph, RAG. Or open the Training catalog and filter by learning path, level, domain or status.

docs.title: 2. Check the status badge
docs.text: At the top of each course page: 🟢 Published/Approved — deliver as-is · 🟡 Under Review — confirm with the course owner first · ⚪ Draft — not ready.

docs.title: 3. Download what you teach from
docs.text: The Start here line links straight to the current deck. The row of links under it takes you to the instructor guide, setup, slides, labs, activities, assessments, datasets, solutions (🔐 trainer-only) and troubleshooting. Download fresh copies for every delivery.

docs.title: 4. Prepare
docs.text: Open Setup: the trainer preparation checklist (T-minus 1 week), the software participants must install, and every environment file in the course (requirements, Docker Compose, doctor scripts). General guidance: classroom preparation · technical setup.

docs.title: 5. Deliver — and tell us what broke
docs.text:
Follow the instructor guide's day-by-day and hour-by-hour plan. If anything is wrong or missing, use Report a problem on the course page or the feedback page. The course owner is notified automatically, and the fix reaches every trainer.

Tip

Bookmark Recently updated to see which courses changed since your last delivery, and read each course's Change history before you teach it again.

docs.title: Learning pathways
docs.text: The Academy organises courses into four learning paths, each climbing from Practitioner (or Beginner) to Expert. Solid arrows are required prerequisites; dotted arrows are recommended.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Pre-test and post-test use the same items to measure learning gain; do not share either in advance.
  • The qualification form checks prerequisite knowledge before admission.
  • For ten programmes (SDA-DSC-311, 312, 313, 390 and all Level-0) the platform questions were generated from the workbook description because no instructor package existed — they are Under Review.
  • Pass marks, attendance criteria and course weights are platform-fixed values; TODO: Information not available in source material.
  • Keep answer keys, solution notebooks and rubric notes away from participants.

docs.title: Classroom preparation checklist
docs.text: A generic T-minus plan. Always complete the course-specific checklist on the course's Setup page as well.

docs.title: T-minus 2 weeks
docs.text:
• Confirm the course status (Published/Approved, or agreed with the owner if Under Review) and read the change history.
  • Confirm cohort size, delivery mode and schedule with the Academy (AthkaX platform entry).
  • Book lab infrastructure: laptops/VMs, GPU access if required, shared model gateway or API keys with per-participant spend caps (for LLM courses).

docs.title: T-minus 1 week
docs.text:
• Download the current slides, handouts and printables from the portal.
  • Dry-run every lab end-to-end on a clean machine and on the fallback environment.
  • Confirm the classroom network allows the package index, container registry and any model gateway — or prepare mirrors / offline mode.
  • Stage datasets on lab machines or the shared drive.
  • Print posters, activity cards and assessment sheets listed in the instructor guide.

docs.title: T-minus 2 days
docs.text:
• Send participants the software installation list from the course's Setup page.
  • Run the course's diagnostic script (e.g. make doctor, check_env.ipynb) on the classroom image.

docs.title: Day 1
docs.text:
• Room/online session opens 30 minutes early; test projector/screen share and audio.
  • Participants run the environment check before Module 1.
  • Explain how to reach you, and the prayer/break schedule.

docs.title: Delivery standards
docs.text: Academy-wide conventions for delivering Hub courses. Items marked (catalog) come from the Module Catalog v2; items marked (packages) recur in the instructor packages' Instructor Guidance Notes and are listed here for consistency pending Academy approval.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text: Standard Source Every module is 2–5 days × 5 learning hours per day and works standalone or inside a certification pathway (catalog) Levels: Practitioner → Specialist → Expert (plus Beginner Level 0) (catalog) Each course follows its instructor guide's day-by-day and hour-by-hour plan (packages) Each learning "hour" is 50 minutes of instruction + 10 minutes buffer (packages) The long break is scheduled around Dhuhr; plan sessions around prayer times (packages)

docs.title: Teaching practice
docs.text: Standard Source Use the course's golden-thread project/dataset throughout — do not swap in toy examples (packages) Rotate pairs daily; pair complementary strengths (e.g. strong Python with strong domain) (packages) Publish checkpoint/solution notebooks so participants who fall behind can fast-forward (packages) Deliver in Arabic or English; keep code, identifiers, column names and notebook headings in English (packages) Every lab has a primary environment (local) and a tested fallback (hosted notebook / container) (packages) Assessment logistics (daily check-offs, capstone demos, rubric scoring) follow the instructor guide (packages)

docs.text:

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Where do I get the slides? — On the course page: the Start here link is always the current deck.

The course says "Under Review". Can I deliver it? — Yes, after confirming with the content owner (listed on the course page). Everything was migrated unchanged from Google Drive; review confirms it is still correct.

Where are the solutions? — Solutions on the course page, and files marked 🔐 inside lab repositories. They are trainer-only.

A lab does not run. — Check the course's Troubleshooting page and diagnostic scripts, then report a broken lab.

Can I edit the slides for my cohort? — Local tweaks for a single delivery are at your discretion, but improvements must go back through the content owner so every trainer benefits. Never distribute an edited deck as the official version.

Why can't I find the Google Drive folder any more? — The Hub replaced it on 2026-09-27. Everything from Drive is here; duplicates and system files were not migrated (see the migration audit).

Who decides what is in a course? — The course's content owner, with reviewers, under the content governance process.

Is the Arabic title or the English title official? — Both are recorded in course metadata. Where older documents use different titles, the Hub uses Module Catalog v2 and lists the others as aliases.

docs.title: Trainer onboarding
docs.text: Welcome to the SDAIA Academy trainer community. This page gets you productive in the Hub in your first week.

docs.title: Day 1 — access
docs.text:
• Sign in to the Trainer Portal with your SDAIA account (URL from the Academy; see portal_url in the Hub settings). If you are refused, ask an Academy Admin to add you to the Academy Trainers group.
  • Optional: a GitHub account in the Academy organisation if you will also edit content.
  • Read the Trainer guide (10 minutes).

docs.title: Days 2–3 — your courses
docs.text:
• Open each course you are scheduled to deliver. Check its status badge and change history.
  • Read the instructor guide end-to-end, including the hour-by-hour plan and the instructor guidance notes.
  • Run every lab yourself on a clean machine using the course's Setup page.
  • Note anything unclear or broken and report it — new eyes find the most issues.

docs.title: Days 4–5 — shadow and rehearse
docs.text:
• Shadow a delivery of the course if one is running. TODO: Information not available in source material. (Academy shadowing policy.)
  • Rehearse the first half-day with the slides from the portal.
  • Agree with the content owner which Under Review items affect your delivery.

docs.title: What the Academy expects from trainers
docs.text:
• Deliver from the current version in the Hub; never from personal copies.
  • Keep trainer-only material (🔐) away from participants.
  • Report problems through the feedback forms so fixes reach everyone.
  • Follow the delivery standards and assessment guidance.
  • TODO: Information not available in source material. (Academy trainer code of conduct / accreditation requirements — see the Instructor Accreditation Framework when published.)

docs.title: Technical setup for labs
docs.text: Cross-course guidance. The authoritative list for each course is its Setup page, which links the course's requirements.txt, environment.yml, docker-compose.yml, Makefile and doctor scripts.

docs.title: Common stack
docs.text: Component Used in Notes Python 3.11/3.12, venv or conda, JupyterLab Almost all technical courses Pin versions from the course's requirements file Git Courses with lab repositories Participants clone the lab repository listed under Labs Docker Desktop (WSL2 on Windows) / Colima SDA-AIE-311, SDA-AIE-214, SDA-DSC-214, SDA-AIE-216 and others Verify docker run hello-world before Day 1 GPU (CUDA) Deep-learning, computer-vision and fine-tuning courses Check the course Setup page for minimums and hosted fallbacks LLM access (model gateway / API keys) Generative-AI and agentic courses Per-participant spend caps; several labs run in a no-cost stub/offline mode — see the lab README Spark (PySpark, Delta Lake) SDA-DSC-214, SDA-DSC-215, SDA-DSC-313 Memory settings for 8 GB laptops are documented in the lab .env.example

docs.title: Offline and restricted networks
docs.text: Several lab repositories are designed to run without internet or paid APIs (for example the SDA-AIE-311 Tawseel repository's stub model mode). Check the lab README for OFFLINE/stub/replay options before requesting network exceptions.

docs.title: Secrets in the classroom
docs.text: Never put real API keys in notebooks, slides or repositories. Use environment variables or the course gateway, and rotate keys after each cohort. See SECURITY.md.

docs.title: General troubleshooting
docs.text:
Course-specific problems and fixes are on each course's Troubleshooting page. This page covers issues that are not tied to one course.

Problem Try Escalate to Cannot sign in to the portal Use your SDAIA account; clear cookies; try another browser Academy Admins (group membership) A download link on the portal returns an error Refresh; the file may have moved in a recent update — check Recently updated Report a missing file Packages fail to install in class Use the course's pinned requirements; switch to the fallback environment; check the network allowlist Classroom IT; report a setup problem Docker fails on Windows Enable WSL2 and virtualisation in BIOS; restart Docker Desktop Classroom IT LLM API calls fail or are slow Check the gateway key and spend cap; switch the lab to its offline/stub mode if available Academy support Numbers in a lab differ from the instructor guide Restart the kernel and run all; check seeds and data version Report a content error
